ai/a2ui-vs-json-render.title: A2UI vs json-render — Generative UI Protocol vs Framework
ai/a2ui-vs-json-render.content:
A2UI vs json-render — Generative UI Protocol vs Framework
Last verified: 2026-08-25 (a2ui.org + its renderers reference, json-render.dev + its docs, the json-render repo README, GitHub API, and the npm registry all fetched and read the same day). Both projects move fast; version, star, and status claims below decay quickly.


                  
                  One claim in the 2026-06-12 version of this note was wrong 
                  
                

It said json-render was “React and React Native only”. It was not, even then — the Vue, Svelte, and Solid renderers were on npm from February and March 2026, months before that verification. The error came from reading the marketing homepage (which still says only “React & React Native”) and not the repo README or the docs sidebar. Corrected throughout below; see bias-aware-verification-protocol for the general failure — verifying against the most prominent source rather than the most complete one.


Two prominent answers to the same problem — letting an LLM/agent produce interactive UI safely, by emitting constrained declarative JSON instead of executable code. They sit at two different layers of the stack, and are not rivals: one is a cross-platform protocol, the other a multi-framework rendering library. As of 2026-08 they explicitly interoperate — see Do they actually compose? below.
What each one is
A2UI (a2ui.org)
A protocol created by Google, with contributions from CopilotKit and the open source community (the site states this outright). Agents emit declarative JSON messages describing UI structure and data; a client-side renderer maps them onto native components — no arbitrary code crosses the trust boundary. The site frames the purpose as a single question: “how can AI agents safely send rich UIs across trust boundaries?”

Spec versions (per the site’s own table): v1.0 “Candidate”, v0.9.1 “Current production release”, v0.9 “Stable”, v0.8 “Legacy”. Unchanged since 2026-06-12 — v1.0 has now sat as a candidate for 2.5+ months. The site notes v1.0 was “previously designated as v0.10 when in draft”.
Maintained renderers: React, Lit, Angular, Flutter (GenUI SDK) — each ✅ Stable for v0.8 and v0.9.1, 🚧 Planned for v1.0. SwiftUI (iOS/macOS) and Jetpack Compose (Android) are listed as Planned only — no shipping spec support. (The homepage prose also names a Markdown renderer; it is not in the maintained-renderers table.)
Ecosystem renderers (community): json-render, A2UI-Android (~15★, v0.8), a2ui-react-native (~9★, v0.8), Lynx A2UI (v0.9), AGenUI — cross-platform iOS/Android/HarmonyOS (v0.9).
Transport: the site names A2A directly — “Transports like A2A which communicate A2UI messages between agents and clients.” (In the 2026-06 version of this note the A2A pairing was flagged as unverified background; it is now verified at source, and the relationship is specifically transport, not sibling branding.)
Repo: a2ui-project/a2ui, 16.2k stars, Apache-2.0, created 2025-09-24, pushed 2026-08-24
Notable: still no formal GitHub releases — only v0.9 and v0.8 tags, and no tag for the v0.9.1 the site designates as current. The release process stays looser than the website’s version table implies.

json-render (json-render.dev)
A framework/library from Vercel Labs. The developer defines a catalog of allowed components and actions with Zod schemas; the LLM streams constrained JSON matching the catalog; the renderer paints progressively as the stream arrives. Can export a generated UI as standalone React code — or as a whole standalone Next.js project.

Renderers — far wider than the homepage advertises. The README’s own summary: “React, Vue, Svelte, Solid (web), React Native (mobile) from the same catalog”. All four web renderers plus React Native are published at 0.20.0.
Non-DOM renderers too: @json-render/next (routes, layouts, SSR), react-three-fiber (3D scenes), remotion (video), react-pdf, react-email, ink (terminal TUIs), image (SVG/PNG via Satori). The same spec format drives all of them.
Integrations with their own docs pages: AI SDK, A2UI, Adaptive Cards, AG-UI, OpenAPI. Plus @json-render/mcp — “MCP Apps integration for Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code” (see generative-ui-security for what hosting MCP-supplied UI entails).
Component counts — two different numbers, often conflated: the homepage catalog demo shows 41 components and 6 actions; the README advertises 36 pre-built shadcn/ui components in @json-render/shadcn. Different things.
npm @json-render/core at 0.20.0 (published 2026-08-16), 30 versions total. 29 of those landed between 2026-01 and 2026-05; only one minor since. The churn has slowed sharply — that’s the single most decision-relevant change since June.
Repo: vercel-labs/json-render, 16.0k stars, Apache-2.0, created 2026-01-14, pushed 2026-08-19. Unlike A2UI, it does cut formal GitHub releases (v0.20.0, v0.19.0, …).
Vercel AI SDK fit is real and documented: the AI SDK integration page pairs useChat with useJsonRenderMessage, in Standalone and Inline modes (see ui-for-ai-products for that surface).

Do they actually compose?
The 2026-06 version of this note speculated that the layers “can even compose”. As of 2026-08 both projects say so in their own docs — with a caveat worth knowing before planning around it.

A2UI’s side: its renderers reference lists json-render under “Ecosystem Renderers” — “Vercel’s React library for rendering A2UI catalogs via Zod schemas”.
json-render’s side: ships a docs/a2ui page showing how to define an A2UI-shaped catalog (BoundValue, adjacency list, surfaceUpdate) against the schema-agnostic core.
The caveat: that page is labelled “Concept: This page demonstrates how json-render can support A2UI. The examples are illustrative and may require adaptation for production use.” There is no @json-render/a2ui package on npm. This is a documented pattern, not a shipped adapter — budget integration work accordingly.

Pros and cons
A2UI

























ProsConsCross-organization by design — the agent and the client can be built by different vendors, which is the case no library solvesMore moving parts: protocol + per-platform renderer + agent integrationVersioned spec with an explicit safety model (declarative data, not code)v1.0 has been a candidate for 2.5+ months, and no maintained renderer supports it yet — every shipping renderer targets v0.9.1Genuine native-mobile story (Flutter GenUI SDK stable; Compose/SwiftUI planned) plus a growing third-party renderer setNative renderer maturity is thin where it isn’t Flutter — the Compose and React Native options are community projects in the ~10★ range, still on v0.8Google backing; A2A named as the transport, so it slots into an agent-interop stackNo formal GitHub releases, not even a tag for the “current” v0.9.1; Google-initiated projects depend on continued investment
json-render

























ProsConsSimple DX inside JS: catalog → stream → render, with first-class streaming/progressive renderingStill JS-ecosystem-bound — no native iOS/Android/Flutter target, so the trust boundary it crosses is process-level, not vendor-levelFive UI frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, React Native) from one catalog, plus PDF/email/video/3D/terminal/image renderers0.x with 30 versions in 7 months — breaking changes on upgrade are the norm, though the pace dropped sharply after MayCode export = escape hatch; generated UI becomes ordinary React (or a whole Next.js project) you own”Vercel Labs” has historically meant experimental, with no commitment to become a supported productDocumented integrations with AI SDK, A2UI, AG-UI, Adaptive Cards, OpenAPI, and MCP AppsNo stability guarantee or explicit production-readiness statement anywhere on the site or README
Production readiness (as of 2026-08-25)
Neither is boring-mature; both are credible with eyes open. Two months of extra evidence moved them closer together, not further apart.

A2UI’s designated production release (v0.9.1) is stable across all four maintained renderers, which is the real readiness signal. The v1.0 stall is the thing to watch: a candidate that hasn’t landed in 2.5 months, with every renderer still marking v1.0 “Planned”, means pinning to v0.9.1 is the only sane choice today — and that a v1.0 migration is deferred work you are taking on, not avoiding.
json-render is fine for internal tools, prototypes, and products that pin versions. The slowed release cadence (one minor in ~3 months against 29 in the prior five) reads as stabilization rather than abandonment — the repo was pushed 2026-08-19 — but 0.x plus Labs status remain real risks for a long-lived customer-facing product, softened meaningfully by code export, which limits lock-in.

Rule of thumb, revised. The old version of this rule said “multiple platforms → A2UI”. That no longer separates them, because json-render covers five UI frameworks plus six non-DOM targets. The axis that actually separates them:

Different organizations on each end (your client renders UI from someone else’s agent), or native mobile without React Native → A2UI. This is the case a library genuinely cannot cover.
You control both ends and you’re in the JS ecosystem → json-render, whatever your framework. Faster, and the code-export escape hatch caps the downside.
Both → viable, via json-render’s A2UI catalog pattern — but that’s a recipe you implement, not a package you install.

Related

generative-ui-security — what it takes to render untrusted interface in a privileged host; relevant to @json-render/mcp and to A2UI’s trust-boundary claim
ui-for-ai-products — the broader UI-for-AI axis; covers the Vercel AI SDK streaming surface json-render builds on
genui-vs-vibe-coding-nng-review — the GenUI-vs-vibe-coding framing debate (NN/g)

Sources

ai/accretive-spec-development.title: Accretive Spec Development
ai/accretive-spec-development.content:
Accretive Spec Development
A development loop for one person and one AI coding agent in which the spec is a byproduct of building, not a prerequisite. You state an intent and what would prove it false, the agent builds the smallest thing that could falsify it, you react to the running artifact, and the agent harvests spec clauses from what survived — each clause pinned to a check that can fail. The spec grows by accretion, one verified clause per loop, and is periodically rewritten into a readable document.
What it tries to accomplish
Spec-first methods (Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenSpec and similar spec-driven development tooling) write requirements, plan, and tasks before code. That buys agreement before building, at the cost of momentum during exploration and of documents that lag the implementation. Building with no spec at all is fast but has no defence against the agent quietly solving a slightly different problem than the one you asked for.
The accretive loop sits between the two. It aims to:

Keep exploration fast. Minutes per loop, reacting to running code rather than to a document. No task list — the next probe is the task.
End with a spec you can trust. Every clause in the spec is an executable claim with a check that has been shown to fail when the behaviour is broken. A clause without a check is not a clause.
Keep the human’s intent as the anchor, not the agent’s reading of it. The agent writes the probe, the check, and the proposed clause, so left alone the check would only ever encode the agent’s own interpretation. Three independence rules put a human-owned falsifier ahead of the agent’s work, lock accepted checks, and demand a mutant rejection with a named failure before a clause is accepted; their normative form is rules 1 to 3 of clause-loop.
Separate what was observed from what is wanted. Harvest records what the artifact does. Promotion to spec is a separate human act, so accidental behaviour — especially in brownfield code — never becomes contract by default.
Know when to stop looping and plan. Hard gates stop irreversible work for permission, and planning heuristics send unstable work into a conventional plan before the expensive probe, not after five failed ones.
Earn a contract. A region of the spec whose clauses are all wanted and currently verified can be frozen, and a frozen region is a spec-driven-development-shaped contract other agents and services build against.

The honest scope of its guarantee, stated normatively in clause-loop: once a region is frozen, a contract guard rejects missing or failing required checks and unapproved changes to the region’s declared verification surface, and it does not prove that the checks express the requirement or the intent. Spec-to-intent drift is bounded — by the human-owned falsifier, the locked checks and the per-clause evidence rule — not prevented. An earlier version of this note called spec-to-test drift “impossible”; that overstated a guard which only sees the surface it was told about.
The loop
Step 0 — Ground
Before the first intent, hand the agent a screen or less of:

Context — prose about the project and its situation.
Constraints — hard facts the agent may never violate (“Node.js only”, “no external network calls”). Each enters the spec at Ground, born there, with a check attached where one is possible; a constraint with no attachable check is written as a guarded invariant (see Two tiers) from day one. A constraint the current code already violates enters as a wanted clause with an open exception — owner, scope, expiry — in the decisions log, rather than being pretended to hold.
Preferences — soft leanings the agent may trade off but must say when it does. A departure is logged as an amendment.
Irreversibility list — what is expensive to get wrong in this project (migrations, payment paths, public contracts, data deletion). It feeds the hard gates directly.

Output is GROUND.md. Probes are validated against it before you see them. Ground is a floor, not a plan: past roughly a screen you are sneaking upfront design back in.
1 — Intent
One sentence of what you want to be true next, plus one line of what would prove it false. That falsifier is the only oracle in the loop the agent did not write — the human owns it, written from scratch or substantively revised from candidate counterexamples the agent proposes — and it anchors the probe’s check before the agent’s reading of the intent exists. No acceptance criteria beyond that.
2 — Probe
The agent builds the smallest thing that could falsify the intent: code plus a runnable check. Before building, it declares an execution envelope and reads it against the hard gates and planning heuristics (below): a hard gate stops for the human’s permission on that action, a heuristic sends the work to a plan instead of a probe. On brownfield code the first probe is “harvest what is already true”.
The agent ends every probe with a short list of what the probe does not exercise. A running artifact shows presence, never absence, so failure-mode coverage has to be explicit.
3 — Confront
Run it. Before it runs, the agent drafts what pass and fail look like from your falsifier and you amend it if you disagree (/predict-then-compare). React to the working artifact and to the not-exercised list. Say what is wrong and what is missing.
4 — Harvest
The agent proposes one to three clauses capturing what you accepted or rejected. Each clause carries:

an oracle type — one of the seven clause-loop defines: test, property, guard, consistency, reader, walk or manual;
a pin — a stable id, its check id and the change it was born in;
a demonstration that the check rejects a deliberate mutant for a named reason — a one-line sabotage of the implementation that fails at the assertion the clause names, not a crash. A check that cannot fail is not a check, and one that fails for an unrelated reason proves nothing.

Clauses arrive in the observed state. You promote a clause to wanted only when you affirm it deserves to exist, not merely that its test passes. Observed clauses must be ruled on before the change closes; Close refuses while one is unruled. Rejecting one is three decisions on one DECISIONS.log line — not contract; whether the behaviour stays in the artifact; whether the check stays as characterization coverage — because “not promised” is not “not worth testing”.
Prune — this note’s name for what clause-loop reports as verification failing — lives inside Harvest: a clause whose check no longer passes is a stop. It stays wanted; a failing check is not a change of mind.
Once a clause is wanted, its check is locked: the agent may change the code but not that check inside the loop. Editing a locked check is a decision the human makes, and once the region is frozen it is recorded through an approval boundary the agent cannot write to. The normative form of this step is clause-loop rules 3 and 6.
5 — Freeze
A region is proposed for freezing when every clause in it is wanted and currently verified — not when it has merely gone untouched, and not on the strength of one recent probe that exercised a corner of it. Freeze and unfreeze are both decisions-log entries. Frozen means something in CI: a manifest written from the region’s pins names its clauses, checks and verification surface, and a contract guard fails the build on an unapproved change to that surface or on a required check that did not run and pass. The mechanism is defined in clause-loop. A frozen region is also exported as a contract test consumers run on their side; that export is what makes “other agents build against it” a mechanism rather than a sentence.
6 — Consolidate
Every ten or so archives, or at every freeze, the agent rewrites the region’s spec by domain structure: merges overlapping clauses, orders by concept rather than by birth iteration, keeps every pin, re-points any pin the rewrite breaks, and runs a clause-versus-clause conflict scan — two clauses whose checks exercise disjoint inputs can both pass while contradicting each other at intent level, and no per-check test can see that. The harvest order is a changelog; the consolidated form is the spec. Without this step the artifact converges on a test index with prose labels.
Artifacts



































FileHoldsChanges howGROUND.mdContext, constraints, preferences, irreversibility list, envelope defaults, approval boundaryWritten at step 0, edited rarelychanges/<name>/proposal.mdOne change’s intent, falsifier with origin, envelope, loop log and decisionsOne per change; archived at Closespecs/<region>/spec.mdWanted clauses only, each scenario carrying a pin; guarded invariants labelled; a status lineGrows at Close, rewritten by consolidateDECISIONS.logAppend-only; nine kinds defined in clause-loop, written by the agent from the human’s decisionsAppend onlyManifestClause ids, check ids, the verification surface and the contract-test export under freeze, enforced by the contract guardWritten from the pins at freeze; a surface change needs an approval the agent cannot write
No task list. No plan document until a heuristic asks for one.
Clause states
A clause has two axes, defined normatively in clause-loop: acceptance — observed, wanted, retired — which is the human’s and changes rarely, and verification — passing, failing, stale, unknown — which is the run’s and is never hand-edited. A Ground constraint the current code violates is a wanted clause with an open, expiring exception rather than a state of its own. Only wanted clauses can freeze. Brownfield harvest therefore produces a visibly provisional characterization layer, not a contract.
Two tiers of spec
Tier one is executable clauses — the ones the contract guard covers once their region is frozen.
Tier two is guarded invariants: requirements you cannot cheaply attach a check to — negative (“never sends PII outbound”), cross-cutting (“degrades gracefully offline”), non-functional (“migration is reversible”). Each has a named manual check, an owner, and a review cadence. They live in the region’s spec file, labelled as tier two, and count as spec. They just do not get the drift guarantee; they get a scheduled re-check instead. Without this tier the executable-only rule would push the most important requirements out of the spec entirely.
Escalation gates
Planning is an escalation the loop expects to make. A cap of about five loops per intent is the backstop. The gates are defined normatively in clause-loop rule 4; they read an execution envelope the probe declares before building, and they are of two kinds:

Hard gates stop for the human’s permission on that specific action, whichever path the work is on: a write to production or a shared environment, a destructive operation, a credential, an externally visible action, anything on the Ground irreversibility list, an edit to a frozen region’s verification surface. Destructive work is never wrapped in a loop’s conditional.
Planning heuristics send the work to a plan instead of a probe, and are judged rather than computed: uncertainty the agent names about the approach; rework — the same region harvested and rejected twice, which is the intent being unstable, not the code, and which is where splitting an intent to dodge the cap shows up; growth — a probe whose budget exceeds the last three building loops combined, a design question wearing a probe’s clothes; cross-domain coordination — an intent spanning two or more regions with at least one under contract; a contract change — an intent that would modify or retire a wanted clause in a region under contract.

What the probe actually touched is compared to the envelope at every loop, because a rule that reads only the agent’s declared plan cannot see undeclared work.
Escalation has a defined target: a plan artifact in spec-driven-development shape (a Spec Kit plan, an OpenSpec change folder, or equivalent) that the next probes execute against. The loop escalates into that pipeline deliberately, because it is the right tool once the work is known to be expensive.
Command set
Four public actions — Start, Probe, Decide, Close — with eleven operations underneath — ground, intent, probe, confront, harvest, propose, archive, freeze, consolidate, explore, converge. Escalation is not an action; it is the gate check inside Probe. The runnable form — the actions, the operations, both paths, the folder layout, reader and walk oracles for non-code work, and a copyable starter kit — is clause-loop, and it is normative where this note and it differ.
When to use it

Good fit: one person, one agent, one repo; reversible work; exploratory or brownfield code where you learn what you want by seeing it run. It is the concrete instance of the verify-and-iterate unit of work in coding-with-agentic-loops, inside the agent-workflow-solo-practitioner niche.
What it is: an exploration-to-contract mode. Run the loop until a region freezes; a frozen region is a spec-driven-development-shaped contract, and change to it should go through a proposal-first process, which is the “agreement before building” guarantee the loop gives up everywhere else.
Relation to spec-driven development: not a replacement. The difference is direction of derivation (harvest from artifacts versus derive from requirements) and granularity (a clause per loop versus a document per phase). As of 2026-09, the mainstream tools also run evolving specs with executable checks, so executability and brownfield support are not what set this apart. How the two run as one system — which affirmation of a clause gates the build, the region transitions, and the mapping of these artifacts onto a Spec Kit or OpenSpec layout — is in spec-driven-development-operating-model.
Relation to intent engineering: the consolidated region spec is the durable, CI-enforceable contract layer intent-engineering-discipline argues for. This loop is one way to earn that artifact instead of drafting it.
Weak fit: multi-team contracts before anything has frozen; regulated audit trails (the log is the agent’s record of an approval; the approval itself lives at whatever boundary the repo host provides, and neither is a formal audit trail); any project where the first probe is itself the expensive part; handoff between sessions or parallel agents, where “no task list” stops holding and a plan file becomes the thread.

Beyond code: architecture and decisions
The loop transfers to design and decision work; the free re-running oracle does not. In code the check is a test. In architecture it is a spike, a fitness function, or a scenario walk, and only the first two re-run for free.








































StepIn codeIn architecture designIntent”X should be true next”, plus a falsifierA quality-attribute scenario — stimulus, response, measure: “under 10× load, checkout p95 stays under 300 ms”ProbeSmallest code plus a checkA throwaway that could falsify it: walking skeleton, load or failure simulation, cost model, or a paper walk of the scenario through the candidate design. The probe is reversible even when the decision is notConfrontRun it, reactRun the spike where one exists; otherwise walk the scenario adversarially (second-order, red-team)HarvestClause pinned to a testA constraint or invariant pinned to a fitness function where possible (“no imports from domain into infra”, a latency budget in CI) and to a dated scenario walk where notPruneCheck fails, clause reported failingA fitness function fails, or a change touches a scenario’s assumptions and the walk is re-run by handFreezeFrozen region, contract guardAn accepted ADR. Unfreeze is a superseding ADR
Structure scans such as dependency-flow-scan, deepen-architecture and structural-trace serve as fitness functions here, so a harvested architecture clause can be pinned to one of them the way a code clause is pinned to a test. The same generalisation carried to documents and specifications — a reader oracle, where a fresh context is given the artifact alone and must complete a task from it — is defined in clause-loop.
For ADRs specifically (architecture-decision-records-ai): write the record after the probe, not before; carry the falsifier from Intent into the ADR as a pre-registered reversal criterion (“supersede this if the scenario fails at N users”); map ADR status onto clause state (proposed is observed, accepted is wanted, superseded is retired); and write the expected spike outcome before running it so the record does not become hindsight narrative.
Where it degrades: if the smallest falsifier of an intent is “build it in production”, the loop does not apply and the work is plan-first. Quality attributes are mostly tier-two guarded invariants, so “drift is bounded” shrinks to “drift is scheduled for re-check”. Decisions with no artifact at all (team topology, build-versus-buy) have no spike; there the loop collapses to intent, adversarial walk, and an ADR with a reversal criterion — a pre-registered decision journal, not accretive spec development.

ai/agent-isolation-hardening.title: Agent Isolation Hardening
ai/agent-isolation-hardening.content:
Agent Isolation Hardening
agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers picks the tier. This note is the next step: making the boundary you picked actually hold. Verified against Claude Code 2.1.220, the reference dev container at anthropics/claude-code@main, and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime as of 2026-07-31.
The recurring failure mode is not a missing boundary — it’s a boundary with one rule that voids it. Everything below is an instance of that.
The reference firewall has three egress holes — tested, not inferred
The published .devcontainer/init-firewall.sh is the artifact most people copy for unattended work. Its shape is sound: ipset allowlist, iptables -P OUTPUT DROP, explicit REJECT tail, and a self-verification step. Three rules undercut it.
I replicated its rule structure in a rootless container and probed it, with the allowlist deliberately narrowed to api.anthropic.com so the results are unambiguous:








































ProbeResultMeaningcurl -4 github.com (off-allowlist, 443)blockedcontrol — the allowlist works as designedcurl -4 example.comblockedcontrolcurl -6 example.comREACHABLEIPv6 bypasses the entire policycurl example.com (default family)REACHABLEand IPv6 is what curl picks by defaultdig @1.1.1.1 <name>SUCCEEDEDarbitrary external resolver reachablessh -4 git@github.com (off-allowlist)reached sshdport 22 egress to anywhere
Hole 1 — the policy is IPv4-only
The script calls iptables and never ip6tables. In the test container, ip6tables -S showed -P OUTPUT ACCEPT with global IPv6 present, so every allowlist rule was void for IPv6 traffic — and since curl prefers IPv6 when available, the default path was the unfiltered one.
Fairness point: the script’s own verification step catches this. It exits 1 if example.com is reachable, so on a dual-stack container it aborts loudly rather than running wide open. The danger is copying the rules without the check, or running where the resolver happens to return IPv4 first — then the hole is silent.
Fix: mirror every rule to ip6tables (including a v6 ipset, hash:net family inet6), or disable IPv6 in the container outright and assert it — the second is easier to get right and easier to verify.
Hole 2 — unrestricted DNS to any resolver
iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT is added before the restrictions and never narrowed. Any host, any resolver. DNS is a well-worn covert channel: data encodes into query names sent to a nameserver the attacker controls, and no allowlist rule ever sees it.
Fix: allow UDP/53 only to the container’s own resolver address, not 0.0.0.0/0. Under Docker that is 127.0.0.11; other runtimes expose their own resolver address. Everything else falls to the REJECT tail.
Hole 3 — unrestricted TCP/22 to any host
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT gives full outbound SSH anywhere. Confirmed: ssh -4 git@github.com reached GitHub’s sshd while curl -4 github.com was blocked. SSH is a general-purpose tunnel, so this is not “git over SSH works” — it is an arbitrary egress channel with encryption included.
Fix: drop the blanket rule. Git-over-SSH to GitHub already works via the api.github.com/meta ranges in the ipset, matched on destination rather than port.
Hole 4 (not tested, structural) — the host /24
HOST_NETWORK is derived by rewriting the last octet of the default gateway to .0/24, then allowed in both directions. That is a whole subnet, reachable in both directions, granted by a line whose apparent purpose is “let the container talk to its host.” In a corporate network segment it is the adjacent infrastructure — internal registries, admin interfaces, other build agents; in a flat network it is considerably more. Narrow it to the specific host address, if host access is needed at all.
The reference allowlist is stale for claude.ai auth
The script resolves: registry.npmjs.org, api.anthropic.com, sentry.io, statsig.anthropic.com, statsig.com, and three VS Code hosts. Compared against the current documented network requirements, it is missing claude.ai, platform.claude.com, downloads.claude.ai, and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com.
Consequence: a container built from this script can reach the API but cannot complete a claude.ai OAuth sign-in, since token exchange and refresh go to platform.claude.com. Conversely sentry.io and the two Statsig hosts no longer appear in the documented requirements at all.
The current required set is api.anthropic.com, claude.ai, claude.com, platform.claude.com, mcp-proxy.anthropic.com, downloads.claude.ai, storage.googleapis.com, bridge.claudeusercontent.com, and raw.githubusercontent.com, plus optional telemetry (http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com, browser-intake-us5-datadoghq.com, disabled together by CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC). Note that variable also disables Remote Control’s feature-flag fetch.
Better pattern than resolve-once: the script digs each domain at boot and pins the returned IPs. CDN-backed hosts rotate addresses, so the allowlist rots during a long session, and pinning a shared CDN edge IP incidentally allows every other tenant on that edge. Prefer a filtering HTTP proxy that decides on hostname over an IP-set firewall — that is what both the built-in sandbox and sandbox-runtime do — and keep iptables as the backstop that forces traffic through it.
sandbox-runtime, done well
Why it fails closed on Linux
On Linux srt removes the sandboxed process’s network namespace entirely; the only egress is HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies on the host, reached over bind-mounted Unix sockets bridged by socat. This is the architectural reason it is a real boundary and not a convention.
A misreading worth pre-empting: the README’s future-work section carries a heading “Linux proxy bypass”, which reads like an escape vector. The body says the opposite: srt uses HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/ALL_PROXY to point tools at the proxies, and a program ignoring those variables ends up “unable to connect to the internet”. With no netns there is no path around the socket. So: fail-closed (breakage), not fail-open (escape). The same section lists proxychains/LD_PRELOAD as future work to make “bypass more difficult”, so treat it as architecturally fail-closed with the authors reserving some doubt — not as a known escape.
Mandatory deny paths, and the Linux gotcha that defeats them
srt always blocks writes to a fixed set regardless of allowWrite: .bashrc, .bash_profile, .zshrc, .zprofile, .profile, .gitconfig, .gitmodules, .ripgreprc, .mcp.json, and the directories .vscode/, .idea/, .claude/commands/, .claude/agents/, .git/hooks/, .git/config. That list is precisely the self-escalation surface — write any of them and you own the next session.
The gotcha: on Linux these are enforced by bind-mount, so they only block files that already exist. A non-existent .git/hooks/pre-commit cannot be blocked and can be created. macOS uses glob patterns and blocks both.
This exact bug class has been exploited in Claude Code’s own sandbox. CVE-2026-25725 (< 2.1.2, CVSS 3.1 10.0 / v4.0 7.7, CWE-501 Trust Boundary Violation, GHSA-ff64-7w26-62rf): bubblewrap protected .claude/settings.local.json read-only, but .claude/settings.json was not protected when it did not exist at startup. Sandboxed code created the file, injected SessionStart hooks, and those executed with host privileges on the next run. Same shape as the srt gap above — a protection expressed as a constraint on an existing path silently does not apply to a path that isn’t there yet. Treat “pre-create the deny-path files” as a mitigation with a CVE behind it, not a fussy precaution.
Fix: pre-create the deny-path files as empty placeholders in any repo you hand to an unattended srt session, so the bind-mount has something to cover. Also note mandatoryDenySearchDepth defaults to 3 — files deeper than three levels inside an allowed write path are not scanned; raise it (max 10) or keep write scope shallow.
Config skeleton
Deny-all by default, so an under-specified file means a session that cannot start. Minimum viable shape:
{
  "network": {
    "allowedDomains": ["api.anthropic.com", "claude.ai", "platform.claude.com",
                       "downloads.claude.ai", "registry.npmjs.org:443"],
    "deniedDomains": []
  },
  "filesystem": {
    "denyRead": ["/home"],
    "allowRead": ["."],
    "allowWrite": [".", "/tmp", "~/.claude"],
    "denyWrite": [".env"]
  },
  "mandatoryDenySearchDepth": 5
}
Two asymmetries that are easy to get backwards, and are intentional: for reads it is deny-then-allow with allowRead winning, so you can carve a readable workspace out of a denied /home. For writes it is allow-only with denyWrite winning, so you can carve protected files out of a writable tree. Domain entries take an optional :port suffix; without one they match any port.
Claude Code also needs write access to ~/.claude and ~/.claude.json — the latter sits outside the directory, and missing it is the usual cause of a wrapped session that won’t hold auth.
Syscall-level enforcement, and its edges
The bundled apply-seccomp binary (static, x64/arm64) blocks AF_UNIX socket creation, and also io_uring_setup/enter/register — because IORING_OP_SOCKET on Linux 5.19+ would otherwise route around the socket() rule. That second block is a good sign that its authors take the threat model seriously; it is the kind of gap most homegrown seccomp policies miss.
Two edges to know: it does not stop operations on descriptors inherited from a parent or passed via SCM_RIGHTS, and on architectures without a pre-built filter you must fall back to allowAllUnixSockets: true, which removes the protection entirely.
Rollout note: srt is distributed via npm, so the effective install location depends on the fleet’s npm prefix. Where that prefix is unusual — a per-application runtime, a version manager, a locked-down image — the binary can land off the login shell’s PATH, which turns “the wrapper is installed” into a false assumption. Pin the invocation (npx, or an absolute path) rather than relying on PATH resolution in any automated context.
Container tier
What the reference Dockerfile does that is worth keeping, independent of Docker:

Non-root remoteUser. Not cosmetic: --dangerously-skip-permissions refuses to start as root or under sudo, so a root container blocks the very thing the container exists to enable.
Narrow sudoers. node ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/init-firewall.sh — exactly one root command, so the agent can raise the firewall at start but cannot lower it afterwards. Copy this precisely; a blanket NOPASSWD hands the agent the ability to flush its own policy.
Firewall at postStartCommand with waitFor set to it, so the container is not usable before the policy is up.
CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR pointed at a named volume together with mounting ~/.claude there — because ~/.claude.json lives outside ~/.claude, mounting the directory alone loses auth on rebuild.

Runtime portability: none of this requires Docker specifically. --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW is sufficient for the iptables/ipset approach under a rootless runtime — verified — so the pattern ports to rootless OCI runtimes without a privileged container. What does not port automatically is the address-family assumption: the rootless container used for these probes had global IPv6, which is what exposed Hole 1. Docker’s default bridge commonly does not. Assert the address families your runtime actually gives the container instead of inheriting the reference script’s IPv4-only assumption.
Layering the built-in Bash sandbox inside the container requires sandbox.enableWeakerNestedSandbox: true, because nested bwrap cannot mount a fresh /proc unprivileged — tested, with the trade-off in agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers.
The caveat that survives all of this: a container does not stop a malicious project from exfiltrating what is inside the container, including the Claude Code credentials in ~/.claude. Don’t mount ~/.ssh or cloud credential files in; prefer short-lived, repository-scoped tokens.
VM tier
The VM is the only tier that gives kernel-level separation, and it is the documented recommendation for genuinely untrusted code. Two things determine whether it is available rather than theoretical:

Hardware virtualization exposed to the workload. Present on bare metal, frequently absent on cloud instances that don’t offer nested virtualization — and cloud instances are where CI runners live. A VM-tier policy that CI cannot satisfy will be quietly downgraded to a container by whoever has to make the pipeline pass.
A hypervisor stack in the image. On image-based and immutable fleets this is a base-image decision made long before the security review, not something a developer installs later.

Neither is a reason against the tier; both are reasons to verify it on the actual target class before mandating it, since the failure mode is a policy that only holds on the machines that were used to write it.
Cross-cutting: verify the boundary, don’t declare it
Every hole above was found by probing, and three of the four contradicted what reading the script suggested. Minimum acceptance test for any boundary before an unattended run:

Negative control, both address families — an off-allowlist host must fail on IPv4 and IPv6, tested with the family forced (curl -4 / curl -6), not the default.
Positive control — api.anthropic.com must succeed, or you have built a boundary that also blocks the work.
Protocol sweep, not just 443 — try DNS to an external resolver and TCP/22 to an off-allowlist host. Both were open in the reference config.
Self-escalation probe — attempt a write to ~/.bashrc, .git/hooks/pre-commit, and the relevant settings.json. Under srt on Linux, create-then-check, since non-existent files aren’t covered.
Re-run after any allowlist edit. Resolve-once designs rot silently.

Counterargument
The holes above are real, but the threat model that makes them urgent is hostile code inside the boundary — a poisoned dependency, an injected instruction acting on the agent. For unattended work on your own repository, the dominant risk is still the agent doing something wrong-but-permitted, and none of this touches that: a perfectly sealed container will happily let the agent rewrite your project’s history. Hardening egress is necessary for the untrusted case and close to irrelevant for the careless case, which is the more common one. If the realistic worry is “it ran overnight and made a mess”, the effort belongs in deny rules, a scratch branch, and reversibility — not in ip6tables.
The counter-counter: egress hardening is cheap and one-time, and it’s the only one of these controls that still works after the agent has been successfully manipulated.
Related

Sources

ai/agent-output-quality-variance.title: Reducing Quality Variance in Agent Output
ai/agent-output-quality-variance.content:
Reducing Quality Variance in Agent Output
The goal this note serves: a framework around a codebase that makes an agent produce higher-quality code and makes that quality consistent, accepting generation time and token cost as the price. deterministic-gates-agent-loop covers the gates, constrained-shape-for-verifiability covers narrowing the code’s shape. This note is the level above both — what the objective is, which control addresses which part of it, and what the whole thing costs.
The framing is worth being precise about, because it is a reliability problem rather than a capability one, and reliability-vs-capability-agents establishes those diverge systematically. Peak quality and consistent quality are different targets with different instruments.
Gates truncate; they do not lift
A gate can only reject. It cannot make acceptable code better. So a gate stack does not shift the quality distribution rightward — it cuts the left tail off, and the mean rises as a consequence of that truncation rather than independently.
For an explicit variance-reduction goal this is good news: gates are the correct instrument, and the instinct to build a framework out of them is right. But two consequences follow immediately.

The floor sits at your weakest gate’s threshold, not at the strength of your strongest one.
Defect classes you do not gate pass through with their full original variance. Truncation is per-class. A stack of eleven gates that all target correctness leaves readability, naming, and architectural fit exactly as variable as they were.

If you want the mean raised rather than the floor, the levers are different ones — better context, better specification, a stronger model — and no amount of gating substitutes.
Five sources of variance, and only one of them is gate-shaped
This is the part most gate-centric frameworks get wrong. Ask where the run-to-run spread actually comes from:



































SourceWhat variesThe control that addresses itSamplingSame input, different roll of the diceGates plus bounded retry — the one gates genuinely fixContextWhich files were loaded, in what order, whether compaction firedDeterministic context assembly; pin what gets loaded (context-repo-loading-patterns)SpecificationAn ambiguous requirement read differently each runSpecification work. Gates cannot see this at allHorizonLong runs degrade — context pressure, compaction loss, self-conditioningTask sizing and checkpointing (agent-autonomy-horizon)SubstrateThe agent imitates whatever surrounds the editExemplar quality in the touched area (ai-friendly-repo-structure, constrained-shape-for-verifiability)
A framework made only of gates addresses one row of five. That is the central design point, and the reason “add more gates” stops paying long before the problem is solved.
Of the four that gates miss, specification variance is the one to worry about most, because it is plausibly dominant in real work and it is invisible to every downstream control. Two runs that interpret “handle the error case” differently both pass every gate you own. The framework’s specification layer is not a nicety on top of the gates; it is doing more of the work.
Substrate variance is the one with compounding returns. An agent’s output regresses toward the local mean of what it can see, so cleaning the exemplar surface reduces variance on every future edit in that area, permanently, at no per-run cost. Gates charge rent forever; substrate work is bought once.
What the stack costs
Gate runtime is not the dominant cost. First-try pass rate is. If a stack has n gates and the agent satisfies each on the first attempt with probability q, the combined pass rate is q^n and expected attempts is 1/q^n — so cost rises superlinearly in gate count.
Expected attempts to clear the whole stack:








































gatesq=0.98q=0.95q=0.90q=0.8051.1×1.3×1.7×3.1×101.2×1.7×2.9×9.3×151.4×2.2×4.9×28.4×201.5×2.8×8.2×86.7×
And the failure mode that ends the loop — probability a task never clears the stack inside a repair budget of B attempts:








































gatesqcombined pB=3B=550.900.596.9%1.2%100.900.3527.6%11.7%150.900.2150.1%31.6%150.950.4615.5%4.5%
Fifteen gates at a 90% per-gate first-try rate means half of all tasks exhaust a three-attempt budget and escalate. At that density the framework has not reduced variance — it has moved the variance onto the human review queue, which is the resource vigilance-decrement-in-ai-oversight says degrades under exactly that load.
Model caveats, because the shape matters more than the digits: gate failures are not independent (a bad diff trips several at once, and one repair often clears several), and q is wildly non-uniform — a compile gate might sit at 0.98 for a competent agent while a bespoke architecture rule it has never been told about sits near 0.5. Read the tables as the shape of the curve, not as calibrated predictions for a real repository.
The highest-return move: give every gate a context-side twin
Because p = q^n is multiplicative, raising q beats reducing n. And the cheapest way to raise q is to stop letting gates be a surprise.
A gate whose rule the agent was never told is being used for discovery — the agent finds out the rule by violating it, and you pay a full generation cycle for information you could have given away for free in the prompt. State the rule up front and the same gate becomes pure verification.
The arithmetic is worth seeing, at n=10:




















first-try rateexpected attemptsq = 0.80 → 0.959.3× → 1.7×5.6× cheaperq = 0.90 → 0.982.9× → 1.2×2.3× cheaper
So the design rule is: every gate gets a context-side twin. The rule is stated in CLAUDE.md, the skill body, or the task prompt; the gate exists to verify it held, not to teach it. A gate with no twin is a tax you chose to pay.
The corollary is that this bounds gate count in a useful way. If a rule cannot be stated compactly enough to sit in context, it is probably too intricate to be a good gate — the agent will keep tripping it, q stays low, and it drags the whole stack’s economics down.
Retry is rejection sampling, and it selects on the proxy
Bounded retry against a gate is rejection sampling: you draw until a sample passes, then keep it. Which means output becomes conditional on passing the gate, and unmeasured quality dimensions move according to how they correlate with the gate.

Positively correlated with the gate (compile, type-check, tests that assert): selection improves them too. Retry is free quality.
Uncorrelated: unchanged.
Negatively correlated: selection actively degrades them. Where satisfying the gate costs the unmeasured property, more retries make it worse.

The negatively-correlated cases are precisely the metric thresholds from deterministic-gates-agent-loop — a complexity threshold traded against natural seams, a coverage threshold traded against test meaningfulness. Retrying harder against those does not converge on good code; it converges on code shaped to the metric.
Practical reading: retry freely against Tier B structural gates and correctness gates. Do not build a retry loop around a metric threshold.
Measure the variance, or the framework is faith
The objective is a distributional property, so a single run cannot confirm it. The instrument is pass^k from reliability-vs-capability-agents: run the same task k times from the same starting commit and look at the spread, not the best result.
Minimum viable measurement — pick five to ten representative tasks, run each k times with and without the framework, and record escaped defects by class, the spread of a quality proxy, attempts-to-pass, escalation rate, and wall-clock and token cost per accepted change. Keep failed attempts in the denominator.
Without this you cannot distinguish a framework that reduced variance from one that merely made the failures quieter, and measuring-own-ai-leverage is blunt that self-report is a broken instrument for exactly this question.
The case against

Truncation cuts the right tail too. Over-tuned gates reject unusual-but-correct solutions along with bad ones. Variance falls, and so does the ceiling. Linters banning valid idioms are the everyday version.
The framework is code. It rots, it has bugs, and a false-positive gate is a permanent tax on every future change plus a standing incentive to suppress.
Escalation is variance, relocated. Past a certain density the human queue absorbs everything the stack could not resolve, and that queue has its own degradation curve.
The strongest objection: if specification variance dominates, almost none of this helps. Every control here operates downstream of the requirement. Two defensible readings of an ambiguous spec both pass everything. Before building the stack, it is worth checking whether the observed variance is actually sampling variance — the kind gates fix — or disagreement about what was being asked, in which case the money belongs in the specification layer instead.

Related

deterministic-gates-agent-loop — the gate layer, its verdict types, and the input-provenance tiering this note prices
constrained-shape-for-verifiability — the substrate lever, and the one with compounding rather than per-run returns
reliability-vs-capability-agents — pass@k versus pass^k; the measurement primitive this note’s objective requires
agent-autonomy-horizon — horizon variance and in-run degradation
oracle-problem-verification — what every gate in the stack silently trusts
vigilance-decrement-in-ai-oversight — why relocating variance onto human review is not a solution
measuring-own-ai-leverage — why the measurement layer cannot be self-report
ai-for-quality-not-quantity — the allocation argument this operationalizes

Sources

Cost and escalation tables computed from the stated model (p = q^n, expected attempts 1/p, escalation (1-p)^B), not drawn from any study. The independence and uniform-q assumptions are stated inline and are both false in practice; the tables illustrate curve shape only.
This note’s own contributions, argued rather than measured: gates-truncate-rather-than-lift, the five-source variance decomposition, the context-side-twin rule, retry-as-rejection-sampling and its correlation cases, and the case-against. No empirical study is cited for any of them.
The underlying reliability primitives (pass@1 / pass@k / pass^k) and their sourcing live in reliability-vs-capability-agents rather than being restated here.

ai/agent-policy-enforcement-gap.title: Agent Policy Enforcement Gap
ai/agent-policy-enforcement-gap.content:
Agent Policy Enforcement Gap
Third of four. agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers asks which boundary; agent-isolation-hardening asks does the boundary hold; this one asks can you make anyone use it, and what does the policy itself guarantee. Verified against Claude Code 2.1.220 docs as of 2026-07-31.
The organizational failure mode is a category error: shipping a configuration policy and believing you have deployed a security boundary.
The central distinction: who holds the authority, and where is it decided
The intuitive split — “configuration is soft, OS enforcement is hard” — is the wrong axis, and it breaks on the first example. The built-in Bash sandbox is enforced by the kernel, but it is switched on by sandbox.enabled, a settings key. A client that ignores that key never calls bwrap, and no kernel mechanism compels it to. The same holds for a developer who simply doesn’t start the container. An isolation tier the subject activates for themselves is not categorically stronger than a setting the subject can edit.
The axis that actually predicts strength is who controls the substrate the decision is made on:






























Subject-controlled substrateSeparately-controlled substrateExamplesSettings on a developer’s laptop; a sandbox or dev container that same developer opts into; hooks and MCP servers they can editMDM-locked policy file; CI runner image; cloud VM the developer can’t reconfigure; egress enforced by a network the workload doesn’t administerDecision made bySoftware running as, and configurable by, the party being constrainedA different principal, out of the constrained party’s reachSurvives a non-compliant or modified client?No — regardless of whether the mechanism is a JSON key or a hypervisorYesFailure modeSilent detachment; nothing looks brokenAvailability — the control can block legitimate work
Anthropic states the limit for server-delivered policy plainly: it “provide[s] centralized policy enforcement, but … operate[s] as a client-side control, not a security boundary. On unmanaged devices, a user doesn’t need admin or sudo access to bypass them.”
That sentence generalizes further than the page it appears on. The same is true of an OS-level sandbox that the constrained party enabled. Isolation strength is a property of the deployment topology, not of the mechanism.
The corollary, which the rest of this note is an argument for: an org’s real enforcement surface is whatever it runs on infrastructure the developer does not administer. Everything else is a strong default that a motivated or merely misconfigured endpoint steps around.
Three delivery channels, and what each is worth

Server-managed settings — from the claude.ai admin console, fetched at startup and polled hourly. Requires Team or Enterprise, Owner/Primary-Owner role, and reachability of api.anthropic.com. Built for orgs without device management.
Endpoint-managed settings — MDM configuration profiles (macOS managed preferences, Windows registry) or files at /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/ (macOS) and /etc/claude-code/ (Linux/WSL). Anthropic’s own guidance: these “provide stronger security guarantees because the settings file can be protected from user modification at the OS level.”
policyHelper — an admin-deployed executable that computes policy at startup from device posture or a remote service. Only honored from MDM or a system managed-settings file; when configured, its output replaces every other managed source, server-managed included.

Precedence has a sharp edge: server-managed and endpoint-managed settings do not merge. Claude Code takes the first source delivering a non-empty configuration — server first, then endpoint. If the server payload has any keys, the endpoint file is ignored. An org running both, expecting union semantics, is mostly running one of them.
But not entirely, and the exception matters operationally. A short list of keys is “honored when any admin-controlled managed source sets them, rather than only the winning source” — with the user-writable HKCU registry tier excluded, and the whole carve-out superseded when a policyHelper is configured. Those keys are sandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnly and sandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly with their allowlists, allowAllClaudeAiMcps, the sandbox binary paths sandbox.bwrapPath / sandbox.socatPath, and forceRemoteSettingsRefresh. Do not decommission an MDM-delivered managed file on the strength of the general rule: it may still be the thing enforcing your sandbox locks and your fail-closed startup.
The managed tier is also five levels, not two — policyHelper > server-managed > MDM/OS-level policy > file-based (managed-settings.d/*.json + managed-settings.json) > HKCU registry. The same non-merge surprise therefore recurs inside the endpoint channel, between an MDM profile and a managed settings file. Note also that the HKCU tier is user-writable, i.e. there is a user-writable rung inside the “managed” hierarchy.
For multi-team policy authoring, file-based delivery supports a managed-settings.d/ drop-in directory on the systemd convention: base file merged first, then *.json sorted alphabetically, scalars overriding, arrays concatenated and de-duplicated, objects deep-merged. Numeric prefixes (10-telemetry.json, 20-security.json) control order.
The keys that lock, and the keys that merely win
Most settings merge across scopes, so a developer can widen an array-valued policy locally. Two different mechanisms push back, and conflating them produces a false map of what is actually locked.
Managed-only — “only read from managed settings. Placing them in user or project settings files has no effect.” The on-thesis subset of the documented list:













































KeyEffectallowManagedPermissionRulesOnlyPrevents user and project settings defining allow, ask, or deny rules; only managed rules applysandbox.filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnlyOnly managed allowRead paths honored; denyRead still merges from all sourcessandbox.network.allowManagedDomainsOnlyOnly managed domains honored; non-allowed domains blocked without promptingallowManagedHooksOnlyOnly managed, SDK, and force-enabled-plugin hooks load; user and project hooks blockedallowManagedMcpServersOnlyOnly managed allowedMcpServers respected; deniedMcpServers still mergesstrictPluginOnlyCustomizationBlocks skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers from user and project sourcesdisableSideloadFlagsRejects --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents, --mcp-config at startup — without it these bypass strictKnownMarketplaces for a single runrequiredMinimumVersionExits at startup below the floor (claude update/install/doctor still work)forceRemoteSettingsRefreshBlocks startup until policy is freshly fetched; exits if the fetch fails
Managed precedence, not a lock — these work from any scope; managed simply wins:





















KeyActual behaviorpermissions.disableBypassPermissionsModeDocs: “typically placed in managed settings … but it works from any scope. A user can set it in their own settings to lock themselves out of bypass mode”permissions.disableAutoModeSettable in any settings file; “most useful in managed settings where they can’t be overridden”sandbox.enabled, sandbox.failIfUnavailable, sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommandsOrdinary booleans: “Claude Code uses the managed value and ignores anything a developer sets locally”
The practical difference: a managed-only key cannot be set locally at all, so finding one in a user’s settings file means something is wrong. A precedence key can sit in a user’s file looking authoritative while the managed value is what applies — and it produces identical observable behavior right up until the managed source stops being delivered.
requiredMinimumVersion is the partial answer to the “user runs an older client” bypass below — partial by construction, since “versions that predate this setting ignore it,” and it fails open on an invalid value by design so a bad policy push can’t brick the fleet.
On the deny/allow asymmetry. In the default configuration, deny is the more robust half: rules are “evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the outcome,” and permission rules merge across scopes rather than override — so a deny added in any scope holds. But this inverts under allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, the first lock in the table above, which blocks user and project settings from contributing deny rules too. Under that lock the org gains total control and simultaneously loses the property that a developer can always tighten their own machine. Choose deliberately; the two goals are in tension.
excludedCommands has no managed-only lock. The docs say so directly: a developer can always append entries that run additional commands outside the sandbox. Keep the managed list narrow, and treat this as a known, unclosable widening path.
The bypass matrix
These are the vendor’s own disclosed limitations, not findings — the full eight-row security-considerations table for server-managed settings, plus two detachment paths from the platform-availability section. They are reproduced here because the set is more instructive than any single row, and because a reader who only skims the delivery docs will not assemble it.









































ScenarioOutcomeUser edits the cached settings fileTampered file applies at startup; correct settings restore on next fetchUser deletes the cacheFirst-launch behavior — brief unenforced window while settings fetch asyncUser runs an older clientVersions predating the feature never fetch or apply it (partly answered by requiredMinimumVersion)User runs a modified binary”A user who can run a modified client can bypass any client-side control”API unreachableCached settings apply if present; otherwise unenforced until next fetchUser authenticates with a different organizationSettings are not delivered for accounts outside the managed orgNetwork traffic intercepted or redirected”Disabled TLS validation or intercepted traffic can alter the settings the client receives”User sets a third-party provider variableServer-managed settings bypassed entirely
Plus two more, from platform availability:

apiKeyHelper — “Keys returned by an apiKeyHelper script don’t trigger the settings fetch.” A user-settings key silently kills delivery, exactly parallel to the provider variable below.
Cloud sessions — “Endpoint-managed settings don’t reach cloud sessions,” so orgs using Claude Code on the web need server-managed settings as well. This partially undercuts the standard remedy of “just use the endpoint channel.”

The provider-variable row is worth stating precisely. Exporting CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_MANTLE, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_ANTHROPIC_AWS, or a non-default ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL makes the client skip the settings fetch. You cannot fix this from server-managed settings, because the block arrives through the fetch the export prevents. An endpoint-managed env block doesn’t restore it either — eligibility is checked before managed env blocks apply. Documented remedies: remove the export, set the variable to "" in user settings, or deliver policy through the endpoint channel. For Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry a self-hosted Claude apps gateway restores equivalent delivery.
The same variable has a CVE against it, from the opposite direction. CVE-2026-21852 (Claude Code < 2.0.65, CVSS 3.1 7.5, CWE-522, GHSA-jh7p-qr78-84p7): a malicious repository’s .claude/settings.json set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an attacker-controlled endpoint, and the client issued authenticated requests before the trust prompt appeared — sending the API key in plaintext to the attacker. Check Point’s write-up: “every request included the authorization header – our full Anthropic API key, completely exposed in plaintext.”
So the endpoint-redirect surface is load-bearing in both threat models at once: a user exports it and silently leaves central policy; an attacker plants it and takes the credential. That convergence is the practical argument for treating API-routing configuration as a locked, managed-only concern rather than an ordinary setting — and it is why the fix deferred all network operations until after explicit consent.
Relatedly, CVE-2025-59536 (< 1.0.111, CVSS 3.1 8.8, CWE-94, GHSA-4fgq-fpq9-mr3g) is why the scope restrictions matter: hooks in a repo’s .claude/settings.json and MCP servers in .mcp.json executed at session start — MCP servers “immediately upon running claude, before the user could even read the trust dialog.” The keys a checked-out project is not permitted to set are a list written in incident response.
Read the matrix structurally rather than as a vulnerability list: two of its paths require no privilege and leave nothing visibly broken. That is the property worth carrying — not that policy can be defeated, but that the common detachment paths are silent. Being defeatable is true of all client-side policy by definition. Who is actually exposed: orgs on server-managed delivery without MDM. The docs steer security-sensitive deployments to endpoint-managed precisely because the file can be OS-protected, so the population most affected is the one that chose the convenience channel — which is also the population the channel was built for.
The startup race. Even in the compliant path, first launch without a cache fetches asynchronously and there is “a brief window before settings load where restrictions are not yet enforced.” forceRemoteSettingsRefresh: true converts this to fail-closed — the CLI blocks until a fresh fetch and exits if it fails. The trade is availability: if api.anthropic.com is unreachable, nobody can start Claude Code. Note claude auth subcommands are exempt so users can re-authenticate.
One hardening worth crediting: since v2.1.198 the cached env block withholds proxy/TLS, API-routing, and credential variables until the server confirms the payload — so a tampered cache can’t redirect the very fetch that would correct it.
Policy robustness details

Tolerant parsing. An invalid entry is stripped with a warning and the rest of the policy still applies; a typo cannot disable an organization’s whole ruleset. /doctor lists stripped entries with source file and field.
Hooks and claudeMd require user approval. Because they execute shell commands or inject context, delivered hooks show a security dialog; rejecting exits Claude Code. Non-interactive runs can’t show it — the settings apply for that run only, are not cached as approved, and the dialog appears in the next interactive session.
Auto-mode trust configuration is policy too. autoMode.environment tells the classifier which repos, buckets, and domains the org trusts, in prose. Without it, a correctly-behaving classifier blocks routine internal work and users hit the fallback threshold.

Detection and audit
Enforcement you can’t observe isn’t enforcement. Three documented layers:

ConfigChange hooks — documented purpose: “To detect runtime configuration changes, use ConfigChange hooks to log modifications or block unauthorized changes before they take effect.” Scope limit worth knowing: it fires on config changes during a session, with matchers for user_settings, project_settings, local_settings, policy_settings, and skills. There is no matcher for the server-managed cache, and a pre-startup tamper is not a during-session change — so this does not cover the cache-editing row above, and it is itself a hook delivered through the same client-side channel.
OpenTelemetry metrics — the documented path for monitoring fleet usage.
Audit log export / compliance API — settings-change events including action type, account, device, and previous/new values. Access via the Anthropic account team.

What this means for the isolation tiers
The recommendation, restated on the authority axis from the top of this note: push enforcement onto substrate the developer does not administer — the CI runner image, the VM template, an MDM-locked policy file, a network that enforces egress independently. Not because OS mechanisms beat config keys, but because a control the constrained party can switch off is not a control regardless of what enforces it.
This is why “commit a dev container to the repo” is a weaker answer than it looks, and the note should not have listed it as a remedy: Anthropic calls dev containers “a convention rather than an enforcement boundary,” and a repo file is squarely subject-controlled substrate. Enforcing one requires device management or software allowlisting — i.e. leaving the product’s control surface entirely, which is precisely the point.
Managed settings remain worth deploying. They are how the sandbox locks, deny rules, and requiredMinimumVersion reach compliant machines, which is most of them. Endpoint-managed delivery on MDM-enrolled devices also genuinely sits on separately-controlled substrate. The error to avoid is treating server-managed delivery to unmanaged laptops as equivalent, or letting either be the only thing standing between a hostile repository and production.
Counterargument
This note treats client-side controls as weak because they’re bypassable by a determined user — but that framing imports a threat model most organizations don’t have. The realistic population is developers who want to ship, not adversaries; for them a managed deny list is fully effective, and the bypass paths above are things nobody stumbles into by accident. Under that model the enforcement gap is close to irrelevant and the effort belongs in making the default path good — sensible allowlists, auto mode configured with real trusted infrastructure so it doesn’t cry wolf.
The gap becomes load-bearing in exactly two cases: when the threat is the code rather than the developer (a hostile dependency, an injected instruction — where the compromised client is the attack, not a policy violation), and when the guarantee is being made to somebody else — a regulator, a customer, an auditor. In the first, client-side controls fail by construction. In the second, “we deployed a setting” and “we enforced a boundary” are different claims, and only one is defensible under scrutiny.
