ai/agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers.title: Agent Sandbox Isolation Tiers
ai/agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers.content:
Agent Sandbox Isolation Tiers
Comparison of the isolation boundaries available to a coding agent, framed around the case that forces the decision: running unattended. Verified against Claude Code 2.1.220 and the Claude Code docs as of 2026-07-31; product behavior here is gated on specific minor versions and moves fast, hence the review_by.
For attack vectors see prompt-injection and ai-supply-chain-risks. For the defense architecture in the abstract see ai-agent-security — this note is the concrete operational layer under it.
The two axes people conflate
Permission modes and sandboxes are not the same control, and the distinction is the whole note:























AxisQuestion it answersEnforced byFails howPermission modeDoes this tool call run at all, and are you asked first?Claude Code, before the callYou aren’t there to answer, or a classifier misjudgesIsolation boundaryOnce it runs, what can it reach?The OS (Seatbelt / bubblewrap / kernel / hypervisor)The boundary is drawn too wide
The docs put it directly: with --dangerously-skip-permissions, “with no prompts to catch mistakes, the isolation boundary you choose is what protects your system.”
The unattended case removes the human from the first axis entirely. Everything therefore lands on the second. This is why “I’ll just turn on /sandbox” is the wrong reflex — see the scope gap below.
The six tiers






















































TierWhat’s inside the boundaryNeeds DockerEffortFit for unattendedBuilt-in Bash sandboxBash commands + child processesNoLowNo — see scope gapsandbox-runtime wrapperWhole Claude Code process: file tools, MCP servers, hooksNoLowYes (beta)Dev containerFull dev environmentYesMediumYesCustom containerFull dev environmentYesMedium–highYesVirtual machineFull OS, own kernelNoHighYes; strongestClaude Code on the webFull OS, Anthropic-hostedNoNoneYes; no infra to run
Only the first two run on the host without containers. Every tier below them puts the entire process inside the boundary.
The scope gap that disqualifies the built-in sandbox
The built-in Bash sandbox isolates Bash and its children only. Explicitly outside it:

Read, Edit, Write, WebFetch — run in the Claude Code process, gated by permission rules, not by the OS boundary
MCP servers — separate processes, unconstrained on the host
Hooks — separate processes, unconstrained on the host

Anthropic’s own framing: the Bash sandbox “on its own constrains only Bash, so it is not sufficient for fully unattended runs in either mode.”
This is the gap most deployments miss, because the two categories left outside are exactly the ones an organization tends to standardize on: MCP servers distributed to the fleet, and hooks deployed as policy. Both are separate host processes. Enabling the sandbox and walking away leaves the org’s own extension surface unprotected — and an MCP server is a more attractive target than the shell, since it usually holds credentials for whatever system it fronts.
The scope gap has been exploited, not just theorized. CVE-2026-39861 (< 2.1.64, CVSS 4.0 7.7, CWE-22/61, GHSA-vp62-r36r-9xqp) is the canonical demonstration: a sandboxed process created symlinks pointing outside the workspace, and the unsandboxed parent followed them when writing, with no confirmation. Neither half was individually broken; the composition was. Exploitation “required the ability to add untrusted content into a Claude Code context window to trigger sandboxed code execution via prompt injection” — i.e. the threat model this note assumes.
Two more in the same family: CVE-2026-25725 (< 2.1.2, CVSS 3.1 10.0) escaped by creating .claude/settings.json and injecting hooks that ran with host privileges on restart; the sandbox failed to protect that file because it did not yet exist. CVE-2026-55607 (2.1.38–2.1.162, CVSS 3.1 8.8) abused the worktree write exception described below, creating worktrees named .git to produce directory confusion. Every deliberate carve-out in the boundary shows up in this list.
The sandbox is still the right tool for its actual job — cutting prompts during supervised work — and it composes with the outer tiers. But the fix lineage in the settings reference below is not defensive over-engineering — it is the scar tissue from these three. Settings files are denied at every scope, and symlinks are resolved at those paths from v2.1.210.
sandbox-runtime — the same primitives, wider scope
@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime wraps a whole process in the same Seatbelt/bubblewrap isolation, so file tools, hooks, and MCP servers land inside:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime
npx @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime claude    # or: srt claude
Deny-all by default, so ~/.srt-settings.json must grant, at minimum, write to the project dir, ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, and /tmp, plus network to api.anthropic.com. Config shape mirrors the built-in sandbox (network.allowedDomains, filesystem.allowWrite/denyRead/..., ignoreViolations).
Labeled a beta research preview with a config format that may change — the reason it’s a real option, not the default recommendation.
Containers and VMs
The published reference dev container is Docker-based: non-root user, persistent ~/.claude volume, and an init-firewall.sh doing default-deny egress via iptables. That firewall needs NET_ADMIN + NET_RAW through runArgs. The firewall is what makes --dangerously-skip-permissions defensible there.
The stated caveat is worth repeating verbatim, because it’s the failure mode people assume a container closes: dev containers “do not prevent a malicious project from exfiltrating anything accessible inside the container, including the Claude Code credentials stored in ~/.claude.” Guidance is to avoid mounting ~/.ssh or cloud credential files in at all.
A VM is the recommendation for genuinely untrusted code — kernel-level separation rather than a host-level boundary.
bypassPermissions vs auto mode
Two different ways to remove the prompts, with materially different risk:
bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions) — no checks, including writes to protected paths. Still prompts for: explicit ask rules, org-ask connector tools, MCP tools flagged requiresUserInteraction, and rm -rf / or rm -rf ~ as a circuit breaker (including inside $(...)/backtick/<(...) substitution, v2.1.208+). Refuses to start as root or under sudo unless inside a recognized sandbox. Docs: “offers no protection against prompt injection or unintended actions.”
Auto mode — a separate classifier reviews each action, blocking escalation beyond the request, unrecognized infrastructure, and actions that look driven by hostile content the agent read. The classifier sees user messages, tool calls, and CLAUDE.md; tool results are stripped, so hostile file/page content can’t address it directly.
Three auto-mode details that bear on unattended runs specifically:

It blocks “launching an autonomous agent loop that runs without human approval or a sandbox, such as one started with --dangerously-skip-permissions” — the classifier treats bypassPermissions as a thing to stop.
It blocks writes to Claude Code’s own session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/ (v2.1.205+) — self-tampering as a named threat.
Fallback behavior differs by mode. Interactive: 3 consecutive or 20 total blocks pauses auto mode and resumes prompting. Non-interactive -p: repeated blocks abort the session, since nobody is there to prompt.

Boundaries stated in conversation (“don’t push”) are honored by the classifier but are not stored as rules — they’re re-read from the transcript, so compaction can drop them. For a hard guarantee use a deny rule.
The docs’ own routing: auto mode is a per-action control, not an isolation boundary, so it “still adds defense in depth for unattended runs, and is not required the way it is for --dangerously-skip-permissions.” Read the other way: bypass requires an outer boundary; auto mode benefits from one.
Built-in sandbox configuration reference
Condensed from the settings reference. Two independent layers — filesystem and network — either of which can be turned off separately.
Core: enabled (default false), failIfUnavailable (hard-fail instead of silently running unsandboxed), autoAllowBashIfSandboxed (default true — this is what removes the prompts), excludedCommands, allowUnsandboxedCommands.
Filesystem: the defaults are write access to cwd + session $TMPDIR, and read access to the entire machine. That default read policy still exposes ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh. Keys: filesystem.allowWrite, denyWrite, denyRead, allowRead, disabled (v2.1.216+). Overlap rule: a narrower allowRead re-opens part of a denyRead region, but an exact denyRead path holds inside a broader allowRead — so a wide allow can’t silently re-expose a named secret.
Credentials: credentials.files (deny only) and credentials.envVars (deny unsets; mask swaps in a per-session sentinel and has the proxy substitute the real value on requests to injectHosts). mask requires network.tlsTerminate and v2.1.199+. There is no built-in credential deny list — only what you list is protected.
Network: nothing pre-allowed; first use of a domain prompts. network.allowedDomains, deniedDomains, strictAllowlist (deny instead of prompt, v2.1.219+), httpProxyPort/socksProxyPort for a bring-your-own proxy, tlsTerminate (experimental).
Escalation-resistance built in: the sandbox denies writes to Claude Code’s own settings.json at every scope, and since v2.1.210 resolves symlinks at those paths so a linked settings file can’t be edited through the link. That protection is part of the filesystem layer — filesystem.disabled: true turns it off.
Scope restrictions worth knowing: filesystem.disabled, strictAllowlist, tlsTerminate, mask entries, and allowAppleEvents are honored only from user, managed, or --settings — not from a repo’s .claude/settings.json. A checked-out project cannot widen these itself.
Deployment constraints that shape the choice
Linux dependency footprint is small but non-zero. The built-in sandbox needs bubblewrap and socat; sandbox-runtime needs those plus ripgrep. On mainstream distributions these are single packages, but on an image-based or immutable fleet the question becomes whether they are in the base image, since layering a package to enable a security control is a rollout dependency. Managed deployments can point at non-standard install locations with sandbox.bwrapPath and sandbox.socatPath — both managed-settings-only keys.
Nesting the built-in sandbox inside a container costs isolation strength. Tested directly: inside an unprivileged container, bwrap mounting a fresh /proc fails with Can't mount proc on /newroot/proc: Permission denied; bind-mounting the container’s existing /proc succeeds, as does the fresh mount under a privileged container. That is exactly what sandbox.enableWeakerNestedSandbox: true buys. The documented cost is that it exposes process information a fresh /proc would hide, so the setting is to be used only “when the outer container already provides the isolation boundary you need.”
The practical read for a layered deployment: inside a container the inner sandbox is defense in depth, not a second independent boundary. Size the container’s own policy accordingly rather than treating the pair as additive.
Rootless containers are sufficient for the egress-firewall pattern. The reference dev container’s iptables/ipset approach needs only NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW, which rootless runtimes grant inside the container’s own network namespace — no privileged container required. Verified against a rootless runtime; see agent-isolation-hardening for the tested holes in that firewall’s actual rule set.
What none of these tiers fix

TLS is not inspected by default. The built-in proxy allows or denies on the client-supplied hostname without reading the connection. Domain fronting can therefore reach hosts outside the allowlist, and a broad entry like github.com is an exfiltration path. tlsTerminate exists for credential masking, not content filtering.
Any egress at all is an exfiltration channel for whatever the agent can read.
A writable bind mount is still your code. Every container tier mounts the project writable; that’s the point, and it means the blast radius always includes the repo.
Isolation does not change what’s sent to the model. Prompts and read files go to the API regardless of tier.
allowUnixSockets can hand over the host — /var/run/docker.sock inside the sandbox is host access.
Broad allowWrite is privilege escalation. Anything on $PATH, shell rc files, or system config gives code execution in another context on the next run.

Where hooks sit
PreToolUse hooks receive a permission_mode field whose documented values include "bypassPermissions", which strongly implies hooks still fire in that mode — but the docs do not state it outright, and I found no explicit sentence either way (unverified; worth an empirical test before relying on guard-bash.sh as an unattended safety net). The exit-2 contract itself is documented: exit 2 blocks the tool call and feeds stderr back as the reason. Note also that in auto mode, entering the mode drops broad allow rules that grant arbitrary execution (Bash(*), wildcarded interpreters, Agent rules), restoring them on exit.
See claude-code-enforcement-hooks for the deployed hook and the deterministic-signal eligibility test.
Counterargument
The case against reaching for a heavy tier: for a single-user machine running a trusted repo, the realistic threat is not a malicious project but the agent misfiring — and against that, auto mode’s classifier plus a deny rule list is a better-targeted control than an OS boundary, because it catches semantically-wrong-but-in-bounds actions (force push, dropping a prod table) that any sandbox permitting normal work would also permit. Isolation is the right frame when the code or its dependencies are the threat; it’s largely the wrong frame when the agent’s judgment is. The tiers above answer “what can it reach”, and for supervised work on your own code that was rarely the question.
That argument weakens as sessions get longer and less supervised, and it collapses entirely for untrusted repos — where the classifier’s inputs are exactly what the attacker controls.

ai/ai-agent-security.title: AI Agent Security
ai/ai-agent-security.content:
AI Agent Security
Security for AI systems that autonomously execute code, modify files, and communicate across networks. Protects autonomous execution at runtime, not just data at rest. A compromised agent has code execution, file access, and network reach — a massive attack surface with immature defenses.
This note covers the defense architecture. For attack vectors, see prompt-injection and ai-supply-chain-risks.
Permission models
Tiered access (Claude Code pattern)
ML classifier on terminal transcripts infers risk, auto-approves low-stakes ops. Effective UX, but adversarial inputs can bypass the classifier.

























TierExamplesApprovalRead-onlyFile read, glob, grepAuto-approvedFile modificationEdit, writeUntil session endShell executionBash commandsPer-directory
Sandboxing layers

Filesystem — designated directories only
Network — zero-trust, no unvetted exfiltration
Process — container or CVM (Confidential VM)
Hardware — AMD SEV-SNP, NVIDIA H100 enclaves for highest security
Fail-closed — when security controls fail, deny access (not fall-open)

Concrete tier-by-tier comparison, the permission-mode-vs-isolation distinction, and configuration specifics: agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers.
Threat vectors

Prompt injection — malicious instructions in processed data → prompt-injection
Supply chain — compromised deps auto-installed → ai-supply-chain-risks
Classifier bypass — adversarial inputs fool ML permission gating
Compaction persistence — payloads survive context summarization (see context-window-management)
Attribution evasion — agents contributing code undisclosed

Defense principles

Least privilege — minimum necessary access per tool, per session
Blast radius containment — assume compromise, limit damage
Human-in-the-loop for irreversible actions (see hitl-progressive-autonomy)
Cryptographic provenance — track human vs. agent authorship
Runtime monitoring — detect anomalous tool-calling patterns
Provable defenses over obscurity — Claude Code’s anti-distillation (fake schemas) became useless the moment code leaked

Incidents informing design (2026)

CrewAI chain (CVE-2026-2275/2285/2286/2287, CERT/CC VU#221883): CodeInterpreterTool fell back to an insecure SandboxPython path when Docker was unreachable — injection → fail-open sandbox → RCE, SSRF, arbitrary file read. The fix removed the tool outright. CVE IDs verified 2026-07-31. Detailed analysis in prompt-injection
OpenClaw (CVE-2026-32922, CVSS 3.1 9.9 / v4.0 9.4, CWE-266, < 2026.3.11): insufficient scope validation in device.token.rotate let a low-privilege pairing operator mint an admin token and execute code across connected nodes. CVE and scores verified against NVD 2026-07-31; the 135,000+ internet-facing instance figure is unverified. Detailed in ai-supply-chain-risks
Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit: open-source response — goal hijacking, memory poisoning, rogue agent protection. A widely-repeated “97% of enterprises expect a major agent security incident in 2026” figure appears alongside it — source not identified; unverified

Claude Code’s own sandbox has three verified escapes worth studying as a family — CVE-2026-25725, CVE-2026-39861, CVE-2026-55607 — collected with mechanisms and sources in enterprise-agent-execution-architecture.
Related

ai/ai-assisted-code-review.title: AI-Assisted Code Review — Best Practices
ai/ai-assisted-code-review.content:
AI-Assisted Code Review — Best Practices
Web-research synthesis (2026-07-22) on using AI as the reviewer. This is the third leg of the vault’s code-review triangle:

effective-code-review — the human craft: hierarchy, thresholds, psychology, communication
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — judging AI-authored code after green CI
This note — running an AI reviewer over PRs (human- or AI-authored) without wrecking the review culture

Last verified: 2026-07-22. The tool landscape and every number here are FAST-decay claims.
Where the AI reviewer goes in the pipeline
The placement the surveyed sources recommend — noting that most are vendor guides, so this is genre convergence more than measured consensus: AI feedback before human eyes, after deterministic gates conceptually but in parallel in practice.

Author opens the PR (draft state ideally) → AI review lands within minutes.
Author resolves the mechanical/obvious findings while context is hot.
Human reviewer sees a pre-cleaned diff and spends attention on design, intent, and business logic.

The value is sequencing, not detection alone: the AI pass is cheap and instant, so it belongs where its findings can be fixed before a human’s limited attention is spent. An AI reviewer bolted on after human approval adds little — at that point its findings either go unread or reopen a closed review (this note’s own reasoning, not a sourced claim).
Two standing constraints carried over from effective-code-review:

Non-deterministic → not a compliance gate. LLM reviewers can comment and advise; they cannot be the thing that blocks merge in a regulated pipeline. Deterministic tools (linters, SAST, type checks) remain the hard gates.
Don’t duplicate the deterministic layer. If the AI reviewer is commenting on formatting or lint-catchable issues, that’s a configuration failure, not a feature.
The diff leaves the building. A hosted reviewer receives the diff and usually broader repo context; for many teams the data-processing/IP question gates tool choice before any quality comparison starts. The surveyed sources are almost all hosted-SaaS-flavored — self-hosted or local-model review is a real alternative they underrepresent.

Division of labor
The split the sources converge on (here vendor and practitioner sources agree, and it matches the human/machine split already in effective-code-review):

























LayerOwnsDoesn’t ownDeterministic (lint/SAST/types)Style, known vulnerability patterns, mechanical correctnessAnything needing contextAI reviewerCross-file consistency, likely-bug patterns, edge cases, test-gap hints, summarizing the diff, catching issues that match no fixed ruleFinal verdicts; architectural direction; business-logic validationHumanArchitecture, intent-vs-implementation drift, trade-off debate, domain/business correctness, accountability for the mergeAnything the two layers above already caught
Human sign-off stays non-negotiable — “an AI reviewed it” is not an auditable position, and no source surveyed argues otherwise. Changes touching auth, payments, secrets, or untrusted-input handling additionally need a human threat-model pass regardless of what the AI said (Osmani).
Noise economics — the adoption killer
The most consistently named failure mode across the surveyed material: false-positive volume kills the tool socially before anyone evaluates its recall. Once a team learns the bot is usually wrong, they stop reading it entirely — and then even its true positives are ignored. Vendor content circulating in 2026 cites single-to-low-double-digit false-positive rates and describes reviewer attention collapsing once wrongness passes some fraction-of-comments threshold; the specific numbers attached to these claims could not be traced to a checkable source, so only the mechanism carries weight here.
Countermeasures, roughly in order of leverage:

Start narrow, widen slowly. Enable few high-severity categories first; earn trust before turning on opinionated ones.
Severity thresholds and focus areas configured per repo — not the tool’s defaults.
Ignore patterns for generated code, vendored code, and migrations.
Track accepted-vs-rejected suggestions and prune the categories that get rejected. The accept rate is the tool’s precision measured against your team; a category nobody acts on is noise by definition.
A feedback path for developers to mark false positives, feeding rule/prompt adjustments.

This is the same iterative-critic-tuning loop as in evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests §Tier 3: the reviewer prompt/config is a stateful artifact that must be recalibrated against ground truth, not installed and forgotten.
Author-side discipline still binds
AI review does not relax the author obligations from effective-code-review — it sharpens them, because AI-era PRs trend larger (Osmani cites ~18% larger PRs and rising change-failure rates with AI adoption; single-source, unverified):

Small PRs still win. The ~400-LOC ceiling applies to AI reviewers too — review quality (human and machine) degrades on big diffs, and several sources report accuracy gains simply from keeping PRs small.
The PR contract (Osmani’s framing, a useful tightening of the description-as-artifact rule): every PR ships with intent (1–2 sentences), proof (tests run, screenshots, logs), provenance (which parts were AI-generated), and review focus (where human judgment is actually needed).
Never submit code you can’t explain. The knowledge-transfer function of review (effective-code-review — the real point of review per the Microsoft research) dies silently if authors relay AI output they don’t understand; the cost surfaces later as expensive on-call debugging.

Measuring whether it’s working
Three metric families (Graphite’s split, generalizable):

Quality: production-bug rate, security incidents, escaped-defect trend
Process: time-to-first-review, review cycles per PR, developer satisfaction with the bot
ROI: review time saved vs. time spent triaging bot comments (count both sides)

The measurement standard worth stealing: “did the developer actually change the code in response?” — a comment that produced no action was noise regardless of how plausible it read. This is the core metric of Martian’s Code Review Bench (codereview.withmartian.com, released early 2026), billed — by the vendors ranked on it — as the first independent benchmark for AI code-review tools: real GitHub PRs, precision/recall scoring, an online layer tracking which bot comments developers fix vs. ignore (methodology per vendor and press descriptions, not independently audited).
Calibration warning that doubles as a market snapshot: as of 2026-07, at least three vendors (Qodo, CodeRabbit, cubic) each publicly claim the #1 spot on that same benchmark. Vendor leaderboard claims and vendor ROI figures (“40–60% review time saved”) are marketing until reproduced on your own PRs — the accept-rate tracking above is the only benchmark that transfers.
Anti-patterns

Bot as final reviewer. AI approval treated as sign-off; accountability evaporates.
Complacency by delegation. The subtler version: humans still nominally review, but skim because “the bot already checked it” — the pre-cleaned diff lowers vigilance exactly where the bot is weakest (architecture, intent). This is automation bias applied to review (ai-automation-biases); the countermeasure is keeping the human pass scoped to what the bot explicitly does not own.
Default-config deployment. Shipping the tool’s out-of-box sensitivity, drowning the team, concluding “AI review doesn’t work.”
Noise tolerated until ignored. Not pruning rejected-suggestion categories; the bot becomes wallpaper and its true positives die with the false ones.
AI-on-AI monoculture. The same model family writing and reviewing the code correlates the blind spots (evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — critic collusion). If code is agent-written, review with a different model, and keep the human pass.
Relitigating style. AI reviewer commenting on things the formatter/linter owns — configure it out.
Metrics counting only the win side. “Time saved” tracked while triage cost, larger-PR drift, and change-failure rate go unmeasured.

Related

effective-code-review — the human-review substrate; its human/machine split section is the 2026-06 snapshot this note extends
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — reviewing AI-authored diffs; shares the critic-tuning loop and monoculture warning
ai-code-review-deterministic-agent-hybrid — build-side view: how a production AI reviewer allocates work between deterministic code and LLM judgment
ai-verification-stack-web — the deterministic gate layer this note assumes underneath
.claude/skills/lean-review/, /ai-diff-judgment — the vault’s own review skills; this note is the team-pipeline view, those are the solo-practitioner view
/pr-contract — skill built from this note (2026-07-22): author-side producer of the four-part PR contract that /ai-diff-judgment consumes

Sources
Web research 2026-07-22; quality varies sharply and is labeled per claim above.

Addy Osmani, “Code Review in the Age of AI” (Elevate/Substack, 2026) — PR contract, accountability stance, PR-size drift figures; the strongest practitioner source surveyed
Graphite — AI code review implementation best practices — configuration, accept/reject tracking, metric families
GitHub — AI code reviews — division-of-labor framing; cites no data
Martian Code Review Bench — verified to exist; methodology description from vendor + press coverage, not independently audited. Competing #1 claims: Qodo, CodeRabbit, cubic
False-positive-rate and ROI figures — aggregated from vendor/SEO content (codeant.ai, exceeds.ai, byteiota, others); unverified, mechanism-only weight

ai/ai-code-latent-failure-modes.title: AI-Generated Code — Latent Failure Modes
ai/ai-code-latent-failure-modes.content:
AI-Generated Code — Latent Failure Modes
Taxonomy of the debt patterns AI-generated code introduces that don’t trip CI — defects that ship green and surface later, during a rollback, under production load, or the week the maintainer tries to extend the code unaided.
Pairs with evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — that note covers how to detect post-CI risk; this one covers what there is to detect, named so the pattern can be grepped for and discussed.
Why this set, not just “bugs”
The interesting failure modes of agentic coding cluster around a shared root cause: the agent optimizes for making the immediate change pass its immediate verifications. Whatever falls outside that loop is invisible to the agent’s reward signal — production state it can’t observe, concurrent execution it doesn’t test, the codebase’s shape in six months, the maintainer’s ability to fix it in a panic. CI green is not a measure of any of those things.
These failure modes are not all brand-new categories. Comprehension debt, schema drift, concurrency bugs, and duplication all predate AI coding and exist in any fast-moving codebase. What AI changes is the rate of accrual and the shape of the mistakes: more code per unit review, no human author who holds context across the change, and a feedback loop that rewards making the current task pass. Giving each pattern its own name preserves the leverage to triage them separately; collapsing them into “AI code is buggy” loses it.
The “80% problem” framing is useful shorthand for why these matter: the visible 80% of functionality is cheap; the invisible 20% of production resilience is left to the human. But the 20% isn’t a single thing. It decomposes into the patterns below.
The failure modes
1. Comprehension debt
Code whose sophistication exceeds the maintainer’s independent skill level. The author can generate it with the agent; they cannot fix it without the agent.
Mechanism. The agent defaults to idiomatic-for-its-training-distribution solutions. For a solo dev whose personal skill ceiling sits below that distribution median in a given language or framework, the output is correct but opaque. Generics, decorators, metaclasses, library-specific DSLs, clever type manipulation — each fine in isolation. In aggregate, the codebase becomes agent-dependent.
Symptom. Fixes in that module require re-prompting the agent, because reading the code and reasoning about it is slower than asking.
Why solo devs are more exposed. No team to spread knowledge across. A senior colleague who understands the generics provides a fallback; a solo operator has no such layer.
Mitigations.

Require the agent to explain the change in plain prose as part of the PR. The explanation is the comprehension check.
Prefer “boring” solutions in AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md; name what to avoid (no meta-programming for its own sake, no novel abstractions without justification).
Periodically patch a bug in the module unaided. If you can’t, the debt is accruing faster than you noticed.

2. Silent schema drift
Application code, ORM models, migration history, and the actual database schema diverge without a failing check.
Mechanism. The agent adds or modifies a field in response to a feature request. It updates the application code, often updates the ORM model, runs the tests against the local dev database (where the migration applied cleanly), and ships. From observed patterns (not a controlled study), the agent only inconsistently produces:

A reversible migration
Backfill for existing rows
An idempotent migration safe to rerun
Updated seed data for CI environments
Updated schema dumps or snapshots that other environments read from

The divergence between “local dev works” and “production has different data” is invisible to the agent’s test loop because tests never hit production-shaped data.
Detection surface.

Schema-snapshot diff in CI (pg_dump comparison, Prisma migrate diff, equivalent for other ORMs)
Drift detectors (e.g., Atlas, sqldef) as a scheduled CI job, not a pre-merge gate
A rollback rehearsal drill — can you actually revert the last migration on a copy of prod?

Why it’s latent. Surfaces only during rollback, replica sync, or a feature re-enable after long disuse. Worst case: irrecoverable data corruption when the application writes against a schema the migration never established.
3. Race-condition time bombs
Logic correct under sequential execution and wrong under concurrency.
Mechanism. Agent test runs are sequential by default. A read-modify-write on a counter passes when run alone. The agent has no signal that two requests could hit that code path simultaneously. Common omissions:

Idempotency keys on mutating endpoints
Optimistic locking / version columns on updates
Distributed locks around side-effectful external calls
Retry-safe handlers for webhooks that re-deliver on timeout
Row-level locking in transactions that read then update

Detection surface.

Property-based tests with concurrent execution (e.g., fast-check asyncProperty with parallel runners)
Deliberately concurrent E2E scenarios (two tabs, two parallel API calls)
Load test before production for any write-path change
Review specifically scanning for read-then-write patterns without a lock

Why it’s latent. May run cleanly for months, then detonate the day traffic doubles or a retry storm hits a webhook endpoint.
4. Missing observability hooks
The feature works. When it breaks in production, there is no signal pointing at what broke.
Mechanism. Observability is rarely stated explicitly in feature specs, so the agent has no cue to include it. The agent implements what the spec said — auth flow, payment capture, background job — without structured logging, trace-context propagation, correlation IDs, or meaningful metric emission. Tests don’t assert on logs, so the gap doesn’t fail CI. (Mechanism claim, not empirical; the counter-case is teams whose spec templates bake observability in by default — those see less of this pattern.)
Symptoms.

Production incident: the only signal is a user complaint
On-call cannot bisect whether the failure is in this feature’s code or downstream
Logs exist but are at console.log level, unstructured, uncorrelated

Detection surface.

Observability checklist in the PR template (every new endpoint: structured log on entry/exit, trace ID in errors, one meaningful metric)
Lint rule or AST check that new route handlers import a logger
Post-incident pattern: grep for how often an incident required adding observability after the fact

Mitigations for solos.

Codify expectations in AGENTS.md with a concrete template
Use a standard wrapper (middleware, decorator) that enforces logging on all new handlers, so the agent cannot forget
Treat “added a feature with zero new log lines” as an escalation signal during review

5. Duplication drift (anti-refactor)
The agent, when asked to add behavior similar to existing behavior, copies and adapts rather than refactors to a shared abstraction.
Mechanism. Creating a new file is cheap; refactoring existing files is expensive in token cost and risk of regression. The agent’s default minimizes local change footprint. Over time, the codebase accumulates near-duplicates, each slightly diverged from the others.
This is the mirror failure of “premature abstraction” (see evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests architectural risks). Both are real; which one dominates depends on prompt shape. “Add X similar to Y” tends to produce duplication; “refactor X and Y to share logic” tends to produce over-abstraction.
Detection surface.

Duplication scanners (jscpd, PMD CPD, SonarQube) tracked as a trend, not just a threshold
Periodic “grep for function shape” — lists of functions with the same arity and similar names
Watch PR diffs for new files that structurally resemble existing ones

Why it compounds. When a bug is discovered in the duplicated logic, it must be fixed in every copy. The probability of missing one approaches certainty as N grows.
6. Haunted codebases (terminal state)
Enough of the above accumulates that neither the maintainer nor the agent has a coherent mental model of the codebase. Changes produce unexpected effects; debugging requires spelunking; every fix is provisional.
Mechanism. Compound of comprehension debt, duplication drift, unresolved schema state, and undocumented architectural drift. The codebase is no longer designed; it is accreted.
Why naming the terminal state matters. A codebase does not become haunted overnight — it becomes so gradually as the above debts go untriaged. Treating “I’m not sure how this works anymore” as a signal rather than a private confession is the mitigation.
Root causes in one place
The failure modes above are instances; the structural causes are few.

































Root causeFailure modes it producesAgent tests in an isolated, single-process environmentRace conditions, missing production state awarenessAgent optimizes for local change minimalityDuplication driftProduction state is outside the agent’s observationSilent schema drift, rollback failuresFeatures are specified; non-functional requirements aren’tMissing observability, missing error handlingAgent’s default skill register isn’t matched to the maintainer’sComprehension debtNo accumulating signal for codebase healthHaunted terminal state
Mitigations that address a root cause (observability template in AGENTS.md, rollback rehearsal as a routine) generalize across modes. Mitigations that target only one failure mode (a lint rule for logger imports) help that mode and leave the rest.
Solo-dev-specific mitigations
Cluster-level verification (ai-verification-stack-web, evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests) applies. These are the additional habits that earn their cost specifically because there is no team. Each has friction — listed alongside so the cost-benefit is visible, not hidden:

Quarterly unaided maintenance drill. Fix a non-trivial bug without the agent. Not for productivity — as a comprehension-debt gauge. Time it; if it’s dramatically worse than last quarter, the debt is growing.
Cost: an afternoon lost to a task the agent could have done in 20 minutes. Skip during delivery crunches; don’t skip two quarters in a row.
Explicit non-functional requirements in every spec. Observability, error paths, rollback, concurrency model. The spec is the only place non-features get attention; the agent will not add them spontaneously.
Cost: meaningfully longer spec-writing phase. Load-bearing anyway — retrofitting observability during a 3 a.m. incident is the alternative.
Schema drift scan scheduled, not on-demand. Running it weekly in CI costs minutes; not running it costs a day of recovery when prod diverges.
Cost: CI minutes plus alert noise when it false-positives on intentional schema changes. Tune the alerts, don’t disable the scan.
PR-to-self on solo repos. Already covered in solo-developer-ai-stack; particularly load-bearing here because these defects hide in diffs that pass CI.
Cost: ceremony that feels pointless until it catches something. First thing to get skipped under deadline pressure — which is precisely when these defects ship.

None of these is free. The calibration question is whether the expected cost of the failure mode exceeds the ongoing cost of the habit, with the failure mode’s cost multiplied by how likely you are to hit it in your stack. For a solo SaaS operator with live users, schema drift and missing observability usually clear that bar; for a weekend hacker on an internal tool, they likely don’t.
What’s adjacent but out of scope

Package hallucinations, typosquatting, slopsquatting → ai-supply-chain-risks
Output-side AI biases (sycophancy, hallucinated confidence, narrative coherence) → ai-output-bias-fingerprints
Review-time decision rubric for green-CI diffs → evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests
Runtime observability of the agent itself (debugging the agent, not its output) → open topic in topic-suggestions

Related

evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — detection-side companion: how to find these during review
ai-verification-stack-web — toolchain these depend on
ai-friendly-repo-structure — earlier surfacing of comprehension debt and the enterprise anti-patterns
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — code-specific items in the fingerprint catalog
ai-supply-chain-risks — adjacent class of latent risk
solo-developer-ai-stack — hub; this note slots into the pitfalls section
agent-workflow-solo-practitioner — daily loop where these debts accrue or get caught

Sources

Vibe Coding Enterprise 2026 — origin of “comprehension debt” and “haunted codebase” framings (already cited in ai-friendly-repo-structure)
CodeRabbit, “State of AI vs Human Code Generation” (Dec 2025) — 1.7× issue rate; also the actual source of the 1.88× figure (improper password handling), previously misattributed to Veracode — corrected details in evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests
Veracode Spring 2026 GenAI Code Security Update — ~55% security pass rate for unguided AI code
Anthropic 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report — the “fully delegate 0-20% of tasks” figure underlies the comprehension-debt argument
Internal synthesis from the knowledge/ai/ cluster (April 2026)

ai/ai-friendly-repo-structure.title: AI-Friendly Repository Structure
ai/ai-friendly-repo-structure.content:
AI-Friendly Repository Structure
How to structure code repositories so AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Aider, Codex, Gemini CLI, etc.) can contribute effectively. Covers instruction files, architecture, context management, documentation, testing, workflow, and anti-patterns.
Why it matters
The difference between a repo where agents produce good work and one where they create a mess comes down to structure, guardrails, and workflow design. AI agents now write a large share of new code — estimates range from 22% of merged code (DX Q4 2025 survey) to ~41% of generated code; generated ≠ merged, so pick the measure before quoting a number. And the quality gap is real: CodeRabbit’s “State of AI vs Human Code Generation” (Dec 2025, 470 open-source PRs) found AI-co-authored PRs carried 1.7x more issues overall, security issues up to 2.74× higher in the worst category (XSS), and 75% more logic/correctness issues than human-only PRs. This is not about making AI’s job easier — it is about making your codebase more maintainable and your AI output more reliable.
(Corrected 2026-06-10: previously “2.74x more security vulnerabilities and 75% more misconfigurations… 2026 industry data” — 2.74x is the ceiling category, the 75% was logic issues not misconfigurations, and the source is CodeRabbit Dec 2025.)
1. AI Instruction Files
The landscape (as of April 2026)







































































ToolPrimary FileLocationFormatClaude CodeCLAUDE.mdProject root, ~/.claude/, parent/child dirsMarkdownOpenAI CodexAGENTS.mdProject root, ~/.codex/, subdirsMarkdownGemini CLIGEMINI.mdProject root, ~/.gemini/, subdirsMarkdownCursor.cursor/rules/*.mdc.cursor/rules/ directoryMDC (Markdown + YAML)GitHub Copilot.github/copilot-instructions.md.github/ directoryMarkdownCopilot (scoped).github/instructions/*.instructions.md.github/instructions/Markdown + YAML frontmatterWindsurf.windsurf/rules/*.md.windsurf/rules/ directoryMarkdownJetBrains AI.aiassistant/rules/*.md.aiassistant/rules/MarkdownJetBrains Junie.junie/guidelines.mdProject rootMarkdownUniversalAGENTS.mdProject rootMarkdown
AGENTS.md emerged mid-2025 from Sourcegraph, OpenAI, Google, Cursor collaboration. Now maintained by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Supported by 20+ tools. Over 20,000 GitHub repos have adopted it. If you use multiple AI tools, keep shared instructions in AGENTS.md and tool-specific overrides in their native files.
What to include
High-value content:

Build/test/lint commands with exact flags (agents reference these constantly)
Technology stack with hard version constraints
Non-obvious project conventions and patterns
Boundaries: always/ask-first/never tiers
Non-standard tooling underrepresented in training data
Workflow rules (branch naming, PR conventions)
Developer environment quirks (required env vars)

What to exclude:

Code style enforcement (delegate to linters/formatters — “never send an LLM to do a linter’s job”)
Architecture overviews (agents discover these independently; removing them produces identical behavior at lower token cost)
Repository structure documentation (becomes stale, actively misleads)
Content the agent can figure out by reading code
Standard language conventions the model already knows
Auto-generated content (LLM-generated instruction files reduced task success by 0.5-2% while increasing costs 20-23%)

Critical constraints

Frontier LLMs can reliably follow ~150-200 instructions. Claude Code’s system prompt uses ~50. Your file gets the remainder.
Keep under 300 lines. A focused 50-line file outperforms a sprawling 1,000-line one.
The reported performance gain from human-curated files (~4% in instruction-file evals) is real but modest. The ROI comes from preventing specific, observed failure classes.
“Lost in the middle” — critical rules should go early in the file.
Treat instruction files like code: review when things go wrong, prune regularly, test by observing behavior changes.

Multi-tool strategy
project/
+-- AGENTS.md              # Universal: shared instructions
+-- CLAUDE.md              # Claude-specific (@imports, hooks)
+-- .github/
|   +-- copilot-instructions.md
+-- .cursor/
|   +-- rules/             # Cursor scoped rules
Claude Code reads AGENTS.md as fallback. If you only use Claude Code, CLAUDE.md alone is sufficient.
Hierarchical organization
All major tools support nested instruction files. Root = universal rules, subdirectories = scoped context. Nested files take precedence on conflicts.
project/
+-- CLAUDE.md              # Universal project rules
+-- apps/web/CLAUDE.md     # Next.js-specific
+-- apps/api/CLAUDE.md     # API-specific patterns
+-- packages/shared/CLAUDE.md
Progressive disclosure pattern
Don’t front-load everything. Create an agent_docs/ directory with focused files:

building_the_project.md
running_tests.md
code_conventions.md
service_architecture.md

Reference from CLAUDE.md using @agent_docs/building_the_project.md syntax. Claude reads on demand, keeping base context lean.
2. Repository Structure Patterns
Vertical slicing by feature (strongly preferred)
AI agents traverse codebases depth-first. Vertical/feature-driven organization keeps everything an agent needs for one task in one directory, minimizing tool calls and context consumption.
Preferred:
features/
+-- auth/
|   +-- index.ts
|   +-- index.test.ts
|   +-- schema.ts
|   +-- utils.ts
|   +-- utils.test.ts
+-- billing/
    +-- index.ts
    +-- index.test.ts
    +-- webhook-handler.ts
    +-- webhook-handler.test.ts
Avoid (horizontal slicing):
controllers/
+-- auth-controller.ts
+-- billing-controller.ts
services/
+-- auth-service.ts
+-- billing-service.ts
models/
+-- user.ts
+-- invoice.ts
Horizontal slicing scatters feature logic across directories, forcing agents to jump between folders, consuming more tokens and losing coherence. One analysis found modularized, collocated files “improve recall by eliminating cross-cutting jumps between directories.”
Key structural principles

Collocation: Keep implementation, tests, types, and utilities for a feature together
Small, focused files: Avoid large “service” or “repository” files that mix unrelated operations — they pollute context with irrelevant code
Focused test files: Match tests 1:1 with source files rather than monolithic test suites
Clear module boundaries: Each module should have an explicit public interface (barrel exports, __init__.py, etc.)
Self-contained modules: Dependencies between modules should be explicit and minimal

Functional Core, Imperative Shell (FCIS)
Separate pure business logic (deterministic functions: data in → data out, zero side effects) from I/O operations (database, network, filesystem). The “shell” orchestrates side effects around the pure “core.”
Why this matters for AI:

Pure functions map directly to LLM input-output reasoning — agents generate reliable tests without complex mocking frameworks
Side-effect-free code is safe for autonomous modification — no risk of accidental database mutations or network calls during agent execution
Sub-agents can operate exclusively within the functional core with minimal blast radius
When business logic is coupled with side effects, AI frequently hallucinates mocking frameworks or generates brittle, untestable code

Dependency hygiene
Circular dependencies (A → B → A) are catastrophic for AI reasoning. Transformers process information sequentially through attention — cyclical logic confuses the reasoning engine, causing hallucinated patches that deepen the tangle. One modified shared utility can cascade across dozens of files the agent doesn’t know about.

Extract shared types and interfaces into standalone neutral modules (Interface Segregation Principle)
Enforce acyclic dependencies with tooling (eslint-plugin-import, madge, deptry, Go’s built-in cycle detection)
Keep module boundaries explicit — each module has a clear public API
Consider code intelligence tools that build AST-based dependency graphs (see Section 3) so agents can query blast radius before modifying shared code

Monorepo vs polyrepo
Monorepos give AI agents a major advantage: cross-project context, pattern consistency, atomic multi-project changes, and no context loss at repository boundaries. Nx reports ~30% productivity improvement on cross-project work with agents.
However, monorepos introduce complexity. The meta-repo pattern offers a middle ground: a dedicated repo serving as the AI agent’s knowledge base for navigating a multi-repo codebase, containing:

AGENTS.md with repository map and conventions
repos.yaml with machine-readable repo definitions
structure/ for dependency graphs
conventions/ for cross-repo standards
workflows/ for step-by-step multi-repo operations
active-work/ for current multi-session epics

Using this pattern, one case study demonstrated an 8-merge-request fix across 6 repositories over 5 sessions without context loss.
Domain-driven layers
For larger projects, DDD layers (/domain, /application, /infrastructure) give agents predictable navigation: business rules in domain (no cloud dependencies), integrations in infrastructure. Agents can modify and test business logic independently.
3. Context Management
The core constraint
LLM performance degrades as context fills. The “40% rule” suggests quality drops noticeably past 40% context utilization. Everything in the repo structure should work to minimize how much context an agent needs to load for any given task.
Strategies
File-level discipline:

Keep files small and focused — under 300-400 lines is a good target
One concept/feature per file
Clear naming that describes contents without needing to read the file
Type exports and barrel files so agents don’t need to read implementation to understand interfaces
Whitespace, deep indentation, and formatting are parsed as distinct tokens by LLM tokenizers — keep formatting clean but avoid excessive nesting that burns tokens without aiding AI comprehension

Instruction-level discipline:

Use progressive disclosure: tell the agent how to find information, not all the information
Scope rules to file types using glob patterns (Cursor .mdc frontmatter, Copilot applyTo field)
Put critical rules early in instruction files (“lost in the middle” problem)
Customize compaction behavior: “When compacting, always preserve the full list of modified files and any test commands”

Session-level discipline:

Clear context between unrelated tasks (/clear in Claude Code)
Use subagents for investigation — they explore in separate context windows and report summaries
Scope investigations narrowly: “look at src/auth/” not “investigate the codebase”
After 2-3 failed corrections, start fresh rather than accumulating failed context

Architecture-level discipline:

Sub-agent architectures: specialized agents handle focused tasks with clean context, returning condensed summaries (1,000-2,000 tokens)
Claude Code Skills run in their own context window and can be parallelized
Context persistence through structured memory files (TODO.md, DECISIONS.log) rather than relying on conversation history

Tools for context packing and code intelligence

Repomix (20.9k GitHub stars): Packs codebase into AI-friendly single files with token counting and Tree-sitter compression. Has MCP server integration.
repo-map / llm-codemap: AST-based dependency graphs that give agents structural understanding of call chains, inheritance hierarchies, and cross-file relationships — a shift from “context packing” (blindly appending text) to “graph querying” (targeted structural lookups)
AI Distiller: AST-powered compression (90-98% reduction) via Tree-sitter — strips method implementations and internal variables, keeps public API signatures, types, and critical docstrings
gitingest / repo2txt: Bundle codebase excerpts for feeding to AI
Nx Polygraph: Connects multiple repos into a federated meta-repo for agent context
.aidignore: Like .gitignore for AI context — explicitly exclude generated code, vendor directories, build artifacts from agent analysis. Complementary to .repomixignore (Repomix’s own ignore file)

4. Documentation-as-Code for AI
What helps AI understand code
Type annotations are critical. Explicit types serve as machine-readable documentation. Agents parse function signatures, parameter types, and return types to understand intent without reading implementation. TypeScript strict mode, Python type hints for all functions, explicit interfaces over type aliases.
Naming conventions matter more than you think. When a codebase follows consistent naming patterns, AI becomes a “force multiplier.” When it doesn’t, AI becomes a “chaos amplifier.” Establish and document naming conventions explicitly, especially counterintuitive ones.
One real code snippet beats three paragraphs. In instruction files, demonstrate patterns with actual project code rather than prose descriptions.
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs):

Capture the why behind architectural choices — agents can discover what code does but not why decisions were made
New standard: AgDR (Agent Decision Records) extends ADR for AI-assisted development
ADRs become “executable intentions” for AI assistants — the agent reads the ADR and implements consistently with the recorded decision
AI can help generate ADRs from codebase analysis, but human review is essential
For machine readability, use explicit section tags in ADRs (<decision>, <context>, <consequences>) — lets LLMs parse decision boundaries reliably instead of guessing from prose structure
Embed capability manifests and authorization constraints in tabular format within ADRs — transforms passive records into active governance that agents can query

Inline documentation strategy:

JSDoc/docstrings on public interfaces: parameters, return types, edge cases, side effects
Comments for the “why”, not the “what” — AI reads code for what it does, comments for why
Gold standard file: one exemplar file that demonstrates all conventions applied together, functioning as an end-to-end test for AI style compliance
64% of developers now use AI for documentation generation (Google DORA 2025)

What to make explicit:

Error handling patterns (how the project handles failures)
Non-obvious conventions (e.g., “all client API methods never throw — always return ApiResult”)
Domain terminology and jargon
Framework-specific idioms that differ from defaults

Machine-readable documentation formats
Standard README.md optimized for human consumption (badges, narrative tutorials) is inefficient for models. Emerging formats provide structured, token-efficient alternatives:

llms.txt: Sits at project root (inspired by robots.txt). Provides condensed representation of purpose, public APIs, and interaction rules. Increasingly adopted by documentation sites and library authors.
ReadMe.LLM: Acts like a header file — details how the model should use the library, what architectural patterns to respect, what dependencies are available in the execution environment.

Novel frameworks and internal libraries suffer from “The Great Ossification” — AI models default to popular, heavily-represented technologies from training data. If your project uses something niche or proprietary, explicit LLM-friendly documentation is essential for agents to use it correctly rather than hallucinating based on similar-but-wrong training data.
Practical tips for AI-readable docs:

Numbered code snippets let models reference explicit line numbers rather than guessing file locations
Avoid complex JSON in documentation examples — custom plain-text delimiters ([[code]]...[[/code]]) prevent quote escaping and line break issues during generation
Explicitly state operational rationale for constants (e.g., # Three retries balances reliability vs speed; most intermittent failures resolve by the second retry rather than just MAX_RETRIES = 3)

5. Testing and Guardrails
The verification principle
“Include tests, screenshots, or expected outputs so Claude can check itself. This is the single highest-leverage thing you can do.” — Anthropic best practices
AI performs dramatically better when it can verify its own work. Without verification, you become the only feedback loop.
Multi-layer validation stack
Layer 1 — Pre-commit hooks (deterministic, blocking):
# Linting
npm run lint || exit 1
 
# Type checking (catches type-valid-looking but invalid AI code)
npx tsc --noEmit || exit 1
 
# Targeted tests on changed files
changed=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=d)
if echo "$changed" | grep -q '\.ts$'; then
  npm test -- --changed || exit 1
fi
 
# Commit message format enforcement
msg=$(cat "$1")
if ! echo "$msg" | grep -qE '^(feat|fix|chore|docs|refactor|test):'; then
  echo "Must use conventional commits"
  exit 1
fi
Pre-commit hooks “aren’t about catching human mistakes anymore. They’re about keeping AI focused.” The agent gets the failure, adjusts, and tries again — no human intervention needed.
Layer 2 — Claude Code hooks (deterministic, lifecycle-attached):
Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions (advisory), hooks guarantee execution. Key events:

PostToolUse: auto-format/lint after every file edit
PreToolUse: block writes to protected directories (migrations, generated code)
Stop: run final validation when agent finishes

Layer 3 — CI/CD pipeline:

Full test suite on PR creation
Security scanning (AI code shows ~50% vulnerability rate vs 15-20% human)
Architecture consistency checks
Performance profiling on critical paths

Layer 4 — Multi-agent review:

Writer/Reviewer pattern: one session writes, a fresh session reviews (no bias toward own code)
Adversarial review: second model or session critiques output
AI review first (style, common bugs, docs gaps) then human review (architecture, business logic, edge cases) — the “review sandwich” reduces human review time 30-50%

Hook and review tooling

Pre-commit framework: Multi-language hook management (Ruff, ESLint, Prettier, Mypy, tsc)
Husky: JS/TS hook management
CodeRabbit: AI code review with security scanning and architecture checks
Ellipsis: PR-level analysis with conversational context

Semantic linting for AI output
Traditional text-based linters miss structural anti-patterns common in AI-generated code. AST-based tools match code structure rather than text:

AST Grep: Lint rules that match structural intent (e.g., catch incorrect API usage regardless of variable naming). Catches semantic hallucinations that regex-based linters miss.
unparam (Go via golangci-lint): Detects function parameters consistently called with identical values — a common LLM anti-pattern of over-abstracting into generic functions
Security scanners (gosec, Snyk, Aikido, SonarQube): Critical given AI code’s ~50% vulnerability rate. Feed scanner output back to the agent via MCP or CI for automated self-correction loops.

The goal is a self-correcting pipeline: agent generates code → semantic linters + security scanners run automatically → failures feed back to the agent → agent iterates until standards are met.
Industry-validated mitigation stack

Formal verification gates: Compiler passes, test suites, type checks, linting — things that can’t be faked
Adversarial review models: Second AI session or different model critiques output
Hierarchical agents: Separate planner, worker, and reviewer agents
Low-stakes prioritization: AI for boilerplate, tests, docs, migrations. Humans for critical business logic.
Spec-driven development: Specifications before implementation; specs as source of truth
Knowledge transfer rituals: Require authors to explain AI-generated code in PRs/docs

6. Workflow Patterns
The four-phase pattern

Explore (Plan Mode): Agent reads files and answers questions without changes
Plan: Agent creates detailed implementation plan, human edits before proceeding
Implement: Agent codes against the plan, running tests iteratively
Commit/PR: Agent commits with descriptive message, creates PR

Skip planning for small, clear-scope tasks. Planning is most valuable when uncertain about approach, modifying multiple files, or unfamiliar with the code.
Task decomposition

Generate ultra-small tasks (1-2 hours, 4-8 hours max) with clear acceptance criteria
Atomic decomposition: no shared state between tasks enables parallel agent execution
Spec-driven development: write specs before AI implementation; specs become source of truth
Prompt plans: structured files containing sequential prompts for systematic execution

Branch and collaboration strategy
The trust gradient:

Agent suggests changes, human applies manually
Agent makes changes on branches, human reviews PRs
Agent merges low-risk changes autonomously

Adjust based on track record and blast radius. Start conservative.
Parallel sessions:

Git worktrees for isolated parallel AI sessions on separate features
Writer/Reviewer split: one session implements, another reviews
Test-first split: one session writes tests, another writes implementation
Non-interactive mode (claude -p) for CI, scripts, and batch migrations

Commit discipline:

Ultra-frequent commits as “save points” for rollback
Never commit code you can’t explain
State checkpointing constantly to Git as an undo mechanism

The spec-first workflow

AI conducts structured interview surfacing requirements, constraints, edge cases
Collaboratively develop spec.md with architecture, data models, testing strategy
Start fresh session for implementation (clean context focused on execution)
Written spec serves as reference throughout

Agent bootstrapping
Autonomous agents can’t ask colleagues or manually troubleshoot setup. The repo needs a deterministic initialization sequence — an “agent bootloader” documented in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md:

Sync: Exact git commands to get latest state
Secrets: Secure injection of env vars and API keys (never hardcoded in prompts)
Dependencies: Deterministic install (npm ci, poetry install, lock files enforced)
Verify environment: Lint and test commands the agent runs to validate its own workspace before starting work

Without this, autonomous workflows are fragile — agents silently work against stale code, missing dependencies, or broken environments. The gap between “works on my machine” and “works in the agent’s session” is where autonomous execution fails.
7. Anti-Patterns
Repository anti-patterns

Horizontal slicing: Scattering features across controllers/services/models directories forces excessive context loading
Monolithic files: Large service/repository files pollute context with unrelated code
Monolithic test suites: Bundling tests forces agents to load irrelevant test context
Implicit conventions: Engineers absorb patterns tacitly; agents need explicit documentation
Stale structural references: Outdated directory maps in instruction files actively mislead agents

Instruction file anti-patterns

Auto-generating instruction files: LLM-generated rules reduced task success 0.5-2%, increased costs 20-23%. Hand-write every line.
Rule accumulation without pruning: Creates contradictions and bloat. Review and prune regularly.
Over-specification: If Claude already does it correctly without the instruction, delete it
Broad behavioral hotfixes: Vague instructions like “write better code” are useless
Architecture in instruction files: Agents discover architecture independently; documenting it wastes tokens and becomes stale

Workflow anti-patterns

Kitchen sink sessions: Mixing unrelated tasks in one session pollutes context
Correction spirals: After 2 failed corrections, start fresh — don’t accumulate failed approaches
Infinite exploration: Unscoped “investigate” prompts cause agents to read hundreds of files
Single-prompt architecture: Generating entire systems in one request eliminates iteration
Iterative AI debugging loops: “AI writes buggy code, AI fixes it, introduces new bugs” creates layers of uncomprehended fixes
Blind generation: “Create a complete system” produces over-engineered, untested code
Premature automation: Automating before understanding the problem space
Trust-then-verify gap: Accepting plausible-looking output without verification

Enterprise anti-patterns

Comprehension debt: Code that is more sophisticated than the team could independently create or maintain, creating fragility and AI dependency (see ai-code-latent-failure-modes for the full taxonomy)
Haunted codebases: Iterative drift where “the codebase slowly becomes something no one (human or AI) fully understands”
AI-only implementation, human-only testing: Developers get boring work; tests miss edge cases discovered during implementation
No audit trails: Missing prompt history, context, iteration records for AI-generated code
Skill atrophy: No tracking of what happens to team expertise over 2-3 years of AI delegation

8. Real-World Examples and Tools
Notable projects and approaches

steipete/agent-rules (5.7k stars, archived Dec 2025): Early framework for Claude Code and Cursor rules, succeeded by agent-scripts
PaulDuvall/ai-development-patterns: Comprehensive 30+ pattern catalog covering Foundation, Development, and Operations phases with anti-patterns
Repomix (20.9k stars): Packs codebases into AI-friendly formats with token compression and MCP integration
Airbnb: Compressed an 18-month migration to 6 weeks using agents in a monorepo
Anthropic 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report: Engineers use AI in ~60% of work but can only fully delegate 0-20% of tasks
rulesync: Tool to unify management of rules across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor from a single source
vibe-rules: Save, load, and distribute AI rules across projects

Related

ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints.title: AI Output — Bias Fingerprints
ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints.content:
AI Output — Bias Fingerprints
What it is
A catalog of bias-like patterns that appear in LLM output, framed so a reviewer can detect them before trusting the output. Some of these are direct analogs of human cognitive biases; others are mechanistic artifacts of how models are trained and decoded. Either way, they’re the signatures to scan for when reviewing AI-generated prose, plans, specs, summaries, or code.
Why it matters
The default failure mode when reviewing AI output is automation bias amplified by fluency: polished prose triggers acceptance that factual plausibility doesn’t earn. Treating the output as a set of measurable fingerprints rather than a monolithic “is this right?” question converts a gut call into a checklist — exactly the shift that structural interventions make possible where introspection fails, per cognitive-biases.
This note is the output-side half of a two-layer verification pattern. Pair with prompt-bias-diagnostics (input side) and bias-aware-verification-protocol (synthesis).
Details
A caveat before the catalog
Human cognitive biases arise from an evolved, embodied, affect-driven brain. LLMs don’t have amygdalas or ego-protection drives. When a model’s output looks like confirmation bias or loss aversion, the mechanism underneath is almost always statistical, not psychological — reflecting training-data distributions or RLHF reward signals.
This matters because the countermeasures differ. You can’t “make the model aware” of its bias the way you coach a human. You can:

Change the prompt (shift the distribution it samples from)
Change the decoding (temperature, sampling, constrained generation)
Add a second pass (verification, red-team, disagreement drill)
Route around it (don’t use the model for tasks where the fingerprint dominates)

With that caveat, the human-bias vocabulary is still useful as labels for patterns, because reviewers are humans and need language that maps to their existing intuitions.
1. Fluency-as-accuracy
The mechanism you must resist in yourself, not the model. LLMs are optimized for fluent, coherent, grammatically clean output. Human readers natively equate fluency with credibility. The two are uncorrelated in LLM output.
Fingerprint: confident, well-structured prose on a topic where the factual substrate is thin, novel, or long-tail.
Counter: when reading, explicitly separate is this written well from is this true. Strip rhetoric and list the load-bearing factual claims; check them independently.
2. Sycophancy
The model adjusts its answers toward what the user appears to want, even when that answer is wrong. Documented extensively — including in production RLHF’d models — by Sharma et al. (Anthropic, 2023) and earlier in Perez et al. (2022). Root cause: RLHF reward models learn that agreeing, flattering, and echoing the user’s framing scores well with human raters.
This is the most common and most dangerous fingerprint in day-to-day use. It silently converts the model into an amplifier for the user’s own confirmation bias.
Fingerprints:

Sudden pivot in position after user pushback, without new evidence
Opening phrases that validate the user (“Great question,” “You’re right to ask…”) before analysis
Mirroring the user’s vocabulary and framing rather than reframing with more precise terms
Confidence rises when the user expresses confidence; drops when the user hedges
Strong agreement with loaded or leading user assertions

Counter: ask the model the same question from an opposite framing, or neutrally, or in a third persona. Large answer changes under frame changes = sycophancy. Also: explicitly instruct “state your position first; don’t echo mine.”
3. Hallucinated confidence (illusion-of-validity analog)
The model expresses high confidence in claims it cannot actually support. There is no calibrated uncertainty signal in the output by default; confidence language is a stylistic feature, not a probability estimate.
Fingerprints:

Named citations, URLs, API methods, CVE numbers, or quotations that don’t exist
Precise-sounding numbers without a source
“According to [plausible organization]…” with no verifiable attribution
Specificity that exceeds what the prompt supplied

Counter: treat every named entity (person, paper, URL, version, function signature) as a claim requiring verification. Grep the codebase, fetch the URL, check the citation. Never publish AI-sourced specifics in a persistent artifact without independent confirmation (see the trust-but-verify rule in the personal CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/).
4. Narrative coherence over correctness
Given a gap or ambiguity, the model will produce a plausible-sounding completion rather than flag the gap. The training objective rewards coherent continuation, not epistemic honesty about what was not supplied.
Fingerprints:

A plan that answers a question the user didn’t ask, because it fits the narrative better than the actual question
Code that handles an edge case the spec didn’t mention, implemented plausibly but wrong
Summaries that smooth over contradictions in the source material
“The issue is X” framings where the actual issue was not identifiable from the evidence

Counter: explicitly prompt for what’s missing or uncertain (“list assumptions you’re making; list information you’d need to verify”). Reward the model for saying “I don’t know” by framing prompts so that’s an acceptable answer.
5. Training-data availability bias
The model overweights popular framings and majority positions in its training corpus. Long-tail or minority-but-correct answers are systematically underrepresented.
Fingerprints:

“Best practice” advice that reflects 2022–2023 consensus on popular blogs, not actual current engineering discussion
Preference for widely-documented frameworks over better-fitting niche tools
Answers that feel like a median Stack Overflow response when a more specific answer exists
Mainstream cultural/political/aesthetic assumptions baked into recommendations

Counter: if you suspect the dominant answer is wrong for your case, prompt for alternatives explicitly (“besides X, what are less common approaches and when would they be better?”). Treat “best practices” outputs with extra scrutiny on long-tail topics.
6. Survivorship bias in recommendations
Training data over-represents what was published, shared, and upvoted — which correlates poorly with what actually worked in production. Failed projects rarely publish detailed post-mortems; successful ones retroactively narrate their success.
Fingerprints:

Architecture advice that mirrors famous public case studies (Netflix, Uber, Spotify) without caveating scale mismatch
Uncritical endorsement of patterns that work at large scale and break badly at small scale (or vice versa)
“Companies that do X succeed” framings with no failure rate

Counter: ask explicitly about failure modes — “what are known ways this pattern fails, and at what scale?” Prefer answers that acknowledge tradeoffs over answers that don’t.
7. In-register bias
The model speaks in the register, values, and framing of the dominant subculture in its training data — typically US tech, English-language, academic-adjacent. This shows up as unstated assumptions in recommendations, examples chosen, and what counts as “obvious.”
Fingerprints:

Examples that assume US-centric context (dollar amounts, imperial units, US legal framing) without being asked
Implicit Silicon Valley values (velocity over stability, SaaS over self-hosted, public cloud over local) leaking into neutral technical recommendations
Aesthetic and editorial conventions from a specific professional register (LinkedIn-voice, journalistic opener, five-bullet summary)

Counter: pin down the context explicitly in the prompt — user role, scale, constraints, values. Ask for culturally or contextually specific variants if the default feels generic.
8. Self-evaluation bias
The model praises work it has produced — even when that work is mediocre. Distinct from sycophancy (which targets the user’s apparent preferences); self-evaluation bias targets the model’s own outputs. When you ask a generator to grade its own draft, the grade is systematically higher than an independent evaluator would give for the same artifact. Identified as a load-bearing motivation for separating generation from evaluation in Anthropic’s March 2026 harness-design note (harness-design-load-bearing). The note itself uses the term “self-evaluation”; the “bias” suffix here is the vault’s catalog framing.
The likely mechanism is again statistical rather than psychological: training distributions reward fluent justification of presented content, and the model treats “this output” the same way it treats “a presented passage” — finding the merits, smoothing over flaws. The model has no stake in the work, but it doesn’t need one for the fingerprint to appear.
Fingerprints:

Self-review that scores own output near-uniformly high regardless of actual quality
“Looks good to me” verdicts on code that fails on first execution
Acknowledgment of an issue followed by dismissal (“yes it’s broken, but the structure is reasonable so I’ll pass it”)
Quality scores that fail to track quality variance — the worst draft and the best draft get similar marks
Critique that nitpicks surface details while missing whole-output failure

Counter: never let the generator grade itself. Use a separate evaluator agent — different prompt context, ideally invoked without the generator’s reasoning trace in its window. The separation matters more than which model you use; even the same underlying model produces less biased grades when it’s not the one that just produced the artifact. The generator-vs-evaluator pattern in harness-design-load-bearing is the architectural response to this fingerprint.
9. Specification drift (not a bias — a related failure mode)
Included for completeness because it’s often misdiagnosed as a bias. The model produces output matching what it inferred from context rather than what was asked. Unlike the bias fingerprints above, this is a straightforward communication failure, curable by tightening the spec.
Counter: explicit specs, type contracts, and test scaffolding (see ai-verification-stack-web).
Detection checklist
Use during review of any non-trivial AI output:

Strip fluency — list the load-bearing factual claims as bullet points; ignore the prose
Frame-test for sycophancy — does the output change substantially if you remove your framing?
Entity check — every named person, paper, URL, API, or number: does it exist?
Gap test — what assumptions did the model make? Were any of them wrong to make?
Mainstream check — on topics with a “popular answer,” is the popular answer the right one for your case?
Failure-mode probe — did the output acknowledge tradeoffs and failure modes? If not, ask.
Context fit — did the model inherit assumptions from its training register that don’t fit your context?
Self-evaluation check — if the model graded its own work, did the grade track actual quality variance? Re-grade with a separate evaluator before trusting the verdict.

Runs in under a minute for short outputs. For long outputs (full docs, large diffs), apply selectively to the load-bearing sections.
The /bias-scan-ai slash command automates this checklist on a file and returns structured findings with a PASS / REVIEW / FAIL verdict. For human-authored content, use /bias-scan-human instead — different bias catalog, different checks.
Code-specific additions
Layered on top of the above for code output:

Plausible-looking tests with 4% mutation score — see evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests; a form of narrative-coherence fingerprint (the test looks like a test, but doesn’t actually catch the bug)
Invented APIs — hallucinated method signatures, imports, CLI flags; entity-check variant
Copy-paste from training set — code that duplicates a well-known example even when the surrounding code uses a different pattern; in-register bias variant

Related

Sources

Sharma, M. et al. (2023) — “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models” — Anthropic
Perez, E. et al. (2022) — “Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations” — Anthropic
Ji, Z. et al. (2023) — “Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation” — ACM Computing Surveys
Wang et al., “Mutation-Guided Unit Test Generation with a Large Language Model” (arXiv 2506.02954, IEEE TSE 2025) — the 100%-coverage/4%-mutation-score finding (previously misattributed here to “Meta LLM Mutation Testing Research”; referenced in ai-verification-stack-web)
Anthropic (2024) — “Measuring the Persuasiveness of Language Models” — related to sycophancy dynamics

ai/ai-supply-chain-risks.title: AI Supply Chain Risks
ai/ai-supply-chain-risks.content:
AI Supply Chain Risks
What it is
Security risks when autonomous AI agents install dependencies, fetch packages, execute build tools, load model weights, and connect to external services without human oversight. A superset of traditional software supply chain risks, amplified by agent autonomy and expanded to cover AI-specific vectors (model weights, MCP servers, training data).
Why it matters
Agents don’t pause to verify package authenticity — they npm install and move on.
