Traditional supply chain attacks (typosquatting, dependency confusion) become dramatically more dangerous when the developer in the loop is an LLM that can’t evaluate trust signals. The attack surface also expands beyond code dependencies to include model weights, tool definitions, and training data.
Details
Attack vectors
1. Package registry attacks (npm, PyPI, crates.io)
Typosquatting: Register recat instead of react. A human might notice; an LLM generating npm install commands frequently won’t, especially for less common packages. LLMs may also hallucinate package names that don’t exist — and attackers can register those names preemptively (“hallucinated dependency attacks”).
Dependency confusion: If an org uses private packages (e.g., @company/utils), an attacker publishes a public package with the same name but higher version. Package managers may resolve the public version. Agents following standard install commands have no way to detect this.
Compromised maintainer accounts: legitimate packages taken over via credential theft. The package name and history look clean. Even a careful human review might miss a subtle backdoor in a minor version bump.
Malicious post-install hooks: npm runs postinstall scripts automatically. These can download and execute arbitrary code. Agents that install packages as part of a coding workflow trigger these hooks in the agent’s execution environment, with the agent’s permissions.
2. Build toolchain attacks
The Claude Code source leak itself was a supply chain failure: Bun runtime bug (#28001, open 20 days) shipped source maps in production despite configuration to exclude them. An unpatched known bug in the build pipeline led to full source code exposure. Lessons:

Known bugs in build tools are supply chain risks
Source maps, debug symbols, and development artifacts are attack surface
Configuration that “should” prevent exposure may not, due to tooling bugs
Time-to-patch matters: 20 days of known exposure is too long for a critical tool

3. Model weight attacks
Backdoored models: a model fine-tuned to produce vulnerable code patterns in specific contexts (e.g., always use eval() when processing user input). Detectable only through behavioral testing, not weight inspection.
Serialization exploits: Pickle-format model files (common in PyTorch) can execute arbitrary code on load. The safetensors format was created specifically to address this. Always prefer safetensors over pickle/PT files for untrusted models.
Quantization poisoning: a model uploaded as “Q4_K_M quantization of Llama 3” may be a different model entirely, or a modified version with behavioral backdoors introduced during the quantization process. Verify model hashes against the original publisher.
4. MCP server attacks
MCP servers are executable code that your AI agent connects to and trusts. A malicious MCP server can:

Return poisoned data that influences the agent’s decisions (prompt injection via tool response)
Request elevated permissions through the MCP capability negotiation
Exfiltrate data from the agent’s context (the agent sends tool calls containing your code/data)
Act as a man-in-the-middle between the agent and legitimate services

With 10,000+ public MCP servers — the figure cited when Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation, announced 2025-12-09 alongside Block’s goose and OpenAI’s AGENTS.md — the registry is becoming an attack surface similar to npm. See model-context-protocol.
5. Training data poisoning
Deliberately injecting vulnerable patterns into training data (public repos, Stack Overflow answers, documentation) so that models trained on this data reproduce the vulnerabilities. This is a slow, indirect attack — hard to attribute and hard to detect.
Real-world incidents
March 2026 — npm RAT injection: Attackers injected Remote Access Trojans into npm packages concurrent with the Claude Code source leak. Agents that were installing dependencies as part of coding tasks pulled poisoned packages immediately. The timing was deliberate — attackers exploited the surge of developer activity around the leak.
August 2025 — Nx “s1ngularity”: the first known case of malware weaponizing developer AI assistants for supply-chain attack. Compromised nx npm versions programmatically invoked Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Amazon Q CLI, prompting them to enumerate the filesystem for credentials, SSH keys, and crypto wallets. GitGuardian counted 2,349 distinct secrets across 1,079 repositories; exfiltration went to ~1,400 public repos named s1ngularity-repository, and a second phase used the stolen tokens to flip victims’ private repositories public. The malicious versions were live for roughly five hours.
This is the incident that makes the agent amplification section below concrete: the agent was not the victim, it was the enumeration tool. A dependency install and a credential-reading assistant in the same session is the whole attack.
September 2025 — postmark-mcp, the first malicious MCP server in the wild (verified 2026-08-07): an npm package impersonating the legitimate Postmark MCP server. The attacker cloned ActiveCampaign/Postmark’s real GitHub repository, published it to npm under the same name, and shipped 15 clean versions first. From v1.0.16 onward a single added line BCC’d every outgoing email to an attacker-controlled address (phan@giftshop[.]club) — password resets, invoices, internal correspondence. Published 2025-09-15, malicious from 2025-09-17, unpublished 2025-09-25 after the discovering researchers (Koi) got no reply from the author ○.
Three things make it the cleanest instance of this note’s thesis. The registry name was the entire attack surface — nothing about the official repo was compromised. The malicious change was one line, well inside what a human skim or an agent’s judgment would pass. And the payload rode the trust built by 15 honest releases, which is a pattern no point-in-time scan catches.
Impact numbers here are commonly over-quoted: the widely-repeated “~300 organizations affected” is Koi’s own estimate, derived by assuming ~20% of ~1,500 weekly downloads were live installs, against 1,643 total downloads before removal. Koi said plainly it could “only guestimate the impact.” No registry or victim telemetry establishes a count — see §4 of reading-quantitative-ai-claims.
March 2026 — CrewAI file read (CVE-2026-2285): JSON loader tool with no path validation allowed agents to read arbitrary files (SSH keys, credentials). Part of a broader injection-to-RCE chain — see prompt-injection for the full analysis.
OpenClaw localhost trust (2026): Local WebSocket gateway with implicit localhost trust. Any website could connect and send commands to the developer’s AI agent. Tracked as CVE-2026-32922 (CVSS 3.1 9.9, CWE-266, fixed in 2026.3.11 — verified against NVD 2026-07-31).
The frequently-cited “135,000+ internet-facing instances” figure was verified 2026-08-07 and should not be quoted in the present tense. It is real but transient: The Register recorded it on 2026-02-09 from SecurityScorecard STRIKE’s live discovery dashboard, and the same article notes STRIKE’s own report published earlier that same day showed “just over 40,000” (STRIKE’s blog: “40,214 (and climbing)”). The count tripled within one news cycle because it is a cumulative discovery counter, not a census — STRIKE’s stated method was internet-wide favicon-hash fingerprinting plus proprietary breach correlation, GitHub API, and direct enumeration. By 2026-08-06 the first-party dashboard reportedly showed ~1.04M cumulative discoveries against only ~68.3K currently responding (dashboard figures from a research ledger; the dashboard returned 403 on direct fetch, so this pair is unverified). Cite it as “135,000+ discovered as of 2026-02-09,” never as a population. The general failure mode is §3 of reading-quantitative-ai-claims.
This is supply chain adjacent — the “trusted local service” pattern is analogous to trusting a local package.
Agent amplification
The core problem: agents execute the full software development lifecycle (install, build, test, deploy) at machine speed without the human pause-and-verify moments that catch supply chain attacks.








































Traditional riskWith agentsAmplification factorMalicious packageAuto-installed, no human reviewHigh — agent trusts registry implicitlyTyposquatted nameAgent won’t catch subtle misspellingHigh — LLMs hallucinate package namesCompromised build scriptExecuted as normal workflowMedium — agent may detect odd outputMalicious post-install hookRuns immediately in agent envCritical — agent’s permissions, agent’s networkBackdoored model weightsLoaded and used without verificationHigh — behavioral backdoors are invisiblePoisoned MCP serverConnected and trusted by agentCritical — full data access via tool protocol
Mitigations
For package dependencies

Lockfile-only installs (npm ci, not npm install): never resolve new versions autonomously. The lockfile is the single source of truth for dependency versions.
Package allowlists: restrict which registries and packages the agent can install from. Tools: npm --registry, .npmrc scope mapping, Artifactory/Nexus proxy registries.
Sandboxed install environments: run npm install in an isolated container with no network access after initial download. Post-install hooks execute in the sandbox, not on the host.
Signature verification: require cryptographic signatures on packages. npm supports --signature-audit; not all ecosystems have this yet.
Human approval for new dependencies: any package.json change that adds a new dependency requires human review. Automate the detection, not the approval.
Reproducible builds: verify that building from source produces identical artifacts. Detects backdoors inserted during the build process.
npm audit in CI: run vulnerability scanning on every change. Block merges with known vulnerabilities.
Socket.dev / Snyk / Dependabot: automated tools that scan for known malicious packages and anomalous package behavior.

For model weights

Prefer safetensors format: avoids arbitrary code execution on model load
Verify hashes: compare SHA-256 of downloaded weights against the publisher’s stated hash
Download from official sources: Hugging Face Hub, Google/Meta official repos — not random mirrors
Behavioral testing: run evaluation suites on downloaded models before deploying to production

For MCP servers

Vet server source code before connecting, especially for servers with filesystem or network access
Principle of least privilege: only grant the permissions the server actually needs
Network isolation: local MCP servers shouldn’t have internet access unless required
Monitor tool call patterns: anomalous requests (reading SSH keys, accessing credentials) should trigger alerts

For agents generally

Least-privilege execution: agents should run with the minimum permissions needed. No root. No access to credentials directories. No unrestricted network.
Ephemeral environments: run agents in disposable containers that are destroyed after each task. No persistent state for attackers to leverage.
Audit logging: log every package install, file write, and network request. Review anomalies.

Related

ai-agent-security — permission models and sandboxing framework
capability-combination-security-frames — why installing one MCP server can flip an agent from a safe capability count to an unsafe one
reading-quantitative-ai-claims — how the incident figures above get over-quoted (snapshots as populations, estimates as counts)
prompt-injection — injection via tool responses is a supply chain vector
agentic-ai-architecture — the agent loop that automates the vulnerable workflow
model-context-protocol — MCP server trust model and emerging registry

Sources

Claude Code source leak (March 2026) — the Bun build toolchain failure
npm security incidents (March-April 2026)
CrewAI CVEs: CVE-2026-2275, CVE-2026-2285, CVE-2026-2286, CVE-2026-2287
OpenClaw CVSS 9.9 privilege escalation (2026)
Nx “s1ngularity” (2025-08-26), verified 2026-07-31: GitGuardian, Wiz, StepSecurity and Trend Micro write-ups
MCP donation to the Agentic AI Foundation, 2025-12-09: Linux Foundation announcement and blog.modelcontextprotocol.io
Bun issue oven-sh/bun#28001 “Source map incorrectly served when in production”, opened 2026-03-11, verified open 2026-07-31
Socket.dev: socket.dev — supply chain security research

ai/ai-verification-stack-web.title: AI Code Verification — Web Development Stack
ai/ai-verification-stack-web.content:
AI Code Verification — Web Development Stack
As of April 2026. Covers the verification gap, the emerging tooling stack for web, market signals, and a concrete skill-building path. Treats verification-as-a-discipline as an object of study — not a personal career prescription.
What it is
A framework for verifying AI-generated web code — the tools and patterns that constitute “verification” as a distinct practice as AI subsumes code generation, architecture, and system design. The interesting question this note explores: whether verification coheres into a defensible discipline as generation commoditizes.
Why it matters
Generation is commoditizing. Verification is getting harder. The structural asymmetry:













































MetricValueSourceAI-authored PRs: avg issues10.83 vs 6.45 human-only (1.7x more bugs)CodeRabbit Dec 2025 (470 PRs)Security issues in AI PRsup to 2.74x higher (worst category: XSS); password handling 1.88xCodeRabbit Dec 2025 (same report)Unguided AI code passing security checks~55% pass rateVeracode Spring 2026OWASP Top 10 in AI code25.1% of samples (best model: 19.1%)AppSec SantaHollow test suites4% mutation score despite 100% coverage (some suites)Wang et al., arXiv 2506.02954 (IEEE TSE 2025)CVEs from AI code (Mar 2026)35 new (up from 6 in Jan, 15 in Feb)CycodeDev speed with AI (experienced devs, own repos)19% slowerMETR RCT, 16 devs / 246 tasks (arXiv 2507.09089)
AI generates a large share of global code — estimates range from 22% (merged, DX Q4 2025) to ~41-42% (generated); generated ≠ merged. The landscape note identifies the defining challenge: verification, maintenance, and governance of non-human logic. This note is the practical playbook.
Why verification is defensible

Oracle problem is irreducible. AI checks AI, but someone must define “correct.” Human judgment at the boundary.
Trust bottleneck. Certifying AI code as safe is a chokepoint role — analogous to auditors in complex financial systems.
Liability mandate. US Copyright Office: no IP protection for purely AI-generated works. EU AI Act: transparency and audit requirements. Someone signs off. They need verification skills.
Compounding expertise. Each verification system teaches failure modes → better specs → better verification. The knowledge compounds.

The Verification Stack (Web-Specific)
Layer 1: Specification-First Development
Write machine-checkable specs. AI implements. Verification checks implementation against specs.
Tools:

GitHub Spec Kit (Sep 2025) — open-source, works with Claude Code, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Cursor
Amazon Kiro (July 2025) — AI-native IDE with built-in spec-driven development
Even a spec.md file with explicit edge cases dramatically improves AI output

Specs execute as BDD scenarios, API contract tests, or model simulations. Implementation cannot drift without failing the build.
Layer 2: Type-Level Verification & Schema Contracts
Web development’s practical formal methods — lightweight but high-impact.
Type systems as verification:

TypeScript strict mode — strict: true, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes. Most teams aren’t using the strictest settings. Free bug prevention.
Zod — runtime schema validation bridging compile-time types to actual data. When AI generates an API handler, Zod schemas are executable specifications.
tRPC — end-to-end type safety. AI can’t generate a mismatched frontend call without the build failing.

API contracts as formal specs:

OpenAPI specs — spec first → generate types and validation → AI implements against the spec. Tools: openapi-typescript, orval, swagger-typescript-api
GraphQL schemas + codegen — schema gates what AI can generate
Pact — consumer-driven contract testing. AI modifies backend → Pact verifies all consumers still work without running them

Layer 3: Mutation Testing & Visual Regression
Proves tests catch bugs, not just touch code.

Stryker Mutator — JS/TS mutation testing. Exposes hollow AI-generated test suites (100% coverage, 4% mutation score)
Chromatic / Percy — visual regression. AI generates UI changes → pixel-level comparison catches unintended breakage
Playwright visual comparisons — screenshot-based regression in E2E suite (free, no third-party)
Storybook — component isolation + visual testing

Recommended mutation thresholds for AI web code: 70% business logic, 50% UI components, 30% utility/glue.
Layer 4: Multi-Agent Verification
AI checking AI with safeguards against collusion.

Adversarial code review — critic agent reviews builder output against spec before human review
Consensus engines — independent tools each verify/reject claims of the previous
Actor-critic — generator → critic → refiner with specialized critics (safety, accuracy, compliance)

Layer 5: Web Architecture Fitness Functions
Automated gates on every PR:

Lighthouse CI — performance, accessibility (WCAG), SEO, best practices. “No merge below 90.”
Bundle size budgets — bundlesize, size-limit, or Vite/webpack limits. AI loves adding deps; this catches bloat.
ESLint architectural rules — eslint-plugin-boundaries for import constraints, dependency-cruiser for layer violations. Fitness functions that prevent AI from breaking architecture.
npm audit / socket.dev — dependency security gates. Catches vulnerable or typosquatted packages.
Core Web Vitals monitoring — post-deploy via CrUX, SpeedCurve, or Vercel Analytics

Layer 6: Human Oversight at Decision Points
Not implementation review. Specification review.

Provenance tracking — what model, what prompt, when
System-level decisions (human) vs micro-decisions (automated)

The Role Shift
The design comes from AI. The constraints, values, and trade-off priorities remain human.
The role becomes: “person who defines what ‘works’ means” — encoding business requirements, security constraints, performance budgets, and compliance mandates into machine-checkable specifications.
Specification writer → AI generates → Verification pipeline gates → Human reviews results
Lead dev experience transfers directly: that role already translates business needs into technical direction. The output shifts from “code and documents” to “specifications and verification pipelines.”
How the Role Could Evolve
A plausible maturation path for the discipline itself, sketched in the abstract — observing how the work might layer up, not prescribing a ladder for anyone in particular:
Directing humans
  → directing AI + spec-driven development
  → designing quality gates (verification architecture)
  → supervising AI systems / leading verification engineering
Market signals (as of April 2026): AI safety/alignment expertise reportedly commands a ~45% salary premium over generalist ML engineering. Axiom raised 200M (1.6B valuation) for AI code verification. Qodo raised $70M for multi-agent code review. These figures signal that the market is pricing the discipline — not that any one person should chase it.
Learning Path (Web-Focused)
Phase 1 — This week:

Spec-driven development (write spec.md before asking AI to implement)
Tighten TypeScript config (strict: true, noUncheckedIndexedAccess)
Set up Lighthouse CI on one project

Phase 2 — Next 1-3 months:

Stryker mutation testing (the eye-opener)
Contract testing (Pact, OpenAPI-first, or Zod schemas as specs)
Visual regression (Playwright screenshots or Chromatic)

Phase 3 — 3-6 months:

ESLint architectural rules (eslint-plugin-boundaries, dependency-cruiser)
Property-based testing with fast-check
Full verification CI pipeline (the capstone)

What to Watch

Qodo 2.0 ($70M) — multi-agent code review with organizational context
GitHub Spec Kit — spec-driven development (open-source)
Stryker Mutator — JS/TS mutation testing ecosystem
Chromatic — visual regression with Storybook
Axiom ($200M) — formal verification for AI code at scale
socket.dev — next-gen dependency security
Lighthouse CI — Google’s web quality gates

Related

deterministic-gates-agent-loop — the machine-facing axis under this stack: determinism as an engineered property (the pin list), gate placement inside the agent’s repair loop rather than after it, the agent-must-not-edit-its-own-oracle rule, and fail-closed reporting so “green” can’t mean “a tool timed out”
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — decision rubric that sits on top of this stack: trust signals, escalation triggers, tiered review
bias-aware-verification-protocol — orthogonal axis on top of every layer in this stack: four-pass protocol (input triage, output scan, disagreement drill, red team) that checks the reasoning behind the artifact, not just the artifact
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — output-side bias patterns (sycophancy, hallucinated confidence, narrative coherence) that survive type checks and test passes — worth scanning even when CI is green
prompt-bias-diagnostics — input-side reframes for specs and prompts; biased specs produce biased implementations at scale
ai-software-dev-2026-landscape — the broader AI dev landscape this sits within
ai-agent-security — runtime security for agents generating this code
ai-frontier-crisis-april-2026 — why verification matters at the frontier level
ai-supply-chain-risks — dependency attack vectors AI amplifies
structured-output-json-mode — Zod/schema validation as a verification layer
agentic-ai-architecture — the agent loop producing code that needs verification

Sources

CodeRabbit, “State of AI vs Human Code Generation” (Dec 2025, 470 PRs) — 1.7×, up-to-2.74× security, 1.88× password handling all from this one report
Veracode Spring 2026 GenAI Code Security Update — ~55% security pass rate (no 1.88× figure; prior misattribution corrected 2026-06-10)
Wang et al., “Mutation-Guided Unit Test Generation with a Large Language Model” (arXiv 2506.02954, IEEE TSE 2025) — 100%-coverage/4%-mutation-score (previously misattributed to Meta)
METR, “Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI…” (arXiv 2507.09089, July 2025) — the 19%-slower RCT
Cycode CVE tracking (Q1 2026)
Axiom Series A ($200M, March 2026) — TechCrunch
Qodo Series B ($70M, March 2026) — TechCrunch
Trail of Bits: “Mutation testing for the agentic era” (April 2026)
Martin Kleppmann: “AI will make formal verification mainstream” (Dec 2025)
Microsoft Research: “Intent Formalization” grand challenge paper
GitHub Blog: “Spec-driven development with AI” (Sep 2025)
Martin Fowler: “Understanding SDD tools” (2026)

ai/architecture-decision-records-ai.title: ADRs in AI-Assisted Repositories
ai/architecture-decision-records-ai.content:
ADRs in AI-Assisted Repositories
Architecture Decision Records are short documents capturing the why behind a load-bearing architectural choice — what forces were at play, what was picked, what alternatives were considered, what becomes harder. In AI-assisted repositories they pull double duty: a letter to future-you, and machine-readable governance the agent reads on every session.
This note consolidates the ADR material scattered across the vault. For the upstream design workflow that produces ADRs, see ai-system-design-workflow. For where ADRs sit in the wider AI-friendly repo structure, see ai-friendly-repo-structure §4.
Why ADRs matter more in AI-assisted repos
Three reasons compound:
1. Agents see code, not intent. “Agents can discover what code does but not why decisions were made” (ai-friendly-repo-structure §4). An ADR is the only artifact that preserves the rejected alternatives — without it, an agent (or future-you) will re-litigate the same decision and may land on a different answer.
2. No team memory to fall back on (solo angle). “Architecture Decision Records sound enterprise, but they’re actually more valuable solo, because there’s no team memory to fall back on. Six months in, ‘why did I pick Remix over Next.js’ has no answer unless you wrote it down” (ai-system-design-workflow).
3. Highest-stakes hallucination surface. “The worst failures aren’t in code (caught by tests) or customer replies (caught on review) — they’re in ADRs, docs, and commit messages that durably mislead future-you. These get written once and read for years” (solo-developer-ai-stack). An LLM-drafted ADR with a plausible-sounding but fabricated rationale will be cited as ground truth for years.
Format
Michael Nygard’s original format (2011) is the widely-used default:
# 0001 — Web framework
 
**Date:** 2026-04-21
**Status:** Accepted
 
## Context
[Two paragraphs — what forces are at play]
 
## Decision
[What we chose]
 
## Alternatives considered
[The other options, one paragraph each]
 
## Consequences
[What's now easier, what's now harder, what we're locked into]
Machine-readable variant
For AI-assisted repos, ai-friendly-repo-structure §4 recommends two additions:

Explicit section tags (<decision>, <context>, <consequences>) so LLMs parse decision boundaries reliably instead of guessing from prose structure
Tabular capability manifests and authorization constraints embedded in the ADR — transforming a passive record into something agents can query (e.g., “is the agent allowed to modify this layer?“)

The same note references AgDR (Agent Decision Records) as an ADR extension for AI-assisted development. The term is referenced rather than defined in the source, and its origin is not independently verified — treat it as a labeling convention pointing at the same artifact with explicit agent-readable structure, not a separate standard.
Filesystem layout
Single file per decision, numbered, in a flat directory:
docs/
├── adr/
│   ├── 0001-web-framework.md
│   ├── 0002-database.md
│   ├── 0003-feature-slicing.md
│   └── template.md
The concrete example in enterprise-frontend-ai-folder-structure places docs/adr/ alongside agent-docs/ (progressive-disclosure imports) and llms.txt (machine-readable project summary), under a top-level docs/.
Agent integration
Two mechanics make ADRs active rather than archival:
1. @import into CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md). The agent reads the relevant ADR on every session, so it doesn’t re-litigate the decision. From ai-system-design-workflow:

adr/*.md → CLAUDE.md can @import these so the agent doesn’t re-litigate decisions

2. ADR violation in a PR is a signal, not a problem to suppress. Same source:

The agent making a PR that violates an ADR is a signal to either (a) update the ADR intentionally, or (b) reject the change. Either way, the decision is surfaced, not drifted into.

This is the active-governance behavior — the ADR is the spec the diff is checked against.
Generating an ADR with the LLM
ai-system-design-workflow Phase 3 contains a forced-alternatives prompt template — ask for three architecturally distinct options, each with its own “death scenario” (what event would force a rewrite), then a recommendation with an “unless X” counter-case. Three options forces real differences; the death scenario forces the model to commit to a weakness rather than hand-wave; the unless-clause gives the model permission to disagree with its own recommendation. See the source note for the full template.
The output of that prompt maps cleanly onto Nygard’s structure (synthesis inference, not in the source): Context ← spec, Decision ← recommendation, Alternatives ← the other two options, Consequences ← death scenario + cheap-at/expensive-at notes. (The template also asks what each option is cheap at vs expensive at, in dev time and dollars.)
Verification
ADRs are a high-leverage target for the vault’s verification skills:

/bias-scan-ai <path> — before committing any AI-drafted ADR. Catches sycophantic agreement with whatever the prompt anchored on, fabricated specifics (versions, benchmarks, “studies show”), and rationales that read confident but cite nothing.
/bias-scan-human <path> — for ADRs you drafted yourself. Different axis: sunk-cost rationalization of a choice already made, confirmation bias in the alternatives, fundamental-attribution-error framing of why a previous approach “failed.”
/red-team <path> — for ADRs covering load-bearing decisions (database, auth, deployment topology). Produces the strongest objections and a pre-mortem before the decision locks in.
/reviewers-map <path> — lighter-weight per-output check; tags [V]/[U]/[I] claims in the draft.

See bias-aware-verification-protocol for which to pick when. The defaults from .claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md apply with extra force here: ADRs are exactly the “synthesis notes, high-stakes claims” the rules call out.
When to skip ADRs
Not every decision deserves a record. From ai-system-design-workflow:

Genuine throwaway prototypes (exploring whether something is possible at all)
Replacing a single function or adding one field to existing well-modeled code
Spike work where the output will be discarded

The test is the six-month one: would I read this in six months? If no, don’t write it. If yes, it’s five minutes now to save an hour of re-derivation later.
Anti-patterns

Compliance theater. ADRs written to look thorough rather than to be read. If you wouldn’t open it again, it’s not load-bearing. From ai-system-design-workflow: “they’re a letter to future-you. If you wouldn’t read it in six months, don’t write it.”
AI-drafted ADRs committed without verification. Highest-impact failure mode. The LLM will confabulate a clean rationale even if the actual decision was “I read a Hacker News comment.” Always run a verification scan (bias-aware-verification-protocol).
ADR as post-hoc justification. Writing the ADR after the implementation locks in, then back-filling Context to fit the Decision. The alternatives section becomes a strawman parade. The fix is the upstream workflow: ADR drafted from a forced-alternatives prompt before implementation, with the rejected options recorded honestly.
Single giant prompt that produces both ADR and code. Context pollution, lost-in-the-middle effects, and the model shortcutting past the design work to the SQL (ai-system-design-workflow anti-patterns).
ADRs as advisory text the agent ignores. Without @import into CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md, the ADR is unread. Without a PR-level check that surfaces ADR violations, the agent will drift past decisions it never knew were made.

Related

ai-system-design-workflow — upstream design phases that produce ADRs; full forced-alternatives prompt template
ai-friendly-repo-structure §4 — ADRs within the documentation-as-code section; AgDR, machine-readable variants
enterprise-frontend-ai-folder-structure — concrete docs/adr/ placement in a Next.js monorepo layout
solo-developer-ai-stack — durable-artifact hallucination risk; why ADRs are the highest-leverage target for /bias-scan-ai
bias-aware-verification-protocol — four-pass framework; which scan to pick when
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — how to check that implementation matches the recorded decision

Sources

Michael Nygard. “Documenting Architecture Decisions.” 2011. (ADR format, originating reference)
Synthesis of the four vault notes listed under Related. The “machine-readable variant” (section tags, capability manifests) and AgDR labeling are drawn from ai-friendly-repo-structure; verify the specific framing against current external sources before adopting AgDR as a published term elsewhere.

ai/autonomous-agent-vs-decomposed-workfl.title: Autonomous Agent vs Decomposed Workflow
ai/autonomous-agent-vs-decomposed-workfl.content:
Autonomous Agent vs Decomposed Workflow
When a task needs several steps, there are two ends of a design axis: hand the whole flow to one agent that decides its own steps in a tool-calling loop, or decompose it into discrete steps you wire together yourself (prompt chain, router, orchestrator). This note frames that as a spectrum, enumerates the intermediate options, and gives the head-to-head pros/cons and the axes that decide which one to reach for.
The governing distinction (from Anthropic’s Building Effective Agents, Dec 2024): a workflow is a system where LLM calls and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths; an agent is a system where the LLM directs its own process and tool use, deciding at each step what to do next. Most production systems are not one or the other — they are workflows with agentic cells.
This is the build-time sibling to task-decomposition-for-ai-plans (which decides whether to split a plan you’re about to issue) and agentic-ai-architecture (the loop mechanics). The reliability case underneath it is reliability-vs-capability-agents.
The core axis — who owns the control flow
The single variable that orders every option below is who decides what the next step is:

You decide, at design time → the control flow is in code. Deterministic, inspectable, testable. The LLM fills in cells; it never chooses the path.
The model decides, at run time → the control flow is in the model’s head. Flexible, handles open-ended tasks, but the path is non-deterministic and only visible after the fact.

Everything else — cost, latency, debuggability, reliability — falls out of where you put that decision.
The option spectrum (low → high agent autonomy)
More options than the binary, ordered by how much control flow you cede to the model:




































































#PatternWho picks the next stepBest whenMain risk0Single augmented callNobody — one shotTask fits one call (+tools/retrieval)Forcing multi-step work into one prompt1Prompt chain (fixed pipeline)You, fixed orderSteps are known and stable; each gates the nextBrittle to inputs that don’t fit the fixed shape2Routing (classify → dispatch)A classifier, then fixedDistinct input classes want different handlingMisroute cascades; needs a fallback class3Parallelization (sectioning / voting)You, fan-out then aggregateIndependent subtasks, or you want N votesAggregation/merge logic; correlated errors in votes4Orchestrator–workersAn LLM orchestrator, per taskSubtasks can’t be enumerated up front but are boundedOrchestrator is a single point of failure5Plan-then-executePlanner once, then fixedCoherent plan worth paying a frontier model forPlan staleness mid-execution; no replanning6Evaluator–optimizer loopGenerator + critic, boundedClear quality bar a critic can check; iteration helpsInfinite/empty loops; critic shares the generator’s blind spots7Fully autonomous agent loopThe model, every stepOpen-ended task, unknowable step count, tools availableNon-determinism, runaway cost, hard to verify
Patterns 1–3 are pure workflows (control flow in code). 4–6 are hybrids — a model makes some routing/iteration decisions inside a structure you bounded. 7 is the agent. The “agent does it itself vs split into steps” choice is the gap between 7 and {1–6}. (The 0–7 ordering onto an autonomy gradient is this note’s synthesis; Anthropic’s essay names the patterns as coordinate options, not a linear rank.)
Head-to-head: autonomous agent (7) vs decomposed workflow (1–3)
Autonomous agent — pros

Handles the unknowable. When you can’t enumerate the steps (the count depends on what the model finds mid-task), the agent adapts where a fixed chain can’t.
Less to build and maintain. One loop + good tools + one prompt, versus a graph of steps, schemas, and glue. Capability rides on the model improving, not on your wiring.
Recovers in-context. A failed tool call, a surprising file — the agent reasons about it and tries another route without you having coded that branch.
Generalizes. The same loop serves many tasks; a workflow is shaped to one.

Autonomous agent — cons

Reliability erodes with horizon. pass@1 ≠ pass^k: it may do the task once and not dependably across runs, and the gap widens as the flow gets longer (reliability-vs-capability-agents). Unattended loops need pass^k, which no single demo measures.
Cost and latency are unbounded and variable. Step count is decided at run time; a task that “should” take 4 steps can take 25. Needs explicit step/token circuit-breakers.
Opaque and hard to debug. The control flow only exists in the transcript. When it goes wrong, you reconstruct why it chose that after the fact (see debugging-agentic-failures).
All-or-nothing verification. One final output to check, with no confirmed-correct intermediate anchors. Errors compound silently across steps.
Larger blast radius. More autonomous tool use = more surface for prompt injection and unintended destructive actions (ai-agent-security).

Decomposed workflow — pros

Deterministic, inspectable control flow. You can read the graph, unit-test each step, set a per-step schema, and log every transition. Observability is built in, not reconstructed.
Verification anchors at every seam. Each step produces a checkable intermediate; a failure is localized and recoverable from the last good anchor (task-decomposition-for-ai-plans “small victories”).
Bounded, predictable cost/latency. Fixed number of calls; you can pick the cheapest model per step (cheap classify, expensive reason).
Higher per-step reliability. A narrow, well-specified step beats an open-ended one; the model executes against your spec, not its training-data prior for a vague instruction.
Lets you mix deterministic code in. Rule-expressible transforms become real code, not prompts — cheaper and exact.

Decomposed workflow — cons

Brittle to inputs outside the designed shape. The fixed path can’t handle a case you didn’t foresee; coverage is your problem.
More to build and maintain. Steps, schemas, routing, aggregation, glue — and it ages as the task changes.
Switching/handoff overhead. Context is re-established at each boundary; over-splitting pays setup cost twice and dilutes the larger goal (task-decomposition-for-ai-plans over-decomposition).
Caps at the wiring’s ceiling. It only does what you composed; it won’t surprise you usefully the way an agent can.

The axes that actually decide it
When unsure, score the task on these — they’re the dimensions the pros/cons collapse into:


















































AxisFavors decomposed workflowFavors autonomous agentStep predictabilitySteps known and stableStep count depends on run-time findingsStakes / reversibilityHigh (irreversible, production)Low (sandboxed, reversible, cheap to retry)Reliability needUnattended, must pass^kHuman-in-loop picks the good run (pass@k)Cost/latency sensitivityTight budget, must be boundedCan absorb variable cost for capabilityVerifiabilityNeeds intermediate anchorsOne end-output is cheaply checkableTask diversityOne narrow task, high volumeMany varied tasks, one harnessMaintenance appetiteWilling to own a graphWant capability to ride model upgradesObservability/complianceAudit trail requiredBest-effort, transcript is enough
Rule of thumb: the more a wrong step costs and the harder it is to undo, the more control flow you keep in code. Reserve full autonomy for open-ended, low-stakes, reversible work — and even there, bound it.
Intermediate and hybrid moves (where most real systems land)
You rarely pick a pure end. The high-leverage options sit in the middle:

Deterministic skeleton, agent in the cells. Code owns sequencing, gating, and irreversible actions; the LLM is reserved for the judgment steps. This is a common production pattern — see ai-code-review-deterministic-agent-hybrid (“keep control flow, routing, resource gating in code; reserve the LLM for judgment”).
Plan-then-execute (“think expensive, act cheap”). A frontier model decomposes the task into a plan once; cheaper models execute each step. The plan supplies the coherence small models lack (agentic-ai-architecture planning/execution separation). Add replanning if mid-execution surprises are likely, or the plan goes stale.
Staged autonomy with human-in-the-loop (HITL) gates at bottlenecks. Let the agent run autonomously between checkpoints, but stop for confirmation at verification seams and before destructive steps. Put the gates at bottleneck states, not arbitrary boundaries. The trust granted should be horizon-indexed and grow as the agent earns it (hitl-progressive-autonomy).
Bounded agent. A full loop with hard circuit-breakers: max steps, token budget, max retries per tool, fail-closed on security-relevant errors. Many nominally “autonomous” production agents are really this.
Implementation intentions for branches. A flow with a single run-time fork need not become a full agent — express the fork as a deterministic IF-trigger-THEN-response so a workflow can carry it without ceding the whole control flow (implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans).

When the autonomous loop is the right call
The cons list shouldn’t read as “always decompose.” The agent wins cleanly when:

The step count genuinely can’t be known up front (research, debugging, exploration).
The task space is too diverse to wire a workflow per case, and one harness must serve all.
The work is reversible and sandboxed, so an off run is cheap.
A human (or a cheap oracle) filters outputs, so you’re operating at pass@k, not pass^k.
You’d otherwise spend more engineering the workflow than the task is worth.

Conversely, decomposition is over-applied when the task is short and single-concern: running an orchestration graph over a 3-step job is its own failure mode (switching overhead, diluted goal). For small, stable tasks, a single augmented call or a short chain beats both a graph and an agent.
Counterargument and nuance

It’s a spectrum, and the binary framing misleads. Treating it as “agent vs workflow” hides the productive middle (patterns 4–6, hybrids). The real question is where on the autonomy gradient and which steps get ceded — not a single global choice.
The line moves with model capability — time-sensitive. As models get more reliable over long horizons, the autonomy that’s safe to grant rises, and tasks that needed decomposition in 2025 may run as a bounded agent later. Re-evaluate per model generation; don’t freeze this decision. (As of 2026-06, long-horizon reliability is still the binding constraint — reliability-vs-capability-agents.)
Decomposition can hurt. Splitting at non-bottlenecks pays setup cost without buying anchor stability; over-decomposed flows drift from the superordinate goal even as each step “succeeds.” Split at seams, keep the why visible at each boundary (task-decomposition-for-ai-plans).
Multi-agent is a different axis, not a higher rung. Decomposing into steps is orthogonal to decomposing across agents. Default to a single agent or a single-process workflow; only go multi-agent when subtasks are genuinely independent and a single agent can’t reach quality (multi-agent-diminishing-returns, multi-agent-coordination-topologies).

Related

agentic-loop-examples — the worked-example companion: a minimal pseudocode skeleton for each of the 0–7 patterns enumerated here, plus the Ralph brute-force variant
task-decomposition-for-ai-plans — the plan-level sibling: five structural signals for whether to split, plus the over-decomposition failure mode
bottleneck-states-as-split-points — where a split or HITL gate should land once you’ve decided to decompose
agentic-ai-architecture — the autonomous loop’s mechanics: tool registry, permissions, planning/execution separation
reliability-vs-capability-agents — pass@1/pass@k/pass^k; the reliability case for keeping control flow in code on unattended tasks
ai-code-review-deterministic-agent-hybrid — worked instance of the “deterministic skeleton, LLM for judgment” hybrid
agent-pipeline-feature-creation — a concrete decomposed workflow (spec → plan → code → test → review) with typed contracts
hitl-progressive-autonomy — staged autonomy and trust calibration for the HITL-gate option
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — carrying a single run-time branch in a workflow without going fully agentic
multi-agent-diminishing-returns / multi-agent-coordination-topologies — the orthogonal across-agents decomposition axis
debugging-agentic-failures — why the autonomous loop’s opacity raises the debugging cost

Sources

Schluntz, E. & Zhang, B. (2024). Building Effective Agents — Anthropic engineering, published 2024-12-19 (anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents). Source of the workflow-vs-agent distinction and the five workflow patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) plus the augmented-LLM building block. Authors, date, definitions, and all five pattern names verified against the live article 2026-06-17.
Internal: the reliability primitives, decomposition signals, and hybrid examples cited above are developed in the linked vault notes; this note synthesizes them into the autonomy-gradient decision rather than re-deriving them.

ai/bdi-architecture-for-coding-agents.title: BDI Architecture for Coding Agents
ai/bdi-architecture-for-coding-agents.content:
BDI Architecture for Coding Agents
Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) is a cognitive architecture for rational agency from late-1980s/early-1990s AI research. Its enduring contribution is the separation of deliberation from means-ends reasoning — deciding whether the current goal is still the right goal is a different activity from deciding the next step toward it, and conflating them is a known failure mode. That separation is directly relevant to LLM coding agents, which routinely either re-deliberate constantly (losing forward momentum) or commit to stale plans (continuing past the point where the goal no longer holds).
This note ports the BDI vocabulary to LLM coding agents and flags what doesn’t transfer cleanly. It is not a claim that classical BDI systems should be rebuilt — they were planning systems, not natural-language ones. The vocabulary is the value: it gives precise names to four moving parts in an agent loop that are otherwise lumped together.
The four parts
The classical BDI decomposition, mapped to a coding agent:






























BDI constituentClassical definitionCoding-agent realisationBeliefsInformational state — what the agent takes to be true of the worldRepository state (AST, dependency graph, file contents), retrieved documentation, observed tool outputsDesiresMotivational state — outcomes the agent is oriented toward, possibly conflictingGoals from the user / spec (“refactor X to use Y”; “maintain backwards compatibility”)IntentionsCommitted-to subset of desires the agent is actively pursuingActive execution threads, the current plan, scheduled tool invocationsEventsExternal triggers for belief revisionTest failures, lint errors, compilation errors, user redirection, file watcher signals
The agent loop, classical-BDI flavour:

Observe environment → update beliefs.
Evaluate desires against current beliefs → select an intention via deliberation.
Use means-ends reasoning to pick the next action toward the selected intention.
Execute. New observations and events feed back to step 1.

Most LLM agent loops today collapse all of this into a single autoregressive turn. The BDI lens is useful precisely because it names where the collapse happens.
Why the deliberation / means-ends split matters
Deliberation answers: is the currently committed intention still the right one given updated beliefs?
Means-ends reasoning answers: given the currently committed intention, what’s the next step?
Two failure modes when the split collapses:

Plan staleness. The agent commits to a plan, executes step-by-step, observes that the underlying belief that justified the plan no longer holds (e.g., a test it relied on was deleted), and continues anyway because nothing triggered re-deliberation.
Decision thrash. The agent re-deliberates on every step, never building forward momentum, often switching plans on noisy signals (one flaky test, one unhelpful tool result).

Classical BDI handles this trade-off with commitment strategies (Rao & Georgeff): blind, single-minded, open-minded — corresponding to never re-deliberate, re-deliberate when blocked, re-deliberate when anything changes. LLM coding agents face the same trade-off without typically naming it. The choice is a tuning parameter.
The hallucinated-beliefs problem
The single most important failure mode when porting BDI to LLM agents: beliefs formed from parametric memory are not grounded.
A classical BDI agent’s beliefs were a structured knowledge base — the agent literally could not believe something not in the KB. An LLM agent’s beliefs leak from training data: it will confidently assert that a library exists, a function is named X, an internal API accepts argument Y — none of it true for the actual repository. Those beliefs then become preconditions for intentions, and the intentions become plans, and the plans fail in ways downstream of the original ungrounded belief.
The structural fix is to decouple belief formation from parametric weights and tether it to verified retrieval:

AST-derived facts (the actual call graph, the actual import tree) — not LLM-summarised descriptions of code.
Metadata-filtered retrieval over docs, not raw vector search (which returns semantically similar but possibly outdated/wrong material). fine-tuning-vs-rag discusses the broader retrieval choice.
Capability-checked tool invocations — if the agent’s “belief” is that tool T exists, the runtime confirms or rejects this before the intention forms. See functional-agent-architecture on typed effects and capability tokens.

In other words: beliefs that are load-bearing for an intention must come from a source the system can verify, not from the model’s internal continuation.
Where BDI vocabulary helps in a real coding-agent pipeline
The BDI separation suggests questions worth asking of any agent design:

Where do beliefs come from? If the answer is “the model decides,” the system is one ungrounded continuation away from a hallucinated belief becoming an intention becoming an action.
Are conflicting desires resolved up front, or at execution time? Resolving at execution time means the agent might pick either branch depending on which retrieved chunk hit attention first. Up-front resolution is what a good intent spec does (see intent-engineering-discipline).
What triggers re-deliberation? “Never” → stale plans. “Anything” → thrash. Pick deliberately. Test failures, lint errors, and user interrupts are the usual concrete triggers; everything else stays in means-ends.
What is an intention’s commitment level? A single tool call? A multi-step plan? Until the next observation? Until the user redirects? This is the commitment-strategy question, and the answer shapes the whole loop.

What BDI doesn’t solve

Deterministic reasoning — LLM token sampling is stochastic; BDI vocabulary doesn’t change that. It only helps name where stochasticity becomes a problem.
Belief grounding by itself — BDI says beliefs should be grounded; it doesn’t say how. The how lives in retrieval, verification, and capability systems (functional-agent-architecture, fine-tuning-vs-rag, ai-verification-stack-web).
Multi-agent coordination — BDI was originally single-agent. Distributed-BDI (dMARS, d’Inverno et al. 1998) extended it, but the topology choices in multi-agent-coordination-topologies aren’t pre-decided by adopting BDI vocabulary.
The empty middle of LLM reasoning — BDI assumes the means-ends reasoner can compute “the next action to achieve intention I.” For complex coding tasks, the LLM is the reasoner, and its competence at that step is the central question — BDI doesn’t answer it.

Tradeoff: vocabulary vs. ceremony
The risk in adopting BDI vocabulary for LLM agents is ceremony — wrapping a normal tool-calling loop in B/D/I/E labels without changing behaviour. The vocabulary is worth carrying only if the labels make a real distinction visible:

A field labelled beliefs should be grounded by mechanism, not just renamed context.
A field labelled desires should expose conflicts; if there’s only one desire, just call it the goal.
A field labelled intentions should be revisable on events; a frozen plan is just a script.
An events channel that doesn’t actually trigger re-deliberation is decoration.

When the labels stop adding distinction, drop them.
Related

agentic-ai-architecture — the basic agent loop that BDI separates into named parts
functional-agent-architecture — typed effects and capability tokens; the mechanism that makes belief grounding enforceable
intent-engineering-discipline — many proposed intent-spec schemas use B/D/I sections
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — Gollwitzer’s if-then construct lives at the boundary between events and intentions
multi-agent-coordination-topologies — where the deliberation/execution split goes when distributed across agents
multi-agent-governance — runtime governance as a separate layer above per-agent BDI
fine-tuning-vs-rag — the retrieval side of belief grounding
context-window-management — belief storage as a context-budget problem

Sources

Bratman, M. E. (1987). Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason. Harvard University Press. The philosophical foundation — practical reasoning as a three-part structure.
Georgeff, M. P. & Lansky, A. L. (1986). “Procedural knowledge.” Proceedings of the IEEE, 74(10), 1383–1398. The Procedural Reasoning System (PRS) — the first major BDI software implementation.
Rao, A. S. & Georgeff, M. P. (1991). “Modeling rational agents within a BDI-architecture.” Proc. KR-91. The formalisation of BDI as a software model.
Rao, A. S. & Georgeff, M. P. (1995). “BDI agents: From theory to practice.” Proc. ICMAS-95. The often-cited applied paper; introduces commitment strategies (blind / single-minded / open-minded).
d’Inverno, M., Kinny, D., Luck, M. & Wooldridge, M. (1998). “A formal specification of dMARS.” ATAL’97. The distributed multi-agent BDI extension.

The recent (2026) literature on BDI-LLM hybrids is emerging and not yet citation-settled (e.g., grounding LLM beliefs via retrieval, hallucinated-belief problem). Treat compound-named “BDI + X” frameworks in current AI writing with the same scepticism as other fingerprints of AI-synthesised text — the underlying questions (where do beliefs come from, what triggers re-deliberation) are real; the specific named methods often are not.
Last reviewed: 2026-05-15.

ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.title: Bias-Aware Verification Protocol
ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.content:
Bias-Aware Verification Protocol
What it is
A concrete, runnable protocol for bias-aware AI interaction. It treats every non-trivial exchange as having two bias layers — one in the user’s prompt, one in the model’s output — and applies explicit passes to each. It then adds two adversarial passes (disagreement drill and red-team) on the resulting answer.
This is the synthesis note. The two atomic layers are documented separately:

prompt-bias-diagnostics — input side (what’s biased in the prompt, and how to reframe)
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — output side (what bias signatures to detect in the response)

Why it matters
The hardest thing about verifying AI output isn’t spotting a wrong answer — it’s deciding when to scrutinize at all. A protocol gives you a cost-calibrated default: which checks to run at which stakes, without having to re-derive the question each time.
For anyone whose role is “the human who verifies AI work” (see ai-verification-stack-web), this protocol is a first-class skill. It sits orthogonally on top of the verification stack — not a new layer, but a discipline that improves every layer’s signal-to-noise.
The four passes
Pass 1 — Input (prompt) triage
Goal: neutralize framing bias before the model sees the prompt.
Trigger: any prompt that will shape a decision with real consequences — production code, specs, research that changes your mind, user-visible outputs, prompts going to a subagent fleet.
What to do: run the prompt-bias-diagnostics triage (under 30 seconds):

Leading question? → reframe to neutral
Embedded estimate? → ask for independent estimate first
Single anecdote? → add base-rate request
Dispositional framing of behavior? → ask for situational first
Hot emotional state? → delay or add cold-state reframe
Alternatives ruled out? → ask for alternatives explicitly

Automation: the /bias-scan-prompt slash command runs this triage on a prompt (file path or literal text) and returns findings plus a suggested rewrite. Use it for prompts that will shape a decision or be baked into a spec.
Cost: 30 seconds of attention, or a cheap auto-prompt-triage subagent ($0.001/prompt with Haiku-tier).
Pass 2 — Output fingerprint scan
Goal: detect bias signatures in the model’s response before acting on it.
Trigger: any output that will be acted on, published, or propagated (committed code, vault notes, PR descriptions, emails, agent decisions).
What to do: run the ai-output-bias-fingerprints detection checklist:

Strip fluency — list load-bearing factual claims
Frame-test for sycophancy
Entity check — every named person, paper, URL, API, number
Gap test — what assumptions did the model make?
Mainstream check — is the popular answer right for your case?
Failure-mode probe — were tradeoffs acknowledged?
Context fit — did training-register assumptions leak in?

Automation: the /bias-scan-ai slash command runs this checklist on a file and returns structured findings plus a PASS/REVIEW/FAIL verdict.
Cost: under a minute for short outputs; selective for long outputs (apply to load-bearing sections).
Pass 3 — Disagreement drill (inversion)
Goal: use the model’s own variance under reframing as a calibration signal.
Trigger: decisions with significant downside, or where the model’s first answer felt suspiciously clean.
What to do: ask the model to argue the opposite position as strongly as it argued the first. Compare.

Large gap (two substantially different answers) → the question is genuinely contested or the model is unreliable here; go to Pass 4 or escalate to human judgment
Small gap (model hedges both ways with the same evidence) → the first answer was probably noise-dressed-as-confidence; treat as uncalibrated
Zero gap (model refuses to engage with the opposite) → strong signal of a value-locked or RLHF-constrained topic; seek independent sources

This is inversion applied to model outputs.
Automation: the /disagree slash command runs this drill on the most recent substantive assistant response.
Cost: one additional model call, plus a minute of reading and comparison.
Pass 4 — Red-team pass
Goal: surface failure modes the primary pass missed.
Trigger: high-stakes outputs — production architecture, security-relevant decisions, public-facing content, automated actions with non-trivial blast radius.
What to do: a second prompt or second agent whose only job is to find the first answer wrong. Concrete prompt patterns:

“Here is an answer: <first output>. Give me the three strongest reasons this is wrong or will fail in practice.”
“A skeptical senior engineer is reviewing this. What is their first objection?”
“Pre-mortem: assume this decision turned out to be a disaster six months from now. List the causes.”

Use a different model if you can — cross-model disagreement is a stronger signal than same-model disagreement. Document the red-team findings; if the primary answer survives them, you have earned trust in it. If not, revise.
This is red teaming operationalized for AI outputs.
Automation: the /red-team slash command runs this pass on a file or artifact and returns three strongest objections, a pre-mortem, and the weakest load-bearing claim.
Cost: one to three additional model calls plus human review time. Not cheap — reserve for high-stakes decisions.
When to run which pass — a cost-calibrated default





























































StakesInput triageOutput scanDisagreement drillRed-teamExploratory / local / throwaway✗✗✗✗Personal work, no audienceoptional✗✗✗Committed to vault / shared doc✓✓optional✗Committed to codebase✓✓optional✗Production / security-relevant✓✓✓✓Public-facing / external comms✓✓✓✓Automated agent action, non-trivial blast radius✓✓✓✓
The protocol is not “run all four every time.” It is “run the right ones for the stakes.” Overhead unmatched to stakes is the main reason verification protocols get abandoned.
Orthogonal: human-authored artifact scan
The four-pass protocol above is about AI interactions — it assumes there’s a prompt and a model-produced output to check. A separate scan exists for artifacts whose reasoning is the author’s own:

/bias-scan-human <path> — runs against a human-drafted decision note, journal entry, plan, retrospective, or synthesis note
Checks the full cognitive-bias catalog: sunk cost, confirmation, anchoring, planning fallacy, fundamental attribution error, self-serving bias, narrative fallacy, survivorship, loss aversion, automation bias, etc.
Draws on cognitive-biases, probability-judgment-biases, social-attribution-biases, ../general/consumer-valuation-biases, ai-automation-biases, debiasing-mental-models

This scan is orthogonal to the four-pass AI protocol — not a fifth pass. The two sets of checks are largely non-overlapping: /bias-scan-ai asks “did the model hallucinate or sycophant,” /bias-scan-human asks “did the author sunk-cost or confirmation-bias.” When an artifact is mixed (human draft + AI edits), run both; their findings typically don’t duplicate.
How this slots into the verification stack
The protocol sits orthogonally to ai-verification-stack-web:








































Existing stack layerWhat it verifiesWhat the bias protocol addsSpecsIntent is capturedWere the specs themselves written under bias (Pass 1)?Type contractsData shapes hold—Tests / mutation testsImplementation passes casesAre the generated tests narrative-coherent fakes (Pass 2)?Visual regressionUI doesn’t break—Fitness functionsArchitecture doesn’t drift—Human reviewJudgment at the boundaryStructured bias passes replace gut-feel review (Pass 2, 3, 4)
Existing layers check the artifact. The bias protocol checks the reasoning that produced the artifact — both yours (input) and the model’s (output). Neither substitutes for the other.
Templates
Bias-aware code review prompt
Use when reviewing an AI-generated PR:
You are reviewing AI-generated code. Before line-by-line review, perform a bias-fingerprint pass:

1. Are there hallucinated APIs, imports, or function signatures? List any you can't verify.
2. Do the tests exist to test behavior, or to pass CI? Identify tests with low mutation value.
3. Was the simplest, most mainstream solution chosen when a better-fitting niche solution exists?
4. Are there confident-looking claims in comments or commit messages that don't match what the code does?
5. What assumptions did the AI make that the spec did not supply? Which are wrong?

Report findings as a bulleted list. Do not proceed to normal review until the fingerprint pass is complete.

Bias-aware research synthesis prompt
Use when asking for a summary of evidence you’ll act on:
Before summarizing, run an input-side check:

1. Did my question embed an answer I'm expecting? Restate it neutrally.
2. Am I asking about a case where the mainstream answer tends to be wrong? Flag this.

Then produce the summary with:
- Load-bearing claims listed as bullets (no prose hiding)
- Base rates where relevant
- At least two counterarguments or failure modes per major claim
- Explicit list of assumptions and information you'd need to verify

End with the strongest argument against your own summary.

Disagreement-drill one-liner
You just gave position A. Now argue position not-A with equal rigor, as if that's what I'd asked. Note where the evidence genuinely supports both and where it only supports one.

Red-team one-liner
Here is a proposed [decision/plan/answer]: <paste>. A hostile but honest reviewer finds three specific ways this fails. What are they?

Anti-patterns

Protocol theater. Running all four passes on every interaction regardless of stakes. Burns budget and attention; erodes the discipline’s credibility when the overhead stops paying off.
Self-serving framing audits. Using Pass 1 to rewrite prompts toward a preferred conclusion rather than toward neutrality. If you know what answer you want before asking, no amount of framing hygiene will save you.
Trusting the red-team output. The red-team pass is itself an AI output and is subject to the same bias fingerprints. Skepticism doesn’t bottom out.
Treating passes as proof. Running the protocol produces better-calibrated reasoning; it does not produce correctness. The output still requires ordinary verification for facts, specs, and contracts.
Skipping Pass 1 because the output scan exists. Biased prompts produce biased outputs that the output scan is less likely to catch (because the output looks internally consistent with the biased question). The cheapest correction is upstream.

Why it stays valuable as models improve
The protocol stays valuable even as models get stronger — because stronger models produce more convincing biased outputs, not fewer. This protocol is part of the verification skill stack that compounds over time (see ai-verification-stack-web). The oracle problem is irreducible; someone has to decide what “correct” means, and bias-aware verification is part of how that judgment is exercised and trusted.
The protocol also addresses the specific failure mode in the personal CLAUDE.md rule (trust-but-verify subagent meta-claims): the incident behind that rule is a textbook Pass 2 miss — a confident, coherent, narrative-consistent subagent output that went un-entity-checked and got relayed.
Related
Slash commands that automate this protocol

/bias-scan-prompt — Pass 1 automation (prompt triage + neutral rewrite)
/bias-scan-ai — Pass 2 automation (output-fingerprint scan on AI-generated artifacts)
/disagree — Pass 3 automation (inversion drill on recent assistant response)
/red-team — Pass 4 automation (adversarial critique of an artifact)
/bias-scan-human — orthogonal (see above section); scans human-authored reasoning, not part of the four-pass AI protocol

Source notes

harari-information-vs-truth — upstream conceptual frame: information’s default function is connection, not representation, which is why the truth-axis has to be enforced externally on LLM outputs
prompt-bias-diagnostics — Pass 1 details
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — Pass 2 details
ai-automation-biases — the human biases this protocol counteracts
ai-verification-stack-web — the stack this sits orthogonally on top of
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — the code-specific review rubric, complementary to Pass 2
cognitive-biases — hub of biases in scope; covered by /bias-scan-human
debiasing-mental-models — Pass 3 (inversion) and Pass 4 (red teaming) originate here
hitl-progressive-autonomy — when to delegate vs. verify; this protocol is the verification side of that trust equation
multi-agent-governance — fleet-scale version of the red-team pass (Superego agents)

Sources

Klein, G. (2007) — “Performing a project premortem” — Harvard Business Review (Pass 4)
Munger, C. T. (1994) — “A lesson on elementary worldly wisdom” — USC Business School speech (Pass 3, inversion)
Sharma, M. et al. (2023) — “Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models” — Anthropic (why Pass 1 matters)
Kahneman, D. (2011) — Thinking, Fast and Slow — structural debiasing as the only reliable countermeasure

ai/bottleneck-states-as-split-points.title: Bottleneck States as Split-Point Heuristics
ai/bottleneck-states-as-split-points.content:
Bottleneck States as Split-Point Heuristics
The plan-split-scan answers whether a plan should be split. This note answers the next question: where should the split land? The structural answer from hierarchical reinforcement learning and human-planning research is consistent: at bottleneck states — points in the state space where many paths converge and through which all forward progress must pass.
Splitting at a bottleneck state truncates the planning tree at a natural seam. Splitting at a non-bottleneck pays the cost of splitting (re-establishing context) without buying its benefit (truncated dependencies). A non-bottleneck here: an arbitrary count of steps, a topical boundary that doesn’t match the state structure.
The graph-theoretic concept
In any state graph, the betweenness centrality of a node is the fraction of shortest paths between all node pairs that pass through it. High-betweenness nodes are bottlenecks — gateway states that most successful paths funnel through.
For planning, the load-bearing property of a bottleneck is dependency truncation: once the executor reaches a bottleneck state, the path from there to the goal can be planned without holding the path from start to bottleneck in working memory. Bottlenecks are where the executor can “forget the past and just go forward.”
Computing exact betweenness centrality requires solving all-pairs shortest paths — intractable for any non-trivial state space and certainly intractable for the human brain or an LLM planning ad hoc. Both biological and artificial planners use heuristics that approximate centrality without computing it directly.
Formal foundations — hierarchical RL
The structural result that bottleneck states are optimal split points was established in computational neuroscience and reinforcement learning:

Sutton, Precup & Singh (1999), “Between MDPs and semi-MDPs” introduced the options framework — temporally extended actions (“macro-actions”) for hierarchical RL. The framework needed a principled way to choose the temporal abstraction; bottleneck states became the canonical answer.
Solway, Diuk, Córdova, Yee, Barto, Niv & Botvinick (2014), “Optimal Behavioral Hierarchy” (PLOS Computational Biology) formalized this: an optimal behavioral hierarchy is one that minimizes the description length of the agent’s policy across task distributions, and the optimal subgoals turn out to be high-betweenness states. The result is structural — it holds independent of what task is being executed, given the state-space structure.
Correa et al. (2020, 2023) cited in the parent note extended this to human planning — humans behaviorally use bottleneck-state proxies when decomposing tasks in gridworld environments, with response-time signatures consistent with the centrality-truncation mechanism.

The human implementation is a memory-based proxy: track which states are frequently visited along successful past paths; treat those as candidate bottlenecks. This avoids the intractable all-pairs computation while capturing the empirical structure of centrality in environments the planner has experience with.
What this looks like in a plan
A plan-state isn’t a literal graph node, but the structural property maps cleanly: a bottleneck in a plan is the state, artifact, or decision that every downstream step depends on. After the bottleneck, the upstream context can be discarded; before it, all downstream work is conditional on its outcome.
Linguistic and structural fingerprints of plan-level bottlenecks:

“After we have X, we can…” — X is the bottleneck; everything downstream branches from it
“Before we can do Y, we need Z” — Z is the bottleneck for Y
An artifact or schema referenced by multiple downstream steps — building it is the bottleneck
A decision that determines the shape of the rest of the plan — making it is the bottleneck (e.g., “choose between SQL and document store” before the data-access layer can be designed)
A verification gate — confirming a result before proceeding (running a migration; receiving a code review; getting a destructive-action approval). Verification seams — the plan-split-scan’s name for these gates — are bottleneck states in graph-theoretic terms; see Signal 4 of the plan-split-scan

Anti-patterns — where splits don’t help
If the plan-split-scan says “split before issue” but the proposed split point is not at a bottleneck, the split pays cost without earning benefit. Common bad split locations:

Arbitrary length boundary — “Plan A: steps 1–5. Plan B: steps 6–10.” If step 6 is mid-flow through a single concern and depends on volatile state from step 4, the split forces re-establishing that state at the boundary. The cost is paid, no truncation is purchased.
Topical boundary that crosses state-carry — “Plan A: backend. Plan B: frontend.” If the frontend plan’s first step depends on a backend schema decision made mid-Plan-A and not yet finalized, the topical boundary cuts state-carry that hasn’t reached a stable point. Wait until the bottleneck (schema finalized) before splitting.
Splitting just before a destructive operation but downstream of the speculative state that produced it — the destructive step depends on the speculative output. If the split is at the destructive boundary but the speculative state is still mid-formation, the bottleneck is upstream of the split point, not at it. Move the split upstream to the point where the speculative state is confirmed.

The corrective: find the bottleneck first, then split there. If no bottleneck is visible within the proposed splitting region, the plan may need work before splitting — surfacing the implicit state structure so the bottleneck can be identified.
Detection heuristic (without running graph algorithms)
For a draft plan being audited:

List the artifacts and decisions the plan produces at each step (schemas, files, decisions, intermediate outputs, confirmations).
For each downstream step, ask which upstream artifact(s) it depends on. Steps that depend on the same upstream artifact are downstream of the same bottleneck.
The artifact with the most downstream dependents is the highest-betweenness state in the plan. That’s the natural split point.
Verification gates are bottlenecks by construction — if the plan has explicit verification steps, those are split candidates regardless of centrality calculation.

This heuristic mirrors the memory-based proxy humans use empirically: tracking which states are referenced by (i.e., “visited along the path to”) many subsequent states. You’re approximating betweenness via citation count rather than computing it.
Mapping to the plan-split-scan signals
The five signals of the plan-split-scan connect to the bottleneck mechanism:

Signal 1 (concern count) — concerns intersect at bottlenecks (the state that connects auth and database is a bottleneck across concerns). Split at the intersection.
Signal 2 (state-carry depth) — long state-carry means there’s a bottleneck the planner didn’t surface. The fix is to make the bottleneck explicit, then split there (or restate the bottleneck content at the point of use).
Signal 3 (decision branches) — the branching decision is a bottleneck. Either resolve it before the plan, split there, or use an implementation intention to bind the branch evaluation to a deterministic trigger.
Signal 4 (verification seams) — verification seams ARE bottleneck states. This signal is the most direct bottleneck-detection move.
Signal 5 (reversibility boundary) — destructive operations sit on the downstream side of a bottleneck (the speculative state that produced the inputs to the destructive operation). Split between the bottleneck (state confirmed) and the destructive step.

Tradeoffs and context-dependence

Bottleneck identification is itself search. For a plan you wrote, the bottlenecks may be obvious — you know what depends on what. For a plan you’re auditing without context, identifying the bottlenecks requires understanding the dependencies, which is non-trivial. The heuristic above is approximation, not algorithm.
Plans aren’t formally state graphs. The betweenness-centrality framing is structural analogy, not literal computation. The analogy is load-bearing where the plan has a state structure — most engineering plans, migration plans, multi-step research plans — and weakens where it doesn’t (creative work, brainstorming, exploratory analysis).
Memory-based proxy fails on first-of-kind plans. Humans use the proxy because they have history with environments they’re planning in. A genuinely novel plan (new system, new domain, no prior runs) has no memory to draw on; bottleneck identification falls back on first-principles dependency analysis. The first-principles analysis is more expensive but more reliable when memory is absent.
Some plans have no dominant bottleneck. A plan with five independent, non-interacting concerns has no high-betweenness state — every step is its own forward-flow. In this case the bottleneck-heuristic answer is “split by concern, not by state” — and Signal 1 (concern count) is the relevant move, not Signal 4.

What this doesn’t cover

Formal computation of betweenness on plan graphs. This note treats bottleneck identification as a heuristic move on a roughly-state-structured artifact. Tools that compute centrality on workflow DAGs (project-management software, task-graph analyzers) exist and could in principle be applied; not addressed here.
Multi-bottleneck plans. A long plan may have several bottlenecks at different scales. Which to split at is a design choice trading off the cost of splitting (more total plans) against the cognitive load of the un-split alternative.
Dynamic bottlenecks. In plans where the structure depends on intermediate results (the bottleneck emerges from a step’s output), bottleneck identification must happen during execution, not before. This is the case where implementation intentions or split-into-separate-plans is the right move — you can’t pre-identify a bottleneck whose existence depends on a not-yet-run step.

Counterargument
The strongest objection: plan structure is rarely tree-shaped or graph-shaped in the formal sense computational frameworks assume. Most engineering plans are loosely sequential with implicit dependencies, not formal DAGs. Importing betweenness-centrality vocabulary into informal plan auditing risks pseudo-quantitative framing — making the audit sound rigorous while doing the same heuristic work that pre-existing terms (“checkpoint,” “milestone,” “phase boundary”) covered.
The honest position: the bottleneck-state lens adds value at the placement layer of plan splitting, where the alternative is unprincipled boundary choice. It does not add value if the planner already knows where the checkpoints belong — in that case “split at checkpoint X” is the same answer the bottleneck heuristic would produce. The lens is useful when planners are unsure which of several candidate split points is the right one, and the dependency analysis disambiguates.
The framework is also potentially overfitted to state-graph-shaped problems. Plans whose structure is genuinely decision-tree-shaped (lots of branching, less linearity) may be better served by the implementation-intentions framing than by bottleneck identification.
Related

task-decomposition-for-ai-plans — parent note; Signal 4 (verification seams) is the most direct bottleneck-detection move
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — alternative move when bottlenecks are dynamic / decision-shaped rather than state-shaped
falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — operational claim shape; bottleneck states correspond to where falsifiability gates land
multi-agent-coordination-topologies — bottlenecks at the multi-agent layer (which agent depends on which other agent’s output) follow the same structural logic
agent-pipeline-feature-creation — concrete pipeline whose stage boundaries (spec → plan → code → test → review) are exactly bottleneck states

Sources
Verified 2026-05-12.
