Sutton, R. S., Precup, D. & Singh, S. (1999). “Between MDPs and semi-MDPs: A framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning.” Artificial Intelligence, 112(1–2), 181–211. The options framework — foundational reference for temporally extended actions in hierarchical RL.
Solway, A., Diuk, C., Córdova, N., Yee, D., Barto, A. G., Niv, Y. & Botvinick, M. M. (2014). “Optimal Behavioral Hierarchy.” PLOS Computational Biology, 10(8). The result that optimal hierarchical decompositions correspond to high-betweenness states; formalizes the bottleneck-as-subgoal intuition.
Correa, C. G. et al. (2020, 2023). Resource-rational task decomposition references; full citation in task-decomposition-for-ai-plans. Documents the memory-based betweenness proxy in human planning behavior.
Botvinick, M. M., Niv, Y. & Barto, A. C. (2009). “Hierarchically organized behavior and its neural foundations: A reinforcement learning perspective.” Cognition, 113(3). Earlier review establishing the bottleneck-state framing in human behavioral neuroscience.
Şimşek, Ö. & Barto, A. G. (2009). “Skill characterization based on betweenness.” NeurIPS. Algorithmic methods for discovering bottleneck states in RL — the engineering side of the same insight.

ai/canonical-evidence-vs-derived-index.title: Canonical Evidence vs Derived Index
ai/canonical-evidence-vs-derived-index.content:
Canonical Evidence vs Derived Index
As of 2026-08-28. The eval-framework citations were verified this session; the security, governance, and vendor claims are attributed to named sources but not independently re-checked — each is marked below.
The distinction
A retrieval system has two kinds of storage, and conflating them is the failure that shows up months later as an unanswerable audit question:

Canonical evidence — the source as captured, plus identity, version, timestamps, permissions, and a content hash. Append-only while retained.
Derived index — chunks, embeddings, lexical postings, extracted entities, graphs, summaries, caches, published copies. Every one of these is a reproducible projection over the canonical plane.

The rule is one sentence: a projection is never the system of record. When the vector index is the only place a document exists, the system has silently taken on obligations it cannot discharge.
This note covers only the governance axis — the part that is verification work. RAG engineering depth (chunk sizing, embedding-model choice, reranker selection) lives in fine-tuning-vs-rag and was deliberately skipped in topic-suggestions as commodity territory. That skip still holds; this is the orthogonal axis it doesn’t cover.
What only the canonical plane can do
Five functions a derived index structurally cannot perform. The grouping into five is this note’s synthesis, not a taxonomy any cited source publishes — treat the boundaries as a working frame. Each is a question to ask of any knowledge system before it carries something that matters.
Deletion that actually completes
Removing a document means removing it from the canonical store and every chunk, vector, lexical posting, summary, cache entry, export, and published mirror derived from it. Then verifying absence. Then keeping a restore-exclusion record until backups age out, so restoring a backup cannot make deleted material searchable again.
An index that holds embeddings of text whose source is gone has no way to know it should forget. Deletion is a canonical-plane operation that fans out; it is not an index operation.
Immutability and retention are separate concerns. Keep payloads in erasable storage, and let a minimal tombstone record that a version existed and was deleted without retaining its content.
Authorization before retrieval, not redaction after
Identity, tenant, and security labels have to reach every index and every query, and the system must fail closed when that metadata is missing or stale. Retrieving broadly and redacting afterward is not equivalent: unauthorized content that reaches the ranker has already influenced ranking, generation, logs, and caches.
Conflict and time
Two sources can disagree, and both can be worth keeping. Storing scope, publication time, valid time, and authority alongside each claim lets the system present the conflict, apply an explicit precedence rule, escalate, or abstain. Overwriting the loser destroys the signal that a conflict existed at all — the same argument knowledge-base-deduplication-costs makes for prose.
Distinguish the world changed from we were wrong earlier. Without that split, historical answers become unreconstructable. knowledge-claim-lifecycle holds the prior-art map for claim-state modeling.
Cache keys that carry authorization
Every derived cache needs its invalidation dimensions named, and the answer-level ones need the caller’s authorization context in the key:





























CacheMinimum invalidation dimensionsParsed documentsource hash + parser/OCR versionChunksnormalized-document hash + chunker configEmbeddingsexact retrieval text + embedding model/versionRetrieval / rerankquery + index generation + identity/policy + filters + retriever versionsGenerated answerevidence hashes + prompt/model versions + policy + answer contract
Never reuse a semantic, retrieval, or answer cache entry across callers whose accessible corpus differs. Prompt-prefix caching is a compute optimization and is not a source-of-truth cache.
Rollback by index generation
Build a complete index generation in shadow, evaluate it, then atomically promote a versioned manifest. This makes rollback possible and stops users querying a half-rebuilt corpus. In-place mutation of a live index has neither property.
The answer contract
Abstention has to be a status the system can return, not a failure it routes around. A structured contract makes the distinctions machine-checkable:
status: answered | not_found | conflicting_evidence | insufficient_authority
claims:
  - text: string
    evidence: [{source_id, version_id, span}]
limitations: [string]
Two things this buys. Citations resolve to a span in a specific version, not a document homepage — so a reader can check the claim rather than the existence of a source. And “the corpus has no answer” is separable from “sources conflict” and “you lack permission to see the evidence,” which are three different problems with three different fixes.
Citation presence is not citation correctness. Provenance proves origin, never truth — the same limit agent-audit-trails-provenance records for agent action logs.
Evaluating the pipeline in layers
A single composite score hides which component failed. Measure separately: corpus coverage and parse failures; retrieval recall and ACL violations; context quality (duplicate ratio, irrelevant-context ratio, conflict representation); answer correctness; claim support and citation correctness; abstention precision and recall; latency and cost. Then triage along the failure tree — corpus, then query and policy, then retrieval, then ranking and context, then generation, then citation, then abstention.
Four peer-reviewed frameworks decompose this, all verified 2026-08-28: RAGAS (reference-free retrieval/context/answer metrics), ARES (fine-tuned judges plus synthetic query generation), RAGChecker (fine-grained retrieval and generation diagnostics), and RAGTruth (a hand-annotated word-level hallucination corpus). Automated judges accelerate iteration but are measurements with bias, not ground truth — calibrate against blinded human ratings and pin grader versions, per the independence axis in llm-evaluation-methodology.
Two optimization traps: maximizing retrieval recall alone floods the model with distractors and can reduce answer quality; maximizing fluency or user ratings rewards confident unsupported answers.
Where this vault stands
This vault has no vector index. Retrieval is grep, glob, and a model reading files, so most of the plane-confusion risk does not apply — the canonical markdown is what gets read.
It has exactly one committed derived plane, and that plane had the predicted defect. snippets/ holds machine-extracted distillations of knowledge/ notes, each carrying a source: path and a generated: date. site/content/ is the other projection and is correctly git-ignored.
Measured 2026-08-28, and the measurement is itself the argument. The date signal flagged 52 of 74 snippets as stale, because their generated: date preceded their source note’s updated: date. That number was close to worthless: the 68-wave prose-surgery sweep bumped updated: on all 333 notes that existed at the time without changing substance, so a date comparison cannot separate a rewritten claim from a moved comma.
Replacing it with checks that verify correspondence rather than recency:






























CheckKindResultSource path resolvesdefinitive0 orphanedquote still a verbatim substringdefinitive0 broken of 7Body hash matches extractiondefinitivefield did not existgenerated: vs updated:heuristic52 flagged, upper bound
Zero definitive failures. The prose sweep preserved every quoted span, which its commit messages claimed and the substring check now confirms independently. Cross-referencing git history narrowed the real candidates from 52 snippets to 9 of 15 source notes carrying substantive commits since extraction.
The heuristic also errs the other way. Six further sources were never flagged, because their updated: field still predated their snippets — yet git showed all six had been committed to since. Checking the diffs cleared them: four gained only a publish tag, which is frontmatter and correctly does not bump updated:, and two gained a single cross-reference line whose authors did not bump it. No claim moved, so this produced no wrong snippet. It is still the failure mode the deletion and cache arguments above turn on. A signal derived from a field a human remembers to update is not a signal about content.
Regenerating those 9 found exactly one snippet that had genuinely gone wrong, and the date signal could never have identified which. A snippet of the design-system governance note presented centralized, federated, and hybrid as three comparable models with hybrid as the target. Its source note was rewritten in August 2026 to record that Nathan Curtis, who published that taxonomy in 2015, retracted it in 2024 — “Favoring federated was and is wrong” — and that across 80+ systems the share thriving without central staffing is “Zero. Zero. Zero percent.” The projection was still confidently serving the framing its source now names as the mistake.
One wrong snippet out of 74 is a small harm. The point is that the derived plane had no way to find it, and a display device was showing it.
The fix is the one the cache table above names. tools/snippet_drift.py now verifies quote substrings and a source_hash, and the extract-snippets skill records that hash — a digest of the note body, so bumping verified: or updated: does not invalidate a projection built from unchanged prose. All 91 snippets across 21 sources now carry one, so the date heuristic no longer fires anywhere and every entry rests on a definitive check. It is a reporter, not a gate, in the same shape as tools/staleness_due.py.
The general lesson outlasts the local fix: a derived plane that records when it was built can only ever guess. One that records what it was built from can answer.
Counterargument
Most of this is enterprise-scale machinery, and applying it to a solo vault would be cargo-culting. A personal knowledge base with one reader has no tenant boundary, no deletion SLA, and no adversary worth a shadow-index build.
There is also no evidence offered here that plane-separated systems outperform conflated ones. Nobody has run that comparison; the argument is structural, not measured.
That is right about the controls and wrong about the distinction. The plane separation costs nothing to hold as a design habit and is expensive to retrofit — the vault already earned it once, in the snippet layer, at 74 files — where a date-based signal produced 52 candidates, 51 of them noise, hid the one that mattered, and silently passed six sources it had no basis to clear. The controls should be added when a second reader or a real obligation appears, not before.
Related

Sources
Verified this session (2026-08-28):

RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation — Es, James, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert; EACL 2024 System Demonstrations (arXiv 2309.15217)

ai/clause-loop.title: Clause Loop
ai/clause-loop.content:
Clause Loop
A development method for one person and one AI agent — plus the fresh contexts that agent dispatches for reader checks and spot-checks — for any work whose output can be checked: code on a greenfield or a brownfield, a feature on a live system, a throwaway prototype, a specification, a document. You say what should be true next and what would prove it false; the agent builds the smallest thing that could settle it inside a declared envelope; you decide, from a short packet, what deserves to become a clause — a requirement pinned to a check that has been shown to fail for the right reason. The spec is a byproduct of building, not a prerequisite, and it grows one chosen clause at a time.
This note is the normative description of the method: where it and its two parent notes disagree, this note wins, and the parents link here rather than restate. The engine it runs is accretive-spec-development; the reasoning for why the requirement gates some builds and the check gates others, and how the loop and spec-driven development run as one system, is spec-driven-development-operating-model. Read those for the argument; read this to do the work.
The idea
The problem it answers. Working with a coding agent, there are two familiar ways to keep the work honest and both cost something. Spec-first methods (Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenSpec and their kin) derive the code from requirements, design and tasks agreed first, a document per phase. That buys agreement before building, at the price of committing to a reading of the problem before anything has run. Their specs do evolve — OpenSpec’s accumulate change by change — so what separates this method from them is the direction of derivation and the grain, not whether the spec grows. Building with no spec at all is fast, but nothing stops the agent from quietly solving a slightly different problem than the one you asked for — and the tests it writes to check its own work only ever encode its own reading of your intent.
The bet. Sit between the two. State an intent plus a falsifier, build the smallest probe that could falsify it, confront the running result, harvest clauses from what held. Exploration stays fast because you react to a running artifact, not a document; the spec you end with can be trusted because every clause in it is pinned to a check that has failed on demand for a named reason. Once a domain of the spec has been exercised and its clauses all chosen, freeze it — and a frozen domain is a contract other agents and services build against, which is where spec-first practice takes over. The loop is the on-ramp to a contract, not a replacement for one. Its distinctive value is turning explored behaviour into an explicitly chosen, evidence-linked contract — not the number of documents or gates it accumulates.
The pieces that make it hold. Each is a rule below; here is why it exists.

A clause is a SHALL sentence, a WHEN/THEN scenario, and a pin. The pin carries a stable id, the check, and the evidence — the mutant the check was watched failing against, with the assertion that caught it named. A check that cannot fail is not a check; a check that fails for an unrelated reason proves nothing; and a requirement with no check drifts from the code the day after it is written. Nothing enters the spec without all three.
Independence comes from the human, at decision boundaries. The agent writes the probe, the check and the proposed clause, so left alone every check would encode the agent’s interpretation of the intent. The human owns the falsifier — writes it, or substantively revises the agent’s candidate counterexamples — at every user-visible outcome and every consequential decision; mechanical tasks inherit it. The human decides which harvested clauses are wanted, and chooses and reads the spot-check of the evidence while a trusted runner executes it. Ownership of intent is not the same as typing every line, and the method asks for the first.
Observed is not wanted. Harvest records what the artifact does; promotion records what you want. The two are separate acts so that accidental behaviour — especially on brownfield code, where the first harvest captures everything that happens to be true — never becomes contract by default. Turning a clause down is three decisions, not one: whether it is contract, whether the behaviour stays in the artifact, and whether its check stays as characterization coverage.
Wanted is not verified. Acceptance is a human decision and changes rarely; verification is what the last run says and changes every run. A wanted clause whose check fails is still wanted — it is wanted and failing, and the failure is a stop, not a change of mind. Keeping the two axes apart is what lets a stale reader check, a flaky dispatch, or a known implementation debt be named without rewriting what was agreed.
Permission and impact gate the build, not file layout. Every probe declares an execution envelope. Hard gates — production writes, destructive operations, credentials, externally visible actions, anything on the irreversibility list, edits to a frozen verification surface — stop for permission whatever the path. Planning heuristics — uncertainty, rework, growth, cross-domain coordination, a contract change — send work to a proposal before the expensive probe. Both stay active inside an approved proposal, and what the agent actually changed is compared to what it declared.
Freeze is a mechanism, not a label. A domain whose clauses are all wanted and all currently verified gets a manifest naming its verification surface, and a guard fails the build on an unapproved change to that surface or on a required check that did not run. This is the guarantee, stated at its honest size: the guard rejects missing or failing required checks and unapproved changes to the declared verification surface. It does not prove that the checks express the requirement, or your intent. Drift between the spec and your intent is bounded by the human-owned falsifier, the locked checks and the evidence rule with its spot-check; it is not prevented.
Consolidate, or the spec becomes a test index. Harvest order is a changelog. Every ten or so archives the domain spec is rewritten by concept, scanned for clauses that contradict each other at intent level while both pass, and its expired re-check dates and exceptions listed.

Why one method for code and prose. A clause is the same object whether the artifact is a service or a quickstart; only the oracle changes — what runs the check and what counts as evidence it can fail. For code that is a test. For a document it is a reader check: a fresh context, given the artifact and nothing else, must complete a task from it, and the mutant is deleting everything that carries the clause’s content and watching the reader fail. The generalisation strains at the grammar — SHALL is borrowed from requirements engineering and sits stiffly on prose. What carries over is the scenario and the pin, so if the SHALL sentence reads as ceremony for a document, keep the scenario and drop the keyword.
Where it comes from. The change-folder skeleton follows the shape of OpenSpec-style tools; the requirement-to-check link follows the shape Kiro-style tools build, run in the opposite direction. The reader and consistency oracles, the mutant-by-deletion rule for documents, the spec rule and the profile table generalise the accretive note’s architecture mapping (spike, fitness function, scenario walk) to non-code work; they are this vault’s own design, precedent check deferred. The 2026-09-05 revision — the envelope and hard gates, the acceptance-versus-verification split, the three-decision rejection, the evidence record, the four-action surface and the contract guard’s approval boundary — came from an external design review of the previous version, applied in one pass and then corrected against three fresh-context reviews of the result.
It has not been run end to end. The first rule of the method is that the human owns the falsifier, so here is this note’s own: the method is wrong if, in the first month of real use, hard gates or heuristics fire on most probes so nothing is ever harvested; if a task you later judge consequential ran on an inherited falsifier because the agent did not flag it; if DECISIONS.log goes unwritten after a few sessions; or if the pilot in What to test next finds, by its independent read, an intent substitution that the loop’s own packet did not surface. The two worked examples below are constructed illustrations — the paths, dates and log lines in them are invented to show the shape, not records of anything that happened.
Vocabulary
Six words carry a loop. About twenty more carry setup, most of them at Ground, once; they arrive as you meet them.

































Day oneMeaningintentOne sentence of what should be true next.falsifierOne line, owned by the human: the observation that would prove the intent false. Written by you, or an agent candidate you substantively revised; the origin is recorded.envelopeWhat a probe may touch: allowed writes, allowed external actions, data and environment, contracts potentially affected, budget in minutes and loops, rollback or disposal.probeThe smallest build that could falsify the intent, plus its check, ending with a not-exercised list of what it does not cover.clauseA SHALL sentence plus a WHEN/THEN scenario plus a filled Pin: line with a stable id.packetThe short record the agent hands you at Decide: what was asked, what ran, what is untested, what is proposed, the evidence and relevant failures, actual-versus-declared, the log lines written since the last packet, and the decision needed.





































































































LaterMeaningartifactWhatever the work produces: the codebase, a prototype, specs/<domain>/spec.md itself, a document. Named in Ground.domainThe unit a spec file and a manifest cover; one folder under specs/. Both parent notes call the same thing a region.GroundGROUND.md: profile, context, constraints, preferences, irreversibility list, domain table, how checks run, envelope defaults, the approval boundary, the contract guard’s behaviour. A screen or less.profileOne line in Ground naming the kind of work, which sets the usual oracles and what the rules relax.hard gate / heuristicA hard gate stops for permission before an action whatever the path; a heuristic sends work to a proposal. Both read the envelope.changeA folder under changes/ holding one intent’s proposal, loop log, decisions and delta spec; archived when done.loopOne probe-confront pass inside a change, logged with predicted and observed outcome, evidence, actual-versus-declared writes, and minutes.pinThe line under a scenario carrying the clause’s id, acceptance, oracle, check id, birth change, and evidence. The one canonical record for now; the manifest is written from it.oracleWhat runs a check: test, property, guard, consistency, reader, walk, manual.evidence / mutantFor a re-runnable check: the four-step record — baseline passes, mutant applied to a scratch copy, the named assertion fails, restore passes. mutant= names the sabotage; the loop log names the assertion.reader checkA file naming a question (locate or complete), a task, a closed list of what a fresh context is given, what is withheld, whether it may execute, a repeat policy, a pass criterion, the mutant, and a Runs table.walk checkA dated hand procedure through the artifact; no mutant, so the pin carries the date of the last walk.acceptanceThe human axis: observed (harvested, provisional), wanted (chosen, check locked), retired (withdrawn, evidence kept in the archive).verificationThe run axis, read from the latest recorded run rather than kept as a pin field: passing, failing, stale, unknown.exceptionA logged, expiring excuse for a wanted clause that is failing or unverifiable while its domain is harvesting: owner, scope, expiry. None may be open at freeze and none exist under contract. Replaces the old debt state.deltaA change’s specs/<domain>/spec.md: ADDED, MODIFIED and RETIRED requirements, merged into the domain spec at Close.guarded invariantTier two: a requirement with no cheap check, carried with an owner and a re-check date instead of a drift guarantee.verification surfaceThe files whose change could weaken a domain’s checks: the check files, the fixtures and helpers they use, runner and discovery config, the CI job, the spec file, the manifest, GROUND.md, and for a reader or walk id the artifact section the check covers.freeze / manifest / under contractFreeze writes a manifest from a domain’s pins — clause ids, check ids, the surface, the export, the approval — and the domain is then under contract, guarded.contract guardTwo halves. The surface guard fails a diff that touches the surface without a permit line, while the boundary itself refuses the merge without your review. The execution guard fails a run in which a manifest-listed check did not execute and pass.approval boundaryNamed in Ground: where a human decision is recorded in a way the agent cannot impersonate — on GitHub a protected-branch review on the exact commit or an environment approval, elsewhere your forge’s equivalent, or a chat decision a separate controller records, which is a design slot, not built here. It holds only if the agent commits under its own identity, not yours, and admins cannot bypass the protection.DECISIONS.logAppend-only, one line per decision or close: reject · retire · permit · freeze · unfreeze · exception · amend · archive · consolidate. Written by the agent from your packet reply, which it quotes verbatim in the proposal; you do not edit it, and the next packet echoes what it wrote.consolidateThe periodic rewrite of a domain spec by concept, with a conflict scan, re-pointed pins, and the list of expired dates and exceptions.
The four actions
Four things you do, in a loop: Start, Probe, Decide, Close. Everything else — grounding, proposals, freezing, consolidating — is machinery the agent runs when one of the four asks for it, listed under Operations in the reference. The action names are steps you write in a prompt, not installed skills.

Start. You give one sentence of intent. The agent copies changes/_template/ to changes/<name>/, copies its specs/_domain/ once per domain the intent touches, renamed, writes the intent into proposal.md, proposes two or three candidate counterexamples marked as its own, and drafts the envelope. You write the falsifier — from scratch or by substantively revising a candidate — and confirm or tighten the envelope. Probe refuses to run while the falsifier’s origin is missing or reads agent, unrevised.
Probe. The agent checks the envelope against the hard gates and the heuristics. A hard gate stops for your permission on that specific action; a heuristic hands the change to a proposal. Otherwise it builds the smallest thing that could falsify the intent, together with the check, runs it against a prediction of pass and fail drafted from your falsifier, records what it actually wrote and did against what the envelope declared, and ends with the not-exercised list. For each check it earns the evidence: baseline passes, mutant on a scratch copy, the named assertion goes red, restore passes. A crash or compile error is logged as an attempt, not as evidence. It logs the loop with minutes.
Decide. The agent hands you a packet: what you asked for, what ran and what happened, what remains untested, the clauses it proposes with their evidence and any relevant failures, the actual-versus-declared envelope, the log lines written since the last packet, and the decisions it needs. You answer in chat. Per clause: contract — wanted or not; if not, whether the behaviour stays in the artifact and whether the check stays as characterization. On a brownfield first harvest you may answer once for the batch — not contract, behaviour kept, checks kept as characterization — and name only the exceptions; the default is yours because you said it. Plus: loop again on a gap the not-exercised list named, escalate, or permit a gated action. The agent writes the pins and the log lines from your answer, quoting the answer verbatim in the proposal’s Decisions section, and you spot-check one piece of evidence per change by choosing which and reading a trusted runner’s re-application of it. Cap about five loops per intent; the cap is a signal the intent should be split or escalated, not extended.
Close. The agent runs every check, reports verification per clause, lists any clause you never ruled on and refuses to close until you have — silence is not a decision — gates on every scenario or invariant outside RETIRED carrying a wanted pin with evidence, compares the change’s total writes and actions to the envelope, reads the intent against the promoted clauses for anything quietly substituted, merges the delta into specs/<domain>/spec.md, writes the archive line, and moves the folder to changes/archive/<date>-<name>/. If the domain was under contract, the manifest is rewritten and the surface change goes through the approval boundary.

When a heuristic fires at Probe, the requirement gates instead: the agent writes a proposal and design, they are red-teamed, you agree the delta spec before the build, and each task then runs Probe and Decide inside the change folder. Tasks inherit the change’s falsifier unless a task introduces a new assumption, trade-off or externally visible behaviour, in which case it gets its own decision; the agent flags which tasks it thinks qualify, and the flag is its judgement, which you can overrule either way. Hard gates and the envelope stay live inside the proposal; exceeding the envelope pauses for an amendment, not a second proposal. Worked example A shows both paths on the same codebase; example B shows a document.
Getting started

Copy the kit. cp -r templates/clause-loop <repo>/clauses — the kit lives at templates/clause-loop/ in this vault and carries its own README with the target tree. Everything the method’s own bookkeeping writes lives under that one root; the artifact and its checks stay wherever the project keeps them.
Ground the project. Fill GROUND.md: the profile (one of greenfield-code, brownfield-code, feature, prototype, specification, documentation) and, for the last three, the artifact — a folder or a single file; two or three sentences of context; constraints, each with a check id, a manual procedure, or an exception reference, which ground writes into their domain specs once step 3 has created them; preferences; the irreversibility list; the domain table; the Checks section — how to run all checks, how to run one, how the runner reports which check ids executed, the command that dispatches a reader check, how a walk is performed, the id form per oracle, and the evidence rule; the Envelope defaults — which environments a probe may touch without permission; and the Approval boundary — where your decisions on gated actions and surface changes are recorded so the agent cannot write them itself. Keep it to a screen: past that you are sneaking upfront design back in.
Create the domains. Copy specs/_domain/spec.md once per domain Ground names, stripping the placeholder requirement and invariant and setting Status: open — then let ground write each constraint into its domain as a wanted clause with born=ground, which moves that domain to harvesting — and leave manifest where it is — it is the template freeze fills, not a file an open domain owns. A file that belongs to no domain leaves the cross-domain heuristic unreadable, and Probe refuses an envelope it cannot read; if two people would draw the boundary differently, settle it in Ground before the first intent.
Wire the contract guard. The kit ships no guard script; you write one for your CI from the behaviour Ground describes, and until it exists rule 6 is a convention like the others. Both halves run in CI on the protected branch. The surface guard reads each frozen domain’s manifest as it stands on the protected branch, so removing an entry is itself a surface change, and fails when a listed surface file changes in a diff that adds no permit line naming it; the boundary — on GitHub, branch protection with required code-owner review on the surface paths — is what refuses the merge without your review. The execution guard compares the manifest’s check ids to the ids the runner reports as executed and passed, and fails on any that are missing, skipped or failing. Define the guard where the candidate diff cannot reach it — a workflow the forge requires from outside the repository, where that exists — because a job defined in the candidate tree can be skipped, and on GitHub a skipped required job reports success (checked 2026-09-05 against GitHub’s documentation). If it must live in the repository, its workflow file is the one surface file the guard cannot protect from a skip, and your review of any change to it is the only enforcer. A pre-push hook is advisory: the agent can edit or skip it. Describe the behaviour in Ground rather than the hook’s path. Outside a version-controlled repo — a standard drafted in a shared drive, a report — there is no diff, so the guard has no enforcer and the consistency oracle usually has no runner; what survives is the pin, the reader check and the log. Say so in Ground rather than pretending the guard exists.
Pick the first intent by profile. On brownfield code it is harvest what is already true — everything lands observed, so nothing accidental becomes contract. On greenfield it is the skeleton runs end to end. On a prototype it is the riskiest assumption, written as a falsifier. On a documentation or specification project the document, not the code, is what the clauses are about; the first intent is a fresh reader can do X from this alone. The profile table in the reference names the usual oracles for each.
Run changes. Copy changes/_template/ per change and follow the four actions. Once Probe reports no heuristic fired, delete design.md, tasks.md and the proposal’s proposal-path sections — they are requirement-first files, and an empty one archived beside a check-gated change is noise.
Run until a domain qualifies for freeze. On code, the bet is that the first freeze is when the method starts paying: before it, this is bookkeeping; after it, the contract guard holds. On a prototype, which never freezes, or a document, which rarely does, the payoff is the pin itself: a claim about the artifact that a fresh reader has been shown to fail without. Walk and manual clauses get a scheduled re-check instead, an unmanifested reader clause is re-dispatched whenever the section it covers changes, and a mutant shows a check is not vacuous, not that it is adequate.

Turn the operations that earn it into skills after a real run, not before. If the method is too heavy, keep the pin, the evidence rule and the manifest and relax everything else first; the bet is that the likeliest failure is not a bookkeeping error but dropping the method.
Reference
The seven rules
Each rule names what it prevents and where it is checked. Only rule 6 is machine-enforced. The rest are conventions the agent follows because the prompt says so — “Probe refuses” means the agent is instructed to refuse, and nothing detects an agent that does not — which is why the loop log, the packet and the actual-versus-declared comparison are mandatory: they are where a human can see that a step was taken.

The human owns the falsifier at every decision boundary. One line in proposal.md, before the agent builds, with its origin recorded: human, or agent, revised when you substantively changed a candidate the agent proposed. An unrevised candidate does not count, and Probe refuses while the origin is missing or unrevised. The boundaries are the change’s intent — a user-visible outcome — and any task inside a proposal that introduces a new assumption, trade-off or externally visible behaviour; every other task inherits the change’s falsifier and says so. The agent flags which tasks it thinks cross that line; the flag is its judgement, and you may overrule it either way. The agent proposes candidate counterexamples first so you are checking for omissions rather than composing from nothing; a narrow falsifier leaves the same interpretation gap an agent’s would, so the candidates are there to widen yours. Prevents the agent authoring both the intent and the test of it. Checked at Probe.
A clause is a SHALL plus a scenario plus a pin with evidence. The Pin: line carries a stable id=, and its evidence field must be filled: mutant= for every oracle that re-runs without a person walking it (test, property, guard, consistency, reader), last= for a walk, owner= and next= for a manual check. mutant= names something that happened — the four-step record in Evidence below, with the assertion that caught it named in the loop log. Anything less is a note, not a clause. A clause you already mean to reject earns none of this; only a clause you promote needs a pin. The agent earns the evidence and reports it, so you are trusting its report on the one piece of evidence every pin rests on: spot-check one per change by choosing which mutant and reading a trusted runner’s re-application, or mutant= decays into a slug. Checked at Decide.
Acceptance is yours; verification is the run’s. Clauses arrive observed, with mutant=pending until you promote them; only you flip one to wanted, and only you retire one. A wanted clause’s check is locked — the agent may change the artifact but not that check — and the lock is a rule the agent follows until freeze makes it machine-enforced. Turning a harvested clause down deletes its block from the delta — the reject line is its record — and is three decisions, recorded on that line: it is not contract; whether the behaviour stays in the artifact or is removed; whether its check stays as characterization coverage or is deleted. “Not promised” does not mean “not worth testing”: a brownfield characterization test may protect callers who depend on the accident, guard a regression while a migration is planned, or cover behaviour a wanted clause shares. Delete a check only when its purpose is obsolete. A kept characterization check is written in the loop that observed the behaviour, so the reject line can name it, and carries a comment with the clause id and the reject date. A reject whose ref is a change name records a deliberate omission from the artifact, not a clause, and carries no decisions. Close refuses while any clause is still observed, so accidental behaviour never becomes contract by default and never leaves by default either: you rule on it, in the packet. Verification — passing, failing, stale, unknown — is not a pin field; it is read off the latest recorded run, and a wanted clause that is failing is a stop until the artifact is fixed, the clause is revised by a new decision, or — while the domain is harvesting — an exception with owner, scope and expiry is logged. Prevents brownfield habits and agent guesses being promoted silently, and prevents a failing check being read as a change of mind. Checked at Decide and Close; the prototype profile is the one exception on promotion.
The envelope gates the build: hard gates stop, heuristics escalate, and actual is compared to declared. Every probe declares an envelope before building. Hard gates read it against Ground and stop for your permission on that specific action, on either path, recorded as a permit line with an approval reference: a write to production or any shared environment; a destructive operation — delete, drop, migrate, overwrite; a credential or secret; an externally visible action — send, publish, pay, deploy; any item on the irreversibility list; any edit to a frozen domain’s verification surface. Heuristics are judged, not computed, and send the change to a proposal: uncertainty the agent names about the approach; rework — two reject lines naming a clause of this domain across the last three changes that touched it, or a wanted clause currently failing; growth — the envelope’s minute budget exceeds the summed minutes of the project’s last three building loops, read from the loop logs of open and archived changes, where a building loop is one that changed the artifact, and it cannot fire until three exist; cross-domain coordination — the intent spans two or more domains and at least one is under contract; contract change — the intent would modify or retire a wanted clause in a domain under contract, which is where spec-first practice takes over. Inside an approved proposal the heuristics are not re-evaluated, but the hard gates and the envelope stay live: exceeding the envelope pauses for an amend decision, not a second proposal. At every loop and at Close the agent lists what it actually wrote and did against what it declared, because a rule that reads only what the agent says it will do cannot see undeclared work. Prevents an irreversible action riding on a small diff, and an unrelated test added to a frozen file being treated as a design question. Checked at Probe and Close.
One spec file per domain; every change is a delta. specs/<domain>/spec.md is the only spec; a change writes changes/<name>/specs/<domain>/spec.md and the merge at Close carries pins verbatim: ADDED blocks are appended under the domain’s Requirements — or, for an ### Invariant: block, under its Guarded invariants — MODIFIED replaces the block of the same name, RETIRED removes it from the domain spec and keeps the block with its last pin in the archived delta, and the delta’s own headings do not survive. The pin is the canonical record: the manifest, the packet’s clause list and the consolidate report are written from the pins, never maintained as a second copy. Ground constraints, written by ground with born=ground, are the one entry that arrives without a delta. Prevents a second set of books. Checked at Close.
A frozen domain has a manifest and a contract guard. Freeze writes the manifest from the domain’s pins — clause id, check id, the verification surface, the contract-test export, the approval reference — and the guard’s two halves enforce it: the surface guard fails a change to any listed surface file that carries no permit line, reading the manifest from the protected branch; the execution guard fails a run in which any listed check id did not execute and pass. Authorization is the boundary Ground names — a review the agent cannot give itself, bound to the exact commit; the permit line is the record, and its approval= is a pointer for the reader, not a credential the guard verifies. A check changed under a permit re-earns its evidence before Close and its clause appears as MODIFIED in the delta. Reader and walk ids count, so freezing a document is expensive in a way freezing code is not: every edit to a section a reader check covers is a surface change. Freeze a document only once it is genuinely a published contract. Prevents check-tampering after the fact, including the indirect kinds — a fixture, a helper, discovery, a runner-level skip, the manifest, the requirement’s wording. Enforced by the guard you wire in Ground.
Every departure is a line in DECISIONS.log, written by the agent from your reply. Kinds: reject · retire · permit · freeze · unfreeze · exception · amend · archive · consolidate. You decide in chat on a packet; the agent records, quoting your reply verbatim in the proposal’s Decisions section. The log trusts that transcription — nothing else in the repository holds your words — so every packet echoes the lines written since the last one, and a mismatch is yours to catch there. Every ~10 archives, and at every freeze, consolidate rewrites the domain spec by concept rather than birth order, runs a clause-versus-clause conflict scan, re-points any check= the rewrite breaks — never an id= — and lists overdue next= and last= dates and expired exceptions. Without it the spec converges on a check index with prose labels.

Evidence
A pin’s mutant= is the one thing every clause rests on, so what counts is defined narrowly.
The record. For every re-runnable check, four steps on a scratch copy, logged in the loop entry:

Baseline. The unmodified artifact passes the check.
Mutant. A sabotage that introduces the specific behavioural violation the scenario forbids — the guard removed, the store moved before the validation, the sentence and the example line deleted.
Named failure. The check fails at the assertion that carries the scenario’s THEN, and the log names it. A THEN with two parts — “the request fails and nothing is stored” — needs an assertion for each, and a mutant that trips only the first leaves the second unproven; either add a second mutant or record the second part as unproven.
Restore. The scratch copy is discarded and the check passes again.

What does not count. A compile error, a missing dependency, a runner crash, a timeout, or a failure in a different check are logged as attempts with their class, never as evidence. A red result is not a mutant kill unless step 3 names the assertion.
A failing baseline. When the check fails before any mutant, that is the falsifier firing — not evidence and not an attempt. Log it as the loop’s observed outcome and start the record once the artifact passes.
The contrast twin. A scenario that forbids something — rejects, refuses, never — carries a companion scenario under the same requirement showing the accepted case, or “reject everything” satisfies the check. The twin has its own pin and its own mutant; one twin per requirement covers every forbidding scenario under it.
Strength by consequence. One targeted mutant per scenario is the baseline and is cheap. Where a clause sits on the irreversibility list or in a domain under contract, add what the consequence warrants: a mutation score over the check (mutation-testing-ai-generated-code), a property oracle, or a hidden test the agent has not seen. A mutant shows a check is not vacuous, not that it is adequate.
Spot-check. Once per change you choose one clause and a trusted runner — a CI job, a script, a second agent with no stake in the result — re-applies its mutant while you read the outcome. Independent selection and interpretation is what the spot-check buys; operating the terminal yourself is not required.
Oracles
Seven types. What separates them is re-run cost and what counts as evidence the check can fail.
