A reader check is a file naming a question, a task, a closed list of what the reader is given, what is withheld, whether the reader may run anything, a repeat policy, a pass criterion, the mutant, and a Runs table. Running it means dispatching a fresh context — an agent, or a person who has not seen the work — with the check file as the task and exactly the files it names, nothing else; every dispatch goes in the check’s Runs table. Six decisions determine whether the check can fail at all and what a pass means, so the file states them:

Which question. locate: can a reader find and interpret the required information from the artifact, with everything that answers the task another way withheld? complete: can a reader finish the real task under realistic conditions, with whatever a real reader would have? Withholding the source makes the locate mutant bite and distorts complete; the two are both legitimate and never share one pass label. A clause about the document pins to locate; a complete run is recorded beside it as a realism check.
What is withheld. A locate check on a document about a system has to withhold the system — including what the reader could reach but must not open, such as a source tree it has just cloned. Give the reader the quickstart and the source and the mutant proves nothing: with the line deleted, the reader reads the source and passes anyway.
Whether the reader may execute. A text-only reader and a reader with a machine can return opposite verdicts on the same document — the first sees a coherent narrative, the second hits the error. Name which this check is.
That the reader states blocking questions instead of guessing. A dispatched agent has nobody to ask, so left alone it invents a plausible value and reports success, and the oracle degrades into whether it bluffed convincingly.
Whose context it is. A fresh context from the same model family that drafted the artifact shares training data and fails in correlated ways (oracle-problem-verification); dispatch cross-family where the clause matters, as diversity, not as a guarantee of independence.
The repeat policy. The check is stochastic in a way test is not. Fix the count before dispatching — three is the kit’s default — and the rule: unanimous is the result; a majority with one dissent is the result marked mixed; anything less is uncertain, which cannot promote a clause. Every dispatch is recorded, so “re-dispatch a disagreement” cannot become “run until it passes”.

The mutant removes everything that carries the clause’s content, not only the one sentence, and is applied to a scratch copy rather than the artifact. In the Runs table mutant-fail means the reader failed under the mutant — the check proving it can fail. Re-run whenever the section the check covers changes, not on every edit: at the default policy a pin costs nine dispatches — baseline, mutant and restore, three each — and each re-check costs three more. A reader completing a task does not establish that the document’s claims are true; a factual document keeps a separate consistency check against its sources for that.
A walk check is a dated procedure: a stimulus, the response the artifact promises, a measure, and the steps you take through the artifact to see whether it holds. It has no mutant because it cannot be re-run for free; the pin carries the date of the last walk instead, and consolidate lists walks that have gone stale.
States
A clause has two axes. Acceptance is the human’s and lives in the pin: observed (harvested, provisional, dropped at Close unless promoted), wanted (chosen by you, check locked, eligible to freeze), retired (withdrawn by you with a retire line; the block and its last pin stay readable in the archived delta). Verification is the run’s and is not a pin field: passing (the latest recorded run passed and nothing the clause covers has changed since), failing (the latest run failed), stale (what the clause covers changed after the latest run — on free oracles a run clears it, on readers and walks a re-dispatch or re-walk does), unknown (no run recorded in this environment). For free oracles the run record is the runner’s output; for readers and walks it is the check file’s Runs table, written by whoever dispatched or walked — usually the agent — and trusted the way the log is, through the packet’s echo. Close reports verification per clause; under contract, failing fails the build.
An exception is the third thing, logged separately and only while the domain is harvesting: a wanted clause that is failing or cannot currently be verified, excused by you with an owner, a scope and an expiry, so the clause stays wanted and the gap stays visible. A Ground constraint is the one clause that does not arrive through a delta: the ground operation writes it into its domain’s spec as a wanted clause with born=ground — evidence earned then if it has a check, a guarded invariant if it has none — and that domain is harvesting from that moment; one the artifact violates carries an open exception from day one. Consolidate lists expired exceptions, and an expired one counts as failing. Freeze requires none open, and under contract there are none: a failing check fails the build until the artifact is fixed or the clause is changed through a proposal, so the agent has no excuse path it can write for itself.
A domain is open (no clauses), harvesting (clauses exist; checks may well run in CI, but no manifest guards them), or under contract (frozen: every clause wanted and verified, a manifest written from the pins, a contract test exported to consumers). The state is the Status: line at the top of specs/<domain>/spec.md: open when the file is copied from the template; a Ground constraint written into it, or the first Close that touches it whether or not that Close promoted anything, moves it to harvesting; freeze and unfreeze move the last edge. Harvesting is a legitimate resting place — a domain with every clause wanted and no consumers to contract with stays there, and most documentation domains never leave it. A domain keeps its state while a proposal runs against it: a frozen domain stays frozen, its surface edits take permits, and it is re-frozen at Close. The full transition table is in spec-driven-development-operating-model.
Retiring is not the same as failing. A failing clause’s check fails; a retired requirement’s check still passes, so retirement is deliberate — a retire line carrying the decisions on behaviour and check, at Close — or a dead clause survives as a green test.
The contract guard
What “under contract” means mechanically, and what it does not.
The surface. Freeze declares, per domain, the files whose change could weaken its checks: the check files; the fixtures, helpers and assertion utilities they import; runner configuration and test discovery; the CI job that runs the execution guard; specs/<domain>/spec.md; the manifest itself; GROUND.md, whose irreversibility list, envelope defaults and approval boundary the hard gates read; and, for a reader or walk id, the artifact section the check covers. Before the first freeze, an amend to those three Ground sections is a packet decision you make, echoed back like any other. The manifest lists the surface explicitly, so the guard is a path check on a diff, not a heuristic.
The approval boundary. A change to the surface needs an approval the implementing agent cannot produce, bound to the exact candidate commit. Ground names which. On GitHub: a protected-branch review by you on that commit, with code owners on the surface paths and stale reviews dismissed on new pushes, or an environment approval; other forges have equivalents. A chat decision you post that a separate controller records with the commit is the headless shape — a design slot, not built here. Two preconditions make any of these hold, and the guarantee is void without them: the agent commits under its own identity, not yours, since an author cannot approve its own pull request and you could not approve one pushed under your account; and administrators cannot bypass the protection, which on GitHub is off by default and must be switched on (both checked 2026-09-05 against GitHub’s documentation). A permit for a gated action rather than a diff — a migration, a send — binds to the reviewed commit that adds the script or the decision reference the boundary provides. You never edit the log or the manifest. The permit line’s approval= field carries the reference; the line is the record, the boundary is the authorization, and the guard does not verify the string.
The execution guard. The CI job on the protected branch reads each frozen manifest as it stands on the base, not in the candidate, and compares the listed check ids to the ids the runner reports as executed and passed. Missing, skipped, or failing fails the build. It is a required status check, defined where the candidate diff cannot reach it wherever the forge allows, because a skipped required job reports success on GitHub. This is what catches a test skipped through the runner’s configuration, a discovery change, a deleted test, and a manifest entry removed in the same diff.
The export. Freeze also writes a contract test for consumers — the domain’s wanted scenarios and the ids of their checks, in whatever form the project’s consumers can run: a test file they import, a schema, a fixture set — and names it in the manifest as export:, or none where consumers have nothing to run, as on most documentation freezes. It is what makes “other agents build against it” a mechanism rather than a sentence: a downstream service runs it on its side and learns of a contract change from a failure, not a message.
What it covers. Unapproved changes to the declared surface, and required checks that did not run or did not pass.
What it does not cover. Whether the checks express the requirement, whether the requirement expresses your intent, a mutant that was weak, a surface file you forgot to declare, its own workflow file if that lives in the repository, an agent committing under your identity, or anything outside a version-controlled repo. Those are bounded by the human-owned falsifier, the locked checks and the evidence rule with its spot-check, and only bounded.
Files and the pin line
The method’s own files live under one root, so adopting it is one copy; the artifact and its checks stay where the project keeps them.
clauses/
├── GROUND.md                       # profile, context, constraints, preferences,
│                                   #   irreversibility list, domains, how checks run,
│                                   #   envelope defaults, approval boundary, contract guard
├── DECISIONS.log                   # append-only; nine kinds; agent-written
├── specs/<domain>/spec.md          # wanted clauses, each scenario carrying a Pin,
│                                   #   plus guarded invariants: the requirements with no
│                                   #   cheap check (negative, cross-cutting, non-functional),
│                                   #   which count as spec but get a re-check date, not a guarantee
├── specs/<domain>/manifest         # written by the agent from the pins at freeze: clause ids,
│                                   #   check ids, the surface, the export, the approval; never hand-edited after
├── checks/readers/<name>.md        # reader checks
├── checks/walks/<name>.md          # walk checks
├── checks/manual/<name>.md         # optional; a manual pin may be a bare slug instead
└── changes/
    ├── _template/                  # copied per change; delete design.md and
    │                               #   tasks.md on a check-gated change
    ├── <name>/
    │   ├── proposal.md             # intent, falsifier with origin, envelope, gates, loop log, decisions
    │   ├── design.md               # proposal path only
    │   ├── specs/<domain>/spec.md  # the delta: ADDED / MODIFIED / RETIRED
    │   └── tasks.md                # proposal path only
    └── archive/<date>-<name>/
The folder shape matches the root an OpenSpec-style tool uses; whether such a tool’s CLI tolerates the extra Pin: line, or RETIRED where it writes REMOVED, is unverified, and nothing here depends on one. Ground and the log sit inside the root rather than beside it.
The Pin: line goes directly under each #### Scenario: and each ### Invariant:, one line, no spaces inside values:
Pin: id=<domain>.<slug> acceptance=<observed|wanted|retired> oracle=<type> check=<id> born=<change-name> mutant=<slug>
id= is assigned at harvest and never changes; consolidate may re-point check= and logs it, and nothing re-points id=. born= names the change that harvested the clause, or ground for a constraint entered at Ground. A THEN with two parts takes two mutants, joined with +. walk swaps mutant= for last=<date>; manual swaps it for owner=<name> next=<date>, and its check= is either a procedure slug or a file under checks/manual/. Two roots are in play and the grammar does not distinguish them: a checks/... or specs/... id or path, and the kit’s own GROUND.md and DECISIONS.log, are relative to the clauses/ root; every other id is relative to the repo root, which is the folder clauses/ sits in. pending is legal for check= and mutant= only inside a delta — an agreed scenario before its task, an observed one before promotion — and Close refuses it. Verification is not a pin field; it is read from the run record. A decisions line is YYYY-MM-DD | kind | domain | ref | text, where ref is a clause id, a check id, a surface file, a change name, a manifest path, a gated action or irreversibility-list item, or -.
The pin is the one record for now. Once tooling exists, the shape to move to is a small structured file per domain from which the readable pins, the manifest and the packet’s clause list are rendered; until then the pin line is that file, one line per clause, and the agent writes the manifest from it at freeze rather than maintaining a second copy.
Operations
The machinery under the four actions. Named steps, not skills: the agent runs them when an action calls for them, and you write only the action name — plus explore or converge when you want one.

























































































OperationCalled fromNeedsThe agent returnsRulegroundbefore the first Startthe project, its constraints, what is expensive to get wrong, where approvals liveGROUND.md filled, and each constraint written into its domain’s spec as a wanted clause with born=ground — evidence earned if it has a check, a guarded invariant if not, an open exception if the artifact violates it2, 4, 6exploreany time; optionala question about the existing artifacta read-only map; no writes—intentStartone sentencechanges/<name>/proposal.md with the intent, candidate counterexamples marked agent, a drafted envelope, the falsifier blank1, 4probeProbethe falsifier with origin, the envelopeeither a stopped hard gate or a fired heuristic, or the smallest falsifier plus its check plus the evidence record plus the not-exercised list plus actual-versus-declared, logged as one loop with minutes1, 2, 4confrontProbenothing; the prediction is drafted from your falsifier and you may amend it (predict-then-compare is one way)the run, against the prediction and against the not-exercised list—harvestDecideyour packet replypins written on promoted clauses with their evidence, reject lines with the three decisions on the rest and their blocks removed from the delta, kept characterization checks commented with the clause id, the spot-check recorded2, 3, 7proposeProbe, when a heuristic firesthe heuristicproposal.md and design.md, adversarially reviewed (red-team) with the strongest objection given a destination; a proposal with no falsifiable scenario is rejected, not improved (intent-check)4archiveClosethe finished changethe run, verification per clause, the gate — no clause still observed, no pending field, every scenario or invariant outside RETIRED carrying a wanted pin with evidence, envelope actual matches declared, and a read of the intent against the promoted clauses that finds nothing quietly substituted (intent-fulfilment-check automates it) — then the merge, the move to changes/archive/<date>-<name>/, and an archive line. Under the prototype profile there is no merge: the findings go into proposal.md instead3, 4, 5freezeClose, when a domain qualifiesa domain you want to contractthe manifest written from the pins, the contract-test export, a freeze line through the approval boundary6consolidateevery ~10 archives and every freezenothingthe domain spec rewritten by concept, a conflict scan, re-pointed check= fields, overdue dates and expired exceptions7convergeany time; optionalnothingthe gaps between the spec and the artifact, as candidate intents you may take or drop—
Converge’s output enters only as new intents with a human-owned falsifier — never as tasks the agent runs.
The proposal path
A heuristic fired inside Probe, so the requirement gates the build.

propose writes proposal.md (why, what changes, the heuristic) and design.md (approach, at least one alternative, files and domains touched, the envelope for the whole change, rollback). red-team runs on both; the strongest objection becomes either a #### Scenario: in the delta or a reject line. A red team whose findings go nowhere is theatre.
You review and agree. The delta spec is written before the build — this is the agreement the check-gated path gives up — with each agreed scenario carrying acceptance=wanted and check=pending mutant=pending until its task earns them; Close refuses a pending. Agreeing also permits the hard-gated items the proposal names, one permit line each with the agreement’s approval reference.
tasks.md decomposes the work (task-decompose shape). Every row names its falsifier as inherited or its own; a row gets its own — human-owned, per rule 1 — when it introduces a new assumption, a trade-off or externally visible behaviour, and the agent flags which rows it thinks do.
Each row runs Probe and Decide inside the change folder until the scenario it names has its check and evidence; it was wanted at agreement. Heuristics are not re-evaluated inside a proposal; the escalation already happened. The hard gates, the envelope and the evidence rule stay live: an action outside the envelope pauses for an amend decision on the proposal, not a new proposal.
Close merges, then re-freezes if the domain was under contract, which kept its state throughout: a permit line per surface change made during the tasks, its ref the check id or file, and one freeze line whose approval covers the rewritten manifest and spec.

For drafting the proposal itself, to-prd produces the requirement shape this path wants.
Profiles
One line in GROUND.md names the kind of work. The rules do not change; what is relaxed is explicit.





























































ProfileArtifactFirst intentUsual oraclesFreeze meansRelaxedGreenfield code (greenfield-code)a walking skeleton, then features”the skeleton runs end to end”test, guardthe domain has consumersGround is thin; domains are added as they are discovered, each addition a Ground edit logged as amendBrownfield code (brownfield-code)the existing system”harvest what is already true” — everything lands observed, and a violated Ground constraint lands wanted with an open exceptiontest, guardonly after every clause is verified in the freeze runnothing; expect most first-harvest checks to be kept as characterization rather than promotedFeature on a live system (feature)the codebasethe feature’s smallest visible effecttest, guard, consistencythe domain’s consumers are live; a touched frozen domain re-freezes at Close, and an unfrozen domain on the same codebase harvests as brownfieldnothing — the proposal path is the common one herePrototype (prototype)a throwaway buildthe riskiest assumption, written as a falsifierreader, walkneverpromotion is not required and nothing freezes; the deliverable is DECISIONS.log plus the findings Close writes; the code is discarded or moved into a real changeSpecification (specification)specs/<domain>/spec.md itselfthe first requirement group a consumer needswalk, reader, re-pointed to test laterthe version consumers build againstred-team per requirement group replaces the probe’s not-exercised listDocumentation (documentation)the document”a fresh reader can do X from this alone”reader (locate for the clause, complete beside it), consistency for factualitythe published versionconsolidate runs per section rewrite; DECISIONS.log records what was deliberately left out as reject lines with the change as ref
The spec rule. If what you are writing will later have executable checks, write it as clauses in specs/<domain>/spec.md, pinned to walk or reader now, and re-point the pin to test when the code lands — an oracle upgrade, logged as consolidate. If instead it is read by people — documentation, a standard, a brief, a report — the document is the artifact and the clauses are about it, pinned to reader and consistency.
Cadences and stop rules

Per loop: the envelope before the build; a prediction before the run; the evidence record; actual-versus-declared; minutes; the not-exercised list.
Per intent: cap about five loops.
Per change: Close refuses while any clause is still observed, then gates on every scenario or invariant outside RETIRED carrying a wanted pin with evidence, envelope actual matching declared, and the intent read.
Freeze eligibility: every clause in the domain is wanted, every free-oracle check executed and passed in the freeze run, every reader check dispatched and every walk walked since the section it covers last changed, no manual next= overdue, and no open exception. One recent probe of the domain is not enough; freeze needs current evidence for every clause it lists.
Consolidate: every ~10 archives and at every freeze.
Re-checks: last= on walks and next= on manual pins are dates that expire, and so is every exception; consolidate lists the overdue ones.
The numbers are starting values, not measurements. Five loops, three changes, ten archives, three building loops, three reader dispatches — none of these has been calibrated against a real project. Recalibrate them after the first one.

Worked example A — a feature on brownfield code
Profile feature — the domains already exist. Ground names comments, auth and api; comments is harvesting, with clauses from earlier changes, and auth was frozen by an earlier change, its manifest listing tests/auth.test.ts, the fixtures it imports, the runner config, the CI job, specs/auth/spec.md, the manifest itself and GROUND.md. Ground names the approval boundary as a protected-branch review on the exact commit. (A fresh adoption has none of this: every domain starts open, and the first brownfield intent is the harvest that the profile table names.)
empty-comment, check-gated. Start. Intent: an empty comment is rejected before it is stored. The agent proposes three candidates, marked agent: posting an empty body returns 201; the request fails but a comment record is still created; a whitespace-only body is accepted. You write the falsifier from the first two — an empty comment is accepted, or any comment record is created by the rejected request — and leave whitespace to the not-exercised list; origin agent, revised. Envelope: writes to the request handler and tests/comments.test.ts; no external actions; local environment; contracts affected none, since comments is harvesting and nothing in auth is touched; budget forty minutes and three loops; rollback is a revert.
Probe. Hard gates: nothing on the irreversibility list, no shared environment, no surface file. Heuristics: no rework lines, forty minutes under the summed minutes of the last three building loops, one domain, no wanted clause touched. L1 adds a validation guard to the handler and two tests: rejects-empty-body, asserting the status and that the store count is unchanged, and stores-non-empty-body, the contrast twin. Evidence for the first: baseline passes; mutant guard-removed fails at the status assertion, which leaves the not-stored assertion unproven, so a second mutant store-before-validate — the store call moved ahead of the guard — fails at the store-count assertion; restore passes. Evidence for the twin, whose THEN also has two parts: mutant reject-all fails at the status assertion and mutant drop-store fails at the stored assertion. Actual writes match the envelope. Not exercised: whitespace-only bodies. While reading the handler the agent also notices existing behaviour — the stored body has its trailing whitespace stripped — and writes a characterization test for it in the same loop, so the packet can name a check.
Decide. The packet lists the three proposed clauses — (a) empty body is refused, its twin non-empty body is stored, and (b) trailing whitespace is trimmed — the evidence, the actual-versus-declared line, and the decisions. You answer: (a) and its twin — contract, yes. (b) trailing whitespace is trimmed — not contract; it is incidental normalisation you never asked for, but callers may depend on it, so the behaviour stays and its check stays as characterization. The agent writes:
2026-06-18 | reject | comments | comments.trailing-whitespace-trimmed | not contract; behaviour kept, callers unknown; check kept as characterization, tests/comments.test.ts::trims-trailing-whitespace
The ref names the clause id: this is a harvested clause turned down, the kind the rework heuristic counts. L2 probes the gap the not-exercised list named and harvests (c) whitespace-only bodies are refused — a second scenario under the same requirement, with the same two-mutant evidence — which you promote; your spot-check this change is store-before-validate, re-applied by the CI scratch job while you read its output.
Close. Every check runs; (a), its twin and (c) are passing; the change’s writes match the envelope; the intent read finds nothing substituted. The delta merges into specs/comments/spec.md and the folder moves to changes/archive/2026-06-18-empty-comment/. The delta header and the promoted pin:
# Delta: comments — empty-comment
 
## ADDED Requirements
 
### Requirement: empty comments are refused
The system SHALL reject a comment with an empty body before storing it.
 
#### Scenario: empty body is refused
- WHEN a client posts a comment whose body is the empty string
- THEN the request fails and nothing is stored
Pin: id=comments.empty-body-refused acceptance=wanted oracle=test check=tests/comments.test.ts::rejects-empty-body born=empty-comment mutant=guard-removed+store-before-validate
 
#### Scenario: non-empty body is stored
- WHEN a client posts a comment with a non-empty body
- THEN the request succeeds and one record is stored
Pin: id=comments.non-empty-body-stored acceptance=wanted oracle=test check=tests/comments.test.ts::stores-non-empty-body born=empty-comment mutant=reject-all+drop-store
 
#### Scenario: whitespace-only body is refused
- WHEN a client posts a comment whose body is only whitespace
- THEN the request fails and nothing is stored
Pin: id=comments.whitespace-only-body-refused acceptance=wanted oracle=test check=tests/comments.test.ts::rejects-whitespace-only-body born=empty-comment mutant=guard-skips-trim+store-before-validate
comments-service, proposal path. Intent: comments are served by their own service with no visible change to callers. Your falsifier: a request that succeeded before the extraction fails after it, or a comment is stored without an authenticated session. Extracting comments names the public API contract, which is on the irreversibility list — a hard gate; spans comments, auth and api with auth under contract — the cross-domain heuristic; and carries a whole-change minute budget over the last three building loops — growth. Probe stops and returns all three. propose writes the proposal and design with a whole-change envelope; the red team’s strongest objection — existing permalinks break when ids change — earns a destination as #### Scenario: existing permalinks resolve after migration in the delta rather than a note in a review thread. You agree the delta, whose scenarios carry check=pending mutant=pending, and the agreement permits the gated contract change:
2026-06-26 | permit | api | public-api-contract | proposal comments-service agreed; approval=pr-review:#40@7e2d9b1
tasks.md holds three rows: the extraction and the routing inherit the change’s falsifier; the id migration introduces externally visible behaviour, so it gets its own, which you write. Task two needs to widen an assertion in tests/auth.test.ts::session-required-for-post, a check on the auth surface, to accept the service’s session header: the agent stops, you approve that commit through the branch review, the log gets 2026-06-27 | permit | auth | tests/auth.test.ts::session-required-for-post | assertion widened for the service session header; approval=pr-review:#41@a1b2c3d, and the check re-earns its evidence before Close. Task three finds it needs a data migration the envelope did not declare: it pauses, you amend the envelope, and the migration — destructive, a hard gate — takes a permit through the same review, bound to the commit that adds the migration script. auth stays frozen throughout. Close merges, rewrites the auth manifest, and re-freezes through the boundary with one freeze line.
Worked example B — documentation
Artifact docs/quickstart.md, domain onboarding, change quickstart-env, check-gated.
Start. Intent: a reader with the quickstart and a clean machine reaches a running server. The agent’s candidates: the reader stops to ask a question; the reader reaches a server that answers on the wrong port; the reader succeeds only by opening the source. You take the first — a fresh reader stops to ask a question before the server responds — and add the third to the withheld list; origin agent, revised. Envelope: writes to the quickstart and a CI script; no external actions; a clean container for dispatches; no contracts affected; budget an hour and three loops; disposal is a revert.
Probe. The agent writes the smallest quickstart it can and the check that could fail it — checks/readers/quickstart-to-running.md, question locate, naming the task (reach a running server), what the reader gets (docs/quickstart.md and a clean machine; it may run what the quickstart tells it to, cloning included, but may not open the source tree, or it would find the answer in the code and the check could never fail), that it must state a blocking question rather than guess a value, a repeat policy of three dispatches, and the pass criterion (the server responds). The first dispatch stops at the first run command, having no value for a required environment variable, and says so instead of inventing one; the other two stop at the same place. That is the falsifier firing, which is the loop working. L2 adds the missing line, and alongside it scripts/doc-commands.sh, which runs the quickstart’s commands in CI; three re-dispatched readers reach a responding server.
Decide. The packet proposes a clause and its scenario, and you promote it. Evidence: baseline three of three pass; on a scratch copy, every line carrying that content is deleted — the prose sentence and the export line in the example block — and three dispatches all stop where they stopped before, the named failure being the reader’s blocking question; three restore dispatches pass. Nine dispatches for one pin:
### Requirement: environment is stated before it is needed
The quickstart SHALL state every required environment variable before the first run command.
 
#### Scenario: fresh reader reaches a running server
- WHEN a reader with the quickstart and a clean machine follows it
- THEN the server responds without the reader asking a question
Pin: id=onboarding.env-vars-before-first-run acceptance=wanted oracle=reader check=checks/readers/quickstart-to-running.md born=quickstart-env mutant=env-line-removed
The packet also proposes a second clause — the quickstart SHALL print commands that execute; WHEN CI runs the quickstart’s commands in order THEN every one exits zero — pinned to consistency as id=onboarding.quickstart-commands-execute check=scripts/doc-commands.sh::quickstart, with mutant=run-command-broken: on a scratch copy of the quickstart, corrupt the run command and the script fails at the exit-code assertion. One clause protects comprehension, the other protects truth, and neither substitutes for the other. A third run, question complete, is recorded beside the clause and not pinned: a reader with the quickstart and the repository on a clean machine, which is what a real newcomer has; it passes, which says the realistic path works, not that the document alone does. What you chose to leave out is logged rather than forgotten:
2026-06-18 | reject | onboarding | quickstart-env | Docker path left out of the quickstart; deliberate omission, belongs in a how-to
Close. L2’s not-exercised list named the Docker path and a Windows shell; the two loops took about fifty minutes; writes matched the envelope; your spot-check was the consistency mutant, re-applied by the CI scratch job. Both clauses are passing, the intent read finds nothing substituted, the delta merges into specs/onboarding/spec.md, and the log gets 2026-06-18 | archive | onboarding | quickstart-env | 2 promoted, 0 rejected; intent read: nothing substituted; envelope matched; onboarding stays harvesting.
What to test next
Do not expand the method into a framework before it has been compared to something. The hypothesis is:

Clause Loop reduces intent drift and undetected regression enough to justify its additional human effort.

Arms. Baseline: intent, tests, code review and a changelog. Thin Clause Loop: the baseline plus the observed-versus-wanted separation, one targeted mutant per clause with a named failure, and protected clause-to-check links. Nothing else from this note.
Changes. Comparable real ones, one of each: an exploratory feature, a brownfield bug fix, a contract-sensitive change, a documentation task.
Measures. Human active time, not agent runtime; end-to-end delivery time; intent substitutions caught; defects found by independent checks; unnecessary escalations and approval friction; whether the records are usable in a fresh session; whether the workflow was followed without reminders.
Controls. Keep failed and abandoned attempts in the record. Strip clauses/ from the loop arm’s artifacts before evaluation so the evaluator cannot tell the arms apart. Give both arms’ artifacts to a fresh context for an intent-fulfilment read against the original intent, so “substitutions caught” has a ground truth that is not the loop’s own instrument. Seed one frozen domain before the contract-sensitive change, or the thin arm’s protected links never come into play. Alternate which arm goes first across the four changes.
What it can show. With one change per cell and one person in both arms this is a pilot, not an experiment: it yields observations — did gates fire, was the log written, minutes per loop, dispatches per pin, what the independent read found — not estimates of effect. Across four changes the expected number of intent substitutions is near zero, so a clean run is weak evidence for the method and one substitution the packet missed is strong evidence against it. The result feeds the falsifier in The idea and recalibrates every number in Cadences.
When not to use it
Against the obvious baseline — a test suite, a changelog and code review — what this buys is the pin and the contract guard: the link from a chosen requirement to a check demonstrated able to fail for the right reason, and a build that breaks when that link is cut or a required check goes missing. If you would not use those two, the remaining ceremony is overhead. The entry cost is real: six words to run a loop, about twenty more to set a project up, and none of the actions is free.

Where the smallest falsifier of an intent is “build it in production”, the work is plan-first and the loop does not apply.
Where the artifact has no checkable output at all — team topology, build-versus-buy — there is no probe; what remains is an intent, an adversarial walk, and a decision record with a reversal criterion, which is a decision journal rather than this method.
The rest of the boundary — multi-team contracts before anything has frozen, regenerate-from-spec practice, regulated audit trails, parallel agents and session handoff — is in spec-driven-development-operating-model.

Related

accretive-spec-development — the engine: why the spec is a byproduct, the architecture mapping this note’s non-code oracles extend; its rules are defined here
spec-driven-development-operating-model — why the requirement gates some builds and the check gates others; domain transitions; the artifact mapping onto spec-driven-development layouts
ai-writing-workflow — the prose pipeline the documentation profile sits inside; a locate reader check is its adversarial final review — the editor who did not write the draft — made a re-runnable oracle, and its factuality audit is what a consistency pin runs
architecture-decision-records-ai — where a prototype’s findings go once the throwaway is discarded
oracle-problem-verification — why an agent-written check is not an independent oracle, which is what rule 1 exists for
mutation-testing-ai-generated-code — the tooled form of mutant= for code oracles: a mutation score, where this method asks for one watched sabotage per scenario and more by consequence
intent-to-retrospective-loop — the lifecycle this method compresses to minutes
to-prd, task-decompose, red-team, intent-check, intent-fulfilment-check, predict-then-compare — the vault skills the operations above delegate to

Sources
The method is original to this vault, assembled 2026-09-04 from the two parent notes and revised 2026-09-05 against an external design review; their sources carry the external tool mechanics. The non-code oracles, the mutant-by-deletion rule, the spec rule and the profile table were designed here and their precedents have not been checked — candidates are queued in knowledge/ai/topic-suggestions.md. No claim is made about any tool’s compatibility with the Pin: line or the folder layout.

ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.title: Cognitive Burden of AI Use
ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.content:
Cognitive Burden of AI Use
The mental cost of working with AI is not what the productivity narrative assumed. Generation got cheap; judgment, verification, integration, and stewardship got expensive. The net effort is often comparable to or greater than doing the work manually — just distributed differently, and in ways the human cognitive system is less well-adapted to sustain.
This note is the hub for how that burden shows up, why it is structurally worse than ordinary computer work, and what design and workflow patterns actually reduce it. It sits alongside ai-automation-biases (which covers the trust side) and hitl-progressive-autonomy (which covers the oversight architecture). As of April 2026.
Why this matters
If AI verification is a candidate for a durable discipline (see ai-verification-stack-web, evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests), then cognitive burden is the load curve anyone in such a role rides for a living. If the work of verifying, integrating, and stewarding AI output is structurally exhausting and structurally underestimated, then (a) the role has durable economic value because organizations cannot easily scale it by simply “adding more reviewers,” and (b) the personal sustainability question — how to do this work for years without burning out — is a first-class engineering problem, not a wellness afterthought.
For day-to-day developer work that uses AI as a tool (without verification being the explicit job), the same load curve still applies in compressed form: every PR review of agent-generated code, every “trust this output or check it” decision, draws on the same cognitive budget.
The shift: from generation to verification-as-default
The most carefully-sourced empirical picture comes from Lee et al. at Microsoft Research / CMU (CHI 2025), who surveyed 319 knowledge workers and analyzed 936 real-world examples of GenAI use. Their central finding, paraphrased:

AI does not replace the need for critical thinking in knowledge work; it relocates it.
Effort moves from information gathering and problem solving toward information verification, response integration, and task stewardship — the downstream, evaluative modes in Bloom’s taxonomy.
The worker’s relationship to the output shifts from author to critical integrator: editor, guide, constrainer, validator.
Higher self-reported trust in the AI correlates with less critical thinking enacted; higher task-specific self-confidence correlates with more.

That last pairing — the confidence-effort inversion — is the practical crux. The more you trust the AI, the less you check it; the more you trust yourself on the task, the more you push back. Both are problematic on their own but in opposite directions, and the bias fingerprint note (ai-output-bias-fingerprints) catalogs why polished AI output preferentially exploits the first.
Longitudinal confirmation (2026). Lee et al. is a cross-sectional survey; Vella & Blincoe (2026) followed professional software engineers over six months (two surveys, 158 → 101 respondents, matched cohort of 95) and found the shift playing out in time. Productivity perception held stable — 84% reported improvement at both time points — while the proportion reporting worsened developer experience nearly doubled, 14% → 27%, with flow state and cognitive load named as what specifically eroded. 82% reported spending less time writing code, and the authors propose a name for what replaced it: supervisory engineering work — the direction, evaluation, and correction of AI-generated output.
That is this note’s thesis measured over a real interval, by a group that did not stop believing it was more productive. It is self-report, so it measures experienced load rather than performance; that limitation is also what makes it the right instrument for this particular claim.
The burden is a slope, not a level
The sharpest experimental result on this note’s core claim also complicates it. Fan et al. (CHI 2026) held the LLM backend fixed (GPT-4o, fixed decoding, no tools) and varied only the interface — Inline completions, Chat, or Structured prompting — across N=60 participants and three Python tasks, with a no-AI control cohort. Per task, AI helped on every conventional measure: workload fell 18.2 RAW-TLX points, completion time fell 22% (25.0 vs 32.1 min), correctness improved (OR 1.71).
Fatigue nonetheless accumulated faster with AI than without it: KSS rose Δ +0.70 from task 1 to task 3 in the AI cohort versus Δ +0.48 in the control (Condition × Index interaction, p=0.041). Their behavioural verification-load composite — compile/test failures, time-to-first-compile, code churn, pauses, context switches — statistically mediated about 26% of that fatigue rise and 24% of the stress rise.
Two consequences matter more than the effect sizes, which are modest:

The load is in the accumulation, not the instance. A per-task workload measure can fall while the day still costs more. Studies that measure one task cannot see this, which is one reason the burden literature disagrees with itself.
Checking and repairing is the mediator, not generating. The design implication is not “generate less” but “schedule the checking” — cap it, batch it, and recover after it.

The same study found interaction mode governs the slope, and inversely to how cheap each mode feels: Inline had the steepest fatigue slope (Δ +1.18) despite being the fastest and lowest-load mode on simple work, with Chat shallowest (+0.92) and Structured between (+1.05); Mode × Index p=0.033. It also isolated a behavioural trigger — rejection streaks of ≥5 within 3 minutes, and pause clusters, predicted mode-switching (OR 2.36, 95% CI [1.33, 4.20]) — the “rejection spiral” participants described unprompted. And it located a calibration point: an Inline acceptance rate near 0.48 was associated with peak correctness, with both over- and under-acceptance degrading outcomes.
Scope discipline. Three ~25–32 minute lab tasks, capped at 40 minutes with 15–20 minute breaks. Extrapolating the slope to a workday is an inference, not their finding. The backend is a 2024-generation model without tool use, and the modes studied are completions and chat — not agent runs, where the ratio of machine output to human attention is far higher. Whether that steepens or flattens the slope is open. The operational schedule derived from this treats the mode and trigger findings as the transferable parts and the timings as conventions to tune.
Mechanisms that make supervisory work harder than it looks
“Supervisory” is not the same as “easier.” Four features of AI oversight consistently push load upward:
Cognitive decoupling. When you write something, you understand it as a byproduct of writing it. When you read something an AI wrote, you must reverse-engineer the reasoning the AI never actually did — and the output’s fluency gives you a false sense that you already grasp it. This is the same trap as the illusion of understanding, applied specifically to reviewing instead of reading for learning.
Accountability without authorship. You carry professional, legal, and in some domains moral responsibility for outputs you did not produce line by line and cannot fully inspect. The legal-accountability version of this is Elish’s moral crumple zone; the daily experienced version is a low-grade, draining background anxiety.
Fragmentation across multiple agents. Modern stacks route work through several specialized tools — IDE autocomplete, chat, code review bots, search-grounded agents, deployment assistants. Each hand-off costs working memory. Context management is a second-order problem that eats first-order attention. Multi-agent systems amplify this (multi-agent-token-efficiency, multi-agent-failure-modes).
The humanness amplifier. Conversational and agentic interfaces trigger the brain’s social-cognition machinery whether you want them to or not. Evaluating a chatty, confidently-worded assistant is not the same cognitive operation as evaluating a JSON response from a microservice, even when the information content is identical. Anthropomorphic design bypasses analytic filters and adds a layer of relational management on top of instrumental evaluation.
Vigilance decrement — the well-documented collapse of sustained attention when a system is usually-but-not-always correct — makes all four worse, and gets worse as the system improves, because rarer defects are missed at higher rates. See hitl-progressive-autonomy for the oversight-architecture response to this (autonomy reduction before escalation, anti-rubber-stamping UX).
The capacity-state axis — the burden is not a constant
Everything above describes the burden as a property of the work. It is also a function of the operator’s current executive capacity, which varies by hour, by day, and by illness. This axis is missing from most of the literature because studies recruit willing participants and measure them once.
Why AI work degrades faster than manual work
The load-floor argument, derived from cognitive decoupling above:
When you write something yourself, understanding is a byproduct — it arrives free with the act of producing. When you review AI output, understanding is a separate deliverable: you must hold the intended spec, construct a model of what the output actually does, and diff the two. Three working-memory objects where manual work needed one.
At full capacity the difference is invisible. As capacity drops, the byproduct path still works and the three-object path collapses. This predicts something the productivity framing misses: AI-assisted work has a higher load floor than manual work for small, well-understood tasks. Below some capacity threshold, writing the function yourself is genuinely cheaper than specifying it, reading it, and verifying it. “Use AI less when depleted” is correct triage rather than a failure of discipline.
The degradation curves are real and modelled
Three independent literatures put numbers on operator-state decay:

Vigilance decrement — measurable decline in sustained monitoring, worse for repetitive work, and reliably faster than intuition suggests: Mackworth’s founding experiment lost 10–15% of detection inside the first half hour, and later work finds decrement within 15 minutes. There is no fixed onset time to schedule against — it moves with signal salience, target prevalence, and task difficulty. The oversight version has a name: out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity, where an operator supervising a usually-correct system disengages and loses sensitivity to anomalies. vigilance-decrement-in-ai-oversight is the full treatment, including the finding that the obvious remedies (cap the block, batch the queue, micro-break) are much less supported than the problem is.
Fatigue-aware deferral — Zhang et al. (2026) argue that human-AI deferral systems fail because they assume static expert performance, and model it instead as a two-phase curve: quadratic warm-up to a peak, then sigmoid decay toward a floor, driven by cumulative workload. Their design detail is the load-relevant one: only tasks routed to the human accumulate fatigue. They validate against mammography data where radiologist recall declines from 78% to 66% over 100 continuous readings.
Acute state suppression — sidi-stress-cognition covers stress-driven dlPFC suppression and decision-fatigue the cumulative version. Illness belongs on the same axis: sickness behaviour is a cytokine-mediated syndrome (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) that includes cognitive impairment, and working memory depends on frontoparietal networks vulnerable to neuroinflammation. (The mechanistic chain from a common respiratory infection to measurable dlPFC hypoactivation is inferred from adjacent literatures — much of the causal work is LPS-challenge studies in rodents — so treat the mechanism as plausible and the phenomenology as the reliable part.)

The practical consequence is that capacity state should route the task, not just pace it. Low-capacity windows suit mechanical work with strong external verification signal — green CI, tight refactors, well-specified changes. They do not suit architecture decisions, “is this agent plan right,” or irreversible commits. This is the operator-side counterpart to the machine-side deferral policy Zhang et al. formalize.
The design implication for tooling and training
Every AI workflow is designed and tested by people at peak capacity, and used by people at median capacity. Tool designers, internal champions, and the person writing the onboarding doc are all in an unrepresentative state. A workflow that only works when the operator is sharp does not work. Design and evaluate against the median state, not the demo.
Why the problem doesn’t self-correct — the broken feedback channel
The burden is largely invisible to the person carrying it, which removes the signal that would normally drive adaptation.
METR’s randomized trial (2025) is the sharpest illustration. Sixteen experienced open-source developers completed 246 real issues on mature repositories they knew well (averaging 22k+ stars, 1M+ lines). With AI tools allowed, tasks took 19% longer (CI +2% to +39%). They had predicted a 24% speedup — and after experiencing the slowdown, still estimated AI had made them 20% faster. Among the contributing factors METR proposes is one squarely in this note’s territory: cognitive distraction from working with the tool.
Vella & Blincoe’s longitudinal cohort (above) shows the same channel from the other side: productivity perception stable at 84% while experienced load worsened.
Read together — the benefit is perceived and stable; the cost accrues on an axis nobody is measuring. Learning-by-doing needs a feedback signal, and here it is inverted for productivity and absent for load.
Scope discipline on METR. Its own February 2026 follow-up contextualizes rather than retracts: a late-2025 re-run gave −18% (CI −38% to +9%) for returning developers and −4% (CI −15% to +9%) for new ones, which METR itself calls “only very weak evidence” because 30–50% of developers declined to submit tasks they wouldn’t attempt manually, systematically excluding the highest-value AI cases. The experiment is being redesigned. The slowdown magnitude is uncertain and probably shrinking with tool generation; the perception gap is the robust part, and it is what this section rests on.
How it actually shows up
Workplace — “AI brain fry”
The term was coined by BCG in a 2026 Harvard Business Review article (Bedard, Kropp, et al., March 2026) based on a survey of roughly 1,488 US workers. It is a consulting-firm coinage, not a peer-reviewed clinical construct — useful as a label, but worth flagging as such. The study’s own reported differentials: AI-heavy oversight work associated with roughly 14% more mental effort, 12% more fatigue, 19% more information overload, and among the most affected (“brain-fry”) cohort, 33% higher decision fatigue and 39% higher intent to quit.
The driver in enterprise contexts is not AI per se, it is what an industry commentary has called the efficiency paradox: AI generates more options per unit time than a human can meaningfully evaluate, expanding the “sphere of accountability” faster than it contracts the sphere of execution.
A 2026 scale estimate, with a vendor caveat. Harness’s State of Engineering Excellence 2026 (700 engineering practitioners and managers across five countries, fielded by Sapio Research in April 2026) puts 31% of a developer’s day on what it calls AI-related invisible work — reviewing AI output, deeper quality scrutiny, and trust/override judgment calls — with 81% of engineering leaders reporting that code-review time has risen sharply since deploying AI. Developers named the top friction sources as reviewing AI code for accuracy (53%), fixing subtle bugs (52%), and explaining AI-generated code to teammates (48%). This is a vendor-published survey supporting a product category that sells into exactly this pain, so treat the direction as informative and the magnitude as unaudited.
The honest counterweight. DORA’s State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025 found no correlation between AI adoption and increased burnout or friction in its survey data — the largest developer dataset addressing the question, returning a null. DORA’s own reading is that strain is accumulating where surveys do not yet look (rising stalled work, restarts, and sharply higher parallel-thread counts), and that AI functions as an amplifier of existing organizational strengths and weaknesses rather than an independent load source. That reading is an inference from operational metrics, not a measurement of burden, and it should be held as one. Anyone citing this note for “AI is exhausting people” needs to also carry the null.
Education — atrophy vs. scaffolding
Two pieces of carefully-cited work:

Gerlich, M. (2025), Societies 15(1), 6 — survey of 666 UK participants using the Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment. Reported correlations: AI use ↔ cognitive offloading r ≈ +0.72, offloading ↔ critical thinking r ≈ -0.75, total effect of AI use on critical thinking r ≈ -0.42. The relationship is mediated through offloading, and the total effect is meaningful but not catastrophic.
Zhai, Wibowo & Li (2024), Smart Learning Environments 11, 28 — PRISMA review of 14 studies on AI dialogue systems and cognitive effects.

The caveat worth holding onto: heavy offloading is not the same as moderate, bounded use. The Gerlich effect is mediated, not direct — the risk is a usage pattern (delegating the productive struggle), not the presence of the tool. Beware the moral-panic register here; the popular press runs with it and the data is softer than the headlines.
Healthcare — ambient integration wins, intrusive CDSS loses
The clearest real-world dichotomy. Ambient scribes (listen passively, generate notes in the background) show strong effects in peer-reviewed work: a multi-center study published in JAMA Network Open (2025) across 263 clinicians and 6 health systems reported burnout dropping from 51.9% to 38.8% in 30 days; Stanford’s Tierney et al. study in JAMIA (2025, 32(2), 375+) found task load down 24 points and measurable burnout reduction.
In contrast, clinical decision-support systems that interject recommendations mid-workflow impose verification friction that can slow care and induce moral distress when AI and clinician disagree — the friction of cross-referencing against EHR and clinical judgment. Cognitive load here is dictated by integration posture, not by how capable the underlying model is.
Personal life — digital housekeeping
Managing a smart-home mesh or a consumer AI stack is increasingly a form of unpaid cognitive labor: onboarding devices, debugging integrations, re-auth’ing services, curating recommendation feeds. Sociology work on “digital housekeeping” shows this load distributes unevenly within households (typically onto the most tech-literate member). Recommendation-driven analysis paralysis is the same phenomenon in miniature: AI multiplies the options presented faster than it improves the decision.
The confidence-effort inversion — the actionable lever
Lee et al.’s finding that trust in AI and enacted critical thinking move in opposite directions is the single most useful design-level insight in this literature. It predicts:

The most fluent, best-marketed AI tools will produce the least critical engagement from their users. Polish is a load-reducer and a verification-reducer.
Domain experts push back more, even when fatigued, because task-specific self-confidence is a separate variable. Non-experts accept more.
Interventions that build earned skepticism (structured disagreement drills, forced counter-drafts, independent re-derivation on critical paths) are more valuable than generic “critical thinking training.”

See bias-aware-verification-protocol for the four-pass protocol that operationalizes this, and ai-automation-biases for the bias-cluster view.
Anthropomorphism as a hidden tax
There is a real and replicated empathy effect: anthropomorphic chatbots elicit longer, deeper, more personal user interactions than neutral ones, and users rate them as more trustworthy. Experimental work on perceived empathy in AI (e.g., Mousavi et al., AAAI 2025, arXiv:2411.12877) has documented the behavioural asymmetry. A Nature Human Behaviour 2025 study on human-vs-AI empathy comparison is another reasonable entry point. Specific numeric claims in popular summaries of these studies should be treated cautiously — the literature is young and the effect sizes vary.
The cost is that empathetic interfaces bypass analytic filters. Affect-laden engagement recruits social-cognitive resources that neutral, tool-like interfaces do not. For instrumental work — code review, factual verification, high-stakes decisions — the conversational register is a load multiplier, not a friendliness feature. The design implication is not “make AI cold” but “match interaction register to task register”: warm for support, neutral for instruments.
What actually reduces the burden
Pulled from HCI research and oxzo’s existing notes. Reduction comes from design changes, not from demanding more human resilience.
Direct manipulation over prompt-juggling. Shneiderman’s 1983 direct-manipulation principles — visible objects, reversible actions, rapid incremental feedback — have been re-applied to LLM interfaces. Masson et al.’s DirectGPT (CHI 2024) layered UI affordances over a chat model and reported users were ~50% faster, used ~50% fewer prompts, and those prompts were ~72% shorter than baseline chat. Prompt-engineering fatigue is a symptom of broken HCI, not an inherent cost of LLMs. See also agentic-vs-autocomplete-coding for the mode-selection version of this argument.
Ambient integration, not intrusive assistance. The healthcare scribe pattern generalizes. AI that fades into the workflow and produces artifacts reviewed at natural breakpoints imposes far less load than AI that interjects mid-task. For web development, the analogue is async code-review bots vs. in-editor autocomplete in a high-stakes file.
ISO 9241-210 principles applied to AI surfaces. Suitability, self-descriptiveness, controllability, error tolerance — the HCI fundamentals predate LLMs and still apply. Self-descriptiveness (clear audit trails, visible reasoning) and error tolerance (undo, prompt-iteration history) are the two most commonly violated by current AI UX.
Structured verification that scales with stakes. Not every AI output needs deep scrutiny. A tiered protocol — light heuristic checks for low-risk outputs, deep audit for high-stakes ones — is how you avoid burning vigilance on cases that don’t warrant it. The bias-aware-verification-protocol encodes this; hitl-progressive-autonomy is the agent-fleet version.
Automated reasoning / external grounding. Pushing factual verification from the human reviewer onto tool-assisted systems (automated-reasoning checks, RAG with source display, test-as-spec) reduces supervisory load by letting the machine carry the proof obligation. AWS Bedrock’s Automated Reasoning Checks advertise up to 99% verification accuracy against formalized domain policies — vendor-marketing figure, not an independent benchmark, but the architectural direction is sound.
Match accountability to authority. If you’re the named human in the loop, your review capacity needs to be real, not nominal. This is a management and staffing question as much as a UX one. Anti-rubber-stamp design is the interface side; adequate review time is the organizational side.
State-triage the task class. Per the capacity-state section: route work by current capacity, and treat “do this manually” and “defer this” as first-class options rather than concessions. The three moves that survive a bad day, in leverage order — pre-commit acceptance criteria before generating (converts depleted-state review from constructing a judgment into matching against a written list, the cheapest working-memory reduction available); externalize the spec into a plan file so it isn’t reloaded from memory on every output; and reduce the number of live surfaces, since each agent hand-off costs working memory.
Cognitive forcing functions — and the reason they need to be structural. Buçinca, Malaya & Gajos (2021) tested interventions that interrupt the reflexive acceptance of an AI suggestion and force deliberate engagement. They reduced overreliance on incorrect AI output — and participants trusted and preferred them less than frictionless explainable-AI interfaces, with the effect strongest among high need-for-cognition users, who are exactly the population most likely to believe they don’t need the friction. The design lesson generalizes past their task: the intervention that works is the one the operator will want to remove, so it has to live in a template, a checklist, a hook, or a plan file — anywhere other than in-the-moment discipline, which is the resource already depleted. This is the empirical backing for the “pre-commit acceptance criteria before generating” lever below.
Break dosing, correctly sized. Albulescu et al. (2022), a meta-analysis of 22 studies, found micro-breaks (≤10 minutes) reliably boost vigor (d=.36) and reduce fatigue (d=.35), both p<.001 — while the effect on performance was not significant (d=.16, p=.116), and a meta-regression showed longer breaks produced larger performance benefits. Micro-breaks manage subjective state; recovering capacity after a depleting verification block needs more than ten minutes. Break protocols that treat all breaks as interchangeable get the wellbeing benefit and none of the capacity one.
Scaffolds over skill. Anand & Idan (2026) report that a conceptual-roadmap scaffold reduced outcome variance across users by ~40% without lowering mean performance. Artifacts carry competence that training has to install per-person and that fatigue removes — the same logic as sidi-stress-cognition’s protocols-over-judgment counter. trainability-of-ai-use develops this into the intervention argument.
Operational counters — skills and persistent infrastructure
The patterns above describe what should exist in tools. Below are two concrete invocable skills plus one persistent file, each tied to a specific mechanism named above. Both skills rely on the AI accurately surfacing its own uncertainty, which is exactly what output-side bias fingerprints flag as unreliable — so these are partial counters, not full fixes. Their purpose is to make the invocation surface cheap so the deliberate act of reviewing happens at all.
They complement each other on different granularities: /reviewers-map runs per substantive output, /commitment-ledger runs per session. The persistent log file attacks the mechanism directly by converting ephemeral chat state into a searchable audit trail over time.
Reviewer’s-map skill — counters cognitive decoupling
Invoke. /reviewers-map [path] — if a path is given, maps that file; otherwise infers the most recent substantive output in the session. Skill definition at .claude/skills/reviewers-map/SKILL.md.
When to use. Any time the AI’s output will be acted on, committed, or published — code diffs, note drafts, research synthesis, PR descriptions. Skip for throwaway queries.
What it does. Produces a verification map alongside the output, so the reviewer does not reverse-engineer the reasoning from fluent text. Fluency decouples “understood the text” from “understood the logic”; the map reattaches them by handing the reviewer a ranked target list instead of an undifferentiated wall of prose.
Underlying template (what the skill tells Claude to produce — reproduced here for reference):
After producing your primary output, append a "Reviewer's map":

1. Load-bearing claims — bullet list of assertions the output depends on
   (names, numbers, dates, API methods, file paths, causal claims).
   Tag each [V] verifiable from provided context, [U] unverified, [I] inferred.
2. Least-confident spots — three places you are least sure, ordered by how
   much the rest of the output leans on them. One sentence each on what
   would falsify them.
3. What to check first — if the reviewer has five minutes, the three
   highest-leverage verifications.
4. What I did not do — files not read, sources not fetched, tests not run,
   steps deferred.

Do not pad. If a section would be empty, say "none."

Failure mode to watch for. A confident-sounding map that mirrors the output’s confidence rather than genuinely surfacing uncertainty. If everything is tagged [V] and nothing is [U] or [I], the map is probably sycophantic rather than honest — re-run with an explicit instruction to tag at least one claim as unverified or inferred, or accept that the output may not warrant the map at all.
Commitment-ledger skill — counters accountability without authorship
Invoke. /commitment-ledger — no arguments; operates on session state (git status, conversation history). Skill definition at .claude/skills/commitment-ledger/SKILL.md.
When to use. End of a working session that produced changes or decisions. Run it before closing the laptop, not at the start of the next day — the point is to lock in the ledger while context is still warm.
What it does. Converts diffuse “what did I just agree to” anxiety into an explicit list of files touched, claims implicitly accepted, and deferrals. The accountability mechanism is that you carry professional responsibility for outputs you did not produce line by line; the ledger makes the responsibility surface concrete rather than a low-grade background load. At the end of its output, the skill offers to append to [[commitments-log|journal/commitments-log.md]] for a persistent audit trail — see the next subsection.
Underlying template (reproduced for reference):
Produce a session closeout. Be factual and terse.

1. Files touched — each file changed or created, ≤10-word description
   of what changed.
2. Claims I stated that you accepted without external verification —
   assertions I stated as fact where you did not independently check
   (library behavior, API shape, benchmark numbers, "this pattern is
   standard"). If none, say "none."
3. Decisions recorded — choices made this session (architecture,
   naming, scope cuts). Name the rejected alternative if one was
   discussed.
4. Deferred items — anything flagged "will need to check later,"
   "assuming for now," or "TODO." If none, say "none."
5. What to check first tomorrow — the two or three highest-stakes
   items from sections 2-4.

Do not rehash the conversation. Do not editorialize. Empty section → "none."

Failure mode to watch for. The ledger sliding into a sycophantic progress narration. The point is load transfer, not accomplishment summary. If section 2 is consistently “none” across sessions, either the work was genuinely low-claim or the AI is underreporting — the latter is more likely, and the fix is to re-prompt with examples of the kinds of implicit claims that got accepted (e.g., “you said Zod’s .parse throws on invalid input — did you actually check?”).
Commitments log — persistent infrastructure
File. journal/commitments-log.md, append-only. Each /commitment-ledger invocation optionally appends under a timestamped section header.
What it does structurally. Converts ephemeral session state into a searchable audit trail. Ledgers that live only in chat history evaporate the moment context clears; a rolling log file makes last week’s assumptions, decisions, and deferrals walkable. This is the move that directly attacks the accountability without authorship mechanism rather than mitigating it per-session — the assistant can grep the log before starting a new session to see what was deferred, and the user has a real audit surface if anything produced a regression.
Rules, summarized (full format in the file’s header):

Append-only. Never rewrite or edit past entries. Corrections go in a new dated entry.
No de-duplication. Repeated claims across sessions are themselves a signal.
Terse, not reflective. The daily note is where reflection lives; this is an audit log.
Per-session opt-in. Not every session warrants persistence.

Failure mode to watch for. A log that grows into wallpaper. Two signs: (a) the user stops reading past weeks when starting new sessions, (b) the ledger gets appended automatically on every trivial session out of habit. Countermeasure: the skill asks per-session before appending; if you find yourself saying “yes” to everything, the threshold is too low.
Counterpoint worth holding onto
The burden framing can overstate the case in two ways. First, the empirical record on aggregate productivity with AI remains mixed-but-positive across most developer-tool studies; the burden is real but it does not wipe out the gains. METR’s slowdown is the sharpest counter-example on record and it is narrow by construction — experienced contributors, mature codebases with high quality bars, early-2025 tooling — with wide confidence intervals and a selection problem METR itself flags. Do not read it as “AI makes developers slower”; read it as “the cost is real, it is context-dependent, and it is not perceived.” Second, the cognitive-atrophy literature is still young, and its effect sizes (Gerlich’s r ≈ -0.42 total effect) are meaningful without being catastrophic. The risk is heavy, unreflective substitution, not any use.
The stronger framing: this is an ergonomic problem with a design solution, not a moral problem requiring users to “use AI less.” Treating it as the former keeps the intervention surface pointed at tools, workflows, and staffing; treating it as the latter tends to collapse into guilt and optimization anxiety, which are themselves forms of cognitive load.
