ai/cognitive-load-theory-for-ai.title: Cognitive Load Theory for AI Prompts and Plans
ai/cognitive-load-theory-for-ai.content:
Cognitive Load Theory for AI Prompts and Plans
Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) decomposes the mental effort demanded during learning or problem-solving into distinct sources, against a fixed working-memory bottleneck (Sweller, 1988; Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas, 1998). The framework originates with John Sweller’s work in the late 1980s and was developed for instructional design; this note ports its diagnostic vocabulary to AI prompt and plan design.
The bridge is not literal — LLMs do not have a Baddeley-style working memory; the binding constraint is attention dilution within the context window rather than a separate short-term store. But the three-load taxonomy is structurally portable: AI executors face load from the inherent difficulty of the task, from the form in which the task is presented, and from the productive synthesis work itself. Naming the three lets prompt and plan designers diagnose which kind of load a failure traces to and apply the right corrective.
The three load types (canonical formulation)

























TypeSourcePropertyIntrinsicThe inherent difficulty of the task or material — irreducible, set by the problem itself given the executor’s prior knowledgeCannot be eliminated; can only be staged or scaffoldedExtraneousThe form, presentation, or organization of the task — load that does not contribute to solving the problemEliminable; the primary target of prompt and plan improvementGermaneThe productive cognitive effort dedicated to schema-building, pattern-recognition, and integrationProductive; the load you want the executor spending capacity on
Working memory capacity is bounded — the classical figure of ~7±2 items (Miller, 1956) has been revised downward to ~4±1 for unrelated items (Cowan, 2001). When the sum of intrinsic + extraneous + germane load exceeds capacity, performance collapses non-gracefully.
Important note on the framework. Sweller and collaborators substantially revised the three-load formulation in later work (Sweller, Ayres & Kalyuga, 2011; Sweller, 2010 onward), reconceptualizing germane load as a redistribution of working-memory resources to intrinsic-load processing rather than a separately measurable third type. This note uses the three-type vocabulary because it remains the most useful descriptive frame for design decisions, while flagging that the underlying construct is contested even within CLT research. Treat the categories as diagnostic labels for design, not as separately quantifiable load measurements.
The LLM mapping
The structural analogs hold. The mechanism differs.
Intrinsic load → problem difficulty for the executor
The task’s irreducible complexity given the LLM’s pre-trained capabilities and the in-context information available.

Asking GPT-4 / Claude / equivalent to do arithmetic on six-digit numbers is high intrinsic load (the operation is poorly represented in training)
Asking the same model to summarize a paragraph is low intrinsic load (well-represented operation)
A reasoning task that requires holding three independent constraints simultaneously is high intrinsic load on attention-allocation

You cannot reduce intrinsic load by reformatting the prompt. You can stage it (chain-of-thought, multi-step plans, scratchpads) — which converts what looked like high intrinsic load into a sequence of lower-load steps each within capacity.
Extraneous load → load from prompt form, not content
The portion of working-memory / attention budget consumed by how the task is presented, not by the task itself. Sources:

Repetition — the same context restated multiple times across a plan, forcing the executor to re-parse it each time
Irrelevant ceremony — boilerplate, system-prompt cruft, retrieval noise, verbose XML markup that doesn’t carry task information
Bad ordering — task statement after the context it operates on, or task scattered across the prompt
Format mismatches — natural-language description of what should be a table; code presented as prose
Position-bias-vulnerable layout — load-bearing instructions in the middle of a long prompt where lost-in-the-middle applies

Extraneous load is the primary actionable target of prompt engineering. Most “the model didn’t follow my instructions” failures trace here.
Germane load → productive synthesis
The cognitive work that actually produces the output — pattern recognition, integration of context with the task, generation of the answer. For LLMs, this is the next-token-prediction process operating over the active context.
You want maximum capacity available for germane load. The path is: reduce extraneous load aggressively, stage intrinsic load when it exceeds capacity, don’t try to “increase germane load” — that’s not a thing you control directly; you control what capacity remains for it.
Chunking — pre-existing schemas expand effective capacity
In human CLT, chunking — organizing disparate elements into a single Gestalt — is the mechanism by which experts process material that overwhelms novices. A grandmaster sees a chess position as a few high-level structures (open file, weak square, attacking formation) where a novice sees 32 individual pieces. The chunk is a single working-memory item; the schema is the long-term-memory structure that produces the chunk.
The LLM analog is well-established empirically: prompts that cue an existing model schema (named pattern, well-known framework, canonical example) execute better than prompts that describe the same structure from scratch. “Apply the Strategy pattern to this code” cues a pre-trained schema; “Create classes such that…” forces the model to reconstruct the same structure from primitives. The first prompt has lower extraneous load not because it’s shorter, but because it leverages a chunk the model already holds.
The corollary: a prompt that uses vocabulary the model doesn’t have a chunk for pays extraneous load for the same task. Stylistic conventions specific to your codebase, jargon from a narrow domain, or invented framework names all force the model to reconstruct schemas from primitives — extraneous load that should have been eliminated. Either use the canonical vocabulary, or lift the schema definition once at the top of the prompt rather than implicitly assuming it.
The granularity paradox
The same load decomposition explains why both under-decomposition and over-decomposition fail — they fail through different load types.

























Decomposition stateFailure load sourceSymptomMonolithic (zero decomposition)Intrinsic load exceeds capacityAttention drift, confabulated state-carry, “the agent did the wrong thing on step 8”Optimal (intermediate)Germane load maximized for capacityClean execution; verification checkpoints land at natural seamsHyper-granular (over-decomposition)Extraneous load exceeds capacityEach step re-establishes context; coordination overhead exceeds task work; “plans of plans” syndrome
This is the load-theoretic restatement of the task-decomposition note’s over-decomposition counter: there is no single “more granular = better” axis. The right granularity is where intrinsic load per step fits the executor’s capacity and the cumulative extraneous load of orchestration doesn’t dominate the productive work.
Diagnostic moves for the three load types
When a prompt or plan is failing, classify the dominant load type before reaching for a fix.
If failure traces to intrinsic load
Symptom: the executor competently follows the structure but produces a wrong answer on the substantive question. Re-prompting in the same shape produces the same wrong answer. The model “doesn’t know” or “can’t reason about” the problem.
Fixes:

Stage the work — split the high-intrinsic step into a chain where each link is within capacity
Add scaffolding — chain-of-thought, scratchpad, intermediate artifacts
Provide the missing schema — example, definition, named pattern reference
Accept and escalate — if intrinsic load exceeds the executor’s reach even after staging, escalate to a more capable executor (larger model, human review, external tool)

Anti-pattern: rewriting the prompt with more emphasis or threatening tone. Intrinsic load isn’t a compliance problem.
If failure traces to extraneous load
Symptom: the executor follows part of the instruction, misses or contradicts another part, or seems to “lose track” mid-execution. The instructions are correct but the executor doesn’t act on them coherently.
Fixes:

Cut repetition — state shared context once, lift it to the top
Drop ceremony — verbose markup that doesn’t carry task information
Reorder — task statement first or last (avoid middle), with position-bias mitigated
Use chunked vocabulary — leverage pre-trained schemas instead of inventing terminology
Run density-scan on the prompt — the six levers there target extraneous-load patterns specifically

Anti-pattern: adding more instructions hoping one will stick. Each addition is more extraneous load.
If failure traces to germane-capacity exhaustion
Symptom: the executor handles each individual instruction correctly but produces a shallow or incoherent synthesis. Surface compliance, missing depth.
Fixes:

Reduce extraneous load to free capacity for synthesis (the primary lever)
Break the synthesis into named sub-syntheses that the executor produces in sequence
Use intermediate artifacts that capture early synthesis output, then feed it back as input to later steps

Anti-pattern: asking for “deeper analysis.” This often increases intrinsic load without freeing germane capacity.
What this does and doesn’t translate from human CLT
Translates well:

The three-load diagnostic vocabulary — useful for naming what kind of failure you’re seeing
The capacity-is-bounded principle — different substrate, same shape: attention dilution as the LLM analog of working-memory capacity
Chunking and schema-leverage — pre-trained patterns reduce extraneous load
The granularity paradox — under- and over-decomposition fail through different load mechanisms

Translates with caution:

Specific numeric capacity claims — “4±1 items” is a human result; LLM equivalents would need entirely separate measurement
The germane-load construct itself — contested within CLT research (Sweller’s own later revisions); use as a label, not a measurement
Worked-example effect, expertise reversal effect, redundancy effect — empirically grounded in human studies; plausibly applicable to LLM prompts but the specifics may differ. Treat as design hypotheses to test, not laws

Does not translate:

The motivational and self-efficacy mechanisms layered on top of CLT in the goal-setting literature — LLMs do not have motivation, fatigue, or affect
“Cognitive overload as protective shutdown” — humans avoid overwhelming tasks; LLMs typically generate confabulated output instead of refusing, which is a different failure shape that CLT does not predict

Composition with related skills

/density-scan on prompt prose — operates on the surface patterns that drive extraneous load (surprisal spikes, monotony, long dependencies). The skill is what you reach for when you suspect extraneous load is the dominant failure source.
/plan-split-scan on multi-step plans — operates on plan structure (concern count, state-carry, branches). The load-theoretic lens is the why behind the signals: each signal flags a structural pattern that drives extraneous load at the orchestration layer.
/reviewers-map on AI output — operates on the receiver side. Where CLT-for-AI is about executor load, reviewers-map is about the load the AI output places on the human reviewer.

The three are non-overlapping in target (prompt prose, plan structure, output verification) and complementary in lens (CLT explains what kind of load each scan addresses).
Tradeoffs and context-dependence

The framework is a diagnostic vocabulary, not a measurement instrument. Don’t try to assign numeric loads to prompt components — the construct doesn’t support that even in human CLT.
Intrinsic load is executor-dependent. What’s intrinsically hard for a 7B local model is intrinsically easy for Claude Opus. The same prompt may need different staging for different executors. The executor declaration in the plan-split-scan (Step 0) is the entry point.
Some “extraneous load” is intentional. Examples, worked solutions, and reference material look extraneous if you measure by token count but are productive scaffolding for intrinsic load. The distinction is functional: does this content help the executor build a schema that reduces total load downstream? If yes, it’s germane scaffolding, not extraneous noise.

What this doesn’t cover

Worked-example effect in detail. The CLT literature has a substantial body on worked examples, expertise reversal, and faded guidance. The plausibility of these transferring to LLMs is high but unmeasured; a separate empirical note would be needed to claim more.
Multi-modal load. Human CLT has substantial work on visual + auditory split-attention effects. LLM analogs (text + image, text + code) are an open area; this note does not address them.
Cross-executor calibration. “How much intrinsic load can model X handle in step Y?” — there is no general answer; calibrate against your own failure data.

Counterargument
The strongest objection: the three-load decomposition is a useful framing, but importing it from human educational psychology to LLM prompt design risks dressing prompt-engineering folklore in scientific vocabulary. The fixes recommended above (“cut repetition,” “use named patterns,” “stage hard problems”) are practitioner consensus anyway; the CLT lens doesn’t add new fixes, it just relabels existing ones.
The honest position: the lens adds value at the diagnostic layer, not the prescriptive layer. The fixes are what they are; the value of CLT-for-AI is letting you say “this failure is extraneous-load-driven, not intrinsic-load-driven” — which changes which fix to reach for. If a designer already knew which fix to apply, the lens is overhead. If they were applying intrinsic-load fixes to an extraneous-load failure (or vice versa), the lens corrects them.
The framework is also vulnerable to the narrative-coherence failure mode — CLT sounds explanatory because it has named categories and authoritative citations. Treat it as a working hypothesis for AI design, not as established science applied to LLMs. The empirical work has not been done.
Related

information-density-for-llm-prompts — surface-density patterns; the lever-level toolkit for reducing extraneous load
cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — receiver-side load (the human reviewing AI output); orthogonal to this note’s executor-side framing
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — companion plan-design move; reduces extraneous load at branch points
context-window-management — position bias and lost-in-the-middle; the attention-dilution mechanism this note’s capacity analog relies on
system-prompt-design-principles — cache-efficient, low-extraneous prompt construction

Sources
Verified 2026-05-12. The framework citations are canonical CLT references; the LLM mapping is this note’s analytical extension and is not empirically grounded in human-CLT research.

Sweller, J. (1988). “Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning.” Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257–285. Foundational CLT paper.
Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G. & Paas, F. G. W. C. (1998). “Cognitive architecture and instructional design.” Educational Psychology Review, 10(3), 251–296. The canonical three-load formulation.
Sweller, J., Ayres, P. & Kalyuga, S. (2011). Cognitive Load Theory. Springer. Textbook-length synthesis incorporating later revisions.
Sweller, J. (2010). “Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load.” Educational Psychology Review, 22(2), 123–138. The revision reconceptualizing germane load as redistribution of working-memory resources rather than a separate type.
Miller, G. A. (1956). “The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information.” Psychological Review, 63(2). Original capacity claim.
Cowan, N. (2001). “The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity.” Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1). Revised capacity claim for unrelated items.
Liu, N. F. et al. (2023). “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts.” TACL. The attention-dilution finding behind the LLM-side mapping.

ai/constrained-shape-for-verifiability.title: Buying Verifiability by Constraining Shape
ai/constrained-shape-for-verifiability.content:
Buying Verifiability by Constraining Shape
deterministic-gates-agent-loop takes the code as given and asks which gates to run against it. This note is the inverse move: change the shape of the code until the gate you want becomes cheap.
The observation underneath it is that analysis cost is a property of the representation, not only of the question. “Can control reach the payment handler without passing an authorization check?” is an interprocedural data-flow problem in free-form async TypeScript — you need CodeQL or equivalent, the analysis is unsound in practice, and it takes minutes. The identical question against an explicit state machine is graph reachability over a finite edge set: milliseconds, and complete rather than merely sound.
Completeness is the part worth pausing on. deterministic-gates-agent-loop’s four-property table notes that practical linters are neither sound nor complete. Constraining the representation is one of the few moves that buys the upgrade outright, because the state space stops being an approximation and starts being an enumeration.
What a state machine makes mechanical
Once a subsystem’s states and transitions are declared rather than implied, a set of questions that were judgment calls become graph queries:

unreachable states — dead code the type checker cannot see;
missing transitions — the enumerable version of “did it handle the error case?”, which is otherwise unanswerable without knowing what the cases are;
terminal states with no exit — deadlock, as a query rather than an incident;
invariant violations — “no transition into charging except from authorized” as a graph assertion instead of an AST heuristic hoping the call is reachable.

The last one matters because it repairs a specific weakness the gates note names: an AST rule can verify a call is present but not that it is reached. Declared transitions collapse that gap.
The oracle payoff
The larger prize is test generation. oracle-problem-verification argues the scarce resource in verification is not analysis but oracles — something that decides whether an output is correct. A finite machine is an oracle generator: enumerate the paths, and each path is a test case with an expected state sequence you did not have to author.
In XState this is getSimplePaths from @xstate/graph. The path set is derived from the machine, so it is not co-authored with the implementation in the way an LLM-written test suite is — which is precisely the independence failure the oracle note catalogs.
Caveat on maturity: as of 2026-08-21 xstate itself is healthy (v5.32.5, ~22M downloads/month, actively pushed), and @xstate/graph is at v3.0.4. But @xstate/test, the model-based-testing package, sits at v0.5.1 and was last published 2026-01-19 while core moved on. The path-generation primitive is solid; the ergonomic wrapper around it is the least-maintained part of the stack, so expect to write the harness yourself.
Why an executing model beats a modeled model
TLA+, Alloy, and the bounded model checkers in the gates note all carry the same structural liability: you verify a model, and model-to-code correspondence is manual. A proof about the model says nothing about the code if the two have drifted, and nothing mechanical prevents that drift.
A statechart in application code does not have this gap, because the machine is the runtime artifact rather than a description of one. That is a meaningful advantage over heavyweight formal methods for exactly the mid-tier properties most web systems care about, and it is the reason to reach for this before reaching for TLA+ — not because the logic is stronger, but because the correspondence is free.
The trade is expressiveness: TLA+ can state properties about unbounded concurrent systems that a statechart cannot.
”Forced” has to mean a gate, not a convention
A convention that the team uses state machines is advisory, and claude-code-enforcement-hooks draws the relevant line: advisory rules describe intent, gates deny actions. An agent under deadline writes an if chain next to the machine, and every individual diff looks locally reasonable.
Making it binding means a layer-2 AST rule in the sense of the gates note: within a designated directory, transitions of the relevant domain type may only be declared in a machine definition, and a handler that mutates that state outside one fails the PR. That is a ast-grep or Semgrep rule, and without it the constraint erodes in the direction of least resistance — which for a generative model is whatever shape its training data made most probable.
Where it earns its keep, and where it is ceremony
Worth it where the domain is genuinely state-shaped and the consequences are asymmetric: authentication and session lifecycle, checkout and money movement, multi-step onboarding, retry/backoff and circuit breakers, connection and subscription lifecycle, and agent loops themselves (functional-agent-architecture).
Not worth it for CRUD endpoints, rendering, data transformation, or anything whose “state” is just the value of a variable. Modeling those as statecharts produces ceremony that makes the code harder to read while verifying nothing anyone doubted.
The test is whether you can name the states without inventing them. If the states are obvious to a domain expert and currently implied by scattered booleans, the machine is recovering structure that already exists. If you have to invent state names to fit the formalism, you are adding structure rather than revealing it.
The general family
Statecharts are one instance of a recurring trade — narrow what can be expressed, and a checkable property falls out:



































ConstraintExpressiveness given upProperty boughtSQL instead of arbitrary traversal codeimperative control flowquery planning, optimization, static analysis of accessDeclarative IaC instead of setup scriptsarbitrary side effectsdiffable plans, drift detection, policy-as-codeSchemas instead of ad-hoc payloadsstructural freedomvalidation, compatibility diffs, codegenPure functions / typed effectsambient side effectstestability without mocks, safe reorderingStatechartsarbitrary control flowreachability, exhaustive transitions, path-derived tests
Recognizing the family is the useful part: when a property keeps being expensive to check, the productive question is often not “which analyzer is strong enough” but “what would have to be true about the code’s shape for this to be trivial”.
The case against

It relocates the oracle problem rather than solving it. The machine definition becomes the specification. A machine that models the domain wrongly gets verified confidently and completely, which is a worse failure than an unverified implementation because it carries more authority. Everything oracle-problem-verification says about circular specifications applies unchanged.
State explosion under composition. Parallel regions and nested machines multiply states. “Finite” stops implying “small”, and the exhaustive path enumeration that made this attractive becomes intractable at exactly the complexity where you wanted it most.
Ecosystem risk is real. XState’s v4→v5 transition was a substantial breaking change, and the model-based-testing surface is the least-maintained part today. Constraining architecture around a library is a bet on that library.
The strongest version of the objection: most defects in web systems are not illegal-state-transition defects. They are wrong business logic inside a legitimate transition, and no amount of state-machine rigor touches those. The gain is real but narrower than the ceremony implies, and it is concentrated in the specific subsystems listed above rather than distributed across the codebase.

Related

agent-output-quality-variance — why this lever is the one with compounding returns: substrate variance is bought once, where gates charge rent per run
deterministic-gates-agent-loop — the gate-side view this inverts; the layer-2 AST rule that makes the constraint binding lives there
oracle-problem-verification — why path-derived tests matter, and the circular-specification failure this inherits
temporal-logic-for-agent-verification — LTL over execution traces of a running agent; adjacent but distinct, this note constrains code shape rather than monitoring runs
functional-agent-architecture — typed effects and behavioral contracts, the same trade applied to the agent loop
ai-friendly-repo-structure — the broader “shape the substrate so generated code lands correctly” argument
claude-code-enforcement-hooks — the advisory-versus-enforced distinction this section depends on
ai-code-latent-failure-modes — the defect classes this does and does not address

Sources

XState package state confirmed 2026-08-21 via the npm registry and downloads API: xstate v5.32.5 (created 2017-05-24, ~22M downloads/month, last modified 2026-08-20), @xstate/graph v3.0.4, @xstate/test v0.5.1 (last published 2026-01-19). The getSimplePaths API is quoted from the @xstate/graph README.
This note’s own contributions, argued rather than measured: the representation-determines-analysis-cost framing, the executing-model-versus-modeled-model advantage over TLA+/Alloy, the constraint-family table, the name-the-states-without-inventing-them test, and the case-against. No study is cited for the claim that statecharts reduce defect rates, because none was found; the argument is mechanical, not empirical.
Not verified: any claim about relative defect rates in state-machine-structured versus conventional code. Treat the value proposition as a reasoned bet.

ai/context-engineering-claude-5-generati.title: Context Engineering for Claude 5-Generation Models
ai/context-engineering-claude-5-generati.content:
Context Engineering for Claude 5-Generation Models
What it is
Anthropic’s July 24, 2026 statement that most prior context-engineering practice was scaffolding for weaker models, and can now be deleted. The headline, quoted exactly from the post:

We removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 with no measurable loss on our coding evaluations.

Six named then→now reversals, plus a four-layer model for where context should live. Author: Thariq Shihipar, member of technical staff at Anthropic.
This is the prompt-layer instance of the thesis in harness-design-load-bearing — every component encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do. That note studied agent topology and found scaffolding relocating; this post studies a system prompt and reports it shrinking. The two are compatible observations at different layers rather than a disagreement — see Relation to “harness moves, not shrinks”.
Why it matters
Several notes in this vault codified 2026-Q1/Q2 prompting practice as durable principle. This post dates that practice and, in two places, reverses it. The reconciliation is recorded in What this supersedes in the vault so the corrections stay traceable to a source rather than becoming quiet drift.
The practical consequence for the seat: the default move on a misbehaving prompt has inverted. It was add a rule. It is now delete a rule and check whether the model already had the judgement.
Details
The six reversals








































ThenNowWhat actually changedGive Claude rulesLet Claude use judgementGuardrails written for worst-case avoidance were wrong for a subset of prompts; newer models handle the call unaidedGive Claude examplesDesign interfacesTool-usage examples constrain the exploration space; expressive parameters do the same work without the ceilingPut it all upfrontProgressive disclosureVerification and code review moved out of the system prompt into selectively-invoked skillsRepeat yourselfSimple tool descriptionsInstructions live in the tool description, not duplicated in the system promptMemory in CLAUDE.md (# hotkey)Auto-memoryClaude saves relevant memories itselfSimple specsRich referencesHTML artifacts, test suites, a function in another codebase, rubrics — all valid specs
The rules→judgement row carries the post’s own worked example. The retired instruction was:

In code: default to writing no comments. Never write multi-paragraph docstrings or multi-line comment blocks — one short line max. Don’t create planning, decision, or analysis documents unless the user asks for them — work from conversation context, not intermediate files.

Its replacement is a single sentence: “Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.” The post is explicit that the old version was a knowingly-accepted tradeoff — without it, “the comments Claude wrote would be incorrect in many cases” on older models.
Two rows deserve scope care:

Examples. The claim is about tool-usage examples constraining exploration. The post does not address output-format examples, and does not claim examples are bad in general. The Todo tool is the given counter-design: a pending | in_progress | completed enum plus a one-item-in-progress instruction communicates the usage pattern through the interface instead of through demonstrations.
Progressive disclosure. Applies to tools as well as skills. Deferred-loading tools require the agent to fetch full definitions via ToolSearch before use, so a large tool surface costs nothing until needed. Directly observable in this harness — the Task, Cron, and MCP tools load this way.

Where context should live
The post’s layer assignment, which no single existing vault note owns:

























LayerAssignmentSystem promptProduct context — what product Claude is operating in and what it’s doing. Claude Code users will “likely never modify this”; harness builders should spend most of their effort hereCLAUDE.mdLightweight. A brief statement of what the repo is for, then most of the tokens on gotchas. Explicitly avoid “the obvious” — anything Claude can learn by reading the file system. Push detailed procedures into skills and reference themSkillsLightweight guides for finding information when needed. Encode opinions and practices particular to you, your team, or your product. Avoid overconstraining “except in highly important areas.” Long skills split into many filesReferences@-mentioned files. Prefer code over description — “a HTML mockup of a design will generally produce better results than a description of the design or a screenshot”
Rubrics get a specific role: they let Claude verify your taste in a domain (the post’s example is what good API design looks like) by spinning up verifier agents carrying the rubric. That is the same generator/evaluator primitive harness-design-load-bearing documents, addressed at a subjective axis.
claude doctor
The post describes a command that helps simplify system prompts, skills, and CLAUDE.md files automatically. (Not verified locally — the behavior described here is the post’s claim, not an observation. claude doctor also predates this post as an install/diagnostics command, so confirm which behavior the local version has before relying on it.)
Relation to “harness moves, not shrinks”
harness-design-load-bearing quotes Anthropic’s March 24, 2026 engineering note: “the space of interesting harness combinations doesn’t shrink as models improve. Instead, it moves.” That note’s evidence was a harness that relocated — sprint decomposition became unnecessary at Opus 4.6 while the evaluator and planner stayed load-bearing.
This post reports the prompt layer shrinking by >80%. That is not a counterexample, and it is worth being explicit about why, because the surface reading (“one says moves, one says shrinks”) is wrong. The March claim is about the space of interesting harness combinations — agent topology. This post is about the token content of one agent’s system prompt. A shrinking prompt does not contradict a relocating topology; the two sources describe different layers and neither addresses the other’s.
What the two do share is the underlying mechanism, and this post refines it by showing that removed scaffolding has two distinct fates:

Relocated. Verification, code review, and tool instructions didn’t vanish — they moved into skills and tool descriptions, loaded on demand. This is the March note’s “moves,” observed at the prompt layer.
Deleted. The rules→judgement and repetition→consolidation reversals have no destination. That content is gone because the model no longer needs it.

Working synthesis: harness components relocate; harness guardrails get deleted. The March note only had occasion to observe the first, because topology components have somewhere to go. Neither source tests the other, and nothing here should be read as one Anthropic team contradicting another.
What the post does not establish

“No measurable loss” is scoped to Anthropic’s coding evaluations. Aggregate eval scores are the wrong instrument for detecting the failure class these guardrails were written against — the post says the original rules existed to avoid “worst case scenarios, such as deleting files,” which is tail behavior an averaged benchmark can miss. The claim is credible for typical coding work and untested for the tail.
Model-scoped, not universal. The reversals are asserted for Opus 5 and Fable 5. The post’s own reasoning implies the old rules remain correct for weaker models — anyone routing to Haiku or an older tier should not delete guardrails on the strength of this post.
Vendor guidance about its own product. Best possible source for what Anthropic did to Claude Code; weaker evidence for what you should do with a different harness, model, or domain. No independent replication documented.
Survivorship. The post reports the removals that held. Removals that were tried and reverted are not discussed, so the 80% is a success rate of unknown denominator.

What this supersedes in the vault
Corrections applied 2026-08-03 across the notes this post dates:





























NoteStatussystem-prompt-design-principles”Examples > explanations” scoped — the tool-usage case now points here. Principle 5 (no duplication) is reinforced by the repetition→tool-descriptions reversal, not contradictedsystem-prompt-assembly~30K tokens / 110+ pieces re-dated to the March–April 2026 reverse-engineering window; flagged as not describing Opus 5-generation Claude Codeclaude-code-architecture, claude-code-prompt-pipeline, llm-cost-optimizationSame figure, same date-scopingclaude-code-effective-use#-to-memory compaction tactic marked superseded by auto-memory; CLAUDE.md guidance aligned to gotchas-over-obviousharness-design-load-bearingCross-linked to the layer distinction above
Deliberately not changed: the ~30K figure is date-scoped, not replaced. “Over 80%” does not license computing a current number, and no source states one.
skill-quality-criteria needs no correction — its progressive-disclosure and degrees-of-freedom criteria already match the post’s skills guidance. Its finding that no vault skill currently uses progressive disclosure (all bodies well under 500 lines) remains the correct call at current sizes.
Related

system-prompt-assembly — the pre-Opus-5 Claude Code prompt structure
skill-quality-criteria — progressive disclosure and overconstraint at the skill layer

Sources

Anthropic — “The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models”, published 2026-07-24, by Thariq Shihipar. Fetched and read in full 2026-08-03; the 80% figure sits in the lede and is absent from reader-mode extractions of the page body.
Linked from that post, not independently read: “A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code” and the “Fable field guide”.

ai/context-repo-loading-patterns.title: Loading a Context Repo into Working Repos
ai/context-repo-loading-patterns.content:
Loading a Context Repo into Working Repos
What it is
A recurring multi-repo pattern: keep durable context (conventions, skills, agent instructions, knowledge notes) in one source-of-truth repo, and get it into each working/project repo where an agent actually edits code. The hard design choice is not what the context contains — it’s the delivery mechanism: how the context physically reaches the working repo and how it stays current.
This is the loading-mechanism axis. It’s distinct from, and downstream of, the instruction-file and repo-layout questions covered in ai-friendly-repo-structure (which treats the meta-repo pattern but not the delivery choice as its own decision).
Why it matters
The mechanism, not the content, decides who can use the context and how stale it gets:

MCP / manual → zero footprint in the working repo, but the context is invisible to anything without the live server (CI jobs, teammates, a clean remote/web session where the server isn’t mounted).
Submodule / sync-copy → real files land in the repo, readable by native Read/Grep and by every consumer, but you inherit a freshness obligation (pinned commit, or a sync step that can drift).

Pick the wrong one and you either (a) build context nobody downstream can see, or (b) vendor a snapshot that silently rots.
The five established patterns
Prior art clusters into five families (sources below). None is universal; they trade footprint against reach and freshness.















































PatternMechanismFootprint in work repoReach (CI / teammates)Freshness modelThin pointer + git submoduleContext repo vendored as a submodule (e.g. .ai-instructions/); root CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md is a one-line pointer; a setup script copies skills into .claude/skills/Medium (submodule tree + pointer files)FullPinned commit; git submodule update --remote to advanceSpine / meta-repoMarkdown-only repo above the project repos; operator loads the relevant files into the session by handNone (lives outside)Manual onlyAlways-latest (no copy); but human-drivenSync-copy tool (knowhub, ai-rules-sync, rulesync)Declare which files each repo wants; tool fetches them from the central source into the repo, run on setup or in CILow–medium (only the declared files)FullRe-run sync on pull/CI; copies can drift between runsMCP cold-memory retrievalContext stays in its own repo, queried on demand via an MCP serverNoneServer-holders onlyAlways-latest; no copy to go staleVirtual monorepoClone every repo into one workspace dir; one top-level instruction file ties them togetherHigh (all repos local)Local workspace onlyPer-repo git pull
A sixth shape — vendored reference snapshot (pull direction)
The five families all deliver your own context repo into work repos. The inverse need
is a distinct shape: pulling an external repo (a library you depend on, an API’s
reference implementation, a docs repo) into the working repo as read-only agent
reference — decoupled like sync-copy, local like the virtual monorepo, but per-consumer,
disposable, and deliberately inert. Closest prior art is degit-style clone-without-history.
Built 2026-07-04 as tools/load-context in this vault (symlinked to ~/.local/bin):
load-context load <url> shallow-clones into the host repo’s context/<name>/, strips
.git (a snapshot, not a repo), writes a .context-meta provenance receipt, regenerates
a context/AGENTS.md stating the read-only contract, and hides the folder via
.git/info/exclude so the host repo’s committed files stay untouched. Command surface
and decisions: projects/load-context/overview.
The tradeoff axes
Reduce the choice to four questions about your situation:

Who consumes it? Only your own agent sessions → MCP/manual is viable. CI or teammates without your server → you need real files (submodule or sync).
Native-file vs server read? Agents read native files faster and more reliably than they round-trip an MCP tool. Files-in-repo also survive when the server isn’t there. (This vault’s own CLAUDE.md already prefers native Read/Grep over MCP for exactly this reason.)
How tightly coupled? A submodule pins an exact commit and couples the work repo’s history to the context repo. A sync-copy decouples (just files) but loses the version pin. MCP couples nothing.
Freshness obligation you’ll actually honor. Pinned-but-stale beats auto-fresh-but-broken only if you advance the pin. A sync step in CI/setup is the most reliable “stays current” story for a solo operator who won’t remember to bump a submodule.

Recommendation — brains as context repo, single-user Claude Code
Given the constraints in play (brains is the context source; the only consumer is your own Claude Code sessions; you lean sync-tools), the strongest setup is a hybrid: synced core + on-demand depth, not a single mechanism.

Synced core (sync-copy). Generate or curate a small, stable bundle from brains — the agent instructions and the handful of skills/conventions a work repo always needs. Sync it into the working repo as real files under a predictable path (e.g. .ai-context/). A root CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md pointer tells the agent it’s there. This is the knowhub/ai-rules-sync shape and it matches your lean. It wins because:

the files are native-readable (faster than MCP, per the vault’s own preference) and present in every session including remote/web where the brains MCP may not be mounted;
a sync step run on setup/CI is the freshness model a solo operator actually sustains, where a submodule pin tends to freeze.


On-demand depth (MCP / manual). Leave the full vault behind the brains MCP. The agent pulls deep notes ad hoc when a task needs them, so you never vendor the whole knowledge base into a code repo. The synced core is the always-loaded floor; the MCP is the searchable ceiling.

Skip the submodule here: it couples the work repo’s git history to brains and the version-pin freezes unless you remember to bump it — friction with no payoff when a single user controls both ends. Skip the virtual monorepo: it solves cross-repo code navigation, not context delivery.
Counter-case (when sync is the wrong call)
If you ever add CI that must reproduce the exact context a past session saw, the sync-copy’s lack of a version pin becomes a liability — that’s the one scenario where a pinned submodule earns its coupling cost. And if consumers were only ever your interactive sessions with the MCP guaranteed present, the synced core is redundant and pure MCP is the lowest-footprint answer. The hybrid is the right default precisely because remote/web sessions break that guarantee.
Concrete shape
brains/  (context source — this vault)
├── context-bundle/        # curated subset meant for syncing out
│   ├── AGENTS.md          # the always-loaded core instructions
│   └── skills/            # the handful of work-repo-relevant skills
└── …                      # the full vault stays here, reached via MCP
 
some-project/  (working repo)
├── AGENTS.md              # thin pointer → read .ai-context/AGENTS.md
├── .ai-context/           # synced from brains/context-bundle (gitignored or committed)
│   ├── AGENTS.md
│   └── skills/
└── src/…
Whether .ai-context/ is committed or git-ignored is a separate call: commit it if teammates/CI need it without running the sync; git-ignore it (and run sync on setup) if only your sessions read it and you want the work repo’s history clean.
A working scaffold of this lives in the vault at context-bundle/ — an authored core AGENTS.md, a manifest.txt declaring which skills ship, and a sync.sh that fetches the declared skills from .claude/skills/ into a target repo’s .ai-context/ and writes a .sync-meta receipt with the source commit (declare-and-fetch, so nothing is duplicated inside the vault). See context-bundle/README.md.

ai/continuous-agent-task-fit.title: Continuous Agents — What the Clock Buys, and What It Doesn't
ai/continuous-agent-task-fit.content:
Continuous Agents — What the Clock Buys, and What It Doesn’t
A standing agent is a process with a persistent identity that is woken repeatedly across weeks, by a schedule or by an event, rather than given a task in a session and exited. This note is about which work fits that shape. It is not about how long a single run may go (a different question with a different evidence base) or how many agents to run at once.

As of 2026-08-28. The vendor primitives cited here are months old and moving fast.

Confidence legend: ✅ = source re-fetched and the quoted text matched verbatim during this pass · ○ = single-source or secondary, not independently corroborated · (est.) = synthesis judgment, not a measured value.
The claim, stated so it can fail

Continuous operation does not deepen what an agent can think. It changes what it can be present for.

That sentence is easy to agree with and hard to test, so here is the operational form. Classify a task by when its inputs arrive:

A depth task has all of its inputs available at the start. A proof, a refactor, a research question with a fixed corpus.
A presence task has inputs that arrive after the start — a new commit, a deadline passing, a page changing, a message landing.

One shape fits neither cleanly and is named below rather than smuggled in: a sweep has all its inputs at the start but more of them than any single session can get through. For a sweep the clock buys windows, not thinking — which is consistent with the claim, and worth saying so the definition is not quietly doing the second disjunct’s work.
The hypothesis forbids one thing: a depth task improving under scheduled operation at equal spend and equal context resets. Same model, same total tokens, same number of fresh context windows and the same progress file — one arm runs its N sessions back-to-back in a day, the other spreads the same N sessions across a week. Only calendar spread differs. If the spread arm wins on a static-input task, the “presence” account is wrong and the clock is buying thinking after all. (est.) Nothing found in this pass reports such a result; that is absence of evidence, and the claim stays a hypothesis.
Two pins, and both matter. Equal spend: a standing agent that spends ten times more is not demonstrating a duration effect. Equal resets: splitting a large task across several fresh sessions with a progress file is standard practice for work that cannot fit one window, and an arm that gets more fresh contexts than the other is testing compaction, not the calendar. A comparison that lets those differ would “falsify” this note for a reason that has nothing to do with presence.
The counterargument first
The strongest case against this note is that there is nothing here — that a “standing agent” is a cron job with a language model in the loop, and cron is a solved problem.
The case is well made and partly right. ○ One practitioner account of replacing a working cron script with an agent doing the same job reports it cost more and ran slower, and frames the pattern as “bolting agents onto workflows that a script already handled.” ○ Two separate commentaries make the same reduction: “In their current form, AI agents are essentially cron jobs with a chatbot interface,” and, in software engineering, “a ‘job’, ‘worker’, and even ‘agent’” have always been things that wait “for a stimuli in the form of an application request or user input” and can “operate on a schedule, in the form of a ‘cron job’.” ✅ Anthropic’s own worked examples for scheduled routines are maintenance jobs, one weeknightly and one weekly — “A schedule trigger runs every weeknight against your issue tracker via a connector. The routine reads issues opened since the last run, applies labels, assigns owners” — which is what a well-written script has done for twenty years.
(est.) What this argument gets right: the trigger is ordinary. Schedules, webhooks, mentions, and queues behave the same whether the consumer is a script or a model, and inherit the same failure modes. What it misses: the argument is about the wakeup, not the work. The question this note asks is narrower — once something wakes on a schedule, is there a step in the work that needs judgment a script cannot supply? For some task shapes there is not, and the honest answer is a script. For others there is, and it is always the same step: the one after the detection.
Six task shapes
The shapes below are the ones where the binding constraint is attention over time rather than thinking capacity. Two columns carry the test the counterargument demands: what the agent adds beyond a script, and where its output lands — because a standing agent that produces continuously delivers into a review queue that is not standing.















































ShapeWhat the clock buysWhat the agent adds beyond a scriptWhere the output landsWatch — detect a delta against a baselineSampling at times nobody is lookingNothing for the detection — a hash, a diff, or a threshold does that. The agent’s value starts after detection: triaging the delta and proposing the fix. Every scheduled example in Anthropic’s routines documentation is this shape: scan merged PRs, flag docs “that references changed APIs”, open “update PRs … for an editor to review”A list a human reads, a ticket, or a draft PRRevisit — surface decay after a half-life elapsesRemembering when something is dueThe re-verification: re-reading a source, deciding whether a claim still holds, rewriting it. A script can only say “this is old”An edit a human reviews, or a reportResolve — close predictions whose deadline has passedNoticing the deadlineThe judgment call on the outcome, and the written reasoning for it. A script can list what is due; it cannot say whether it came trueA log entry a human samplesAccumulate — build evidence no session can holdMany samples across weeksReading and summarising each sample into a running record; the state is the productA dossier a human reads at intervalsWait — act on an external event when it arrivesBeing there when it happensInterpreting a natural-language event (a message, an issue, a review comment) and deciding what it asks forA pull request, a reply — something with an approverSweep — grind large-N work no session would finishEnough windows to get through the listThe per-item edit or judgment itself, when it is not mechanicalMany small changes, each needing review
(est.) Read the third column as a filter. Watch without triage is a script, and an agent that wakes on the clock to check for a delta spends tokens confirming nothing changed. Watch with triage, Revisit, Resolve, Accumulate, and Wait need an agent for the second half — detection is mechanical, but what follows detection is a reading-and-judging step, and that is what the model supplies. Sweep depends on the item: renaming is a script, rewriting is not.
That gives the corrected shape of the hypothesis: the clock buys the detection, the agent buys the judgment, and the two are separable. The mistake is putting the agent on the clock. Put the script on the clock and the agent behind the script — and at least one runtime already does exactly that: ✅ OpenClaw’s heartbeat reads a scratch file first; if it “is effectively empty,” the runtime “skips the heartbeat run to save API calls,” reported as reason=empty-heartbeat-file, with other pre-model gates marked “(no model call).” The gate fires only on a file that exists and is empty; the same page says that if no scratch file exists, the heartbeat still runs.
What continuous operation costs that a session does not
Four costs are specific to the standing shape. They are what an operating design has to answer, and they are the reasons the cron-job reduction is not the whole story.
1. An exit code is not a result. A cron monitor treats exit 0 as success. A standing agent can exit 0 having done nothing, or having decided nothing needed doing, or having produced a confident wrong answer. ✅ Anthropic’s routines documentation says this outright: “A green status in the run list means the session started and exited without an infrastructure error. It does not mean the task in your prompt succeeded.” ✅ One personal-agent runtime builds the empty case into its default heartbeat prompt: “If nothing needs attention, reply NO_REPLY.” (est.) That is a third run state that a cron monitor only sees if the run reports it as a metric, and nothing found on the agent side reports it by default. Liveness monitoring for a standing agent therefore needs a task-level assertion in the ping, not just the ping. The assertion has to be on something the task was supposed to change, or it passes forever.
2. The empty wake still spends — unless something cheaper runs first. A script that finds nothing costs a process spawn. A model that wakes to find nothing has paid for the context it loaded to find out, and the size of that context is a design choice: ✅ OpenClaw’s cost guidance says a fresh session per heartbeat takes the load “from ~100K tokens down to ~2-5K per run” against carrying the conversation history in. The floor is a few thousand tokens per wake, or zero if a pre-model gate decides there is nothing to look at. Where no such gate exists the cost is uncapped in aggregate. ✅ Anthropic’s scheduled deployments cap each run separately and say so: the budget “bounds every run separately rather than acting as a cumulative ceiling across runs: a deployment with a ‘2000’ cap can spend up to about $20 on every run.” ✅ The per-session SDK cap defaults to “No limit.” Per-period ceilings exist only at the account level — ✅ a daily cap on routines, ✅ per-user monthly limits on one workspace type, ✅ monthly hard limits that return a 429. (est.) Nothing found in this pass offers, as a default, a cumulative budget scoped to one standing agent across its runs. (est.) There is a workaround, an API gateway key per agent with a per-period cap, but it is a deployment the operator builds, and nothing found gives a lifetime ceiling that does not reset. The integral over time is the operator’s to compute.
3. Unattended means unapproved. ✅ “Routines run autonomously as full Claude Code cloud sessions: there is no permission-mode picker and no approval prompts during a run,” and included connectors can be used “including writes, without asking for permission during a run.” A session agent has a human at the prompt to say no; a standing agent has whatever scope it was given, for as long as it is given. (est.) This is the time-integrated form of the authority question agent-policy-enforcement-gap asks at session altitude: a control that merely wins during a session can be re-argued in the next one, while a key that locks is the only kind that holds at 03:00. And where the agent can install its own trigger, the scope includes the schedule itself: ✅ OpenAI’s scheduled-task documentation says “Skills can also create or update scheduled tasks.” ✅ The one counter-design found is a session-scoped recurring task that “automatically expire[s] 7 days after creation,” which its documentation justifies as bounding “how long a forgotten loop can run.” A trigger that dies on its own is the cheapest answer to authority that would otherwise integrate without limit.
4. The intake is a trust boundary. Work arrives at a standing agent through channels that outsiders can write to: an issue, a pull-request comment, a message in a channel. ✅ Anthropic’s own guidance for the GitHub integration warns that “External contributors may include hidden instructions through HTML comments, invisible characters, hidden attributes, or other techniques,” and for the Slack integration that Claude “may follow directions from other messages in the context.” ✅ A 2026 systematisation of 78 studies on prompt injection against agentic coding assistants reports “attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses exceed 85% when adaptive attack strategies are employed.” A job queue with a trusted producer does not have this property. Intake design for a standing agent is who may write to it before it is what format the message takes.
The review queue is the ceiling
The fourth column of the shapes table is the load-bearing one. Every row lands its output somewhere that is not standing: a human, or a gate a human configured. (est.) The capacity a standing agent adds is the production cost of each item minus the cost of checking it — so where checking an item costs about what producing it would have, a 24/7 producer aimed at a 9-to-5 reviewer is a capacity transfer dressed as a capacity gain. That is the case for output that must be read in full, judged, and possibly redone. Where checking is cheap relative to producing, the gain is real, and that gap is the whole design lever.
Two things follow. First, any task shape adopted has to state where its output lands and who absorbs it, in the design, not afterwards. Second, the shapes that fit best are the ones whose output is machine-verifiable or sampled rather than read: a resolved prediction with a stated criterion, a drift report with a hash, a change with a test, a go/no-go posted to a channel. Where the output must be read in full, the standing agent’s cadence should be set by the reader’s cadence, not the clock’s. ✅ GitHub’s coding agent enforces a version of this at the approval step. “The person who created the issue can’t be the final approver” is separation of duties, and also an admission that the agent’s output is a review item, not a result.
hitl-progressive-autonomy holds the mechanism for lowering per-item review cost as trust accrues; delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix argues the missing axis in most task-fit judgments is verification cost and blast radius, which is exactly the axis the fourth column tracks. autonomous-agent-vs-decomposed-workflow settles a related question, who owns control flow inside a task. Its answer, keep the loop bounded and gate at seams, carries over: a standing agent’s schedule is a control-flow decision made once and then never looked at.
What would revise this note

A controlled comparison where a static-input task improves under scheduled operation at equal spend. The hypothesis is dead and the note is retitled.
A vendor shipping a cumulative budget scoped to a standing agent across its runs. Cost 2 becomes a configuration problem.
A cron-monitoring product adding a task-level assertion state distinct from “missed” and “failed.” Cost 1 becomes ordinary SRE.
Pre-model gating becoming the default in every scheduling product. Cost 2 shrinks to the gate’s false-negative rate, and the Watch row’s caveat goes.

Limits

Vendor documentation is the main evidence base. It describes what products do, not what practitioners experience; the practitioner sources here are ○ secondary and few. Several of the surfaces cited are in preview or being retired; the routines page carries a research-preview label and the Slack integration page a retirement notice, so the ✅ marks date faster than the arguments they support.
The six shapes are a partition chosen for this note, not a taxonomy found in the literature. A different partition would move some judgments; Anthropic’s own examples, for instance, are four event-triggered and two scheduled, which is Wait-heavy relative to this table.
“Equal spend and equal resets” is the pin that makes the hypothesis testable and also the reason no evidence was found: this pass found no such comparison, and did not search for one directly.
The only number found for the empty-wake cost is one vendor’s own “~100K tokens down to ~2-5K per run” figure, which measures conversation-history carry-in rather than the wake itself. The claim that the aggregate is material is (est.).

Related

Sources

ai/delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix.title: Agent Fit at Task Granularity — the Delivery-Org Matrix, Re-judged
ai/delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix.content:
Agent Fit at Task Granularity — the Delivery-Org Matrix, Re-judged
The vault’s prediction cluster argues at the level of skills and roles (skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age, human-role-roadmap-under-ai) or occupations (ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms). This note works one level lower: 87 concrete delivery-org tasks, each scored for AI-agent fit, held against the vault’s framework. The task granularity is what’s new; the framework is not.
As of 2026-07-17. Fit scores are capability-relative and will drift. The re-judgments age more slowly — but not uniformly: re-judgments #1, #2, and #4 (below) are themselves indexed to the 2026 state of verification tooling, and the revise triggers at the bottom say when they fall.
Provenance and epistemic status
Source: two third-party PDF matrices (“Designer Task × Phase Matrix”, 48 tasks with per-task rationales; “Delivery Org Task × Phase Matrix”, 87 tasks — a superset adding engineering, data, security, and ops), produced outside this vault with AI assistance, against references not available to us. The artifact itself invites this treatment: “a starting hypothesis, not a verdict — filter and re-judge against your own framework.”
Consequences for how to read this note:

Every fit score is an unverified hypothesis. None traces to a source we can inspect. The scores are kept because the classification judgments are interesting, not because they are evidence.
The matrix’s own vocabulary (“re-encoding”, “origination”, “will-bound”) is close enough to this vault’s that independent convergence can’t be assumed — the same 2025–2026 consensus corpus likely sits under both. Agreement between the matrix and the vault is a consensus echo, not confirmation (skills-to-train-for-ai-future flags the identical risk).

The axis, and its mapping onto vault vocabulary
The matrix scores each task on a single axis:

























ScoreMatrix definitionNearest vault conceptHigh”Re-encoding existing decisions; structured output”Depreciating translation-layer work — spec→code, data→report (skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age depreciation list, item 5)Partial”Agent drafts, human directs/calibrates”The L2–L4 middle of the autonomy ladder (human-role-roadmap-under-ai)Low”Origination, tacit/non-verbal, or permission-bound”The principal’s residue: originating purpose, bearing accountability (appreciating-position-vs-skill); plus the tacit/embodied bottleneck (ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms)
The mapping is nearly one-to-one. That’s the note’s first finding: “re-encoding vs. origination” is a compressed restatement of the vault’s valuation logic — value migrates off re-encoding because generation is cheap, and pools where someone must originate or answer for the result.
What the matrix shows (accepting its scores at face value)
Distribution across the 87 delivery-org tasks (counts computed from the PDF, not quoted from it). Read every number here as a property of this enumeration, not a measurement of delivery work: the 87-row task list is one AI’s slicing of a delivery org, and the counts are not stable under re-slicing — split the implementation tasks finer and the High share grows; merge the strategy tasks and the Low share doubles. The patterns are only as real as the classification judgments behind them (which is what the re-judgments below attack).




































































PhaseTasksHighPartialLowDiscovery & Research11452Definition & Strategy160115Ideation & Concept7061Design & Production191171Validation & Testing13661Delivery & Handoff9450Monitoring & Iteration12651Total87314511
Three patterns:

The phase gradient. Agent fit rises as decisions get made: Definition & Strategy and Ideation contain zero High-fit tasks between them (0 of 23), while Design & Production is majority-High (11 of 19). Fit tracks how much of the task is downstream of already-made decisions.
The 11 Lows sort into two families. (a) Origination / will-bound: business model design, problem reframing, vision, scope & MVP, backlog prioritization, roadmap & portfolio shaping, voice & tone — seven tasks that are the principal seat wearing different hats. (b) Live-human / tacit: qualitative research, requirements elicitation, workshop facilitation, usability testing — four tasks whose moat is in-the-room human reading. (Sorting caveat: the designer PDF supplies rationales for 9 of the 11 and those sort cleanly; the two without — requirements elicitation and backlog prioritization — are sorted here by task nature, our judgment, not the source’s.) Two different moats, and (argued below) of different durability.
The entire engineering production layer scores flat High — frontend, backend, database, data pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, CI/CD, plus test authoring and automation. Directionally consistent with the entry-level-attrition evidence in ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms: the High column at task level is the “junior-shaped work” the occupation-level data shows thinning. (That source is deliberately two-sided — aggregate employment effects are ~null so far and the Jevons expansion story remains live — so this is one strand of it agreeing, not the note’s verdict.)

Where the vault re-judges
This is the “do our own analysis” part — five places the vault’s framework disagrees with or restructures the matrix.
1. The missing second axis: verification cost and blast radius
The matrix’s single biggest structural gap. human-role-roadmap-under-ai’s core claim is that delegation is per-workflow, indexed by stakes and reversibility — you are L4 on test generation and L2 on schema migrations simultaneously. A one-dimensional fit score per task type can’t express that. “Backend implementation: High” is true for the median reversible ticket and false for the auth flow or the payment path — same task type, different verification cost, different honest rung. Re-judged: fit = f(task type, verification cost, blast radius), and the matrix only models the first argument. This re-judgment is executed on the desk-relevant subset in delivery-org-matrix-desk-rescoring: no High keeps a single unconditional label, and the oracle-layer rows turn out to be delegable only under seat-governed independence.
2. “Partial” is 52% of the matrix and carries no information
45 of 87 tasks land on “agent drafts, human directs/calibrates” — which describes essentially all AI-assisted knowledge work in 2026 and therefore discriminates nothing. The vault’s ladder gives the middle its structure: which rung (L2 co-planning / L3 consult / L4 approve-by-exception), and who authors the escalation policy. Operationally, the interesting question about every Partial task is not “human in the loop?” but “what oracle does the human own, and what escalates?” (An oracle here is an independent verification check — tests, property checks, cross-model review.)
3. The High scores are near-circular — and the circularity hides origination inside production tasks
Tasks score High because they’re classified as “re-encoding existing decisions” — the score restates the classification. The classification is where the contestable judgment lives, and it bakes in an idealized decisions-then-encoding pipeline. Counter-example from the matrix itself: “Wireframing: High — re-encoding decided flows into layout” assumes the flows arrive decided; in practice wireframing is often where the deciding happens (the sketch is the argument). Real delivery work interleaves origination inside nominally-productive tasks; the waterfall framing systematically over-scores High.
4. Code review’s “Partial” collides with the rubber-stamping base rate
The matrix scores code review Partial — which, per its legend, means “agent drafts, human directs/calibrates” (no per-task rationale is given; code review appears only in the delivery-org PDF, which has none). Read through the legend, the score keeps a human judgment layer inside code review. The vault’s hardened finding says that layer is precisely what fails: automation complacency hits experts, survives practice, and is worst on highly-reliable systems (Parasuraman & Manzey 2010, via human-role-roadmap-under-ai) — rubber-stamping is the modal outcome, not a tail risk. Re-judged: code review of machine output is not a stable Partial; it’s either backed by an independent oracle the reviewer didn’t author (tests, property checks, cross-model review — making it honest) or it degrades toward an unacknowledged High with a human fig leaf.
5. Low is two claims of different durability — split it
Family (a) Lows (will-bound: vision, scope, roadmap, business model) rest on a position — someone must want the outcome and answer for it. Per appreciating-position-vs-skill, that survives capability growth by construction; these Lows are durable. Family (b) Lows (tacit/live: usability testing, qualitative research, facilitation) rest on a capability claim — “AI can’t read humans live” — and capability-based safe lists have aged badly: creativity, Go, art, and natural-sounding prose all fell off 2015-era safe lists within a decade (skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age’s counterargument section; what-survived-machine-conquest documents translation’s fall as the in-progress warning case). AI-moderated interviews and synthetic-user testing are already marketed claims (unverified here, but the direction of pressure is visible). Re-judged: family (a) Low is a floor; family (b) Low is a forecast — track them separately.
Two qualifications on the floor, so the positional argument isn’t quietly converted into a task-count argument it can’t support. First: the floor guarantees the function survives — someone originates and answers — not that seven tasks’ worth of principal-work persists, or any given seat’s. Will-bound work can consolidate into fewer chairs. Second: even the position carries appreciating-position-vs-skill’s own live erosion trigger, AI systems bearing real institutional accountability. The same split applies inside the Low rationale “origination of brand identity” (voice & tone): the identity decision is family (a); the generation of candidate voices is already Partial.
The split’s most uncomfortable product comes from pointing it at the Partial column. “Agent drafts, human directs/calibrates” is itself a capability claim — a statement about what agents can’t yet do unassisted — so every Partial whose human half is not will-bound is family (b) by construction. On this matrix’s own terms, the only floor is the seven will-bound Lows. The 45-task Partial middle is a forecast wearing a reassuring label.
Where the matrix pushes back on the vault
Re-judging in one direction only would be its own bias — the task granularity does expose two things the vault’s skill/role-level cluster can’t do. Both inherit the provenance discount: they come from the same unverifiable source the re-judgments discount when it agrees with the vault. So they are framed as questions the vault should answer, not findings the matrix established:

The vault has no task inventory. Every cluster note argues about which skills appreciate, but none can answer “which of the tasks on my desk this week are delegable, and at what rung?” The matrix’s contribution is the census structure, honestly labeled: a genre-typical delivery-org enumeration — consultancy-shaped task names, waterfall phases — not anyone’s verified inventory. As a scaffold to inventory real work against, it is still the first of its kind here. human-role-roadmap-under-ai says rungs are per-workflow; this is the first artifact that enumerates candidate workflows to point that question at.
A denominator question no vault note poses. Taken at face value, 11 of 87 tasks (~13%) are origination-bound — a small share against the vault’s reassuring prose about value migrating to judgment and accountability. The number is demoted on arrival: task counts are not time or value weights, and the count is unstable under re-slicing. It is a property of this enumeration, not a measurement. What survives the demotion is the question. The vault argues the migration’s direction without ever stating a denominator, and under any plausible slicing the origination-bound share of a delivery org’s task list is a minority. One rationale from the designer PDF is worth keeping verbatim as this point’s sharpest instance: documentation & artifact maintenance as “the durable, illegible job — agents keep it current.”

The read for an architecture-owning engineering seat
What the matrix implies for the seat that owns solution architecture, tech-stack selection, data modeling, and estimation — stated with re-judgment #5 applied consistently rather than comfortably:

Every task nearest that seat sits Partial, and every one of those Partials is capability-bound — family (b). None is will-bound; the will-bound Lows (scope, backlog, roadmap, vision) read as sitting one seat up, with product/PO roles. (Role attribution is our inference from task nature — the PDFs advertise role tags but the rendered tables don’t show per-row roles.) The uncomfortable conclusion the split forces: the architecture seat’s moat is a forecast, not a floor. skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age already carries the sentence that applies here, and it is easy to leave behind in that note: senior judgment is “an appreciating asset built on a depreciating ladder… better verification tooling erodes the moat from the other side.”
The strategic implication is therefore a choice, not reassurance. One option is to move toward the will-bound seat: own outcomes — scope, priority, the answer-for-it role — not only the technical decisions. The other is to make the Partials survivable by owning the oracle: per human-role-roadmap-under-ai, the seat that authors the verification architecture keeps a durable function even as its tasks drift from Partial toward High-with-oracle. “Keep doing architecture and stay Partial” is not one of the stable options this matrix’s own logic leaves open.
The actionable cut from re-judgment #2: for each Partial task actually on the desk, the move is not “use AI more” but “decide the rung and build the oracle” — the roadmap note’s per-workflow question restated at task level.
Re-judgment #3 is the working caution in the other direction: tasks where origination hides inside production (architecture decisions made while “just implementing” a spike) are exactly where a flat High/Partial label would misprice the seat’s work — some of the moat is real but mislabeled by the taxonomy.

What would revise this note

A verified source list from the matrix’s author materially different from the 2025–2026 consensus corpus → the consensus-echo caveat weakens; the matrix becomes independent evidence rather than a restatement.
Family (b) Lows falling in practice (AI-moderated usability/qual research producing decisions teams actually ship on) → the Low family split is confirmed in the uncomfortable direction and the remaining Lows compress to the will-bound seven.
Verification tooling maturing to where the engineering-High column routinely ships unreviewed (skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age’s second falsifier) → re-judgment #1’s second axis collapses; fit really does become one-dimensional, and the matrix was right ahead of schedule.
Field evidence that the phase gradient inverts — agents doing well-bounded strategy drafting while production stalls on integration cost → the re-encoding definition of High was wrong, not just circular.
Will-bound work visibly consolidating into fewer seats (one principal plus agents holding vision + scope + backlog + roadmap across what were several roles) → family (a) held as a function but failed as a headcount floor; strip any remaining reassurance-reading from the floor language.

Desk Rows Re-scored — the Verification-Cost Axis Applied
delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix re-judgment #1 says the matrix models only one of three arguments: fit = f(task type, verification cost, blast radius). This note executes that re-judgment on the rows actually on this desk, using the machinery from human-role-roadmap-under-ai: the honest score is a rung (L1–L5) per workflow, set by how cheap an independent oracle is (a check the human didn’t author) and how large the aggregate blast radius is (per the roadmap’s aggregation caveat — individually-reversible actions can aggregate into consequential outcomes). Source data: delivery-org-task-matrix-data; row numbers refer to it.
Desk-row selection is an inference, not given by the source: the 21 rows below are what an architecture-owning lead-web-developer seat (TypeScript/JS) plausibly touches. The matrix’s PDFs advertise role tags but don’t render them per-row, so no source-side attribution exists to check against. Defensible variants of the cut exist (accessibility implementation, IaC, and production monitoring are arguable inclusions). That is one reason the findings below are stated as patterns, not counts. The headline, up front: under the two added columns no High keeps a single unconditional label — each splits by blast radius, holds only while an independence condition is maintained, or demotes.
Red-teamed same day (2026-07-17, clean-context pass); two corrections applied and kept visible below — the count-based headline was replaced with a pattern statement, and the oracle-layer demotion was rebuilt around governing independence rather than keeping authorship.
Method — the two added columns

Verification cost — cost of an independent oracle for the task’s output. Low means a check exists that the human didn’t author and that fails loudly (tests, types, contract suites, “the spike runs”). High means the only check is the human re-deriving the judgment, or feedback arrives months later, confounded.
Blast radius — aggregate consequence of an undetected failure, not per-action reversibility.
Re-score — the honest fit under both columns, stated as fit + rung. Δ marks the divergence from the matrix: = holds · ↑ promotes · ↓ demotes · ⇄ splits into cases the single label conflated.

In the table, the Matrix column carries the source’s original fit label — H for High, P for Partial.
