The differences, marked — what the added axis systematically changes
Of the 21 desk rows the matrix scores 9 High / 12 Partial. Under the added columns, no High keeps a single unconditional label — every one splits by blast radius, holds only while an independence condition is maintained, or demotes. (The first draft stated this as a count: “1 of 9 Highs survives”. The same-day red-team broke that count on three fronts: the survival criterion was applied inconsistently across rows, the sole survivor’s blast-radius cell violated this note’s own definition, and the seat-relative row cut makes any count unstable — the same instability-under-re-slicing the parent note already warns about. The pattern statement is what survives.) The divergences sort into five patterns:

The oracle layer cannot be delegated the way the matrix implies — the biggest single difference. The matrix scores CI/CD setup, test-case authoring, and automated-test implementation flat High: they are re-encoding, so by the matrix’s axis they’re maximally delegable. But these rows are the oracle infrastructure every other High’s re-score depends on, and what governs them is human-role-roadmap-under-ai’s independence requirement: the protecting check is one the output’s author didn’t write. So the demotion is conditional, not absolute — same-agent-writes-code-and-tests is self-undermining. The hollow-suite evidence — 100% coverage, 4% mutation score — shows that failure is real, not hypothetical. By contrast, cross-agent authorship under a verified mutation floor and seat-held required-checks config satisfies independence with no human authorship at all. What the seat must keep is governance of oracle independence — who checks whom, floors, sampling, escalation policy — not the authoring. (The first draft claimed authorship itself must stay with the seat; the red-team showed that contradicts the roadmap’s own definition of the protecting oracle, and the cited mutation-testing trajectory has agents driving the oracle layer as the mainstream direction.)
The implementation Highs split rather than hold. Frontend, backend, database: H is true of the median reversible ticket and false of auth, payments, identity, write-path migrations — same task type, different blast radius, different honest rung. No row keeps a single unconditional label.
Two promotions the matrix missed. Technical spike artifacts (self-verifying + throwaway; the feasibility inference stays human) and bug reproduction/clustering. Estimation is a third, conditional on running the calibration loop the vault already has — an owned feedback loop the matrix’s axis can’t see (delayed and scope-confounded, but scoreable, which is more than the other strategy Partials have).
The strategy Partials hold but their moat gets re-labeled. Solution architecture, stack selection, schema design stay P — pinned at L2 not by tacit human skill but by oracle absence plus delayed feedback. That matters for durability: it makes them exactly the family-(b) forecast the parent note warns about (a moat resting on a capability claim, not a position). If verification tooling reaches architecture decisions (fitness functions, executable architecture tests), the pin releases and these rows drift toward the High column.
Spec authoring demotes from High. The matrix reads “developer handoff & specs” as re-encoding decided design. But the spec is the one artifact with no external oracle — it is the source of intent that all other verification checks against, and writing it is the L2→L3 binding skill. Delegate the drafting; the intent must stay authored.

The compressed conclusion: on this desk, the matrix’s High column is really three different things — honest Highs (cheap oracle, contained blast radius: median tickets, spike artifacts, perf-test execution), conditional Highs (High only while an independence check holds: tests-with-mutation-floor, docs-with-sampling), and oracle-layer Highs (rows where the output is the checking infrastructure, so delegation is safe only under seat-governed independence — check-author ≠ output-author, plus meta-monitors). The single-axis matrix cannot distinguish them, and the third category is the dangerous one — it looks most delegable on the re-encoding axis while being exactly where ungoverned delegation is self-undermining.
What would revise this note

Architecture-level oracles maturing from constraint-guards (the Layer 5 fitness functions that already exist) into checks on the decision itself → the strategy Partials un-pin from L2; finding #4’s durability warning fires.
Agent-authored test suites with verified mutation floors becoming routine → the conditional Highs (#59, #60) collapse back to plain High, and finding #1 reduces to a governance checklist rather than a demotion.
Field evidence that sampled-review + escalation-policy regimes fail like uniform review does → the code-review restructure (#62) was a rearrangement, not a fix, and the rubber-stamping base rate wins regardless of structure.
The desk changing — the row selection is seat-relative and should be re-cut if the seat’s task mix shifts.

ai/design-side-ai-adoption-stall.title: Why Design-Side AI Adoption Stalls — a Structural Trace
ai/design-side-ai-adoption-stall.content:
Why Design-Side AI Adoption Stalls — a Structural Trace
Output of /structural-trace, run 2026-07-29. The pattern: on a delivery team, designers are not adopting AI while the engineers have; the designers’ stated objections are (1) AI output is bad quality and (2) source control and technical tooling are too hard — “we’re not programmers”; and the prevailing explanation on the deciding side is that the designers are simply behind.
Instanced on a real team, generalized here. The specifics are stripped because they are not what the diagnosis turns on — the structure below is the claim, and the situation is one instance of it. What the generalization costs is recorded in the Sources section and in objection B: this is a single-vantage account with no adoption history behind it.
This note is a diagnosis, not a plan. The skill deliberately produces no recommendation; picking an intervention is a separate step (/second-order on a candidate, then /red-team). The designer-seat-under-ai note is the forecast companion — what design work becomes; this is the structure companion — why the transition stalls where it does.
The generalizable claim: the adoption asymmetry between engineering and design is not a willingness gap. It is an accumulated-verification-capacity gap, and the dispositional explanation is itself a load-bearing part of the structure that sustains it.
Pattern
Attempts to increase design-side AI adoption produce objections rather than uptake, while the same push on the engineering side compounds — and each cycle strengthens the explanation that the designers are the problem.
Stocks and flows
Two stocks, coupled. Naming them separately matters: the usual framing (“we have an adoption problem”) collapses a stock and a flow into one phrase and hides where the accumulation actually is.
Directions below were originally stated as fact and are downgraded to hypothesis after the adversarial pass (objection B): no adoption history was available, so “shrinking” and “running toward collapse” are inferences from a single conversational report, not measurements.

Stock A — constraint substrate: machine-readable design decisions the generator can be held to (tokens, component contracts, DESIGN.md-style identity rules, documented do/don’t). Direction (hypothesised): low and roughly static.

Inflow: designer-hours spent authoring system-level artifacts
Outflow: drift as the product changes; untokenized one-offs shipping; turnover


Stock B — trust in generated output: the per-person credit that gates whether a next attempt happens at all. Direction (hypothesised): shrinking — but see objection B, which notes we cannot know it was ever high enough to shrink from.

Inflow: generation runs whose output clears the designer’s quality bar
Outflow: exposures to slop, drift, and off-system output — draining disproportionately, since a first bad run costs far more credit than a good one adds



Stock A is the deeper driver; Stock B is what’s visible and what people argue about.
Loops

Correction kept visible (adversarial pass, objection C). B1 and B2 were originally labelled balancing loops. They are not: a balancing loop requires closure — the stock’s level must feed back to change the flow that changes the stock — and neither does. B1 is a decision rule (designer sees generic output → declines to proceed); B2 is a threshold test (entry cost vs. expected benefit). Nothing accumulates and gets corrected. They are kept below under their original names because they are real mechanisms that shape the behavior, but the “level 8 — balancing-loop strength” leverage claim rests on the mislabel and is re-ranked in the adversarial section. R1 and R2 survive as genuine reinforcing loops.

R1 — Substrate starvation [reinforcing]

Actors / mechanism: low constraint substrate → generator has nothing to be held to → output shows slop and drift (visual-ai-slop-fingerprints) → designers judge the tool unusable → they don’t use it → authoring tokens and identity rules has no consumer, so the hours are never spent → substrate stays low.
Currently running: toward collapse.
Delay: significant and asymmetric — the crux of the whole system. Substrate investment pays off only after enough accumulates for output quality to visibly cross the bar (weeks to months). The disconfirming evidence — a bad screen — arrives in seconds. Fast negative evidence beats slow positive evidence, so the loop resolves toward non-adoption long before the investment could have paid.

R2 — Divergent returns [reinforcing]

Actors / mechanism: engineering arrived with a large pre-existing oracle stock (types, tests, CI, code review, linters — decades of accumulated verification infrastructure). Generated code gets checked cheaply → failures caught before they hurt → trust accrues → more use → more visible wins → the lead’s finite attention, tooling budget, and onboarding effort flow toward the side showing returns → the design side gets comparatively less → the gap widens, confirming the reading that produced the allocation.
Currently running: toward growth on the engineering side, toward starvation on the design side.
Delay: moderate — attention and budget reallocation lags visible wins by roughly a quarter.

B1 — Quality-bar defense [balancing loop → decision rule, per objection C]

Actors / mechanism: the designer’s trained discrimination fires on generic output and rejects it. This pulls shipped quality back toward a standard.
Implicit goal / setpoint: the designer’s internalized quality bar — never written down, acquired over a career, and the thing they are actually paid for.
Delay: none — this is the fastest loop in the system, which is why it dominates. A squint at a screen resolves in under a second.
Note: this loop is functioning correctly. It is the system’s quality regulator, not a pathology. Its structural problem is timing, not direction: because it fires faster than any other loop, it terminates trials before the slow accumulating loops (R1’s substrate, B2’s familiarity) can run at all.

B2 — Entry-cost gate [balancing loop → threshold test, per objection C]

Actors / mechanism: on-ramps routed through developer infrastructure (git, CLI, PRs) impose a fixed entry cost. Designers weigh it against expected benefit, which R1 has already driven low, so the gate holds.
Implicit goal / setpoint: effort proportional to expected return — “don’t pay a programmer’s entry fee for a non-programmer’s payoff.”
Delay: none significant.
Note: this is the legible objection, and therefore the one interventions target — but it is not the binding constraint. It binds only because R1 has already suppressed the expected benefit. Remove the git barrier entirely and R1 still produces non-adoption.

Archetype
Match: Growth and Underinvestment.

Why it fits: all three of the archetype’s required elements are present. (a) A growth engine — AI adoption — that stalls. (b) A capacity stock (the oracle and the constraint substrate) that must be built ahead of demand, with a delay before it shows returns. (c) An eroding performance standard that justifies not investing. The third element is the diagnostic one, and in this pattern it takes a recognizable form: a dispositional claim about the non-adopting group — “the designers are just behind the engineers” and its variants. That sentence is the eroded standard. The dispositional explanation is not a commentary on the structure — it is the component that licenses the underinvestment and closes the loop. Where the stall appears, expect the sentence; it is a structural marker rather than a character assessment, and it is worth noticing in one’s own mouth and not only in other people’s.
Standard intervention (per the archetype, stated as the archetype’s playbook, not as advice): invest in capacity ahead of demand, and hold the performance standard constant — refuse to let the standard drift down to match observed performance.
What the obvious response does instead: pushing harder on adoption — more training, more evangelism, mandates, better prompts — raises demand against unchanged capacity, generates more bad first-runs, further erodes the standard (“see, they’re just behind”), and accelerates the stall. The obvious response is the archetype’s named failure mode.

A second shape co-occurs on the resource-allocation side: Success to the Successful (R2), where two parties draw on a shared limited resource — the lead’s attention and tooling budget — and early advantage compounds. It is secondary here because it explains the divergence rate, not the stall itself.
Leverage scan























































Candidate interventionMeadows levelNotesGit / CLI training for designers12 — ParameterTargets B2, the legible-but-non-binding constraintMore seats, better models, prompt training12 — ParameterWhere current action concentratesDesign-tool-native surface (Dev Mode MCP), no terminal required10 — Stock-and-flow structureReroutes who can touch what; dissolves B2 rather than training past itShorten the delay between substrate investment and visible quality gain9 — Delay lengthR1’s crux; rarely attempted because the delay is usually treated as fixedBuild a design-side oracle — visual regression, token conformance, slop scan8 — Balancing-loop strengthConverts B1 from a trial-terminator into an automatic gate: quality regulation stops depending on a human catching slop in the momentMake the constraint substrate an owned, resourced, measured deliverable5 — RulesChanges what the job is, not how much of it is doneFirst exposure routed to non-identity H-column work (localization, all-states, a11y annotation)6 — Information flowChanges which evidence enters the system first; near-free, large effect on Stock BRestate the goal from “designers use AI” to “designers own the constraint system it generates against”3 — GoalsChanges what the system is trying to doDrop the dispositional model for the structural one2 — ParadigmThis is the element the archetype names as licensing the underinvestment
Where action is currently concentrated: level 12 — parameters. Training, licenses, tooling, exhortation.
Where leverage actually sits, given the diagnosis: levels 8 and 3, with 2 as the enabling condition. Strengthening the balancing loop (an automated design-side oracle) is what stops B1 from killing trials at second one, because it moves quality regulation off the human eye and onto a gate. Changing the goal from tool-adoption to constraint-ownership is what makes the substrate investment in R1 rational for the person being asked to make it. And the paradigm level matters here not for philosophical reasons but mechanically: while “they’re behind” holds, the archetype’s eroded standard stays eroded and capacity investment stays unjustified.
Boundary flag
Flagged — not a routine internal dynamic. The parties bearing the consequences of this transition (the designers, whose craft column is the exposed one per designer-seat-under-ai, and whose junior on-ramp is the one being cut) are not represented in the framing of the problem. “Adoption” is set as the goal by someone outside that group, and the affected group’s objection is currently coded as resistance rather than as input — which structurally removes the only channel through which the goal itself could be contested.
Note the specific asymmetry: objection (1), the output is bad, is a substantive claim about the system that happens to be largely correct, and coding it as resistance discards real information. A boundary-critique or SSM pass (soft-systems-methodology, CATWOE) is warranted before acting, because the question “is adoption the right goal, and whose?” is genuinely contested and this diagnosis takes the goal as given.
What this diagnosis depends on

The constraint substrate really is low or absent. If a governed design system with real tokens already exists and the output is still bad, R1 is not the driver and the diagnosis is wrong — the cause would be tool configuration (prompt-to-markup rather than map-to-library, per ai-design-to-code-pipeline), which is a level-12 fix after all.
The designers’ quality judgments are accurate — they are seeing real slop, not novelty aversion. If they would reject good output as readily, B1’s setpoint is identity defense rather than quality regulation, and the leverage moves to level 3 alone.
Engineering’s adoption is explained by pre-existing oracle stock, not by selection. If programmers simply self-select as more tool-curious, R2 weakens substantially and the asymmetry is partly dispositional after all — the one reading this diagnosis is built to exclude, so it deserves the hardest check.
Adoption has actually been attempted and stalled, rather than never seriously resourced. If the latter, there is no stall dynamic to diagnose — it is an unfunded initiative, and none of the loops above are load-bearing. (Objection B argues this is not merely an assumption but an open question the note has no evidence on.)
The asymmetry is about verification capacity rather than product-market sequencing — added after the adversarial pass, and the note’s most vulnerable point. The competing explanation is that coding assistants were trained, benchmarked, sold, and shipped for developers first, so programmers adopted because the tools were built for them, not because they held oracles. That explanation is simpler, predicts a different action (“wait, or buy better design tools”), and this note holds no evidence separating the two. Distinguishing test: find a discipline with weak verification infrastructure but first-class tooling (marketing copy, support, sales enablement). Fast adoption there favors the tooling explanation; a similar stall favors this note’s.

Forward simulation — the level-8 intervention (/second-order, 2026-07-29)
Action traced: build a design-side verification oracle (visual-regression baselines, token-conformance check, slop scan) and gate generated output on it, before pushing further adoption. Chosen over the level-3 goal restatement because it is the concrete action; level 3 is an enabling condition without a cascade of its own. Sign-neutral by design — [+] favorable, [-] unfavorable, [~] mixed.
First order: (1) generated output acquires a pass/fail signal not dependent on a designer noticing slop in the moment; (2) building the oracle forces substrate work, since rules must exist to encode; (3) engineering effort is spent on a design-side deliverable before any adoption gain is visible.
Second order — who responds

Designers, subset one [+] — test the gate against their own judgment (“does it catch what I catch?”). Where it agrees, trust accrues to the gate even while trust in the generator stays low. This is the intended conversion.
Designers, subset two [-] — recognise the gate as an encoding of their discrimination and read it as automating the judgment that makes them valuable. Not paranoia: designer-seat-under-ai argues exactly that negative taste commoditizes. Expect withholding of the rules that would make the gate good.
Programmers [~] — inherit a design gate in CI they didn’t ask for. Noisy → they mark it non-blocking and it silently becomes advisory. Tight → false positives escalate to designers, raising designer interrupt load before lowering it.
The lead [+] — gets the first legible design-side adoption metric (pass rates, drift counts), which changes what can be resourced. See the Goodhart branch below.
CI/build owner [-] — visual regression is slow and storage-heavy per breakpoint and theme; build times rise, creating pressure to sample or disable.
Design-system maintainer, if one exists [+] — gets a forcing function and, for the first time, a downstream consumer for substrate work. This is the intended R1 fix. If no such role exists, that absence is the finding.
Delivery/product managers [-] — substrate work has no user-visible output for weeks; under delivery pressure it is cut first, yielding a half-built oracle.
Designers, on the costly signal [~] — the org spending engineering effort on a design-side deliverable before demanding adoption is itself evidence the objection was heard. This may move adoption more than the oracle does.

Third order — what changes structurally

Gate-testing scales → the rule set becomes a written encoding of house taste — the first time the quality bar exists outside individual heads. That makes it transferable (onboarding, contractors, agents) and contestable (arguable, which instinct never was). Note the collision: this is the same structural change subset two feared, valued oppositely. Favorable and unfavorable branches converge on one outcome with opposite signs.
Withholding scales → the oracle encodes only what is safe to give away (spacing, contrast, token conformance) and never what constitutes taste. Still useful as a drift-catcher, but the leverage claim degrades: B1 keeps terminating trials on the axis the gate doesn’t cover.
Non-blocking scales → advisory gates get ignored per the automation-complacency base rate the vault already carries (human-role-roadmap-under-ai). The system returns to its pre-intervention state while believing it has a gate — strictly worse than no gate, because the belief suppresses further investment.
Half-built oracle scales → coverage correlates with what was easy to encode, so the gate is strong on spacing and contrast and blind on layout, hierarchy, and register — exactly the axes carrying the slop signal. Confidence rises precisely where discrimination is weakest.
Metrics scale → Goodhart: pass rate becomes the adoption KPI, and the cheapest way to raise it is to loosen rules or generate only inside the well-covered zone — a rising number attached to falling ambition. [speculative — stop]; depends on whether anyone is rewarded on the number.

Temporal triple





























HorizonDominant effectNon-obvious consequenceSign flip?10 minAn engineering ticket, and a request to designers for rulesThe request itself repositions designers from objectors to authorsNo10 monthsEither the gate exists with a floor under generation, or the investment was cut and the standard eroded furtherEither way the org now holds a written quality bar or a demonstrated inability to write one — and the second is decision-relevant information it did not previously havePossible — this is where the branch resolves10 yearsQuality regulation is infrastructural rather than personalDesigners who authored the bar hold the constraint-ownership seat; those who withheld are competing on the axis that commoditizedYes — the branch that felt protective at 10 minutes is the costly one at 10 years
Speculation flags: the Goodhart branch assumes pass rate becomes a rewarded metric (org-specific, unverified); “costly signal beats the oracle” is plausible but unmeasured; the 10-year designer branch inherits designer-seat-under-ai’s constraint-ownership claim, which is a forecast, not a floor.
Worth base-rate checking (/reference-class), both signs — favorable: do automated gates accrue trust in the tool among skeptical practitioners, or only in the gate? do forcing functions get design-system substrate built where direct requests failed? Unfavorable: how often do slow/noisy CI gates get marked non-blocking within a year? how often does delayed-payoff capacity investment survive delivery pressure (this is the Growth-and-Underinvestment base rate itself)? do experts withhold tacit rules when encoding them into systems that could replace their judgment?
Adversarial pass (/red-team, 2026-07-29) — three hits, kept visible
The diagnosis was attacked on its own structure. Two objections landed hard enough to change the note (corrections applied above); the third reframes what the note is for.
Objection A — the diagnosis is self-sealing. The move that declares “designers are behind” to be the archetype’s eroded standard converts the strongest evidence against a structural reading into evidence for it. If the deciding side voices it, that confirms the archetype; if they stop, that is the recommended paradigm shift; adoption confirms the fix, non-adoption means the substrate wasn’t built. No observation disconfirms. Note also that the original load-bearing assumption #3 offers a falsifier scoped to R2, the secondary loop — the core (R1, B1, the archetype) is left unfalsifiable. Protecting the core and offering a falsifier on the periphery is the shape /falsifiability-scan files under self-sealing.
Objection B — there may be no loop at all. A stock’s direction requires history, and none exists. The evidence is one conversational report of two objections: we do not know how many attempts were made, what was shown, or whether trust was ever high enough to shrink from. The Sources section admitted this and the body then stated directions as fact anyway — naming the “modeling fetish” anti-pattern is not avoiding it. Correction applied: both stock directions downgraded to hypothesis.
Objection C — B1 and B2 are not loops. Balancing loops require closure; these don’t have it. B1 is a decision rule, B2 a threshold test. This matters because level 8 — “balancing-loop strength” — was the top-ranked leverage point, and you cannot strengthen a loop that is not one. Relatedly, R1’s “asymmetric delay” is two signals with different arrival times — an information-timing property, not a stock-flow lag — so calling it Meadows level 9 imports the vocabulary without the mechanic. Correction applied: labels fixed above. Re-ranked: the oracle intervention is better read as level 6 — information flow (it changes what evidence about generated output reaches whom, and how fast) than as level 8. It may still be the right action; the structural justification originally given for it was wrong.
Pre-mortem — how this note ages badly by mid-2027

The oracle gets built, adoption still doesn’t move, and the real blocker turns out to be operational — allocation, contractor status, nobody scheduling the work. Four real-sounding loops, elegantly mapping the wrong system.
“Designers are behind” turns out to be about two specific people, not a discipline. The generalization from a small interpersonal situation to a structural claim about design-vs-engineering is what aged worst.
The boundary flag was the most valuable section and got ignored, because it sits after the leverage table and readers act on tables.
The note becomes the thing it warned about: a sophisticated vocabulary for explaining designer non-adoption without ever asking the designers. “It’s structural, not dispositional” is more comfortable than either “they’re lazy” or “I might be wrong about what they need,” and it licenses another six months of not asking.
Assumption #2 breaks — the quality judgments were partly novelty aversion, designers reject good output in a blind test, B1’s setpoint was identity defense, and the oracle addressed the wrong mechanism.

Weakest load-bearing claim — not the archetype. It is the note’s own headline: “the adoption asymmetry is not a willingness gap, it is an accumulated-verification-capacity gap.” Everything downstream points at the stock that claim names. It rests entirely on the analogy that engineering’s oracles caused engineering adoption — asserted, never argued — and there is a simpler competing explanation the note never engages: the tools were built for programmers first. Coding assistants were trained on code, benchmarked on code, sold to developers, and shipped inside developer tools; design tooling lags because vendors aimed at code first. Under that explanation the asymmetry is a product-market fact with nothing to do with verification capacity, and the implied action is “wait, or buy better design tools” — not “build an oracle.” The note holds no evidence that distinguishes the two, and the competing explanation is arguably simpler.
Verdict: revise, don’t discard. The two reinforcing loops and the boundary flag survive. The leverage ranking needed re-grounding (done), the stock directions needed demotion (done), and the headline claim needs the competing explanation stated beside it rather than assumed away — which is now recorded as assumption 5 below.
What this trace did not do

Did not recommend an intervention — the leverage scan is a map, not a plan
Did not verify that the diagnosed loops produce the observed history (that needs outcome data over time, which does not exist here)
Did not trace any specific action forward (/second-order after picking one)
Did not run an adversarial pass (/red-team before this drives a decision)

Related

systems-thinking-engineering — the canonical vocabulary: stocks/flows, the eight archetypes, Meadows’ leverage points
soft-systems-methodology — the follow-up lens the boundary flag calls for, where the problem statement itself is contested
visual-ai-slop-fingerprints — why objection (1) is substantially correct; the catalog B1 fires on
ai-design-to-code-pipeline — the map-to-library vs. emit-fresh-markup distinction that decides whether a first run confirms or disconfirms the objection
dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model — the amplifier effect: AI magnifies existing organizational strengths and weaknesses, and none of the seven capabilities is about which assistant you buy. The org-level statement of this note’s structural claim
design-system-failure-modes — the substrate’s own decay dynamics; why Stock A has an outflow even when nobody touches it

cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — the load B1 carries when quality regulation runs on a human rather than a gate

Sources
/structural-trace run 2026-07-29, instanced on a real delivery team and generalized for publication — the situational specifics are stripped because the structure, not the instance, is the claim. The situational inputs are a single-vantage account — the designers’ own framing is not represented here, which is precisely what the boundary flag records. Loop structure, archetype match, and leverage ranking are analytic output, not measurement: no outcome history was available to test whether the diagnosed loops actually generate the observed behavior, so anti-pattern one in the skill body (“modeling fetish”) is live and the load-bearing assumptions above are the honest counterweight.
Vocabulary and archetype/leverage definitions from systems-thinking-engineering (Senge’s archetypes; Meadows’ twelve leverage points). Supporting claims about slop, the design-to-code distinction, and the amplifier effect inherit the verified/unverified status of their source notes.

ai/design-side-ai-onramp.title: A Design-Side AI On-Ramp — the Intervention Companion
ai/design-side-ai-onramp.content:
A Design-Side AI On-Ramp — the Intervention Companion
Third note in a set. designer-seat-under-ai forecasts what design work becomes; design-side-ai-adoption-stall diagnoses why the transition stalls; this one is what to actually do — the part the diagnosis was structurally forbidden from producing, since /structural-trace ends at the map.
Read the epistemic warning before the sequence. The diagnosis this builds on survived its adversarial pass only partially: its headline claim (the asymmetry is an accumulated-verification-capacity gap) has an undefeated simpler competitor — that coding assistants were trained, benchmarked, sold, and shipped for developers first, so programmers adopted because the tools were built for them. Nothing in that note distinguishes the two.
So this sequence is deliberately built in two tiers: moves that are correct under either explanation, and moves that bet on the capacity explanation. Front-load the first tier; gate the second on the test in step 0c. An intervention plan that assumed its own diagnosis would be repeating the error the diagnosis was written to catch.
Step 0 — three checks, any of which can kill the plan
Do these before spending anything. They are ordered by how cheap they are and how completely they can invalidate what follows.
0a. Ask the designers, on the record. The diagnosis’s own pre-mortem names the failure mode this guards against: a sophisticated vocabulary for explaining designer non-adoption without ever asking the designers. “It’s structural, not dispositional” is more comfortable than either “they’re lazy” or “I might be wrong about what they need,” and it will license months of not asking. Three questions that produce decision-relevant answers rather than agreement:

What exactly did you see that was bad? — get the artifact. If it was raw prompt-to-markup output, the objection is about configuration and not about AI, and ai-design-to-code-pipeline’s map-to-library vs. emit-fresh-markup distinction is the whole fix.
What would have had to be true for that output to be acceptable? — this is a specification of the constraint substrate, elicited from the people who hold it.
What’s the last thing you did by hand that you’d have been glad to hand off? — this is the on-ramp task, self-selected. Strictly better than choosing for them, and it makes step 2 nearly free.

0b. The substrate check. Do governed tokens exist? Component contracts? A written definition of done for a screen? If not, the quality objection is correct, the blocker is not the designers, and they are simply the people positioned to notice first. This is dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model’s amplifier effect at the team level: AI magnifies existing organizational strengths and weaknesses, and none of its capabilities is about which assistant you buy.
0c. The distinguishing test. Find a discipline in the org with weak verification infrastructure but first-class AI tooling — marketing copy, support, sales enablement. Fast adoption there favors the tools-were-built-for-programmers explanation, and the tier-2 moves below are mis-aimed: the right response is to wait or buy better design tooling. A comparable stall favors the capacity explanation. Caveat that matters: if no such comparison group exists in your org, this test does not resolve, and tier 2 stays a bet rather than becoming a conclusion. Don’t launder an absent comparison into a green light.
Tier 1 — correct under either explanation
Cheap, robust, and worth doing even if the diagnosis is wrong.
1. Separate AI adoption from developer-infrastructure adoption. Nobody should be onboarded through a git CLI. That filters on terminal comfort rather than on taste, which is the opposite of what the seat needs. Use design-tool-native surfaces (Dev Mode MCP — tool surface verified in designer-seat-under-ai) so no terminal is required. The skill actually wanted is diff literacy — read a generated change, call drift or no-drift — which is a far lower bar than authoring commits or resolving conflicts.
2. First exposure from the High column, outside the identity zone. Localization stress, all-states generation, accessibility annotation, content audit, documentation maintenance. Not “generate a UI.” The reason is mechanical rather than diplomatic: the quality-bar decision rule is the fastest-firing element in the whole system, so a first exposure on the axis where it fires terminates the trial before anything else can run. If 0a produced a self-selected task, use that instead.
3. Don’t pitch speed to seniors. The call-center RCT in ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms: novices +34%, experienced agents ~unchanged. Telling a senior designer they’ll be faster at their current work is a promise that observably will not pay, and when it doesn’t you have spent the credibility that tier 2 needs. The honest pitch is coverage they cannot currently reach — every state, every locale, every variant.
Tier 2 — bets on the capacity explanation
More expensive, higher payoff, and wrong-footed if 0c comes back favoring the tooling explanation.
4. Ship one narrow oracle — and name its boundary in its own output. The forward simulation found the specific failure mode here, and it is nastier than “incomplete”: coverage tracks what was easy to encode, so a half-built gate ends up strong on spacing and contrast and blind on layout, hierarchy, and register — exactly the axes carrying the slop signal (visual-ai-slop-fingerprints). Confidence rises precisely where discrimination is weakest. Two rules follow:

Pick one axis and say so. A check that announces “this validates tokens and nothing else” is honest. A “design quality gate” that only validates tokens is actively harmful.
Blocking, or don’t build it yet. Advisory gates get ignored per the automation-complacency base rate (human-role-roadmap-under-ai), and the failure compounds: the belief that a gate exists suppresses further investment, making a half-hearted gate worse than none.

Ranking note: the diagnosis originally rated this Meadows level 8 (balancing-loop strength). The adversarial pass corrected that — the mechanism it strengthens is not a loop — and re-ranked it to level 6, information flow. It changes what evidence about generated output reaches whom and how fast. Still worth doing; the original justification was wrong.
5. Hand over the constraint system as territory, with authority attached. Tokens, DESIGN.md, the escalation policy naming what must reach a human (design-tokens, ai-verification-stack-web). Two findings shape how:

The request repositions before the artifact delivers. Asking designers to author the rules moves them from objectors to authors, and the forward simulation suggests that repositioning may move adoption more than the oracle does. But framing decides the sign entirely: arriving as tooling chores, it is a cost; arriving as “you decide what the machine is allowed to do,” it is authority.
Expect withholding, and don’t argue it away. Some will read encoding their taste as automating themselves — and they are not wrong that negative taste commoditizes (skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age). The honest counter is the ten-year sign flip the forward simulation found: whoever authors the bar holds the constraint-ownership seat; whoever withholds ends up competing on the axis that commoditized. Protective at ten minutes, costly at ten years.

6. Hold the standard. The archetype’s prescribed intervention is to invest in capacity ahead of demand and refuse to let the performance standard erode to match observed performance. Operationally: write down what “adopted” means before starting, and do not revise it downward when the delay runs long. This is the hardest item and the most load-bearing, because the eroded standard in this pattern has a recognizable form — a dispositional claim about the group that hasn’t adopted, of the shape “the designers are just behind the engineers.” Treat that sentence as a structural marker rather than a conclusion, including when it is your own.
What not to do
The archetype’s named failure mode is pushing harder: more training, more evangelism, mandates, prompt coaching. That raises demand against unchanged capacity, produces more bad first runs, further erodes the standard, and accelerates the stall. It is also where action naturally concentrates, because it is the visible end.
Three specific traps from the forward simulation:

Don’t make pass rate a KPI. The cheapest way to raise it is to loosen rules or generate only inside the well-covered zone — a rising number attached to falling ambition.
Don’t build the oracle from what’s easy to encode. See step 4.
Don’t ship an advisory gate. See step 4.

Leading indicators at ~3 months
Both directions, because watching only for confirmation is how this note would fail.
Working: designers test the gate against their own judgment unprompted · someone asks for a rule to be added · the first hand-off request originates from a designer rather than from you · a rejected output gets discussed in terms of which rule it broke rather than “it looks wrong.”
Failing: the gate gets marked non-blocking · substrate work is the first thing cut in a pressured sprint · adoption metrics rise while the work gets visibly blander · you catch yourself explaining designer non-adoption structurally to someone who didn’t ask. That last one is the pre-mortem’s failure mode arriving on schedule, and it is the earliest signal available.
The boundary this note inherits
design-side-ai-adoption-stall carries a boundary flag, and it applies with more force here because this note acts. The people bearing the consequences of the transition are not represented in the framing; “adoption” was set as the goal from outside the affected group; and their objection is currently coded as resistance when objection (1) — the output is bad — is largely correct. Step 0a is the minimum response to that, not a full one. If the goal itself deserves contesting rather than assuming, that is soft-systems-methodology territory and this note does not do it.
Related

design-side-ai-adoption-stall — the diagnosis this acts on, including the /second-order cascade and /red-team findings quoted throughout, and the competing explanation that gates tier 2
designer-seat-under-ai — the forecast: which task columns are exposed, the learn-instead-of-Figma table, the verified toolchain step 1 and step 5 draw on
dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model — the amplifier effect behind check 0b
ai-design-to-code-pipeline — map-to-library vs. emit-fresh-markup, the fix if 0a shows a configuration problem
visual-ai-slop-fingerprints — the axes a narrow oracle will not cover, and why that matters more than the coverage it has
human-role-roadmap-under-ai — the owned-oracle machinery and the rubber-stamping base rate behind “blocking or don’t build it”
ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms — the novice/experienced productivity split behind step 3
soft-systems-methodology — the follow-up the boundary flag calls for

Sources
Internal synthesis (2026-07-29). This note is recommendation, unlike its two companions — the forecast note is argument and the diagnosis note is explicitly recommendation-free. Its content derives from the /second-order and /red-team passes recorded in design-side-ai-adoption-stall; every claim inherits the status recorded there, and the two-tier structure exists specifically because that note’s headline claim did not survive the adversarial pass intact.
Not validated in practice. No step below has been run and measured; the leading indicators are the proposed test, not evidence. Situational inputs are a single-vantage account of one team, generalized for publication, and the affected group’s own framing is absent — see the boundary section.

ai/designer-seat-under-ai.title: The Designer Seat Under AI — the Task Census Read Against the Prediction Cluster
ai/designer-seat-under-ai.content:
The Designer Seat Under AI — the Task Census Read Against the Prediction Cluster
delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix ends with “the read for an architecture-owning engineering seat,” and delivery-org-matrix-desk-rescoring executes it on 21 engineering rows. The designer seat never got the same treatment — even though the source artifact was a Designer Task × Phase Matrix first and a delivery-org superset second. This note is that read: the vault’s role-prediction cluster pointed at design work, at task granularity, with the comfortable answers tested rather than repeated.
It is a forecast, and the note’s job is to make it falsifiable rather than plausible. Written 2026-07-29 in response to “speculate what designers’ work will look like.”
Epistemic status — the discounts this note inherits
Carried forward from the matrix cluster, because they matter more here than in the engineering read (the design rows are where the source’s own reasoning was thinnest):

Every fit score below is an unverified third-party hypothesis. The source PDFs were AI-assisted, produced outside this vault, against references not available to us. The artifact’s own framing: “a starting hypothesis, not a verdict.”
The 48-task Designer matrix was never transcribed into the vault. Only the 87-task delivery-org superset lives in delivery-org-task-matrix-data. The designer PDF supplied per-task rationales; those are unavailable here, so the designer-specific reasoning below is reconstructed from the superset plus the vault’s design cluster.
The row selection is our inference. The PDFs advertise role tags but don’t render them per-row, so “which rows are the designer’s” has no source-side attribution to check against — same caveat delivery-org-matrix-desk-rescoring carries for its desk cut.
Counts are properties of one enumeration, not measurements of design work. Slice the production tasks finer and the High share grows.
Consensus echo. “The designer becomes a director/curator” is the mainstream 2026 take. The matrix and this vault likely sit on the same 2025–2026 corpus, so their agreement is correlation, not confirmation.
“Designer” here means product/UX designer in a software delivery org — the register the source matrix and the vault’s front-end cluster both assume. Brand, editorial, motion, and industrial design are not covered, and the predictor would sort them differently: they sit closer to the authorship-premium destination (speculation #6) and further from the constraint-system one (#1). Reading this note as “designers” full stop is a scope error it would otherwise invite.
The design-specific labor evidence is one row. ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms has exactly one graphic-design line — restructuring; commodity assets near-term; image freelancers’ work declined post-DALL-E/Midjourney ○ (extracted, not verified). Everything else below is inference from general mechanisms, not measured design outcomes.

The two instruments
The predictor (what-survived-machine-conquest): a role died where the human was a pipe — an input→output transformation fully specifiable as procedure, with nothing else bundled in. It survived where judgment, trust, liability, presence, or authorship was inseparable from the transformation.
The census (delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix): agent fit is scored on a re-encoding-vs-origination axis (High = re-encoding decided things; Partial = agent drafts, human calibrates; Low = origination, tacit, or permission-bound). Its phase gradient is the finding: fit rises as decisions get made.
The designer cut of the census
Designer-relevant rows from the 87, grouped by phase. Fit letters are the source’s; family marks are this vault’s re-judgment #5 split — (a) = will-bound, a floor; (b) = tacit/live, a capability claim and therefore a forecast. † marks rows the cluster disputes.

Discovery & Research — qualitative research L (b) · requirements elicitation L (b) · synthesis into insights P · ecosystem & stakeholder mapping P · research transcription & coding H · content & competitor audit H
Definition & Strategy — problem reframing L (a) · vision & north-star L (a) · scope & MVP L (a) · information architecture P · content strategy & modeling P · metric & KPI definition P
Ideation & Concept — workshop / co-creation facilitation L (b) · ideation / concept generation P · service concept development P · journey mapping P
Design & Production — voice & tone L† (identity decision is (a); candidate generation already P) · UI / visual design P · design system components P · UX writing / microcopy P · service blueprinting P · user flows & task analysis P · wireframing H† · prototyping H · localization / readability H · accessibility implementation H · content production & entry H
Validation & Testing — usability testing L (b) · heuristic / design review P · A/B test design & analysis P · accessibility audit H · content & QA validation H
Delivery & Handoff — stakeholder communication / decks P · developer handoff & specs H · documentation & artifact maintenance H
Monitoring & Iteration — journey / service performance review P · KPI monitoring H · content effectiveness analysis H · user feedback triage H · governance & content maintenance H

Two structural facts fall straight out:

Design & Production is the only phase in the whole 87-task matrix that is majority-High (11 of 19). Definition & Strategy and Ideation contain zero High tasks between them (0 of 23).
The designer’s exposure is almost perfectly inverted from the profession’s self-image. The craft phase is the exposed one; the phase most designers treat as overhead — definition, scope, identity — is where the only durable floor sits.

Six speculations
1. The deliverable stops being the artifact and becomes the constraint system. What ships is a token dictionary (design-tokens’s three tiers), component contracts, Code Connect mappings, a DESIGN.md-style identity spec, and — the new one — an escalation policy naming which generated screens must reach a human. Mockups become disposable probes. ai-design-to-code-pipeline already calls this the “upstream” move; the sharper claim is that upstream becomes the only durable artifact, because everything downstream of it regenerates for free.
2. Volume explodes and review becomes the job — but review alone doesn’t hold. Forty variants, every state, twelve locales at zero marginal cost. Then human-role-roadmap-under-ai’s hardened finding bites: rubber-stamping is the modal outcome of a retained human gate, not a tail risk (Parasuraman & Manzey 2010 — complacency in experts, not fixed by practice, worst on highly-reliable systems). So the designer who survives owns an independent oracle they didn’t author: perceptual-diff baselines, a11y regression gates, a brand-conformance linter, the squint test as an actual gate. Predicted artifact of this: a real title around it — design-system oracle owner, design QA lead.
3. The middle hollows out, and it takes the junior rung with it. Wireframing, prototyping, redlines, spec production, asset variation — the High column — are exactly the tasks that trained juniors. The documented mechanism in ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms is entry-level attrition, not role death: 22–25-year-olds in the most-exposed jobs −16% relative while experienced workers held steady ✅ (the vault also carries a differently-scoped ~20%-from-peak figure for software developers specifically in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age — same paper family, different cut; don’t merge them). Corollary: the portfolio-of-screens dies as a hiring signal — anyone can generate forty screens. The signal moves to “show me a system you governed, and a call you made that turned out wrong.”
4. Taste splits into two goods, and only one stays a designer skill. visual-ai-slop-fingerprints is already the automation of negative taste — untinted neutrals, reflexive gradient headlines, glassmorphism with nothing behind it — and it ships as a CLI scanner. That layer commoditizes. The catalog’s own limits section is the load-bearing sentence: “avoiding all ten still leaves a vast space of forgettable interfaces.” What remains is positive taste — committing to a specific non-obvious direction and defending it — which is not a checklist skill and is exactly what the catalog says it cannot produce.
5. The most defensible ground is what designers currently file under overhead. Voice & tone is the single Low in the entire production phase, and the cluster splits even that: the identity decision is family (a), the generation of candidate voices is already Partial. Same shape for problem reframing, vision, scope. The durable work is the decision, not the exploration — and exploration is the part most designers enjoy.
6. An authorship-premium tier appears — as a market segment, not a career. what-survived-machine-conquest’s measured mechanisms: the handmade effect (~17% price premium, Fuchs et al. J. Marketing 2015) and AI-label devaluation (identical artworks rated lower when labeled AI-made, d=0.57, even though >70% couldn’t tell them apart — Horton, White & Iyengar, Scientific Reports 2023). Expect a small high-margin “designed by a person, provenance attached” tier alongside abundant machine-composed interface work. But the same note supplies the cold water: Swiss watch employment went 90,000 → 28,000 while value concentrated into mechanicals (~86% of export value on shrinking units). Value migration is not headcount preservation.
Where the cluster contradicts the standard designer reassurance

“AI can’t do research, empathy, facilitation.” These are family (b) — qualitative research, requirements elicitation, workshop facilitation, usability testing. Family (b) rests on a capability claim, and capability-based safe lists have aged badly (creativity, Go, art, natural-sounding prose all fell off 2015-era lists within a decade). On the cluster’s own logic, the most-repeated designer reassurance is the least durable claim in the set.
“Design-system work is safe.” Design system components score Partial. What’s durable is the governance — and design-system-failure-modes says the modal org underfunds exactly that (the “done” illusion, TCO underfunding, drift, shadow systems). Safety here is conditional on doing the unglamorous half.
“I’ll move into product/strategy.” That is family (a), the real floor — but the floor guarantees the function survives, not the headcount. The cluster’s own qualification: will-bound work can consolidate into fewer chairs.
The one correction running the designer’s way is re-judgment #3. Wireframing scores High because it’s classified as re-encoding decided flows — but in practice wireframing is often where the deciding happens; the sketch is the argument. Origination hides inside nominally-productive design tasks, so the waterfall framing systematically over-scores High. Designers who can make that visible keep more than the census says.

What to learn instead of Figma craft
Sequenced by which crossing it binds, following human-role-roadmap-under-ai’s ordering (oracle first, because the base rate says willpower loses) and the operationalized format of skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age — every row gets a test you could fail, so the list isn’t a horoscope.















































SkillConcretely isTest you could failIs notVisual verification architecture (build first)Perceptual-diff baselines, a11y regression gates, a slop/brand linter, and a written escalation policy naming what must reach a humanSeed defects — a token drift, a contrast break, a slop tell — into a batch of generated screens; measure catch rate without the diff list”I’ll review it carefully.” The base rate says you won’tConstraint-system authorshipThree-tier semantic tokens, component contracts, Code Connect mappings, a DESIGN.md-style identity spec — the design system as the API the agent programs againstHand an agent your system plus a feature brief and nothing else: does the output compose your components, or emit fresh markup and raw hex?Maintaining a Figma component librarySpec / intent writing (compress — absorbed up-stack)A brief precise enough that output is judged against it, not against taste-in-the-momentSame feature, agent run with your spec vs. a raw ask — the spec must measurably cut iterationsA mood board, or a rationale written after the factPositive taste, made defensibleCommitting to a specific non-obvious direction and defending it in one sentence tied to contextFor your last ten visual decisions, name the alternative rejected and why. “It looked better” = a default, not a decisionKnowing the ten slop fingerprints — that’s the half being automatedDiff literacyReading a generated PR: did it compose the library or fork it? Running the app; working the design-tool→repo loopGiven a generated PR, call drift or no-drift without asking an engineerBecoming a frontend engineerProblem selection & scope (the will-bound seat)Killing a direction early; the one-paragraph why-this-why-now; owning the scope callTrack record — did what you chose to design get used?”Strategic thinking” as a slide
Stop over-investing in: high-fidelity mockup production, redlines and handoff specs, variation generation, per-locale layout by hand, and the portfolio-of-screens as the career artifact. All sit in the High column; all are the skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age “first-draft production of anything” row wearing design clothes.
The hedge on research craft. Because family (b) is a forecast, don’t drop interview and facilitation skill — but bank on the half that isn’t capability-bound: deciding which question is worth asking and owning the decision that follows, not being the one in the room.
How to run each task with AI
The how is set by the fit score, not the task name. Four modes:






























ModeAI doesYou doHThe workOwn an oracle you didn’t author. Without one it’s an unacknowledged handoff with a human fig leafPDraftsPick the rung and write what escalatesL (a)Attacks your answerMake the call — delegating here is delegating the goalL (b)Preps and synthesizes around the live partBe in the room, while that lasts
Discovery & Research. Qualitative research L(b) — AI drafts the discussion guide and does first-pass thematic coding; never accept a theme without re-reading raw quotes, because models produce coherent themes from noise. Requirements elicitation L(b) — pre-generate the question set from existing docs and flag contradictions between stakeholders’ written statements. Synthesis into insights P — demand a raw-quote citation per insight and check the quotes exist (rule 1 of bias-aware-authoring, applied to research). Stakeholder mapping P — agent drafts from docs; the power/influence reading is tacit and it will get it wrong confidently. Transcription & coding H — delegate; oracle is a random-k% spot-check against audio, since codebook drift is the failure. Content & competitor audit H — your rubric must exist first or the audit reflects the model’s priors.
Definition & Strategy (zero Highs — treat accordingly). Problem reframing / vision / scope L(a) — write your answer first, then have AI attack it (/disagree, /assumption-reversal, /second-order for cut consequences). Generating these for you is the one delegation the position argument says isn’t available. Information architecture P — model IA is training-corpus convention; validating against real users is the difference between your nav and the median site’s. Content strategy & modeling P — strong fit, it’s schema inference. Metric & KPI definition P — always ask for the gaming path of each metric.
Ideation & Concept. Ideation P — the trap is median collapse; a bare “brainstorm ideas for X” returns the training-data centre of mass. Use structured divergence (/scamper) and produce your own set first, then diff (augmented-vs-trained-thinking). Journey mapping P — excellent at current-state from tickets/analytics/session data; future-state is a design decision, not a summary. Facilitation L(b) — AI preps the stimulus set; reading the room is the moat, and it’s the moat that’s a forecast.
Design & Production (the exposed phase). Voice & tone L† — you write “what we sound like / never sound like,” agent generates at volume, a linter checks conformance. UI / visual design P — the whole game is whether it composes your library or emits fresh markup; gate with the slop checklist and a squint test. Design system components P — best genuine fit in the phase, but the prop API review is yours: a bad API is expensive and invisible in a screenshot. User flows & task analysis P — one of the strongest wins available, because completeness is exactly what models are good at and humans are bad at. Wireframing H† — if the flow is genuinely decided, delegate; if you’re still thinking, sketch it yourself, or you’re delegating the argument. Prototyping H — the real change is working code against real state instead of a clickable illusion. Localization H — render German / Arabic RTL / CJK before code exists; cheapest defensible win on the list. Accessibility implementation H — automated tooling catches only ~30–50% of WCAG issues (the vault’s own notes disagree inside that range); focus order, meaningful alt text and error-to-field association are the judgment remainder.
Validation & Testing. Usability testing L(b) — synthetic-user testing is marketed; treat its output as a hypothesis generator, never as evidence a design works. This is the family (b) bet in its purest form. Heuristic / design review P — strong fit, and it is negative taste automating in front of you. A/B design & analysis P — own the decision rule before seeing data; it will p-hack on request.
Delivery & Handoff. Developer handoff & specs H — this task is dissolving, not automating: the artifact becomes the PR, and still producing redlines is itself the signal. Documentation & artifact maintenance H — the quiet high-value win; the source matrix’s sharpest line is worth keeping verbatim, “the durable, illegible job — agents keep it current.” Stakeholder decks P — information transfer automates, trust-bearing communication doesn’t.
Monitoring & Iteration. KPI / content-effectiveness / feedback triage H — scheduled agents producing digests, but summarization smooths outliers and outliers are where design problems live; demand raw examples per theme. Governance & content maintenance H — the strongest automation case on the whole list (drift detection, orphan components, stale tokens), and the constraint-system deliverable in operational form.
Three rules across all of it: every H needs an oracle you didn’t author; produce first wherever your judgment is the product; what escalates is a design decision.
The toolchain — verified 2026-07-29
Named tools are the most perishable content here, and this cluster has a documented instance of the failure: two research briefs ~4 weeks apart both confidently listed the same wrong Figma MCP tool names (ai-design-to-code-pipeline). Every entry below was checked against its primary source on the date given. Categories are durable; product names are claims to re-verify at point of use.























































ToolStatus (checked 2026-07-29)What changed vs. the vault’s prior recordFigma Dev Mode MCP server✅ All seven previously-recorded tools still present (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_variable_defs, get_metadata, get_code_connect_map, get_code_connect_suggestions, add_code_connect_map)Surface has grown to 24 tools with a local/remote split — new: get_motion_context, get_figjam, generate_figma_design, search_design_system, send_code_connect_mappings, shader tools, asset up/download. The vault’s list is a correct subset, not the full surfaceThe confabulation trap✅ get_file / get_file_nodes / get_file_styles still absent — REST endpoint shapes, not MCP toolsWarning holds; keep distrusting briefs that list themDESIGN.md (Google Labs)✅ Exists, Apache 2.0, version alpha, spec under active developmentMaterially matured from “weeks old, emerging”: now ships a linter (11 rules — broken refs, contrast, orphaned tokens) and exports to Tailwind v3/v4 and W3C DTCGDTCG Design Tokens Format Module✅ 2025.10, Final Community Group Report, published 2025-10-28 — stable and intended for implementation, but not a W3C Standard and not on the Standards TrackNew to the vault. The token interchange format now has a stable spec; this is the durable layer under every token toolStyle Dictionary / Tokens Studio✅ SD v4 has first-class DTCG support; 2025.10 not fully supported — WIP in v5Prior status was “coverage unverified.” Pipeline shape: Tokens Studio (define) → DTCG JSON (exchange) → Style Dictionary (build)pbakaus/impeccable⚠️ The vault’s command was wrong. It is npx impeccable install, then /impeccable <command> (audit, polish, init) — not npx impeccable detectGrew from a scanner to 60 deterministic detector rules across 23 commands; /impeccable init generates PRODUCT.md + DESIGN.md, tying it to the format aboveAxe MCP server (Deque)✅ Upgraded from reported to verified — official (dequelabs/axe-mcp-server-public), bundled into Axe DevTools for Web, supports Claude Code / Cursor / Copilot / VS CodeWas “reported” in ai-augmented-ui-development; now confirmed. Coverage ceiling unchangedPlaywright Test Agents✅ Planner / Generator / Healer, introduced v1.56; current line 1.61 (2026-07-14); setup npx playwright init-agentsVersion moved; the three-agent model is intactv0 · Builder.io Visual Copilot · ShadCN Figma plugins⚠️ Not checked this pass — still vendor claims from a 2026-05 briefUnchanged. The durable content is the distinction, not the products: tools that map to your existing library fight drift; tools that emit fresh markup cause it
Learning order, if only some of it happens: (1) token architecture and semantic naming, because every other tool consumes it; (2) DESIGN.md and the agent-context layer, where taste becomes machine-readable; (3) the Figma MCP bridge plus Code Connect, which closes the loop so runs don’t restart from zero; (4) one oracle, actually gated on; (5) generation tools last — most marketed, least durable.
The tension worth keeping visible: a tools list is a depreciating-asset answer by construction, since tool proficiency is the exposed column this whole note describes. The durable read is the categories and the format specs, not the products.
What would revise this note

Jevons. Interface production gets 10× cheaper and product/surface/locale count expands enough to hold design headcount → the hollowing-out claim is about price, not employment. Genuinely live; the same falsifier skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age carries for code.
Visual oracles mature to where generated UI routinely ships without human visual review → speculation #2 collapses and the oracle-owner role never forms. This is skill-valuation’s second falsifier applied to the visual axis.
AI-label devaluation shrinks in newer cohort studies → the authorship premium was generational taste, not structure → speculation #6 dies.
Family (b) holds — AI-moderated research and synthetic-user testing demonstrably fail to produce decisions teams ship on → the research/facilitation moat is a floor after all, and the “least durable reassurance” claim inverts.
Will-bound design work visibly consolidates into fewer seats (one principal plus agents holding vision + scope + identity across what were several roles) → family (a) held as a function but failed as a headcount floor; strip any reassurance-reading from speculation #5.
The toolchain table goes stale faster than the argument. It is dated for that reason: the Figma MCP surface grew from 7 recorded tools to 24 in seven weeks, and one vault-recorded command (npx impeccable detect) was already wrong on first check. Treat a >6-month-old row as unverified, not as record.
The designer PDF’s rationales, once transcribed, turn out to disagree with the reconstruction here → the row-level reasoning above was our inference filling a gap, and should be replaced rather than defended.
