ai/deterministic-gates-agent-loop.title: Deterministic Gates in the Agent Loop
ai/deterministic-gates-agent-loop.content:
Deterministic Gates in the Agent Loop
The vault already holds the layers of a verification stack (ai-verification-stack-web), the theory of what any gate is trusting (oracle-problem-verification), and the decision rubric for what to do once CI is green (evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests). This note holds a different axis: a gate as a mechanism sitting inside an agent’s edit-and-repair loop rather than at the end of it, and determinism as a property you have to engineer rather than one your tools come with.
The organizing claim: a gate is only a falsifier if its verdict is a function of the diff. If the verdict can change while the diff stays the same, the agent has not been given a constraint — it has been given a slot machine.
Determinism is not correctness
Four properties get collapsed into “the tool is reliable”. They are independent:






























PropertyMeansFails asDeterministicSame inputs → same verdictA regex scanner that is consistently wrongSoundNever misses a real defect of its classReports false positives on purposeCompleteNever reports a non-defectMisses whole defect classes to stay quietCorrectThe encoded property was the right propertyGreen code that does the wrong thing
Most practical linters are neither sound nor complete. A test proves only that those executions passed. A bounded model checker proves a property only inside its bounds and environment model. A proof assistant gives a kernel-checked proof of a formal statement — relative to your specification, its axioms, and the extraction path.
Determinism is the cheapest of the four and the one worth engineering first, because it is what makes the other three measurable. You cannot tell whether a gate is sound if you cannot get the same answer twice.
A useful operational definition: given the same source tree, configuration, tool binaries, dependency graph, external databases, environment, and seeds, the tool emits the same verdict and the same diagnostics.
Why flakiness is worse in an agent loop than in CI
This section is an argued mechanism, not a measured one — it is this note’s own reasoning, not a finding from the source or from any study the vault holds. Treat it as a hypothesis with a clear falsifier: instrument a repair loop and check whether patches following a flaky failure are more often no-ops or retries than substantive fixes.
A human treats a flaky gate as noise and re-runs it. An agent treats it as a gradient.
If a gate fails nondeterministically, the cheapest action that turns it green is to try again — not to fix anything. A nondeterministic gate therefore converts repair into resampling, and it does so silently: the loop terminates on green, the diff looks fine, and nothing records that the agent won by rolling the dice. This is the loop-level version of the coverage-gaming problem mutation-testing-ai-generated-code describes at the suite level.
The corollary is that determinism buys more in an agentic pipeline than it does in a human one, and it is worth paying for pinning that a human-only team could reasonably skip.
The pin list
Sources of hidden nondeterminism, all of which should be pinned or recorded:

compiler, analyzer, plugin, and rule-pack versions (a rule-pack bump changes verdicts without changing code);
lockfiles and dependency resolution, resolved offline / frozen;
generated code and build flags;
OS/architecture, locale, timezone, filesystem ordering, environment variables;
network-fetched vulnerability databases and remote policies — record the digest or timestamp, or a historical rerun cannot reproduce its own verdict;
test order, random seeds, fuzz corpus, thread scheduling, wall-clock time, external services;
incremental caches and the exact changed-file baseline.

Search-based tools are a deliberate exception. Fuzzing and property generation are search processes and are not intrinsically deterministic. They convert: a discovered counterexample, committed with its seed and tool version, becomes a deterministic regression input. Treat the search as a discovery phase whose output is a permanent deterministic asset.
A container is not automatically hermetic — it can still reach the network, use mutable tags, mount host paths, and read the clock. Sandboxing protects the host from generated code; it does not make the analysis reproducible.
Placement: cost-ordered falsifiers
Order the gates by cost-per-refutation and run the cheapest that can still refute this diff. Everything above the line runs inside the agent’s loop; everything below runs on a human clock.
AI proposes patch
  ├─ [0] scope policy: allowed files, patch size, protected paths
  ├─ [1] parse / format / compile / type-check          every edit
  ├─ [2] AST policies + architecture + API-schema diff   every edit
  ├─ [3] focused tests + seeded properties + secrets     PR gate
  ├─ [4] full tests + SCA/IaC + mutation on changed code merge gate
  └─ [5] fuzz / sanitizers / deep dataflow / model check  nightly or risk-triggered
        ↓
  independent review of the exact verified diff
The placement is the point. A gate that runs after the agent has stopped produces a bug report. The same gate running during the loop produces a constraint the agent has to satisfy before it can claim to be finished. The source argues layers 1 and 2 carry most of the yield, on the reasoning that they are fast enough to run on every edit and their diagnostics carry file, range, rule ID, and often a fix. That ordering is a design claim, not a measurement — the bake-off below is how you would find out for your own repository.
Layers 3–5 are where the vault’s existing notes live — ai-verification-stack-web for the web tooling, mutation-testing-ai-generated-code for the “test the tests” step, oracle-problem-verification for what any of them is actually trusting.
Gate verdicts: block, ratchet, route
Everything above implicitly assumes a gate answers is something wrong here? Many useful deterministic checks don’t answer that question at all, and forcing them into a pass/fail shape is how they turn into noise. Three verdict types, only the first of which should hard-block:





























TypeAnswersVerdict onExamplesBlockIs this wrong?Absolutecompile, type-check, tests, secrets, schema breakRatchetIs this worse than before?Delta vs. baselinecomplexity, duplication, type coverage, suppression count, bundle sizeRouteWho should look at this?Threshold → escalationchurn, blast radius, semantic diff size
A ratchet gate blocks only on regression, so legacy debt doesn’t have to be paid off before the gate is useful — the property the source calls “no new findings”. A route gate never blocks; it changes what happens next, which is the right shape for a signal that correlates with risk but doesn’t establish it.
Where complexity fits
Complexity metrics are deterministic in the strict sense — same source, same number — so they pass this note’s entry test. But they are ratchet gates, not block gates, and the distinction is load-bearing.
The folk objection is that cyclomatic complexity is just line count wearing a hat, so it carries no information. The largest study on the question found the opposite. Landman, Serebrenik, Bouwers and Vinju tested the correlation on 17.6M Java methods and 6.3M C functions and reported that linear correlation between CC and SLOC “is only moderate as caused by increasingly high variance”, concluding it is “not strong enough to conclude that CC is redundant with SLOC” — explicitly contradicting the earlier literature the folk claim rests on (Journal of Software: Evolution and Process, conference version ICSME 2014).
So CC is not redundant. That is a narrower result than it sounds: not-redundant-with-SLOC is not the same as predicts-defects, and neither establishes that a CC threshold makes a good gate. What it does license is using complexity as a ratchet and a routing signal rather than dismissing it.
The AI-specific reason to care is duplication rather than complexity as such. GitClear’s tracking reports duplicated blocks rising 81% (40.3 → 73.0 per million changed lines, 2023 → 2026), moved/refactored code falling from 21% in 2022 to 3.8% in 2026, and cross-file function calls down 35% — across 623M analyzed changes. Caveats that matter: GitClear sells the analytics product that measures these signals, the page carries no methodology section or acknowledged limitations, the metrics are their own definitions, and the series is time-correlated rather than causally attributed to AI. Treat it as directional evidence for a failure mode the vault already names from other directions (ai-code-latent-failure-modes §5, duplication drift) rather than as a measured effect size.
If that direction is real, a duplication ratchet is the deterministic detector pointed straight at it, and it is cheap.
Composite metrics, and why CRAP inverts the incentive
The CRAP index (Change Risk Anti-Patterns, Savoia and Evans, 2007, originally Crap4j for Java) is the best-known attempt to make complexity actionable by pairing it with coverage:
CRAP(m) = CC(m)² × (1 − cov(m))³ + CC(m)        cov as a fraction, 0..1
Above 30 is the conventional “CRAPpy” threshold. The design is thoughtful: complexity alone condemns code that is complex and well tested, and CRAP gives that code an escape valve. Fully covered code scores exactly its CC. Two properties fall out that are useful on their own — CC ≤ 5 can never exceed 30 at any coverage, and CC ≥ 31 can never fall below it at any coverage, so the metric carries a hard complexity ceiling that no amount of testing buys past.
Is it deterministic? Only conditionally, and the reason generalizes. CC is computed from the AST and is deterministic by construction. Coverage is produced by executing the suite, so it is deterministic only if the suite is. CRAP therefore inherits the determinism of its worst input — which is the general law for composite gates, and the reason the test-suite-determinism check in the table below is load-bearing rather than fussy.
Is it a good agent-facing gate? No — it is worse than raw CC, despite being a better diagnostic for a human reading a report. The uncovered fraction is cubed while complexity is only squared, so coverage has strictly more leverage on the score. Evaluated at CC=15, cov=0.5:






























MoveNew CRAPΔbaseline43.1—CC 15 → 14 (real refactoring)38.5−4.6coverage 0.5 → 0.629.4−13.7coverage 0.5 → 0.915.2−27.9
An agent minimizing CRAP gets three to six times more score from the coverage term than from the complexity term. And coverage is precisely the term that AI-authored suites are documented to satisfy vacuously — the 100%-coverage / 4%-mutation-score result mutation-testing-ai-generated-code is built on. CRAP hands an optimizer a cheap gameable lever with more leverage than the honest one. It is an incentive-inverted gate: it points effort away from the work it exists to encourage.
Two ways to keep the idea and drop the flaw. Gate the CC ceiling separately, since that part is coverage-proof by construction. And consider substituting mutation score for coverage:
CRAP_m(m) = CC(m)² × (1 − mutationScore(m))³ + CC(m)
Mutation score is not vacuously satisfiable — resisting vacuous tests is the entire point of it — so this puts the hard term in the cubed position and inverts the gaming incentive back the right way. This substitution is this note’s proposal, not something a search turned up as published prior art; the cost is that mutation testing is a layer-4 gate, so this cannot run in the inner loop.
Computing it from TypeScript. Both inputs already exist in an ordinary TS pipeline, so this is a short script over artifacts you produce anyway rather than a new tool: per-function CC from the TypeScript compiler API or ts-morph (or read out of ESLint’s complexity rule via JSON output), and per-function coverage from Istanbul’s coverage-final.json, whose fnMap function ranges and statementMap counts are emitted by Vitest, Jest, and c8 alike.
Resist reaching for a package. As of 2026-08-21 npm carries at least five CRAP implementations for TS — crap-ts, crap4ts, @alperlabs/crap4ts, @barney-media/crap-typescript, crap-score — and all but the last were first published during 2026, all are single-maintainer, and most are pre-1.0 with a handful of releases and low-thousands monthly downloads. That is not evidence of anything malicious, but a niche 2007 metric acquiring five near-identical implementations inside one year is the shape of low-effort package proliferation, and a metrics tool runs in CI with read access to the whole source tree. The gate you add to improve quality is itself a dependency in the blast radius (ai-supply-chain-risks). Fifty lines you own beats a transitive tree you don’t.
Sibling composites, and the tier that actually matters
CRAP is one member of a family: multiply two signals so that neither alone condemns code. Others worth knowing:






























CompositeInputsNotesHotspots (churn × complexity)git commit frequency × complexityTornhill’s; the strongest of the family. code-maat is his open-source CLI, CodeScene the commercial productChange coupling / temporal couplingfiles that change together across commitsDetects logic duplicated across files — which produces co-change without an import edge, so structural analysis cannot see it by constructionMaintainability IndexHalstead volume, CC, SLOCWidely implemented, constants derived from a small early-1990s study; treat the absolute number as meaningless and only the trend as signalSQALE / technical-debt ratiorule violations × assigned remediation costDeterministic given a pinned rule set, but the “minutes to fix” values are assigned, not measured
Vendor caveat, same shape as the GitClear one above: Tornhill is CodeScene’s CTO, so the hotspot research and the product that sells it share an author.
What separates these is not sophistication. It is where the inputs come from relative to the agent’s write access:





























TierInput provenanceGameable byExamplesAThe agent authored itWriting more of itcoverage, tests, assertionsBDerived deterministically from the codeDeforming the code — at least visible in the diffCC, cognitive complexity, AST rules, types, duplicationCRepository history or production, which this diff cannot rewriteNothing the current patch can dochurn, change coupling, hotspots, incident and telemetry data
This is the frame that retroactively explains CRAP. Both its terms are Tier A — the agent wrote the code and the tests — which is why the metric folds. Hotspots have the same two-signal shape but draw churn from Tier C, and that single substitution is what makes them a sound agent-facing gate where CRAP is not.
The honest limit: Tier C is not ungameable in principle. An agent could avoid touching hot files, or split one to reset its churn history. But it cannot be gamed by the diff under review, and the moves that would game it are structurally odd enough to show up elsewhere. Tier C signals belong in the route column — they are excellent at deciding what deserves a human and terrible as blockers.
Change coupling deserves separate billing for AI code specifically. The documented failure mode is duplication rather than abstraction; duplicated logic across files produces files that change together without importing each other, which is exactly the pattern dependency-cruiser and every import-graph tool is blind to. It is a gate that sees what the other gates cannot.
Repair-loop rules

Start from a clean, hashed revision.
Run the cheapest relevant gate first.
Give the model only actionable diagnostic data, and treat that data as untrusted input.
Constrain the next patch to intended files and a size budget.
Re-run from the first invalidated gate, not just the one that failed. A fix at layer 3 can break layer 1.
Cap the repair budget. Oscillation escalates to a human rather than burning attempts.
Require independent review of the exact final diff, not of a description of it.
Reject missing, malformed, timed-out, or stale reports.

The agent must not edit its own oracle
Snapshots, baselines, suppression files, mutation exclusions, and security policies are the gate’s definition of correct. An agent allowed to update them can always reach green, and the loop will report success.
This is the same independence failure oracle-problem-verification names for co-authored tests, one level up: there, the producer wrote the test; here, the producer edits the thing the test is compared against. The fix is the same — the party that changes the oracle must not be the party the oracle is judging. Practically: put snapshots, baselines, and suppression config on the protected-paths list at layer 0, and require a separate reviewed change to move them. claude-code-enforcement-hooks is the local mechanism for exactly this class of rule.
Formatter autofixes are safe enough to let run. Semantic autofixes are patches and deserve diff review.
And it will deform code to pass the ones it can’t edit
Oracle-editing is the direct attack. Metric gaming is the indirect one: the agent can’t move the threshold, so it deforms the code until the number complies. Told CC < 10, it splits a function at whatever line makes the metric pass rather than at a seam that means anything. Told to raise coverage, it writes tests that execute without asserting.
Agents do this more reliably than humans, because the human writing to a threshold still has some stake in the result and some taste about where a natural seam is. An agent has neither, and a metric is a far more legible target than “good code”.
This is the argument for ratchets over thresholds. A ratchet’s target is “no worse than the baseline”, which is satisfied by not making things worse — a much smaller space of deforming moves than “get this number under 10”. It is also the argument for keeping complexity out of the inner repair loop entirely and running it at PR time, where a human sees the shape of the fix.
Green has to mean something
The failure mode that undoes all of the above: reporting “all checks passed” when a tool timed out, skipped files it could not parse, lacked build context, or never ran.
Fail closed. A green verdict should assert that every expected gate ran, over the changed surface, and produced a parseable report. That needs a declared inventory of expected outputs and a nonzero exit on anything missing, extra, unparsed, or stale — the report inventory is itself a gate. Preserve raw tool output as evidence; normalizing to SARIF or an internal record schema must not silently discard unsupported-file and parse-error entries, which is precisely where the coverage gap hides.
Two related things “green” never means:

Zero findings is not zero defects. It is zero findings of the classes you enabled, in the files that parsed.
A dependency advisory match is not an exploitability finding. SCA reports that a resolved version matches an advisory. Reachability analysis improves prioritization and has its own limits.

Selecting tools: one per failure class
Running every available scanner produces overlapping low-quality findings and alert fatigue, which degrades the human review the whole stack terminates in (vigilance-decrement-in-ai-oversight on why that degradation is not a discipline problem). Pick one tool per distinct failure class, then measure yield and drop what does not earn its noise.
A repository-specific bake-off is the honest way to choose: collect real historical defects and representative clean changes, add seeded defects across the classes you care about (auth bypass, unsafe shell/SQL, nullness, resource leak, schema break, vacuous test, dependency vulnerability, IaC exposure, architecture violation), pin every version, and measure detection by category, false-positive burden, skipped-file rate, latency, and agent repair success. Keep failed attempts in the denominator.
What this adds over the web stack note
ai-verification-stack-web already covers specs, type/schema contracts, mutation testing, visual regression, and fitness functions for a TS/web seat. The gaps this axis points at, for that same seat:























































Failure classGateNoteRepo-specific banned/required patternsast-grep or Semgrep rulesStructural match, not regex; the article’s rule ideas — authorization must dominate sensitive ops, no raw SQL interpolation, no blanket eslint-disable, tests must assert not merely executeConsumer-visible API breakAPI Extractor, oasdiff, Buf breakingCompare before/after artifacts; never ask a model whether a change “looks backward compatible”CI workflow securityzizmorGitHub Actions permissions, triggers, expression injection, pinning. GitHub-specific; other CI systems need an equivalent or a policy-as-code ruleDependency advisoriesOSV-ScannerPin the advisory DB digest or reruns are not reproducibleType-gate escape hatchestype-coverage, counted @ts-ignore / @ts-expect-error / eslint-disableRatchet. The hole layer 1 cannot see by construction: an agent under type pressure satisfies tsc by widening to any or suppressing. The type gate reports green because it is greenDead code and unused exportsknipAI adds; it rarely removes. Deterministic, low false-positive, and it compounds — unused exports keep dead paths alive for the next agent to read and imitateDuplicationjscpd (PMD CPD outside JS)Ratchet, pointed at the duplication-drift failure mode aboveMigration safetysquawk for Postgres, plus dry-run against a representative prior schemaBlast-radius shaped: a bad function is revertible, a dropped column is not. Worth blocking, not ratchetingThe suite’s own determinismRun tests twice with randomized order and seeds, diff the resultsThe artifact-side mirror of this note’s whole argument. A suite that isn’t order-independent makes every gate above it unreliable, and agents introduce shared-state coupling readily
AST presence is not runtime behavior. A required call can be unreachable, shadowed, rebound, or sitting after an early return — structural rules need control/data-flow analysis or execution behind them where behavior actually matters.
Maintenance status, checked at source 2026-08-21

Terrascan is archived. The Tenable repository is archived (last push 2025-11-20). Do not start new IaC scanning on it; Checkov, KICS, Trivy config, or explicit OPA policy cover the ground.
Gitleaks is feature-complete by declaration. Its README carries a warning that no new features will be merged, future releases are security patches only, and the author has shifted focus to Betterleaks. The repository is still actively pushed to. Usable now; not a safe long-horizon standardization without a migration view.

The case against
Drafted deliberately, because a note assembled from a source that already concluded “layered deterministic gates” will otherwise just restate that conclusion.

The costs are real and land on you, not the vendor. Ten to thirty repo-specific AST rules are code: they rot, they false-positive, and someone maintains them. A rule that fires wrongly twice teaches the team to suppress rather than fix, which converts a gate into a formality.
Layers 1–2 tax every edit. Running compile plus type-check plus AST policy on each agent edit is only free if it is fast. On a large TS monorepo it is not, and a slow inner loop is itself a quality cost.
Specification quality may bind harder than gate coverage. The gates check encoded contracts. If the spec is the weak link — which “The limit” below concedes — then the marginal hour buys more in the spec than in a sixth scanner. The layered-stack framing quietly assumes gate coverage is the constraint.
“Not one more AI reviewer” is inherited, not tested here. The source opens with it and this note carried it. ai-assisted-code-review holds the other side; the honest position is that deterministic gates and an AI reviewer catch different classes, and the split is an empirical question per repository rather than a settled ranking.

What survives the objections: the pin list (cheap, and flakiness is a cost you pay whether or not you believe the rest), the agent-must-not-edit-its-own-oracle rule (near-zero cost, removes a whole class of false green), and fail-closed reporting. The elaborate middle of the stack is where the cost-benefit genuinely depends on the repository.
The limit
No analyzer proves that a requirement was the right requirement. A fully green deterministic pipeline means the code satisfied the encoded contracts, under the analyzed model, in the pinned environment. Everything the specification failed to say remains unchecked, and that gap is where ai-code-latent-failure-modes lives.
The shift the whole stack is aiming at: from “AI writes code and humans inspect it” to AI proposes, deterministic tools falsify, AI repairs within bounds, independent review approves the exact verified artifact.
Related

evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — the human-facing rubric after the gates are green; this note is the machine-facing half before that

Sources

Primary input: “Deterministic code analysis for AI-assisted coding” (research snapshot dated 2026-08-20, local AI News Tracker instance). An AI-generated research artifact; its structure, gate architecture, pin list, and tool landscape are the basis for this note. Sampled claims were checked at source rather than assumed.
Verified independently 2026-08-21: Terrascan repository archive status and Gitleaks README maintenance warning (GitHub API + raw README). Both matched the source.
This note’s own contributions, not from the source and not otherwise sourced: the four-property table framing, the flakiness-as-resampling mechanism, the cost-per-refutation ordering, the mapping of “agent edits its own oracle” onto the vault’s co-authorship independence failure, the block/ratchet/route verdict taxonomy, the metric-gaming-as-indirect-oracle-attack framing, the composite-gates-inherit-their-worst-input rule, the mutation-adjusted CRAP variant, the A/B/C input-provenance tiering, and the case-against section. Argued, not measured.
Named tools confirmed to exist and be actively maintained on 2026-08-21 (GitHub API): ast-grep, Semgrep, zizmor, OSV-Scanner, oasdiff, Buf, API Extractor (rushstack).
Landman, D., Serebrenik, A., Bouwers, E., Vinju, J. — “Empirical analysis of the relationship between CC and SLOC in a large corpus of Java methods and C functions”, Journal of Software: Evolution and Process (conference version ICSME 2014). Abstract read verbatim from the authors’ preprint 2026-08-21; the “only moderate” and “not strong enough to conclude that CC is redundant” phrasings are quoted from it. Note the search-engine summary of this paper states the opposite conclusion — the abstract does not.
GitClear, “The Maintainability Gap” (released January 2026, 623M analyzed changes 2023–2026) — duplication, moved-code, and function-connectivity figures. Vendor-authored: GitClear sells the analytics product measuring these signals, the page carries no methodology section or stated limitations, metric definitions are its own, and the series is time-correlated rather than causally attributed. Directional only.
Tornhill, A. — Your Code as a Crime Scene and Software Design X-Rays; hotspots (churn × complexity), change/temporal coupling, code-maat (open-source CLI, 2.6k stars, last pushed 2025-07-03, no license file detected). Attribution and concept definitions confirmed via CodeScene documentation and blog 2026-08-21. Tornhill is CodeScene’s CTO — same author for the research and the product.
CRAP metric: formula, 2007 origin (Alberto Savoia and Bob Evans, Google Testing Blog / Crap4j), and the >30 threshold confirmed across independent secondary sources 2026-08-21. The published worked examples (CC=10 needs 42% coverage; CC=25 needs 80%) were reproduced independently from the formula before being cited, which is what establishes the formula is transcribed correctly here.
CRAP leverage table and the CC≤5 / CC≥31 boundary properties: computed directly from the published formula, not quoted.
npm CRAP-package maturity figures (publish dates, version counts, maintainer counts, last-month downloads) pulled from the npm registry and downloads API 2026-08-21.
Tool existence and maintenance confirmed 2026-08-21 (npm registry / GitHub API): knip, type-coverage, jscpd, squawk.
Not independently verified: the per-tool capability and limit claims in the source’s landscape tables (compiler/SAST/fuzzing/formal-methods rows). Treat as a map for evaluation, not as measured results.

ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model.content:
DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
What it is
DORA’s 2025 report, State of AI-assisted Software Development, centers AI-assisted engineering in its title and framing (earlier reports treated it as one chapter). Its headline thesis is the amplifier effect: “AI’s primary role is as an amplifier, magnifying an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses.” AI does not repair broken engineering cultures or rescue poor architecture — it accelerates whatever system it lands in. For example: a team with strong review culture and automated pipelines ships faster, while a team with manual testing and ambiguous leadership generates unmaintainable code at higher velocity (my gloss, not report wording).
This is consistent with what the vault’s front-end cluster observes at code level: AI output quality is downstream of the constraints around it (ai-friendly-repo-structure, ai-code-latent-failure-modes). As survey evidence, though, the report is weaker than “proof of” that observation.
The seven capabilities
Alongside the report, DORA introduced its inaugural AI Capabilities Model — seven organizational practices that determine whether AI amplifies strength or dysfunction. The capability names below are verbatim from the announcement; the rationale column is interpretive gloss (mine + the research brief’s), not quoted report text:





































CapabilityWhy it matters under AI (gloss)Clear and communicated AI stanceAmbiguity about permitted AI use stifles adoption and invites shadow IT; boundaries on data, IP, and agent autonomy must be explicitHealthy data ecosystemsLLMs can’t reason over fragmented, contradictory internal documentationAI-accessible internal dataGeneric assistance plateaus fast; connecting AI to internal APIs, codebases, and trackers (MCP, RAG) is where returns compoundStrong version control practicesDisciplined VCS is the failsafe against runaway agentic change as code volume spikesWorking in small batchesHumans can’t review thousand-line AI PRs; small incremental commits keep peer review functionalQuality internal platformsAI interfacing with standardized pipelines amplifies throughput; fragmented legacy infrastructure amplifies chaosUser-centric focusSpeed without user feedback just ships irrelevant features faster
On the last capability, the announcement itself makes the sharpest negative claim in the model: without user-centric focus, AI adoption “can have a negative impact on team performance” — amplification with a flipped sign, not merely diminished returns. DORA’s materials also state that user-centric teams have 40% higher organizational performance — though that figure appears on dora.dev’s user-centric-focus capability page and reads as a longer-standing DORA finding, not necessarily a 2025-report result (attribution unconfirmed; verified 2026-07-18 that the capability page states the figure without naming a comparison group or performance measure).
How to read the model
The model’s implicit claim: successful AI adoption is a systems-engineering problem, not a tooling-acquisition problem. None of the seven capabilities is about which assistant you buy; all seven are about the surrounding system the assistant amplifies. The practical corollary for a team lead: before scaling agent autonomy, audit the amplifier inputs — review batch size, pipeline automation, data accessibility — because those, not the model choice, set the sign of the multiplication.
The “working in small batches” capability connects directly to the verification-economics theme: AI shifts the bottleneck from generation to review (cognitive-burden-of-ai-use), so practices that keep review tractable are now throughput practices, not hygiene.
Limits
DORA’s evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported survey data — the amplifier effect is an interpretive frame over correlations, not a causal result. DORA is also a Google Cloud research program, and Google Cloud sells the AI tooling whose (well-supported) adoption the model encourages; the findings are widely respected but not vendor-neutral.
Related

ai-software-dev-2026-landscape — broader 2026 landscape this report sits in (productivity paradox, agentic workflows)
ai-friendly-repo-structure — the repo-level version of “make the system worth amplifying”
ai-code-latent-failure-modes — what amplified dysfunction looks like at code level
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — keeping review meaningful under AI code volume
hitl-progressive-autonomy — calibrating agent autonomy, the “clear AI stance” capability in practice

Sources

DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development (2025) — dora.dev/research/2025/dora-report/ (verified 2026-06-10)
Google Cloud, “Introducing DORA’s inaugural AI Capabilities Model” — cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/introducing-doras-inaugural-ai-capabilities-model (verified 2026-06-10; the seven-capability list above matches this announcement)
DORA capability page, user-centric focus (the 40% figure) — dora.dev/capabilities/user-centric-focus/

Surfaced by a user-provided research brief on AI in front-end development (2026-06-10); report title, amplifier framing, and capability list were independently verified against the sources above before this note was written.

ai/enterprise-agent-execution-architectu.title: Enterprise Agent Execution Architecture
ai/enterprise-agent-execution-architectu.content:
Enterprise Agent Execution Architecture
The platform-agnostic layer under the Claude-Code-specific trio (agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers, agent-isolation-hardening, agent-policy-enforcement-gap). Those ask which boundary, whether it holds, and whether an org can mandate it for one tool. This asks what a production agent platform looks like when no single vendor’s feature set is assumed.

Provenance. Synthesized from an external AI-generated research report (dated 2026-07-31) supplied by oxzo, not from primary research by this vault. Four of its roughly forty checkable vendor and standards claims were verified against source before writing; those are marked ✅ below. The report’s own product-landscape section is deliberately not carried over — it is the part that rots fastest and the part least worth inheriting unverified. Structural claims here are argument, not measurement, except where this vault’s own probes are cited.

The thesis

A sandbox is necessary but insufficient. The sandbox should be assumed compromisable; its job is to limit the first blast radius.

The security objective is not “the agent cannot do anything harmful.” It is: no single model decision, prompt injection, sandbox process, dependency, credential, network path, or human approval can create an unbounded enterprise impact.
This is the same conclusion agent-policy-enforcement-gap reaches from the opposite direction — that note starts from one vendor’s policy system and finds it can’t bind a non-compliant endpoint; this one starts from architecture and concludes the endpoint was never the right place to put the guarantee.
Why agent execution is not ordinary application execution
A normal application runs developer-authored code on predefined inputs. An agent synthesizes new commands, interprets untrusted natural language as instructions, chooses tools dynamically, installs packages, retains state across long horizons, and can modify files that execute later somewhere else.
That produces three simultaneous problems, and most deployments solve only the first:

Untrusted-code isolation — generated code may attack the kernel, runtime, parser, or helper services.
Confused-deputy prevention — a perfectly isolated process can still misuse legitimate APIs, credentials, and repositories. Isolation does nothing here.
Output and supply-chain containment — the agent plants changes in source, CI config, Git hooks, IDE tasks, skills, or lockfiles that execute later on a trusted machine, outside the boundary entirely.

A sandbox that protects the host kernel addresses (1) partially and does nothing about (2) or (3).
Trust assumptions
Assume adversarial: the model’s own output and trajectory; retrieved content, repository text, issues, documents, logs, and tool descriptions; packages and build scripts; the sandbox user including root inside the guest; outbound destinations reached via redirect, DNS change, or allowed SaaS APIs; persisted workspace, memory, snapshots, caches, and shared skills; other tenants; and a mistaken or malicious human request.
Protect: host and hypervisor; the orchestration plane; model and tool credentials; source, customer, and regulated data; cloud/K8s/CI/identity/secrets infrastructure; other tenants; the audit evidence and policy configuration themselves; and downstream consumers of generated artifacts.
The planes
The core structural claim is that these five planes must be separate, and that the agent sits inside only the second:



































PlaneHoldsAgent’s accessOrchestration & policyModel gateway, deterministic policy engine, approval service, tool broker, credential exchange, budgets, kill switchNone — it proposes, the plane decidesExecutionDisposable microVM/sandbox, no ambient identity, read-only input, ephemeral scratch, quotasThis is the agentCapability brokersEgress proxy, package mirror, Git/DB/email/cloud brokers with destination and action policy, DLPOnly through typed callsEvidenceAppend-only/tamper-evident run log, hashes of policy, image, inputs, actions, outputsWrite-only, out-of-guestVerification & releaseClean image, hidden tests, scanners, exact-diff review, signingNone — cannot modify the verifier
Hard separation requirements: the sandbox cannot reach the hypervisor, container runtime socket, orchestrator API, cloud metadata service, secrets manager, policy store, evidence store, or approval database. The agent cannot modify its own network policy, identity, quotas, base image, verifier, hidden tests, audit sink, or termination conditions. The verifier consumes a content-addressed output — it never trusts a “tests passed” claim from the agent.
Policy enforcement lives outside the sandbox. An out-of-process reference monitor decides; the model only proposes. This is the architectural expression of the authority axis in agent-policy-enforcement-gap.
Isolation primitives


















































PrimitiveFitMaterial limitationOrdinary container (runc)Trusted internal code, single tenantShares host kernel; not a sole boundary for arbitrary agent-generated codeRootless containerDefense in depthStill shares the kernel — does not justify a lower risk tiergVisorMedium-risk, high densityUser-space kernel intercepts many syscalls; compatibility and performance vary by workloadKata ContainersHigh-risk Kubernetes workloadsPer-pod VM boundary with container workflow; operational and memory/startup overheadConfidential ContainersHost/operator outside the trust boundaryAdds TEE attestation and policy-gated secret release; inherits TEE and side-channel limits. Complements containment, doesn’t replace itFirecracker-style microVMEphemeral high-risk jobsA strong primitive, not a control plane — you build orchestration, images, identity, policy, logging, forensicsFull/confidential VMRegulated or tenant-dedicatedHighest cost and startup overheadWasm/WASI componentNarrow deterministic toolsHost imports define real authority; not a general POSIX replacement
✅ Verified: kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox is real — a Sandbox CRD and controller under SIG Apps, supporting gVisor and Kata as isolation backends, with v0.2.1 moving to a “secure by default” networking architecture. It is the most direct standardization effort for this pattern.
A caveat from this vault’s own testing, relevant when layering: nested bwrap inside an unprivileged container fails to mount a fresh /proc, so an inner sandbox requires a documented weaker mode — see agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers. Layered isolation is defense in depth, not two independent boundaries.
Network is the most underestimated boundary
Default should be deny-all for both address families, no public ingress, enterprise-controlled or absent DNS, an immutable internal package mirror, and broker access only to named APIs. Block link-local, private ranges, node-local services, cloud metadata, cluster ranges, control planes, and other sandboxes.
Domain allowlists are structurally insufficient. Bypasses: compromised or user-content-hosting allowed services, redirects and alternate endpoints, DNS rebinding and raw-IP access, broad cloud API domains fronting many services, TLS/SNI vs HTTP Host ambiguity, non-HTTP protocols, QUIC/HTTP3, WebSockets, tunnels and CONNECT, and allowed APIs that themselves accept attacker-chosen destinations.
This vault has measured the claim rather than only citing it. Probing a replica of Anthropic’s published reference dev-container firewall found IPv6 traffic bypassing the entire IPv4-only policy, unrestricted DNS to any external resolver, and unrestricted TCP/22 to any host — with controls confirming the allowlist worked on IPv4/443. IPv6 is also what curl reaches for by default, so the unfiltered path was the default one. Details in agent-isolation-hardening. Three independent egress channels in an artifact whose shape is otherwise correct.
✅ Verified independently, from a different vendor: E2B’s documentation states internet access is enabled by default; domain filtering “only works for HTTP traffic on port 80 (via Host header inspection) and TLS traffic on port 443 (via SNI inspection)”; other ports use CIDR filtering only; “UDP-based protocols like QUIC/HTTP3 are not supported for domain filtering”; and “when both allow and deny rules are specified, allow rules always take precedence over deny rules.”
That last clause deserves attention on its own — allow-over-deny inverts the usual security default, so a broad allow silently defeats a narrow deny. Three sources now agree that hostname-based egress control leaks at the protocol edges. Treat “egress filtering: yes” in any product matrix as a claim to test, not a control to rely on.
Filesystem and persistence
Safe default: immutable base image; read-only content-addressed input; ephemeral writable scratch; an initially-empty export directory; no secrets mount; no host mount; no runtime socket.
Do not mount a developer checkout read-write into a high-risk sandbox. The agent can alter Git hooks, CI configuration, IDE tasks, build scripts, agent instructions, lockfiles, or generated binaries that later execute on a trusted host — problem (3) above. Prefer an immutable snapshot or private clone plus explicit patch export, and review hooks separately from ordinary diffs.
Interlock worth noting: sandbox-runtime implements exactly this defense as a mandatory deny list (.bashrc, .gitconfig, .mcp.json, .git/hooks/, .claude/agents/, …) — but on Linux it only blocks files that already exist, so a non-existent .git/hooks/pre-commit can still be created. A control this architecture treats as essential has a documented hole in at least one implementation. See agent-isolation-hardening.
Persist only what is required. Snapshots, caches, memories, package directories, browser profiles, and shared skill stores all carry state across runs; bind them to one tenant and never share writable state between trust domains.
Identity, brokered tools, and approval
Each run gets a unique short-lived workload identity, exchanged for narrowly scoped, audience-restricted, destination-bound credentials only when a permitted tool call occurs. That identity carries tenant, run/task ID, risk tier, data class, initiating human, approved tool set, expiry, and policy and image digests. Broad reusable credentials never enter the sandbox.
Prefer typed business tools over shell access to enterprise APIs. A git.create_pull_request tool taking a repository, base commit digest, patch digest, and branch lets the broker independently check tenant, branch pattern, changed paths, secret scan, policy, approval, and idempotency — then act with its own credential. The agent never holds the Git token.
Human approval is not a sandbox. Approvals are defeated by fatigue, misleading summaries, race conditions, and post-approval mutation. Bind approval to canonical bytes or a content digest, exact target, action, policy version, expiry, and maximum count; require re-approval when any bound field changes; show the reviewer the exact diff and an independently generated risk summary, not the agent’s own explanation.
The general form of a finding in agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers: boundaries stated conversationally (“don’t push”) are re-read from the transcript and can be dropped by context compaction. Durable authorization must be a rule, not a sentence.
Fail-closed conditions
For high-impact operations the orchestrator must deny, terminate, or quarantine when identity/attestation/tenant binding is invalid; a policy decision is deny, unavailable, timed out, indeterminate, or untraceable to a version; a tool request fails schema, canonicalization, or object-level authorization; approval is absent, expired, revoked, or doesn’t match the action digest; egress enforcement or destination validation is unavailable; classification/residency/DLP outcome is unknown for a sensitive sink; image or artifact signature, provenance, or SBOM is missing or invalid; the required runtime class or tenant boundary can’t be proven; the durable evidence sink is unavailable; the identity broker can’t mint the narrow scope; or persistent state lacks valid tenant and integrity metadata. It must never guess, retry through a weaker path, or fall back to a broader credential.
Availability exceptions must be preauthorized, named, and limited to low-risk read-only paths.
Risk tiers



































TierExampleMinimum isolation and authority0 AdvisorySummarize supplied documentsNo execution; scoped read-only retrieval; output filtering1 Bounded developmentAnalyze trusted repo, draft a patchDisposable gVisor/microVM; read-only input or private clone; no secrets; restricted mirror; PR draft only2 Untrusted code/dataExecute generated code or third-party reposmicroVM; no network by default; no persistent state; brokered tools; full audit; independent verification3 Sensitive enterprise actionModify internal systems, regulated data, cloud resourcesTier 2 plus tenant-dedicated boundary, workload identity, typed tools, DLP, exact-action approval, separate release authority4 Hostile evaluationCyber agents, malware analysis, containment testsOffline or one-way; dedicated hardware; no enterprise credentials or routes; tripwires; external kill controls; post-run rebuild
Authority should expand within a run only after objective evidence passes. Don’t provision a Tier-3 identity because a task might eventually need one.
Acceptance tests
The operational counterpart to “verify the boundary, don’t declare it.” The platform should fail closed against: host access via runtime sockets, device nodes, host namespaces, hostPath, or nested virtualization; egress via raw IP, IPv6, alternate DNS, DNS rebinding, redirects, QUIC/UDP, WebSocket, CONNECT, cloud metadata, or exfiltration through allowed code-hosting, logs, package names, or model APIs; identity attacks using expired/wrong-audience/replayed tokens, post-approval parameter changes, or splitting a denied transaction into permitted small ones; required-control outages; filesystem attacks via symlinks, path traversal, archive extraction, and writes to .git/hooks, CI config, or lockfiles; and evidence attacks — dropping or reordering events, making tests green by editing tests or fixtures, or closing a run as successful after a policy denial. Required-control outages cover: policy engine returning deny/timeout/stale, credential minting unavailable, egress enforcement disabled, and evidence sink dropping events — each must stop consequential work rather than degrade.
Standards mapping
✅ Verified: the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 exists — released 2025-12-09, peer-reviewed by 100+ contributors, taxonomy ASI01–ASI10. Named categories include Agent Goal Hijack (ASI01), Tool Misuse & Exploitation (ASI02), Agent Identity & Privilege Abuse (ASI03), Agentic Supply Chain Compromise (ASI04), Unexpected Code Execution (ASI05), Memory & Context Poisoning (ASI06), Insecure Inter-Agent Communication (ASI07). (ASI08–ASI10 not verified — do not cite specific names for those without checking.)
Also referenced by the source report, not individually re-verified here: NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile), SP 800-190 (container security), SP 800-207 (zero trust), SP 800-53r5, Kubernetes Pod Security Standards, MITRE ATLAS, SLSA, Sigstore, SPIFFE/SPIRE. All are well-established documents; the risk in citing them is misattributing specific content, not existence.
Compliance mapping does not prove containment. The decisive evidence is effective configuration plus repeated adversarial tests.
Incidents that ground the architecture
Every row below was verified against a primary source (NVD, GitHub Security Advisory, or CERT/CC) during authoring on 2026-07-31 — not from a secondary summary. Scores are given with their CVSS version because several differ sharply between v3.1 and v4.0.


















































IncidentMechanismWhat it groundsCVE-2026-25725 — Claude Code < 2.1.2, CVSS 3.1 10.0 / v4.0 7.7, CWE-501 Trust Boundary Violation (GHSA-ff64-7w26-62rf)The bubblewrap sandbox protected .claude/settings.local.json read-only but failed to protect .claude/settings.json when that file did not exist at startup. Sandboxed code created it, injected SessionStart hooks, and those ran with host privileges on restart.Problem (3): the sandbox held, and the escape still happened later, outside it. Also that absence-based protections fail — see below.CVE-2026-39861 — Claude Code < 2.1.64, CVSS 4.0 7.7, CWE-22/CWE-61 (GHSA-vp62-r36r-9xqp)A sandboxed process created symlinks pointing outside the workspace; the unsandboxed parent process then followed them when writing, with no confirmation. Reliable exploitation “required the ability to add untrusted content into a Claude Code context window to trigger sandboxed code execution via prompt injection.”The boundary is only as strong as the least-sandboxed component in the loop. A partially-sandboxed architecture composes into an escape.CVE-2026-55607 — Claude Code 2.1.38–2.1.162, CVSS 3.1 8.8, CWE-22/59/78 (GHSA-7835-87q9-rgvv)Worktrees could be named .git and navigated to outside the sandbox context, producing git-directory confusion.Write exceptions punched for a legitimate workflow become the escape. Every carve-out is attack surface.CVE-2025-59536 — Claude Code < 1.0.111, CVSS 3.1 8.8 / v4.0 8.7, CWE-94 (GHSA-4fgq-fpq9-mr3g)Hooks in a repository’s .claude/settings.json and MCP servers in .mcp.json executed on session start — MCP servers “immediately upon running claude, before the user could even read the trust dialog.""Treat repository text as hostile” is not hygiene advice. Config files in a repo are an execution vector.CVE-2026-21852 — Claude Code < 2.0.65, CVSS 3.1 7.5, CWE-522 (GHSA-jh7p-qr78-84p7)A malicious repo’s .claude/settings.json set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an attacker endpoint; the client issued authenticated requests before the trust prompt, sending the API key in plaintext.No ambient credentials in the execution environment. A credential present at startup is exfiltrable before any policy runs.CrewAI — CVE-2026-2275 / 2285 / 2286 / 2287 (CERT/CC VU#221883)CodeInterpreterTool fell back to an insecure SandboxPython path when Docker was unreachable, chaining prompt injection into RCE, SSRF, and arbitrary file read. The fix removed the tool entirely and directed users to external sandboxes.The fail-closed requirement, concretely. A sandbox that degrades to “no sandbox” on infrastructure error is worse than none, because the operator believes it is present.Nx “s1ngularity” — 2025-08-26Malicious npm versions programmatically invoked Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Amazon Q CLI with prompts instructing them to enumerate the filesystem for credentials, SSH keys, and wallets. GitGuardian counted 2,349 distinct secrets from 1,079 repositories; exfiltration went to ~1,400 public s1ngularity-repository repos. A second phase used the stolen tokens to flip private repos public.The agent itself as a lateral-movement tool — the confused-deputy problem in the wild, and the first known case of weaponizing developer AI assistants for supply-chain attack.OpenClaw — CVE-2026-32922 — < 2026.3.11, CVSS 3.1 9.9 / v4.0 9.4, CWE-266Insufficient scope validation in device.token.rotate let a low-privilege pairing operator obtain an admin token and execute code across connected nodes.Brokered identity with narrow, audience-bound scopes; and that implicit local trust is not a boundary.
Two patterns worth extracting, because they recur across the set:

Three of these are escapes from a correctly functioning sandbox. In 25725, 39861, and 55607, bubblewrap did its job; the escape came from the seam between sandboxed and unsandboxed components, or from a write exception granted deliberately. This is the strongest available evidence for the thesis that isolation is the first blast-radius limit and not the guarantee.
Two independent attacks target the same configuration surface from opposite directions. CVE-2026-21852 is an attacker placing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in a repo to steal a key; the policy-detachment path in agent-policy-enforcement-gap is a user exporting the same variable to silently drop out of central policy. A config key that redirects the API endpoint is load-bearing in both threat models, which is a good general signal for where to look in any agent platform.

Not verified and therefore not cited above: aggregator claims of a specific total CVE count for Claude Code, and the frequently-repeated “two CVSS 10.0 sandbox escapes” — only CVE-2026-25725 reaches 10.0, and only under CVSS 3.1.
Where this framework is weak
Three criticisms of the source report, recorded because the note would otherwise read as endorsement:

It is documentary, not empirical. Built from vendor documentation and standards; its own evidence caveats concede vendor pages “do not independently prove isolation” — a concession that applies to the report itself. It prescribes adversarial acceptance tests without running any. This vault’s egress probe is one small counterweight and covers a single artifact.
It never prices anything. The “minimum viable secure configuration” — fresh microVM per run, deny-all egress, internal mirror, brokered identity, tamper-evident evidence, independent verifier — is a platform team, not a config file. Calling it “intentionally inconvenient” is honest but is not a degraded-but-real tier for an org with two engineers. The gap between Tier 1 and “nothing” is where most real deployments sit and the report is silent there.
It assumes the org owns the execution substrate. Every architecture is a cluster or managed service. The dominant actual deployment — agents in developers’ local IDEs on machines the org only partly controls — is out of scope, and that is exactly where agent-policy-enforcement-gap finds the enforcement gap bites hardest.

Counterargument
The architecture is correct and mostly unaffordable, and an unaffordable control set has a predictable failure mode: it gets declared, partially built, and then relied upon at full strength. Consider an org that implements the microVM and the egress broker but skips the evidence plane and the independent verifier. It has covered problem (1) and left (2) and (3) — the ones isolation never addressed — while feeling considerably safer. On that reading, the highest-value first move is not the microVM at all but the verification plane: a clean-room CI the agent cannot write to, which catches bad output regardless of how the sandbox performed, and which most orgs already have.
The counter to that: the verification plane only catches what reaches it, and problems (2) and (3) include actions that never produce a reviewable artifact — a credential used, data exfiltrated, a ticket closed. Verification is the cheapest high-value plane, not a substitute for brokered authority.
Related

Sources

External AI-generated research report, “Running AI Agents Safely in Enterprise Sandboxes,” dated 2026-07-31, supplied by oxzo. Primary structural source; not independently authored by this vault.
Verified during authoring, 2026-07-31: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (genai.owasp.org); kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox (GitHub); E2B internet-access and domain-filtering behavior (e2b.dev docs)

ai/evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests.title: Evaluating AI-Generated Code Beyond Tests
ai/evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests.content:
Evaluating AI-Generated Code Beyond Tests
A decision rubric for “green CI, now what?” When every automated gate passes, what do you actually check next — and how do you decide whether to ship, return to the agent, or escalate to human review?
Extends ai-verification-stack-web, which enumerates the tools. This note covers the judgment layer that sits on top.
Why green CI isn’t enough
Green pipelines prove the code doesn’t break the things you thought to test. For AI-authored code, the gap between “tests pass” and “behaves correctly” is wider than for human code:

Hollow tests. Test suites can hit 100% line coverage with only a 4% mutation score — Wang et al.’s mutation-guided test-generation study found exactly such suites (arXiv 2506.02954, IEEE TSE 2025; “some test suites achieve 100% coverage but only 4% mutation score”). The tests exist to satisfy the CI contract, not catch bugs. (Attribution corrected 2026-06-10: previously credited to “Meta LLM mutation research” — Meta’s ACH paper (arXiv 2501.12862, FSE 2025) is a different work and does not contain this figure.)
Spec drift. The AI implemented what it inferred from context. Tests check the inferred spec, not the actual spec.
Local correctness. A change can be internally consistent — types align, tests pass, linter clean — while violating an invariant the test suite doesn’t encode.
Novel failure surface. AI-co-authored PRs carry 1.7× more issues than human-only PRs, with security issues up to 2.74× higher in the worst category and improper password handling 1.88× more likely (all CodeRabbit, Dec 2025); Veracode’s Spring 2026 GenAI report separately finds ~45% of AI-generated code fails security checks absent explicit security guidance. Familiar review intuitions undercalibrate. (Corrected 2026-06-10: 1.88× was previously stated as the overall vulnerability rate co-attributed to Veracode — it is CodeRabbit’s password-handling figure.)

What green CI does not prove:








































ClaimGate that would prove itTypical statusCode matches intentSpec review + property testsAbsent or informalNo architectural driftFitness functions, import lintingRarely enforcedPerformance under loadBudgets + load testsMissing for changes <100 LOCSecurity invariants holdThreat-modeled tests, SASTIncompleteExisting features still workFull E2E + visual regressionPartialFuture maintainabilityHuman judgmentSkipped under deadline
Trust signals
Before reading the diff line-by-line, scan for signals that raise or lower the prior that this change is safe.
Positive signals (lower skepticism)

Small, focused diff. <50 LOC, <3 files, single concern.
Uses existing patterns. Imports established helpers instead of reinventing them.
No new abstractions. No new classes, interfaces, hooks, middleware, or utility modules.
Tests behavior, not implementation. Assertions are on observable outputs, not internal calls.
Touches non-critical code. No auth, permissions, payments, persistence, or public API surface.
Agent expressed uncertainty where appropriate. The reasoning log flags edge cases and asks clarifying questions rather than confidently guessing.
Clear mapping from spec to diff. Every changed line traces to a line in the spec or ticket.

Negative signals (raise skepticism)

Large diff, scope creep. Touches files unrelated to the stated task.
Fresh abstractions. New classes, wrappers, adapters, or “utility” modules.
Defensive code without reason. try/catch blocks that swallow errors, null checks on values the type system guarantees, fallback values for impossible states.
Test edits without behavior change. Test assertions weakened or deleted without a corresponding code change. This is the single strongest tampering signal.
Parallel implementations. A second function that does what an existing function already does.
Over-confident reasoning. The agent declares the change “complete” without flagging edge cases that obviously exist.
Layer violations. Business logic in UI components, DB access in route handlers, presentation concerns in domain code.
New dependency added. Especially unfamiliar packages. Check ai-supply-chain-risks.

Architectural-risk heuristics
Where AI-generated web code goes wrong architecturally. Use these as a checklist when the change is non-trivial.

Premature abstraction. AI reaches for classes, factories, and generics before the duplication justifies them. Three similar lines is better than a hook.
Inventing types. Introduces a new User or Order type parallel to the existing one because it didn’t grep for the existing one.
Error-handling theater. Wraps everything in try/catch and returns null or a stringified error, turning compile-time guarantees into runtime mysteries.
Implicit coupling. Module A reads from a context or store that Module B writes to, without either side declaring the relationship.
Wrong layer. Fetch calls in components, validation in routes, formatting in domain models. AI will match whatever layer the request mentioned, not the layer the logic belongs in.
Fake convergence. Tests edited until they pass rather than code fixed until tests pass. Especially suspect when both tests and code changed in the same pass.
Deleted invariants. Assertions, type constraints, or validation removed “to make the test pass” without a comment explaining why the invariant was wrong.

The tiered decision rubric
Think of review as a cascade. Each tier is cheaper than the next. Escalate only when lower tiers leave uncertainty.
Tier 1 — Mechanical gates (cost: seconds)
Type check, lint, unit tests, mutation score threshold, bundle size, dependency audit. See ai-verification-stack-web layers 2–3 and 5. Non-negotiable; failure blocks everything.
Tier 2 — Semantic automated gates (cost: minutes)
Schema/contract validation, visual regression, fitness functions (import boundaries, perf budgets), E2E smoke. Catches whole classes of “green CI but wrong behavior” bugs.
Tier 3 — AI critic review (cost: cents to dollars)
A separate agent with the spec and the diff, prompted as a skeptical reviewer. Useful for scanning for the negative signals above at scale. Not a replacement for human review — collusion risk is real (see multi-agent-failure-modes).
Two operational details that make the difference between a critic that catches bugs and one that rubber-stamps:

Sprint contracts. Where possible, the critic is grading against an explicit contract the generator agreed to before coding — scope, acceptance criteria, behavior to demonstrate. This is the upstream-prevention move from harness-design-load-bearing: a critic with a contract verifies; a critic without one improvises. Without a contract, the critic ends up grading whatever the diff happens to do, which means spec drift slips through.
Iterative critic tuning. Early versions of any critic agent identify legitimate issues and then dismiss them (“yes it’s broken, but the code looks reasonable so I’ll pass”). Treat the critic prompt as a stateful artifact: read its logs, compare verdicts against your own on a sample, and rewrite the prompt when the verdicts diverge. The critic that ships PR #100 should not have the same prompt as the one that shipped PR #1. See harness-design-load-bearing for the operational pattern.

Both moves attack self-evaluation bias from different angles — sprint contracts make the critic’s job mechanical enough to short-circuit the bias; iterative tuning calibrates the critic against ground truth.
Tier 4 — Human spec review (cost: minutes)
Not line-by-line code review. The question: does this change match what I asked for? Read the spec, then the PR description, then the diff summary. If they tell the same story, the code is probably close. If the diff touches files the spec didn’t mention, stop and ask why.
Tier 5 — Human architectural review (cost: 15+ minutes)
Required for any change that trips an escalation trigger below. This is where the lead dev’s judgment pays off — read the diff with the mental model of “what will this look like in six months when the next AI change touches it?”
Escalation triggers
Any of these force Tier 5 review, regardless of what lower tiers said:

Change crosses a module boundary or touches a shared interface
New runtime dependency added
Modifies auth, permissions, persistence, payments, or PII handling
Introduces a new abstraction (class, interface, hook, middleware, service)
Diff exceeds 200 LOC or 10 files
Mutation score below threshold for the file’s tier (70% business logic, 50% UI, 30% utilities)
Test files edited in the same pass as implementation files without new behavior added
Public API surface changes (exports, route shapes, event payloads)
Agent’s own reasoning log expresses uncertainty about correctness
Fitness function / architectural rule warning suppressed rather than resolved

Review protocol for AI diffs
When you do pull up the diff, the order matters. Humans reviewing AI code with human-code habits miss the AI-specific failure modes.

Read the spec or ticket first. You’re checking the diff against intent, not against your aesthetic preferences.
Read the PR description / agent reasoning log. Note any hedges, flagged assumptions, or “I chose X because Y” decisions. Those are the places to focus.
Look at the test diff before the code diff. If tests were weakened or removed, stop and investigate. This is the highest-signal check for AI self-deception.
Grep for new abstractions. Search the diff for class , interface , function , export const, type . Every new abstraction should have a justification.
Check cross-file consistency. If the change modifies a shared type or function, verify callers still make sense. AI often updates the definition and misses one caller.
Run the feature. Not just the tests. See ai-verification-stack-web layer 3 for visual verification. Human perception catches regressions tests miss.
Cross-check the diff against the escalation trigger list. If any trigger fires, route to architectural review.

Decision outputs
Every review ends with one of these. Pick explicitly — “LGTM” is not a decision.

Ship. All gates green, no escalation triggers, trust signals positive.
Ship with monitoring. Green but non-trivial. Add observability; review metrics post-deploy.
Ship behind a flag. Risky area, bounded blast radius. Gradual rollout.
Return to agent with specific feedback. Cite the failing gate or signal. Vague feedback produces vague fixes.
Escalate to human architect. A trigger fired. Not a judgment on the code — a policy requirement.
Reject. Fundamental mismatch with spec, security concern, or architectural violation that can’t be fixed by iteration.

Anti-patterns

Rubber-stamping after green CI. The whole point of this note. Green CI is a floor, not a ceiling.
Line-by-line review of every AI diff. You’ll burn out and miss the patterns. Use signals to triage, then deep-read the suspicious changes.
Accepting “all tests pass” as the agent’s completion signal. Tests passing is table stakes; the agent should also report what it verified beyond tests.
Letting the agent edit its own tests unchecked. The single highest-leverage guardrail is: test changes require stronger justification than code changes.
Suppressing a fitness function rather than resolving the violation. If the ESLint rule or bundle budget complains, the rule is usually right.
Trusting AI critic reviews as independent. Same model family = correlated blind spots. Critic agents catch surface issues; they don’t replace Tier 4/5.

Related

Sources

CodeRabbit, “State of AI vs Human Code Generation” (Dec 2025, 470 PRs) — 1.7× issue rate; also the source of the up-to-2.74× security-category and 1.88× password-handling figures (one report, not independent corroboration)
Veracode Spring 2026 GenAI Code Security Update — ~55% security pass rate for unguided AI code, i.e. the ~45% fail rate cited above (this report does not contain a 1.88× figure)
Wang et al., “Mutation-Guided Unit Test Generation with a Large Language Model” (arXiv 2506.02954, IEEE TSE 2025) — the 100%-coverage/4%-mutation-score finding (previously misattributed here to Meta)

Martin Fowler: “Reviewing AI-generated code” (2026)

ai/explore-dispatch-routing.title: Explore-Dispatch Routing
ai/explore-dispatch-routing.content:
Explore-Dispatch Routing
What it is
A default routing rule for which tool calls go through a Task/Explore subagent (cheap, separate context window, Haiku-class model) versus which stay in main context (expensive but stateful). The pattern formalises the principle: search noise lives in cheap subagent tokens; decisions live in main-context tokens.
The rule is paired with a context-discipline rule: every Explore dispatch carries explicit context — file paths, errors, prior decisions — because the subagent has no access to prior conversation turns.
Why it matters
Two failure modes this avoids:

Main-context bloat from search. Glob, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch, and multi-file Read produce verbose tool output. When that output lands in main context, it stays there for the rest of the session, displacing room for actual reasoning and accelerating compaction. The raw output volume usually far exceeds the information extracted.
Subagent confabulation from missing context. A subagent dispatched with “check the auth flow” but no file paths, no recent errors, no prior decisions, is forced to reason from base knowledge — and will confidently report findings that don’t correspond to this codebase. The fix is structural: dispatch carries context; subagent reads code; subagent reports against the provided frame.

The first failure mode is the source repo’s core efficiency argument (see Sources); the second — subagent confabulation from missing context — is my synthesis pairing the source with the trust-but-verify rule for subagent outputs, not a claim the source makes directly.
The pattern fits one layer above tool selection — it’s a routing discipline, not a tool discipline.
Default routing
Through Explore (subagent)





























Tool / operationWhy subagentGlob across many pathsOutput is large, signal is smallGrep over the codebaseSame — most matches are noiseWebSearchResult lists are verbose; subagent extracts the relevant claimWebFetch (large pages)Page is long; main only needs the synthesised answerMulti-file Read for survey purposes”Read these 8 files and tell me what’s similar” — fits subagent shape
Stay in main context





























Tool / operationWhy mainBash / gitSubagents typically can’t run shell commands; also, output is usually load-bearing and smallSingle-file Read of a user-named fileThe file is the actual subject; main needs to read it itselfTargeted Read of a known locationCost is small, hop to subagent doesn’t payAskUserQuestionThe clarification is a main-context conversational beatSynthesis, decisions, planningCannot delegate; this is the work
Borderline cases

WebFetch on a short, known page — fine in main if the result is the actual deliverable
Multi-file Read of 2-3 files — main if you’ll need them in working memory anyway; subagent if you only need a summary
Grep for a single pattern with a known small match set — main if you’ll act on each match; subagent if you’re surveying

The dividing question: will the raw output be load-bearing in my next step, or only the synthesis? If raw → main. If synthesis → Explore.
The “carry context per dispatch” rule
The most common failure when delegating to Explore is dispatching with too little context. The subagent has no access to:

Prior conversation turns
Files the user has named in this session
Errors already shown
Decisions already made
The project’s CLAUDE.md unless re-loaded

A dispatch that says “find the auth bug” will produce a confabulated answer at non-trivial cost. A dispatch that says “in src/auth/, find the function that handles session refresh — the user reported it throws AccessDenied after 30 minutes; check whether the JWT exp claim is being compared to a wall-clock or a monotonic time” produces a real answer.
Minimum per-dispatch payload:

What — the actual question or task, specified concretely
Where — file paths, directories, or named external sources
Frame — the relevant errors, decisions, or constraints from this session
Stop condition — what counts as enough information to return

Net effect

Search-and-survey tokens land on cheap subagent context, not the user-visible main context
Main context stays uncrowded for reasoning, synthesis, and decisions
The subagent’s report is shaped by frame from the dispatching turn, so it doesn’t confabulate against this codebase
Tools that must stay in main (Bash, AskUserQuestion, file edits) are not displaced by search noise

Anti-patterns

Dispatching Explore with no context. Produces fluent but wrong-codebase findings. The whole point of routing through a subagent is undermined.
Putting Bash in Explore. Most subagent configurations can’t execute shell commands. Bash is intrinsically main-context.
Reading 12 files in main “just in case”. That output stays in context for the rest of the session. If you don’t need them as working memory, dispatch the read and ask for synthesis.
Treating the subagent’s report as raw evidence. It is a claim about the raw evidence. For load-bearing claims, verify against the actual source — see reliability-vs-capability-agents for the trust-but-verify protocol.

When the routing itself is the wrong tool
Routing through Explore is a discipline with costs, not a free win. Cases where main context is the better choice even for searches:

Small dispatches with known small payload. A grep for a single identifier with maybe three callers — by the time you have written the dispatch with frame and stop condition, you have spent more attention than the raw output would have cost.
Exploratory reads where the synthesis is uncertain. If you do not yet know what you are looking for, a subagent’s synthesis will compress out the exact unfamiliar detail that matters. Main-context Read keeps the raw material accessible.
Search where the raw evidence is the deliverable. If the user asked “show me every place X is called”, dispatching the search and reporting a count loses what the user wanted. Run it in main and present the raw matches.
Context-carrying overhead exceeds the search savings. A short search with a long required context payload costs more in dispatch construction than in tokens saved — the payload being paths, errors, prior decisions, stop condition.

The routing rule trades volume-of-output cost for ceremony cost. Apply where the trade is favourable; not as a blanket rule.
Related

context-window-management — the broader cost model this pattern optimises against
claude-code-prompt-pipeline — where in the pipeline subagent dispatches happen
multi-agent-token-efficiency — the same waste-reduction principle at multi-agent scale
feedback_subagent_trust in the auto-memory — verification discipline for subagent meta-claims; pairs directly with this routing rule

Sources
