ai/external-skills/mattpocock/index.title: Matt Pocock Skills — Collection Analysis
ai/external-skills/mattpocock/index.content:
Matt Pocock Skills — Collection Analysis
Comparative capture of the public mattpocock/skills repo — a set of Claude/agent skills authored by Matt Pocock (Total TypeScript). Each note records what the skill does, its key mechanism (the part worth stealing), when it fires, and how it relates to this vault’s owned skill toolkit under skills.
Scope: 25 of the repo’s 29 skills — all active + in-progress. The 4 deprecated skills (design-an-interface, qa, request-refactor-plan, ubiquitous-language) were excluded by design. Captured 2026-06-08 against HEAD; this is a time-sensitive snapshot of an evolving repo.
Headline finding: the two collections barely overlap. This vault’s skills are thinking / verification / cognitive-burden tools; Pocock’s are engineering-workflow tools (TDD, triage, PRD/issue generation, debugging, repo setup). So 21/25 are novel (new capability area), and only the 4 below are flagged as direct adoption-candidates — novel and worth considering for the owned set.

Implementation backlog: adoption-plan — actionable grafts of these mechanisms onto specific owned skills, with a resume point and recommended order.

Adoption candidates (review these first)



































SkillCategoryWhy it’s worth adoptingRelates to ownedgrill-meproductivityMinimal one-question-at-a-time interview that walks a plan’s decision tree, each question with a recommended answer, exploring the codebase instead of asking when possible. A tighter, lower-ceremony cousin of clarify-first.clarify-first, starburst, red-teamhandoffproductivityCompacts a conversation into a portable handoff doc for a fresh agent: saved to OS temp dir, mandatory “suggested skills” routing section, de-dups by referencing existing artifacts, redacts secrets. Mechanism complements commitment-ledger.commitment-ledger, retrospective, context-budget-scanwrite-a-skillproductivityA generator for SKILL.md (structure, progressive disclosure, description rules, review checklist). The owned set has only auditors (skill-quality-audit, skill-trigger-audit) — this fills the authoring-side gap.skill-quality-audit, skill-trigger-audit, which-skillreviewin-progressDiff review split into two axes — Standards vs Spec — run as parallel isolated sub-agents with a no-merge aggregation rule so one axis can’t mask the other. The orchestration pattern is the steal; owned skills run these checks sequentially in one context.ai-diff-judgment, lean-review, intent-fulfilment-check, reviewers-map
All skills by category
engineering (10) — all novel

diagnose — Six-phase debugging loop; builds a fast deterministic pass/fail signal before touching code, then ranked falsifiable hypotheses + one-variable instrumentation. (rel: falsifiability-scan, verify, red-team)
grill-with-docs — One-question-at-a-time interview that stress-tests a plan against the project glossary (CONTEXT.md) and ADRs, updating both inline. (rel: clarify-first, intent-check, contradiction-scan)
improve-codebase-architecture — Surfaces shallow-module/coupling friction; proposes “deepening” refactors via an interactive HTML report + design grilling loop.
prototype — Throwaway question-answering code; branches between an interactive TUI (logic/state questions) and toggleable UI variants (?variant=).
setup-matt-pocock-skills — One-time conversational bootstrap that writes per-repo config so the other skills know the issue tracker, triage labels, domain-doc layout.
tdd — Strict red-green-refactor in vertical slices (bans horizontal slicing); tests verify public behavior not implementation.
to-issues — Breaks a plan/PRD into independently-grabbable tickets shaped as tracer-bullet vertical slices. (rel: task-decompose, plan-split-scan, branch-resolve)
to-prd — Synthesizes the current conversation into a structured PRD, seam-first test design, anti-staleness rule (no file paths). (rel: intent-check, falsifiability-scan, plan-options)
triage — Issue category/state role machine ending in a durability-over-precision agent brief (interfaces not file paths, testable acceptance criteria).
zoom-out — Three-sentence human-only prompt: shift abstraction level, map modules + callers in domain vocabulary.

productivity (5) — 3 adoption-candidates

caveman — Persistent output-style mode stripping filler (~75% token cut) with exact-preservation carve-outs and an auto-clarity exception for safety/destructive steps. (rel: density-scan, context-budget-scan)
grill-me ★ — see adoption table.
handoff ★ — see adoption table.
teach — Stateful multi-session teaching workspace; externalizes pedagogical state into named files (MISSION.md, learning-records, per-lesson HTML). Promoted in-progress→productivity upstream by 2026-06-11; already runs here as the vault-adapted teach port. Novel capability, not a mechanism-graft. (rel: calibration-loop — both externalize incrementing dated records across sessions)
write-a-skill ★ — see adoption table.

misc (4) — all novel

git-guardrails-claude-code — PreToolUse hook that blocks destructive git commands (push/reset —hard/clean -f/branch -D) by exiting 2 with a reason.
migrate-to-shoehorn — Migrates TS test as assertions to @total-typescript/shoehorn partial-data helpers via a fixed three-way mapping + grep-driven checklist.
scaffold-exercises — Scaffolds a course exercise tree that passes the ai-hero-cli linter; encodes the linter’s hidden rules as an explicit naming grammar.
setup-pre-commit — Wires Husky + lint-staged (Prettier/typecheck/test) into a JS/TS repo; lockfile-based PM detection, fail-soft missing scripts.

personal (2) — all novel

edit-article — Topologically orders an article’s sections (DAG of prerequisites), then rewrites each for clarity at ≤240 chars/paragraph. (rel: density-scan, structural-trace)
obsidian-vault — Thin convention sheet teaching Claude one specific Obsidian vault’s layout (path, Title Case, no-folders/index-notes, wikilinks) + grep/find commands. (Direct analogue of this vault’s own CLAUDE.md + conventions.)

in-progress (4) — 1 adoption-candidate, experimental

review ★ — see adoption table.
writing-beats — Choose-your-own-adventure article assembly; offers 2-3 candidate next beats, writes one at a time.
writing-fragments — Grilling interview that mines heterogeneous writing fragments into a flat append-only markdown file.
writing-shape — Turns a pile of raw notes into an article via conversational paragraph-by-paragraph shaping with per-beat format rubric.

Recurring mechanisms worth stealing
The cross-cutting patterns that repeat across the collection — the real harvest for “further analysis”:

One-question-at-a-time grilling (grill-me, grill-with-docs, triage, setup-*) — strict turn discipline, a recommended answer attached to every question, and “explore the codebase instead of asking when the answer is there.” More disciplined than the owned clarify-first’s batched AskUserQuestion.
Vertical slices / tracer bullets (tdd, to-issues) — explicitly ban “horizontal slicing” (all tests then all code) in favor of thin end-to-end slices.
Durability over precision in written artifacts (triage, to-prd, to-issues) — an anti-staleness rule: briefs/PRDs describe interfaces and behavior, never file paths or code snippets (except prototype-derived shapes), so they don’t rot.
CONTEXT.md glossary + ADR as shared state (grill-with-docs, improve-codebase-architecture, to-prd, setup-*) — a persistent project vocabulary and decision log that multiple skills read and write, with a three-gate ADR test (hard-to-reverse, surprising, real trade-off).
Re-read the file from disk before every append (writing-fragments, writing-beats, writing-shape) — preserves the user’s mid-session manual edits; never overwrites.
Context isolation via parallel sub-agents (review, improve-codebase-architecture) — separate questions into disjoint sub-agent contexts so they can’t cross-contaminate or mask each other.
Throwaway artifacts with capture-then-delete (prototype) — build to answer one question, record the answer durably, then delete.
Guardrails as hooks, not instructions (git-guardrails-claude-code, setup-pre-commit) — enforce safety via PreToolUse / pre-commit hooks the harness runs, not prose the model may ignore.

Related

skills — the owned skill toolkit these are compared against
verification-stack-operational-map — decision tree across the owned skills
skill-quality-criteria — what makes a good SKILL.md (used as the lens for mechanism capture)
skill-pack-design-constraint-pattern — the structured-skill-bundle pattern; this repo is another worked example


Time-sensitive: captured 2026-06-08 against mattpocock/skills@HEAD. The repo is actively evolving (note the in-progress and deprecated folders) — re-verify before treating any specific mechanism as current.
Re-verified 2026-06-11 against current main (latest upstream commit 2026-06-10). Skill set unchanged — still 29 skills, same 4 deprecated, same names. One drift: teach promoted in-progress→productivity and developed heavily 06-08…06-10, adding four pedagogy mechanisms (fluency-vs-storage-strength, one-primary-source-per-lesson, same-length quiz answers, HTML anchor cross-linking) — all grafted onto the owned teach port this pass; details in teach. No other skill changed category or gained adoption-relevant mechanisms. The adoption-plan backlog remains complete.

ai/falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.title: Falsifiability — Claim-Shape Fingerprints and Operational Tests
ai/falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.content:
Falsifiability — Claim-Shape Fingerprints and Operational Tests
Backing catalog for the /falsifiability-scan skill. The skill tags load-bearing claims by shape (could this even be wrong, and how would we know?) — a different axis from /reviewers-map (is each claim true?), /bias-scan-ai (is the output contaminated?), and /red-team (is the argument wrong?). A claim can pass /reviewers-map’s [V] (verified) check because nothing rules it out — that vague-but-confident shape is the failure mode this catalog targets.
The note is organised so the skill can reference it cheaply: taxonomy and fingerprints come first; the philosophy that constrains the taxonomy follows.
Why a separate axis from existing skills






























Existing skillQuestionWhat it misses/reviewers-mapIs each claim true / verifiable?Claims so vague nothing rules them out tag as [V] — they have no specific to verify/bias-scan-aiIs the output contaminated by output-side bias fingerprints?Tests for hallucination, sycophancy, narrative coherence — but not whether well-supported claims are shaped such that they could be refuted/red-teamIs the argument wrong?Adversarial truth, not testability of claim shape/disagreeCould the opposite be defended?Inversion drill on most recent response, not per-claim shape
The dangerous case: a fluent AI-drafted note where every claim sounds confident, the entity check (/bias-scan-ai) passes, the inversion (/disagree) has weak purchase — yet the load-bearing claims (“more robust,” “users will prefer,” “scales better”) have no specifiable falsifying observation. Verified-and-unfalsifiable is the gap.
The six-category taxonomy
Each load-bearing claim about the world gets exactly one tag:








































TagMeaningExample[OP] OperationalStated falsifying observation, measurement, deadline”build time < 2s on commit X by date D”[DEF] Deferred-testFalsifiable in principle; currently untestable for cost / instrumentation / scope reasons”this approach scales to 10k req/s” — testable, not in this session[VAGUE] SharpenableFalsifiable shape latent but unspecified; needs operationalization to become [OP]”more robust” — robust against what, measured how[SEAL] Self-sealingCounter-evidence reframed away by the claim’s own structure”in the right context X works” / “that’s not real X”[PROB] Bayesian-disconfirmableProbabilistic; updates posterior but cannot be strictly refuted by any finite evidence”this prompt usually produces better output”[DEFN] Definitional / tautologicalAnalytic, terminological, or value-laden; not an empirical claim”the verification protocol is the four-pass workflow”
Three categories deserve emphasis:

[DEFN] and [PROB] are not failures. Definitions and probabilistic claims fall outside Popper’s strict criterion of falsifiability as a logical property; that does not make them defective. Probabilistic claims need the Tetlock operationalization (probability + resolution criteria) instead of the strict-falsification one.
[SEAL] is the rhetorical-failure mode. A claim is degenerating in Lakatos’s sense when it was risky but is now being patched after each disconfirmation. This is distinct from [VAGUE]: a [VAGUE] claim could be sharpened into [OP]; a [SEAL] claim is structured to absorb every counterexample.
[VAGUE] is the actionable middle case. Most AI-drafted prose lives here. The constructive output of the scan is the operationalization checklist that converts [VAGUE] into [OP] or [DEF].

Fingerprints of unfalsifiable / self-sealing claims
The patterns below are diagnostic. Not all are bad — definitions need to be tautological, hedges have legitimate uses — but in load-bearing claims about the world, each pattern is the signature of [VAGUE] or [SEAL].
Vacuous universals. “X always works in the right context” / “with proper implementation” / “for the right team.” The qualifier is unbounded and absorbs every counter-case. Compare with operational form: “X reduced p99 latency by ≥30% in benchmark suite Y on hardware Z.”
Self-sealing reframe. Any counter-example is reclassified as “not real X” or as evidence of denial / repression / immaturity / wrong fit. The standard taxonomy includes the no-true-Scotsman move, the Marxist-false-consciousness move, the repressed-Oedipus move. Cf. the Logically Fallacious entry on self-sealing arguments — “wherever you go, there you are” is the limiting case.
Postdiction dressed as prediction. Claim explains what already happened (“the framework predicts last year’s outcome”) without committing to a future observation it forbids. Popper’s distinction: a scientific claim must forbid possible observations, not retro-fit accomplished ones.
Hedge-stacked claims. “Generally,” “tends to,” “in many cases,” “could,” “may” — combined so densely the conjunction survives any observation. One hedge is calibration; a stack of hedges is camouflage.
Operationally empty comparatives. “More robust,” “scales better,” “users will prefer,” “more aligned” — no measurement procedure, threshold, or population. These are the dominant [VAGUE] shape in AI-drafted technical prose.
Definitional retreat. When evidence challenges the claim, the key term is silently redefined (“that’s not really intelligence / learning / understanding”) and the claim re-asserted. The definition was load-bearing all along; the claim was [DEFN] masquerading as [OP].
Tautology. The claim is true by virtue of its own form. “Two weeks from today you will be doing what you’ll be doing.” Legitimate as a [DEFN]; failure mode as a load-bearing prediction.
Operationalization checklist
For each [VAGUE] and [DEF] claim, demand four items. This four-item checklist mirrors the operational moves in pre-registration, Lean Startup, and forecasting communities — the cash value of the criterion in everyday prose.

Falsifying observation — what would count against this claim?
Measurement procedure — how would the observation be captured?
Deadline / commitment point — by when, against what artifact?
Auxiliary bundle — what background assumptions are pinned alongside it (toolchain version, dataset, environment, prompt, hardware)?

Item 4 is the Quine–Duhem holism move: a falsification verdict is against the bundle, not the claim alone. Naming the auxiliaries makes the verdict honest.
For [PROB] claims, use the Tetlock variant
Probabilistic claims are technically unfalsifiable in strict Popper (Sober’s point: no finite outcome sequence refutes a probability claim). The honest operationalization is forecaster-shaped:

Numeric probability — translate verbal hedges (“usually,” “often,” “tends to”) into a number. “Usually” is not a probability; 0.7 is.
Resolution criterion — the question must resolve unambiguously yes/no on observable evidence. “User satisfaction improves” does not resolve; “NPS ≥ +20 in survey instrument Y on date D” resolves.
Deadline — by when does the question resolve.
Scoring posture — Brier score / log-score commitment, or at minimum a recorded prediction the future-self can grade against. The Annie Duke move: separate process from outcome at scoring time.

A [PROB] claim with all four is honestly testable; a [PROB] claim missing any of them is [VAGUE] wearing probabilistic clothing.
Theoretical foundations (brief)
Popper introduced falsifiability in The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934 / 1959 English) and developed it in Conjectures and Refutations (1963). A theory is scientific if and only if it is incompatible with possible empirical observations. Three load-bearing distinctions:

Falsifiability vs falsification. Falsifiability is a logical property (the statement has potential falsifiers). Falsification is a methodological act (accepting that one of those falsifiers has been observed). The skill targets the first; only the user can perform the second.
Risky predictions. “The more a theory forbids, the better it is.” Eddington’s 1919 eclipse test of general relativity is the paradigm case — a prediction that could have failed spectacularly. The [OP] tag corresponds to claims that forbid specific observations.
The asymmetry. No finite observation set verifies a universal law (Hume’s induction problem); a single genuine counter-instance refutes one. This logical asymmetry licenses falsifiability as the criterion.

Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Karl Popper (Stephen Thornton, 2022); Wikipedia “Falsifiability”; Conjectures and Refutations.
Critical guardrails — what the scan must NOT claim
Five constraints derived from the philosophical literature. The skill prompt must not violate any of these:
1. Unfalsifiable ≠ meaningless or unscientific. Popper rejected the verificationists’ meaning criterion — definitions, ethics, mathematics, and probabilistic claims fail strict falsifiability without being defective. The scan flags shape, not value.
2. Falsification is never binary in practice (Quine–Duhem holism). A hypothesis H entails an observation E only conjoined with auxiliaries B. So ¬E entails ¬(H ∧ B), not ¬H — we cannot tell which conjunct to blame. The scan output must name the bundle, not pretend the claim falsifies in isolation.
3. In-principle falsifiable ≠ operationally testable now (Lakatos). A claim can be falsifiable in logic but currently untestable for cost, instrumentation, or scope reasons. Lakatos’s distinction between progressive and degenerating research programmes (hard core + protective belt) is more honest than “unscientific.” The [DEF] tag captures this — deferred test, not failure.
4. Probabilistic claims are technically unfalsifiable in strict Popper (Sober). A probability claim is never refuted by any finite outcome sequence. The honest move is to call them [PROB] (Bayesian-disconfirmable), not [SEAL] or [VAGUE]. The Tetlock operationalization is the appropriate test, not the strict-falsifiability one.
5. Demarcation, not meaning (Popper vs verificationism). Popper’s criterion separates empirical-scientific from non-empirical-scientific, not meaningful from meaningless. Yudkowsky’s “make your beliefs pay rent in anticipated experiences” is a recognisable cousin from the meaning lineage (closer to Peirce’s pragmatic maxim) — useful as a second-order check when the four-item checklist is ambiguous, but distinct from Popper’s demarcation.
Boundary against neighboring concepts

Testability is broader than falsifiability. A confirmation-only test (probabilistic prediction that becomes more or less likely) is testable but not strictly falsificatory.
Refutability vs disconfirmability. Refutation is binary and decisive; disconfirmation is graded probabilistic update. Bayesians replace one with the other; the scan should not call a claim [SEAL] when it is honestly [PROB].
Verificationism (Vienna Circle) is a meaning criterion Popper explicitly opposed. Do not conflate.
Predictiveness vs falsifiability. Orthogonal. A claim can be predictive but unfalsifiable (“something noteworthy will happen this year”) or vague but falsifiable (“the bridge will not collapse under load X by date D”).
Pragmatic maxim (Peirce / James). A theory of meaning, not of demarcation. “Beliefs pay rent” is the modern descendant of this lineage.

Operational descendants outside philosophy
The taxonomy converges with several practitioner traditions. Each gives the skill a non-philosophical vocabulary for the same moves:

Pre-registration (replication crisis). Hypotheses, predictions, and analyses committed before data collection — institutionalised falsifiability against HARKing and p-hacking. Caveat: many preregistrations are too vague to actually constrain analyses; low-falsifiability preregistrations don’t deliver the epistemic benefit.
Lean Startup (Eric Ries). Every product change requires “a falsifiable hypothesis” testing a “leap-of-faith assumption”; build–measure–learn is the operational falsification cycle (“validated learning”).
Tetlock superforecasting. Vague verbal forecasts must be translated into numeric probabilities over precisely-resolved questions with deadlines, scored by Brier score. Source for the [PROB] operationalization.
Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets. Generalises Tetlock: state probabilities and resolution criteria so outcomes can update beliefs; separate process quality from outcome quality at scoring time.
ML construct validity (Freiesleben & Zezulka, The Benchmarking Epistemology, 2025, arXiv 2510.23191). Capability claims unaccompanied by an extensional task definition are unfalsifiable in operational terms; benchmark scores without methodology footnotes are unfalsifiable claims.
“Beliefs pay rent” (Yudkowsky). “Every belief should flow from a question of anticipation … what experience will happen to you?” Cousin from the pragmatic-maxim lineage; useful as a second-order anticipation check.

How to use this catalog
When invoked by /falsifiability-scan:

Extract load-bearing claims about the world (skip definitions, decisions, preferences).
Tag each with one of the six categories using the taxonomy table.
For [VAGUE] and [DEF] claims, run the four-item operationalization checklist.
For [PROB] claims, run the Tetlock variant.
Name the auxiliary bundle for the most load-bearing [OP] or [DEF] claim (Quine–Duhem holism).
Verdict: falsifiable enough to commit if load-bearing claims are [OP], [DEF], honest [PROB], or [DEFN]; sharpen before commit if any load-bearing claim is [SEAL] or load-bearing [VAGUE].

Related

ai-output-bias-fingerprints — output-side bias catalog (different axis: contamination, not testability)
bias-aware-verification-protocol — four-pass framework this skill plugs into
cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — why fluent prose feels verified when it isn’t (the failure mode this scan exists to catch)
prompt-bias-diagnostics — input-side reframing (upstream)

Sources

Karl Popper — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Thornton, 2022)
Falsifiability — Wikipedia
Conjectures and Refutations — full text PDF (Popper, 1963; PDF host unverified — original is canonical)
Duhem–Quine thesis — Wikipedia
Imre Lakatos — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Bayesian Epistemology — Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
What Did Karl Popper Really Say About Evolution? — NCSE
Self-Sealing Argument — Logically Fallacious
Lean startup — Wikipedia
Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters — Good Judgment
The Benchmarking Epistemology: Construct Validity for Evaluating Machine Learning Models (Freiesleben & Zezulka, 2025)
Making Beliefs Pay Rent (in Anticipated Experiences) — LessWrong (Yudkowsky)
Sober, Philosophy of Biology — for the argument that probabilistic theories are technically unfalsifiable in Popper’s strict sense, and that “unfalsifiable = unscientific” overstates Popper

ai/generative-ui-landscape.title: Generative UI — Runtime Landscape and Evidence Base
ai/generative-ui-landscape.content:
Generative UI — Runtime Landscape and Evidence Base
Last verified: 2026-08-25 (npm registry + GitHub API queried directly; arXiv metadata via the arXiv API; spec, vendor, and ACM pages fetched same day, with paywalled ACM abstracts via tools/snapshot). Version, star, and status claims below decay fast. The libraries in the table shipped releases the same week this was written.
The vault already holds two narrow slices of this: a2ui-vs-json-render (one head-to-head, re-verified 2026-08-25) and ui-for-ai-products (streaming and failure affordances). Neither covers the field, and neither carries the research. This note is the anchor: the two axes that organize the space, the current runtime options, and what the evidence actually shows.
Scope boundary, kept sharp throughout: design-time builders (v0, Bolt, Lovable — a human prompts, a human reviews, code lands in a repo) are a different problem from runtime generative UI (an agent produces interface for an end user, live, with no human in the loop). They share a name and almost nothing else. Most confusion in this space is the two being discussed as one thing.
Two axes, not one
Every runtime approach answers what crosses the trust boundary. But what a failure costs depends on what the host is holding — and that second question does more predictive work than the first. Treating this as one axis is the common mistake, and it produces guardrail advice that is either ignored or over-applied.
Axis 1 — what crosses the boundary. CopilotKit’s 2026 developer guide splits it three ways (vendor-authored, and it positions CopilotKit as the answer at all three tiers); restated around the boundary rather than around their product:





























TierWhat crossesThe model choosesCharacteristic failureStaticNothing. A tool-call name + validated args.Which of your components to show, and with what dataWrong component; bounded and inspectableDeclarativeA JSON tree naming components from a fixed catalogComposition and layout, within the catalogCatalog too narrow → generic output; too wide → unbounded surfaceOpen-endedHTML/CSS/JS, or a whole UI surfaceEverythingArbitrary code from a probabilistic source; XSS, exfiltration, silent side effects
Axis 2 — what a compromise costs. A browser tab in your own web app is a low-privilege host: the web’s threat model already assumes hostile content, and an escape costs you that tab. What this means for the guardrail everyone repeats
Practitioner guardrail lists near-universally open with “give the model a whitelisted component registry, not arbitrary HTML or JavaScript” — stated flatly, as a rule. The condition is what matters, and it is almost always omitted.
Google ships open-ended code generation to consumers and violates nothing: presentational surface, low-privilege host, no privileged actions. That is not a counterexample to the rule; it is the rule’s scope, made visible. Two failure modes, and they are opposite. Repeating the guardrail unconditionally gets it ignored, because a very large visible counterexample exists. Abandoning it because Google does otherwise throws away the cases where it holds. The grid above is the condition. Know which cell you are in before you decide the rule applies.

Migration is npx @ai-sdk/codemod v7. Generative UI in the SDK remains the tool-call→React-component binding, i.e. the static tier.
MCP Apps — the one with a finished spec
SEP-1865 reached Final status on the Extensions Track (created 2025-11-21; authored by Ido Salomon, Liad Yosef, Olivier Chafik and six others; shipped as the first official MCP extension, per secondary sources, on 2026-01-26 — a date the ext-apps repo path specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx corroborates).
It sits in the grid’s worst cell, open-ended content in a high-privilege host. The design answers that directly:

UI ships as predeclared resources under a ui:// URI scheme, typed text/html;profile=mcp-app — not embedded in tool results. The SEP is explicit that this was chosen over MCP-UI’s embedded-resource approach specifically so hosts can prefetch, cache, and security-review the HTML before anything runs.
Bi-directional traffic reuses MCP’s JSON-RPC, so every UI→host message is loggable and auditable rather than a bespoke postMessage channel.
Mandatory iframe sandboxing; hosts may require explicit user consent for UI-initiated tool calls.
Optional, negotiated, backwards-compatible.

The provenance is worth keeping. It unifies two prior systems, community MCP-UI (adopters cited in the SEP: Postman, HuggingFace, Shopify, Goose, ElevenLabs) and OpenAI’s Apps SDK (launched November 2025). This is the “UI runs inside someone else’s AI client” case, and it is the only one here with a finalized standard.
What the research actually shows
Six papers, all metadata confirmed against the arXiv API on 2026-08-25. A community index at awesomegenerativeui.com tracks ~28 and is a better entry point than any single reading list.
The capability is real — and it’s shipped
“Generative UI: LLMs are Effective UI Generators” (arXiv 2604.09577, Leviathan et al., Google; arXiv metadata reports 2026-02-24 — note the 2604 ID prefix would normally imply April, an inconsistency left unresolved. Author count is not stated here: the arXiv API returns 13 author nodes while the abstract page lists 12). Claims, verbatim from the abstract: results are “overwhelmingly preferred by humans over the standard LLM markdown output”; worse than human experts but “at least comparable in 50% of cases”; the capability is “emergent, with substantial improvements from previous models.” Releases PAGEN, an expert-crafted evaluation dataset.
The important part is not the paper — it is that Google shipped this before publishing it. The Google Research blog post (2025-11-18) predates the arXiv posting and describes it live in the Gemini app (dynamic view, visual layout) and in Search AI Mode for AI Pro/Ultra subscribers in the US. The implementation: Gemini 3 Pro, a server exposing tools (image generation, web search), heavy system instructions, and post-processing to fix common issues — generating HTML/CSS/JS that runs in the user’s browser. Stated limitation: generation “can sometimes take a minute or more.”
So the most visible consumer deployment of runtime generative UI is raw code generation with a post-processing cleanup pass — bottom-left cell of the grid above. Not a violation of the registry guardrail; outside its scope. Worth stating what is inference rather than fact: Google does not say “we ship this because the surface has no privileged actions.” That reading is mine, and it is the load-bearing assumption behind treating this deployment as safely replicable in a low-privilege host.
Two independent corroborations, so the capability claim does not rest on Google evaluating Google:

“Generative Interfaces for Language Models” (arXiv 2508.19227v3, Chen, Zhang, Zhang, Shao et al. — SALT-NLP; ACL 2026 Findings). LLMs respond by generating a task-specific UI rather than prose, via structured interface representations plus iterative refinement. Reports up to 72% improvement in human preference over chat, across a multidimensional framework covering functional, interactive, and emotional dimensions. Independent team, independent evaluation, same direction as Google’s result.
“The Keyhole Effect: Why Chat Interfaces Fail at Data Analysis” (arXiv 2602.00947, Mohan Reddy, 2026-02-01) is the mechanistic case, and the most useful framing here for anyone who has to justify the work. It argues chat degrades multi-step analytical tasks through five named mechanisms — content displacement defeating spatial memory, hidden state exceeding working memory (~4 chunks under load), forced verbalization triggering verbal overshadowing that degrades visual pattern recognition, linear text blocking epistemic action and cognitive offloading, and serialization penalties scaling with data dimensionality. Generative UI appears as one of eight proposed remedies. Note what this reframes: the argument for generative UI is not “prettier than markdown” but “markdown is a cognitive bottleneck for state-dependent work.” That is a falsifiable claim about tasks, which tells you where generative UI earns its cost — and by implication where it does not. It also connects the whole axis to cognitive-load-theory-for-ai and how-much-information-at-once.

The explanations are unreliable — measured
“Design Theater: Evaluating the Gap Between User-Facing Design Reasoning and Implementation in Generative UI Tools” (arXiv 2607.22928v2, Imteyaz et al., 6 authors, 2026-07-24, accepted at AAAI/AIES). The strongest result in the set and the one to actually act on.
24 benchmark tasks × 5 tools = 120 interfaces. Tools evaluated: ChatGPT, Claude, Firebase Studio, Vercel v0, and Bolt. Findings:

~25% of user-facing design rationales are not implemented in the interface produced.
34% for functional requirements.
Tools recognize roughly half the UX principles embedded in prompts (mean = 0.54).
Four of the five tools implemented ≤6% of functional principles.
Interfaces converge across tools in appearance and layout, varying mainly in color.

“Design Theater” names the failure precisely: “plausible and confident design rationales that have little relationship to the actual implementation.”
Note the scope carefully — these are design-time builders, not the runtime frameworks in the table above. The paper does not measure json-render or Tambo. What transfers is the mechanism, not the number: an LLM’s stated reasoning about its own UI output is not evidence about that output. That indicts one specific workflow, reading the rationale instead of testing the interface. It is the same generation-vs-verification asymmetry as cognitive-burden-of-ai-use and the oracle-problem-verification framing. The convergence finding also lands squarely on visual-ai-slop-fingerprints.
”Good UI” has no single ground truth
“Efficient Personalization of Generative User Interfaces” (arXiv 2604.09876, Peng, Das, Bigham, Wu — CMU/Purdue, 2026-04-10). 20 trained designers made pairwise judgments over the same 600 generated UIs. Average kappa = 0.25 — substantial disagreement among trained designers, and written rationales show they diverge on how they define and prioritize shared concepts like “hierarchy” or “cleanliness.”
This is the quiet load-bearing result for anyone building evals here. A fixed design rubric encodes one designer’s preferences and calls it quality. Their method instead represents a new user in terms of prior designers, and beat both a pretrained UI evaluator and a larger multimodal model. Direct read-through: an LLM-as-judge for UI quality inherits whichever designer population its rubric was written from. But do not over-read the disagreement — the paper’s actual contribution runs the other way. Low inter-rater agreement did not mean preference was arbitrary; their model learned it from sparse feedback and beat both baselines. The lesson is that “good UI” is learnable but not universal: a single fixed rubric asserting global quality is the thing that fails, while a judge calibrated to a named population can work. Pairs with llm-evaluation-methodology.
Accessibility — two separate bodies of work, deliberately not merged
There are two literatures here. They are often cited together as if one answered the other. They do not: they use different tools, tasks, output artifacts, metrics, and populations, and neither is positioned to confirm or contradict the other. Kept apart on purpose.
(a) Generation used as a remediation layer over existing pages
“Generative UI as an Accessibility Bridge: Lessons from C2C E-Commerce” (arXiv 2604.25455, Bektur Ryskeldiev, Mercari R4D / Univ. of Tsukuba, 2026-04-28) synthesizes six studies (2022–2025) with blind, low-vision, and older-adult users. Its ASSETS ‘25 browser extension used GPT-4o to restructure existing e-commerce HTML for screen-reader users; 15 screen-reader users rated three conditions:





















ConditionOverall browsing experience (5-pt Likert)Fully regenerated, text-only5.0Tag-level reorganization (visual layout unchanged)4.57Original Mercari site3.14
Median task-completion time fell from ~130 s to ~25 s. Semantic similarity between original and regenerated pages averaged 96.3% (range 91.60–99.36%), so content meaning was largely preserved. Scope: n=15 on one site class, and the author states the wider program’s samples run 8–15. This is a promising result on a narrow task, not a general finding about accessibility.
What makes this case tractable is structural and worth naming: the system has a source document to be faithful to, so fidelity is measurable, and it inherits content rather than inventing it. That property does not transfer to generation from a prompt.
(b) Accessibility of interfaces generated from a prompt
Three results, and they need their scopes attached — the headline number in particular is weaker than it reads:

“Generated Inaccessible: Measuring WCAG Violations in AI UI Design Tools” (W4A 2026). Reports 29.0% compliance across 21,880 assessments (color contrast 26.8%, use of color 19.2%), and 39% of AI violations needing “major redesign” versus 22% for manual. Read the scope before quoting the number: the tools are design-mockup tools (Figma Make, Google Stitch, Visely, UXPilot, Banani, SketchFlow AI) — not runtime generative UI and not code generation; the 54 participants were “primarily students and early-career designers”; and the five WCAG criteria were chosen because participants lacked the background to assess code-dependent criteria like semantic structure, keyboard operability, or ARIA correctness. So this is what novices could see by visual inspection of mockups, not a WCAG audit. It is real evidence about a real tool class, and it is not evidence about generated code.
“Measuring the Semantic Accessibility Gap in LLM-Generated Web UIs” (CHI 2026 EA, Calò et al.). The stronger result for our purposes, because it works at code level: 300 UIs from three frontier models (Claude, Gemini, GPT) yielded 541 semantic violations that pass automated checks — alt="image", “Click here” links. Detection by LLM-as-judge, validated by controlled fault injection at 80–92% recall, triangulated against four expert annotators over 324 components.
A11YN (arXiv 2510.13914, Yoon et al., Yonsei/SNU, 2025-10-15). RL (GRPO) against an axe-core-severity-weighted reward cut a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B baseline inaccessibility rate from 0.38 to 0.15 on RealUIReq-300, reportedly beating GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4. Those baselines are two model generations old — treat the comparison as historical and the method (severity-weighted automated signal as an RL reward) as the transferable part.

The one claim that survives from both
Not a synthesis of the two literatures — a finding each reaches separately about the same instrument. The automated accessibility gate is the wrong gate here. From (a): “every test page passed some automated audits while still failing real users.” From (b): an image with alt="image" “passes every check yet conveys nothing.” Axe-core’s ~30–40% WCAG coverage is already noted in ai-augmented-ui-development; the semantic-gap paper is direct code-level evidence that generated UI fails predominantly in the uncovered remainder. A green axe run on generated UI is weak evidence. See visual-verification-ai-ui and design-system-accessibility.
And one counterintuitive result, scoped to its tool class: in the W4A mockup-tool study, explicitly specifying accessibility requirements in the prompt decreased compliance — prompts naming 4.5:1 contrast, 44×44px touch targets, and no-color-alone did worse than prompts that did not. The authors read it as misalignment between how designers express accessibility and how these systems operationalize constraints. Whether it generalizes to code-generating models is untested. Within that tool class, “just put it in the prompt” is falsified.
The definitional work
“The GenUI Study” (arXiv 2501.13145v3, Chen, Knearem, Li — UCLA/Google/DeepMind, DIS 2025): 37 UX professionals across four roles, week-long mini-projects with journals and interviews. The field’s main empirical account of practitioner adoption, which is the axis relevant to design-side-ai-adoption-stall and designer-seat-under-ai.
“Towards a Working Definition of Designing Generative User Interfaces” (arXiv 2505.15049, Kyungho Lee, DIS 2025 companion): 127-publication review + 18 expert interviews + 12 case studies. Its definition is the useful export — humans and AI collaborate at design time to generate interfaces; users interact with AI-generated interfaces at runtime. That is the boundary this note opens with, and the reason to trust it is that a 127-publication review landed on it, not that this note asserts it.
The security surface
Extracted to its own note: generative-ui-security — the isolation stack flag by flag, what the MCP Apps spec actually mandates versus leaves to hosts, A2UI’s double-iframe pattern, and a review checklist. The short version, because axis 2 depends on it:
Where the host-privilege axis comes from. Backslash Security’s analysis of the 2026-07-28 MCP spec (published 2026-05-28), on MCP Apps rendering in IDE iframes:

“A sandbox escape in a tab costs you that tab. A sandbox escape here is a full IDE compromise.”

Vendor blog, architectural analysis, no disclosed exploit. The framing is the origin of axis 2; the mechanics are independently checkable and carry more weight.
The one mechanism to remember: the question is not whether allow-same-origin is set, it is whose origin the frame has. allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin gives no containment when the frame shares the embedder’s origin — it can reach the parent DOM or delete its own sandbox attribute. On a different origin the same pair is fine, and MCP Apps requires exactly that: “The Host and the Sandbox MUST have different origins”, and the Sandbox “MUST have the following permissions: allow-scripts, allow-same-origin.”
The spec is also more prescriptive than “mandates sandboxing and leaves the rest to hosts” — it specifies the sandbox-proxy contract, a mandatory CSP built from declared domains, and a restrictive default policy (default-src 'none', connect-src 'none') when an app declares none. On confirmation the Final spec is blunt: a View-initiated tool call is governed by a bare “MAY … subject them to further user approval.” A server cannot assume the host prompts. (An agent-invokes-app-tool direction with stronger language exists only in the draft — it is not in the shipped standard.) Either way, do not use the host’s confirmation UI as your authorization boundary; that is guardrail 3.
One scope trap worth carrying: the sandbox-proxy contract binds “if the Host is a web page” — so it does not bind for the Electron desktop hosts that make up the high-privilege case, where the spec prescribes nothing beyond “sandbox the iframe” and Electron’s own process controls do the real work. Detail and a corrections log in generative-ui-security.
Evaluating generated UI — what actually exists
“Evaluate task success, not screenshot plausibility” is easy to say. Three things now make it doable.

PAGEN — Google’s released dataset of expert-crafted reference results, from the Leviathan paper. Reference set, not a metric.
FlowEval (arXiv 2605.04165, Wu, Vaithilingam, Schoop, Nichols — Apple-affiliated, 2026-05-05). The most useful idea in the set. It measures whether a generated UI supports realistic interaction flows, by driving a computer-use agent through validated tasks on a real site and its generated analog, then comparing navigation traces with reference-based similarity metrics (e.g. dynamic time warping). Expert-evaluator study reports strong correlation with human judgment and better-aligned rankings than an MLLM-judge baseline. This is the closest thing to “task success, measured, at scale” — and note it evaluates behavior under interaction, not appearance, which is precisely the axis Design Theater found tools failing on.
LLM-as-judge, validated by fault injection — the semantic-accessibility method above: inject known faults, measure recall (80–92%), then trust the judge proportionally on unmodified samples. Worth stealing as a general technique for any LLM judge, well beyond accessibility. Pairs with llm-evaluation-methodology.

The constraint on all of it remains the kappa = 0.25 ceiling: trained designers agree with each other weakly, so a judge aligned to “human preference” is aligned to some humans. FlowEval partly sidesteps this by measuring flow support rather than design quality — a reason to prefer behavioral metrics where the task allows.
Cost and latency — the constraint nobody’s guardrail list mentions
Hard numbers, from the bridge paper’s ASSETS ‘25 study: full-page HTML regeneration took one to five minutes per page and consumed roughly 220,000 tokens per session. Google’s own blog concedes generation “can sometimes take a minute or more.”
The author’s conclusion is the one to carry: “For a screen reader user browsing quickly, minute-scale latency is a regression, not an improvement.” Practical deployment needs caching, smaller specialized models, or regeneration only on first visit. The companion failure from the same program runs the other way — an object-detection loop at every 100 ms for responsive audio framing, bounded by battery and thermal headroom, not by tokens.
Two design consequences:

Generative UI has a latency floor that conventional UI does not, and it lands in exactly the range where interactive use breaks. This is a stronger argument for the static tier than any safety argument — the static tier renders your components at component speed.
Output tokens are the expensive ones. A UI response is billed as output. Full-page HTML regeneration at ~220k tokens per session is not a rounding error, and it recurs per user per session. llm-cost-optimization applies directly.

Guardrails, and which ones survive contact
The standard list is sound but under-specified about when each item is load-bearing. Sharpened:

Whitelisted component registry, not arbitrary markup. Non-negotiable when the generated surface can trigger actions, and non-negotiable when the host is high-privilege (IDE, desktop AI client, agent shell) regardless of actions — that is the trust inversion above. Google’s consumer deployment shows the rule is negotiable for a purely presentational surface in a browser tab; neither exemption transfers to an IDE. Be able to state which case you are in.
Validate every prop (Zod / JSON Schema) at the render boundary. Cheap, catches malformed and partial streams, and is the mechanism structured-output-json-mode already covers.
Separate rendering from authorization. The single most important item. Generated UI must never be the thing that authorizes a side effect — see vibe-coding-authorization-flaws for what this looks like when it fails. Confirmation gates on purchases, deletion, publishing, account changes.
Deterministic fallback, on a latency budget. Text or conventional UI when generation fails, times out, or validates badly. Measured generation is one-to-five minutes for a full page — set the timeout from a real interaction budget and fall back, rather than letting the user watch a spinner. This is an availability requirement, not an error path.
Persist the spec, the tool calls, the validation result, and the user’s action. Without it, a generative UI bug is unreproducible by construction. This is agent-audit-trails-provenance applied to the render path; MCP Apps’ JSON-RPC choice bakes it into the protocol.
Test the stream, not just the output — malformed, partial, delayed, duplicated, out-of-order.
Evaluate task success and workload, not screenshot plausibility. Design Theater and the kappa = 0.25 result are the two reasons: convincing-looking output and unreliable self-reported reasoning are exactly what these systems produce well. FlowEval’s trace-comparison approach is the concrete method; an MLLM judge scoring screenshots is the thing it beat.
Do not treat a green accessibility audit as evidence. The load-bearing measurement is the code-level one: 541 semantic violations across 300 UIs from three frontier models, all passing automated checks. Automated a11y tooling covers the syntactic layer; generated UI fails predominantly in the semantic layer beneath it. Manual assistive-tech testing is not optional here in the way teams have learned to pretend it is elsewhere. (The 29.0%-compliance figure is about design-mockup tools assessed visually by novices — real, but not about generated code; don’t use it to carry this guardrail.)
Give untrusted UI an origin that is not yours — either opaque (omit allow-same-origin) or a separate real origin behind a sandbox proxy, which is what MCP Apps mandates. With allow-scripts on your origin there is no containment at all. Full checklist in generative-ui-security.

Guardrail 7 deserves its own line: do not accept the model’s design rationale as evidence. It is the specific thing that was measured and found ~25–34% detached from implementation.
The failure record, such as it is. One documented content-integrity failure in a deployed system: the bridge paper’s HTML-regeneration extension silently dropped a link to an extended-warranty option on an Amazon product page while condensing promotional sections (the author’s own disclosure; mitigated with a semantic-similarity threshold and targeted link re-insertion). Plus a substantive security-analysis literature on the MCP Apps surface, architectural, with no disclosed exploit. This pass found no public post-mortem of a runtime generative-UI system attacked or failing at scale, and no CVE against MCP Apps or A2UI; that is a statement about what one search pass found, not about what exists.
The dropped-warranty-link failure is worth holding onto as the canonical shape: not a crash, not a refusal, not a visible error — a silent omission inside output that looked entirely correct. That is what generative UI failure looks like, and it is invisible to every automated gate in the stack.
How to choose
Answer the two axis questions first — they narrow the field faster than any feature comparison.
1. What must cross the boundary? If your components can express the output, nothing needs to. 2. What is the host holding? If it holds credentials, treat every open-ended option as a security project, not a UI project.

ai/generative-ui-security.title: Generative UI Security — Rendering Untrusted Interface in a Privileged Host
ai/generative-ui-security.content:
Generative UI Security — Rendering Untrusted Interface in a Privileged Host
Extracted from generative-ui-landscape, which covers the field, the options, and the research. This note covers one question in the depth it needs: when a model or a third-party server supplies interface markup, what stops it from doing whatever it likes?
Last verified: 2026-08-25. Every normative quote below is from a raw source file fetched and read directly — not a summary. See Corrections for why that is stated rather than assumed.


                  
                  Which spec, and why it matters 
                  
                

ext-apps ships two files. specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx is the Final one — what shipped as MCP’s first official extension, and what a host implements against. specification/draft/apps.mdx is the work in progress; it carries 73 normative statements to Final’s 56. Everything below is sourced to Final, with draft-only material labelled as such and never counted as an obligation. An earlier version of this note quoted the draft throughout while its sibling advertised MCP Apps as a finalized standard.


Different layer from the vault’s other isolation notes. agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers and agent-isolation-hardening contain a coding agent at the OS boundary, with containers and VMs. This note is further in: containing rendered markup inside a client the user already trusts.
The browser’s primitives are not the only tools available. The high-privilege hosts in question are Electron apps, which have process-level controls sitting underneath the iframe. Because this premise carries the whole section, here is what actually backs it per product, at three different evidence grades:

























HostElectron?How this note knowsVS CodeYes — verified first-handA local install ships the Chromium/Electron runtime: chrome_crashpad_handler, v8_context_snapshot.bin, libffmpeg.so, resources.pak, LICENSES.chromium.html. Upstream package.json carries @vscode/gulp-electron and an electron build script. Checked 2026-08-25.CursorYes, by inheritance — secondaryConsistently reported as a VS Code fork retaining its extension/runtime ecosystem. No vendor-documentation quote obtained; the fork claim is universal in coverage but not verified at Cursor’s own docs.Claude DesktopYes — secondary, multi-sourceMultiple independent commentators discuss it as an Electron app, several critically. No Anthropic documentation states it. Treat as well-corroborated, not vendor-confirmed.
And a caveat that matters more than the table. Establishing that a host is Electron says the controls below are available. It says nothing about whether they are switched on — an Electron app can ship nodeIntegration: true and have none of them. “Is it Electron” is the question that makes the next questions worth asking; it is not itself an assurance.
Quoted from Electron’s own security docs, read directly 2026-08-25:

Process sandboxing — “Starting from Electron 20, the sandbox is enabled for renderer processes without any further configuration.” The checklist restates it: “This recommendation is the default behavior in Electron since 20.0.0.”
Context isolation — “Context Isolation is the default behavior in Electron since 12.0.0.” It runs preload and Electron APIs in a dedicated JS context, so renderer scripts cannot modify globals like Array.prototype.push out from under the preload.

The coupling is the part worth knowing, and it is a single-flag cascade. These defaults are not independent, and one setting silently removes both:

“Enabling Node.js integration for a renderer process by setting nodeIntegration: true disables the sandbox for the process.”
“Disabling context isolation (see above) also disables process sandboxing, regardless of the default, sandbox: false or globally enabled sandboxing!”

So nodeIntegration: true → context isolation off → process sandboxing off, even if you enabled it globally. A host can believe it has three layers and have one. Electron’s own verdict on that state: “Loading, reading or processing any untrusted content in an unsandboxed process, including the main process, is not advised.”
VS Code additionally moved its extension host out of the renderer into a separate utility process and replaced the Electron webview tag with a plain iframe — reported in its process-sandboxing write-up, not verified against VS Code source.
Electron’s full security checklist is twenty items, not the handful summarised here; treat this as the subset that interacts with rendering untrusted UI.
So there are three layers, not one: OS/process sandbox → renderer configuration → iframe isolation. This note owns the third and the seams around it. If you are building an Electron host, the first two are yours too and they are stronger controls than any sandbox token — verify them, and verify the cascade above has not quietly collapsed them, before spending effort on flags.
Why this is not the usual iframe problem
Embedding untrusted third-party content in a web page is a solved-ish problem with well-worn answers. What changes here is what the embedding process is holding.

























Browser tabIDE, desktop AI client, agent shellAssumed hostile contentYes, by designNo, historicallyAmbient authoritySite-scoped cookies and storageSSH keys, cloud tokens, repo write, shellCost of an escapeThat tabEverything the user has
Backslash Security’s analysis of the 2026-07-28 MCP spec (published 2026-05-28) puts it in one line:

“A sandbox escape in a tab costs you that tab. A sandbox escape here is a full IDE compromise.”

Provenance matters: that is a security vendor’s blog, it is architectural analysis, and it describes no disclosed exploit. The framing is useful and the risk is real in principle; treat the urgency as marketing-adjacent until an incident exists. The web-platform mechanics in the rest of this note are independently checkable and carry more weight than the framing does.
This is ambient-authority-and-blast-radius applied to a render path. The blast radius is not a property of how carefully the UI was generated. It is a property of what the host process can reach.
What the attacker controls
Assume the markup is fully attacker-chosen. The Final spec’s threat model, verbatim:


Malicious server delivers harmful HTML content
Compromised View attempts to escape sandbox
View attempts unauthorized tool execution
View exfiltrates sensitive host data
View performs phishing or social engineering


Note what that list assumes, and what this note inherited from it. Every entry names a third party — a hostile server, or a View compromised by one. It is the right model for MCP Apps, where markup arrives across an organizational boundary.
It is not the model for the case generative-ui-landscape identifies as the largest deployment: a first-party model generating raw HTML/CSS/JS for its own host, with no server in the loop. There the markup is authored by a component you trust, and the failure modes are different — output steered by injected content that reached the model’s context (prompt-injection), or simply wrong markup with no adversary at all. Neither a server allowlist nor predeclared-resource hashing applies, because there is no predeclaration and no server.
What still applies to the first-party case: the origin rule (§2), CSP as destination containment (§3), and the process layer. What does not: everything premised on reviewing a template before it arrives. This note is scoped to the third-party case. The first-party case needs its own treatment and does not have one here.
UI mimicry — the threat no sandbox flag addresses
The spec files this under “Other risks” and its advice is one line: “UI can still display misleading content. Hosts should clearly indicate sandboxed UI boundaries.”
A server ships HTML that renders as a pixel-accurate copy of the host’s own authentication prompt or permission dialog. The sandbox works perfectly. The user types their credentials into it anyway. Defenses are presentational, not technical: visible provenance on every server-supplied surface, host chrome that generated content cannot reproduce, and never rendering third-party UI in a region where native dialogs also appear.
The isolation stack
Five controls. They are not alternatives — each covers what the others miss, and the common failure is shipping one and assuming it is the sandbox.
1. The sandbox attribute, flag by flag
A bare sandbox is the strictest setting: no scripts, no forms, no storage, opaque origin. Every flag you add gives something back.
All fourteen tokens defined for the sandbox attribute, enumerated from MDN’s <iframe> reference source (fetched 2026-08-25) rather than from memory — an earlier version listed eight without saying so, and a partial list reads as a completed check:
















































































FlagGrantsFor untrusted UIallow-scriptsJS executionRequired for interactive UI. See the origin rule below.allow-same-originThe frame keeps a real originDepends entirely on whose origin. See below — this is the subtle one.allow-formsForm submissionConstrain with CSP form-action; do not assume CSP reaches the frame (see §3).allow-modalsalert/confirm/promptWorkable; mild phishing surface.allow-popupswindow.openPopups inherit the sandbox unless the next flag is set.allow-popups-to-escape-sandboxPopups open unsandboxedNever. A documented escape hatch, not a convenience.allow-top-navigationNavigate the whole host awayNo.allow-top-navigation-by-user-activationSame, gated on a real gestureOnly if genuinely needed.allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocolsInvoke registered protocol handlersNo on a desktop host — custom protocols are a route out of the web sandbox entirely.allow-downloadsTrigger file downloadsNo reason to grant. (The Final spec says nothing about downloads at all; a host-mediated ui/download-file flow exists only in the draft.)allow-storage-access-by-user-activationRequest storage accessNo.allow-presentationPresentation APINo reason to grant.allow-pointer-lockPointer Lock APIGrant only for a genuine canvas/game surface.allow-orientation-lockScreen orientation lockNo reason to grant.
2. allow-scripts + allow-same-origin is only unsafe relative to the embedder’s origin
The single most important mechanic here, and the one most often stated wrongly — including by an earlier version of this note. The wrong version is the absolute one: “allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin is not a sandbox; always omit allow-same-origin.” Stated that way it would lead you to reject the MCP Apps spec’s own required design.
Content granted both flags keeps a real origin. If that origin is the embedder’s, the content can reach the parent DOM or locate its own <iframe> element and delete the sandbox attribute — no containment at all. If the frame is served from a different origin than the host, the same flag pair is fine: same-origin policy separates it from the host, and it can hold its own storage without that meaning anything to the embedder.
So the control doing the work is origin separation, not the flag in isolation. Two ways to get it:

Opaque origin — omit allow-same-origin. The frame gets a unique origin and cannot touch localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies at all. Strongest, and correct for content you never want to persist anything.
A different real origin — serve the frame from a separate origin you control. Keeps storage working, which a proxy layer needs. This is what ext-apps mandates (§5).

Ask “which origin, relative to what?” rather than “is allow-same-origin set?“.
3. Content Security Policy
The sandbox governs capabilities. CSP governs destinations — and exfiltration is a destination problem. A frame with scripts and no network policy can encode whatever it can read into a request to a server the attacker controls.
ext-apps makes this a host obligation rather than advice. Verbatim from the spec’s host-behavior section: “Host MUST construct CSP headers based on declared domains”; “Host MAY further restrict but MUST NOT allow undeclared domains”; “Host SHOULD log CSP configurations for security review.”
When ui.csp is omitted the host MUST apply this default, which is worth reading closely because it is a good starting policy for any untrusted-UI frame:
default-src 'none';
script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
img-src 'self' data:;
media-src 'self' data:;
connect-src 'none';

connect-src 'none' is the exfiltration control — no fetch, no XHR, no WebSocket. default-src 'none' denies everything not listed. 'unsafe-inline' is present for scripts and styles, which is unavoidable for srcdoc-injected content and is exactly why the sandbox and origin controls have to carry the weight.
One gap worth catching if you copy this: the Final spec’s restrictive default omits object-src 'none', while the CSP-construction example a few lines later in the same document includes it (and font-src, and base-uri). The draft’s default has object-src and Final’s does not. Add it yourself — a policy with default-src 'none' covers object-src by fallback, but do not rely on reading that subtlety correctly under time pressure.
The spec’s construction example also maps declared permissions (camera, microphone, geolocation) onto the inner iframe’s allow attribute — Permissions Policy, a separate mechanism from both CSP and sandbox tokens. Three policy systems on one frame; know which one you are editing.
Note that CSP also offers a sandbox directive as a header-level equivalent of the attribute, though coverage differs — some sandbox tokens are implemented only for the iframe attribute. Use the attribute as the primary control.
4. postMessage origin validation
The channel out of the sandbox is the channel in. A handler that does not check event.origin accepts messages from anything that can get a handle on the window. Validate the sender origin on every inbound message, and treat the message body as untrusted input rather than as a command — the same discipline prompt-injection demands of model input.
Reusing a structured protocol helps here. ext-apps routes UI-to-host traffic over MCP’s JSON-RPC precisely so every message is typed and loggable, rather than a bespoke postMessage shape that nobody audits.
5. The sandbox-proxy pattern — and who it actually binds
Read the first clause before the rest, because it inverts who this section is for:

“If the Host is a web page, it MUST wrap the View and communicate with it through an intermediate Sandbox proxy.”

“The Host and the Sandbox MUST have different origins.”
“The Sandbox MUST have the following permissions: allow-scripts, allow-same-origin.”


The proxy is sandboxed, with allow-same-origin, and its safety comes from sitting on a different origin than the host — exactly the case §2 describes. The frame holds a real origin; that origin just is not the host’s.
The rest of the proxy’s obligations, from the Final spec:









































RequirementLevelSandbox announces readiness (sandbox-proxy-ready); Host then sends the raw HTML (sandbox-resource-ready)MUST (both — the draft has these as SHOULD; Final is stricter)Load the View’s raw HTML with CSP enforcing the domains declared in ui.cspMUSTframe-src 'none' unless frameDomains declared; base-uri 'self' unless baseUriDomains declared; object-src 'none'MUSTRestrictive defaults when no CSP metadata is providedMUSTForward messages both ways, except methods starting ui/notifications/sandbox-MUSTHost must not send any request or notification to the View before receiving initializedMUST NOTProxy originates no requests of its own (it would have to synthesize request ids)SHOULD NOTSet the inner iframe’s allow attribute from declared permissionsMAY
The scope problem, stated plainly. That conditional — if the Host is a web page — means this entire contract binds for browser-based hosts, which this note’s own trust table calls the low-privilege case. For an Electron desktop host (VS Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop — the high-privilege case this note exists for), the sandbox-proxy MUST does not apply, and the spec prescribes nothing in its place.
That is a genuine gap in the standard, not an omission in this note, and it is worth knowing before you cite the spec as your desktop containment story. What fills it:

The process layer documented at the top of this note — renderer sandboxing, context isolation, and not tripping the nodeIntegration cascade. This is the desktop host’s real containment, and it is Electron’s contract, not MCP’s.
The origin rule in §2 holds regardless of host type: an opaque origin, or a real origin that is not yours. A desktop host is free to adopt the proxy pattern voluntarily and probably should; it simply is not obligated to.
Mitigation 1 does bind universally: “All View content MUST be rendered in sandboxed iframes with restricted permissions.” That MUST has no host-type conditional. It just does not say which tokens.

So the honest summary for a desktop host: one unconditional MUST (sandbox the iframe), no prescribed token set, no prescribed origin model, and the Electron layer doing the actual work.
What MCP Apps mandates, and what it leaves to you
From the Final spec. The gaps are where hosts differ and where a review should focus.





















































ControlFinal spec positionAll View content rendered in sandboxed iframesMUST — unconditional, no host-type caveatSandbox-proxy contract (different origins, allow-scripts+allow-same-origin, CSP construction, message forwarding)MUST — but only “if the Host is a web page”CSP constructed from declared domains; block undeclaredMUSTRestrictive default CSP when ui.csp is absentMUSTWarn users when UI requires external domain accessSHOULDValidate incoming messages, reject malformed types, log View-initiated RPCSHOULD-level host behaviorPredeclared review: inspect HTML at connection setup, hash/sign resources, allowlist or blocklist by hashSHOULD-level host behaviorIndicate sandboxed-UI boundaries clearly (social-engineering mitigation)“Other risks” — advisoryResource limits against CPU/memory exhaustion”Other risks” — advisoryUser confirmation before a View-initiated tool callMAYApproval granularity, allowlists, audit-log persistenceHost discretion
Confirmation: one direction, and it is a bare MAY
The only relevant flow in the Final spec is the View calling out — the app’s UI triggering a tool. It is governed by sandbox-proxy item 8:

“The Host MAY forward any message from the View (coming via the Sandbox) to the MCP Apps server, for any method that doesn’t start with ui/. While the Host SHOULD ensure the View’s MCP connection is spec-compliant, it MAY decide to block some messages or subject them to further user approval.”

MAY on both blocking and approval, with no recommendation attached. A server cannot assume the host will prompt. That is the whole answer for the shipped standard.
Draft-only, and this note previously presented it as an obligation. The draft adds app-registered tools — an agent invoking a tool the app declared — under a 5. App-Provided Tools Security section carrying SHOULD-level host protections, “Require explicit user approval for tools with readOnlyHint: false”, and a “user confirmation required” safe default for unannotated tools. None of that exists in Final. Grepping Final for readOnlyHint, app tool, or register their own tools returns nothing; its Mitigations run 1–4 plus “Other risks”, with no fifth section. If app tools land as specified, that second direction becomes real. Today it is not something a host is obligated to do or a server can rely on.
The practical rule is the same either way and does not depend on the spec: do not use the host’s confirmation UI as your authorization boundary. That is guardrail 3 in generative-ui-landscape.
Predeclared review — the control most likely to go unused
Worth pulling out because it is the spec’s most distinctive idea and the easiest for a host to skip silently. UI ships as ui:// resources referenced by tool metadata rather than embedded in tool results, specifically so hosts receive templates during connection setup, before tool execution. The spec’s host behaviors: review HTML for obviously malicious patterns, generate a hash or signature per resource, warn users about suspicious content, and allowlist or blocklist by resource hash.
Hashing is the part that turns this from a vague “review the HTML” into something operable — it gives you a stable identity for a template, so an approved template that later changes is detectable. If you are auditing a host, ask whether it does that or merely renders what arrives. The review window exists only if someone uses it.
Review checklist
Split by role, because most of these controls are only actionable by one of the two.
If you are building or auditing a host (the controls actually live here):

How privileged is this process? Per-session, not per-product — the same IDE differs with and without cloud credentials loaded.
If Electron: is the renderer genuinely sandboxed? sandbox: true, contextIsolation: true, nodeIntegration: false — and confirm the cascade above has not silently collapsed all three.
Whose origin does the frame have? Not “is allow-same-origin set” — an opaque origin or a different real origin both work; the embedder’s own origin does not.
Are the dangerous tokens absent? allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox, allow-top-navigation, allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols (this one matters more on desktop than on web).
Is there a CSP, and does it block undeclared destinations? connect-src is the exfiltration control.
Does every postMessage handler validate event.origin
Is the predeclared-review window actually used — templates inspected and hashed at connection setup — or does the host just render what arrives?
Is a View-initiated tool call gated by something the host controls? The spec only says MAY; the decision is yours and nobody makes it for you.
Is server-supplied UI visually distinguishable from host chrome?
Are View-initiated RPC calls logged? Post-incident this is the only record — agent-audit-trails-provenance, post-breach-investigability.

If you are shipping a server that supplies UI (you control almost none of the above):

Assume no host prompts before your tool calls. MAY is the spec’s word.
Do not let the UI be your authorization boundary. Enforce server-side; treat anything arriving from a View as an untrusted request regardless of which UI produced it.
Declare the narrowest CSP domains you can. Hosts may tighten what you declare but must not loosen it, so a tight declaration is a control you actually own.
Assume your template is inspected and hashed — and that changing it may invalidate an allowlist entry.

What this note does not cover

No incident data. No CVE against MCP Apps, MCP-UI, or A2UI surfaced in this pass, and no public post-mortem of an attacked generative-UI system. Everything here is architectural.
No implementation was checked. This is the sharpest limit and it deserves stating first among them. Every claim here describes what a document requires. Nothing in this note establishes that Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, or any other host actually implements the sandbox-proxy contract, the CSP default, or the predeclared-review window. A reviewer could complete every checklist item against an architecture no shipping product implements. Treat the checklist as questions to ask an implementation, not as a description of one.
First-party generation. Covered in the threat-model section: the model-generates-its-own-markup case needs separate treatment this note does not provide.
Server-side compromise. Contained markup from a malicious server is still a malicious server; this note bounds the damage the UI can do.
Model-level defenses. Stopping a model from being steered into hostile output is prompt-injection; this note assumes that failed.
OS-level containment of the agent itself — agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers, agent-isolation-hardening. The host process layer is now covered above; the agent-in-a-container layer is not.
Supply chain. A compromised renderer library, or a malicious UI template in a registry, sits upstream of every control listed here and defeats all of them. ai-supply-chain-risks, supply-chain-security.

Corrections
Kept in the note rather than only in git, because this is security guidance: a reader may have acted on an earlier version, and each of these was wrong in a way that would change what someone built. Four errors across two revisions, and the pattern in them is the useful part.


The sandbox-proxy architecture was described backwards. An early version said the outer proxy is same-origin with the host and unsandboxed, with an opaque-origin inner frame. The spec requires the opposite: different origins for Host and Sandbox, and the Sandbox holding allow-scripts and allow-same-origin.


The origin mechanic was stated as an absolute — “allow-scripts + allow-same-origin is never a sandbox.” True only relative to the embedder’s origin. Stated absolutely it would lead a reader to reject the spec’s own mandated design as insecure.


The consent claim was wrong twice, in opposite directions. First flatly (“the spec does not mandate consent”). Then the correction quoted the App-Provided Tools Security recommendations — which govern the agent invoking app tools — to overturn a claim about View-initiated calls, a different flow with a bare MAY. The second version sounded better-sourced and was wrong about which question it answered.


An A2UI inner-frame sandbox flag list was published from a documentation summary. It is not what the specification requires. Removed rather than corrected.


The wrong specification file was quoted throughout. Every normative claim was sourced to specification/draft/, while the sibling note advertised MCP Apps as a finalized standard. The load-bearing requirements — sandbox proxy, CSP — turn out to be identical in Final, so most of the note survived on luck. Two things did not: the app-registered-tools consent model (draft-only; absent from Final entirely) and the ui/download-file flow (same). This also means error 3’s “correction” was arguing about a feature that has not shipped, and the original blunt claim was right for the Final spec all along.


The Electron premise was asserted about three named products without a source, in the very section added to fix an earlier premise error. Caught before it was wrong — all three check out — but it was the last unsourced specific in a note that had made a virtue of sourcing everything, and it was asserted from background knowledge, which is exactly what produced errors 1, 2 and 4. Now carries per-product evidence grades, two of which are secondary.


The pattern, revised. Errors 1, 2 and 4 came from treating an LLM summary of a page as a source read — a diagnosis this note published after round two, which then made error 5 harder to see, because provenance had been so visibly fixed that nobody asked which file. Error 3 came from a confident correction of an earlier error; error 5 was underneath it the whole time and was the actual root cause. Error 6 is the interesting one because it was a near-miss rather than a mistake: the claim was true, and it was still unsourced in a note whose entire credibility rests on sourcing. Being right by luck reads identically to being right by method until someone checks.
Four lessons, in order of how much they cost: name the document version, not just the document; fetch the raw file and grep normative keywords; when correcting, re-verify what question the new citation answers; and an unsourced specific is a defect even when it turns out to be true.
A reader is entitled to ask what this record implies about the claims that remain. The honest answer: every normative statement above is now quoted from the Final spec file and can be checked against it in a minute, which is the only assurance worth offering. The architectural reasoning around those quotes — the three-layer framing, the origin rule, the first-party gap — has not been tested against any implementation, and that limit is stated below rather than buried.
Related
