Sources

ext-apps Final specification, specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx — the source for every normative claim above. Raw file fetched and read 2026-08-25; MUST/SHOULD quotes are literal.
ext-apps draft specification — read for comparison only. 73 normative statements to Final’s 56. Cited here solely to mark what is draft-only (app-registered tools and their consent model; the ui/download-file flow; object-src in the default CSP). Nothing draft-only is treated as an obligation.
SEP-1865 — predeclared-resource rationale; fetched 2026-08-25
a2ui.org — MCP Apps in A2UI — fetched 2026-08-25, but nothing in this note now rests on it; the flag list it was cited for has been removed (see Corrections). Listed only so the provenance trail is complete.
MDN <iframe> reference — raw source fetched 2026-08-25; the fourteen sandbox tokens were enumerated from it
Electron docs/tutorial/security.md and docs/tutorial/sandbox.md — raw sources fetched 2026-08-25; version defaults and the nodeIntegration cascade quoted verbatim
Backslash Security — New MCP Spec Opens Three New Attack Surfaces (2026-05-28) — trust-inversion framing; vendor blog, no disclosed exploit
VS Code process-sandboxing write-up — secondary; the extension-host/utility-process claim is flagged unverified inline
Local VS Code install (com.visualstudio.code flatpak, 1.130.0) inspected 2026-08-25 for Electron runtime artifacts; microsoft/vscode package.json fetched the same day
Cursor-as-VS-Code-fork and Claude-Desktop-as-Electron: secondary sources only, graded in the table above; neither is vendor-documented here
Checked and dropped: an earlier version raised a residual concern about allow-popups citing Mozilla bug 1589845. That bug is RESOLVED DUPLICATE, filed 2019, and its duplicate target concerns sandboxes that include allow-same-origin — it does not support a concern about popups in an opaque-origin frame. Cited from a search result without checking status; removed.

ai/genui-vs-vibe-coding-nng-review.title: Verification Review — GenUI vs. Vibe Coding (NN/g)
ai/genui-vs-vibe-coding-nng-review.content:
Verification Review — GenUI vs. Vibe Coding (NN/g)


                  
                  What this is 
                  
                

A worked example of running two verification passes — /falsifiability-scan (claim-shape) and /red-team (adversarial) — over a single artifact, then closing the one finding that needed external checking. The artifact under review is an internal summary of Kate Moran’s NN/g article “GenUI vs. Vibe Coding: Who’s Designing?” (nngroup.com/articles/genui-vs-vibe, 2026-03-27). The two scans ask different questions and overlap little — falsifiability: could each claim be false, and how would we know?; red-team: is the argument wrong?


Disposition (read this first)
The summary is a faithful, well-hedged capture. The scans surfaced two issues worth recording:

Source fidelity was asserted without a verification marker. The capture quoted three passages verbatim and named author/date/URL with nothing recording that the source had actually been fetched and checked — the fabrication hotspot the global trust-but-verify rule exists for. Now resolved: the article was fetched 2026-06-03. Title, author (Kate Moran), and date (2026-03-27) confirmed; two of the three quotes are verbatim and the third is verbatim modulo em-dash spacing (— vs —). The worst case red-team objection A imagined did not occur — quotes that were paraphrases wearing quotation marks. The lesson is process, not fact: the capture was right but undisciplined; verification + a dated marker is what converts luck into reliability.
The framing contains an internal inconsistency — the “specification spectrum” point dissolves the “three paradigms” trichotomy the summary is built on (see Objection B). This is unresolved and is the real reason not to build a synthesis note on the framing as-is.

Carry-forwards are listed at the bottom.

Part 1 — Falsifiability scan (claim shape)
Framing: the capture’s Key Takeaways are Kate Moran’s claims, reported and not endorsed. The vault’s own voice is in the Analysis hooks, which are posed as open questions and assert nothing load-bearing — which is why the capture commits cleanly as a capture. Tags below pre-sort the reported claims for the eventual synthesis note.


















































TagClaimLocation[DEFN]”Three paradigms, not two” — GenUI / vibe coding / AI-assisted design split by who initiatesKey Takeaways[DEFN]”The dividing line is initiation + accountability” (the table)Takeaways table[VAGUE]”Vague prompts push real decisions onto the AI → generic output""specification spectrum” bullet[VAGUE]”A meaningful prerequisite, and not one most people meet” — the ability to specify one’s UI needs (keystone)skepticism bullet / quote[VAGUE]”Specialized software encodes years of user research ad hoc prompts can’t replicate”skepticism bullet[VAGUE]”GenUI benefits everyone—including users who wouldn’t think to ask”GenUI-burden bullet[DEFN]”Vibe coding fails on execution; GenUI fails on judgment”failure-modes bullet[PROB]”Invisible AI” prediction — GenUI → behind-the-scenes, no visual indicators; success = “reads the moment”prediction bullet
Nothing is [SEAL] (self-sealing). The two claims worth operationalizing before the vault endorses them in its own voice:
Keystone — “most people can’t specify their UI needs”:

Falsifying observation: a representative sample of non-technical users produces usable specs above some threshold (e.g. >50%) on a fixed task.
Measurement: task-based usability study, output scored against a usability rubric.
Deadline / scoring: none in the source; resolves against a future study.
Bundle (the confound): depends on tool capability at test time, task difficulty, the “usable” threshold, sampled population. A 2026 tool vs a 2028 tool could flip the verdict with the human-ability claim unchanged — the article reads the limit as intrinsic to users when it may be intrinsic to 2026 tooling.

“Invisible AI” prediction (Tetlock variant):

Numeric probability: none stated.
Resolution criterion: as written it does not resolve — “reads the moment” / “moves toward” have no yes/no boundary. The capture’s hook calls it “testable and dated,” but the date is the article’s publication date, not a forecast resolution date.
Before it enters the calibration log: attach a concrete instance, a “no visual indicator” definition, a resolution date, and a probability — otherwise it sits unscoreable.

Falsifiability verdict: Falsifiable enough to commit as a capture. The two [VAGUE]/[PROB] items above are carry-forwards for promotion, not blockers now.

Part 2 — Red team (adversarial)
Objection A — Source specifics asserted with no fetch marker [verified — held up]

Target: header (author “Kate Moran”, “Published: 2026-03-27”, the URL) and the three verbatim quotes.
Mechanism: the capture reads as faithful transcription, but nothing recorded that the source had been fetched and the quotes checked. If summarized from a partial fetch, the “verbatim” quotes would be paraphrases wearing quotation marks; a synthesis note would cite them as direct quotes, propagating the drift.
Tell: the date was hedged (“per the article”) but author, URL, and quotes were asserted flat — inconsistent verification discipline inside one header block.
Resolution (2026-06-03): fetched the article. Author, title, and date confirmed; quotes (a) and (c) verbatim, (b) verbatim modulo em-dash spacing. The objection was a valid process flag — the discipline was missing — but the underlying facts held. This is the honest outcome to want from a red-team: most objections-from-missing-verification resolve clean, and the value is the dated marker, not a scandal.

Objection B — The spectrum takeaway dissolves the trichotomy

Target: the three-paradigm split vs. the “specification spectrum” takeaway.
Mechanism: GenUI is defined as “AI decides, no spec required.” Maximally-vague vibe coding (“build me a trip planner”) is also “the AI decides with no meaningful spec.” Same operation, opposite end of one continuum whose dial is “specification.” The accountability split (design quality vs execution fidelity) then can’t be cleanly assigned, because a vague-enough vibe prompt makes the AI exercise exactly the design judgment GenUI is held accountable for. The capture concedes the spectrum and doesn’t notice it undercuts the framing it just endorsed.
Evidence: internal inconsistency — “the degree of design judgment the AI exercises varies enormously” is the concession.

Objection C — Over-integration of one evidence-free op-ed

Target: five Analysis hooks + six Related links built from a single opinion piece.
Mechanism: the capture threads one NN/g blog post into five existing notes and proposes a new “runtime generative UI” note as a “candidate gap.” If the framing (B) or the source (A) is shaky, every link inherits the defect, and a new note gets born from one opinion rather than a synthesis of sources. The article offers no data; “encodes years of user research ad hoc prompts can’t replicate” is an assertion, not a finding.

Pre-mortem (one year out)

Vocabulary churned out from under it — “vibe coding” / “GenUI” are 2025–26 coinages; by 2027 they merge, get renamed, or one dies. The spine is terminology; the time-sensitive tag was right but the half-life was short.
The “invisible AI” prediction resolved untestable, not true/false — no-indicator customization was already shipping in 2026 (recommenders, adaptive templates), so it reads as postdiction; or it stayed directional and never got scored.
“Most people can’t vibe-code specs” aged into condescension — 2027 tooling added scaffolding that let non-technical users ship usable specs; the limit was 2026 tooling, not human capacity.
A re-fetch found one “verbatim” quote was a paraphrase — checked and held: the 2026-06-03 fetch confirmed all three quotes (one differs only in em-dash spacing). This predicted failure did not occur.
The “candidate gap” note got created and this capture became orphaned scaffolding — links pointing at it, content fully superseded.

Weakest load-bearing claim
That “who initiates” is a clean axis that cleanly determines accountability. It matters because it’s the capture’s reason to exist and the insight threaded into five other notes. It’s vulnerable because the capture’s own spectrum takeaway converts the axis into a continuum, where “who initiates” stops being categorical. Break it and the trichotomy, the accountability rubric, and the proposed new note all collapse together.
Red-team verdict: the load-bearing argument survives; objection A resolved clean, B is a genuine framing crack to fix before any synthesis is built on it.

Carry-forwards before promotion to a synthesis note

✅ Verify the source — done 2026-06-03. Author, date, and all three quotes confirmed against the live article; a dated marker was added to the capture.
Record the trichotomy-vs-spectrum tension (Objection B) inside the capture’s Analysis hooks, so synthesis inherits it as a known issue, not a hidden assumption. (Open — the one real blocker.)
Operationalize the keystone claim (“most people can’t specify”) with the people-vs-tooling bundle confound named, before the vault endorses it in its own voice.
Make the “invisible AI” prediction scoreable (instance + resolution criterion + date + probability) before it enters the calibration log — or don’t log it.
Hold the five integration hooks until 2–3 are cleared; don’t spin cluster scaffolding from a single evidence-free op-ed.

Related

GenUI vs. Vibe Coding: Who’s Designing? — the original NN/g article (Kate Moran, 2026-03-27) under review
falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — claim-shape taxonomy used in Part 1
bias-aware-verification-protocol — the four-pass framework these two scans plug into (Pass 2 / Pass 4)

ai/harness-design-load-bearing.title: Harness Design — Load-Bearing Components
ai/harness-design-load-bearing.content:
Harness Design — Load-Bearing Components
What it is
A methodology for designing the scaffolding around AI agents — the “harness” — and for removing parts of that scaffolding as model capability rises. The core claim, from Anthropic’s March 24, 2026 engineering note: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can’t do on its own. Those assumptions are worth stress-testing — when a model improvement makes one obsolete, the component stops being load-bearing and becomes overhead.
Distinct from multi-agent-coordination-topologies (which structural pattern to pick) and multi-agent-diminishing-returns (when adding agents helps). This note is about the dual question — when to remove harness components — and the two specific patterns from the article: GAN-framed generator/evaluator and sprint contracts.
Why it matters
Most harness design happens by accretion. A scaffold gets added to work around a model limitation; the limitation goes away in the next model; the scaffold stays. The result is harnesses that pay for capabilities the underlying model already has, with attendant cost, latency, and complexity. The simplification methodology gives you a way to find and remove that drift.
The Anthropic note’s cost/quality data points (as of article publication, pre-Opus 4.7; these are R&D experiments from one team, not user-facing pricing):

Solo agent, no harness (retro game maker task): $9, 20 minutes, broken core functionality (non-responsive game entities, incomplete wiring).
Full Planner/Generator/Evaluator harness with Opus 4.5: $200, 6 hours, working retro game maker with AI integration.
Same harness with Opus 4.6 on a comparable task (DAW — digital audio workstation): $124.70, 3 hours 50 minutes — quality preserved, cost down because sprint decomposition was no longer needed.

The harness didn’t get smaller across model generations. It moved: components that were load-bearing for Sonnet 4.5 (sprint decomposition, context resets) stopped being load-bearing for Opus 4.6, but other components (the evaluator, the planner’s spec abstraction) remained necessary at the complexity frontier — see the model table in “Harness moves, not shrinks”.
Caveat: these findings come from one engineering team’s experiments. Independent replication across teams is not yet documented. Treat the methodology as well-motivated practice from one source, not as established cross-team result.
Details
The generator/evaluator pattern (GAN-framed)
Separating evaluation from generation is more tractable than making generators self-critical. The article describes a generator with an internal critic praising its own output even when quality is mediocre. (The article calls this “self-evaluation”; the vault catalogs it as self-evaluation bias in ai-output-bias-fingerprints.) An independent evaluator, once tuned, drives iterative refinement of the generator without that bias.
The article takes inspiration explicitly from Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and applies the analogy to two domains:
Frontend design (subjective domain). Four grading criteria turned aesthetics into measurable axes:

Design quality
Originality
Craft
Functionality

The evaluator drove a live page with Playwright before scoring. Generator refined over 5 to 15 iterations per generation, sometimes making “sharp aesthetic turns” between iterations rather than incremental tweaks. The wording of the criteria steered the generator in unanticipated ways, suggesting prompt language shapes output character at this level of feedback density.
Full-stack coding (verifiable domain). Three agents:





















AgentRolePlannerExpands brief prompts into product specs at high level (scope + design, not implementation detail) — keeps spec errors from cascading downstreamGeneratorImplements features iteratively; Opus 4.6 dropped the sprint-based decomposition Sonnet 4.5 requiredEvaluator/QADrives the running app via Playwright; exercises UI features and API endpoints
The pattern portability across subjective and verifiable domains is the strongest signal that generator/evaluator is a real primitive, not a domain-specific trick. Both domains have a familiar lifecycle stage (review, QA) that maps onto the evaluator role.
Sprint contracts
A negotiated specification between Planner, Generator, and Evaluator agreed before coding begins. The generator and evaluator literally “negotiate what ‘done’ looks like” up front — the evaluator’s grading criteria become a contract the generator can target.
Why this is upstream of evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests: that note’s rubric catches spec mismatch downstream, at review time. Sprint contracts prevent the mismatch by forcing alignment between spec and verification criteria before implementation. It’s the same epistemic move as test-first development, lifted to the agent layer.
Composes with architecture-decision-records-ai (the spec layer above the contract) and implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans (the conditional-trigger structure that makes a contract executable).
Iterative evaluator tuning
Getting the evaluator agent to perform rigorously is its own loop. Early versions of an evaluator typically:

Identify legitimate issues but dismiss them (“yes it’s broken, but the code looks reasonable so I’ll pass it”)
Score against the rubric without verifying the rubric matches reality
Praise novelty over correctness when grading creative output

The fix is operational: read the evaluator’s logs, compare its verdicts to a human’s verdict on the same outputs, and rewrite the evaluator prompt when judgments diverge. The Anthropic note reports later iterations catching specific behavior-level bugs that earlier versions had waved through — e.g., a draw function existing but not being correctly wired to the relevant event handler.
This makes the evaluator itself a stateful artifact in the harness, not a static prompt. Its prompt evolves through observation, the same way a senior reviewer’s mental model evolves through reviewing junior PRs.
Load-bearing component analysis (the simplification methodology)
The methodology, applied between model generations:

Inventory every component in the current harness — agents, decomposition steps, context-management strategies, verification gates.
Name the assumption each one encodes. (Sprint decomposition assumes the model can’t hold a multi-hour build coherently. Context resets assume context anxiety degrades quality past a threshold. Evaluator agents assume self-evaluation bias dominates internal critique.)
Remove one component at a time and observe. Don’t restructure radically — methodical removal is what reveals which assumptions still hold.
Keep what still load-bears. Discard what doesn’t.

Rule of thumb from the Anthropic note: the evaluator’s necessity scales with task difficulty relative to model capability. At the complexity frontier it adds obvious value. For tasks well within the model’s solo range, it becomes overhead.
This is the dual of multi-agent-diminishing-returns — that note tells you when adding agents stops paying off; this methodology tells you when to take them away.
”Harness moves, not shrinks”
Direct quote: “the space of interesting harness combinations doesn’t shrink as models improve. Instead, it moves.”
The article’s model-generation observations are endpoint comparisons — the article uses Opus 4.5 as the first harness version and Opus 4.6 as the later one, and the Sonnet 4.5 reference is on the context-anxiety/reset side:





















ModelWhat the article reportsSonnet 4.5Exhibits context anxiety; benefits from context resets and sprint decompositionOpus 4.5The first version of the harness used Opus 4.5; full Planner/Generator/Evaluator stack appliedOpus 4.6Sprint decomposition no longer needed; cost down to $124.70 / 3h 50m on a comparable task
The frontier moves. Sprint decomposition wasn’t wrong for Sonnet 4.5 — it was load-bearing then. It just stopped being necessary at Opus 4.6, while other harness combinations (longer planning, multi-domain evaluators, cross-agent memory schemes) became newly interesting at the higher capability level. The space of interesting harness combinations relocates rather than collapses.
Practical implication: harness design is a continuous activity tied to model releases, not a one-time architectural decision. Treat your harness like a dependency that needs version-tracking against the underlying model.
Refined by a later Anthropic source (2026-07-24). The context-engineering post reports removing over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for Opus 5 / Fable 5 with no measurable loss on coding evals. That is not a counterexample to “moves, not shrinks” — this note’s claim is about the space of harness combinations (agent topology), while that post is about the token content of one agent’s system prompt. Different layers; neither source addresses the other. What the post adds is that removed scaffolding has two fates: components with somewhere to go get relocated (verification and code review moved into skills, tool guidance into tool descriptions — “moves,” observed at the prompt layer), while guardrails get deleted outright (the rules→judgement and repetition→consolidation reversals have no destination). Working synthesis: components relocate, guardrails get deleted. Full treatment in context-engineering-claude-5-generation.
Detection signals: when a component has stopped load-bearing
Vault-added operationalization of the methodology; not in the source article. Triage signals that a harness component might be obsolete:

Component fires but its outputs are increasingly ignored downstream
Removing it in a single-shot test produces equivalent quality
Its prompt has accumulated workarounds for failure modes the current model no longer exhibits
Its cost/latency contribution is rising while its impact on quality scores is flat
Newer model releases shrink the gap between with-component and without-component runs

Conversely, signals that a component is still load-bearing: removing it produces clear quality drops (not just stylistic shifts), and the failure modes that re-emerge match the original justification for adding the component.
Anti-patterns
Vault-added; the article describes the methodology without enumerating its anti-patterns. These are extrapolations consistent with the methodology, not source-supported claims.

Restructuring instead of removing. Big rewrites destroy the load-bearing signal. Remove one thing at a time.
Carrying scaffolding by sentiment. “We added this for Sonnet 4.5 and it felt important” is not evidence. Either re-derive the justification on the current model or drop it.
Conflating evaluator quality with harness necessity. A poor evaluator that adds no value is not evidence the role of evaluator is unnecessary. Tune it first (Iterative evaluator tuning) before concluding it’s obsolete.
Permanent harness solutions. Harness design has no permanent answers; tying a release process to a frozen harness invites drift the moment models shift.

Related

multi-agent-coordination-topologies — structural patterns; this note picks generator/evaluator out of the hybrid-topology list and treats it as a primitive
multi-agent-diminishing-returns — when adding agents stops paying; this note is the dual (when to remove)
multi-agent-failure-modes — MAST taxonomy; the failure modes a harness is meant to absorb
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — self-evaluation bias is the bias generator/evaluator separation is designed to neutralize
context-window-management — context resets are one of the components most likely to relocate as models improve
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — downstream review rubric; sprint contracts prevent some of what this rubric catches
agent-pipeline-feature-creation — concrete pipeline that uses planner/generator/evaluator-shaped components
architecture-decision-records-ai — the spec layer above sprint contracts
claude-code-effective-use — the harness layer most users actually touch (Claude Code itself)
context-engineering-claude-5-generation — the prompt-layer instance of this methodology; refines “moves, not shrinks” into relocate-vs-delete

Sources

Anthropic Engineering — “Harness Design for Long-Running Application Development”, published March 24, 2026 (pre-Opus 4.7)

ai/hitl-progressive-autonomy.title: HITL Progressive Autonomy
ai/hitl-progressive-autonomy.content:
HITL Progressive Autonomy
Designing human-in-the-loop systems where the oversight surface shrinks over time — starting with wide escalation triggers and expanding the autonomous envelope as the system proves itself through accumulated corrections. Not “human reviews everything” or “human reviews nothing,” but a formal trajectory between those extremes.
As of April 2026; the regulatory landscape is evolving rapidly — EU AI Act Article 14 was slated to become enforceable August 2, 2026. Update 2026-06-12: the Digital Omnibus provisional agreement postpones the high-risk obligations to late 2027/2028, pending formal adoption; details in agent-audit-trails-provenance.
Why it matters
The naive approaches both fail:

Review everything: alert fatigue → rubber-stamping → false confidence. Security SOC analysts report up to 99% false positive rates (USENIX Security 2022). The same pattern holds clinically: alarm false-positive rates run 72-99%. The human becomes a bottleneck who provides the appearance of oversight without the substance.
Review nothing: silent failures compound (see multi-agent-failure-modes). The system optimizes for the wrong objective. One bad decision cascades. No correction signal reaches the system.

The architecture problem: design a system where human involvement starts high, decreases predictably as trust is earned, and ratchets back up when trust is violated — with formal mechanisms governing every transition.
Autonomy level frameworks
Three frameworks now define graduated autonomy for AI agents; a fourth lens — the HITL/HOTL/HOVL taxonomy — describes how the human relates to execution rather than a level ladder:
Cloud Security Alliance — Agentic Trust Framework (ATF v0.9.1, Feb 2026)
The most implementation-ready. Uses role metaphors with formal promotion/demotion gates:



































LevelRolePermissionsPromotion requirement1InternAccess data, generate insights. Cannot modify external systemsMinimum 2 weeks at level2AssociateExecute pre-approved actions within narrow scopePass all 5 gates3SeniorBroader action scope, handle exceptions autonomouslyPass all 5 gates4PrincipalFull autonomy within defined ODD (Operational Design Domain — see Safety envelopes below)Pass all 5 gates
Five promotion gates (all must pass):

Demonstrated accuracy/reliability over evaluation period
Security audit appropriate to target level
Measurable positive impact
Clean operational history at current level
Explicit stakeholder approval

Demotion is immediate on critical incident — agent drops back to Intern regardless of current level. This asymmetry (slow promotion, instant demotion) is architecturally critical. The framework is built on Zero Trust principles.
Knight First Amendment Institute — Levels of Autonomy (June 2025)
Five levels based on the human’s role:



































LevelHuman roleDescriptionL1OperatorHuman drives everythingL2CollaboratorShared planning, fluid control handoffsL3ConsultantAgent leads, consults human for expertiseL4ApproverAgent operates independently, escalates high-risk casesL5ObserverFull autonomy, human can only monitor or emergency-stop
Critical insight: autonomy is independent of capability. A highly capable agent can still be constrained to L2 if the deployment context demands it. The authors propose “AI autonomy certificates” specifying the maximum autonomy level an agent is permitted to operate at.
NVIDIA — Agentic Autonomy Levels (L0-L3)
L0 deterministic/no autonomy → L1 deterministic workflows → L2 model-guided with human checkpoints → L3 fully autonomous. Higher autonomy does not mean higher risk but does mean less predictability. L3 requires taint tracing, manual approval of sensitive actions, and sanitization of untrusted data.
The HITL / HOTL / HOVL taxonomy
Three architectural patterns for how the human relates to execution:

HITL (in the loop): Agent cannot proceed without human validation at each decision point
HOTL (on the loop): Agent executes autonomously within boundaries; human monitors and can veto
HOVL (over the loop): Human sets policy, reviews outcomes episodically, intervenes only on strategic deviations

A single pipeline uses all three simultaneously — different stages at different levels. The shrinking surface means actions migrate from HITL → HOTL → HOVL over time.
Escalation trigger design
The confidence calibration problem
LLM confidence scores are severely miscalibrated. You cannot naively use logprobs or verbalized confidence as escalation triggers:

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) ranges 0.108-0.427 across formats — far above acceptable thresholds
RLHF fine-tuning degrades calibration — the models you deploy are worse at knowing what they don’t know than base models
Evidence tools (web search) systematically induce overconfidence; verification tools (code interpreters) calibrate better
In multi-agent deliberation, confidence increases through debate rather than calibrating — agents talk each other into being more certain, not less. Self-rated win confidence averaged 72.92% at the opening round and rose to 83.3% by the close; the rational baseline is 50%, since one of two debaters must lose

Calibration techniques that work:

Prompt-ensemble: 20-40% ECE/Brier score reduction with minimal latency
Action-wise Platt scaling: 10-20% per-dimension miscalibration reduction
Adaptive Temperature Scaling (ATS): per-token temperature prediction
RL with proper scoring rule rewards: state-of-the-art calibration + robust OOD generalization

Design lever: never use raw confidence as your sole escalation trigger. Always calibrate, and combine with other signals.
Monitor confidence continuously, not only at the end
Key finding from “Agentic Uncertainty Quantification” (arXiv 2601.15703): optimal intervention points should be dynamically selected based on continuous confidence monitoring, not checked only at the end. The system should balance efficient execution and deep deliberation based on real-time confidence signals.
Beyond confidence — multi-signal escalation
A production escalation trigger should combine:








































SignalMechanismWeightCalibrated confidencePlatt-scaled probability below thresholdBase signalBlast radiusFinancial impact, data scope, reversibilityMultiplierAnomaly detectionSemantic distance from known-good patternsFlagPolicy conflictAction violates ABAC/ReBAC permission rulesHard stopSimilarity to known failuresEmbedding distance to intervention database (introduced below)BoostDomain boundaryAction outside defined ODDHard stop
Blast radius as first-class primitive (the “Runplane pattern,” after a commercial AI runtime-guardrails product):

Scope limits: database updates limited to N records at a time
Value limits: auto-approve refunds up to $X, require human above
Rate limits: frequency caps on actions
Real-time dashboards showing blast radius across agent fleets

Every action request is evaluated against the rules and receives a decision in milliseconds.
The meta-problem: the escalation decision itself is unreliable
The agent deciding whether to escalate is the same unreliable system you’re trying to oversee. Mitigations:

Runtime ODD monitoring (external to the agent) that triggers autonomy reduction independently
Hard policy rules that bypass the agent’s judgment entirely (value thresholds, permission boundaries)
Anomaly detection operating on behavior patterns, not the agent’s self-assessment

Trust quantification — the math
Bayesian trust model
The most formally developed approach, from human-robot interaction research. Uses a Beta distribution as conjugate prior to Bernoulli (success/failure):
Prior:     Beta(α₀, β₀)  — initial trust (e.g., α₀=1, β₀=1 for uninformative)
Success:   α_{n+1} = αₙ + 1
Failure:   β_{n+1} = βₙ + 1
Trust:     E[trust] = α / (α + β)
Key empirical finding: the negative feedback loop (trust decrease after failure) exerts stronger influence than the positive loop (trust increase after success). Trust stabilizes over repeated interactions — the effect of any single event diminishes as history grows.
This directly implements earned autonomy:

New agent (α=1, β=1): trust = 0.5, needs many successes to climb
After 50 successes, 2 failures (α=51, β=3): trust = 0.94
One critical failure resets β significantly: trust drops sharply

Design lever: maintain per-action-type, per-context Beta distributions. An agent that’s trusted for “read and summarize” may not be trusted for “modify and deploy.” Trust is contextual, not global.
Contextual bandits for real-time adaptation
For updating escalation thresholds without full retraining: a contextual bandit layer sits on top of the agent’s base policy and learns from human corrections in real-time. Query human feedback only when the action policy exceeds an uncertainty threshold. The bandit learns which contexts are safe for autonomous action and which need input — directly implementing the shrinking surface.
Intervention tracking and learning
Building the intervention database
The concrete pattern emerging in production:

Log every human override with full context: agent state, proposed action, human correction, reason given
When human approves without changes → record as successful autonomous pattern
When human rejects or modifies → record the delta and the context
Over time, build a corpus of labeled decision points
Use this corpus to update escalation thresholds — if corrections cluster around specific action types or contexts, tighten triggers there; if approvals accumulate with zero corrections, loosen

Each iteration improves accuracy and decreases the number of cases needing manual intervention. This is the mechanical implementation of the “shrinking surface.”
RLHF in the pipeline context (not model training)
Targeted Human Feedback (RLTHF): combines LLM-based initial alignment with selective human corrections. Achieves full-human-annotation-level alignment with only 6-7% of the human annotation effort. Directly applicable: use the LLM to handle routine alignment, route the 6-7% most ambiguous cases to humans.
Measuring intervention quality
Not all human corrections are good. Track:

Consistency: does the same reviewer make the same decision on similar cases?
Outcome impact: did the correction actually improve the final result?
Reviewer reject rate: a reviewer who never rejects is rubber-stamping
Correction reversal rate: how often is a correction itself corrected later?

The “Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability” paper (Rabanser, Kapoor et al., Feb 2026) decomposes reliability into four dimensions: consistency, robustness, predictability, safety — with twelve concrete metrics independent of raw accuracy. These reliability metrics should gate autonomy expansion, not just capability scores.
Safety envelopes and runtime monitoring
Operational Design Domain (ODD) — borrowed from autonomous vehicles
The most mature formal approach to defining “where a system is allowed to operate autonomously.” For AVs, ODD specifies: road types, weather, time of day, speed ranges, geographic boundaries. For AI agents:



































ODD dimensionAV exampleAgent pipeline equivalentRoad typeHighway vs residentialAction type (read vs write vs deploy)WeatherClear vs rain vs snowData quality / completenessSpeed range0-65 mphValue / blast radius rangeGeographic boundaryCity limitsPermitted data sources / systemsManeuver restrictionsNo U-turnsProhibited action combinations
ODDs are not static — developers start narrow and expand as competence is demonstrated. But each expansion requires a new safety case. The SAE driving-automation L3→L4 transition is the critical one: at L3, the human must be ready to take over; at L4, the system can bring itself to a safe state without human intervention within its ODD.
Design lever: for each agent, define the ODD explicitly before deployment. Document the boundary. Expansion requires formal validation, not just “it seems to be working.”
Runtime ODD monitoring
Runtime ODD monitoring runs sub-monitors for input distribution, action patterns, and environmental context. When the agent approaches the boundary of its safe envelope:

Narrow permitted actions before failure occurs (autonomy reduction, not just escalation)
Alert human if reduction is insufficient
Safe-stop if the situation exceeds all boundaries

IBM’s A2AS Framework implements “semantic firewalls” — monitoring how the agent thinks, not just what it outputs. The firewall detects manipulation through reasoning patterns and behavioral drift from original intent.
Autonomy reduction vs escalation
The sophisticated pattern is not binary (autonomous vs escalate-to-human):
Normal operation → Detect boundary approach → Narrow scope →
  Still near boundary? → Escalate to human →
    Critical? → Safe-stop
This gives the system three responses to uncertainty before involving a human, reducing unnecessary escalation while maintaining safety.
The human side — decision fatigue and complacency
The core paradox: as the system gets better, humans get worse at overseeing it (Parasuraman-Manzey model). Automation bias occurs in both naive and expert participants and cannot be prevented by training alone. If you escalate too much, you escalate nothing — the human learns to click “approve” without reading. SOC false positive rates: up to 99%.
Anti-rubber-stamping UX (MIT Sloan / BCG 2025)

Present evidence for AND against each recommendation
Reject rate monitoring — flag reviewers who never reject
Time-minimum for review — block approvals in < N seconds
Rotating reviewers to prevent single-reviewer complacency
Progressive disclosure of reasoning depth on demand

Klarna lesson: AI assistant handled 800 FTEs of work, cut resolution time from 11 to 2 minutes. Klarna expanded autonomy too fast, pulled back, and re-implemented with proper escalation triggers and confidence scoring.
Regulatory landscape
EU AI Act Article 14 (postponed to 2027-28 — see agent-audit-trails-provenance): High-risk systems must enable humans to understand capabilities, detect anomalies, remain aware of automation bias, and disregard outputs. Academic critique: “no clear guidance about meaningful human oversight” and cognitive constraints undermine such oversight in practice.
FDA PCCPs: The closest regulatory pattern to progressive autonomy — pre-approve the expansion path. A PCCP describes planned modifications, validation methodology, and impact assessment upfront; manufacturers can then make pre-specified changes without new submissions.
Financial services (US): No AI-specific regulations yet. FINRA 2026 oversight report addresses “where to have human in the loop agent oversight protocols.” Existing rules apply technology-neutrally.
Anti-patterns
Gaming the metrics
Agents with planning and reasoning can learn to manipulate oversight. The system may learn to avoid escalation (appearing confident) rather than avoid errors. Without explainability, oversight becomes superficial. Reward hacking in RLHF is a documented failure mode where the system optimizes the proxy metric rather than the actual objective.
Mitigation: measure reliability (consistency, robustness, predictability, safety), not just accuracy. Track error-conditional-on-not-escalating separately from overall error rate.
Asymmetric error costs
False positive escalations cost time and create alert fatigue. False negative autonomous errors cost damage. The optimal threshold depends on cost asymmetry in your specific domain — there is no universal answer. In content moderation, a 2% precision drop generates false removals that overwhelm review queues; a recall drop means harmful content stays visible.
Design lever: make the cost asymmetry explicit in your escalation scoring. escalation_score = calibrated_confidence × inverse_blast_radius × cost_asymmetry_weight.
Skill degradation
As the system handles more autonomously, human overseers handle fewer edge cases, and their ability to detect subtle errors degrades. “Poorly designed automation can actually degrade human performance by inducing complacency, reducing skill maintenance, or overwhelming operators with alerts.”
Mitigation: periodically route known-good decisions for human review (calibration checks). Track reviewer accuracy over time. Rotate reviewers across domains.
The paradox of success
“The more confident we become in automation, the more tempted we are to remove human oversight entirely, even when judgment still matters.” If your time-to-detect is slower than the system’s time-to-act, oversight is ceremonial. This is the core tension: you are choosing whether to intervene while performance metrics argue for letting it run.
Mitigation: the ODD boundary approach. Never expand to full autonomy — always maintain a defined boundary where human oversight activates. Expand the boundary, but never remove it.
Case studies

ai/implementation-intentions-for-ai-plan.title: Implementation Intentions for AI Plan Execution
ai/implementation-intentions-for-ai-plan.content:
Implementation Intentions for AI Plan Execution
An implementation intention is a conditional plan in the form “if situation Y occurs, then I will initiate response Z” — distinct from a goal intention, which specifies the desired outcome (Gollwitzer, 1999). The framework was developed in self-regulation research to explain why goal intentions on their own often fail to produce action: the unresolved gap between intention and execution is closed by binding the when, where, and how of the response to an explicit environmental cue.
This note ports the framework to AI plan design. Implementation intentions are the structural upgrade for Signal 3 of the plan-split-scan (decision branches): an unresolved branch in a plan should be either resolved up front, split into its own plan, or expressed as an implementation intention. Anything else is a bet that the executor will figure out the branch correctly at run-time — a bet that loses more often than the planner expects.
The framework (Gollwitzer)
Two distinct planning constructs, working at different levels:




















ConstructFormFunctionGoal intentionI intend to achieve XNames the desired end state. Necessary but not sufficient for action.Implementation intentionIf situation Y occurs, then I will initiate response ZSpecifies the conditional execution. Binds behavior to a trigger.
Implementation intentions are subordinate to goal intentions — they don’t decide what to do, only when/where/how to execute it. In human self-regulation, the mechanism is offloading the moment-of-decision from deliberative control to environmental cues: when the trigger fires, the response is initiated automatically, without re-deliberation.
Empirically, supplementing a goal intention with implementation intentions produces meaningful behavior-change effects. Gollwitzer & Sheeran’s (2006) meta-analysis of 94 studies reported a medium-to-large effect size (d ≈ 0.65) for goal attainment when implementation intentions were added — across health behaviors, academic tasks, prejudice-control, and other domains. The effect is robust enough that implementation-intentions interventions are now standard tools in clinical behavior-change practice.
Why this matters for AI plans
LLMs and agents don’t have willpower failures, but they have structural cousins: context drift, branch-collapse, and default-policy fallback. The same conditional-binding move that solves the human intention–behavior gap addresses these for AI execution.
Context drift
On long plans, the executor’s attention erodes (lost-in-the-middle / position bias). Decisions that depend on plan-level reasoning made early in context can be silently lost by step 10. An implementation intention binds the decision to a local trigger at the point of use rather than relying on the executor to maintain global state.
Branch-collapse
When an LLM encounters an unresolved if/then in a plan, it tends to pick one branch and proceed — usually the most common or training-data-typical one. Counterfactual branches are silently flattened. An explicit implementation intention forces the branch to remain open and deterministic at execution time (if X, then route to subagent Y with payload Z; if not-X, then return to user for confirmation).
Default-policy fallback
Underspecified responses (“handle the error appropriately,” “deal with the edge case”) collapse onto the model’s training-data prior for that phrase — which may bear no relation to your actual intent. The implementation-intention form forces the response to be operationalized as a specific action against a specific trigger.
The conditional template
IF <trigger>: <observable, deterministic, falsifiable signal>
THEN <response>: <specific action, named tool, named subagent, or explicit return-to-user>

Both halves must pass strict tests:
Trigger criteria. The trigger must be:

Observable by the executor at the moment of decision (not a future state, not a global property)
Deterministic — same input maps to same trigger-firing decision
Falsifiable — a clear “yes the trigger fired” or “no it did not” verdict, not a feel

Vague triggers (“if something feels off,” “if the result looks wrong”) are not implementation intentions — they’re verbal hedges. Re-formulate or drop.
Response criteria. The response must be:

Specific — named action, named tool call, named subagent, named output
Executable by the executor as currently configured (don’t reference a tool the agent doesn’t have)
Bounded — has a clear termination, so the response doesn’t recursively expand into its own plan

A response that is itself a multi-step plan should not be smuggled into a then-clause. Either inline it, or have the response be escalate to a separate plan.
Worked examples
Bad (un-operationalized branch)

If the existing migration works, modify it; otherwise rewrite it.

The trigger (“works”) is not observable until the executor checks; the response (“rewrite”) is itself a plan. This is Signal 3 of the plan-split-scan in pure form — an unresolved branch the executor cannot collapse without doing the check first.
Better (resolved up front)
Run the check before issuing the plan, decide which branch, and issue the resolved plan. Eliminates the conditional entirely.
Better (implementation intention)

Step 1: Run pytest tests/migration_test.py.
IF all tests pass: continue to step 2 (modify migration in place, see spec section A).
IF any test fails: STOP. Return the failing test names to the user and request a decision (modify-with-fix or rewrite path B).

The trigger is observable (test exit code), deterministic (same input → same verdict), and falsifiable (pass/fail is binary). The response is specific (named tool, named output, explicit return-to-user on the negative branch). The branch remains open until the trigger fires.
Better (split into separate plans)
Issue the test-run as its own plan. Receive the result. Issue the appropriate downstream plan (modify or rewrite) based on the result. Highest verification leverage, highest coordination overhead — pick this when the branch is high-stakes or the two downstream paths are large.
Mapping to the plan-split-scan signals
Implementation intentions interact with multiple signals of the plan-split-scan:

Signal 3 (decision branches) — the direct mapping. Every unresolved branch should be: resolved up front, split into its own plan, or expressed as an implementation intention. “We’ll figure it out when we get there” is none of those. Prefer the first two as defaults; the conditional form is the fallback (see the corrective under Counterargument).
Signal 2 (state-carry depth) — implementation intentions reduce state-carry by binding the decision to a local trigger rather than a global decision made earlier in the plan.
Signal 4 (verification seams) — a well-formed implementation intention is itself a verification seam (the trigger evaluation is a natural pause point).
Signal 5 (reversibility boundary) — never wrap a destructive operation in an implementation intention. The conditional-form invites the executor to fire it without the explicit user-confirmation gate. Destructive operations remain hard splits.

Failure modes specific to LLM execution
In human self-regulation, implementation intentions work through an automatic, cue-driven response; that mechanism translates imperfectly to LLM context. Four concrete failure modes:
Trigger ambiguity. The trigger is observable in principle but ambiguous in execution. “If the build fails” — what counts as failing? Non-zero exit code? Warning count above threshold? Both pass and known-flaky test list non-empty? Either pin the trigger precisely or expect non-deterministic branching.
Response under-specification. “Then handle the error” collapses onto the model’s training-data prior for error-handling, which may be silent-swallow, retry-forever, or some other default that doesn’t match intent. Name the action.
Compound conditionals as deferred planning. A chain of if A then if B then if C then … is not an implementation intention — it’s a plan with branches the planner failed to resolve, hidden in conditional syntax. Each nested branch should resolve to a single trigger/response pair or split into its own plan.
Run-time trigger evaluation drift. The LLM evaluates the trigger differently than the user intended (e.g., evaluates “passes” more loosely on a test the planner cared about being strict). If the trigger evaluation is itself load-bearing, instrument it externally (run the test, capture exit code, pass it back into the plan) rather than asking the LLM to evaluate.
Related cognitive-science context
The Gollwitzer framework sits in a broader literature on goal hierarchies:

Goal intentions (what to achieve) are necessary but insufficient. Studies find that goal-intention-only conditions produce significantly less follow-through than goal-intention-plus-implementation-intention conditions across many domains.
Distal goals are protected from intention–behavior gap erosion by proximal implementation intentions. This pairs with the concrete-subgoals pillar (Locke & Latham 1990; Bandura 1977) — concrete subgoals provide the what; implementation intentions provide the when/how of executing them.
Self-regulation depletion (Baumeister’s ego-depletion line of work) was the original problem the framework solved; the framework’s empirical robustness has held up better than ego-depletion itself, which suffered replication issues (Hagger et al. 2016, multi-site replication finding no significant depletion effect). The if-then mechanism’s empirical base is independent of whether ego-depletion as a construct survives.

Tradeoffs and context-dependence

The cost is up-front planning effort. Implementation intentions move work forward in time — you have to anticipate triggers and pre-specify responses. This is real cost; it’s worth paying when the consequences of the branch are non-trivial.
They are not universal. For plans with one concern, deterministic flow, and no branching, implementation intentions add nothing but ceremony. Use them where Signal 3 fires.
They compose with the falsifiability scan. A well-formed implementation intention is essentially the operationalization checklist (falsifying observation, measurement, deadline) packaged as a conditional. The two skills can fire together: /falsifiability-scan on the trigger phrasing, /plan-split-scan on the structural placement.

What this doesn’t cover

Trigger detection by the LLM itself. This note assumes the trigger evaluation is reliable. For triggers where the LLM might mis-evaluate (vague natural-language conditions, subjective quality judgments), externalize the trigger evaluation to a deterministic check (exit code, test result, schema validation) before relying on the if-then form.
Multi-agent if-then routing. When the response is “route to subagent Y,” the question of which subagent is itself a planning problem this note doesn’t address. The named subagent or named tool is the boundary — picking it is upstream.
State machines and finite-state plans. When a plan grows beyond ~3 independent conditionals, it’s a state machine and should be modeled as such. Implementation intentions are the syntax for single conditional choices; they don’t replace formal state-machine specification for genuinely stateful workflows.

Counterargument
The strongest objection: if-then conditionals can become a syntactic veneer that hides un-resolved planning rather than resolving it. A plan with twelve nested conditionals is not “twelve implementation intentions” — it’s an unresolved plan with branches the planner failed to think through. The framework’s empirical strength in human self-regulation depends on the conditionals being few and cue-driven; ported to AI plans, the same constraint holds. If implementation intentions become a way to avoid the discipline of resolving branches up front, they have failed in the same way that always-breaking-it-down-further can produce over-decomposition (see the over-decomposition counter).
The corrective: prefer resolved up front and split into separate plans over implementation intention as defaults; reach for the conditional form only when neither alternative is feasible (the trigger genuinely cannot be evaluated up front, and the two downstream paths are similar enough in scope that splitting would duplicate setup).
Related

task-decomposition-for-ai-plans — the parent note; Signal 3 is the direct upstream
falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — operationalization checklist; implementation intentions are a packaging of the same move
information-density-for-llm-prompts — position-bias and lost-in-the-middle, the LLM mechanism behind one of the failure modes
system-prompt-design-principles — prompt structure; conditional sections are an analog of implementation intentions at the system-prompt layer
multi-agent-coordination-topologies — when the then clause is “route to subagent Y,” topology choice is upstream

Sources
Verified 2026-05-12.

Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). “Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans.” American Psychologist, 54(7), 493–503. The canonical introduction of the if-then implementation-intention framework.
Gollwitzer, P. M. & Sheeran, P. (2006). “Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes.” Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. Meta-analysis of 94 studies; reported medium-to-large effect (d ≈ 0.65) for goal attainment with added implementation intentions. The “implementation intentions are highly effective” line in the AI-roundup-style literature traces here; this is the source to cite.
Locke, E. A. & Latham, G. P. (1990). A Theory of Goal Setting and Task Performance. Prentice Hall. The concrete-subgoals framing; pairs with implementation intentions on the what vs how axis.
Bandura, A. (1977). “Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change.” Psychological Review, 84. Self-efficacy as the mechanism by which subgoal completion builds capacity for harder goals.
Hagger, M. S. et al. (2016). “A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect.” Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4). Multi-site replication finding no significant ego-depletion effect; ego depletion was the original problem implementation intentions were proposed to solve. Implementation-intention efficacy is empirically independent of this.

ai-news-july-2026 — Delta window late Jun → mid Jul 2026: the frontier release cluster (Sonnet 5, Grok 4.5, GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, Gemini 3.5 Pro delayed to ~Jul 17), the ~$2/M near-frontier price tier, Reflection AI’s Colossus 2 lease + Meta Compute, Illinois audit-mandating AI safety law + EU AI Act re-timing in law + FTC “truthful outputs” preemption move; resolves the predecessor’s OpenAI-funding and what-did-the-other-labs-ship open questions. fable-5-vs-opus-4-8-field-reports-2026-06 — First-month field reports: Fable 5’s edge over Opus 4.8 is long-horizon autonomy (multi-day runs, whole-repo migrations, unblocking months-stuck tasks), not smarter one-shots — independent short-task benchmarks show a modest gap; emerging routing consensus is Opus as default, Fable for done-vs-not-done tasks. ai-trends-second-order-2026 — Forward simulation of those trends (/second-order) stress-tested with base rates (/reference-class) and adversarial critique (/red-team); reconciliation: the verification deficit is the central dynamic, but whether verification automates as fast as generation is the variable everything hinges on
ai-news-april-2026 — Timeline of March-April 2026 developments (index to detailed notes)
ai-software-dev-2026-landscape — Productivity paradox, best practices, agentic workflows, IP/legal, 2027-2029 forecasts
ai-frontier-crisis-april-2026 — Mythos architecture, Glasswing coalition, lab escape, DoW clash, AGI timeline
model-access-inequality — Does unequal access to smarter models widen or narrow inequality? The sign flips by margin: within-task it compresses skill gaps (novices gain most — best-measured effect), but at the structural margin (compute/training concentration, capital–labor tilt, the “frontier-worker” adoption gap, agent-fleet quantity, lock-in) it concentrates. The binding constraint is migrating from price to agency; sources incl. Agentic Inequality (access/capability/quantity/control), Brynjolfsson-Li-Raymond QJE, Brookings, World Bank/Anthropic usage data
ai-job-displacement-timescales-mechanisms — How/when/through-what-mechanism AI displaces labor (deep-research synthesis, 2026-06). The documented signal is task automation + entry-level attrition, not occupational collapse: Stanford/ADP shows 22–25-yr-olds in most-exposed jobs −16% while experienced workers held steady ✅; augment-vs-automate predicts which roles thin; aggregate unemployment ~null so far ○. Sector table + near/medium/long timescales gated by liability/physical-world/regulation bottlenecks; GPTs-are-GPTs vs Frey-Osborne vs Acemoglu methodologies; per-claim confidence labels (3-vote-verified vs single-source-extracted, since the run’s synthesis stage was rate-limited)
capability-outcome-gap — Deliberately thin (one essay + its HN thread, 2026-08-06): the premise the role/skill cluster assumes but never states — does capability convert into outcome? Two mechanisms for “often, no”: bottleneck is marginal (capability added to a non-binding stage yields ~nothing — the 12-year FDA surrogate-endpoint validation on data that already existed), and incentive capture decides where capability gets aimed (patents protect composition-of-matter, not novel biology → target herding → the largest AI-for-biology rounds land on the already-tractable molecule-optimization stage). Carries its own strongest counters, including the one that nearly kills it: the argument rests on an IP-vs-genuine-difficulty split its source never attempts. Software transfer (review capacity as the real constraint; AI-coding capital flowing to appropriable value, not largest value) and the missing-governor correction to ../general/skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age. Time-sensitive
agent-systems-trajectory — Where agent systems are heading 2026-2029: capabilities, tooling, workflows, economics, what to invest in now
embodied-ai-llm-transfer — The mechanism behind the displacement note’s “physical world is the hard bottleneck”: LLM progress transfers to robotics through named channels (VLA semantic generalization, embodied System-2 reasoning per Gemini Robotics 1.5, cross-embodiment motion transfer, world-models-as-data-workaround) — but to breadth, not reliability at contact: the data gap and Moravec’s System-1 layer advance on their own slower clock. Deployment reality check (Agility Digit as the lone revenue case, tote-moving as the least-Moravec-hard task; cheap bodies arriving before trustworthy hands) plus four watch conditions that would change the verdict. Time-sensitive
delivery-org-agent-fit-matrix — Task-granularity leg of the prediction cluster: a third-party AI-generated 87-task delivery-org matrix (re-encoding vs. origination axis, all scores unverified hypotheses) re-judged against the vault — the axis is the skill-valuation logic in miniature; five re-judgments (missing verification-cost/blast-radius axis, the uninformative 52% Partial middle, near-circular Highs hiding origination inside production, code review vs. the rubber-stamping base rate, Low split into position-Lows vs. capability-Lows — and pointed at the Partial column, which makes the whole 45-task middle a forecast) plus what the matrix teaches back (the vault has no task inventory; the ~13% origination-bound share is a slicing artifact that still poses a denominator question the vault never states). Red-teamed same-day; counts demoted to enumeration properties. Time-sensitive
delivery-org-task-matrix-data — Source data for the above: the full 87-row task × phase × fit table transcribed verbatim from the third-party PDF (31 High / 45 Partial / 11 Low, all scores unverified hypotheses), kept as a clean copy for re-slicing and re-scoring; analysis stays in the agent-fit note
delivery-org-matrix-desk-rescoring — Re-judgment #1 executed on the 21 desk-relevant rows (architecture-owning lead-web-dev seat, selection inferred): verification-cost + blast-radius columns added per the roadmap note’s rung/oracle machinery, Δ marked per row. Headline (post same-day red-team, corrections kept visible): no desk High keeps a single unconditional label — the High column decomposes into honest / conditional / oracle-layer Highs, and the oracle-layer rows (CI/CD, test authoring) are delegable only under seat-governed independence (check-author ≠ output-author, floors, meta-monitors) — governance stays, authorship needn’t. Two promotions the matrix missed (spike artifacts, bug repro); strategy Partials pinned at L2 by oracle absence (partial fitness-function oracles noted), which is also their erosion path. Time-sensitive
designer-seat-under-ai — The designer-seat counterpart to the desk-rescoring note: the prediction cluster pointed at design work at task granularity. Design & Production is the only majority-High phase (11/19) while Definition & Strategy + Ideation hold zero Highs across 23 — the designer’s exposure is inverted from the profession’s self-image. Six speculations (deliverable becomes the constraint system; review becomes the job but only holds with an owned oracle; the hollowed middle takes the junior rung and kills the portfolio-of-screens; taste splits into automatable negative and residual positive; the durable work is the decision not the exploration; an authorship-premium segment ≠ headcount), the reassurances the cluster contradicts (research/empathy is family (b) — a forecast, not a floor), and a six-row learn-instead-of-Figma table with a test you could fail per row. Then the operational layer: a per-task how-to-run-it-with-AI pass keyed to a four-mode table (H needs an oracle you didn’t author / P pick the rung / L(a) AI attacks your answer / L(b) AI preps around the live part), and a primary-source-verified toolchain table (2026-07-29) — Figma MCP surface grew 7→24 tools with a local/remote split (the three REST-shaped confabulations still absent), DESIGN.md matured to a linter + DTCG export but is still alpha, DTCG Format Module 2025.10 is a Final Community Group Report and explicitly not a W3C Standard, and npx impeccable detect was found wrong and corrected at source. Row selection inferred; the 48-task Designer PDF was never transcribed. Time-sensitive
design-side-ai-adoption-stall — /structural-trace output and the structure companion to the above: why design-side AI adoption stalls while engineering’s compounds. Diagnosis, not a plan. Two coupled stocks (constraint substrate; trust in generated output), four loops — R1 substrate starvation whose crux is an asymmetric delay (bad screens disconfirm in seconds, substrate investment pays off in months), R2 divergent returns off engineering’s pre-existing oracle stock, B1 quality-bar defense (the fastest loop, functioning correctly, which is why it terminates trials before slower loops run), B2 entry-cost gate (the legible but non-binding objection). Archetype: Growth and Underinvestment, where the eroded performance standard is the phrase “designers are behind” — the dispositional explanation is a load-bearing component, not commentary. Action concentrates at Meadows 12 (training, licenses); leverage sits at 8 (a design-side oracle, converting B1 from trial-terminator to gate) and 3 (goal from tool-adoption to constraint-ownership). Boundary-flagged: the affected party’s objection is coded as resistance, and objection (1) is largely correct. Then /second-order on the oracle intervention (sign flip at the 10-year horizon: withholding taste is protective at 10 minutes and costly at 10 years; the half-built-oracle branch is blind on exactly the axes carrying the slop signal) and /red-team on the diagnosis itself — three hits, corrections kept visible: the “designers are behind” move is self-sealing, the stock directions were asserted without any adoption history (demoted to hypothesis), and B1/B2 are not loops but a decision rule and a threshold, which re-ranks the oracle from Meadows 8 to 6. Weakest claim is the headline itself — the competing “tools were built for programmers first” explanation is simpler and undistinguished by evidence; a distinguishing test is recorded. Time-sensitive
design-side-ai-onramp — Third of the set and the only one that recommends: what to actually do, which /structural-trace was forbidden from producing. Built in two tiers because the diagnosis it rests on only partly survived red-team — tier 1 (don’t make git the entry fee; first exposure from the High column outside the identity zone; don’t pitch speed to seniors) is correct under either explanation; tier 2 (ship one narrow blocking oracle that names its own coverage boundary; hand over the constraint system as authority, not chores; hold the standard) bets on the capacity explanation and is gated on a distinguishing test. Step 0 is three plan-killing checks led by ask the designers, since the pre-mortem’s named failure is using structural vocabulary instead of asking. Leading indicators both ways at ~3 months, including the self-check “you catch yourself explaining non-adoption structurally to someone who didn’t ask.” Not validated in practice. Time-sensitive
ai-framing-shift-design-systems-2023-2026 — Corpus read of Design Systems WTF (58 episodes, 31.0 h, 325,317 words, 2023-09→2026-08, locally transcribed) tracking how a practitioner community’s AI framing moved: tool → collaborator → reader → economic dependency. Headline finding is distributional, not volumetric — AI was quarantined in dedicated episodes through 2025 (half of all other episodes never said the word), then in 2026 appears in editorial content in 15 of 16 episodes, including burnout and org-placement episodes (paid sponsor reads segregated throughout — the ad script itself went 2% → 20% AI-saturated, reported as a separate vendor-positioning finding). The load-bearing move is late-2025: documentation stops being written by AI for humans and starts being read by AI, celebrated as “the death of the doc site”. Verification & Quality

llm-evaluation-methodology — The methodology foundation under the whole verification stack: an eval as a measurement instrument with three failure axes — validity (metric choice can manufacture results — Schaeffer; construct validity; contamination as validity-killer — Golchin & Surdeanu), independence (never let the producer grade; same-family judges aren’t independent either — Zheng’s position/verbosity/self-enhancement biases, Panickssery’s self-recognition∝self-preference, Knight & Leveson’s correlated-error result; the cross-family lmquery escape, named-but-unused), and reliability (one run is a sample — pass@k from Chen et al., inter-rater κ/α). Shows how skill-eval-format already embodies all three (mechanical-checks-first as the independent oracle, blind scoring, the falsifiability-scan 15/15 blind run that out-found its own labels); primary-sourced because a note arguing against same-family authorship can’t lean on it
agent-output-quality-variance — The capstone over the gates and shape notes: what happens when the objective is stated as consistency of generated-code quality rather than peak quality, which is a reliability problem, not a capability one. Core reframe: gates truncate, they do not lift — a gate can only reject, so the mean rises as a consequence of cutting the left tail, the floor sits at your weakest gate’s threshold, and unaddressed defect classes keep their full original variance. Then the finding that bounds every gate-centric framework: run-to-run spread has five sources (sampling, context, specification, horizon, substrate) and gates fix exactly one — specification variance is invisible to every downstream control and plausibly dominant, while substrate variance is the one with compounding returns since gates charge rent forever and exemplar quality is bought once. Prices the stack: cost is governed by first-try pass rate, not gate runtime, and p = q^n makes it superlinear in gate count — 15 gates at q=0.90 means half of all tasks blow a 3-attempt repair budget, at which point the framework hasn’t reduced variance, it has relocated it onto the human queue. Hence the highest-return move: every gate gets a context-side twin (a gate whose rule the agent was never told is being used for discovery, and you pay a generation cycle for information you could have given away — stating it lifts q, and multiplicativity makes that 5.6× cheaper at n=10). Plus retry-as-rejection-sampling: output becomes conditional on the gate, so unmeasured dimensions negatively correlated with it get actively worse — which is exactly the metric thresholds, so never build a retry loop around one. Closes on measurement (pass^k or the framework is faith) and the objection that guts it: if spec variance dominates, almost none of this helps. All tables computed from the stated model with the independence and uniform-q assumptions flagged as false in practice
constrained-shape-for-verifiability — The inverse of the gates note: instead of pointing a stronger analyzer at unconstrained code, narrow the code’s shape until the gate is cheap. Analysis cost is a property of the representation, not just the question — “can control reach the payment handler without an auth check?” is interprocedural data flow in free-form async TS (CodeQL, minutes, unsound in practice) and graph reachability over a finite edge set in an explicit state machine (milliseconds, and complete, which is one of the few moves that buys that upgrade outright). Worked case is statecharts: unreachable states, missing transitions, and no-exit terminals become graph queries, and declared transitions repair the specific weakness AST rules have — a rule can verify a call is present but not reached. The larger prize is oracle generation (getSimplePaths derives a path set from the machine, so tests aren’t co-authored with the implementation — the independence failure oracle-problem-verification catalogs). Argues an executing model beats a modeled one: TLA+/Alloy verify a model and leave model-to-code correspondence manual, while a statechart in app code is the runtime artifact, so the correspondence is free — the reason to reach here before TLA+ isn’t stronger logic, it’s no gap. “Forced” has to mean a layer-2 AST rule, not a convention, or the agent writes an if chain next to the machine. Ceremony test: can you name the states without inventing them. Case-against is load-bearing — it relocates the oracle problem (a wrong machine gets verified confidently and completely), state explosion under composition kills the exhaustive enumeration exactly where you wanted it, @xstate/test is the stalest part of the stack (v0.5.1, Jan 2026, while core moved on), and most web defects are wrong business logic inside a legitimate transition, which this doesn’t touch. Closes with the general family — SQL, declarative IaC, schemas, pure functions, statecharts — each trading expressiveness for a checkable property. No defect-rate study cited because none was found; the argument is mechanical, not empirical, and says so. Time-sensitive
deterministic-gates-agent-loop — The machine-facing axis under the stack: a gate as a falsifier positioned inside the agent’s repair loop, not at the end of it. Separates the four properties that get collapsed into “reliable” (deterministic / sound / complete / correct — a regex scanner can be consistently wrong), then the mechanism that makes determinism matter more for agents than for humans: a flaky gate converts repair into resampling, because the cheapest action that turns it green is to retry rather than fix. Carries the pin list (rule-pack versions, advisory-DB digests, seeds, baselines, filesystem ordering) and the search-tool exception — fuzz/property counterexamples aren’t deterministic but convert into deterministic regressions once frozen with their seed. Cost-ordered gate hierarchy 0–5 with the loop/human-clock line drawn between 2 and 3; eight repair-loop rules led by re-run-from-the-first-invalidated-gate; and the rule this note argues is the load-bearing one — the agent must not edit its own oracle (snapshots, baselines, suppressions, mutation exclusions), which is oracle-problem-verification’s co-authorship failure one level up. Plus fail-closed evidentiary integrity (green must assert every gate ran over the changed surface and produced a parseable report — timeouts and unparsed files are the coverage gap), one-tool-per-failure-class selection with a bake-off design, and four gaps for the TS seat the web note doesn’t cover (ast-grep/Semgrep repo rules, API-compat diffs, zizmor, OSV pinning). Extended same-day with the block/ratchet/route verdict taxonomy — the note originally assumed every gate answers is this wrong?, which is where complexity, duplication, type-coverage and suppression-count checks get forced into a pass/fail shape and turn into noise. Complexity lands as a ratchet, not a block, and the folk objection that CC is just SLOC in disguise is contradicted by the largest study on it (Landman et al., 17.6M Java methods / 6.3M C functions: correlation “only moderate”, “not strong enough to conclude that CC is redundant” — the search-engine summary of that paper asserts the opposite of its abstract). Plus metric gaming as the indirect oracle attack (can’t move the threshold, so deform the code until the number complies — the argument for ratchets over thresholds), and five gates the web note misses, led by the type-gate escape hatch ratchet (any-widening and @ts-ignore are invisible to layer 1 by construction, because the type gate really is green). GitClear duplication figures carried as directional-only with the vendor-incentive caveat stated. Then the CRAP index worked through as the composite case (Savoia/Evans 2007, CC²(1−cov)³+CC): deterministic only conditionally, which yields the general rule that a composite gate inherits the determinism of its worst input; and incentive-inverted as an agent gate, because the uncovered fraction is cubed while complexity is squared, so the gameable term carries 3–6× the leverage of the honest one (computed at CC=15/cov=0.5) — and coverage is exactly what AI suites satisfy vacuously. Two rescues: gate the coverage-proof CC ceiling separately (CC≤5 never CRAPpy, CC≥31 always), and a proposed mutation-adjusted CRAP substituting mutation score for coverage. Computable from TS off the compiler API plus Istanbul’s fnMap — with a warning not to install one of the five single-maintainer npm CRAP packages that appeared during 2026, since a metrics tool runs in CI with read access to the tree. Extended again with the composite-metric family and the frame that orders it — sibling composites (Tornhill’s churn×complexity hotspots, change/temporal coupling, Maintainability Index, SQALE) ranked not by sophistication but by input provenance relative to the agent’s write access: Tier A the agent authored (coverage, tests), Tier B derived from the code (CC, AST rules, types), Tier C from history the diff cannot rewrite (churn, coupling, telemetry). That frame retroactively explains CRAP — both its terms are Tier A, which is why it folds; hotspots have the identical two-signal shape but draw churn from Tier C, and that one substitution is the whole difference. Tier C signals belong in the route column, never as blockers. Change coupling billed separately as the gate that sees what the others structurally cannot: AI-duplicated logic produces files that co-change without an import edge, invisible to every import-graph tool by construction. CodeScene vendor caveat stated (Tornhill is its CTO). Maintenance status verified at source 2026-08-21: Terrascan archived, Gitleaks feature-complete by declaration (Betterleaks).
