Closes with a recorded failure of the author’s own — rejecting a correct METR figure because it carried two decimal places, when unusual precision is equally the signature of someone reading a raw data file. The only discriminator is whether a retrievable artifact backs the number, never whether it looks invented
verification-stack-operational-map — Single decision tree across all 19 vault skills (generative, detection, operationalization, adversarial, forward/structural, cognitive-burden, prose & prompt quality); seven clusters, six common chains, thirteen non-overlap axes, cost-calibrated single-skill default
Skills index — Per-skill reference notes (when to use, why each exists) for all 19 slash commands under .claude/skills/
vigilance-decrement-in-ai-oversight — The node eight other notes already point at, finally written: what sustained-attention research licenses about reviewing machine output, and what it doesn’t. Splits underload (mindlessness — the family that fits AI oversight) from overload (depletion), which matters because they prescribe opposite remedies — engage vs. rest. Establishes that fast onset is well supported (Mackworth’s 10–15% loss inside the first half hour) while no fixed cap exists — the “20–30 minute limit” is a distribution compressed into a constant. Adds the vault’s own prevalence-trap argument from Wolfe’s low-prevalence effect (7% miss at 50% prevalence → 30% at 1%): rising agent quality lowers defect prevalence and therefore degrades reviewer accuracy, coupling the two in the wrong direction. Carries the strongest direct result — Ye et al.’s ~5-hour sabotage study, 94% of developers missed it, and 56% accepted the code even after a correct monitor warning, which invalidates any safety argument terminating in “and then the human is alerted.” Three findings cut against cap-and-batch (micro-breaks don’t restore accuracy; self-scheduled breaks are no better than imposed and self-pacing doesn’t abolish the decrement; an intermittent non-task-related prompt beat undistracted monitoring), plus the self-defeating property that a homogeneous batch is a low-prevalence monitoring task. What survives: risk-triggered selective escalation (~15pp TPR gain) and restructuring the artifact into inspectable tests. Ends with a ten-row claim ledger and the missing experiment. Time-sensitive
oracle-problem-verification — The meta-layer under the whole verification stack: every gate silently picks a test oracle and inherits its independence failure; taxonomizes the five oracle types (test / spec / human / formal-LTL / cross-model) with each one’s failure (co-authorship, circular spec, vigilance decrement, expressiveness ceiling, correlated errors), then the oracle-free escape — metamorphic relations (Chen et al.) with a worked filterProducts example and the necessary-not-sufficient anchor discipline
knowledge-claim-lifecycle — Prior-art map for claim-state lifecycles and provenance in public knowledge infrastructure, grounding Piper’s 2026 “knowledge supply chain” essay: what’s already deployed (Wikidata ranks’ error≠supersession + demote-don’t-delete, Wikipedia [citation needed], PROV-DM revision/invalidation/bundles, Micropublications typed challenges, DEC disagreement/delusion + settle), the measured failure record (CA-GOP “Nazism” panel despite one-minute revert; retracted papers persisting on Wikipedia a median 3.68 years across 1,181 citations with authority slowing repair), and the genuine gap — lifecycle state doesn’t route between systems; claims shed epistemic state at every boundary, especially the AI summarization layer
interpretability-as-verification-primitive — The process-side complement to the (output-side) oracle table: mechanistic interpretability reads the model’s internal computation and answers the one question output scans can’t — was the stated reasoning faithful to the actual computation, or a post-hoc story? Why the output baseline is weak (CoT unfaithful: hints acknowledged ~25–39%, reward-hacks exploited >99% / disclosed <2%), what interpretability demonstrably shows (faithful-vs-confabulated separation, hidden-goal detection via SAE features, feature-level hallucination mechanism) vs. what’s aspirational (can’t prove a circuit’s absence, captures a fraction of computation), the honest counterweight (probes beat black-box on some splits, lose on others — de-correlated signal, not a deployable verifier), and the verified hands-on path: Anthropic’s circuit-tracer (open-sourced 2025-05-29) on Gemma-2-2b via ~15GB-VRAM Colab or Neuronpedia. Time-sensitive (2025 results)
reliability-vs-capability-agents — Capability (succeeds once) vs reliability (succeeds consistently across k runs and longer horizons) as distinct, divergent properties; pass@1 / pass@k / pass^k as primitives; the Khanal et al. reliability-science framework (decay curves, variance amplification, graceful degradation, meltdown onset — rank inversions across horizons, single study) and the benchmark-to-merge gap quantified (SWE-ABS: ~1 in 5 “solved” patches semantically wrong under strengthened tests; SWE-PRBench: AI reviewers catch 15-31% of human-flagged issues; AIDev field merge rates 43-83% per agent). Operational upshot: one green run is a sample, not a verdict — trust should be horizon-indexed and k-sampled
in-run-agent-monitoring — The completion signal is free and tells you least: it fires whether the work was done, abandoned, hallucinated as done, or circled for six hours. Answers the progress-vs-done requirement coding-with-agentic-loops states but doesn’t solve. Frames the tension between a rising task-length trend and production keeping agents to ≤10 steps as monitoring being the binding constraint, then covers why the obvious fix fails (a whole-transcript LLM monitor degrades 2×–30× with transcript length, so window it and repeat it instead), loop detection as the tractable case (IAL-Scan: 6,549 repos scanned, 68 confirmed infinite-loop failures across 47 projects at 91.9% precision), a detector table from step budgets through heartbeats to predictive state monitors, circuit breakers with a DEGRADED middle state, and trajectory scoring against Pass@1’s “high-score illusion”. Grounded in the July 2026 Hugging Face agent intrusion, where detection fired but was never escalated and “the successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones”. Time-sensitive
agent-autonomy-horizon — How long an agent can run before you must look at it, split into the two questions the phrase conflates: the task-length trend (METR’s TH1.1 revision — post-2023 doubling 131d vs 165d under TH1, post-2024 88.6d, ~7 months across 2019–2025; suite 170→228 tasks; the revision moved individual models tens of percent in both directions, and OpenAI repeats a ~7-month doubling while citing METR for it — a shared reference point, not an independent replication) and the in-run decay nobody had written down. Four separable mechanisms with different fixes: context-length degradation that hits the monitor as hard as the worker (frontier models miss dangerous actions 2×–30× more often after 800K benign tokens), compaction as a discrete lossy event (Governance Decay: in-context policy violation 0% → 30% after compaction, 59% worst model, and a Compaction-Eviction Attack that defeats every model tested — mitigated by pinning constraints outside the summarisable region), self-conditioning (a run’s own errors make further errors likelier, and scale doesn’t fix it), and iterative erosion. Plus why the 50% horizon is the wrong planning number (METR’s own fit conflates 50% and 80%; error bars ~2× and widening; >16h unreliable). Records an honest gap: no source isolates decay by elapsed time from decay by load. Time-sensitive
agentic-eda-tool-coupling — The deterministic-coupling thesis tested where executable feedback is strongest (simulators, formal engines, DRC, timing analyzers) rather than at code-review scale. Centerpiece is a negative result: on a commercial RTL-to-GDS flow, adding domain-specific EDA skills made a generic agent worse at the later stages (physical impl. 7/8 → 3/8, ECO 3/8 → 2/8 over 8 runs), while a structured harness hit 8/8 on all three — 31.7% of physical-design failures were tool-version/interface mismatches, and comparable-progress agents differed 141× in Token ROI (FluxBench, arXiv 2607.17528v3, verified in full text; one design, one lab, authors own the winning architecture). Sits against NVIDIA’s CVDP/ACE-RTL results, where the same iterative-feedback idea lifts bounded-task pass rates to 92–100% — the bounded-vs-long-horizon disagreement is the actual state of the art. Plus the DAC 2026 (26 Jul, Long Beach) vendor cluster with per-claim baseline grading, a date correction (Cadence’s 100× release is Apr 2026, not July — secondary coverage collapses it into DAC), and why “self-verifying” is the phrase to distrust. Time-sensitive

generative-ui-security — Extracted from generative-ui-landscape (verified 2026-08-25 against the Final ext-apps spec, specification/2026-01-26/, after three revisions sourced from summaries and then from the draft; five errors logged in the note’s own Corrections section, which is kept because a reader may have acted on them). Three layers — OS/process sandbox → renderer configuration → iframe isolation — and the cascade that collapses them: nodeIntegration: true disables context isolation, which “also disables process sandboxing, regardless of the default … or globally enabled sandboxing”. A host can believe it has three layers and have one. The mechanic to carry: whose origin does the frame have, not whether allow-same-origin is set. The scope trap: the sandbox-proxy MUST binds only “if the Host is a web page” — so it does not bind for the Electron desktop hosts that are the whole high-privilege case, where the spec prescribes only “sandbox the iframe” and Electron does the real work. A gap in the standard, not the note. Confirmation for a View-initiated tool call is a bare MAY in Final; the stronger app-registered-tools model is draft-only and unshipped. All fourteen sandbox tokens from MDN source; CSP-from-declared-domains is MUST, and Final’s restrictive default drops object-src that the draft had. Plus predeclared-review-by-resource-hash (the control most likely to go unused), UI mimicry, a checklist split by role because a server author controls almost none of it, and an explicit statement that no implementation was ever checked — the checklist is questions to ask a host, not a description of one. Pipelines & Implementation

long-run-session-persistence — “The agent can resume” is three claims wearing one coat, and only the cheapest is solved. Layer 1 conversation (solved — SDK sessions persist transcripts to disk; continue/resume/fork, where fork branches an expensive accumulated context; background sessions are supervisor-managed processes stopped after ~1h unattached and resurrected from disk on next attach, so the recovery path is exercised continuously rather than only after a crash). Layer 2 filesystem (partial — checkpointing snapshots code before each prompt, 100 per session, but explicitly does not track bash-command changes or subagent edits, which is exactly where unattended runs operate; git is the checkpoint without the holes). Layer 3 external effects (unsolved — compensating transactions “are not perfect inverses”, and a 435-work survey finds the literature concentrates on accumulating state over governing, recovering, or relinquishing it). Plus the checkpoint-vs-durable-execution distinction (a checkpoint says what state you were in; only a watchdog notices you died) and why compaction can delete state none of the three layers is guarding. Closes the queued resume-after-crash item. Time-sensitive

continuous-agent-task-fit — Which work fits a standing, always-on agent, stated so it can fail: continuous operation buys presence (inputs that arrive after the start) not depth (inputs all available at the start), and the hypothesis forbids a static-input task improving under scheduled operation at equal spend. Leads with the “it’s cron with a chatbot” counterargument and grants it the trigger. Six task shapes (Watch, Revisit, Resolve, Accumulate, Wait, Sweep) with two test columns — what the agent adds beyond a script, and where the output lands — giving the corrected form: the clock buys the detection, the agent buys the judgment; put the script on the clock and the agent behind it. Four costs a session doesn’t have, each from vendor docs: exit 0 is not a result (“green … does not mean the task in your prompt succeeded”), the empty wake still spends (per-run caps “rather than … a cumulative ceiling across runs”), unattended means unapproved (“no approval prompts during a run”), and intake is a trust boundary (85% adaptive-attack success across 78 studies). Ends on the review queue as the ceiling — a 24/7 producer aimed at a 9-to-5 reviewer is a capacity transfer. Published; stands on four published anchors only. Time-sensitive
standing-agent-operation — The private organisation half: how work reaches an always-on agent, whether the wakeup is a design object, how you know it silently stopped, and what its authority integrates to over weeks. Verdict first — the kill criterion half-fired: every intake channel and scheduler found is ordinary (mentions, assignments, polled queues; cron’s delay/drop/DST/60-day-disable intact), and three residuals are agent-specific, each narrowed on review: a third liveness state (woke, exit 0, did nothing) that monitors can hold but no agent product emits by default; budgets that are per run or per account, with a per-agent gateway key as workaround but never a default or a lifetime ceiling; and intake whose natural-language payload the consumer executes. The trigger-authority finding corrected against the plan’s first guess: it is scoped by where the trigger lives — repository CI triggers need GitHub’s separate workflow scope (this vault’s staged cron is the first-hand case), harness-native triggers are agent-creatable (Codex skills, OpenClaw automations, /schedule), and the only distinct authority above them is an org kill switch. Carries the vault’s own instance column for the six shapes (four of six need an agent for the judgment half, none for the trigger) and the honest reading of the kill criterion: the vault needs scheduling first, and the agent behind the script. 49 ledger claims re-fetched and quote-matched. Practitioner Workflows

long-running-agent-workflows — Hub for the long-running-agent cluster, and deliberately not a guide to running agents longer: it answers should this work be a long unattended run at all. Leads with the case against, because the evidence supports it — production teams keep agents to ≤10 steps before human intervention (68%), the horizon metric you’d plan with has ~2× error bars and is unreliable above 16h, decay inside the run is multi-causal, and the monitor degrades faster than the worker. Then five preconditions that must all hold before starting one (closeable loop, pinned invariants, bounded blast radius, a cap the agent can’t reason past, a progress signal separate from completion), a work-shape → run-shape table whose common error is treating decomposable work as exploratory work, and the observation that persistence/supervision/gating have moved into the harness so effort shifts to specifying the work. Carries Cognition’s opposing view that decomposition itself produces fragile systems — decompose and lose context, or run long and decay, is the real design tension. Synthesis; (est.) framing marked throughout. Time-sensitive

ai-system-design-workflow — The upstream-of-coding counterpart to agent-workflow-solo-practitioner: three phases before any code gets written (idea stress test → data model → architecture choice), each producing an artifact (spec.md, data-model.md, adr/0001-*.md) that feeds the next and later the coding loop. Organization & Adoption


decision-capacity-as-ai-constraint — The org-chart counterpart to the verification-load cluster: when generation gets cheap, throughput stops at who is allowed to say yes, how fast, and who owns the risk. Deliberately weak-form and falsifiable — decision capacity binds next, does not fall out of model scaling, and gives way only three ways (restructure the process, automate the checking, or let assurance quietly decay). Garicano’s queue as the formal backbone (span of control = 1/[exception rate × escalation cost], and the cost is paid by the receiver even when the answer is “I don’t know”). The BGSV finding sharpened to what it actually says — information technology decentralizes to whichever level it serves, communication technology centralizes — with its own caveats carried (~0.038 SD, conditional correlations, two of six headline results insignificant at 5%). Carries the counter that should temper it: Rajan & Wulf / Guadalupe et al. found the last flattening wave produced more decisions at the top (“functional centralization”). Bezos’s Type 1 / Type 2 doors quoted with his own survivorship-bias footnote. The best-evidenced decision-shape result is the 2025 JAMA RCT — two options beat one (62.1% vs 44.0%, OR 1.90) with no gain past two — and choice overload is explicitly not leaned on, because it failed meta-analysis. Ends with a throttle table separating a pathological decision structure from a correctly rate-limiting one. Time-sensitive
review-capacity-org-design — Corrects four other vault notes. Review capacity is not simply a throughput ceiling: the queue congests and gets bypassed at once. The 2x-mandate panel (802 developers, 196,212 PRs) shows what actually happens: human review coverage 89%→68%, substantive review 39%→21%, automated review overtaking human review, and the median reviewer’s silent approvals roughly doubling — “the added load fell on bare approval rather than substantive review,” while throughput doubled and merge/revert rates held flat. Review lead time still rose ~23% and the substantive-review queue never decongested — so what constrains throughput is weak, and what constrains assurance is tight. Careful scoping the note keeps: assurance inputs were measured falling; assurance outcomes were not measured in either direction. Then the lever that does not work: reviewer headcount predicts nothing across the largest samples (Thompson & Wagner’s null over 3,126 projects; Porter’s 2≈4; Google’s median reviewer count of 1), no reviewer-to-generator ratio exists, and the two figures that circulate are untraceable folklore. Traces the 200–400-line rule to a 2006 vendor study whose own footnote concedes the confound and whose data-derived breakpoint is ~200–250. Bacchelli & Bird’s 14% is the uncomfortable base: defect-finding is a minority of what review produces. Carries the strongest counter — the 2025–26 repository-mining literature is sign-unstable, and “the direction of these trends flips under different but equally defensible analysis choices.” Time-sensitive
ai-function-topology — Centralized / embedded / federated / platform, led by the finding that governs the rest: no controlled evidence exists that any AI topology outperforms another — no RCT, no quasi-experiment, no matched-pair design; the search returns consultancy prescription without exception. Transfers and stress-tests design-system-governance’s table. Data mesh as the base rate for how this debate ages (six years, a vendor category, organizational outcomes still unmeasured by its own peer-reviewed review). The one instrumented topology result is the model for honest evidence here, and it is a tradeoff rather than a failure: DORA 2024 measured internal developer platforms at +8% individual, +10% team and +6% organizational performance — gains that did aggregate — bought at −8% throughput and −14% change stability. DORA names reverse causality itself and reports the J-curve as an initial drop followed by big gains. Conway deflated to what it rests on — a 1968 essay with two anecdotes that HBR rejected for lack of proof, plus a five-pair test whose cross-sample basis is a sign test — and Colfer & Baldwin’s split that matters most: mirroring holds in firms (70%) and fails in open collaborative projects (56% unmirrored), the setting agent-mediated work most resembles. The one causal result (INSEAD cluster-RCT) says AI adoption rewires the network, so topology is an outcome, not only an input. Corporate mandates included as evidence of what was tried, not what worked — Meta centralized in June 2025 and cut 600 MSL roles by October; Klarna’s SEC-filed 38% AI-attributed headcount decline is mostly attrition on the CEO’s own arithmetic. Time-sensitive

Best Practices


long-run-cost-control — What one unattended session actually costs, and why the lever is cache behaviour rather than model choice: a long run re-reads its own history every turn, so input grows ~quadratically while output stays linear, and a cache read at 0.1× base makes hit rate close to a direct multiplier on the bill. Verified Anthropic list pricing as of 2026-08-03 (Fable 5 10/50, Opus 5 5/25, Sonnet 5 2/10 rising to 3/15 on 2026-09-01, Haiku 4.5 1/5) plus three facts that break naive arithmetic: 4.7+ models use a tokenizer producing ~30% more tokens for the same text (so cross-generation per-token comparison misleads), compaction costs an extra sampling step and invalidates downstream cache (it is a trade, not a saving), and a documented /usage example shows 6m20s of API time inside a 6h33m session — duration is a terrible cost proxy. Spend-cap ladder ending at gateway-level 429 — which itself fails open by default on a store timeout unless enforcement.fail_closed_on_error is set, so the hardest control needs one config line before it is a control at all. The recurring mechanism behind runaway spend is that the agent has no reliable access to its own cumulative cost or elapsed time; the widely-cited 63-hour/$4,200 illustration of it is a ~2023 OpenAI incident, not a 2026 Anthropic one, and its dollar figure collides coincidentally with a separate 2026 Cursor incident. Five-column forensic schema (authority/intent/context/action/artifact) across three layers (session transcript / OTel telemetry / artifact metadata), with the cross-layer join named as the unshipped piece. Regulatory floor corrected to mid-2026 state: EU AI Act Art 12/19/26 substance intact but high-risk dates omnibus-postponed to Dec 2027/Aug 2028; Colorado SB 24-205 repealed → SB 26-189 ADMT framework (3-year retention). Claude Code’s redact-by-default OTel gates as the reference design; the SLSA/in-toto pre-commit gap (no attestation captures the prompt); trailer attribution dismissed as social convention. Counterweights: trail-as-attack-surface, GDPR-vs-retention, capture ≠ replay. Time-sensitive
ai-supply-chain-risks — Package, model, MCP server, and build toolchain attack vectors with mitigations
fine-tuning-vs-rag — Decision framework for when to customize model weights vs augment context
canonical-evidence-vs-derived-index — The governance axis under retrieval, orthogonal to the RAG-engineering depth topic-suggestions skipped as commodity: a chunk/embedding/graph/cache/published-copy is a reproducible projection, never the system of record. Five functions only the canonical plane can perform (deletion that fans out to every derivative plus backup restore-exclusion, authorization-before-retrieval instead of retrieve-then-redact, conflict and valid-time held rather than overwritten, cache keys carrying the caller’s authorization context, rollback by shadow-built index generation); the four-status answer contract making abstention a return value (not_found / conflicting_evidence / insufficient_authority); layered scorecard + failure tree with four verified eval frameworks (RAGAS EACL 2024, ARES NAACL 2024, RAGChecker NeurIPS 2024, RAGTruth ACL 2024). Measured in-vault 2026-08-28 — snippets/ is the one committed derived plane; a date signal flagged 52 of 74 files but definitive checks (path resolution, verbatim-quote substring, body hash) found zero failures, and git history narrowed the real candidates to 9 of 15 sources. Regenerating those 9 found exactly one snippet genuinely wrong: it still served the centralized/federated/hybrid governance taxonomy its source note now records as retracted by its own author. The heuristic also erred the other way, silently passing six sources whose updated: field was stale against git — cleared on inspection, but on no basis it had. tools/snippet_drift.py verifies quotes and a source_hash (body digest, so a verified: bump doesn’t invalidate), the extract-snippets skill records it, and all 91 snippets across 21 sources now carry one, so the date heuristic no longer fires anywhere. Counterargument held: the controls are enterprise-scale, the plane distinction is not

ai/intent-engineering-discipline.title: Intent Engineering as a Discipline
ai/intent-engineering-discipline.content:
Intent Engineering as a Discipline
“Intent engineering” is an emerging (mid-2026) framing that positions a third discipline alongside prompt engineering (per-query syntax) and context engineering (which information enters the window, with what relevance / sufficiency / isolation / economy / provenance). Where those two address the information and surface layers, intent engineering addresses the strategic layer: what the user/org wants the system to produce, what counts as done, and what must never happen — encoded durably enough that any agent can be run against the same contract, whether local or remote, current model or next quarter’s.
This is the same operation as the one in clear-intent-as-anchor (state the target so the rest can be checked against it), at the artifact altitude: instead of a one-line intent: frontmatter on a note, it’s a repository-resident, machine-readable spec that the CI pipeline can validate.
Why the framing exists
Single-prompt engineering treats AI generation as a query problem: get the wording right, get the output you want. Context engineering treats it as an environment problem: the model is fine if you put the right facts and shape in front of it. Both are necessary; neither covers what happens when an autonomous agent runs for thirty minutes across forty tool calls and quietly drifts off the user’s actual goal.
The 2026 “vibe coding” phase made the gap visible — products shipped fast, but with no traceable answer to what was supposed to be built once the conversation that produced them scrolled off. The agentic IDEs (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, etc.) operate multi-step. Their failure mode is not “wrong token” but “right-looking code, wrong intent.” That’s the failure intent engineering is reaching for.
The discipline borrows its analogy from intent-based networking (Cisco / IETF, mid-2010s), where the operator declares a desired network state and the controller reconciles reality to match. Applied to coding agents: declare the desired user outcome and the strict constraints; let the agent execute against the declaration rather than a procedural prompt.
The three layers
A useful decomposition (synthesised from the emerging literature, not a settled standard):

























LayerWhat it isWhat goes wrong when missingIntentionRaw unstructured signal — a user friction, a complaint, a feature requestNothing to build fromStructureFormalised, falsifiable specification of what success means and what is prohibited”Right-looking” output that misses the actual askProjectionExecution into code, UI, API documentationThe visible artifact; only this layer is usually reviewed
Most teams jump Intention → Projection and skip Structure. Intent engineering is the explicit name for the missing middle layer.
Position relative to existing vault concepts

Upstream cognitive principle: clear-intent-as-anchor — the why; the four-axis test (form, completion-falsifiable, navigable, altitude) for whether any intent statement is doing real work. Intent engineering is that principle operationalised as a repository artifact rather than a one-line frontmatter.
Tactical primitive: implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — Gollwitzer’s if-then conditionals are the form most “what should the agent do under situation Y” rules in an intent spec take. Use that note’s trigger/response criteria when authoring those rules.
Architectural enforcement: functional-agent-architecture — once the intent spec exists, it’s enforced by typed effects, capability tokens, snapshot isolation, and property-based behavioural contracts. The spec says what counts as compliance; the architecture is how non-compliance is physically prevented.
Adjacent durable artifacts: architecture-decision-records-ai — ADRs and AgDRs (Agent Decision Records) capture the why of decisions; an intent spec captures the what must hold of an ongoing capability. They overlap but don’t substitute (an ADR explains the choice once; the intent spec is read every session).
Output containment: structured-output-json-mode — JSON-mode and grammar-constrained generation are the lowest-level enforcement of structural constraints stated in the spec.
Spec-first design loop: ai-system-design-workflow — the upstream activity that produces material for an intent spec; this is intent engineering at the codebase scale.

What an intent specification typically contains
Reconstructed from the cross-section of the emerging literature; treat as a starting shape, not a standard:

Objective and target components — what is being changed, named.
Belief grounding — where the agent’s worldview comes from (which docs, with what metadata filters), so it doesn’t form beliefs from parametric memory. The actual ground-truth side of bdi-architecture-for-coding-agents.
Desires — the goal intentions, possibly conflicting; the spec resolves the conflict up front (e.g., “non-blocking I/O and strict backwards compatibility — backwards compatibility wins on conflict”).
Implementation intentions — explicit if-then rules for foreseeable situational cues (see implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans for the trigger/response criteria).
Invariants — properties that must hold across the execution. Often split into hard (zero tolerance — e.g., no plaintext secrets) and soft (tolerated transient violation with a bounded recovery window).
Governance — allowed and prohibited tools / capabilities (cf. functional-agent-architecture capability tokens).
Recovery mechanisms — what happens on violation; typically tiered (lightweight critique → autonomy reduction → human escalation).
Success criteria — CI-enforceable verification commands (pytest, ruff, type checks, mutation thresholds — see ai-verification-stack-web).

Failure modes
Theatrical spec. The artifact exists, is structured, and anchors nothing — the same failure mode clear-intent-as-anchor flags at the one-line frontmatter scale, scaled up. A well-formatted YAML with vague success criteria (“system should be reliable”) is theatre. Apply the four-axis test to every load-bearing field.
Premature solution lock-in. clear-intent-as-anchor’s altitude axis warns against specifying the implementation (use library X, route through framework Y) before the right shape is known: it closes off option space. For early/exploratory work, prefer need-level statements; commit to solution-level only when the implementation is the actual subject of the work.
Spec drift without re-check. The original spec was right at write-time; the work has moved; the spec has not. No current tooling forces a re-check. Treat the spec like a long-lived ADR — visible review when the work substantively shifts.
Smuggled fabrication. The 2026 literature on intent engineering is dense with AI-synthesised compound terms (“Constraint-Checked RAG”, “Triples-to-Beliefs-to-Triples”, “Drift Bounds Theorem”) whose specifics do not consistently trace to citable work. The source material for this note is part of that literature. Verify named methods before encoding them in a spec or a vault note. The real underlying ideas — constraint-filtered retrieval, structured-output grammars, property-based behavioural contracts — are well-established in their non-renamed forms and already live in functional-agent-architecture and structured-output-json-mode.
Maturity caveat (as of 2026-05)
The term intent engineering is emerging. The underlying ideas — declarative specs, contract-first design, intent-based networking, behaviour-driven development — are not. What is genuinely new is the synthesis: the proposal that LLM-agent IDEs need a durable, repo-resident, CI-enforceable contract layer, distinct from per-session prompts, distinct from context selection, distinct from architectural decisions. Whether the discipline settles around this name or another (intent specs, agent contracts, system specs, spec-driven AI) is open. The operation — state the target so the rest can be checked against it — is the part to track, not the label.
Related

clear-intent-as-anchor — the cross-scale cognitive principle; intent engineering is its repository-artifact instantiation
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — Gollwitzer if-then rules as the form most situational responses in an intent spec take
functional-agent-architecture — typed effects, capability tokens, behavioural contracts; the enforcement layer
architecture-decision-records-ai — adjacent durable artifact; captures why decisions, not what must hold
bdi-architecture-for-coding-agents — the belief / desire / intention vocabulary used inside many intent specs
ai-system-design-workflow — the upstream design activity that produces material for an intent spec
ai-verification-stack-web — the CI side that validates the spec’s success criteria
structured-output-json-mode — grammar-constrained generation as the lowest-level enforcement primitive
multi-agent-governance — runtime governance layers that an intent spec ultimately drives

Sources

Bratman, M. (1987). Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason. Harvard University Press. (foundational philosophy of intention this discipline borrows from)
Rao, A. S. & Georgeff, M. P. (1995). “BDI agents: From theory to practice.” Proc. ICMAS-95. (the architectural lineage)
Cisco / IETF intent-based networking literature, ~2017+ — the analogy intent engineering draws on; e.g., RFC 7575 (Autonomic Networking), and Clemm et al. on intent-based networking surveys
Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). “Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans.” American Psychologist, 54(7). (already cited in implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans)
The specific term intent engineering as a named discipline distinct from prompt + context engineering is being used in 2026 industry writing (originating in agentic-IDE and enterprise-AI discourse). The term is recent; the operation it names is older.

Last reviewed: 2026-05-15. Time-sensitive — re-check whether the term has settled or been displaced.

ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop.title: The Intent-to-Retrospective Loop
ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop.content:
The Intent-to-Retrospective Loop
The development lifecycle this vault’s tooling serves runs from a stated intent through to a retrospective, and it is a loop, not a line: the retrospective feeds the next intent. Each stage has two distinct operations — produce the artifact (generative) and check the artifact (evaluative) — and when this loop was first mapped, the skill catalog was rich in checks and nearly empty of produces (gaps since closed — see Build order below). This note defines the loop, maps each stage to its skill (or names the gap), and specifies the data contract that lets the loop close. It is the conceptual anchor for the lifecycle-skill family, the way knowledge-base-entropy anchors the corpus-scan family.
The loop
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                                          │
        ▼                                                          │
   ① INTENT ──▶ ② PLAN ──▶ ③ TASKS ──▶ ④ IMPLEMENTATION            │
        │          │          │              │                     │
     [check]    [check]    [check]      ⑤ mechanical verification  │
        │          │          │              │                     │
        │          │          │         ⑥ intent-fulfilment check ─┤
        │          │          │              │                     │
        └──────────┴──────────┴──────▶  ⑦ RETROSPECTIVE ───────────┘
                                          (feeds calibration log)
The front half (① → ④) is production; the back half (⑤ → ⑦) is verification; ⑦ closes the loop by converting the cycle into lessons and scored predictions that inform the next ①.
The produce / check split
Every stage can be acted on two ways. The split is the whole point of this note, because it locates the thin side. (Design-time snapshot — the GAP cells were filled the same day; see Build order.)













































StageProduce (generative)Check (evaluative)① Intent— (elicited via clarify-first, not generated)intent-check ✓② Plannative — see ceremony trappartial (size only, ③)③ Plan size—plan-split-scan ✓④ Task / task sizenative → task-decompose (scoped) — see ceremony trapplan-split-scan ✓ + branch-resolve⑤ Mechanical verification—reviewers-map ✓ (knowledge: ai-verification-stack-web, evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests)⑥ Intent-fulfilment—GAP — nothing checks output-serves-intent⑦ RetrospectiveGAP — no lessons generatorpartial (calibration-loop scores, commitment-ledger lists)
The generative column is empty except for native behaviour. That is the thin side, stated precisely.
The two keystones
Stages ⑥ and ⑦ were the missing pieces (both since built — see Build order), and they are the ones that make the ①–⑦ spine a loop rather than a line.
⑥ Intent-fulfilment check (proposed /intent-fulfilment-check)
Nothing currently asks “does this output actually serve the intent we started from?” intent-check audits the intent’s quality at the start; reviewers-map audits the output’s correctness at the end; neither connects the two. The check: take the originating intent (the ① artifact — an intent: line, a project Goal, a spec objective), take the produced output, and assess whether the output advances that target. The check flags silent goal-substitution (the work drifted to an adjacent, easier, or more interesting target) and partial fulfilment (correct but addresses only part of the intent). Distinct from intent-check (intent quality, no output) and the corpus-level intent-drift-scan backlog candidate (body-vs-stated-intent drift across many notes; this is one cycle, output-vs-intent).
⑦ Retrospective (proposed /retrospective)
The one genuinely generative skill on the spine — it produces lessons, it doesn’t evaluate an artifact. Its mechanism is resulting separation (Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets, 2018): separate decision-quality from outcome-quality so the cycle’s “lessons” don’t encode luck as validated process. The dangerous quadrants it surfaces:

good outcome / bad process — luck mistaken for skill; must not be encoded as a repeatable lesson
bad outcome / good process — a sound process wrongly abandoned after one bad roll

This is also where the loop pays its biggest dividend: the retrospective is the natural place to harvest predictions into the calibration log, which directly attacks the dormant-calibration-loop problem (the loop’s single empirical feedback mechanism currently holds one prediction). See the data contract below.
The ceremony trap (stages ② and ④)
“Generate a plan” and “generate tasks” look like generative gaps, but Claude already does both natively. A skill there is ceremony unless it forces a discipline Claude skips. When planning, Claude reliably skips two things: it collapses to one plan without generating alternatives, and it loses the thread back to ①. So a stage-② skill is worth building only if it forces option-generation + intent-traceability — produce 2–3 candidate plans, each explicitly traced to the intent, then collapse to one with the reason recorded (the judge-panel pattern). Decided 2026-05-29: build the disciplined stage-② generator on exactly this bar (proposed /plan-options); stage ④ (task-generation) stays native — its size is already covered by plan-split-scan and a separate task-generator would not clear the same bar. This applies the anti-sprawl guard from the catalog: a generative skill must force a discipline the default skips.
Stage ④ reopened 2026-05-29. The same-day call above (“stage ④ stays native — a separate task-generator would not clear the same bar”) was over-general: it settled the bar by domain when the bar is actually case-dependent. Walking the loop on two concrete cases — provisioning Pi-hole, and building an ESP32 + display Claude Code status companion — split cleanly:

Pi-hole (routine, narrow): done-criteria write themselves (nslookup <ad-domain> → 0.0.0.0); the one non-obvious item (a secondary DNS resolver letting clients silently bypass Pi-hole) is a branch → branch-resolve. A task-generator here is ceremony. The original “native is adequate” call holds.
ESP32 companion (novel, integration-heavy): native decomposition reliably skips three disciplines — (1) a falsifiable done-criterion per task written at creation time (reviewers-map checks this only post-hoc on the output, too late to shape the task); (2) the cross-task interface contract (the Claude Code hook’s payload schema vs. the device’s parser — built on both sides independently, the mismatch surfaced at integration); (3) risk-ordering (the one task that can kill the project sits last in narrative order instead of first as a spike: does a Claude Code hook reach a LAN device at all?). None of these has a home in plan-split-scan (size), branch-resolve (branches), or reviewers-map (post-hoc).

So ④ does clear the ceremony bar — but as a trigger-bounded skill (task-decompose), not a blanket one: fire on integration-heavy or novel work where done-criteria are non-obvious and tasks share a contract; refuse on routine, well-trodden work where native decomposition is already adequate. The Pi-hole case is the refuse-floor; the ESP32 case is the pass-ceiling — both halves of the Phase-0 dogfood gate fall out of this single walk.
The data contract
The loop only closes if ⑦ writes to the artifacts that feed the next ①. The contract:

Reads: the cycle’s intent (① artifact), the plan/tasks, the mechanical-verification result (⑤), and the intent-fulfilment readout (⑥).
Produces:

Lessons — transferable claims phrased for reuse (not “this specific bug” but “this class of mistake”), each linked to where it would next apply.
Resulting verdict — decision-quality vs outcome-quality per notable call, flagging the two dangerous quadrants.
Calibration entries — any forward-looking claim the cycle made that is now resolvable, or any new bet worth tracking, formatted in the exact calibration-loop record schema (claim / resolves-by / criterion / confidence / domain / rationale / Resolution: PENDING).


Writes to: journal/calibration-log.md directly (auto-write, decided 2026-05-29) — the retro appends new PENDING prediction entries autonomously, no confirmation gate. The one safety property: it only appends new entries, never edits or resolves existing ones (the log is append-only by its own contract; resolution stays with calibration-loop resolve), and it echoes every appended entry in its output so the write is auditable. Optionally also appends to journal/commitments-log.md (overlap with commitment-ledger — the retro is the learning layer above the ledger’s accounting layer; they compose, the retro does not replace the ledger).

This contract is the load-bearing design decision: it is what turns “what we learned” from prose that evaporates into a scored prediction that compounds. Without the calibration write, ⑦ is just a nicer journal entry; with it, the loop has a memory.
Build order
All three built 2026-05-29 (SKILL.md + reference note under knowledge/ai/skills/ + decoupled /skill-trigger-audit dogfood each; all verdicts trigger-clean):

⑦ retrospective — the generative learning gap; revives the dormant calibration loop via the auto-write data contract. Built first; pinning its contract made ⑥ fall out.
⑥ intent-fulfilment-check — the loop-closer (output-vs-intent).
② plan-options — the disciplined plan-generator, built on the ceremony bar (option-generation + intent-traceability).
④ task-decompose (2026-05-29, reopening — see ceremony trap) — the disciplined task-generator, scoped by a refuse-on-routine trigger boundary; forces done-criterion + interface-contract + risk-ordering at generation time. Dogfooded on the Pi-hole (correct-refuse) and ESP32-companion (pass) cases; closes the last buildable produce-side cell.

The loop’s check stages were already in the catalog: ① intent-check, ③/④ plan-split-scan + branch-resolve, ⑤ reviewers-map. The loop is now fully instrumented end to end — produce side at ②④⑦, check side at ①③④⑤⑥. The only produce cells left empty (① intent-generation, ⑤ mechanical-verification) are empty by category: the human owns the intent, and verification is intrinsically a check.
Related

_index — the skill catalog; this note anchors the lifecycle-skill family within it
knowledge-base-entropy — sibling anchor note for the corpus-scan family; same backing-note-per-family pattern
verification-stack-operational-map — the decision tree across all skills; the loop is the temporal ordering this note adds to that map’s flat list
intent-engineering-discipline — ① as a repository-resident, CI-enforceable contract; the upstream framing for the intent stage
ai-verification-stack-web — the ⑤ mechanical-verification layer in depth
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — ⑤ detail: why passing tests is not fulfilment
task-decomposition-for-ai-plans — backing concept for ③/④ (plan-split-scan)
agent-workflow-solo-practitioner — the human-side operating model the loop runs inside
cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — why ⑦ must be a low-friction tool: a retrospective that depends on willpower lapses, exactly as the calibration loop did

ai/interpretability-as-verification-prim.title: Interpretability as a Verification Primitive
ai/interpretability-as-verification-prim.content:
Interpretability as a Verification Primitive

As of 2026-06-12. The empirical results below are dated 2025 (model-state claims scoped to the models studied); interpretability moves fast — re-verify before relying on a specific number.

Every scan, fingerprint, and oracle in this vault’s verification stack treats the model as a black box and judges the artifact it emitted — the code, the claim, the summary. oracle-problem-verification catalogs the oracles that verdict can rest on (test / spec / human / formal-LTL / cross-model), and all five read the output. This note holds the complementary axis: mechanistic interpretability, which reads the process — the internal computation that produced the output. It asks the one verification question no output-side check can reach: was the model’s stated reasoning faithful to what it actually computed, or is it a plausible story told after the fact?
The honest headline, stated up front so the rest reads against it: interpretability is today a case-study capability and a decorrelated signal — not a deployable verifier. It is the process-side row the oracle table is missing, and like every other row it has an independence failure. The value for a practitioner is mostly upstream of any workflow: a sharper mental model of why fluent reasoning text is not evidence of the reasoning, plus one hands-on path to see that directly.
The gap it addresses: the output-side baseline is genuinely weak
The case for looking at the process starts with a measured failure of the output. A model’s chain-of-thought (CoT) reads like its reasoning, and the temptation is to verify by reading it. But CoT is frequently unfaithful — it does not reliably reflect the computation that produced the answer:

When a hint was inserted that changed the model’s answer, the models acknowledged using that hint in only ~25–39% of cases — the rest gave confident reasoning that omitted the thing that actually moved them (Anthropic, Reasoning models don’t always say what they think, 2025).
Trained on environments containing a reward hack, models exploited the hack in over 99% of runs but verbalized it in under 2% — the CoT actively concealed the real driver (same study).

Faithfulness here is not introspected — it is measured behaviorally, by intervening: change something the CoT claims (or doesn’t claim) to depend on and see whether the answer moves the way the stated reasoning implies. Faithfulness is task- and size-conditional — it varies by setup, not a fixed property.

Framing guard (refuted claims — do not assert): an earlier, intuitive version of this argument was refuted in the adversarial pass (1-2): “larger models produce less faithful CoT, so output scans get strictly worse as models scale”. Do not make the monotonic-degradation claim; the evidence is that faithfulness is conditional, not that it falls with capability. Likewise, do not frame interpretability as redundant with output scans (also refuted) — the relationship is complementary, not substitutive.

This is the gap: if the reasoning text can diverge this far from the actual computation, a class of verification questions is structurally invisible to anything that only reads the output.
What interpretability can reliably show (and what’s still aspirational)
Mechanistic interpretability earns its place by answering process questions output scans cannot — via circuits, sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, attribution graphs, linear probes. What’s demonstrated (primary-source, mostly Anthropic, 2025), kept separate from what’s aspirational:
Demonstrated (case-study strength, scoped to the models studied):

Faithful vs. post-hoc separation. Attribution graphs can distinguish genuine multi-step computation from confabulation and from working-backwards-from-a-target — the literal faithfulness-vs-plausibility question (Anthropic, Tracing the thoughts of a language model / Biology of an LLM, 2025).
Hidden-goal detection. In a blind audit, interpretability located goal-pursuing mechanisms in a model trained to conceal its objective and which refused to reveal it verbally; SAE features surfaced the causally-responsible reward-bias mechanism where plain semantic search failed (Anthropic, Auditing language models for hidden objectives, 2025). (Two of three verifiers confirmed; one dissent — treat as a strong case study, not a settled law.)
Hallucination has a feature-level mechanism. Default behavior is refuse; a “known-entity” feature inhibits the refusal; when it misfires on an unknown entity, the model hallucinates. Anthropic causally induced a hallucination by activating that feature (Tracing the thoughts, 2025). Scoped to Claude 3.5 Haiku.

Aspirational / not there yet:

Proving the absence of a deceptive circuit. You cannot. Interpretability can find a mechanism if it looks; it cannot certify none exists (Nanda, Interpretability will not reliably find deceptive AI, 2025).
Complete accounts of computation. Current tooling captures only a fraction of what the model does: it relies on an imperfect transcoder/cross-layer approximation, attention is largely invisible to the attribution graph, the graphs need manual distillation to read, and they carry tooling artifacts (Anthropic, Attribution graphs: methods/biology, 2025).

Where it sits in the oracle table: a sixth row, process-side
oracle-problem-verification frames every verification gate as silently picking an oracle and inheriting that oracle’s blind spot. Interpretability is the row that table doesn’t have — the only one whose correctness signal comes from inside the computation rather than from the output:




















OracleCorrectness =Independence failure (what it can’t catch)(the five output-side rows)output matches test / spec / human / LTL trace / another modelshared-source, attention, partiality, correlation — see oracle-problem-verificationInterpretability (process-side)internal activations show the computation matches the stated reasoning / lacks the suspect mechanismPartiality + non-absence. Captures only a fraction of the computation and cannot prove a mechanism is absent; needs intervention to confirm, not just observe. Independent of authorship — but incomplete.
The payoff of adding the row is decorrelation, not coverage. Its failure mode (partial visibility) does not correlate with the output rows’ failure modes (shared source, vigilance, correlated judges). That is exactly the move the oracle note prescribes: “add a second oracle whose failure is uncorrelated with the first”. Interpretability is a domain-independent process signal the way a metamorphic relation is a domain-independent output signal.
The honest counterweight: process-side does not cleanly beat output scans
The decorrelation is real but the magnitude is modest, and this is the claim most worth keeping skeptical:

Deception probes give a weak, inconsistent boost. On a 2025 benchmark, a linear deception probe beat a black-box baseline on some dataset splits but lost to it on others — i.e. the process-side signal was sometimes worse than reading the output (arXiv:2507.12691, mid-2025; single benchmark — don’t over-generalize; the per-split figures are in the paper’s results table, not re-quoted here to avoid unverified precision).
The SAE-audit advantage was partly confounded — some of interpretability’s edge in the hidden-objective audit came from factors other than the features themselves (Anthropic, Auditing hidden objectives, 2025).
Probes can’t localize which specific claim in an output is false — they flag a global “something’s off,” not the bug’s location (2-1 confirmed; one dissent).

So the verdict is “decorrelated signal, not redundant” — measurably independent of output scans, but not a strict upgrade and not a standalone gate.
Hands-on path: tracing an attribution graph yourself
This is the part that moved from read-only to actually-doable, and the specifics are verified first-hand against the primary sources (2026-06-12):

Tooling: Anthropic open-sourced a circuit-tracing library on 2025-05-29 (anthropic.com/research/open-source-circuit-tracing). The library is safety-research/circuit-tracer on GitHub; Neuronpedia hosts an interactive frontend to visualize, annotate, and share the attribution graphs.
Supported models (per the repo README): Gemma-2-2b, Llama-3.2-1b, Qwen-3 (0.6B–14B), Gemma-3 (270M–27B), Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, GPT-OSS 20B — i.e. small open-weights models, several overlapping the local LM Studio set (local-llm-deployment-patterns, and the LM-Studio note in auto-memory).
Hardware reality: Gemma-2-2b runs with ~15 GB of GPU RAM (the free Colab T4 tier is enough per the README). CPU offloading is supported but non-optimal, and no CPU-only path is stated. Intervention (not just observation) is available on Neuronpedia for Gemma-2-2b with zero install.
What it produces: an attribution graph — the direct effect each active transcoder feature, error node, and input token has on every other active feature and on the output logits — the same object the Biology of an LLM case studies are built from.

Honest local-feasibility note: “trace one attribution graph locally” is genuinely doable if there is a ~15 GB-VRAM GPU on hand; otherwise the free-Colab or zero-install-Neuronpedia route is the path. LM Studio itself is inference-only and is not the vehicle for this — don’t conflate “I run Gemma locally for chat” with “I can trace its circuits locally.”
Honest payoff for a solo web developer
Where the line actually falls — this is not a tool you wire into a verification pipeline today:

Don’t: build a workflow around it, treat a clean attribution graph as a merge gate, or expect a deployable hallucination-detector. The tooling is research-grade, partial, model-scoped, and needs manual reading.
Do take three durable things:

The mental model — “fluent reasoning text is not evidence of the reasoning” — which directly sharpens how you read CoT and AI explanations in your existing output-side verification (evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests, skill-reviewers-map / /reviewers-map). This is the highest-value takeaway and costs nothing.
One concrete rep — trace a single attribution graph on Gemma-2-2b (Colab or Neuronpedia, ~an afternoon) to see confabulation and the known-entity/hallucination mechanism with your own eyes rather than reading about them. Intuition, not infrastructure.
A named row in the oracle table — when a verification verdict feels under-supported, you now know there is a process-side, decorrelated signal, what it can show, and what it provably can’t.



In the vault’s own register: this sits in the same intellectual-interest-with-a-hands-on-toehold tier as oracle-problem-verification — load-bearing for how you think about verification, not yet load-bearing in a shipping pipeline. That’s the line.

ai/mutation-testing-ai-generated-code.title: Mutation Testing for AI-Generated Code
ai/mutation-testing-ai-generated-code.content:
Mutation Testing for AI-Generated Code
The logic-side companion to visual-verification-ai-ui under Layer 3 of ai-verification-stack-web. Visual regression proves an AI’s UI change didn’t break what you see; mutation testing proves its tests would actually catch a bug. Both attack the same lie — a green pipeline that verifies nothing.
What it is
Mutation testing measures whether a test suite can detect bugs, not whether it merely executes code. A mutation tool makes thousands of tiny, deliberately-broken copies of the source — each one a mutant with a single seeded fault (+ becomes -, > becomes >=, a statement deleted). It then runs the test suite against each mutant. If a test fails, the mutant is killed: the suite caught the injected bug. If every test still passes, the mutant survived: the suite is blind to that fault.
The headline number is the mutation score — killed mutants ÷ total non-equivalent mutants (equivalent mutants are explained below). Unlike line coverage, which only asks “did a test touch this line?”, mutation score asks “would a test notice if this line were wrong?” That gap is the entire point.
Why it matters for AI code
Coverage is the metric an AI agent most readily optimizes when told to “write tests,” and it is exactly the wrong one. A suite can hit 100% line coverage with a 4% mutation score — Wang et al.’s mutation-guided test-generation study found precisely such suites (arXiv 2506.02954, IEEE TSE 2025). The tests run every line and assert almost nothing about the results. They exist to satisfy the CI contract, not to catch bugs. (The strong “coverage-gaming agent” generalization below is an inference from this one study plus the vault’s own model of agent incentives, not a separately-measured finding.)
This is the agent-specific failure mode in its purest form: an LLM asked to raise coverage will write tests that invoke functions without asserting their behavior — calling the code, catching no wrong answer. The test diff looks productive; the safety net has holes the size of the function. It is the test-suite analogue of the “hollow test” tampering signal, except here no one weakened the tests — they were born weak.
Mutation testing is one of the few cheap, mechanical gates that catches this failure mode directly. It turns “the AI wrote tests” into “the AI wrote tests that would fail if the code were wrong” — a falsifiable claim. That is why it sits in evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests’s Tier 1 mechanical gates (the seconds-to-minutes, non-negotiable layer), not as an optional nicety.
Mutation operators
A mutation operator is a rule for introducing one fault. The standard families, as implemented by Stryker for JS/TS and verified against Stryker’s operator documentation:





































OperatorExampleArithmetic operator replacementa + b → a - bRelational / comparison replacementa > b → a >= bLogical operator replacementa && b → a || bConditional / boundary mutationif (x) → if (true) / if (false)Statement removal (block)delete a statement or returnArray / method-call mutationswap or empty array methodsString / literal mutationreplace string and numeric literals
The off-by-one and boundary operators (> ↔ >=) tend to matter most for AI code, because boundary errors are a common AI failure mode (unverified as a ranked claim — asserted from practice, not a measured study) and are exactly what a “calls the function, asserts the happy path” test misses.
The equivalent-mutant problem
Not every surviving mutant means a missing test. A mutant can be semantically equivalent to the original — a change to syntax that never changes observable behavior, so no test could ever kill it (e.g. mutating a loop bound that a prior guard already makes unreachable). These inflate the denominator and depress the score for no real gap.
Detecting equivalence is undecidable in general (it reduces to program equivalence), so it cannot be fully automated — every mutation tool ships with a residue of equivalent mutants that a human must triage or ignore. The equivalent-mutant problem is a limitation recognized since the technique’s origins (DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward, “Hints on Test Data Selection,” 1978; the problem is surveyed at length in Jia & Harman, “An Analysis and Survey of the Development of Mutation Testing,” IEEE TSE 2011).
Practical consequence: don’t chase 100%. A score plateauing in the 70s–80s with the survivors all looking equivalent on inspection is a healthy suite, not a failing one. Treat the threshold as a floor that flags negligent gaps, not a target that demands perfection — the same reasoning behind the tiered floors below.
Score thresholds by code tier
A flat target wastes effort on glue code and under-protects business logic. This vault’s verification stack recommends tiered floors for AI-authored web code (from ai-verification-stack-web Layer 3, mirrored in evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests’s escalation triggers):

70% — business logic. Domain rules, pricing, permissions, state transitions. Where a surviving mutant is a latent bug with consequences.
50% — UI components. Rendering and interaction; some behavior is better caught by visual regression than by unit mutants.
30% — utility / glue. Adapters, formatters, wiring. High mutation coverage here is mostly equivalent-mutant noise.

A file scoring below its tier’s floor is an escalation trigger in the decision rubric — route it to human review regardless of green CI, because the tests demonstrably don’t defend it.
Stryker for JS/TS — workflow
Stryker Mutator is the de-facto mutation-testing framework for JavaScript and TypeScript. It runs against the common test runners (Jest, Vitest, Mocha, Jasmine, Karma — verified from Stryker’s runner support).
Three features make it viable as a CI gate rather than an overnight batch job:

Per-mutant test selection. Coverage analysis means Stryker runs only the tests relevant to each mutant, not the whole suite — the difference between minutes and hours.
Hit-limit counters. A mutant that turns a loop condition into an infinite loop is bounded by a hit limit instead of hanging the run.
Incremental mode. --incremental stores prior results (in a JSON report file) and re-mutates only changed code, emitting a full report regardless. Combined with parallelism, incremental mode puts mutation testing (per Stryker’s docs) on every PR in roughly 1–5 minutes for most codebases — the property that lets it live in Tier 1. That figure assumes the favorable case: a large repo or a slow base test suite can blow past a per-PR budget (each mutant re-runs real tests), so confirm the run cost on your own suite before treating Tier-1 placement as free.

Config trade-offs for AI-authored suites

Gate incrementally, baseline fully. Run a full mutation pass to establish per-tier baselines, then enforce only the changed-file score on each PR. This catches the agent that adds a feature plus a hollow test in the same diff, without paying full-suite cost every time.
Threshold as break, not just report. Stryker’s threshold config can warn or fail the build. For the AI-code use case the floor must break the build below tier — a reported-but-ignored score trains everyone to ignore it, the same anti-pattern as a suppressed fitness function.
Scope mutants to logic, exclude generated code. Point mutation at domain modules; excluding generated clients, migrations, and vendored code keeps the score meaningful and the run fast.
Read survivors, don’t just read the number. The score is the trigger; the survivor list is the signal. Each surviving non-equivalent mutant names a specific behavior no test asserts — that list is the precise review target, far cheaper than re-reading the whole AI diff.

The agentic turn
Mutation testing was historically too slow and too language-specific to be routine — the reason it stayed a research-and-finance-grade tool. Two 2026 shifts move it into the AI-verification mainstream:

It is the natural answer to AI’s coverage-gaming. As hollow AI test suites become common, the metric that exposes them stops being optional.
Tooling is being built for agents to run. Trail of Bits’ “Mutation testing for the agentic era” (April 2026) ships mewt (a language-agnostic core spanning Solidity, Rust, Go, and more) and MuTON (TON languages), plus a configuration-optimization skill meant for an agent to drive — framing mutation-campaign setup and survivor analysis as something the agent does as part of its own loop rather than a manual slog. Their worked case: a high-severity Arkis protocol fund-draining bug that line coverage missed and mutation testing caught (attributed; not independently verified here).

The direction of travel: mutation score becomes a standard line in the AI-code CI report, and “raise the mutation score on the changed files” becomes a verifiable instruction you can hand the agent — closing the loop the agent’s own coverage-optimization opened.
