ai/skills/skill-ai-diff-judgment.title: Skill: ai-diff-judgment
ai/skills/skill-ai-diff-judgment.content:
Skill: ai-diff-judgment
Decide whether to merge an AI-authored git diff after green CI — the human-judgment layer machines can’t run. The organizing spine is intent: recover what the change was supposed to do (ticket → PR description + agent reasoning log → commits → diff self-evidence), decompose it into checkable clauses, and verify the implementation clause-by-clause. Around that spine it reads the test diff before the code diff (the highest-signal AI-specific check), hunts failure modes a passing suite can’t see (spec drift, goal substitution, test tampering, hollow coverage-theater tests, error-handling theater, deleted invariants), and rations depth by a trust-signal prior. Output is altitude-ordered — intent verdict before any Conventional-Comments line finding — ending in a six-way net-improvement decision (Ship → Reject) with hard escalation triggers.
When to use

An agent / Claude / Copilot / Cursor wrote the change, CI is green, and you must decide: merge, return to the agent, or escalate
“Did the agent actually implement the spec?” / “Can I trust this AI PR?”
Signing off agent output where the risk is plausible-but-wrong, not broken

Skip when:

Provenance-irrelevant correctness review → lean-review (cheap) or built-in /code-review (broad)
Verifying an AI text artifact’s claims → reviewers-map
Bias fingerprints in an AI artifact → bias-scan-ai
You need to run the change to confirm behavior → built-in /verify
CI is not green — the skill stops by design; fix the machine layer first

Why it exists
Counters automation-bias merging: AI code that passes every gate can still be internally consistent yet implement the wrong spec — tests check the inferred spec, not the actual one (evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests). General review skills hunt correctness; nothing else makes intent fidelity the spine. It also carries an honest self-limit: an AI reviewer sharing a model family with the author has correlated blind spots, so it escalates readily and never claims to replace human architectural sign-off.
First live run (2026-06-05)
/ai-diff-judgment on the tikkuukko diff — 15 LOC / 3 files of uncommitted working-tree changes (boil-runtime.ts, boil.tsx, level1-cave.tsx). How each step played out:

Intent recovery fell to the lowest-priority source (diff self-evidence — no ticket/PR/commit message) and was presented back as an explicit assumption, exactly the fallback path the build-time dry-run forced into the skill. Three clauses recovered: animation-cycle bug fix (seed % 3 could never index a length-4 pose cycle), magic-number naming, redundant-condition cleanup.
Trust triage → low prior (small diff, existing patterns, 2 of 3 clauses behavior-preserving), so steps 9–10 ran as spot-check only. Total cost: ~4 tool calls — the depth-rationing did its job.
Verdict: Ship; clause table all-implemented; one non-blocking issue: (visible behavior change, project has no test suite → recommend /verify), one suggestion: (a useBoilFrame() hook instead of subscription-only useBoilSeed() + direct singleton read), one praise: (why-comment on SPIKE_HIT_H).

Calibration lessons:

The grep-to-confirm discipline prevented a false positive. First instinct was to flag the direct Boil.frame read as the step-9 “React data-flow escape”; reading useBoilSeed’s implementation showed force-update reads of the singleton are the module’s established idiom — finding correctly demoted from issue: to suggestion:. Pattern-match alone would have shipped the false positive.
The “assume CI green” premise is weak on hobby projects with no test infra — the skill noted it inline rather than pretending the machine layer existed. Watch whether this needs a first-class “no machine layer” branch if it recurs.

Provenance
Built 2026-06-05 by a multi-agent workflow (3 forced-angle designs → judge synthesis → adversarial verify incl. dry-run on a live diff; 14 findings applied, 2 blocking). Backing notes: evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests (trust signals, failure modes, escalation triggers) and effective-code-review (altitude order, Conventional Comments, net-improvement standard). Skill at .claude/skills/ai-diff-judgment/SKILL.md.
Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/ai-diff-judgment/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: ai-diff-judgment
description: Decide whether to merge an AI-AUTHORED git diff after green CI — the human-judgment layer machines can't run. Use when an agent / Claude / Copilot / Cursor wrote the change and you must sign off — can I trust this AI PR, is this AI change safe to merge, vet agent-written code, review machine-written changes, post-CI judgment on AI changes. Recovers intent, decomposes it into checkable clauses, verifies clause-by-clause, reads the TEST diff before the code diff, and hunts the failure modes a passing suite cannot see (spec drift, goal substitution, test tampering, hollow tests); rations depth by a trust-signal prior. Assumes CI passed; if not green it stops. Distinct from `/lean-review` (token-frugal correctness pass on ANY diff, not AI-provenance/intent verification), built-in `/code-review` (maximum-coverage correctness, provenance-agnostic), `/reviewers-map` (claim map of an AI text output, not code findings), and `/bias-scan-ai` (bias fingerprints, not spec fidelity). Counters automation-bias merging.
---
 
Review the AI-authored diff identified by `$ARGUMENTS` as the human-judgment layer that runs **after** green CI. The organizing spine is **intent**: recover what the change was supposed to do, break it into checkable clauses, and verify the implementation clause-by-clause — because spec drift and goal substitution (did the agent implement the ACTUAL spec, or one it inferred?) are the central AI-specific judgments a passing test suite cannot make. Around that spine, run the full AI-failure-mode checklist, rationing depth by a trust-signal prior.
 
Motivate every check from the failure-mode mechanics below, never from a vendor/lab statistic. Backing rationale: `knowledge/ai/evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests.md` and `knowledge/tech/effective-code-review.md`. Consult if you need the why; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope — what this is NOT
 
- **Assume CI/lint/type-check/SAST/coverage already passed.** This is the post-green layer. If CI is not green, say so and stop.
- Do **not** re-do general correctness/style/formatting or anything a linter/formatter/type-checker/SAST/coverage gate catches — defer to `/lean-review` and the built-in `/code-review`. Spend tokens only where automation is weak: logic edge cases, concurrency, intent drift, coupling, hollow tests.
- Never run CI, tests, mutation testing, or the app — reason over the diff, do not execute it. To run the feature, recommend `/verify` as a follow-up.
- Route siblings: a new dependency is flagged inline (step 9) — do not perform supply-chain depth; security threat-modeling depth (flag the surface, escalate, don't perform it) → `/security-review`; bias-fingerprint scanning → `/bias-scan-ai`; claim-verification mapping of an AI text output → `/reviewers-map`. It does not replace human Tier 4/5 architectural review — it escalates instead.
 
## Resolve the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` selects the diff:
- empty → working-tree + staged changes against `HEAD` (or the largest staged diff in `git status`)
- a ref / branch / `PR#` → that base vs the current branch
 
## Investigation order — load-bearing, do not reorder
 
**1. Scope gate.** Take AI-authorship as given from the invocation context; if no agent reasoning log or AI provenance signal is present anywhere, note that provenance is unverified and proceed. CI is assumed green. Route general/correctness/security/run-the-app requests to the named siblings. Skip anything a gate already catches.
 
**2. Size guard FIRST, before reading code.** Run `git diff --stat`. If >~400 changed LOC or >10 files, emit a decomposition finding naming the applicable split strategy (stacked / file-based / horizontal / vertical / refactoring-separation) and state that one pass cannot honestly cover it. The ~400-LOC line is an operational convention, **not** an empirical law. It is deliberately distinct from the >200-LOC escalation trigger (step 10): ~400 LOC = "one pass cannot cover, split"; >200 LOC = escalate. A 200–400 LOC diff therefore escalates without a decomposition flag. Proceed on the reviewable slice.
 
**3. Recover intent**, in fixed order: linked issue/ticket/spec → PR description AND agent reasoning log → commit messages → (lowest priority, e.g. an uncommitted working-tree diff, the step-target default) infer intent from diff self-evidence (code comments, symbol names, structural change) and **present it back as an explicit assumption for confirmation**, flagging that no intent artifact existed. Reserve the hard **STOP and ask the user** for diffs where even self-evidence is ambiguous. A missing or vague PR description is itself a finding. Mine the reasoning log for hedges and every "I chose X because Y" — those are where to focus review. If the PR description carries an explicit review-focus or provenance section (the `/pr-contract` shape), take the declared focus areas as priority review inputs and feed the provenance statement into the trust-signal triage (step 5) — declared sections don't *replace* your own hunt, they seed it.
 
**4. Decompose intent** into checkable spec clauses. This clause list is the spine of the review. For refactor/cleanup diffs with no feature spec, collapse the clause table to a single "behavior-preserving?" row per logical change and state explicitly that intent was inferred.
 
**5. Trust-signal triage** — set the skepticism prior AND the read depth.
   - *Positive* (lower prior): small focused diff (<50 LOC / <3 files), reuses existing patterns, no new abstractions, tests assert on behavior, non-critical surface, agent flagged its own uncertainty, clear spec→diff mapping.
   - *Negative* (raise prior): scope creep, fresh abstractions, defensive code without reason, **test edits without a behavior change** (single strongest tampering signal), parallel implementations, over-confident "complete" reasoning, layer violations, new dependency.
   - Low-risk prior → lean clause-trace + test-diff pass only, and **skip steps 9–10** except for a one-line confirmation that no escalation trigger is present. High-risk prior (any negative signal, or non-trivial logic) → add the full deep-hunt in steps 7–10.
 
**6. Read the TEST diff before the code diff** — highest-signal AI-specific check.
   - (a) Flag any assertion weakened or deleted without a matching behavior change.
   - (b) Flag tests AND implementation edited in the same pass with no new behavior — strongest test-tampering / fake-convergence signal: **stop and investigate** before continuing.
   - (c) Hollow / coverage-theater check: do tests assert on observable outputs, or merely on internal calls / trivially-true conditions? Would they catch a planted bug? This is mutation-resistance *reasoning*, not running coverage. If you cite mutation-score conventions (e.g. 70% business logic / 50% UI / 30% utilities, or "~4% mutation score at 100% line coverage"), present them as hedged heuristics / motivation, **never** as validated standards.
   - (d) No test delta? If the diff changes behavior but touches no tests, emit a (non-blocking) issue noting the untested behavior change and recommend `/verify`. If the diff is pure refactor (behavior-preserving), absent test changes is expected — not a finding.
 
**7. Read the code diff against the clauses.** Every changed line must trace to a clause. Detect **spec drift** (actual vs inferred spec; any file the spec never mentioned = stop-and-ask) and **goal substitution** (internally consistent — types align, tests pass, lint clean — yet not what was asked). Mark each clause: implemented / drifted / unaddressed / substituted.
 
**8. Hunt where tests can't see** (run fully on high-risk prior; spot-check on low-risk):
   - error-handling theater — try/catch returning null or a stringified error, fallback values for impossible states, null checks the type system already guarantees;
   - deleted invariants — assertions/validation/type constraints removed with no comment justifying why the invariant was wrong;
   - unencoded invariants — race conditions / read-then-write without a lock, concurrency, idempotency on mutating endpoints.
 
**9. Architectural-risk checklist** (non-trivial changes): premature abstraction (classes/factories/generics/hooks before duplication justifies them); invented parallel types (grep to confirm no second `User`/`Order` beside an existing one); duplication drift (copy-and-adapt instead of refactoring to a shared abstraction); wrong-layer logic (fetch in components, validation in route handlers, formatting in domain models); implicit coupling (module A reads a store module B writes, neither declaring it) — **including a component reading mutable module-global state outside the subscribed/returned value (React/signal data-flow escape)**; silently added new dependency.
 
**10. Escalation triggers.** ANY ONE forces an *Escalate to human architect* verdict regardless of other findings: module-boundary / shared-interface crossing; new runtime dependency; auth / permissions / persistence / payments / PII touched; new abstraction introduced; >200 LOC or 10 files (operational threshold, not law); public API surface change; agent reasoning expressed uncertainty; suppressed fitness-function / arch-rule warning; test+impl edited together without new behavior.
 
**11. Emit altitude-ordered output** (format below). The intent verdict precedes every line finding. **Priority-inversion guard:** if the verdict is Reject or Return-to-agent, suppress `nitpick:` lines entirely. On a clean Ship with no blocking/should-fix findings, emit at most 1–2 non-issue lines; do not manufacture `question:`/`thought:` lines to demonstrate effort.
 
**12. Terminal decision** in net-improvement semantics ("does this improve code health", not "is it perfect"). "LGTM" is not a decision. Return-to-agent MUST cite the specific failing gate/signal — vague feedback produces vague fixes.
 
## Output format
 
Report findings; do not edit files. Single fenced block, altitude order top to bottom:
 
```text
[SIZE GUARD: <N> LOC / <M> files exceeds ~400 LOC / 10-file convention — split via <strategy>; one pass cannot honestly cover this.]   ← only if triggered
 
## Intent verdict
Intent source: <ticket / PR / commit / inferred-from-diff / asked-user>
| Clause | Status |
| --- | --- |
| <clause 1> | implemented / drifted / unaddressed / substituted |
Spec drift / goal substitution: <explicit line, or "none observed">
Judgment: <one line — does the diff implement the ACTUAL spec?>
 
## Findings
issue: (blocking) path:line `offending fragment` — <finding in one clause from the taxonomy: spec drift / goal substitution / hollow test / test tampering / swallowed error / deleted invariant / race / invented parallel type / wrong-layer logic / premature abstraction> — fix: <concrete fix>
suggestion: (non-blocking) path:line — <…>
question: path:line — <…>
nitpick: (non-blocking) path:line — <…>   ← omit entirely if Decision is Reject/Return
thought: path:line — <…>
praise: path:line — <…>   ← ≥1 when warranted
 
## Escalation triggers hit
- <any fired trigger, or "none">
 
## Decision
<Ship | Ship with monitoring | Ship behind a flag | Return to agent with specific feedback | Escalate to human architect | Reject>   (Return-to-agent cites the specific failing gate/signal)
 
## Caveat
<one line: same-model-family correlated blind spots; catches surface issues, does not replace human Tier 4/5 review.>
```
 
- `issue:` is blocking and MUST carry a concrete fix. Ground `issue:`/`suggestion:` lines with a ≤1-line verbatim fragment of the offending code — a line number is a coordinate counted against external state and drifts; the fragment keeps the finding locatable (rationale: `knowledge/ai/llm-grounding-via-deterministic-positioning.md`). Beyond that fragment, do not paste code back — the reader has the diff.
- Critique the code, not the author; prefer "we" over "you"; include ≥1 sincere `praise:` when warranted.
- Zero findings with a clean intent verdict is a valid result — no quota padding.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Reviewing a never-green diff as if it passed.** The skill trusts the machine layer for correctness/lint/types. If CI is not actually green, stop — do not simulate it.
- **Line findings before the intent verdict.** Altitude inversion teaches the reader to skim nits and miss spec drift. Verdict first, always.
- **Asserting caveated statistics as fact.** Mutation-score figures, the ~400-LOC guard, the >200-LOC/10-file threshold, and any vendor multiplier (CodeRabbit, Veracode, SmartBear, "AI dev 19% slower", "41–42% of code") are operational heuristics / calibrated folklore — hedge and attribute, never state as law. Motivate from the failure mechanism, not the number.
- **Vague return-to-agent feedback.** "Tighten this up" produces a vaguer diff. Cite the failing gate/signal.
- **Trusting an AI critic as independent.** If this reviewer shares a model family with the author, it has correlated blind spots — escalate readily, do not treat the pass as a Tier 4/5 sign-off.
- **Padding to a quota.** No finding count target — clean is clean (operationalized in step 11).
 
## Scope — when not to use this
 
- A token-frugal correctness pass on ANY diff (provenance-irrelevant) → `/lean-review`.
- Maximum-coverage / uncertain-but-possible correctness on any diff → built-in `/code-review`.
- A claim-verification map of an AI *text* output (what to check, not what's wrong in code) → `/reviewers-map`.
- Bias fingerprints in an AI artifact (epistemic shape, not functional correctness) → `/bias-scan-ai`.
- Running the feature to confirm behavior → `/verify`.
 
## Known tradeoffs (keep honest)
 
- Falls back to diff-self-evidence intent on artifact-less diffs (presented as an assumption); hard-stops only when even self-evidence is ambiguous.
- Correctness-floor bugs are deliberately deferred to `/lean-review` and `/code-review`.
- Trusts the green checkmark for the machine layer while distrusting it for intent — a never-actually-passed diff would be reviewed as if it had.
- Test-diff-first weighting under-scrutinizes a clean-tests-but-subtly-wrong implementation that lacks a tampering signature.
- Degrades when the agent's reasoning log is terse or misleading.
- The self-eval caveat caps the ceiling and makes it escalate readily.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests.md` — trust signals, failure modes, escalation triggers, decision outputs
- `knowledge/tech/effective-code-review.md` — altitude order, Conventional Comments, human/machine split, net-improvement decision
- `knowledge/ai/ai-assisted-code-review.md` — team-pipeline view: where this judgment layer sits relative to an AI reviewer bot; the PR-contract input this skill consumes
- `/pr-contract` — author-side producer of the intent/proof/provenance/review-focus artifact step 3 reads
- `knowledge/ai/llm-grounding-via-deterministic-positioning.md` — why findings carry a verbatim fragment, not a bare line number
- `/lean-review` · built-in `/code-review` · `/reviewers-map` · `/bias-scan-ai` — the four near-neighbors disambiguated above
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — run on this description before publishing to confirm it fires here and not on the siblings
- `.claude/workflows/axis-review.js` — when you want the Spec lens (this skill) and the Standards lens (`/code-review` / `/lean-review`) run in **isolated parallel contexts** with no-merge aggregation, rather than blended in one pass here; this skill is the single-context Spec-spine review, that workflow is the two-axis split

ai/skills/skill-api-surface-scan.title: Skill: api-surface-scan
ai/skills/skill-api-surface-scan.content:
Skill: api-surface-scan
Audit a codebase’s exported surface against actual consumption via the unexport test (make it private: who breaks?): dead exports (nobody imports), test-only exports (the declared interface isn’t the test surface — cross-referenced to /test-shape-scan), wholesale barrels (export * from turning every internal into accidental surface), and reach-pasts (consumers importing deep paths around the entry point — converging ones indict the entry point, scattered ones indict discipline). Emits a markdown report to the OS temp dir with named-but-not-performed repairs; published-contract symbols (plugin hooks, library API with invisible downstream consumers) are exempted or held, never convicted.
The consumption lens on skill-deepen-architecture’s depth ratio: that skill asks how much behaviour hides behind an interface; this asks whether each exposed symbol has anyone on the other side at all. Every export is a promise — an unconsumed one is a promise nobody asked for, still constraining every future change.
When to use

A package’s public API has sprawled and nobody remembers what is actually used
Pruning dead exports, tightening barrels, or fixing deep-path imports
Before extracting or publishing a package — deciding what the entry point should promise
Making internals private again after “temporary” exports froze into de-facto contracts

Skip when:

The question is depth behind the surviving surface — /deepen-architecture
Import direction and cycles — /dependency-flow-scan
What the suite reveals about seams — /test-shape-scan
Executing the shrink — downstream; /lean-review the diff

Why it exists
Surface sprawl is a ratchet: exporting is one keystroke, unexporting is an archaeology project, so surfaces only grow — and every needless export both widens the interface readers must learn (the denominator of /deepen-architecture’s depth ratio) and freezes an internal as a de-facto contract someone will eventually depend on. Dedicated tools (knip, ts-prune) find dead exports mechanically; the skill’s added judgment is everything around the mechanical census — published-contract exemptions, the promote-vs-fence reading of reach-pasts, the barrel-lie correction (tracing consumption to the symbol, not the barrel line), and the library caveat that downgrades unprovable deaths to hold.
Related

.claude/skills/api-surface-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-deepen-architecture — depth behind the surface; this audits who consumes it
skill-test-shape-scan — receives the test-only-export cross-references
skill-dependency-flow-scan, skill-churn-hotspot-scan, skill-error-topology-scan, skill-concept-drift-scan — the static-structure family
skill-lean-review — reviews the eventual shrink diff

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/api-surface-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-22. Re-sync on every body edit.

---
name: api-surface-scan
description: Audit a codebase's exported surface against actual consumption — dead exports nobody imports, exports consumed only by tests, barrels re-exporting wholesale, and consumers reaching past declared entry points — via the unexport test (make it private: who breaks?), ranked as a markdown report with a reachable "surface is earned" clean verdict. Use when a package's public API has sprawled, you want to shrink what a module exposes, prune dead exports, or tighten entry points before extracting a package. Stops at the ranked report; does not perform the unexporting. Distinct from /deepen-architecture (how much behaviour hides behind an interface — this measures who actually consumes each exposed symbol) and /dependency-flow-scan (edge direction between modules, not surface width). Counters surface sprawl — every needless export widening the interface readers must learn and freezing internals as de-facto contracts.
---
 
Audit the exported surface at `$ARGUMENTS` against actual consumption and rank **shrink candidates** — symbols whose export status is unearned. The skill is a diagnostic-scan: it produces a ranked report and stops. It does not perform the unexporting (downstream execution; `/lean-review` the diff) and it does not redesign interfaces (`/grill`, usually via `/deepen-architecture`). The output is a markdown report written to the OS temp dir, never into the repo.
 
This is the consumption lens on `/deepen-architecture`'s depth ratio: that skill asks how much behaviour hides *behind* an interface; this asks whether each exposed symbol has *anyone on the other side at all*. Every export is a promise — an unconsumed one is a promise nobody asked for, still constraining every future change.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the surface to audit, as any of:
 
- A repo root, a package, or a subtree path (`packages/core/`) — the scan audits that unit's exports against consumers outside it
- A free-text area name ("the SDK's public API") to be resolved against the working repo
- Empty → the current working repo; if it is large, scope to the package most recently discussed this session
 
If no codebase is in scope, say so and ask for a path — do not invent a target.
 
## The fixed glossary (low-freedom — drift is forbidden)
 
Every finding must use these terms **verbatim**.
 
- **Export** — a symbol reachable from outside its module: public function, type, class, constant, or a barrel re-export.
- **Consumer** — an import of that symbol from outside the module that declares it.
- **Earned export** — has at least one non-test external consumer.
- **Dead export** — zero external consumers.
- **Test-only export** — the only external consumers are tests.
- **Entry point** — the declared public face: `package.json` `exports`/`main`, an index barrel, `__init__.py`, a `pub` facade.
- **Reach-past** — a consumer importing a deep path around the entry point.
- **Unexport test** — the battery's core move: make the symbol private; enumerate exactly who breaks.
 
## The test battery (low-freedom — apply each verbatim)
 
1. **Unexport test.** For every export in scope, census external consumers. Prefer a dead-export tool already present in the repo (`knip`, `ts-prune`, compiler dead-code flags) — do not install one; otherwise Grep for the symbol across the codebase outside its module. Zero consumers → **dead export**. Tests only → **test-only export** — the declared interface is not the test surface, which is evidence for `/test-shape-scan`'s axis; record the cross-reference, don't re-scan here.
2. **Entry-point test.** Where barrels or declared entry points exist: flag symbols re-exported through the barrel but never consumed *via* the barrel, and barrels that re-export entire modules wholesale (`export * from`), which turn every internal symbol into accidental surface.
3. **Reach-past census.** Find consumers importing deep paths around the entry point. Read the pattern before convicting: many reach-pasts converging on the *same* symbol mean the surface is under-declared — the repair is **promote** (add it to the entry point); scattered one-off reach-pasts mean discipline slipped — the repair is **fence** (route them through the entry point).
 
## The procedure
 
Three bounded phases.
 
1. **Establish the surface.** Identify the unit's declared entry points and enumerate its exports (bounded: for a large package, the exports of the declared entry points plus the modules with the most fan-in — state the scope). Public-by-published-contract symbols (documented plugin hooks, framework lifecycle methods, reflection targets) are exempt from the unexport test — list them as exemptions, don't count them dead.
2. **Apply the battery & rank.** Run the three tests. Badge each surviving candidate: **strong-buy** (dead export with no contract exemption, or a wholesale barrel), **consider** (test-only exports, promote/fence calls), **hold** (published-contract ambiguity — might have external consumers this repo can't see, e.g. a library's downstream users). For a *published library*, external consumers are invisible by definition — downgrade dead-export findings to hold and say why. **Stop here — do not unexport anything.**
3. **Report & hand off.** Emit the report (next section) to `<tmpdir>/apisurface-<timestamp>.md`, computing the timestamp at run time. Route onward: the shrink itself is downstream execution with `/lean-review` on the diff; if shrinking reveals a module that is *all* surface, route it to `/deepen-architecture`.
 
Clean-verdict reachability: if every export is earned, barrels are deliberate, and reach-pasts are absent, return the **clean verdict** ("the surface is earned"). Do not manufacture findings.
 
## Output format
 
A markdown report written to the temp dir:
 
```text
# API surface review — <unit>   (<timestamp>)
 
## Surface scope
<entry points: <list> · exports enumerated: N · method: <tool | grep census> · exemptions (published contract): <list or none> · library caveat: <applies | n/a>>
 
## Verdict
<strong-buy: N · consider: N · hold: N>   |   <clean: the surface is earned — every export has a non-test external consumer>
 
## Top recommendation
<the single strongest shrink in one paragraph. Omit if clean.>
 
## Finding <n> — <symbol or barrel>   [strong-buy | consider | hold]
- **Type:** <dead export | test-only export | wholesale barrel | reach-past>
- **Unexport test:** <who breaks: nobody | tests only: <which> | N consumers via deep paths>
- **Repair (named, not performed):** <unexport | unexport + fix test to use the interface | enumerate the barrel | promote to entry point | fence through entry point>
- **Risk note:** <published-contract exposure, if any>
 
## What this scan did not do
- Did not unexport or move any symbol (downstream; `/lean-review` the diff).
- Did not judge depth behind the surviving surface (`/deepen-architecture`).
- Did not audit the test suite's shape (`/test-shape-scan`) — test-only exports are cross-referenced there.
```
 
Definition of done: every finding carries a type, an unexport-test result, a named repair, and a risk note where relevant; exemptions and the library caveat are stated up front; the report is in the temp dir.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Killing published contracts.** Plugin hooks, framework lifecycle methods, and documented library API have invisible consumers. Exempt or hold — a "dead" export that ships in a published package is not provably dead from this repo.
- **Trusting the barrel.** `export * from` makes the census lie — symbols look consumed via the barrel while nothing imports them. Trace consumption to the symbol, not to the barrel line.
- **Convicting every reach-past.** Converging reach-pasts indict the entry point (promote), not the consumers. Read the pattern before assigning the repair.
- **Performing the shrink.** The scan stops at the report. "I removed the obviously dead ones while I was there" is the anti-pattern with a diff.
- **Ignoring dynamic consumption.** String-keyed lookups, DI containers, and reflection consume without importing. State the census's blind spots in the scope line.
- **Writing the report into the repo.** Temp dir only.
- **Padding.** The clean verdict is reachable and correct — use it.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A package's public API has sprawled and nobody remembers what is actually used
- Pruning dead exports, tightening barrels, or fixing deep-path imports
- Before extracting or publishing a package — deciding what the entry point should promise
- Making internals private again after "temporary" exports froze into de-facto contracts
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Depth of behaviour behind the interface — `/deepen-architecture`
- Direction and cycles of the import graph — `/dependency-flow-scan`
- What the test suite reveals about seams — `/test-shape-scan` (test-only exports are handed there)
- Executing the shrink — downstream; review the diff with `/lean-review`
 
## Related
 
- `/deepen-architecture` — depth behind the surface; this skill audits who consumes the surface
- `/test-shape-scan` — receives the test-only-export cross-references
- `/dependency-flow-scan`, `/churn-hotspot-scan`, `/error-topology-scan`, `/concept-drift-scan` — the static-structure family
- `/lean-review` — reviews the eventual shrink diff

ai/skills/skill-assumption-reversal.title: Skill: assumption-reversal
ai/skills/skill-assumption-reversal.content:
Skill: assumption-reversal
Surface five unstated assumptions in a problem or plan, then invert each as a one-line design brief.
When to use

Ideation keeps cycling through variants of the same idea — the frame is the constraint, not the solution space
Before writing a spec, to test that the problem statement isn’t baking in the solution
A decision feels forced by constraints — inverting them may reveal they aren’t real
After /scamper produces uniformly conservative output

Skip when:

Ranking already-generated candidates (use /red-team or /disagree)
The problem genuinely has one framing (“which of these five libraries”)
Low-stakes choices where frame-level reversal wastes tokens

Why it exists
Most stuck ideation is stuck on the frame, not the solution space. Generic brainstorming explores within the inherited assumptions; assumption reversal attacks the assumptions themselves. It’s the generative cousin of /disagree (diagnostic inversion of the last response) and /red-team (adversarial critique of a committed artifact) — same inversion mechanic, but pointed at the problem statement instead of an answer.
Related

.claude/skills/assumption-reversal/SKILL.md — operational definition
solo-ideation — operating model the skill plugs into
heuristic-ideation-prompts — assumption reversal alongside SCAMPER and starbursting
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/assumption-reversal/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: assumption-reversal
description: Surface 5 unstated assumptions in a problem or plan, then invert each as a one-line design brief. Use when a problem feels stuck inside a frame — assumption reversal attacks the problem's frame rather than its surface. Generative, not diagnostic (for diagnostic inversion use `/disagree` or inversion in `/red-team`).
---
 
Surface and invert the unstated assumptions in `$ARGUMENTS`.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently discussed problem statement, plan, or design brief. If nothing fits, ask the user what to reverse rather than guess.
 
## Your role
 
A frame-attacker. Your job is to make visible the assumptions the user is treating as background conditions, then imagine each one inverted and describe what that new problem looks like.
 
Assumption reversal works because most stuck ideation is stuck on the frame, not the solution space. "Customers want fast checkout" treats the speed-preference as a given; inverting it ("customers want slow checkout") generates a different problem whose best solution is obvious (luxury goods, craft coffee) and usually unreachable from inside the original frame.
 
This skill is generative, not diagnostic. For diagnostic inversion ("argue the opposite of the last assistant response"), use `/disagree`. For adversarial critique of a committed artifact, use `/red-team`.
 
## What to produce
 
**5 unstated assumptions**, ranked by load-bearing weight (1 = most load-bearing; these are the ones whose inversion yields the biggest frame shift). For each:
 
- **Assumption** — the assumption stated as a declarative claim, as the user would likely endorse it
- **Why it's likely unstated** — one line on why this is treated as background (e.g., "inherited from industry default", "true in most cases the user has encountered")
- **Inverted brief** — the new problem statement if the assumption is false: "Design as if [inverted assumption] — [what that implies, one sentence]"
- **Real-world precedent** (if any) — cases where the inverted assumption is true and produced something interesting; if none comes to mind, say so rather than invent
 
After the five, a one-line summary: **Which inversion is most likely to yield a useful new direction, and why** — not a recommendation to adopt the inversion, just a read on which is most generative.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Assumption reversal — <problem name>
 
## Context
<one-line restatement>
 
## Assumption 1 (most load-bearing)
- **Assumption:** <declarative claim>
- **Why unstated:** <background condition>
- **Inverted brief:** Design as if <inverted claim> — <implication>
- **Precedent:** <example or "none obvious">
 
## Assumption 2
...
 
## Assumption 5
...
 
## Most generative inversion
<which assumption-reversal yields the biggest frame shift and why — one line>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Surface features as "assumptions."** "We assume users have internet" is trivially true and inverting it produces a boring problem. Target assumptions about *purpose*, *order*, *audience*, *success criteria*, *constraint direction* — the load-bearing frame elements.
- **Inverting a technical constraint.** "We assume the database is relational" → "assume it's not" is a technology swap, not a frame reversal. Reserve this skill for frame-level inversions; leave tech swaps to `/scamper` Substitute.
- **Self-canceling inversions.** If the inverted brief is absurd in every direction ("design as if users don't exist"), the inversion failed. Good inversions produce coherent alternative problems, not nonsense.
- **Recommending adoption.** The skill surfaces and inverts; it does not tell the user which frame to adopt. The "most generative" verdict is about which yields the biggest shift, not which is correct.
- **Padding with obvious assumptions.** Five strong inversions is better than five plus three weak ones. If you can only find three load-bearing assumptions, produce three and say so.
 
## When to invoke
 
- When ideation cycles through variants of the same idea — the frame is the constraint, not the solution space
- Before writing a spec, to test that the problem statement isn't baking in the solution
- When a decision feels forced by constraints — inverting the constraints may reveal they aren't real
- After `/scamper` produces uniformly conservative output — the frame is probably the problem
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Concrete solution selection (already-generated candidates being ranked)
- Problems with one genuine framing (some decisions really are "which of these five libraries")
- Low-stakes choices where frame-level reversal wastes tokens
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation.md` — hub, operating model
- `knowledge/general/heuristic-ideation-prompts.md` — assumption reversal alongside SCAMPER and starbursting
- `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md` — inversion as a diagnostic tool; this skill is its generative cousin
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation-prompt-library.md` — manual templates and session recipe

ai/skills/skill-bias-scan-ai.title: Skill: bias-scan-ai
ai/skills/skill-bias-scan-ai.content:
Skill: bias-scan-ai
Scan an AI-generated artifact (LLM-drafted note, AI research output, AI-produced code, agent-generated summary) for output-side bias fingerprints.
When to use

Before committing AI-drafted content to the vault, a spec, or a PR description
LLM-written research summaries about to be propagated into a decision
Agent-generated artifacts before they’re acted on

Skip when:

The artifact is human-authored (use /bias-scan-human — different fingerprints)
You’re scanning an inbound prompt, not an outbound output (use /bias-scan-prompt)
A targeted check is enough; /reviewers-map is the lighter-weight alternative

Why it exists
AI outputs have characteristic failure modes that human outputs don’t: hallucinated specifics, sycophancy, narrative coherence without evidence, training-data availability and survivorship bias, in-register defaults, missing failure-mode analysis. These are different in kind from human reasoning biases, so a single bias scan can’t cover both axes well. This skill operationalizes Pass 2 of the bias-aware verification protocol.

---
name: bias-scan-ai
description: Scan an AI-generated artifact (LLM-drafted note, AI research output, AI-produced code, agent-generated summary) for output-side bias fingerprints — hallucinated specifics, sycophancy, narrative coherence without evidence, training-data availability, survivorship, in-register assumptions, missing failure modes. Use before committing AI-drafted content. For human-authored artifacts use `/bias-scan-human`; for prompts use `/bias-scan-prompt`; for stylistic AI tells rather than epistemic ones (puffery, em dashes, chatbot phrases) use `/unslop`.
---
 
Scan the AI-generated artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for output-side bias fingerprints. This is the output-side counterpart to `/bias-scan-prompt` (input side) and `/bias-scan-human` (human-reasoning side).
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently written/edited AI-drafted file in this session, or the largest staged diff in `git status` if nothing was written this session.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on content that was **generated by a model** (LLM or agent):
 
- Knowledge notes drafted by the assistant
- Research summaries produced by subagents or the assistant
- AI-generated code diffs or test suites
- Agent-generated PR descriptions, commit messages, architecture proposals
- Transcripts or outputs from multi-agent pipelines
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Human-authored notes (use `/bias-scan-human`)
- Prompts (use `/bias-scan-prompt`)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` entries (explicit scratchpad)
- `journal/` entries (personal reflection)
- Frontmatter-only or formatting-only changes
- `.claude/` configuration files
 
If you can't tell whether an artifact is AI- or human-authored (mixed edits, retroactive AI passes on a human draft), default to running **both** `/bias-scan-ai` and `/bias-scan-human` — the checks are largely non-overlapping.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Read the target file** in full.
2. **Run each of the seven checks below.** The canonical definition lives in `knowledge/ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints.md` — consult if you need the full rationale, but do not re-read it on every invocation.
3. **Report structured findings** in the format shown at the bottom of this file.
4. **Do not modify the target.** This is a review pass, not an edit.
 
## The seven checks
 
These target **AI-output-specific** failure modes, not the author's reasoning (that's `/bias-scan-human`) or the prompt's framing (that's `/bias-scan-prompt`).
 
### 1. Entity check (hallucinated confidence)
 
List every named specific in the note: people, paper titles, URLs, API/method signatures, CVEs, version numbers, dates, precise statistics. For each, classify:
 
- ✓ **Verifiable** — either a well-established canonical reference or something you can confirm exists
- ? **Uncertain** — plausible but you cannot confirm from your knowledge; flag for user verification
- ✗ **Likely fabricated** — specifics that look invented (suspiciously round numbers, dates that don't match known events, URLs that look templated, API signatures that don't exist in the named library)
 
This is the highest-priority check. Hallucinated specifics are the dominant failure mode for AI-authored notes (see the trust-but-verify rule in user CLAUDE.md).
 
### 2. Fluency strip
 
Extract the load-bearing factual claims as bullets, ignoring prose quality. For each claim, note whether evidence is actually cited or whether the prose is carrying it. "Beautifully written but unsupported" is the failure mode — LLMs are optimized for fluent output; readers natively equate fluency with credibility. Separate the two explicitly.
 
### 3. Sycophancy check
 
Does the note structure mirror the prompt that produced it, rather than re-examining the question? Signs:
 
- Note opens by restating a user premise as though it were settled
- Section headers use user vocabulary instead of domain vocabulary
- Confidence level matches the prompt's confidence, not the evidence
- Alternatives the user didn't mention are absent
- Strong agreement with loaded or leading user assertions
 
This is the most common AI-output bias in day-to-day use; it silently converts the model into an amplifier for the user's own confirmation bias.
 
### 4. Narrative-coherence gap test
 
What assumptions did the draft make that its sources didn't supply? List them. The model rewards coherent continuation over epistemic honesty — gaps get filled with plausible-sounding content rather than flagged.
 
Specific signatures:
 
- A plan that answers a question the user didn't ask, because it fits the narrative better
- Summaries that smooth over contradictions in the source material
- "The issue is X" framings where the actual issue wasn't identifiable from the evidence
 
### 5. Training-data mainstream check
 
On topics with a "popular answer," is the popular answer right for this context? LLMs over-weight dominant framings in their training corpus; long-tail-but-correct answers are systematically under-represented.
 
Fingerprints:
 
- "Best practice" advice that reflects 2022–2023 blog consensus rather than current engineering discussion
- Preference for widely-documented frameworks over better-fitting niche tools
- Answers that feel like a median Stack Overflow response when a more specific answer exists
 
### 6. Survivorship and failure-mode probe
 
Two related checks:
 
- **Survivorship** — do the examples cited all come from publicly-visible successful cases (Netflix, Uber, Stripe architectures) without caveating that the failure distribution is invisible?
- **Failure modes** — are tradeoffs, caveats, and failure modes acknowledged? One-sided notes read as advocacy rather than knowledge.
 
Training data over-represents what got published and upvoted, which correlates poorly with what worked in production. Flag sections where a fair critic would expect pushback but none is present.
 
### 7. In-register / context-fit check
 
Do unstated assumptions from the training-data register leak in? Examples:
 
- US-centric examples where local context matters
- SaaS/cloud defaults where self-hosted or local alternatives exist
- Academic register where practitioner register would be clearer
- Tech-industry values (velocity, scale, SaaS-first) presented as universal
- Aesthetic conventions from a specific professional register (LinkedIn-voice, journalistic opener, five-bullet summary)
 
### Code-specific additions
 
When the artifact is AI-generated code, layer these on top:
 
- **Tests with low mutation value** — tests that look like tests but don't actually exercise the behavior (narrative coherence variant). See `knowledge/ai/evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests.md`.
- **Invented APIs** — hallucinated imports, method signatures, CLI flags (entity-check variant)
- **Copy-paste-from-training-set** — code duplicating a well-known example even when surrounding code uses a different pattern (in-register variant)
 
## Output format
 
```text
# AI bias scan — <filename>
 
## 1. Entity check
- ✓ <verified entity>
- ? <uncertain entity> — <line or section>
- ✗ <likely fabricated> — <line or section>
 
## 2. Fluency strip
- <load-bearing claim 1> — evidence present / missing
- <load-bearing claim 2> — evidence present / missing
 
## 3. Sycophancy check
<findings, or "no signs detected">
 
## 4. Narrative-coherence gap test
<assumptions the draft made that its sources didn't supply>
 
## 5. Training-data mainstream check
<cases where popular answer was defaulted to without fit check>
 
## 6. Survivorship and failure modes
<missing failure modes; survivorship-biased examples>
 
## 7. In-register / context-fit
<training-register leakage>
 
## Code-specific (if applicable)
<low-mutation tests, invented APIs, copy-paste artifacts>
 
## Verdict
**PASS** | **REVIEW** | **FAIL**
<one-line rationale>
```
 
**Verdict meaning:**
 
- **PASS** — all checks cleared or only trivial issues; safe to commit
- **REVIEW** — findings worth addressing before commit; list is actionable
- **FAIL** — fabrication detected (any ✗ entry), or substantial bias that makes the note unsafe to ship; do not commit without correction
 
A single ✗ in the entity check is enough for FAIL. Hallucinated specifics are the load-bearing failure this scan exists to catch.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Skipping the entity check.** The most common way this scan fails to catch a real problem is by rushing past named specifics. Read every person, paper, URL, and number explicitly.
- **Treating fluency as evidence.** If the prose is confident and coherent, you should be *more* suspicious, not less. Fluent output is the bias-exploiting shape, not the safe shape.
- **Passing because nothing obvious is wrong.** Most AI-output bias is subtle — sycophantic framing, mainstream defaulting, survivorship examples. Look for the checks, don't wait for glaring errors.
- **Inventing findings.** If a check genuinely turns up nothing, write "no signs detected" and move on. A scan that manufactures findings erodes its own credibility.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing an AI-drafted knowledge note
- Before merging AI-generated code that will ship
- When a research summary from a subagent is going to be relayed in a persistent artifact
- When reviewing any AI output whose content you'll act on

Skip when:

The artifact is a prompt, not a finished argument (use /bias-scan-prompt)

Why it exists

A scan tuned for AI fingerprints will silently miss most of them. Authoring this as a separate skill enforces target-specific scanning rather than a generic “check for bias” pass.

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/bias-scan-human/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: bias-scan-human
description: Scan a human-authored artifact (decision note, journal entry, plan, project overview, argument) for cognitive biases in the author's reasoning. Covers the full bias catalog — commitment, evidence-selection, estimation, attribution, selection, valuation, and AI-interaction biases — plus a structural debiasing-procedure check (did the artifact use a decision journal, pre-mortem, inversion, or reference-class anchor?). Use before committing a decision or a synthesis note that the user wrote.
---
 
Scan the human-authored artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for cognitive biases in the **author's reasoning**. This is the human-side counterpart to `/bias-scan-ai` and `/bias-scan-prompt`.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently written/edited file in this session, or the largest staged diff in `git status` if nothing was written this session.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on human-authored content where the author's reasoning is the product:
 
- Decision notes / architecture decision records
- Project overviews (`projects/*/overview.md`)
- Synthesis notes or `_connections.md` entries the user drafted themselves
- Journal entries with self-diagnostic framing (what happened, why, what to do)
- Retrospectives and post-mortems
- Investment theses or plans in `finance/`
- Training plans or self-diagnostic notes in `health/`
- Arguments or conclusions in knowledge notes the user authored (not AI-drafted)
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- AI-generated notes (use `/bias-scan-ai` instead)
- Prompts about to be sent (use `/bias-scan-prompt` instead)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` quick captures (explicit scratchpad)
- Frontmatter-only or formatting-only changes
- Reference notes that merely catalog external facts
 
## Your role
 
Read the artifact as a skeptical but charitable reviewer whose job is to find where the author's **reasoning** went off the rails, not whether the conclusion happens to be right. A conclusion can be correct and still have biased reasoning behind it — flag that case, because the reasoning is what generalizes.
 
Do not modify the artifact. This is a review pass, not an edit.
 
## The checklist
 
Grouped by bias family. The canonical definitions live in:
 
- `knowledge/general/cognitive-biases.md` (hub)
- `knowledge/general/probability-judgment-biases.md`
- `knowledge/general/social-attribution-biases.md`
- `knowledge/general/consumer-valuation-biases.md`
- `knowledge/general/ai-automation-biases.md`
- `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md`
 
Consult only as needed — don't re-read on every invocation.
 
### 1. Commitment and continuation
 
How does the artifact treat **past investment** in a position, tool, or path?
 
- **Sunk cost fallacy** — does prior time/money/effort appear as a reason to continue? ("We've already spent three weeks on this.") Forward cost is the only rational input.
- **Status quo bias** — is the current state the implicit default, with change needing to justify itself harder than continuation does?
- **Escalation of commitment** — is the plan to double down on a failing approach framed as "seeing it through"?
- **Loss aversion** — are potential losses weighted more heavily than equivalent gains? Look for asymmetric language around "risk" that only points one direction.
 
### 2. Evidence selection
 
How does the artifact pick which evidence counts?
 
- **Confirmation bias** — does the evidence cited uniformly support the author's conclusion? Are counter-examples, dissenting sources, or failure cases absent? This is the single highest-frequency bias in human writing.
- **Availability heuristic / recency** — does a recent or vivid event carry more weight than its actual statistical importance? ("Last week's incident shows we need to rebuild X.")
- **Narrative fallacy** — is a clean causal story imposed on events that might be noise, randomness, or multi-causal? Look for single-cause explanations of complex outcomes.
- **Survivorship bias** — do the examples cited all come from successful cases, ignoring the invisible failure distribution? ("Company X did Y and it worked" without "and here are ten companies that did Y and failed").
- **Illusion of validity** — does the author express high confidence in a prediction about a domain where their past predictions' hit rate is unknown or poor?
 
### 3. Estimation and probability
 
How does the artifact handle numbers, probabilities, and forecasts?
 
- **Anchoring** — is an early number (estimate, budget, deadline) carried through without independent re-derivation? Was the anchor actually informative, or just the first number said?
- **Planning fallacy** — are time/cost estimates for project-shaped work, and do they include a reference-class check? No 50th–75th percentile spread is a fingerprint.
- **Base rate fallacy** — when making a probability claim about a specific case, does the artifact anchor to the base rate for similar cases first?
- **Representativeness** — is a specific case matched to a prototype ("classic X case") without checking how common X actually is in this population?
- **Gambler's / hot-hand fallacy** — are streaks of outcomes treated as predictive in contexts where they're independent? ("The last three incidents were all deploys, so the next one will/won't be.")
- **Hard-easy effect** — is the confidence level uniform across claims, or does it track with claim difficulty? Novel / complex claims should carry more uncertainty than routine ones; flag when they don't.
- **Dunning-Kruger signature** — is the author expressing high confidence in a domain they've recently entered, or dismissive confidence about what experts find difficult?
 
### 4. Attribution and social reasoning
 
How does the artifact explain **other people's** behavior and **its own**?
 
- **Fundamental attribution error** — are other people's failures explained by character ("they're careless/lazy/difficult"), while similar failures in the author's own work get situational explanations ("the spec was unclear, the tools broke")?
- **Self-serving bias** — are successes attributed to the author's skill and failures to external factors?
- **Extrinsic incentive bias** — does the artifact assume others are driven by money/status while the author is driven by meaning/curiosity?
- **In-group / out-group framing** — are teammates or allies given charitable readings while outsiders get suspicious ones, on the same evidence?
- **Halo / horn** — is a single strong trait (a prestigious employer, a past failure) generating blanket judgments across unrelated dimensions?
- **Illusion of transparency** — does the artifact assume an audience "obviously" knows something the author feels strongly but hasn't stated?
- **False consensus** — does "obviously everyone prefers X" appear without evidence?
- **Empathy gap (hot-cold)** — was the artifact drafted in a hot emotional state (angry, anxious, sleep-deprived, frustrated) and is it making commitments that bind a cold-state future self?
 
### 5. Selection and social influence
 
How does the artifact treat what "everyone" does?
 
- **Bandwagon effect** — is the recommendation driven by "everyone is doing X" rather than fit-to-context?
- **Survivorship-driven convention** — is a practice recommended because famous successful cases use it, without asking what the failure rate of that practice is?
 
### 6. Valuation (if the artifact decides between options)
 
- **Endowment effect** — is something the author already owns/built given higher value than an equivalent alternative?
- **Disposition effect** — is an underperforming asset (code, tool, position, contract) being held because selling would "make the loss real"?
- **Decoy / asymmetric dominance** — if options are presented, is an artificial third option framing the choice?
 
### 7. AI-interaction specific
 
Only apply if the artifact is a decision **about using AI**, delegating to an agent, or reviewing AI output:
 
- **Automation bias** — is AI output being treated as the answer rather than as a piece of evidence?
- **Delegation creep** — is the scope of AI authority being expanded based on past low-stakes successes, without updating governance?
- **Accountability diffusion** — does the artifact leave unclear who is answerable if the AI path fails?
- **Google effect** — is the author remembering *which prompt to use* instead of *the underlying reasoning*?
- **Verification asymmetry** — does the plan assume AI-accelerated generation without budgeting matching verification effort?
 
### 8. Debiasing-procedure check
 
Did the artifact use any structural debiasing? (From `debiasing-mental-models.md`.)
 
- Decision journal style — explicit "what would change my mind"?
- Pre-mortem — has the author considered "imagine this failed disastrously — why"?
- Inversion — "what would guarantee failure"?
- Base-rate or reference-class anchor used?
 
Absence isn't a failing flag on its own — but for high-stakes artifacts (architecture, investment, major career move), absence of any debiasing procedure is itself a finding.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Human bias scan — <filename>
 
## 1. Commitment and continuation
- <finding, cited line or section>  → <bias name>
- <or: no signs detected>
 
## 2. Evidence selection
- <finding>  → <bias name>
 
## 3. Estimation and probability
- <finding>  → <bias name>
 
## 4. Attribution and social reasoning
- <finding>  → <bias name>
 
## 5. Selection and social influence
- <finding>  → <bias name>
 
## 6. Valuation
- <finding>  → <bias name>
- <or: N/A — artifact does not decide between options>
 
## 7. AI-interaction specific
- <finding>  → <bias name>
- <or: N/A — artifact is not about AI use>
 
## 8. Debiasing-procedure check
- Pre-mortem: present / absent
- Inversion: present / absent
- Base-rate anchor: present / absent
- Decision-journal framing: present / absent
 
## Verdict
**PASS** | **REVIEW** | **FAIL**
<one-line rationale; name the top 1–2 biases to address if REVIEW or FAIL>
```
 
**Verdict meaning:**
 
- **PASS** — no meaningful bias signatures, or only minor ones; reasoning is sound
- **REVIEW** — findings worth addressing before committing the artifact; list is actionable
- **FAIL** — a load-bearing conclusion is standing on biased reasoning; the argument should be rebuilt, not patched
 
## What "finding" looks like
 
A good finding cites the specific line or section, names the bias, and explains the mechanism in one line. A weak finding is generic.
 
**Weak:** "Some confirmation bias present."
 
**Strong:** "§ Rationale cites three blog posts supporting the RSC migration; no dissent from the SPA-stays-fine camp is acknowledged. → confirmation bias. The mainstream answer may be right, but the artifact hasn't shown its work."
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Bias-naming as critique.** Labeling something "confirmation bias" without pointing at the specific line and explaining the mechanism is theatre. A finding must be falsifiable.
- **Treating absence of bias markers as endorsement.** Passing this scan does not mean the conclusion is right — it means the reasoning doesn't show bias signatures. The artifact still needs ordinary fact-checking.
- **Inventing biases to look thorough.** If only two or three of the seven sections have real findings, the verdict should reflect that — don't manufacture findings to fill the template.
- **Pattern-matching the author.** Biases live in the **artifact**, not in inferred author psychology. Do not speculate about why the author might be biased; scan what's on the page.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing an architecture decision, investment decision, or major plan
- Before publishing a journal retrospective or post-mortem
- On a synthesis note you drafted yourself before running `/red-team`
- When you notice you're strongly committed to a conclusion and want a structural check on your reasoning

- `knowledge/general/probability-judgment-biases.md` — §3 source

- `knowledge/general/ai-automation-biases.md` — §7 source

Skill: bias-scan-prompt
Scan a prompt (draft or already-written) for input-side framing bias before it’s sent to a model or baked into a spec.
When to use

High-stakes prompts you’ll act on the result of (specs, subagent briefs, research queries that drive decisions)
Prompts about to be baked into a skill body, system prompt, or recurring agent
Reviewing an existing prompt that’s been producing characteristically wrong output

Skip when:

Conversational, low-stakes prompts
Prompts whose output you’ll obviously sanity-check anyway
The artifact is an output, not a prompt (use /bias-scan-ai or /bias-scan-human)

Why it exists
Input framing constrains output more than the model does. Leading questions, embedded anchors, single-anecdote generalization, dispositional framing, hot-state drafting, and ruled-out alternatives bake bias into the answer before the model sees it. A scan at Pass 1 of the verification protocol catches this before the bias propagates downstream and gets re-laundered through fluent prose.

---
name: bias-scan-prompt
description: Scan a prompt (draft or already-written) for input-side framing bias before it's sent to a model or baked into a spec. Detects 15 input-side patterns including leading questions, anchored estimates, single-anecdote generalization, dispositional framing, hot-state drafting, and ruled-out alternatives (full catalog in body). Returns findings plus a neutral rewrite. Use on high-stakes prompts — specs, subagent briefs, research queries you'll act on.
---
 
Scan the prompt at `$ARGUMENTS` for input-side framing bias. This is the input-side counterpart to `/bias-scan-ai` (output side) and `/bias-scan-human` (human-reasoning side).
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A file path — read the file and treat its contents as the prompt
- A path-and-section ref (e.g., `projects/foo/spec.md#research-query`) — read the section
- Literal prompt text, usually quoted
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most recent prompt-shaped content the user drafted this session (a message, a spec section, a subagent brief)
2. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it contains prompt-shaped content (e.g., a `projects/*/prompts.md` or `.claude/` agent definition)
3. If nothing fits, ask the user what prompt to scan rather than guess.
 
## Your role
 
You are a neutrality reviewer who returns **Clean** for clean prompts and only flags signatures from the catalog below. You are not the answer-giver here.
 
The cheapest place to correct for bias is upstream. A biased prompt produces a biased answer that looks internally consistent with the biased question — so the output-side check is weaker for biases that were baked into the input.
 
## The checklist
 
Drawn from `knowledge/ai/prompt-bias-diagnostics.md`. Do not re-read the source note on every invocation — consult only if you need the full rationale for a specific pattern.
 
### 1. Leading question
 
Signatures:
 
- "Why is X the best…"
- "Confirm that X…"
- "Don't you think…"
- "Since we already know X, …"
- Any question whose surface form presupposes the answer
 
**Reframe:** "What are the arguments for and against X? Is it the best approach for this context?"
 
### 2. Embedded estimate (anchoring)
 
Signatures:
 
- "I'm thinking 2 weeks — does that sound right?"
- "Budget is $50k — can we do it?"
- Any numeric anchor stated before asking for the model's independent view
 
**Reframe:** "Give an independent estimate first, then compare to my prior of <N>."
 
### 3. Sunk-cost framing
 
Signatures:
 
- "I've built it this way for months — how do I make it work?"
- "We've already invested X, so the question is just…"
- Past investment used as a reason to continue rather than as a forward-cost input
 
**Reframe:** "Should this be salvaged or rewritten? Evaluate both paths on forward cost only."
 
### 4. Single-anecdote generalization (availability)
 
Signatures:
 
- One vivid recent event expanded into a general rule
- "Last week X happened — so we should always…"
- A base rate is required but not requested
 
**Reframe:** "What's the base rate for this outcome across similar cases? Adjust from the base rate."
 
### 5. Dispositional framing (FAE)
 
Signatures:
 
- "My coworker is being difficult — how do I handle them?"
- "The engineer keeps missing edge cases — how do I coach them?"
- Behavior framed as character-driven without situational context
 
**Reframe:** "List situational factors that could explain this behavior (spec clarity, tooling, time pressure, missing context) before recommending a dispositional intervention."
 
### 6. Hot state
 
Signatures:
 
- Angry email drafts, late-night refactor plans
- High-intensity language ("this is broken," "we have to fix this now") when the real deadline is not urgent
- Emotional load leaking into technical framing
 
**Reframe:** Delay if the stakes allow. Otherwise annotate: "Assume I am tired / frustrated / under pressure. What would a rested, calm version of me notice that I'm missing?"
 
### 7. Planning fallacy signature
 
Signatures:
 
- "Can we ship this in two sprints?" with no reference-class mention
- Duration estimates without 75th-percentile variance
 
**Reframe:** "What's the reference-class estimate for projects of this scope? Give me a median and 75th-percentile estimate with the main risk drivers."
 
### 8. Self-diagnostic (Barnum)
 
Signatures:
 
- "Is this imposter syndrome?"
- "Am I burning out?"
- Vague self-labeling invited
 
**Reframe:** "What specific observable behaviors would distinguish this from the closest alternatives?"
 
### 9. Bikeshedding
 
Signatures:
 
- Deep dive on a trivial detail inside a larger decision
- Proxy issue getting disproportionate attention
 
**Reframe:** "What's the load-bearing decision here? Rank issues by actual impact on outcome before answering."
 
### 10. False consensus
 
Signatures:
 
- "Obviously everyone would prefer X"
- "No one would argue for Y"
- Unstated consensus used as evidence
 
**Reframe:** "Who would reasonably prefer not-X, and why?"
 
### 11. Representativeness (prototype fitting)
 
Signatures:
 
- "This looks like a classic Y case"
- Prototype invoked without base-rate check
 
**Reframe:** "Before fitting to the Y prototype, list the base rate of Y in this context and three alternatives."
 
### 12. Narrative fallacy
 
Signatures:
 
- "We wiped because X"
- "The market dropped because Y"
- Single-cause story for a multi-causal or noisy event
 
**Reframe:** "List the top five candidate causes. Weight by evidence rather than narrative fit."
 
### 13. Status quo bias
 
Signatures:
 
- "What's the minimal change to keep things working?"
- Incremental-only framing
- No blank-slate alternative requested
 
**Reframe:** "What would you do if you were starting fresh? Compare against the minimal-change path."
 
### 14. Alternatives ruled out
 
Signatures:
 
- Question frames a binary that excludes a third option
- "Should we do A or B?" when C, D, E exist
 
**Reframe:** "Before answering A vs. B, list the alternatives this binary rules out and say whether any of them fit better."
 
### 15. Sycophancy setup
 
A meta-pattern: combinations of validation language ("you're great at this"), confident opening ("I know the answer is X"), and a question that allows the model to simply agree. This primes sycophancy before the model even responds.
 
**Reframe:** strip validation language; state the open question without signaling the expected answer.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Prompt bias scan — <source>
 
## Original prompt
<verbatim or summarized; quote the load-bearing sentence if long>
 
## Signatures detected
 
- <bias name> — <signature line or phrase from the prompt> — <one-line mechanism>
- <or: no signatures detected>
 
## Severity
**Clean** | **Annotate** | **Rewrite** | **Delay**
 
## Recommended action
 
### If "Annotate"
Append the following instruction to the prompt:
> <exact annotation text>
 
### If "Rewrite"
Suggested neutral version:
> <full rewritten prompt>
 
### If "Delay"
<why delay is the right move — typically hot-state drafts>
 
## What the original prompt would pull from the model
 
<one sentence on what a sycophantic or framing-responsive model would likely produce from the original — this is the bias payload>
```
 
**Severity meaning:**
 
- **Clean** — no signatures, or only mild ones that won't meaningfully shape the output; send as-is
- **Annotate** — one or two signatures; cheap to counteract with a counter-framing instruction appended to the prompt
- **Rewrite** — multiple signatures or a load-bearing framing problem; the prompt should be neutralized, not patched
- **Delay** — hot-state drafting detected; the right move is not to rewrite but to defer, unless stakes force action now
 
## When to escalate to rewrite vs. annotate
 
- **Annotate** when the prompt's core question is neutral but a framing signature is layered on top (e.g., a reasonable question that opens with "Obviously X…")
- **Rewrite** when the question itself presupposes the answer, or when the prompt contains three or more framing signatures that won't be absorbed by a single counter-instruction
- **Delay** specifically for hot-state drafts; neutral framing doesn't fix a decision made under emotional load — only a cold-state revisit does
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Over-reframing low-stakes prompts.** If the user's prompt is "what's the syntax for a Python list comprehension," this skill should return **Clean** and stop. Reserve full rewrites for prompts that will shape a decision.
- **Rewriting toward a preferred answer.** The goal is neutrality, not steering. If the reframe quietly biases the prompt toward a different conclusion, you've just replaced one bias with another.
- **Meta-hedging reframes.** A rewrite that demands the model consider every angle, list every alternative, and weight all evidence produces vague hedged output. Neutrality is the goal; paralysis is not.
- **Inventing signatures.** If the prompt is genuinely clean, return **Clean**. A scan that manufactures findings to look thorough erodes the discipline.
- **Treating the reframe as the answer.** A neutral prompt is a prerequisite, not a correct answer. `/bias-scan-ai` still applies to whatever the model produces in response.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before sending a prompt that will shape a production decision, spec, architecture choice, or research conclusion you'll act on
- Before committing a prompt to a subagent brief, agent definition, or workflow file where it will run many times
- When a prompt in a spec is about to be propagated to a downstream fleet
- When reviewing someone else's prompt for research quality
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Throwaway exploratory questions
- Command-line or syntax-lookup prompts
- Prompts inside already-committed docs unless you're about to modify them
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/prompt-bias-diagnostics.md` — the source catalog
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — Pass 1 context
- `knowledge/ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints.md` — why input-side catch beats output-side correction for framing biases
- `knowledge/general/cognitive-biases.md` — the human biases being diagnosed in the author of the prompt
- `knowledge/general/social-attribution-biases.md` — FAE, false consensus, transparency in prompt framing
- `knowledge/general/probability-judgment-biases.md` — base-rate and representativeness reframes

ai/skills/skill-branch-resolve.title: Skill: branch-resolve
ai/skills/skill-branch-resolve.content:
Skill: branch-resolve
Operationalize each unresolved decision branch in a multi-step plan — route every branch to one of three resolutions in preference order: (1) resolve up front before issuing, (2) split into separate plans at the determinant, (3) express as a Gollwitzer implementation intention. Apply trigger criteria (observable, deterministic, falsifiable) and response criteria (specific, executable, bounded) when producing option 3. Force a hard split with a user-confirmation gate on any branch whose downstream contains a destructive or production-touching operation.
When to use

After /plan-split-scan flags a Signal-3 finding (unresolved branches) — this skill is the action step
Before issuing a multi-step plan that contains conditional syntax to an agent or subagent
Before confirming an ExitPlanMode draft with embedded “if X then Y otherwise Z” structure
Before committing a projects/**/plan.md document with run-time branches
Whenever a plan reads coherent but contains determinants whose evaluation falls to the executor at run time

Skip when:

The plan has no branches — nothing to resolve (run /plan-split-scan for structural audit instead)
Every branch is already in valid implementation-intention form (the skill will refuse)
The artifact is descriptive rather than prescriptive
Work is throwaway / exploratory

Why it exists
When an LLM encounters an unresolved if/then in a plan, it tends to pick one branch and proceed — usually the most training-data-typical one. The counterfactual branch is silently flattened. This skill exists to keep branches open and deterministic at execution time: by routing each unresolved branch to either an up-front resolution, a split into separate plans, or a Gollwitzer implementation intention with observable trigger and named response. The destructive-branch safety rule (never wrap a destructive op in conditional syntax) closes the asymmetric-cost case where a conditional firing produces irrecoverable state.
Related

.claude/skills/branch-resolve/SKILL.md — operational definition
implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans — canonical Gollwitzer if-then framework; trigger/response criteria; LLM-specific failure modes
task-decomposition-for-ai-plans — parent decomposition framework; Signal 3 is the upstream diagnostic
skill-plan-split-scan — the diagnostic that flags Signal 3; this skill is the action step on that signal
intent-engineering-discipline — many intent specs encode situational rules as implementation intentions; this skill is the per-rule authoring tool
bdi-architecture-for-coding-agents — implementation intentions live at the boundary between events and intentions in BDI vocabulary
skill-falsifiability-scan — adjacent operationalization move on claims about the world; composes with this skill on plans containing both
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/branch-resolve/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: branch-resolve
description: Operationalize each unresolved decision branch in a multi-step plan — route it to one of three resolutions in preference order: (1) resolve up front before issuing, (2) split into separate plans at the determinant, (3) express as a Gollwitzer implementation intention (IF observable trigger THEN named response). Apply the trigger criteria (observable, deterministic, falsifiable) and response criteria (specific, executable, bounded) when producing option 3. Force a hard split on any branch whose downstream contains a destructive or production-touching operation — never wrap those in conditional syntax. Use after `/plan-split-scan` flags a Signal-3 finding, or directly when a plan contains "if X then Y otherwise Z" or "depending on X, do Y or Z" branches whose evaluation will fall to the executor at run time. Counters branch-collapse — the failure mode where the LLM picks the most training-data-typical branch and silently flattens the counterfactual one.
---
 
Operationalize each unresolved decision branch in the plan at `$ARGUMENTS`. This skill is the **action** side of Signal 3 in `/plan-split-scan`: the diagnostic scan flags unresolved if/then branches; this skill routes each branch to one of three concrete resolutions in preference order. The dangerous case it targets: a plan with "if X exists then modify it; otherwise rewrite" that reads coherent on paper, where the executor at run time picks whichever branch the most training-data-typical reading suggests, and the counterfactual branch silently never runs.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most recently drafted plan in this session containing if/then conditional syntax
2. A Signal-3 finding emitted by a recent `/plan-split-scan` run
3. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it contains plan-shaped conditional content
4. Ask which plan to scan rather than guess
 
The canonical framework (Gollwitzer goal-vs-implementation intentions, trigger/response criteria, LLM-specific failure modes) lives in `knowledge/ai/implementation-intentions-for-ai-plans.md`. The parent decomposition framework lives in `knowledge/ai/task-decomposition-for-ai-plans.md`. Consult for rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke when a plan contains decision branches whose evaluation will fall to the executor:
 
- Multi-step plans with "if X then Y otherwise Z" conditional syntax
- ExitPlanMode drafts with unresolved branches before user confirmation
- `projects/**/plan.md` files containing run-time conditionals
- Signal-3 findings from a `/plan-split-scan` run
- Agent briefs that prescribe conditional execution
- Long Claude Code TODO lists with embedded branches
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Plans without branches — nothing to resolve (run `/plan-split-scan` for structural audit instead)
- Plans where every branch is already in valid implementation-intention form (observable trigger + specific response)
- Hypothetical / illustrative branches in knowledge notes (descriptive, not prescriptive)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` quick captures
- `journal/` entries
 
**Refuse-to-scan condition.** If the plan contains zero unresolved branches (every conditional is already either resolved, split, or in valid implementation-intention form), emit a one-line "no branches to resolve" and stop. Running the resolution exercise on already-resolved branches is itself an over-decomposition pattern.
 
## The three resolutions, in preference order
 
| # | Resolution | When to prefer | When not |
|---|---|---|---|
