```text
## 4. Deferred items
- <item> — <where deferred from>
- ...
OR
none
 
## 5. What to check first tomorrow
1. <highest-stakes item>
2. <next item>
3. <next item>
```
 
## Optional: append to persistent log
 
After producing the ledger, ask the user: "Append to `journal/commitments-log.md`?"
 
If yes, append the ledger to `journal/commitments-log.md` under a new `## <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM>` section header. The file is rolling and append-only — do not rewrite earlier entries, do not de-duplicate. **Re-read the file from disk immediately before appending** — the user hand-edits this log, and writing from a copy read earlier in the session can clobber a manual edit. If the file does not exist, create it with the format documented in its header.
 
If no, leave the ledger in chat only.
 
The user decides per-session whether the ledger warrants persistence. Not every session needs an audit trail.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Sycophantic progress narration.** The ledger is a load-transfer instrument, not an accomplishment summary. Do not write "Successfully completed X, Y, Z" — write what changed, what was assumed, what was deferred.
- **Section 2 always "none."** If section 2 is consistently empty across sessions, either the work was genuinely low-claim or the skill is underreporting. The latter is more likely. Re-check the conversation for phrases like "that library does X" or "the API returns Y" where no verification happened.
- **Rehashing the conversation.** Do not summarize turns. Extract state. The reader should be able to pick up from the ledger without re-reading the chat.
- **Editorializing.** No "great progress on," no "we accomplished." Factual and terse.
- **Padding to fill sections.** Empty section → say "none" and move on.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md` — the mechanism this skill operationalizes (accountability without authorship)
- `journal/commitments-log.md` — persistent rolling ledger, if the user opts to append
- `/reviewers-map` — per-output counterpart to this session-level skill

ai/skills/skill-concept-drift-scan.title: Skill: concept-drift-scan
ai/skills/skill-concept-drift-scan.content:
Skill: concept-drift-scan
Scan a codebase’s vocabulary for concept integrity — one concept, one name. A grep-based term census convicts synonym drift (one concept under several interchangeably-used terms) and homonym collisions (one term bound to unrelated concepts), ranks findings by blast radius, and recommends a canon per drifted concept chosen in fixed priority order: project glossary → boundary usage (API/schema) → majority. Never invents a fresh term. Emits a markdown report to the OS temp dir and stops before any rename.
The vocabulary lens on the locality axis skill-deepen-architecture scans: that skill flags one concept scattered across modules; this flags one concept scattered across names. Both taxes are paid by every reader — human or AI — who must learn that two things are actually one.
When to use

Naming feels inconsistent; readers must learn several words for one thing
Recurring rename debates that never settle for lack of a census
Before writing a project glossary or CONTEXT.md — the scan produces the evidence for it
Making a codebase more AI-navigable: synonym drift misleads retrieval and grep alike

Skip when:

The scattering is structural (one concept across modules) — /deepen-architecture
The term rotation is in prose, not identifiers — /prose-surgery
Vault notes disagree about an empirical claim — /contradiction-scan
You want the rename executed or its diff reviewed — downstream; /lean-review

Why it exists
Ubiquitous-language decay is gradual and unowned: each contributor’s synonym feels harmless, but every drifted term is a permanent tax on every future reader, and for AI navigation it is worse — retrieval and grep both miss half the concept’s occurrences. The scan’s core discipline is that interchangeability must be proven (same value under both names, converters that only rename), because the seductive failure mode is convicting a legitimate distinction — user vs customer may be two concepts, and a naming scan that flattens real distinctions does more damage than the drift. Convicted distinctions are recorded as legitimate so future runs don’t re-litigate them, mirroring the vault’s rejected-suggestions convention.
Related

.claude/skills/concept-drift-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-deepen-architecture — locality of code; this owns locality of vocabulary
skill-prose-surgery — the prose counterpart (term-reuse operation)
skill-contradiction-scan — cross-note disagreement; different corpus, same one-truth instinct
skill-lean-review — reviews the eventual rename diff

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/concept-drift-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-22. Re-sync on every body edit.

---
name: concept-drift-scan
description: Scan a codebase's vocabulary for concept integrity — one domain concept under several names (synonym drift, e.g. user/account/customer for the same entity) and one name doing double duty (homonym collision) — via a grep-based term census, ranked by blast radius as a markdown report with a reachable "vocabulary is coherent" clean verdict. Use when naming feels inconsistent, readers must learn several words for one thing, renames keep getting debated, or before writing a project glossary or CONTEXT.md. Recommends a canonical term per concept but stops at the report; does not perform renames. Distinct from /deepen-architecture (code locality — this is vocabulary locality), /prose-surgery (fixes term rotation in prose, not identifiers in code), and /contradiction-scan (vault notes disagreeing, not code naming). Counters ubiquitous-language decay — each new synonym taxing every future reader and misleading AI navigation.
---
 
Scan the vocabulary at `$ARGUMENTS` for concept integrity — one concept, one name — and rank drifted concepts by blast radius. The skill is a diagnostic-scan: it produces a ranked report with a recommended canon per drifted concept and **stops before any rename**. Executing renames is downstream work; reviewing the rename diff is `/lean-review`. The output is a markdown report written to the OS temp dir, never into the repo.
 
This is the vocabulary lens on the same locality axis `/deepen-architecture` scans: that skill flags one concept *scattered across modules*; this flags one concept *scattered across names*. Both taxes are paid by every reader — human or AI — who must learn that two things are actually one.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the codebase to scan, as any of:
 
- A repo root or a subtree path (`src/billing/`) to scope the census
- A free-text area name ("the checkout domain") to be resolved against the working repo
- Empty → the current working repo; if it is large, scope to the subtree most recently discussed this session
 
If no codebase is in scope, say so and ask for a path — do not invent a target.
 
## The fixed glossary (low-freedom — drift is forbidden)
 
Every finding must use these terms **verbatim** — a naming scan that drifts its own naming has no standing.
 
- **Concept** — one domain idea the code manipulates (an entity, an operation, a state).
- **Term** — a name used for it: identifier, type, file name, schema column, API field, doc heading.
- **Census** — the grep-based count of where each term occurs, and in which modules.
- **Synonym drift** — one concept carried by two or more terms used interchangeably.
- **Homonym collision** — one term bound to two or more unrelated concepts.
- **Canon** — the single term a drifted concept should converge on.
- **Blast radius** — occurrence count and module spread of the terms that would change if the canon won.
 
## The test battery (low-freedom — apply each verbatim)
 
1. **Synonym test.** For each core concept, census its candidate terms. Two or more terms are **drift only if used interchangeably** — the conviction requires evidence: the same value flowing under both names, converter functions that only rename, the same schema field surfaced under different identifiers. If the terms encode a real distinction (`user` the login vs `customer` the payer), that is *not* drift — record it as a legitimate distinction so it isn't re-flagged next run.
2. **Homonym test.** One term bound to two or more unrelated concepts (`order` = purchase and sort sequence). Evidence: two unrelated type definitions or usage clusters for the same word.
3. **Canon test.** For each convicted drift, pick the canon in fixed priority order: (1) the project glossary / `CONTEXT.md` term if one exists, (2) the term used at the outermost boundary (public API, schema, URL), (3) the majority term in the census. Never invent a fresh third term — the canon must already be in use.
 
## The procedure
 
Three bounded phases.
 
1. **Discover the concepts.** Read the domain's spine — core type/model definitions, schema, public API — plus `CONTEXT.md`/glossary if present, and list the core concepts (bounded: the ~10 most load-bearing, not an ontology of everything). High freedom here: what counts as core is discovered from the code, not from a checklist.
2. **Census & rank.** Grep the candidate terms per concept, apply the battery, and rank convicted findings by blast radius. Badge each: **strong-buy** (clear drift, canon obvious, radius manageable), **consider** (drift real but canon contested or radius large), **hold** (drift at a boundary you don't own — external API names, wire formats). **Stop here — recommend the canon, do not start renaming.**
3. **Report & hand off.** Emit the report (next section) to `<tmpdir>/conceptdrift-<timestamp>.md`, computing the timestamp at run time. If the user wants the canons recorded, offer to append a glossary section to the *target repo's* `CONTEXT.md` — only with their go-ahead, and never in this vault. Rename execution is downstream; `/lean-review` reviews the resulting diff.
 
Clean-verdict reachability: if each core concept has one term and each term one concept, return the **clean verdict** ("vocabulary is coherent"). Legitimate distinctions recorded in phase 2 do not count against it. Do not manufacture drift.
 
## Output format
 
A markdown report written to the temp dir:
 
```text
# Concept drift review — <repo / subtree>   (<timestamp>)
 
## Census scope
<concepts examined: N · glossary/CONTEXT.md: <present and honored | absent> · census method: grep over <file kinds>>
 
## Verdict
<strong-buy: N · consider: N · hold: N>   |   <clean: vocabulary is coherent — one term per concept, one concept per term>
 
## Legitimate distinctions (not drift — do not re-flag)
- <termA vs termB — the real difference they encode>
 
## Finding <n> — <concept>   [strong-buy | consider | hold]
- **Type:** <synonym drift | homonym collision>
- **Terms & census:** <term (N uses, M modules) · term (N, M) · …>
- **Interchangeability evidence:** <the converter / shared field / dual definition, quoted briefly>
- **Canon:** <term> — chosen by <glossary | boundary usage | majority>
- **Blast radius:** <total occurrences to change, modules touched>
 
## What this scan did not do
- Did not perform any rename (downstream; `/lean-review` the diff).
- Did not judge code structure (`/deepen-architecture`) or import direction (`/dependency-flow-scan`).
- Did not invent terms — every canon is already in use in the repo.
```
 
Definition of done: every finding carries a type, quoted interchangeability evidence, a canon with its selection rule, and a blast radius; legitimate distinctions are recorded; the report is in the temp dir.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Convicting a real distinction.** `user` vs `customer` may be two concepts. No interchangeability evidence, no finding — and record the distinction so future runs don't re-litigate it.
- **Inventing a canon.** Proposing a clean new term nobody uses. The canon comes from the glossary, the boundary, or the majority — in that order.
- **Keyword-only census.** Counting string matches without checking they refer to the concept (`state` the noun vs `state` the machine). The census counts *referring* uses.
- **Starting the rename.** The scan stops at the report. A drive-by rename of "just the easy ones" is the anti-pattern with a diff.
- **Ontology sprawl.** Cataloguing fifty concepts. Bounded: the ~10 load-bearing ones.
- **Writing the report into the repo.** Temp dir only; the optional glossary append goes to the target repo's `CONTEXT.md` with user go-ahead.
- **Padding.** The clean verdict is reachable and correct — use it.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Naming feels inconsistent; readers must learn several words for one thing
- Recurring rename debates that never settle for lack of a census
- Before writing a project glossary or `CONTEXT.md` — this scan produces the evidence for it
- Making a codebase more AI-navigable: synonym drift misleads retrieval and grep alike
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Structural locality — one concept scattered across modules — `/deepen-architecture`
- Term rotation in *prose* artifacts — `/prose-surgery` (its "reuse rotated terms" operation)
- Vault notes that disagree about a claim — `/contradiction-scan`
- Reviewing a rename diff — `/lean-review`
 
## Related
 
- `/deepen-architecture` — locality of code; this skill owns locality of vocabulary
- `/prose-surgery` — the prose counterpart of the synonym test (term reuse operation)
- `/dependency-flow-scan`, `/churn-hotspot-scan`, `/error-topology-scan`, `/test-shape-scan`, `/api-surface-scan` — the static-structure family
- `/lean-review` — reviews the eventual rename diff

ai/skills/skill-context-budget-scan.title: Skill: context-budget-scan
ai/skills/skill-context-budget-scan.content:
Skill: context-budget-scan
Three-mode scan of context-window economics — artifact (a static prompt, agent brief, CLAUDE.md fragment, or system-prompt section), architecture (an agent loop or design doc), or session (a conversation transcript) — for cache-unfriendly ordering, lost-in-middle placement, verbatim-instead-of-reference inclusion, memory-hierarchy misses, tool-output bloat, cross-layer redundancy, and missing compaction strategy. Operates on the token-economy axis: how the context budget is being spent against what it buys.
When to use

Before issuing a long prompt or agent brief that will run many times — cost compounds
Before deploying or substantially editing an agent loop / system prompt — Signal 7 (missing compaction) is cheapest to catch at design time
Before growing a persistent layer (CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/*.md, MEMORY.md) — Signal 4 (memory hierarchy) findings here pay every turn forever
When a Claude Code session has crossed a context-pressure stage (microcompaction triggered, response latency rising, output quality dropping)
After a session that produced poor output, to retrospectively identify the bloat

Skip when:

Short prompts (<500 tokens, single concern, no cache implication, no persistent layer) — token-economy is not the bottleneck
The question is comprehension (use density-scan)
The question is plan structure (use plan-split-scan)
The question is per-output verification (use reviewers-map)
Throwaway / exploratory work

Why it exists
Prompts and sessions grow monotonically — each addition feels like “just one more thing” until token cost, response latency, attention degradation, or autocompact damage the output. The failure is silent: each addition was individually justified, the aggregate violates cache boundaries, scatters load-bearing content into the lost-in-middle zone, duplicates persistent memory in-turn, or has no plan for what to evict. The scan names the seven structural signals (and the per-mode refuse-to-scan floors) so the budget decision is auditable, not vibes-based. Distinct axis from /density-scan (comprehension), /plan-split-scan (executor structure), /reviewers-map (output verification) — a prompt can be density-clean and budget-bloated, or vice versa.
Related

.claude/skills/context-budget-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
context-window-management — canonical backing note (compaction pipeline, lost-in-middle, memory hierarchy, cache-efficient structure)
information-density-for-llm-prompts — per-prompt density (comprehension axis); sibling note
system-prompt-design-principles — cache-efficient prompt structure (Signal 1 mechanism)
multi-agent-token-efficiency — cross-agent duplication; relevant for multi-agent architectures
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/context-budget-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: context-budget-scan
description: Three-mode scan of context-window economics — artifact mode (a static prompt, agent brief, CLAUDE.md fragment, or system-prompt section), architecture mode (an agent loop or design doc), or session mode (a conversation transcript) — for cache-unfriendly ordering, lost-in-middle placement, verbatim-instead-of-reference inclusion, memory-hierarchy misses, tool-output bloat, cross-layer redundancy, and missing compaction strategy. Returns ranked findings with mode-specific verdicts. Use when a prompt, brief, or CLAUDE.md feels bloated, when token cost or latency is rising, when a session approaches context overflow, or before deploying an agent design that hasn't decided what to evict. Different axis from `/density-scan` (reader comprehension cost inside a prompt), `/plan-split-scan` (executor-side plan structure), and `/reviewers-map` (per-output verification) — this is the token-economy axis on the context budget. Counters prompts and sessions growing until cost, latency, or autocompact damage output.
---
 
Scan the target at `$ARGUMENTS` for context-budget pathology — token spending that does not buy proportional value, cache-unfriendly structure, or accumulated noise that degrades attention. This skill operates on the **token-economy** axis: how the context budget is being spent against what it buys. Sibling axes: `/density-scan` (comprehension cost inside a prompt — orthogonal: a prompt can be density-clean and budget-bloated, or budget-clean and density-bloated), `/plan-split-scan` (executor-side plan structure), `/reviewers-map` (per-output verification). The dangerous case this skill targets: a prompt, brief, or session whose content all looks individually justified yet whose aggregate violates cache boundaries, scatters load-bearing content into the lost-in-middle zone, duplicates persistent memory in-turn, or has no plan for what to evict — paid for in money, latency, and silently-degraded output quality.
 
The canonical mechanism research (compaction pipeline, lost-in-middle U-curve, memory hierarchy, cache-efficient prompt structure) lives in `knowledge/ai/context-window-management.md`. Companion notes: `knowledge/ai/information-density-for-llm-prompts.md` (per-prompt density), `knowledge/ai/system-prompt-design-principles.md` (cache-efficient structure), `knowledge/ai/multi-agent-token-efficiency.md` (cross-agent duplication). Consult for rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Three modes
 
Invoke with an explicit mode or let the target infer it:
 
- **artifact** — a static prompt, agent brief, CLAUDE.md fragment, system-prompt section, or any text artifact that will be issued as context. Easiest to scan statically.
- **architecture** — an agent loop, design doc, or system spec describing how context accumulates across turns. Catches structural failures (no per-tool budget, no compaction strategy, missing memory hierarchy).
- **session** — a conversation transcript or current session state. Detects accumulated bloat, redundant re-reads, missed compaction opportunities, and degraded-response signals.
 
Modes share signal vocabulary but have different scoping rules and verdicts.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- `artifact <path>` or just `<path>` — a file or section; read and scan
- `architecture <path>` — a design doc, agent spec, or `.claude/skills/<n>/SKILL.md`-like configuration
- `session` (no path) — the current conversation
- Literal text, usually quoted or fenced (defaults to artifact mode)
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty and no mode is named, infer in this order:
 
1. The most recent draft prompt, brief, or `.claude/**/*.md` file edited in this session → **artifact**
2. A `projects/**/agent-*.md` or design-doc style file in the largest staged diff → **architecture**
3. If a long-running session is visible and the user just asked about token cost → **session**
4. If nothing fits, ask which target rather than guess
 
This is a review pass. **Do not modify the target.**
 
## Scope per mode
 
### Artifact mode — invoke on
 
- Long prompts (>2K tokens) about to be sent or baked into a spec
- Agent briefs being passed to subagents via the Agent tool
- `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, or other persistent context files being grown or restructured
- System-prompt fragments in API-based agent code
- Any context file where size growth has been monotonic and a trim is overdue
 
### Architecture mode — invoke on
 
- Agent design docs (loop, tool inventory, memory strategy)
- New skill SKILL.md files that prescribe tool-output handling
- Multi-agent coordination plans (where cross-agent duplication is a known failure mode)
- Refactor proposals for existing agents that touch context-management
 
### Session mode — invoke on
 
- A Claude Code session that has crossed a context-pressure stage (microcompaction triggered, response quality dropping, latency increasing)
- A long session where the user is debating whether to continue, compact, or restart
- An audit of a recent session that produced poor output, to retrospectively identify what bloated the context
 
**Do not invoke on:**
 
- Short prompts (<500 tokens) with one purpose — token-economy is not the bottleneck
- Pure prose where readability is the question (route to `/density-scan`)
- Per-claim verification of an already-produced output (route to `/reviewers-map`)
- Plan structure questions (route to `/plan-split-scan`)
- Frontmatter-only or formatting-only changes
- Throwaway / exploratory artifacts
 
**Refuse-to-scan conditions:**
 
- **Artifact**: <1K tokens, single concern, no cache implication, no persistent layer (CLAUDE.md/MEMORY.md) involved
- **Architecture**: trivial agent (single tool, no loop, no memory layer)
- **Session**: <20 turns, no tool output >2K tokens, no degraded-response observation, model still well under window pressure
 
If the refuse condition fires, emit a one-line "no scan needed — context budget is not the bottleneck for this target" and stop. The refuse exists because over-applying budget advice is itself an extraneous-load pattern.
 
**Override the refuse if any of these are present** (regardless of size): explicit user request for the scan, a prompt that will run many times (cost compounds), a persistent layer being grown, or a session with observed quality degradation.
 
## Step 0 — declare model + window
 
Budget pressure is model-dependent. Before scanning, declare in one line (model names as of 2026-06 — the window-size classes are the durable anchor if the lineup has shifted):
 
- **Claude Opus / Sonnet 4.x (1M window)** — pressure starts ~200K input tokens; quality cliff much later. Tolerates more bloat but cost is real per turn.
- **GPT-4o / similar 128K models** — practical pressure ~50K; "lost in the middle" already biting at 64K. Findings tighten significantly past 30K.
- **Local 32K models** — pressure starts ~8–10K; quality cliff sharp. Strictest envelope; every signal applies; verbatim-instead-of-reference findings are near-always high severity.
- **Cache-bound** — model is API-cached (Anthropic prompt cache, OpenAI cached prefix). Signal 1 (cache-unfriendly ordering) becomes the dominant axis; cache miss is paid in dollars every variant.
 
The model declaration sets which findings are real and which are noise. Findings without a declared model are uncalibrated.
 
## The seven structural signals
 
Each signal names a pattern that wastes context budget, causes cache miss, degrades attention, or accelerates context pressure. Mode-applicability noted per row.
 
| # | Signal | Detection signature | Modes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Cache-unfriendly ordering** | Variable / dynamic content placed before static / cached content (system prompt, tool definitions, persistent rules). Every dynamic variation invalidates the downstream cache. | artifact, architecture |
| 2 | **Lost-in-middle placement** | Load-bearing instructions or constraints positioned in 30–70% of total content. U-curve attention decay means middle content is effectively de-weighted. | artifact, session |
| 3 | **Verbatim-instead-of-reference** | Inline blobs (full files, log dumps, large data, prior outputs) included verbatim when a reference (path + line range, fetch-on-demand pointer, summary) would suffice. | artifact, session |
| 4 | **Memory-hierarchy miss** | Cross-session-stable content (project rules, identity, conventions) in turn-by-turn context, paying token cost every turn, instead of in a persistent layer (CLAUDE.md, MEMORY.md, project rules). | artifact, architecture |
| 5 | **Tool-output bloat** | Tool design or invocation that returns raw output without summarization, truncation, or structured filtering. `grep` returning 200 lines; `git diff` against the whole repo; `find /` etc. | architecture, session |
| 6 | **Cross-layer redundancy** | Same constraint, instruction, or fact stated across multiple layers (system prompt + CLAUDE.md + agent brief + per-message instruction). Each restatement pays tokens; net informational gain is near-zero past the second mention. | artifact, architecture |
| 7 | **Missing compaction strategy** | No plan for what to evict as context grows. Architecture assumes infinite window. Session has no summarize-and-continue checkpoint. Stage 4 autocompact becomes the only line of defense and damages output unpredictably. | architecture, session |
 
**Signal 1 is special when cache is in scope.** A single cache-unfriendly ordering finding can dominate the verdict for an artifact that will run thousands of times — the dollar cost compounds where other signals do not.
 
**Signal 7 is special for architecture and long sessions.** Missing compaction strategy is not a token-bloat finding per se; it is an *absence of a stage transition*. The failure mode is delayed (manifests at context overflow, not on the next request) and asymmetric in cost (autocompact silently summarizes and may drop the part you needed).
 
**Signal 3 is the most common artifact finding** and the easiest to fix surgically: replace inline content with a reference. The user's MCP filesystem can fetch on demand; the in-context blob almost never earns its tokens.
 
## Severity per finding
 
- **low** — token waste of <5% of the target's total budget, or signal-1 ordering issue on uncached usage; routine optimization
- **medium** — noticeable cost, latency, or quality loss; clear win to fix before issuing/deploying
- **high** — likely cache miss with compounding cost, imminent context-pressure stage transition, load-bearing instruction in lost-in-middle zone, or memory-hierarchy violation that will pay every turn forever
 
**Signal 1 findings on cached usage are at least medium.** Signal 4 findings on persistent layers are at least medium (the cost is per-turn-forever). Signal 7 findings are at least medium in architecture mode (missing strategy doesn't bite until it does, and then it's expensive).
 
## Verdicts per mode
 
### Artifact mode
 
- **Budget-clean** — zero high-severity findings, no Signal 1 hits on cached usage, no Signal 4 hits on persistent layers. Token spend is proportional to value.
- **Tune** — surgical fixes. Convert one or two inline blobs to references; reorder one section for cache. The artifact's structure is sound.
- **Restructure** — Signal 1 (cache ordering) or Signal 4 (memory hierarchy) findings require moving content across layers, not just trimming. Name the layer move explicitly.
 
### Architecture mode
 
- **Design-clean** — agent loop has named eviction/summarization policy, tool-output budgets, and memory hierarchy. Signal 7 explicitly addressed.
- **Strategy-gap** — one or more stage transitions missing (e.g., no microcompaction policy, no per-tool output cap). Name the missing stage.
- **Restructure** — load-bearing memory-hierarchy or tool-output discipline issue requires redesigning a layer, not just adding a policy.
 
### Session mode
 
- **Continue** — context still well under pressure for the declared model; observed response quality unaffected; no high-severity bloat findings.
- **Compact** — recommend summarize-and-continue checkpoint. Name what to preserve verbatim (last 3–5 turns + active file refs + load-bearing constraints) and what to summarize (older tool outputs, completed-and-shipped subtasks).
- **Restart** — context past quality cliff for the declared model, or autocompact has triggered and meaningfully degraded output. Recommend new session with explicit carry-forward (state summary, open todos, next-action commitment). This is the rare verdict; default to Compact when uncertain.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Identify the mode** (explicit `$ARGUMENTS` prefix, or inferred from target).
2. **Read the target.** For artifact: full content, skip frontmatter. For architecture: the design / loop / tool inventory sections. For session: the conversation transcript or visible session state.
3. **Apply the refuse-to-scan check** for the identified mode. If under threshold and no override condition fires, emit the one-line refuse and stop.
4. **Declare the model + window** from Step 0.
5. **Scan for each applicable signal** (table above; not every signal applies to every mode).
6. **Estimate token cost where load-bearing** — for Signal 3 (verbatim blobs) and Signal 4 (persistent-layer misses), estimate the per-instance or per-turn cost. Use the 4-chars-per-token heuristic if no precise counter is available; label as estimate.
7. **Compile findings.** Dedupe across signals (one span may hit multiple — assign the dominant one).
8. **Rank by severity, then by load-bearingness within severity.** Cap at 8 findings.
9. **For each finding**, give: signal number, severity, location (line range or quoted span), one-line reason with token-cost estimate where relevant, recommended action (convert to reference / move to persistent layer / reorder for cache / cap tool output / add compaction stage / consolidate restatement / leave alone).
10. **Issue verdict** for the identified mode. Two-line max rationale.
11. **Note explicitly what you checked and didn't find.** Signals with no findings get one line of "checked: clean — <one-line reason>".
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Context-budget scan — <target> (<mode>)
 
## 0. Model + window
<Opus 1M | Sonnet 1M | GPT-4o 128K | local 32K | cache-bound> — <one-line cue>
 
## 1. Findings (ranked)
1. **[Signal N | severity]** <location>
   <one-line reason; include ~<N> tokens estimate where load-bearing>
   *Action:* <convert to reference (fetch path X) | move to persistent layer Y | reorder section Z before cache boundary | cap tool output to N tokens | add summarize-and-continue checkpoint | consolidate restatement of constraint W | leave alone>
2. **[Signal N | severity]** <location>
   ...
[cap at 8]
 
## 2. Signals checked, no findings
- Signal <N>: <one-line note on what you scanned for and why it's clean>
- ...
 
## 3. Verdict
**<mode-appropriate verdict>**
<one or two-line rationale; if Restructure or Strategy-gap, name the layer move or missing stage>
```
 
If the refuse-to-scan check fires at step 3, emit only:
 
```text
# Context-budget scan — <target> (<mode>)
 
**No scan needed.** <one-line reason: under token threshold, no cache implication, no persistent layer, no pressure observed>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing findings to look thorough.** If the target is budget-clean, report it clean. A scan that pads erodes the discipline. Two real findings beat eight manufactured ones.
- **Confusing this with `/density-scan`.** Density-scan asks "would the reader struggle to parse this?" — comprehension axis. Budget-scan asks "are tokens being spent that would buy more elsewhere?" — economy axis. A prompt can be density-clean and budget-bloated (good prose, 50KB of irrelevant boilerplate). A prompt can be budget-clean and density-bloated (short but with surprisal spikes). If the artifact is being scanned for readability, route to `/density-scan`.
- **Running on prompts below the refuse threshold.** A 300-token prompt with one purpose and no cache implication does not have a context-budget problem worth scanning.
- **Treating all signals as equally weighted.** Signal 1 (cache) dominates on cached high-volume usage. Signal 4 (memory hierarchy) compounds per turn. Signal 7 (missing compaction) is delayed-bite. Calibrate severity against the consumption pattern, not signal count.
- **Recommending in-context content where reference-by-pointer is cleaner.** The MCP filesystem and the Claude Code project context exist precisely so that load-bearing content can live on disk and be fetched. If a finding's fix is "move this paragraph elsewhere in the prompt," check whether the real fix is "move it out of context entirely."
- **Skipping the model declaration.** Step 0 is load-bearing. A 50K-token prompt is comfortable on Opus 1M and disastrous on a local 32K. Findings without a declared model are uncalibrated.
- **Confusing total length with budget pathology.** Long context is not automatically a problem on 1M-window models. The signals are the rubric, not the line count.
- **Conflating cache misses with bloat.** Signal 1 (cache-unfriendly ordering) is not about content size; it's about content *position*. A 2KB section in the wrong position can invalidate 50KB of cached content downstream. The fix is ordering, not trimming.
- **Recommending Restart when Compact would do.** Restart is destructive; Compact is recoverable. Default to Compact; reserve Restart for sessions where the model has demonstrably degraded (wrong answers on previously-correct material, persistent confusion about state). The cost asymmetry favors Compact unless the evidence for irrecoverable degradation is strong.
- **Treating Signal 7 (missing compaction) as urgent.** Missing-compaction findings are *design debt*, not active fires. They become urgent at context-pressure stages but are otherwise medium severity. Don't escalate them past evidence.
- **Tagging tool-output bloat in a session as architecture failure.** Mode-appropriate framing matters. In session mode, Signal 5 is "this conversation accumulated tool noise — compact it." In architecture mode, Signal 5 is "this tool's design lacks a budget — change the design." Same signal, different fix family.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before issuing a long prompt or agent brief that will run many times — cost compounds
- Before deploying or substantially editing an agent loop / system prompt — Signal 7 (missing compaction) is cheapest to catch at design time
- Before growing a persistent layer (`CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, `MEMORY.md`) — Signal 4 (memory hierarchy) findings here pay every turn forever
- When a Claude Code session has crossed a context-pressure stage (microcompaction triggered, response latency rising, output quality dropping) — session mode
- After a session that produced poor output, to retrospectively identify the bloat — session mode retrospective
- Composes with `/density-scan` on instructional artifacts: density is comprehension, budget is economy; both can fire
- Composes with `/plan-split-scan` on agent briefs: plan-structure × budget are different axes; both apply
- Composes with `/reviewers-map` *after* execution when investigating quality degradation: this scan checks the input budget; reviewers-map checks the output
 
Skip when: the target is below the refuse threshold, the question is comprehension (use `/density-scan`), the question is plan structure (use `/plan-split-scan`), the question is per-output verification (use `/reviewers-map`), or the work is throwaway / exploratory.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/context-window-management.md` — canonical backing note (compaction pipeline, lost-in-middle, memory hierarchy, cache-efficient structure, model-specific envelopes); consult for rationale
- `knowledge/ai/information-density-for-llm-prompts.md` — per-prompt density (comprehension axis); sibling note to this skill
- `knowledge/ai/system-prompt-design-principles.md` — cache-efficient prompt structure (Signal 1 mechanism)
- `knowledge/ai/multi-agent-token-efficiency.md` — cross-agent duplication; relevant when scanning multi-agent architectures
- `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md` — receiver-side load; orthogonal axis (reviewer load, not budget)
- `/density-scan` — comprehension cost in a prompt, orthogonal axis
- `/plan-split-scan` — executor-side plan structure, orthogonal axis
- `/reviewers-map` — per-output verification, orthogonal axis
- `/red-team` — adversarial truth, not budget

ai/skills/skill-contradiction-scan.title: Skill: contradiction-scan
ai/skills/skill-contradiction-scan.content:
Skill: contradiction-scan
Scan a cluster of notes — a seed note’s link/tag neighborhood, a topic folder, or a tag — for pairs that silently disagree about the same fact, number, or claim. The skill assembles the note-neighborhood, extracts load-bearing empirical claims across the set, matches same-proposition pairs, and classifies each as agreement / tension / direct-contradiction / stale-superseded. It emits a conflict ledger — both note paths, both claims quoted, the reconciling regime (if any), and a resolution prompt — and stops. It reports; it never rewrites. The only skill in the catalog that ingests more than one note and reasons over the pair.
When to use

Auditing an aging, high-traffic topic cluster (folder or tag) for internal consistency
Integrating a new or substantially-edited note into a dense cluster — does it contradict what’s already there?
Before treating a belief that recurs across several notes as settled enough to build a decision on
Periodic corpus-maintenance, paired with /staleness-decay-scan (this catches disagreement; that catches expiry)

Skip when:

The input is one artifact (use /red-team, /reviewers-map, /bias-scan-human, /falsifiability-scan)
Claim-type triage on one note (use /claim-function-scan)
The artifact is a task queue (use /whittle-scan)
The assembled neighborhood has fewer than 2 notes, or no two share an overlapping empirical claim (refuse-to-scan)

Why it exists
Distributed inconsistency is the failure mode the scan counters — the memory-layer-specific decay where two notes written months apart each assert something about the same proposition, they disagree, and because you only ever read one note at a time the conflict is invisible. The vault asserts both X and not-X, a retriever surfaces whichever ranks higher, and the contradiction is trusted precisely because it lives in the persistent memory layer. No single-note skill can reach this: the unit of analysis is the note-pair across a retrieved set, and assembling that set is the mechanical work the skill automates. Three disciplines keep it from generating noise — report-don’t-rewrite (a ledger, never an edit, so one wrong inference can’t propagate corpus-wide), empirical-only (only truth-dependent claims can contradict; framing differences and deliberately-held alternatives don’t), and name-the-regime (two claims true in different contexts aren’t in conflict — a forced contradiction is the corpus analogue of a fabricated finding). See knowledge-base-entropy for the backing concept.
Related

.claude/skills/contradiction-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
knowledge-base-entropy — backing concept; this skill operationalizes decay mode 1 (distributed inconsistency)
skill-staleness-decay-scan — sibling corpus scan; this catches cross-note disagreement, that catches single-note expiry
skill-claim-function-scan — run its empirical/non-empirical cut first; only empirical claims can contradict
skill-red-team, skill-reviewers-map — single-artifact axis; route there when the input is one document
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/contradiction-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: contradiction-scan
description: Scan two or more notes — a seed note's link/tag neighborhood, a topic folder, or a tag — for pairs of different notes that silently disagree about the same fact, number, or claim. Pairwise-classifies same-proposition claims (agreement / tension / direct-contradiction / stale-superseded) and emits a conflict ledger with both paths and claims quoted — a ledger, never a rewrite. Use when auditing an aging cluster for internal consistency, before integrating a new note into a dense cluster, or before treating a repeated vault belief as settled. The only skill that reasons over note-pairs — distinct from `/claim-function-scan` (claim type on one note), `/red-team` (one artifact's adversarial critique, incl. a single note's self-contradiction), `/bias-scan-human` (one author's biases), and `/staleness-decay-scan` (single-note expiry over time). Skip for single-artifact review, a queue of tasks (`/whittle-scan`), or fewer than 2 notes sharing an overlapping claim. Counters distributed inconsistency.
---
 
Scan a cluster of notes for pairs that silently disagree about the same proposition — the distributed-inconsistency decay mode in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`. The dangerous case: two notes written months apart each assert something about the same fact (a number, a date, a capability, a causal claim), they disagree, and because you only ever read one note at a time the conflict is invisible — the vault asserts both X and not-X, a retriever surfaces whichever ranks higher, and the contradiction is trusted because it lives in the memory layer. This skill assembles the note-neighborhood, extracts the load-bearing empirical claims, finds the pairs that conflict, and emits a **conflict ledger** — both paths, both claims, a classification, and a resolution prompt. It reports; it never rewrites.
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is a seed note path, a folder, or a `#tag`. If empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. A note or cluster named in the current session
2. The most-recently-modified note's neighborhood
3. Ask which cluster to scan rather than guess
 
## Assembling the neighborhood
 
The unit of analysis is the **note-pair across a retrieved set**, not a single artifact. Build the set first:
 
- **From a seed note:** its outbound `[[wiki-links]]`, its backlinks (grep the vault for links *to* it), and same-`tags:` notes. Cap at ~15 notes; if larger, scope to the seed's direct link neighborhood and say so.
- **From a folder or tag:** all notes in it (e.g. `knowledge/finance/`, or every note tagged `solana`).
 
Use Glob/Grep/Read to assemble the set. Read the relevant sections, not necessarily whole files.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A topic cluster being audited for internal consistency (a folder, a tag, a seed note's neighborhood)
- A new or just-edited note about to join a dense cluster — does it contradict the existing notes?
- A frequently-repeated vault belief, before building on it as settled
- A periodic consistency pass over an aging, high-traffic cluster
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A single artifact under review (use `/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`, `/bias-scan-human`, `/falsifiability-scan`)
- Claim-type triage on one note (use `/claim-function-scan`)
- A queue of tasks/projects (use `/whittle-scan`)
- Prose readability or density (use `/density-scan`)
 
**Refuse-to-scan condition.** If the assembled neighborhood has fewer than 2 notes, or no two notes share an overlapping empirical claim, there is nothing to compare — say so in one line and stop. Do not manufacture a conflict to justify the run.
 
## What counts as a conflict
 
Only **empirical, truth-dependent claims** can contradict in the sense this skill cares about. Apply the `/claim-function-scan` cut first: a difference in framing, emphasis, recommendation, or a deliberately-held alternative view is **not** a contradiction. Classify each same-proposition pair into one of four states:
 
| State | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct contradiction** | Both claims are empirical, about the same proposition, and cannot both be true in the same regime | *(illustrative)* Note A: "X is ~400ms"; Note B: "X is ~2.5s" with no version/regime distinction |
| **Tension** | The claims pull against each other but a regime, scope, or date distinction may reconcile them | A says a tool is "the standard"; B treats a different tool as standard — possibly different contexts |
| **Stale-superseded** | One claim explicitly or by date supersedes the other; not a contradiction, a versioning event | An older "as of 2026-Q1" figure vs a newer "as of 2026-Q2" figure |
| **Agreement** | The claims corroborate — recorded only to confirm the pair was checked, not flagged | — |
 
The load-bearing discipline: **name the regime.** Two claims each true in a different context (different time, scope, assumption, or version) are not in conflict — say what distinguishes them rather than forcing a contradiction. A forced contradiction is the corpus-scan analogue of a fabricated finding.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Assemble the neighborhood** per the section above. Count notes. If fewer than 2, refuse-to-scan.
2. **Extract load-bearing empirical claims** from each note — the factual, numeric, dated, or causal assertions, not the framing. Skip non-empirical claims (coordination, narrative, identity) per the `/claim-function-scan` cut.
3. **Match same-proposition pairs.** Group claims that are *about the same thing* across notes. Only matched pairs can conflict; unmatched claims are not findings.
4. **Classify each matched pair** into direct-contradiction / tension / stale-superseded / agreement.
5. **For each non-agreement pair, write a ledger entry** — both note paths, both claims quoted verbatim, the classification, the regime that might reconcile it (or "none — genuine conflict"), and a one-line **resolution prompt** (which note is likely correct, or what to check). Never edit the notes.
6. **Order by severity** — direct contradictions first, then tensions, then stale-superseded.
7. **State coverage honestly.** If you capped the neighborhood or read only sections, say which notes/sections were *not* compared. Silent truncation reads as "checked everything" when it didn't.
 
## Verdict states
 
Pick one:
 
- **Contradictions found** — at least one direct contradiction between two empirical claims with no reconciling regime.
- **Tensions only** — pairs pull against each other but each may be reconcilable by a named regime; no hard contradiction.
- **Stale-superseded only** — the only conflicts are versioning events (older fact vs newer); route the stale side to `/staleness-decay-scan`.
- **Consistent** — matched claims corroborate or are cleanly regime-separated; no flags.
- **Neighborhood too small** — fewer than 2 notes or no overlapping empirical claims; refuse-to-scan.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /contradiction-scan — <seed/folder/tag> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Neighborhood
<N notes>: <list paths>
<Coverage note: capped at X / read sections only / full — name what was NOT compared>
 
## Conflict ledger
### Direct contradictions
1. **<proposition>**
   - `<note A path>`: "<claim A quoted>"
   - `<note B path>`: "<claim B quoted>"
   - Reconciling regime: <none — genuine conflict | the distinction that would reconcile>
   - Resolution prompt: <which is likely right / what to verify>
 
### Tensions
1. **<proposition>** — `<A>` vs `<B>`: <one line>. Likely reconciled by: <regime>. Resolution prompt: <one line>
 
### Stale-superseded
1. **<proposition>** — `<older>` superseded by `<newer>`. Route to `/staleness-decay-scan`.
 
## Checked-and-consistent
<count> matched claim-pairs corroborated (not listed individually unless useful).
 
## Verdict
**<Contradictions found | Tensions only | Stale-superseded only | Consistent | Neighborhood too small>**
<one-line rationale>
```
 
If the verdict is **Neighborhood too small**, emit only:
 
```text
# /contradiction-scan — <target>
 
**Neighborhood too small.** <N notes / no overlapping empirical claims>; nothing to compare.
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Rewriting instead of reporting.** The skill emits a ledger and stops. It never edits a note to resolve a conflict — resolution is a human judgment, and an auto-rewrite is how one wrong inference propagates corpus-wide. (Decay-discipline #1 in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`.)
- **Flagging framing as contradiction.** Two notes emphasizing different things, recommending different approaches, or holding different non-empirical views are not contradicting. Only truth-dependent claims about the same proposition qualify. Run the `/claim-function-scan` cut first.
- **Forced contradiction (regime blindness).** Two claims true in different regimes (different dates, versions, scopes, assumptions) are not in conflict. Name the regime instead of forcing a flag. This is the corpus analogue of the fabricated-finding failure mode.
- **Treating supersession as contradiction.** An older fact and its newer correction are a versioning event, not a disagreement — classify stale-superseded and route the stale side to `/staleness-decay-scan`. Flagging it as a contradiction creates noise and implies a problem the author already fixed.
- **Unmatched-claim padding.** A claim that appears in only one note cannot conflict with anything. Only matched same-proposition pairs are findings; don't list singletons.
- **Silent truncation.** If the neighborhood was capped or only sections were read, say so. A ledger that looks complete but skipped half the cluster is worse than one that admits its bound.
- **Whole-vault scanning.** This is a *cluster* tool. Pointing it at all 200+ notes produces a shallow, low-precision pass. Scope to a neighborhood, tag, or folder.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Auditing an aging, high-traffic topic cluster (a folder or tag with many notes accreted over months) for internal consistency
- Integrating a new or substantially-edited note into a dense cluster — check it doesn't contradict the existing set before committing
- Before treating a belief that recurs across several notes as settled enough to build a decision on
- Periodic corpus-maintenance, paired with `/staleness-decay-scan` (this catches disagreement; that catches expiry)
 
Skip when: the input is one artifact (use `/red-team` / `/reviewers-map` / `/bias-scan-human`), it's a task queue (use `/whittle-scan`), or the neighborhood is too small to have a pair.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy` — the backing concept; this skill operationalizes decay mode 1 (distributed inconsistency). The report-don't-rewrite, empirical-only, name-the-regime disciplines are defined there.
- `/staleness-decay-scan` — the sibling corpus scan; this catches cross-note *disagreement*, that catches single-note *expiry*. Stale-superseded findings route there.
- `/claim-function-scan` — run its empirical/non-empirical cut first; only empirical claims can contradict. That works on one note; this works on the pair.
- `/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`, `/bias-scan-human` — single-artifact axis; route there when the input is one document, not a cluster.
- `/falsifiability-scan` — per-claim testability on one artifact; orthogonal to cross-note consistency.
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-contradiction-scan` — the reference note for this skill.

ai/skills/skill-deepen-architecture.title: Skill: deepen-architecture
ai/skills/skill-deepen-architecture.content:
Skill: deepen-architecture
Diagnose a codebase’s static module structure and rank deepening refactors — turning shallow modules (interface nearly as complex as the implementation) into deep ones (a lot of behaviour behind a small interface). Uses a fixed glossary and a three-test battery (deletion test, interface-is-the-test-surface, one/two-adapter rule), emits a markdown + Mermaid report of ranked candidates to the OS temp dir, and stops at the design boundary — it hands the chosen candidate to /grill and /plan-options rather than designing or writing code itself.
House-native port of Matt Pocock’s improve-codebase-architecture (see the source capture): it keeps the two transferable mechanisms that note flags — the fixed glossary (anti-synonym-drift) and the deletion test — translates his HTML report into a markdown+Mermaid one, makes the per-repo CONTEXT.md/ADR glossary optional-if-present, and delegates his hand-rolled grilling loop and “design it twice” pass to the owned /grill and /plan-options.
When to use

The user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, or reduce tight coupling
Consolidating modules that leak across their seams; making a codebase more testable through its interfaces
Making a codebase more AI-navigable — fewer shallow modules to bounce between to understand one concept
The user names “shallow modules”, “deep modules”, “deepening”, or pure functions extracted only for testability

Skip when:

Behaviour recurs over time and the issue is standing structure, not static code shape — /structural-trace
You want a correctness review of a diff (/lean-review) or a merge call on an AI-authored diff (/ai-diff-judgment)
A candidate is already chosen and you want to design its interface — /grill (and /plan-options)
You want the refactor actually performed — this skill stops at the ranked report

Why it exists
A codebase drifts into many shallow modules — interfaces nearly as wide as the implementations behind them — that leak across their seams, can’t be tested through their declared interface, and force a reader (human or AI) to bounce between files to understand one concept. Nothing in the owned catalog diagnosed static code structure: the toolkit is thinking/verification-focused, /structural-trace diagnoses system behaviour over time, and the code-review skills judge a diff for correctness rather than the whole codebase for new structure. The source-skill capture tagged this capability “novel — no analogue in the owned set”; this skill fills that gap, prescriptively (ranked candidates with a recommendation badge) and with a reachable clean verdict so it doesn’t manufacture findings on an already-deep codebase.
Related

.claude/skills/deepen-architecture/SKILL.md — operational definition
improve-codebase-architecture — the source skill this ports (glossary, deletion test, dependency-category taxonomy)
skill-structural-trace — the dynamic-behaviour sibling; this is its static-code-structure counterpart
skill-lean-review, skill-ai-diff-judgment — per-diff correctness; this proposes whole-codebase structure
skill-grill — the interactive design loop this hands the chosen candidate to
skill-plan-options — the multi-constraint “design it twice” generator for the chosen candidate
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/deepen-architecture/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08. Re-sync on every body edit.

---
name: deepen-architecture
description: Diagnose a codebase's static module structure and rank deepening refactors — turning shallow modules (interface ≈ implementation) into deep ones (much behaviour behind a small interface), via a fixed glossary and the deletion test, as a markdown report of ranked candidates with a reachable "already deep" clean verdict. Use when you want to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, reduce tight coupling, make a codebase more testable or AI-navigable, or hunt shallow modules and leaky seams. Stops at the ranked report; does not write code. Distinct from /structural-trace (system behaviour over time via loops and archetypes, not static code), /lean-review and /ai-diff-judgment (judge a diff for correctness, not the whole codebase for new structure), and /grill and /plan-options (the design-phase skills it hands the chosen candidate to). Counters shallow-module sprawl — many thin modules that leak across their seams and can't be tested through their interface.
---
 
Diagnose the architecture at `$ARGUMENTS` and rank **deepening** candidates — shallow modules worth consolidating into deep ones. The skill is a diagnostic-scan: it produces a ranked report and **stops at the design boundary**. It does not design the new interfaces (that's `/grill`) and it does not write or review code (that's `/lean-review`). The output is a markdown report written to the OS temp dir, never into the repo.
 
This is the static-code-structure counterpart to `/structural-trace`: that skill diagnoses *system behaviour over time* (loops, archetypes, leverage) and stays non-prescriptive; this one diagnoses *static module shape* and is explicitly prescriptive — it ranks candidates with a recommendation badge.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the codebase to diagnose, as any of:
 
- A repo root or a subtree path (`src/payments/`) to scope the walk
- A free-text area name ("the auth layer") to be resolved against the working repo
- Empty → the current working repo; if it is large, scope to the subtree most recently discussed this session
 
If no codebase is in scope (e.g. invoked inside this knowledge vault with no target repo), say so and ask for a path — do not invent a target.
 
## The fixed glossary (low-freedom — drift is forbidden)
 
Every finding must use these eight terms **verbatim**. Synonym drift ("component", "service", "API", "boundary", "layer") is the cardinal failure mode — consistent language is what makes candidates comparable across a report and across sessions.
 
- **Module** — a unit with an interface and an implementation behind it. The thing under diagnosis.
- **Interface** — what a caller must understand to use the module: signatures, names, required call order, leaked types.
- **Implementation** — everything behind the interface the caller does *not* need to understand.
- **Depth** — the ratio of hidden implementation to exposed interface. *A lot of behaviour behind a small interface = deep.* Adopt depth-**as-leverage**, not Ousterhout's lines-of-code ratio.
- **Seam** — a place where the module is substituted for testing or for an alternate implementation.
- **Adapter** — a concrete implementation that sits across a seam (the production one, the test one).
- **Leverage** — how much a caller accomplishes per unit of interface it must learn. Deep modules have high leverage.
- **Locality** — how much of one concept lives in one place versus being scattered across modules a reader must bounce between.
 
If the target repo has a `CONTEXT.md` glossary or area ADRs, read them first and **extend** this glossary with the project's domain terms — do not require their existence and do not create them.
 
## The test battery (low-freedom — apply each verbatim)
 
1. **Deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module and inlining it at every caller. If complexity *vanishes*, it was a pass-through — flag it as shallow. If complexity *reappears*, duplicated across K callers, the module was concentrating it — it earns its keep. "Concentrates complexity across many callers" is the buy signal for *keeping and deepening*; "evaporates on inlining" is the buy signal for *collapsing it away*.
2. **The interface is the test surface.** If you must reach *past* the interface to test the module (poke internals, stub private collaborators), the module is the wrong shape — its real interface is wider than its declared one.
3. **One adapter = hypothetical seam; two = real seam.** Don't propose a port/seam unless something genuinely varies across it — typically a production adapter *and* a test adapter. A seam with one adapter is speculative generality; flag proposals that introduce it.
 
## The procedure
 
Three bounded phases. Do not skip ahead — phase 2 must not design interfaces.
 
1. **Explore.** If `CONTEXT.md` / area ADRs exist, read them first. Then spawn a native `Explore` subagent to walk the code **organically**, noting friction — shallow modules, tight coupling, untestable seams, scattered locality — rather than running a rigid checklist. The walk surfaces friction sites; it does not yet judge them. (High freedom here: what counts as friction is discovered, not enumerated.)
2. **Diagnose & rank.** For each friction site, apply the test battery. Classify each surviving candidate's seam by dependency category — **in-process** (merge and test directly), **local-substitutable** (a real stand-in, e.g. an in-memory store), **remote-but-owned** (ports & adapters, in-memory adapter for tests), **true-external** (injected mock) — because that determines how the deepened module would be tested across its seam. Assign each a badge: **strong-buy** (clear deletion-test signal + real seam + high leverage), **consider** (mixed signal), or **hold** (friction is real but deepening is risky or speculative). **Stop here — do not design the new interface.**
3. **Report & hand off.** Emit the report (next section) to `<tmpdir>/arch-review-<timestamp>.md`, computing the timestamp at run time. Then route the chosen candidate out: `/grill` to design the deepened interface interactively, and `/plan-options` for the "design it twice" pass (2–3 designs under different constraints — minimise interface / maximise flexibility / optimise the common caller). If the user wants the chosen module's name recorded in the target repo's `CONTEXT.md`, offer to append it — only with their go-ahead, and only in the target repo, never in this vault.
 
Clean-verdict reachability: if the walk finds no shallow modules — interfaces are already small relative to their implementations and seams are real — say so and return the **clean verdict** ("architecture is already deep"). Do not manufacture candidates to fill the report.
 
## Output format
 
A markdown report (renders in Obsidian; before/after via Mermaid), written to the temp dir:
 
```text
# Architecture review — <repo / subtree>   (<timestamp>)
 
## Verdict
<strong-buy: N · consider: N · hold: N>   |   <clean: architecture is already deep — no shallow modules found>
 
## Top recommendation
<the single strongest candidate in one paragraph — what's shallow, what deepening buys, why it ranks first. Omit if clean.>
 
## Candidate <n> — <module name>   [strong-buy | consider | hold]
- **Deletion test:** <complexity reappears across K callers → earns its keep, deepen | evaporates on inlining → collapse away>
- **Why shallow:** <interface ≈ implementation, leaks across its seam, or scattered locality>
- **Seam category:** <in-process | local-substitutable | remote-but-owned | true-external> → tested by <merge | stand-in | in-memory adapter | injected mock>
- **Proposed depth:** <described, not designed — what behaviour would move behind what smaller interface>
- **Before/after:** emit a Mermaid `flowchart LR` — before: `caller --> shallow --> shallow --> shallow`; after: `caller --> [deep module]`.
 
## Next step — design phase (not done here)
- `/grill` <module> — design the deepened interface interactively, one decision at a time.
- `/plan-options` — generate 2–3 designs under different constraints; collapse to one with the reason recorded.
 
## What this scan did not do
- Did not design any interface (`/grill`).
- Did not verify a refactor is correct (`/lean-review` or `/ai-diff-judgment` on the eventual diff).
- Did not trace runtime behaviour over time (`/structural-trace`).
```
 
Definition of done: every candidate carries a badge, a deletion-test result, and a seam category; the report is in the temp dir (not the repo); the clean verdict is used when nothing is shallow.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Synonym drift.** Writing "component / service / API / boundary" instead of the eight glossary terms. The cardinal sin — it destroys comparability, which is the whole point of the fixed vocabulary.
- **Designing during diagnosis.** Proposing the new interface in phase 2. The diagnose phase ranks *what to deepen*; designing *how* is `/grill`'s job and runs after the user picks a candidate.
- **Forcing a buy.** Tagging a module strong-buy when the deletion test says pass-through (complexity evaporates). A pass-through is collapsed away, not deepened — don't invert the signal to produce a recommendation.
- **Speculative seams.** Recommending a port/adapter where only one adapter exists. One adapter is a hypothetical seam; flag it, don't bless it.
- **Reimplementing the grilling loop.** Drifting into an interactive design Q&A inside this skill. Hand off to `/grill` — it owns that loop; duplicating it here makes one skill do two jobs.
- **Writing the report into the repo.** The report goes to the OS temp dir. Don't commit an `arch-review-*.md` into the target codebase or this vault.
- **Padding to fill the report.** Manufacturing weak candidates when the architecture is already deep. The clean verdict is reachable and correct — use it.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, or reduce tight coupling
- Consolidating modules that leak across their seams, or making a codebase more testable through its interfaces
- Making a codebase more AI-navigable — fewer shallow modules to bounce between to understand one concept
- The user names "shallow modules", "deep modules", "deepening", or pure functions extracted only for testability while the real bugs live in how they're called
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Behaviour that recurs over time where the issue is standing structure, not static code shape — `/structural-trace`
- Correctness review of a specific diff — `/lean-review`; merge judgment on an AI-authored diff — `/ai-diff-judgment`
- Designing the deepened interface once a candidate is chosen — `/grill` (and `/plan-options` for the multi-design pass)
- A request to actually perform the refactor — this skill stops at the ranked report; execution is downstream
 
## Related
 
- `/structural-trace` — the dynamic-behaviour counterpart; this skill is its static-code-structure sibling
- `/lean-review`, `/ai-diff-judgment` — per-diff correctness; this operates on the whole codebase to propose new structure
- `/grill` — the interactive design loop this skill hands the chosen candidate to (replaces a hand-rolled grilling loop)
- `/plan-options` — the multi-constraint "design it twice" generator for the chosen candidate
- `knowledge/ai/external-skills/mattpocock/improve-codebase-architecture.md` — the source skill this is the house-native port of (glossary, deletion test, dependency-category taxonomy)

ai/skills/skill-deepen-thinking.title: Skill: deepen-thinking
ai/skills/skill-deepen-thinking.content:
Skill: deepen-thinking
Training-layer skill: a single-session Socratic walk up the higher-order tiers (Understand → Analyze → Evaluate → Create → metacognitive close) on a subject the user already partly holds, where the user produces at every rung and the AI scaffolds and adversarially checks but never climbs a rung for them. On a request like “analyze X for me” it reframes to produce-first rather than handing over a take. The schemas being built live in the user — the foundation-paradox defense from higher-order-thinking-under-ai, applied as a ladder.
When to use

Wanting to think harder about a subject rather than be handed a take — “help me think about X more deeply”, “go deeper on this”, “push my thinking on X”, “think at a higher level”
A request to “analyze / give a deep take on” a subject you clearly hold — invoke and let it reframe to produce-first, instead of consuming an AI take
Building the deliberate-practice habit of producing higher-order analysis rather than offloading it

Skip when:

You don’t yet hold the subject — that’s a knowledge gap; use /teach (the skill routes there if rung 1 reveals this)
The “subject” is an in-progress plan or design with decisions to resolve — use /grill
You genuinely want the AI to just produce the analysis right now — answer normally; don’t force the ladder

Why it exists
The default move — ask the AI to analyze a subject and read the result — is augmentation: the analyze/evaluate/create work happens in the model, and the user’s own schemas for the subject never get built (augmented-vs-trained-thinking: who produces decides whether you trained or offloaded; higher-order-thinking-under-ai: the Evaluate tier only appreciates on schemas you actually built, and the same automation that makes it valuable cuts the reps that build it). This skill forces the inversion — the human climbs, the AI belays — and sequences the tiers explicitly because the evidence says explicit + practiced + adversarially-checked beats immersion (teaching-higher-order-thinking).
Related

.claude/skills/deepen-thinking/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-grill — interactive resolution of an in-progress plan’s decisions; the plan-side sibling to this subject-side skill
skill-disagree — single adversarial inversion of the AI’s answer; the move Rung 3 borrows, aimed at the user instead
skill-predict-then-compare — the metacognitive close hands falsifiable predictions here
higher-order-thinking-under-ai — why the Evaluate tier appreciates only on schemas you built
augmented-vs-trained-thinking — the who-produces-decides principle the integrity rule enforces
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/deepen-thinking/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-16. Re-sync on any later body edit.

---
name: deepen-thinking
description: Walk a subject the user already partly holds up the higher-order tiers — they produce at every rung while the AI scaffolds and attacks their output but never climbs a rung for them. On "analyze X for me" it reframes to produce-first; doing the thinking for them is the trap it avoids. Use when the user wants to think harder about a subject rather than be handed a take — "help me think about X more deeply", "go deeper on this", "push my thinking on X", "think at a higher level", "develop my own take on X" — substantive subjects only. Distinct from /grill (resolves a plan's decisions — this elevates a subject with no decision to settle), /teach (acquires new knowledge across sessions — single-session on a subject already held, routing there if not), and /disagree (one inversion of the AI's own answer — this sequences five tiers against the user's output). Counters the augmentation default — ask the AI and consume the result — which never builds your own analyze/evaluate/create schemas.
---
 
Scaffold the user *up* the higher-order tiers on a subject they already partly hold — Understand → Analyze → Evaluate → Create → metacognitive close — with one non-negotiable rule that separates this from every "explain X to me" interaction: **at each rung the human produces first, and the AI never climbs the rung for them.** The AI prompts, flags gaps, and attacks the user's output; it does not supply the analysis, the evaluation, or the synthesis. The capability being built — the schemas for analyzing and judging this subject — lives in the user, which is the whole point ([[higher-order-thinking-under-ai]]: the Evaluate tier appreciates only if you actually built the schemas it runs on; [[augmented-vs-trained-thinking]]: who produces decides whether you trained or just offloaded).
 
The trap to refuse: a request like "analyze X for me" or "give me a deep take on X" is a request for augmentation. **Reframe it** — "I'll scaffold *you* to analyze it; you produce each step and I'll pressure-test it" — and only proceed if the user wants that. If they just want the take, this is the wrong skill; answer normally instead.
 
## How to locate the subject
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the subject to think harder about — a topic, a claim, a body of ideas, a concept the user holds an opinion on. If empty, infer it: the subject the user just raised. If nothing fits, ask what subject to work, rather than invent one.
 
Then run two gates **before** climbing:
 
- **Held-enough gate.** Does the user actually hold the subject well enough to think *about* it? One probe (rung 1 doubles as this). If the honest answer is "they need to learn it first," this is a knowledge gap, not a thinking gap — **route to `/teach`** and stop. A ladder built on a subject the user doesn't hold is just teaching wearing a costume.
- **Subject-not-plan gate.** If "the subject" is really an in-progress plan or design with decisions to resolve, this is the wrong tool — **route to `/grill`**.
 
## The ladder
 
Five rungs, climbed in order (you cannot evaluate what you haven't analyzed). **Adaptive**: compress or skip a rung that doesn't fit the subject — many subjects have no genuine Create payoff, and forcing one manufactures slop. Name which rungs you're running at the start. Per rung, keep the AI's contribution to *probing and testing*, never producing.
 
### Rung 1 — Understand (and the held-enough check)
 
Ask the user to state their current grasp of the subject in their own words — Feynman-style, no notes. Do **not** supply or correct content with answers; instead surface gaps as questions ("you said X drives Y — by what mechanism?"). If the gaps are large and structural, the user doesn't hold the subject yet → offer `/teach` and stop.
 
### Rung 2 — Analyze
 
Ask the user to decompose: the parts, how they relate, and the **load-bearing assumptions** underneath. The AI points at what's missing — a part not named, a relationship not traced, an assumption left implicit — as a prompt, never by handing over the decomposition. Push until the structure is the user's, not yours.
 
### Rung 3 — Evaluate
 
Ask the user to judge the subject against explicit criteria: strengths, weaknesses, evidence quality, where it breaks, what it's good and bad for. Then **play adversary against the user's evaluation** — the `/disagree` move aimed at the human: steelman the opposite of their judgment, find the weakest link in their reasoning, and make them defend or revise. The output is *their* sharpened evaluation, not yours.
 
### Rung 4 — Create
 
Ask the user to synthesize something the subject didn't hand them: a novel connection, a reframe, a cross-domain transfer, an extension or application. Then **pressure-test for genuine novelty** — is this a real synthesis or a recombination of the obvious? Does it survive a counterexample? Do not generate the synthesis; test the user's.
 
### Rung 5 — Metacognitive close
 
Ask the user three things: confidence now (a number), where they're still weak, and what would change their mind. Hand any falsifiable prediction that surfaced to `/predict-then-compare`. If something durable emerged (a reframe, a connection worth keeping), offer to seed a normal knowledge note — but only if it earns it; don't manufacture a note to close the session.
 
## The integrity rule (low freedom — do not bend)
 
At every rung the human produces **first**; the AI must not supply the rung's substantive content before the human has attempted it. This is the analogue of `/predict-then-compare`'s withhold rule and it is what makes the skill train rather than augment. If the user asks the AI to "just do" a rung, offer the exit — this is a training ladder; if they want the rung done for them, that's a different request — rather than silently switching to producing it. The AI's allowed moves are: prompt, probe, flag a gap, attack the user's output. Producing the analysis/evaluation/synthesis is not on the list.
 
## Stop conditions
 
- The metacognitive close is done → ladder complete.
- The user taps out partway → fine; a partial ladder is still reps. Summarize what was climbed.
- Rung 1 reveals the subject isn't held → route to `/teach`, stop.
- The subject turns out to be a plan/decision → route to `/grill`, stop.
 
## Output format
 
Maintain a running ladder as you climb; render the compact summary at the close:
 
```text
# Thinking ladder — <subject>
Rungs run: <e.g. Understand · Analyze · Evaluate · (Create skipped — no synthesis payoff)>
 
Rung 1 · Understand — your grasp: <one line> · gaps surfaced: <…>
Rung 2 · Analyze — your decomposition: <…> · missed → you added: <…>
Rung 3 · Evaluate — your judgment: <…> · adversary pushed: <…> · you held/revised: <…>
Rung 4 · Create — your synthesis: <…> · novelty verdict: <genuine | recombination>
Rung 5 · Metacog — confidence <0.NN> · still weak on <…> · would change mind if <…>
 
Handoffs: <prediction → /predict-then-compare> · <durable? → seed note: y/n>
```
 
## Definition of done
 
- The subject was elevated through the named rungs, **in order**, with the user producing each one.
- The AI never supplied a rung's substantive content before the user attempted it (the integrity rule held).
- Rung 3 actually pushed back on the user's evaluation (an evaluation nobody attacked wasn't evaluated).
- The metacognitive close named confidence, a remaining weakness, and a mind-changer — or the user tapped out and the partial climb was summarized.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Climbing the rung for them.** The fatal one. "To be helpful" the AI produces the analysis or the synthesis and asks the user to react — that is augmentation, the exact thing the skill exists to prevent. Withhold the content; supply only the probe.
- **Skipping the reframe on "analyze X for me."** Silently giving the take instead of scaffolding the user to produce it. Reframe and confirm first, or decline and answer normally — don't run a fake ladder around an AI-produced answer.
- **Faking a ladder over a knowledge gap.** If the user doesn't hold the subject, this is `/teach`, not a thinking ladder. The held-enough gate exists to catch this; honor it.
- **Forcing all five rungs.** Manufacturing a Create rung on a subject with no synthesis payoff produces slop. Name the applicable rungs up front and skip the rest.
- **A toothless Evaluate rung.** Accepting the user's first judgment without adversarial push. Rung 3's whole value is the attack on *their* reasoning; an unchallenged evaluation is just an opinion logged.
- **Grading novelty leniently at Create.** Calling a recombination of the obvious "novel" to flatter the user. Name it recombination when it is one — the honest verdict is the lesson.
- **Letting it sprawl.** This is a focused single-session climb, not an open-ended seminar. Five rungs, then close.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user wants to think harder about a subject rather than be handed a take — "help me think about X more deeply", "go deeper on this", "push my thinking on X", "think this through at a higher level", "understand X more rigorously".
- The user asks the AI to "analyze / give a deep take on" a subject they clearly hold — invoke and **reframe** to produce-first, rather than answering as augmentation.
- Building the deliberate-practice habit of producing higher-order analysis instead of consuming it.
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- A subject the user doesn't yet hold — that's learning; use `/teach`.
- An in-progress plan or design with decisions to resolve — use `/grill`.
- One adversarial inversion of the AI's own last answer — that's `/disagree` (this sequences five tiers and aims the adversary at the user's output).
- A genuine request for the AI to just produce the analysis (the user doesn't want to train right now) — answer normally; don't force the ladder.
 
## Related
 
- `/grill` — interactive resolution of an in-progress plan's decisions; the plan-side sibling to this subject-side skill
- `/teach` — multi-session knowledge acquisition; the route when the held-enough gate fails
