- `/disagree` — single adversarial inversion of the AI's answer; the move Rung 3 borrows, aimed at the user instead
- `/predict-then-compare` — the metacognitive close hands falsifiable predictions here
- `knowledge/general/higher-order-thinking-under-ai.md` — why the Evaluate tier appreciates only on schemas you built, and the foundation paradox this skill defends against
- `knowledge/general/higher-order-thinking-skills.md` · `knowledge/general/teaching-higher-order-thinking.md` — the Bloom tiers and the explicit-beats-immersion evidence the ladder operationalizes
- `knowledge/ai/augmented-vs-trained-thinking.md` — the who-produces-decides principle the integrity rule enforces

ai/skills/skill-density-scan.title: Skill: density-scan
ai/skills/skill-density-scan.content:
Skill: density-scan
Scan written text for information-density failure modes that increase reader cognitive load: surprisal spikes (missing connectives), sentence-length monotony, propositional density mismatched to channel, long-distance dependencies, lexical density mismatch, and the “shorter is better” compression trap.
When to use

Before publishing prose where comprehension matters — knowledge notes, specs, instructions, agent briefs
Prompts that will run many times (small density wins compound)
Reviewing edits that aggressively shortened existing prose

Skip when:

Throwaway scratch text or chat-message prose
Density-tolerant readers (LLMs handle higher density than humans on some axes — see backing note)

Why it exists
Short text isn’t always better. Cuts that drop connectives, raise propositional density, or create long-distance dependencies cost the reader more than they save in length. The compression trap is the dominant failure mode: confidently-edited prose that looks tighter but reads worse. Density-scan finds where compression actually damaged comprehension, not whether to compress at all.
Related

.claude/skills/density-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
information-density-for-llm-prompts — LLM-receiver levers
information-density-in-written-text — human-reader sibling
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/density-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-18.

---
name: density-scan
description: Scan written text for information-density failure modes that increase reader cognitive load — surprisal spikes (missing connectives), sentence-length monotony, propositional density mismatched to channel, long-distance dependencies, lexical density mismatch, and the "shorter is better" compression trap. Returns ranked findings with locations and minimum-cost rewrite suggestions. Use before publishing prose where comprehension matters — knowledge notes, specs, instructions, agent briefs, prompts that will run many times. Distinct from /readability-scan, which owns the word- and document-level axes (headings, point placement, word choice). Counters the heuristic that shorter is always better — short text whose density rose disproportionally to the cut damages the reader.
---
 
Scan the prose at `$ARGUMENTS` for information-density failure modes — patterns that increase reader cognitive load even when the surface looks tight. This is a different axis from `/bias-scan-prompt` (epistemic framing), `/bias-scan-ai` (output contamination), `/falsifiability-scan` (claim shape), and `/reviewers-map` (per-claim verification). The dangerous case it targets: prose that scores easy on Flesch, passes the entity check, and inverts cleanly under `/disagree` — yet forces the reader to repeatedly re-parse, infer missing logical links, or hold long dependencies in working memory. Tight surface, expensive parse.
 
The canonical lever definitions and contested-finding flags live in `knowledge/general/information-density-in-written-text.md`. Consult if you need the rationale for a specific lever; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A file path — read the file and scan its body (skip frontmatter)
- A path-and-section ref (e.g., `projects/foo/spec.md#instructions`) — scan that section
- Literal prose, usually quoted or fenced
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most recently written or edited prose-bearing file in this session
2. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it contains prose changes (not pure code)
3. If nothing fits, ask which artifact to scan rather than guess
 
This is a review pass. **Do not modify the target.**
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on prose where cognitive load matters to the reader's downstream use:
 
- Knowledge notes about to be committed (especially synthesis / hub notes)
- Specs, ADRs, design docs, instruction documents
- Long prompts or agent briefs that will run many times
- Article / blog drafts (notes tagged `publish`)
- Project overviews and `_connections.md` entries
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Code (this scan is about prose density, not code complexity — different axis)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` quick captures
- `journal/` entries (personal voice; density tuning is not the bar)
- Frontmatter-only or formatting-only changes
- Trivial questions or syntax-lookup prompts
- Poetry or aphorism (intentional high density)
 
## Step 0 — identify the channel
 
Density tunes against a channel. Before scanning, declare the inferred register in one line. Cues:
 
- `knowledge/**`, `projects/**/overview.md`, ADRs → **reference register**: high lexical density and moderate-to-high propositional density are appropriate; cohesion (lever 1) is the dominant tuning target.
- Long prompts, agent briefs, instruction docs → **instructional register**: explicit predictive cues matter most (levers 1, 4, 6); compression-trap is the dominant failure mode.
- Articles and `publish`-tagged notes → **public register**: variation (lever 2) and channel-density match (lever 5) become first-class targets alongside cohesion.
- `journal/` would be **conversational**; the scope rules already exclude this, but if a borderline case is forced, low lexical density and short dependencies are correct.
 
The channel determines which levers are scored stricter. State the channel up front in the output.
 
## The six levers
 
Each lever names a pattern that can be detected (in a draft) and modulated (in a rewrite). Full definitions in the companion note; the table below is the working detection rubric.
 
| # | Lever | Detection signature |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Surprisal spike | Missing complementizer ("that") before unexpected embedded clause; deleted causal/contrastive connective ("because", "however", "therefore", "while"); asyndetic clause boundary where the logical link must be inferred; deleted determiner before long modifier |
| 2 | Sentence-length monotony | 4+ consecutive sentences within ±20% of each other in word count, in either direction |
| 3 | Propositional density mismatch | Many predicate-argument units packed into few words, where the channel doesn't justify the density (or, conversely, sparse content in reference register) |
| 4 | Long-distance dependency | Subject-to-main-verb separation >7 words; nested clauses without a top-level break; pronoun separated from its antecedent across multiple clauses |
| 5 | Lexical density mismatch | Heavy nominalization in conversational/instructional register, or sparse content words in reference register |
| 6 | Compression trap | Text reads short but ideas were not reduced proportionally — symptoms include unexplained referent jumps, deleted causal links, single sentences compressing what should be three |
 
**Honest about what this is**: pattern detection on the surface, not surprisal measurement. The skill flags candidates that *look like* spike-causing or load-increasing patterns. It does not compute true surprisal (which would require a reference language model and per-token probability access). Findings are evidence-suggestive, not measurements.
 
## Severity per finding
 
- **low** — fix would benefit the reader but absence does not damage comprehension; consider during routine editing
- **medium** — discrete cognitive load increase that an attentive reader notices; fix before publishing in public register
- **high** — likely to cause misparse, structural forgetting, or local comprehension failure on first pass; fix before commit regardless of register
 
## Verdict states
 
Pick one based on the finding profile:
 
- **Density-clean** — load matches channel, no severe spikes, sentence variation present, cohesion intact. Zero high-severity findings; at most three low-severity findings.
- **Tune** — surgical fixes. Multiple low/medium findings, or one high. The text is structurally sound; spot-fixes restore it.
- **Rework** — structural mismatch. Pervasive issues across multiple levers, or density fundamentally wrong for the channel (e.g., reference-register prose with conversational lexical density throughout, or a long prompt that's been compressed past the comprehension floor). The artifact needs reauthoring at the paragraph level, not line edits.
 
**Rework is rare** and should be reserved for cases where surgical fixes won't add up. If in doubt between Tune and Rework, pick Tune and list the top fixes.
 
## Format-fit rubric (constructive counterpart for fix suggestions)
 
This skill diagnoses; it does not rewrite. But several findings — propositional-density mismatch (lever 3), sentence-length monotony (lever 2), the compression trap (lever 6) — are best repaired by a *format* change, not a word-level edit. When a suggested fix is a format change, apply these firing conditions. Each format must earn its use; **prose is the default** and the burden is on the alternative.
 
| Format | Use only when |
|---|---|
| List | The items are genuinely parallel / enumerable — a set or sequence the reader scans, not an argument with connective logic between steps |
| Table | The same shape repeats **3+ times** (same fields per row). Fewer than three → repeated bold-lead lines read lighter than table scaffolding |
| Callout (`> [!NOTE]` / `[!TIP]`) | The aside is worth keeping but would derail the main argument if left inline |
| Block quote | The exact wording is the point (a definition, a claim being challenged) — otherwise paraphrase |
| Code block | Multi-line, or it encodes a decision more precisely than prose (schema, type, state machine); short single references stay inline code |
 
The trap this guards against: reaching for a list or table as *decoration* when prose carried the logic better. A list of non-parallel items destroys the connective tissue lever 1 works to preserve — so a format "fix" can raise density if its firing condition isn't met. Suggest the format change as a fix; do not apply it (this remains a review pass).
 
## What to do
 
1. **Read the target** in full. Skip frontmatter.
2. **Declare the channel** from Step 0.
3. **Scan for each of the six levers.** Note candidate spans for each.
4. **Compile findings.** Dedupe across levers (one phrase may hit multiple — assign the dominant one).
5. **Rank by severity, then by load-bearingness within severity.** Cap at 10 findings.
6. **For each finding**, give: lever number, severity, location (line range or quoted span), one-line reason, minimum-cost suggested fix if obvious. If the fix isn't obvious, say "no surgical fix — see verdict."
7. **Issue verdict.** Two-line max rationale.
8. **Note explicitly what you checked and didn't find.** Levers with no findings get one line of "checked: no spikes / variation present / etc."
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Density scan — <target>
 
## 0. Channel
<reference | instructional | public | conversational> — <one-line cue>
 
## 1. Findings (ranked)
1. **[lever N | severity]** <location>
   <one-line reason>
   *Fix:* <minimum-cost restoration, or "no surgical fix">
2. **[lever N | severity]** <location>
   ...
[cap at 10]
 
## 2. Levers checked, no findings
- Lever <N>: <one-line note on what you scanned for and why it's clean>
- ...
 
## 3. Verdict
**<Density-clean | Tune | Rework>**
<one or two-line rationale; if Rework, name the structural issue>
```
 
If the artifact is genuinely clean across all six levers, write a short scan with the channel declaration, an empty findings section, the "levers checked" recap, and the **Density-clean** verdict. Do not pad.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing findings to look thorough.** If the prose is clean, report it clean. A scan that pads erodes the discipline. Two real findings beat ten manufactured ones.
- **Confusing low Flesch with low cognitive load.** The Hemingway trap: short sentences, easy words, propositional density at 0.99. Surface ease ≠ parse ease. The lever-3 detector exists specifically to catch this.
- **Recommending wholesale style changes.** This skill is targeted. The fix for a finding is the minimum-cost restoration of a function word or the splitting of one over-compressed sentence — not "rewrite this paragraph in a different voice."
- **Demanding density reduction in registers where high density is correct.** Reference notes, technical specs, and condensed agent briefs are *meant* to be dense. The lever-3 mismatch fires when density is wrong *for the channel*, not when density is high.
- **Pretending to measure surprisal.** Findings are pattern-suggestive, not surprisal-quantitative. Phrase them as "candidate" or "likely" if the inference is uncertain. Reserve "high" severity for clear cases.
- **Over-restoring connectives.** Lever 1 fixes the cases where a missing function word forces re-parse. It does not mandate "that" / "because" / "however" everywhere they could syntactically fit. Restoration is for predictive load, not completeness.
- **Suggesting fixes that violate the channel.** Adding chatty connectives to terse reference material trades one density problem for another. The fix has to fit the register declared in Step 0.
- **Treating Tune as a near-default.** Most committed vault notes should land on **Density-clean**. If Tune is your default verdict, calibrate down — many findings should be omitted as too low to act on.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing a knowledge note to the vault, especially synthesis or hub notes
- Before publishing an article-register draft (notes tagged `publish`)
- Before saving a long prompt or agent brief that will run many times
- Before propagating a spec section to a downstream fleet
- After a heavy edit pass that reduced word count by ≥20% — the compression trap is exactly this case
- Composes with `/bias-scan-prompt` on instructional artifacts (different axes: framing vs. cognitive load; both can fire)
- Composes with `/reviewers-map` on AI-drafted synthesis notes (verifiability vs. cognitive load)
 
Skip when: throwaway / exploratory work, code-only diffs, frontmatter-only changes, journal entries, or content where dense surface is the deliberate craft choice (poetry, aphorism).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/information-density-in-written-text.md` — canonical lever definitions, contested-finding flags, prompt-pattern templates including the smoothing-pass and compression-check companions to this scan
- `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md` — broader account of receiver-side cognitive load
- `/unslop` — fix-mode sibling on the register axis (AI-writing tells); orthogonal to density
- `/readability-scan` — sibling scan owning the word- and document-level axes (headings, point placement, word choice); routes density symptoms here
- `/bias-scan-prompt` — input-side framing, orthogonal axis; both can fire on a high-stakes prompt
- `/bias-scan-ai` — output-side bias contamination, orthogonal axis
- `/falsifiability-scan` — claim-shape testability, orthogonal axis
- `/reviewers-map` — per-claim verification map, orthogonal axis

ai/skills/skill-dependency-flow-scan.title: Skill: dependency-flow-scan
ai/skills/skill-dependency-flow-scan.content:
Skill: dependency-flow-scan
Diagnose a codebase’s import-graph edges — cycles (strongly connected components), inversions (edges from stable modules to volatile ones, convicted only with git-churn corroboration), and skips (edges bypassing a layer the project itself declares) — and rank edge-repair candidates with a named-but-not-designed repair move (break / merge / re-point / promote). Emits a markdown + Mermaid report to the OS temp dir and stops at the design boundary, handing interface design to /grill.
The edge counterpart to skill-deepen-architecture: that skill judges the nodes of the module graph (is there enough behaviour behind each interface?); this judges the edges (do the arrows point the right way?). Together they cover most of what “architecture review” means for static structure.
When to use

Circular-dependency build errors, or “everything imports everything” complaints
Enforcing or auditing a layering (UI → service → storage) before or after a refactor
A change in one module keeps rippling into rebuilds or breakages across the graph
The user names “dependency direction”, “import cycles”, “layer violations”, or “module boundaries”

Skip when:

The question is module depth, not edge direction — /deepen-architecture
You want to know where change and cost actually concentrate — /churn-hotspot-scan
Behaviour recurs over time via runtime feedback loops — /structural-trace
You want a correctness review of a diff — /lean-review

Why it exists
Dependency rot is the edge-side failure /deepen-architecture can’t see: a codebase can be made of perfectly deep modules whose import arrows still form cycles, point from stable code into volatile code, or skip declared layers — and every change then ripples across the graph regardless of how good the individual modules are. Nothing in the catalog audited the import graph. Two design guards keep it honest: the metric alone never convicts (instability formulas must be corroborated by actual git churn), and the skip test refuses to run against a layering the project never declared — no invented architecture to convict against.
Related

.claude/skills/dependency-flow-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-deepen-architecture — the node sibling; shared module/interface glossary
skill-churn-hotspot-scan — supplies the volatility evidence the direction test requires
skill-structural-trace — dynamic feedback loops; explicitly out of scope here
skill-grill, skill-plan-options — the design-phase skills a chosen finding routes to

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/dependency-flow-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-22. Re-sync on every body edit.

---
name: dependency-flow-scan
description: Diagnose a codebase's import-graph edges — cycles, dependencies pointing from stable modules to volatile ones, and layer-skipping imports — and rank edge-repair candidates as a markdown report with a reachable "flow is clean" verdict. Use when you want to untangle circular dependencies, enforce layering, check dependency direction, find out why a change ripples across imports/rebuilds everywhere, or audit module boundaries before a refactor. Stops at the ranked report; does not redesign interfaces or write code. Distinct from /deepen-architecture (judges the nodes — module depth; this judges the edges between them), /structural-trace (runtime feedback loops, not static imports), and /churn-hotspot-scan (where change happens, not where imports point). Counters dependency rot — cycles and wrong-direction edges that make every change ripple across the graph.
---
 
Diagnose the import graph at `$ARGUMENTS` and rank **edge-repair** candidates — cycles to break, inverted dependencies to re-point, layer skips to close. The skill is a diagnostic-scan: it produces a ranked report and **stops at the design boundary**. It does not design the inversion interfaces (that's `/grill`) and it does not write code. The output is a markdown report written to the OS temp dir, never into the repo.
 
This is the edge counterpart to `/deepen-architecture`: that skill judges the *nodes* of the module graph (is there enough behaviour behind each interface?); this one judges the *edges* (do the arrows point the right way?). Together they cover most of what "architecture review" means for static structure.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the codebase to diagnose, as any of:
 
- A repo root or a subtree path (`src/payments/`) to scope the walk
- A free-text area name ("the auth layer") to be resolved against the working repo
- Empty → the current working repo; if it is large, scope to the subtree most recently discussed this session
 
If no codebase is in scope (e.g. invoked inside this knowledge vault with no target repo), say so and ask for a path — do not invent a target.
 
## The fixed glossary (low-freedom — drift is forbidden)
 
Every finding must use these terms **verbatim**. Synonym drift ("reference", "link", "usage", "coupling") destroys comparability across a report and across sessions.
 
- **Module** — a unit with an interface and an implementation behind it (same definition as `/deepen-architecture`); here, a vertex in the import graph.
- **Edge** — a static import/require/use from one module to another. `A → B` means A must know about B to compile or load.
- **Cycle** — a set of modules mutually reachable along edges (a strongly connected component larger than one module).
- **Fan-in / fan-out** — the count of edges arriving at / leaving a module.
- **Stability** — resistance to change implied by position: high fan-in, low fan-out. Instability `I = fan-out / (fan-in + fan-out)`.
- **Volatility** — how often the module *actually* changes (git history); the empirical check on the stability metric.
- **Inversion** — an edge from a more stable module to a less stable one: the thing everyone depends on now depends on the thing that changes most.
- **Skip** — an edge that bypasses a layer the project itself declares (folder convention, lint boundary rule, architecture doc).
 
If the target repo has a `CONTEXT.md` or area ADRs declaring layers or allowed dependencies, read them first — they define what counts as a skip.
 
## The test battery (low-freedom — apply each verbatim)
 
1. **Cycle test.** Compute strongly connected components over the import graph. Every SCC with more than one module is a finding — there is no benign cycle. Rank by member count × combined fan-in (how much of the codebase the tangle can drag).
2. **Direction test.** For each edge `A → B` where A is clearly more stable than B (instability margin, not a hair's difference), check volatility: does B actually churn (git log)? Metric + churn together convict an **inversion**; the metric alone does not — a "volatile" module that never changes in practice is a hold, not a finding.
3. **Skip test.** Only if the repo *declares* layers. An edge bypassing a declared intermediate layer is a **skip**. If no layering is declared anywhere, skip this test entirely — do not infer a layering the project never claimed and then convict against it.
 
## The procedure
 
Three bounded phases. Do not skip ahead — phase 2 must not design interfaces.
 
1. **Build the graph.** Prefer a graph tool already present in the repo (`madge`, `dependency-cruiser`, `go list`, `cargo tree`, language equivalents) — do not install one. Otherwise derive edges by scanning import statements with Grep. The graph does not need to be perfect; it needs to be honest — record the extraction method and its blind spots (dynamic imports, DI containers, reflection) in the report.
2. **Apply the battery & rank.** Run the three tests. For each surviving finding, *name* the repair move without designing it — **break** (cut the edge by inverting: interface at the stable side), **merge** (cycle members that are one module in denial — route to `/deepen-architecture`), **re-point** (move the edge to the declared layer), or **promote** (the skipped-to symbol belongs in the intermediate layer's interface). Assign each a badge: **cut** (clear violation + churn corroboration), **consider** (metric signal, weak corroboration), **hold** (real but risky or load-bearing to touch). **Stop here — do not sketch the new interface.**
3. **Report & hand off.** Emit the report (next section) to `<tmpdir>/depflow-<timestamp>.md`, computing the timestamp at run time. Route onward: `/grill` to design an inversion interface, `/deepen-architecture` when a cycle's members look like one module split too thin, `/churn-hotspot-scan` to check whether a suspect edge actually costs anything in practice.
 
Clean-verdict reachability: if the graph is acyclic, edges point toward stability, and no declared layer is skipped, say so and return the **clean verdict** ("dependency flow is clean"). Do not manufacture findings to fill the report.
 
## Output format
 
A markdown report (renders in Obsidian; graphs via Mermaid), written to the temp dir:
 
```text
# Dependency flow review — <repo / subtree>   (<timestamp>)
 
## Graph provenance
<extraction method (tool or grep), module count, edge count, known blind spots>
 
## Verdict
<cut: N · consider: N · hold: N>   |   <clean: dependency flow is clean — acyclic, arrows point toward stability, no skips>
 
## Top recommendation
<the single strongest finding in one paragraph. Omit if clean.>
 
## Finding <n> — <cycle | inversion | skip>   [cut | consider | hold]
- **Edges:** <the offending edges verbatim, `path/a → path/b`>
- **Evidence:** <SCC members | instability values + churn counts | the declared layer rule violated>
- **Repair move (named, not designed):** <break | merge | re-point | promote>
- **Blast radius:** <combined fan-in of involved modules>
- **Graph:** Mermaid `flowchart LR` — before (with the offending edge marked) and after (with the repair move applied).
 
## Next step — design phase (not done here)
- `/grill` — design the inversion interface for a chosen finding.
- `/deepen-architecture` — when cycle members should merge into one deep module.
 
## What this scan did not do
- Did not design any interface (`/grill`).
- Did not measure where change actually happens (`/churn-hotspot-scan`).
- Did not judge module depth (`/deepen-architecture`).
```
 
Definition of done: every finding carries a type, a badge, quoted edges, and a named repair move; the report is in the temp dir; the clean verdict is used when the flow is clean.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Inventing layers.** Convicting a "skip" against a layering the project never declared. No declaration, no skip test.
- **Metric-only convictions.** Calling an inversion on the instability formula alone. Volatility (git evidence) must corroborate — a stable-in-practice module invalidates the finding.
- **Designing during diagnosis.** Sketching the inversion interface inside the report. Name the repair move; `/grill` designs it.
- **Perfect-graph paralysis.** Refusing to proceed because grep-derived edges miss dynamic imports. State the blind spots and scan what the graph shows.
- **Synonym drift.** "Coupling", "reference", "usage" instead of the glossary terms. Edge, cycle, inversion, skip — verbatim.
- **Writing the report into the repo.** Temp dir only.
- **Padding to fill the report.** The clean verdict is reachable and correct — use it.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Circular-dependency build errors, or "everything imports everything" complaints
- Enforcing or auditing a layering (UI → service → storage) before or after a refactor
- A change in one module keeps rippling into rebuilds or breakages across the graph
- The user names "dependency direction", "import cycles", "layer violations", or "module boundaries"
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Module depth — is there enough behaviour behind each interface? — `/deepen-architecture`
- Where change and maintenance cost actually concentrate — `/churn-hotspot-scan`
- Runtime feedback loops and system behaviour over time — `/structural-trace`
- Correctness review of a specific diff — `/lean-review`
 
## Related
 
- `/deepen-architecture` — the node sibling (module depth); this skill owns the edges
- `/churn-hotspot-scan` — the evolutionary sibling; corroborates the direction test's volatility check
- `/grill`, `/plan-options` — the design-phase skills a chosen finding is handed to
- `/structural-trace` — dynamic system behaviour; out of scope here

ai/skills/skill-disagree.title: Skill: disagree
ai/skills/skill-disagree.content:
Skill: disagree
Inversion drill on your most recent substantive response — argue the opposite position with equal rigor. The gap between the two answers is a calibration signal for whether the original was well-supported or confidently-stated noise.
When to use

After a substantive answer that’s load-bearing for a decision
Before propagating an answer into a persistent artifact (vault note, PR, spec)
When the original felt fluent enough that you can’t easily tell if it was right

Skip when:

Trivial or factual answers where opposite is obviously absurd
Answers already paired with explicit counterarguments

Why it exists
Confident-sounding text and well-supported text look identical in fluent prose. Forcing the inverse with equal rigor surfaces whether the original was reasoning or noise — if the opposite holds up almost as well, the original wasn’t load-bearing reasoning, just register. Pass 3 of the bias-aware verification protocol; complementary to /red-team (which critiques an artifact, not an answer).
Related

.claude/skills/disagree/SKILL.md — operational definition
bias-aware-verification-protocol — four-pass protocol this is Pass 3 of
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/disagree/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: disagree
description: Inversion drill on your most recent substantive response. Argue the opposite position with equal rigor; the gap between the two answers is a calibration signal for whether the original was well-supported or confidently-stated noise. Use after a substantive answer when you want a calibration check before treating the original as settled — particularly when it's load-bearing for a decision or about to be propagated into an artifact.
---
 
Argue the **opposite** of your most recent substantive answer in this session, with equal rigor — not as a devil's-advocate exercise, but as if the opposite is what the evidence actually supports.
 
Ignore `$ARGUMENTS`. This skill operates on conversational context, not a file path.
 
## Purpose
 
The gap between your first answer and the inverted answer is a calibration signal:
 
- **Large gap** (two substantially different, evidence-backed positions) → the question is genuinely contested; the first answer should acknowledge both
- **Small gap** (same evidence hedged in both directions) → the first answer was probably noise dressed as confidence; downgrade your confidence
- **Zero gap** (you refuse to engage with the opposite, or the opposite argument is obviously thin) → value-locked or RLHF-constrained topic; flag and seek independent sources
 
This is Pass 3 of the bias-aware verification protocol (`knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md`), and an application of inversion (`knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md`).
 
## What to produce
 
### 1. The opposite claim
 
State the opposing position crisply in one sentence. Do not soften. "The opposite of X" should be a real position, not a strawman.
 
### 2. Strongest case for the opposite
 
Argue it with the same rigor you used for the original:
 
- Use the same evidence where you can, interpreted the other way
- Bring in evidence the original answer ignored or underweighted
- Identify assumptions the original treated as fixed that are actually contestable
 
If after genuine effort the opposite argument is noticeably weaker, say so — but only after making the effort.
 
### 3. Where the evidence supports both
 
Honestly identify the parts of the question where both positions are defensible given current evidence. This is often more useful than either answer alone.
 
### 4. Where one position only has rhetoric
 
Which side is backed by actual evidence, and which is held up by narrative fluency or convention? Be specific about which claims on each side are evidence-backed vs. assertion.
 
### 5. Calibration verdict
 
Pick one and explain:
 
- **Large gap** — both positions are defensible; the original should be revised to acknowledge the contested nature
- **Small gap** — same hedge both ways; original was overconfident; downgrade
- **Zero gap** — could not genuinely engage the opposite; original may reflect a value lock or training constraint, not evidence
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Disagreement drill
 
## Original claim (summary)
<one sentence>
 
## Opposite claim
<one sentence>
 
## Case for the opposite
<argued with the same rigor as the original>
 
## Where evidence supports both
- <point 1>
- <point 2>
 
## Where one side is rhetoric
- <point, and which side>
 
## Calibration verdict
**<Large gap | Small gap | Zero gap>**
<explanation; what should the user do with this?>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Strawmanning the opposite.** Defeats the purpose; a weak inversion produces false confidence in the original.
- **Refusing to engage.** "The opposite isn't defensible" is a valid conclusion only after you've tried hard. If you reach it instantly, that's the Zero-gap signal, not an answer.
- **Treating this as balance.** The goal is calibration, not balance. Sometimes the original answer was right and the inversion reveals that; say so.
 
## When to invoke
 
- After any substantial recommendation the user might act on
- When a first answer felt suspiciously clean
- Before committing contested claims to a persistent note
- When the user asks "are you sure?" — this is the structured version of "are you sure?"
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — Pass 3 context
- `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md` — inversion background (Jacobi, Munger)

ai/skills/skill-error-topology-scan.title: Skill: error-topology-scan
ai/skills/skill-error-topology-scan.content:
Skill: error-topology-scan
Diagnose how failures move through a codebase: a swallow census (caught and neither decided nor re-raised — log-and-continue included), a wrap-and-layer test on representative failure paths (more than two wraps between origin and handling layer is ceremony; a catch at a layer that can’t decide anything is wrong-layer), and Ousterhout’s define-out test (could a small interface change make this error a non-event?). Emits a markdown report to the OS temp dir with named-but-not-designed repairs, and stops at the design boundary — /grill designs the define-out.
A failure-path lens on the same static structure skill-deepen-architecture scans: error surface is interface width. A module whose callers must know five exception types is wider than its signatures admit, and a layer that catches everything but decides nothing is a shallow module wearing a try/catch.
When to use

Error handling feels scattered: caught everywhere, handled nowhere, logs full of noise
Auditing failure paths before hardening a service or adding retries
Repeated incidents where a failure was “logged but nothing happened”
The user names “swallowed exceptions”, “error handling mess”, or “who actually handles this?”

Skip when:

The question is module depth in general — /deepen-architecture
You want correctness review of one diff — /lean-review; an AI-authored merge call — /ai-diff-judgment
You want consequence simulation of a decision — /second-order
You want runtime resilience testing (chaos, load) — out of scope for a static scan

Why it exists
Error-handling sprawl is the failure mode where every layer catches, wraps, and logs while the actual decision — retry, degrade, abort, tell the user — is made nowhere; it hides from diff review because each individual catch block looks responsible. The scan’s two calibration guards define its character: logging is not handling (a log-and-continue is a swallow whatever the log level), and top-level boundaries that catch-all-and-report are the sanctioned pattern, not a finding — the scan hunts mid-layer swallows, not try/catch as such. The define-out test adds the one genuinely architectural move in error handling: redesigning the interface so the error case stops existing.
Related

.claude/skills/error-topology-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-deepen-architecture — error surface as interface width; swallow clusters route there
skill-dependency-flow-scan, skill-churn-hotspot-scan, skill-test-shape-scan — the static-structure family
skill-grill — designs the define-out or the relocated handling layer
skill-lean-review — per-diff correctness, including new error handling in a change

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/error-topology-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-22. Re-sync on every body edit.

---
name: error-topology-scan
description: Diagnose how failures move through a codebase — swallowed errors (caught and discarded or logged-and-continued), excessive wrapping between origin and handling layer, catches at layers that can't decide anything, and errors that could be defined out of existence by a small API change — ranked as a markdown report with a reachable "topology is sound" clean verdict. Use when error handling feels scattered, exceptions are caught everywhere and handled nowhere, logs are full of noise, or you want to audit failure paths before hardening a service. Stops at the ranked report; does not rewrite handlers. Distinct from /deepen-architecture (module depth — this scans the failure paths crossing those interfaces), /lean-review (correctness of one diff), and /second-order (consequence cascades of a decision, not code). Counters error-handling sprawl — every layer catching, wrapping, and logging while the actual decision is made nowhere.
---
 
Diagnose the error topology at `$ARGUMENTS` — where failures originate, how they travel, and where (if anywhere) something is actually decided about them. The skill is a diagnostic-scan: it produces a ranked report and **stops at the design boundary**. It does not rewrite handlers and does not design the define-out API changes (that's `/grill`). The output is a markdown report written to the OS temp dir, never into the repo.
 
This is a failure-path lens on the same static structure `/deepen-architecture` scans: error handling is interface width. A module whose callers must know five exception types is wider than its signatures admit, and a layer that catches everything but decides nothing is a shallow module wearing a try/catch.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the codebase to diagnose, as any of:
 
- A repo root or a subtree path (`src/payments/`) to scope the walk
- A free-text area name ("the ingestion pipeline") to be resolved against the working repo
- Empty → the current working repo; if it is large, scope to the subtree most recently discussed this session
 
If no codebase is in scope, say so and ask for a path — do not invent a target.
 
## The fixed glossary (low-freedom — drift is forbidden)
 
Every finding must use these terms **verbatim**.
 
- **Origin** — where a failure is first detected and raised.
- **Error surface** — the set of errors an interface can emit toward its callers. Part of interface width, exactly as `/deepen-architecture` defines it.
- **Handling layer** — the place where a *decision* changes behaviour: retry, fallback, degrade, map to a status code, abort, tell the user. Logging alone is not a decision.
- **Swallow** — caught and neither decided nor re-raised. Includes log-and-continue.
- **Wrap** — caught and re-raised as a different type or message.
- **Crash path** — a failure that propagates to the top of the process or request with no handling layer on the way.
- **Define-out** — an interface change that makes the error case a non-event (delete-missing = success, absent config = documented default), per Ousterhout's "define errors out of existence".
 
## The test battery (low-freedom — apply each verbatim)
 
1. **Swallow census.** Find catch/except/rescue blocks (Grep by language idiom). Classify each: **decides** (handling layer), **re-raises**, or **swallows**. Every swallow is a finding unless it sits at a documented top-level boundary (request handler, worker loop, main) *and* the failure is surfaced to monitoring. "We log it" does not clear a mid-layer swallow.
2. **Wrap-and-layer test.** Trace 2–3 representative failure paths from origin to handling layer (pick the paths the code's own tests or docs treat as important). More than two wraps between origin and decision is ceremony; a catch at a layer that cannot decide anything is a wrong-layer finding — the catch belongs above or below.
3. **Define-out test.** For the most frequent error classes surfaced by tests 1–2, ask verbatim: *could a small interface change make this case a non-event?* If yes, the finding names the define-out (described, not designed). If the error is genuinely exceptional and must surface, say so — not every error can or should be defined out.
 
## The procedure
 
Three bounded phases. Do not skip ahead — phase 2 must not redesign APIs.
 
1. **Map.** If `CONTEXT.md` / area ADRs document an error-handling policy, read them first — they define where the sanctioned top-level boundaries are. Then locate origins (throw/raise/Err sites) and catches (Grep), and sketch which layers exist between them. High freedom here: the map is discovered, not enumerated.
2. **Apply the battery & rank.** Run the three tests. Badge each surviving finding: **strong-buy** (mid-layer swallow on a real failure path, or a define-out with an obvious small change), **consider** (ceremony wraps, wrong-layer catches), **hold** (real but load-bearing — e.g. a swallow compensating for a flaky dependency that needs its own fix first). **Stop here — do not design the new API or rewrite a handler.**
3. **Report & hand off.** Emit the report (next section) to `<tmpdir>/errtopo-<timestamp>.md`, computing the timestamp at run time. Route onward: `/grill` to design a chosen define-out; `/deepen-architecture` when swallows cluster around one module (the module's shape, not its handlers, is the problem).
 
Clean-verdict reachability: if failures are decided at few, sanctioned layers, mid-layers pass errors through untouched, and no frequent error begs to be defined out, return the **clean verdict** ("error topology is sound"). Do not manufacture findings.
 
## Output format
 
A markdown report written to the temp dir:
 
```text
# Error topology review — <repo / subtree>   (<timestamp>)
 
## Map
<origins found: N · catches found: N · sanctioned top-level boundaries: <list or "none documented">>
 
## Verdict
<strong-buy: N · consider: N · hold: N>   |   <clean: error topology is sound — decisions at few right layers, no mid-layer swallows>
 
## Top recommendation
<the single strongest finding in one paragraph. Omit if clean.>
 
## Finding <n> — <swallow | ceremony wrap | wrong-layer catch | define-out | crash path>   [strong-buy | consider | hold]
- **Where:** <file:line of the catch or origin>
- **Path:** <origin → wraps → where it dies or is decided>
- **Evidence:** <the catch block or trace, quoted briefly>
- **Repair (named, not designed):** <delete the catch | move decision to <layer> | define-out: <one sentence>>
 
## Next step — design phase (not done here)
- `/grill` <finding> — design the define-out interface change.
- `/deepen-architecture` <module> — when swallows cluster around one module's seam.
 
## What this scan did not do
- Did not rewrite any handler or design any API (`/grill`).
- Did not judge a diff for correctness (`/lean-review`).
- Did not assess runtime failure behaviour under load — this is a static scan.
```
 
Definition of done: every finding carries a type, a badge, a quoted location, and a named (not designed) repair; the report is in the temp dir; the clean verdict is used when the topology is sound.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Counting logs as handling.** Logging is not a decision. A log-and-continue is a swallow, whatever the log level.
- **Zealotry about top-level boundaries.** A worker loop or request handler that catches-all, reports to monitoring, and continues is the *sanctioned* pattern, not a finding. The scan hunts mid-layer swallows.
- **Define-out absolutism.** Forcing a define-out onto genuinely exceptional failures. Some errors must surface loudly; the test allows "no — this one should stay an error".
- **Designing during diagnosis.** Sketching the new API or the rewritten handler in the report. Name the repair; `/grill` designs it.
- **Synonym drift.** "Ignore", "eat", "suppress", "rethrow" instead of swallow and wrap. Glossary terms verbatim.
- **Writing the report into the repo.** Temp dir only.
- **Padding.** The clean verdict is reachable and correct — use it.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Error handling feels scattered: caught everywhere, handled nowhere, logs full of noise
- Auditing failure paths before hardening a service or adding retries
- Repeated production incidents where a failure was "logged but nothing happened"
- The user names "swallowed exceptions", "error handling mess", or "who actually handles this?"
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Module depth and interface size in general — `/deepen-architecture`
- Correctness review of a specific diff — `/lean-review`; AI-authored merge call — `/ai-diff-judgment`
- Forward consequence simulation of a decision — `/second-order`
- Runtime resilience testing (chaos, load) — out of scope for any static scan
 
## Related
 
- `/deepen-architecture` — error surface is interface width; swallow clusters route there
- `/dependency-flow-scan`, `/churn-hotspot-scan`, `/test-shape-scan` — the static-structure family; this owns the failure-path axis
- `/grill` — designs the define-out or the relocated handling layer
- `/lean-review` — per-diff correctness, including new error handling in a change

ai/skills/skill-extract-snippets.title: Skill: extract-snippets
ai/skills/skill-extract-snippets.content:
Skill: extract-snippets
Extract screen-sized, self-contained snippets from a vault note (or a folder / the whole knowledge/ tree) and write each as its own file under snippets/, in three shapes — claim, definition, quote — for the Snippet Puck display. Generation happens at authoring time; the puck publish-service only rotates over the stored files.
When to use

Extracting snippets from a single note, a folder, or the whole knowledge/ tree
Building or rebuilding Snippet Puck content ahead of display time (batch generation)
Refreshing one note’s snippets after editing it — re-run on that note; it replaces the old files

Skip when:

You want a summary of a note for reading/research (a normal answer, not stored display snippets)
You want teaching material — /teach owns multi-session lessons under learning/
You want to audit or critique a note — the bias scans / /red-team judge; this skill produces

Why it exists
The Snippet Puck needs a pool of distilled, glance-readable snippets, and the quality-critical part is selection and faithful compression — which lines from a 200-word note are worth showing alone, compressed without inventing specifics. Doing that at display time would mean a model call per rotation; doing it at authoring time, once, stores the judgment as data the device can serve dumbly.
The two failure modes it counters are invention (a snippet gaining a number, name, or definition the source never stated — the vault’s rule-1 violation) and padding (manufacturing a weak snippet because a note “should have one”). Both pollute the rotation silently: a fabricated snippet reads as authoritative on the screen, and a padded one crowds out a real one. The skill makes zero-snippets an expected, clean result for index/stub/pointer notes, and binds quote to exact-substring verbatimness so the one type whose contract is exactness can’t be quietly softened. Glyph sanitization is deliberately not done here — it’s the publish-service’s serve-time job, because an ASCII-flattened quote is no longer verbatim.
Related

.claude/skills/extract-snippets/SKILL.md — operational definition
projects/snippet-puck/overview — the project this feeds; defines the publish-service that consumes snippets/
.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md — rule-1 (no fabricated specifics), the faithfulness spine of all three snippet types
skill-teach sibling skill — also reads notes, but builds stateful lessons under learning/, not display snippets (distinct output + workspace)
skill-write-a-skill — authored this skill
skill-quality-criteria — the criteria this skill was authored against

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/extract-snippets/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-09. Re-sync on any SKILL.md body edit.

---
name: extract-snippets
description: Extract screen-sized, self-contained snippets from a vault note (or a folder / the whole knowledge tree) and write each as its own file under `snippets/` for the Snippet Puck display. Claude reads the note and distills up to ~5 snippets per note in three shapes — claim (a standalone idea), definition (term + crisp meaning), quote (a verbatim source line) — storing faithful text with original glyphs; zero snippets is a valid result for index/stub/thin notes and the skill must not pad to a count. Regenerating a note replaces its old snippet files. Use when you want to extract snippets, generate or rebuild snippet-puck content from notes, or refresh a note's snippets after editing it. Distinct from /teach (builds multi-session lessons under learning/, not display snippets) and the bias scans (which audit, not extract); follows the vault's no-fabricated-specifics rule — quotes must be exact substrings, distillations invent nothing. Counters snippet generation drifting into invention or padding.
---
 
You extract display-ready snippets from vault notes and write each to its own file. Generation happens here, at authoring time — the downstream puck publish-service only rotates over the stored files and never calls a model. Your job is faithful compression and honest selection, not invention and not volume.
 
## Configurable assumptions (vault-specific)
 
Two paths are vault-specific; treat them as the only place to change if this skill is reused elsewhere:
 
- **Content root:** `knowledge/` — where source notes live.
- **Output root:** `snippets/` — where snippet files are written, mirroring the source's sub-path under the content root.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be:
 
- A single note path (`knowledge/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary.md`) — extract from that note.
- A folder (`knowledge/ai/`) — extract from every `.md` note under it, skipping index/special files.
- `knowledge/` or empty-with-intent-to-batch — the whole tree.
- Empty — infer from session: the note most recently read or edited this session. If none is recoverable, ask which note or folder; do not guess.
 
For a folder/tree run, process notes one at a time and accumulate the report. Special files are never sources: `_index.md`, `_connections.md`, `_inbox.md`, `topic-suggestions.md`, and any `templates/` file.
 
## The extraction procedure
 
Per note:
 
1. **Read the whole note.** Snippets must reflect the note as it stands, not its title or a skim.
 
2. **Decide eligibility — zero is a valid answer.** Produce no snippets, and record the note as *skipped (reason)*, when the note is: a special/index file; a `stub`-tagged or near-empty note; purely structural/navigational (a map-of-content, a link list); or a note whose content is entirely a pointer to other notes. Do **not** pad a thin note to reach a count — a forced snippet is the primary failure mode here.
 
3. **Select candidates — at most 5, fewer when the note is thin.** Pick the ideas that survive out of context: the load-bearing claims, the sharp definitions, the one or two lines worth quoting verbatim. A dense synthesis note may yield 4–5; a focused note 1–2; many notes 0. Quality of selection is the high-judgment part of this skill — spend it here.
 
4. **Assign each candidate a type** (`claim` / `definition` / `quote`) and apply that type's faithfulness rule below. Drop any candidate that fails a check rather than weakening the rule.
 
5. **Apply the budget + self-containment checks** (below) to every survivor. Trim or drop.
 
6. **Regenerate cleanly: delete this note's existing snippet files first.** Before writing, remove any prior snippets for this source (glob the source-derived prefix in the mirrored output folder — see Storage). This makes a re-run a replace, not an accumulation, so a note that now yields 2 snippets doesn't leave a stale third behind.
 
7. **Write one file per surviving snippet** in the Storage format.
 
8. **Report** per the Output format.
 
## Snippet types and their faithfulness rules
 
The vault's rule-1 (no fabricated specifics, `.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md`) is the spine of all three: extraction, never invention.
 
- **`claim`** — a self-contained idea or assertion, distilled in your words. May paraphrase, but every specific it contains (name, number, date, API, CVE, version) must appear in the source, and if the source hedges ("reportedly", "as of X"), the snippet keeps the hedge. No specific that isn't in the note.
- **`definition`** — a term plus a crisp statement of its meaning, drawn from how the note defines or uses it. Same no-invented-specifics rule. Don't import a textbook definition the note didn't give.
- **`quote`** — a striking line lifted **verbatim**: it must be an exact substring of the source text. Verify by locating it in the note before writing. Preserve the original glyphs and punctuation unchanged (see Faithful storage). If you cannot reproduce it exactly, it is not a quote — reclassify it as a `claim` (paraphrase) or drop it.
 
## Budget and self-containment
 
Every snippet, regardless of type:
 
- **≤ ~60 words.** It has to be readable at a glance on a 480×480 screen. Treat 60 as a ceiling, not a target; shorter is better when it stays faithful.
- **Self-contained.** It must make sense alone, with no surrounding note. No "as above/below", no "this approach", no pronoun whose referent lives outside the snippet, no abbreviation the note introduced earlier but the snippet doesn't. If making it self-contained would require inventing context, drop it instead.
 
## Faithful storage (do not sanitize here)
 
Store the snippet **as written**, with original glyphs — em-dashes, smart quotes, arrows (`→`), accents. Do **not** ASCII-flatten at extraction time:
 
- The puck's font cannot render every glyph, but that is the **publish-service's** serve-time concern, not this skill's. Flattening belongs at the transport edge so the stored note stays readable in Obsidian.
- A `quote` that has been ASCII-mangled is no longer verbatim — sanitizing here would silently break the one type whose contract is exactness.
 
## Storage format
 
One file per snippet, mirroring the source's sub-path under the content root.
 
- **Path:** strip the content root from the source path and mirror the rest under the output root, then name `<source-stem>-<type>-<n>.md` with `<n>` a 1-based counter per (source, type).
  - Source `knowledge/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary.md` with two claims and one quote →
    `snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-claim-1.md`,
    `snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-claim-2.md`,
    `snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-quote-1.md`.
  - The delete-before-write glob for that note is `snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-*.md` — scoped to the mirrored folder, so two same-named stems in different topics don't collide.
- **File contents:**
 
```markdown
---
source: knowledge/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary.md
title: "KMP ↔ JS Interop Boundary"
type: claim
generated: <today's date, YYYY-MM-DD>
---
<the snippet text — faithful, ≤ ~60 words, self-contained>
```
 
`source` is the path to the origin note; `title` is that note's frontmatter title; `type` is one of claim/definition/quote; `generated` is the run date.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Snippets extracted
 
## <source note path>  —  <N written | skipped: reason>
- claim-1: "<first ~10 words…>"
- definition-1: "<first ~10 words…>"
- quote-1: "<first ~10 words…>"   (verbatim ✓)
 
## <next note> — skipped: index file
...
 
## Summary
notes processed: <n> | snippets written: <n> (claim <n> / definition <n> / quote <n>) | notes skipped: <n>
output: snippets/<topic>/…
```
 
For a single-note run, the summary line alone is enough. When nothing qualified, say so plainly — "0 snippets: note is an index/stub/pointer" is a clean, expected result, not a failure.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Padding to a count.** Producing a weak snippet because a note "should have one". Zero is a valid, common result; a forced snippet pollutes the rotation.
- **Inventing specifics.** Adding a number, name, date, or definition the note doesn't contain, to make a snippet sound sharper. This is the rule-1 violation the skill exists to avoid.
- **Fake-verbatim quotes.** Labelling a paraphrase as `quote`, or "lightly cleaning up" a quote (smart-quote → straight, trimming a word) so it's no longer an exact substring. If it isn't exact, it isn't a quote.
- **Sanitizing at extraction.** ASCII-flattening glyphs here — it breaks quote-verbatimness and makes the Obsidian-side note ugly. Leave it to the publish-service.
- **Context-dependent snippets.** Leaving a "this", "the above", or an undefined abbreviation in the snippet. It will display alone with no source in view.
- **Accumulating stale files.** Writing new snippets without deleting the note's old ones first, so a shrunk note leaves orphaned snippets behind.
- **Over-long snippets.** Blowing past ~60 words because the idea is "too good to cut" — if it won't fit the screen, it isn't a snippet.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user wants to extract snippets from a note, folder, or the whole `knowledge/` tree
- Building or rebuilding Snippet Puck content ahead of display time
- Refreshing a note's snippets after editing it (re-run on that one note)
 
Do not invoke for:
 
- Summarizing a note for reading or research (that's a normal answer, not stored display snippets)
- Building teaching material — `/teach` owns multi-session lessons under `learning/`
- Auditing or critiquing a note — the bias scans / `/red-team` do that; this skill produces, it doesn't judge
- Writing snippets to anywhere but the output root, or inventing content not in the source
 
## Related
 
- [[projects/snippet-puck/overview]] — the project this feeds; the publish-service that consumes `snippets/` and does serve-time glyph sanitization
- `.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md` — rule-1 (no fabricated specifics) is the faithfulness spine of all three snippet types
- `/teach` — also reads notes, but builds stateful lessons under `learning/`, not single-glance display snippets
- `knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md` — the criteria this skill was authored against

ai/skills/skill-falsifiability-scan.title: Skill: falsifiability-scan
ai/skills/skill-falsifiability-scan.content:
Skill: falsifiability-scan
Scan a draft note, plan, decision, or prediction for the falsifiability shape of its load-bearing claims. Tags each claim by category (operational / deferred / vague / self-sealing / probabilistic / definitional) and produces an operationalization checklist for the ones worth sharpening.
When to use

Before committing artifacts that make load-bearing claims about the world (predictions, plans, decision rationale)
Synthesis notes where every claim sounds confident in fluent prose
Strategy docs where you suspect some claims have no specifiable falsifying observation

Skip when:

Pure narrative or instructional content
After /claim-function-scan already separated empirical from non-empirical claims, only re-run on the empirical half

Why it exists
Every confident claim sounds true in fluent prose. Tagging by falsifiability category makes visible which claims could be wrong and how — separating operational claims (testable) from vague, self-sealing, or definitional ones that masquerade as empirical. Without this pass, narrative coherence reads as evidence; with it, the load-bearing claims become an operationalization checklist.
Related

.claude/skills/falsifiability-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — backing six-category catalog
skill-claim-function-scan sibling skill — triage pass when claims may be bundled
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/falsifiability-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: falsifiability-scan
description: Scan a draft note, plan, decision, or prediction for the falsifiability shape of its load-bearing claims. Tags each claim by category (operational / deferred / vague / self-sealing / probabilistic / definitional) and produces an operationalization checklist for the ones worth sharpening. Use before committing artifacts that make load-bearing claims about the world. Counters narrative coherence without testability — the failure mode where every claim sounds confident yet has no specifiable falsifying observation.
---
 
Scan the artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for the falsifiability *shape* of its load-bearing claims about the world. This is a different axis from `/reviewers-map` (is each claim true?), `/bias-scan-ai` (is the output contaminated?), and `/red-team` (is the argument wrong?). The dangerous case it targets: a fluent draft where every claim sounds confident, the entity check passes, the inversion has weak purchase — yet "more robust," "users will prefer," "scales better" have no specifiable falsifying observation. Verified-and-unfalsifiable is the gap.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently written/edited file in this session, or the largest staged diff in `git status` if nothing was written this session.
 
The canonical catalog (taxonomy, fingerprints, philosophical guardrails) lives in `knowledge/ai/falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.md`. Consult if you need the rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on artifacts that make **load-bearing claims about the world** — predictions, capability assertions, causal claims, comparative judgments:
 
- Knowledge notes that argue for a position
- Plans, ADRs, design docs with claims about how systems will behave
- Research syntheses with empirical conclusions
- PR descriptions / commit messages with performance or behavior claims
- Decision notes with predicted outcomes
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Pure definitions, terminology, or value judgments (these are honestly `[DEFN]`; the scan adds nothing)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` quick captures
- `journal/` entries (personal reflection)
- Frontmatter-only or formatting-only changes
- `.claude/` configuration
- Code diffs without prose claims about behavior (use `/reviewers-map` instead)
 
## What to do
 
1. **Read the target file** in full.
2. **Extract load-bearing claims about the world.** Skip definitions, decisions, preferences, and value judgments. Only world-claims get tagged.
3. **Tag each claim with one of the six categories** (table below). Exactly one tag per claim.
4. **Run the operationalization checklist** for `[VAGUE]` and `[DEF]` claims (four items); run the Tetlock variant for `[PROB]` claims (four items).
5. **Name the auxiliary bundle** for the most load-bearing `[OP]` or `[DEF]` claim — Quine–Duhem holism: a falsification verdict is against the bundle (toolchain, dataset, environment), not the claim alone.
6. **Verdict** — two-state.
7. **Do not modify the target.** This is a review pass.
 
## The six-category taxonomy
 
| Tag | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `[OP]` Operational | Stated falsifying observation, measurement, deadline | "build time < 2s on commit X by date D" |
| `[DEF]` Deferred-test | Falsifiable in principle; currently untestable for cost / instrumentation / scope reasons | "this approach scales to 10k req/s" — testable, not in this session |
| `[VAGUE]` Sharpenable | Falsifiable shape latent but unspecified; needs operationalization to become `[OP]` | "more robust" — robust against what, measured how |
| `[SEAL]` Self-sealing | Counter-evidence reframed away by the claim's own structure | "in the right context X works" / "that's not real X" |
| `[PROB]` Bayesian-disconfirmable | Probabilistic; updates posterior but cannot be strictly refuted by any finite evidence | "this prompt usually produces better output" |
| `[DEFN]` Definitional / tautological | Analytic, terminological, or value-laden; not an empirical claim | "the verification protocol is the four-pass workflow" |
 
**`[DEFN]` and honest `[PROB]` are not failures.** Definitions and probabilistic claims fall outside Popper's strict criterion as a *logical property*; that does not make them defective. **`[SEAL]` is the rhetorical-failure mode.** **`[VAGUE]` is the actionable middle case** — most AI-drafted prose lives here.
 
## Fingerprints (diagnostic patterns)
 
Use these to disambiguate `[VAGUE]` from `[SEAL]` and to recognise `[DEFN]` masquerading as `[OP]`:
 
- **Vacuous universals** — "X always works in the right context" / "with proper implementation." Unbounded qualifier absorbs every counter-case. → `[VAGUE]` or `[SEAL]` depending on whether the qualifier could be specified.
- **Self-sealing reframe** — counter-examples reclassified as "not real X" or as denial / wrong fit / immaturity. No-true-Scotsman shape. → `[SEAL]`.
- **Postdiction dressed as prediction** — explains accomplished facts without forbidding future observations. → `[VAGUE]`; sharpen by demanding a future commitment point.
- **Hedge-stacked claims** — "generally," "tends to," "in many cases," "could," "may" — combined so the conjunction survives any observation. → `[VAGUE]` or `[PROB]` depending on whether a numeric probability is recoverable.
- **Operationally empty comparatives** — "more robust," "scales better," "users will prefer," "more aligned." Dominant `[VAGUE]` shape in AI-drafted technical prose.
- **Definitional retreat** — when challenged, the key term is silently redefined ("that's not really intelligence / learning / understanding"). → `[DEFN]` masquerading as `[OP]`; flag explicitly.
- **Tautology** — true by virtue of form. Legitimate as `[DEFN]`; failure mode as a load-bearing prediction.
 
## Operationalization checklist — for `[VAGUE]` and `[DEF]`
 
For each, demand four items:
 
1. **Falsifying observation** — what would count *against* this claim?
2. **Measurement procedure** — how would the observation be captured?
3. **Deadline / commitment point** — by when, against what artifact?
4. **Auxiliary bundle** — what background assumptions are pinned alongside it (toolchain version, dataset, environment, prompt, hardware)?
 
A `[VAGUE]` claim with all four becomes `[OP]`. A `[DEF]` claim with the first three but the fourth deferred is honestly deferred. A claim missing the first item is `[SEAL]` in disguise — flag as such.
 
**Prefer the cheapest deterministic signal (item 2).** When a claim admits several possible falsifying observations, rank them by cost and pick the cheapest one that is still *deterministic* (same conditions → same verdict). A claim whose only proposed test is slow, manual, or expensive usually has a faster proxy that falsifies the same thing — "build time < 2s, measured by a one-line timing script on commit X" beats "users report the build feels faster." A fast deterministic check is what makes a claim actually get tested rather than deferred forever; a test that's expensive by construction is a `[DEF]` claim wearing `[OP]` clothing (falsifiable in principle, never run in practice) — tag it `[DEF]`, not `[OP]`. This generalizes the feedback-loop-first instinct: build the cheap pass/fail signal before the expensive work.
 
## Operationalization — Tetlock variant for `[PROB]`
 
Probabilistic claims are technically unfalsifiable in strict Popper (Sober: no finite outcome sequence refutes a probability claim). The honest test is forecaster-shaped:
 
1. **Numeric probability** — translate verbal hedges into a number. "Usually" is not a probability; 0.7 is.
2. **Resolution criterion** — must resolve unambiguously yes/no on observable evidence. "User satisfaction improves" does not resolve; "NPS ≥ +20 in survey instrument Y on date D" resolves.
3. **Deadline** — by when does the question resolve.
4. **Scoring posture** — Brier / log-score commitment, or at minimum a recorded prediction the future-self can grade.
 
A `[PROB]` claim with all four is honestly testable. A `[PROB]` claim missing any of them is `[VAGUE]` wearing probabilistic clothing — re-tag.
 
## Bundle / holism note
 
For the most load-bearing `[OP]` or `[DEF]` claim, list the auxiliaries it depends on (toolchain version, dataset, environment, prompt, hardware, library). Quine–Duhem in operational form: a falsification verdict is against the bundle, not the claim alone. Naming the auxiliaries makes the verdict honest and prevents claim-blame when the auxiliary was the broken link.
 
If only one or two `[OP]`/`[DEF]` claims exist, do this for each. If many, do it for the single most load-bearing one and note the rest are similar.
 
## Verdict
 
Pick one:
 
- **Falsifiable enough to commit** — load-bearing claims are `[OP]`, `[DEF]`, honest `[PROB]`, or `[DEFN]`. Any `[VAGUE]` claims present are peripheral, not load-bearing.
- **Sharpen before commit** — at least one load-bearing claim is `[SEAL]`, or load-bearing `[VAGUE]` claims are doing work the artifact won't survive without. List the top two sharpenings.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Falsifiability scan — <filename>
 
## 1. Load-bearing world-claims
 
- `[OP]` <claim> — <location>
- `[DEF]` <claim> — <location>
- `[VAGUE]` <claim> — <location>
- `[SEAL]` <claim> — <location>
- `[PROB]` <claim> — <location>
- `[DEFN]` <claim> — <location>
 
## 2. Operationalization for [VAGUE] / [DEF]
 
### <claim 1>
- Falsifying observation: <one sentence>
- Measurement: <one sentence>
- Deadline: <one sentence>
- Auxiliary bundle: <one sentence>
 
### <claim 2>
...
 
## 3. Operationalization for [PROB] (Tetlock variant)
 
### <claim 1>
- Numeric probability: <p>
- Resolution criterion: <one sentence>
- Deadline: <one sentence>
- Scoring posture: <one sentence>
 
## 4. Bundle / holism note (most load-bearing claim)
 
<claim>: depends on <auxiliaries>. A falsification verdict here is against the bundle, not the claim in isolation.
 
## 5. Verdict
 
**<Falsifiable enough to commit | Sharpen before commit>**
<one-line rationale; if "Sharpen," list the top two sharpenings>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Conflating unfalsifiable with meaningless or unscientific.** Popper rejected the verificationists' meaning criterion. Definitions, ethical claims, and probabilistic claims fail strict falsifiability without being defective. The scan flags claim *shape*, not value.
- **Tagging probabilistic claims as `[SEAL]`.** Probabilistic claims are honestly `[PROB]` — Bayesian-disconfirmable, not self-sealing. Re-tag if you find this.
- **Pretending falsification is binary.** Quine–Duhem holism: the verdict is always against a bundle. The bundle/holism note exists to keep the output honest about this.
- **Treating `[OP]` as easy.** The four-item checklist is the bar. A claim is `[OP]` only when all four are present in the artifact (or supplied as part of the operationalization output).
- **Manufacturing findings.** If the artifact is honestly `[OP]` and `[DEFN]` only, write a short scan with no `[VAGUE]`/`[SEAL]` and verdict "Falsifiable enough to commit." Do not pad.
- **Demanding falsifiability of decisions or value judgments.** "We will adopt approach X" is a decision, not a world-claim. "Approach X reduces p99 latency" is a world-claim. Tag only the second.
- **Skipping the bundle note.** A scan that lists `[OP]` claims without naming auxiliaries pretends the claims falsify in isolation. That is the failure shape this scan exists to counter.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing a knowledge note that argues for a position
- Before publishing an ADR / design doc with claims about how systems will behave
- Before relying on AI-drafted research syntheses with empirical conclusions
- Before quoting a prediction or probabilistic claim in a persistent artifact
- Composes well with `/reviewers-map`: that one checks "could each claim be true?", this one checks "could each claim be false?". Two axes, no overlap.
 
Skip when: the artifact is exploratory / throwaway, the claims are honestly definitional, or you are working in `_inbox.md` / `journal/`.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.md` — canonical catalog (taxonomy, fingerprints, philosophical guardrails); consult for rationale
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — four-pass framework this skill plugs into
- `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md` — the failure mode this scan exists to catch (fluent prose feels verified when it isn't)
- `/reviewers-map` — different axis: per-claim verification targets `[V]`/`[U]`/`[I]`. Composes with this one.
- `/red-team` — adversarial truth, not testability of claim shape
- `/bias-scan-ai` — output-side bias contamination, not claim-shape testability

ai/skills/skill-field-report.title: Skill: field-report
ai/skills/skill-field-report.content:
Skill: field-report
Capture a one-line structured field report about a vault-built skill’s notable real-world behavior — caught something real, misfired, chafed, created value, or sparked an idea — and append it to journal/skill-field-log.md, degrading gracefully to a local file plus an emitted line when invoked outside the vault.
When to use

A vault-built skill just did something notable in any repo — a real catch, a misfire, friction at the deploy target, a concrete win, an improvement idea
A quick “anything notable?” pass at the end of an external-repo session where vault skills ran
Backfilling a remembered field event

Skip when:

Wrapping a whole session (files, claims, decisions) — commitment-ledger
The lesson needs paragraphs — retrospective
Recording a prediction — calibration-loop record

Why it exists
The vault is the lab; skills run and earn their value in external repos — and until this skill existed, none of that field evidence flowed back. Trigger audits simulated queries instead of replaying real ones, and there was no usage data to weigh skills for iteration or retirement. /field-report is the capture half of the field→lab feedback loop (development plan, Phase 1); the Phase-2 field review is the consumption half. The design constraint is habit survival: capture must cost under 30 seconds, so the skill is zero-interrogation — one line in, done, unknown context degrades to ? rather than blocking.
Phase-0 dogfood status
Conditional pass (2026-06-09). The structural gate holds — a filed line feeds a named consumer (the Phase-2 review) and so changes a future action by construction — but the log ships empty: no real field event was recoverable at build time specific enough to file without fabricating details, and padding the log at birth would violate its own notability gate. The gate completes when the first real entry lands from an external session. If the log is still empty at the Phase-2 review, that is the index-theater verdict on this skill and it should be retired by its own standard.
Related

.claude/skills/field-report/SKILL.md — operational definition
journal/skill-field-log.md — the log it appends to (schema in its header)
skill-catalog-development-plan — the plan this skill instruments (Phase 1 builds, Phase 2 consumes)
skill-commitment-ledger — session-scope sibling; same re-read-before-append discipline
skill-retrospective / skill-calibration-loop — the other journal-writing loops

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/field-report/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-09. Re-sync this block on any body edit.

---
name: field-report
description: Capture a one-line field report about a vault-built skill's notable real-world behavior — caught something real, misfired, chafed (friction), created value, or sparked an idea — and append-and-commit it to the lab's field log (journal/skill-field-log.md) from any repo; outside the vault it falls back to a local log to carry home. Zero-interrogation — one line in, done; unknown context becomes "?", never invented. Use when a skill just earned or lost its keep — "log a field report", "field-log this", "that scan caught a real bug", "that scan just paid for itself", "/x misfired", "note this friction with /x" — or as a quick anything-notable pass ending an external-repo session. Distinct from /commitment-ledger (whole-session closeout ledger) and /retrospective (multi-paragraph cycle lessons) — this files one line about one skill event. Counters the missing field→lab feedback loop, where external use produces zero evidence for skill iteration.
---
 
File a **field report**: one structured line about a vault-built skill's notable behavior during real work, appended to the lab's field log. The vault crafts skills; external repos run them; this skill carries the evidence home. The boundary that keeps it from bleeding into siblings: one line about one skill event — not a session closeout (`/commitment-ledger`), not cycle lessons (`/retrospective`).
 
The capture must cost under 30 seconds. Everything in this skill bends toward that: a habit too expensive to keep produces an empty log, and an empty log means the lab iterates on simulated evidence instead of field evidence.
 
## Input resolution
 
`$ARGUMENTS` may carry one event ("/lean-review caught a real N+1 in the api repo"), several events (each becomes its own line), or nothing — then recover the event from the current conversation: which vault-built skill just ran, and what happened.
 
No-guess fallback: the **skill name** and the **event** are mandatory. If either is unrecoverable from arguments and conversation, reply with the single missing piece in one line and stop — never run a multi-question interview. All other fields degrade to `?` rather than blocking.
 
## Line schema
 
One line per event, pipe-separated, grep-able:
 
```text
- <YYYY-MM-DD> | /<skill> | <context> | <event> | <summary>
```
 
- **date** — today, the filing date. Backfills included: put the remembered timing inside the summary ("~last week: …") rather than guessing a calendar date.
- **skill** — the vault-built skill the report is about. Mandatory (see above).
- **context** — repo or project name (the git-root directory name is fine); `vault` when the event happened inside brains; `?` when unclear.
- **event** — exactly one of five (two events = two lines):
  - `caught` — found something real (bug, bad claim, contradiction) that would otherwise have shipped
  - `misfire` — fired when it shouldn't, failed to fire when it should, or fired and produced noise
  - `friction` — ran but chafed: vault-coupled reference, awkward output contract, missing context at the deploy target
  - `value` — concrete usefulness not tied to a single catch (changed a decision, saved a rework)
  - `idea` — field use sparked an improvement to a skill or a candidate for a new one
- **summary** — one line, ≤140 characters, plain words, the specific thing that happened. No narrative.
 
**Notability gate.** Log events that would change how a skill is built, triggered, or routed. "Ran fine, nothing notable" is not an entry — when invoked as an end-of-session sweep and nothing qualifies, report that as the clean outcome and write nothing. The Phase-2 field review reads this log as evidence; padding destroys its signal.
 
## Write-path resolution
 
Deterministic order; stop at the first hit:
