ai/skills/skill-metacog-check.title: Skill: metacog-check
ai/skills/skill-metacog-check.content:
Skill: metacog-check
Augmentation-layer orchestrator for the metacognition operation — the fourth of the four higher-order operations the appreciating-position-vs-skill session decomposed, and the gate that decides whether the other three engaged honestly. The AI self-monitors its own most recent substantive answer — calibrated confidence + a mind-changer, an inversion via /disagree, a claim map via /reviewers-map, and a competence-edge check — while the user stays the principal who decides whether to trust the self-report, because self-assessed competence is where a model is least reliable.
When to use

An answer is load-bearing and you want its reliability priced before acting — “how confident are you really”, “what would change your mind”, “are you sure”, “check your reasoning on that”
Before propagating an AI answer into a decision or an artifact
After a fluent, confident-sounding answer in a domain where rubber-stamping is the risk

Skip for one adversarial inversion (/disagree), a claim map of an output (/reviewers-map), bias fingerprints in an AI-authored file (/bias-scan-ai), or adversarial critique of a committed artifact (/red-team).
Why it exists
One of the four “AI performs, you stay principal” operation-skills built from the appreciating-position-vs-skill conclusion. It counters automation-bias rubber-stamping — accepting fluent output whose confidence was never priced — which higher-order-thinking-under-ai names as the characteristic failure mode of the appreciating Evaluate tier. The discriminating move is the competence-edge check (the note’s “is my schema strong enough to judge this, or am I about to rubber-stamp it?”), which no single sibling runs. The honest limit it bakes in: a model judging its own competence boundary is least reliable exactly there — so the skill reports, and the principal decides trust. The augmentation counterpart to /deepen-thinking’s metacognitive close.
Related

skill-disagree — the inversion this composes (packaged with confidence + competence-edge)
skill-reviewers-map — the claim-verification map this pulls the weakest claim from
skill-calibration-loop — receives any binary prediction so the confidence gets Brier-scored
skill-bias-scan-ai · skill-red-team — the artifact-facing siblings (files, not the AI’s own reasoning)
skill-deepen-thinking — the training sibling (user’s own metacognitive close; this performs the AI’s)
appreciating-position-vs-skill — metacognition as the gate; the method finding (catalogued belief vs lived model)
higher-order-thinking-under-ai — “Metacognition becomes the gate” under automation bias

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/metacog-check/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-16. Re-sync on any later body edit.

---
name: metacog-check
description: Self-check the AI's own most recent substantive answer — state a calibrated confidence, name what would change it, and judge whether the AI's schema is strong enough to answer or it's about to rubber-stamp. The AI monitors its own reasoning; you stay the principal who decides whether to trust the self-report — self-assessed competence is where models are least reliable. Use when an answer is load-bearing and you want it checked before acting — "how confident are you really", "what would change your mind", "are you sure", "check your own reasoning". Thin orchestrator: composes /disagree (invert the answer) and /reviewers-map (tag claims), and feeds a binary prediction to /calibration-loop. Distinct from /disagree (one inversion — this adds confidence + competence-edge), /reviewers-map (claim map — one input here), and /bias-scan-ai (artifact fingerprints, not a reasoning-confidence self-report). Counters automation-bias rubber-stamping — accepting fluent output whose confidence was never priced.
---
 
Self-monitor the AI's own last substantive answer — the metacognition operation (the fourth of the four in `knowledge/general/appreciating-position-vs-skill.md`, and the *gate* that decides whether the other three engaged honestly). The AI performs the self-check; the boundary that keeps you the principal is that **a model judging its own competence boundary is at its least reliable exactly there — so the AI reports, and you decide whether to trust the report.** Thin by design: it drives `/disagree` and `/reviewers-map` and synthesizes their output into one calibrated read rather than reimplementing them.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS`, if present, names which answer to check; otherwise the target is **the AI's own most recent substantive response** in this session. Not a hand-in artifact — for that, the bias scans apply. If there's no substantive prior answer to check, say so and stop; don't manufacture one to check.
 
## The procedure
 
Four moves, then the gate. Keep it tight — this is a check on one answer, not a re-derivation.
 
1. **Calibrated confidence.** State a number (0–1) for the answer's core claim, and — the calibration discipline — name explicitly what observation would move it. A high confidence paired with a concrete, *unresolved* mind-changer is incoherent; reconcile it (usually by lowering the number), and show the reconciliation.
2. **Invert it** via **`/disagree`** — argue the opposite of the answer with equal rigor (steelman, not strawman). The size of the gap between the original and its inversion is the signal: a strong inversion means the original was confidently-stated noise.
3. **Map the claims** via **`/reviewers-map`** — tag the answer's load-bearing claims `[V]` verified / `[U]` unverified / `[I]` inference, and pull out the single weakest load-bearing one.
4. **The competence-edge check** (the discriminating move — the note's "is my schema strong enough to judge this, or am I about to rubber-stamp it?"). Judge honestly whether the AI holds enough domain schema to have actually reasoned here, or merely produced fluent in-distribution text. Name which. This is the check no single sibling skill runs.
5. **Run the principal gate** and, if a falsifiable binary prediction surfaced, hand it to **`/calibration-loop`** so the confidence gets scored over time.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Metacog check — <the answer being checked, one line>
 
## Confidence
<0.NN> on <the core claim> · would change if: <concrete observation>
Reconciled? <yes — lowered from X because the mind-changer is open | n/a>
 
## Inversion (/disagree)
Strongest opposite case: <one line> · Gap verdict: <well-supported | confidently-stated noise>
 
## Claim map (/reviewers-map)
Weakest load-bearing claim: <claim> — <[V]|[U]|[I]>
 
## Competence edge
<reasoned from real schema | fluent in-distribution text only> — <why>
Rubber-stamp risk: <low | high>
 
## You own (principal gate)
- The self-confidence above is the AI's, and self-assessed competence is where it's least reliable — decide whether to trust it.
- If rubber-stamp risk is high, the schema to judge this may need to be yours, not the AI's.
 
## Handoff
Prediction → /calibration-loop: <binary prediction + deadline, or "none surfaced">
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Self-flattering confidence.** Reporting 0.9 because the answer *sounds* settled. The mind-changer test exists to catch this — if something concrete and open would flip it, the number was wrong.
- **A toothless inversion.** Strawmanning the opposite case so the original wins. `/disagree`'s value is a real steelman; a weak one fakes the calibration signal.
- **Skipping the competence-edge check.** Running confidence + inversion + claim-map and stopping. The "am I rubber-stamping" judgment is the move that distinguishes this from its siblings — omitting it makes this just /disagree with a number.
- **Checking a hand-in artifact.** This monitors the AI's *own* reasoning. For a user-authored or AI-authored file, use the bias scans / `/red-team`, not this.
- **Deciding trust for the user.** Declaring the answer reliable. The skill reports the self-assessment; whether to trust it is the principal's call.
 
## When to invoke
 
- An answer is load-bearing and you want its reliability priced before acting — "how confident are you really", "what would change your mind", "are you sure", "check your reasoning on that"
- Before propagating an AI answer into a decision or an artifact
- After a fluent, confident-sounding answer in a domain where rubber-stamping is the risk
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- One adversarial inversion with no confidence/competence wrapper — `/disagree`
- A claim-by-claim verification map of an output — `/reviewers-map`
- Bias fingerprints in an AI-authored *artifact/file* — `/bias-scan-ai`
- Logging a binary prediction over time — `/calibration-loop` (this feeds it)
- Adversarial critique of a committed note or plan — `/red-team`
 
## Related
 
- `/disagree` — the inversion this composes (and packages with confidence + competence-edge)
- `/reviewers-map` — the claim-verification map this pulls the weakest claim from
- `/calibration-loop` — receives any binary prediction so the confidence gets Brier-scored
- `/bias-scan-ai` · `/red-team` — the artifact-facing siblings, for files rather than the AI's own reasoning
- `/deepen-thinking` — the *training* sibling: scaffolds the user's own metacognitive close rather than performing the AI's
- `knowledge/general/appreciating-position-vs-skill.md` — metacognition as the gate; the method finding (catalogued belief vs lived model)
- `knowledge/general/higher-order-thinking-under-ai.md` — "Metacognition becomes the gate" under automation bias

ai/skills/skill-note-value-scan.title: Skill: note-value-scan
ai/skills/skill-note-value-scan.content:
Skill: note-value-scan
Value the notes in a corpus so that something can finally leave it. The skill places each note in the irreplaceability × activation quadrant — could a frontier model regenerate this content today, and does anything actually use it — then checks whether the body still serves its stated intent:, flags redundant near-neighbours, and emits a ranked action table: keep / invest / merge / demote-to-snippet / re-verify / archive. It reports the actions; it does not perform them. In this vault the deterministic narrowing pass is tools/note_value.py; outside it, the same narrowing is done by hand.
When to use

A deliberate corpus-strategy review — the “what should leave?” pass, especially where nothing has ever been archived
A folder that has grown lopsided, bloated, or full of near-duplicates
Before a restructure, to decide what merges and what splits
The inverse question — which notes deserve deepening, splitting, or promotion to a hub
Paired with /staleness-decay-scan on a maintenance day — that one catches expiry, this one catches irrelevance

Skip when:

The target is a single artifact you want critiqued (use /red-team or /reviewers-map)
The scope is a queue, backlog, or commitment ledger (use /whittle-scan)
The problem is a perishable fact in one note (use /staleness-decay-scan)
The corpus is under ~30 notes — the thresholds are corpus-relative and meaningless on a handful (refuse-to-scan)

Why it exists
The vault is append-mostly, and git confirms it: zero note deletions and zero renames in knowledge/ across the entire history. knowledge-base-entropy named the stock-and-flow problem — capture is the inflow, and there is no outflow — and built two scans for decay inside notes. Neither decides which notes should leave. That gate is what this skill closes, and it is decay mode 5, commodity drift: the frontier moves, yesterday’s synthesis becomes today’s zero-shot answer, and a note’s value erodes without the note changing at all. No per-note read can catch that, because nothing about the note looks wrong.
Three design moves carry the weight:

Quadrant, not ranking. Irreplaceability and activation are orthogonal, and the off-diagonal cells hold the decisions: irreplaceable-but-unused work nobody links to (surface it, never bin it), and heavily-linked commodity content (an anchor, or a hub by habit?). A single score collapses both.
Being mentioned is not being used. In a densely cross-linked vault the median note already carries 9 editorial inbound links, so “is linked” separates nothing. Activation counts active channels — depended on by tooling, deliberately revisited, harvested for snippets, hub-scale linkage. Ordinary linkage is treated asymmetrically: it vetoes an archive verdict, but never counts as use.
The proxy shortlists; the read decides. Marker density can rank candidates, but assigning the irreplaceability band requires reading the note. A hub note can be pure commodity content and score low on every marker while being load-bearing.

The known limitation is stated in the skill body rather than designed away: the regeneration test is a model judging what a model could produce, so every verdict must quote its evidence and a human overrules per note.
Related

.claude/skills/note-value-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
knowledge-base-entropy — backing concept; this skill operationalizes the outflow gate and decay mode 5 (commodity drift)
skill-staleness-decay-scan — the boundary partner; owns perishable facts whose authority expired. re-verify items route there
skill-contradiction-scan — sibling corpus scan; catches cross-note disagreement, orthogonal to whether a note earns its place
skill-whittle-scan — owns queue items with a per-week cost of inaction, not notes
skill-extract-snippets — the mechanism behind a demote-to-snippet verdict
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/note-value-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-07-29.

---
name: note-value-scan
description: Value the notes in a knowledge corpus to decide what to keep, deepen, merge, or delete — the outflow gate for a vault that only ever grows. Places each note in the irreplaceability × activation quadrant (could a model regenerate this today? does anything actually use it, or is it unused and unlinked?), checks whether the body still serves its stated `intent:`, flags near-duplicate neighbours, and emits a ranked action table. Use for a corpus-strategy review, when a folder feels bloated, when deciding what to prune or archive before a restructure, or when asking which notes deserve deepening. Owns whether a note still earns its place — distinct from `/staleness-decay-scan` (facts that expired), `/contradiction-scan` (notes that disagree), and `/whittle-scan` (queue items with a per-week cost of inaction). Skip for single-artifact critique (`/red-team`) or a corpus under ~30 notes. Counters commodity drift and the no-outflow ratchet.
---
 
Value the notes in a corpus so that something can finally leave it — the outflow gate named but not built in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`. The dangerous case is not a wrong note; it is a corpus that only grows. Capture is continuous, archival never fires, and every note still reads fine on its own, so the cost is invisible: retrieval dilutes, maintenance load rises, and content that was worth writing in 2025 quietly becomes something any model emits on demand. This skill decides, per note, whether it still earns its place, and emits an **action table** — keep, invest, merge, demote, re-verify, archive.
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is a folder, a note path, or empty (= the corpus's main knowledge root). Scanning is cheap to start and expensive to finish: narrow deterministically first, then read.
 
## Boundary table (read first)
 
Four skills touch corpus decay. They own different questions:
 
| Skill | Owns | Decay it sees |
|---|---|---|
| **This skill** (`/note-value-scan`) | Does this note still earn its place? | Value erosion — commodity drift, or work nothing ever used |
| `/staleness-decay-scan` | Is this dated claim still true? | A fact silently expired |
| `/contradiction-scan` | Do two notes disagree? | Distributed inconsistency |
| `/whittle-scan` | What is it costing me not to act? | Per-week cost of inaction on a queue item |
 
**Do not re-derive staleness here.** A note whose only problem is an aged figure is a `/staleness-decay-scan` item: emit `re-verify` and route it. This skill asks whether the note should exist at all, which is a different question from whether its numbers are current — a perfectly fresh note can be worthless, and a stale one can be irreplaceable.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A deliberate corpus-strategy review — the "what should leave?" pass
- A folder that has grown lopsided, bloated, or full of near-duplicates
- A pre-restructure prune, before splitting or merging a cluster
- The inverse question: which notes deserve deepening, splitting, or promotion to a hub
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A single artifact you want critiqued (`/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`)
- A queue, backlog, or commitment ledger (`/whittle-scan`)
- Perishable facts in one note (`/staleness-decay-scan`)
- A corpus under ~30 notes — the thresholds are corpus-relative and meaningless on a handful of notes; say so and stop
 
**Refuse-to-scan condition.** If the target is too small for relative ranking, or is a mirror of content authored elsewhere, say so in one line and stop. "This corpus is too small to rank against itself" is a correct verdict, not a failure.
 
## The value model
 
Two axes that are genuinely orthogonal, plus two flags that ride alongside.
 
**Axis A — irreplaceability. The regeneration test: would a frontier model today produce this note's load-bearing content from a one-line prompt?**
 
| Band | What it looks like | Storage value |
|---|---|---|
| `proprietary` | The author's own decisions, measurements, configs, first-hand observations, project-specific architecture | Irreplaceable — cannot be regenerated at any price |
| `synthesis` | Resolves a tension between sources, or carries verified primary citations that cost real work | Regenerable in *form*, not in *verified content* |
| `commodity` | A competent explainer of a public topic | ≈ 0 — a model emits an equal or better version on demand, while the note still costs maintenance |
 
This is the axis that decides prune-vs-keep in an AI-authored corpus, and the one that moves without the note changing: **commodity drift**. Every capable-model release reclassifies some `synthesis` notes as `commodity`. Assign the band by reading the note — a marker-density proxy can shortlist candidates, but it cannot make this call.
 
**Axis B — activation. Does anything actually use it?** Count independent channels of *active* use: depended on by tooling or rules, deliberately revisited after creation, harvested for snippets, or hub-scale inbound linkage.
 
Ordinary inbound links are weak evidence in a densely-linked corpus — being *mentioned* is not being *used*. Treat linkage asymmetrically: below-median linkage is not evidence against a note, but above-median linkage **vetoes an archive verdict**. Report the raw count either way so the reader can overrule.
 
**Flag C — intent fidelity.** Where notes carry an `intent:` field (a stated optimization target, re-evaluatable by design), classify: `on-target` / `body-drifted` (the note moved and its target didn't) / `fulfilled` (target achieved, the note is now a record → archive candidate) / `no-intent`.
 
**Flag D — redundancy.** Near-neighbour overlap that suggests a merge. **Exempt parallel-template families** — a set of notes applying one template per instance (one per spec, per model, per client) overlaps by construction. Seven notes at 90% structural overlap is a template, not seven redundant notes.
 
### The quadrant
 
|  | **Unused** | **Used** |
|---|---|---|
| **Commodity** | `archive` — the clearest case | `anchor-check` — is it earning the links, or a hub by habit? Often `demote-to-snippet` |
| **Irreplaceable** | `latent-value` — hard-won work nothing points at; usually `invest` (surface and link it), never archive | `keep` / `invest` — working as intended |
 
The off-diagonal cells are the point. A ranking collapses them into one axis and hides both.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Narrow deterministically.** In this vault, run `python3 tools/note_value.py` (`--json` for structured output, `--root <folder>` to scope). It classes notes, computes axes B/C/D, and shortlists on an axis-A proxy. **Outside this vault the script will not exist** — do the same narrowing by hand with Glob/Grep/`git log` and say in the output that the pass was manual.
2. **Class out what must not be valued as authored content**: mirrors of external material, catalog/reference notes whose value lives in the thing they describe, and structural maps (`_index.md` and friends). They dominate the low-value tail on every naive metric and are false positives. State the counts.
3. **Read the shortlist.** Full read per note — the axis-A band cannot be assigned from a proxy.
4. **Assign band, channels, and flags** per note. Quote the load-bearing claim you are judging.
5. **Sample the keep band.** Read ~10–15 notes the narrowing pass did *not* shortlist and check whether any should have been. Report the miss rate. An unvalidated proxy is what turns a corpus scan into a noise generator.
6. **Assign a verdict** per shortlisted note (see below), with the evidence that drove it.
7. **Rank by value at risk** — an irreplaceable note nobody can find outranks a commodity note nobody reads.
8. **State coverage**: how many notes valued, how many classed out, what was not reached.
 
## Verdicts
 
- **`invest`** — deepen, split, or promote to a hub
- **`keep`** — earns its place as-is; no action
- **`merge → <path>`** — name the target note, not just "merge"
- **`demote-to-snippet`** — one durable claim inside a commodity wrapper; extract the claim, archive the wrapper
- **`re-verify`** — value hinges on a claim that has aged; route to `/staleness-decay-scan`
- **`archive`** — commodity, unused, and either intent-fulfilled or intent-absent
 
Every `archive` and `merge` verdict must quote the note's load-bearing claim and name a path. A verdict without evidence is not a finding.
 
## Verdict states
 
- **Outflow candidates found** — at least one `archive` or `merge`.
- **Reshaping only** — no archives; `invest`, `demote`, and `re-verify` items only.
- **Corpus earning its place** — every note valued lands on `keep` or `invest`.
- **Too small to rank** — under ~30 notes; refuse-to-scan.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /note-value-scan — <target> — reference date <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Scope
<N valued>; <M classed out: mirrors/catalog/structural>; <thresholds used>
<coverage note — what was not reached>
 
## Action table
| Note | Band | Activation | Intent | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<path>` | commodity/synthesis/proprietary | <channels or none> | on-target/drifted/fulfilled/— | archive / merge → `<path>` / demote / re-verify / invest / keep | "<quoted load-bearing claim>" |
 
## Latent value (irreplaceable, unused)
- `<path>` — <what is in here that nothing points at, and where it should be linked from>
 
## Routed elsewhere
- `<path>` → /staleness-decay-scan (aged claim, not a value question)
 
## Proxy validation
<K keep-band notes sampled; J should have been shortlisted — miss rate J/K>
 
## Verdict
**<Outflow candidates found | Reshaping only | Corpus earning its place | Too small to rank>**
<one-line rationale + the single highest-value action>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Assigning the irreplaceability band from a proxy.** Marker density shortlists; it does not decide. A hub note can be pure commodity content and score low on every marker while being load-bearing — read it.
- **Auto-archiving.** Like every corpus scan, this emits a ledger and stops. Removing a note is the author's judgment, and a wrong inference applied corpus-wide is unrecoverable. (Decay-discipline #1 in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`.)
- **Pruning template families.** Notes that share a structure because they instantiate one template per case are not duplicates. Check for a family before flagging redundancy.
- **Treating "not linked" as "not valuable".** The `latent-value` cell exists precisely because unused and worthless are different. The action there is to surface it, not to bin it.
- **Ranking instead of quadranting.** Collapsing irreplaceability and activation into one score hides the two cells that carry the actual decisions.
- **Scoring the whole corpus.** Emitting 300 rows with numbers reproduces the invisibility the skill exists to counter. Shortlist, then read, then rank what survives.
- **Grading your own kind without saying so.** The regeneration test is a model judging what a model could produce. Name that limitation in the output and quote the evidence so a human can overrule it per note.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A deliberate corpus-strategy review, especially where nothing has ever been archived
- After a burst of capture, when a folder has visibly outgrown its shape
- Before a restructure, to decide what merges and what splits
- Paired with `/staleness-decay-scan` on a maintenance day — that one catches expiry, this one catches irrelevance
 
Skip when: the corpus is tiny, the target is one artifact (`/red-team`), or the question is about queue items (`/whittle-scan`).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy` — the backing concept; this skill operationalizes the outflow gate and decay mode 5 (commodity drift)
- `/staleness-decay-scan` — the boundary partner; owns perishable facts. `re-verify` items route there
- `/contradiction-scan` — catches cross-note disagreement; orthogonal to whether a note earns its place
- `/whittle-scan` — owns queue items with a per-week cost of inaction, not notes
- `/extract-snippets` — the mechanism behind a `demote-to-snippet` verdict
- `tools/note_value.py` — the deterministic narrowing pass this skill reads
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-note-value-scan` — the reference note for this skill

ai/skills/skill-option-premium-check.content:
Skill: option-premium-check
Scan a proposed action, a chosen path, or a list of deferred-but-unresolved items for flexibility-burning commitments (irreversible moves where an equal-EV reversible alternative exists) and optionality-hoarding patterns (deferred items whose carrying cost has overtaken the preserved option’s value — Pandora override). Claude names options-preserved, options-destroyed, and concrete carrying-cost mechanisms from the artifact; the user supplies felt lock-in pressure via AskUserQuestion. Mismatch between the formal option structure and felt lock-in surfaces the flags. Returns flags with implied next actions — take the flexibility-preserving alternative, or close the held-open option in one direction.
When to use

A proposed action is being framed as obvious or low-cost but you suspect it’s a one-way door
Two paths look roughly equivalent on expected payoff but you can’t tell which preserves more flexibility
A list of deferred items in a project, commitments log, or backlog has been sitting unresolved for a week or more
A roadmap branch point or ADR is approaching commit
Before a planning block where multiple lock-in moves are queued (schema decisions, API surface, naming conventions)
After a stretch of optionality-preserving moves, as a check on whether you’ve drifted into optionality hoarding

Skip when:

The queue’s failure mode is invisible per-week decay (use /whittle-scan — different lens on the same item type)
The artifact is a single draft needing adversarial review (use /red-team)
The question is about forward consequences across actors and time horizons (use /second-order)
The estimate to correct is numeric (use /reference-class)
The artifact contains no decision and no deferred-item list
You’re depleted — the option-structure enumeration is deliberation-heavy

Why it exists
The two failure modes are symmetric and both invisible to intuition. One-way-door blindness — committing to a path that destroys options when an equal-EV alternative would have preserved them. Naive expected-value calculation under-counts variance; flexibility has positive value under uncertainty (the option premium), and the premium rises with uncertainty — the opposite of how intuition treats variance. Optionality hoarding — keeping an option open at a carrying cost that exceeds its preserved value, dressing avoidance as prudence. Deferring commitment delays integration, blocks downstream work, and creates drift between artifact and world.
The skill’s most insidious failure mode is reproducing optionality hoarding via the scan itself — “preserve all options pending further analysis” is exactly what it exists to counter. The constraint that every flag must point at a specific next action (close the option, take the preserving alternative, or accept the lock-in explicitly) is the structural guard against that drift. The Step 0 routing discriminator (decay-dominant items → /whittle-scan; blocked-downstream-work-dominant items → stay here) prevents cross-skill cannibalization on deferred-list artifacts where both lenses would otherwise fire. The MEDIUM calibration anchor on Q3 (felt lock-in) — requiring the user to name one concrete reversal scenario before MEDIUM is recorded — guards against MEDIUM-default drift.
Related

.claude/skills/option-premium-check/SKILL.md — operational definition
index-policies-for-prioritization — canonical four-index framework; this skill operationalizes the Real Options column
prioritization-architecture-synthesis — Layer 3 (valuation) home alongside /whittle-scan
skill-whittle-scan — adjacent skill on the same valuation layer; decay valuation rather than flexibility valuation
skill-second-order — forward consequence cascade; complementary axis (this skill values flexibility at the commit moment; /second-order projects consequences across actors and time horizons after)
skill-red-team — adversarial truth-testing; use after option-premium has flagged a flexibility-burning move and you want the case-against surfaced before deciding
skill-branch-resolve — for plans with conditional branches needing operationalization; route there when the question is “how do I express this branch?” rather than “is committing flexibility-burning?”
skill-commitment-ledger — pairs naturally; ledger captures what was decided, this skill values what flexibility was burned or preserved
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/option-premium-check/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: option-premium-check
description: Scan a decision, proposed action, or list of deferred-but-unresolved items for flexibility-burning commitments and optionality-hoarding. Names the options each decision preserves and destroys; signs it flexibility-creating, flexibility-burning, dominant, or optionality-hoarding (carrying cost exceeds preserved value — Pandora override); returns flags with implied next actions. Use when proposing a one-way-door / irreversible action, when reversibility is unclear, when two similar-payoff paths differ in reversibility, when a deferred-items list has sat unresolved long enough to feel stale, or when a commitment feels like lock-in but you can't name what it gives up. Skip for per-week queue decay (`/whittle-scan`), adversarial truth-testing of a draft (`/red-team`), forward consequence cascades (`/second-order`), numeric base-rate estimation (`/reference-class`), session closeout (`/commitment-ledger`), or goal-statement quality (`/intent-check`). Counters optionality hoarding and one-way-door blindness.
---
 
Scan the decision-shaped or deferred-list artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for **flexibility-burning** commitments and **optionality-hoarding** patterns. The two failure modes are symmetric and both are surfaceable from outside the decision-maker's intuition:
 
- **Flexibility-burning:** committing to a path that destroys options when an equal-expected-payoff alternative would have preserved them. Naive expected-value calculation under-counts variance; flexibility has positive value under uncertainty (the "option premium"), and the premium rises with uncertainty — the opposite of how intuition treats variance.
- **Optionality-hoarding:** keeping an option open at a carrying cost that exceeds the option's preserved value. Deferring commitment delays integration, blocks downstream work, accumulates cognitive load, and creates drift between the artifact and the world it's meant to act on. At some point Pandora's stopping rule overrides the option premium and the right move is to close the option in one direction or the other.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most-recently-modified decision-shaped artifact (`projects/*/overview.md`, `journal/commitments-log.md`, a roadmap, an ADR, a plan note)
2. A decision named in the current session
3. Ask which decision or deferred-list to scan rather than guess
 
The canonical mental-model framework lives in `knowledge/general/index-policies-for-prioritization.md` — the **Real Options** section is the load-bearing one for this skill, and the note's anti-pattern list (optionality hoarding, false precision) maps directly onto this skill's anti-patterns. Consult for rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A proposed action where reversibility is not obvious (e.g., "should I commit to framework X for the next 6 months?")
- A choice between two or more paths whose expected payoffs are roughly similar but whose option structure differs
- A list of deferred-but-unresolved items (e.g., the **Deferred items** section of a `/commitment-ledger` entry, a project's "open questions," a backlog of unstaged changes)
- A roadmap branch point or a plan's conditional fork (where committing to a branch closes the counterfactual)
- An ADR or decision note before it's signed
- A multi-step plan whose early steps lock in later structure (e.g., schema decisions, API surface, naming conventions)
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A queue where the failure mode is invisible per-week decay rather than reversibility (use `/whittle-scan`)
- A single artifact under adversarial review (use `/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`)
- A forward consequence-cascade trace (use `/second-order` — that skill projects consequences across actors and time horizons; this one valuates flexibility at the commit moment)
- A numeric prediction needing outside-view base-rate correction (use `/reference-class`)
- A session-end audit of what was committed today (use `/commitment-ledger`)
- A goal or intent statement (use `/intent-check`)
- A plan with conditional branches that need operationalization (use `/branch-resolve`)
- A clarification loop (use `/clarify-first` — Pandora's stopping rule applies but is encoded there)
 
**Refuse-to-scan conditions.** Refuse and say so in one line if:
 
- The artifact contains no decision and no deferred-item list (e.g., a pure description, a knowledge note, a finished change-log) — there is no flexibility valuation to perform.
- The "decision" is so vague that options-preserved and options-destroyed cannot be named in one line each. Ask for sharpening rather than synthesize a confabulated option structure.
- The decision is fully irreversible by construction and has already been executed. Surfacing what was given up is `/red-team` territory, not flexibility valuation.
 
## The core questions
 
For each decision under scan, three questions. The first two are answerable from the artifact and Claude's reasoning; the third must come from the user.
 
> **Q1. What options does this action preserve?** (The right to abandon, scale, pivot, defer, revise, narrow, widen.)
>
> **Q2. What options does this action destroy?** (Sunk commitments, locked-in dependencies, foreclosed alternatives, written-into-stone choices.)
>
> **Q3. How much does this commitment feel like a one-way door to you?** (LOW = easily reversed, MEDIUM = reversible with effort, HIGH = irreversible-in-practice, UNKNOWN = no working-memory read.)
 
The third question is the **felt lock-in pressure** — the user's read on how reversible the commitment is *right now*. Could they walk it back this week with bounded effort? Two formally-similar decisions can sit very differently on this axis. The question is deliberately present-state: prospective affective forecasts ("how trapped will this feel in six months?") are systematically miscalibrated (Wilson & Gilbert on affective forecasting), so the question asks about the present reversibility surface, not the future felt state. Claude has no working memory in this sense and cannot pattern-match from descriptions to produce it without confabulating.
 
The signal lives in the **mismatch** between the formal option structure (Q1, Q2) and the felt lock-in (Q3):
 
| Pattern | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Many options destroyed, felt lock-in LOW | One-way-door blindness — the **primary flag** for flexibility-burning. The user is underestimating irreversibility. |
| Few options destroyed, felt lock-in HIGH | Phantom lock-in — the **inverse flag**. The user feels trapped by a decision that's actually reversible; surfacing it unlocks the move. |
| Options preserved, carrying cost > preserved value | Optionality hoarding — the **second primary flag**. Pandora override applies; close the option in one direction. |
| Options preserved at low carrying cost | Dominant choice — informational; no flag. |
| An alternative path preserves strictly more options | Surface the alternative + ask the user whether expected payoffs are roughly comparable — **conditional flag** that fires only on the user's "yes, roughly comparable" judgment. |
 
Sign is **directional, not numerical.** "Carrying cost = $1,200/wk in cognitive load" is theater; the framework values directionally (LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH) and names the mechanism.
 
## What to do
 
**Estimator axis (Mode 3 split, carried forward from `/whittle-scan`).** This skill estimates two columns from different sources: Claude names *options preserved*, *options destroyed*, and *carrying-cost mechanism* by reasoning about the decision's structure from artifact content; the *user* supplies *felt lock-in pressure* and *EV-comparability judgments* directly via `AskUserQuestion`, because only the user can judge present-state reversibility and whether two paths' expected payoffs are roughly comparable. Do not impute felt lock-in from project descriptions or decision language — that is confabulation, and the primary-flag pattern (one-way-door blindness vs. phantom lock-in) requires the user's read to detect. Collect felt lock-in one question per decision if N ≤ 6, or top-3-by-options-destroyed plus any deferred items past N days if N > 6. **MEDIUM calibration anchor:** if the user picks MEDIUM, follow up with "name one concrete reversal scenario — what specifically would you do this week to walk it back?" If no concrete scenario comes to mind, downgrade the answer to UNKNOWN rather than recording MEDIUM. This guards against MEDIUM-default drift, where the answer slides to MEDIUM to avoid both LOW (dismissive) and HIGH (committing). If the user answers "I don't know" or skips, record `unknown-lock-in` and exclude that decision from primary-flag classification — never default to LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH.
 
0. **Route deferred items by dominant cost type before scanning them as option-premium items.** For each held-open / deferred item, ask: is the dominant cost *decay of the value at stake* (compounding cost over time, expiring window, eroding relationship, calibration data lost on resolution-date pass) or *blocked downstream work / integration drift* on a value that isn't itself decaying (waiting commit blocks dependent commits, unstaged convention creates doc-code drift, open decision blocks a specific named next task)? If decay-dominant, route to `/whittle-scan` instead — don't fake the lens. If blocked-work-dominant, stay here. Items where *both* costs are material get scanned by both skills; flag the doubling explicitly in the verdict. Items where neither cost is concretely nameable are correctly deferred — exclude from the scan.
1. **Identify the decision(s) under scan.** Count. If zero decisions and zero deferred items remain after the routing step, refuse-to-scan.
2. **For each decision, name options preserved (Q1) in one line.** If none, write "none" — don't invent. *(Claude estimates.)*
3. **For each decision, name options destroyed (Q2) in one line.** If none, write "none" — don't invent. *(Claude estimates.)*
4. **For each held-open / deferred item that survived routing, name the concrete carrying-cost mechanism.** Acceptable mechanisms must be concrete and nameable: drift between artifact and world, *specific* downstream work that is blocked and can be named, integration window with a stated closing date, accumulating implementation tax with a named compounding source. **"Cognitive load of holding the open question" is acceptable only when tied to specific blocked downstream work the user can name** — generic "this is on my mind" load is too cheap a mechanism and would fire the Pandora override indiscriminately. If no concrete mechanism is real, the item is correctly deferred — write "none" and move on. *(Claude estimates; the user confirms or rejects in Step 5.)*
5. **Ask the user for felt lock-in per decision (Q3) via `AskUserQuestion`** per the spec above (including the MEDIUM calibration anchor). Record LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / unknown-lock-in. *(User supplies. Do not impute.)*
6. **Sign each decision.** Apply the pattern table above. Flexibility-burning, optionality-hoarding, dominant choice, phantom lock-in, alternative-preserves-more, or no flag.
7. **For each flag, name the implied next action in one line.** For flexibility-burning when an alternative was found: surface the alternative explicitly and ask the user via `AskUserQuestion` whether the two paths' expected payoffs are roughly comparable. If "yes, roughly comparable" → recommend the alternative. If "no, primary path is clearly better" → "accept the lock-in explicitly; the EV gap dominates the option premium." If "I don't know" → mark `unknown-EV-comparability` and exclude from this flag's recommendation. For optionality-hoarding: name which direction to close (commit or abandon). For one-way-door blindness or phantom lock-in: name the concrete next move. If no concrete next action follows, the flag is theater — demote or drop.
8. **Aggregate-hoarding check on deferred-item lists.** If three or more deferred items that survived Step 0 routing show carrying cost > preserved value individually, flag the pattern — the failure mode is not item-by-item, it's the aggregate of "preserving revisability" across the whole list. Note that items routed out to `/whittle-scan` in Step 0 do not count toward the aggregate (their cost was decay, not held-open carrying cost).
9. **Mark restatements.** If a flag duplicates something already named in the artifact itself (an ADR's stated trade-offs, a roadmap's explicit Branch-A/B framing, a deferred-items section that already calls out the carrying cost), mark `(restate of <source>)`. Restatements are still useful (they consolidate the read) but they are not the primary value the scan adds.
10. **Compute restatement ratio.** If ≥ 80% of flags are restatements, verdict is **Restatement scan** and the deferral line is emitted verbatim.
 
## Record-durably gate (which flagged decisions warrant a durable record)
 
After signing, apply a three-gate test to each flagged decision to decide whether it should be written down as a durable record — a `/commitment-ledger` Decisions entry or a standalone decision note — rather than just resolved in the moment. Record only if **all three** gates hold:
 
1. **Hard to reverse** — felt lock-in (Q3) is HIGH. This gate reuses the reversibility read the scan already collected; a LOW/MEDIUM decision rarely earns a durable record.
2. **Surprising without context** — a reader six months out could not reconstruct *why* this was chosen from the artifact alone.
3. **Result of a real trade-off** — a genuine alternative was given up (the options-destroyed column is non-empty).
 
Missing any gate → do not manufacture a record; the decision is either reversible, self-evident, or forced (no trade-off). This is the durable-record *filter*, adapted from the ADR three-gate test; it pairs with — does not replace — `/commitment-ledger`, which logs *what* was decided regardless of durability. Emit the gate result as a one-line recommendation per flagged decision (e.g., "record durably — all three gates hold" / "skip — reversible, gate 1 fails"), not a fourth verdict state.
 
## Verdict states
 
Pick one:
 
- **Action-changing scan** — at least one flag produces a next action the user was not already going to take, or surfaces a one-way-door / phantom-lock-in / aggregate-hoarding pattern not visible in the artifact itself.
- **Restatement scan** — at least 80% of flags duplicate framing already explicit in the artifact (or in a related roadmap / ADR / project gate). **Emit verbatim:** *"this scan added no novel signal beyond what the artifact already names; the next run should be deferred or the skill deprecated for this artifact."*
- **No flags** — the decision's option structure and the user's felt lock-in track each other; no flexibility-burning or optionality-hoarding pattern surfaces.
- **Refused** — no decision shape, no deferred items, or the decision was too vague to scan. State which refusal condition triggered.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /option-premium-check — <artifact path or decision> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Decision(s) under scan
<N decisions and/or deferred items entering the scan; M items routed out to `/whittle-scan` in Step 0; K items excluded (correctly deferred — no concrete carrying cost)>
 
## Per-decision table
| Decision | Options preserved | Options destroyed | Carrying cost (if held open) | Felt lock-in (user) | Sign |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| <name> | <one line or "none"> | <one line or "none"> | <concrete mechanism or "none" or "—"> | LOW/MED/HIGH/unknown | <flexibility-burning / optionality-hoarding / dominant / phantom-lock-in / alternative-preserves-more / no-flag> |
 
## Routed-out items
<list items where the dominant cost was decay, sent to `/whittle-scan` instead — surfacing the routing decision itself is part of the output>
 
## Flags
1. **<decision>** — Sign: <flexibility-burning / optionality-hoarding / phantom-lock-in / alternative-preserves-more>. Mechanism: <one line>. <If alternative-preserves-more: name the alternative and quote the user's EV-comparability answer.> Implied action: <one line>. <Mark "(restate of <source>)" if applicable>
2. ...
 
## Aggregate-hoarding flag (if applicable)
<one paragraph naming the pattern across deferred items that survived Step 0 routing, with the Pandora-override implication. Items routed to `/whittle-scan` do not count toward this flag.>
 
## Dominant choices (informational, not action-changing)
<list — preserve options at low/no carrying cost>
 
## Items without a user lock-in read (unknown-lock-in)
<list any — surfacing the absence is itself a finding>
 
## Items without a user EV-comparability read (unknown-EV-comparability)
<list any alternative-preserves-more flags where the user could not judge whether the alternative's EV was roughly comparable>
 
## Restatement ratio
<N restatements> / <M total flags> = <%>
 
## Verdict
**<Action-changing scan | Restatement scan | No flags | Refused>**
<one-line rationale>
 
<If Restatement scan, emit verbatim on the next line:>
> this scan added no novel signal beyond what the artifact already names; the next run should be deferred or the skill deprecated for this artifact.
```
 
If **Refused**, emit only:
 
```text
# /option-premium-check — <artifact>
 
**Refused.** <Which condition triggered: no decision shape / decision too vague / fully-executed irreversible action.>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Optionality hoarding via the scan itself.** The most insidious failure mode this skill can produce: invoking the scan to defer commitment indefinitely by surfacing yet more options to weigh. If the scan output is "preserve all options pending further analysis," it has reproduced the failure mode it was supposed to counter. Every flag must point at a specific next action (close the option, take the preserving alternative, or accept the lock-in explicitly). The source note's "optionality hoarding" anti-pattern is explicit about this — Pandora's stopping rule eventually overrides.
- **Confabulated option structure.** If the decision is too vague to name options preserved and options destroyed in one line each, refuse-to-scan rather than synthesize. Specificity is not optional — the entire skill rests on naming what flexibility is at stake.
- **Imputing felt lock-in from artifact content.** Felt lock-in is the user's working-memory read; Claude has no working memory in this sense and cannot pattern-match from decision language to produce it without confabulating. The Mode 3 split exists to enforce this — the user supplies lock-in pressure via `AskUserQuestion`, not Claude. If the user is unavailable, refuse-to-scan rather than synthesize the column.
- **False precision in carrying cost.** "Carrying cost = $X/wk in cognitive load" is theater. The framework values directionally and *names the mechanism* (drift, blocking, integration window). The source note's "false precision" anti-pattern applies directly.
- **Decay-smuggling.** "If I don't pick this option soon, I lose the flexibility" — that frame conflates carrying cost (option-premium reasoning) with decaying value (Whittle reasoning). Use `/whittle-scan` for invisible per-week decay; option-premium is about the *flexibility itself*, not about how the underlying value decays over time.
- **Cognitive-load as universal carrying cost.** "This is on my mind" or "holding the open question takes attention" is too cheap a mechanism — every undecided question carries some attention load. If accepted as a legitimate carrying cost, the Pandora override fires on every deferred item and the skill becomes a "close everything" generator (the mirror failure of the optionality hoarding it's supposed to counter). Cognitive load is only a legitimate mechanism when tied to *specific named blocked downstream work* — if no concrete blocked task can be named, the load is generic and the item is correctly deferred.
- **Smuggling EV-equality past the user.** Step 7 surfaces a flexibility-preserving alternative and asks the user whether expected payoffs are roughly comparable. Do not skip this question and recommend the alternative on the user's behalf — "the lower-EV option happens to preserve flexibility" is a flag the user might rationally reject because the EV gap dominates the option premium. The skill surfaces alternatives; the user judges EV-comparability. If the user is unavailable for the EV-comparability question, mark `unknown-EV-comparability` and exclude from the recommendation.
- **Treating reversibility as binary.** A decision is rarely fully reversible or fully irreversible. The dimensions are: cost to reverse, time window for reversal, signaling cost, sunk-investment carry. Name the relevant axis when signing.
- **Survivorship in option enumeration.** Listing the options preserved is easy; listing the options destroyed requires imagining branches you're committing against. The destroyed-options column is where confabulation risk is highest. If the destroyed-options column is "none" on every decision, suspect the enumeration step.
- **Running it on fully-executed actions.** This skill is for the *commit moment* (or before it). Post-hoc "what flexibility did we give up?" is `/red-team` adversarial review, not option-premium valuation. Refuse on shipped artifacts unless a follow-up decision is still open.
- **Restatement laundering.** If every flag duplicates framing already explicit in the artifact (a roadmap that already names Branch A / Branch B with their lock-in costs, an ADR that already articulates the trade-off), the scan is restating, not surfacing. Say so in the verdict; do not dress restatements as findings.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A proposed action is being framed as obvious or low-cost but you suspect it's a one-way door
- Two paths look roughly equivalent on expected payoff but you can't tell which preserves more flexibility
- A list of deferred items in a project, commitments log, or backlog has been sitting unresolved for more than a week or two
- A roadmap branch point is approaching and committing to one branch will close the counterfactual
- An ADR is drafted but not signed; before signing, check what flexibility it burns
- Before a planning block where multiple lock-in moves are queued (e.g., schema decisions, API surface choices)
- After a stretch of optionality-preserving moves, as a check on whether you've drifted into optionality hoarding
 
Skip when: the artifact contains no decision (use a knowledge-scan tool instead), the failure mode is invisible per-week decay (use `/whittle-scan`), the artifact is a single draft needing adversarial review (use `/red-team`), the question is about forward consequences across actors (use `/second-order`), the estimate to correct is numeric (use `/reference-class`), or you're depleted (the option-structure reasoning is deliberation-heavy; see `knowledge/general/decision-fatigue.md`).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/index-policies-for-prioritization` — canonical four-index framework; this skill operationalizes the **Real Options** column. The note's anti-pattern catalogue (optionality hoarding, false precision, decay-smuggling-as-Whittle) maps directly onto the anti-patterns above.
- `knowledge/general/decision-fatigue` — capacity floor; the option-structure enumeration is deliberation-heavy and produces noise under depletion.
- `knowledge/general/prioritization-architecture-synthesis` — Layer 3 (valuation) is where this skill sits alongside `/whittle-scan`; together they operationalize two of the four valuation lenses, with the other two refused as non-skill-shaped on this vault.
- `/whittle-scan` — adjacent skill on the same valuation layer; decay valuation rather than flexibility valuation. Don't smuggle option-premium reasoning into a Whittle scan or vice versa — the lenses answer different questions about the same queue.
- `/second-order` — forward consequence cascade; complementary axis. Use `/second-order` to project what happens *after* a chosen action; use this skill to value the action's *preservation of future choice* at the commit moment.
- `/red-team` — adversarial truth-testing of an artifact; use after option-premium has flagged a flexibility-burning move and you want the case-against the move surfaced before deciding.
- `/reference-class` — outside-view base-rate forecasting; orthogonal axis to flexibility valuation. Numeric estimates go there; flexibility structure goes here.
- `/branch-resolve` — for plans with conditional branches needing operationalization; route there when the question is "how do I express this branch?" rather than "is committing to this branch flexibility-burning?"
- `/clarify-first` — Pandora's stopping rule for clarification loops specifically; this skill applies the same stopping rule to optionality hoarding more generally.
- `/commitment-ledger` — pairs naturally with this skill on the same artifact: ledger captures what was decided; option-premium values what flexibility was burned or preserved in the deciding. Run after a `/commitment-ledger` entry has accumulated deferred items.
- `projects/prioritization-skills/overview` — the project this skill is Phase 2 of; Phase 0 dogfood result on `journal/commitments-log.md` is recorded there, and surfaced the aggregate-optionality-hoarding pattern that the body above leans on.

ai/skills/skill-persona-cluster-check.title: Skill: persona-cluster-check
ai/skills/skill-persona-cluster-check.content:
Skill: persona-cluster-check
For a persona prime in a prompt or skill (“You are an expert X”, “Acting as senior Y”), surface the cluster of register, defaults, and biases the persona likely invokes from training data, then check whether those defaults match the actual job.
When to use

Before baking a persona prime into a system prompt, agent brief, or skill body
When a prompt’s outputs feel characteristically wrong in a register you can’t name
Reviewing an existing skill whose persona prime predates the rest of the body

Skip when:

Prompts without persona priming
Persona is the explicit point (creative writing, role-play) rather than a task-shaping move

Why it exists
Persona priming is the densest move in a prompt — a few words import an entire cluster of register, defaults, and biases from training data. The silent failure mode is when those defaults don’t match the task and the mismatch only surfaces as characteristically-wrong outputs that the prompt author can’t predict from the persona label alone. Surfacing the cluster makes the bet explicit before it ships.
Related

.claude/skills/persona-cluster-check/SKILL.md — operational definition
system-prompt-design-principles — patterns for composable, cache-efficient system prompts
system-prompt-assembly — how Claude Code assembles its own prompt
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/persona-cluster-check/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: persona-cluster-check
description: For a persona prime in a prompt or skill ("You are an expert X", "Acting as senior Y"), surface the cluster of register, defaults, and biases the persona likely invokes from training data, then check whether those defaults match the actual job. Use before baking a persona prime into a system prompt, agent brief, or skill body. Counters the silent failure mode where persona priming — the densest prompt move — invokes a learned cluster whose defaults don't match the task, and the mismatch only surfaces when outputs are characteristically wrong.
---
 
Surface and audit the persona cluster invoked by `$ARGUMENTS`. This is lever 6 from `knowledge/ai/information-density-for-llm-prompts.md` — persona priming as the densest compression move available, with an opaque cluster as its silent failure mode.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A literal persona prime, usually quoted (e.g., `"You are a senior security engineer reviewing a PR"`)
- A file path containing a persona prime — extract the persona line and audit it
- A path-and-section ref (e.g., `.claude/skills/foo/SKILL.md#role`) — audit the persona prime found in that section
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most recently drafted prompt or skill body in this session that contains a persona prime
2. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it adds a persona line to a `.claude/` or `projects/*/prompts.md` file
3. If nothing fits, ask the user which persona prime to check rather than guess
 
## Your role
 
A cluster reviewer. Your job is to make the invoked cluster's defaults explicit so the user can decide whether those defaults match the job, and to flag the silent mismatch — the case where the cluster's defaults bias outputs in a direction the user didn't intend and won't notice without the audit.
 
You are not auditing prose density (`/density-scan`), or framing bias (`/bias-scan-prompt`), or trigger-match (`/skill-trigger-audit`). The axis is: *what learned cluster does this persona prime invoke, and does it fit the task?*
 
This skill is generative-diagnostic — it surfaces hidden cluster content and judges fit, but does not score severity numerically and does not rewrite the prompt. The user decides what to do with the findings.
 
## What a persona cluster is
 
A persona prime ("You are an expert X") is a label that invokes a learned cluster of associations from training data — a register, a tone, a set of default recommendations, a refusal pattern, a jargon set, a risk posture. The cluster is dense (one phrase invokes a vast prior) and opaque (the user doesn't see what's been invoked).
 
Two failure modes:
 
- **Register mismatch** — the cluster's default tone is wrong for the job (e.g., "academic researcher" cluster invoked when the job needs operational brevity).
- **Default mismatch** — the cluster's default *recommendations* or *priorities* are wrong (e.g., "senior security engineer" defaults to conservative recommendations when the job is rapid prototyping; "lawyer" defaults to risk-aversion when the job is creative drafting).
 
The mismatch is silent because outputs match the cluster's distribution and look reasonable in isolation. The mismatch only surfaces when outputs are wrong in characteristic ways, repeatedly.
 
## The check procedure
 
1. **State the persona prime verbatim.** Quote the exact line.
2. **State the actual job in one line** — what the prompt or skill is meant to accomplish. If the job isn't named in the surrounding context, ask the user rather than guess.
3. **Name the invoked cluster** in one short paragraph — the kind of person, where they typically work, what they typically produce, what register they typically use.
4. **List 5–7 cluster defaults** across these axes (skip an axis if it doesn't apply):
   - **Register / tone** — formal, casual, terse, expansive, hedged, decisive
   - **Risk posture** — conservative, balanced, aggressive
   - **Recommendation pattern** — what they typically suggest first; what they refuse to suggest
   - **Jargon use** — domain-heavy, plain-language, mixed
   - **Priority ordering** — what they treat as most important by default
   - **Failure mode** — how they typically fail (over-cautious, over-confident, scope-creeping)
5. **For each default, judge match against the job:** **aligned** (helps), **neutral** (doesn't matter), **silent risk** (could bias outputs in the wrong direction without being noticed).
6. **Flag the highest-leverage mismatch** — the single default that is most likely to produce wrong outputs at this job, and what those wrong outputs would look like.
7. **Propose alternatives** — pick one or more:
   - **Narrow the persona** — "senior X reviewing Y" beats "expert X" if the cluster narrows usefully
   - **Add a qualifier** — "...who prefers minimal solutions" or "...with a bias toward shipping" to override the default
   - **Switch to role-only frame** — "Acting as code reviewer with focus on Z" — names the function without invoking a person-cluster
   - **Drop the persona** — sometimes the density move costs more than it earns; the prompt is clearer without it
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Persona cluster check — <skill or prompt name>
 
## Persona prime
> <verbatim quote>
 
## Actual job
<one line>
 
## Invoked cluster
<one short paragraph naming the cluster>
 
## Cluster defaults vs. job
 
| # | Axis | Default | Match |
|---|------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Register | <default> | aligned / neutral / silent risk |
| 2 | Risk posture | <default> | ... |
| 3 | Recommendation pattern | <default> | ... |
| 4 | Jargon use | <default> | ... |
| 5 | Priority ordering | <default> | ... |
| 6 | Failure mode | <default> | ... |
 
## Highest-leverage mismatch
<one or two sentences naming the silent risk default and what wrong-but-plausible output it would produce>
 
## Suggested alternatives
- **Narrow:** <tighter persona prime, if one fits>
- **Qualify:** <persona + qualifier, if a qualifier fixes the mismatch>
- **Role-only:** <function-named alternative without persona invocation>
- **Drop:** <one-line case for removing the persona prime entirely, if applicable>
 
## Verdict
**Cluster-fit | Adjust | Mismatch**
<one or two-line rationale>
```
 
**Verdict states:**
 
- **Cluster-fit** — defaults align with or are neutral to the job; no silent risks identified. Keep the persona prime as written.
- **Adjust** — one default is a silent risk; a narrowing or qualifier closes the gap. Apply one of the alternatives.
- **Mismatch** — multiple defaults are silent risks, or the persona's primary register is wrong for the job. Switch to role-only framing or drop the persona prime.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing cluster defaults to look thorough.** If a persona genuinely invokes only three defaults that matter for this job, list three. Padding to seven dilutes the signal.
- **Treating every default as a silent risk.** Most defaults are neutral or aligned; the audit's value is finding the one or two that aren't. Calibrating "silent risk" too loosely makes the verdict useless.
- **Recommending persona-removal as the default fix.** Persona priming earns its density; removing it loses that compression. Drop only when the cluster is genuinely fighting the job, not as a routine cleanup move.
- **Inventing cluster content from no evidence.** Claims about what a cluster contains are hypotheses about training-data distributions. Hedge appropriately ("likely defaults to...") and don't fabricate specifics. If you can't name a default with reasonable confidence, leave the axis blank.
- **Auditing role-only frames as if they were persona primes.** "Acting as code reviewer" is a function-frame, not a persona prime; it doesn't invoke a person-cluster the same way "You are a senior code reviewer" does. The cluster check doesn't apply, or applies much weaker.
- **Ignoring the surrounding prompt.** A persona prime followed by tight task-specific instructions may have the cluster mostly overridden. Audit the persona prime in context, not in isolation.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before publishing a SKILL.md or system prompt that contains a persona prime
- When a skill or prompt is producing characteristically biased outputs (over-cautious, over-formal, jargon-heavy) and the persona prime is suspected
- When borrowing a persona prime from another prompt — the cluster that worked for that job may not fit yours
- During the recursive-calibration project on existing vault skills
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Prompts without a persona prime — there's no cluster to audit
- Role-only or function-only frames — these don't invoke person-clusters
- Bundled skills the user can't modify
- Throwaway one-shot prompts — the audit's cost outweighs the benefit
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/information-density-for-llm-prompts.md` — lever 6, the source concept
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — retrieval-match axis on the description field; sibling skill for SKILL.md auditing
- `/density-scan` — prose density axis
- `/bias-scan-prompt` — input framing bias; orthogonal axis on user-side prompts

ai/skills/skill-plan-options.title: Skill: plan-options
ai/skills/skill-plan-options.content:
Skill: plan-options
Generate 2–3 genuinely different candidate plans for a task or intent — each traced clause-by-clause to the intent and labelled with its tradeoff — then collapse to one with the choice reason recorded and the best ideas from the runners-up grafted in. The ② stage of the intent-to-retrospective-loop and the disciplined plan-generator that clears the ceremony bar: it forces the two disciplines the default planning pass skips — option-generation (not collapsing to the first plan that comes to mind) and intent-traceability (each plan mapped to what the intent actually asked for).
When to use

The start of a non-trivial cycle, after the intent is set, before committing to an approach
When the first plan that came to mind feels obvious — the median-collapse risk is highest exactly there
A decision between approaches where you want each fairly developed and traced to the goal
Upstream of /plan-split-scan and /branch-resolve — this picks the approach, those shape and de-risk it

Skip when:

The task is trivial with one obviously-right approach (generating 3 plans is ceremony — refuse, and say so)
The approach is already constrained or decided
You want to audit an already-drafted plan’s size (use /plan-split-scan)
You’re doing open-ended ideation not aimed at a set intent (use /scamper, /assumption-reversal)

Why it exists
Median-collapse is the failure mode it counters: the default planning pass silently settles on the most training-data-typical approach without generating alternatives or checking any against the actual intent. A generative planning skill only earns its slot if it forces a discipline the default skips — so this one is built on exactly that bar (option-generation + intent-traceability), and it self-guards against the inverse failure (refuse on trivial tasks where three plans would be ceremony). The collapse step is as important as the divergence: generating options without choosing is brainstorming, not planning, so the skill converges on one plan with a recorded reason and grafts the runners-up’s best ideas in. It hands the chosen plan downstream to /plan-split-scan (right size?) and /branch-resolve (unresolved branches?).
Related

.claude/skills/plan-options/SKILL.md — operational definition
intent-to-retrospective-loop — backing concept; this skill is the loop’s ② stage, the disciplined plan-generator
skill-intent-check — audits the intent this skill consumes; route there if the intent is too vague to trace plans against
skill-plan-split-scan — the downstream check on the chosen plan’s decomposition size; this picks the approach, that sizes it
skill-branch-resolve — operationalizes unresolved branches in the chosen plan; runs after this
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/plan-options/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: plan-options
description: Generate 2-3 genuinely different candidate plans for a task or intent — each traced clause-by-clause to the intent and labelled with its tradeoff — then collapse to one, recording why and grafting the runners-up's best ideas. Forces the two disciplines the default planning pass skips: option-generation and intent-traceability. Use at the start of a non-trivial cycle after the intent is set, before committing to an approach — especially when the first plan feels obvious (exactly when the training-data median gets chosen unexamined). Distinct from `/plan-split-scan` (checks an already-drafted plan's decomposition/size), `/scamper` and `/assumption-reversal` (divergent ideation, not plans toward a set intent), `/branch-resolve` (operationalizes branches in one plan), and `/intent-check` (audits the intent this skill consumes). Skip — and say so — when one approach is obviously right, already constrained or decided, or when auditing an existing plan rather than generating one. Counters median-collapse.
---
 
Generate candidate plans for a task and converge on one with the reasoning recorded — the ② stage of the loop in `knowledge/ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop.md`, built to clear the ceremony bar (a generative planning skill is only worth it if it forces a discipline the default skips). The default planning pass does two things badly: it **collapses to one plan** — the first, most-typical approach — without generating real alternatives, and it **loses the thread back to the intent**, optimizing for a plausible-looking plan rather than the stated target. This skill forces divergence (2–3 genuinely different plans), intent-traceability (each mapped to the intent's clauses), then disciplined convergence (pick one, record why, graft the rest).
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the task/intent to plan. If empty, use the cycle's stated intent (`intent:` line, project Goal, objective). The intent should already have passed `/intent-check`; if it's vague, route there first — you cannot trace plans to a target that isn't set.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- The start of a non-trivial cycle, after the intent is set, before committing to an approach
- A task where the first plan that came to mind feels obvious — the median-collapse risk is highest exactly there
- A decision between approaches where you want each fairly developed and traced to the goal, not strawmanned
- A plan about to be issued to an agent or session, when the *approach* (not just the structure) hasn't been deliberately chosen
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A trivial task with one obviously-right approach (generating 3 plans is ceremony — refuse)
- A task whose approach is already constrained or decided (nothing to diverge over)
- An already-drafted plan you want to check for size/decomposition (use `/plan-split-scan`)
- Conditional branches inside one plan (use `/branch-resolve`)
- Open-ended idea generation not aimed at a set intent (use `/scamper`, `/assumption-reversal`, `/starburst`)
 
**Refuse-to-generate condition.** If the task has one obviously-correct approach, say so in one line and stop — manufacturing two weaker alternatives to fill the format is exactly the ceremony this skill exists to avoid. The honest output is "one approach; no real alternatives worth developing."
 
## What to do
 
1. **Pin the intent** and decompose it into clauses (the targets each plan will be traced against). If unstated/vague, route to `/intent-check`.
2. **Generate 2–3 genuinely different plans.** Different *along a named axis*, not three dressings of the same approach — e.g. risk-first vs MVP-first vs reuse-existing; or different architectures, build-vs-buy splits, or sequencing. At least one should be non-obvious (resist all three converging on the training-data default).
3. **Trace each plan to the intent clauses** — which clauses it serves well, which it serves weakly. A plan that doesn't map to the intent is off-target regardless of elegance.
4. **Name each plan's tradeoff** — what it optimizes and what it sacrifices (speed, reversibility, surface, risk, cost).
5. **Collapse to one.** Pick the plan, record *why* (against the intent + tradeoffs), and **graft** the best ideas from the runners-up into the chosen plan. Convergence with a recorded reason is the point; divergence without it is just brainstorming.
6. **Hand off.** The chosen plan is now ready for `/plan-split-scan` (is its decomposition the right size?) and `/branch-resolve` (any unresolved branches?).
 
## Verdict states
 
- **Plan chosen** — 2–3 real alternatives generated, traced, and collapsed to one with a recorded reason.
- **Converged early** — the alternatives were developed but one clearly dominates on the intent; recording *why the others lost* is the value.
- **One approach (refused)** — the task genuinely has a single right approach; generating alternatives would be ceremony. Say so and stop.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /plan-options — <task/intent> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Intent (clauses)
1. <clause>  2. <clause>  …
 
## Candidates
### A — <name / the axis it takes>
- Plan: <2-5 step sketch>
- Serves clauses: <which, how well>  ·  Weak on: <which>
- Tradeoff: optimizes <x>, sacrifices <y>
 
### B — <name>
…
 
### C — <name>
…
 
## Chosen: <A/B/C>
- Why: <against intent + tradeoffs>
- Grafted from runners-up: <the best idea(s) pulled in>
 
## Hand-off
Ready for /plan-split-scan (size) and /branch-resolve (branches).
 
## Verdict
**<Plan chosen | Converged early | One approach (refused)>**
```
 
If **One approach (refused)**, emit only:
 
```text
# /plan-options — <task>
 
**One approach.** <the obvious plan in a line>; no real alternatives worth developing — generating them would be ceremony.
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Fake alternatives.** Three variations of the same plan (same approach, different ordering) is not divergence — it's the median collapse wearing a costume. Each candidate must differ along a *named* axis, and at least one should be non-obvious.
- **Skipping the intent-trace.** The discipline that earns this skill its slot is mapping each plan to the intent's clauses. A candidate set with no intent-trace is `/scamper` output, and `/scamper` already exists.
- **Skipping the collapse.** Generating options and stopping is brainstorming, not planning. The skill must converge — pick one, record why, graft the rest. Options without a decision multiply work instead of focusing it.
- **Ceremony on trivial tasks.** If one approach is obviously right, refuse. The whole reason this skill cleared the bar to exist is that it forces a *missing* discipline; applying it where the discipline isn't needed reintroduces the sprawl tax.
- **Median collapse survived.** If all candidates turn out to be the same training-data default, the divergence failed — regenerate with an explicit constraint that forces a contrarian approach (e.g. "one plan that uses no new dependencies", "one that is reversible in a day").
- **Planning the decomposition here.** This skill picks the *approach*; the right *size* of the chosen plan's steps is `/plan-split-scan`'s job. Don't merge them — hand off.
 
## When to invoke
 
- At the start of a non-trivial cycle, once the intent is set, before locking an approach
- When the obvious plan feels *too* obvious — the median-collapse tell
- When choosing between approaches and you want each developed fairly and scored against the goal
- Upstream of `/plan-split-scan` and `/branch-resolve`: this picks the approach, those shape and de-risk it
 
Skip when: the task is trivial (one right approach — refuse), the approach is already decided, you're auditing an existing plan (`/plan-split-scan`), or you're doing open-ended ideation not aimed at a set intent (`/scamper`, `/assumption-reversal`).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop` — the backing concept; this skill is the loop's ② stage, the disciplined plan-generator that clears the ceremony bar (option-generation + intent-traceability).
- `/intent-check` — audits the intent this skill consumes; route there if the intent is too vague to trace plans against.
- `/plan-split-scan` — the downstream check on the *chosen* plan's decomposition size; this picks the approach, that sizes it.
- `/branch-resolve` — operationalizes unresolved decision branches inside the chosen plan; runs after this.
- `/scamper`, `/assumption-reversal` — divergent ideation on a problem rather than candidate plans toward a set intent; use those when there's no intent to trace to yet.
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-plan-options` — the reference note for this skill.

ai/skills/skill-plan-split-scan.title: Skill: plan-split-scan
ai/skills/skill-plan-split-scan.content:
Skill: plan-split-scan
Scan a draft multi-step plan for structural over- or under-decomposition signals — concern count, state-carry depth, decision branches, verification seams, reversibility boundary — and recommend split, consolidate, or leave-alone per finding. Operates on the executor-side load axis: the plan’s shape against the executor’s capacity, before execution.
When to use

Before issuing a multi-step plan to an agent or subagent via the Agent tool
Before confirming an ExitPlanMode draft, especially across multiple concerns or production state
Before committing a projects/**/plan.md style document executed across sessions
Before a migration plan, a multi-file refactor, or any sequence mixing speculative and destructive operations

Skip when:

Plan is under ~5 steps, single concern, no destructive operation, no unresolved branch — monolithic execution is the right default and the scan refuses
Artifact is a description of a process rather than a prescription to execute
Throwaway / exploratory work, or the user has explicitly opted into monolithic execution

Why it exists
Under-decomposition produces attention drift, flattened branches, verification debt, and confabulated state-carry — the executor gets through it, but the output is unreviewable. Over-decomposition produces switching overhead, lost goal coherence, and plans of plans. Both failure modes are real and both are silent: fluent plans hide them. The scan names the structural signals (and the over-decomposition counter-signs) explicitly so the decision is auditable, not vibes-based.
