Imagine it is one year from now and this artifact has aged visibly badly. Write 3–5 bullets on what aged worst and why:
 
- Which claims became obviously wrong?
- Which recommendations turned out to be bad advice?
- Which assumptions the author relied on quietly broke?
- Which "current state" claims dated the fastest?
 
This is prospective hindsight (see `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md`). Commit to the failure frame — don't hedge with "if it failed."
 
### 3. Weakest load-bearing claim
 
Identify the single claim the artifact most depends on that a motivated critic would attack first. Not the worst claim in isolation — the weakest one that **matters**. Explain why that specific claim is both important and vulnerable.
 
### 4. Verdict (one line)
 
Pick one:
 
- **Survives red-team** — objections are real but peripheral; the load-bearing argument holds
- **Revise before commit** — specific fixes would make it solid; list the top two
- **Load-bearing claim does not hold up** — the argument's foundation fails under critique; rethink, don't patch
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Red team — <artifact name>
 
## 1. Three strongest objections
 
### Objection A: <one-line statement>
- **Target:** <cite>
- **Mechanism:** <how it fails>
- **Evidence:** <what a critic would point to>
 
### Objection B: ...
 
### Objection C: ...
 
## 2. Pre-mortem
- <aged-badly bullet 1>
- <aged-badly bullet 2>
- ...
 
## 3. Weakest load-bearing claim
<the claim, why it matters, why it's vulnerable>
 
## 4. Verdict
**<Survives red-team | Revise before commit | Load-bearing claim does not hold up>**
<one-line rationale; if "Revise," list the top two fixes>
```
 
## Scope notes
 
- **Do not modify the artifact.** Critique only.
- **Do not water down for politeness.** A soft red-team is worse than no red-team — it produces false confidence.
- **Do not invent attacks.** If a claim is actually well-supported, say so in Verdict rather than manufacturing synthetic objections.
- **Use a different register than the artifact.** If the artifact hedges, the critique should be direct. If the artifact is confident, the critique should probe the evidence.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Synthesis notes: hubs, cluster summaries, `_connections.md` additions
- High-stakes decisions: architecture, career, financial, infrastructure
- Research conclusions you'd act on
- Any artifact where the user explicitly says "is this right?"
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md` — inversion and red-teaming background
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — Pass 4 context

ai/skills/skill-reference-class.title: Skill: reference-class
ai/skills/skill-reference-class.content:
Skill: reference-class
Apply outside-view / reference-class forecasting to the quantitative estimates in a draft plan, ADR, prediction, or scoping note. For each estimate, identify a reference class of comparable past cases, build the distribution, and locate the inside-view estimate against it.
When to use

Artifacts containing numeric predictions: durations, costs, sizes, throughput, percentages
Plans where the estimates are the load-bearing claim (scoping, project sizing, ADRs)
Predictions about counts or magnitudes rather than binary outcomes

Skip when:

Estimates that are obviously intuitions, not commitments
Binary predictions (use /calibration-loop for those)
One-off magnitude calls where there’s no useful reference class

Why it exists
Bottom-up estimation is systematically optimistic — the planning fallacy is well-replicated and not curable by trying harder. Outside-view forecasting locates the inside-view estimate against a distribution of comparable past cases, converting “feels reasonable” into “lies at the X percentile of similar work.” That’s the only correction known to actually shift estimates closer to outcome.
Related

.claude/skills/reference-class/SKILL.md — operational definition
reference-class-forecasting — backing catalog: outside-view procedure, distribution-building rules, planning-fallacy correction
skill-calibration-loop sibling skill — multi-session calibration on binary predictions
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/reference-class/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: reference-class
description: Apply outside-view / reference-class forecasting to the quantitative estimates in a draft plan, ADR, prediction, or scoping note. For each estimate, identify a reference class of comparable past cases, build the distribution, and locate the inside-view estimate against it. Use before committing artifacts that contain numeric predictions (durations, costs, sizes, throughput, percentages). Counters the planning fallacy — the systematic optimism of bottom-up estimation that ignores base rates.
---
 
Scan the artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for the **calibration** of its quantitative estimates against base rates. This is a different axis from `/bias-scan-human` (full bias catalog — detects planning fallacy as one item; this skill runs the *correction*), `/falsifiability-scan` (claim shape, not magnitude — an `[OP]` estimate can still be 3× too low), and `/reviewers-map` (per-claim verification — an estimate has nothing to verify until the future arrives). The dangerous case it targets: a plan with falsifiable, verifiable, well-argued estimates that are nonetheless systematically optimistic because every estimate was built bottom-up from the specific case.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently written/edited file in this session, or the largest staged diff in `git status` if nothing was written this session.
 
The canonical catalog (procedure, fingerprints, philosophical guardrails, sources) lives in `knowledge/ai/reference-class-forecasting.md`. Consult if you need rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on artifacts that make **quantitative predictions about the future**:
 
- Project plans, sprint plans, scoping notes
- ADRs and design docs with predicted performance, cost, or timeline
- Roadmap entries with delivery dates
- Cost / capacity estimates
- Predicted impact statements ("this will reduce p99 by 30%")
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Artifacts with no quantitative claims (decisions, design choices, value judgments — nothing to calibrate)
- Measured / past data (the estimate has already been observed)
- `knowledge/_inbox.md` quick captures
- `journal/` entries (personal reflection)
- `.claude/` configuration
- Pure code diffs without prose claims
 
## What to do
 
1. **Read the target file** in full.
2. **Extract every quantitative estimate** about the future. A quantitative estimate is any number-shaped claim that predicts a future state: duration, cost, size, throughput, count, percentage, ratio. Quote each one verbatim with location.
3. **Tag each estimate** with one of three categories (table below). Exactly one tag per estimate.
4. **For `[INSIDE]` estimates: propose a reference class** using the specificity-gradient heuristic. Apply the four-part operationalization checklist.
5. **Build the distribution honestly** — empirical numbers if available, qualitative outside view if not, "no data" if neither. Never fabricate percentiles.
6. **Compare and recommend** — locate the inside-view estimate in the distribution; recommend an adjustment (or "calibrated").
7. **Verdict** — two-state.
8. **Do not modify the target.** This is a review pass.
 
## The three-category taxonomy
 
| Tag | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `[ANCHORED]` | Estimate already cites or implies a reference class | "Similar refactors in this codebase have taken 3–6 weeks; we estimate 4 weeks" |
| `[INSIDE]` | Inside-view-only — no reference class in the artifact | "We estimate 2 weeks based on the planned steps" |
| `[NO-CLASS]` | Genuinely novel — no comparable past cases plausibly exist | "First-of-its-kind migration to runtime X (released last month)" |
 
**`[ANCHORED]` is not automatically a pass.** Check that the cited reference class is appropriate — not too narrow, not too broad, and the cited distribution is plausible.
 
**`[NO-CLASS]` is rarer than it feels.** Most cases that feel novel from the inside have a reference class one specificity-gradient step up. Apply the gradient before accepting `[NO-CLASS]`.
 
## Operationalization checklist — for `[INSIDE]` estimates
 
For each, deliver four items:
 
1. **Proposed reference class** — what category of past cases is this an instance of? Specific enough to be informative, broad enough to give multiplicity (≥3 cases ideally; ≥5 for any quantitative claim).
2. **Distribution** — range, median, p10/p90 if available; or qualitative outside view ("historically these take 1.5–3× the inside-view estimate"); or honest "no data available."
3. **Inside-view position** — where does the inside-view estimate sit in the distribution? *Below p10 / within central range / above p90 / outside.*
4. **Recommended adjustment** — anchor on the outside view (e.g., the median) and justify any deviation explicitly. If "no data," recommend treating the estimate as low-confidence inside-view-only and either finding data before committing or accepting the uncertainty.
 
A `[NO-CLASS]` estimate gets only items 1 (the failed search — "I considered classes X, Y, Z; each failed because…") and 4 (recommendation: flag as low-confidence; consider whether the artifact needs the number at all, or whether a range / scenario set would serve better).
 
## Specificity-gradient heuristic
 
Picking the reference class is the load-bearing choice. Apply the gradient:
 
- Start specific: "frontend refactors of similar scope on this codebase by this team."
- If N < 3 at that level, broaden one step: "frontend refactors of similar scope on this codebase," then "frontend refactors of similar scope across teams I've seen," then "refactors of similar scope across software domains."
- Stop broadening when heterogeneity becomes obvious — when the broader class includes cases that are clearly not informative for the specific case (e.g., backend rewrites at a different company in a different language).
- If even the broadest plausible class still has N < 3, the estimate is honestly `[NO-CLASS]`.
 
The right level is **the most specific class with enough cases to support inference**.
 
## Fingerprints (diagnostic patterns)
 
Use these to identify `[INSIDE]` estimates and to suspect over-optimistic `[ANCHORED]` ones:
 
- **Round-number anchors** — "2 weeks," "10x," "$50k," "a quarter." Round numbers are usually mental-arithmetic stopping points, not central tendencies of historical distributions.
- **Best-case decomposition** — the estimate is a sum of step durations, each estimated assuming nothing goes wrong. The variance the historical distribution captures is exactly what step-by-step decomposition leaves out.
- **"This time it's different"** — the case is described as exceptional in ways that defeat reference-class membership. Sometimes true; usually a narrative that licenses ignoring inconvenient base rates.
- **Single-anecdote base** — "last time we did this it took N." N=1 is not a base rate. Variance across multiple cases is the relevant quantity, almost always larger than the single recalled case.
- **Inside-view confidence** — "we've thought through every risk." The systematic feature of the planning fallacy is that the planner does not know what they do not know. The unknown unknowns are precisely what reference-class variance encodes.
- **No comparable cases mentioned** — the estimate stands alone, no "similar to X / Y / Z" anchoring. Strong fingerprint.
 
## Verdict
 
Pick one:
 
- **Estimates calibrated** — load-bearing estimates are `[ANCHORED]` against appropriate reference classes, or `[INSIDE]` estimates sit inside the central range of the proposed reference class, or honest `[NO-CLASS]` flags are present with appropriate low-confidence framing.
- **Outside-view treatment needed** — at least one load-bearing estimate is `[INSIDE]` and below p10 of its reference class, or `[ANCHORED]` against a class that's too narrow / too broad to support the estimate, or `[NO-CLASS]` with confident-sounding precision the framing doesn't earn. List the top two adjustments.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Reference-class scan — <filename>
 
## 1. Quantitative estimates
 
- `[ANCHORED]` <estimate quote> — <location>
- `[INSIDE]` <estimate quote> — <location>
- `[NO-CLASS]` <estimate quote> — <location>
 
## 2. Reference-class analysis (for [INSIDE] estimates)
 
### <estimate 1>
- Proposed reference class: <one or two sentences; specificity level reached>
- Distribution: <numeric range/median/p10–p90, OR qualitative outside view, OR "no data available — flag as low-confidence inside-view-only">
- Inside-view position: <below p10 | within central range | above p90 | outside | unknown — no data>
- Recommended adjustment: <anchor + justification, OR "treat as low-confidence; find data before committing">
 
### <estimate 2>
...
 
## 3. Reference-class check (for [ANCHORED] estimates)
 
### <estimate 1>
- Cited / implied reference class: <one sentence>
- Appropriateness: <too narrow | too broad | appropriate>
- Cited distribution plausibility: <plausible | suspicious | not specified>
- Note: <one sentence, or "no concerns">
 
## 4. No-class flags (for [NO-CLASS] estimates)
 
### <estimate 1>
- Classes considered and rejected: <X failed because…; Y failed because…; Z failed because…>
- Recommendation: <flag as low-confidence; consider replacing point estimate with range or scenario set>
 
## 5. Verdict
 
**<Estimates calibrated | Outside-view treatment needed>**
<one-line rationale; if "treatment needed," list the top two adjustments>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing distributions.** Without actual data for the reference class, do not invent percentiles. Honest output: "no empirical data available; flag as inside-view-only, low confidence." A fabricated "p10/p90 of 6–14 weeks" is worse than no outside view because it puts authoritative-looking precision on epistemic emptiness. This is the dominant failure mode for the scan.
- **Treating one similar case as a reference class.** N=1 is an anchor without spread. Demand multiplicity (≥3, ideally ≥5) or admit there isn't a class.
- **Over-narrowing.** "Projects exactly like this one" is small-N and over-fits. Apply the specificity-gradient heuristic until the class has enough cases.
- **Over-broadening.** "All software projects" is too heterogeneous to constrain a specific frontend refactor estimate. Find the most specific class with enough cases.
- **Mechanical correction.** The outside view is an anchor, not the answer. Specific reasons to deviate from the base rate exist (genuinely novel constraints, well-understood learning effects); they should be named and small, not the default move.
- **Tagging artifacts that have no estimates.** If the target makes no quantitative predictions about the future, write a short scan: "no quantitative estimates to analyze; this skill does not apply." Do not manufacture estimates from prose.
- **Demanding reference classes for measured quantities.** "p99 latency was 142ms in the staging benchmark on commit X" is a measurement, not an estimate. Tag only forward-looking quantities.
- **Confusing decisions with estimates.** "We will use Postgres for X" is a decision. "Postgres will handle 5k req/s for our workload" is an estimate. Tag only the second.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing a plan, ADR, or scoping note containing duration, cost, or performance estimates
- Before quoting a numeric prediction in a persistent artifact (PR description, roadmap, decision log)
- Before signing off on a multi-week timeline that was estimated step-by-step
- After a `/bias-scan-human` flags planning fallacy or anchoring as a finding — this skill is the operational correction
- Composes well with `/falsifiability-scan`: that one checks the *shape* of claims (could each be wrong?), this one checks the *magnitude* of estimates (is each calibrated?). Two axes, no overlap.
 
Skip when: the artifact is exploratory / throwaway, contains no quantitative predictions, or the predictions describe past measurements rather than future states.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/reference-class-forecasting.md` — canonical catalog (Kahneman/Lovallo, Flyvbjerg, Tetlock; full procedure, philosophical guardrails)
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — four-pass framework this skill plugs into
- `knowledge/ai/falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.md` — sibling skill on claim shape; composes cleanly
- `knowledge/general/cognitive-biases.md` — the broader bias catalog including the planning fallacy
- `/bias-scan-human` — broader detection (catalog scan); this skill is the deeper correction for one bias
- `/falsifiability-scan` — different axis: shape testability, not magnitude calibration
- `/reviewers-map` — different axis: per-claim verification of present claims, not future estimates

ai/skills/skill-retrospective.title: Skill: retrospective
ai/skills/skill-retrospective.content:
Skill: retrospective
Run a learning retrospective on a completed development cycle, project phase, or substantial working session. The skill separates decision-quality from outcome-quality (Duke’s “resulting”), extracts transferable lessons phrased for reuse, and auto-appends any resolvable or new prediction to journal/calibration-log.md. It is the ⑦ stage and the only genuinely generative skill of the intent-to-retrospective loop — it produces lessons and scored predictions rather than evaluating an artifact.
When to use

At the close of a development cycle, project, or phase that began from a stated intent
At the end of a substantial working session that made real decisions
Before reusing a past outcome as evidence — to check the “lesson” isn’t a resulting artifact
Periodically, to keep the calibration loop fed (the retro is the main inflow to journal/calibration-log.md)

Skip when:

The cycle is mid-flight, before outcomes are known
The session was trivial or purely mechanical (refuse-to-retro)
You only need accounting (use /commitment-ledger)
You’re resolving or scoring existing predictions (use /calibration-loop resolve / review)

Why it exists
Two failure modes. Resulting (Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets, 2018) — judging a decision by how it turned out rather than by the process given what was knowable — makes a cycle’s “lessons” encode luck as validated process; the resulting 2×2 forces the two axes apart and flags the dangerous quadrants (good-outcome/bad-process must not graduate to a repeatable lesson; bad-outcome/good-process must not trigger a recant). Hindsight + evaporation — what-we-learned, left as prose, decays and is never tested; harvesting forward-looking claims into the calibration log turns a lesson into a scored prediction that compounds. The auto-write to journal/calibration-log.md is the design decision (2026-05-29) that makes the loop close: the retro is the calibration loop’s main inflow, which is the structural fix for the dormant-calibration problem (the log having sat at a single prediction). The skill sits in the learning layer above /commitment-ledger (accounting) and feeds /calibration-loop (scoring) — append-only, never resolving.
Related

.claude/skills/retrospective/SKILL.md — operational definition
intent-to-retrospective-loop — backing concept; this skill is the loop’s ⑦ stage; the auto-write data contract is defined there

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/retrospective/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: retrospective
description: Run a learning retrospective (post-mortem / lessons-learned / after-action review) on a completed development cycle, project phase, or substantial working session — separate decision-quality from outcome-quality (Duke's "resulting"), extract transferable lessons, and harvest the cycle's forward-looking claims into the calibration log in bulk. Auto-appends predictions to journal/calibration-log.md in the /calibration-loop record schema. Use at the end of a cycle that started from a stated intent, when closing a project phase, or before citing a past outcome as evidence for a current decision. Distinct from /commitment-ledger (accounting: what changed, what's deferred — no learning), /calibration-loop (scoring: record/resolve/review binary predictions, Brier), and /reviewers-map (per-output verification). Skip mid-cycle before outcomes are known, for pure session accounting, or for resolving existing predictions (/calibration-loop resolve). Counters resulting and hindsight.
---
 
Run a learning retrospective on a completed cycle — the ⑦ stage of the loop in `knowledge/ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop.md`. The cycle ran from a stated intent through plan, tasks, implementation, and verification; the retrospective converts it into two things that compound: **transferable lessons** (phrased as reusable claims, not outcome restatements) and **scored predictions** (harvested into the calibration log so the next cycle's judgment is empirically anchored). The discipline that makes it more than a nicer journal entry is **resulting separation** — rating the *process* given what was known at decision time, separately from how the outcome happened to land.
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the cycle to retro — an intent/project path, a session description, or empty (= this working session). If empty, reconstruct the cycle from the conversation and any artifacts touched.
 
## The boundary with the adjacent journal skills (read first)
 
Three skills write to or near `journal/`; they own different layers:
 
| Skill | Layer | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| `/commitment-ledger` | **accounting** | files touched, claims accepted unverified, decisions, deferred items, what to check tomorrow |
| `/calibration-loop` | **scoring** | record / resolve / review of binary predictions; Brier score |
| `/retrospective` (this) | **learning** | resulting verdict, transferable lessons, and *new* predictions auto-appended to the calibration log |
 
The retro **composes with** the other two — it does not replace them. It sits above the ledger (learning, not accounting) and feeds the calibration loop (it appends new PENDING predictions; it never resolves them — resolution stays with `/calibration-loop resolve`).
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- The end of a development cycle that started from a stated intent (the loop's ⑦)
- A completed project or project phase
- A substantial working session that produced decisions and outcomes
- A past outcome about to be cited as evidence for a current decision (run the resulting check on it before trusting the "lesson")
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A cycle mid-flight, before outcomes are known (nothing to learn from yet)
- Pure session accounting with no decisions to learn from (use `/commitment-ledger`)
- Resolving or scoring existing predictions (use `/calibration-loop resolve` / `review`)
- A single artifact's correctness (use `/reviewers-map`, `/red-team`)
 
**Refuse-to-retro condition.** If the cycle produced no decisions or outcomes to learn from — a trivial or purely mechanical session — say so in one line and stop. A retro with no real call to examine manufactures lessons, which is worse than none.
 
## Resulting separation (the core mechanism)
 
For each notable call, rate two axes independently (Annie Duke, *Thinking in Bets*, 2018):
 
- **Decision quality** — given *only what was knowable at the time*, was this a good call? (Not: did it work out.)
- **Outcome quality** — how did it actually land?
 
Place each call in the 2×2 and flag the two dangerous quadrants:
 
| | Good outcome | Bad outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **Good process** | ✓ skill — encode the lesson | **⚠ don't recant** — sound process, unlucky roll; resist over-correcting |
| **Bad process** | **⚠ luck — do NOT encode** as a repeatable lesson | learn the process fix |
 
The two ⚠ quadrants are the whole reason the skill exists. A cycle that "succeeded" via bad process must not graduate luck into a validated pattern; a cycle that "failed" via good process must not trigger a recant.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Establish the cycle boundary.** Name the intent it started from (the ① artifact, if any), what was built, and the outcome. If there are no decisions/outcomes, refuse-to-retro.
2. **List the notable calls** — the decisions, bets, and judgment moments that mattered, with their outcomes.
3. **Resulting pass.** Rate decision-quality vs outcome-quality per call; place in the 2×2; flag the ⚠ quadrants.
4. **Extract lessons.** Phrase each as a *transferable* claim — a class, not an instance ("deploys without a rollback step fail expensively", not "the Tuesday deploy broke"). Each lesson carries where it would next apply. Drop any "lesson" that is an outcome restatement, a hindsight ("should have known") that wasn't actionable at the time, or a luck-quadrant pattern.
5. **Harvest predictions → calibration log.** Any forward-looking claim the cycle made that is now resolvable, or any new bet worth tracking, gets formatted in the `/calibration-loop record` schema and **auto-appended to `journal/calibration-log.md`**. Append-only — never edit or resolve existing entries. **Re-read the log from disk immediately before appending** — the user (and `/calibration-loop`) hand-edits it between sessions; writing from a stale in-context copy can clobber a manual edit. Echo each appended entry in the output. A claim that cannot be made binary + dated is a *lesson*, not a calibration entry — don't append vague predictions.
6. **Intent-fulfilment readout.** One line: did the cycle's output serve the originating intent? (The full check is `/intent-fulfilment-check`; the retro just records the readout.)
7. **Name the headline** — the single highest-value lesson and the single most-overconfident call of the cycle.
 
## Calibration-log append schema
 
Append new entries to `journal/calibration-log.md` in exactly this form (matching `/calibration-loop record`):
 
```text
## <YYYY-MM-DD> — <short claim title>
 
- Claim: <falsifiable statement>
- Resolves by: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Resolution criterion: <how it will be checked, by whom, against what source>
- Confidence: <0.00–1.00>
- Domain: <markets | project | ai-capability | …>
- Rationale: <one or two lines>
- Resolution: PENDING
- Resolved on: —
- Notes: —
```
 
## Verdict states
 
- **Lessons recorded** — produced at least one transferable lesson and/or appended at least one calibration entry.
- **Resulting-only** — outcomes examined but no transferable lesson survived (a luck-dominated cycle); recording *that* is itself the finding.
- **Nothing to retro** — no decisions or outcomes; refuse.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /retrospective — <cycle> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Cycle
Intent: <the ① it started from, or "none stated">
Built: <one line>  ·  Outcome: <one line>
 
## Resulting 2×2
| Call | Decision quality | Outcome | Quadrant | Flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <call> | good/bad (given what was known) | good/bad | quadrant | ⚠ luck / ⚠ don't-recant / — |
 
## Lessons (transferable)
1. **<class-level lesson>** — applies next at: <where>.
 
## Calibration entries appended to journal/calibration-log.md
- <YYYY-MM-DD — title> · conf <x> · resolves <date> · domain <…>  [echo of what was written]
 
## Intent-fulfilment
<one line — did the output serve the originating intent? full check: /intent-fulfilment-check>
 
## Headline
- Highest-value lesson: <one line>
- Most-overconfident call: <one line>
 
## Verdict
**<Lessons recorded | Resulting-only | Nothing to retro>**
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Resulting.** Rating a decision "good" because it worked out is the exact failure the skill counters. Rate the process against what was knowable at the time; the outcome is a separate column.
- **Hindsight lessons.** "I should have known X" is hindsight bias unless X was actionable with the information available at decision time. A lesson must point at a forward-applicable change, not a retroactive scolding.
- **Outcome-restatement as lesson.** "The deploy failed" is an outcome, not a lesson. The lesson is the transferable class ("no-rollback deploys fail expensively"). If you can't state the class, there's no lesson.
- **Luck encoded as process.** The good-outcome/bad-process quadrant must not generate a repeatable lesson — that is survivorship dressed as wisdom. Flag it and stop.
- **Auto-write overreach.** Only **append** new PENDING predictions, in the exact calibration-log schema, and echo every write. Never edit, re-date, or resolve an existing entry — resolution is `/calibration-loop resolve`'s job and the log is append-only by its own contract.
- **Vague predictions.** A harvested prediction with no binary resolution criterion and date is noise in the calibration log. If it can't be made falsifiable + dated, record it as a lesson, not a calibration entry.
- **Accounting masquerading as learning.** Listing files changed and decisions made is `/commitment-ledger`. If the retro produces no lesson and no scored prediction, it added nothing — say "Nothing to retro" rather than dress the ledger as a retro.
 
## When to invoke
 
- At the close of a development cycle, project, or project phase that began from a stated intent
- At the end of a substantial working session that made real decisions
- Before reusing a past outcome as evidence — to check the "lesson" isn't a resulting artifact
- Periodically, to keep the calibration loop fed (the retro is the main inflow to `journal/calibration-log.md`)
 
Skip when: the cycle is mid-flight, the session was trivial/mechanical, you only need accounting (use `/commitment-ledger`), or you're resolving existing predictions (use `/calibration-loop resolve`).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop` — the backing concept; this skill is the loop's ⑦ stage and its data contract (auto-write to the calibration log) is defined there.
- `/calibration-loop` — the scoring layer this skill feeds; the retro appends new predictions, `/calibration-loop resolve`/`review` scores them. The retro is the inflow; the loop is the ledger.
- `/commitment-ledger` — the accounting layer below this one; they compose (accounting + learning), the retro does not replace it.
- `/intent-fulfilment-check` (loop stage ⑥) — the retro records a one-line intent-fulfilment readout; this skill is the full check.
- Annie Duke, *Thinking in Bets* (2018) — source of the resulting / process-vs-outcome distinction; not yet a dedicated vault note (adjacent cluster: `knowledge/general/decision-making-frameworks`).
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-retrospective` — the reference note for this skill.

ai/skills/skill-reviewers-map.title: Skill: reviewers-map
ai/skills/skill-reviewers-map.content:
Skill: reviewers-map
Produce a reviewer’s verification map for a substantive AI output (note draft, code diff, research synthesis, PR description). Surfaces load-bearing claims with [V] / [U] / [I] tags, least-confident spots, a five-minute check list, and what was not done.
When to use

Before committing AI-drafted content that will be acted on
PR descriptions, research syntheses, code diffs, note drafts
When you need a targeted review and a full /bias-scan-ai seven-check sweep would be overkill

Skip when:

Trivial content or throwaway artifacts
Artifact requires the full bias-scan (use /bias-scan-ai instead)

Why it exists
Fluent prose tricks the reviewer into reverse-engineering reasoning instead of testing claims — cognitive decoupling, the per-output failure mode in the cognitive-burden-of-ai-use stack. A pre-mapped target list (tagged claims, least-confident spots, five-minute checklist) replaces effortful reading with structured verification, reducing the reviewer’s load from “read it all” to “check the items.”
Related

.claude/skills/reviewers-map/SKILL.md — operational definition
cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — backing concept; the per-output counter
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — full sweep alternative
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/reviewers-map/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: reviewers-map
description: Produce a reviewer's verification map for a substantive AI output (note draft, code diff, research synthesis, PR description). Surfaces load-bearing claims with [V]/[U]/[I] tags, least-confident spots, a five-minute check list, and what was not done. Use before committing AI-drafted content that will be acted on. Counters cognitive decoupling — the reviewer reads a ranked target list instead of reverse-engineering reasoning from fluent prose.
---
 
Produce a **reviewer's map** for a substantive AI output, so the reviewer can target their verification effort instead of reverse-engineering reasoning from fluent text.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is a file path, scan that file. If empty, infer the target: the most recent substantive output in this session — last AI-drafted note written or edited, largest staged diff in `git status`, or (if neither) the assistant's most recent substantive message in the current conversation.
 
This skill counters **cognitive decoupling** (see `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md`). It is the operational form of Pass 2 of the bias-aware verification protocol, narrowed to per-output review rather than full bias scanning. For the wider output-bias sweep use `/bias-scan-ai`.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing AI-drafted code that crossed more than one file
- Before saving an AI-drafted knowledge note to the vault
- Before merging a PR where the AI wrote most of the description
- Before citing or acting on AI research output (quoting, passing to someone, basing a decision)
- Before pasting AI output into a user-facing artifact (email, spec, doc)
 
Skip when: the output is exploratory / throwaway, you already know the domain well enough that reading the output *is* verification, or the artifact is a frontmatter-only or formatting-only change.
 
## What to produce
 
### 1. Load-bearing claims
 
Bullet list of assertions the output depends on: names, numbers, dates, API methods, file paths, causal claims, specific statistics. Tag each:
 
- **[V]** — verifiable from provided context, or canonically well-established
- **[U]** — unverified; plausible but not confirmed from session context or your knowledge
- **[I]** — inferred or extrapolated from other claims; not directly evidenced
 
Include the line or section reference where each claim appears.
 
### 2. Least-confident spots
 
Three places you are least sure, ordered by how much the rest of the output leans on them. One sentence each on what would falsify the claim. If fewer than three exist, say so — do not pad.
 
### 3. What to check first
 
If the reviewer has five minutes, the three highest-leverage verifications. These should be concrete actions ("grep for `foo_bar` to confirm it exists in the `baz` crate", "open `path/to/file.md` line 42 and check the cited statistic against the Sources section"), not vague advice.
 
### 4. What I did not do
 
Files not read, sources not fetched, tests not run, steps deferred. If the scope of the output exceeded what was actually verified during generation, name the gap explicitly.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Reviewer's map — <target>
 
## 1. Load-bearing claims
- [V] <claim> — <location>
- [U] <claim> — <location>
- [I] <claim> — <location>
 
## 2. Least-confident spots
1. <claim>. Falsified by: <one sentence>
2. <claim>. Falsified by: <one sentence>
3. <claim>. Falsified by: <one sentence>
 
## 3. What to check first
1. <concrete action>
2. <concrete action>
3. <concrete action>
 
## 4. What I did not do
- <gap>
- <gap>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Sycophantic maps.** Tagging everything `[V]` to match the output's confidence. If nothing is `[U]` or `[I]`, you either scanned a trivial output (in which case the map wasn't warranted) or you are underreporting uncertainty. Re-run with an explicit instruction to tag at least one load-bearing claim as `[U]` or `[I]`.
- **Padding to fill sections.** "Three least-confident spots" is a target, not a quota. If only one exists, say "one" and move on. A padded map teaches the reviewer to skim.
- **Abstract "check this area" advice.** Section 3 must be executable — a grep target, a file path, a test to run. "Verify the factual claims" is not a check.
- **Treating this as a full bias scan.** For the seven-check output-bias sweep, use `/bias-scan-ai`. This skill is narrower and cheaper.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.md` — the mechanism this skill operationalizes (cognitive decoupling)
- `knowledge/ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints.md` — the bias catalog this skill partially implements
- `knowledge/ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol.md` — Pass 2 context
- `/bias-scan-ai` — heavier-weight output-bias sweep; invoke this for deeper review
- `/commitment-ledger` — session-level counterpart to this per-output skill

ai/skills/skill-scamper.title: Skill: scamper
ai/skills/skill-scamper.content:
Skill: scamper
Apply SCAMPER (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put-to-another-use, Eliminate, Rearrange) to a problem or candidate idea to generate structured divergent alternatives.
When to use

Divergent phase of solo ideation where a generic “brainstorm ideas for X” would collapse toward the training-data median
When you have a candidate idea and want axes-of-variation rather than free-association alternatives
Early-stage design before constraints have hardened

Skip when:

You’re evaluating or selecting between candidates (use /red-team or /disagree)
The problem is frame-stuck, not solution-stuck (use /assumption-reversal)
Tight constraints already determine the solution space

Why it exists
Undirected brainstorming converges on the obvious — the “training-data median” failure mode for both humans and LLMs. Seven structured prompts force exploration along axes you wouldn’t naturally hit (especially Eliminate and Put-to-another-use, which violate normal idea-generation defaults). Generation-only by design; pair with adversarial skills for selection.
Related

.claude/skills/scamper/SKILL.md — operational definition
solo-ideation — operating model the skill plugs into
heuristic-ideation-prompts — SCAMPER alongside assumption reversal and starbursting
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/scamper/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: scamper
description: Apply SCAMPER (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put-to-another-use, Eliminate, Rearrange) to a problem or candidate idea to generate structured divergent alternatives. Pass a single SCAMPER letter as the first argument to run that one axis at depth. Use during the divergent phase of solo ideation when a generic "brainstorm ideas for X" would collapse toward the training-data median. For evaluating or selecting between candidates, use `/red-team` or `/disagree` instead — this skill is generation only.
---
 
Apply SCAMPER to the problem or candidate at `$ARGUMENTS`.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recent problem statement, spec, or candidate idea in this session. If nothing fits, ask the user what to apply SCAMPER to rather than guess.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` starts with a single letter from {S, C, A, M, P, E, R} followed by a space, run only that letter at higher depth (see *Single-letter mode* below).
 
## Your role
 
A divergent-phase generator. Your only job is to produce structurally distinct alternatives along each of the seven SCAMPER axes. You are not evaluating, ranking, or recommending. A narrow, polished three-idea answer is the wrong output; a wide, uneven seven-pass scan is the right one.
 
SCAMPER works because each letter forces the semantic network to activate along a specific direction — "what could be swapped" hits different memory than "what could be merged." Collapsing the letters into a single generic pass defeats the mechanism.
 
## What to produce
 
### Full-pass mode (default)
 
For each of the seven letters, generate **3–5 candidates**. For each candidate:
 
- **Idea** — one line
- **What changes** — specifically: what is being substituted / combined / adapted / etc.
- **Failure mode** — the most likely way this idea goes wrong
 
Keep the candidates within a letter structurally distinct. Five variants of "swap React for Vue" is not five Substitute ideas; it is one.
 
### Single-letter mode
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` begins with a letter {S/C/A/M/P/E/R}, run that letter only, with **7–10 candidates** and a one-sentence rationale per candidate in addition to the failure mode. Use this when the user wants depth on a specific axis.
 
## The seven letters
 
| Letter | Probe | Typical leverage |
|---|---|---|
| **S — Substitute** | What material, person, rule, step, assumption can be swapped? | Forces reconsideration of any component taken as given |
| **C — Combine** | What can be merged — features, processes, roles, workflows? | Generates hybrids and coupling |
| **A — Adapt** | What works elsewhere that could be imported? | Pulls in cross-domain patterns |
| **M — Modify / Magnify / Minify** | What if this were larger, smaller, more frequent, reshaped, inverted in scale? | Explores the parameter dimensions of the existing design |
| **P — Put to another use** | Where else could this work, as-is or with minor changes? | Reveals latent utility and re-purposing |
| **E — Eliminate** | What can be removed and the thing still function? | Forces confrontation with non-essential complexity |
| **R — Rearrange / Reverse** | What if the order, roles, or direction were swapped? | Attacks the sequence as an assumption |
 
## Output format
 
```text
# SCAMPER — <problem or candidate name>
 
## Context
<one-line restatement of the target>
 
## S — Substitute
- <idea> · <what changes> · <failure mode>
- <idea> · <what changes> · <failure mode>
- ...
 
## C — Combine
- ...
 
[... A, M, P, E, R ...]
 
## Notes
<optional: any probes that returned weak output and why — e.g., "Eliminate produced thin output because the system is already minimal">
```
 
For single-letter mode, just the one section with 7–10 candidates and rationale.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Bundling letters.** Do not produce three generic ideas that loosely span SCAMPER. Each letter gets its own pass with its own distinct ideas.
- **Evaluating or ranking.** Divergent phase only. If the user wants a recommendation, point them at `/red-team` or the contradiction-pass prompt in `knowledge/general/solo-ideation-prompt-library.md`.
- **Sycophantic gravity.** If every idea sounds like the user's stated favorite, the model is mirroring, not generating. The output should contain ideas the user would probably reject on first read.
- **Training-data median.** "Wild" ideas that are actually textbook industry recommendations are not wild. Calibrate against what a sensible senior practitioner would reject, not what a junior one would.
- **Uniform depth.** If one letter genuinely has nothing to offer (e.g., Eliminate on an already-minimal system), say so in *Notes*. Do not manufacture weak candidates to hit a count.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Divergent phase of a real decision where the default option set feels too narrow
- After writing a spec but before freezing it — SCAMPER the spec's core design choices
- When stuck cycling through the same 3–4 obvious alternatives
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Decisions already in the convergent phase — use `/red-team` instead
- Trivial design choices (naming, formatting) where divergence adds no value
- Problems that are actually search-for-a-fact questions dressed up as design
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation.md` — the hub, operating model
- `knowledge/general/heuristic-ideation-prompts.md` — SCAMPER's place in the broader toolkit
- `knowledge/general/divergent-convergent-thinking.md` — why per-letter passes work
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation-prompt-library.md` — manual templates including the contradiction-pass follow-up

ai/skills/skill-second-order.title: Skill: second-order
ai/skills/skill-second-order.content:
Skill: second-order
Neutral forward simulation of a proposed action’s consequence cascade across three orders, with named actors and time horizons. Produces a sign-neutral map (1st → 2nd → 3rd) surfacing both favorable and unfavorable branches without filtering, and flags speculation creep.
When to use

Before committing to an action whose first-order effect is the only effect that’s been examined
Policy decisions, system changes, or interventions with named stakeholders
When the proposal feels obviously good — that’s the System-1 closure signal this skill is for

Skip when:

Actions with single, contained effects (no second-order surface)
Reversible local changes where forward simulation costs more than re-doing

Why it exists
System-1 stops at the first plausibly-good consequence and treats deliberation as finished. Forced three-order simulation with named actors and time horizons surfaces favorable AND unfavorable downstream branches without filtering, before commitment. Pairs with /red-team (which weaponizes the unfavorable branches) and /reference-class (which base-rates the load-bearing links).
Related

.claude/skills/second-order/SKILL.md — operational definition
second-order-thinking — backing concept
systems-thinking — broader frame
skill-structural-trace sibling skill — diagnoses the standing structure that this skill traces forward through
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/second-order/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: second-order
description: Neutral forward simulation of a proposed action's consequence cascade across three orders, with named actors and time horizons. Produces a sign-neutral map (1st → 2nd → 3rd) surfacing both favorable and unfavorable branches without filtering, and flags speculation creep. Use for clarity of thinking before committing to an action whose first-order effect is the only effect that's been examined; pairs with `/red-team` (which weaponizes the unfavorable branches) and `/reference-class` (which base-rates the load-bearing links). Counters System-1 closure — the failure mode where the brain stops at the first plausibly-good consequence and treats deliberation as finished.
---
 
Trace the consequence cascade of the action at `$ARGUMENTS`. `$ARGUMENTS` is either a file path (decision note, plan, ADR) or a free-text action statement.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recent action / decision / plan in this session. If nothing fits, ask rather than guess.
 
The canonical write-up (rationale, prompt patterns, failure modes) lives in `knowledge/general/second-order-thinking.md`. Consult if you need the why; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Your role
 
A forward-simulator. Trace what happens at t+1, t+2, t+n given that the action triggers reactions. You are not recommending, not evaluating, not compressing branches into a verdict. The output is a cascade map; the user decides what to do with it.
 
Distinct from neighbouring skills:
 
- `/red-team` — adversarial critique of the case made *for* the action; this skill simulates *forward* without taking a side
- `/starburst` — gap-finding questions; this skill produces consequence chains
- `/assumption-reversal` — attacks the frame; this skill accepts the frame and traces consequences
- `/reference-class` — base-rate check; runs *after* this skill on the most load-bearing cascade links
- pre-mortem (inside `/red-team`) — generates failure scenarios; this skill produces the cascades that *cause* those failures
 
## What to produce
 
A three-order cascade map with named actors per branch, a three-horizon temporal check, and an explicit list of links worth verifying with `/reference-class`. No recommendation.
 
### Discipline rules
 
These are the four discipline rules that distinguish this skill from "just write a good prompt":
 
1. **Named actors, not placeholders.** "The market will adjust" / "users will respond" are non-answers — they specify no actor and no mechanism. Each 2nd-order response names a specific actor (role / segment / system) and a specific action.
2. **Stop at speculation creep.** When the next link in the chain requires too many unverified assumptions, mark the chain `[speculative — stop]` and do not extend. Padding to a target depth is the failure mode this guards against.
3. **Hand off, don't self-validate.** The skill produces cascades; it does not check whether they actually happen. The "verify with /reference-class" section names the 3-5 load-bearing links the user should base-rate-check before acting on the cascade.
4. **Both signs, no filtering.** Surface favorable and unfavorable branches with equal weight. The skill is sign-neutral by design — failure-only cascade-tracing is a pre-mortem, which is `/red-team`'s job. Drift toward listing only failure modes is the most common way this skill collapses into a worse version of `/red-team`; resist it. Tag each 2nd-order response with `[+]` (favorable to the action), `[-]` (unfavorable), or `[~]` (mixed / depends).
 
## Structure
 
1. **Name the action.** One sentence, neutral phrasing. Strip recommendation language.
2. **First-order effects.** 1-3 immediate, intended consequences. This is where most thinking stops; here it's the input, not the output.
3. **Second-order responses.** For each first-order effect, name 3-5 actors who notice it and what each does. Branches are listed separately, not merged.
4. **Third-order structural shifts.** For each second-order response, name what changes structurally if the response repeats or scales. Stop here unless a fourth order is clearly load-bearing — usually it is not.
5. **Temporal triple.** How does the action look at 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years? Flag any horizon where the sign of the net effect flips.
6. **Speculation flags.** Mark every link where extension required unverified assumptions. Do not silently extrapolate past these.
7. **Verify-with-reference-class list.** 3-5 most load-bearing cascade links — the ones the action stands or falls on. These are the inputs to a follow-up `/reference-class` run.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Second-order cascade — <action>
 
## Action
<one-sentence neutral restatement>
 
## 1st order — immediate effects
- <effect 1>
- <effect 2>
 
## 2nd order — actor responses
### From <effect 1>
- **<actor A>** (role/segment) `[+|-|~]`: <specific response>
- **<actor B>** `[+|-|~]`: <specific response>
- **<actor C>** `[+|-|~]`: <specific response>
 
### From <effect 2>
- **<actor D>** `[+|-|~]`: <specific response>
- ...
 
> Sign tags: `[+]` favorable to the action, `[-]` unfavorable, `[~]` mixed / depends. If all branches end up the same sign, the simulation is probably filtering — re-examine.
 
## 3rd order — structural shifts
### If <actor A>'s response repeats / scales
- <structural change>
 
### If <actor B>'s response repeats / scales
- <structural change> `[speculative — stop]`
 
[...]
 
## Temporal triple
| Horizon | Dominant effect | Non-obvious 2nd-order consequence | Sign-flip? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 minutes | <effect> | <consequence> | <yes/no> |
| 10 months | <effect> | <consequence> | <yes/no> |
| 10 years | <effect> | <consequence> | <yes/no> |
 
## Speculation flags
- <link>: <what assumption is unverified>
- <link>: <what assumption is unverified>
 
## Verify with /reference-class
The cascade links the action stands or falls on. Both sides — the favorable cascades are as load-bearing as the unfavorable ones, and confirmation bias on either side is the failure mode.
 
### Favorable links the success case rests on
1. <link> — base-rate question: <how often does this kind of favorable response actually materialize?>
2. <link> — base-rate question: ...
 
### Unfavorable links the failure case rests on
1. <link> — base-rate question: <how often does this kind of unfavorable response actually materialize?>
2. <link> — base-rate question: ...
 
> If one side has zero links, the simulation was sign-filtered. Re-run.
 
## What this skill did not do
- Did not evaluate whether the action is good
- Did not check base rates on the cascades (run `/reference-class` on the list above)
- Did not extend chains past speculation flags
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **"The market will adjust" / "users will respond."** Disembodied effects with no named actor. Force a specific role, segment, or system. If you cannot, mark the link speculative and stop.
- **One-strand fixation.** Following only one chain of consequence. The starting structure (3-5 actors per first-order effect) exists to prevent this; do not collapse to one branch because it's the most interesting.
- **Performative second-order.** Adding "but in the long run…" rhetorically without naming the cascade. The output is a list of named actors and named responses, not a vibe.
- **Padding to depth.** Extending a chain to third or fourth order to look thorough. Mark `[speculative — stop]` instead.
- **Self-validating cascades.** Concluding "and therefore the action is bad/good" within the skill. The skill produces the map; the user runs `/reference-class` on the load-bearing links and then decides.
- **Recommending.** The note is explicit: do not recommend. The cascade map is the output.
- **Confusing this with pre-mortem.** Pre-mortem assumes failure and works backward. This skill traces forward without assuming a sign. Run `/red-team` after this skill if you want adversarial pressure on the cascades.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing to an action whose first-order effect is the only effect that's been examined
- On a decision note whose recommendation rests on a single immediate consequence
- When evaluating a plan in a Complex domain (Cynefin) — second-order is most necessary where causes and effects interact non-linearly
- As an upstream input to `/red-team` (which can then attack the cascades) or `/reference-class` (which can then base-rate-check them)
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Clear-domain problems where first-order suffices (deterministic, low-interaction)
- Decisions already taken — use `/red-team` for post-commitment critique instead
- Pure ideation phase — use `/scamper` or `/starburst` instead; second-order is for examining a candidate, not generating one
- Trivial choices where cascade-tracing is more expensive than the decision
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/second-order-thinking.md` — canonical write-up: rationale, prompt patterns, failure modes
- `knowledge/general/decision-making-frameworks.md` — systems-thinking neighbour (steady-state, not temporal)
- `knowledge/general/cognitive-biases.md` — System-1 closure is the bias this counters
- `/reference-class` — outside-view base rates on the cascade links this skill produces
- `/red-team` — adversarial critique; can run on the cascade map after this skill
- `/starburst` — gap-finding questions on the candidate before this skill traces consequences
- `/assumption-reversal` — frame attack; orthogonal axis to forward simulation

ai/skills/skill-skill-output-eval.title: Skill: skill-output-eval
ai/skills/skill-skill-output-eval.content:
Skill: skill-output-eval
Runner for the catalog’s output evals: stages a skill’s fixtures into a temp dir, executes each case in a fresh-context subagent, then grades mechanical checks before judge checks against the planted-finding labels in the skill’s co-located eval/eval.md. Completes the audit family — skill-quality-audit reads the body, skill-trigger-audit reads the description, this one executes the skill and scores the output.
When to use

After substantially editing the body of a skill that has an eval (regression check)
Before exporting a skill outside the vault, when an eval exists
After a frontier-model change, on the evaled subset — the catalog’s model benchmark
When a skill triggers fine but its output feels weak and an eval exists

Skip when:

The question is whether the skill fires (use /skill-trigger-audit) or whether its body is well built statically (use /skill-quality-audit)
The skill has no eval/eval.md — the runner refuses; author the eval first per skill-eval-format
You want to write an eval — the format note owns authoring; this skill only runs

Why it exists
The catalog audited structure and triggers but never measured outputs: a skill could pass both audits and still pad findings on clean artifacts or miss planted problems — and body edits shipped with no regression signal. Golden reference outputs were rejected as the grader (free-form prose; similarity scoring rewards mimicry), so the ground truth is planted-finding fixtures plus binary contract checks, with mechanical checks (greps, counts) anchoring the LLM-judge ones. The runner’s job is the discipline that makes a score mean something: fresh-context execution, label isolation (staged fixtures, no eval.md in the brief), verbatim collection, mechanical-first grading, and the label-gap rule so the eval improves instead of punishing the skill for being right.
Related

skill-eval-format — the format this skill runs: layout, eval kinds, fixture rules, label-gap rule, coverage table
skill-quality-audit / skill-trigger-audit — the sibling audit axes
which-skill — owner of the catalog’s first eval set (router kind), which seeded the format
journal/eval-which-skill-run-2026-05-11.md — the pilot run whose mechanical-first methodology the runner generalizes

Operational reference
Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/skill-output-eval/SKILL.md (re-sync on every body edit):
---
name: skill-output-eval
description: Execute a skill's co-located output eval (.claude/skills/<name>/eval/) end to end — stage fixtures to a temp dir, run each case in a fresh-context subagent, grade mechanical checks before judge checks against the planted-finding labels, write a dated run report to journal/. Use when you want to run, score, test, or re-run a skill's eval, check for output regression after editing a skill body, validate a new skill's output quality before exporting it, benchmark the catalog against a new model, or when a skill's output feels weak and an eval exists. Runs evals, never writes them — requires an eval authored per knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md and refuses with a pointer when none exists. Distinct from /skill-trigger-audit (would it fire — this assumes it fired), /skill-quality-audit (static body audit — this executes the skill), and /which-skill (routes a request). Counters unmeasured skill quality — body edits shipping on vibes because outputs are never scored against ground truth.
---
 
Run the output eval for the skill named in `$ARGUMENTS` and grade the results against its labels. This skill completes the audit family: `/skill-quality-audit` reads the body, `/skill-trigger-audit` reads the description, this one **executes the skill and scores what comes out**. The format the evals follow — layout, eval kinds, fixture rules, the five-binary-check shape — is `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md`; this skill is its runner, not its author. If the named skill has no `eval/eval.md`, stop and say so, pointing at the format note — do not improvise an eval on the fly.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be:
 
- A skill name (e.g. `falsifiability-scan`) — resolve to `.claude/skills/<name>/eval/eval.md`
- An `eval.md` path — use directly
- A name plus a case subset (e.g. `bias-scan-ai C1 C3`) — run only those cases
 
If empty, infer: the skill whose SKILL.md or eval was most recently edited this session. If nothing fits, ask which skill to run rather than guess.
 
## The run procedure
 
Isolation steps (1–3) are low-freedom — exact discipline, because a contaminated run grades nothing. Judge matching (step 5b) is high-freedom — finding→label matching legitimately requires judgment.
 
### 1. Read the instruments
 
Read the eval's `eval.md` in full, then the target `SKILL.md` in full. Note the kind (diagnostic-scan / generative / router), the cases, each case's checks, recall bars, and expected verdicts.
 
### 2. Stage fixtures
 
Create a temp dir (`mktemp -d`) and copy each case's fixture into it, keeping the neutral filenames. Two reasons, both load-bearing: a subagent pointed at `.claude/skills/<name>/eval/fixtures/` can list the directory and read the labels next door, and several scan skills refuse `.claude/` paths by their own scope rules. Router-kind evals (inline queries) skip this step.
 
### 3. Execute cases in fresh contexts
 
One subagent per case, run in parallel where cases are independent (they almost always are). The brief contains the skill name and the staged fixture path (or the inline query) — **never** the labels, the eval path, the exemplar, or any hint of expected findings:
 
- **Diagnostic-scan kind**, skill in clean-reviewer's in-scope list → `clean-reviewer` subagent: name the skill and the staged artifact path, per its dispatcher contract.
- **Generative kind**, or any skill clean-reviewer declines → general-purpose subagent: "Read `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and apply it to `<staged path>` as its argument. Run to completion; do not use AskUserQuestion; return the skill's output verbatim as your final message."
- **Router kind** → general-purpose subagent per query: invoke the skill with the query, return the verbatim output.
 
Collect every output verbatim before grading anything. If a subagent dies or returns a refusal, record the case as **not run** — an unrun case is not a 0/5; it is missing data, reported as such.
 
### 4. Grade — mechanical first
 
Run the eval's mechanical checks as actual commands before forming any opinion: grep the verdict string against the skill's fixed verdict set, grep the required section headers, regex the tag set, count the bullets, `grep -F` quoted evidence against the staged fixture. Record pass/fail per check, per case. A mechanical check is never "close enough" — that is what makes it the calibration anchor.
 
### 5. Grade — judge second
 
- **a. Recall** — match each output finding to the label list; count planted items found with the expected classification against the case's recall bar.
- **b. Precision** — for each finding outside the label list, apply the label-gap rule from the format note: either it is a precision miss, or it is a genuine fixture defect the eval author missed. Confirming the latter requires checking the fixture content itself, not the output's say-so. A confirmed gap **amends the labels** (edit `eval.md`, bump `updated:`) and re-scores the case; record the amendment in the run report.
 
### 6. Score and persist
 
- Per-case score = checks passed / 5. Eval score = mean across run cases.
- Write the run report to `journal/eval-<skill>-run-YYYY-MM-DD.md` (template below).
- Update the target row's **Last run** in the coverage table of `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md`. Re-read the note from disk before editing — other sessions write it too.
- If `eval.md` marks its exemplar **pending** and a case scored 5/5, offer that output as the exemplar candidate: write it to `eval/exemplar.md` with the run date and the exemplar-not-gold marker.
- Remove the temp dir.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Eval run — /<skill> — YYYY-MM-DD
 
## Setup
- Eval: <path> (cases run: …)  |  Skill under test: <SKILL.md path>
- Isolation: fixtures staged to <temp dir>; subagents had no access to labels
- Subagent types per case: <clean-reviewer | general-purpose>
 
## Results
| Case | Check 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | ✓/✗ | … | … | n/N vs bar | ✓/✗ | x/5 |
(label columns 4–5 per the eval's kind: recall/precision for
diagnostic-scan, contract checks for generative, accept-set
match for router)
 
Eval score: <mean>. Not run: <cases, with reason — or "none">.
 
## Per-case notes
<per case: what was found vs planted, misses, precision rulings, label-gap amendments>
 
## Label amendments
<eval.md edits made under the label-gap rule, or "none">
 
## Verdict
**Clean run | Findings | Eval defect**
<one-line rationale; for Findings, the actionable list; for Eval defect, what to fix in the eval before trusting scores>
```
 
**Verdict states:**
 
- **Clean run** — every run case at full score. This is the expected steady state for a healthy skill; reporting it is the eval working, not wasted effort.
- **Findings** — one or more check failures that implicate the *skill* (or the model running it). Each failure listed with the case, the check, and what the output did instead.
- **Eval defect** — the failure implicates the *instrument*: wrong labels, a defective fixture, an unrunnable check, contamination discovered mid-run. Takes precedence over Findings — fix the eval before trusting any score it produces.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Leaking labels.** If the subagent brief, the staged directory, or anything the subagent could plausibly read contained the labels or exemplar, the run is void — rerun it; do not grade and caveat.
- **Grading from memory.** Mechanical checks are commands, not impressions. Run the greps; paste nothing into the report you didn't verify against the actual output text.
- **Diffing against the exemplar.** The exemplar calibrates the judge's register; similarity to it is never a score. The format note demoted golden outputs deliberately.
- **Punishing the skill for being right.** An unlisted-but-real finding is a label gap, not a precision miss. The label-gap rule exists so the eval improves instead of penalizing correctness.
- **Running cases in the dispatching context.** The drafting/dispatching context knows the labels; an in-context run is contaminated by construction. Fresh subagent, always.
- **Score inflation by reruns.** One run per case per report. If you rerun a flaky case, report both outcomes — distribution is data, not noise to discard.
- **Editing the skill under test mid-run.** Finish the run, report, then edit. Interleaving edits with cases makes the score mean nothing.
 
## When to invoke
 
- After substantially editing the body of a skill that has an eval (regression check)
- Before exporting a skill outside the vault, when an eval exists
- After a frontier-model change, on the evaled subset — the catalog's model benchmark
- When a skill triggers fine but its output feels weak and an eval exists (if none exists, `/skill-quality-audit` is the static first look)
- On the development plan's cadence for eval-covered skills
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- "Will this skill fire on the right queries" — `/skill-trigger-audit`
- Static structure/contract review of a SKILL.md — `/skill-quality-audit`
- Authoring a new eval — follow `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md` by hand; this skill runs evals, it does not write them
- Skills without an `eval/eval.md` — the correct output is the refusal with the format-note pointer
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md` — the format this skill runs: layout, eval kinds, fixture rules, label-gap rule, coverage table
- `/skill-quality-audit` — sibling axis: static body/contract audit (its axis 9 reports trigger-eval existence informationally; output-eval coverage lives in the format note's coverage table)
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — sibling axis: description retrieval-match
- `.claude/agents/clean-reviewer.md` — the fresh-context executor for diagnostic cases
- `journal/eval-which-skill-run-2026-05-11.md` — the pilot run whose mechanical-first methodology this skill generalizes

ai/skills/skill-skill-quality-audit.title: Skill: skill-quality-audit
ai/skills/skill-skill-quality-audit.content:
Skill: skill-quality-audit
Deep structural audit of one skill’s SKILL.md — body, structure, output contract, and metadata conformance. The complement of skill-trigger-audit: that skill asks “will it fire on the right queries”, this one asks “when it fires, is it built to produce reliable output”.
When to use

Before publishing a new skill to .claude/skills/
After substantially editing a skill body
When a skill triggers correctly but its output is weak, wandering, or unverifiable
As the per-skill lens in a catalog-wide review (fan-out, one audit per skill)

Skip when:

The concern is retrieval matching (use /skill-trigger-audit) or prose density (use /density-scan)
The target is a bundled built-in skill the user can’t modify
The artifact is a non-skill prompt or agent brief (/context-budget-scan, /bias-scan-prompt)

Why it exists
The catalog had a trigger-axis instrument but nothing auditing the body — the procedure, the output contract, the truthfulness of the description against what the body delivers. A skill can fire perfectly and still underperform: an unreachable clean verdict turns a scan into a noise generator, an unbounded procedure makes two runs diverge, an over-1024-char description gets its routing clauses truncated out of the router’s view. Nine axes, severity traced to the verification labels in skill-quality-criteria ([V] primary-source-confirmed / [U] community practice / [O] locally observed), verdicts Sound / Tune / Restructure with Sound defined as reachable.
Built 2026-06-05 from a deep-research pass distilled into skill-quality-criteria; draft was red-teamed (three findings fixed: mis-specified reference-note path, unearned verification labels on axes 8–9, unreachable Sound verdict) and trigger-audited (Trigger-clean) before commit.
Related

.claude/skills/skill-quality-audit/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-quality-criteria — the criteria base with verification labels; the note this skill operationalizes
skill-skill-trigger-audit — sibling axis: retrieval-match simulation on the description
skill-density-scan — sibling axis: prose density on the body
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/skill-quality-audit/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: skill-quality-audit
description: Deep structural audit of one skill's SKILL.md — its body, structure, contract, and metadata, not whether it fires. Checks metadata conformance (1024-char description cap and truncation risk, third person, what+when, pushiness), description↔body truthfulness, body structure, procedure executability (deliberate degrees of freedom, bounded counts, stop conditions), output contract with a reachable clean verdict, rigidity without rationale, terminology consistency, handoff and catalog-sync integrity, and trigger-eval existence. Use before publishing a new skill, after substantially editing a skill body, when a skill fires correctly but produces weak or unverifiable output ("is this skill well built", "audit this skill"), or as the per-skill lens in a catalog-wide review. Hands retrieval-match query simulation to /skill-trigger-audit and prose density to /density-scan. Counters the failure mode where a skill triggers fine yet underperforms because its body was never audited.
---
 
Audit the skill at `$ARGUMENTS` for structural quality. The criteria base is `knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md` — read it before auditing; it carries the verification labels ([V] primary-source-confirmed, [U] community practice, [O] locally observed) that determine finding severity. This skill owns the axes between "does it fire" (`/skill-trigger-audit`) and "is the prose dense" (`/density-scan`): whether the skill, once fired, is built to produce reliable output.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A SKILL.md file path — audit it directly
- A skill name (e.g., `density-scan`) — resolve to `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The SKILL.md most recently edited in this session
2. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it touches `.claude/skills/**/SKILL.md`
3. If nothing fits, ask the user which skill to audit rather than guess
 
This is a review pass. **Do not modify the target.** Edits are proposed in the output for the user to apply.
 
## Your role
 
A structural reviewer of skill artifacts. The question is not "will this skill trigger" but "when it triggers, will it reliably do its job" — and "will its catalog neighbors and metadata stay truthful about it." Findings cite the criterion they violate and its verification label; severity follows the label, because a [V] criterion broken is a defect while a [U] criterion missed is a suggestion. Two axes rest on house catalog conventions rather than the criteria note — the catalog-sync clause of axis 8 and all of axis 9 — and are labeled [O]; they support low-severity or informational findings only.
 
## The nine axes
 
### 1. Metadata conformance
 
Measure the description's character count against the 1024-char platform cap [V]. If it exceeds the cap, quote the tail that falls beyond it — in this harness the tail is what gets truncated from the router's view, and house style puts the "distinct from X" routing clauses there [O]. Also check: third person [V], states both what and when [V], includes user-vocabulary trigger terms [V], pushy enough to combat undertriggering [V]. Name field: lowercase-hyphenated, not vague (`helper`, `utils`) [V].
 
### 2. Description↔body truthfulness
 
Every job the description advertises must map to a body section that performs it; every substantial body capability should be advertised. Over-advertising is the defect (the skill fires and disappoints); under-advertising is a trigger loss — note it and hand it to `/skill-trigger-audit`.
 
### 3. Body structure
 
Line count against the 500-line limit [V] and against the catalog band (77–251, median ~145 [O] — context, not law). Presence of the house anatomy: `## Output format`, `## Anti-patterns`, `## When to invoke`, `## Related` — absence needs a reason, not a reflex finding. Recommend progressive disclosure (split to referenced files, one level deep [V]) only when the body actually approaches the limit.
 
### 4. Procedure executability
 
Would two independent runs of this skill converge on similar output? Check for: bounded counts ("7–10 queries", not "some queries"), explicit stop conditions, defined `$ARGUMENTS` resolution with a no-guess fallback, validation/feedback loops on quality-critical steps [V], and a *deliberate* degrees-of-freedom choice [V] — high freedom where approaches legitimately vary, low freedom (exact steps) where the operation is fragile. The defect is defaulting to prose without choosing.
 
### 5. Output contract
 
A diagnostic skill needs: a specified output format, per-finding fields that include location and quoted evidence, a fixed verdict set with mutually exclusive states, and — decisive for scan-type skills — a **reachable clean verdict** with defined criteria. A scan that cannot return clean is a noise generator: its finding count measures invocation, not the artifact. For generative skills, the analogue is a definition-of-done [U].
 
### 6. Rigidity without rationale
 
ALL-CAPS ALWAYS/NEVER and rigid structures without explanation are a yellow flag [V] — the model follows reasoning better than rote rules. But absolute directives are *correct* at low-freedom fragile steps; flag only rigidity that carries no why.
 
### 7. Consistency and perishability
 
One term per concept throughout [V]. No time-sensitive claims in the body (versions, model state, "currently") unless quarantined with a date [V] — a skill body is read for months.
 
### 8. Handoff and catalog integrity
 
Every sibling skill the body names ("use /X instead") must exist in `.claude/skills/`. Every `## Related` entry must resolve — vault paths exist, skill names match. Stale handoffs silently re-create the overlapping-trigger anti-pattern [U] the clauses were written to prevent. House convention [O]: the catalog reference note exists and agrees with the SKILL.md about scope — the path is `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-` + the full skill name + `.md` (e.g. `skill-density-scan.md`; for `skill-trigger-audit` it is `skill-skill-trigger-audit.md` — the prefix stacks).
 
### 9. Trigger-eval existence (informational)
 
Does a labeled should-fire / should-not-fire query set exist for this skill anywhere in the vault? The official recipe is ~20 queries, 8–10 each way [V] — but the recipe being verified does not make per-skill eval sets a criteria-note requirement; their absence is a catalog-wide condition today [O]. Report a missing set as an informational handoff to `/skill-trigger-audit`, never as a severity finding — this axis cannot block a Sound verdict, or it would turn every audit into the noise generator axis 5 warns about.
 
## The audit procedure
 
1. **Read the criteria note** (`knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md`), then the target SKILL.md in full.
2. **Measure the mechanical facts** — description char count, body line count, section presence — before judging anything. Numbers first, so impressions don't anchor the audit.
3. **Walk the nine axes in order.** For each: pass, or a finding with quoted evidence and the criterion's verification label.
4. **Check the catalog surfaces** (axis 8) with actual lookups — Glob the sibling skills and the reference note; do not assert existence from memory.
5. **Rank findings by severity:** high = [V] criterion broken with user-visible consequence; medium = [V] criterion broken with the consequence contained; low = [U] criterion, [O] convention break, or style; info = axis 9 and other catalog-wide conditions. When a finding's criterion isn't actually in the criteria note, say so and cap it at low — unearned labels collapse trust in every other label.
6. **Propose surgical edits per finding.** If the fixes amount to reauthoring, that is a Restructure verdict, not a fifteen-item edit list.
7. **Emit handoffs** for everything observed outside these axes — retrieval simulation, prose density, persona primes — rather than auditing it here.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Skill quality audit — <skill name>
 
## Mechanical facts
description: <N> chars (cap 1024) | body: <N> lines (limit 500) | anatomy: <present/missing sections>
 
## Axis findings
- [axis N | high|medium|low | V|U|O] "<quoted evidence>" — <issue> — <proposed fix>
- ...
(axes that pass: one line each, "axis N — pass")
 
## Handoffs
- /skill-trigger-audit — <reason, e.g. retrieval simulation for reworked description>
- ...
 
## Proposed edits
- **<file>**: <surgical edit>
- ...
 
## Verdict
**Sound | Tune | Restructure**
<one or two-line rationale>
```
 
**Verdict states:**
 
- **Sound** — no high- or medium-severity findings; low and informational findings are allowed and expected. A well-built skill should land here; reporting Sound is the audit doing its job, not the audit failing to find.
- **Tune** — bounded findings with surgical fixes; the skill's architecture is right.
- **Restructure** — a truthfulness break (axis 2), a missing or unreachable-clean output contract (axis 5), or a procedure two runs couldn't follow the same way (axis 4). The skill needs reauthoring around its actual job.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing findings.** The audit's value is calibration, not finding count. If the skill is well built, say Sound and stop.
- **Re-running sibling axes.** Query simulation, density rewrites, and persona-cluster analysis belong to their own skills; emitting a handoff is the correct output, duplicating the analysis is not.
- **Treating [U] criteria as hard rules.** Community practice supports low-severity suggestions only; high severity requires a [V] criterion, named.
- **Punishing length per se.** 500 lines is the limit; the catalog band is context. A 240-line skill that needs 240 lines is not a finding.
- **Wholesale rewrites.** Surgical edits per finding; if surgery isn't enough, the verdict is Restructure.
