- **Self-exemption.** When this skill is itself the target, the same nine axes apply — including the 1024-char cap on its own description.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before publishing a new SKILL.md to `.claude/skills/`
- After substantially editing a skill body (not frontmatter typo fixes)
- When a skill triggers correctly but its output is weak, wandering, or unverifiable
- As the per-skill lens inside a catalog-wide review (one audit per skill, fan-out)
- Periodically on heavily-used skills, paired with `/staleness-decay-scan` on their backing notes
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- "Will this skill fire on the right queries" — that is `/skill-trigger-audit`
- Prose-density concerns on the body — that is `/density-scan`
- Bundled built-in skills the user can't modify (`/init`, `/review`, `/security-review`)
- Non-skill prompts and agent briefs — `/context-budget-scan` or `/bias-scan-prompt` own those
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md` — the criteria base with verification labels; this skill is its operational form
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — sibling axis: retrieval-match simulation on the description
- `/density-scan` — sibling axis: prose density on the body
- `/persona-cluster-check` — sibling axis: persona primes in skill bodies
- `/context-budget-scan` — token economy of prompts and briefs generally; this skill is the skill-specific structural audit

ai/skills/skill-skill-trigger-audit.title: Skill: skill-trigger-audit
ai/skills/skill-skill-trigger-audit.content:
Skill: skill-trigger-audit
Audit a SKILL.md’s description field for retrieval-match quality — whether the skill will fire when it should and not when it shouldn’t.
When to use

Before publishing a new skill
After observing a skill misfire (fired when it shouldn’t, or didn’t fire when it should)
When two skills look at risk of overlapping in their trigger surfaces

Skip when:

Stable skills with known good trigger behavior
Skill content quality is the concern (use /density-scan for prose; this targets retrieval matching)

Why it exists
A well-written skill that doesn’t fire on its target queries fails silently — the user types something it should match, gets a generic response, and never knows the skill existed. The retrieval-match axis is distinct from skill content quality: a skill body can be excellent while its description is invisible to the queries it was built for. This skill targets that axis specifically.
Related

.claude/skills/skill-trigger-audit/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-pack-design-constraint-pattern — broader pattern for structured skill bundles
system-prompt-design-principles — composability and matching
skill-density-scan sibling skill — distinct axis (prose density vs retrieval matching)
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/skill-trigger-audit/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: skill-trigger-audit
description: Audit a SKILL.md's `description` field for retrieval-match quality — whether the skill will fire when it should and not when it shouldn't. Targets the description-as-trigger axis (will Claude match user queries to this description?), distinct from `/density-scan` which targets prose density. Generates should-fire and should-not-fire test queries against the description and flags weak trigger phrases, missing user vocabulary, and overlap with competing skills. Use before publishing a new skill, after observing a skill misfire, or when two skills look at risk of overlapping. Counters the silent failure mode where a well-written skill doesn't trigger on the queries it was built for.
---
 
Audit the SKILL.md at `$ARGUMENTS` for retrieval-match quality. The `description` field is the retrieval target — Claude matches user phrasing against it to decide which skill to invoke. A skill can be internally well-designed and still misfire because its description fails to advertise the jobs it does, or advertises jobs it doesn't do, or overlaps a competing skill's description.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A SKILL.md file path — read it and audit the `description` field
- A skill name (e.g., `density-scan`) — resolve to `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
- A literal description block, usually quoted
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The SKILL.md most recently edited in this session
2. The largest staged diff in `git status` if it touches `.claude/skills/**/SKILL.md`
3. If nothing fits, ask the user which skill to audit rather than guess
 
This is a review pass. **Do not modify the target.** Edits are proposed in the output for the user to apply.
 
## Your role
 
A retrieval-match reviewer. Your job is to predict, before deployment, which user queries will hit this skill's description and which will miss. The audit produces evidence: a list of test queries with predicted match/miss outcomes and the specific phrases responsible.
 
You are not auditing prose density (`/density-scan`), or claim shape (`/falsifiability-scan`), or framing bias (`/bias-scan-prompt`). The axis is: *would the right user query, in the user's own words, plausibly invoke this skill?*
 
## The five failure modes
 
### 1. Vague trigger verbs
 
The description leads with verbs that don't say *what* fires the skill. "Scan", "check", "review", "analyze" with no object or no domain marker.
 
Signature: open the description and ask — could this verb fire on twenty other skills? If yes, the verb is doing no work.
 
### 2. Missing user vocabulary
 
The description names the mechanism in domain jargon, but users phrase the same job differently. "Operationalize load-bearing claims" vs. "make this claim testable". Users won't search for the jargon.
 
Signature: list the user phrasings the skill is meant to handle. Are any of them present in the description? If the user's words don't appear, retrieval has no anchor.
 
### 3. Competing-skill overlap
 
Two skills' descriptions both plausibly match the same query. Claude picks one — possibly the wrong one. The fix is on whichever description is broader; tighten its scope to disambiguate.
 
Signature: list 2–3 sibling skills in the same area. Generate a query that should fire only this skill. Would the sibling's description also match? If yes, name the overlap span.
 
### 4. Abstract framing
 
The description names the mechanism (what the skill does internally) rather than the user-visible job (the problem the user is trying to solve). Users describe their problems, not your mechanism.
 
Signature: does the description's first sentence mention a user-facing problem, or only an internal procedure? If only procedure, retrieval depends on the user knowing the procedure name.
 
### 5. Negative-only framing
 
The description is heavy on "do not invoke for..." with weak positive triggers. Negative framing doesn't help retrieval — the user query has to match positive content to fire at all.
 
Signature: count the positive trigger sentences vs. the exclusions. If exclusions outweigh positives, the description is configured for after-fire scope-narrowing, not for firing in the first place.
 
## The audit procedure
 
1. **Read the SKILL.md.** Extract the `description` field verbatim. Skim the body for context on the actual job.
2. **State the claimed job in one line** — what the skill is meant to do, in plain user-facing language.
3. **Generate 7–10 should-fire queries** — diverse phrasings of the job, including: a casual phrasing, a jargon-free phrasing, a phrasing that mentions a competing concept, a phrasing that names the artifact being acted on, a phrasing that names the symptom that triggers the need.
4. **Generate 4–5 should-not-fire queries** — adjacent jobs the skill doesn't do, things a sibling skill should handle.
5. **List 2–3 competing skills** — skills whose descriptions might also match should-fire queries.
6. **Score each query** as **fire** / **maybe** / **miss**, based on whether the description's vocabulary would plausibly match the query. Note the matching span when fire/maybe; note the missing anchor when miss.
7. **Flag specific weak phrases** in the description against the five failure modes.
8. **Propose minimum-cost edits** — phrases to add (user vocabulary, concrete artifact names) or remove (jargon, abstract mechanism descriptions, redundant exclusions). Do not rewrite the whole description; surgical edits only.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Skill trigger audit — <skill name>
 
## Claimed job
<one-line plain user-facing description>
 
## Description (verbatim)
> <description field>
 
## Test queries
 
### Should fire
- [fire | maybe | miss] "<query>" — <matching span or missing anchor>
- ...
 
### Should not fire
- [correctly-miss | incorrectly-fires] "<query>" — <reason>
- ...
 
## Competing skills checked
- `<skill-name>` — <one line on overlap risk>
- ...
 
## Weak phrases (mode | location | issue)
- [mode N] "<quoted phrase>" — <one-line issue>
- ...
 
## Proposed edits
- **Add:** "<phrase>" — <one-line reason>
- **Remove:** "<phrase>" — <one-line reason>
- **Replace:** "<old>" → "<new>" — <one-line reason>
 
## Verdict
**Trigger-clean | Tune | Rework**
<one or two-line rationale>
```
 
**Verdict states:**
 
- **Trigger-clean** — should-fire queries hit, should-not-fire miss, no competing-skill collision, weak-phrase findings are cosmetic.
- **Tune** — one or two should-fire misses or one competing-skill collision; surgical edits restore retrieval.
- **Rework** — three or more should-fire misses, or the description's framing is fundamentally abstract/mechanism-only and needs reauthoring around user-facing jobs. Rare.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Manufacturing test queries to inflate failure count.** The query set should reflect plausible user phrasings, not stress-tests designed to fail. If the description matches a wide range of natural phrasings, report it clean.
- **Recommending wholesale rewrites.** This skill produces surgical edits. If the description needs full rewriting, that's a **Rework** verdict, not a list of fifteen edits.
- **Ignoring the body.** The description is the retrieval target, but the skill body holds the actual scope. Edits to the description must remain truthful to what the skill body does — never propose a phrase that overstates capability.
- **Confusing density with retrieval-match.** A description can be informationally dense and still miss retrieval. Density-axis problems belong to `/density-scan`. Don't fix density problems here.
- **Treating "user vocabulary" as colloquialism.** The user's vocabulary is whatever phrasings real users will produce — for a technical skill, that includes technical terms. The fix is matching the *register* the user will write in, not lowering the register.
- **Generating one phrasing seven times.** Diversity across the should-fire query set is the point. Seven near-identical phrasings of the same query don't test retrieval.
- **Flagging exclusions as failure mode 5 when they're load-bearing.** Some skills genuinely need strong exclusion clauses (e.g., the `claude-api` SKIP rules). Mode 5 fires only when exclusions outweigh weak positive triggers.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before publishing a new SKILL.md to `.claude/skills/`
- After observing a skill misfire — wrong skill fired, or right skill didn't
- When two skills are reported by the user as overlapping or ambiguous
- After substantially editing a skill description (not just frontmatter typo fixes)
- As part of the recursive-calibration project on existing vault skills
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Bundled skills the user can't modify (`/init`, `/review`, `/security-review`)
- Skills whose body is being edited but description is unchanged
- Brand-new skills before the body is drafted — there's nothing for the description to be truthful to yet
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/information-density-for-llm-prompts.md` — sibling axis (density vs. retrieval-match); the note flags tool-description density as decisive but does not address retrieval-match directly
- `/density-scan` — prose density axis on the body
- `/bias-scan-prompt` — input framing bias on prompts the user writes
- `/persona-cluster-check` — persona-prime cluster invocation, another silent skill-failure axis

ai/skills/skill-skill-trigger-eval.title: Skill: skill-trigger-eval
ai/skills/skill-skill-trigger-eval.content:
Skill: skill-trigger-eval
Runner for the catalog’s trigger evals: strips the answer key from a skill’s co-located eval/trigger-eval.md, routes each should-fire / should-not-fire query cold in a fresh-context subagent (via which-skill against the live catalog), then scores the actual pick against the ground truth. The empirical counterpart to skill-trigger-audit — the audit predicts match from the description statically; this measures what fires. Trigger-axis sibling of skill-output-eval, which runs the output eval.md.
When to use

After editing a skill’s description (retrieval regression check)
Before publishing or exporting a new skill with a trigger eval — confirm it fires on its jobs and stays off its siblings
After a frontier-model change, on the trigger-eval-covered subset — the catalog’s routing benchmark
When a skill is reported to misfire and a trigger eval exists

Skip when:

No persisted set exists — use /skill-trigger-audit (static prediction) or author a set first per skill-eval-format (trigger bullet)
The question is what the skill produces once it fires — /skill-output-eval
The question is static body/contract quality — /skill-quality-audit

Why it exists
Axis 9 of /skill-quality-audit reported trigger-eval existence but nothing ran the sets, and /skill-trigger-audit only predicts firing from the description — a prediction never checked against an actual cold routing. So a description could be edited (as the six code-structure scans were, 2026-07-22) on faith that the right queries still fire and the wrong ones still miss, with no empirical signal. This runner closes that loop with the same discipline as the output-eval runner: fresh-context execution, answer-key isolation (anchor-span and routes-to columns stripped, queries interleaved and unlabeled), verbatim collection, and a verdict that separates a description defect (route the surgical edit to /skill-trigger-audit) from an eval defect (an ambiguous query or wrong predicted sibling — fix the set). Batched single-subagent routing is the lightweight default; per-query isolation is the higher-fidelity fallback.
Related

skill-eval-format — shared eval format home; the trigger bullet defines the trigger-eval.md layout this skill runs
skill-trigger-audit — sibling axis: static description prediction; owns the surgical edits this runner’s Findings route to
skill-output-eval — sibling axis: runs the output eval on the same fresh-context, ground-truth-scored discipline
which-skill — the routing oracle this skill drives per query
skill-quality-audit — Axis 9 reports trigger-eval existence; this skill is what makes the set pay off

Operational reference
Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/skill-trigger-eval/SKILL.md (re-sync on every body edit):
---
name: skill-trigger-eval
description: Execute a skill's co-located trigger eval (eval/trigger-eval.md) — route each should-fire/should-not-fire query cold against the live catalog, score the actual pick against the expectation, and write a dated run report to journal/. Use to run, score, or re-run a skill's trigger eval, catch retrieval regression after a description edit, confirm a new skill fires on its jobs and stays off its siblings before publishing, or benchmark routing on a new model. Runs trigger evals, never writes them — requires a set authored per knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md; refuses with a pointer when none exists. Distinct from /skill-trigger-audit (statically predicts match from the description — this empirically routes a persisted set), /skill-output-eval (runs the output eval — this runs the routing eval), and /which-skill (routes one request — this scores many against ground truth). Counters unverified triggering — descriptions edited on faith that the right queries still fire and the wrong ones still miss.
---
 
Run the trigger eval for the skill named in `$ARGUMENTS` and score the routing against its ground truth. This is the empirical counterpart to `/skill-trigger-audit`: the audit *predicts* match from the description statically; this **routes a persisted query set cold and measures what actually fires**. It is the trigger-axis sibling of `/skill-output-eval` (which runs `eval.md`); the shared format home is `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md` (trigger bullet). If the named skill has no `eval/trigger-eval.md`, stop and say so, pointing at the format note — do not improvise a query set on the fly.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be:
 
- A skill name (e.g. `dependency-flow-scan`) — resolve to `.claude/skills/<name>/eval/trigger-eval.md`
- A `trigger-eval.md` path — use directly
- Several skill names — run each as its own scored report
 
If empty, infer: the skill whose SKILL.md or trigger-eval was most recently edited this session. If nothing fits, ask which skill to run rather than guess.
 
## The run procedure
 
Isolation (steps 2–3) is low-freedom — exact discipline, because a router that sees the answer key grades nothing. Verdict adjudication (step 5) is high-freedom — telling a skill failure from an instrument defect requires judgment.
 
### 1. Read the instruments
 
Read `trigger-eval.md` in full and the target `SKILL.md` description. Note the two query lists, the target skill, and — for each should-not-fire query — the sibling the eval predicts should win.
 
### 2. Strip the answer key
 
Extract only the bare query strings. The **anchor-span** column (should-fire) and the **routes-to-instead** column (should-not-fire) are the answer key — they must never reach the router. Assign each query its stable id (F1–F10, N1–N10) for scoring, then interleave should-fire and should-not-fire into one unlabeled list: a router that can tell which queries are "supposed" to fire is contaminated by construction.
 
### 3. Route cold in a fresh context
 
Dispatch the unlabeled list to a general-purpose subagent (routing is not in `clean-reviewer`'s scope). The brief: for each query, run `/which-skill "<query>"` against the live catalog and return only `id → top pick` plus ranks 2–3 if any — **not** the rationale. The brief contains the bare queries and nothing else: no `trigger-eval.md` path, no target-skill name framed as "the skill under test," no expected picks. `/which-skill` reads `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` (descriptions, not `eval/` dirs), so the answer key stays unreachable.
 
Default to one subagent for the whole list (the lightweight path — 20 short routings in one context). Per-query subagents are more faithful (zero cross-query priming) but heavier; use them only when a batched run shows suspicious clustering. Collect the id→pick table verbatim before scoring. A query the router fails to answer is **not run** — missing data, not a miss.
 
### 4. Score — mechanical mapping
 
Map each returned pick against the ground truth. This is table lookup, not judgment:
 
- **should-fire Fi** — **fire** if top pick == target skill; **weak** if the target appears only at rank 2–3; **miss** if absent. Fire rate = fires / (should-fire run).
- **should-not-fire Ni** — **correct-reject** if top pick != target skill; **misfire** if top pick == target skill. Correct-reject rate = correct-rejects / (should-not-fire run). Separately, for each correct-reject record whether the pick == the predicted sibling (**sibling-hit**) or some other non-target skill (**off-target reject**). Sibling-accuracy = sibling-hits / correct-rejects — a secondary signal on whether the eval's *predicted* winner is right, never a pass/fail on the skill.
 
### 5. Adjudicate misses and misfires
 
Every miss (F) and misfire (N) is one of two things, and the distinction sets the verdict:
 
- **Skill/description defect** — the description under-advertises a job it does (miss) or over-claims into a sibling's territory (misfire). The fix is a surgical description edit → hand off to `/skill-trigger-audit`. Do **not** edit the description here.
- **Eval defect** — the query is genuinely ambiguous (two skills legitimately fit and the eval demanded one), or a should-not-fire's predicted sibling loses for a sound reason. The fix is in `trigger-eval.md`: reword the query, or correct the predicted routing. Confirming this requires reading the competing descriptions, not the router's say-so.
 
An **off-target reject** (correct-reject whose pick ≠ predicted sibling) is never a skill failure — the should-not-fire bar is "not us." It is at most an eval-prediction note in `trigger-eval.md`, worth correcting only if the actual winner is clearly right.
 
### 6. Persist
 
- Write the run report to `journal/trigger-eval-<skill>-run-YYYY-MM-DD.md` (template below).
- Bump `last_run: YYYY-MM-DD` in the eval's frontmatter (add the field if absent). Re-read `trigger-eval.md` from disk before editing — other sessions write it too.
- Any `trigger-eval.md` query/prediction correction made under step 5 is a content edit: bump its `updated:` and record it in the report's amendments section.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Trigger-eval run — /<skill> — YYYY-MM-DD
 
## Setup
- Eval: <path> (should-fire run: <n>/<F>, should-not-fire run: <n>/<N>)  |  Skill under test: <SKILL.md path>
- Router: /which-skill via <one batched | per-query> general-purpose subagent
- Isolation: answer-key columns stripped; queries interleaved + unlabeled
 
## Results
- Fire rate: <n>/<F>   (weak: <ids>, miss: <ids>)
- Correct-reject rate: <n>/<N>   (misfire: <ids>)
- Sibling-accuracy: <n>/<correct-rejects>   (off-target rejects: <id → actual pick>)
 
(<F>, <N> = the eval's should-fire and should-not-fire counts — 10 and 10 for the seed sets, but do not hardcode.)
 
| id | query (abbrev) | expected | actual top pick | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | … | fire /<skill> | <pick> | fire / weak / miss |
| N1 | … | not /<skill> (→ <sibling>) | <pick> | correct-reject / misfire |
 
Not run: <ids, with reason — or "none">.
 
## Adjudication
<each miss/misfire: skill-defect (→ trigger-audit edit) or eval-defect (→ eval fix); each off-target reject noted>
 
## Eval amendments
<trigger-eval.md query/prediction edits made, or "none">
 
## Verdict
**Clean run | Findings | Eval defect**
<one-line rationale; for Findings, the description edits to route to /skill-trigger-audit; for Eval defect, the query/prediction to fix before trusting scores>
```
 
**Verdict states:**
 
- **Clean run** — every should-fire fires top-1 and every should-not-fire correctly rejects. Sibling-accuracy short of 100% with a clean fire/reject sweep is still a clean run (the skill routes right; only the eval's predicted winner was off).
- **Findings** — one or more misses or misfires that implicate the *description*. Each listed with the id, the query, what fired instead, and the surgical edit for `/skill-trigger-audit`.
- **Eval defect** — the failure implicates the *instrument*: an ambiguous query, a wrong predicted sibling, contamination discovered mid-run. Takes precedence over Findings — fix the eval before trusting any score it produced.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Leaking the answer key.** If the router brief, or anything the subagent could read, contained the anchor-span or routes-to columns, the target-skill "under test" framing, or the `trigger-eval.md` path, the run is void — rerun; do not grade and caveat.
- **Routing in the dispatcher's context.** The dispatching context has read the answer key; an in-context routing is contaminated by construction. Fresh subagent, always.
- **Lenient fire scoring.** Fire means the target is the *top* pick. "It appeared in the ranked list" is **weak**, not fire — record it honestly; a description that only ranks 2nd on its own core query has a real retrieval problem.
- **Punishing an off-target reject.** A should-not-fire that lands on a different non-target skill than predicted still passes — the bar is "not us." Correct the prediction in the eval if warranted; never score it as a skill failure.
- **Editing the description mid-run.** Finish the run and report; route description edits to `/skill-trigger-audit` after. Interleaving edits with routing makes the score mean nothing.
- **Reruns for score inflation.** One run per report. If you rerun a flaky query, report both outcomes — distribution is data.
- **Confusing this with the audit.** `/skill-trigger-audit` generates queries and predicts from the description; this executes a fixed set and measures. If you find yourself inventing new queries, you are auditing, not running.
 
## When to invoke
 
- After editing a skill's `description` (retrieval regression check)
- Before publishing or exporting a new skill that has a trigger eval — confirm it fires on its jobs and stays off its siblings
- After a frontier-model change, on the trigger-eval-covered subset — the catalog's routing benchmark
- When a skill is reported to misfire and a trigger eval exists (if none exists, `/skill-trigger-audit` is the static first look)
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- "Is this description well-phrased for retrieval" without a persisted set — `/skill-trigger-audit`
- Static structure/contract review of a SKILL.md — `/skill-quality-audit`
- Scoring what a skill *produces* once it fires — `/skill-output-eval`
- Authoring a trigger eval — follow the trigger bullet of `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md` by hand; this skill runs sets, it does not write them
- Skills without an `eval/trigger-eval.md` — the correct output is the refusal with the format-note pointer
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/skill-eval-format.md` — shared eval format home; the trigger bullet defines the `trigger-eval.md` layout this skill runs
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — sibling axis: static description prediction; owns the surgical edits this runner's Findings route to
- `/skill-output-eval` — sibling axis: runs the output eval (`eval.md`); same fresh-context, ground-truth-scored discipline on the other axis
- `/which-skill` — the routing oracle this skill drives per query
- `/skill-quality-audit` — Axis 9 reports trigger-eval existence informationally; this skill is what makes the set pay off

ai/skills/skill-staleness-decay-scan.title: Skill: staleness-decay-scan
ai/skills/skill-staleness-decay-scan.content:
Skill: staleness-decay-scan
Scan a note, folder, or the vault for time-sensitive notes whose perishable factual claims (version numbers, prices, model/capability state, benchmarks, “current best practice”, NCT IDs, dated statistics) have aged past their half-life and now read as authoritative while possibly being false. The skill globs notes carrying time-sensitive markers, parses their as-of/updated dates against today, assigns each perishable claim a volatility class (FAST / MEDIUM / SLOW), buckets fresh/aging/stale on half-life thresholds, and emits a ranked action table — re-verify / re-date / archive / promote-durable per stale claim. It reports the actions; it does not perform them.
When to use

A periodic corpus-maintenance pass — the vault has no archival outflow (git-confirmed), so staleness accumulates silently and needs a deliberate sweep
Before citing or building on an aging note in new work
After a fast-moving domain has likely shifted (a new model release, a market move, a framework major version) — scan that folder
Paired with /contradiction-scan on a maintenance day — this catches expiry, that catches disagreement

Skip when:

The scope is a queue or backlog (use /whittle-scan)
The item is a forecast/prediction with a resolution date — it has a per-week cost of inaction, not silently-expiring authority (use /whittle-scan or /calibration-loop)
The material is evergreen — a conceptual note with no dated or perishable claims is correctly out of scope (refuse-to-scan)
The axis is cross-note disagreement (use /contradiction-scan)

Why it exists
Silent staleness is the failure mode the scan counters — a dated claim keeps reading as current because its as-of date is invisible when you’re scanning the corpus for an answer, so the rot is never felt until a stale fact propagates into a decision. The structural reason it accumulates: the vault is append-mostly and has zero archival outflow (git-confirmed over 60 days), so the staleness stock only rises. The key design move is the volatility class — age alone is a bad signal, because a six-month-old AI-tooling claim is stale while a six-month-old physiology mechanism isn’t. Classifying FAST / MEDIUM / SLOW and bucketing against a class-specific half-life keeps the scan from flagging durable claims as noise. The load-bearing boundary is with /whittle-scan: this skill owns perishable static facts whose authority expired; /whittle-scan owns dated commitments and forecasts with a per-week cost of inaction. Forecast-resolution-dates route there, not here — the two are description-scoped apart so they don’t collide on retrieval. See knowledge-base-entropy for the backing concept.
Related

.claude/skills/staleness-decay-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
knowledge-base-entropy — backing concept; this skill operationalizes decay mode 2 (fact staleness); the no-outflow stock/flow framing motivates the archive action
skill-contradiction-scan — sibling corpus scan; this catches single-note expiry, that catches cross-note disagreement
skill-whittle-scan — the boundary partner; owns dated commitments and forecast-resolution-dates with per-week cost; forecast items route there
skill-calibration-loop — owns dated binary predictions and their resolution
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/staleness-decay-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: staleness-decay-scan
description: Scan a note, folder, or the vault for time-sensitive notes whose perishable factual claims (version numbers, prices, model/capability state, benchmarks, "current best practice", "as of" figures) have aged past their half-life and now read as authoritative while possibly being false. Assigns each claim a volatility class, buckets fresh/aging/stale on half-life thresholds, and emits a ranked re-verify / re-date / archive / promote-durable action table. Use for a periodic corpus-maintenance pass, before relying on an aging note in new work, or after a fast-moving domain (AI tooling, crypto, model state) has likely shifted. Owns perishable STATIC facts whose authority silently expired — distinct from `/whittle-scan` (dated commitments/forecasts with a per-week cost of inaction — hand those there), `/contradiction-scan` (cross-note disagreement), and `/falsifiability-scan` (claim testability on one artifact). Skip when nothing in scope carries a time-sensitive marker or date. Counters silent staleness.
---
 
Scan time-sensitive notes for perishable factual claims that have aged past their half-life — the fact-staleness decay mode in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`. The dangerous case: a note states a version number, price, model capability, benchmark, or "current best practice" with an "as of" date, the fact has since changed, but the note still reads as authoritative because the per-note date is invisible when you're scanning the corpus for an answer — so the stale fact gets propagated into a decision. This skill finds dated/perishable claims, computes their age against today, buckets them by a volatility-adjusted half-life, and emits a ranked **action table** — re-verify, re-date, archive, or promote the durable idea out before the wrapper decays.
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is a note path, a folder, or empty (= scan the whole vault's time-sensitive notes). If scanning broadly produces too many results, scope to the most-relevant folder and say so.
 
**Preventive counterpart.** This skill detects staleness after it has set in; the authoring-time defense is rule 7 ("durability over precision — describe behavior, not paths or snippets") in `.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md`. When a scan turns up a note stale because it hard-coded a path or snippet that moved, the durable fix is often to re-author it as a behavior description per that rule, not just to re-date it.
 
## The whittle-scan boundary (read first)
 
This skill and `/whittle-scan` both involve decay and dates; they own **different** decay:
 
| This skill (`/staleness-decay-scan`) | `/whittle-scan` |
|---|---|
| Perishable **static facts** in a note body | **Queue items / commitments** with a cost of inaction |
| Decay = the fact silently became false | Decay = compounding cost of *not acting* per week |
| A version number, price, "as of" figure, model-state claim | A forecast with a resolution date, a task, a thesis to re-bet |
| Action: re-verify / re-date / archive the note | Action: do the thing before its window closes |
 
**A dated forecast or prediction with a resolution date is a `/whittle-scan` item, not a staleness item** — it has a per-week cost of inaction, not silently-expiring authority. If you encounter one here, route it and don't bucket it. Likewise a queue, backlog, or commitment item goes to `/whittle-scan` even if it "feels stale" — this skill owns perishable *facts in a note body*, not *items in a list*.
 
## Finding time-sensitive material
 
Assemble the candidate set with Glob/Grep:
 
- Notes tagged `time-sensitive`
- Notes with an `as of <date>` / "Last verified" line in the body
- Notes whose filename or title encodes a timeframe (e.g. `solana-2026-outlook`, `…-april-2026`)
- Notes with an `updated:` date well in the past *and* containing perishable claim patterns
 
Within each candidate, grep for **perishable claim patterns**: semantic version numbers, currency/price figures, "$N", percentages presented as current, "current best / standard / state of the art", model names + capability/cost/limit claims, benchmark scores, NCT IDs, "latest", "now", "recently".
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A periodic corpus-maintenance pass over the vault's time-sensitive notes
- A single aging note you're about to rely on in new work
- A fast-moving folder (`knowledge/ai/`, `knowledge/finance/`) after the domain has likely shifted
- A note flagged stale by another process, to decide re-verify vs archive
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A queue, backlog, or commitment ledger (use `/whittle-scan`)
- A dated forecast/prediction with a resolution date (use `/whittle-scan` or `/calibration-loop`)
- Cross-note disagreement (use `/contradiction-scan`)
- Per-claim testability on one artifact (use `/falsifiability-scan`)
- An evergreen note with no dated or perishable claims (nothing to scan)
 
**Refuse-to-scan condition.** If nothing in scope carries a time-sensitive marker, date, or perishable claim pattern, say so in one line and stop. Evergreen conceptual notes are correctly out of scope — not a finding.
 
## Volatility classes and half-life
 
Age alone doesn't determine staleness — a six-month-old AI-tooling claim is stale; a six-month-old physiology mechanism isn't. Assign each perishable claim a volatility class, then bucket against its half-life:
 
| Class | Examples | Half-life | Stale past |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FAST** | AI model state, tool/framework versions, prices, benchmarks, "current best practice" | ~3 months | ~6 months |
| **MEDIUM** | Ecosystem/landscape surveys, org/project status, roadmaps, regulatory state | ~6 months | ~12 months |
| **SLOW** | Mechanisms, definitions, durable research findings, math | ~18 months+ | rarely — usually evergreen, drop from scan |
 
Bucket each claim by **age relative to its class half-life**: `fresh` (< half-life), `aging` (1–2× half-life), `stale` (> 2× half-life, i.e. past the "stale past" column).
 
Today's date is the reference point — compute age from the claim's as-of date (or the note's `updated:` if no inline date). State the reference date in the output.
 
## What to do
 
1. **Assemble the candidate set** per "Finding time-sensitive material". If empty, refuse-to-scan.
2. **Extract perishable claims** from each note with their inline as-of date (fall back to `updated:`).
3. **Route out forecast/commitment items** to `/whittle-scan` — list them under a separate heading, do not bucket them.
4. **Assign a volatility class** (FAST / MEDIUM / SLOW) per claim. SLOW claims that are effectively evergreen drop from the scan — note the count, don't list each.
5. **Compute age and bucket** fresh / aging / stale against the class half-life.
6. **Assign an action** per aging/stale claim:
   - **re-verify** — likely changed; check the current value before trusting
   - **re-date** — probably still true; confirm and bump the as-of date
   - **archive** — the note's value was entirely time-bound and has passed (route to the no-outflow problem the backing note names)
   - **promote-durable** — the wrapper is stale but holds a durable idea worth extracting into an evergreen note (a not-yet-built `evergreen-promote-scan` skill is on the backlog for this; until then, do the extraction manually)
7. **Rank by staleness × stakes** — a stale FAST claim in a note that feeds decisions ranks above a mildly-aging one in a rarely-read note.
8. **State coverage** — how many notes scanned, how many SLOW/evergreen dropped, anything not reached.
 
## Verdict states
 
- **Stale items found** — at least one claim past 2× its class half-life still presented as current.
- **Aging items only** — claims in the 1–2× half-life band; worth a re-date pass, no hard staleness.
- **All fresh** — every dated claim is within its half-life.
- **Nothing time-sensitive in scope** — no dated or perishable claims; refuse-to-scan.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /staleness-decay-scan — <target> — reference date <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Scope
<N notes scanned>; <M SLOW/evergreen claims dropped>; <coverage note — what was not reached>
 
## Routed to /whittle-scan (forecast/commitment items — not staleness)
- `<note>`: "<forecast claim>" — has a resolution date; route to /whittle-scan.
 
## Stale (past 2× half-life)
| Note | Claim (quoted) | As-of | Age | Class | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<path>` | "<perishable claim>" | <date> | <Nmo> | FAST/MED | re-verify / re-date / archive / promote-durable |
 
## Aging (1–2× half-life)
| Note | Claim | As-of | Age | Class | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
 
## Verdict
**<Stale items found | Aging items only | All fresh | Nothing time-sensitive in scope>**
<one-line rationale + the single highest-priority action>
```
 
If the verdict is **Nothing time-sensitive in scope**, emit only:
 
```text
# /staleness-decay-scan — <target>
 
**Nothing time-sensitive in scope.** No dated or perishable claims found; the material is evergreen.
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Bucketing forecasts as stale facts.** A dated prediction with a resolution date has a per-week cost of inaction — it's a `/whittle-scan` item. Routing it here mislabels "I should resolve this bet" as "this fact expired". Keep the boundary.
- **Age without volatility class.** Flagging every six-month-old claim is noise — a six-month-old mechanism is fine. Always classify FAST/MEDIUM/SLOW before bucketing; SLOW/evergreen claims drop out.
- **Auto-editing the note.** Like all corpus scans, this reports an action table and stops. Re-verifying a value or archiving a note is a human decision — the scan names the action, it doesn't perform it. (Decay-discipline #1 in `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy.md`.)
- **Scanning evergreen notes.** A conceptual note with no dated or perishable claims is correctly out of scope. "Nothing time-sensitive in scope" is the right verdict, not a failure — don't invent staleness to produce findings.
- **Confusing `updated:` churn with freshness.** A recent `updated:` date means the file was touched, not that its perishable claims were re-verified. Check the inline as-of date of the *claim*, not just the frontmatter.
- **Whole-vault dumps with no ranking.** Scanning broadly is fine, but emit a *ranked* table (staleness × stakes), not an undifferentiated list — an unranked dump reproduces the invisibility the skill exists to counter.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A periodic corpus-maintenance pass — the vault has no archival outflow (git-confirmed), so staleness accumulates silently and needs a deliberate sweep
- Before citing or building on an aging note in new work
- After a fast-moving domain has likely shifted (a new model release, a market move, a framework major version) — scan that folder
- Paired with `/contradiction-scan` on a maintenance day — this catches expiry, that catches disagreement
 
Skip when: scope is a queue (use `/whittle-scan`), the item is a forecast with a resolution date (use `/whittle-scan` / `/calibration-loop`), or the material is evergreen.
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/ai/knowledge-base-entropy` — the backing concept; this skill operationalizes decay mode 2 (fact staleness). The no-outflow stock/flow framing motivates the archive action.
- `/whittle-scan` — the boundary partner; owns dated commitments and forecast-resolution-dates with per-week cost of inaction. This skill owns perishable static facts. Forecast items route there.
- `/contradiction-scan` — the sibling corpus scan; this catches single-note *expiry*, that catches cross-note *disagreement*.
- `/calibration-loop` — owns dated binary predictions and their resolution; a forecast found here belongs to its record/resolve flow.
- `/falsifiability-scan` — per-claim testability on one artifact; orthogonal to time-decay.
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-staleness-decay-scan` — the reference note for this skill.
- `.claude/rules/knowledge-conventions.md` — the `time-sensitive` tag and "Last verified" convention this skill enforces.
- `.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md` — rule 7 (durability over precision) is the authoring-time preventive counterpart to this detection scan.

ai/skills/skill-starburst.title: Skill: starburst
ai/skills/skill-starburst.content:
Skill: starburst
Generate gap-finding questions around a candidate idea or decision, distributed across Who / What / Where / When / Why / How. Questions, not answers — pre-commitment gap analysis, not evaluation.
When to use

Before committing to a candidate idea, when the unknowns aren’t yet cataloged
Pre-spec gap analysis — the thing the spec needs to answer before it can be written
Decisions that feel ready but you suspect have un-asked questions

Skip when:

Post-decision evaluation (use /red-team or /disagree to attack the answer)
Cases where the unknowns are already cataloged
The idea is fully explored and the bottleneck is selection, not gap-finding

Why it exists
Confident ideas conceal their gaps — the same fluency that makes an idea pitchable hides what hasn’t been asked about it. Forced question-generation across the six interrogatives surfaces unknowns distributed across actor, scope, location, timing, motivation, and mechanism, instead of the two or three a free brainstorm would have hit. Generative, like /scamper and /assumption-reversal, but oriented to questions rather than alternatives.
Related

.claude/skills/starburst/SKILL.md — operational definition
solo-ideation — operating model the skill plugs into
heuristic-ideation-prompts — starbursting alongside SCAMPER and assumption reversal
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/starburst/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: starburst
description: Generate gap-finding questions around a candidate idea or decision, distributed across Who/What/Where/When/Why/How. Use before committing to an idea to surface what you don't yet know. Questions, not answers — this is pre-commitment gap analysis, not evaluation.
---
 
Generate a starburst of questions around the candidate at `$ARGUMENTS`.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recently discussed candidate idea, decision, or plan in this session. If nothing fits, ask the user what to starburst rather than guess.
 
## Your role
 
A question-generator. Your job is to surface the gaps the user would be embarrassed to encounter after committing. You are not evaluating the idea, not recommending alternatives, not answering the questions you raise.
 
Starbursting works because most failure modes are invisible from inside the enthusiasm phase of an idea. Forcing structured question-generation across the six journalism axes recruits the parts of the problem the user hasn't engaged with.
 
## What to produce
 
**~20 questions total**, distributed approximately evenly across the six probes. Quality criterion: prefer questions whose answers would change the decision if surfaced now but would be costly to discover after commitment.
 
### The six probes
 
- **Who** — is affected, uses it, opposes it, benefits, is excluded, needs to approve, will resent it, is missing from the room?
- **What** — is it actually, breaks it, changes it, depends on it, becomes true once it exists, stops being true?
- **Where** — does it work, fail, belong, spread, run, get stored, need to integrate?
- **When** — does it apply, not apply, need to happen, fail, become obsolete, matter?
- **Why** — does it matter, work, fail, exist, need to exist, not exist already?
- **How** — is it done, measured, scaled, reversed, abandoned, debugged?
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Starburst — <candidate name>
 
## Context
<one-line restatement of the candidate>
 
## Who
- <question>
- <question>
- <question>
 
## What
- ...
 
[... Where, When, Why, How ...]
 
## The three most uncomfortable questions
<pick three from above that the user is most likely to be avoiding — explain in one line each why they sting>
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Answering the questions.** The output is the question list. If the user wants answers, a separate turn runs each answerable question. Mixing raises and answers collapses the mechanism.
- **Generic questions.** "How will we measure success?" is a prompt, not a starburst output. Good questions name specifics: "How will we distinguish success from a low-traffic month?"
- **Skewed distribution.** If 12 of 20 questions are "How" questions, the starburst failed. Rebalance — the point is coverage across probes, not depth in the user's comfortable probe.
- **Softball questions.** Questions whose answer is obvious or self-serving fail the mechanism. Prefer questions that would embarrass the user if asked at a review.
- **Evaluating the idea.** Even indirect evaluation ("this raises concerns about X") is out of scope. State the concern as a question.
 
## When to invoke
 
- Before committing to a candidate idea you generated divergently
- Before writing a spec around an idea — surface gaps the spec should close
- When an idea feels too clean — starburst is a cheap test for "what am I not seeing"
- Before a stakeholder meeting where the idea will be presented
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Decisions already committed (use `/red-team` for post-commitment critique)
- Questions that are actually gap-analysis already done (re-asking creates false thoroughness)
- Low-stakes choices where gap-finding is not worth the token cost
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation.md` — hub, operating model
- `knowledge/general/heuristic-ideation-prompts.md` — starbursting alongside SCAMPER and morphological analysis
- `knowledge/general/debiasing-mental-models.md` — pre-mortem (diagnostic cousin); `/red-team` for adversarial evaluation after gaps are surfaced
- `knowledge/general/solo-ideation-prompt-library.md` — manual templates and session recipe

ai/skills/skill-structural-trace.title: Skill: structural-trace
ai/skills/skill-structural-trace.content:
Skill: structural-trace
Diagnose the structural behavior of a recurring pattern using stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays, Senge archetypes, and Meadows leverage points. Produces a structural map — what’s accumulating, which loops produce the observed behavior, where delays sit, where leverage actually is — not a recommendation.
When to use

Behavior recurs over time and the issue is the standing structure (not a discrete action)
“We keep doing this” / “every time we fix X, Y comes back” patterns
Before trying to act on a chronic problem — diagnosing structure first prevents fix-symptom errors

Skip when:

One-off events with no recurrence pattern
Clearly actor-driven failures (skill or process problems, not structural ones)
You need a recommendation; this skill diagnoses, doesn’t prescribe

Why it exists
Structural pathology gets blamed on actors when the loops, stocks, and delays of the system would produce the same behavior with different people in the seats. Diagnosing the structure (Senge archetypes, Meadows leverage points) before acting prevents fix-the-person errors that leave the structure intact. Pairs with /second-order (which traces a chosen action forward through the structure this skill diagnoses).
Related

.claude/skills/structural-trace/SKILL.md — operational definition
systems-thinking — backing concept
skill-second-order sibling skill — forward simulation through the structure this diagnoses
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/structural-trace/SKILL.md as of 2026-05-12.

---
name: structural-trace
description: Diagnose the structural behavior of a recurring pattern using stocks, flows, feedback loops, delays, Senge archetypes, and Meadows leverage points. Produces a structural map — what's accumulating, which loops produce the observed behavior, where delays sit, and where leverage actually is — not a recommendation. Use when behavior recurs over time and the issue is the standing structure, not a discrete action; pairs with `/second-order` (which traces a chosen action forward through the structure this skill diagnoses). Counters dispositional explanation — the failure mode where structural pathology gets blamed on the actors inside the system.
---
 
Diagnose the structural pattern at `$ARGUMENTS`. `$ARGUMENTS` is either a file path (situation note, retro, postmortem, policy doc) or a free-text description of recurring behavior.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target: the most recent recurring problem, organisational dysfunction, or system-level symptom in this session. If nothing fits, ask rather than guess.
 
The canonical write-up (full vocabulary, archetypes, leverage points, sources) lives in `knowledge/general/systems-thinking-engineering.md`. Consult if you need the why; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Your role
 
A structural diagnostician. Your job is to name what's accumulating, which loops produce the observed behavior, where the delays are, and where leverage actually sits. You are not recommending, not solving, not evaluating actions. The output is a structural map; the user decides what to act on.
 
Distinct from neighbouring skills:
 
- `/second-order` — traces a chosen action *forward* in time; this skill diagnoses the *standing structure* the action will land in
- `/red-team` — adversarial critique of a recommendation; this skill produces a diagnosis, not a recommendation
- `/reference-class` — base-rate check on outcomes; this skill explains *why* outcomes recur
- `/disagree` / `/assumption-reversal` — attack the frame; this skill takes the situation as observed and explains it structurally
 
## What to produce
 
A four-part structural diagnosis: stock/flow inventory, loop dynamics, archetype match (or explicit no-match), and leverage-point ranking of candidate interventions. No recommendation.
 
### Discipline rules
 
These distinguish the skill from "describe the system informally":
 
1. **Stock and flow named separately.** A stock is what's accumulating (inventory, trust, bug count, fatigue). A flow is the rate that changes it (hires/quarter, new bugs/week). Confusing the two is the dominant reasoning error structural diagnosis exists to prevent — name them as separate items, not "we have a hiring problem."
2. **Loops have polarity, actors, and a goal.** Each loop is tagged R (reinforcing) or B (balancing). A balancing loop has an *implicit goal / setpoint* — name it, even if the system has never written it down. A reinforcing loop is currently running in some direction — name which.
3. **Delays are flagged explicitly.** Long delays relative to system response time are where most counterintuitive behavior lives. If a loop has a non-trivial delay, mark it; if not, say so.
4. **Archetype match is yes/no, not vibe.** Either the situation matches one of the eight named archetypes (Limits to Growth, Shifting the Burden, Fixes That Fail, Tragedy of the Commons, Eroding Goals, Escalation, Success to the Successful, Growth and Underinvestment) or it does not. If yes, name what the archetype's *standard* intervention is and how it differs from the obvious response.
5. **Leverage points ranked, with where action currently concentrates.** Tag candidate interventions by Meadows level (parameters / buffers / information flows / rules / goals / paradigm). Flag if existing action is concentrated at the low-leverage end (it usually is — that's the visible end).
6. **No dispositional bailout.** "The team needs to be more disciplined / focused / accountable" is not a structural diagnosis — it's the failure mode this skill counters. If the output reduces to actor character, you have not done structural analysis. Try again or declare no structural diagnosis.
 
## Structure
 
1. **Name the pattern.** One sentence describing the recurring behavior, neutrally. Not "we keep failing at X" — "X output declines after each attempted fix."
2. **Stocks and flows.** What is the accumulation that drives the behavior? What flows change it?
3. **Loops.** Identify at least one reinforcing and one balancing loop, with polarity, named actors / mechanism, the implicit goal of any balancing loop, and any non-trivial delay.
4. **Archetype check.** Match against Senge's eight or declare no match.
5. **Leverage scan.** List candidate interventions and tag each by Meadows level. Note where current action concentrates and what level it would shift to under a leverage-optimised stance.
6. **Boundary flag (optional).** If the situation has distributional consequences — externalities falling on parties without voice in the system, contested goals, decisions about whose interests are inside the boundary — flag for follow-up boundary-critique work. Skip if it's a routine internal dynamic.
7. **What this diagnosis depends on.** Name 2-4 structural claims that, if wrong, invalidate the diagnosis. These are the load-bearing assumptions for follow-up checking.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Structural trace — <pattern name>
 
## Pattern
<one-sentence neutral restatement of the recurring behavior>
 
## Stocks and flows
- **Stock**: <what's accumulating> — current direction: <growing | shrinking | oscillating>
- **Inflow(s)**: <rate(s) adding to the stock>
- **Outflow(s)**: <rate(s) draining the stock>
 
## Loops
### R1 — <short name> [reinforcing]
- **Actors / mechanism**: <who does what>
- **Currently running**: <toward growth | toward collapse>
- **Delay**: <where, how long relative to response time | none significant>
 
### B1 — <short name> [balancing]
- **Actors / mechanism**: <who does what>
- **Implicit goal / setpoint**: <what level the loop pulls the stock toward, even if unstated>
- **Delay**: <where, how long | none significant>
 
[... add R2, B2 if the system genuinely has them; do not pad]
 
## Archetype
**Match**: <Limits to Growth | Shifting the Burden | Fixes That Fail | Tragedy of the Commons | Eroding Goals | Escalation | Success to the Successful | Growth and Underinvestment | none>
 
If matched:
- **Why it fits**: <the structural shape>
- **Standard intervention**: <what the archetype's playbook says to do>
- **What the obvious response would do instead**: <the failure mode the archetype names>
 
## Leverage scan
| Candidate intervention | Meadows level | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| <intervention 1> | 12 — Parameter | <e.g., "where current action concentrates"> |
| <intervention 2> | 6 — Information flow | <often near-free, large effect> |
| <intervention 3> | 5 — Rules | <changes incentives, not just amounts> |
| <intervention 4> | 3 — Goals | <changes what the system is trying to do> |
 
**Where action is currently concentrated**: <level>
**Where leverage actually sits, given the diagnosis above**: <level + why>
 
## Boundary flag
<Skip — routine internal dynamic, OR: this situation has distributional consequences. Externalities fall on <parties> who are not represented in the boundary as drawn. Suggest follow-up CST / boundary-critique pass before acting.>
 
## What this diagnosis depends on
1. <load-bearing assumption 1> — if wrong: <how the diagnosis fails>
2. <load-bearing assumption 2> — if wrong: <...>
 
## What this skill did not do
- Did not recommend an intervention
- Did not check whether the diagnosed loops actually drive the observed behavior (would need outcome history)
- Did not trace the consequences of any specific action (run `/second-order` after picking one)
- Did not run an adversarial pass on the diagnosis (run `/red-team` if it will drive a decision)
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Modeling fetish.** Producing an elaborate stock-and-flow inventory that doesn't match the actual observed behavior. The test: does the diagnosed structure produce the *historical* dynamics, or only a plausible-sounding story? If untested, the load-bearing-assumptions section must say so.
- **False precision.** Implying any rate or magnitude is forecastable from the diagnosis. The skill produces a directional sketch of structure, not numbers.
- **Reductionism creep.** Forcing a stock-and-flow shape onto a reflexive social system that doesn't have one (markets that read forecasts, organisations whose self-model changes their behavior). When the diagnosis stops fitting, say so — do not pad.
- **Dispositional bailout.** Concluding "the team needs better discipline / leadership / focus." If the diagnosis reduces to actor character, you have not done structural analysis.
- **Leverage-point misranking.** Treating Meadows' 12-to-1 ordering as a theorem. The ordering is a default sensibility — for a specific system, parameter changes (12) sometimes outperform paradigm work (2) on practical timescales. Tag levels honestly; do not promote interventions to higher levels for narrative reasons.
- **Archetype forcing.** Naming an archetype because the skill's structure expects one. If none fits, say "no match" — that is information.
- **Recommending.** The skill produces a diagnosis. Picking the intervention is the user's job — usually after `/second-order` and `/red-team` on candidate interventions.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A pattern keeps recurring despite repeated attempts to fix it (Shifting the Burden / Fixes That Fail signal)
- A growth dynamic is hitting a ceiling no one named (Limits to Growth signal)
- Two parties' "reasonable" responses are escalating (Escalation signal)
- A team's standards or output have drifted down without a discrete decision (Eroding Goals signal)
- Before running `/second-order` on a candidate intervention — the structural map names which loops the cascade will flow through
- After a postmortem whose root causes all describe actor behavior — structural diagnosis usually finds the loop they're inside
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Discrete one-off decisions where structure isn't the issue — use `/red-team` or `/second-order`
- Clear-domain (Cynefin) problems with deterministic, low-interaction dynamics
- Chaotic-domain situations where there's no time to model — act first, diagnose later
- Pure interpersonal / single-actor situations — that's the operator lens (`knowledge/general/systems-thinking.md`), not this one
- Stakeholder-disagreement messes where the *problem statement itself* is contested — that's SSM territory (`knowledge/general/soft-systems-methodology.md`); a CATWOE-style pass fits better
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/systems-thinking-engineering.md` — canonical write-up: full vocabulary, the eight archetypes, Meadows' twelve leverage points, CST / boundary-critique extension
- `knowledge/general/systems-thinking.md` — sibling lens (operator's inner conditions); this skill optimises structure, that note optimises the actor
- `knowledge/general/soft-systems-methodology.md` — third lens, for stakeholder-disagreement situations this skill cannot resolve
- `knowledge/general/cynefin-framework.md` — domain check; this skill fits Complicated and partially Complex
- `/second-order` — runs *after* this skill on a chosen intervention to trace its cascade through the diagnosed structure
- `/reference-class` — base-rate check on whether the diagnosed archetype's standard intervention has historically worked in comparable cases
- `/red-team` — adversarial pass on the diagnosis if it will drive a decision

ai/skills/skill-synthesize.title: Skill: synthesize
ai/skills/skill-synthesize.content:
Skill: synthesize
Augmentation-layer orchestrator for the creation/synthesis operation — the third of the four higher-order operations the appreciating-position-vs-skill session decomposed. The AI generates a novel synthesis (a reframe, a cross-domain transfer, a new connection) by composing the ideation skills to diverge, then converges to a candidate and stress-tests its novelty, while the user stays the principal who decides whether to adopt it and answers for it. Sits squarely on the generate/adjudicate line: it takes the generate side (cheap), the principal keeps adjudicate (scarce).
When to use

Wanting something new made from a subject — “synthesize X and Y”, “a novel take/reframe”, “create something new from this”, “a new connection”
A problem stuck in its frame, wanting a genuinely different angle generated rather than scaffolded
Fusing two bodies of ideas into one structure neither had alone

Skip for a single divergent technique (/scamper, /assumption-reversal, /starburst directly), candidate plans toward a set goal (/plan-options), or training yourself to synthesize (/deepen-thinking Create rung).
Why it exists
One of the four “AI performs, you stay principal” operation-skills built from the appreciating-position-vs-skill conclusion. It counters recombination-as-novelty — shipping a confident remix of the obvious dressed up as new. The novelty test (borrowed from /deepen-thinking’s Create rung but aimed at the AI’s own output) is the discriminating value the bare ideation skills don’t carry: it names a candidate as recombination when it is one, instead of flattering it. The most augmentation-slop-prone of the four, which is exactly why the converge-and-test discipline and the principal gate are load-bearing here.
Related

skill-scamper · skill-assumption-reversal · skill-starburst — the divergent-ideation skills this composes
skill-plan-options — the sibling generator aimed at plans-toward-a-goal rather than free synthesis
skill-deepen-thinking — the training sibling (user synthesizes; this performs it)
appreciating-position-vs-skill — the four-operation decomposition; the generate/adjudicate split pinning adoption to the principal
augmented-vs-trained-thinking — the generate-vs-adjudicate line this sits on the generate side of

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/synthesize/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-16. Re-sync on any later body edit.

---
name: synthesize
description: Generate a novel synthesis for a subject — a reframe, a cross-domain transfer, a new connection it didn't hand you — by diverging through the ideation skills then converging to one candidate, stress-tested for genuine novelty versus recombination of the obvious. The AI produces it; you stay the principal who decides whether to adopt it and answers for it. Use when you want something new made — "synthesize X and Y", "a novel take/reframe", "create something new from this", "a new connection". Thin orchestrator: composes /scamper, /assumption-reversal, /starburst to diverge, then converges and runs a novelty test. Distinct from /scamper, /assumption-reversal, /starburst (single divergent techniques — this sequences them and converges to one tested artifact), /plan-options (plans toward a set goal, not free synthesis), and /deepen-thinking's Create rung (which trains you to synthesize — this performs it). Counters recombination-as-novelty — shipping a confident remix of the obvious as new.
---
 
Produce a novel synthesis and adjudicate its novelty — the creation/synthesis operation (the third of the four in `knowledge/general/appreciating-position-vs-skill.md`). The AI *generates*; the boundary that keeps the principal in the seat is the note's split of Bloom's Create tier — *generating* the artifact is cheap, *deciding what to create and owning the result* is the scarce residual, so **the AI synthesizes but only you adopt and answer for it.** Thin by design: it drives the existing ideation skills to diverge, then converges and tests, rather than reinventing ideation.
 
## How to locate the subject
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the subject to synthesize from — a topic, a pair of ideas to fuse, a problem wanting a reframe, a body of material to extend. If empty, infer the subject just discussed. If nothing fits, ask what to create *from* rather than invent a subject.
 
## The procedure
 
Diverge, converge, test — never skip the test.
 
1. **Diverge** (compose the ideation skills; pick by fit, don't run all three by reflex):
   - **`/scamper`** — when the subject is an existing thing to transform (Substitute / Combine / Adapt / Modify / Put-to-another-use / Eliminate / Rearrange).
   - **`/assumption-reversal`** — when the subject feels stuck in a frame; invert its unstated assumptions into design briefs.
   - **`/starburst`** — when the subject is under-explored; open the Who/What/Where/When/Why/How gaps first.
   Generate a spread of candidate syntheses — aim for ~5 genuinely different ones, not five phrasings of one.
2. **Converge.** Select the 1–2 candidates with the most load-bearing newness and state each as a crisp synthesis: the new connection / reframe / transfer, in one or two lines.
3. **Run the novelty test** (the discriminating step — borrowed from `/deepen-thinking`'s Create rung, aimed at the AI's own output):
   - Is this a genuine synthesis, or a recombination of the obvious? Name which, honestly.
   - Does it survive one counterexample?
   - What does it *cost* — what does adopting this reframe give up?
   A candidate that fails the test is reported as recombination, not dressed up as novel.
4. **Run the principal gate.** Hand the adopt/own decision back — see Output.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Synthesis — <subject>
 
## Diverged via
</scamper | /assumption-reversal | /starburst> — <one line on what it surfaced>
 
## Candidate synthesis
1. <the new connection / reframe / transfer — 1–2 lines>
2. <…>  (optional second candidate)
 
## Novelty verdict
Candidate 1: <genuine synthesis | recombination of the obvious> — <why>
Survives counterexample? <yes/no — the counterexample> · Costs: <what it gives up>
 
## You own (principal gate)
- Adopt, adapt, or reject — and if you adopt it, you answer for it, not the AI.
- The AI can generate the artifact; deciding it's worth making is yours.
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Grading novelty leniently.** Calling a recombination of the obvious "novel" because it sounds good or to please. The honest verdict — "this is a remix" — is the deliverable's most valuable line.
- **Diverging without converging.** Dumping twenty raw ideas and stopping. The user can do brainstorm-sludge themselves; the value is the convergence plus the novelty test.
- **Running all three ideation skills by reflex.** Pick the one(s) that fit the subject. Forcing /starburst on a well-explored subject manufactures filler.
- **Skipping the test.** Handing a candidate over with no novelty verdict, no counterexample, no cost. An untested synthesis is just a confident guess.
- **Adopting on the user's behalf.** Presenting the synthesis as the answer rather than a candidate for the principal to adopt and own.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user wants something new made from a subject — "synthesize X and Y", "novel take on this", "create something from this", "a fresh reframe", "a new connection between these"
- A problem is stuck in its frame and wants a genuinely different angle, generated rather than scaffolded
- Fusing two bodies of ideas into one structure neither had alone
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- A single divergent technique — `/scamper`, `/assumption-reversal`, or `/starburst` directly
- Generating candidate *plans* toward a set goal — `/plan-options`
- Training yourself to synthesize (you produce, AI belays) — `/deepen-thinking` (Create rung)
- A factual answer or a summary — answer normally; this is for novel synthesis, not retrieval
 
## Related
 
- `/scamper` · `/assumption-reversal` · `/starburst` — the divergent-ideation skills this composes
- `/plan-options` — the sibling generator aimed at plans-toward-a-goal rather than free synthesis
- `/deepen-thinking` — the *training* sibling: scaffolds the user to synthesize (Create rung) rather than performing it
- `knowledge/general/appreciating-position-vs-skill.md` — the four-operation decomposition; the generate/adjudicate split that pins adoption to the principal
- `knowledge/ai/augmented-vs-trained-thinking.md` — the generate-vs-adjudicate line this skill sits on the generate side of

ai/skills/skill-task-decompose.title: Skill: task-decompose
ai/skills/skill-task-decompose.content:
Skill: task-decompose
Decompose a chosen plan into implementation tasks with their specs attached — each task carries a falsifiable done-criterion written at creation, the interface it exposes and consumes, and a risk-rank that front-loads the project-killing unknown. The ④ stage of the intent-to-retrospective-loop and the produce-side sibling of plan-options (which picks the approach this skill then decomposes). It clears the ceremony bar by forcing the three disciplines the default task-breakdown skips: done-criteria at creation, the cross-task interface contract, and risk-ordering.
When to use

After the approach is chosen (e.g. via /plan-options), before issuing implementation work, on integration-heavy or novel material — build-both-sides-and-integrate shapes, hardware/firmware bring-up, cross-service wiring
When the seam between tasks is the real risk — a payload schema or protocol two tasks must agree on before either is built
When “is this task done?” is a non-trivial question for most tasks in the list
Upstream of /branch-resolve (branches) and /plan-split-scan (size); downstream of /plan-options (approach)

Skip when:

The work is routine and well-trodden, done-criteria write themselves, and nothing shares a contract (provisioning a standard service, a CRUD endpoint, a config change) — refuse, and say so
The approach isn’t chosen yet (use /plan-options)
You’re checking an already-drafted task list’s size (use /plan-split-scan)
You’re verifying a produced output (use /reviewers-map — post-hoc, not generation-time)

Why it exists
Silent-underspecification is the failure mode it counters: a plan gets broken into a narrative-ordered task list whose done-criteria are unstated (so “done” means “worked once”), whose cross-task contracts are discovered only at integration, and whose riskiest task is back-loaded behind cheap visible progress. None of the existing loop skills closes this at generation time — /plan-split-scan audits size, /branch-resolve operationalizes branches, and /reviewers-map verifies the output post-hoc, too late to shape the task.
The skill was the last buildable produce-side cell of the loop. Stage ④ was originally left native (2026-05-29) on the judgment that a task-generator couldn’t clear the ceremony bar; it was reopened the same day after walking the loop on two concrete cases that split the bar by case, not domain:

Pi-hole (routine, narrow): done-criteria write themselves (nslookup <ad-domain> → 0.0.0.0); the one non-obvious item (secondary-DNS bypass) is a branch for /branch-resolve. Task-generator = ceremony → correct refuse (the refuse-floor).
ESP32 + display Claude Code companion (novel, integration-heavy): native decomposition skipped all three disciplines — fuzzy done-criteria, the hook-payload-vs-device-parser contract built blind on both sides, and the project-killing unknown (does a Claude Code hook reach a LAN device at all?) sitting last instead of first. Task-generator clears the bar → pass (the pass-ceiling).

So the skill ships trigger-bounded: fire on integration-heavy/novel work where done-criteria are non-obvious and tasks share a contract; refuse on routine work. The refuse condition is what keeps it from competing with native decomposition everywhere — the same self-guard /plan-options carries against generating three plans for a one-approach task.
Related

.claude/skills/task-decompose/SKILL.md — operational definition
intent-to-retrospective-loop — backing concept; this skill is the loop’s ④ stage, reopened and re-scoped 2026-05-29 (see the ceremony-trap section for the two-case dogfood)
skill-plan-options — the upstream ② stage; picks the approach this skill decomposes
skill-plan-split-scan — the sibling check on the task list’s size; this generates the list, that audits its decomposition
skill-branch-resolve — operationalizes branches surfaced during decomposition; runs after this
skill-reviewers-map — the ⑤ post-hoc verification; this writes done-criteria at creation so that check has targets
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/task-decompose/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: task-decompose
description: Decompose a chosen plan into implementation tasks, forcing the three disciplines the default task-breakdown skips — a falsifiable done-criterion per task written at creation time, the cross-task interface contract (what each task exposes and consumes), and risk-ordering (spike the project-killing task first). Use after the approach is chosen (via `/plan-options`) and before issuing implementation work, on integration-heavy or novel work where done-criteria are non-obvious and tasks share a contract — any "build both sides and integrate" shape. Distinct from `/plan-split-scan` (checks an already-drafted task list for size — not a generator), `/plan-options` (picks the approach this skill then decomposes), `/branch-resolve` (operationalizes conditional branches), and `/reviewers-map` (post-hoc output verification). Skip — and say so — on routine work where native decomposition already yields adequate tasks with free done-criteria; the spec'd table there is ceremony. Counters silent-underspecification.
---
 
Decompose a chosen plan into implementation tasks with their specs attached — the ④ stage of the loop in `knowledge/ai/intent-to-retrospective-loop.md`, built to clear the ceremony bar (a generative task skill is only worth it if it forces a discipline the default skips). The default task-breakdown does three things badly: it **leaves done-criteria unstated** (tasks read as activities, not as falsifiable completions, so "done" silently means "worked once"), it **flattens cross-task contracts** (two tasks that must agree on a schema or protocol get built independently and the mismatch surfaces at integration), and it **orders by narrative, not risk** (the one task whose failure kills the project sits last, behind cheap visible progress). This skill forces a done-criterion per task at creation time, surfaces the interface each task exposes and consumes, and re-orders by uncertainty so the project-killing unknown is spiked first.
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the chosen plan to decompose. If empty, use the plan just produced (e.g. the `/plan-options` chosen plan, a project's approach section). The approach should already be chosen; if it isn't, route to `/plan-options` first — you cannot decompose a plan that hasn't been picked.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A chosen plan about to become implementation work, on **integration-heavy or novel** material — build-both-sides-and-integrate shapes, hardware/firmware bring-up, cross-service wiring, anything where the seam is the risk
- Work where **done-criteria are non-obvious** — where "is this task actually finished?" can't be answered by a one-line observable without thought
- Work where **tasks share a contract** — a payload schema, a protocol, an API surface two tasks must agree on before either is built
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- Routine, well-trodden work where native decomposition is already adequate and done-criteria write themselves (provisioning a standard service, a CRUD endpoint, a documented config change) — generating a spec'd task table is ceremony; **refuse**
- A plan whose approach hasn't been chosen yet (use `/plan-options` first — nothing to decompose)
- An already-drafted task list you want to check for size/over-decomposition (use `/plan-split-scan`)
- Conditional branches inside the plan (use `/branch-resolve`)
- A produced output you want to verify (use `/reviewers-map` — that's post-hoc; this is generation-time)
 
**Refuse-to-generate condition.** If native decomposition already yields adequate tasks with free done-criteria — the routine case — say so in one line and stop. Manufacturing an interface table and a risk-ranking for `nslookup → 0.0.0.0`-grade tasks is exactly the ceremony this skill exists to avoid. The honest output is "native decomposition is adequate here; no skipped discipline to force."
 
## What to do
 
1. **Pin the chosen plan.** If the approach isn't chosen, route to `/plan-options`. If the plan is trivial/routine (free done-criteria, no shared contract), apply the refuse condition and stop.
2. **Decompose into tasks at uniform altitude, sliced vertically.** Each task is a unit of work with a single owner-concern. Resist mixing a 30-second config edit and a multi-day integration in the same list. Prefer **vertical slices** — each task a thin end-to-end increment that can be demoed and verified on its own — over **horizontal layers** (all schema, then all API, then all UI), which defer integration risk to the end and leave early tasks with no observable done-state. A horizontal task whose done-criterion (step 3) can only be "the code exists" rather than "a user/test can exercise it" is the tell; recut it by capability. Carve-out: an irreducible foundational layer with no thinner vertical expression (a whole-schema migration, a shared library every later slice consumes) may stay horizontal — spike it first per the risk-ordering step.
3. **Write a falsifiable done-criterion per task — at creation.** The observable that proves the task is *correctly* complete, not merely attempted. "Connect WiFi" → *reconnects within 10s after a router reboot*, not "WiFi code written." **If a task's done-criterion can't be stated, the task is underspecified** — split or sharpen it until it can. This is the load-bearing discipline.
4. **Surface the interface each task exposes and consumes.** Name the cross-task contracts — the schema, protocol, or signature two tasks must agree on. Flag the **load-bearing contract**: the seam where building both sides independently would produce an integration-time mismatch. Pin that contract *before* either side is built.
5. **Risk-order.** Rank tasks by uncertainty, not narrative flow. Identify the **highest-uncertainty task — the one whose failure kills the project** — and mark it to spike *first*, before any cheap/visible work. Narrative order back-loads risk; this front-loads it.
