ai/skills/skill-unslop.content:
Skill: unslop
Rewrites a prose artifact to strip AI-writing tells and put voice back in, working from a fixed 31-pattern catalog: puffery, AI vocabulary, “not just X but Y”, em-dash and boldface overuse, inline-header lists, chatbot phrases, stacked hedging, filler, abstract metaphor nouns, passive voice, generic conclusions. It edits in place and logs every change before→after.
House-native port of cursor/plugins, pstack/skills/unslop, fetched 2026-08-19. The 31-pattern catalog is reproduced substantially verbatim — it is the substance of the skill. Four house changes:

A preservation floor (Step 0). Upstream has none, and two of its patterns are a fabrication trapdoor: pattern 5 says “name the source or delete” and pattern 21 says “find sources or remove”. Under house rules both resolve to delete or flag, never to supply a source you do not have. Facts, numbers, hedge strength, citations, quotes, and wiki-link targets survive verbatim, matching skill-prose-surgery’s floor.
A change log and a reachable clean verdict. Upstream rewrites silently. The port emits before→after per change, a needs-verification list for spans a fix would require knowing something to close, and a Clean verdict that leaves the file untouched — so “found nothing” is a successful run rather than a prompt to manufacture edits.
A register gate on patterns 27–31 (added 2026-08-19). The plain-speech block — “shorten dense sentences”, “active voice”, “cut adverbs”, “prefer the plain word” — is general prose-quality advice, not AI-tell detection, and fires on competent human writing. It now fires only in a paragraph where a register pattern (1–26) already fired; elsewhere the symptom is routed to /prose-surgery, /density-scan or /readability-scan and the span is left alone. Evidence: the head-to-head run logged 11 changes on the lowest-tell note in an eight-note sample, 5 of them from 27–31 alone — making the Clean verdict unreachable in practice, the exact axis-5 failure /skill-quality-audit passed the skill on because the contract defined one.
House calibration on three patterns. Em dashes (13), inline-header lists (16), and abstract metaphor nouns (26) collide with this vault’s established register. See below.

Upstream’s description read “Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.” That was replaced. An always-fires rewrite skill is a standing hazard to every note in the vault, and the house description formula wants triggers plus a distinctness clause, not a mandate.
When to use

A draft reads like an LLM wrote it: “make this sound human”, “this is slop”, “de-AI this”, “strip the AI tells”, “less ChatGPT”
Before committing an AI-drafted note, README, or PR description that a human will read as authored
On external-facing prose (publish-tagged notes, external repo docs) where register is part of the deliverable
After skill-bias-scan-ai — that scan clears the epistemic layer, this one clears the register layer, and both can fire on the same artifact

Skip when:

The symptom is a hallucinated specific or unearned narrative — skill-bias-scan-ai, different layer
The reader has to re-parse sentences (referents, dependency distance, given-new) — skill-prose-surgery
You want a diagnosis without an edit — skill-readability-scan or skill-density-scan
The target is a journal entry, an inbox capture, or code

The three house calibrations
The reason this port needed adapting rather than dropping in:

























PatternUpstream ruleHouse resolution13, em dashesAvoid entirelyTwo modes. Vault-internal: fire on overuse only (>1 per paragraph, or two in one sentence) — em dashes are this vault’s standing device and voice is protected. External: apply as written, and external means leaving the vault’s voice (external repo, PR description, someone else’s publication) — not a publish tag, which ~216 notes carry as the site-visibility flag. Declare the mode before editing.16, inline-header listsConvert bold-label-colon lines to proseUpstream already exempts the bold-lead-in-with-new-detail form, which is the form the vault uses throughout. Fire only on the restating kind.26, abstract metaphor nounsReplace with the concrete wordSeveral listed words are canonical vault terms: “surface” (in skill-api-surface-scan), “harness”, “primitive”, “vector”, “scaffolding”. A word naming an established concept is vocabulary, not slop — replacing it manufactures exactly the drift skill-concept-drift-scan exists to catch. Fire only where no established term is invoked.
Why it exists
Every existing prose skill in the catalog either diagnoses without editing (skill-density-scan, skill-readability-scan) or edits a different axis (skill-prose-surgery, which owns parse load under hard meaning preservation). None of them own register — the vocabulary, punctuation, formatting habits, and absent point of view that make a passage read as machine-written even after it survives every correctness check. An AI-drafted note can be factually clean, well-cited, structurally sound, calibrated, and still unmistakably AI. That gap is what this skill closes.
The second half of the skill matters as much as the first. Upstream is explicit that removing patterns is half the job and voiceless prose is just as obvious a tell. The house limit on that: voice gets sharpened, not supplied. On someone else’s note, an inserted opinion is a fabricated claim, which puts it back under the vault’s authoring rules rather than its style rules.
Related

.claude/skills/unslop/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-prose-surgery — the other fix-mode prose skill; parse-load axis where this one owns register
skill-bias-scan-ai — detection sibling on the epistemic layer; composes before this
skill-readability-scan, skill-density-scan — diagnostic siblings that route fixes here or to prose-surgery
skill-concept-drift-scan — the reason pattern 26 is calibrated
prose-revision-operations — evidence base for the sentence-level operations this skill defers to
Source: cursor/plugins, pstack/skills/unslop/SKILL.md

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/unslop/SKILL.md as of 2026-08-19. Re-sync this block on any body edit.

---
name: unslop
description: Edit a prose artifact to strip AI-writing tells and restore human voice — the register-and-vocabulary fix pass, worked from a fixed 31-pattern catalog (puffery, buzzwords, AI vocabulary, "not just X but Y", em-dash and boldface overuse, chatbot phrases, hedging, filler, passive voice). Edits in place when tells are found, under a preservation floor — facts, numbers, hedges, unverified-labels, citations and wiki-links survive verbatim, and every change is logged before→after. Use when text reads like an LLM wrote it or sounds robotic, when asked to make writing sound human or less like ChatGPT, to de-slop or de-AI a draft, strip AI tells, or clean up an AI-drafted note, README, or PR description before committing. Distinct from /bias-scan-ai (detects epistemic fingerprints, never edits), /prose-surgery (repairs parse-load structure, not register), and /density-scan and /readability-scan (diagnose only). Counters the AI register that survives every correctness check.
---
 
Rewrite the prose at `$ARGUMENTS` to remove AI-writing tells and put voice back in. This is a **fix-mode** skill: it edits. The boundary that keeps it from bleeding into its siblings — `/prose-surgery` operates on *parse load* (referents, given-new order, dependency distance) and `/bias-scan-ai` operates on *epistemic contamination* (hallucinated specifics, sycophancy, unearned narrative). This skill operates on **register**: vocabulary, punctuation, formatting habits, filler, and the absence of a human point of view. If a symptom is structural or epistemic, name it in one line and route it; do not fix it here.
 
House-native port of `cursor/plugins`, `pstack/skills/unslop` (fetched 2026-08-19). The 31-pattern catalog below is upstream's and is reproduced substantially verbatim — it is the substance of the skill. Four house changes: a **preservation floor** before any edit (upstream has none, and two of its patterns invite fabrication), a **change log** in the output, an explicit **house calibration** for the three patterns that collide with this vault's established voice, and a **register gate** on patterns 27–31 (added 2026-08-19 after a head-to-head run showed those five firing on prose with no AI tells at all, which made the clean verdict unreachable). Upstream's `description` read "Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply." — replaced, because an always-fires rewrite skill is a standing hazard to every note in the vault.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A file path — operate on the body, never frontmatter values
- A path-and-section ref (e.g. `knowledge/ai/foo.md#the-read`) — operate on that section
- Literal prose, quoted or fenced — return the rewritten text instead of editing a file
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. A note or draft written by an AI earlier in this session
2. The most recently edited prose-bearing file in this session
3. If nothing fits, ask which artifact to unslop rather than guess
 
## Scope
 
Operate on prose a human will read as someone's writing: knowledge notes, article and `publish`-tagged drafts, PR descriptions, READMEs, project overviews, external-facing docs, anything an LLM drafted and nobody has since rewritten.
 
Do **not** operate on:
 
- Code, or code blocks inside prose (never touched)
- Frontmatter values, `journal/` entries, or `knowledge/_inbox.md` captures — personal voice and raw capture are not the bar
- Skill bodies and their catalog verbatim copies (byte-sync contract; route to `/skill-quality-audit`)
- Quoted source material, block quotes, and citations — the point of a quote is that it is unedited
- Poetry, aphorism, or prose whose difficulty is craft
- Text where the AI register is the deliverable (a note *about* AI writing, a fixture, an eval input)
 
## Step 0 — preservation floor
 
Before any edit, inventory what must survive verbatim. This is the hard floor, not a preference. It exists because two upstream patterns (5, vague attributions; 21, cutoff disclaimers) instruct you to "name the source or delete" — and inventing a source to satisfy a style rule is the worst failure this skill can produce.
 
- **Facts**: numbers, dates, named entities, statistics, and their labels
- **Hedge strength**: "unverified", "reportedly", "~", "as of" — an edit may not make a claim stronger or weaker. Cutting a hedge as "excessive hedging" (pattern 24) is only legal when the hedges are stacked and redundant, never when one hedge is carrying a real uncertainty.
- **Citations, quotes, and their placement** relative to the claim they support
- **Wiki-link targets** — display text may change only to the note's established term
- **Claim set**: nothing new is asserted. Pattern 5 resolves to *delete the vague attribution* or *leave it flagged*, never to supply a plausible-sounding source.
 
Anything a fix would require you to *know* — who the expert was, what the missing number is — is not a rewrite. Report it as needs-verification and leave the span.
 
## Process
 
1. Read the target in full. Run Step 0.
2. Declare the mode: **vault-internal** or **external** (see house calibration).
3. Scan for patterns 1–26. Then scan for 27–31 **only in paragraphs where 1–26 fired** (see the gate).
4. Rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
5. Add voice (next section).
6. Self-audit: "what still makes this obviously AI-generated?" Fix the remaining tells.
7. Emit the change log and verdict.
 
## Adding voice
 
Removing patterns is half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious.
 
- **Have opinions.** React to facts instead of neutrally listing pros and cons.
- **Vary rhythm.** Short sentences. Then longer ones that take their time. Mix it up.
- **Acknowledge complexity.** "Impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "impressive."
- **Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional.
- **Let some mess in.** Perfect structure looks machine-made.
- **Be specific.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am."
 
One house limit on this section: voice is added *by the author's own commitments*, not invented for them. If the artifact is the user's note, an opinion you insert is a claim they did not make. Sharpen the opinions already present; flag where the draft is voiceless and say what a stance would need to commit to.
 
## Patterns to detect and fix
 
### Content
 
1. **Puffery.** "pivotal moment", "testament to", "evolving landscape", "setting the stage for", "indelible mark", "deeply rooted". Cut puffery, state what happened.
2. **Name-dropping.** Listing media outlets without context. Pick one, say what was said.
3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
4. **Promotional language.** "nestled", "vibrant", "breathtaking", "groundbreaking", "renowned", "stunning", "must-visit". Use neutral descriptions.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete. *(House: delete or flag. Never supply a source you do not have — Step 0.)*
6. **Formulaic challenges.** "Despite challenges... continues to thrive." Replace with specific facts.
 
### Language
 
7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Just say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Forcing ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
 
### Style
 
13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). Em dashes are an AI tell, and reaching for parentheses instead just trades one tell for another. If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma. *(House-calibrated — see below.)*
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example. Not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Replace with straight quotes.
 
### Communication artifacts
 
20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
21. **Cutoff disclaimers.** "While specific details are limited..." Find sources or remove. *(House: remove, or leave the claim explicitly labeled unverified. Do not manufacture the missing source.)*
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
 
### Filler
 
23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". "It is important to note that" gets deleted.
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may". *(House: stacked hedges collapse to one. A single hedge carrying real uncertainty stays — Step 0.)*
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
 
### Jargon
 
26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate, wedge, vector, locus, vantage, nexus, primitive (as noun), harness (as metaphor), surface (as in "API surface"), bedrock, scaffolding (as metaphor), modality, paradigm, gold-plating, ratchet (as metaphor), evacuate (for moving code), endgame, north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. "Substrate" becomes "base". "Wedge in" becomes "add". "Vector" becomes "way" or "method". "Gold-plating" becomes "more than the job needs". "Ratchet" becomes the mechanism's real name or "a limit that only tightens". "Evacuate" becomes "move out". "Endgame" becomes "the last phase". Pick the concrete word. *(House-calibrated — see below.)*
 
### Plain speech — gated
 
**Firing condition for 27–31.** These five are general prose-quality rules, not AI tells: they fire on
competent human writing too. Apply them **only in a paragraph where at least one of patterns 1–26 has
already fired.** In a paragraph carrying no register tell, a plain-speech symptom is a sibling's finding,
not yours — name it under *Routed elsewhere* and leave the span:
 
| Pattern | Owner when the gate is shut |
|---|---|
| 27 — feeling instead of mechanism | `/readability-scan` (concrete core claims) |
| 28 — dense sentence needing a split | `/density-scan` diagnoses it, `/prose-surgery` splits it |
| 29 — passive with a recoverable actor | `/prose-surgery` (actor restoration) |
| 30 — propping adverb | `/readability-scan` (word choice) |
| 31 — fancier synonym | `/readability-scan` (audience-familiar terms) |
 
The gate is per paragraph, not per document: a slopped paragraph opens it for that paragraph only. On
genuinely AI-drafted text patterns 1–26 fire almost everywhere, so the gate is open almost everywhere and
this section works as upstream wrote it. On human prose it stays shut, which is the point.
 
27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number. "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" becomes "use", "leverage" becomes "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
 
## House calibration
 
Three upstream patterns collide with this vault's established register. Resolve them this way, and say which mode you are in before editing — never silently.
 
- **13, em dashes.** Upstream's rule is absolute. This vault's notes, skill bodies, and `CLAUDE.md` use em dashes as a standing device, and `/prose-surgery`'s preservation floor protects voice. **Vault-internal mode**: fire on *overuse* only — roughly more than one per paragraph, or any sentence carrying two. **External mode** (external repos, PR descriptions, READMEs, a piece written for someone else's publication — anything going to a reader who did not choose this voice): apply the rule as written. **A `publish` tag is not an external-mode signal in this vault**: it is the site-visibility flag, carried by ~216 notes as of 2026-08-19, and the published voice is the vault voice. Four separate runs had to reason around the earlier wording before proceeding. When in doubt, ask which mode; do not de-dash the whole vault on your own authority.
- **16, inline-header lists.** Upstream already exempts the bold-lead-in-with-new-detail form, which is the form this vault uses throughout. Fire only on the restating kind.
- **26, abstract metaphor nouns.** Several listed words are canonical vault terms — "surface" in `/api-surface-scan`, "harness", "primitive", "vector", "scaffolding". A word that names an established concept or a skill is vocabulary, not slop, and replacing it manufactures exactly the drift `/concept-drift-scan` exists to catch. Fire only where no established term is invoked and a plainer concrete word exists.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Unslop — <target>
 
## Mode
<vault-internal | external> — <one-line reason>
 
## Changes
1. **[pattern N]** <location>
   before: <quoted span>
   after:  <rewritten span>
2. ...
 
## Needs verification (not rewritten)
- <span> — <what a fix would require knowing>
 
## Routed elsewhere
- <symptom> → `/prose-surgery` | `/readability-scan` | `/bias-scan-ai` | `/density-scan`
 
## Verdict
**<Clean | Unslopped | Rewrite recommended>**
<one or two lines>
```
 
Verdict states:
 
- **Clean** — no tells worth acting on. The file is unchanged. Report it and stop; do not manufacture edits to look useful. Gated-out plain-speech symptoms never block Clean — a document with zero register tells and any number of 27–31 symptoms is **Clean**, with those symptoms routed to their owners.
- **Unslopped** — tells found and fixed in place, all logged above.
- **Rewrite recommended** — the tells are not spans but the whole shape (the draft is a voiceless summary of nothing in particular). Surgery will not save it. Say so, name what the piece would have to commit to, and leave the file alone.
 
If the artifact is clean, the output is the mode line, an empty changes section, and the verdict. Do not pad.
 
Done when: the mode is declared; the gate was evaluated per paragraph before any 27–31 edit; every edit appears in the change log as a before→after pair; every protected item from Step 0 is present in the file unchanged; no claim was added, strengthened, or weakened; and the verdict is one of the three states.
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Opening the gate by reflex.** Patterns 27–31 fire only where a register tell already fired in the same paragraph. Applying them everywhere is how this skill turns into a generic style-checker that can never report clean — the measured failure the gate was added to fix.
- **Manufacturing edits.** Clean prose reported clean is a successful run. A skill that always finds 20 tells is a skill nobody trusts on the note that mattered.
- **Inventing the source.** Patterns 5 and 21 are the fabrication trapdoor. "Experts believe" becomes deleted or flagged. It never becomes "Anthropic's 2025 report found".
- **Softening or hardening a claim.** Filler-cutting that removes "may" turns a calibrated sentence into an assertion. That is the house's core authoring sin arriving as a style fix.
- **Inserting opinions the author does not hold.** "Add voice" means sharpen the stance that is there, not supply one. On someone else's note, an invented opinion is a fabricated claim.
- **Register laundering.** Removing every tell until the prose reads as competent, anonymous, and empty. Upstream says this outright: voiceless is as obvious as sloppy.
- **De-dashing the vault.** Pattern 13 in vault-internal mode is an overuse check, not a purge. See house calibration.
- **Editing quotes.** A quote you unslopped is a misquotation.
- **Doing `/prose-surgery`'s job.** Referent repair, given-new reorder, and dependency-closing are that skill's seven operations. Route the symptom, do not absorb it.
- **Self-exemption.** This skill's own output — the change log, the verdict lines — follows the same 31 patterns. No "I hope this helps", no puffery in the verdict.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A draft reads like an LLM wrote it: "make this sound human", "this is slop", "de-AI this", "strip the AI tells", "less ChatGPT"
- Before committing an AI-drafted note, README, or PR description that a human will read as authored
- After a heavy AI-assisted writing session, on the artifact rather than the transcript
- On external-facing prose (`publish`-tagged notes, external repo docs) where the register is part of the deliverable
- Composes after `/bias-scan-ai` — that scan clears the epistemic layer, this one clears the register layer. Both can fire on the same artifact.
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Detecting hallucinated specifics, sycophancy, or unearned narrative — `/bias-scan-ai` (detection, different layer)
- Sentences the reader has to re-parse (referents, dependency distance, given-new) — `/prose-surgery`
- Diagnosing *why* prose is hard, without editing — `/readability-scan` (document and word axes), `/density-scan` (sentence axis)
- A message that did not land in chat — `/re-pitch`
- Code style, or any code block
- Journal entries and inbox captures — the personal register is not a defect
 
## Related
 
- `/prose-surgery` — the other fix-mode prose skill; parse-load axis under hard meaning preservation, where this one owns register
- `/bias-scan-ai` — detection sibling; epistemic fingerprints rather than stylistic ones, and never edits
- `/readability-scan`, `/density-scan` — diagnostic siblings; both route their fixes here or to `/prose-surgery`
- `/concept-drift-scan` — the reason pattern 26 is calibrated: established terms are vocabulary, not jargon
- `knowledge/general/prose-revision-operations.md` — evidence base for the sentence-level operations this skill defers to
- `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-unslop.md` — catalog reference note
- Source: `cursor/plugins`, `pstack/skills/unslop/SKILL.md`

ai/skills/skill-which-skill.title: Skill: which-skill
ai/skills/skill-which-skill.content:
Skill: which-skill
Recommend which skill(s) from the local catalog to invoke given a situation, an artifact, or an intent. Returns 1–3 ranked candidates with quoted trigger phrases plus 1–2 rejected near-misses.
When to use

The catalog is too large to hold in your head and you want a routed recommendation
Two skills look adjacent and the choice between them isn’t obvious
You want the routing decision made explicit and auditable rather than silently picked
A skill recently misfired and you want to confirm the catalog still routes a class of requests correctly
Before publishing a new skill — alongside /skill-trigger-audit, check whether the new skill overlaps existing routes

Skip when:

The matching skill is obvious — just invoke it
The request is clearly outside the skill catalog (regular code edits, vault note authoring)
For built-in Claude Code commands (/init, /review, /security-review)

Why it exists
Claude already matches user phrasings against skill descriptions silently — picks one and runs. As the catalog grows, the silent pick becomes less reliable: descriptions overlap, user vocabulary drifts from skill vocabulary, two adjacent skills both plausibly fit. /which-skill makes that implicit routing visible. The output (ranked candidates with quoted trigger phrases and rejected near-misses) is an artifact the user can correct, and the rejection reasons teach the catalog — two-thirds of the value is in the near-misses, not the recommendation.
The skill is the dynamic counterpart to verification-stack-operational-map: the map is the static decision tree, /which-skill routes a specific request. Use the map when you can hold the catalog in view; use /which-skill when the catalog is too large or the choice is ambiguous.
Related

.claude/skills/which-skill/SKILL.md — operational definition
verification-stack-operational-map — static decision tree across the full catalog (the complement to this skill)
skill-skill-trigger-audit sibling skill — distinct axis (audits one skill’s description; this routes to a skill)
information-density-for-llm-prompts — why description retrieval is decisive for tool selection

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/which-skill/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: which-skill
description: Recommend which skill(s) from the local catalog to invoke given a situation, an artifact, or an intent. Reads `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` live, ranks 1–3 candidates, and for each returns the matching trigger phrase quoted from its description, a one-line rationale, and what the skill won't do — plus 1–2 rejected near-misses with reasons. Use when you can't tell which scan applies, when two skills look adjacent, when you want help picking a tool, when you want to find one for a specific job, when you want to triage a failing prompt/plan by failure type, or when you want the routing decision made explicit and auditable rather than silently picked. Returns a "no skill fits" verdict when honest. Distinct from `/skill-trigger-audit` (which audits one skill's description for retrieval-match quality); this skill routes a request to a skill.
---
 
You are a skill router with a high bar for matching — return 1–3 candidates with rejected near-misses, or "no skill fits" when honest.
 
This skill makes implicit routing explicit. Claude already matches user phrasings against skill descriptions silently — this skill turns that into a visible artifact the user can correct.
 
## How to locate the target
 
`$ARGUMENTS` can be one of:
 
- A situation description in prose ("I just drafted a synthesis note that makes load-bearing claims about base rates")
- An artifact path (`projects/foo/overview.md`, `knowledge/ai/some-note.md`)
- An intent verb plus object ("scan a prompt", "ideate alternatives", "review a draft")
- Empty — infer from session context: the most recently edited file, the user's last substantive request, the current task
 
If no signal is recoverable, ask one clarifying question. Do not guess.
 
## Read the live catalog
 
Do not rely on memory of which skills exist. Each invocation:
 
1. List `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`.
2. For each, extract `name` and `description` from the frontmatter.
3. Match against the user's job using the description text — the description IS the retrieval surface, the body is not.
 
Skills get added, renamed, and rescoped. A cached catalog goes stale silently.
 
## The matching procedure
 
1. **State the user's job in one line** in plain language. If the input is an artifact path, state what the user appears to want done with it (scan? plan? review? ideate?). Make this explicit so a wrong inference is visible.
 
2. **Generate candidate matches.** For each skill in the catalog, predict whether the user's job matches its description's positive trigger spans. Rank by:
   - Direct match on the artifact type (e.g., "AI-generated note" → `/bias-scan-ai`; "prompt about to be sent" → `/bias-scan-prompt`)
   - Direct match on the verb-object pair the user used ("scan a prompt", "audit a description", "ideate alternatives")
   - Direct match on the failure mode the skill addresses (the "Counters X" clause in many descriptions)
   - If the input *describes a failure* (model didn't follow, agent went wrong on step N, output is shallow), classify the dominant cognitive-load type first — see "Load-type diagnostic hints" below. The same failure language routes to different skills depending on type.
 
3. **Return top 1–3.** If four or more skills plausibly fit, the user's intent is too vague — ask one clarifying question instead of dumping the catalog.
 
4. **Surface 1–2 near-misses.** Skills that look adjacent but were rejected, with the reason. This is two-thirds of the value — it teaches the catalog and prevents the user from invoking the wrong thing next time.
 
5. **Optional workflow chain.** If the situation calls for multiple skills in sequence (e.g., draft → `/density-scan` → `/bias-scan-human` → `/red-team`), name the chain. Don't force this — most requests fit one skill.
 
6. **"No skill fits" is a valid output.** Don't force-match. If the request is outside the catalog, say so and suggest what to do instead (a regular tool, a manual procedure, or that the user write a new skill).
 
## Load-type diagnostic hints
 
When the input signals a failure rather than a forward-looking scan, classify the dominant load type before ranking. The three patterns and their routes:
 
| Symptom | Dominant load | Route toward | Anti-route |
|---|---|---|---|
| Executor follows the structure but is substantively wrong; re-prompting the same shape repeats the failure; "the model can't reason about X" | **Intrinsic** | `/plan-split-scan` (stage the hard step into within-capacity links); escalate executor; provide a missing schema / worked example | Reformatting or "stronger" prompts — intrinsic load isn't a compliance problem |
| Executor follows part of the instruction, contradicts another part, "loses track" mid-execution; instructions are correct but execution is incoherent | **Extraneous** | `/density-scan` (prompt surface), `/context-budget-scan` (token economy), `/plan-split-scan` (orchestration extraneous) | Adding more instructions — each addition is more extraneous load |
| Executor handles each step correctly but produces shallow / incoherent synthesis; surface compliance, missing depth | **Germane-capacity exhausted** | `/density-scan` to free capacity; `/plan-split-scan` to break synthesis into staged sub-syntheses; intermediate artifacts | Asking for "deeper analysis" — that raises intrinsic load without freeing germane capacity |
 
Treat the three types as **diagnostic labels** for picking the right fix, not as measurements. Rationale: `knowledge/ai/cognitive-load-theory-for-ai.md`. If the failure could plausibly be either intrinsic or extraneous, name both in the recommendation and let the user pick.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# Skill recommendation
 
## User's job
<one-line plain description>
 
## Recommended
 
### 1. /<skill-name> — <strong fit | likely fit | weak fit>
- Matches: "<trigger phrase quoted verbatim from the description>"
- Why: <one line — what this skill does for the user's job>
- Won't do: <one line — scope boundary, quoted or paraphrased from the skill's "do not invoke for" / anti-patterns / related sections>
 
### 2. /<skill-name> — <verdict>
...
 
## Near-misses
- /<skill-name> — <one-line reason rejected; quote the trigger span that almost matched>
- /<skill-name> — <one-line reason rejected>
 
## Workflow (optional)
/<skill-a> → /<skill-b> → /<skill-c>
<one-line rationale for the chain>
 
## Verdict
<one or two lines; what to invoke next>
```
 
If no skill fits:
 
```text
# Skill recommendation
 
## User's job
<one-line plain description>
 
## No skill fits
<one-line reason — the catalog covers X, Y, Z; this request is about W, which is outside scope>
 
## Suggested alternative
<a regular tool, a manual procedure, or "this would warrant a new skill — sketch?">
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Paraphrasing descriptions back to the user.** Quote the matching trigger span verbatim from the description. Paraphrase loses the audit value — the user can't tell whether the match is real or invented.
- **Force-matching.** If nothing fits, say so. A weak match recommended confidently is worse than "no skill fits" — it creates noise and trains the user to ignore your recommendations.
- **Recommending without rejecting near-misses.** Always name 1–2 skills that look close but were rejected, with reasons. The teaching value is in the rejected siblings.
- **Recommending more than three.** If four+ skills plausibly fit, ask a clarifying question. A long ranked list is the same as no recommendation.
- **Recommending /which-skill recursively.** Don't.
- **Hardcoding the catalog from memory.** Read the live SKILL.md files every invocation. The catalog drifts.
- **Treating the workflow chain as default output.** Most requests fit one skill. Only suggest a chain when there's a genuine sequencing reason — otherwise the chain is invented structure.
- **Inventing trigger phrases.** If the description doesn't actually contain a phrase that matches the user's job, that skill isn't a match — even if you "know" it does the job. Either the description is broken (separate problem; flag it for `/skill-trigger-audit`) or the skill isn't right.
- **Recommending bundled / built-in skills.** `/init`, `/review`, `/security-review` and other Claude Code defaults are out of scope — this skill routes among user-authored skills in `.claude/skills/`.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user describes a situation but isn't sure which scan/tool applies
- Two skills look adjacent and the user wants the routing decision auditable
- The user asks "what should I run on this?" or "is there a skill for X?"
- After observing a misfire — confirm the catalog still routes the situation correctly
- Before publishing a new skill (alongside `/skill-trigger-audit`) — check whether the new skill overlaps existing routes
 
Do not invoke for:
 
- One-off requests with an obviously matching skill (just invoke the skill)
- Requests clearly outside the skill catalog (regular code edits, vault note authoring, conversation)
- Built-in Claude Code commands (`/init`, `/review`, etc.)
 
## Related
 
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — audits one skill's description for retrieval-match quality (description-as-trigger axis); use when a skill misfires or before publishing a new one
- `/density-scan` — audits one skill's body for prose density (density axis)
- `knowledge/ai/verification-stack-operational-map.md` — static decision tree across the catalog; this skill is the dynamic complement (routes a specific request rather than mapping the whole stack)

ai/skills/skill-whittle-scan.title: Skill: whittle-scan
ai/skills/skill-whittle-scan.content:
Skill: whittle-scan
Scan a queue-shaped artifact (project index, inbox, backlog, commitment ledger) for items where the cost of inaction is being underweighted because decay is invisible per week — the Whittle-indifference pattern. For each item, Claude estimates the decay mechanism and a directional subsidy (LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH); the user supplies felt urgency via AskUserQuestion. The gap between the two is the load-bearing signal — subsidy >> urgency surfaces decay the user isn’t feeling, urgency >> subsidy surfaces novelty-pull. Returns flags with implied next actions, not a full ranking.
When to use

A project queue, backlog, or inbox has been sitting more than a week without re-evaluation against capacity
Before a planning block — catch decay that “what’s urgent?” thinking won’t surface
After a stretch of novelty-driven work, as a check on whether novelty-pull crowded out genuinely high-cost items
A calibration loop, thesis-tracking artifact, or commitment ledger has resolution dates that do not fire deadline alarms

Skip when:

The queue has fewer than 3 items (refuse-to-scan)
You’re reviewing a single artifact (use /red-team or /reviewers-map)
The artifact is an intent statement (use /intent-check)
The failure mode is held-open optionality, not decay (use /option-premium-check)
You’re depleted — the scan is deliberation-heavy and produces noise under decision fatigue

Why it exists
Hyper-discounting and urgency illusion are the failure modes the scan counters. Intuition under-rates items whose cost compounds slowly and silently — technical debt, eroding client relationships, calibration windows that pass — because decay does not fire a deadline alarm. Symmetrically, intuition over-rates novel low-stakes items because they bid harder for prefrontal attention. The structural fix is to externalize the question: name the decay mechanism explicitly, then check whether felt urgency tracks the named cost. The Mode 3 estimator split (Claude estimates decay mechanism + subsidy; user supplies felt urgency) prevents the confabulation failure where Claude imputes urgency from artifact tone — the inverse-flag pattern would collapse under that. The restatement-frequency gate (≥ 80% restatement triggers a verbatim deferral line) prevents the skill from laundering existing roadmap text as fresh signal.
Related

.claude/skills/whittle-scan/SKILL.md — operational definition
index-policies-for-prioritization — canonical four-index framework; this skill operationalizes the Whittle column
kurzban-opportunity-cost-effort — biological isomorph; the felt sensation of “tired of this” computes the same indifference threshold in dopaminergic territory
prioritization-architecture-synthesis — Layer 3 (valuation) is where this skill sits alongside /option-premium-check
skill-option-premium-check — adjacent skill on the same valuation layer; flexibility valuation rather than decay valuation
skill-commitment-ledger — pairs well with weekly /whittle-scan on the same ledger artifact
skill-calibration-loop — different axis; this skill produces flags, not predictions
verification-stack-operational-map — placement in the full toolkit

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/whittle-scan/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-05.

---
name: whittle-scan
description: Scan a task list, project queue, project index, inbox, backlog, or commitment ledger for items where the cost of inaction is being underweighted because decay is invisible per week — the Whittle-indifference pattern. For each item, surface the subsidy you'd need to be bribed into ignoring it for another week; flag a large subsidy with low felt urgency (decay you're not feeling), and the inverse where felt urgency exceeds real cost-of-inaction (novelty-pull, urgency illusion). Returns flags with implied next actions, not a full ranking. Use when a queue feels long or stale, when deciding what to work on next, before a planning block, or when a calibration or thesis-tracking artifact has resolution dates that don't fire deadline alarms. Skip for single-artifact reviews (`/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`), goal-statement quality (`/intent-check`), session closeout (`/commitment-ledger`), clarification loops (`/clarify-first`), or queues of fewer than 3 items. Counters hyper-discounting and urgency illusion.
---
 
Scan the queue-shaped artifact at `$ARGUMENTS` for items where the cost of inaction is being underweighted because the decay is invisible per-week — the Whittle-indifference pattern. The dangerous case: a queue where the items you'd naturally pick next are not the items with the highest cost-of-inaction, because decay (compounding technical debt, calibration windows passing without resolution, client-relationship erosion, stale data losing value) does not fire a deadline alarm and intuition hyper-discounts it. The skill surfaces those items and the inverse — items whose felt urgency exceeds their real cost-of-inaction, typically via novelty-pull.
 
If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, infer the target in this order:
 
1. The most-recently-modified queue-shaped artifact in this vault (`projects/_index.md`, `knowledge/_inbox.md`, `journal/commitments-log.md`)
2. A queue named in the current session
3. Ask which queue to scan rather than guess
 
The canonical mental-model framework lives in `knowledge/general/index-policies-for-prioritization.md` — the Whittle section is the load-bearing one for this skill, and the note's own anti-pattern list (index theater, false precision, optionality hoarding, hyper-discounting reframed as Whittle) maps directly onto this skill's anti-patterns. The biological isomorph — why "tired of this" computes the same indifference threshold in dopaminergic territory — lives in `knowledge/general/kurzban-opportunity-cost-effort.md`. Consult for rationale; do not re-read on every invocation.
 
## Scope
 
Invoke on:
 
- A project queue or project index page (e.g., `projects/_index.md`)
- A task list, kanban export, or TODO list
- An inbox or backlog with multiple pending items
- A commitment ledger (`journal/commitments-log.md` or equivalent)
- A reading list, watch list, or thesis-tracking artifact with implicit resolution dates
- A backlog of half-finished items where compounding cost is plausible
 
Do **not** invoke on:
 
- A single artifact under review (use `/red-team`, `/reviewers-map`, `/falsifiability-scan`)
- A goal or intent statement (use `/intent-check`)
- A session-end closeout (use `/commitment-ledger`)
- A clarification loop (use `/clarify-first` — Pandora's stopping rule is the relevant lens, not Whittle)
- A binary prediction (use `/calibration-loop`)
- A plan with conditional branches (use `/branch-resolve`)
 
**Refuse-to-scan condition.** If the queue has fewer than 3 items, there is no meaningful prioritization gap to surface — say so in one line and stop.
 
## The core question
 
For each item, the Whittle mental-model line:
 
> What hypothetical weekly subsidy would I need to be bribed into ignoring this for another week?
 
Pair it with a felt-urgency estimate. The gap between the two is the load-bearing signal:
 
| Pattern | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Subsidy >> felt urgency | Decay you're not feeling — the **primary flag** this skill exists to surface. |
| Felt urgency >> subsidy | Novelty-pull or urgency illusion — the **inverse flag**; a project that feels active but has no real cost-of-inaction. |
| Subsidy ≈ felt urgency | Correctly calibrated — no flag. |
 
The subsidy is **directional, not numerical**. Writing "$2,400/wk" implies precision the framework does not deliver. Use LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH or qualitative descriptors of what would decay.
 
## What to do
 
**Estimator axis (Mode 3 split).** This skill estimates two columns from different sources: Claude names *decay mechanism + subsidy* by reasoning about compounding cost from artifact content; the *user* supplies felt urgency directly via `AskUserQuestion`, because only the user knows how much an item tugs at attention. Do not impute felt urgency from project descriptions — that is confabulation, and the inverse-flag pattern breaks under it. Collect felt urgency one question per item if N ≤ 6, or top-3-by-subsidy plus 3 random items if N > 6. If the user answers "I don't know" or skips, record `unknown-urgency` and exclude that item from gap calculation — never default to LOW or MED.
 
1. **Read the queue.** Count items. If fewer than 3, refuse-to-scan.
2. **For each item, name the decay mechanism if any** — compounding cost, expiring window, relationship erosion, technical-debt interest, data going stale, calibration data lost on resolution-date pass. If no decay is real, write "none" — don't invent one to justify ranking. *(Claude estimates this column.)*
3. **Estimate subsidy directionally** (LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH) based on the named decay mechanism. No decay → LOW. *(Claude estimates this column.)*
4. **Ask the user for felt urgency per item** via `AskUserQuestion` per the spec above. Record LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / unknown-urgency. *(User supplies this column. Do not impute.)*
5. **Flag items where the two diverge** — both directions. Subsidy >> urgency is the primary flag; urgency >> subsidy is the inverse. Items marked `unknown-urgency` are not flagged but listed separately — surfacing that the user has no working-memory read on them is itself a finding.
6. **For each flag, name the implied next action in one line.** If no concrete action follows from the flag, the flag is theater — demote or drop it.
7. **Mark restatements.** If a flag duplicates something already named in a roadmap, a project's own gate text, or another artifact's explicit discipline, mark it `(restate of <source>)`. Restatements are still useful (they remind) but they aren't the primary value the scan adds.
8. **Compute restatement ratio.** Count flags marked `(restate of ...)` and divide by total flags. If the ratio is ≥ 80%, the verdict is **Restatement scan** (see Verdict states) and the deferral line must be emitted verbatim.
 
## Verdict states
 
Pick one:
 
- **Action-changing scan** — at least one flag produces a next action the user was not already going to take, or surfaces decay they did not have in working memory.
- **Restatement scan** — at least 80% of flags duplicate existing roadmap text or project-gate discipline. **Emit verbatim:** *"this scan added no novel signal beyond existing written discipline; the next run should be deferred or the skill deprecated for this artifact."* The queue may be correctly prioritized in writing, but the scan is not adding value on this artifact.
- **No gaps found** — felt urgency and cost-of-inaction track each other on every item; the queue is calibrated.
- **Queue too small** — fewer than 3 items; refuse-to-scan.
 
## Output format
 
```text
# /whittle-scan — <artifact path> — <YYYY-MM-DD>
 
## Queue
<N items>
 
## Per-item table
| Item | Decay mechanism | Subsidy/wk | Felt urgency (user) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <name> | <mechanism or "none"> | LOW/MED/HIGH | LOW/MED/HIGH/unknown | <"subsidy >> urgency" / "urgency >> subsidy" / "unknown-urgency" / "—"> |
 
## Flags (subsidy >> urgency)
1. **<item>** — Decay: <one line naming the mechanism>. Implied action: <one line>. <Mark "(restate of <source>)" if applicable>
2. ...
 
## Inverse flags (urgency >> subsidy)
1. **<item>** — Why it bids hard for attention despite low decay cost: <one line>. Implied action: <one line, usually "don't let this crowd out the primary flags">
 
## Items without a user urgency read (unknown-urgency)
<list any — surfacing the absence is itself a finding>
 
## Restatement ratio
<N restatements> / <M total flags> = <%>
 
## Verdict
**<Action-changing scan | Restatement scan | No gaps found | Queue too small>**
<one-line rationale>
 
<If Restatement scan, emit verbatim on the next line:>
> this scan added no novel signal beyond existing written discipline; the next run should be deferred or the skill deprecated for this artifact.
```
 
If the verdict is **Queue too small**, emit only:
 
```text
# /whittle-scan — <artifact path>
 
**Queue too small.** Only <N> items; no meaningful prioritization gap to surface.
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **False precision.** "Subsidy = $2,400/wk" is theater. The framework is directional. LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH or qualitative descriptors. The source note (`index-policies-for-prioritization`, "false precision" anti-pattern) makes this explicit.
- **Constructed decay.** Don't invent decay to justify ranking a task higher because you want to do it (or to procrastinate something else). Decay must be real and nameable in one line. If you cannot name the mechanism, the item's decay is LOW or none.
- **Imputing felt urgency from artifact content.** Felt urgency is the user's working-memory tug; Claude has no working memory in this sense and cannot pattern-match from project descriptions to produce it without confabulating. The Mode 3 split in "What to do" exists to enforce this — the user supplies felt urgency via `AskUserQuestion`, not Claude. If the user is unavailable, refuse-to-scan rather than synthesize the urgency column.
- **Hyper-discounting reframed as Whittle.** Telling yourself an urgent low-value task has high Whittle index because it "decays" if not addressed today is the failure mode this skill is supposed to *counter*, not reproduce. Decay must be compounding or window-expiring, not "I feel like doing this now."
- **Optionality hoarding via decay claims.** "If I don't keep this option open, I lose flexibility" is not Whittle decay — that's Real Options reasoning, a different lens. Use `/option-premium-check` for flexibility valuation; don't smuggle it into a Whittle scan.
- **Restatement laundering.** If every flag duplicates something already written in a roadmap or project-gate text, the skill's output is restating, not surfacing. Say so in the verdict; do not dress restatements as findings.
- **Ranking the whole queue.** This skill produces flags, not a full ranked list. A ranked list with no gaps highlighted reverts to artifact-shaped review and loses the cost-of-inaction axis the skill exists to surface.
- **Single-artifact application.** If the input is one artifact rather than a queue, route to `/red-team` or `/reviewers-map`. Refuse the scan; don't fake a queue from sections of a document.
- **Running it under depletion.** The Whittle reasoning is deliberation-heavy; running it after a long cognitive-demand day produces noise. Schedule the scan into a morning block. See `knowledge/general/decision-fatigue`.
- **Index fetishism.** The skill is a lens, not a solver. The synthesis note (`prioritization-architecture-synthesis`) flags the architecture as descriptive-not-buildable; the Whittle scan is one of its few buildable parts and only because the failure mode it counters (invisible per-week decay) is concretely operationalizable.
 
## When to invoke
 
- A project queue or backlog has been sitting more than a week without re-evaluation against capacity
- You're about to pick a next action and want a check on what you're skipping
- A periodic project list could be quietly accumulating items whose ignored-cost is invisible
- A calibration loop, thesis-tracking artifact, or commitment ledger has resolution dates that do not fire deadline alarms (the failure mode the dogfood pass caught)
- Before a planning block, to catch decay that "what's urgent?" thinking won't surface
- After a stretch of novelty-driven work, as a check on whether the novelty-pull was crowding out genuinely high-cost items
 
Skip when: queue has <3 items, you're reviewing a single artifact, the failure mode is clarification rather than action (use `/clarify-first`), you're auditing an intent statement (use `/intent-check`), or you're depleted (the scan needs deliberation capacity).
 
## Related
 
- `knowledge/general/index-policies-for-prioritization` — canonical four-index framework; this skill operationalizes the Whittle column. The note's anti-pattern catalogue maps directly onto the anti-patterns above.
- `knowledge/general/kurzban-opportunity-cost-effort` — biological isomorph; the felt sensation of "tired of this" computes the same indifference threshold in dopaminergic territory.
- `knowledge/general/decision-fatigue` — capacity floor; don't attempt the scan under depletion.
- `knowledge/general/prioritization-architecture-synthesis` — Layer 3 (valuation) is where this skill sits; the note flags Layers 1 and 4 as non-skill-shaped on this vault.
- `knowledge/general/dynamic-context-routing` — adjacent lens (Layer 3 routing); this skill picks *what*, routing picks *when*.
- `/option-premium-check` (Phase 2 of `projects/prioritization-skills`) — adjacent skill; flexibility valuation rather than decay valuation. Don't smuggle option-premium reasoning into a Whittle scan.
- `/commitment-ledger` — session-end closeout; pairs well with weekly `/whittle-scan` on the same ledger artifact.
- `/calibration-loop` — different axis; this skill produces flags, not predictions.
- `/clarify-first` — Pandora's stopping rule for clarification loops; orthogonal lens, not a substitute.
- `/red-team`, `/reviewers-map` — single-artifact axis; route there when the input is one document, not a queue.
- `projects/prioritization-skills/overview` — the project this skill is the first phase of; Phase 0 dogfood result is recorded there and surfaced the "decay invisible per-week" framing that the description above leans on.

ai/skills/skill-write-a-skill.title: Skill: write-a-skill
ai/skills/skill-write-a-skill.content:
Skill: write-a-skill
Authors a new skill for .claude/skills/ from scratch to the vault’s house conventions, then stops at a draft routed to the auditors rather than self-grading. The generation front-half of the owned meta-trio — which was all audit/route (skill-quality-audit, skill-trigger-audit, which-skill) with no authoring scaffold.
When to use

The user wants to create, write, build, or scaffold a new skill or slash command for .claude/skills/
Drafting a SKILL.md and unsure of the required structure, frontmatter, or house conventions
Turning a procedure repeated by hand into a reusable skill
Deciding the contract (kind, output format, degrees of freedom) for a skill not yet written

Skip when:

Auditing or fixing an existing skill — that is /skill-quality-audit (body/contract) or /skill-trigger-audit (description/firing)
Routing a request to an existing skill — /which-skill
A one-off task an existing skill already covers (run /which-skill first if unsure)

Why it exists
The owned skill-authoring loop had only the back half: instruments that grade a finished SKILL.md. Nothing generated one. The result was that new skills got drafted ad hoc — from training-data defaults that reproduce the generic Anthropic skill shape but skip this vault’s house conventions: the catalog reference note, the _index.md entry, the verbatim-copy sync, the Counters <X> closing clause, the 1024-char-in-both-units cap whose tail (the distinctness clause) is what truncates first.
The design constraint, set in adoption-plan (T3.1), is that generation hands off to the existing, more rigorous auditors rather than duplicating their checks — the auditors run decoupled from the drafting context, so a same-context self-review would repeat the drafting blind spots. So the skill authors to skill-quality-criteria and then emits handoffs to /skill-quality-audit, /skill-trigger-audit, and /which-skill (the last as a catalog-collision test) instead of inlining a verdict. Its output contract is a definition-of-done (generative), not a Sound/Tune verdict.
Built 2026-06-08 as the cleanest single addition from the Matt Pocock skills adoption pass (source: the public write-a-skill skill in mattpocock/skills); the steal is the requirements → draft → review scaffold, not its lighter checklist, since the owned auditors already exceed it on rigor.
Related

.claude/skills/write-a-skill/SKILL.md — operational definition
skill-skill-quality-audit — structural auditor this skill authors against and hands off to
skill-skill-trigger-audit — retrieval-match auditor for the new description
skill-which-skill — catalog router; used here as the post-draft collision test
skill-quality-criteria — the criteria base the draft is authored to pass
mattpocock/write-a-skill — external source of the scaffold mechanism
adoption-plan — T3.1, the backlog item this implements

Operational reference

Verbatim copy of .claude/skills/write-a-skill/SKILL.md as of 2026-06-08.

---
name: write-a-skill
description: Author a new owned skill (SKILL.md) from scratch to this vault's house conventions, then route it to the existing auditors instead of self-grading. Pins the skill's contract first (what it does, when it fires, kind — diagnostic-scan / generative / router, degrees of freedom, adjacent skills), drafts the SKILL.md to the house anatomy, writes the matching catalog reference note plus an _index.md entry, and hands off to /skill-quality-audit, /skill-trigger-audit, and /which-skill for verification. Use when you want to create, write, build, make, or scaffold a new skill or slash command for .claude/skills/, draft a SKILL.md, or turn a recurring procedure into a skill. Distinct from /skill-quality-audit and /skill-trigger-audit (which grade a finished skill) and /which-skill (which routes to an existing one) — this authors a new one. Counters median-collapse authoring: drafting a skill from training-data defaults that skip the vault's catalog wiring and the audit stage.
---
 
This skill authors a new skill for `.claude/skills/` and **stops at a draft routed to the auditors** — it does not grade its own output. The owned meta-trio is all audit/route (`/skill-quality-audit`, `/skill-trigger-audit`, `/which-skill`); this is the missing generation front-half. The discipline is **author to the criteria, then hand to the instruments that check them** — the auditors are more rigorous and run decoupled from the drafting context, so a self-audit here is both weaker and contaminated.
 
Criteria base: `knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md`. Read it before drafting — you are authoring an artifact that must pass it. House anatomy comes from the live catalog, not memory: open two or three existing SKILL.md files (e.g. `skill-quality-audit`, `which-skill`) and match their shape.
 
## How to locate the input
 
`$ARGUMENTS` is the skill to build, in any of:
 
- A one-line description of the job ("a scan that flags X before committing Y")
- A recurring procedure the user wants captured as a reusable command
- Empty → infer from the session: a procedure repeated by hand this session, or the user's last "we should make this a skill"
 
If the job isn't recoverable from the request or the session, ask one grounded question — do not invent a skill to fill the slot.
 
## Phase 1 — Pin the contract before drafting
 
Six fields the description must encode and the auditors will check. Recover each from the request or the codebase first; ask (via AskUserQuestion, grounded options only) **only** for the ones still genuinely undetermined — don't interrogate when the request already answers a field.
 
1. **What it does** — one line, the mechanism.
2. **When it fires** — the triggering situations *and the user vocabulary* that names them (artifact types, symptoms, verb-object pairs). The description is the sole trigger surface.
3. **Kind** — this picks the output contract (Phase 2): **diagnostic-scan** (returns findings + a fixed verdict set incl. a reachable clean), **generative** (returns an artifact + a definition-of-done), or **router/meta** (returns a ranked recommendation + a "none fits" escape).
4. **Degrees of freedom** — low (exact steps) where the operation is fragile, high (heuristics) where approaches legitimately vary. Choose deliberately; defaulting to prose is the defect.
5. **Adjacent skills** — read the live catalog (`ls .claude/skills/`, scan descriptions) and name the 1–3 skills closest in scope. These become the description's real distinctness clause and the overlap risk `/skill-trigger-audit` will probe.
6. **Persisted state** — does it append to or read a shared journal/log file? If so it inherits the re-read-from-disk discipline; note it.
 
Stop and confirm the contract with the user before drafting if any of {kind, scope boundary vs an adjacent skill} is still ambiguous — these are expensive to fix after the body is written.
 
## Phase 2 — Draft the SKILL.md
 
Low freedom on **structure**, high freedom on **content**. The house anatomy (omit a section only with a reason, not by reflex):
 
- **Frontmatter** — `name` lowercase-hyphenated and specific (never `helper`/`utils`); `description` written **last** (see formula below).
- **Opening role paragraph** — what the skill is and the one boundary that keeps it from bleeding into a sibling.
- **`$ARGUMENTS` resolution** — what the input can be and a no-guess fallback, *if* the skill takes input.
- **The procedure** — bounded counts ("5 questions", not "some"), explicit stop conditions, and validation/feedback loops on quality-critical steps.
- **`## Output format`** — a fenced template matching the kind's contract from Phase 1.
- **`## Anti-patterns`** — the failure modes a runner will actually hit, including self-exemption where relevant.
- **`## When to invoke`** + a **Do not invoke for** list routing the near-misses to their owning skills.
- **`## Related`** — sibling skills (`/name`) and the backing concept note.
 
Keep the body <500 lines (the catalog median is ~145); references one level deep. One default with an escape hatch, never a menu of approaches. No time-sensitive claims in the body unless dated — a skill body is read for months.
 
**Description formula** (write last, then measure): sentence 1 = what it does · middle = the contract and triggers in user vocabulary · `Use when …` (pushy — list contexts it should fire on even if not explicitly asked) · `Distinct from /X …` boundary against the real adjacent skills from Phase 1 · closing `Counters <failure mode>.` Keep **≤1024 in both characters and bytes** (the cap's unit is unverified; house keeps both safe). The distinctness clause lands in the tail, exactly where truncation bites — so staying under the cap is what keeps it visible to the router.
 
## Phase 3 — Wire the catalog
 
House conventions a generic generator omits — a SKILL.md alone is half-installed:
 
- **Catalog reference note** at `knowledge/ai/skills/skill-<name>.md` (the prefix stacks: `skill-` + the full skill name). Frontmatter per `knowledge-conventions.md`; sections: a one-line summary, **When to use**, **Why it exists** (the failure mode it counters), **Related**, and an **Operational reference** holding a *verbatim* fenced copy of the SKILL.md. This copy must be re-synced on every later body edit — flag that to the user.
- **`_index.md` entry** — add `[[skill-<name>]]` under the right section of `knowledge/ai/skills/_index.md` with a one-line hook.
 
## Phase 4 — Route to the auditors (do not self-grade)
 
Emit handoffs; do not run the audits inline.
 
- `/skill-quality-audit <name>` — structure, contract, executability, catalog sync.
- `/skill-trigger-audit <name>` — will it fire on its target queries; overlap with the adjacent skills.
- `/which-skill "<the job>"` — collision test: does the catalog now surface the new skill, or an existing one? A surfaced existing skill means the new one may be redundant.
 
## Output format
 
A definition-of-done, not a verdict (this skill is generative):
 
```text
# New skill — <name>
 
## Contract
what: <one line> | when: <triggers> | kind: <scan|generative|router>
freedom: <low|high, where> | adjacent: </a, /b> | state: <none|appends to X>
 
## Files created
- .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
- knowledge/ai/skills/skill-<name>.md (with verbatim operational copy)
- knowledge/ai/skills/_index.md — entry under "<section>"
 
## Handoffs (run before publishing)
- /skill-quality-audit <name>
- /skill-trigger-audit <name>
- /which-skill "<job>"
 
## Done when
all three handoffs return clean (Sound · Trigger-clean · no collision); reference-note copy matches the SKILL.md
```
 
## Anti-patterns
 
- **Self-grading.** Don't inline the audit — emit handoffs. The decoupled auditors are the point; a same-context self-review repeats the drafting blind spots.
- **Skipping the catalog wiring.** The reference note and index entry are house conventions; a lone SKILL.md is half-installed and goes uncited.
- **Inventing a distinctness clause.** The `Distinct from /X` boundary must name a real adjacent skill from the live catalog — not a plausible-sounding one. If you can't name one, the skill may not be distinct enough to exist.
- **Drafting before the contract is pinned.** Kind drives the output contract; deciding it after the body is written means a reauthor, not an edit.
- **A menu of approaches in the body.** One default plus an escape hatch — offering many is a named anti-pattern in the criteria note.
- **Over-cap description.** Measure chars and bytes; the routing tail is what gets cut first.
- **Generating on routine.** If the job is a one-off, or `/which-skill` shows an existing skill already covers it, say so and stop — don't manufacture a skill.
 
## When to invoke
 
- The user wants to create, write, build, or scaffold a new skill or slash command for `.claude/skills/`
- Drafting a `SKILL.md` and unsure of the required structure, frontmatter, or house conventions
- Turning a procedure repeated by hand into a reusable skill
- Deciding the contract (kind, output format, degrees of freedom) for a skill not yet written
 
Do **not** invoke for:
 
- Auditing or fixing an *existing* skill — `/skill-quality-audit` (body/contract), `/skill-trigger-audit` (description/firing)
- Routing a request to an existing skill — `/which-skill`
- A one-off task an existing skill already covers (run `/which-skill` first if unsure)
- Editing this vault's notes, rules, or non-skill prompts
 
## Related
 
- `/skill-quality-audit` — the structural auditor this skill hands off to (and authors against)
- `/skill-trigger-audit` — the retrieval-match auditor for the new description
- `/which-skill` — catalog router; used here as the post-draft collision test
- `knowledge/ai/skill-quality-criteria.md` — the criteria base you are authoring to pass
- `knowledge/ai/skills/_index.md` — the catalog this skill registers the new skill into

ai/spec-driven-development-operating-mod.title: Spec-Driven Development and the Accretive Loop as One Operating Model
ai/spec-driven-development-operating-mod.content:
Spec-Driven Development and the Accretive Loop as One Operating Model
Tool specifics verified 2026-09-04 against Spec Kit’s evolving-specs guide, Kiro’s specs and correctness docs, and the OpenSpec README, concepts and existing-projects docs. The combined model is original to this vault.
accretive-spec-development positions the loop beside spec-driven development (SDD) as a different mode: agree-then-build versus build-then-harvest. Under both, every clause ends up affirmed twice by a human — once as a requirement (this is what we want) and once as a check (this is how we would know). The models differ in which affirmation comes first and which one gates the build. This note gives the rule for that, the region transitions that follow from it, and how the loop’s artifacts sit inside a tool’s layout without a second set of books. It is also the vault’s SDD note: it carries only the SDD mechanics the combination needs, not a tool comparison. The runnable method built on this reasoning is clause-loop, which also carries it to prototypes, specifications and documentation and which is normative — where this note and it differ, it wins; this note stays the why.
One shape, two orders
The three verified tools share a core: specify or propose → design or plan → tasks → implement. Spec Kit and OpenSpec wrap it with a clarify or explore step in front and a consistency or verify step behind, and OpenSpec archives at the end. Spec Kit runs it as /speckit.specify, /speckit.clarify, /speckit.plan, /speckit.tasks, /speckit.analyze, /speckit.implement, /speckit.converge; Kiro as requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md; OpenSpec as /opsx:explore, /opsx:propose, /opsx:apply, /opsx:archive, with /opsx:verify (“check implementation matches specs”) optional in its expanded profile. The loop’s shape is intent plus falsifier → probe → confront → harvest → freeze → consolidate.
What differs:

Which affirmation gates the build. SDD gates on the requirement — “Agree before you build”, in OpenSpec’s words. The loop gates on the check: it pre-registers a falsifier, builds, and affirms the harvested clause afterwards.
What the human authors upstream. A requirement with WHEN/THEN scenarios bounds many failure directions; one falsifier line bounds one. Both are agent-drafted otherwise, so this is the only place independence enters — which is why the loop asks the human to own the falsifier at every outcome boundary, not to type one per task.
A design gate. SDD puts a design.md or plan.md in front of the human before the build. The loop has no design step: “how” is the agent’s probe choice, seen first at Confront.
Enforcement point. SDD checks its artifacts against each other before implementation (/speckit.analyze across spec, plan and tasks). The loop enforces after, in CI, through the contract guard on a frozen region’s manifest.
Granularity. A change per SDD cycle; a clause per loop.

What does not differ is accumulation or brownfield fit. OpenSpec’s openspec/specs/ “starts nearly empty and accumulates”; “you write specs only for what you’re about to change”; “the spec for auth/ becomes thorough only after you’ve made several auth changes”. That is accretion at change granularity — a design claim from the tool’s own docs; no non-vendor evidence on brownfield behaviour is cited here. The loop is accretion at clause granularity with an executable pin. So “SDD for frozen regions, the loop for open ones” is the wrong cut: OpenSpec runs on regions that have no spec yet by design, and the loop already sends work in regions without a contract to a plan when a heuristic fires. Region state is an input to the rule below, not the boundary between the models.
The operating rule
Which affirmation gates the build. The requirement gates it — agree, then build — when a planning heuristic fires on the envelope the probe declares: uncertainty about the approach, rework in the region, growth past the last three building loops, cross-domain coordination with at least one region under contract, or a contract change that would modify or retire a wanted clause in a region under contract. Separately, a hard gate — an irreversibility-list item, a production or shared-environment write, a destructive operation, a credential, an externally visible action, or an edit to a frozen region’s verification surface — stops for the human’s permission on that action whichever affirmation is gating, and a bare surface edit needs a permit, not a proposal. Otherwise the check gates it — build, harvest, then promote. The heuristics and gates are defined normatively in clause-loop rule 4; this note only places them. The surface gate is the pre-build half of test-tamper protection; a code-only probe that breaks a listed check without editing its surface is caught after the fact by the execution guard (the failing row below). Under this rule, “spec is the source of truth, code is a regenerable artifact” (writing-loops-not-prompts) is true of a region under contract and false of a region that is harvesting, where the running artifact is the truth and every clause is provisional.
Three honest notes on the rule. Its output drifts: as regions go under contract, the cross-domain heuristic and the surface gate fire more often, and a mature project is requirement-first by construction — the loop is the on-ramp, not the steady state. And the growth heuristic has a cold start: after three trivial probes, any real one is longer than the previous three combined. Read it against the last three probes that built something. And the model has not been run: what would show the rule wrong is the heuristics or the gates firing on most probes within the first month, so harvesting never happens, or DECISIONS.log going unwritten after a few sessions.
Region states and transitions
A region is the unit a manifest covers: a domain folder under openspec/specs/ (a feature directory in Spec Kit). An intent that spans two folders is two regions and hits the cross-domain heuristic once either is under contract. Three states:

open — no clauses.
harvesting — the loop is running; clauses are observed or wanted; checks may well run in CI, but no manifest guards them.
under contract — frozen: every clause wanted and verified, a manifest written from the pins naming clauses, checks and the verification surface, a contract test exported to consumers — other agents, future sessions, downstream services.

Rows two to four below are the phases of a requirement-first change; the region keeps its state while the change runs.



























































From → toTriggerWhat gets writtenAffirmationopen → harvestinga Ground constraint written into the region, or the first Close that touches it; on brownfield the first probe harvests observed clauses into the deltathe region spec, via ground or the merged deltathe check, at promotionharvesting → proposala heuristic fires inside Probe; the agent refuses to build and returns itchanges/<name>/proposal.md, design.md, a delta spec, tasks.md with each row as intent plus falsifierthe requirement; adversarial review (/red-team) of the proposalproposal → applyingdelta agreed, gate passednothing new: each task runs Probe and Decide, inheriting the change’s falsifier unless it introduces a new assumption, trade-off or visible behaviour, and harvest pins the delta’s scenarios to check idsper task — falsifier before, check and evidence after; acceptance was given at agreementapplying → archivedevery scenario has a pinned check that rejects a mutant for a named reason; a clause-level fulfilment check (/intent-fulfilment-check) reports nothing unaddressed or substitutedthe archive folder; the delta merged into specs/<region>/spec.md with pins carried; consolidate when due. The manifest is updated only if the region was under contract before the change (a re-freeze, with a decisions entry); otherwise the region returns to harvesting with the change’s clauses wanted and freeze-eligibleat archive — the record of what was agreed, which the decisions log does not keepharvesting → under contractfreeze: every clause wanted and currently verified in the freeze run, no open exceptionmanifest written from the pins, contract-test export, decisions entry through the approval boundaryat freezeunder contract → proposalthe cross-domain heuristic, or any intent whose delta would modify a listed clause; a bare surface edit takes a permit insteadas the second rowthe requirementunder contract → harvestingunfreeze: decisions entry, consumers toldmanifest removedthe requirementany → failing clausea pinned check failsverification failing, acceptance unchanged; under contract the build fails until the artifact is fixed or the clause is changed through a proposal; expiring exceptions exist only while harvestingnone — it is a stop
Two rows need a note. A requirement-first change does not suspend the loop: inside it, every task is intent plus falsifier, and the mutant gate still runs before a scenario counts as pinned. And retiring is not failing. A failing clause’s check fails; a retired requirement’s check still passes, so retirement is a deliberate decision at archive — a retire entry saying whether the behaviour stays and whether the check stays as characterization coverage — rather than an automatic deletion, and a check is deleted only when its purpose is obsolete. The first is clause-loop rules 1, 2 and 4; the second is rule 3.
Artifacts: one layout, three additions
The rule that prevents a second set of books: the region’s spec file is specs/<region>/spec.md and there is no other. The loop’s files map onto the tool’s layout, inside its root; nothing lives beside it. Three additions carry the loop’s guarantees, because no verified tool has them in this form:

The pin — under each #### Scenario:, one trailing line with a stable id, acceptance, oracle type, check id, birth change and evidence. Whether OpenSpec’s tooling tolerates the extra line is unverified.
The manifest written from the pins, the contract guard and the contract-test export — the CI mechanism behind “under contract”.
DECISIONS.log — nine kinds, defined in clause-loop, written by the agent from the human’s decisions.
