Reference layout, OpenSpec-shaped; + marks the additions:
openspec/
  GROUND.md                      # + context, constraints, preferences, irreversibility list, envelope defaults, approval boundary
  DECISIONS.log                  # + append-only; nine kinds; agent-written
  specs/<region>/spec.md         # wanted clauses only; each scenario carries a Pin line: id, acceptance, oracle, check, evidence
  specs/<region>/manifest        # + written from the pins: clause ids, check ids, verification surface; the contract guard reads it
  changes/<name>/
    proposal.md                  # check-first change: intent + falsifier · requirement-first: why, what, red-team result
    design.md                    # requirement-first changes only: how
    specs/<region>/spec.md       # delta ADDED / MODIFIED / RETIRED; observed clauses live here until promoted
    tasks.md                     # requirement-first changes only; each row names its falsifier as inherited or its own
  changes/archive/<date>-<name>/
Spec Kit is feature-keyed (specs/<feature>/spec.md). Treat a feature directory as a region when the feature is one. When a feature spans regions, the per-feature directories stay as the historical record the guide wants and the region file is consolidated from them; the two will diverge, and the region file wins.
The vault’s own skill chain is this pipeline without the name: to-prd is specify or propose, plan-options is plan or design, task-decompose is tasks with a falsifiable done-criterion per row, the loops are implement, intent-fulfilment-check is converge’s completion assessment at intent level, and pr-contract is the archive-time record.
Which Spec Kit persistence model, when
Spec Kit’s guide names three ways to keep specs/ aligned with code. The combined model uses two of them, by phase, and declines the third:

Flow-back while harvesting. The guide lets “the first useful edit … happen wherever the insight lands” and then realigns the artifact set, with /speckit.analyze to check for gaps; its discipline is “do not leave a lower-level change in tasks.md or code if spec.md still says something different and the spec is meant to remain trustworthy”. An observed clause is that first edit, captured in the artifact closest to the work. The loop adds what the guide does not have: the clause is not trustworthy until promoted, and promotion needs the pin, the locked check and the mutant gate — this vault’s additions, not the guide’s.
Living spec under contract. “Revise the existing spec.md first. Then regenerate or manually revise downstream artifacts so they match”, with /speckit.analyze before implementation resumes and /speckit.converge to assess completion. A change to a region under contract starts in the delta spec, which is this model.
Flow-forward, declined. “Each feature directory should remain a historical record” — a new directory per follow-up change. That conflicts with one spec file per region; the model keeps the per-change record in the archive folder instead, which is OpenSpec’s mechanism, not Spec Kit’s.

The oracle bridge
Kiro extracts properties from EARS-formatted requirements during design, before implementation, and calls the result “a clear, traceable link between your requirements and the tests that validate them”. The loop builds the same link in the opposite order: probe, then check, then clause. In both, the agent authors the check, so independence comes only from what the human authored upstream — a requirement in one direction, a falsifier in the other, and the requirement reaches further. That is oracle-problem-verification’s circular-spec row stated as a workflow rule.
The completeness rule that makes either order acceptable: a clause is complete only when it has both a requirement form and a pinned check shown to reject a mutant for a named reason, whichever was born first. Requirement-first clauses have the form and must earn the pin; harvested clauses have the pin and must earn the form before promotion.
Kiro’s on-failure choice — fix the implementation, adjust the tests, or refine the requirements — maps onto the loop’s rules one to one: fixing code is free inside the loop; adjusting a test is an edit to a locked check and needs the human’s permission — through the approval boundary once the region is under contract; refining a requirement is a change to a wanted clause and needs a decision, or a proposal if the region is under contract. The mutant gate is the addition: Kiro’s docs name neither it nor the test library that runs the properties.
Two critique gates
A falsifier is a pre-registration — how we would know it is not working — not a critique. The critique asks whether this is the wrong thing to build, and it sits where the cost is:

Before the build, red-team on proposal.md and design.md, because a requirement-first change is expensive by definition. The output has a destination: the strongest objection becomes a #### Scenario: in the delta or a rejection in DECISIONS.log. A red team whose findings go nowhere is theatre.
After the probe, Confront: the human reacts to the running artifact and to the not-exercised list, after committing to what pass and fail look like — pre-registered criteria, predict-then-compare. Cheap probe, cheap gate. OpenSpec’s optional /opsx:verify is the tool slot for this; the loop makes it mandatory.

Failure modes of running both

Double bookkeeping. A SPEC.md beside openspec/specs/. The one-file-per-region rule exists for this.
Theatrical proposal. A proposal structured to pass the gate that anchors nothing. Run a four-axis intent audit (intent-check) on the SHALL lines; a proposal with no falsifiable scenario is rejected, not improved.
Independence collapse. The agent writes the proposal, the design, the tasks and the properties, and the human only approves. The floor is a human-owned falsifier at every outcome boundary — the change’s intent, and any task that introduces a new assumption, trade-off or visible behaviour — with the other tasks inheriting it and saying so; below that, every check encodes the agent’s reading of the intent — intent-engineering-discipline’s “theatrical spec” with tests attached.
Harvest-only SDD. Building on a region under contract and back-filling a proposal from the harvest. The surface gate stops it before the build when the envelope names the edit; the surface guard fails CI when it does not, and the execution guard when a listed check breaks without its surface being touched.
Converge as the gap oracle. Letting /speckit.converge’s generated tasks replace the not-exercised list removes the human falsifier from failure-mode coverage — the agent then names both the gap and its fix.
Consolidate and archive drifting. An archive-merge can break pins the same way a consolidate rewrite can. Re-point any pin the rewrite breaks — the consolidate rule — applies to both.
Undefined regions. The cross-domain heuristic, the manifest and the spec file are all keyed on the region. If auth/ is one region to one person and three to another, the heuristic fires on everything. Fix the folder taxonomy in Ground.
Retirement handled as failure, or a rejected clause’s check deleted by reflex. A passing check silently kept, or useful characterization coverage thrown away; see the transition table.
Too heavy for one person. Per clause: a pin, an evidence record, a decision; per proposal: a red team; plus the contract guard. The public surface is four actions and a packet the human answers in chat, which is the thinning already applied. The likeliest failure is not a bookkeeping error but dropping the model. If it must be thinned further, keep the pin, the evidence rule and the manifest and relax the rest first.

When not to combine

Multi-team contracts before anything has frozen: SDD alone.
Regenerate-from-spec practice, where code is rebuilt from the spec rather than edited: harvest is idle; SDD plus the mutant gate.
Work where the first probe is itself the expensive part: plan-first, as the loop already says.
Regulated audit trails: permit and freeze lines carry an approval reference from the boundary, but the log is agent-written and the boundary is whatever the repo host provides; add a formal approval step at archive.
Parallel agents or session handoff: a plan file is the thread and “no task list” stops holding.

ai/task-decomposition-for-ai-plans.title: Task Decomposition for AI Plans
ai/task-decomposition-for-ai-plans.content:
Task Decomposition for AI Plans
The cognitive-science research on task decomposition — why humans intuitively break large tasks into smaller subtasks — has direct analogs in LLM and agent execution. This note bridges the research basis to the design problem: when should a plan or prompt be split into multiple, what structural signals indicate a split is overdue, and when does decomposing actually hurt.
This is the plan-structure sibling to information-density-for-llm-prompts (which addresses density inside a single prompt) and the executor-side sibling to cognitive-burden-of-ai-use (which addresses load on the human reviewer). As of 2026-05.
Why this matters
Whether the executor is a human, an LLM agent, or a Claude Code session, a plan that is too large for it fails in characteristic ways: attention drift on later steps, confabulated state-carry (earlier decisions mis-recalled by later steps), decision branches that flatten into one arbitrary path, and verification debt that accumulates until the final output is unreviewable. A plan that is too small fails differently: switching overhead, lost context across handoffs, and dilution of the larger “why.”
Choosing plan size is a design decision, not a stylistic preference. The choice is load-bearing for whether the executor can hold the plan and whether the reviewer can verify the output.
Three research pillars
The cognitive-science literature on task decomposition rests on three findings, each pointing at a different mechanism. The citations supplied as starting material are listed in the Sources section below with verification status; the mechanism each names is the load-bearing content here, not the specific citation.
1. Resource-rational decomposition — minimize planning runtime
Humans decompose tasks to reduce the computational cost of planning, not because larger plans are intrinsically harder, but because the cost of figuring out what to do next dominates as plan size grows. Decomposition trades one expensive global planning step for several cheaper local ones (Correa et al., 2020 / 2023).
LLM analog. Long context dilutes attention (position bias / lost-in-the-middle); state-carry across many concerns hits effective working-memory limits even when the nominal context window is large. A 200K-token model can still execute a 4K plan poorly if the plan demands holding three independent mental models simultaneously. The binding constraint is concurrent concerns, not token count.
2. Small victories — early wins build verification anchors
In behavioral-economics framings of motivation, ordering subtasks from easiest to hardest produces early “small victories” that build momentum and reduce the probability of abandonment (Brown & Lahey, 2014 — the specific effect is over task size, smallest-to-largest, not over difficulty per se). For human executors this is largely a motivation effect.
LLM analog. No motivation curve, but a structurally equivalent design move: each verification checkpoint converts a “maybe-correct” intermediate state into a confirmed-correct anchor. A 5-step plan executed sequentially with verification at each step produces 5 anchors, any of which can be a recovery point if later steps fail. The same work compressed into one monolithic prompt produces a single output whose correctness is all-or-nothing. The mechanism differs (anchor stability vs. motivation), but the design move (verification at every subgoal) is identical.
The easiest-to-hardest ordering itself matters less for LLMs (no fatigue curve) and more for information dependency — earliest subtasks should establish the state later subtasks depend on, so each step can be specified concretely rather than in terms of “whatever the previous step decides.”
3. Concrete subgoals — falsifiable done-states build self-efficacy
In goal-setting theory, abstract long-term goals feel distant and intimidating; concrete subgoals provide proximal markers of accomplishment, building self-efficacy and reducing procrastination (Locke & Latham, 1990, on goal-setting; Bandura, 1977, on self-efficacy). Each subgoal needs a clear done-state to function as a marker.
LLM analog. Each subtask in a plan must have a falsifiable done-state — what observation indicates this step succeeded? Vague subtasks (“refactor for clarity,” “improve error handling”) fail this test; concrete subtasks (“rename X to Y across files A, B, C; tests still pass”) pass it. This is the direct bridge to falsifiability-claim-fingerprints: a well-decomposed plan is a sequence of operationalized done-states.
The self-efficacy mechanism has no LLM analog (no belief-in-own-ability variable), but the operationalization requirement is sharper for LLMs: an agent given a vague subtask will execute against its training-data prior for that phrase rather than against your actual intent.
Structural signals — when a plan needs splitting
The right plan size is not a length measure. A 300-line plan touching one concern often executes better than a 60-line plan spanning three. The load-bearing signals are structural.
Signal 1 — Concern count
Number of distinct mental models the executor must hold simultaneously. Auth + DB schema + frontend routing = three concerns. Pure CSS work on one component = one concern.
Threshold heuristic. More than two simultaneous concerns is a split candidate. Each additional concern multiplies the state the executor must keep coherent across the plan.
Signal 2 — State-carry depth
How far back later steps reference earlier decisions. A plan where step 10 must recall a naming choice made in step 1 has deep state-carry; a plan where each step is locally complete has shallow state-carry.
Threshold heuristic. If any step requires verbatim recall of a decision made more than ~3 steps earlier, the state-carry is too long. Either re-state the decision at the point of use, or split before the recall.
Signal 3 — Decision branches
If/then forks that can’t be resolved up front. “If the existing migration works, modify it; otherwise rewrite” is a branch the executor cannot collapse without doing the check first.
Threshold heuristic. Each unresolved branch is its own plan. A plan with N independent branch-points is structurally 2^N plans masquerading as one. Three valid resolutions, in order of preference: (a) resolve the branch up front before issuing the plan; (b) split into separate plans at the branch point; (c) express as an implementation intention — a deterministic if-then with an observable trigger and a named response. Reach for (c) only when the trigger genuinely cannot be evaluated up front and the two downstream paths are similar enough in scope that splitting would duplicate setup; otherwise (a) and (b) are the defaults. “We’ll figure it out when we get there” is none of the three.
Signal 4 — Verification seams
Places where a human reviewer would want to pause and confirm before proceeding — typically after a schema change, before a destructive operation, or where downstream steps depend on a non-obvious intermediate state.
Threshold heuristic. Every verification seam is a natural split candidate. If you’d want to manually check before continuing, the executor should also stop and report there.
Signal 5 — Reversibility boundary
Destructive or irreversible operations are natural stopping points. Putting speculative work and destructive work in the same plan is the failure mode where exploratory edits accidentally land in production state.
Threshold heuristic. Never put a destructive step after speculative work in the same plan. Split immediately before the destructive step, with explicit confirmation as the first action of the next plan.
The split-or-consolidate heuristic
Combining the signals:

Concern count > 2 and state-carry shallow across concerns → split by concern boundary
Decision branches present and branching decision not resolvable up front → split per branch
Verification seam between unrelated subtasks → split at the seam
Destructive step preceded by speculative work → split before the destructive step

Conversely, do not split when:

State-carry is high across the candidate boundary — the split forces re-establishing context, paying the setup cost twice
Tight coupling — step B is only meaningful given step A’s specific output, and that output cannot be summarized without losing the structure step B operates on
One verification covers all steps — splitting adds overhead without buying anchor stability
Plan is short enough that switching cost dominates coherence cost — for plans under ~5 steps with one concern, monolithic execution is usually correct

Over-decomposition — the symmetric failure mode
The research on small victories and concrete subgoals creates a one-directional bias in popular advice (“always break it down further”). The symmetric failure mode is real: tiny subtasks accumulate switching overhead, dilute the larger goal, and produce a sequence of locally-correct outputs that don’t compose into the intended whole.
The motivational-psychology research itself contains the counter: Höchli, Brügger & Messner (2018) argue that superordinate goals — abstract, identity-based, long-horizon — are crucial motivators alongside concrete subgoals. Over-focus on subgoal granularity at the expense of the larger purpose loses motivational coherence, complicating the goal-setting-theory framing in pillar 3.
Signs of over-decomposition:

Each subtask requires re-stating the same shared context (high duplication across plans)
Plans become outlines of outlines — the unit of execution is smaller than the unit of decision-making
The reviewer can’t tell from the subtask whether it’s on-strategy without reconstructing the larger plan
Total token cost (including re-setup) exceeds the original monolithic plan

The corrective: subtasks should be sized to the unit at which a decision changes the plan. If two adjacent subtasks always succeed or fail together, they’re one subtask.
Goal-architecture safeguards — equifinality and cross-context compensation
The five signals above address plan structure. Two additional failure modes emerge from how the goal architecture is layered — and a well-split plan can still fail if these safeguards are missing. The vocabulary comes from Höchli, Brügger & Messner (2018), whose paper complicates the pure-subgoals story from pillar 3 in two specific ways.
Equifinality — multiple paths to the same end
A superordinate goal (“the migration is safe in production”) admits many subordinate paths (canary rollout, blue/green, dual-write, …). When the current subordinate path fails or hits an unexpected blocker, equifinality is the property that lets the planner pivot to an alternative path without abandoning the goal. The superordinate goal acts as an anchor; the subordinate paths are interchangeable means.
A plan structured only as a sequence of subordinate steps loses this property silently: when step 5 blocks, the plan looks dead because no alternative is visible. The fix is stating the superordinate purpose at each split point so the executor (or the planner on resume) can navigate to an alternative path without rebuilding the goal-architecture from scratch.
The applied move: at each split boundary, the next plan’s preamble names the superordinate purpose it serves, not just the local subordinate task. “Plan B: deploy the migration” is fragile; “Plan B: deploy the migration as one path toward making the migration safe in production; if blocked, the alternative paths are dual-write rollout or canary” preserves equifinality at the boundary.
Cross-context compensation — local victories licensing later slack
In human self-regulation, pure-subgoal architectures produce a known failure mode: completing a hard subordinate task licenses reduced effort on subsequent tasks (“I had a productive morning, so I can disengage this afternoon”). The local victory is the entire goal; cumulative progress decouples from the superordinate purpose.
LLMs have no motivation curve, but the structural analog is real and applies to mixed human + AI execution: a plan that surfaces only subordinate steps can be executed locally-correctly while drifting from the original purpose. Each step’s done-state is met; the cumulative output doesn’t add up to the superordinate intent. The human reviewer accepts each subtask’s output and the drift accumulates unobserved.
The corrective is the same as for equifinality: maintain visible superordinate purpose alongside subordinate steps. At verification seams, the question is not just “did this step succeed?” but “is this step contributing to the superordinate goal, or is it now optimizing for something else?” Without the second question, cross-context drift is invisible.
The composite design move
Both safeguards point to the same architectural principle: the goal architecture should be dual-layered, not single-layered. Subordinate steps without superordinate anchoring are vulnerable to both failure modes; superordinate goals without subordinate operationalization are vulnerable to procrastination and abstract paralysis. The pair is the design unit.
For plans about to be issued to an agent: name the superordinate purpose in the preamble and refer back to it at verification seams and split boundaries. For plans that span sessions or hand off across agents, the superordinate statement is what survives the handoff; without it, each new session reconstructs the local plan and loses the larger purpose.
Audit template — plan-split scan
This template operationalizes the structural signals as a checklist. Use as a prompt for the model to audit a draft plan, or as a manual checklist before issuing a plan to an agent.
Audit the following plan for split-or-consolidate signals.

For each finding, give: (a) which signal, (b) location (step number or
quoted span), (c) one-line reason, (d) recommended action: split at
boundary X (naming the bottleneck), consolidate steps Y-Z, resolve
branch up front, convert to implementation intention, lift setup, or
leave alone.

Structural signals:
1. Concern count — more than two distinct mental models held
   simultaneously.
2. State-carry depth — later steps requiring verbatim recall of a
   decision made more than ~3 steps earlier.
3. Decision branches — if/then forks that cannot be resolved before
   the executor starts.
4. Verification seams — points where a human would pause to check
   before continuing.
5. Reversibility boundary — destructive step preceded by speculative
   or exploratory work in the same plan.

Also check for the symmetric failure (over-decomposition):
- Are adjacent subtasks always succeed-or-fail together? → consolidate.
- Does each subtask re-state the same shared context? → consolidate.
- Is the subtask smaller than the unit at which a decision changes
  the plan? → consolidate.

Cap at 8 findings. Rank by severity. Note explicitly what you checked
and didn't find. Output a single split-or-consolidate verdict plus
recommended split points.

Plan:
[paste]

This template was the seed of the /plan-split-scan slash command, which now lives at .claude/skills/plan-split-scan/. The slash command is the canonical operational form (executor declaration, severity calibration, refuse-to-scan threshold, output format); this template remains here as the research-level statement of the same audit, useful for understanding why the signals are what they are without invoking the skill.
Tradeoffs and context-dependence

Plan size is executor-dependent. A senior developer with deep project context can execute a larger plan than a fresh agent. A vault-aware Claude Code session can execute a larger plan than a stateless API call. The right size shifts with the executor; a plan-split-scan should ideally take executor capacity as input rather than applying a fixed threshold.
The signals are heuristic, not measured. “Concern count > 2” and “state-carry > 3 steps” are operational rules of thumb extracted from prompt-engineering practice, not numbers backed by an experiment on AI plan execution. Treat them as starting calibration; adjust against your own failure data.
The verification-seam signal overlaps with falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — both name the same move (each subtask has a quotable done-state) from different angles. Verification seam is the plan-structure framing; falsifiability is the claim-shape framing.

What this doesn’t cover

Cross-session plan continuity — how to hand off a long plan across multiple sessions or agents. The commitments-log infrastructure is the persistence side; the plan-decomposition side of session handoff is unaddressed here.
Plan generation by AI itself. This note assumes the plan exists. An LLM-drafted plan has its own failure modes — over-decomposition is more common in AI-generated plans than human-generated ones, in informal observation. A separate analysis of AI plan-drafting would be its own note.
Quantitative measurement of plan-execution success. The signals here predict difficulty; they don’t predict success rate. A study correlating structural-signal scores with execution success would convert this from heuristic to empirical.

Counterargument
The decomposition framing risks an availability-driven over-application. Many short, simple plans do not need a split scan; running the audit on them is itself a form of over-decomposition. The honest position:

For plans under ~5 steps with one concern, default to monolithic execution.
For plans with any destructive operation, irreversible step, or unresolved branch, always scan regardless of length.
For long, single-concern plans, the bottleneck is usually density (position bias, compression trap), not decomposition.

The plan-split scan is most useful at the medium-complexity layer where neither default applies — multi-concern plans of 5-20 steps with mixed reversibility. This is plausibly where agent failures concentrate in informal observation, but the distribution has not been measured, so the leverage is conjectural — the tool is not universal.
Related

Sources
Verified 2026-05-12. The three citations supplied as starting material were each checked against primary literature; one (the original Höchli attribution on pillar 3) was found to be misattributed and has been corrected — see note below.

Correa, C. G. et al. (2023) — Humans decompose tasks by trading off utility and computational cost — PLOS Computational Biology, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011087. Canonical journal version of the same line of work; received Oct 2022, published Apr 2023 (which likely explains the “2022” date in some secondary summaries).
Brown, A. L. & Lahey, J. N. (2014) — Small Victories: Creating Intrinsic Motivation in Savings and Debt Reduction — NBER Working Paper #20125, link. Later published as Brown & Lahey (2015), Journal of Marketing Research. The specific effect: faster completion when sub-parts are arranged smallest-to-largest by size — an effect study participants did not spontaneously prefer when offered the choice.
Locke, E. A. & Latham, G. P. (1990) — A Theory of Goal Setting and Task Performance — Prentice Hall. Canonical goal-setting source for the concrete-subgoals → performance claim in pillar 3. See also Locke & Latham (2002), American Psychologist, for the 35-year review.

Cited in the over-decomposition section as a counter to pillar 3: argues superordinate (abstract, identity-based) goals are also crucial motivators, complicating the pure concrete-subgoals story. Note: an earlier draft of this note attributed pillar 3 to Höchli et al.; that was incorrect — the paper complicates rather than supports the pillar-3 framing.

ai/temporal-logic-for-agent-verification.title: Temporal Logic for Agent Runtime Verification
ai/temporal-logic-for-agent-verification.content:
Temporal Logic for Agent Runtime Verification
Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) is a modal logic over linear sequences of states, introduced by Amir Pnueli in 1977 for reasoning about reactive systems. Its relevance to AI agents is direct: an agent’s execution is a sequence of states and effects, and many of the safety / correctness properties we care about are temporal — “always X”, “if X happens then eventually Y”, “no Z until W”. LTL gives those properties a precise, machine-checkable form.
This note covers what LTL can and cannot do for agent supervision, with concrete examples for a coding agent. It is not an introduction to LTL as a logic; it is a decision aid for when reaching for the formalism is worth the cost.
The operators (just enough)
LTL extends propositional logic with operators over future states in an execution trace — the sequence of states or actions the agent moves through:



































OperatorReadingHolds iff◯ φ”Next”φ holds in the immediate next stateφ U ψ”Until”φ holds in every state until ψ becomes true (and ψ must eventually become true)□ φ”Globally” / “Always”φ holds in every state of the trace◇ φ”Eventually”φ holds in some future state◇≤k φ”Bounded eventually”φ holds within k steps
A constraint is satisfied by a trace iff the trace makes the LTL formula true.
What kinds of agent properties become LTL formulas
The natural fit is trace-level safety and liveness properties — properties that quantify over the sequence of actions or observable states, not over the content of generated text.
Concrete coding-agent examples:

Globally safety. “The agent never writes outside the project directory.”
□ (¬write_outside_workspace)
Globally with implication. “Every install of a third-party dependency is preceded by a vulnerability-database check.”
□ (install_dep → vuln_check_was_run_first)
Until. “No commit until all tests pass.”
¬commit U all_tests_pass
Bounded eventually. “After a tool error, a recovery action occurs within 3 steps.”
□ (tool_error → ◇≤3 recovery_action)
Mutual exclusion / sequencing. “Read-only mode persists until the human approves write capability.”
read_only U human_approves_write

The structural test for “is this an LTL property”: you can describe it as a constraint on the sequence of events without needing to evaluate the content of any natural-language artifact in the sequence.
Runtime verification (RV)
The agent is non-deterministic and unbounded; you cannot verify the entire state space. So LTL’s most useful realisation for AI agents is not offline model-checking but runtime verification: a monitor evaluates the LTL formula step-by-step against the actual execution trace. When the trace is about to violate the formula, the monitor intercepts.
In a typical agent pipeline, the monitor sits between the agent’s plan (what it intends to do next) and the effect handler (what actually touches the world):

Agent proposes effect e (write file, run shell, install dep).
Monitor projects the effect against the LTL formula given the trace so far.
If e would cause violation, monitor intercepts — denies the effect, signals back to the agent, optionally triggers a recovery rule.
Otherwise, effect proceeds and the monitor advances its automaton.

This is where LTL meets functional-agent-architecture: typed effects give the monitor a clean alphabet — a fixed set of observable event types — over which to evaluate the formula. Untyped string-prompt-to-string-output agents don’t give a monitor anything to observe except the surface text.
What LTL cannot do
Recognising the limits is half the value. LTL is the right tool for trace-level safety. It is the wrong tool for:

Content-of-generated-output properties. “The generated code contains no SQL injection.” LTL has nothing to say about whether a string of Python is or isn’t injection-vulnerable. You need a different tool (taint analysis, static analyser) at the content layer; LTL can then enforce “static analyser was run and passed before the code is committed” as a trace property.
Properties requiring LLM judgment to evaluate. “The agent’s reasoning was sound.” Not expressible without grounding “sound” externally first. Same for “the diff is a refactor, not a rewrite.”
Probabilistic compliance. Classical LTL is binary — a trace satisfies the formula or doesn’t. LLM agents are stochastic and may transiently violate soft constraints. Extensions exist (Probabilistic CTL, statistical model checking, runtime-quantitative LTL), but they require committing to a specific extension; the 2026 literature on this for LLM agents is unsettled — recent papers proposing (p, \delta, k)-style soft compliance frameworks have not yet stabilised into a citable standard, so treat compound-named variants in current writing with scepticism.
Real-time deadlines in wall-clock terms. LTL counts in steps of the trace, not seconds. For wall-clock real-time, MTL (Metric Temporal Logic) or TLTL (timed LTL) is the variant; wall-clock real-time is usually not the constraint that matters for coding agents.

Where the formalism is worth the cost
LTL has a tooling burden — you need a monitor, a trace alphabet, and a way to map agent effects to atomic propositions. The cost is worth paying when:

The safety property is load-bearing — getting it wrong is expensive or unrecoverable (production data, secret exposure, force-push).
The property is trace-shaped — expressible as “always/eventually/until” over a sequence, not as a content predicate on a single output.
The atomic propositions are observable — the monitor can determine if each one holds without LLM judgment.
The agent runs long enough that the temporal structure matters; for a single-turn completion, LTL is overkill.

For all other safety properties, lighter tools usually suffice — capability tokens that simply can’t issue the forbidden effect, pre-commit hooks, structured-output schemas. LTL is the right tool when the constraint is genuinely about the sequence, not the single action.
Tooling

Spin (Holzmann) — classic LTL model-checker; useful for offline verification of protocol-shaped agent designs, less so for runtime.
MOP / JavaMOP (Meredith & Roşu) — runtime monitoring framework supporting LTL and related logics; the closest match to “drop a monitor in front of an arbitrary system.”
Runtime Verification libraries — Bauer, Leucker, Schallhart’s runtime-LTL work is the citation backbone; specific libraries (e.g., LamaConv, AspectLTL) exist but vary in maintenance.
Domain-specific monitors — for typical coding-agent uses (no write outside workspace; no commit before tests pass), a hand-rolled state machine is often simpler than wiring a general LTL monitor. The LTL formula then lives as documentation and tests for the hand-rolled monitor.

Where this sits in the verification stack
Different from the content-level checks already in the vault:

ai-verification-stack-web — content-level verification (types, tests, mutation, visual regression). LTL doesn’t replace any of these.
evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — heuristics for evaluating the output; LTL evaluates the trace that produced the output.
functional-agent-architecture — provides the typed-effect alphabet that an LTL monitor needs; the architectural prerequisite.
multi-agent-governance — runtime governance layers; LTL monitors are one mechanism within the broader governance stack.
ai-agent-security — permission tiers and capability classification; LTL constraints often formalise the rules these tiers approximate.

What this doesn’t cover

Encoding standard policies as LTL. That is a per-policy authoring exercise; this note doesn’t catalogue them.
Performance overhead of monitors. Runtime monitoring is cheap relative to LLM inference but not free; for high-throughput pipelines this needs measurement.
Composition of monitors. Multiple LTL formulas form a conjunction; their joint monitor is constructable but engineering-non-trivial.
Branching-time logics. CTL and CTL* reason over branching futures, useful for would-have analysis; LTL is the linear cousin and the right starting point for runtime monitoring.

Related

ai-verification-stack-web — content-level verification; LTL is the orthogonal trace-level layer
multi-agent-governance — runtime governance, where LTL monitors live as one enforcement mechanism
