Sources

Pnueli, A. (1977). “The temporal logic of programs.” Proc. 18th FOCS, 46–57. The foundational paper introducing LTL for program verification; Pnueli later received the Turing Award (1996) in part for this work.
Manna, Z. & Pnueli, A. (1992). The Temporal Logic of Reactive and Concurrent Systems: Specification. Springer. The standard reference for LTL applied to reactive systems.
Holzmann, G. J. (2003). The SPIN Model Checker: Primer and Reference Manual. Addison-Wesley. SPIN remains the canonical LTL model-checker.
Bauer, A., Leucker, M. & Schallhart, C. (2011). “Runtime verification for LTL and TLTL.” ACM TOSEM, 20(4). The reference for runtime (rather than offline) LTL verification.
Meredith, P. & Roşu, G. (2010). “An overview of the MOP runtime verification framework.” Software Tools for Technology Transfer, 12(3). The MOP / JavaMOP framework — practical runtime monitoring.

The application of LTL-style runtime monitoring specifically to LLM agents is an emerging 2025-2026 research area; recent compound-named frameworks are not yet citation-settled (probabilistic LTL extensions, drift-bounded compliance, agent behavioural contracts with explicit (p, \delta, k) tuples). Use the classical LTL + runtime-verification base; add probabilistic / soft-compliance layers only against a specific verified paper.
Last reviewed: 2026-05-15.

ai/three-level-repo-documentation.title: Three-Level Repository Documentation: docs, ADR, intent
ai/three-level-repo-documentation.content:
Three-Level Repository Documentation: docs, ADR, intent
A plan for layering three kinds of documentation into a code repository, each answering a different question at a different altitude. Two of the three — docs and ADR (architecture decision records) — are established practice; the third, per-file intent, is an explicit hypothesis being tested here, not a settled standard. This note is the methodology and the rollout plan; it is language-agnostic and meant to be adapted per repo.
It assembles existing vault material rather than inventing new theory: clear-intent-as-anchor (the four-axis test for whether an intent does real work), intent-engineering-discipline (the same anchoring move at repo scale), architecture-decision-records-ai (the ADR layer), ai-friendly-repo-structure §4 (the docs layer), and the intent-to-retrospective-loop / /intent-fulfilment-check machinery (the drift check).
The three levels
Each level answers a distinct question. The unifying idea (clear-intent-as-anchor): state the target so the rest can be checked against it — at three altitudes.

































LevelQuestion it answersAltitudeLifetimeLives wheredocsWhat does it do, and how do I use/build/operate it?repo / packageliving, present-tenseREADME, llms.txt/AGENTS.md, agent_docs/, API docsADRWhy was this decision made, over which alternatives?one decisionpoint-in-time, append-only statusdocs/adr/NNNN-*.mdintentWhat is this file for — what would be lost if it vanished?one fileliving, edited with the filea marker inside each source file
The gap intent fills: code shows what it does; docs explain how to use it; ADRs explain why a choice was made. Nothing at the file level states what this unit is supposed to accomplish, such that drift away from that purpose can be noticed. That missing fine-grained anchor is the hypothesis this plan tests.
How the three stay distinct (anti-duplication):

intent ≠ docs. Intent is the file’s one-line target, for drift-checking and navigation — not usage instructions. Usage goes in docs.
intent ≠ ADR. An ADR is written once and records a decision; a file’s intent is read every session and moves with the file. A file’s intent may cite an ADR (implements ADR-0003) but does not restate it.
docs stays durable. Describe behavior and interfaces, not file paths or line numbers (.claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md rule 7); paths rot on the next refactor, behavior survives it.

The file-intent hypothesis (the unsettled part)
Hypothesis: a one-line intent on (nearly) every source file produces enough value — agent navigation, drift detection, a forcing function against dead/bloated files — to justify the authoring and maintenance cost.
Why it might pay off:

Agents see code, not intent — the same argument that makes ADRs matter more in AI-assisted repos (architecture-decision-records-ai §1), pushed down to the file. A file-intent tells an agent what a file is for before it spends context reading 400 lines.
Drift detection at file grain. /intent-fulfilment-check asks “does this output still serve its stated intent?” Run per-file, it catches scope creep, god-objects, and files that quietly became something else.
A deletion test. If you can’t write a non-trivial intent for a file, that is evidence the file shouldn’t exist (the deletion test from /deepen-architecture).
Navigation. Grepping intents finds “the file that does X” faster than reading directory trees.

Why it might not (failure modes, surfaced deliberately):

Intent theater. Most file intents on trivial files will restate the filename — @intent: handles auth on auth.ts. That is noise, and noise trains readers to ignore the marker that matters (clear-intent-as-anchor “Theater” failure mode). Intent theater is the dominant risk of the all files choice, and the main reason the layer is a hypothesis rather than a recommendation.
Granularity mismatch. Many files are too small to have an intent distinct from their module’s. Per-file may be the wrong unit; per-module may be right. (This is the open question — see Phase 5.)
Drift / rot. The intent goes stale as the code moves. Mitigation: phrase it as a durable target, not an implementation description (rule 7 again).
Distributed maintenance cost. Every substantive file edit may need an intent edit; the cost is small but paid constantly, and the benefit is diffuse and hard to attribute back.

Form discipline (from the four-axis test, clear-intent-as-anchor): an intent is a target, not a description. “the file that resolves a raw config blob into a validated, typed settings object” works; “config code” does not. Run the Form axis on a sample of intents during the hypothesis review — if they read as filename restatements, the layer is theatrical and the pre-registered fork in Phase 5 fires.
How to implement file-intent
Mechanism — in-file header marker (recommended). A single canonical, greppable token at the top of each file:
@intent: <one-line target, in the file's native comment syntax>
Compared against the alternatives:








































MechanismCollocationSurvives refactorCI-greppableDrift riskIn-file header marker (recommended)✅ with the code✅ moves with the file✅ one regex finds allmediumDocstring / KDoc / JSDoc tag✅✅✅mediumSidecar file (foo.ts + foo.intent.md)✗ scatters, doubles file count✗ orphans easily✅highCentral registry (INTENTS.yaml)✗ far from code✗ stale on any rename✅ easiesthighest
The header marker wins on the axes that matter for AI-assisted repos: collocation (keep what an agent needs in one place — ai-friendly-repo-structure §2), durability (it moves when the file moves, unlike a path-keyed registry), and greppability (the presence gate is a single regex). Use one token across all languages so a single scan finds every intent regardless of comment syntax. A docstring tag is a fine variant where the language’s doc tooling should pick it up; sidecars and registries are not recommended — they drift worst and fight collocation.
Enforcement — presence + drift (the chosen level). Two gates, deliberately split by cost and trust:

Presence gate — deterministic, cheap, blocking. A script scans tracked source files; any non-exempt file missing the marker fails CI (and a pre-commit hook). This is grep-level and maps to the deterministic Layer-1/Layer-3 gates in ai-friendly-repo-structure §5. Maintain an explicit exemption list: generated code, vendored/third-party, config, test files, barrel/index files, and trivially short files. The exemption list is itself a load-bearing artifact — record its rules in the establishing ADR.
Drift gate — LLM judgment, periodic, advisory. A scheduled job (not per-commit — too costly) runs /intent-fulfilment-check at file granularity over files changed since the last run: does the file still serve its stated intent? It flags Drifted / Over-built / Substituted and emits a report or PR comment for a human to triage. It is advisory, not blocking, because LLM judgment is not a deterministic oracle (oracle-problem-verification). Scope it to changed files to bound token cost (agent-context-budget-as-admission-control).

Sequence matters: stand up presence first, add drift once the marker is habitual. The drift gate is the expensive, less-proven half — and it is also the instrument that falsifies or validates the whole hypothesis, so it is where the evidence comes from, not where you start.
Phased rollout








































PhaseDeliverableRisk0 — Decide & dogfoodWrite ADR-0001 establishing this system: the canonical @intent token, the exemption rules, the per-file granularity bet and its fork condition. This ADR is the gold-standard example for the ADR layer.low1 — docs layerREADME (human), llms.txt or AGENTS.md (machine), agent_docs/ progressive-disclosure files, an empty docs/adr/ with template.md. Mostly known practice (ai-friendly-repo-structure §1, §4).low2 — ADR layerNygard + machine-readable template.md (<context>/<decision>/<consequences> tags), @import active ADRs into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, adopt “ADR violation in a PR = signal, not problem to suppress” (architecture-decision-records-ai). Backfill only decisions that pass the six-month test.low3 — intent presence gateConvention doc + exemption list + presence-check script wired into pre-commit and CI. Apply to new and changed files first; backfill existing files opportunistically rather than in one big-bang pass.medium4 — intent drift gateScheduled per-file /intent-fulfilment-check over changed files, advisory output. This is the hypothesis’s measurement instrument.medium5 — review the hypothesisAfter a set period / N PRs, run the validation signals below and decide: keep all-files, fall back to per-module, or restrict to public-interface files. Record the outcome as a new ADR.—
Validating the hypothesis (Phase 5 criteria)
Pre-register what would change the decision, so the review is evidence-driven rather than vibes (clear-intent-as-anchor axis 2; /calibration-loop):

Falsified if: a Form-axis sample shows intents are mostly filename restatements; the drift gate rarely fires meaningfully; authors route around it; the intents are demonstrably never read.
Validated if: the drift gate catches real scope-creep / dead-file cases; agents demonstrably navigate faster; the deletion test removes real cruft.
Pre-registered fork: if per-file proves theatrical on small files, fall back to per-module intent (one per package/directory) plus per-file intent only on public-interface files. Both fallbacks were live options at the start; the bet is that all-files beats them, and Phase 5 is where that bet resolves.

Authoring the docs themselves
ADRs and docs are a high-stakes hallucination surface — written once, read for years (architecture-decision-records-ai, solo-developer-ai-stack). Any AI-drafted ADR gets /bias-scan-ai before commit; load-bearing decisions (auth, persistence, deployment topology) get /red-team. See .claude/rules/bias-aware-authoring.md.
Related

clear-intent-as-anchor — the four-axis test (form, completion-falsifiable, navigable, altitude) the file-intent layer must pass to avoid theater
intent-engineering-discipline — the same anchoring move at repo scale (CI-enforceable contract); file-intent is its smallest-grain instance
architecture-decision-records-ai — the ADR layer: format, machine-readable variant, @import governance, when to skip
ai-friendly-repo-structure — the docs layer (§4) and the multi-layer validation stack (§5) the presence/drift gates plug into
intent-to-retrospective-loop — the develop-and-verify loop whose ⑥ stage is the drift gate’s /intent-fulfilment-check
ai-system-design-workflow — the upstream design activity that produces ADRs
oracle-problem-verification — why the LLM drift gate is advisory, not blocking

Sources
Synthesis of the vault notes listed under Related (each carries its own sourcing). The @intent token, the exemption-list approach, and the two-gate presence/drift split are design proposals made here, not external standards — adopt by deciding (Phase 0 ADR), not by citing. ADR format: Michael Nygard, “Documenting Architecture Decisions,” 2011 (via architecture-decision-records-ai). The deletion test is from /deepen-architecture (Ousterhout-derived).
Last reviewed: 2026-06-17. The file-intent layer is an open hypothesis; revisit after Phase 5.

ai/trainability-of-ai-use.title: Trainability of AI Use
ai/trainability-of-ai-use.content:
Trainability of AI Use
“Train the team to use AI effectively” is sold as one problem. It is at least three, with training economics that differ by orders of magnitude, and the industry prices all three at the cost of the cheapest one.
This note answers how hard is it to train people — the question cognitive-burden-of-ai-use raises but doesn’t address, and the question the design-adoption cluster (design-side-ai-adoption-stall, design-side-ai-onramp) hits from the organizational side. As of August 2026.
The three-component split





























ComponentWhat it isTraining horizonWho teaches itInteraction literacyPrompt formulation, tool selection, mode choice, context managementDays–weeksThis is what workshops teachVerification capacityDomain expertise sufficient to judge whether the output is rightYearsNobody, as “AI training” — it is the domainState managementRecognizing your own current capacity and matching task class to itNever taught—
Almost all commercial AI training targets row 1. Row 2 is the binding constraint. Row 3 is invisible.
The split matters because the three fail differently. Bad interaction literacy produces frustration and abandonment — visible, self-correcting, cheap to fix. Missing verification capacity produces confident acceptance of wrong output — invisible, self-reinforcing, and the failure lands downstream of the person who caused it.
Row 1 is real and separable — the AIC evidence
The strongest case that interaction literacy is a genuine, distinct skill comes from Anand & Idan (2026), who name it AI Interaction Competence (AIC): the ability to elicit, filter, and verify model outputs, decomposed into prompt formulation, output evaluation, and iterative refinement.
Their reported finding: GenAI access improved mean performance ~17%, but the distribution of gains was highly uneven — and the gains were not predicted by GPA or prior knowledge. They were predicted by AIC. High-AIC participants realized outsized gains; low-AIC participants saw limited or negative marginal returns.
Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions:

Optimistic: if the predictor is a skill rather than a trait or a credential, it is in principle trainable, and the population that gains most is not the population that already had the most.
Pessimistic: the negative-marginal-returns tail means there is a competence threshold below which AI subtracts. Deploying AI to an untrained population is not “some gain for everyone, more for some.” For part of the distribution it is a loss.

Caveat that matters. This is a working paper, in education and knowledge-work settings, and AIC is a construct its own authors defined. “People good at using AI gain more from AI” is close to tautological unless AIC is measured independently of the outcome it predicts. Treat the shape as informative and the effect size as provisional. This is the note’s weakest load-bearing evidence.
Row 2 is the constraint, and it isn’t AI training
Verification capacity is domain expertise. You cannot workshop it.
The distributional evidence makes this concrete. Dell’Acqua et al.’s pre-registered field experiment with 758 BCG consultants (~7% of the firm’s individual-contributor workforce) found that on 18 realistic tasks within AI’s capability frontier, consultants below the average performance threshold improved 43% against their own baseline while those above it improved 17%. The same inversion appears across the literature — the call-centre and writing studies in model-access-inequality report the same direction.
The uncomfortable reading: training returns are highest exactly where verification capacity is lowest. The people who gain most from AI are the people least equipped to catch it when it’s wrong. That is not an argument against training novices; it is an argument that the gain and the risk arrive on the same people at the same time, and the interventions have to be designed together.
The same paper supplies the reason this can’t be solved by task selection alone. Its central concept is the jagged technological frontier: AI performs excellently on some tasks and poorly on others that look, to a human, comparably difficult. The boundary is irregular and it is not visible from the outside. Deciding which side of it a given task falls on is itself a verification-capacity judgment — which is why “just use AI where it’s good” is not advice a novice can act on.
This is also the mechanism under the design-adoption stall. The designers’ quality objection isn’t resistance — it’s the correct output of people who can verify visual quality being handed a tool whose output they can’t verify in the code domain. design-side-ai-onramp’s step 0b (does the constraint substrate exist?) is asking the row-2 question.
Row 3 — the capacity-state component nobody teaches
The burden is not a constant. It’s a function of the user’s current executive capacity, and it has a floor. See cognitive-burden-of-ai-use for the mechanism and the load-floor argument; the training implication is what belongs here:
Every AI workflow is designed and tested by people at peak capacity, and used by people at median capacity. Tool designers, internal champions, and the person writing the onboarding doc are all in an unrepresentative state — engaged, rested, motivated by novelty. The workflow that only works when you’re sharp doesn’t work.
The training move this implies is not more training. It is scaffolding that survives low capacity — see the intervention section below.
The feedback channel is broken
The most damaging finding for any self-directed learning model: people cannot perceive their own AI-induced cost.

METR’s RCT (2025) — 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 real issues on mature repositories they knew well. With AI tools allowed, tasks took 19% longer (CI +2% to +39%). The developers had predicted a 24% speedup, and after experiencing the slowdown still estimated AI had made them 20% faster.
Vella & Blincoe (2026) — longitudinal, two surveys six months apart, matched cohort of 95 professional engineers. Productivity perception held stable at 84% reporting improvement at both time points, while the proportion reporting worsened developer experience nearly doubled, 14% → 27%, with flow state and cognitive load specifically named as what eroded. 82% reported spending less time writing code, and the authors name a new category — supervisory engineering work — for the direction, evaluation, and correction that replaced it.

Read together: the benefit is perceived and stable; the cost accrues on an axis the person isn’t measuring. Ordinary learning-by-doing requires a feedback signal. Here the signal is inverted for productivity and absent for load.
Honest scope on METR. Its own 2026-02 follow-up contextualises rather than retracts the result: a late-2025 re-run gave −18% (CI −38% to +9%) for returning developers and −4% (CI −15% to +9%) for new ones, which METR itself calls “only very weak evidence” because 30–50% of developers declined to submit tasks they wouldn’t attempt manually, systematically excluding the highest-value AI cases. The experiment is being redesigned. The slowdown magnitude is genuinely uncertain and probably shrinking; the perception gap is the robust part and is what this section rests on.
The pipeline erodes itself
The training problem has a second-order version. The capacity that row 2 requires is degraded by the tool that requires it.

Gerlich (2025) — AI use → cognitive offloading → reduced critical thinking, mediated rather than direct (see cognitive-burden-of-ai-use for figures and the moral-panic caveat).
Liu et al. (2026) — participants given AI assistance showed reduced persistence and worse independent performance on similar tasks afterward. The proposed mechanism is that immediate availability of a solution atrophies willingness to struggle, which is the process that builds durable capability. (Preprint; direction reported, effect sizes not extracted.)

If verification capacity is the binding constraint, and heavy unreflective AI use erodes the struggle that produces it, then scaling AI adoption faster than you build verification capacity is a self-limiting strategy. augmented-vs-trained-thinking is the personal-practice version of this trade; higher-order-thinking-under-ai is the skills version.
What actually works — scaffold, don’t train
The single most actionable finding in this literature: Anand & Idan’s scaffolding intervention (conceptual roadmaps) reduced outcome variance by ~40% without lowering mean performance.
That is the intervention shape. Not “make everyone competent” — make the workflow tolerant of varying competence. It converts a skill problem into an artifact problem, and artifacts survive states that skills don’t. The same logic drives sidi-stress-cognition’s counter to stress-degraded decisions: pre-built protocols are the cognition still available when capacity is low.
Ordered by leverage:

Ship the roadmap, not the workshop. A written scaffold — acceptance criteria, a review checklist, a worked example of a good and a bad output — carries competence that training has to install per-person and that fatigue removes.
Pre-commit verification criteria before generating. Written while fresh, the depleted-state task becomes matching against a list (recognition) rather than constructing a judgment. Cheapest available working-memory reduction.
Assign first tasks where the person’s existing verification capacity already reaches. This is design-side-ai-onramp’s “first exposure from the High column” restated in row-2 terms: never make someone’s first AI task one they cannot judge.
Teach the abstain condition explicitly. “Don’t use it below this capacity, above this stakes level, or outside your verification range” is a teachable rule and is almost never taught, because it doesn’t look like adoption.
Build the org-side oracle. Tests, linters, gates — machine-carried proof obligations reduce how much verification capacity each individual must personally hold. dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model’s amplifier effect: AI magnifies existing organizational strengths and weaknesses, so the substrate has to exist first.

Note the direction: every item moves load out of the person and into an artifact or a system. None of them is “be better at prompting.”
What the market is selling instead
DataCamp’s 2026 survey of 500+ enterprise leaders (US/UK) reports that organisations with a structured upskilling programme are roughly twice as likely to report significant AI ROI (42% vs 21% overall), that only 35% have a mature organisation-wide AI-literacy programme, and — the interesting pair — that 77% offer some kind of AI training while 59% still report an AI skills gap. (Vendor survey; DataCamp sells AI training. Treat the ROI correlation as interested, and note it cannot separate “training causes ROI” from “organisations that are good at this do both.“)
That last pair is what the three-component split predicts: most organisations are buying row 1 and needing row 2, so the training is delivered, absorbed, and the gap stays open. The survey’s own explanation is different — it blames training models built for slower-moving skills — which is a claim about delivery format where this note’s is about which capacity was the constraint. Both could be true; they are not the same diagnosis, and only one of them is fixed by buying more courses.
Counterargument
The strongest objection is that this is a snapshot artifact. Every study cited runs on 2023–2026 tools. The whole framing rests on verification being expensive. If models improve to where verification collapses to spot-checking — or where self-verification is reliable enough to carry its own proof obligation — then row 2 stops being the constraint, the training problem becomes row 1 only, and it is a workshop. ai-capability-watch-log tracks the indicators that would signal this; self-verification is the one to watch. METR’s own follow-up already suggests the 2025 measurement may not describe 2026.
Second objection: consensus echo. “Verification and judgment are what survive” is simultaneously this vault’s position and the mainstream consulting position. skills-to-train-for-ai-future flags that agreement as a yellow flag rather than confirmation. The three-component split is vulnerable to the same critique — it is a satisfying frame, and satisfying frames get adopted for reasons unrelated to being true.
Third: measurement quality. Two of the four load-bearing studies are preprints, one key survey is self-report, one is vendor-interested, and the strongest construct (AIC) has a circularity risk named above. The direction is consistent across independent designs, which is the main reason to credit it. No individual figure here should be quoted as settled.
Related

cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — the load this note asks how to train people to carry; the capacity-state and load-floor mechanisms row 3 depends on
design-side-ai-adoption-stall — the organizational instance: why row-2 absence reads as designer resistance
design-side-ai-onramp — the intervention sequence this note’s scaffolding argument supports
model-access-inequality — the novice-compression finding from the other direction (who gains, structurally)
skills-to-train-for-ai-future — the personal roadmap; source of the consensus-echo counter
augmented-vs-trained-thinking — offload-vs-train as a per-task decision, the personal version of the pipeline-erosion problem
higher-order-thinking-under-ai — what the durable capacity is made of
sidi-stress-cognition — protocols-over-judgment under degraded capacity
dora-2025-ai-capabilities-model — amplifier effect behind the org-side oracle recommendation
cognitive-load-theory-for-ai — executor-side load; this note and the burden hub are the human side

Sources
Verified 2026-08-05. Publication status flagged per source — three of these are preprints and one is a vendor survey.

Anand, B. & Idan, L. (2026) — “Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work” — working paper, May 2026. arXiv:2605.18143. Source of AIC, the ~17% mean gain, the negative-marginal-returns tail, and the ~40% variance reduction from conceptual-roadmap scaffolding. Not peer-reviewed.
Dell’Acqua, F., McFowland, E. III, Mollick, E. R., Lifshitz-Assaf, H., Kellogg, K., Rajendran, S., Krayer, L., Candelon, F. & Lakhani, K. R. — “Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality” — Organization Science 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838; originally HBS working paper 24-013, 2023. Study summary: HBS AI Institute. 758 BCG consultants (~7% of the IC workforce), pre-registered, 18 within-frontier tasks; below-average +43% / above-average +17% against own baseline; within-frontier gains of >25% speed, >40% human-rated quality, >12% completion. The jagged-frontier concept and the 758/7% figures are primary-verified; the 43/17 split is consistent across secondary summaries but was not read in the primary (SSRN and the HBS PDF are bot-blocked).
METR (2025) — “Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity.” metr.org. 16 developers, 246 issues, 19% slowdown (CI +2% to +39%), 24% predicted / 20% perceived speedup.
METR (2026-02-24) — “We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design.” metr.org. Late-2025 re-run figures, the 30–50% task-selection bias, and METR’s own “only very weak evidence” characterisation.
Vella, A. & Blincoe, K. (2026) — “The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on Software Engineering: A Longitudinal Study,” May 2026. arXiv:2605.23135. 158 → 101 respondents, 95 matched; 84% stable productivity perception, 14% → 27% worsened experience, “supervisory engineering work.” Self-report.
Liu, G., Christian, B., Dumbalska, T., Bakker, M. A. & Dubey, R. (2026) — “AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance.” arXiv:2604.04721. Preprint; direction reported here, effect sizes not extracted.
Gerlich, M. (2025) — “AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking” — Societies 15(1), 6. MDPI. Figures and caveats carried in cognitive-burden-of-ai-use.
DataCamp (2026) — “The State of Data & AI Literacy 2026.” datacamp.com. 500+ enterprise leaders, US/UK; no further methodology published. Vendor survey, interested party. Figures read at source 2026-08-05.
Dantzer, R., O’Connor, J. C., Freund, G. G., Johnson, R. W. & Kelley, K. W. (2008) — “From inflammation to sickness and depression: when the immune system subjugates the brain” — Nature Reviews Neuroscience 9(1), 46–56. PubMed 18073775. Cited via cognitive-burden-of-ai-use’s capacity-state section for the illness axis; the AI-relevant inference is the vault’s, not the paper’s.

ai/verification-stack-operational-map.title: Verification Stack Operational Map
ai/verification-stack-operational-map.content:
Verification Stack Operational Map
What it is
A single decision tree across the 38 per-task skills installed in this vault (verification, ideation, planning, review, cognitive-burden, authoring-quality, valuation, and corpus-maintenance) — when to run which, in what order, what each catches the others miss — plus the meta-router /which-skill that selects among them. The skills exist; the integrated picture didn’t.
The 38 per-task skills (as of 2026-06-08, source: .claude/skills/ directory): ai-diff-judgment, assumption-reversal, bias-scan-ai, bias-scan-human, bias-scan-prompt, branch-resolve, calibration-loop, claim-function-scan, clarify-first, commitment-ledger, context-budget-scan, contradiction-scan, density-scan, disagree, falsifiability-scan, grill, handoff, intent-check, intent-fulfilment-check, lean-review, option-premium-check, persona-cluster-check, plan-options, plan-split-scan, red-team, reference-class, retrospective, reviewers-map, scamper, second-order, skill-quality-audit, skill-trigger-audit, staleness-decay-scan, starburst, structural-trace, task-decompose, whittle-scan, write-a-skill.
The 39th, /which-skill, sits outside the per-task taxonomy as a meta-router — given a request, it ranks 1–3 candidate skills with quoted trigger phrases and rejected near-misses. This map and /which-skill are complementary: the map is the static decision tree (read top-down to find an entry skill); /which-skill is the dynamic counterpart (describe the situation, get routed). At 38 per-task skills the catalog has outgrown casual scanning — in practice /which-skill is increasingly the working entry point, and this map is the auditable reference it routes against.
Revision history: first revision mapped 15 skills; the 2026-05-10 revision added claim-function-scan, density-scan, persona-cluster-check, skill-trigger-audit, and the /which-skill meta-router (19+1). This revision (2026-06-05) adds fifteen: the work-cycle set (intent-check, plan-options, plan-split-scan, branch-resolve, task-decompose, intent-fulfilment-check, retrospective), the request-side clarify-first, the code-review pair (lean-review, ai-diff-judgment), the token-economy context-budget-scan, the valuation pair (whittle-scan, option-premium-check), and the corpus-maintenance pair (contradiction-scan, staleness-decay-scan). The taxonomy grows from seven clusters to twelve. A same-day addendum (2026-06-05) adds skill-quality-audit (35+1) — the body/structure complement to skill-trigger-audit, built from the deep-research note skill-quality-criteria. A further revision (2026-06-08) adds three more, each folding into an existing cluster: grill (interactive plan interrogation → plan & decomposition), handoff (next-agent continuation → cognitive-burden, beside commitment-ledger), and write-a-skill (the generative front of the skill-authoring trio → authoring-side). 38+1. The twelve clusters absorb all three — no new top-level mode.
Why this exists
Two narrower maps already cover part of the surface:

bias-aware-verification-protocol — four-pass framework (/bias-scan-prompt → /bias-scan-ai → /disagree → /red-team) plus the orthogonal /bias-scan-human. Five of 38.
cognitive-burden-of-ai-use — three cognitive-burden counters (/reviewers-map, /commitment-ledger, /calibration-loop). Three of 38.
intent-to-retrospective-loop — the develop-and-verify loop across the seven work-cycle skills. Seven of 38.

Together: fifteen. The other twenty-three sit outside those anchors and have no shared decision surface. The existing notes also do not answer the cross-cutting question: which skill fits this exact moment?
The cost of not having this map is invocation-surface friction. Per cognitive-burden-of-ai-use (Lee et al., CHI 2025), the deliberate act of choosing to run a verification step is where verification dies. A decision tree replaces “remember which skill” with “what stage am I in.”
The skills, by purpose
Twelve functional clusters across the 38 per-task skills. A per-task skill belongs to exactly one — the cluster captures what mode the skill puts you in, not what topics it can touch. /which-skill is the meta-router and is described separately below; it does not belong to a cluster because it does not put you in a working mode — it picks one for you.
Pre-action clarification — request-side
The only cluster that runs before the task itself is settled. Single member by design — it has no neighbor in invocation shape.

/clarify-first — research-then-ground-then-ask protocol on a vague but load-bearing request: mine the conversation and codebase first, then ask multiple-choice questions where every option traces to a real finding. Counters ungrounded clarification (options confabulated from training-data priors).

Generative — pre-commitment ideation
Used before you have committed to a frame, an option set, or a problem definition. Output is divergent: alternatives, questions, frame breaks. None of these evaluate or select.

/assumption-reversal — surface 5 unstated assumptions in a problem; invert each as a one-line design brief. Frame attack.
/scamper — Substitute / Combine / Adapt / Modify / Put-to-another-use / Eliminate / Rearrange — structured divergent variants on a candidate idea.
/starburst — Who / What / Where / When / Why / How questions around an idea. Pre-commitment gap analysis.

Intent anchoring & loop closure — the cycle’s bookends
Bracket a work cycle: audit the goal before work starts, check the output against it after, convert the cycle into lessons. See intent-to-retrospective-loop.

/intent-check — four-axis test (form, completion-falsifiable, navigable, altitude) on a stated intent, goal, or objective. Counters theatrical intent — a goal too vague to anchor anything.
/intent-fulfilment-check — decompose the originating intent into clauses; mark each served / partial / substituted / unaddressed against the produced output; flag scope inflation. Counters silent goal-substitution. Requires both an intent and an output — route to /intent-check if the intent is missing.
/retrospective — convert a completed cycle into transferable lessons plus a resulting (process-vs-outcome) verdict; auto-feeds the calibration log.

Plan & decomposition — before execution
Operate on plans, not artifacts. Two generative (produce the plan), two diagnostic (audit it), one interactive (interrogate it).

/plan-options — generate 2–3 genuinely different candidate plans, each traced clause-by-clause to the intent, then collapse to one with the choice reason recorded. Counters median-collapse. Skips (and says so) on trivial tasks.
/task-decompose — decompose the chosen plan into tasks with a done-criterion + interface contract + risk-ordering at generation time. Refuses on routine work.
/plan-split-scan — scan a draft multi-step plan for five structural signals (concern count, state-carry depth, decision branches, verification seams, reversibility boundary); recommend split / consolidate / leave-alone. Executor-side load axis.
/branch-resolve — operationalize each unresolved decision branch: resolve up front, split at the determinant, or express as an IF-trigger-THEN-response implementation intention; hard split on branches with destructive downstream. Counters branch-collapse.
/grill — sustained one-question-at-a-time interview that walks an in-progress plan’s decision tree in dependency order, attaches a recommended answer to each question, and explores the codebase to settle a point rather than asking. Produces a resolved-decisions ledger, not an execution. The interactive member — distinct from the static scans, which read a finished draft.

Detection scans — bias fingerprints on a specific artifact
Each scans one axis of bias on one target.

/bias-scan-prompt — input-side framing in a prompt about to be sent. Pass 1 of the verification protocol.
/bias-scan-ai — output-side fingerprints in an AI-drafted artifact. Pass 2; full seven-check sweep, backed by ai-output-bias-fingerprints.
/bias-scan-human — full cognitive-bias catalog (sunk cost, confirmation, FAE, narrative fallacy, planning fallacy, anchoring, etc.) on a human-authored artifact. Orthogonal to the four-pass AI protocol.

Operationalization — claim triage, sharpening, numeric grounding
Take a draft and improve the testability or grounding of specific elements within it. Tag-and-fix shape, not whole-artifact verdict.

/claim-function-scan — triage claims into empirical / non-empirical / bundled. The actionable failure mode is the bundled case: an empirical claim wrapped in an identity or coordination frame, immune to challenge until split. Triage pass before /falsifiability-scan or /reviewers-map when claims may be bundled.
/falsifiability-scan — categorize claims by testability ([OP] / [DEFER] / [VAGUE] / [SEAL] / [PROB] / [DEFN]); operationalization checklist for the ones worth sharpening. Backed by falsifiability-claim-fingerprints.
/reference-class — apply outside-view forecasting to numeric estimates in a draft (durations, costs, sizes, percentages). Tag inside-view estimates against base-rate distributions. Backed by reference-class-forecasting.

Adversarial — post-draft
Run after a draft exists. Goal is to find it wrong, not improve it from inside.

/disagree — inversion drill on the most recent substantive assistant response. Argue the opposite. The variance under reframing is the calibration signal. Pass 3.
/red-team — adversarial critique of an artifact. Returns strongest objections, pre-mortem, weakest load-bearing claim. Pass 4.

Code review — diffs, not prose
The only cluster whose target is code. Pick by what question you’re asking, not by diff size alone.

/lean-review — token-frugal correctness review of the current diff: scope with --stat first, read only changed hunks, bounded severity · file:line findings. Provenance-irrelevant. The cheap default.
/ai-diff-judgment — post-green-CI merge judgment on an AI-authored diff: recover the originating intent, verify it clause-by-clause, read the test diff before the code diff, hunt spec drift / hollow tests / test tampering; altitude-ordered verdict ending in a net-improvement decision. Counters automation-bias merging.

Built-in neighbors (not vault skills, but in the same routing space): /code-review (maximum-coverage correctness, effort-tiered) and /verify (run the app and observe behavior — the empirical complement both vault skills explicitly defer to).
Forward and structural — action / system tracing
These don’t scan an artifact for bias — they trace a behavior or action through time and structure.

/second-order — neutral forward simulation of a proposed action’s consequences across three orders, sign-neutral. Pairs with /red-team (which weaponizes the unfavorable branches).
/structural-trace — stocks-flows-feedback diagnosis of a recurring pattern. Senge archetypes, Meadows leverage points. Diagnostic, not prescriptive. Counters dispositional explanation (blaming actors when structure is the cause).

Valuation — queues, options, commitments
Price what the other clusters don’t: the cost of not acting, and the flexibility a choice destroys.

/whittle-scan — surface queue items whose cost-of-inaction is invisible per-week (decay valuation): dated commitments and forecast-resolution-dates rotting quietly.
/option-premium-check — sign a proposed action or deferred-item list as flexibility-creating / flexibility-burning / dominant / optionality-hoarding; flags one-way doors with equal-payoff two-way alternatives, and deferral sets whose carrying cost exceeds the preserved option’s value.

Cognitive-burden counters — per-output / per-session / multi-session
Address the load of verification and continuation, not the verification itself. Each operates at a different granularity.

/reviewers-map — per-output verification map: load-bearing claims tagged [V] / [U] / [I], least-confident spots, five-minute check list, what was not done. Lighter than /bias-scan-ai. Counters cognitive decoupling.
/commitment-ledger — per-session closeout: files touched, claims accepted without verification, decisions, deferrals, what to check first tomorrow. Counters accountability without authorship. Optionally appends to journal/commitments-log.
/handoff — per-session continuation doc for the next agent or session: compacts the conversation into carry-forward state (decisions, open threads, a mandatory suggested-skills routing section), dedup-by-reference, written to the OS temp dir out of version control. The next-agent-facing counterpart to /commitment-ledger (human-audit-facing). Counters continuation amnesia across a context boundary.
/calibration-loop — multi-session loop. record captures a binary prediction with resolution criterion; resolve closes predictions whose deadline has passed; review reports Brier score and calibration buckets. Reads/writes journal/calibration-log. Counters uncalibrated confidence.

Authoring-side scans — prose form, invocation surface, token budget
These mostly don’t verify the content of an artifact — they audit the form, the invocation surface, and the budget. The cluster also holds one generator (/write-a-skill) that produces a skill the two audits then check. Each targets an axis where a fluent-looking artifact silently fails to do its job.

/density-scan — information-density failure modes in prose: surprisal spikes, sentence-length monotony, propositional density mismatched to channel, long-distance dependencies, the “shorter is better” compression trap. Reader-comprehension axis.
/context-budget-scan — token-economy scan in three modes (artifact / architecture / session): cache-unfriendly ordering, lost-in-middle placement, tool-output bloat, missing compaction strategy. Explicitly a different axis from /density-scan — what the artifact costs the model, not the reader.
/persona-cluster-check — for “You are an expert X” primes, surface the cluster of register, defaults, and biases the persona invokes from training data, then check fit to the actual job.
/write-a-skill — generator for a new SKILL.md from a capability description: produces the frontmatter (third-person what+when description), body structure, and output contract. The generative front of the skill-authoring trio — feed its output to /skill-trigger-audit then /skill-quality-audit before publishing.
/skill-trigger-audit — audit a SKILL.md description for retrieval-match quality (will the skill fire on the queries it was built for?).
/skill-quality-audit — deep structural audit of a SKILL.md body and metadata: description↔body truthfulness, procedure executability, output contract with a reachable clean verdict, catalog-sync integrity. The complement of /skill-trigger-audit — that one asks “will it fire”, this one asks “when it fires, is it built to do its job”.

Corpus maintenance — cross-note scans
The only skills that ingest more than one note and reason over the set. They counter the silent decay an append-mostly vault accumulates (see knowledge-base-entropy). Report-only: ledger or action table, never a rewrite.

/contradiction-scan — surface note-pairs that silently disagree about the same empirical claim (distributed inconsistency); emits a conflict ledger with both claims quoted.
/staleness-decay-scan — surface time-sensitive notes whose perishable claims have aged past a volatility-adjusted half-life; ranked re-verify / re-date / archive / promote-durable table. Owns perishable static facts; dated commitments go to /whittle-scan.

Meta-router — selection across the catalog
Outside the per-task taxonomy. Operates one level above: given a request, returns the per-task skill(s) to invoke.

/which-skill — given a situation, artifact, or intent, ranks 1–3 candidate skills with quoted trigger phrases, one-line rationales, and what each won’t do — plus 1–2 rejected near-misses. Returns a “no skill fits” verdict when honest.

Common chains — in what order
Eight chains cover most non-trivial work. Skills are listed in execution order. Stop early if the artifact is exploratory; run the full chain only at high stakes.
Chain 1 — Pre-commit an AI-drafted artifact
/bias-scan-prompt  →  drafting  →  /reviewers-map  →  /bias-scan-ai  →  /red-team  →  /calibration-loop record
   (Pass 1)                         (light, fast)      (deep, 7-check)   (if high-stakes)   (if a prediction)

/reviewers-map is the cheap default; /bias-scan-ai is the deep dive. Don’t run both by default — pick by stakes. Add /falsifiability-scan if the draft has load-bearing prose claims; add /reference-class if it has numeric estimates.
Chain 2 — Pre-commit a human-authored synthesis
drafting  →  /bias-scan-human  →  /claim-function-scan (if mixed)  →  /falsifiability-scan  →  /reference-class (if numbers)  →  /red-team

/bias-scan-human covers the cognitive-bias side; /claim-function-scan triages bundled claims before they reach the next pass; /falsifiability-scan and /reference-class cover the operational-shape side; /red-team covers the adversarial side. Skip /claim-function-scan if the artifact is purely technical or purely narrative.
Chain 3 — Pre-commit a decision
/starburst  →  /second-order  →  /option-premium-check (if one-way door)  →  /red-team  →  /calibration-loop record
  (gaps)        (consequences)     (what flexibility it burns)               (objections)    (close the loop)

/starburst surfaces what you do not know; /second-order traces the cascade neutrally; /option-premium-check prices the reversibility; /red-team weaponizes the unfavorable branches; /calibration-loop record makes the decision a falsifiable prediction.
Chain 4 — Diagnose a recurring problem
/structural-trace  →  /second-order
  (diagnose the         (test the proposed action through the
   standing system)     structure just diagnosed)

Don’t reverse the order. You need the structure first, or the action’s consequences are traced through the wrong system.
Chain 5 — Break a stuck frame
/assumption-reversal  →  /scamper (or) /starburst
  (frame attack)         (variants)     (gaps)

After /assumption-reversal, pick whichever next step matches what you have less of — options or questions.
Chain 6 — Authoring quality on a prompt or skill artifact
[draft prompt or SKILL.md]  →  /persona-cluster-check (if persona prime)  →  /bias-scan-prompt (if runnable)  →  /density-scan  →  /context-budget-scan (if it will run many times)  →  /skill-quality-audit + /skill-trigger-audit (if SKILL.md — body/structure, then trigger surface)

Runs orthogonally to chains 1–5 — they verify content, this chain checks form, budget, and invocation surface. Apply the relevant content chain first, then run this on the final draft.
Chain 7 — Full work cycle (develop-and-verify loop)
/clarify-first (if request vague)  →  /intent-check  →  /plan-options  →  /plan-split-scan (+ /branch-resolve on flagged branches; + /grill to interrogate the plan interactively)  →  /task-decompose  →  [execute]  →  /lean-review or /ai-diff-judgment (if the output is a diff)  →  /intent-fulfilment-check  →  /retrospective

The skeleton of intent-to-retrospective-loop. Most stages are skippable on routine work — /plan-options and /task-decompose refuse trivial tasks by design; the load-bearing minimum is /intent-check at the front and /intent-fulfilment-check at the back, which together catch silent goal-substitution.
Chain 8 — Corpus maintenance pass
/staleness-decay-scan  →  /contradiction-scan  →  /whittle-scan
  (which dated claims        (which note-pairs          (which dated commitments
   expired silently)          silently disagree)          are decaying in the queue)

Periodic, vault-level. The three are disjoint by design: perishable static facts / cross-note disagreement / dated commitments. Run when a fast-moving domain shifted or before relying on an aging cluster in new work.

Anti-patterns

Map theater. Running every skill in every chain because the map says so. Per bias-aware-verification-protocol: “overhead unmatched to stakes is the main reason verification protocols get abandoned.” The same applies at this meta level — and applies harder at 38 skills than it did at 19.
Forcing a skill outside its cluster. /red-team is adversarial, not generative — running it for ideation gives objections to options that don’t exist yet. /starburst does not evaluate; it asks. /lean-review does not hunt intent drift; /ai-diff-judgment does not maximize correctness coverage.
Skipping the map. Picking by name-recognition (“/red-team sounds right”) instead of by trigger. The trigger language above is the entry point; the skill names are the exit.
Treating skill output as authoritative. Each skill is itself an AI output and is subject to the bias fingerprints /bias-scan-ai exists to detect. Skepticism does not bottom out. The map reduces friction; it does not produce correctness.
Letting the chain replace engagement. Running Chain 1 mechanically on an AI-drafted thesis without adjusting any probability table or rewriting any framing is the failure mode the augur project explicitly guards against. Skills do not substitute for substantive editing.
Map-as-end-state. This map is unmeasured opinion until someone actually scores artifacts before/after the protocol and produces a delta. Until then, treat the operational picture as a working hypothesis and revise when chains fail in practice.

Open questions for the next revision

Does the static map still scale at 38? The 2026-05-10 revision asked whether authoring-side checks deserved a higher-level split; the answer that growth gave is that the catalog now has at least four top-level modes (verify content / shape the work cycle / audit form & budget / maintain the corpus). The 2026-06-08 additions folded into existing clusters without a new mode, so the four-mode structure held — but /which-skill is now the only practical per-request entry point, and if the count keeps growing the map may need to become a map of cluster-maps.
Are Chain 1 and Chain 2 actually different chains, or is “AI-drafted” vs “self-drafted” a distinction without a difference once the artifact exists? Watch in practice; collapse if both behave the same.
Should /disagree move out of the adversarial cluster? It targets the last assistant turn, not an artifact. Currently grouped with /red-team because they share the inversion intent.
The code-review cluster routes by provenance (/lean-review any diff, /ai-diff-judgment AI-authored). As AI-authored becomes the default provenance, does the distinction collapse into cheap-vs-deep — and if so, does /lean-review survive as the cheap tier or fold into the built-in /code-review effort levels?
Chain 7 (full work cycle) is nine skills end-to-end; nobody will run it whole. Which two-or-three-skill sub-chains of it actually recur in practice? Log real usage before prescribing more.
