general/feynman-technique.title: Feynman Technique
general/feynman-technique.content:
Feynman Technique
What it is
A four-step iterative loop for converting a topic from “I think I get it” into “I can teach it without notes.” Named after Richard Feynman, who repeatedly emphasized that if you can’t explain something simply you don’t actually understand it. The technique is essentially a high-effort form of active-recall applied to conceptual integration rather than fact memorization.
Why it matters
Most knowledge gaps hide behind jargon. As long as you’re allowed to say “the Hamiltonian acts on the wave function,” you can keep the gap covered. Forcing yourself to explain the same idea in plain language — to a 12-year-old, on a blank page, without notes — surfaces every place where you’re moving symbols around without understanding.
Two compounding effects:

Gap surfacing: Every stumble, jargon retreat, or vague hand-wave marks a specific place to study next. The technique is its own diagnostic.
Protégé effect: The act of preparing to teach forces structural reorganization of the material — finding the load-bearing claims, removing redundancy, building the explanatory through-line. That reorganization is itself the learning.

It’s the strategy of choice when the goal is understanding rather than retention. For sheer volume of facts, spaced-repetition is faster.
Details
The four steps


Pick the topic and study it. Read the primary sources, attend the lecture, work through the textbook chapter. Build a baseline of context. Don’t skip this — Feynman is for consolidating understanding, not generating it from scratch.


Explain it in plain language, on a blank page, as if to a child. Out loud or in writing. Aim for declarative sentences, no jargon, concrete examples. The 12-year-old framing is a constraint, not a literal audience — it forces you to ground every term in something more basic.


Find the gaps. Wherever you stumbled, retreated to jargon, glossed over a “why,” or felt the explanation get hand-wavy — that’s a specific gap. Mark it. Return to the source and study only that.


Simplify, refine, archive. Iterate on the explanation until it flows from start to finish without notes and without ambiguity. The final version goes into your notes for later spaced review.


When to use it

New conceptual frameworks (a new theorem, a new economic model, a new architectural pattern)
Material you’ll need to use generatively, not just recognize on a test
Cross-disciplinary synthesis where you need to bridge two domains
Before writing or presenting — Feynman before draft saves time later
Diagnosing whether you understood something you read

When not to use it

Pure rote material (vocabulary, anatomy, dates) — use spaced-repetition
Skills that are mostly procedural (typing, riding a bike, sight-reading) — use interleaving-practice and deliberate practice instead
Time-constrained recall before an imminent test — Feynman is too slow; drill the flashcards

Stacking with other strategies
The high-leverage workflow:

Feynman first to build understanding of a concept cluster
Extract atomic facts from the resulting clear explanation into SRS cards
Interleave when reviewing if the topic shares features with adjacent topics

Feynman builds the structure; SRS keeps the structure populated; interleaving keeps you able to discriminate it from neighbors.
Common failure modes

Skipping step 1 and bluffing: Without primary-source study you’ll just write a confident-sounding empty page.
Stopping at step 2: Producing a draft explanation feels like the work, but the gap-fixing iteration (step 3 → 2 → 3) is where most of the learning happens.
Optimizing the prose, not the understanding: A polished explanation is not the same as a clear one. If a 12-year-old can’t follow it, it’s still too dense.
Using it on the wrong material: Don’t Feynman a vocabulary list.

Related

active-recall — Feynman is a high-effort case of retrieval applied to whole concepts
spaced-repetition — Pair: Feynman to understand, SRS to retain
note-taking-systems — The “archive” step typically lands here
evidence-based-learning — Hub

Sources
Preliminary research synthesis (AI-drafted, 2026-04-25). The technique is widely attributed to Feynman based on his teaching style and the “Lectures on Physics” preface; popularized in self-study contexts by Scott Young and others. The “protégé effect” is documented in Fiorella & Mayer (2013, Contemporary Educational Psychology).
Last verified: 2026-04-25

general/flow-state.title: Flow State
general/flow-state.content:
Flow State
What it is
Flow is Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of optimal experience — a mental state of complete absorption in a task where action and awareness merge, self-consciousness disappears, and time perception distorts. It is not relaxation or passive enjoyment; flow occurs during active, challenging engagement that stretches current skill level without exceeding it. The “flow channel” sits between boredom (skill exceeds challenge) and anxiety (challenge exceeds skill).
Why it matters
Flow is where the best work happens — whether that’s writing code, pushing watts on the bike, or executing a high-key Mythic+ (M+) dungeon. Research consistently shows that people in flow are more productive, more creative, produce higher-quality output, and report greater life satisfaction. Understanding flow’s triggers lets you engineer the conditions for it rather than waiting for it to randomly occur. Cal Newport’s “deep work” framework is essentially a practical methodology for creating flow-compatible work environments.
Details
Flow Triggers (Conditions for Entry)
Csikszentmihalyi identified several conditions that facilitate flow:


Clear goals — You must know exactly what you’re trying to accomplish. Vague objectives (“make progress on the project”) prevent flow. Specific targets (“implement the authentication middleware and write tests for it”) create the directional clarity flow requires.


Immediate feedback — You need to know whether what you’re doing is working, in real time. Test suites passing/failing, power numbers on the bike computer, health bars moving in a dungeon — all provide the tight feedback loop flow depends on.


Challenge-skill balance — The task must be approximately 4% beyond your current ability (Csikszentmihalyi’s rough heuristic). Too easy triggers boredom and mind-wandering. Too hard triggers anxiety and withdrawal.


Deep concentration — Undivided attention on a single task. This is the prerequisite most often violated in modern work environments.


Physiological and Psychological Markers

Altered time perception — Hours feel like minutes (or occasionally, seconds feel expanded during peak moments)
Reduced self-consciousness — The inner critic goes quiet. You stop monitoring yourself and just do.
Intrinsic motivation — The activity becomes rewarding in itself, independent of external outcomes
Sense of control — Not that you’re forcing the outcome, but that you’re capable and responsive
Merging of action and awareness — No gap between deciding and doing

Neurologically, flow involves transient hypofrontality — reduced activity in the prefrontal cortex, which normally handles self-monitoring, time awareness, and inner criticism. This deactivation is what produces the ego-dissolution and time-distortion effects.
Flow in Specific Domains
Coding:

Complex problem-solving where the solution isn’t immediately obvious but is tractable
Test-driven development provides the immediate feedback loop (red-green-refactor cycle)
Refactoring sessions where you’re reshaping code architecture — skill-appropriate challenge with clear progress signals
Debugging deep issues can trigger flow when you’re following a trail of evidence
Flow killers: Slack notifications, unclear requirements, waiting for CI, meetings breaking up blocks

Cycling (Zwift / outdoor):

Sustained intervals at or near threshold — the effort demands full attention
Zwift races where you’re in a competitive group, reacting to attacks and managing effort
Outdoor climbing — long sustained grades require constant power management and body awareness
Sweet spot and threshold work is ideal for flow; Z2 endurance is often too easy to demand full engagement (podcasts fill this gap, which is fine)

Gaming (WoW M+):

Dungeons at the right key level — hard enough to require full attention, achievable enough to not feel hopeless
Progression raiding on a boss that’s within reach — each pull provides feedback, each wipe teaches something
Key level is the literal “challenge-skill dial” — too low = autopilot, too high = frustration
The healer role is particularly flow-compatible: constant decision-making, immediate feedback (health bars), high consequence

Designing for Flow
Time architecture:

Minimum 15-25 minutes of uninterrupted focus to enter flow. The deeper you go, the richer the experience — 90-120 minute blocks are ideal.
Schedule deep work blocks during peak cognitive hours (typically morning). Protect these blocks aggressively.
Batch shallow work (email, Slack, admin) into designated windows so it doesn’t fragment deep blocks.

Environment:

Eliminate notification sources. Phone on DND, Slack closed or snoozed, email tabs closed.
Consistent environmental cues can accelerate flow entry over time (same music, same desk setup, same pre-work ritual).
Physical comfort matters — hunger, cold, or discomfort pulls attention away from the task.

Task design:

Break ambiguous projects into concrete, skill-appropriate sub-tasks
Define “done” clearly before starting
If a task feels too easy, add constraints (time limit, higher quality bar). If too hard, decompose further.

Flow Blockers








































BlockerWhy it kills flowMitigationNotificationsBreaks concentration; 23 minutes average to recover (Gloria Mark research)DND, notification batchingContext switchingPrevents the depth of engagement flow requiresSingle-task blocks, time-boxingUnclear goalsNo direction = no engagementDefine goals before startingFatigueDepleted cognitive resources can’t sustain attentionSleep, caffeine timing, restAnxiety about other tasksMental load from unfinished obligationsCapture everything in a system (GTD-style)PerfectionismSelf-monitoring prevents hypofrontality”Ship the draft, iterate later” mindset
Connection to Deep Work
Cal Newport’s Deep Work (2016) is essentially a practical framework for maximizing flow in knowledge work:

Deep work = professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free concentration (i.e., flow conditions)
Shallow work = logistical tasks that don’t require deep concentration
Newport’s thesis: the ability to perform deep work is becoming simultaneously more rare and more valuable — making it a career superpower
His scheduling methods (time blocking, shutdown rituals, quit social media) are all flow-enablement strategies

The Group Flow Phenomenon
Flow is not limited to solo activities. Csikszentmihalyi and later Keith Sawyer (2007) documented group flow — a state where an entire team enters flow simultaneously through collaborative interaction.
Conditions for group flow:

Shared goals — everyone knows and cares about the objective
Close listening — participants build on each other’s contributions
Equal participation — no single person dominates
Autonomy within structure — clear rules/roles but freedom within them
Familiarity — groups that have worked together before enter group flow more easily

Where this applies:

WoW M+ groups: A well-coordinated group running a key at the right difficulty level frequently enters group flow. Communication is minimal but precise, cooldowns are used without being called, and the run “just works.” This is why pushing with a consistent team produces better results than pugging — you’re building the conditions for group flow.
Pair programming: Two developers solving a problem together can enter a shared flow state where the solution emerges faster than either could produce alone.
Music: Improvising musicians are Csikszentmihalyi’s original example of group flow in action.

Quantifying Flow
Steven Kotler’s Flow Research Collective has attempted to measure flow’s productivity impact — the specific numbers below are contested, the direction less so:

People in flow report being up to 500% more productive (McKinsey study cited by Kotler, though methodology is debated)
More conservatively, a 2019 study in the Journal of Happiness Studies found flow experiences correlated with a 25-30% increase in creative output compared to non-flow work sessions
Flow frequency correlates with higher job satisfaction and lower burnout across occupations (Bakker, 2005)

These numbers should be taken with appropriate skepticism — flow research has measurement challenges (self-report bias, selection effects). But the directional claim is robust: flow states produce meaningfully better output than non-flow states.
Flow and Deliberate Practice
Flow and deliberate practice (Ericsson, 1993) are related but distinct:

Deliberate practice focuses on targeted improvement at the edge of ability, with coaching feedback. It is often effortful and not enjoyable.
Flow occurs when challenge and skill are matched and the experience is intrinsically rewarding.
The overlap: both require tasks at the edge of current ability. The difference is that deliberate practice deliberately targets weaknesses (uncomfortable), while flow rides the sweet spot (feels good).
Practical implication: Use deliberate practice to build skills (e.g., isolated log analysis and targeted improvement), then ride those skills into flow during actual performance (the M+ key itself, the race, the coding session).

general/friendship-formula-schafer.title: Friendship Formula and Exchange vs Communal Relationships
general/friendship-formula-schafer.content:
Friendship Formula and Exchange vs Communal Relationships
What it is
Two complementary models of how relationships develop and how they operate once developed.
The Friendship Formula, attributed to former FBI behavioral analyst Jack Schafer (presented in his 2015 book The Like Switch):

Friendship = Proximity + Frequency + Duration + Intensity

A working model — not a tested equation in the strict experimental-psychology sense — for what inputs produce relationship depth.
Exchange vs communal relationships, from Margaret Clark and Judson Mills (originally 1979, JPSP; extensive follow-on work). A formal distinction between two fundamentally different rule-sets that can govern an interaction:

Exchange relationships — strict reciprocity, tracked balance of inputs and outputs
Communal relationships — response to need without expectation of equivalent return

The two models go together because Schafer’s formula describes how a relationship develops intensity, while Clark and Mills describe how the rules of exchange shift as that intensity grows.
Why it matters
Two practical questions these models answer:

Why do some relationships feel stuck? Usually one or more of the four formula inputs is missing. Most often: frequency without intensity (you see them often but never go deep), or intensity without frequency (one great conversation a year)
Why do some interactions go badly even between people who like each other? Often because one party is operating on exchange rules and the other on communal rules. Offering to repay your spouse for cooking dinner is offensive precisely because it imposes exchange logic on a communal context — it downgrades the relationship

Details
The Friendship Formula — four inputs
Proximity — physical or virtual distance. The opportunity for interaction. Without proximity, the other three inputs cannot fire. This is why long-distance friendships decay even between people who genuinely like each other, and why colleagues who sit near each other develop bonds that geographically dispersed teammates do not.
Frequency — how often the encounters happen. Capitalizes on the mere exposure effect. High frequency is the default for coworkers and household members; low frequency for friends from previous chapters of life.
Duration — how long each encounter lasts. There’s an inverse relationship between frequency and duration: people who see each other daily can sustain a bond on short interactions, but people who see each other once a year need extended sessions to maintain the same depth. This is why annual visits with old friends feel “compressed” — the duration is doing the work that frequency normally would.
Intensity — psychological depth of the interaction. Governed by the exchange of vulnerabilities and the satisfaction of psychological needs. A 30-minute conversation that surfaced something real outweighs five hours of small talk for relationship depth. Intensity is the input most under deliberate control — you can choose to bring up the harder topic.
The four interact: high frequency makes intensity easier (each conversation is one of many, so each carries less individual weight), and high duration creates space for intensity to surface naturally.
Schafer’s “Golden Rule of Friendship”
Schafer summarizes much of his FBI behavioral-analyst work into a single principle: if you want people to like you, make them feel good about themselves. This is not flattery — flattery is detected and resented. It is creating conditions in which the other person experiences themselves as competent, interesting, valued, or heard. The mechanisms in conversational-responsiveness are the operationalization.
Exchange relationships — the default for new contacts
Exchange rules:

Inputs and outputs are tracked
A favor creates an immediate obligation to repay at roughly equivalent value
Equity is judged by ledger
Emotional expression is moderate
Default for new acquaintances, business contexts, transactional interactions

Clark and Mills tested the exchange/communal distinction in a series of clean experiments. In one canonical setup, subjects were paired with a partner on a joint task and given pens of multiple colors. Subjects in the exchange condition (where they had been induced to view the relationship transactionally) reliably picked different-colored pens from their partner — a behavior that preserved the legibility of who contributed what. Subjects in the communal condition (induced to view the relationship as based on mutual care) chose the same color, deliberately blurring individual contribution.
Communal relationships — what mature bonds become
Communal rules:

Inputs and outputs are deliberately not tracked
Help flows in response to need, not in response to past favors
Equity is judged by attentiveness to need over long horizons, not by per-transaction balance
Emotional expression is significantly higher
Default for family, close friends, long-term partners

Imposing exchange norms on a communal relationship is corrosive. Offering to “repay” a partner for emotional support, keeping score of household chores down to the task, or invoicing a friend for a favor all transmit the message: I do not see this as a communal relationship. Clark and Mills’ subjects rated such moves as actively offensive, not merely awkward.
How a relationship transitions from exchange to communal
This transition is under-specified in the original literature but the practical pattern is consistent: trust accumulates through a series of small, asymmetric, unrequited acts of care that aren’t immediately reciprocated, and aren’t expected to be. Each unrequited act is a credible signal that the giver has shifted toward communal rules. Over time, both parties update.
This is why early relationship-building can feel inefficient — it requires repeated small gifts of attention, time, or help with no near-term return. It is also why the rush to “balance the books” early kills the transition: enforcing exchange in the formative phase signals that you are not, in fact, ready to move past it.
Failure modes

Frequency without intensity — the colleague you eat lunch with daily for years and never know
Intensity without frequency — the friend you have one great conversation with annually that produces less depth than expected
Asymmetric exchange/communal coding — one party thinks “we’re close, I can call them about anything,” the other party is keeping a ledger and resents the imbalance
Premature communal claim — treating a new acquaintance as if you were already in a communal relationship; reads as presumptuous or transactional-by-overcompensation
Long-term exchange enforcement — the spouse who calculates fairness per-transaction; the friend who tracks who paid for dinner last

Practical counters

For stuck relationships: identify which of the four formula inputs is missing and whether you can supply it. Frequency is often the cheapest fix
For depth: bring up the harder topic in one out of every five conversations rather than waiting for it to surface naturally
For communal-stage relationships: consciously stop tracking. Notice when you reach for a ledger and let it drop
For early-stage relationships: assume exchange rules apply, and let the asymmetric small gifts of attention do the work of moving the relationship along

Related

Sources

Clark, M. S., Mills, J. (1979) — “Interpersonal attraction in exchange and communal relationships” — Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Clark, M. S., Mills, J. (1993) — “The difference between communal and exchange relationships: What it is and is not” — Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

general/harari-information-vs-truth.title: Harari: Information vs Truth
general/harari-information-vs-truth.content:
Harari: Information vs Truth
What it is
In Nexus (2024), Yuval Noah Harari argues that information and truth are distinct categories that the modern “naive view” routinely conflates. The naive view holds that information → truth → wisdom → power, with more data automatically improving each downstream step. Harari claims this reverses the actual function of information: most information that has ever existed — myths, scripture, brand stories, currency, propaganda, bureaucratic records — was never trying to represent reality. Its defining function is connection (tying minds, institutions, and behaviors into coordinated wholes), not representation (accurately depicting how things are). Truth-tracking is a special case of what information does, not its default.
The often-quoted formulation: “information has no essential link to truth.”
Why it matters
Carrying this distinction into AI use disarms a common implicit assumption — that an LLM, being an information-generation engine, is therefore a truth-generation engine. LLMs are optimized for coherence, fluency, and stylistic fit (the connection-function); world-representation accuracy is something that has to be enforced from outside, by verification. The naive view is precisely the assumption the vault’s bias-aware verification stack exists to counter.
The same frame clarifies which claims in any artifact actually need truth-tests. Many claims in organizational, social, and personal artifacts are non-empirical by design (identity, coordination, narrative); applying truth-tests to them is a category error in the other direction. This is the same cut claim-function-scan makes at the document level.
Details
The two functions of information























FunctionWhat it doesExamplesBound by truth?RepresentationDepicts reality accuratelyScientific paper, weather forecast, sensor readingYes — falsifiable in principleConnectionCoordinates a network of minds and institutionsMoney, nation, scripture, brand, party platform, corporate missionNo — coherence + adoption suffice
Most information operates on the connection axis. The representation axis is a special case whose value happens to depend on empirical accuracy. The naive view conflates the two, assuming all information is representation-information, or that “more representation-information automatically wins.” As a result, it gets the failure modes of large information systems wrong.
Three reality registers
Harari distinguishes three registers (drawing on a long social-science lineage, not original to him; see Sources):

Objective — true regardless of belief; physics, biology, the contents of an empty room.
Subjective — exists if one mind believes it; pain, preference, mood.
Intersubjective — exists because a network of minds believes it; money, nations, corporations, gods, laws, scientific paradigms. Not “false” — real in their effects — but not objective.

Most powerful information operates in the intersubjective register. Treating intersubjective claims as objective (or vice versa) is the central pathology Harari is naming.
Why truth loses a free fight — the cost asymmetry
The mechanism beneath “no essential link.” Truth and fiction don’t compete on equal terms; the asymmetry runs three ways (Harari’s argument as given in interviews around the book’s release; presumably also in the book itself, not checked against the text):

Truth is costly — research, evidence, expertise take time and money. Fiction is nearly free to produce.
Truth is complicated — reality rarely fits a clean narrative. Fiction can be exactly as simple as its audience wants.
Truth is often painful — unflattering to persons and nations. Fiction can be shaped to flatter ingrained beliefs.

So in an unregulated information market the equilibrium favors fiction: “more information” doesn’t drift toward truth, it drifts toward cheap, simple, and flattering. The connection-function wins by default economics, not only by historical accident. Generative AI collapses the production cost of fiction-shaped content still further, widening an asymmetry that was already lopsided.
Self-correcting mechanisms — Harari’s positive thesis
Harari’s prescription follows from the cost asymmetry: since truth loses a free fight, truth-tracking has to be paid for via self-correcting mechanisms (SCMs) — institutionalized error-detection that is empowered to revise the network’s own canon. Peer review, appellate courts, a free press, constitutional amendment. His running contrast: the US Constitution’s Article V acknowledges the document’s human, fallible origin and builds in a revision procedure; scripture that claims infallibility structurally cannot self-correct.
The predictive claim: what distinguishes truth-tracking networks is not how much information they process but how strong and independent their SCMs are. His AI worry, restated in these terms: AI-scale networks may generate and propagate content faster than human-speed SCMs can correct. A further vault inference (ours): because SCMs are pure cost on the order axis, they are the first thing competitive pressure trims.
There is pushback on the AI half: Johnson (2025) argues that AI development already embeds feedback loops (iterative deployment, user feedback, evals) and that Harari’s “alien intelligence” framing underplays them. The vault counter-reading (ours, not Johnson’s): those loops mostly optimize engagement and helpfulness — connection-axis metrics — so whether they count as SCMs in Harari’s sense depends on whether anything in the loop rewards representation-accuracy specifically.
Truth vs order — the standing tension
Every durable information network has to do two things at once: discover truth and create order. These pull against each other:

Pure truth-seeking erodes shared fictions, weakening the network’s coordination capacity.
Pure order-keeping suppresses inconvenient truths, weakening the network’s grip on reality.

Historical institutions have mostly optimized for order and treated truth as a side-effect when it was cheap. The exceptions — scientific institutions, market-pricing systems, adversarial legal/journalistic systems — are explicit attempts to build truth-seeking infrastructure that doesn’t immediately collapse under order pressure.
Implication for AI (vault reading)
This section is the vault’s bridge, not a direct quote from Harari. LLMs and recommender systems sit squarely on the connection axis. Their training objectives reward engagement, coherence, and stylistic fit; they have no built-in mechanism that rewards representation-accuracy as such. A naive “more LLM throughput → more truth” expectation misreads what the system is optimizing.
This is Harari’s frame applied to the same mechanism that ai-output-bias-fingerprints describes at the artifact level: fluent + coherent + confident is the production-target, not a byproduct of accuracy. The bias-aware verification stack exists because the truth-axis has to be enforced externally — the model doesn’t enforce it.
The per-utterance version: LLM output as Frankfurtian “bullshit”
Academic philosophy reached the same conclusion through a different door. Hicks, Humphries & Slater (2024) argue LLM falsehoods are best understood as bullshit in Harry Frankfurt’s sense — speech produced with indifference to truth — rather than lies (which require intent to deceive) or “hallucinations” (which imply a perceptual malfunction in an otherwise truth-tracking system). They distinguish hard bullshit (active deception about the nature of the enterprise) from soft bullshit (mere unconcern for truth) and argue LLMs meet at least the soft definition. This is the per-utterance restatement of Harari’s network-level claim: the system’s production target is truth-apt-looking text, not truth.
The framing is contested: Gunkel & Coghlan (2025) reply that Frankfurt’s bullshitter has attitudes and motives LLMs lack, so “bullshit” anthropomorphizes in its own way, and that “hallucination”/“confabulation” may remain useful metaphors. Note what the dispute is about — which anthropomorphism misleads least. Neither side claims the system is truth-tracking by design, which is the load-bearing point for verification practice.
The policy operationalization: epistemic security
The truth-vs-order tension is becoming a security field. The epistemic security literature treats reliable information supply chains as infrastructure a democracy needs to deliberate and respond to crises (Elizabeth Seger and colleagues; Demos reports Epistemic Security 2029, 2025, and Epistemic Security for Crisis Resilience, 2026) — i.e., it frames defending self-correcting mechanisms as a national-security problem rather than an academic virtue. Adjacent: Coeckelbergh (2022) argues AI threatens citizens’ epistemic agency — the capacity to control how one forms and revises beliefs — via recommender bubbles and pressure to defer to AI-equipped experts, and that losing epistemic agency erodes political agency itself.
The note’s own frame predicts the failure mode here: securitizing the truth-axis is an order-axis move. Whoever defines what counts as a threat to “epistemic security” holds order-keeping power over the information network, so the field carries its own truth-vs-order tension rather than escaping it.
Is the slogan even right? The veridicality debate
“Information has no essential link to truth” is contested terrain in philosophy of information — a literature Nexus doesn’t appear to engage (unverified negative; based on reviews, not a bibliography check). Luciano Floridi’s veridicality thesis defines semantic information as well-formed, meaningful, and truthful data: on this view false “information” is not information at all but misinformation, and the factivity requirement is doing real work (it dissolves the Bar-Hillel–Carnap paradox, where contradictions would otherwise count as maximally informative). Dretske (1981) held a similarly factive view; Primiero (2009) and others reject the thesis.
Part of the disagreement is terminological — Harari uses “information” in the everyday/engineering sense (whatever flows through networks), Floridi in the factive sense (what you can learn from). But the translation is instructive in both directions: under Floridi’s usage Harari’s slogan is false by definition; under Harari’s usage Floridi’s definition concedes the empirical point — most of what circulates in information networks isn’t (Floridian) information at all. Either way the operational lesson survives intact: truth-boundness is a property to be checked, never assumed.
Limits and criticisms
Harari’s broad-historical-synthesis style draws standard objections that apply here too:

He compresses multi-century debates into legible binaries. The truth/order tension is real but more textured in any specific institution than the chapter-length summary admits.
The “intersubjective” register is not original to Nexus. Searle’s The Construction of Social Reality (1995) and Berger & Luckmann’s The Social Construction of Reality (1966) are direct upstream sources. Harari popularizes; he does not originate.
The book’s prescriptive sections (what AI governance should look like) are weaker than the descriptive frame and have drawn skeptical reviews. The framing-of-the-problem is the more durable contribution.
The “alien intelligence” framing of AI draws specific criticism: reviewers argue it commits the dehumanization-of-the-other move Harari himself warns against, and that “aggregate human intelligence” (a system reflecting human training data, steered by human feedback) describes current systems better.

For vault use, the value is the framing — information ≠ truth, function determines verification regime — not the specific historical narratives or policy proposals.
Related

falsifiability-claim-fingerprints — shape-of-claim catalog that the empirical half routes into
bias-aware-verification-protocol — per-output protocol that enforces the truth-axis externally on LLM outputs
ai-output-bias-fingerprints — production-target framing (fluent + coherent ≠ true) at model-output level
ai-automation-biases — human-side biases that make the naive view sticky (fluency-as-accuracy illusion, automation bias)

Sources

Harari, Y. N. (2024). Nexus: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI. Penguin Random House.
Wink, C. (2025-02-02). “Information has no essential link to truth”: Yuval Noah Harari in Nexus. christopherwink.com/2025/02/02/information-has-no-essential-link-to-truth-yuval-noah-harari-in-nexus/

general/higher-order-thinking-skills.title: Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS)
general/higher-order-thinking-skills.content:
Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS)
Hub note for the higher-order-thinking cluster — the umbrella term for cognitive processes above recall and routine application: analysis, evaluation, synthesis/creation, argumentation, analogical reasoning, and metacognitive self-regulation. The companion note teaching-higher-order-thinking holds the intervention evidence (what actually moves the needle); this note holds the conceptual frameworks, the cognitive constraints, and the measurement problem.
Drafted from an incoming AI-generated research report (2026-06-16). The taxonomies and the domain-specificity argument are well-established; the effect sizes that report carried are handled in the companion note, where each is verified or flagged. One implausible figure in the source (a metacognition effect of d ≈ 3.29 in statistics) was dropped as almost certainly a misread.
Why this is in the vault
The user’s working hypothesis is that higher-order thinking is the skill that appreciates most as AI capability compounds. That bet is plausible but not free — it’s the cognitive-science twin of the appreciating-skills argument in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age and skills-to-train-for-ai-future (“verification, judgment, problem selection survive; production depreciates”). This cluster exists to supply the grounding those notes lean on — and the counterweight: HOTS research says these skills are real and trainable, but also that they ride on deep domain knowledge and transfer poorly, which complicates any “train general thinking and you’re safe” reading. See the Future-skill framing section, which is deliberately written against the premise rather than around it.
What counts as “higher-order” — four taxonomies
There is no single agreed definition; there are competing classification systems, each measuring a different axis. The useful move is to know which axis each one measures.



































FrameworkMeasures”Higher-order” isKey limitationBloom (Revised, Anderson & Krathwohl 2001)Type of cognitive processApplying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating (vs. Remembering, Understanding)Verb-based; the same verb (“describe”) can be recall or deep analysis. Original 1956 model assumed a strict prerequisite ladder that cognitive science has since softened.Webb’s Depth of Knowledge (DOK, 1997)Complexity/depth of processing a task demandsStrategic Thinking (L3), Extended Thinking (L4)Measures cognitive rigor, not content difficulty — explicitly orthogonal to Bloom.SOLO (Biggs & Collis 1982)Structural quality of the observed responseRelational (integrates parts), Extended Abstract (generalizes to new domains)Assesses what the learner actually produced, not the intended objective — strong for formative diagnosis.Marzano’s New Taxonomy (2000)Interaction of three mental systemsAnalysis + Knowledge Utilization, gated by the Metacognitive and Self-SystemsAdds motivation, self-efficacy, and self-regulation as preconditions for cognition, not just the cognition itself.
Two structural points worth keeping:

Bloom and Webb are orthogonal, not redundant. Karin Hess’s Cognitive Rigor Matrix crosses them deliberately: an “Evaluate” task (Bloom) can be low-depth (rate a story by preference) or high-depth (critique a paper’s statistical validity). The verb tells you the process; DOK tells you the rigor. You need both to specify a task.
The strict-ladder assumption is the part to drop. The original Bloom claim that you must master lower tiers before higher ones is the most-critiqued piece — foundational knowledge and higher-order reasoning are acquired intertwined, not sequentially. This matters because it’s the assumption behind “teach all the facts first, then think” curricula.

The cognitive constraint: why HOTS is hard to deploy
Higher-order reasoning runs against a fixed bottleneck — working-memory capacity (~4±1 unrelated items; see cognitive-load-theory-for-ai for the full intrinsic/extraneous/germane decomposition, which this vault already ported to AI prompt design). Analogical reasoning and complex problem-solving are working-memory-intensive: you must hold multiple concepts, compare their relational structure, and evaluate candidates simultaneously. When total load exceeds capacity, reasoning doesn’t degrade gracefully — it collapses.
Two consequences the research emphasizes:

Executive function is the gate. Relational thinking requires inhibiting the pull toward surface similarity and directing attention to deep structure. Stress, anxiety, and poor emotional regulation deplete exactly this control — they hijack working memory with rumination. (This connects to sidi-stress-cognition.)
Schemas in long-term memory are the workaround. Experts “chunk” — compressing many facts into single conceptual units — which frees working memory for evaluation. This is the same chunking mechanism described in cognitive-load-theory-for-ai. It’s also the hinge of the domain-specificity debate below: chunking only works on knowledge you already hold.

Higher-order thinking correlates strongly with fluid intelligence (Gf) — domain-general reasoning over novel problems — and childhood working-memory capacity predicts later complex problem-solving. But the functional efficiency of working memory is improvable through better schemas, even where raw capacity is fixed. So the pessimistic read (“it’s mostly innate Gf”) and the optimistic read (“it’s trainable”) are both partly right: baseline capacity is largely given; the schemas that let you use it are built.
The domain-specificity debate (and its resolution)
The most-contested question: is critical thinking a general, transferable skill (learn logic/fallacies/probabilistic reasoning once, apply everywhere) or domain-specific (inseparable from deep background knowledge of the subject)?

General view: critical thinking is a set of overarching strategies — spot fallacies, evaluate sources, reason about probability — teachable in isolation.
Domain-specific view (Willingham and others): you cannot critically evaluate an argument without deep factual knowledge of its subject, and what counts as “good thinking” differs by discipline (historical interpretation vs. mathematical proof vs. experimental method). A novice without background knowledge overloads working memory just holding the facts, leaving nothing for evaluation.

The evidence resolves toward a both/and, and it has a direct pedagogical consequence (carried into teaching-higher-order-thinking): general heuristics exist and help, but they only deploy when the reasoner already holds the domain knowledge to chunk against. Transfer to genuinely novel domains is rare without explicit bridging instruction. The practical upshot — the “mixed” approach — is to teach the general strategy explicitly and immediately practice it inside specific content, not one or the other.

This is the single most important takeaway for the “future-skill” bet: “general higher-order thinking” that floats free of domain knowledge is mostly a myth. The transferable part is real but thin; the powerful part is welded to expertise.

Measuring it is genuinely contested
Assessment is where the field is weakest, which matters if you want to track whether practice is working.

Standardized critical-thinking tests — Watson-Glaser (WGCTA), California (CCTST), Cornell (CCTT) — share a recurring psychometric criticism: at the subscale level their factor structure is unstable, and they load heavily on general verbal/reading ability rather than cleanly separable critical-thinking sub-skills. They predict academic aptitude (correlate with SAT/GRE) but may be measuring a unidimensional reasoning-plus-reading construct.
The Halpern assessment (HCTA) is the structural standout: it mixes constructed-response (recall) and forced-choice (recognition), so it measures both the capacity to spot a flaw and the disposition to do the effortful reasoning. Its strongest validity evidence is that scores predict real-world decision outcomes — avoiding the consequences of poor everyday judgment — rather than just other test scores (Butler and colleagues; framing reported in the source, the real-world-outcome link is well-attested).
Large-scale (PISA): the 2015 Collaborative Problem-Solving module had students “collaborate” with scripted computer agents via restricted menus — a documented design choice. Critics argue this measured human-computer interaction and reading comprehension, not genuine collaboration (no real social interdependence, trust, or unstructured conflict). It’s a clean cautionary case of ecological validity lost when a fluid skill is forced into a computer-scorable format.

The durable lesson: there is no clean, uncontested instrument for higher-order thinking. Any self-assessment of “am I getting better at this” should lean on real-world decision outcomes and produced-artifact quality (the SOLO axis), not on a single test score.
Future-skill framing — read against the counterargument
The reason this cluster exists is the hypothesis that HOTS is the appreciating skill under AI. The honest version:

Supporting it: the appreciating column in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age — verification, judgment, problem selection, architecture — is operationally higher-order thinking (analyze/evaluate/create, applied to machine output you didn’t produce). AI collapses the cost of lower-order production (recall, routine application, first drafts), which is exactly the LOTS band. If production is free, the residual value is in the evaluation and synthesis layers HOTS names.
Against it (keep this): (1) HOTS research says higher-order thinking is welded to domain knowledge — so “train general thinking” is not a substitute for deep expertise, it’s a multiplier on it. A person with strong general reasoning and no domain depth has little to evaluate with. (2) Lists of “AI-proof skills” have aged badly (creativity, prose, Go were all on 2015 safe-lists). Evaluation and judgment are themselves active automation targets — see the consensus-echo and discontinuous-jump counters in skills-to-train-for-ai-future. what-survived-machine-conquest is the empirical record this point gestures at — which human practices actually died vs survived past machine conquest, and the pipe/bundle property that predicted which. And it cuts both ways: the practice usually migrated up the judgment layer (supporting the bet), but the incumbent whose skill was the automated function was downgraded anyway (the warning the bet hides). (3) The skills here are real and trainable, which is the genuinely good news — but trainable-by-deliberate-practice, not absorbed-by-exposure (the central finding of teaching-higher-order-thinking).

The defensible position is not “bet everything on general higher-order thinking” but: higher-order thinking is the appreciating layer when fused with domain depth and kept on a feedback loop — and that fusion is exactly what the evidence-based interventions in the companion note are designed to build.
higher-order-thinking-under-ai takes this section further by reading the AI-future question from the taxonomy down rather than from the labor market: which Bloom tiers a machine in the loop absorbs (both ends — recall and the generative half of Create), why the pyramid’s difficulty ordering stops predicting value, and the foundation paradox — that the Evaluate tier appreciates while the same automation cuts the lower-tier reps that build the domain schemas Evaluate depends on.
Related

general/higher-order-thinking-under-ai.title: Higher-Order Thinking Under AI
general/higher-order-thinking-under-ai.content:
Higher-Order Thinking Under AI
Third note in the higher-order-thinking cluster, and the one that turns the cluster toward the working-alongside-AI question directly. The hub higher-order-thinking-skills establishes the taxonomies and the domain-specificity constraint; teaching-higher-order-thinking holds the intervention evidence. This note asks the AI-era question from the taxonomy down: when a machine sits inside the cognitive loop, which tiers of higher-order thinking does it absorb, which become the human’s residual job, and does the difficulty ordering the taxonomies encode still predict where value lands?
The vault already answers the labor-market version of this in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age and ai/skills-to-train-for-ai-future (“verification, judgment, problem selection appreciate; production depreciates”). This note is the cognitive-science restatement of that bet, plus the place where the restatement breaks it. The point of writing it taxonomy-first is that the taxonomy makes a prediction the labor-market framing doesn’t: it says exactly which mental operations should appreciate, and it carries its own counterexample (the foundation paradox below) inside the same vocabulary.
The reallocation across Bloom’s ladder
Take Bloom’s revised tiers (Anderson & Krathwohl 2001; full sourcing in the hub) and ask, for each, who performs it now in an AI-assisted workflow. The answer is not “AI takes the low tiers, humans keep the high ones.” It’s stranger — AI absorbs from both ends.















































Tier (revised Bloom)The operationWho does it nowThe human residualRememberRecall facts, syntax, APIsAI, fullyKnowing which recall is worth distrustingUnderstandExplain, summarize, paraphraseAI (this is translation-layer work it natively is)Checking the explanation is faithful, not fluent-but-wrongApplyRun a known procedure on a new caseAI (routine implementation)Choosing which procedure, and catching off-distribution misapplicationAnalyzeDecompose, find relational structureShared / contestedFraming the decomposition; owning what the parts meanEvaluateJudge an artifact against criteriaMaximally humanThe load-bearing residual — judging output you didn’t produceCreateGenerate a novel artifactAI generates; human directsDeciding what to create and answering for it — not generating it
Two tiers don’t behave the way Bloom’s pyramid trains you to expect:

Create — the top tier — splits, and its production half falls to the bottom of the value stack. Bloom puts Create at the apex. But “Create” bundles two operations that AI separates cleanly: generating the artifact (now nearly free) and deciding what to generate and owning the result (still scarce). This is the generate/adjudicate line cutting straight through Bloom’s highest tier. The generative half — the literal pinnacle of the taxonomy — is the single cheapest thing in the AI workflow.
Evaluate — one tier below the apex — is where the human value concentrates. Judging machine output you didn’t produce, at volume, without the comprehension that producing it used to force. This is exactly “verification & taste” in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age, arriving here as a specific Bloom tier rather than a labor-market category.

This is the same cut that what-survived-machine-conquest finds across two centuries of automation, under a different name. Its one-line predictor: a role died where the human was a pipe — a pure input→output transformation fully specifiable as a procedure — and survived where judgment, liability, or authorship was bundled in. Bloom’s lower tiers plus Create’s generative half are the pipe; the Evaluate-and-own residual is the bundle. The taxonomy and the casualty record are describing the same boundary from two directions — which is the strongest external check this note’s reallocation has, since the historical pattern was derived without reference to Bloom.
The value-inversion: Bloom’s pyramid is a difficulty ranking misread as a value ranking
The reallocation table only looks paradoxical because of an assumption baked into how the pyramid is usually read. Bloom’s ordering is a ranking of difficulty-for-humans — Create sits on top because synthesizing something novel was the hardest thing an unaided human mind did. Over decades that difficulty ranking quietly became a value ranking: “higher on the pyramid = more valuable thinking.”
AI breaks the coupling. It collapses the cost of the operations that were hard for humans (generation, synthesis, fluent production) while leaving hard the operations that are hard to automate (judging against criteria you hold, deciding what is worth making, owning the outcome). So under AI:

Value tracks resistance to automation, not height on Bloom’s pyramid. The two used to correlate because both were proxies for “hard.” AI decouples them — generation was high-on-Bloom and hard-for-humans, but it is not hard-to-automate. Read the pyramid by the automation axis and it partly inverts: the apex (Create’s generative half) drops, and the Evaluate band rises above it.

This is the same claim skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age makes with “generation cost fell faster than verification cost,” restated in the taxonomy’s own units. The taxonomy adds precision the labor-market version lacks: it names which cognitive operation appreciates (Evaluate-against-held-criteria, plus the metacognitive gate below) rather than the fuzzy “judgment.”
The foundation paradox
Here is where the taxonomy-native reading earns its place — it carries the counterexample to its own optimism inside the same framework.
The hub’s domain-specificity finding is that higher-order thinking is welded to domain knowledge: you cannot meaningfully Evaluate an artifact without the schemas to chunk it against, and a novice without those schemas overloads working memory just holding the facts, leaving nothing for evaluation. The Evaluate tier — the one that appreciates — requires deep domain schemas as its input.
Those schemas were historically built by doing the lower tiers: Understand and Apply, performed many times, until the facts compress into chunks (the hub’s chunking mechanism). The lower tiers are the developmental supply chain for the upper ones. And those lower tiers are exactly what AI now absorbs.
So the automation that makes evaluative thinking valuable is the same automation that cuts the pipeline that produces the capacity to do it:

A practitioner who already holds the schemas gets a multiplier — they can Evaluate machine output fast and well, the leverage skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age describes.
A practitioner who offloaded the lower-tier reps before the schemas formed has nothing to evaluate with. They can run the Evaluate ritual — read the diff, nod at the output — without the chunked domain knowledge that makes the judgment real. The result is rubber-stamping that looks like evaluation.

This is the taxonomy-level version of skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age’s “senior judgment is an appreciating asset built on a depreciating ladder,” and of augmented-vs-trained-thinking’s offloading-mediation evidence (Gerlich 2025: AI use degrades critical thinking through offloading, not through mere presence). Stated as a taxonomy claim it is sharper: the appreciating tier depends on inputs the same technology removes. The honest limit — this is an argument about a developmental pipeline, not a measured long-run effect; the offloading-mediation evidence is cross-sectional and adult-classroom, and whether it compounds into eroded expertise over a career is unproven (the same transfer caveat teaching-higher-order-thinking flags).
what-survived-machine-conquest supplies both the historical warning and its sharpest counter-case. The warning is its incumbent asymmetry: across past automation shocks the labor market recovered — future cohorts did fine — while the individuals whose specific skill was the automated function were permanently downgraded (the cleanest case being the Feigenbaum–Gross switchboard-operator result). That is the foundation paradox at the scale of a career rather than a tier. The counter-case is the live datum that the paradox is not inevitable: after AlphaGo, serious Go players’ decision quality rose sharply because they trained against the superhuman engine rather than offloading to it — and a companion study found the gains largest for younger and weaker players (both findings sourced in that note). So superhuman AI in the loop need not starve schema-building; whether it does turns on the generate/adjudicate split — offload the reps and the schemas never form; produce against the machine and they do. The foundation paradox is the default, not the destiny.
Metacognition becomes the gate
Marzano’s taxonomy (hub) elevates the metacognitive system above cognition: it decides whether and how the lower systems engage at all. Under AI that gate carries the heaviest load, because the characteristic failure mode is automation bias — accepting fluent output without engaging Evaluate at all (ai-automation-biases: verification asymmetry, accountability diffusion).
The load-bearing metacognitive question shifts from “how do I solve this” to “is my domain schema strong enough to judge this output, or am I about to rubber-stamp it?” That is calibration about one’s own competence boundary — knowing the edge of what you can actually evaluate versus what merely looks evaluated. It is the cheapest high-leverage rep in the cluster: the predict-then-compare move (commit your own answer before querying, then diff) is exactly a metacognitive-gate drill, and it feeds the calibration loop. The foundation paradox is what makes this tier load-bearing rather than optional — when the schemas may be thin, the only defense against rubber-stamping is a calibrated read of whether they’re thin.
Counterargument worth keeping
The bias-aware default: draft the case against before committing.

Consensus-echo. “Evaluation and judgment appreciate” is the comfortable answer for people who already hold domain expertise — which is exactly when to distrust it (the same flag ai/skills-to-train-for-ai-future raises). Evaluate is itself an active automation target: LLM-as-judge, self-verification, and cross-model checking all aim straight at it. If they mature, the inversion doesn’t stop at Evaluate — it keeps climbing, and there is no stable human tier, just a receding frontier.
The taxonomy may be the wrong unit. Bloom describes operations inside one human mind. Human-plus-AI is a distributed cognitive system, and the extended-mind reading (augmented-vs-trained-thinking, Clark & Chalmers) says “which tier does the human hold” is the wrong question — system capability is the unit, and asking who performs Evaluate is like asking which neuron holds the thought. Partial concession: this is right for permanently-available, low-stakes work; it fails precisely where the AI’s output is the thing being judged and a human must answer for it, because there the unaided evaluative capacity is the load-bearing one.
The inversion assumes the asymmetry holds. The whole value-inversion rests on generation staying cheap and evaluation staying hard. That gap is a premise, not a law (it’s the same load-bearing premise flagged in skill-valuation-in-the-ai-age). If evaluation cost falls toward generation cost, the taxonomy stops predicting anything useful about where human value sits.

The defensible position is the cluster’s throughout: higher-order thinking is the appreciating layer when fused with domain depth and kept on a feedback loop — and the foundation paradox means that fusion is now something you have to protect against your own tooling, not something AI delivers for free.
A live stress-test of this thesis (appreciating-position-vs-skill, 2026-06-16) pushed it one step further and partly against itself: if AI can perform all four higher-order operations, the residue that survives may not be a thinking tier at all but a position — the principal who originates purpose and bears accountability. That would mean this note still names the wrong unit (a cognitive operation rather than a stance), and it’s the sharpest open challenge to the cluster’s framing.
Related

Sources
Drafted 2026-06-16. This note is an argument built on the cluster’s already-sourced foundations rather than a new evidence synthesis, so it cites internally rather than re-introducing external figures:

general/how-much-information-at-once.title: How Much Information to Give at Once
general/how-much-information-at-once.content:
How Much Information to Give at Once
The sender-side question — how much can I put in this message? — has no absolute answer, and the number people reach for (7±2) is the wrong instrument for it. The binding constraint is not how many items you sent. It is how many of them the receiver has to hold simultaneously to make sense of any one of them, and how many of those they already have a schema for.
This is the human-receiver counterpart to information-density-in-written-text (surface density of the text itself) and cognitive-load-theory-for-ai (load on an AI executor). Same load decomposition, different substrate.
The unit that binds: element interactivity
Cognitive Load Theory’s actual predictor of intrinsic difficulty is element interactivity — whether elements can be understood one at a time or only in relation to each other (Sweller, 2010).

Low interactivity: ten independent facts. Each lands or doesn’t, independently. Cheap, and the count barely matters.
High interactivity: four facts where each only makes sense given the other three. Expensive, and four may already be too many.

Vocabulary lists are low-interactivity; the grammar that combines them is high. A status update listing five unrelated items is low; a design rationale where the constraint, the tradeoff, and the chosen mechanism only cohere together is high. Count interacting elements, not sentences or bullets.
This is why “make it shorter” so often fails to help. Cutting a high-interactivity explanation in half doesn’t halve the load — it removes the connective material that let the pieces cohere, and the receiver now has to reconstruct it.
What the capacity numbers do and don’t say

Miller (1956) — “the magical number seven, plus or minus two” — measured immediate serial recall of unrelated items (digits, letters). It was never a comprehension budget, and Miller’s own paper is substantially about chunking as the escape hatch.
Cowan (2001) — revised the figure to ~4±1 once rehearsal and chunking are experimentally controlled.

Neither number tells you how many ideas to put in an email. What transfers is the shape of the constraint, plus the mechanism that relaxes it:
A chunk is expertise-relative. Chase & Simon (1973) found chess experts reconstructed real board positions far better than novices — and that the advantage largely collapsed for randomly arranged pieces. The expert wasn’t holding more; they were holding fewer, larger units, and only where their schemas applied. The same message is literally a different quantity of information to two people.
The often-repeated version of that result — that the expert advantage vanishes on random boards — is overstated. Gobet & Simon (1996) reviewed the random-position control conditions and found stronger players retain a small but reliable superiority even there, just far smaller than on game positions. The correction matters for the argument: schema-leverage explains most of the capacity difference between two receivers, not all of it. Some of the gap is general skill you can’t hand someone in a paragraph.
The practical consequence: the number that predicts overload is novel, interacting elements — not total elements. Anything the receiver already has a chunk for is close to free.
The receiver-dependence problem
Three findings say the right amount cannot be set once and reused:

Expertise reversal (Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler & Sweller, 2003): instructional support that measurably helps novices measurably hurts experts. The extra scaffolding becomes material the expert must process and reconcile against a schema they already hold. This isn’t “experts don’t need it” — it’s that the same content actively degrades their performance.
The redundancy effect (Chandler & Sweller, 1991): restating content the receiver already has — narrating a self-explanatory diagram, re-explaining a known concept — impairs rather than reinforces. Kalyuga et al. treat expertise reversal as a form of this effect rather than a separate mechanism: the support isn’t neutral-but-wasted, it’s redundant, and redundant material still has to be processed and reconciled.
The curse of knowledge (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989): once you know something, you cannot accurately model what it’s like not to know it. Your estimate of what the receiver needs is systematically wrong, and the error does not feel like an error.

Together these mean you cannot introspect your way to the right amount. You can only get feedback. See also social-attribution-biases on the illusion of transparency — the same failure applied to whether your intent came across at all.
Two kinds of compaction — only one of them works
This is the actionable core. “Be more compact” names a goal, not a method, and the two available methods have opposite effects.



































Cut scopeCut cohesionWhat you removeIdeas, sections, tangents, the third exampleConnectives, context, transitions, explicit referentsEffect on word countDownDownEffect on densityFlat — fewer ideas in fewer wordsUp — same ideas in fewer wordsEffect on the receiverEasierHarder, while looking more professionalHow it feels to writeLike giving something upLike tightening
The second is the compression trap (lever 6 in information-density-in-written-text): deleting “that,” “because,” “however,” and explicit antecedents raises the inference burden on every clause. The author saves characters; the receiver pays with re-reads. Because it feels like craft, it’s the failure mode that survives editing passes.
The test after a compaction pass: did the idea count drop proportionally to the word count? If you cut 30% of the words and 0% of the ideas, you made it denser, not lighter. Cutting scope is almost always the right move; cutting cohesion almost never is. Fix-mode operations for the second case are in prose-revision-operations.
Channel sets the ceiling
The same payload has very different capacity limits depending on the channel, because channels differ in whether the receiver controls the pace and whether they get a second pass.



































ChannelReceiver-paced?Re-readable?Relative capacityWritten docYesYesHighestAsync message / emailYesYesHigh, but competes with a queueMeeting / callNo — you set the paceNoLowInterruption / hallwayNoNoLowest
Speech also runs at much lower lexical density than writing (Halliday, 1985) — spoken language spreads the same content across more words, which is a feature, not sloppiness. Reading a written-register paragraph aloud in a meeting is a common way to overload people who would have absorbed it fine as a document.
The move: match channel to interactivity. High-interactivity material (architecture rationale, tradeoffs, anything where the pieces only cohere together) goes in writing, and the meeting is for the decision. Low-interactivity material (status, ack, one fact) is fine spoken.
Working heuristics
These are heuristics for design decisions, not findings — the empirical literature above constrains them but does not produce them.

3–4 genuinely new, interacting ideas per document, meeting, or message. “New” means the receiver has no existing schema for it. Familiar material doesn’t count against the budget.
One decision per ask. Bundling two decisions reliably returns one answer and one deferral — and the deferral usually takes the whole message with it. Related: decision-fatigue.
Put the ask first. Point-first structure means the receiver knows what to hold the rest against; the mechanics are in readability-mechanics.
Available, not absent. Everything past the budget goes into an appendix, a link, or “ask me about X” — not deleted. This is what makes cutting scope safe.
Front and back, not middle. Serial-position effects (Murdock, 1962) mean the middle of a long list is where items get dropped. Load-bearing content goes at the top or the end.
Ask for the read-back. “What are you taking away from this?” beats any estimate you make of their capacity, because the curse of knowledge makes your estimate unreliable in a direction you can’t feel.

The failure-mode asymmetry
Under-informing and over-informing fail differently, and that asymmetry should drive the default.

Too little → they ask. You find out immediately, and the correction is cheap.
Too much → they don’t tell you. They silently drop items, act on the part they retained, or defer the whole thing. You find out weeks later, when the dropped item surfaces as a surprise.

Over-informing produces no error signal at the moment it fails. That argues for erring low and keeping the remainder reachable — the combination, not either alone. (This asymmetry is a design argument from the mechanisms above, not a measured result.)
Contested or thin

The tappers-and-listeners study — the widely-repeated demonstration that tappers predicted ~50% of listeners would identify a tapped song while ~2.5% actually did — traces to Elizabeth Newton’s 1990 Stanford dissertation, popularized by Heath & Heath’s Made to Stick. It is an unpublished dissertation with no independent replication established here. Treat the figures as illustrative of the curse-of-knowledge mechanism (which has stronger support), not as an established effect size.
The 3–4 idea heuristic has no direct empirical warrant. It’s an analogy from Cowan’s chunk figure to a domain (multi-paragraph comprehension) the chunk literature does not cover. It’s a reasonable starting default that should be recalibrated against your own receivers, not a finding.
Optimal quantity as a pragmatic norm. Grice’s maxim of quantity (1975) — be as informative as required for the current purposes of the exchange, and no more — states the target correctly but defines it circularly. It’s a good frame for asking the question (“required for what?”), not a procedure for answering it.

What this doesn’t cover

Group vs. individual receivers. A room has heterogeneous prior knowledge, so no single density is right for everyone in it. The expertise-reversal literature implies you’re degrading someone either way; how to handle that tradeoff is a separate question.
Motivation and trust. Capacity is not the only reason people drop information — disagreement, low stakes, and low trust in the sender all look identical to overload from the outside. Compacting a message that’s being ignored for political reasons won’t help.
Persuasion. This note is about transmission and comprehension. How much information to give when the goal is to change someone’s mind is a different literature with partly opposing recommendations.
Multi-session accumulation. Everything here is per-exchange. How much someone absorbs over a week of exchanges involves consolidation and spacing — see evidence-based-learning.

Counterargument
The strongest objection is that this note dresses ordinary communication advice in citations. “Lead with the ask, cut tangents, don’t over-explain to experts” is what any decent editor says; element interactivity and Cowan’s chunk figure don’t generate that advice, they decorate it.
The honest position, same as cognitive-load-theory-for-ai takes about itself: the value is diagnostic, not prescriptive. The mechanisms tell you which fix a given failure needs — that a message landing badly is an organization problem, not a length problem; that adding an explanation for a senior reviewer will make things worse rather than neutral; that the tightening pass just made comprehension harder. Someone who already knows which lever to pull gains nothing here.
A second objection cuts against the note’s whole direction: under-informing is a real failure too, and often the more expensive one. Withheld context reads as evasive, forces round-trips that cost far more than the paragraph you saved, and in low-trust settings compaction is indistinguishable from concealment. The instinct to compact is not self-evidently correct — it should be checked against whether the receiver is actually dropping things, or whether you’re optimizing for how the message looks to you.
Related

Sources
Capacity and load references are shared with cognitive-load-theory-for-ai (verified 2026-05-12); the additions below carry their own attribution. The synthesis into a sender-side procedure — the two-kinds-of-compaction table, the channel-capacity table, the heuristics, and the failure-mode asymmetry — is this note’s analytical extension and is not an empirical result.

Miller, G. A. (1956). “The magical number seven, plus or minus two.” Psychological Review, 63(2). Original capacity claim; also the origin of chunking as the escape hatch.
Cowan, N. (2001). “The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity.” Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1).
Chase, W. G. & Simon, H. A. (1973). “Perception in chess.” Cognitive Psychology, 4, 55–81. Expert recall advantage on real positions, largely absent on random ones — chunk relativity. [verified 2026-08-10]
Gobet, F. & Simon, H. A. (1996). “Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill.” Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 3, 159–163. The correction to the above: the expert advantage on random positions shrinks sharply but does not vanish. [verified 2026-08-10]
Sweller, J. (2010). “Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load.” Educational Psychology Review, 22(2). Element interactivity as the driver of intrinsic load.
Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P. & Sweller, J. (2003). “The expertise reversal effect.” Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23–31. [verified 2026-08-10] — note the authors frame expertise reversal as a form of the redundancy effect, not a separate mechanism.
Chandler, P. & Sweller, J. (1991). “Cognitive load theory and the format of instruction.” Cognition and Instruction, 8(4), 293–332. Redundancy and split-attention effects. [verified 2026-08-10]
Camerer, C., Loewenstein, G. & Weber, M. (1989). “The curse of knowledge in economic settings: An experimental analysis.” Journal of Political Economy, 97(5).
Murdock, B. B. (1962). “The serial position effect of free recall.” Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5).
Grice, H. P. (1975). “Logic and Conversation.” In Syntax and Semantics, Vol. 3. The maxim of quantity.
Halliday, M. A. K. (1985). Spoken vs. written lexical density.
Newton, E. (1990). Stanford PhD dissertation — tappers and listeners. Unpublished; see the Contested section before citing the figures.
