cognitive-bias-neuroscience — amygdala and mPFC activity behind in-group vs. out-group empathy gaps
debiasing-mental-models — the ladder of inference directly addresses attribution errors
ai-automation-biases — accountability diffusion is FAE applied to algorithmic systems

Sources

Ross, L. (1977) — “The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings” — Advances in Experimental Social Psychology
Tajfel, H. (1970) — “Experiments in intergroup discrimination” — Scientific American (minimal group paradigm)
Heath, C. (1999) — “On the social psychology of agency relationships: Lay theories of motivation overemphasize extrinsic incentives” — Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
Gilovich, T., Savitsky, K., Medvec, V. H. (1998) — “The illusion of transparency” — Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Loewenstein, G. (2005) — “Hot-cold empathy gaps and medical decision-making” — Health Psychology
Ross, L., Greene, D., House, P. (1977) — “The ‘false consensus effect’” — Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

general/soft-systems-methodology.title: Soft Systems Methodology
general/soft-systems-methodology.content:
Soft Systems Methodology
Scope of this note
A third systems-thinking tradition that sits between the engineering lens ([[systems-thinking-engineering]]) and the human / inner-conditions lens ([[systems-thinking]]). Where the engineering lens diagrams the structure of an external system and the human lens cultivates the operator, Soft Systems Methodology (SSM) sits in the middle: it treats the situation as perceived as the primary object of inquiry — including the disagreement between stakeholders about what the system even is.
Developed by Peter Checkland and colleagues at Lancaster University from the late 1960s onward; canonical reference is Checkland’s Systems Thinking, Systems Practice (1981), with practical refinements in Soft Systems Methodology in Action (Checkland & Scholes, 1990) and a compact restatement in Learning for Action (Checkland & Poulter, 2006).
What it is
A structured method for navigating “messes” — complex, ill-defined human situations where stakeholders hold conflicting views about what is wrong, what would count as improvement, and even what the relevant system is. Where hard systems engineering presupposes a known goal and optimises toward it, SSM treats the goal itself as part of what’s being inquired into.
The methodology is interpretive rather than prescriptive. A practitioner using SSM is not solving the situation; they are facilitating a structured comparison between the situation as it is and purposeful activity systems that different stakeholders can imagine, with the explicit goal of surfacing where those imaginings differ and producing changes that are systemically desirable and culturally feasible — both, not either.
The vocabulary “messes” comes from Russell Ackoff, who argued that managers rarely face isolated problems; they face dynamic, interacting sets of problems where attempting to solve each component independently does not optimise the whole. SSM is one practical response to that diagnosis.
Why it matters
The vault’s existing decision tools — [[wrap-framework]], [[ooda-loop]], [[recognition-primed-decision]] — assume the decision-maker has a roughly stable understanding of the problem. The engineering systems lens assumes the analyst can sketch a structurally honest map of the system. Both fail in the situations SSM was designed for: where ten people in the room would draw ten different maps and disagree about which one is “the” system.
SSM is the right tool when:

Stakeholders disagree about what the problem is, not just how to solve it.
“The system” is partly a social construction that different actors hold different versions of.
A purely structural or quantitative model would either lose what matters or pretend an agreement that does not exist.

It is the wrong tool when the system is genuinely Complicated rather than Complex (in [[cynefin-framework]] terms), when stakeholders agree on goals and differ only on means, or when speed dominates — SSM is deliberate by design and slow under time pressure.
Details
CATWOE — the mnemonic for a root definition
The most portable artefact of SSM. Used to construct a “root definition” of a purposeful activity system — a one-sentence specification of what some stakeholder holds the system to be doing, from their worldview. CATWOE forces the practitioner to name each component explicitly, which is where unstated disagreement surfaces.








































LetterElementQuestion it forcesCCustomersWho are the beneficiaries or victims of this transformation?AActorsWho carries it out?TTransformationWhat input is converted into what output?WWeltanschauung (worldview)What worldview makes this transformation meaningful?OOwnerWho has the power to stop or fundamentally redirect it?EEnvironmentWhat constraints does the system take as given?
The W is the most consequential and most often skipped. Two stakeholders can agree on C, A, T, O, and E but hold incompatible Ws — and the disagreement that drives the mess will usually live in the W.
Rich pictures and root definitions
Two SSM-specific artefacts worth knowing:

Rich pictures — informal, often hand-drawn diagrams capturing the situation including its political, emotional, and cultural texture (who has power, who is frustrated, what the implicit conflicts are). Deliberately not a systems diagram. The point is to capture what a structured model would lose.
Root definitions — precise statements of what a chosen system is to do, conventionally expressed in a “do P, by Q, in order to contribute to achieving R” form. Multiple root definitions are usually constructed for the same situation, each from a different worldview, and explicitly compared.

The seven-stage model (and why Checkland later loosened it)
The classical SSM presentation is a seven-stage cycle: (1) enter the problem situation, (2) express it (rich pictures), (3) formulate root definitions, (4) build conceptual models from them, (5) compare models with reality, (6) identify culturally feasible and systemically desirable changes, (7) act.
Checkland later moved toward a more fluid “two-stream” formulation (a logic-driven stream of analysis and a cultural stream of accommodation) in part because practitioners were turning the seven stages into a checklist, which defeated the purpose. The seven-stage version is still useful as a teaching scaffold; the two-stream version is closer to how mature practitioners actually deploy it.
Systemically desirable and culturally feasible
SSM’s distinctive criterion for a “good” change is both systemically desirable (it would actually improve the situation) and culturally feasible (the people in the situation can accept and operate it). Most failed organisational change is one of these without the other: technocratic reorganisations that solve the structural problem but the culture rejects, or culturally palatable reshuffles that change nothing structural. Holding both criteria simultaneously is the methodology’s central discipline.
Where this composes with vault tools








































LayerQuestionNoteDomain diagnosisWhat kind of problem is this?[[cynefin-framework]] — SSM is for the Complex domainStructureWhat loops, stocks, delays?[[systems-thinking-engineering]]Multiple worldviewsWhose system, in whose terms?This note (CATWOE, rich pictures, root definitions)OperatorWho is acting, in what state?[[systems-thinking]]CascadeAnd then what?[[second-order-thinking]]ProcessHow will I act?[[decision-making-frameworks]] cluster
The three “systems” notes carve the territory cleanly: engineering for the structure, soft systems for the perceived situation and its multiple framings, human-systems for the operator. A thorough analysis of a real organisational mess usually needs all three.
Failure modes

Method-as-checklist — running the seven stages mechanically while skipping the disorienting work (especially the W). Produces SSM-shaped output with none of its insight. Checkland’s pivot to the two-stream model was a direct response.
CATWOE as a single-author exercise — the value of CATWOE is comparing CATWOEs from different stakeholders. A practitioner filling one in alone is doing structured introspection, not SSM.
Rich picture as deliverable — rich pictures are working artefacts, not output documents. Polishing one for a slide deck strips the texture that justified drawing it.
Drift to consensus — SSM’s emphasis on “accommodation between worldviews” can collapse into pressure for false agreement. The point is to make disagreement legible and actionable, not to dissolve it.
Wrong-domain application — using SSM where the situation is Complicated (knowable structure, expert diagnosis available) wastes time and frustrates the experts. Diagnose with [[cynefin-framework]] first.

Prompt patterns
Situation: [the messy situation, especially one with stakeholder disagreement].

For each of three different stakeholders involved, write a one-sentence
root definition in the form "a system to do P by Q in order to achieve
R", and a CATWOE breakdown (Customers, Actors, Transformation,
Weltanschauung, Owner, Environment). Where do the Ws differ? What does
the disagreement on W make visible that a single shared problem
statement would have hidden?

Rich-picture pass: list the elements of [the situation] that an
organisational chart, a process diagram, or a stocks-and-flows model
would all leave out — power, frustration, history, unspoken conflicts,
who avoids whom, what topics never make it onto the agenda. These are
what a rich picture is for.

Desirable-and-feasible test: for each candidate change to [the
situation], answer two questions separately. (1) Would this actually
improve the situation if implemented? (2) Will the people involved
accept and operate it? A change that scores yes/no or no/yes is the
typical failure mode; only yes/yes is worth pursuing.

Related

[[systems-thinking]] — sibling lens; the operator’s inner conditions
[[systems-thinking-engineering]] — sibling lens; structural / cybernetic tradition. The CST extension covered there is the natural follow-on to SSM
[[cynefin-framework]] — domain check; SSM fits the Complex domain
[[decision-making-frameworks]] — cluster this composes with for the deliberation step that follows the inquiry
[[wrap-framework]] — presupposes a stable problem statement, where SSM treats the problem statement itself as in question
[[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]] — adjacent posture: a practitioner running SSM in soldier mode (defending a preferred root definition) gets the form without the substance

Sources

Checkland, P. — Systems Thinking, Systems Practice (1981, John Wiley). Canonical formulation of SSM and the seven-stage model.
Checkland, P., & Scholes, J. — Soft Systems Methodology in Action (1990, John Wiley). Practical refinements; the source most commonly cited for CATWOE in its mature form.
Checkland, P., & Poulter, J. — Learning for Action: A Short Definitive Account of Soft Systems Methodology and Its Use for Practitioners, Teachers and Students (2006, John Wiley). Checkland’s later compact restatement; introduces the two-stream framing more explicitly.
Reynolds, M., & Holwell, S. (eds.) — Systems Approaches to Managing Change: A Practical Guide (2010, Springer / Open University). Comparative treatment placing SSM alongside system dynamics, the viable system model, strategic options development and analysis, and critical systems heuristics.
Ackoff, R. L. — work on “messes” vs problems; the framing referenced in the What it is section. The clearest single statement is in Redesigning the Future (1974) and the essay collection The Art of Problem Solving (1978). (unverified — listed by reputation; specific page references not independently confirmed for this note.)

Synthesis note (2026-04-29). The framing of SSM as a “third tradition” sitting between the engineering and human-systems lenses, and the six-row mapping in Where this composes with vault tools, are vault-internal; treat them as my framing, not as Checkland’s. CATWOE, rich pictures, root definitions, the seven-stage model, and the systemically-desirable / culturally-feasible criterion are presented in their canonical form.
Last verified: 2026-04-29 (canonical sources cited from established systems-thinking literature; Checkland’s two-stream refinement and Ackoff’s “messes” framing paraphrased — primary sources not re-checked for this draft)

general/solo-ideation.title: Solo Ideation
general/solo-ideation.content:
Solo Ideation
What it is
Structured idea generation and selection done alone — increasingly with an LLM as a thinking partner rather than a team. Most brainstorming literature is about groups; this note adapts the useful parts for a solo practitioner.
Why it matters
A 1958 Yale study (Taylor, Berry & Block) and the productivity-loss literature that followed (notably Diehl & Stroebe, 1987) found that nominal groups — individuals generating ideas alone and pooling them later — consistently outproduced interacting groups on both quantity and quality. This is usually framed as a problem for brainstorming. For a solo practitioner, it is a license: the best-documented ideation format is already the one you can run.
The hard part shifts. Group ideation loses productivity to production blocking (waiting to speak), evaluation apprehension, and social loafing — none of which apply to you. But group ideation also provides built-in dissent, which you lose entirely. Your failure mode is not under-generation but under-contested convergence: you are both the generator and the judge, and nothing pushes back on your first-pass filter.
The divergent → convergent cycle
Alex Osborn (co-founder of advertising agency BBDO) formalized brainstorming in Applied Imagination (1953), building on his 1942 How to Think Up and the four-stage creative-process model of Graham Wallas (The Art of Thought, 1926: preparation → incubation → illumination → verification). The useful structural claim underneath the method is J. P. Guilford’s divergent vs. convergent thinking distinction, which splits idea generation from idea selection. He introduced it in his 1950 APA presidential address. See divergent-convergent-thinking.
For solo work, separating the two phases matters more, not less, because the same brain is doing both. Blending them in one sitting collapses divergence — you start self-editing before you have enough to pick from.
Osborn’s four rules, reframed for solo use
Osborn’s original rules were disinhibitors for groups. Adapted:

Go for quantity. The quantity-breeds-quality heuristic applies whether or not you are alone. Set a target (20 ideas, 30 probes) and hit it before stopping.
Withhold criticism. Your inner critic is now the whole group. Defer evaluation to a later session — ideally a different day — so Wallas’s incubation stage can do its work.
Welcome wild ideas. Toning down a wild idea is cheaper than generating a conservative one from scratch. This matters more with LLMs: if you prompt for reasonable ideas, you get the training-data median.
Combine and improve. “Combine” is where remote-association work happens. See divergent-convergent-thinking for the semantic-distance mechanism.

A fifth “include visuals” rule is sometimes added by modern practitioners (e.g., the consulting firm ImageThink). It is not part of Osborn’s canon, though visual capture during a session is independently sensible.
AI as a divergent-phase partner
Sarnoff Mednick’s 1962 associative theory holds that creativity depends on connecting semantically distant concepts, and that highly creative individuals have flat associative hierarchies — many weak links between distant nodes. LLMs, trained on vast heterogeneous corpora, behave like flat associative hierarchies on demand: they will produce links between domains you would not have bridged alone. This is not a mystery about why “AI helps with brainstorming” — it is spreading activation across a wider graph.
Useful patterns:

Generator, not judge. Use the LLM for divergent breadth; do convergent selection yourself, or hand off to a different session, model, or framing. See bias-aware-verification-protocol.
Heuristic prompts scale. SCAMPER, starbursting, morphological analysis, and assumption reversal are prompt scaffolds as much as solo-thinking tools. See heuristic-ideation-prompts.
Beware sycophantic convergence. A sycophantic LLM narrows toward your stated preference during the divergent phase — the opposite of what you need. See prompt-bias-diagnostics for neutralizing prompt framing before a session.

Convergent-phase risks (amplified for solo)
The creative paradox — generating original ideas and then selecting the most familiar ones — hits harder alone. You have no one to argue for the weird option. Counters you already have in this vault:

Pre-mortem before commitment — see debiasing-mental-models.
Inversion on the selected idea: what would have to be true for this to be the wrong choice?
Red-team pass for high-stakes selections: /red-team on the decision note.
Bias-aware verification protocol once you move from “chosen” to “committed” — see bias-aware-verification-protocol.

Working model: divergent phase is where you want an AI; convergent phase is where you want anything but an AI that agrees with you.
Slash commands and prompt library
Three divergent-phase scaffolds are wired as slash commands:

/scamper — full 7-letter pass (or single-letter with depth)
/starburst — gap-finding questions around a candidate idea
/assumption-reversal — surface and invert unstated frame assumptions

Additional copy-pasteable templates (pre-register frame, morphological enumeration, register push, cross-domain adapt, contradiction pass) live in solo-ideation-prompt-library.
A minimum viable session

Reframe the prompt first. Run /bias-scan-prompt on your framing or rewrite leading questions neutrally. Anchors set here determine everything downstream.
Diverge alone (5–10 min). Write ideas by hand, no AI, to avoid being anchored by the model’s first output.
Diverge with the LLM. Ask for more ideas using a heuristic scaffold (SCAMPER or morphological analysis). Then ask for ideas that contradict your first batch.
Stop. Let it rest. Wallas’s incubation stage is not optional. Come back the next day.
Converge. Score candidates (feasibility × novelty is a reasonable template) and apply the convergent-phase counters above.
Hand off to verification. Once selected, the idea enters the verification pipeline — see bias-aware-verification-protocol.

Related

general/spaced-repetition.title: Spaced Repetition (Distributed Practice)
general/spaced-repetition.content:
Spaced Repetition (Distributed Practice)
What it is
A schedule that distributes review of the same material across expanding intervals rather than packing it into a single session — review today, then in a few days, then a week later, then a month. The opposite of cramming (massed practice). Best paired with active-recall as the operation being scheduled.
Why it matters
Hermann Ebbinghaus’s 1885 forgetting-curve experiments showed that newly memorized material decays exponentially: most of it is gone within hours to days unless reinforced. Each properly-timed review flattens the curve — the memory decays more slowly the next time, so the next review can be further out. Over a few months, an item that originally needed daily review becomes one you can skip for years.
Two compounding mechanisms:

Just-in-time retrieval: Reviewing right when you’re about to forget forces the brain to work harder than reviewing while it’s still fresh. The harder retrieval signals biological importance and produces deeper consolidation. (See memory-consolidation.)
Decoupling exposure from time: Cramming gives you many exposures across one timeline; spaced practice gives you the same exposures across many. Sleep and consolidation can do their work between reviews.

Massed practice can boost short-term test performance, but the gains evaporate quickly. Spaced practice trades small short-term losses for large long-term retention.
Details
Simple manual schedules (good for a small number of high-priority items):

The “2-3-5-7” pattern: review 1 day after first exposure, then 3 days, 5 days, 7 days
“1-3-7-21”: one day, three, seven, twenty-one — easier to remember, similar dynamics
Any expanding sequence works as long as intervals grow

Algorithmic SRS (spaced-repetition software) is the standard at scale:

Anki — Open-source, multi-platform, the de facto choice for medical-board prep, language learning, and serious self-study. Uses the SM-2 algorithm by default with newer FSRS option.
SuperMemo — The original, with the most sophisticated algorithm (SM-18 family). Steeper learning curve.
Mnemosyne — Lighter alternative, also research-grounded.
Modern options layer LLM-generated cards or contextual sentence acquisition on top of these cores.

The algorithm tracks each item’s recall difficulty and predicts the next-review date that maximizes retention per review minute. After grading a card (forgot / hard / good / easy), the next interval adjusts accordingly.
What makes a good card (the bottleneck is card quality, not algorithm):

One concept per card; minimum information principle
Cloze deletions over open-ended prompts when possible
Cards built from material you already understand — SRS is for retention, not first-pass learning
Re-write cards that consistently fail; don’t grind through bad cards

When SRS shines: Large volumes of factual or vocabulary material with clear right answers — medical terminology, language vocabulary, legal codes, anatomical structures, programming syntax.
When SRS struggles: Conceptual integration and skill transfer. SRS will keep you from forgetting individual facts but won’t build the structural understanding that connects them — for that, layer feynman-technique and interleaving-practice on top, then extract the resulting nuggets into cards.
Failure modes:

Reviewing too aggressively → burnout and review-debt avalanches
Adding cards faster than retention stabilizes → overwhelming queue
Treating SRS as a substitute for understanding → cards memorized in isolation, knowledge fragmented
Massed re-study before a deadline labeled as “spaced” — calendar matters

Related

active-recall — The retrieval operation that SRS schedules
interleaving-practice — Mix card decks rather than blocking single-topic reviews
feynman-technique — Use to build understanding first, then extract cards
memory-consolidation — Why the intervals work biologically
evidence-based-learning — Hub

Sources
Preliminary research synthesis (AI-drafted, 2026-04-25). Spacing-effect literature traces to Ebbinghaus (1885) and was rated the highest-utility strategy alongside retrieval practice in Dunlosky et al. (2013). SuperMemo’s algorithm history is well-documented at supermemo.com. Anki’s FSRS algorithm is documented in its open-source repository. Specific SRS performance claims from the source draft (e.g., named recent platforms) were not imported.
Last verified: 2026-04-25

general/systems-thinking-engineering.title: Systems Thinking — Engineering Lens
general/systems-thinking-engineering.content:
Systems Thinking — Engineering Lens
Scope of this note
Sibling to [[systems-thinking]], which covers the human / philosophical lens (the practitioner’s inner conditions as the system to cultivate). This note covers the engineering / cybernetic lens rooted in Forrester’s system dynamics and popularized by Meadows (Thinking in Systems) and Senge (The Fifth Discipline). It treats organizations, ecologies, supply chains, and economies as objects that can be diagrammed in terms of stocks, flows, feedback loops, and delays — and intervened in at differentially-leveraged points.
The two traditions are not interchangeable. They give different recommendations on the same problem; conflating them under the unmarked label “systems thinking” is the failure mode that prompted splitting the topic.
What it is
A vocabulary and a set of diagramming conventions for representing how a system’s structure produces its behavior over time. The core claim is that most pathological behavior in complex systems — overshoot, oscillation, collapse, addiction-to-quick-fixes — comes from structural features (loop polarity, delays, stock dynamics) rather than from the dispositions of the actors inside the system. Change the structure and behavior changes; exhort the actors and behavior usually does not.
The minimum vocabulary:

Stock — an accumulation. Inventory in a warehouse, water in a reservoir, trust in a relationship, bug count in a codebase.
Flow — a rate of change in a stock. Hires per quarter, water flowing in or out, bugs created or fixed.
Feedback loop — a closed chain where a stock’s level influences the flows that change it.

Balancing (negative) loop — drives the stock toward a goal or equilibrium. Thermostats, predator-prey limits, code review catching defects.
Reinforcing (positive) loop — amplifies; produces exponential growth or collapse. Compound interest, viral spread, runaway technical debt.


Delay — time lag between a flow change and its observable effect on a stock, or between a signal and a corrective action. Long delays relative to a system’s response time are the dominant cause of oscillation and overshoot.
Leverage point — a place in the structure where a small change yields a large change in behavior. Meadows ordered these from lowest to highest leverage (see below).

Why it matters
Most non-trivial dysfunction in organizations, codebases, and infrastructure is structural. A team that is “always firefighting” is usually not lazy or bad at prioritizing — they are inside a Shifting the Burden archetype where symptomatic relief atrophies the capacity for fundamental solutions. Naming the structure is what unlocks the intervention; addressing only the visible symptom feeds the loop.
This lens is also the structural counterpart to vault tools that operate at adjacent layers:

[[second-order-thinking]] — Marks’s “and then what?” is the temporal-cascade question. The engineering lens supplies the structure through which the cascade flows: which loops amplify, which absorb, where the delays sit. Without structure, second-order thinking is an unconstrained branching exercise.
[[cynefin-framework]] — system dynamics dominates the Complicated domain (structure is knowable and analyzable by experts) and is partially useful in Complex (structure is real but maps are unreliable). It is the wrong tool in Clear (overkill) and in Chaotic (no time to model).
[[systems-thinking]] (human lens) — the actor inside the system. The two lenses cover different blind spots: the engineering lens optimizes structure but ignores the operator; the human lens optimizes the operator but ignores the structure. A practitioner with neither sees neither.

Details
Stocks, flows, and the rate-vs-level confusion
Most reasoning errors about systems come from confusing a flow (rate) with a stock (level). A budget cut reduces the rate at which a deficit grows; the deficit (the stock) keeps growing until the rate goes negative. Cooling the climate requires net-negative emissions, not slowing emissions growth. Reducing hiring slows team growth but doesn’t shrink the team. The intuitive language (“we cut the deficit”) routinely conflates the two and produces policy that misses by years.
Feedback loops
Reinforcing loops produce exponential dynamics in either direction — they don’t care whether the runaway is “good” (compounding savings, network effects, momentum on a project) or “bad” (technical debt, hostility spirals, bank runs). Their character is determined by which direction the system is currently running and what bounds it.
Balancing loops produce goal-seeking behavior. The goal isn’t always intentional — a thermostat has an explicit setpoint, but a code review process has an implicit defect-tolerance setpoint that emerges from team norms and is rarely written down. Identifying the implicit goal of a balancing loop is often where leverage hides.
Delays inside loops are where most counterintuitive behavior lives. A long delay in a balancing loop produces oscillation — over-corrections that themselves require correction. A long delay in a reinforcing loop produces overshoot — the runaway exceeds the bound before the bound becomes visible.
Meadows’ twelve leverage points
From Meadows, “Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System” (1999, The Sustainability Institute; expansion of an earlier 9-point version in Whole Earth, 1997). Conventionally listed from lowest to highest leverage:

Constants, parameters, numbers — tax rates, interest rates, minimum wage. Where most policy debate happens; where the least leverage actually lives.
Sizes of buffers and stabilizing stocks — inventory levels, savings, reservoirs.
Structure of stocks and flows — physical infrastructure; once built, hard to change.
Length of delays — relative to the rate of system change.
Strength of balancing feedback loops — gain on corrective mechanisms relative to the impacts they’re trying to correct.
Strength of reinforcing feedback loops — usually higher leverage to weaken a runaway than to add another corrector.
Structure of information flows — who has access to what, when. Often a near-free intervention with large downstream effects.
Rules of the system — incentives, punishments, constraints. Higher leverage than the parameters those rules govern.
Power to add, change, evolve, or self-organize — capacity to alter rules and structure from within.
Goals of the system — the actual goal, which may differ from the stated one.
Paradigm out of which the system arises — the shared mental model that makes the goals seem natural.
Power to transcend paradigms — the meta-recognition that the paradigm is one of many.

The ordering is intuitively useful, not exact — Meadows herself flagged that the relative leverage of points often depends on the specific system. The signal she insisted on: most action and debate happens at points 12–10, where leverage is lowest, because those are also the most visible and least threatening to existing power.
Senge’s system archetypes
Recurring structural patterns described in The Fifth Discipline (Senge, 1990) and refined in subsequent system-dynamics literature. A short list of the most commonly invoked:

Limits to Growth — a reinforcing loop runs into a balancing constraint. The fix is rarely to push harder on the reinforcing loop; it is to find and address the constraint.
Shifting the Burden — a symptomatic fix relieves pressure on the fundamental solution, which then atrophies. Common in “we don’t have time for tests right now” cycles, in chronic personal coping patterns, in organizational reliance on heroic individuals.
Tragedy of the Commons — individually rational use of a shared resource produces collective irrationality. Hardin’s 1968 Science essay predates Senge; the archetype generalizes.
Fixes That Fail — a short-term fix worsens the long-term problem (painkiller masking a fracture). Distinct from Shifting the Burden in that the fix here is actively counterproductive, not merely lazy.
Eroding Goals — drift toward low performance as goals are gradually lowered to match degraded performance. Often invisible because each individual concession is small.
Escalation — two parties’ corrective actions strengthen each other’s reinforcing loops (arms races, price wars, escalating arguments).
Success to the Successful — initial advantage gets reinforced; resources flow toward those already winning. Underlies Matthew-effect dynamics in research funding, careers, platform economics.
Growth and Underinvestment — capacity grows below demand because the standards used to plan capacity drift down with realized performance.

The archetypes are pedagogical, not exhaustive. Their value is as recognizable templates: when a situation matches the shape, the standard interventions are usually right and the obvious ones are usually wrong.
The Critical Systems Thinking turn — who benefits
A practical critique levelled at the engineering lens by the strand of literature called Critical Systems Thinking (CST). The lens, taken on its own, is technically rigorous but normatively quiet: the practitioner picks the system boundary, the variables, and the goal, then reasons inside that frame. CST’s claim is that those choices are themselves interventions — drawing the boundary in one place rather than another decides whose interests are inside the system and whose are externalities.
Key questions CST adds to a structural analysis (drawn primarily from Werner Ulrich’s Critical Systems Heuristics, 1983):

Who benefits from the system as currently bounded?
Who decides what counts as improvement, and on what mandate?
Whose knowledge is treated as expertise, and whose is dismissed as anecdote?
Who is affected by the system but not represented in its design?

Ulrich frames each of these in both an “is” mode (how the situation actually stands) and an “ought” mode (how the practitioner would defend it). The gap between the two is where the boundary judgments are doing political work that a stocks-and-flows diagram would leave invisible. The shorthand “boundary critique” is the move of treating the system boundary as itself something to argue about, not something to fix at the start of the analysis.
For most engineering-lens applications inside an organisation — capacity planning, debt dynamics, reliability — the CST questions are rarely load-bearing and adding them adds friction. For analyses with distributional consequences (public policy, platform design, resource allocation across teams, anything where externalities fall on parties without voice in the system), skipping CST means producing a structurally clean recommendation that quietly encodes whose problem is being solved.
The “three waves” framing often used in this literature comprises hard / functionalist (first wave), soft / interpretive (second wave; see [[soft-systems-methodology]]), and critical / emancipatory (third wave). The framing is most associated with Michael C. Jackson’s pedagogical schema rather than a settled historical fact about the field. It is useful as a map; treat the dates and ordering as approximate.
Where this composes with vault tools








































LayerQuestionEngineering-lens contributionDomain diagnosisWhat kind of problem is this?Use [[cynefin-framework]] first; engineering lens fits Complicated, partially ComplexStructureWhat loops, stocks, delays are in play?This noteCascadeWhat follows from that structure over time?[[second-order-thinking]] traces; this lens supplies the railsCalibrationHas this archetype produced the behavior I’m guessing at, in comparable cases?[[ai/reference-class-forecasting]]OperatorWho is acting in the system, and in what state?[[systems-thinking]] (human lens)ProcessHow will I act on the diagnosis?[[decision-making-frameworks]] cluster
Failure modes

Modeling fetish — building elaborate causal-loop diagrams that don’t match the actual system, then defending the diagram instead of revising it. Symptom: the diagram has been edited many times but the predictions haven’t been checked against outcomes.
False precision — treating system-dynamics simulation output as a forecast rather than a directional sketch. The numbers feel earned by the modeling work; they usually aren’t.
Reductionism creep — assuming any complex social system can be diagrammed as stocks and flows. Reflexive, agent-saturated systems resist closed-form structure — markets where participants read forecasts, organizations where the model itself changes behavior. The lens degrades gracefully here; treating it as exact does not.
Ignoring the operator — the inverse blind spot of the human lens. A correct structural model of an organization, applied by a leader whose inner conditions are scattered or status-protective, produces correct diagnosis and incoherent action. Pair with [[systems-thinking]].
Quick-fix despite the lesson — even practitioners trained on Shifting the Burden still shift the burden. Knowing the archetype reduces the hit rate; it does not eliminate it. The robust counter is making the fundamental-solution work visible enough that abandoning it has political cost.
Leverage-point misranking — treating Meadows’ 12-to-1 ordering as universal. The ordering is a default sensibility, not a theorem; specific systems sometimes reward parameter changes (point 12) more than paradigm shifts (point 2) on practical timescales.

Prompt patterns
For analyzing a structural situation. Compose with the convergent-prep section of [[decision-prompt-library]].
Situation: [the system or recurring pattern].

Identify the stocks, the flows that change them, and at least one
reinforcing and one balancing loop. Where are the delays? Which
behavior of the system over time is best explained by structure
rather than by the dispositions of the people inside it?

Archetype check: does [the situation] match Limits to Growth,
Shifting the Burden, Fixes That Fail, Tragedy of the Commons,
Eroding Goals, Escalation, Success to the Successful, or Growth
and Underinvestment? If yes, what does the archetype's standard
intervention say to do that the obvious response would not?

Leverage scan: list the candidate interventions for [the situation]
and tag each by Meadows' rough leverage level (parameters, buffers,
information flows, rules, goals, paradigm). Where is the action
currently concentrated? Where would it be concentrated if the
team were optimizing for leverage rather than visibility?

Related

[[systems-thinking]] — sibling note; the human / philosophical lens. The two together form the structure-and-operator pair the decision cluster otherwise lacks.
[[soft-systems-methodology]] — third sibling; Checkland’s interpretive method for messy situations where stakeholders disagree on what the system even is. CATWOE, rich pictures, root definitions. Natural follow-on when the engineering lens hits a worldview disagreement it cannot resolve internally.
[[second-order-thinking]] — temporal-cascade discipline; uses this lens’s structural primitives implicitly.
[[cynefin-framework]] — domain check; the engineering lens fits Complicated and partially Complex.
[[decision-making-frameworks]] — cluster this composes with on the structural-diagnosis side.
[[levin-research-program-implications]] — biological systems thinking as a third tradition; the loop-and-stock vocabulary maps onto Levin’s bioelectric circuits more directly than onto Saarinen’s lens.
[[probability-judgment-biases]] — base-rate and representativeness errors are common when reasoning informally about loop dynamics; the engineering lens forces explicit quantities that resist those errors.
/structural-trace — slash-command operationalisation of this lens; produces a stock/flow/loop/archetype/leverage diagnosis on a recurring pattern. Pairs with /second-order (which traces a chosen action forward through the diagnosed structure).

Sources

Meadows, D. — Thinking in Systems: A Primer (2008, edited posthumously from her unfinished manuscript by Diana Wright). The accessible primer; canonical introduction to stocks, flows, loops, and delays.
Meadows, D. — “Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System” (1999, The Sustainability Institute). The 12-point list. Expansion of a 9-point version in Whole Earth (1997).
Senge, P. — The Fifth Discipline: The Art and Practice of the Learning Organization (1990; revised edition 2006). Source for the system archetypes in their popularized form and for systems thinking as the integrating “fifth” of his five disciplines (personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, systems thinking).
Forrester, J. — Industrial Dynamics (1961), Urban Dynamics (1969), World Dynamics (1971). Foundational system-dynamics work at MIT; differential-equation-based simulation methodology that underlies the lens.
Meadows, D., Meadows, D. L., Randers, J., and Behrens III, W. W. — The Limits to Growth (1972; 30-year update 2004). Application of Forrester-style world modeling to global resource dynamics; the public on-ramp that shaped the lens’s reception.
Sterman, J. — Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World (2000). Standard practitioner textbook for those who want to build models, not just read about them. (unverified — listed by reputation; specific edition details not independently confirmed.)
Ulrich, W. — Critical Heuristics of Social Planning: A New Approach to Practical Philosophy (1983, Haupt). Source for the “boundary critique” / who-benefits framing in the CST section. The twelve boundary questions in their “is / ought” pairing are the canonical artefact.
Jackson, M. C. — Systems Thinking: Creative Holism for Managers (2003, John Wiley). Practitioner-oriented overview that popularised the “three waves” pedagogical framing (functionalist / interpretive / emancipatory) used in the CST section. (unverified — title and year cited from established literature; not re-checked against the volume for this draft.)

Synthesis note (2026-04-29). The mapping table in Where this composes with vault tools and the failure-modes ranking are vault-internal contributions; treat them as my framing, not as Meadows’ or Senge’s. The leverage-point list is paraphrased; for citation purposes consult the 1999 Meadows essay directly. Senge’s archetypes are listed in their popularized form — academic system-dynamics literature often uses different names and finer-grained variants.
Last verified: 2026-04-29 (canonical sources cited from established literature; Sterman text edition flagged as unverified)

general/systems-thinking.title: Systems Thinking
general/systems-thinking.content:
Systems Thinking
Scope of this note
“Systems thinking” names at least two distinct traditions that often get conflated:

The engineering / cybernetic lens — stocks and flows, feedback loops, delays, leverage points. Rooted in Forrester’s system dynamics, popularized by Meadows (Thinking in Systems) and Senge (The Fifth Discipline). Treats organizations, ecologies, and economies as objects to be modeled.
The human / philosophical lens — the self, attention, values, and the stance from which one acts as the system worth understanding. Less concerned with diagramming an external world and more concerned with the inner conditions that produce the actor.

This note primarily covers the second lens, framed through Esa Saarinen’s “Philosophy and Systems Thinking” tradition at Aalto University. The engineering lens is a separate topic, written up in the sibling note [[systems-thinking-engineering]].
What it is (the human-systems lens)
The discipline of treating the person doing the thinking — their mental models, attention, emotional state, values, and posture toward the world — as a system that can be cultivated, observed, and reorganized. Tools and techniques target the inner environment rather than the external problem.
As described in publicly available Aalto course materials, Saarinen’s framing organizes around five themes (paraphrased from a user-provided summary, 2026-04-29 — specific phrasings have not been independently verified against primary teaching materials):

Independent and forward-looking thinking — capacity for broad, creative, life-philosophical reasoning that isn’t borrowed from the prevailing register.
Personal relevance and self-reflection — the system being analyzed is the practitioner’s own behaviors, mental models, and values, on the terms of their actual life.
Mental growth and attitude — tools that strengthen the foundation of one’s everyday stance toward life rather than producing topical knowledge.
Navigating change — the practical objective is to remain creative and value-driven during periods of transition.
Holistic, experiential integration — pedagogically, the goal is to spark a “movement of thought” in the individual rather than transfer information; integrates Western and Eastern philosophical sources with modern human-research findings.

The unifying claim: the highest-leverage system to operate on, for most life and work outcomes, is the human one.
Why it matters
Most decision and reasoning tools in this vault — [[cognitive-biases]], [[debiasing-mental-models]], the entire [[decision-making-frameworks]] cluster — treat the person as a roughly mechanical decision-maker who can install techniques to improve outputs. They presuppose, but do not address, the self that runs those techniques.
Saarinen’s lens insists that this presupposition is the actual leverage point. A person whose inner conditions are scattered, defensive, or value-incoherent will run pre-mortems and inversions performatively without genuine update. A person whose inner conditions are clear will improvise good decisions even without named frameworks.
This is a structural complement, not a replacement. The frameworks remain necessary for adversarial and high-stakes domains where the inner-conditions discipline alone won’t catch a Bayesian error. But the inner conditions determine whether the frameworks get applied honestly.
There’s also a domain claim worth keeping. For genuinely complex situations — relationships, careers, raising children, leading organizations through change — closed-form analysis under-delivers because the system is reflexive: your model of it changes how you act in it, which changes what it does. The human-systems lens is built for exactly that reflexivity. See [[cynefin-framework]] for why this is the Complex domain.
Details
What “movement of thought” means in practice
Saarinen’s pedagogy reportedly emphasizes experiential, emotionally engaged learning over information transfer. The asserted distinction: information about a concept can leave behavior unchanged, while a genuine shift in how one perceives a situation alters action automatically.
The vault analogue: this is [[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]] operating one layer up. Galef’s distinction is about epistemic posture — am I trying to see what’s true, or to defend what I believe? Saarinen’s “movement of thought” is the broader experiential shift that produces and sustains scout posture across domains, not just in argument.
The composing layer beneath the frameworks
A useful way to locate this lens against the rest of the vault:








































LayerQuestionVault notesInner conditionsWho is doing the thinking?This note; [[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]]Posture toward evidenceAm I open to being wrong?[[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]]; [[debiasing-mental-models]]Domain diagnosisWhat kind of problem is this?[[cynefin-framework]]ProcessHow will I decide / deliberate?[[decision-making-frameworks]], [[ooda-loop]], [[wrap-framework]]CascadeAnd then what?[[second-order-thinking]]CalibrationHow often does this kind of thing actually happen?[[ai/reference-class-forecasting]]
Inner conditions are the most invisible layer — when they’re working, it looks like the practitioner is “just good at this.” When they fail, the more visible layers fail in ways that look like technique problems but aren’t.
Where this composes with vault tools

Cynefin ([[cynefin-framework]]) — Saarinen’s lens is most necessary in the Complex domain (where the observer affects the observed and there are no repeatable cause-effect chains). Less necessary in Clear or Complicated, where the engineering lens or expert analysis dominates.
Scout vs soldier ([[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]]) — these are siblings. Galef’s frame is sharper for argument hygiene; Saarinen’s is broader for life orientation. They don’t conflict.
Second-order thinking ([[second-order-thinking]]) — the inner system has its own feedback loops over time. A pattern of avoidance produces narrowing options that produce more avoidance. Second-order thinking applied to one’s own behavior is a bridge between the temporal-cascade tool and this lens.
Levin’s research program ([[levin-research-program-implications]]) — biological systems thinking, a third tradition (cells as goal-directed agents, anatomy as collective behavior). Conceptually adjacent to both lenses on this page; useful as a reminder that “system” cuts across scales.
Decision-making-frameworks cluster ([[decision-making-frameworks]]) — this lens is the precondition the cluster doesn’t otherwise name. Without it, the cluster’s tools work for already-clear practitioners and fail silently for everyone else.

Failure modes

Self-help drift — without anchoring, “personal growth” framings lose specificity and become aesthetic. The discipline survives only if it produces named, observable changes in how one acts. If a year of practice has produced no behavioral evidence, the practice is performative.
Verification gap — the experiential / “movement of thought” register is intrinsically hard to falsify. This is exactly the failure mode [[ai/ai-output-bias-fingerprints|the bias-fingerprint checklist]] and /falsifiability-scan push against in other contexts. Apply the same standard here: if a claim about inner work cannot be checked against any observable signal, treat it as poetry, not method.
Inner-only blind spot — the lens optimizes the actor but not the system the actor is embedded in. A practitioner with excellent inner conditions inside a structurally broken organization will still produce broken outcomes. Pair with the engineering lens when the bottleneck is structural.
Charismatic-teacher dependency — experiential pedagogies tend to encode tacit knowledge in the teacher. Students who don’t replicate the teacher’s stance often don’t actually internalize the practice; they collect quotes. Watch for citation-of-the-master in place of demonstrable change in oneself.
Conflation with the engineering lens — using “systems thinking” rhetorically to mean either tradition without specifying which. The two frames give different recommendations on the same problem; collapsing them produces confusion.

Prompt patterns
Templates for invoking the inner-conditions lens explicitly. Compose with the convergent-prep section of [[solo-ideation-prompt-library]] and the templates in [[decision-prompt-library]].
Situation: [the situation I'm reasoning about].

Before analyzing the situation itself, describe the system that I am
right now — what state am I in, what am I avoiding noticing, what
outcome am I already attached to, what would I have to be willing to
see for my reasoning here to be honest. Do not analyze the situation
until that inventory is complete.

Stance check: list three responses I could give to [the situation]
that would be the responses of a person whose inner conditions are
clear, value-driven, and not defensive. List three responses that
would be the responses of a scattered, anxious, or status-protecting
version. Which set does my current draft response actually belong to?

Movement-of-thought test: name one perception about [topic / person /
project] that has shifted in the last six months in a way that has
changed my behavior. If I cannot name one, what does that suggest
about whether my "thinking" on this topic is actually moving, or just
recirculating?

For decisions where the dominant uncertainty is structural (markets, technical systems, organizational dynamics), promote to the engineering systems-thinking lens at [[systems-thinking-engineering]].
Related

[[decision-making-frameworks]] — the cluster this note composes with rather than belongs in
[[scout-vs-soldier-mindset]] — sibling lens; epistemic posture as the narrower analogue
[[cynefin-framework]] — domain check; the human-systems lens fits the Complex domain
[[second-order-thinking]] — temporal-cascade tool; applied to oneself, becomes a bridge into this lens
[[debiasing-mental-models]] — the named techniques whose efficacy depends on the inner conditions this lens addresses
[[levin-research-program-implications]] — biological systems thinking; a third “systems” tradition for context
[[ai/bias-aware-verification-protocol]] — the verification ethos that the experiential register has to be reconciled against
[[systems-thinking-engineering]] — sibling note; the structural / cybernetic tradition (stocks, flows, feedback loops, Meadows’ twelve leverage points, Senge’s archetypes). Pair with this note when both the operator and the structure are in question.
[[soft-systems-methodology]] — third sibling; Checkland’s interpretive method for messy situations where stakeholders disagree on what the system even is. CATWOE, rich pictures, root definitions. Sits between the engineering lens (structure) and this note (operator) by treating the perceived situation as the primary object.

Sources

Saarinen, E. — “Philosophy and Systems Thinking” course, Aalto University. The five-theme summary in this note is paraphrased from a user-provided summary of Aalto course-page material (2026-04-29). Specific phrasings (“movement of thought”, “Western and Eastern philosophy”, “life-philosophical thinking”) are attributed to that summary and have not been independently verified against primary course materials or Saarinen’s published writing.
