health/exercise-for-longevity.title: Exercise for Longevity — The Four-Pillar Prescription
health/exercise-for-longevity.content:
Exercise for Longevity — The Four-Pillar Prescription
What it is
The exercise pillar of geroscience. Where longevity-foundations covers the nutritional and pharmacological levers, this note covers the physical ones — the modalities, dosing, and intensity thresholds that the contemporary literature converges on for healthspan and lifespan extension.
The framing is the four-pillar model popularized in clinical longevity work (Peter Attia and others): stability, aerobic base (Zone 2), aerobic ceiling (VO₂max), and strength. No single one is sufficient; each addresses a distinct failure mode of aging.
Why it matters
Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF, measured as VO₂max) is one of the strongest single predictors of all-cause mortality known — competitive with or stronger than most clinical risk factors. Skeletal muscle mass and strength independently predict mortality in older adults. Falls — driven by neuromuscular decline — are a leading cause of injury death after 60 and the typical entry point to the terminal cascade (fracture → hospitalization → atrophy → infection).
Importantly, exercise is the only known intervention that simultaneously hits all four nutrient-sensing pathways in nutrient-sensing-pathways (AMPK activation, transient mTOR pulse, sirtuin activation via NAD⁺ flux, autophagy/mitophagy induction) — see Cross-Domain Connections on this point.
For the user’s profile (cyclist with FTP ~270W, indoor trainer, training 5–8 hours/week per cycling-profile): the aerobic side is well-covered by existing training. The gaps are deliberate Zone 2 volume, structured strength work, and stability — see Practical implications below.
The four pillars
1. Stability and mobility (the foundation)
The pillar most often skipped, and the one that gates everything else in the marginal decade. Without postural stability, strength and aerobic capacity cannot be safely deployed.

Why: Falls are mechanical mortality. A hip fracture in an 80-year-old is rarely just an orthopedic event — it triggers immobilization, sarcopenia, and infection.
Predictive marker: The 10-second single-leg balance test (Araujo et al. 2022, BJSM) — inability to balance on one leg for 10 seconds is associated with substantially elevated all-cause mortality risk in the following decade. Useful as a self-check.
Modalities with evidence:

Tai Chi — meta-analyses consistently show meaningful reductions in fall incidence in older adults; effect sizes vary across studies but the direction is robust
Single-leg / unilateral strength work — Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDLs, step-ups; trains stabilizers the bilateral lifts skip
Perturbation-based reactive training (clinical settings) — conditions automatic stepping reflexes


Dose: 2–3 sessions/week, 10–20 minutes; integrates well as warm-up or finisher

2. Aerobic base — Zone 2 (the metabolic engine)
Steady-state aerobic work below the first lactate/ventilatory threshold (~LT1 / VT1). Predominantly fat-oxidative; minimal lactate accumulation.

Mechanism: Drives mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α), capillary density, and metabolic flexibility. AMPK activation during sustained low-intensity work is the primary lever for autophagy/mitophagy — the cellular cleanup pathway.
Heart rate target: ~60–70% HRmax is the typical estimate. Note that fixed percentages have wide individual variation; the talk test is the most reliable field metric — full sentences with noticeable but not labored breathing. If you can sing easily, too low. If you can only speak in fragments, too high.
Volume: Common longevity-focused recommendations target ~150–200+ minutes/week. The user’s existing Zwift Z2 work falls into this bucket.
Note for cyclists: Per cycling-profile, this corresponds to Coggan Zone 2 (56–75% FTP, ~150–200W at 270W FTP). Easy spinning that feels like recovery is closer to Zone 1 — actual Zone 2 is “comfortable but I’m doing something.”

3. Aerobic ceiling — VO₂max work (the protective ceiling)
High-intensity interval training (HIIT) targeting near-maximal oxygen uptake. The pillar most clearly associated with raising the absolute CRF ceiling.

Why VO₂max matters: Each ~1-MET increase in CRF is associated with substantial reductions in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality across multiple large meta-analyses (Kodama 2009, Mandsager 2018, others). Moving from the lowest CRF quintile to the next quintile up shows particularly large mortality benefits — the floor is more lethal than the ceiling is protective.
Protocol: The Norwegian 4×4 (Helgerud et al. 2007) is the canonical protocol — 4 minutes near-maximal effort (~90–95% HRmax) / 4 minutes active recovery, repeated 4 times. Robust evidence for VO₂max gains.
Dose: 1–2 sessions/week is typical. Diminishing returns and recovery cost climb fast above that.
Caveat: The Generation 100 trial (NTNU, 2020) ran five years of HIIT vs MICT vs control in older Norwegians. It found a non-significant trend favoring HIIT for all-cause mortality but no decisive superiority over moderate-intensity work at sufficient volume. So Zone 5 is valuable but not a substitute for Zone 2 base.

4. Strength and muscle mass (the structural armor)
Resistance training to preserve muscle mass, type II fiber recruitment, bone density, and metabolic capacity.

Why: Sarcopenia is one of the dominant aging phenotypes. Muscle is the body’s main amino-acid reservoir and largest postprandial glucose sink — losing it accelerates frailty and metabolic dysfunction. See protein-paradox-aging for the nutrition side.
Independent mortality benefit: Meta-analyses (e.g., Momma et al. 2022, BJSM) report ~10–20% reductions in all-cause and cancer mortality from any muscle-strengthening activity vs none. Combined with aerobic work, the effect is meaningfully larger than either alone.
The J-shape: Same Momma meta-analysis suggests benefits peak around 30–60 minutes/week of resistance training and attenuate or reverse beyond ~140 min/week. The mechanistic explanation is debated (chronic Valsalva-induced BP spikes, maladaptive cardiac remodeling, or — equally plausibly — confounding by anabolic-steroid use and other behaviors in extreme-volume populations). Either way: more is not better here. (unverified — meta-analysis exists; the precise inflection-point claim is one interpretation of the dose-response curve)
Dose: 2–3 sessions/week of compound full-body work; 30–60 minutes per session; focus on heavy-ish loads with good form. Two productive sessions beat five mediocre ones.

Volume thresholds at the aggregate level

WHO baseline: 150–300 min/wk moderate or 75–150 min/wk vigorous physical activity
Optimal protective range (from Lee et al. 2022 Circulation, Nurses’ Health Study + HPFS, ~30 years follow-up): 2–4× the WHO minimums shows the largest mortality reductions, with diminishing returns above that. (the specific hazard-ratio numbers in the source draft are not reproduced here pending direct citation check)
Weekend warrior pattern: Multiple recent cohort analyses (including in diabetic populations) suggest that compressing weekly MVPA into 1–2 days produces mortality reductions comparable to evenly distributed activity, provided total weekly volume is achieved. Aggregate dose appears to dominate distribution.
The extreme-exercise hypothesis: Earlier work suggested a U-shaped curve where ultra-endurance volumes might erase or reverse benefits. More recent large cohorts (Cooper Center Longitudinal Study and others) find that while high-volume athletes show more coronary calcification, the calcium is predominantly stable plaque, and all-cause mortality remains lower than in lower-volume populations. The J-curve concern appears more applicable to resistance training at extreme volumes than to aerobic work.

Molecular mechanism — why this works
Exercise hits the same hallmark-of-aging machinery covered in longevity-foundations and nutrient-sensing-pathways:

AMPK ↔ mTOR cycling — exercise depletes ATP, activates AMPK, transiently suppresses mTOR (cleanup phase); recovery + protein restores mTOR pulse (rebuild phase). This is the pulsing principle applied to physical activity.
Mitophagy — high-intensity work fragments dysfunctional mitochondria via PINK1/Parkin and ULK1; recovery rebuilds via fusion. Selectively culls the inefficient organelles.
Senescent cell clearance — exercise upregulates immune surveillance (NK and CD8⁺ T cells) and reduces accumulation of senescent fibro-adipogenic progenitors in muscle. See cellular-senescence-and-senolytics — exercise functions as a continuous, mild senomorphic.
Telomere preservation — meta-analyses associate higher CRF with longer leukocyte telomere length, mediated through TERT activation and reduced oxidative stress on telomeric ends.
BDNF and neuroplasticity — covered in bdnf-exercise-cognition; the cognitive pillar of the same exercise dose.

Variety as an independent variable
Recent observational work suggests that breadth of movement patterns independently predicts lower mortality, even controlling for total volume — i.e., a person doing 200 min/wk across cycling, lifting, swimming, and racquet sports appears to do better than a person doing 200 min/wk of cycling alone. (specific 2026 BMJ Medicine study cited in source draft — unverified; the broader principle that varied stressors prevent overuse injury and recruit more motor units is well-supported)
The implication: a rigid single-modality routine is biologically inferior to a cross-trained matrix even at matched total volume. For a cyclist, this means deliberately adding strength + a different aerobic modality (rowing, walking under load, hiking) is not just injury insurance — it may itself be a longevity lever.
Practical implications for the user’s profile
Given cycling-profile (270W FTP, Zwift TT Tune-Up, 5–8 hr/wk):

Aerobic base is well-covered. The Coggan Zone 2 work in the cycling plan is the longevity Zone 2 work. No additional volume needed for the longevity case if the cycling volume is hit.
Aerobic ceiling: VO₂max intervals are already in any structured FTP-build plan (the 4×4 lives in cycling literature too — Ronnestad et al.). The cycling-side and longevity-side prescriptions converge here.
Strength is the gap. Cycling is non-weight-bearing; bone density and upper-body strength are not maintained by it. 2 sessions/week of compound resistance work (squat/hinge/push/pull pattern, 30–45 min each) covers both the longevity J-curve sweet spot and the cycling-power benefit (Ronnestad has multiple papers showing strength work supports FTP). Topic-suggestions has this flagged as high-priority — see topic-suggestions.
Stability is the second gap. A 10-minute single-leg / balance circuit before strength sessions, plus the occasional 10-second balance self-check, addresses the highest-leverage intervention for the marginal decade. Currently absent from the routine.
Variety: Indoor cycling is one stressor pattern. Walking under load, hiking, occasional rowing, or a recreational sport (racquet, climbing) would round out the modality matrix without large time cost.

The aggregate weekly target is 5–8 hours cycling (Z2 base + threshold/VO₂ work) + 2 × 30–45 min strength + 2 × 10 min stability. That sits comfortably in the “2–4× WHO baseline” optimal envelope and addresses all four pillars.
What this note deliberately does not promise

Specific hazard ratios are not reproduced. Many of the precise percentages in the source draft (e.g., “26–31% reduction at 300–599 min MPA”) are real findings from real cohorts but the exact numbers vary by analysis and population. The directional pattern is robust; the digits should be looked up if cited.
The 4.7-year-longer-life claim for sub-4-minute milers from the source draft is (unverified) — possibly real but I have not confirmed the citation.
Tai Chi fall-reduction figures of “50–75%” in the source draft are at the high end of the range; published meta-analyses typically show smaller but still meaningful effects (~20–40%). (unverified specific number; effect direction is well-supported)
The “BMJ Medicine 2026 variety study” is (unverified); the variety principle has supporting evidence but the specific study claim should be checked before citing.

Related

longevity-foundations — hub note; this is the exercise pillar previously marked “not in scope”
nutrient-sensing-pathways — AMPK/mTOR mechanism that exercise modulates
cellular-senescence-and-senolytics — exercise as continuous mild senomorphic

cycling-profile — athletic-performance angle on the same training; Coggan zones map to longevity zones
training-load-tss-tracking — TSS/CTL discipline keeps the longevity dose from becoming the overtraining dose
protein-paradox-aging — nutrition complement; without adequate protein, resistance training cannot defend muscle mass

Sources

Verified or well-established underlying literature:

Lee, I.-M. et al. — Physical activity and mortality dose-response work in the Nurses’ Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study (multiple papers, Circulation and JAMA Internal Medicine)

health/fasting-guide.title: Fasting Guide — Durations, Benefits, and Protocols
health/fasting-guide.content:
Fasting Guide — Durations, Benefits, and Protocols
What it is
Fasting is the deliberate, time-bounded cessation of caloric intake. Unlike continuous caloric restriction, it manipulates the timing of nutrient availability, driving the body to switch from glucose to fat/ketone metabolism. That switch triggers a cascade of evolutionarily conserved repair pathways that modern ad libitum eating patterns suppress: autophagy, stem cell renewal, anti-inflammatory signaling, and endocrine recalibration.
Why it matters
Fasting is one of the few interventions that simultaneously improves insulin sensitivity, reduces systemic inflammation, triggers cellular repair, and requires no equipment, prescription, or cost. Benefits scale with duration but so do risks — different fast lengths unlock different biology. The practical question isn’t “should I fast?” but “which fast serves which goal?”
For a cyclist balancing training-load-tss-tracking with metabolic health, fasting can be a potent tool if timed around training load. It is not universally appropriate and interacts with caffeine-and-performance, hydration, and sleep.
The Fasting Timeline — What Happens Hour by Hour
The timeline below is approximate. Individual variation is large (3–7h shifts are common). Metabolic flexibility, prior diet, activity level, and body composition all affect the curve.
0–4 hours (Fed / postprandial)
Insulin is elevated, digesting the last meal. Glucose is the primary fuel. mTOR is active — anabolic, growth-oriented signaling dominates. No fasting benefits yet.
4–8 hours (Postabsorptive)
Blood glucose normalizes. Insulin drops toward baseline. Liver begins breaking down stored glycogen to maintain blood sugar. This is “between meals” for most people — no particular benefit, but the body is no longer in digestion mode.
8–12 hours (Early fasting / glycogen depletion)
Hepatic glycogen stores draw down. Glucagon rises; insulin falls further. Lipolysis begins — free fatty acids start trickling into circulation. Fasting insulin measurements taken here are already meaningfully lower than postprandial values. Most overnight fasters never go past this window.
12–16 hours (Metabolic switching begins)
Glycogen approaches depletion. The liver starts converting fatty acids to ketone bodies (primarily beta-hydroxybutyrate, BHB). BHB typically rises above 0.3–0.6 mmol/L. AMPK — the energy-sensor kinase — activates, beginning to inhibit mTOR and initiate early autophagy. Human studies show autophagy markers (ATG5, ULK1) start trending up in this window. This is the minimum effective dose for most metabolic benefits.
16–24 hours (Deepening ketosis, autophagy ramps)
BHB climbs to 0.5–1.0 mmol/L — nutritional ketosis. Fat oxidation is now the dominant fuel pathway. Growth hormone begins rising (it roughly doubles in this range). Noradrenaline rises to sustain alertness and energy output. Autophagy intensifies — damaged mitochondria, misfolded proteins, and senescent components start being cleared. Arachidonic acid rises, directly suppressing the NLRP3 inflammasome and dampening innate inflammation.
24–36 hours (Autophagy peaks, ketones dominate)
BHB reaches 1–2 mmol/L. Autophagic flux markers (LC3 up, p62 down) reach a meaningful peak in animal and limited human data. Gluconeogenesis plateaus — the liver makes just enough glucose for obligate glucose-users (brain, RBCs). IGF-1 starts dropping. Insulin is at its nadir. Hunger is typically lower here than at 20 hours — “hunger waves” come and go rather than building linearly.
36–48 hours (HGH spike, deep autophagy)
Human growth hormone secretion increases up to ~400% over baseline, with more frequent pulses across the day. HGH preserves lean mass even during caloric void, mobilizes adipose tissue, and supports muscle repair. Autophagy remains elevated. Ketones climb toward 2–3 mmol/L. Cortisol patterns shift — the cortisol awakening response is amplified, supporting metabolic flexibility without triggering muscle breakdown. This is where “you feel weirdly good” for many people — the ketone-adapted clarity phase.
48–72 hours (Stem cell priming, immune remodeling)
IGF-1 drops to its lowest sustainable levels. PKA (protein kinase A) signaling declines — a key regulator of stem cell dormancy. Hematopoietic stem cells begin shifting from dormant to regenerative states. Ketones reach 3–6 mmol/L. AgRP hunger neurons in the hypothalamus actively orchestrate a redistribution of circulating monocytes, reducing pro-inflammatory populations. The immune system is now in an active remodeling phase, not just a quiescent one.
72+ hours (Immune regeneration, deep therapeutic window)
Longo’s work (USC, 2014 and onward) showed 72h+ fasts trigger near-complete immune system rejuvenation via hematopoietic stem cell-driven renewal. BHB can reach 6–8 mmol/L. Arachidonic acid-mediated NLRP3 suppression is deeply established. Thyroid T3 drops 20–30% — a hypometabolic, longevity-mimetic state. This is the clinical-research zone: strong benefits for autoimmune remission, chemo-patient protection, and metabolomic age reversal. Also the zone where medical supervision starts to matter.
5–10 days (Clinical / supervised prolonged fasting)
Maximum depth of autophagy, stem cell activation, and immune reset. Used in Buchinger-Wilhelmi clinics and research settings for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and metabolic syndrome. Muscle strength is preserved (lean tissue loss is ~60% water, ~14% glycogen+water, minimal contractile protein). VO2max drops by ~13% after 7 days. Electrolyte derangement (especially sodium/chloride) becomes the primary risk. Refeeding must be staged carefully to avoid refeeding syndrome.
Summary Table — Duration vs Primary Benefit













































































DurationPrimary BiologyPractical BenefitDifficulty12hInsulin drop, digestive restMetabolic baseline, circadian alignmentTrivial14hEarly lipolysisModest weight management, sleep-alignedEasy16hKetogenesis onset, early autophagy, AMPK activationFat loss, insulin sensitivity, mental clarityModerate — most popular protocol18hKetosis established, autophagy risingDeeper metabolic effects, steadier energyModerate20hMeaningful autophagy, noradrenaline elevationStronger fat loss, appetite bluntingHard — sustainability questionable24hAutophagic flux peaks, deep ketosisInflammation reduction, cognitive resetHard36hHGH spike (+400%), IGF-1 droppingLean mass preservation, repairHard48hMax autophagy, stem cell primingImmune prep, metabolic resetVery hard72hStem cell regeneration, immune resetAutoimmune modulation, immune rejuvenationClinical5d FMDEngineered fast mimicryAutophagy + micronutrients, safer long-fast proxyModerate (with kit)7–10dDeep therapeutic stateDisease-modifying in RA/psoriasis/MSMedical supervision required
Fasting Protocols
12:12 — Circadian baseline
12 hours eating, 12 hours fasting (e.g., 7pm–7am). This is essentially a disciplined “don’t eat at night.” Minimal difficulty. Good entry point for women, older adults, or anyone with a history of disordered eating. Locks meals to the light cycle and improves sleep quality more than it drives fat loss.
14:10 — Gentle TRE
14 hours fasting, 10 hour eating window. Easier on women’s hormonal axes than 16:8 and still delivers most cardiometabolic benefits. The “minimum effective dose” for metabolic health in many 2024–2025 TRE trials.
16:8 — The classic (Leangains)
16 hour fast, 8 hour eating window (typical: 12pm–8pm, or 11am–7pm). The most-studied TRE protocol. Highest probability-ranked intervention for reducing IL-6, TNF-α, and leptin in network meta-analyses. The Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation TRE trial achieved 40% reduction in Crohn’s disease activity using this protocol over 12 weeks.
Compliance is higher than calorie counting because it only asks “when,” not “how much.” Good default for most adults.
18:6 — Intermediate
18 hour fast, 6 hour window. Noticeably deeper ketosis than 16:8, with autophagy markers meaningfully higher. Still sustainable daily for metabolically flexible individuals. A reasonable endpoint if 16:8 stops producing results.
20:4 — Warrior Diet territory
20 hour fast, 4 hour window (often afternoon/evening). Harder to hit protein/caloric targets in 4 hours. Works for some; most people struggle to sustain without undereating or bingeing. Best used intermittently (2–3 days/week) rather than daily.
OMAD / 23:1 — One Meal A Day
Single meal, ~1 hour window. The longest daily TRE variant. Delivers weight loss and modest metabolic benefit but carries risks: LDL elevation in some individuals, delayed insulin response the next morning, and the highest risk of drifting into disordered eating patterns. Lean mass preservation is harder than with moderate TRE. Not recommended as a daily long-term protocol — more defensible 1–2x/week.
24-hour fast / Eat-Stop-Eat (Pilon)
Fast from dinner to dinner (or breakfast to breakfast) once or twice a week. Pushes into meaningful autophagy territory without the sustainability challenges of daily 20:4. Reasonable add-on to a baseline 14:10 or 16:8. Pair with an easy training day — fasted Zone 2 is tolerable; intervals are not.
36-hour “Monk Fast”
Skip a full day entirely — e.g., dinner Monday, no food Tuesday, breakfast Wednesday. Hits the HGH surge window. Run once per week or every other week for repeated benefit without cumulative stress. Popular in the Jason Fung protocol for insulin resistance reversal.
5:2 Diet (Mosley)
Five days of normal eating, two non-consecutive days at ~500 kcal (women) or ~600 kcal (men). Ranks highest among IF variants for sustained CRP reduction. Gentler than ADF; easier long-term adherence. Produces deep immunophenotyping shifts — reduces effector memory T cells, increases naive T cell populations.
Alternate-Day Fasting (ADF)
Fast day, feast day, repeat. Two variants: true ADF (zero calories) and “modified” ADF (~25% intake on fast days). Strong weight-loss tool but highest dropout rate among IF protocols. Better for short, defined interventions (8–12 weeks) than as a permanent pattern.
Fasting-Mimicking Diet (Longo / ProLon)
Five consecutive days per month of a calibrated low-calorie, low-protein, high-fat plant-based intake (~1100 kcal day 1, ~800 kcal days 2–5). Designed to keep the body metabolically in a fasting state — inhibited mTOR, suppressed IGF-1, active autophagy — while providing essential micronutrients.
The only consumer protocol clinically shown to trigger measurable autophagy in humans. Three monthly cycles reduce trunk fat, lower blood pressure, and reduce biomarker-estimated biological age by 1+ years. Used clinically in MS trials showing reduced metabolomic age and pathogenic T-cell depletion. Safer than a water fast for the same 5 days; costs ~$250/cycle if using the ProLon kit, or can be DIY’d with strict macro discipline.
Prolonged water-only fast (5–10 days)
The deepest therapeutic window. Used for rheumatoid arthritis (7–10 day protocol followed by Mediterranean/plant-based diet), psoriasis (7-day + plant-based transition per RiseFast protocol), and severe metabolic disease. Requires medical supervision — electrolyte monitoring, blood pressure tracking, and a structured refeeding plan. Not a self-serve intervention.
Breaking the Fast
The refeeding phase is non-trivial and often underestimated. The longer the fast, the higher the stakes.
Short fasts (≤24h): Any reasonable meal will do. Protein + non-starchy vegetables + moderate fat is lowest-risk. Avoid sugar bombs — they spike insulin on a sensitized system and cause energy crashes.
Medium fasts (24–72h): Start small. Bone broth or a few bites of eggs and avocado, wait 30–60 min, then a proper meal. Avoid high fiber and high fat on the first meal. Don’t celebrate-feast — many people eat more the day after a fast than they would normally, negating most of the caloric benefit.
Long fasts (72h+): This is the danger zone for refeeding syndrome — rapid shifts in phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium that can cause cardiac arrhythmias or death in extreme cases.

Day 1: bone broth, small amounts every 2–3 hours
Day 2: bone broth + steamed non-starchy vegetables
Day 3: soft proteins (eggs, fish), small portions
Continue electrolytes; plan to refeed for half as many days as you fasted
Do not attempt 5+ day fasts with self-directed refeeding if BMI is low or lean mass is already depleted

The regenerative vulnerability caveat: Recent stem cell research (2024–2025) shows that the refeeding phase is a hyper-proliferative state where intestinal stem cells switch to lipid metabolism and divide rapidly. Mutagenic or genotoxic exposures during this window (certain dietary carcinogens, alcohol, processed meats) may be amplified. Keep the first refeeding meals clean and plant-forward — not the time for cheat-day indulgence.
What Breaks a Fast
Strict rule: any measurable insulin response, any significant caloric intake, or any protein/amino acid signal to mTOR breaks the biochemical fast.
Does not break a fast:

Water (plain, sparkling, mineral)
Black coffee (no milk, no sweetener)
Plain tea (green, black, herbal)
Zero-calorie electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium without sugars or sweeteners — LMNT, Redmond Re-Lyte, DIY with salt)
Small amounts of pink/sea salt

Grey zone:

Artificial sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose) — technically zero-cal, but can trigger a modest insulin response in some people and affect gut microbiota
Apple cider vinegar — minimal caloric load, probably fine
MCT oil / bulletproof coffee — breaks autophagic fasting but maintains ketosis; acceptable for “metabolic” fasts, not “cellular cleanup” fasts

Breaks a fast:

Anything with calories above trace amounts
BCAA/EAA supplements — directly activate mTOR
Protein shakes, collagen
Gum with sugar alcohols (minor but real insulin signal)
Diet sodas with reformulated sweeteners

Anti-Inflammatory and Immune Mechanisms
Fasting reduces systemic inflammation through five interconnected pathways, not one:

NLRP3 inflammasome suppression via arachidonic acid. Fasting elevates circulating arachidonic acid, which directly inhibits the NLRP3 complex — the primary sensor that matures IL-1β and IL-18. Mechanism parallels NSAIDs.
Autophagy of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy). Clears ROS-leaking mitochondria that would otherwise activate the cGAS-STING and NLRP3 pathways. mTOR is inhibited, AMPK and FOXO are activated.
NRF2-driven antioxidant response (mitohormesis). Transient mild oxidative stress upregulates SOD, GPx, CAT, and glutathione — the body builds more defenses than it consumes.
HPA-axis and AgRP hunger-neuron modulation. Cortisol dampens peripheral inflammation; the hypothalamic hunger signal itself reduces circulating pro-inflammatory monocytes (demonstrated in mice even without actual caloric deficit).
Gut microbiome reorganization. Favors SCFA (butyrate, propionate) producers, which inhibit NF-κB. Tight-junction integrity improves, reducing LPS endotoxemia that drives TLR-mediated systemic inflammation.

The biphasic immune response
Prolonged fasting (≥48h) can transiently increase hsCRP and some cytokines in the first 24–72 hours. This is not a deterioration — it’s an adaptive hormetic signal mobilizing cellular defenses. Long-term, inflammation normalizes well below baseline, especially in individuals starting from pathologically elevated levels. Don’t test CRP on day 2 of a 7-day fast and panic.
Clinical Applications



































ConditionProtocolEvidenceRheumatoid arthritis7–10 day modified fast → Mediterranean/plant-basedTransient ESR/CRP drop; benefit lost if diet reverts; conditional ACR endorsement for the Med-diet phaseCrohn’s disease16:8 daily for 12 weeks40% reduction in disease activity, 50% less abdominal pain, enriched SCFA microbiome (Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation trial)Multiple sclerosisFMD monthly cyclesReduced metabolomic age; depletion of Th1/effector-memory T cells; reduced fatigue/depression scoresPsoriasis16:8 for 28 weeksPASI50 response in >54%; VEGF, IL-6, hsCRP all down; waist circumference reducedMetabolic syndrome / T2D16:8, 5:2, or ADFWeight loss, HbA1c drops, insulin sensitivity gains — most established clinical use
Exercise and Fasting
Key rule: fasted low-intensity work is beneficial; fasted high-intensity work is counterproductive.
Fasted Zone 2 / endurance (fine-to-beneficial):

6 weeks of fasted endurance training yields ~21% increase in FATmax vs 6% with fed training
Increases β-HAD and citrate synthase activity — foundational for fat oxidation capacity
Good for base-building in early cycling-profile season; supports “train low, race high” adaptation

Fasted intervals / threshold / race efforts (avoid):

Carbohydrate availability is rate-limiting for high-power output
Performance drops meaningfully; session quality suffers
Not an appropriate context to “get tough” — the adaptation stimulus is lower, not higher

After a long fast (48h+):

VO2max drops measurably (~13% after 7 days of fasting)
Do not expect race-quality sessions for 2–3 days post-refeed
Plan fasts during rest weeks or after a heavy training block, not during a build phase

Practical cycling integration:

14:10 or 16:8 daily: fine, pair morning caffeine with fasted Z2, break fast post-ride
24–36h occasional fast: schedule on a rest day, not before a hard Zwift session
FMD or 5+ day: treat as a recovery/rest block; resume intensity gradually

Women and Fasting
The evidence base for fasting in women is thinner and more contentious than for men. Key nuances:

Premenopausal women are generally more hormonally sensitive to energy deficit. Aggressive TRE (20:4, OMAD) can suppress LH pulsatility, affect menstrual regularity, and interact with thyroid function.
72h fasts in follicular phase did not disrupt menstrual cycling in one controlled study — but that’s a narrow, supervised condition.
PCOS shows clear benefit from 8h TRE — reduced total testosterone, higher SHBG, improved eumenorrhea.
Pragmatic recommendation: start with 12:12 or 14:10, not 16:8. Consider cycling the fast — more aggressive in the follicular phase, gentler in the luteal phase. Back off if menstrual patterns change.
Postmenopausal women tolerate standard TRE protocols similarly to men.

Safety and Contraindications
Absolute contraindications:

Type 1 diabetes — severe hypoglycemia / DKA risk
Pregnancy and breastfeeding — fetal/infant nutrient deprivation
Active eating disorders or history of anorexia/bulimia
BMI under 18.5
Children and adolescents under 18

Relative contraindications — medical supervision required:

Type 2 diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas (dose adjustments needed)
Chronic kidney disease
Gout (uric acid spikes during ketosis can trigger flares)
Hypotension or on BP-lowering medication
History of gallstones (long fasts can precipitate stones in susceptible individuals)

Muscle preservation — largely a non-issue. DEXA studies on 6–10 day fasts show ~60% of “lean tissue” lost is water, ~14% glycogen + bound water, with structural muscle protein spared. Isometric and isokinetic strength are preserved after 6–10 day water fasts. Plasma 3-methyl-histidine (a muscle breakdown marker) drops sharply by day 5, confirming protein-sparing.
Electrolyte risk is real. Sodium and chloride drop significantly during multi-day fasts. Supplement ~2–3g sodium/day on fasts >24h; add potassium (~1g) and magnesium (~300mg) for fasts >48h.
Controversies Worth Knowing
The AHA 2024 “16:8 = 91% higher CV death” poster. Widely reported; methodologically fatal. Based on two 24-hour dietary recalls from NHANES, projecting 8 years of mortality from a single snapshot of eating times. Reverse causality dominates — people with tiny eating windows in NHANES were often sick (cancer, psychiatric illness) rather than deliberately doing IF. Current consensus: no credible CV mortality signal from properly implemented TRE in healthy populations, but long-term RCTs are still needed.
Stem cell refeeding and cancer risk. The same regenerative signal that heals the intestinal epithelium during refeeding can accelerate oncogenesis if mutagenic exposures coincide. Relevant for anyone timing fasts around chemotherapy or high-genotoxic exposures. Keep refeeding meals clean; this is not hypothetical-only research.
Autophagy thresholds in humans are less certain than the marketing suggests. Most detailed data come from rodent models. Human studies (Bensalem 2025, Jordan 2025) show autophagy gene expression (ATG5, ULK1) rising during 16:8 and 17–19h daily fasts, but direct human autophagic flux measurements remain limited. The “autophagy kicks in at exactly 16 hours” claim is a simplification — it’s a rising curve, not a switch.
Practical Starting Protocol
For a metabolically healthy adult new to fasting:

Week 1–2: 12:12. Establish a clean overnight fast with no bedtime snacks. Sleep improves.
Week 3–4: 14:10. Push breakfast later or dinner earlier. Most people don’t notice hunger once habituated.
Week 5+: 16:8 if desired. Hold here long-term for most metabolic benefit with minimal downside.
Occasional: Once comfortable with 16:8, add a single 24h fast per week or a 36h fast every other week for deeper autophagy.
Advanced: Consider a 5-day FMD (ProLon or DIY) quarterly for the stem cell / autophagy deep-benefit without the risk profile of water-only 5-day fasts.
Don’t: Jump to OMAD, a 72h fast, or a 7-day water fast without building up. Adverse events cluster in unprepared fasters.

Track: morning bodyweight, HRV (morning), sleep quality, subjective energy, and — if available — a quarterly lipid panel + hsCRP + fasting insulin. The biomarkers tell you what the scale doesn’t.
Related

caffeine-and-performance — black coffee is the primary fasting-compatible ergogenic tool
training-load-tss-tracking — don’t fast during build phases; fast in recovery weeks
cycling-profile — fasted Z2 is legitimate base-building; fasted intervals are self-sabotage
meditation-practice — HPA-axis work complements fasting’s cortisol dynamics

Sources

Longo, V.D. et al. (2014) — “Prolonged fasting reduces IGF-1/PKA to promote hematopoietic-stem-cell-based regeneration” — Cell Stem Cell
Cheng, C-W. et al. (2014) — USC study on 72h fasting and immune regeneration
de Cabo, R. & Mattson, M.P. (2019) — “Effects of intermittent fasting on health, aging, and disease” — NEJM
Wei, M. et al. (2017) — “Fasting-mimicking diet and markers/risk factors for aging, diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease” — Science Translational Medicine
Bensalem, J. et al. (2025) — “Intermittent time-restricted eating may increase autophagic flux in humans” — Journal of Physiology
Jordan et al. (2025) — fasting and autophagy gene expression in healthy young males
Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation TRE trial (2023–2024) — 16:8 in Crohn’s disease, 40% activity reduction
Ho, K.Y. et al. (1988) — 48h fasting and HGH secretion (~400% increase)
Van Proeyen, K. et al. (2011) — “Beneficial metabolic adaptations due to endurance exercise training in the fasted state” — J Appl Physiol
Pietrocola, F. & Kroemer, G. (2019) — autophagy signaling in fasting
American Heart Association 2024 EPI Lifestyle poster (widely critiqued) — TRE and cardiovascular mortality claims
Cahill, G.F. (2006) — “Fuel metabolism in starvation” — foundational on ketogenesis timeline
Nature Communications (2024) — 7-day fast effects on physical performance, VO2max decline
Dr. Alexis Shields, Liv Hospital, BodySpec, LMNT Science (public-facing fasting timelines and refeeding guides)
Goodrick, C.L. et al. (various) — ADF mortality/longevity models
Sutton, E.F. et al. (2018) — early TRF trial in prediabetes

health/forest-bathing.title: Forest Bathing (Shinrin-Yoku) and Nature Exposure
health/forest-bathing.content:
Forest Bathing (Shinrin-Yoku) and Nature Exposure
What it is
Shinrin-Yoku (森林浴, “forest bathing”) is the practice of slow, sensory immersion in a forested environment — walking unhurriedly, attending to sights, sounds, smells, and textures rather than covering distance or photographing landmarks. The term was coined and popularized in Japan in the 1980s, initially by the Japanese Forest Agency, and has since evolved into a body of medical research (“forest medicine”) and a clinical adjunct in some healthcare systems.
The framing is important: forest bathing is not a hike, not exercise, not a guided meditation in a forest setting. It is sustained, low-arousal, multisensory exposure to a biodiverse natural environment, typically over at least 1–2 hours, ideally with phone silenced and pace deliberately slow.
Why it matters
Across Japanese, Korean, Scandinavian, and increasingly North American studies, the replicated finding is that this kind of nature exposure produces measurable physiological and psychological effects with a time course that is faster than expected:

Cortisol reduction — typically a 10–20% drop in salivary cortisol after a forest session compared to matched urban-walk controls
Lower sympathetic and higher parasympathetic activity — measured via heart rate variability and blood pressure
Reduced rumination — most strikingly, reduced neural activity in the subgenual prefrontal cortex, the brain region associated with self-referential rumination and a known marker of depression risk (Bratman et al., 2015, Stanford — 90-min nature walk vs. matched urban walk; effect was specific to nature exposure)
Mood improvement — reductions in tension, anger, fatigue, and depressive affect on the standard Profile of Mood States (POMS) scale, replicated across many studies
Modest immune effects — increased natural killer (NK) cell activity reported in Li et al.’s forest-bathing studies, attributed in part to inhalation of phytoncides (volatile organic compounds released by trees, particularly conifers). Effect size and durability of the immune signal are contested

The effects do not require a wilderness setting. Urban green space (parks, tree-lined streets, gardens) shows attenuated but real versions of the same effects, which matters more for daily life than the headline forest studies.
The mechanism, briefly
Several plausible pathways operate in parallel; they’re not mutually exclusive:

Reduced stimulus load — natural environments lack the temporally unpredictable, high-information visual and auditory stimulation of cities. The cognitive system gets to operate in a lower-arousal default mode (the attention restoration theory of Kaplan & Kaplan)
Phytoncides — airborne terpenes from evergreen trees specifically; some evidence for direct effects on immune cells and possibly on stress hormones via inhalation
Visual fractal structure — natural scenes have fractal complexity in a range (D≈1.3–1.5) that is associated with reduced physiological arousal and lower stress markers in lab studies (Taylor et al.)
Auditory environment — natural sounds (water, wind, birdsong) preferentially activate parasympathetic-associated networks compared to anthropogenic noise
Microbial exposure — soil and plant microbes contribute to immune training and may have downstream mood effects through the gut-brain axis
Awe and self-transcendence — nature exposure reliably produces awe responses, which are associated with reduced self-focused rumination and increased prosocial behavior in lab work

The mechanism question matters less practically than the consistent observation that exposure produces effects, with the dose and duration mattering more than the precise biology.
Dose-response, in practice
Rough guidance from the empirical literature, with the usual caveat that individual variance is high:

Single session — ~1–2 hours of mindful, slow forest exposure produces measurable effects on cortisol, mood, and rumination markers immediately and for several hours afterward
Weekly cadence — weekly forest visits produce sustained effects on resting blood pressure and self-reported wellbeing in trials lasting several weeks
Daily small dose — even short (~20 min) daily exposures to urban green spaces produce smaller but real effects on stress markers; cumulative weekly green-space minutes appear to matter as much as session intensity
The “120 minutes per week” threshold — a 2019 White et al. analysis of UK survey data (~20,000 respondents) found that ≥120 min/week of contact with nature was associated with a reported well-being benefit; below the threshold, effects were inconsistent. The specific threshold is observational and shouldn’t be treated as a precise dose, but the order of magnitude is useful

Practical applications
For someone who already exercises outdoors (cycling, walking) the forest-bathing-specific value is the slow, attentional, non-performance quality of the exposure. A Zwift session and a forest walk produce different effects on the same nervous system; both are useful.
Specific applications worth considering:

Active recovery days — a long, slow walk in a forest area substitutes for a recovery ride and adds the rumination-reducing effect on top
High-stress weeks — frontload nature exposure rather than deferring it to the weekend; the “medicine” is more useful prophylactically than as treatment
Pre-decision wind-down — the SIDI mechanism makes high-stakes decisions under stress unreliable; deliberate nature exposure before such decisions is one of the few interventions that demonstrably restores prefrontal capacity (rather than just feeling like it does)
Sleep adjunct — afternoon or early evening nature exposure improves subsequent sleep onset and quality in several studies; bright outdoor light early in the day also anchors the circadian rhythm (see sleep-hygiene)
For Finnish context — forests are abundant and the cultural infrastructure for nature use (everyman’s right / jokamiehenoikeus) is uniquely well-developed; year-round access including winter is feasible and widely practiced. The cold-and-snow forest exposure has its own specific characteristics but the core mechanism still operates

What’s overhyped
The forest-bathing literature has its share of marketing on top of weaker evidence:

Specific phytoncide-product claims (“guided forest-bathing tour with measured immune boost”) — the immune effects are real in aggregate but the per-session magnitude is small and not reliably attributable to specific tree species
“Forest as cure” framings — useful adjunct for anxiety, mild depression, stress-related complaints; not a treatment for major psychiatric conditions, and should never be presented as substituting for evidence-based therapies
Specific colorimetric claims (“the green wavelength has direct calming effect”) — the visual aspect matters but the specific-wavelength framing oversimplifies the actual mechanism (which involves scene complexity, fractal structure, and meaning, not raw wavelength)

Related

meditation-practice — overlapping mechanism (parasympathetic activation, attentional restoration); forest bathing is closer to “open monitoring” meditation than to focused-attention practice
sleep-hygiene — outdoor light exposure timing is one of the highest-leverage circadian levers; forest walks combine multiple sleep-supporting inputs
sidi-stress-cognition — nature exposure as one of the few interventions that restores rather than just alleviates the prefrontal-suppression state
bdnf-exercise-cognition — outdoor aerobic exercise combines BDNF effects with the nature-exposure effects; the interaction is plausibly synergistic
loneliness-health-risk — group-based nature activities (walking groups, conservation volunteering) stack social-connection benefits with nature-exposure benefits; “green social prescribing” is a recognized category in some health systems
gut-brain-axis — soil and plant microbial exposure is a hypothesized mechanism, though not yet well-quantified
cycling-profile — the user’s cycling is currently indoor/Zwift-dominant; an outdoor green-space cadence is a different stimulus and arguably worth scheduling separately

Counterargument
The forest-bathing evidence base is heterogeneous — many studies are small, short, run by practitioners with promotional interests, or not well-controlled against the simpler hypothesis “any non-urban walk produces some of these effects.” Several effects (cortisol, mood, rumination) do appear robust across different study traditions, but the more enthusiastic claims (specific cancer-protective phytoncide effects, durable immune benefits) rest on thinner evidence than the popular literature suggests.
A simpler, more defensible framing: outdoor activity in green or blue space, away from urban stimulus density, in a slow attentive mode, produces measurable stress-physiology and mood benefits. The Japanese “Shinrin-Yoku” name and ritualized form is one valid way to access these benefits; it is not the only way, and the cultural-import branding can obscure the simpler underlying mechanism.
The honest practitioner position: this is a low-cost, low-risk, evidence-supported adjunct intervention. Treating it as a marketing-laden “forest medicine” specialty obscures its main virtue — that it’s free, requires no equipment, and works for almost everyone who does enough of it.
Sources

Bratman, G.N. et al. (2015) — “Nature experience reduces rumination and subgenual prefrontal cortex activation” — PNAS — the rumination/sgPFC finding
Li, Q. et al. — multiple papers on forest bathing, NK cells, and phytoncides; collected in Li, Q. (2018) Forest Bathing
Park, B-J. et al. (2010) — “The physiological effects of Shinrin-yoku” — Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine — early synthesis of cortisol and HRV evidence
White, M.P. et al. (2019) — “Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing” — Scientific Reports — the 120-min/week threshold
Kaplan, R. & Kaplan, S. (1989) — The Experience of Nature: A Psychological Perspective — the attention-restoration-theory foundation
Taylor, R.P. et al. — fractal analysis of natural scenes and stress response, multiple papers
Kuo, F.E. & Taylor, A.F. (2004) — “A potential natural treatment for ADHD” — American Journal of Public Health — the children-and-nature line of work

health/geroprotective-foods.title: Geroprotective Foods — Functional Compounds in Whole Foods
health/geroprotective-foods.content:
Geroprotective Foods — Functional Compounds in Whole Foods
What it is
A short list of bioactive compounds has credible mechanistic links to the aging pathways. These compounds are concentrated enough in specific whole foods that dietary intake can plausibly move biomarkers. None of these is a miracle on its own; the evidence is strongest when they’re consumed as part of a broader dietary pattern rather than chased in isolation.
This note covers the food-side of these compounds. Concentrated supplement forms are in longevity-supplements-2026.
Why it matters
Most of the “longevity foods” lists circulating online are either marketing or vague. There is a tighter, mechanism-grounded subset that is worth integrating into actual meal planning. Knowing which compound a food is for makes substitution and prioritization easy: if you don’t like one source of spermidine, swap to another, rather than chasing the food itself.
Ergothioneine (ERGO) — the “longevity vitamin” candidate
A sulfur-containing amino acid antioxidant produced by fungi and some bacteria, transferred up the food chain to plants and animals. Humans have a dedicated transporter (OCTN1/SLC22A4 / ETT) that concentrates ergothioneine in tissues with high oxidative stress: erythrocytes, bone marrow, liver, lens, skin, brain. The presence of a dedicated transporter is the main argument for treating it as conditionally essential — animals don’t usually invest in transporters for compounds they don’t need.
Mechanism: powerful, mitochondria-protective antioxidant; resistant to autoxidation at physiological pH; scavenges hydroxyl and peroxyl radicals; protects mitochondrial DNA.
Best dietary sources — by far, mushrooms:


















































SourceApproximate ERGO contentNotesOyster mushrooms (golden, pearl)very highHighest practical dietary sourceShiitakehighCommon, easy to eat regularlyKing oysterhighMeaty texture, good substitute for meat in dishesMaitakemoderate-highComplex flavor; supplemental use less commonPorcinimoderateSeasonal; dried form keepsWhite button / creminimoderateLower density but still meaningful at typical portionsBlack beans, kidney beanslow-moderateDistant second to mushroomsWhole oats, oat branlowMinor contributor, but daily
Exact mg/kg figures vary heavily by species, soil, and cultivation method (cultivation on grape marc and similar substrates can dramatically raise content). (Specific concentration tables in the source material are unverified; the species ranking is broadly correct.)
Practical: 80–100g of mushrooms several times a week is a low-effort way to maintain meaningful ERGO intake. Cooking does not destroy ergothioneine.
Aging signal in humans: lower plasma ergothioneine has been associated with frailty, mild cognitive impairment, and all-cause mortality in older-adult cohorts. Whether raising it via diet or supplementation extends healthspan is the open clinical question.
Spermidine — autophagy inducer
A natural polyamine present in all cells, declining with age. The most-studied dietary autophagy inducer; works in part by inhibiting EP300 (a histone acetyltransferase that normally suppresses autophagy) and by interacting with AMPK and SIRT1 signaling.
Best dietary sources:

Wheat germ — by far the densest dietary source. A few tablespoons daily delivers a meaningful dose.
Soy products (especially natto, tempeh, and aged soy)
Mushrooms, particularly aged or dried
Aged cheeses (parmesan, aged cheddar, blue cheeses)
Mature legumes — lentils, chickpeas, beans
Whole grains and bran
Green peas, broccoli, cauliflower
Mangoes, grapefruit

Aging signal: in the Bruneck Study (Italian cohort), higher dietary spermidine intake was associated with lower all-cause mortality and lower cardiovascular events. The effect size was meaningful in observational terms but the study is not a randomized trial. (Direction of effect is replicated; magnitude warrants the standard observational caveats.)
Practical: a daily pattern that includes wheat germ on yogurt or oatmeal, plus regular legumes, soy, and aged cheese, hits the same intake range as the high-spermidine quartile in observational cohorts. Direct supplementation (1–2 mg/day) is also available; food intake gets you most of the way there.
Fisetin — the strawberry senolytic
A flavonoid that selectively induces apoptosis in senescent cells in preclinical models. Most of the pre-clinical and early human work is in supplement form (longevity-supplements-2026); the dietary signal is much weaker because intake from food alone is well below the doses that show senolytic effects in trials.
Dietary sources (per ~100g):

Strawberries — the densest readily available source
Apples (with skin)
Persimmons
Onions (some varieties)
Cucumbers, grapes — minor

Practical: eating strawberries regularly is fine and probably beneficial for the broader polyphenol load. Treating dietary fisetin as a senolytic intervention is overreach — supplement doses in trials are roughly 100–500 mg/day; you cannot eat enough strawberries to reach that.
Sulforaphane — Nrf2 activator from broccoli sprouts
A potent activator of the Nrf2-Keap1 pathway, which in turn upregulates a broad array of endogenous antioxidant and detoxification enzymes (HO-1, NQO1, glutathione synthesis enzymes). Acts more like a “training stimulus” for the cell’s defense systems than a direct antioxidant — the hormetic mechanism.
Source density:

Broccoli sprouts (3-day) — ~10–100x the sulforaphane precursor (glucoraphanin) of mature broccoli
Mature broccoli, cauliflower, kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts — moderate
Mustard greens, watercress, arugula — lower but contribute

The active compound is generated by myrosinase enzyme activity when the plant tissue is damaged (chewing, chopping, blending). Cooking deactivates myrosinase. Tactics to preserve activity:

Eat raw or lightly steamed (not boiled)
Chop and let sit 30–40 minutes before cooking — myrosinase acts during the rest, releasing sulforaphane that survives cooking better than the precursor
Add a little raw mustard or daikon (myrosinase source) to a cooked cruciferous dish to “rescue” the conversion

Practical: a small amount of broccoli sprouts (30–50g, ~3 tbsp) several times a week is the most concentrated practical food-based source. Mature crucifers daily are a fine substitute.
Urolithin A — postbiotic, mostly via supplement
Urolithin A is not present in food. It’s produced by certain gut bacteria from ellagitannins, the precursor compound found in:

Pomegranates and pomegranate juice
Walnuts
Strawberries, raspberries, blackberries
Aged red wine, oak-aged spirits (small)

Whether you produce urolithin A from these depends on your gut microbiome composition. A meaningful fraction of the population does not produce significant urolithin A from ellagitannins — estimates around one-third (unverified, varies by cohort and methodology). For non-producers, dietary intake of pomegranate has weaker effects than direct supplementation (longevity-supplements-2026).
Practical: pomegranate, walnuts, and berries are worth eating regardless (good polyphenol load, fiber, healthy fats in walnuts), but if mitophagy induction via urolithin A is the goal, the dietary route is unreliable across individuals. Supplement is the controlled-dose option.
Other notable food-based actors

Extra-virgin olive oil — oleocanthal and other phenolics (anti-inflammatory, mild COX-2 inhibitor, ibuprofen-like signaling). Foundational to Mediterranean effects.
Green tea — EGCG; modest mTOR modulation, AMPK activation, polyphenol load. Synergizes with caffeine; see caffeine-and-performance.
Coffee — chlorogenic acids, polyphenols; consistent observational signal for lower all-cause and CV mortality at moderate intake. The “coffee is bad” priors from older literature have not held up.
Dark chocolate (cocoa flavanols) — endothelial function, blood pressure modulation. The signal is real but the typical dose is small per serving and easy to overshoot in calories.
Berries (blueberries, strawberries, raspberries) — anthocyanins; cognitive aging signal, polyphenol delivery.
Cruciferous vegetables (beyond broccoli) — cabbage, kale, Brussels sprouts; the Nrf2-active baseline.
Allium family (garlic, onions, leeks) — sulfur compounds; CV signal in observational cohorts.
Fatty fish — omega-3 (EPA, DHA); anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, cardiovascular.
Nuts and seeds — magnesium, polyphenols, unsaturated fats; among the most consistent mortality signals in cohort data (PREDIMED especially).
Fermented foods — yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, miso; microbiome diversity → SCFA production → systemic anti-inflammatory effect.

How to combine without overthinking
A weekly rotation that hits most of the above without effort:

Mushrooms (oyster or shiitake) in 2–3 meals/week
Wheat germ on yogurt or oatmeal most days
Legumes daily (soup, salad, side, hummus)
Broccoli or cabbage 3–4 times/week, with at least one raw or lightly cooked
Berries most days
Pomegranate or walnuts a few times/week
Olive oil as the default cooking and dressing fat
Fish 2–3 times/week
Green tea or coffee daily; not late afternoon

This is also approximately the Mediterranean / Blue-Zone template. The functional-food framing isn’t an alternative — it’s a lens on why the pattern works.
What this is not

Not a substitute for the dietary pattern. The base diet matters more than any single food.
Not a replacement for TRE and other levers.
Not a license to add concentrated supplements on top without thinking about doses; many of the food-form compounds become more risky at supplement-level intakes (e.g., high-dose isolated quercetin, see longevity-supplements-2026).

health/gut-brain-axis.title: Gut-Brain Axis and Nutritional Neuroscience
health/gut-brain-axis.content:
Gut-Brain Axis and Nutritional Neuroscience
What it is
The gut-brain axis is the bidirectional communication system linking the enteric nervous system with the central nervous system. The enteric nervous system is the network of ~500 million neurons embedded in the gastrointestinal tract. Communication runs through three main channels:

Neural — the vagus nerve carries afferent signals from gut to brainstem (about 80–90% of vagal fibers are afferent, despite the popular framing of vagus as a “control” nerve)
Endocrine and metabolic — hormones and metabolites produced by gut tissue and gut bacteria (short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan derivatives, bile acids) cross into circulation and act centrally
Immune — the gut hosts most of the body’s immune tissue; gut-resident microbes shape systemic immune tone, which feeds back into neuroinflammation

The microbiome — the trillions of bacteria, archaea, viruses, and fungi resident in the gut — is now widely treated as a metabolically active “organ” rather than passive flora.
Why it matters
For mental health and cognitive performance specifically:

~90% of the body’s serotonin is produced in the gut (mostly by enterochromaffin cells, modulated by microbial signals). The popular “gut serotonin = mood serotonin” framing oversimplifies — peripheral serotonin doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier — but tryptophan availability, microbial production of precursors, and vagal signaling all influence central serotonergic tone
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) — butyrate, propionate, acetate — produced by bacterial fermentation of fiber, fortify the gut barrier, modulate inflammation, and act on enteroendocrine cells and the vagus nerve
Systemic inflammation is a known modifier of mood and cognition. Diets that promote dysbiosis (low diversity, high pathobiont load) raise inflammatory markers, which are independently associated with depressive symptoms
Diet effects on mental health appear to operate substantially through microbiome-mediated pathways, on top of the direct nutrient effects (B vitamins, omega-3s, choline, etc.) on neural tissue itself

The framing matters: “diet affects mental health” is not new, but the mechanism — modifiable microbial ecology rather than just macro/micronutrient adequacy — opens different intervention points.
How the microbiome is shaped
Modifiable inputs, in rough order of impact:

Dietary fiber diversity — the dominant lever. Different fibers feed different bacteria; a narrow diet narrows the microbiome. Ranges from soluble fermentable (oats, legumes, onions) to insoluble structural (whole grains, leafy greens) to resistant starch (cooled potatoes, green bananas)
Plant-food variety — the American Gut Project observation: people who report ≥30 distinct plant species per week show meaningfully more diverse microbiomes than those reporting ≤10. Variety beats specific super-foods
Fermented foods — yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, miso, kombucha provide live microbes plus their fermentation byproducts. The Sonnenburg lab’s 2021 trial showed a 10-week fermented-food intervention raised microbiome diversity and lowered inflammatory markers more than a high-fiber arm did — for a baseline-Western population (the high-fiber arm needed a longer ramp to convert)
Antibiotics — dramatic microbiome perturbation; recovery takes weeks to months and may be incomplete. Avoid casual use; necessary courses are obviously fine
Stress and sleep — chronic stress and sleep loss shift microbial composition (mechanism includes altered gut motility, mucus production, and bile acid signaling). The gut-brain axis is bidirectional in practice
Exercise — modest but real effects on microbial composition; partly mediated by changes in transit time, mucosal immunity, and SCFA production

Probiotics and prebiotics, briefly

Probiotic — live microorganisms intended to colonize or transiently support gut function. Common strains in supplements and fermented foods: Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species
Prebiotic — fermentable substrates that feed beneficial microbes. Common: fructooligosaccharides (FOS), galactooligosaccharides (GOS), inulin (chicory root), resistant starch
Synbiotic — combination products
Postbiotic — bacterial metabolites or inactivated cells (newer, less established)

The pragmatic guidance: food sources beat supplements for most people. The supplement industry sells specific strains as targeted “psychobiotics” (e.g., for anxiety, depression). The evidence for specific strains improving specific psychiatric outcomes is mixed and frequently overstated in marketing — the underlying mechanism is plausible and meta-analyses show small-to-moderate effects on mood for some strains, but effects are heterogeneous and don’t replicate consistently across studies.
Dietary patterns with evidence for mental health
The research signal is stronger at the pattern level than at the single nutrient level.

Mediterranean pattern — see blue-zones-dietary-patterns for the full pattern. The SMILES trial (Jacka et al., 2017) showed that a Mediterranean-style dietary intervention reduced depressive symptoms significantly more than a social-support control in moderate-to-severe depression — a small RCT, but a meaningful proof-of-concept that diet is causally relevant, not just correlated
Whole-food, plant-predominant patterns generally — DASH, Nordic, Blue Zones share the skeleton outlined in blue-zones-dietary-patterns and are similarly associated with lower depression incidence in observational data
Western pattern — high in ultra-processed foods, refined carbohydrates, industrial seed oils; consistently associated with higher depression and anxiety in observational studies. Causal direction debated (depression also changes eating patterns) but reverse-causation alone doesn’t account for the effect size

The honest version: dietary intervention in mental-health treatment is supported as an adjunct to first-line treatments (psychotherapy, medication where indicated), not as a replacement.
What’s overhyped

Specific “anti-anxiety” or “anti-depression” foods — bananas for serotonin, dark chocolate for mood, etc. Mostly marketing on top of weak signal
High-dose probiotic supplements as a depression treatment — preliminary, heterogeneous, frequently confounded by industry-sponsored trials. Reasonable to try as a low-risk adjunct; do not stop evidence-based treatment for it
Leaky-gut narratives in popular media — increased intestinal permeability is a real phenomenon in some clinical conditions (IBD, celiac, severe stress) but the consumer “leaky gut” framing dramatically overgeneralizes
Composite Dietary Antioxidant Index (CDAI) and similar indices — they exist in the research literature, but using them to predict individual mental-health outcomes is preliminary; they are population-level associations, not validated personal metrics

Practical implications
For someone already eating a Mediterranean-style diet (see personal-eating-plan) the gut-brain angle adds a few small lenses, not a new program:

Plant-species count as a tracking metric: aim for variety across the week rather than the same five vegetables. The Whole-Plate weekly target of 30+ distinct plants is a useful framing
One fermented food daily — the single most defensible single addition. Yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi rotated through the week
Fiber as a non-negotiable — most adults under-consume. 30g+ daily from food (not supplements) supports SCFA production
Skip targeted “psychobiotic” supplements unless a specific clinical indication and product evidence are present; the supplement market is poorly regulated

Related

health/loneliness-health-risk.title: Loneliness as a Health Risk Factor
health/loneliness-health-risk.content:
Loneliness as a Health Risk Factor
What it is
The replicated finding that chronic loneliness and social isolation produce health effects on a scale comparable to major medical risk factors — not metaphorically, but in terms of measured all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease incidence, and cognitive decline. The effect is large enough that the U.S. Surgeon General formally framed it as a public health “epidemic” in the 2023 advisory Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation; the WHO Commission on Social Connection (launched 2023) is pursuing analogous work at the global level.
This note is the health-risk-factor frame on the same problem the likability-and-social-connection cluster addresses from the social-skills side. The two are complements: the likability cluster is about how to build connection; this note is about why the stakes are large and what systemic interventions exist when individual effort isn’t enough.
Two distinct constructs
The literature is careful — and popular framing usually isn’t — to separate two related but non-identical phenomena:

Social isolation is objective: an absolute count of social contacts, network size, frequency of interaction. Measurable from outside.
Loneliness is subjective: the perceived gap between the connection one has and the connection one wants. Self-reported.

The two correlate but don’t coincide. People with rich networks can feel chronically lonely if those relationships lack depth. People living alone can be entirely un-lonely if their existing ties feel sufficient. Both isolation and loneliness independently predict adverse health outcomes, with somewhat different effect sizes and somewhat different mechanisms.
A third construct — living alone — overlaps with both but is separable; a stable single-person household with strong outside ties looks very different from one without.
The mortality data
The headline number people quote — that loneliness raises mortality risk by an amount comparable to smoking — traces primarily to Holt-Lunstad et al.’s meta-analyses (2010, 2015), which pooled hundreds of thousands of participants across longitudinal cohorts:

The 2015 meta-analysis reported increased odds of mortality of roughly 26% for loneliness, 29% for social isolation, and 32% for living alone, after adjustment for typical confounders
These effect sizes are similar in magnitude to (not identical to) those for obesity and physical inactivity, and have been popularly compared to “smoking 15 cigarettes a day” — a rhetorical compression that captures the order of magnitude even though the underlying biology is different

Beyond all-cause mortality, the same family of studies and subsequent reviews link chronic disconnection to higher incidence of:

Cardiovascular disease and stroke
Type 2 diabetes
Dementia and Alzheimer’s disease
Depression and anxiety (bidirectional — disconnection both predicts and is predicted by these)
Compromised immune function and slower wound healing

The mechanism is consistent with what we know about chronic stress biology: prolonged unmet social needs maintain elevated HPA-axis activity, sympathetic tone, and inflammatory signaling — the same axis described in sidi-stress-cognition but kept chronically activated rather than phasically.
Why this is more than “be sociable”
Three reasons the public-health framing matters even for someone who is broadly socially connected:

The relationship between network size and quality is non-linear. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, running since 1938, is the longest such longitudinal cohort. It consistently finds the strongest predictor of late-life health and happiness is not the number of relationships but the perceived quality of close ones. Optimizing for network breadth at the cost of depth is a known failure mode
Modern infrastructure creates ambient isolation that doesn’t feel like isolation. Remote work, food delivery, on-demand entertainment, and curated digital social feeds reduce friction for solo functioning to the point where the feedback loop that used to push people back into in-person contact is muted. The loneliness epidemic was already detectable pre-2020 and accelerated through the pandemic
Risk distribution is uneven. Older adults, immigrants, marginalized groups, people with disabilities, and rural residents face structurally higher loneliness risk for reasons beyond individual behavior. Population-level responses are warranted, not just individual ones

Social prescribing as a clinical response
A practice developed in the UK’s NHS over the past two decades and now spreading internationally: a healthcare practitioner refers a patient not to medication or therapy but to a link worker, who develops a personalized plan involving community-based activities — typically a patient with mild-to-moderate mental health issues, isolation, or stress-related somatic complaints.
The model is interesting because it acknowledges a category of presenting complaint that traditional clinical infrastructure handles poorly: distress that originates in social, practical, or environmental conditions rather than in pathophysiology, and where pharmaceutical or psychotherapeutic intervention is mismatched to the actual problem.
Common categories of social prescription:

Arts and culture — singing groups, choirs, craft workshops, community theatre
Nature-based — community gardens, conservation volunteering, walking groups
Physical activity — local sports clubs, yoga groups, walking groups (overlap with the above)
Practical and peer support — debt or housing advice, befriending services, bereavement support, intergenerational programs

Evidence base: heterogeneous studies, many small, but converging signals on reduced GP visit frequency, improved subjective wellbeing, and reasonable cost-effectiveness for specific patient categories. Less evidence for severe mental illness as a stand-alone treatment, but useful as adjunct.
For Finland specifically, parallel community-based efforts exist (kulttuuriresepti / cultural prescription pilots, MIELI Mental Health Finland’s peer support and community programs), though the formal “social prescribing” framework is not as institutionalized as in the UK.
What this implies for personal practice
Beyond what the likability-and-social-connection cluster covers:

Track relationships as a real load, not as something that just happens. The friendship-formula factors (friendship-formula-schafer — proximity, frequency, duration, intensity) require deliberate scheduling, especially for adults whose proximity-based ties (school, workplace) have decayed
Quality > quantity for close ties; the mortality effect tracks closer to perceived support than to network size. A few high-quality ties is not a fallback option, it’s the more defensible target
Variety of tie types matters — close ties (family, partner, close friends), affinity ties (clubs, hobby groups, professional communities), and weak ties (regulars at the gym, neighbors, repeated baristas). Mark Granovetter’s “strength of weak ties” finding generalizes to wellbeing as well as job-finding: the count of casual recurring contacts buffers against subjective loneliness even when it doesn’t substitute for close ties
Loneliness is feedback, not failure — chronic loneliness is information the current configuration is mismatched to actual social need; treat it as a signal to investigate rather than as a personal flaw to be willpowered through
Solo-functioning skills (calm-by-yourself, productive-by-yourself, fine-with-silence) are good but should not be confused with not needing connection — the “I’m an introvert who needs alone time” framing is real and useful, but at the population level, self-described introverts who report strong close ties still show better health outcomes than self-described introverts who don’t

Related

likability-and-social-connection — hub for the “how” of building connection; this note is the “why it matters” complement
friendship-formula-schafer — the proximity/frequency/duration/intensity model is the operational counterpart to the public-health framing here
likability-paradox — the failure modes (spotlight effect, hyper-vigilance) that block people from acting on what they know about connection
sidi-stress-cognition — chronic loneliness is a chronic stressor; the prefrontal-suppression mechanism is the same one acute stress triggers
longevity-foundations — social connection is a longevity lever the longevity cluster has not previously addressed in depth and arguably belongs alongside exercise, sleep, and nutrition
bdnf-exercise-cognition — group-based physical activity stacks the social-connection benefit on top of the BDNF benefit
meditation-practice — solo-practice; useful but not a substitute for relational ties

Counterargument
The “loneliness equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes” framing has been criticized as rhetorically compelling but technically loose — the underlying RR/HR comparisons depend heavily on which cohorts are being compared, what confounders are adjusted for, and whether the smoking comparison is current vs. former smokers. The order-of-magnitude claim survives scrutiny; the precise numerical equivalence does not.
Additionally, the causal arrow between loneliness and adverse health is partly bidirectional: chronic illness, depression, and disability shrink networks too. Most of the longitudinal evidence supports loneliness as causally upstream in at least some pathways, but the effect-size estimates from observational data probably overstate the pure causal impact.
The intervention literature is thinner than the descriptive epidemiology suggests. Recommending that lonely people “just connect more” is not actionable for the structural conditions that produce isolation in the first place; this is why the social-prescribing and community-infrastructure framings exist.
Sources

Holt-Lunstad, J. et al. (2015) — “Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: A meta-analytic review” — Perspectives on Psychological Science
Holt-Lunstad, J. et al. (2010) — “Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review” — PLoS Medicine
Office of the U.S. Surgeon General (2023) — Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation — advisory framing the public-health stakes
WHO Commission on Social Connection — ongoing global work, 2023–
Waldinger, R. & Schulz, M. (2023) — The Good Life — popular synthesis of the Harvard Study of Adult Development findings
Bickerdike, L. et al. (2017) — “Social prescribing: less rhetoric and more reality. A systematic review of the evidence” — BMJ Open — sober assessment of the social-prescribing evidence base
Granovetter, M. (1973) — “The Strength of Weak Ties” — American Journal of Sociology — the structural-tie point

The mortality effect-size figures are widely-cited from Holt-Lunstad’s meta-analyses; the popular smoking-equivalence framing originated there but should be treated as an order-of-magnitude rhetorical device rather than precise.
