password-key-hygiene — bearer-secret handling, which capabilities inherit
linux-hardening-checklist — host-level containment mechanics
agent-sandbox-isolation-tiers — the same containment question for agent workloads
../ai/agent-identity-delegated-authority — delegated authority across a network, agent-side
agent-policy-enforcement-gap — why a control the subject administers isn’t a boundary
../ai/capability-combination-security-frames — which capabilities may co-occur in one session

Sources

Google Chrome Security (July 2018) — “Mitigating Spectre with Site Isolation in Chrome” — security.googleblog.com/2018/07/mitigating-spectre-with-site-isolation.html. ✅ Fetched 2026-08-07; the 99% rollout, the 10–13% memory overhead, and the fully-compromised-renderer limitation quoted verbatim. Measures rollout and overhead plus argued exposure reduction — not prevented breaches.
Miller, M., Yee, K.-P. & Shapiro, J. (2003) — “Capability Myths Demolished” — papers.agoric.com/papers/capability-myths-demolished/full-text/. Clarifies capability misconceptions including the confused deputy; does not show capability systems are operationally cheaper.
Watson, R. N. M. et al. (2010) — “Capsicum: Practical Capabilities for UNIX” — USENIX Security. Capability-oriented sandboxing; system evaluation, not web-authorization outcome data.
AWS Well-Architected — “Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture” — docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture/what-is-a-cell-based-architecture.html. First-party operational doctrine; not independent causal evidence. Not re-fetched in this pass.
Framing derived from a user-supplied research synthesis, “The reasoning layer of software security” (2026-08-07), produced by another AI system; the Chrome figures were re-verified against the primary source here.

security/authorization-as-a-protocol.title: Authorization as a Protocol
security/authorization-as-a-protocol.content:
Authorization as a Protocol
Authorization is the layer that resists tooling hardest, and the reason is worth stating exactly: an authorization bug is usually a valid program implementing the wrong relation. Nothing is malformed. The types check, the tests pass, the scanner is quiet, and the code does precisely what it says — which is the wrong thing.
That makes it the residue left over after designing-out-defect-classes (which removes representation errors) and after ambient-authority-and-blast-radius (which bounds consequence). This note is about the relation itself.
Confidence legend: ◐ = corroborated across independent secondary sources, primary not obtained in this pass · ○ = mechanism argued, not a measured result.
Three properties that defeat static tooling
○ Authorization defects have a shape that is hostile to every tool that works on one artifact at a time:

Cross-file and cross-service. Identity is established in one place, resource ownership in another, policy in a third, and the effect in a fourth. No single file contains the bug; the bug is the relation between four files.
Temporal. Roles, consent, suspension, delegation, and object state all change. “User A may edit this” is true until a revocation lands, and a cached decision, a group snapshot, or an in-flight retry can carry the old answer past it.
Contextual. The same action may be permitted only below a threshold, within a region, during an incident, or subject to separation of duties.

What each tool actually sees: SAST sees code; DAST sees the executions its crawler happened to generate; an LLM sees whatever was retrieved into its context. ○ None of them possesses the authoritative business relation, because in most systems that relation is not written down anywhere — it lives in a product manager’s head, a Jira thread, and four handlers that disagree. This is the specification ceiling from adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning in its most concrete form.
The protocol
○ The response is to stop treating authorization as a check and start treating it as a protocol with a stated contract:

One decision shape: principal × action × resource × context → decision. Every enforcement point speaks it.
Centralize the semantics and version them. One place defines what the rules mean. The version is part of every decision.
Enforce at every effect boundary, not only at the UI or API edge. The edge is where requests arrive; effects happen deeper, and background jobs, queue consumers, admin tools, and migrations never pass the edge at all.
Bind cached decisions to policy version and relevant state, so a revocation invalidates rather than waits out a TTL.
Generate negative and metamorphic tests from the policy (below).
Log decision inputs and committed effects out of band — see post-breach-investigability.
Deny on missing tenant, stale identity, or indeterminate policy. Fail-closed is only real if “I don’t know” is on the deny side.

Note that centralizing semantics is not centralizing enforcement. The decision object should be minted centrally and then carried — which is exactly where this meets capabilities: central policy decides whether to mint; the capability constrains what the holder may then do. Either layer alone has a characteristic failure — a central engine alone creates an online dependency and a single semantic failure domain; local grants alone become ungoverned bearer authority with no way to change policy globally.
○ The honest cost: a policy service can become a latency bottleneck and a single point of semantic failure. The answer is not scattering ad-hoc checks back through the handlers; it is replicated enforcement with explicit policy-version and cache semantics, so you know what a stale replica is allowed to answer.
Testing a relation: metamorphic properties
○ This is the practical payoff, and it is underused. You usually cannot write down the whole policy as an oracle — but you can write down invariants the policy must satisfy under transformation, which is testable without knowing every rule:

Monotonicity of privilege — removing a privilege must never increase the set of reachable effects.
Tenant substitution — changing the tenant in a request must never preserve a resource handle’s validity.
Idempotency — replaying an idempotency key must not multiply a value transfer.
Revocation liveness — after revocation lands, no cached path may still commit the effect.
Self-approval — no principal may satisfy both sides of a separation-of-duties requirement.

These are the tests that stay green in a codebase with the bug and go red the moment someone refactors authorization badly. Unlike a fuzzer’s crash oracle, they have a real oracle for “valid but forbidden” — which is precisely the class security-assurance-tooling-ceilings shows fuzzing structurally cannot see.
Automation is possible — under one condition
○ “Authorization cannot be automated” is too strong, and the exceptions teach the rule.
◐ Two older research systems found genuine, previously-unreported authorization flaws at scale. RoleCast (Son, McKinley & Shmatikov, 2011) inferred role-consistency patterns across PHP/JSP applications — if most handlers in a role perform a check and one does not, that inconsistency is a signal. AuthScope (Zuo, Zhao & Lin, 2017) used differential traffic analysis across thousands of Android apps — substitute a protocol field, observe whether the response changes in a way that indicates the substitution was honored.
(Both papers report specific counts of flaws found; those figures were not re-verified in this pass and are deliberately omitted rather than quoted.)
The condition they share is the transferable part: each had a narrow inconsistency oracle or a substitutable protocol field. Neither infers arbitrary unwritten policy, and neither proves absence when no differential appears. So the automation question for your own system is not “can a tool check authorization” but “is there an internal consistency I can make a tool compare against?” Where handlers should be uniform, deviation is machine-findable. Where every rule is bespoke, it is not.
Where this meets generated code
The AI-specific instance is already in the vault and is the sharpest illustration of the whole note: vibe-coding-authorization-flaws documents generated applications whose front-end code is flawless while server-side enforcement was never configured — the flaw is an absence, in a system the diff never touches. This note is the design-side answer to it. If authorization is a protocol with an explicit decision shape and metamorphic tests, “nobody wrote the policy” becomes a failing test rather than an invisible omission.
The caveat that note raises applies here too and should not be waved away: an agent that omitted the enforcement will just as cheerfully omit the negative test, or write one that passes against its own assumptions. The metamorphic properties above are more resistant than hand-written negative tests precisely because they are stated over transformations rather than over specific expected answers — but they still have to come from someone who wants the system to be secure.
Counterargument
The strongest case against this note is that most teams should not build any of it. A single-tenant application with three roles gets more security from a well-reviewed middleware and a couple of integration tests than from a policy service, a version field, and a metamorphic suite — and the elaborate version introduces its own outage mode, where a policy-engine failure takes down a system that would otherwise have been merely wrong for one user.
It also assumes the business relation is knowable at design time. Frequently it is not: the rules are genuinely under negotiation, and encoding them prematurely produces a versioned, audited, precisely-enforced encoding of a policy nobody agreed to — the “verifier proves the wrong policy perfectly” failure with extra infrastructure.
The threshold worth naming: multi-tenancy and irreversible effects. Once one customer’s data can be reached through another customer’s request, or an action moves money or deletes state, the relation becomes load-bearing and ad-hoc checks stop being defensible. Below that line, steps 1, 3, and 7 alone (one decision shape, enforce at effects, deny on unknown) capture most of the value.
Related

adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning — cluster hub; the specification ceiling this note instantiates
designing-out-defect-classes — removes representation errors; cannot reach relation errors
ambient-authority-and-blast-radius — capabilities as the enforcement half of this protocol
security-assurance-tooling-ceilings — why fuzzers and scanners structurally miss this class
post-breach-investigability — logging decision inputs, step 6
web-application-security — broken access control as the symptom catalog
threat-modeling-basics — where authorization boundaries get found before code exists
vibe-coding-authorization-flaws — the generated-code instance of the whole problem

Sources

Son, S., McKinley, K. S. & Shmatikov, V. (2011) — “RoleCast: Finding Missing Security Checks When You Do Not Know What Checks Are” — OOPSLA. Role-consistency inference; convention-relative oracle on an older PHP/JSP corpus. Reported flaw counts not re-verified here.
Zuo, C., Zhao, Q. & Lin, Z. (2017) — “AuthScope: Towards Automatic Discovery of Vulnerable Authorizations in Online Services” — ACM CCS. Differential traffic and response analysis; depends on substitutable protocol fields. Reported flaw counts not re-verified here.
Pang, R. et al. (2019) — “Zanzibar: Google’s Consistent, Global Authorization System” — USENIX ATC — www.usenix.org/conference/atc19/presentation/pang. Production relation-based authorization at scale; demonstrates architecture and consistency, not that central policy eliminates policy mistakes.
Cutler, J. W. et al. (2024) — “Cedar: A New Language for Expressive, Fast, Safe, and Analyzable Authorization” — arxiv.org/abs/2403.04651. ✅ Title, lead author, and subject verified 2026-08-07. Policy-language design and analyzability; correctness still depends on the intended rules.
Structure derived from a user-supplied research synthesis, “The reasoning layer of software security” (2026-08-07), authored by another AI system. Its per-paper flaw counts were not independently verified and were dropped rather than hedged, per this vault’s authoring rules.

security/designing-out-defect-classes.title: Designing Out Defect Classes
security/designing-out-defect-classes.content:
Designing Out Defect Classes
The strongest security move is not teaching people to remember more forbidden patterns. It is making the dangerous state unavailable — deleting a class of decisions from ordinary programming so that the reviewer’s memory is no longer load-bearing.
This is the construction half of adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning. That note argues why detection-based evidence is weak against an opponent who selects the tail; this one covers the response.
Confidence legend: ✅ = primary source fetched and quoted text matched verbatim during this pass · ○ = mechanism argued, not a measured result.
The rare fleet evidence: Android memory safety
Class elimination is usually argued, not measured. Android is the exception worth knowing precisely, because it is production-scale and first-party rather than a microbenchmark.
✅ Google’s Memory Safe Languages in Android 13 (Dec 2022) reports, on vulnerabilities in the Android security bulletin:

“From 2019 to 2022 the annual number of memory safety vulnerabilities dropped from 223 down to 85.”
“From 2019 to 2022 it has dropped from 76% down to 35% of Android’s total vulnerabilities.”
“Android 13 is the first Android release where a majority of new code added to the release is in a memory safe language.”
“In Android 13, about 21% of all new native code (C/C++/Rust) is in Rust,” roughly 1.5 million lines across AOSP.
“To date, there have been zero memory safety vulnerabilities discovered in Android’s Rust code.”

✅ Google states the causal limit itself: “While correlation doesn’t necessarily mean causation … Of course there may be other contributing factors or alternative explanations.” Language migration, code age, review intensity, hardening, and attacker attention were not randomized. The post also notes that hardening tools deployed in the same window (Scudo, HWASAN, GWP-ASAN, KFENCE, more fuzzing) “do not account for the large shift.”
Two readings matter. The absolute count (223 → 85) is the more decision-relevant number; the share (76% → 35%) partly reflects that non-memory-safety vulnerabilities held roughly steady, so a share can fall without any absolute improvement. And Google’s own strategy note is the transferable part: the goal was never to rewrite existing C/C++ but to shift new code, because vulnerability density concentrates in new code.
What actually transfers to TypeScript/JavaScript
○ The lesson is not “use Rust.” It is: identify which defect family can be removed at the narrowest durable boundary, and put a constructor there. For a web system that boundary is rarely the language and usually the type of a domain value.
Concrete moves, in rough order of payoff:

Opaque, validated identifiers instead of free-form strings. A UserId that cannot be constructed from an arbitrary string ends the entire family of “wrong id in the right slot.”
Tenant-scoped resource handles instead of (tenantId, resourceId) passed as separate parameters. The two-parameter form makes cross-tenant access a typo; the handle form makes it unrepresentable. This is the single highest-value one for multi-tenant systems.
State-specific types — PendingOrder and SettledOrder as distinct types rather than one Order with a status flag whose combinations include nonsense.
Bounded and non-empty collections as constructors, not as comments.
One canonical representation of a URL, path, or policy selector, produced once before any policy decision reads it.
A policy decision object carrying principal, action, resource, context, policy version, expiry, and decision — not a boolean named isAllowed. (Why this one is load-bearing: authorization-as-a-protocol.)

The TypeScript-specific caveat, from the source
✅ TypeScript’s own design document lists as non-goals: “Apply a sound or ‘provably correct’ type system. Instead, strike a balance between correctness and productivity,” and “Add or rely on run-time type information in programs, or emit different code based on the results of the type system.”
That is not a criticism of TypeScript; it is the contract. But it fixes where the real boundary sits. any, type assertions, hand-written declaration files, mutation, and plain-JavaScript callers all bypass the compile-time story, and there is no runtime type metadata to fall back on. So the enforceable pipeline is:
unknown bytes → runtime parser → controlled constructor → precise domain value
Types are what keeps the value precise after the parse. They are not what establishes it. A schema validator at the edge (the vault’s existing stack note covers the tooling — ai-verification-stack-web) is the thing doing the actual work; the type is how the result stays trustworthy on the way in.
Parse, don’t validate
○ Alexis King’s formulation is a practitioner argument, not a controlled result, and its security force comes from information preservation:

A validator returns the original weak value plus a transient fact — “this string looked valid, here, once.” Every downstream caller must remember which checks ran.
A parser returns a stronger value whose constructors encode the accepted grammar. Downstream code cannot forget, because the weak form is no longer in its hands.

This matters most at ambiguity boundaries: URLs, filesystem paths, Unicode identifiers, money, dates, signatures, hostnames, policy selectors. Parse once, canonicalize once, reject the leftovers, carry the typed result.
○ Language-theoretic security generalizes it: permissive, context-sensitive recognizers expand attack surface because producer and consumer can disagree about where the input language ends. Parser differentials are that disagreement being exploited. The secure move is a small, explicit input language — never a growing blacklist.
The cost is real and worth stating: versioning parsers and preserving compatibility become explicit product work. That is the trade — you are choosing to do that work centrally and visibly instead of letting every call site improvise a dialect.
Saltzer & Schroeder, audited
The 1975 principles are design heuristics, not independently quantified laws. ○ How each has held up, with the cost each imposes:


















































PrincipleVerdictCost of applying itFail-safe defaultsSurvived strongly. Absence, timeout, parse failure, unknown tenant, indeterminate policy should deny or quarantineAvailability and operational friction during control-plane outagesComplete mediationSurvived, but caches and distributed systems make “every access” a protocol-design problemLatency, policy-version management, invalidation complexityLeast privilegeSurvived, but static roles drift into privilege warehouses; capabilities and short-lived grants make it operationalGrant lifecycle and harder debuggingEconomy of mechanismSurvived as pressure toward a smaller trusted computing base — but small ≠ understandableFeature pressure works against it continuouslyLeast common mechanismSurvived as blast-radius reasoning: shared queues, identity brokers, caches, build runners, admin planes create shared fateDuplication and lower utilizationSeparation of privilegeSurvived where the conditions genuinely fail independently. Two approvals behind one compromised identity provider are one controlProcess friction, and the independence is easy to lose silentlyOpen designSurvived as rejection of secrecy-as-primary-defense. Openness enables scrutiny; it does not perform itNone directly — but it is often over-claimedPsychological acceptabilityBecame more important. A secure API that developers routinely bypass is an unmeasured aspirationDesign effort, and sometimes weaker theoretical guarantees
The durable meta-principle across all eight: minimize what must go right at the moment of use.
Counterargument
Typed domain modelling has a real ceiling and a real bill. Richer types and constructors slow local edits, complicate serialization, and force migration work at every boundary — and in a TypeScript codebase the guarantee stops at the first any, the first untyped dependency, the first JS caller. A team can pay the full cost of branded identifiers and still ship the cross-tenant bug, because the leak was in a query builder that never saw the brand.
The honest scope: this technique eliminates representation errors — wrong value, wrong shape, wrong state, wrong slot. It does nothing for relation errors, where every value is well-formed and the policy is wrong (authorization-as-a-protocol is that gap), and nothing for what happens after a component is compromised (ambient-authority-and-blast-radius). Treating “we have strong types” as a security posture is exactly the category error adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning warns about, one layer up.
Related

adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning — the epistemics this responds to; hub for the cluster
authorization-as-a-protocol — the relation errors types cannot reach
ambient-authority-and-blast-radius — bounding what a compromised component can do
web-application-security — the vulnerability classes; parsing once is the structural defense behind several of them
ai-verification-stack-web — the concrete TS/JS tooling layer (schema validation, contract tests, mutation testing)
typescript-for-ai-tooling — TypeScript’s role in this vault’s tooling work
ai-code-latent-failure-modes — what generated code does when the boundary is only a convention

Sources

Google Android Security (Dec 2022) — “Memory Safe Languages in Android 13” — security.googleblog.com/2022/12/memory-safe-languages-in-android-13.html. ✅ Fetched 2026-08-07; all quoted figures verbatim. First-party observational evidence, explicitly not causal.
Microsoft TypeScript team — “TypeScript Design Goals” — github.com/microsoft/TypeScript-wiki/blob/master/TypeScript-Design-Goals.md. ✅ Non-goals quoted verbatim, fetched 2026-08-07. A mutable design document.
King, A. (2019) — “Parse, don’t validate” — lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/. Practitioner mechanism, not security-outcome research.
Bratus, S. et al. (2016) — “The Seven Turrets of Babel” — IEEE SecDev. Language-theoretic account of input-language errors; taxonomy/design paper, not a deployment effect estimate.
Saltzer, J. H. & Schroeder, M. D. (1975) — “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems” — web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/protection/Basic.html.
Structure and the survival audit derived from a user-supplied research synthesis, “The reasoning layer of software security” (2026-08-07), authored by another AI system; its Android and TypeScript claims were re-verified against primary sources here and its unverifiable numeric claims dropped.

security/incident-response-basics.title: Incident Response Basics
security/incident-response-basics.content:
Incident Response Basics
What it is
Incident response (IR) is the structured process for handling a security incident — a confirmed or suspected breach, compromise, or misuse — from the moment it is detected through to recovery and lessons learned. Its goal is to limit damage, restore normal operation, and preserve the evidence and understanding needed to prevent a repeat, all while making decisions under time pressure and incomplete information.
Why it matters
Incidents are decided in the first hours, and those hours are exactly when panic, improvisation, and well-meaning but destructive actions do the most harm. Someone who wipes a compromised machine to “clean it” before anyone images it has destroyed the evidence needed to understand the breach. Someone who tips off an attacker by clumsily probing may trigger data destruction. A rehearsed process replaces panic with sequence: it tells you what to do first, what not to touch, and who decides.
The difference between a contained incident and a sprawling breach is rarely the sophistication of the attacker; it is how quickly and calmly the defender moves through detection, containment, and recovery. Having thought about this before the incident is most of the value.
Details
The lifecycle
A widely-used framing breaks IR into phases that run roughly in order but loop back as understanding improves:

Preparation — The work done before an incident: an inventory of systems and data, a contact and escalation list, logging and backups that actually exist and are tested, and a written plan people have read. Preparation is the phase that most determines how the others go.
Detection and analysis — Recognizing that something is wrong and characterizing it: what is affected, how, since when, and how confident you are. Distinguish a true incident from a false alarm before triggering disruptive response, but do not let analysis paralysis delay containment of an obvious active compromise.
Containment — Stopping the spread and limiting further damage. Often split into short-term containment (isolate the affected system now — e.g., remove it from the network) and longer-term containment (apply controls that let you keep operating safely while you eradicate the root cause).
Eradication — Removing the attacker’s foothold: the malicious code, the unauthorized accounts, the exploited vulnerability, the leaked-and-still-valid credentials. Eradication is incomplete if the entry path or any persistence mechanism remains.
Recovery — Returning systems to normal, validated operation: restoring from known-good backups, rotating affected secrets, and monitoring closely for signs the attacker returns. Recovery is gated on eradication — restoring a system while the foothold remains just re-infects it.
Post-incident review — A blameless retrospective: what happened, what the timeline was, what worked, what did not, and what concrete changes reduce the chance or impact of a recurrence. This is where an incident pays for itself by improving the next preparation phase.

Preserve evidence before you change anything
The instinct to “fix it” fights with the need to understand it. Where feasible, capture state before altering it:

Collect the most volatile evidence first. Some evidence vanishes the instant a machine is powered off or rebooted — running processes, network connections, memory contents, logged-in sessions — while disk contents persist. Capture the volatile and ephemeral before the durable, because you can always image a disk later but you cannot recover RAM after a shutdown.
Prefer isolation over destruction. Disconnecting a compromised host from the network often contains the threat while keeping the evidence intact, which is usually better than wiping it.
Preserve logs early. Logs are a prime target for an attacker covering tracks and are also easy to lose to rotation. Copy relevant logs to safe storage as soon as the incident is suspected.
Keep a timeline as you go. Note what you observed and what you did, with timestamps. The post-incident review and any external reporting depend on this contemporaneous record, and memory under stress is unreliable.

Decide containment trade-offs deliberately
Containment forces a judgment call: act now and tip off the attacker, or watch longer to understand scope while risking further damage. There is no universal right answer — it depends on what is at stake, how active the threat is, and how confident you are. The point is to make that call consciously, ideally with a named decision-maker, rather than defaulting into it.
Roles and communication

Name a coordinator. Someone must own the incident and the decisions, even in a small team. Diffuse ownership produces both duplicated effort and untaken decisions.
Decide who needs to know, and when. Internal stakeholders, affected users, and (depending on jurisdiction and data) regulators may need notification. Plan the communication path before the incident so it is not invented during one.
Communicate facts, hedge the unknowns. Early in an incident much is uncertain. State what is known, label what is not, and resist the pressure to over-commit to a narrative that later evidence contradicts.

Connection to ongoing hygiene
Most of incident response is won in preparation, which overlaps heavily with everyday security work: tested backups, an asset inventory, working logs, and the ability to rotate and revoke credentials quickly (see password-key-hygiene). A threat model (see threat-modeling-basics) tells you in advance which incidents are most likely and most damaging, so preparation can be aimed rather than generic.
A minimal plan beats no plan
A solo developer or small team does not need a heavyweight program. A short written document turns a 3am scramble into a checklist — who to contact, where backups are and how to restore them, how to take a system offline, how to rotate each kind of secret, and the phase order above. The act of writing it surfaces gaps (no backups, no logs, no idea who owns a system) while there is still time to fix them.
Related

password-key-hygiene — Rotating and revoking compromised credentials during eradication and recovery
threat-modeling-basics — Anticipating which incidents to prepare for
linux-hardening-checklist — Logging, auditing, and backups that make detection and recovery possible
supply-chain-security — Responding to a compromised dependency or build pipeline

Sources

Synthesis of widely-established incident-response practice; the six-phase lifecycle reflects the common preparation / detection / containment / eradication / recovery / lessons-learned structure used across the field. No specific external source.

security/linux-hardening-checklist.title: Linux Hardening Checklist
security/linux-hardening-checklist.content:
Linux Hardening Checklist
What it is
A practical, prioritized guide for securing a Fedora workstation (or server). Covers the layers that matter most — from firewall and SELinux through SSH, disk encryption, auditing, and container isolation. Focused on Fedora and the Red Hat ecosystem but most concepts transfer to any systemd-based Linux distribution. A quick-reference checklist for periodic review sits at the end of this note.
Why it matters
A default Fedora install is reasonably secure out of the box — SELinux is enforcing, firewalld is active, and the kernel has modern exploit mitigations. But “reasonably secure” isn’t enough when the machine holds SSH keys, GPG keys, API tokens, and access to production systems. Every layer you harden reduces the blast radius when (not if) something gets compromised.
Use threat-modeling-basics to decide which layers to prioritize. Not every system needs every item here — a personal workstation has different risks than a public-facing server.
Details
Fresh Fedora Install — First Steps
Do these before connecting to untrusted networks:


Full-disk encryption (LUKS) — Enable during installation. You can’t retrofit this without pain.


Set a firmware/BIOS password — Prevents boot-order tampering.


Update everything: sudo dnf upgrade --refresh


Review running services: systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running — disable anything you don’t need.


Create a non-root user and use sudo exclusively. Fedora does this by default but verify.


Verify Secure Boot is enabled: mokutil --sb-state — Ensures only signed kernels and modules load. Fedora supports Secure Boot out of the box.


Set a boot loader password (GRUB): Prevents single-user mode access without credentials.
# Generate a PBKDF2 hash
grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2
# Add to /etc/grub.d/40_custom:
# set superusers="admin"
# password_pbkdf2 admin grub.pbkdf2.sha512.10000.<hash>
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg


Firewall (firewalld)
Fedora uses firewalld with zone-based rules. The default zone is typically FedoraWorkstation.
# Check current zone and rules
firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
firewall-cmd --list-all
 
# For a workstation, drop to the "home" or "drop" zone
firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=home
 
# Remove services you don't need
firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=mdns
firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=samba-client
 
# Allow only what you need (example: SSH)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh
 
# Apply changes
firewall-cmd --reload
Zone strategy: Use drop zone for public WiFi (drops all incoming), home for trusted networks, and work for office networks. Switch zones per-interface or per-connection via NetworkManager.
Rich rules for fine-grained control:
# Allow SSH only from a specific subnet
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" service name="ssh" accept'
 
# Rate-limit incoming connections (anti-brute-force at firewall level)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule service name="ssh" accept limit value="5/m"'
 
# Log dropped packets (useful for monitoring)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" log prefix="DROPPED: " level="info" drop'
nftables — firewalld uses nftables as its backend on modern Fedora. For advanced users, writing nftables rules directly gives finer control:
# View the actual nftables ruleset behind firewalld
nft list ruleset
 
# Check if firewalld is using nftables backend
firewall-cmd --get-backend  # Should say "nftables"
SELinux
SELinux is Fedora’s mandatory access control system. Never disable it. If something breaks, fix the policy — don’t set it to permissive.
# Verify enforcing mode
getenforce        # Should say "Enforcing"
sestatus          # Detailed status
 
# If something is denied, check the audit log
ausearch -m avc -ts recent
 
# Use audit2why to understand denials
ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2why
 
# If the denial is legitimate, use audit2allow to generate a policy module
ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow -M mypolicy
semodule -i mypolicy.pp
SELinux booleans control common policy decisions without writing custom modules:
# List all booleans
getsebool -a
 
# Example: allow httpd to connect to the network
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
 
# Example: allow user home directories to be served by httpd
setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on
File contexts: When files get mislabeled (e.g., after moving them instead of copying):
# Restore default context for a path
restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
 
# Check a file's context
ls -Z /path/to/file
 
# Define a custom file context for a non-standard path
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/website(/.*)?"
restorecon -Rv /srv/website
Confining users with SELinux: SELinux can restrict what regular users can do, beyond standard Unix permissions:
# Map a Linux user to a confined SELinux user
semanage login -a -s user_u dangeroususer
 
# SELinux user types (from most to least restricted):
# user_u     — No sudo, no su, no network server access
# staff_u    — Can sudo to specific roles
# sysadm_u   — Full admin (only use for actual admins)
# unconfined_u — Default, minimal SELinux restriction
Troubleshooting workflow: When SELinux blocks something, follow this sequence: (1) ausearch -m avc -ts recent to find the denial, (2) audit2why to understand the reason, (3) check if a boolean already exists for the use case with sesearch, (4) only generate a custom module with audit2allow as a last resort.
SSH Hardening
Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config (or add a drop-in file at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf):
# Key-only authentication
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
 
# Restrict access
PermitRootLogin no
AllowUsers your_username
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
 
# Protocol and algorithm hardening
KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org
HostKeyAlgorithms ssh-ed25519
Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com
 
# Other hardening
X11Forwarding no
AllowAgentForwarding no
AllowTcpForwarding no
MaxSessions 3
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2
Fail2ban for brute-force protection:
sudo dnf install fail2ban
sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
 
# Create /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
# [sshd]
# enabled = true
# port = ssh
# filter = sshd
# maxretry = 3
# bantime = 3600
# findtime = 600
Key management: Use Ed25519 keys (ssh-keygen -t ed25519). Store keys with a passphrase and use ssh-agent to avoid retyping. Consider hardware keys (YubiKey via FIDO2: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk).
SSH certificate-based authentication — For environments with multiple hosts, SSH certificates scale better than distributing authorized_keys:
# Create a CA key (do this once, guard this key)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ssh_ca -C "SSH CA"
 
# Sign a user's public key (valid for 52 weeks)
ssh-keygen -s ssh_ca -I user@host -V +52w -n username ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
 
# On the server, trust the CA in sshd_config:
# TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/ssh_ca.pub
Audit your SSH config against known weaknesses:
# Test your server's SSH config remotely
ssh-audit your-server.example.com
 
# Test locally (install via: pip install ssh-audit)
ssh-audit localhost
Two-factor authentication for SSH — Combine key-based auth with TOTP using google-authenticator-libpam:
sudo dnf install google-authenticator
google-authenticator  # Run as the user, follow prompts
# In sshd_config:
# AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive
# In /etc/pam.d/sshd, add:
# auth required pam_google_authenticator.so
Filesystem Permissions and ACLs
Lock down default permissions and audit for risky files:
# Ensure home directory is not world-readable
chmod 700 /home/yourusername
 
# Set umask to restrict default permissions (add to ~/.bashrc)
umask 027  # Files: 640, Directories: 750
 
# Find world-writable files (potential risk)
find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -ls 2>/dev/null
 
# Find SUID/SGID binaries (potential privilege escalation)
find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f -ls 2>/dev/null
 
# Use ACLs for fine-grained sharing
setfacl -m u:collaborator:rx /shared/project
getfacl /shared/project
Sticky bit on shared directories: chmod +t /shared/ prevents users from deleting each other’s files.
Immutable files — Protect critical configs from modification even by root:
# Make a file immutable (cannot be modified, deleted, or renamed)
sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf
 
# View file attributes
lsattr /etc/resolv.conf
 
# Remove immutable flag when you need to edit
sudo chattr -i /etc/resolv.conf
tmpfiles.d hardening — Ensure temp directories have restrictive permissions:
# Verify /tmp and /var/tmp have sticky bit and correct ownership
ls -ld /tmp /var/tmp
# Should show: drwxrwxrwt (1777)
 
# Consider mounting /tmp as tmpfs with noexec,nosuid,nodev
# In /etc/fstab:
# tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev,size=2G 0 0
Automatic Security Updates (dnf-automatic)
Have security patches install themselves on a timer:
sudo dnf install dnf-automatic
sudo systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic-install.timer
 
# Edit /etc/dnf/automatic.conf:
# [commands]
# upgrade_type = security    # Only security updates
# apply_updates = yes
# 
# [emitters]
# emit_via = stdio           # Or "email" for notifications
For a workstation, upgrade_type = security is conservative enough. For servers, keep the same upgrade_type but stage updates through a canary host before they reach the fleet.
Verify updates are working:
# Check last time dnf-automatic ran
systemctl status dnf-automatic-install.timer
journalctl -u dnf-automatic-install.service --since "7 days ago"
 
# List installed security updates
dnf updateinfo list --installed --security
Kernel Hardening (sysctl and boot parameters)
Beyond network sysctls (see Network Hardening below), several kernel parameters improve exploit resistance:
# Add to /etc/sysctl.d/99-kernel-hardening.conf
 
# Restrict access to kernel logs (prevents info leaks)
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1
 
# Hide kernel pointers from unprivileged users (blocks bypass of KASLR,
# the kernel's address-space randomization)
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
 
# Restrict eBPF to root only
kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1
 
# Restrict user namespaces (mitigates container escape classes)
# WARNING: This breaks rootless Podman. Only enable on servers without rootless containers.
# user.max_user_namespaces = 0
 
# Restrict ptrace (prevents process snooping)
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 2
 
# Restrict performance events
kernel.perf_event_paranoid = 3
 
# Disable magic SysRq key combinations (prevents local DoS)
kernel.sysrq = 0
Kernel boot parameters — Add to GRUB command line in /etc/default/grub:
# GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX additions:
# init_on_alloc=1         — Zero-fill allocated memory pages (mitigates use-after-free info leaks)
# init_on_free=1          — Zero-fill freed pages (stronger but ~1-2% performance cost)
# slab_nomerge            — Prevent slab cache merging (hardens heap exploitation)
# page_alloc.shuffle=1    — Randomize page allocator free lists
# randomize_kstack_offset=on  — Randomize kernel stack offset per syscall
 
# Apply:
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
Audit Framework (auditd)
Auditd is the kernel-level audit system. It records system calls, file access, and security events.
sudo systemctl enable --now auditd
 
# Add rules to /etc/audit/rules.d/custom.rules:
 
# Watch sensitive files for changes
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers_changes
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config -p wa -k sshd_config
 
# Watch for privilege escalation
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F euid=0 -F auid>=1000 -k privilege_escalation
 
# Watch for unauthorized access attempts
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open -F exit=-EACCES -k access_denied
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open -F exit=-EPERM -k access_denied
 
# Load rules
sudo augenrules --load
Searching audit logs:
# Recent authentication events
ausearch -m USER_LOGIN -ts recent
 
# Failed access attempts
ausearch -k access_denied -ts today
 
# Generate a summary report
aureport --summary
aureport --auth       # Authentication report
aureport --failed     # All failed events
 
# Watch audit events in real-time (useful for debugging policy)
tail -f /var/log/audit/audit.log | ausearch --interpret
Audit log integrity — Ensure attackers can’t tamper with logs after compromise:
# Enable immutable audit rules (requires reboot to change)
# Add as the LAST line in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-finalize.rules:
-e 2
 
# Forward logs to a remote syslog server for tamper-resistance
# In /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf:
# remote_server = logserver.example.com
# port = 60
Useful pre-built audit rule sets: The audit package includes rule sets in /usr/share/audit/sample-rules/. The 30-stig.rules file implements many requirements from DISA STIG, the US DoD security baseline. Copy and adapt rather than writing from scratch.
Disk Encryption (LUKS)
Full-disk encryption protects data at rest — critical for laptops that might be lost or stolen.

Enable during Fedora install — The Anaconda installer offers LUKS encryption on the storage configuration screen. Use a strong passphrase (6+ random words).
Verify it’s active: lsblk -f will show crypto_LUKS type for encrypted partitions.
Backup the LUKS header: sudo cryptsetup luksHeaderBackup /dev/sda3 --header-backup-file luks-header.img — Store this securely offline. If the header is corrupted, all data is lost.
Add a recovery key: sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/sda3 --recovery-key — Gives you a printable recovery key separate from your passphrase.

Performance: LUKS2 with AES-XTS on modern CPUs with AES-NI has negligible performance impact (< 3% in most workloads). Verify hardware acceleration is available: grep -o aes /proc/cpuinfo | head -1.
LUKS with TPM2 auto-unlock — Decrypt at boot without typing a passphrase, while still protecting against offline disk theft:
# Enroll TPM2 as an additional unlock mechanism
sudo systemd-cryptenroll /dev/sda3 --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7
 
# PCR 7 binds to Secure Boot state — if Secure Boot config changes, TPM won't unlock
# Keep the passphrase as a backup unlock method
Encrypted swap: Ensure swap is also encrypted. If you used full-disk encryption during Fedora install, swap is inside the LUKS volume. Verify: swapon --show should point to a device inside the LUKS container, not a raw partition.
Network Hardening
Kernel network parameters via sysctl — add to /etc/sysctl.d/99-hardening.conf:
# Disable IP forwarding (unless this is a router)
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0
 
# Disable source routing
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
 
# Enable SYN flood protection
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
 
# Ignore ICMP redirects (prevent MITM)
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
 
# Ignore broadcast pings (prevent smurf attacks)
net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1
 
# Log martian packets (spoofed source addresses)
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
 
# Enable reverse path filtering (anti-spoofing)
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1
Apply: sudo sysctl --system
Disable unused services:
# List listening ports
ss -tlnp
 
# Disable services you don't need
sudo systemctl disable --now avahi-daemon  # mDNS — rarely needed on a workstation
sudo systemctl disable --now cups          # Only if you don't print
DNS security: Consider using DNS-over-TLS or DNS-over-HTTPS via systemd-resolved:
# /etc/systemd/resolved.conf
# [Resolve]
# DNS=1.1.1.1#cloudflare-dns.com 9.9.9.9#dns.quad9.net
# DNSOverTLS=yes
# DNSSEC=yes
 
sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved
# Verify DoT is working:
resolvectl status
WiFi security: When connecting to public networks:
# Use MAC address randomization (NetworkManager):
# In /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/99-random-mac.conf:
# [device]
# wifi.scan-rand-mac-address=yes
# [connection]
# wifi.cloned-mac-address=random
# ethernet.cloned-mac-address=random
 
sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
USB Security
USB devices are a common attack vector (BadUSB, USB Rubber Ducky). Restrict which USB devices are allowed:
# USBGuard — whitelist-based USB device authorization
sudo dnf install usbguard
sudo usbguard generate-policy > /etc/usbguard/rules.conf  # Whitelist currently connected devices
sudo systemctl enable --now usbguard
 
# List connected USB devices and their authorization status
usbguard list-devices
 
# Allow a new device permanently
usbguard allow-device <device-id> --permanent
 
# Block all new USB devices by default (already the default policy)
# To temporarily allow a device (e.g., plugging in a new keyboard):
usbguard allow-device <device-id>
For a simpler approach without USBGuard, disable USB storage only:
# Blacklist the USB storage kernel module
echo "blacklist usb-storage" | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/no-usb-storage.conf
Container Isolation (Podman Rootless)
Fedora ships Podman instead of Docker. Rootless containers run as your user with no daemon, providing better isolation by default.
# Run containers rootless (no sudo needed)
podman run --rm -it fedora:latest /bin/bash
 
# Containers are isolated by:
# - User namespaces (UID mapping)
# - Network namespaces (separate network stack)
# - Mount namespaces (filesystem isolation)
# - seccomp profiles (syscall filtering)
 
# Don't run containers as --privileged unless absolutely necessary
# Don't mount the host filesystem with -v /:/host
 
# Scan images for vulnerabilities before running
podman pull docker.io/library/nginx:latest
# Use trivy or grype for scanning:
# trivy image nginx:latest
Podman auto-update: Keep container images patched:
# Label containers for auto-update
podman run -d --name web --label io.containers.autoupdate=registry nginx:latest
 
# Enable the timer
systemctl --user enable --now podman-auto-update.timer
Container hardening flags:
# Drop all capabilities, add back only what's needed
podman run --cap-drop=ALL --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE myapp:latest
 
# Read-only root filesystem (forces explicit writable mounts)
podman run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp:latest
 
# Limit resources (prevent container DoS of host)
podman run --memory=512m --cpus=1 myapp:latest
 
# Custom seccomp profile (restrict syscalls)
podman run --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json myapp:latest
 
# No new privileges (prevent setuid escalation inside container)
podman run --security-opt no-new-privileges myapp:latest
See supply-chain-security for container image scanning and provenance verification.
Hardening Quick-Reference Checklist
Summary checklist for periodic review. Not every item applies to every system — use threat-modeling-basics to prioritize.
Boot and Physical:

 LUKS full-disk encryption enabled
 Firmware/BIOS password set
 Secure Boot enabled (mokutil --sb-state)
 GRUB boot loader password configured
 USB device restrictions (USBGuard or module blacklist)

OS and Kernel:

 System fully updated (dnf upgrade --refresh)
 Automatic security updates enabled (dnf-automatic)
 Unnecessary services disabled (systemctl list-units)
 Kernel hardening sysctls applied
 Kernel boot parameters hardened

Access Control:

 SELinux enforcing (getenforce)
 No direct root login (SSH and console)
 sudo configured with least privilege
 Home directories 700
 umask 027 set

Network:

 Firewall active with minimal open ports
 Network hardening sysctls applied
 DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS enabled
 Unused network services disabled
 WiFi MAC randomization enabled

SSH:

 Password authentication disabled
 Root login disabled
 Strong algorithms only (Ed25519, ChaCha20)
 Fail2ban or equivalent active
 SSH config tested with ssh-audit

Monitoring:

 auditd running with custom rules
 Audit log integrity protected
 Failed login monitoring active

Related

threat-modeling-basics — Framework for deciding what to harden and why
supply-chain-security — Securing the software you install on this system

Sources

CIS Benchmarks for Fedora — www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/fedora
Red Hat Security Guide — docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/security_hardening/
Fedora Security Lab — fedoraproject.org/wiki/Security_Lab
NIST SP 800-123, Guide to General Server Security
SSH Audit — www.ssh-audit.com/ (test your SSH config)
Arch Wiki Security Guide — wiki.archlinux.org/title/Security (much of it applies to Fedora)

security/password-key-hygiene.title: Password and Key Hygiene
security/password-key-hygiene.content:
Password and Key Hygiene
What it is
Password and key hygiene is the set of habits and controls that keep authentication secrets — passwords, API tokens, SSH keys, GPG keys, signing keys — secret, usable only by their owner, and revocable when they leak. It spans how secrets are generated, where they are stored, how access to them is gated, and how they are rotated or retired over their lifecycle.
Why it matters
Most account compromises do not require breaking cryptography; they exploit weak, reused, or carelessly stored secrets. A single password reused across services turns one breach into many, because attackers replay leaked credential pairs against unrelated sites (credential stuffing). A private key checked into a repository or left in a plaintext config file is a standing liability that no amount of network hardening offsets. Good hygiene shrinks both the chance a secret leaks and the blast radius if one does.
The asymmetry is stark: generating and storing a secret well costs minutes once; cleaning up after a leaked secret can mean rotating dependent systems, auditing access logs, and rebuilding trust. Hygiene is cheap insurance against an expensive incident.
Details
Passwords

Length and randomness beat complexity rules. A long passphrase or a randomly generated string resists guessing far better than a short password padded with symbols to satisfy a policy. Entropy comes from unpredictability and length, not from a mandatory punctuation character.
Never reuse passwords across services. Reuse is the mechanism that converts an unrelated site’s breach into a compromise of your important accounts. Unique-per-service is the single highest-leverage password habit.
Use a password manager. A reputable password manager generates unique high-entropy passwords, stores them encrypted behind one strong master secret, and removes the incentive to reuse or simplify. The master secret and the manager’s own recovery path then become the things you protect most carefully.
Layer on a second factor. Multi-factor authentication means a leaked password alone is not enough to log in. Hardware-backed factors (security keys implementing public-key challenge-response) resist phishing in a way that one-time codes typed into a page do not, because the key will only authenticate to the legitimate origin. App-generated time-based codes are a strong middle tier; SMS codes are the weakest common factor because they are interceptable and SIM-swappable.

Cryptographic keys

Generate keys with strong, modern algorithms and adequate key sizes; prefer well-reviewed defaults over hand-tuned parameters. The reasoning is the same one that governs all cryptographic choices: avoid rolling your own, and prefer authenticated, well-vetted primitives over clever custom schemes.
Protect private keys at rest. Encrypt private keys with a passphrase, restrict file permissions so only the owner can read them, and prefer storing them in a hardware token or OS keystore over a bare file when the threat model warrants it. A private key with world-readable permissions on a shared host is effectively public.
Separate keys by purpose and scope. Distinct keys for distinct roles (per-host, per-service, per-environment) mean compromising one does not compromise all, and revoking one is surgical rather than catastrophic. The same logic applies to API tokens: scope each token to the least privilege it needs.
Keep signing keys offline where practical. Keys whose job is to vouch for identity or releases — code-signing keys, root certificate keys — gain disproportionate value to an attacker. Keeping them off general-purpose, network-connected machines is proportionate to that value; keep them instead on hardware tokens, or in air-gapped or dedicated signing environments.

Secret storage anti-patterns

Plaintext secrets in config files or environment files committed to version control are the classic leak. Once a secret enters git history, deleting the file does not remove it — the secret must be treated as compromised and rotated, and the history scrubbed.
Secrets pasted into chat, tickets, or logs spread copies you cannot track or revoke. Treat any secret that lands in an unencrypted shared channel as leaked.
Long-lived secrets that are never rotated accumulate exposure: every backup, every former employee, every prior leak window is a chance the secret escaped. Prefer short-lived, automatically issued credentials where the platform supports them.

Rotation and revocation

Rotate on a schedule and on suspicion. Periodic rotation bounds how long a silently-leaked secret stays useful; immediate rotation on any suspected exposure stops an active attacker.
Make revocation fast and rehearsed. The value of being able to revoke a key is only realized if you can actually do it under pressure — know in advance how to revoke each key type and what depends on it, so revocation is a known procedure, not an improvisation during an incident. This ties directly into incident-response-basics.
Maintain an inventory. You cannot rotate or revoke secrets you have forgotten exist. Knowing what secrets exist, where they live, and what they grant is a prerequisite for the rest.

The mental model
Treat every secret as something that will eventually leak, and design so that when it does, the leak is detectable, contained to a small scope, and recoverable by revocation and rotation rather than by hoping no one noticed. Hygiene is less about preventing every leak and more about ensuring no single leak is catastrophic or permanent.
Related

incident-response-basics — What to do when a secret is suspected leaked (containment, rotation, recovery)
web-application-security — Where credentials and session secrets are exercised at the app boundary
linux-hardening-checklist — Host-level controls (file permissions, key storage) that protect secrets at rest
supply-chain-security — Signing keys and CI credentials as supply-chain trust anchors
threat-modeling-basics — Identifying which secrets are highest-value to an attacker

Sources

Synthesis of widely-established credential and key-management practice; no specific external source.

security/post-breach-investigability.title: Post-Breach Investigability
security/post-breach-investigability.content:
Post-Breach Investigability
Prevention without investigability leaves an organization unable to do the three things that actually determine the cost of a breach: bound the impact, revoke precisely, and learn. All three depend on evidence that had to exist before the incident, in a form the attacker could not edit.
This is the forensic row of adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning’s claim-layer table, and blast-radius question five from ambient-authority-and-blast-radius — which evidence plane can this component rewrite? — developed in full.
Confidence legend: ◐ = corroborated across independent secondary sources, primary not obtained in this pass · ○ = mechanism argued, not a measured result.
Debug logs are not evidence
○ Application logs optimized for debugging answer “why did this request fail.” Investigation asks a different question: which principal, under which policy version, holding which grant, caused which committed effect, on whose data. A log line reading request failed is fully adequate for the first and useless for the second, which is why teams discover their logging gap during the incident rather than before it.
The distinction that organizes the rest of this note: detection and root-cause establishment are separate assurance properties. A system can be excellent at one and incapable of the other, and most are.
The case that makes it concrete
◐ The 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online intrusion (Storm-0558) is the clearest published illustration. Corroborated across independent reporting on the U.S. Cyber Safety Review Board’s April 2024 review:

Detection came from the customer, not the platform. The U.S. State Department detected anomalies using a custom alert rule over the MailItemsAccessed audit log.
That log was a paid entitlement. State could build the rule because it had licensing that included enhanced auditing (Microsoft Purview Audit, Premium tier). Organizations without it did not have the same signal available.
Scope: roughly 60,000 emails downloaded from State alone; the intrusion affected 22 organizations and over 500 individuals.
Root cause was never established. The actor used tokens signed with a Microsoft signing key created in 2016; the Board reported that months into the investigation there was still no definitive account of how the key was obtained.

Three lessons, in descending order of how often they are missed:

Evidence availability can be a product entitlement rather than a default. The capacity to detect this class of intrusion was, at the time, something you bought. When you evaluate a platform, “what is logged, at which tier, retained how long” is a security requirement, not a procurement footnote.
Detection succeeded and root-cause analysis still failed. Being alerted is not the same as being able to explain, and only the second bounds the problem — you cannot say which other systems the key touched if you cannot say how it was taken.
The detection that worked was a custom rule written by the customer against a raw log, not a vendor alert.

(This is a retrospective incident review, not a controlled evaluation; it does not isolate the causal effect of premium logging. The specific figures above are corroborated across secondary sources; the Board’s report itself was not fetched in this pass.)
What the evidence plane should record
○ Per consequential action, aiming at reconstruction rather than volume:

















































FieldWhy it is neededHuman, service, workload, and delegated identities — separately”The service did it” cannot answer on whose behalfCanonical action and resource identifiersNon-canonical forms make correlation unreliable at exactly the wrong momentTenant and purposeBounds impact per customer without re-deriving it from dataPolicy decision, policy version, and the attributes it readLets you replay whether the decision was correct under the rules then in forceApproval / action digest binding and expiryDistinguishes an authorized action from a replayed or substituted oneArtifact and configuration hashesTies the effect to what was actually deployedAttempted and committed effect, including the provider’s resultThe gap between these two is where partial compromises liveCapability or credential identifier and scopeMakes precise revocation possible instead of rotating everythingTrace linkage across queues and retriesAsync boundaries are where causal chains normally breakEvidence completeness / sequence signalsLets you detect that evidence is missing, which is itself the finding
Two rules that make the schema worth having:

○ Send evidence somewhere outside the workload’s rewrite authority. A component that can edit its own audit trail has no audit trail. This is the same argument as agent-policy-enforcement-gap’s: a control the constrained party administers is not a boundary.
○ Deny or quarantine consequential actions when required audit cannot be produced. Otherwise “audit required” silently degrades to best-effort on exactly the days it matters — a broker outage becomes an unlogged window.

○ The costs are not small and should be stated: storage, latency, privacy exposure, insider sensitivity, and schema governance. There is also a genuine second-order risk — a good evidence plane is itself a high-value dataset, concentrating who-did-what-to-whom in one place. Minimize content while preserving attribution and decision reconstruction; that tension does not resolve, it gets managed.
Counterargument
The failure mode of this note is a team that builds a beautiful evidence schema and never runs an investigation. Fields are cheap to specify and expensive to keep correct: an unused audit pipeline drifts, loses fields in refactors, and is discovered to be broken during the incident it existed for — which is strictly worse than knowing you had nothing, because it was budgeted as coverage. Comprehensive audit also collides with data-minimization obligations, and the “log everything consequential” instinct can create the privacy incident it was meant to investigate.
The discipline that keeps it honest is not more fields, it is rehearsal: periodically pick a past action and try to reconstruct it end-to-end from the evidence plane alone. That exercise finds the broken pipeline, prunes fields nobody used, and is the only thing that distinguishes a working evidence plane from a schema. incident-response-basics is where that rehearsal belongs.
Related

adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning — cluster hub; the forensic claim layer
ambient-authority-and-blast-radius — blast-radius question 5, which this expands

../ai/agent-audit-trails-provenance — the agent-side capture mechanics
agent-policy-enforcement-gap — the substrate-control argument reused here

Sources

Cyber Safety Review Board (April 2024) — “Review of the Summer 2023 Microsoft Exchange Online Intrusion” — www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/CSRB-Review-Summer-2023-MEO-Intrusion. ◐ Details corroborated across independent secondary reporting on 2026-08-07 (detection via a custom MailItemsAccessed rule, Purview Audit Premium entitlement, ~60,000 State emails, 22 organizations and 500+ individuals, signing key unexplained). The Board’s PDF was not successfully fetched in this pass — the 2024 URL path 404s and the report now sits under a 2025 path. Retrospective review, no control group.
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (final, April 2025) — Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile — csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final. ✅ Title, revision, and final status verified 2026-08-07. Consensus guidance on the incident/evidence lifecycle; not causal proof for the specific event schema recommended here.
Evidence-plane schema derived from a user-supplied research synthesis, “The reasoning layer of software security” (2026-08-07), produced by another AI system; it is a mechanism argument, not a measured result.

security/security-assurance-tooling-ceil.title: Security Assurance Tooling — Ceilings and Economics
security/security-assurance-tooling-ceil.content:
Security Assurance Tooling — Ceilings and Economics
Assurance tools pay when three things are narrow: the question, the oracle, and the workflow. Without all three, “coverage” is mostly activity. This note is what each major tool family can be asked, what it structurally cannot see, and what the finding actually costs once a human has to act on it.
It is the measurement half of adversarial-vs-reliability-reasoning’s claim-layer table — each row there needs a different oracle, and this is which tool supplies which.
Confidence legend: ✅ = primary source fetched and quoted text matched verbatim during this pass · ○ = mechanism argued, not a measured result.
There is no portable “SAST precision”
○ Precision varies by rule, language, framework, repository, configuration, and — most of all — whether findings are filtered to changed code. Published tool comparisons often use seeded or labeled corpora that behave nothing like production. A vendor precision number is a claim about their corpus, not about yours.
What generalizes is the workflow, and Google’s Tricorder is the best-documented instance.
✅ From Sadowski et al., Tricorder: Building a Program Analysis Ecosystem (ICSE 2015), fetched and quoted verbatim:

Scale and staffing: Tricorder “generates some 93,000 analysis results each day. A small team of 2-3 people maintain TRICORDER and the ecosystem around it.”
The code-review threshold: “We still enforce a very low effective false positive rate here (< 10%). Additionally, we only display results for most analyses on changed lines by default.”
Latency: “we typically expect analyses to complete in less than 5 − 10 minutes (ideally much less), as developers may be waiting for results.”
The stricter bar for build-integrated analyses: “the effective false positive rate must be essentially zero. They also cannot significantly slow down compiles, so must have < 5% overhead.”
The contract: they reserve the right to disable an analyzer if nobody fixes bugs filed against it, if it hurts performance, or if “the analyzer results are annoying developers.”

✅ The most transferable idea is a redefinition, not a threshold. Tricorder measures the effective false positive: “any report from the tool where a user chooses not to take action to resolve the report.” That is a developer-perspective metric, deliberately not a correctness metric — as the paper puts it, “developers will decide whether an analysis has high impact, and what a false positive is.” A technically-correct finding nobody acts on counts against the tool.
✅ One more design choice worth stealing: they “got rid of all priority or severity ratings for analysis results,” on the reasoning that only high-value results should be shown at all, and that letting users filter hides broken analyzers instead of fixing them.
○ Meta’s published account of deploying Infer at scale reaches similar workflow conclusions from a different codebase. Neither establishes that any scanner works on your TypeScript service. What they establish is the mechanism for adoption: findings arrive on the responsible change, while the author still has context and ownership; checks are fast enough that no bypass market forms; noisy analyzers get demoted or repaired; and fixes are measured, not alerts.
DAST and SCA, briefly
○ DAST buys runtime realism and can expose deployment and configuration behavior that source analysis never sees. It loses source-level causality, and it only sees states its crawler, accounts, test data, and timing actually reach — which is a much smaller set than the reachable state space.
○ SCA is excellent at inventory and version matching. “Package present” is not “vulnerable path reachable,” and the gap between those two is where nearly all the wasted triage time goes. The economic win comes from reachability, exploit evidence, exposure, ownership, and upgrade feasibility — not from another undifferentiated alert. (The vault’s dependency-risk note is supply-chain-security; the AI-amplified version is ai-supply-chain-risks.)
The metric to actually track
○ Replace “findings” with:
accepted consequential findings per reviewer-hour
  + recall on seeded severe defects
  + escaped defects
All three, because the first alone is gameable by suppressing everything hard. ○ And note the cost of aggressive noise suppression: it hides rare severe findings. Keep a non-gating research channel for lower-confidence detectors, and periodically seed known-hard cases to measure what the gate is missing rather than assuming.
What fuzzing structurally misses
○ A fuzzer needs four things: a generator, reachability, an execution budget, and an oracle. Crashes and sanitizer violations are strong, generic oracles — which is why fuzzing is so effective on parsers and so weak elsewhere. “User A can read User B’s draft after role revocation during a retry” is not a crash.
The structural blind spots follow directly:

semantically valid but unauthorized outcomes;
long, stateful, multi-service sequences;
rare identity, clock, queue, and cache combinations;
environment-dependent behavior absent from the harness;
economic abuse with no crisp threshold;
anything whose wrongness requires external business knowledge to recognize.

○ The Magma ground-truth benchmark makes a related point that matters more than any leaderboard: it distinguishes reaching a bug from triggering it, and finds no universally best fuzzer across targets. The lesson is not that fuzzing is weak — it is that harness and oracle design dominate tool choice.
○ For a web system the split is clean: fuzz parsers and pure state machines hard; use property-based and metamorphic testing for authorization and workflows. The metamorphic relations for authorization are in authorization-as-a-protocol, and they exist precisely because that class has no generic oracle.
Where formal methods paid
○ AWS reported using TLA+ to find subtle design errors in distributed systems that survived ordinary design review, code review, and testing. seL4 established machine-checked refinement between a formal specification and a C implementation under explicit assumptions. These are strong existence proofs and weak universal ROI estimates — both are heavily selected cases.
○ The conditions under which a target becomes tractable are the useful part:

the state machine is smaller than the implementation;
semantics and interfaces are stable;
invariants can be written without encoding the whole business;
the verified component is reused enough to amortize the proof;
the consequence of a subtle error justifies specialized labor;
assumptions about compiler, hardware, crypto, configuration, and operations are made explicit.

○ And when they fail economically: when the specification changes as fast as the code, when intent is still contested, or — the common one — when a team verifies a clean core while unverified adapters hold the real authority. For a TypeScript organization the right target is almost never “verify the application.” It is the policy algebra, the money/state transition, the token-minting rule, or the replication protocol whose error would dominate loss.
Counterargument
This note’s framing — narrow question, narrow oracle, ruthless noise control — optimizes for developer acceptance, and developer acceptance is not the same as security. Tricorder’s effective-false-positive metric makes that explicit: a finding developers decline to fix is scored against the tool, which is exactly backwards when the finding is a real vulnerability that is merely tedious to fix. A regime tuned to sub-10% annoyance will systematically demote the noisy, high-recall, hard-to-triage detectors — and those are disproportionately the ones that find authorization and injection flaws rather than style issues.
The reconciliation is the non-gating research channel plus seeded-defect recall above; without both, “our static analysis has high acceptance” describes a tool that has been tuned into harmlessness. It is also worth being clear that Tricorder’s numbers come from an organization with a dedicated platform team, a monorepo, and a strong review culture — the thresholds transfer as a design pattern, not as targets a small team can hit.

Sources

Sadowski, C., van Gogh, J., Jaspan, C., Söderberg, E. & Winter, C. (2015) — “Tricorder: Building a Program Analysis Ecosystem” — ICSE. PDF: research.google/pubs/tricorder-building-a-program-analysis-ecosystem/. ✅ Fetched and read 2026-08-07; all quoted figures and definitions verbatim from the paper. Google-specific; measures tool use and fixes, not breach reduction.
Distefano, D. et al. (2019) — “Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook” — CACM. First-party deployment account; no portable precision rate. Not re-fetched in this pass.
Hazimeh, A., Herrera, A. & Payer, M. — “Magma: A Ground-Truth Fuzzing Benchmark” — ACM POMACS / SIGMETRICS. Reach-vs-trigger distinction; native-code benchmark, so the oracle lesson transfers but absolute rates do not. Venue and year not re-verified in this pass; cited here only for the reach-vs-trigger distinction and the no-universal-winner finding.
