Klein, G. et al. (2009) — “seL4: Formal Verification of an OS Kernel” — SOSP. Machine-checked refinement; guarantees bounded by stated assumptions and verified scope.
Structure derived from a user-supplied research synthesis, “The reasoning layer of software security” (2026-08-07), produced by another AI system. Its Tricorder figures were re-verified against the primary paper here — a web search summary had reported different numbers, and the paper confirmed the synthesis rather than the summary.

security/threat-modeling-basics.title: Threat Modeling Basics
security/threat-modeling-basics.content:
Threat Modeling Basics
What it is
Threat modeling is a structured process for identifying, quantifying, and addressing security threats to a system. Rather than reacting to vulnerabilities after they’re exploited, threat modeling forces you to think like an attacker during the design phase — systematically decomposing a system into components, mapping data flows, and asking “what could go wrong?” at every boundary.
Why it matters
Most security breaches exploit architectural weaknesses, not exotic zero-days. A system that was never threat-modeled tends to accumulate implicit trust assumptions that attackers love to violate — “the database is only reachable internally” or “users won’t modify the request body”. Threat modeling surfaces these assumptions early, when fixing them is cheap. It also gives you a rational basis for prioritizing security work instead of chasing the latest CVE.
The case for it is primarily temporal: before implementation, the architecture is still cheap to change, and cross-boundary authority errors have not yet been buried in code. That is a strong argument, and it is not the same as an evidence-backed one — see Does it work? The cost and coverage evidence below before treating threat modeling as a control rather than a design activity.
Details
The Threat Modeling Process
The core loop, regardless of framework:

Decompose the system — Draw a data flow diagram (DFD) showing processes, data stores, external entities, and trust boundaries.
Identify threats — For each element and data flow, enumerate what could go wrong using a structured framework (STRIDE, PASTA, attack trees, etc.).
Rate severity — Score each threat by likelihood and impact. DREAD (Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability) or CVSS can help here, but even a simple High/Medium/Low matrix works for small teams.
Plan mitigations — For each threat, decide: mitigate (fix it), accept (risk is tolerable), transfer (insurance, SLA), or avoid (remove the feature).
Validate — Verify mitigations actually address the threats. Re-model when the system changes.

Data Flow Diagrams (DFDs)
DFDs are the starting artifact. They use four element types:

External entities (rectangles) — Users, third-party APIs, anything outside your control.
Processes (circles) — Code that transforms data. Your application logic.
Data stores (parallel lines) — Databases, files, caches, queues.
Data flows (arrows) — How data moves between elements. Label with protocol and data type.

The critical addition is trust boundaries (dashed lines). Every place where the trust level changes is a trust boundary — between your frontend and backend, between your backend and a third-party API, between user input and your parser. Most threats live at trust boundaries.
Start with a Level 0 DFD (context diagram) showing the whole system as one process, then expand to Level 1 showing major subsystems. You rarely need to go deeper than Level 2 for threat modeling.
Tooling for DFDs:

draw.io / diagrams.net — Free, works offline, exports to SVG/PNG. The Threat Modeling shape library has DFD elements built in.
Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool — Windows only, generates STRIDE threats automatically from DFDs. Free.
OWASP Threat Dragon — Open-source, browser-based, generates threat reports from DFDs.
Mermaid diagrams — If you prefer text-as-code: embed DFDs in markdown and render in Obsidian or CI.
threagile — Threat model as YAML, auto-generates risk reports and DFDs. Good for infrastructure-heavy models.

STRIDE Framework
Developed at Microsoft as part of the SDL (Security Development Lifecycle). Each letter maps to a category of threat and its corresponding security property:








































ThreatViolated PropertyExampleSpoofingAuthenticationAttacker impersonates a legitimate user via stolen credentials or forged tokensTamperingIntegrityAttacker modifies data in transit (MITM) or at rest (SQL injection altering records)RepudiationNon-repudiationUser denies performing an action and there are no logs to prove otherwiseInformation DisclosureConfidentialityError messages leak stack traces; API returns fields the user shouldn’t seeDenial of ServiceAvailabilityResource exhaustion, algorithmic complexity attacks, or simply flooding endpointsElevation of PrivilegeAuthorizationUnprivileged user gains admin access via IDOR, path traversal, or broken access control
STRIDE-per-element: Apply STRIDE to each DFD element. External entities are primarily susceptible to Spoofing. Processes are susceptible to all six. Data stores are susceptible to Tampering, Information Disclosure, and Denial of Service. Data flows are susceptible to Tampering, Information Disclosure, and Denial of Service.
STRIDE-per-interaction: Apply STRIDE to each data flow crossing a trust boundary. This is more focused and scales better for complex systems.
Beyond STRIDE — Other Frameworks
PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) — A seven-stage, risk-centric methodology that starts with business objectives and works down to technical threat enumeration. Better than STRIDE when you need to tie threats directly to business impact and present findings to non-technical stakeholders. Stages: (1) Define objectives, (2) Define technical scope, (3) Application decomposition, (4) Threat analysis, (5) Vulnerability analysis, (6) Attack modeling, (7) Risk/impact analysis.
LINDDUN — Privacy-focused threat modeling framework. Six categories: Linkability, Identifiability, Non-repudiation (in privacy, non-repudiation is a threat — users want plausible deniability), Detectability, Disclosure of information, Unawareness, Non-compliance. Use when GDPR or other privacy regulations apply.
VAST (Visual, Agile, and Simple Threat modeling) — Designed for Agile/DevOps environments. Produces two types of models: application threat models (for developers) and operational threat models (for infrastructure teams). Integrates into sprint workflows rather than being a separate phase.
MITRE ATT&CK — Not a threat modeling methodology per se, but a comprehensive knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics and techniques. Use it to validate your threat model: for each STRIDE threat you identify, check ATT&CK for known techniques an attacker would use. This grounds your model in reality rather than theory. Browse at attack.mitre.org/.
Attack Trees
Attack trees model threats as a hierarchical goal structure:

Root node: The attacker’s goal (e.g., “Steal user credentials”).
Child nodes: Ways to achieve the parent goal, connected by AND/OR gates.
Leaf nodes: Concrete attack steps.

Example (simplified):
Steal user credentials (OR)
├── Phish the user (AND)
│   ├── Craft convincing email
│   └── Host fake login page
├── Exploit password reset flow (OR)
│   ├── Enumerate valid emails via timing
│   └── Intercept reset token (weak randomness)
└── Dump the database (AND)
    ├── Find SQL injection point
    └── Exfiltrate via error-based or blind technique
Attack trees are powerful because they let you assign costs and probabilities to leaf nodes and propagate them up. If phishing costs 50 and has an 80% success rate while a SQL injection requires a 10K exploit toolkit, you know where to focus defenses.
Quantitative risk scoring with attack trees: Assign each leaf node three values — cost to attacker, probability of success, and impact to defender. Propagate up: OR gates take the max probability (attacker picks the easiest path), AND gates multiply probabilities (attacker must succeed at all steps). This gives you a rational basis for security investment — spend on mitigations where the attacker’s cost-to-benefit ratio is most favorable.
Tools for attack trees: ADTool (open-source, graphical), SecuriCAD (commercial, simulation-based), or simply a markdown outline with annotations.
Threat Modeling Real-World Examples
Example 1: Self-hosted web app with API

Draw DFD: Browser → Nginx reverse proxy → Node.js API → PostgreSQL. Trust boundaries: internet/DMZ (at Nginx), DMZ/internal (at API), API/database.
STRIDE at each boundary:

Internet/DMZ: Spoofing (forged JWTs), DoS (HTTP flood), Information Disclosure (server version headers).
DMZ/Internal: Tampering (SSRF from API to internal services), Elevation of Privilege (API escape to host).
API/Database: SQL injection (Tampering), excessive data returns (Information Disclosure).


Mitigations: Rate limiting at Nginx, JWT validation with iss/aud claims, parameterized queries, network segmentation, Server header removal.

Example 2: CI/CD pipeline (a la the xz-utils attack)

DFD: Developer workstation → GitHub → GitHub Actions → Container registry → Kubernetes.
Key trust boundaries: developer identity (SSH/GPG keys), CI runner (shared infrastructure), registry upload credentials.
STRIDE analysis reveals: Spoofing (compromised maintainer account), Tampering (malicious PR modifying build scripts), Information Disclosure (secrets leaked in CI logs).
Mitigations: Branch protection rules, required code review, SLSA provenance, secret scanning, ephemeral CI runners.

Does it work? The cost and coverage evidence
Threat modeling is one of the most confidently recommended practices in security and one of the least measured. The evidence that exists is worth knowing because it is encouraging about validity and discouraging about completeness.
Scandariato, Wuyts & Joosen’s descriptive study of Microsoft’s technique (Requirements Engineering, 2015) is the standard reference. It ran STRIDE with 57 final-year master’s students and measured productivity, precision, and recall against a researcher-constructed baseline. The headline results: precision ≈ 0.81, recall ≈ 0.36.
Read those two numbers together:

Most threats identified were real. Four in five findings were valid, so the output of a session is not noise.
Roughly two-thirds of the baseline threats were missed. A completed threat model is not a coverage claim.

(Precision and recall corroborated across two independent secondary sources on 2026-08-07; the paywalled paper was not read directly. Per-hour productivity figures circulate for this study but were not verified and are deliberately omitted here. Scope: students, one method, one modeled system, an expert-built baseline — not a production breach study.)
The practical consequence is not “don’t threat model.” It is: treat the output as a set of leads with a known miss rate, never as the reason a design is safe. A model that finds five real threats and misses ten is still worth the afternoon; a model treated as an assurance artifact is average-case evidence against an adversary who selects the tail.
Make it an executable design review
The failure mode this evidence points at is ceremony — a diagram and a taxonomy that create confidence without changing anything. The counter is a completion rule: every accepted threat must produce at least one of —

a removed authority,
an architectural boundary,
an invariant or type that makes the state unrepresentable (designing-out-defect-classes),
a negative or metamorphic test (authorization-as-a-protocol),
an observable event in the evidence plane (post-breach-investigability),
a recovery action,
or an explicitly accepted, dated residual risk.

If a session produces none of these, it produced a document. Re-run the model on boundary-changing diffs rather than on a calendar, and stop when new scenarios stop changing the design or the tests.
When to Threat Model

During initial design — Before writing code. The DFD doesn’t need to be perfect; even a whiteboard sketch helps.
Before major changes — New authentication flow? New external integration? New data store? Re-model the affected area.
After incidents — A breach reveals gaps in your model. Update it.
Periodically — Systems drift. Annual reviews catch creeping assumptions.

Lightweight Threat Modeling for Solo Developers / Small Teams
You don’t need a formal process or expensive tools. The minimum viable threat model:

Sketch the DFD on paper or in a tool like draw.io. 15 minutes.
Walk each trust boundary and ask the STRIDE questions. Write threats in a markdown file or issue tracker. 30 minutes.
Rank by gut feel — High/Medium/Low. Don’t overthink scoring.
File issues for the High and Medium threats. Accept the Lows explicitly (write it down so future-you knows it was deliberate).
Timebox it — A 1-hour session per quarter is infinitely better than never modeling.

Minimal threat model template (copy into a markdown file or issue):
## Threat Model: [System/Feature Name]
Date: YYYY-MM-DD | Participants: [names]
 
### System Description
[1-2 sentence summary of what it does and who uses it]
 
### Data Flow Diagram
[Link to draw.io/Mermaid diagram, or ASCII sketch]
 
### Trust Boundaries
1. [Boundary 1]: [what changes across this boundary]
2. [Boundary 2]: ...
 
### Threats Identified
| # | Category | Threat | Severity | Mitigation | Status |
|---|----------|--------|----------|------------|--------|
| 1 | Spoofing | ... | High | ... | Open |
 
### Accepted Risks
- [Risk]: [Reason for acceptance] — Reviewed [date]
 
### Next Review Date: [date]
Adam Shostack’s “four question” framing is useful for teams new to threat modeling:

What are we building?
What can go wrong?
What are we going to do about it?
Did we do a good enough job?

Connection to AI Security
LLM-based systems introduce novel threat modeling challenges. Mapping STRIDE to AI agents:

Spoofing: Prompt injection can make an agent impersonate system instructions — the model can’t reliably distinguish user input from system instructions.
Information Disclosure: Prompt extraction attacks leak system prompts and tool configurations. Indirect injection can exfiltrate context window contents.
Elevation of Privilege: An attacker’s injected prompt can escalate from “user message” trust level to “system instruction” trust level, gaining access to tools and data the attacker shouldn’t control.
Tampering: Poisoned training data or compromised tool outputs alter agent behavior.
Denial of Service: Context window exhaustion, infinite tool-calling loops.

When threat modeling an AI system, treat the model itself as an untrustworthy process — it’s a probabilistic component that can be manipulated. Draw trust boundaries around every tool the model can call, and assume injected content can cross those boundaries. See prompt-injection and ai-agent-security for deeper treatment.
Threat Modeling Checklist
Quick-reference checklist to run through during a threat modeling session:

 System scope defined — Clear boundary of what’s in/out of scope for this model
 DFD drawn — All processes, data stores, external entities, and data flows mapped
 Trust boundaries identified — Every point where privilege, ownership, or network zone changes
 STRIDE applied — Each trust boundary examined for all six threat categories
 Severity rated — Each threat scored (at minimum High/Medium/Low)
 Mitigations assigned — Each High/Medium threat has a planned mitigation or explicit acceptance
 Third-party dependencies reviewed — Threats from external APIs, libraries, and services considered (see supply-chain-security)
 Authentication and authorization flows traced — Token lifecycle, session management, privilege boundaries mapped
 Data classification done — Sensitive data (PII, credentials, keys) identified and their flows traced
 Findings documented — Threats, mitigations, and accepted risks recorded in a persistent, reviewable format
 Review date set — Next scheduled review on the calendar

Related

Sources

Adam Shostack, Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (Wiley, 2014) — The definitive book on the subject
Scandariato, R., Wuyts, K. & Joosen, W. (2015) — “A descriptive study of Microsoft’s threat modeling technique” — Requirements Engineering — doi.org/10.1007/s00766-013-0195-2. 57 final-year master’s students; measured productivity, precision, and recall. Precision ≈ 0.81, recall ≈ 0.36 corroborated across independent secondary sources 2026-08-07; primary paywalled and not read. Academic setting, one system, expert-constructed baseline.
Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle — Original home of STRIDE
OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet — cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Threat_Modeling_Cheat_Sheet.html
Bruce Schneier, Attack Trees (Dr. Dobb’s Journal, 1999) — Original formalization of attack trees

MITRE ATT&CK Framework — attack.mitre.org/ — Real-world adversary tactics and techniques
LINDDUN privacy threat modeling — www.linddun.org/
Threagile (threat model as code) — github.com/Threagile/threagile

security/web-application-security.title: Web Application Security
security/web-application-security.content:
Web Application Security
What it is
Web application security is the practice of protecting web-facing applications from attackers who reach them over the same channels legitimate users do. Because a web app accepts input from anyone on the internet and acts on it — rendering it, storing it, querying a database with it, making requests on its behalf — most web vulnerabilities reduce to a single theme: untrusted input crossing a trust boundary and being treated as trusted. The discipline is largely about identifying those boundaries and ensuring input is validated, encoded, or isolated as it crosses each one.

The vulnerability classes below are described generically. The community-maintained “top risks” lists (such as OWASP’s) re-rank these categories periodically; treat the categories as durable and any specific ranking or year as a snapshot, not a constant.

Why it matters
A web application is, by design, reachable by every attacker on the planet, continuously, at no cost to them. A flaw that a desktop app might expose only to a local user, a web app exposes to automated scanners within hours of deployment. The common vulnerability classes are well-understood and largely preventable, which means most real-world web breaches exploit known categories of mistake rather than novel research. Knowing the categories — and the structural defenses against each — lets a developer design them out instead of discovering them in a breach report.
Details
The recurring theme: trust boundaries and input
Whenever data moves from a less-trusted zone to a more-trusted one — browser to server, server to database, server to another backend service — it crosses a trust boundary. Each crossing is a place where input must be handled defensively. The vulnerability classes below are different faces of failing to do so.
Injection (SQL, command, and relatives)
Injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a command or query that an interpreter then executes — a database, a shell, a template engine. The input smuggles in control syntax and changes the meaning of the command. The structural defense is to separate code from data: use parameterized queries / prepared statements so input can never be parsed as query structure, and avoid passing untrusted input to shells or interpreters at all. Escaping by hand is fragile; let the interpreter’s own parameter mechanism keep the boundary.
Cross-site scripting (XSS)
XSS is injection aimed at the browser: untrusted input is reflected into a page and executed as script in another user’s session, letting an attacker run code with that user’s privileges. The variants differ by path: reflected (echoed straight back from a request), stored (persisted and served to others later), and DOM-based (assembled unsafely by client-side code). But the defense is the same shape: contextual output encoding so data is rendered as text, never as markup or script, plus avoiding APIs that interpret strings as code. A Content Security Policy adds defense in depth by constraining what scripts may run even if encoding fails.
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach a user’s credentials (cookies) automatically: an attacker’s page can cause the victim’s browser to send an authenticated state-changing request to a site the victim is logged into. The defense is to require a value the attacker cannot supply — an anti-CSRF token tied to the session, and/or cookie attributes that prevent the cookie from being sent on cross-site requests. The principle: authenticated state changes must prove they originated from your own application, not just that a valid cookie rode along.
Broken access control and authorization
This class is failing to enforce what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Examples include letting a user access another user’s record by changing an identifier in a request (insecure direct object reference), trusting a client-supplied role, or exposing administrative functionality without a server-side check. The defense is to enforce authorization on the server for every request, against the authenticated identity, denying by default. Authorization is per-action, per-object; checking it once at login is not enough.
Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
SSRF tricks the server into making requests to destinations the attacker chooses — often internal services the attacker cannot reach directly. It arises when the app fetches a URL supplied or influenced by the user. Defenses include validating and constraining destinations to an allowlist, refusing to follow redirects into private ranges, and isolating outbound-fetch capability. SSRF is a reminder that the server’s own network position is a trust asset an attacker will try to borrow.
Authentication and session weaknesses
Even with strong authorization, weak authentication undermines everything: predictable or unprotected session identifiers, missing protection against credential stuffing and brute force, secrets transmitted or stored poorly, and tokens that never expire. Sessions should use unguessable identifiers, be invalidated on logout and on credential change, and be carried only over encrypted transport. Credential handling ties directly to password-key-hygiene — store password verifiers with a slow, salted password-hashing function, never reversibly.
Security misconfiguration and exposure
Many breaches need no clever exploit — just a default left in place: verbose error messages leaking stack traces and internal structure, debug endpoints exposed in production, overly permissive cross-origin sharing, missing security headers, or unnecessary services left listening. The defense is conservative defaults, removing what is not needed, and treating the deployed configuration as part of the attack surface. Relevant HTTP response headers are cheap, broad-spectrum mitigations: a strict Content Security Policy, transport security, and restrictive cross-origin settings.
Cross-cutting principles
These structural habits cut across every class above:

Validate input, encode output. Validate that input matches what you expect on the way in; encode it for the specific context (HTML, SQL, shell, URL) on the way out. The two are complementary, not interchangeable.
Least privilege everywhere. The database account, the service token, the fetch capability — each should hold the minimum it needs, so a successful injection or SSRF yields less.
Defense in depth. No single control is trusted to be perfect; a CSP backs up output encoding, network segmentation backs up SSRF validation, server-side checks back up hidden UI.
Fail closed and quietly. On error, deny rather than allow, and avoid leaking internal detail in the response.
Keep dependencies current. A large share of web risk lives in third-party components; see supply-chain-security.

Where AI-backed web apps add surface
Applications that route untrusted input into a language model inherit a new injection class: the model cannot reliably separate instructions from data, so attacker-controlled content can subvert its behavior. Treat model input and output as untrusted across a trust boundary just like any other input. See prompt-injection and ai-agent-security.
Related

Sources

Synthesis of widely-established web application security practice. The vulnerability categories correspond to the long-standing common-risk taxonomy maintained by the security community (e.g., OWASP); specific rankings change over time and are deliberately not pinned here.

snippets/index.title: Snippets — Index
snippets/index.content:
Snippets
Machine-generated, screen-sized distillations of knowledge/ notes for the Snippet Puck — the idle ESP32-S3 desk display that rotates one vault-sized idea at a glance.
Purpose
Each file is a single self-contained snippet in one of three shapes — claim (a standalone idea), definition (term + crisp meaning), or quote (a verbatim source line). One snippet per file, with frontmatter (source, title, type, generated) plus the snippet text in the body. The host publish-service rotates over these files and pushes them to the puck over MQTT; glyph-folding and markdown-stripping happen at publish time, so the stored text keeps its original glyphs.
Structure
Files mirror the source note’s topic path under knowledge/, named <source-stem>-<type>-N.md. Two subfolders, matching the source topics distilled so far:

ai/ — 13 snippets from 3 source notes
tech/ — 61 snippets from 18 source notes

Generated and regenerable
These files are produced by the extract-snippets skill, not hand-authored. Re-running the skill on a note glob-deletes that note’s old snippets and rewrites them, so the contents are disposable and rebuildable from the source notes at any time. For that reason this index tracks purpose and structure only — there is no hand-maintained per-file list to keep in sync (the file counts above are the one thing to refresh after a regeneration). To inspect or regenerate, go to the source note and run the skill rather than editing snippet files directly.
Related

Snippet Puck — the project these serve
extract-snippets skill — the generator

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: DORA’s AI Capabilities Model implies that successful AI adoption is a systems-engineering problem, not a tooling-acquisition problem: none of the seven capabilities is about which assistant you buy — all seven are about the surrounding system the assistant amplifies.

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: DORA’s 2025 announcement makes its sharpest negative claim about user-centric focus: without it, AI adoption “can have a negative impact on team performance” — amplification with a flipped sign, not merely diminished returns.

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: Before scaling agent autonomy, audit the amplifier inputs — review batch size, pipeline automation, data accessibility. Those, not the model choice, set the sign of the multiplication.

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: Read DORA’s amplifier effect with its limits attached: the evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported survey data, so the frame is an interpretation of correlations, not a causal result. DORA is also a Google Cloud research program, and Google Cloud sells the tooling the model encourages.

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: AI Capabilities Model — DORA’s 2025 set of seven organizational practices that determine whether AI amplifies strength or dysfunction: clear AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control, working in small batches, quality internal platforms, and user-centric focus.

snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.title: DORA 2025 — The Amplifier Effect and the AI Capabilities Model
snippets/ai/dora-2025-ai-capabilities-mo.content: AI’s primary role is as an amplifier, magnifying an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses.

snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.title: Playwright Test Agents — Planner, Generator, Healer
snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.content: Playwright’s Test Agents never guess from source code alone — each observes a real browser session, which grounds the generated selectors and heals in actual application behavior rather than plausible-looking hallucination.

snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.title: Playwright Test Agents — Planner, Generator, Healer
snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.content: Playwright ships agent definitions consumed by your own LLM client — VS Code, Claude Code, opencode. Playwright supplies the instructions and MCP tools while you supply the model; Test Agents is not a self-contained autonomous product.

snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.title: Playwright Test Agents — Planner, Generator, Healer
snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-claim.content: ZeroStep’s plain-text AI assertions for Playwright are a durable idea in a dormant library: last release December 2023, docs still targeting GPT-3.5 (checked 2026-06-10). Treat the pattern as the takeaway, not the library.

snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-defin.title: Playwright Test Agents — Planner, Generator, Healer
snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-defin.content: Playwright Test Agents (v1.56, October 2025) — three AI roles that drive a real browser via MCP: the Planner explores the live app and writes a markdown test plan, the Generator turns the plan into executable .spec.ts files, and the Healer takes a failing test, finds the equivalent element, patches, and re-runs.

snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-quote.title: Playwright Test Agents — Planner, Generator, Healer
snippets/ai/playwright-test-agents-quote.content: an agent that auto-heals tests can also auto-heal them into asserting the wrong thing — a heal is a diff to review, not a green light to trust

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: The characteristic security failure of vibe coding is not injected vulnerable patterns but structurally flawless code that silently fails to enforce authorization at runtime — the flaw is an absence, often in configuration the generated diff never touches.

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: The canonical vibe-coding hole: an agent wires a Supabase or Firebase client flawlessly, but the server-side enforcement — RLS policies, security rules — never gets configured. Code-diff review finds nothing wrong, because nothing in the front-end is wrong.

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: Negative authorization tests (“user A cannot read user B’s rows”) only work if the requirements are operator-supplied — the agent that omitted enforcement will just as cheerfully omit the negative test. The mitigation quietly reintroduces the operator that vibe coding removed.

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: “Agents can’t touch config outside the repo” does not survive checking: Supabase ships an MCP server, RLS can live in an in-repo migration, and Firestore rules are repo files. The durable claim is the removed operator, not the visibility boundary.

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: The person best positioned to notice missing enforcement is exactly the person the workflow removed.

snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.title: Vibe Coding's Authorization Blind Spot
snippets/ai/vibe-coding-authorization-fl.content: Audit the boundaries, not the diff.

snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.content: Shift-left accessibility moves a11y responsibility upstream — into tokens, component APIs, and design annotations — so the system emits accessible output by default rather than hoping product teams remember to add ARIA attributes.

snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.content: A design system is where accessibility work has the highest leverage, because one correct component is consumed by hundreds of pages. Retrofitted accessibility is expensive: findings ship weeks after the code and fixes require refactors.

snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.content: The order of operations for accessible components is semantic HTML first, ARIA only to patch the gap. Nested meaningless divs with click handlers are the single most common source of screen-reader unreadability.

snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.content: Dark mode, high-contrast, and forced-colors are accessibility features, not visual preferences. Under Windows High Contrast the browser overrides all colors, so a system must use system-color keywords rather than assume its custom backgrounds render.

snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-accessibilit.content: WCAG 2.1 AA contrast minimums: 4.5:1 for normal text, and 3:1 for large text, UI components, and graphical objects.

snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.title: Design System Component APIs — Conventions and Anti-Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.content: Representing a component variant as a boolean is the common early mistake — booleans compose into illegal states like isSmall && isLarge and collapse under growth. The durable shape is a string enumeration (variant=“primary” size=“small”), which makes the legal state space explicit.

snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.title: Design System Component APIs — Conventions and Anti-Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.content: The durable escape hatch for a too-rigid component is composition, not a new prop. Named slots (Card.Header), asChild/Slot primitives, and render props let consumers inject custom content without the system growing a prop for every edge case.

snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.title: Design System Component APIs — Conventions and Anti-Patterns
snippets/tech/design-system-component-ap.content: Headless component libraries (Radix, React Aria) ship behavior and accessibility and leave styling to the consumer; styled libraries (Material UI, Polaris) ship visual defaults with theming hooks. Headless is slower to start but has a higher ceiling for custom brand work.

snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.title: Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.content: The most common and corrosive design-system failure is drift — Figma-vs-code bifurcation. Components get updated on one side only; over time designers produce specs the codebase can’t match, and both sides maintain parallel mental models of the same system.

snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.title: Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.content: Forking is the most severe design-system failure: a fork inherits no upstream bug fixes, security patches, or a11y improvements, its visual drift is invisible to the central system, and forks tend to multiply once one team starts.

snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.title: Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.content: Coverage ≠ success. A design system can have 100% coverage of core components and still fail if the components are used but hated (adoption by coercion, not choice), or style-overridden so heavily the visual system is effectively broken.

snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.title: Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
snippets/tech/design-system-failure-mode.content: A design system in “maintenance mode” without dedicated funding becomes a liability within 12–24 months (a rule-of-thumb estimate): framework versions lag, accessibility regresses, and product teams abandon it to keep their own velocity.

snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.content: Nathan Curtis, who popularized the centralized/federated/hybrid taxonomy in 2015, retracted it in 2024: “Favoring federated was and is wrong.” Federated is not a model you choose but a phase you earn — and getting there is central-team work.

snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.content: Across 80+ design systems, Curtis reports the share thriving without centrally allocated people as “Zero. Zero. Zero percent.” His correction is not “always centralize” but to shift the or to an and: always a central team, and also federated participation.

snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.content: Design systems die from governance failures — bottlenecked core teams, shadow forks, uncommunicated breaking changes — far more often than from code issues. Governance is also the hardest thing to retrofit later.

snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.content: The deprecation rhythm that keeps consumer trust: formally deprecate in a minor release (console warnings), remove only in the next major. That gives consumers one full major cycle to migrate; skipping it is how you lose trust.

snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
snippets/tech/design-system-governance-c.content: Read a mature contribution pipeline as a ceiling, not a starting point. Every gate is also a place a contributor gives up, and the characteristic failure is a team that hardens the flow to fix low-quality contributions and ends up with none.

snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.title: Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.content: A Minimum Viable Design System is core tokens + 5–10 atomic components (Button, Input, Checkbox, Select, Grid, Modal…) + a single source of truth. What NOT to build at MVDS scale: multi-brand theming engines, deep visual-regression CI/CD, and heavy governance layers.

snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.title: Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.content: The Radix + shadcn/ui + Tailwind combination is a common 2026 MVDS stack: headless behavior and accessibility, copy-into-your-repo components you own outright, and utility CSS — getting you to “design system-ish” in days, not months.

snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.title: Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-clai.content: Four inflection points signal it’s time to scale up a design system: org growth beyond one cohesive unit, platform bifurcation (web + iOS + Android), multi-brand/white-label needs, and compliance mandates. Hitting two or more means it’s already overdue.

snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-quot.title: Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
snippets/tech/design-system-scaling-quot.content: Copying Material Design at 5 engineers is how good systems fail.

snippets/tech/design-systems-claim-1.title: Design Systems — Hub
snippets/tech/design-systems-claim-1.content: A design system is a product, not a deliverable: shared tokens, components, accessibility baselines, documentation, and governance that replace ad-hoc UI with a single source of truth. Once built, it needs ongoing staffing, versioning, and adoption work to keep producing value.

snippets/tech/design-systems-claim-2.title: Design Systems — Hub
snippets/tech/design-systems-claim-2.content: For a small team with a single product and one brand, a formal design system can be premature optimization. shadcn/ui plus Tailwind plus a short convention doc is a design system too, and often the right one.

snippets/tech/design-systems-quote-1.title: Design Systems — Hub
snippets/tech/design-systems-quote-1.content: The interesting question is rarely “do we need one?” but “what scale of system is honest for our stage?”

snippets/tech/design-systems-quote-2.title: Design Systems — Hub
snippets/tech/design-systems-quote-2.content: The failure mode isn’t only “no system” — it’s also “too much system, too early.”

snippets/tech/design-tokens-claim-1.title: Design Tokens — Three-Tier Architecture and Theming
snippets/tech/design-tokens-claim-1.content: The mature token pattern is a three-tier taxonomy: reference (raw palette values), system (semantic purpose — the theming layer), and component (maps a semantic to one component property). A dark-mode or brand swap changes only the system layer; components don’t care.

snippets/tech/design-tokens-claim-2.title: Design Tokens — Three-Tier Architecture and Theming
snippets/tech/design-tokens-claim-2.content: Hardcoded hex values and pixel magic numbers are the root cause of most design-system drift. Once tokens exist as a layered hierarchy, theming (dark mode, multi-brand, high contrast) becomes swapping one layer’s mapping, not rewriting components.

snippets/tech/design-tokens-definition-1.title: Design Tokens — Three-Tier Architecture and Theming
snippets/tech/design-tokens-definition-1.content: Design tokens — platform-agnostic variables that store visual decisions (color, typography, spacing, radii, motion) as data, so one source of truth can emit the same decision to CSS, Swift, XML, Figma variables, and JSON SDKs.

snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.title: Effective Code Review
snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.content: Developers say code review is for defect detection, but only ~15% of review comments point to actual defects (a figure usually attributed to Czerwonka et al. 2015). The dominant real outcomes are knowledge transfer, team awareness of changes, and alternative-solution discussion.

snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.title: Effective Code Review
snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.content: Code-review defect discovery drops sharply beyond 200–400 lines of code per session; at ≥1,000 LOC review degrades into rubber-stamping. (SmartBear/Cisco vendor study — calibrated folklore, not peer-reviewed law.)

snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.title: Effective Code Review
snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.content: The Ego Effect: the expectation of review improves submitted code even before anyone looks. Spot-checking just 20–33% of changes lowered defect density across the whole codebase — a 1-in-3 chance of scrutiny is enough.

snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.title: Effective Code Review
snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.content: Review top-down, broadest concern first: design and system integration, then functionality and security, then complexity, then tests, then naming. Never read line-by-line from the top — that’s how priority inversion buries a “rewrite” verdict under typo nits.

snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.title: Effective Code Review
snippets/tech/effective-code-review-clai.content: In code review, comments should explain why, never what. A comment that restates what the code does is a refactoring signal — the code itself should be clear enough that a what-comment is unnecessary.

snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.title: Fedora Workstation Setup
snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.content: Don’t disable SELinux — learn to work with it. When a legitimate app is blocked, read the denial with ausearch -m avc and generate a targeted policy with audit2allow, rather than switching enforcement off.

snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.title: Fedora Workstation Setup
snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.content: Rule of thumb for Flatpak vs native packages: if a tool links against system libraries or you develop against it, install it native (dnf); if it’s a desktop app you just run, Flatpak’s sandbox is fine.

snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.title: Fedora Workstation Setup
snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.content: Fedora keeps the last three kernels by default (installonly_limit=3), so a kernel update that breaks something is recoverable by rebooting into an older entry from GRUB rather than by rescuing the system.

snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.title: Fedora Workstation Setup
snippets/tech/fedora-workstation-setup-c.content: Fedora defaults to Btrfs, where snapshots are cheap. Take one with snapper or btrbk before a major version upgrade — and note that df misreports Btrfs, so use btrfs filesystem usage / for real numbers.

snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.title: KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.content: JetBrains lists 70+ named KMP adopters (as of 2026-06), but only a handful — Quizlet, Memrise, Mirego, Cash App — involve a web target at all; the large majority are mobile-only Android+iOS. Production web-target use is the rare exception, not the norm.

snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.title: KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.content: Quizlet migrated its shared code from JavaScript to KMP in early 2019 and runs it in production at 50M+ monthly active users, compiling shared Kotlin business logic to JS for web clients — the cleanest public match to a logic-only shared core with native and web UI on top.

snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.title: KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.content: Financial-services Kotlin at scale is on the backend (ING, N26, Kakao Pay), not shared-core-to-web. No named financial-services company is publicly recorded shipping a Kotlin shared core consumed by a web-native JS/TS frontend in production. (as of 2026-06)

snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.title: KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
snippets/tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-ev.content: Cash App/Block has run KMP in production since 2018 and uses Kotlin/JS for shared presentation since 2021 — but through its Zipline/Redwood stack rendering to each platform’s native UI, not a generic React/TS frontend. A different consumption model than React-consumes-Kotlin-core.

snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.title: The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.content: JetBrains recommends Kotlin/JS over Kotlin/Wasm for a logic-only Kotlin core handed to a JS frontend, because Kotlin/JS provides a better interop experience. Wasm’s strengths — near-native compute, faster UI — are irrelevant when you only ship a library that must hand rich typed objects across the boundary. (as of 2026-06)

snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.title: The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.content: Idiomatic Kotlin doesn’t cross the JS boundary cleanly, so the shared-core team must build a DTO-flattened, annotation-disciplined facade rather than expose the rich domain model. That facade is the public API the web team consumes — the contract that needs semver and .d.ts-diff review.

snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.title: The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-cl.content: On Kotlin/JS, collections (List/Map/Set), Long, unsigned ints, suspend functions, Flow/StateFlow, and sealed hierarchies with object subclasses all fail to export cleanly — each needs flattening or a hand-written wrapper at the boundary. (as of 2026-06)

snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-qu.title: The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
snippets/tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary-qu.content: Anything not marked @JsExport is not supported across the boundary.

snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.title: Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.content: The web facade is a convenience boundary, not a trust boundary. Anything in the shared core that compiles to web ships to the browser, where the user can read and modify it — so validation, authorization, and fraud rules enforced in the core are advisory; the server must re-validate everything.

snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.title: Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.content: Flatten 64-bit values to String, never Double, at the JS boundary. A JS Double is exact only to 53 bits, so a 64-bit amount or account/transaction ID flattened to Double silently loses precision — a corrupt-integrity bug that no exception flags.

snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.title: Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.content: Everything marked @JsExport is callable by any script on the page, including injected XSS payloads, so keep the export surface minimal — least-privilege, not just cheaper to review. Name mangling (hello_sv8swh_k$) is not obfuscation and must not be treated as a protection.

snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.title: Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
snippets/tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-exampl.content: Measured 2026-07: Kotlin/JS tree-shaking is zero by default, but per-file granularity plus a hand-added sideEffects: false prunes a DTO-only consumer to under 1 KB gzip in both Vite and webpack. Each lever alone does nothing; only the combination works.

snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.title: KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.content: The architecture: a shared Kotlin module compiles to a JS library (.js + .d.ts + package.json), is published to npm, and is imported by a React/TypeScript app like any other JS dependency — while the same Kotlin core also serves true-native Android and iOS clients.

snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.title: KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.content: KMP shared-core / web-native UI is the right call only when there’s a genuine true-native Android/iOS client. If “mobile” means React Native, a TypeScript-first shared-core monorepo dominates on hiring, tooling, and zero interop tax — and KMP adds little.

snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.title: KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.content: The most important counterfactual to a shared Kotlin core is thin clients plus server-side logic via generated (OpenAPI/gRPC) clients — the classic finserv pattern. It beats every client-sharing approach on auditability; shared-core wins only on offline capability, latency, and client-side UX.

snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.title: KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
snippets/tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-e.content: Dropbox abandoned its C++ shared core (~2019) for native, after custom-tooling overhead, a C++/Java deadlock that took weeks to debug, and a sustained inability to hire C++ mobile engineers. The failure modes KMP should be stress-tested against: bridging overhead and niche-skill hiring.

snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.title: Mature Design Systems — Comparative Survey
snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.content: Each mature design system is optimized for a different failure mode, which is why “pick the best one” is the wrong framing. Read Material, Polaris, GOV.UK, Carbon, Primer, and Spectrum as examples of what fits a given operational mandate.

snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.title: Mature Design Systems — Comparative Survey
snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.content: GOV.UK’s identity is uncompromising progressive enhancement — components work perfectly without JavaScript, then JS layers on non-essential enhancements — because citizens file taxes and register for healthcare on old devices, flaky networks, and forced-colors mode.

snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.title: Mature Design Systems — Comparative Survey
snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.content: Borrowing a design system’s surface without understanding the constraint that shaped it is how cargo-cult design systems get built. M3’s dynamic color, GOV.UK’s no-JS fallback, and Primer’s annotation toolkit are rational consequences of their audience and distribution model.

snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.title: Mature Design Systems — Comparative Survey
snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.content: IBM Carbon’s deliberate architectural bet is multi-framework parity — shipping first-party React, Angular, and Web Component implementations (plus Vue and Svelte, which have historically lagged) — because a multinational enterprise cannot force one JS framework on every product team.

snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.title: Mature Design Systems — Comparative Survey
snippets/tech/mature-design-systems-surv.content: Adobe Spectrum 2 treats the token system as a shared API across C++, React, and Web Components — the decoupling that lets one color change propagate from Photoshop’s pixel-perfect desktop UI to a Marketing Cloud dashboard. (survey as of 2026-04)

snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-cla.title: MCP Server Development
snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-cla.content: MCP solves the “N×M” integration problem: instead of building a custom integration between every AI client and every tool, you build one MCP server and it works with all MCP clients — the same pattern LSP brought to editors.

snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-cla.title: MCP Server Development
snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-cla.content: In an stdio-transport MCP server, never use console.log — it corrupts the JSON-RPC stream. Write debug output to stderr or a file instead, and return tool errors as isError content blocks rather than throwing, so the AI can see the error and recover.

snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-def.title: MCP Server Development
snippets/tech/mcp-server-development-def.content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools, data, and services. A server exposes tools (functions the agent calls), resources (data it reads), and prompts (reusable templates) over JSON-RPC.

snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.title: TypeScript for AI Tooling
snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.content: Force structured JSON output from an LLM by using tool_choice with a specific tool name, then parsing the tool input against a schema. This is more reliable than asking for JSON in the prompt.

snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.title: TypeScript for AI Tooling
snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.content: Never throw from an agent’s tool handler — return the error back to the model as an is_error tool result so it can self-correct, and always cap the agent loop (e.g. 20 iterations) to prevent runaway costs.

snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.title: TypeScript for AI Tooling
snippets/tech/typescript-for-ai-tooling-.content: For LLM tool schemas, prefer flat structures over deeply nested ones — the model produces more accurate output. If you need nested data, consider splitting into multiple tool calls.

snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.title: Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.content: Most “bad” web pages aren’t ugly — they’re misaligned: a transactional checkout designed like an informational article, or a landing page with homepage navigation bleeding attention. Knowing which typology applies is upstream of layout, copy, and component choice.

snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.title: Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.content: For goal-directed catalog browsing, “Load More” or pagination tends to beat infinite scroll — infinite scroll disrupts spatial memory and hides footer content. Infinite scroll is fine only for hedonic feeds (social, discovery) where there’s no return trip.

snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.title: Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.content: A landing page is engineered for a low attention ratio (interactive links ÷ conversion goals, ideally 1:1): strip global nav and competing CTAs, and enforce message match with the ad or email that drove the click.

snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.title: Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.content: Treat any percentage in web-design literature as directionally useful, not authoritative. Most precise-looking figures trace loosely to Baymard, Nielsen Norman Group, or vendor A/B posts — rerun the measurement on your own funnel before citing it.

snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.title: Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
snippets/tech/web-page-typologies-claim-.content: Zero-results search states must offer alternatives — curated recommendations, popular categories, parameter suggestions — never a dead end.

snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.title: Wine, Proton, and Gaming on Linux
snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.content: Wine is not an emulator — it reimplements the Windows API at the syscall level, translating Win32 calls (CreateFile, Direct3D) through DLL replacements down to Linux syscalls. No Windows code is emulated instruction-by-instruction.

snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.title: Wine, Proton, and Gaming on Linux
snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.content: Anti-cheat is the biggest remaining barrier for Linux gaming. EasyAntiCheat and BattlEye work when developers opt in, but kernel-level anti-cheat like Riot’s Vanguard does not work on Linux — which is why there’s no Valorant on Linux. (as of early 2026)

snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.title: Wine, Proton, and Gaming on Linux
snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.content: Each Wine prefix is an isolated virtual Windows installation — its own C:\ drive, registry, and DLLs — and is just a directory on your filesystem, so you can manage game files (like WoW addons) directly from Linux.

snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.title: Wine, Proton, and Gaming on Linux
snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.content: Gamescope is the better route to FSR upscaling than WINE_FULLSCREEN_FSR=1, which requires true fullscreen. Gamescope wraps any game — windowed included — in its own micro-compositor, and also gives a frame limiter and independent resolution control.

snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.title: Wine, Proton, and Gaming on Linux
snippets/tech/wine-proton-gaming-linux-c.content: Shader compilation stutter is expected on first encounter, not a misconfiguration: DXVK compiles shaders as it meets them and writes a .dxvk-cache beside the game. The cache persists between sessions, so the stutter fades as it fills.

tech/design-system-accessibility.title: Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
tech/design-system-accessibility.content:
Design System Accessibility — Shift-Left and Annotation Patterns
What it is
The practice of moving accessibility responsibility upstream — from end-of-cycle QA into tokens, component APIs, and design annotations — so that the system emits accessible output by default rather than hoping product teams remember to add ARIA attributes.
Why it matters
Retrofitted accessibility is expensive: audit findings ship weeks after the code, fixes require refactors, legal exposure grows with each non-compliant surface. A design system is where a11y work has the highest leverage, because one correct component is consumed by hundreds of pages.
The baseline — what a system should guarantee

Algorithmic contrast — color roles pair background and text automatically, enforcing minimum ratios across light/dark/high-contrast modes. WCAG 2.1 AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, UI components, and graphical objects (source article cited “3:1 minimum” for Material Design 3 — likely referring to the large-text / UI-component tier; verify against M3 spec before citing a universal guarantee).
Semantic HTML by default — components emit <button>, <nav>, <dialog>, <ul> etc., not nested <div> stacks with click handlers. Nested meaningless divs are the single most common source of screen-reader unreadability.
ARIA only where semantic HTML isn’t enough — custom comboboxes, menus, and tabs need ARIA roles and state attributes. The order of operations is semantic HTML first, ARIA to patch the gap.
Focus management — visible focus rings that survive CSS resets; focus traps inside modals; focus restoration on close; keyboard-operable menus, dropdowns, and comboboxes.
Console-level enforcement — Polaris logs developer warnings when required ARIA props are missing. A system that fails loud at dev time prevents regressions at review time.

The shift-left pattern — annotation toolkits
GitHub Primer’s Annotation Toolkit is the canonical example. It’s a Figma asset library designed to document UI anatomy and non-visual behavior directly on the design canvas:

Focus order (numbered arrows between interactive elements)
Keyboard shortcuts
ARIA live region boundaries
Heading semantics (h1 vs h2 vs visual-only heading style)
Structural landmarks (main, nav, complementary, contentinfo)
Announcements for dynamic state changes

Source claims GitHub’s internal research found ~48% of accessibility audit issues could have been prevented if intent had been documented before engineering handoff (specific figure unverified — the shift-left-via-annotation pattern is documented in Primer’s public materials but the 48% number should be confirmed against Primer’s blog posts before citing).
The mechanism: a11y requirements stop being verbal agreements in Slack threads and become visible artifacts that travel with the Figma file into engineering.
User testing with assistive technology
IBM Carbon’s standout claim is integrating actual screen-reader users, keyboard-navigation experts, and AT advocates into component engineering — not just running automated WCAG scans.
This matters because automated tools catch maybe ~30–40% of a11y issues (specific percentage varies by study and tool; widely cited figures from Deque/WebAIM but treat as directional). Screen-reader usability — whether a component is comprehensible, not just technically compliant — requires human feedback.
Accessible theming
Dark mode, high-contrast mode, and forced-colors mode are accessibility features, not visual preferences:

High-contrast mode: used by low-vision users; system must not rely on color alone for meaning
forced-colors (Windows High Contrast): browser overrides all colors; system must use system-color keywords and not assume custom backgrounds will render
Reduced motion: prefers-reduced-motion should disable non-essential animation system-wide

Token-based theming (see design-tokens) is what makes these modes implementable without per-component rework.
What needs more research

The ~48% Primer annotation figure — find the original Primer blog post and confirm
Current state of accessibilityRole and React Native accessibility primitives in 2026
Whether AI-assisted a11y auditing (e.g., LLM review of Figma annotations → generated WCAG checklist) is now production-ready or still experimental

Related

mature-design-systems-survey — Primer, Carbon, GOV.UK are the a11y reference points

Sources

The shift-left pattern, annotation toolkits, and semantic-HTML baseline are widely documented across Primer (primer.style/accessibility), Carbon (carbondesignsystem.com/guidelines/accessibility), and WCAG 2.1. tech/design-system-component-apis.title: Design System Component APIs — Conventions and Anti-Patterns
tech/design-system-component-apis.content:
Design System Component APIs — Conventions and Anti-Patterns
What it is
The prop surface, naming scheme, and state model that a design-system component exposes to consuming product code. API design is the part of a system most likely to rot quietly: a bad choice at v1 becomes a migration hazard at v10.
Why it matters
Components live for years and are imported by hundreds of files. The tension is strictness (enforce the system) vs flexibility (handle edge cases without forking). An API that’s too rigid drives forking; one that’s too permissive becomes a grab-bag with no enforced invariants.
Anti-pattern: boolean flags for variants
The common early mistake is representing a variant as a boolean:
// v1
<Button isPrimary isSmall />
// v3, after "medium" and "secondary" are needed
<Button isPrimary={false} isSecondary isMedium={!isSmall && !isLarge} />
Boolean flags compose into illegal states (isSmall && isLarge) and collapse under growth. The durable shape is a string enumeration:
<Button variant="primary" size="small" />
Enums make the legal state space explicit and survive the addition of new variants without breaking existing callers.
Managing variant styling — CVA and its limits
Class Variance Authority (CVA) has become the common pattern for mapping enum values to Tailwind / utility classes without scattering conditional logic across the component body. It centralizes the variant/size matrix and plays well with IntelliSense.
Tradeoff: CVA adds runtime class-string generation and can introduce real overhead if used on hot paths or with dozens of variants per component. Lean on it for the public component API surface, not for every internal styling decision. (Performance caveat paraphrased from source; measure on your own app before cutting.)
Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs
Design-system form components typically need to support both:

Controlled — caller owns state via value + onChange. Good when the parent needs to observe or transform input in real time.
Uncontrolled — component owns state internally; caller reads via ref or onSubmit. Lower boilerplate for simple forms.

Polaris’s pattern is to use defaultValue to track “dirty” state — whether the user has modified the input relative to its initial value. This lets the app cleanly distinguish “user has made unsaved changes” from “field still holds server state” (specific Polaris API paraphrased from source; verify against current @shopify/polaris docs before implementing).
Providing both modes is standard; the discipline is documenting which is the default and not silently switching based on prop presence in a way that surprises consumers.
Slot / composition patterns for flexibility
The durable escape hatch for “component is too rigid” is composition, not a new prop. Named slots (<Card.Header>, <Card.Footer>), asChild / Slot primitives from Radix, and render props let consumers inject custom content without the system growing a customHeaderClassName prop for every edge case.
Radix + shadcn/ui popularized this pattern in the React ecosystem; it generalizes: expose the shape, let the consumer fill the content.
State modeling beyond inputs

Interaction states — hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error — are part of the API surface even when not exposed as props. Components should emit all of them consistently so themes and focus rings work without per-instance overrides.
Focus management — modal dialogs, menus, and comboboxes must trap focus, restore it on close, and expose onOpenChange-style hooks so apps can integrate with routing. Headless-UI libraries do this heavy lifting; rolling your own is where a11y bugs breed.

Headless vs styled — the architectural fork
Two philosophies:

Styled libraries (Material UI, Polaris React) ship visual defaults with theming hooks. Fastest to pick up; slower to deviate from.
Headless libraries (Radix, Headless UI, React Aria) ship behavior and a11y, leave styling to the consumer. Slower to start; higher ceiling for custom brand work.

shadcn/ui’s influence has been to normalize owning headless + Tailwind-generated components in your own repo — a hybrid that trades versioning pain for customization freedom. For MVDS work this is often the right starting point; see design-system-scaling.
What needs more research

Empirical comparison of CVA overhead vs alternatives (tailwind-variants, cva, manual clsx composition) at scale
How Server Components / RSC shift the controlled-vs-uncontrolled question
Current best-practice API for AI-consumed components (MCP tool-calling, structured generation) — plausibly becoming a real axis by 2026

Related

design-tokens — component tokens feed component APIs

design-system-failure-modes — rigid APIs drive forking

Sources

Condensed from AI-drafted research brief (2026-04-20). Boolean-vs-enum, CVA, and headless-vs-styled patterns are widely documented in React/design-system ecosystem blogs; specific vendor API claims labeled unverified inline.

tech/design-system-failure-modes.title: Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
tech/design-system-failure-modes.content:
Design System Failure Modes — Drift, Forking, and Atrophy
What it is
The systemic ways design systems stop delivering ROI: not dramatic collapses, but slow drift and erosion that turn an accelerator into a tax. Understanding these modes before building is more valuable than documenting them after autopsy.
Why it matters
A design system’s actual ROI is realized over years. The investment front-loads; the returns depend on continued adoption. Most failure modes are quiet — nothing breaks, the system just stops being the path of least resistance, and product teams route around it.
Drift — Figma vs code bifurcation
The most common and most corrosive failure. Components get updated in the engineering repo but not in Figma (or vice versa). Tokens get remapped on one side only. Over time:

Designers produce specs the codebase cannot match without overrides
Engineers visually approximate measurements — margin: 16px instead of var(--spacing-md)
Trust erodes: designers stop treating Figma as a constraints engine; engineers stop treating it as specification
Both sides maintain parallel mental models of the same system

Prevention: treat Figma ↔ code as a bidirectional programmable API (see design-tokens and design-system-governance). Detection: visual regression tests against Figma snapshots, periodic audit of production CSS for token usage vs hardcoded values.
The “done” illusion — underfunded TCO
Many organizations treat a design system as a finite capital project — fund the build, declare victory, cut staffing. Then total cost of ownership (TCO) work is unowned:

CI maintenance and dependency upgrades
Upstream framework churn (React 18 → 19, Vue 3 → 4, new CSS features)
Browser deprecations and evolving web standards
Routine accessibility audits
Documentation freshness
IT support for consuming teams

A system in “maintenance mode” without dedicated funding becomes a liability within 12–24 months. Framework versions lag, a11y regresses, and product teams eventually abandon it to maintain their own velocity. (Time-to-rot estimate is a rule-of-thumb rather than a measured figure — varies with framework choice and organizational size.)
Adoption gaps and shadow systems
A system returns zero ROI if product teams don’t adopt it. Gaps open when:

The system is too rigid for legitimate edge cases
The contribution process is too slow for delivery timelines
The technology choice was theoretical (“React is most popular”) rather than grounded in consuming-team constraints
Documentation is weak enough that building-from-scratch feels faster than learning the API

Teams respond by building shadow systems — parallel component libraries inside product code. Shadow systems create permanent integration breakpoints: global redesigns stall; accessibility fixes need to be applied in multiple places; users encounter inconsistent UX moving between product surfaces.
Detection: coverage tracking (what % of production UI uses system components) is necessary but insufficient. Also track:

Developer sentiment (surveys, friction logs)
PR patterns — how often product teams import a system component vs copy-paste a similar one
Deprecation compliance — how fast consumers migrate off deprecated APIs

Forking — when flexibility fails
When a component is too rigid to handle a legitimate use case and contribution is too slow, product teams copy the component source into their own repo and mutate it locally. Forking is the most severe failure because:

The fork inherits no upstream bug fixes, security patches, or a11y improvements
The fork’s visual drift is invisible from the central system’s perspective
Forks tend to multiply — once one team does it, others follow

Prevention is a flexibility-first API (see design-system-component-apis — slots, composition, named subcomponents) plus a fast-track contribution path for common extensions.
Over-abstraction — the other direction
The mirror failure of rigid-and-forked is hyper-flexible-and-bloated. In an attempt to serve every use case, architects pack components with hundreds of optional props and complex internal conditional logic. Consequences:

Massive JavaScript bundles with unused code paths
Performance regressions visible to end users
API surfaces too large for consumers to learn
Internal code too complex for the core team to maintain

The antidote is composition (see design-system-component-apis) — expose the pieces, let consumers assemble edge cases, resist adding prop #47.
Coverage ≠ success
A system can have 100% coverage of core components and still fail if:

The components are used but hated (adoption by coercion, not choice)
The system captures atomic elements but no product-level patterns
Teams use components but style-override them so heavily that the visual system is effectively broken

Sentiment metrics and pattern-level (not component-level) coverage are the honest measures.
What needs more research

Empirical data on fork rate by system type (permissive vs opinionated APIs)
TCO benchmarks — realistic per-engineer-year cost to maintain a mid-size system
Metrics that correlate with design-system health beyond coverage (sentiment, PR velocity, a11y regression rate) — partly addressed in design-system-value-measurement, which separates penetration metrics from value metrics and proposes UX/UI/a11y ticket volume against a pre-adoption baseline as the one concrete lagging measure

Related
