design-system-component-apis — rigid APIs drive forking, bloated APIs drive abandonment
design-tokens — untokenized values are the substrate of drift
design-system-scaling — premature systemization is itself a failure mode

Sources

Condensed from AI-drafted research brief (2026-04-20). Failure-mode taxonomy is consistent with practitioner writing in the design-system community (Nathan Curtis / EightShapes blog, Sparkbox’s annual design systems survey) — specific vendor figures labeled unverified inline.

tech/design-system-governance.title: Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
tech/design-system-governance.content:
Design System Governance — Models, Versioning, and Contribution
What it is
The organizational and release-process layer that decides who owns the system, how changes are proposed and merged, and how breaking changes are signalled to consumers. Governance is what separates a component library from a working design system.
Why it matters
A design system’s code quality is necessary but not sufficient. Systems die from governance failures — bottlenecked core teams, shadow forks, uncommunicated breaking changes — far more often than from code issues. Governance is also the hardest thing to retrofit later; the model you pick early shapes the organization’s relationship with the system for years.
The three governance models





























ModelOwnershipStrengthFailure modeCentralizedDedicated core team owns all developmentVisual consistency, coherent architectural vision, quality controlCore team becomes bottleneck; loses touch with product-level frictionFederated / decentralizedRepresentatives from product teams govern collectivelyStays close to real product needs; fast adaptation to edge casesArchitectural fragmentation; product engineers lack bandwidth for systemic workHybridSmall core team owns infrastructure (tokens, tooling, CI); product teams contribute componentsCore stability + product-driven innovationRequires sophisticated PR review and communication to avoid degradation
Hybrid is the mature-organization target. Pure centralized works at MVDS scale (see design-system-scaling).
The federated model has been publicly withdrawn by the person who popularized it
The table above presents three models as comparable options. That framing is the specific mistake the taxonomy’s author has since disavowed, and this note carried it until 2026-08-25.
Nathan Curtis set out the original models — solitary, central, federated — in Team Models for Scaling a Design System (2015). In The Fallacy of Federated Design Systems (2024-09-13) he retracted the recommendation:

“Favoring federated was and is wrong.” … “federated is not a choice, it’s a facet. In practice, it’s never pursued first and never without central investment.”

Across 80+ design systems he reports that the number thriving without centrally allocated people is “Zero. Zero. Zero percent.” His correction is not “always centralize” but “Shift that or to an and” — successful systems always have a central team and also seek federated participation; the 2015 diagram’s error was implying you pick one. Six stakeholder myths he says the diagram anchors are worth knowing before any governance conversation, the sharpest being “Federated gets you a design system for free.”
Practical consequence: treat federated as a phase you earn, not a model you choose. Contribution becomes viable once a system has adoption, community, and maturity — and getting there is central-team work. See design-system-governance-how-much for the practitioner evidence.
Semantic Versioning — Polaris as the reference
Shopify Polaris is the commonly-cited template for codified SemVer rules. The structure:
Major (X.0.0) — breaking changes:

Removing a component
Removing a prop
Changing the data type a prop accepts
Structural changes to public Sass variables / CSS custom properties that would invalidate downstream selectors

Minor (1.X.0) — backward-compatible additions:

New components
New props on existing components
Formally deprecating an element (deprecation in a minor release lets consumers see console warnings before removal in the next major)

Patch (1.0.X) — non-breaking fixes:

Bug fixes
Private Sass variable changes
Internal HTML class rename (e.g., BEM internals) that doesn’t affect public APIs

(Specific rule set paraphrased from source; Polaris’s actual release-process doc on polaris.shopify.com is authoritative — verify edge cases there before building a release pipeline on this summary.)
The deprecation-via-minor-then-removal-in-major rhythm is the critical detail: consumers get console warnings for one full major cycle to migrate. Skipping that rhythm is how you lose trust.
Contribution flow
A frictionless-but-gated contribution pipeline typical of mature systems:

Proposal / triage — product team opens an issue describing the missing pattern. Core team assesses whether it’s globally applicable or idiosyncratic to one feature. Idiosyncratic → stays in product code; globally applicable → goes to step 2.
Design + API spec — designers and engineers collaboratively draft visual states, a11y requirements (see design-system-accessibility), and the prop surface (see design-system-component-apis).
Pull request with automation — CI runs linters, unit and integration tests, and visual regression tests (pixel snapshots compared against baseline to catch unintended downstream changes).
Human review + release — governance review for alignment with design philosophy; merge triggers automated release pipeline.

For the usability, research, and accessibility side of testing — which this pipeline doesn’t cover — see design-system-testing-scope.
The visual regression step is the one most commonly skipped and most expensive to retrofit. Tools: Chromatic, Percy, Lost Pixel (vendor list not exhaustive; verify against current tool landscape).
Read this pipeline as a ceiling, not a starting point. Every gate above is also a place a contributor gives up, and practitioners report the characteristic failure as a team that hardens this flow to fix low-quality contributions and ends up with none — losing the contributors’ trust in the system along with their PRs. Two counterweights from design-system-governance-how-much: publish light / medium / heavy contribution tiers so a documentation fix is visibly legitimate, and consider prove-it-in-production promotion (ship the component in the product; promote it only if it survives months of real use and a second team wants it) instead of upfront approval.
Documentation as governance
A documentation site is part of governance, not a deliverable separate from it:

Live interactive sandboxes with prop toggles and framework-specific copy-paste snippets
Anatomy diagrams showing internal structure, padding, and nested elements
Usage guidelines + anti-patterns (“do this, not this”) — explicit anti-patterns reduce decision fatigue
Content design integration — microcopy rules, tone of voice, internationalization standards
Changelog + migration guides — what changed, why, and how to upgrade

Without live docs, consumers read source code to guess prop behavior, and the system loses the ability to course-correct usage patterns.
Figma-to-code parity as governance
The design system is a programmable API across two disciplines. Keeping Figma and the codebase in sync is governance, not tooling trivia:

Figma Variables → JSON tokens via REST API / MCP in CI (see design-tokens)
Figma Code Connect surfaces real compiled snippets inside the design tool
Storybook-Figma integrations expose component state matrices both directions

When this loop breaks, Figma devolves into a “visual snapshot” — a source of inspiration rather than specification — and design system debt accumulates.
What needs more research

Real adoption rate of Figma Code Connect (mid-2025 launch) vs Storybook integrations as of 2026
Whether AI-driven governance (LLMs reviewing PRs for token compliance, automated migration scripts) is production-ready or still experimental. One practitioner position, 2026-07: agent guardrails are not governance but “a documentation and connection tooling problem” — the artifacts agents need are instructions, and filing them under governance imports gates that were built for humans who can be trusted to read
Empirical data on hybrid-model staffing ratios — how many core engineers per N contributing product teams

Related

Sources

tech/design-system-scaling.title: Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
tech/design-system-scaling.content:
Design System Scaling — MVDS to Enterprise Continuum
What it is
The continuum between a Minimum Viable Design System (MVDS) for small teams and a full enterprise-scale design infrastructure. The goal is matching system scope to organizational scale — neither premature optimization (building Material Design at day one) nor terminal procrastination (never systemizing at all).
Why it matters
Both ends of the continuum have sharp failure modes: premature systemization smothers a small team with governance overhead; delayed systemization at enterprise scale produces design debt too expensive to pay down. The right question is “where on this continuum are we, and what’s the next inflection point?”
Minimum Viable Design System (MVDS)
For early-stage startups, mid-sized teams, or organizations with a single product and brand, an MVDS is typically:

Core tokens — primary brand colors, typography scale, standardized spacing grid
5–10 atomic components — Button, Text Input, Checkbox, Select, Layout Grid, Modal, and a few others — the elements used on nearly every screen
Single source of truth — a shared Figma library and a lightweight documentation page
Build time — source article estimates ~8–10 weeks (rule-of-thumb, unverified; varies widely with team experience and starting stack)

What not to build at MVDS scale:

Multi-brand theming engines
Deep CI/CD visual regression pipelines
Heavy governance layers with formal proposals and review boards
Custom documentation sites

Each of these adds maintenance burden disproportionate to the consistency gain at small scale.
Accelerators:

shadcn/ui — headless component templates you copy into your repo and own outright. Source cites ~75,000 GitHub stars (time-sensitive, unverified at this exact figure — shadcn is clearly one of the dominant 2025–2026 patterns regardless of exact count).
Radix Primitives — headless behavior + a11y, no styling
Tailwind — utility CSS that pairs cleanly with the above

The combination (Radix + shadcn + Tailwind) is a common 2026 MVDS stack: gets you to “design system-ish” in days, not months.
Inflection points — when to scale up
Not arbitrary. These signals indicate the cost of not having a formal system has crossed the cost of maintaining one:

Organizational scaling — the design + engineering org grows beyond a single cohesive unit. Implicit knowledge, Slack threads, and ad-hoc communication start breaking.
Platform bifurcation — the product must natively support web + iOS + Android (or any multi-platform combination). Cross-platform token architecture becomes mandatory; see design-tokens.
Multi-brand / white-label — acquisition, distinct product lines, or serving the same software under different brand aesthetics. Hardcoded values must be refactored into a systematic theming engine.
Compliance mandates — entering enterprise B2B, government, regulated healthcare, or financial markets triggers strict WCAG compliance tracking (see design-system-accessibility). Ad-hoc a11y doesn’t survive audit.

Hitting any one of these is usually a signal to move from MVDS toward a formal system. Hitting two or more is a signal it’s already overdue.
Enterprise-scale execution
At enterprise scale the system transforms from UX toolkit to critical organizational infrastructure serving hundreds of product teams:
Architectural shifts:

Headless / Web Components — supporting multiple frontend frameworks simultaneously often forces a shift away from framework-specific components (e.g., pure React + CSS-in-JS) toward Web Components (Custom Elements + Shadow DOM) or headless + wrappers per framework. Both Polaris and Spectrum show this transition.
Design Ops + Dev Ops resources — dedicated roles maintain tooling, documentation sites, contribution pipelines, and automated CI/CD. Not “extra headcount” — the governance budget line.
Programmatic brand enforcement — visual parity enforced by code, not review. Token generation, visual regression, cross-platform asset compilation fully automated. Source mentions tools like Outfit for encoding brand rules into templates (product name unverified — confirm exists and is current before citing; the general pattern of automated brand rules is established, specific vendors change).

Governance shifts — see design-system-governance:

Formal hybrid model (core team + federated product-team contributions)
SLAs for contribution review and release
Public roadmap and deprecation policy

The decision matrix








































DimensionMVDSEnterpriseTarget1–3 teams, single brand100+ teams, multi-brand portfolioComponent countCore tokens + 5–10 atoms60+ components, composed patterns, page templatesGovernanceInformal, maintained by lead designers/engineersDedicated core team with federated contribution + SLAsToolingShared Figma file, basic StorybookAutomated token CI/CD, visual regression, custom lintersDocsSingle markdown page / NotionCustom interactive site with live code sandboxesPrimary failure riskPremature over-engineering stifling velocityAdoption gaps, forking, governance bottlenecks
The honest middle
Most organizations sit between MVDS and enterprise for years. That’s fine. The intermediate pattern:

Keep tokens and 15–30 components; don’t chase the 60+ number
One informal maintainer role at first, moving to a part-time core team as adoption grows
Storybook + a markdown docs site is enough until it isn’t
Visual regression testing enters the picture when the system has enough consumers that “someone else will catch it” stops being true

Scale the system to match the organization. Copying Material Design at 5 engineers is how good systems fail.
What needs more research

Whether the ~8–10 week MVDS estimate holds under 2026 tooling (shadcn/Radix/Tailwind stack may compress this further)
Empirical inflection-point data — what team size / product count actually triggers the transition in practice
Post-MVDS intermediate patterns — the source article skips the messy middle where most systems live

Related

tech/design-systems.title: Design Systems — Hub
tech/design-systems.content:
Design Systems — Hub
What it is
A design system is shared infrastructure — tokens, components, accessibility baselines, documentation, and governance — that replaces ad-hoc UI production with a single source of truth coupling designers and engineers. It is a product, not a deliverable: once built, it needs ongoing staffing, versioning, and adoption work to keep producing value.
Why it matters
Well-run systems cut feature-build cost, hold cross-platform parity, and make accessibility enforceable at the component layer instead of in review. Poorly-run ones accumulate design system debt — forks, shadow systems, Figma-vs-code drift — and can become a net tax on velocity. The interesting question is rarely “do we need one?” but “what scale of system is honest for our stage?”
Scope caveat
This cluster is biased toward commercial web / SaaS / enterprise B2B contexts. Content-first sites, internal tools with a single product surface, and consumer apps with a single tight brand rarely need the full governance apparatus described here. Apply pillar-by-pillar, not as a checklist.
The pillars (summary)
The nine evaluation pillars the source article catalogues fall into three natural clusters:
Foundations — what the system is:

design-tokens — three-tier token architecture, multi-brand theming, mode switching

design-system-accessibility — shift-left accessibility, annotation toolkits, algorithmic contrast

Operations — how the system runs:

Documentation and Figma-to-code parity (folded into governance note)

Trajectory — how the system grows:

The counterargument
Worth saying plainly: for a small team with a single product and one brand, a formal design system can be premature optimization. shadcn/ui + Tailwind + a short convention doc is a “design system” too, and often the right one until the inflection points in design-system-scaling actually hit. The failure mode isn’t only “no system” — it’s also “too much system, too early.”

tech/design-tokens.title: Design Tokens — Three-Tier Architecture and Theming
tech/design-tokens.content:
Design Tokens — Three-Tier Architecture and Theming
What it is
Design tokens are platform-agnostic variables that store visual decisions — color, typography, spacing, radii, motion — as data, so the same decision can be emitted to CSS, Swift, XML, Figma variables, and JSON SDKs from one source. The mature pattern is a three-tier taxonomy that separates raw values, semantic purpose, and component usage.
Why it matters
Hardcoded hex values and pixel magic numbers are the root cause of most design-system drift. Once tokens exist as a layered hierarchy, theming (dark mode, multi-brand, high contrast) becomes a matter of swapping one layer’s mapping, not rewriting components.
The three tiers





























TierAliasRoleExampleReference (primitive)Raw paletteSemantic-free baseline values; the full palette the system could useblue.500 = #0066ccSystem (semantic)ContextualAssigns purpose; the theming layercolor.primary = blue.500ComponentHyper-specificMaps semantics to a single component propertybutton.background = color.primary
Components reference component tokens; component tokens reference system tokens; system tokens reference primitives. A dark-mode or brand swap changes the system layer — components don’t care.
Example token name paraphrased from Material Design 3: md.comp.fab.primary.container.color (component tier). (Exact token name format unverified against current M3 spec; the three-tier pattern itself is well-established across Material, Carbon, Polaris, and Spectrum.)
Naming convention — structured namespaces
Large organizations prevent token sprawl with structured names that encode namespace, category, concept, property, variant, and scale. The EightShapes and Salesforce Lightning Design System conventions are the frequently-cited reference points (original source article cited $esds-color-feedback-background-error = #B90000 as an EightShapes-style example — naming scheme pattern is widely documented; exact value unverified).
The point isn’t the exact separator (., -, /) — it’s that every token name tells you where it sits in the hierarchy without reading the definition.
Multi-brand theming
Overriding the system tier is how one codebase serves multiple brands:

IBM Carbon is the canonical example — IBM Cloud and IBM Watson share the same React/Web Component architecture but swap token dictionaries. (Deep token theming across IBM sub-brands is documented; the specific phrase “Carbon for AI” / “Carbon MCP” appeared in the source research but was not verified here — flag for follow-up if specifically needed.)
Mode switching (light / dark / forced-colors / high-contrast) works the same way: a CSS media query or JS context provider swaps the active token dictionary at the application root, and every component updates simultaneously because nothing is hardcoded.

Figma-to-code parity
Tokens are the contract between Figma and the codebase. Mature workflows:

Sync Figma Variables → JSON token dictionaries via REST API (or MCP servers) in CI
Emit per-platform outputs (CSS custom properties, Swift constants, Android XML, Compose, Kotlin) from one source — Style Dictionary and Tokens Studio are the common tools (specific tool coverage unverified against current releases)
Surface compiled production snippets inside Figma via Code Connect, so designers see what the engineer will actually ship

When this loop is broken, designers specify 16px and engineers ship var(--spacing-md)-approximate pixel values by eye — the first step toward the drift described in design-system-failure-modes.
What needs more research

Current best-practice tooling for token sync as of 2026 (Style Dictionary v4, Tokens Studio, Figma’s native variable APIs, MCP-based flows)
Whether the three-tier model is holding up or whether teams are collapsing to two tiers for small systems
Empirical data on multi-brand cost savings vs single-theme systems

Related

design-systems — hub
mature-design-systems-survey — how Material, Carbon, Polaris implement tokens
design-system-component-apis — component tokens are consumed by component APIs
design-system-failure-modes — untokenized drift is the dominant debt mechanism

Sources

Condensed from AI-drafted research brief (2026-04-20). Three-tier pattern corroborated across Material, Carbon, Polaris public documentation; specific token names and product sub-features labeled unverified inline.

tech/effective-code-review.title: Effective Code Review
tech/effective-code-review.content:
Effective Code Review
Synthesis of preliminary deep research (2026-06-05) on what makes code review effective: empirical findings, the Google eng-practices standard, author-side discipline, reviewer hierarchy, review psychology, communication conventions, and the human/machine split. Captured to feed a future code-review skill — see Implications for a code-review skill.
What review is actually for

Developers say the goal is defect detection, but only ~15% of review comments point to actual defects (Microsoft research: Bacchelli & Bird 2013; the 15% figure is usually cited from Czerwonka et al. 2015, “Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs”).
The dominant real outcomes: knowledge transfer, team awareness of changes, and alternative-solution discussion. Understanding the rationale behind a change is the hardest and most valuable part.
With CI, tests, and static analysis catching mechanical defects, human review has moved up the abstraction gradient: from code-centric (is this line correct?) to intent-centric (does this solve the right problem maintainably?). Humans are poor compilers but good architectural validators.

Cognitive limits (SmartBear/Cisco study)
Source: SmartBear’s study of a Cisco team, ~10 months / ~2,500 reviews (Cohen, Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review). Caveat: vendor research (SmartBear sells a review tool), not peer-reviewed — treat thresholds as calibrated folklore, not law. They are nonetheless the most-cited numbers in the field.






























MetricThresholdBeyond itReview size200–400 LOC per sessionDefect discovery drops sharply; ≥1,000 LOC → rubber-stampingDuration≤60 min uninterruptedAnalytical fatigue, missed edge casesVelocity<500 LOC/hourSuperficial readingDefect yield70–90% when within limitsDecays as size/speed/duration grow

Ego Effect: the expectation of review improves submitted code. Spot-checking 20–33% of changes lowered defect density across the whole codebase — a 1-in-3 chance of scrutiny is enough.
Lightweight asynchronous tool-based review found as many bugs as formal Fagan-style inspection in ~20% of the time. Heavyweight inspection meetings are empirically dead.

The standard: code health strictly improving
From Google’s eng-practices (google.github.io/eng-practices):

Senior principle: approve once the change definitely improves overall code health, even if not perfect. There is no perfect code, only better code.
Two failure modes it balances: gatekeeping perfectionism (disincentivizes incremental improvement) vs. permissive approval (death by a thousand cuts).
Only hard exception: feature appropriateness — a reviewer may reject a well-built feature they don’t want in the system.
Conflict resolution: technical facts and data overrule opinion; the style guide is absolute authority on style; anything not in it is personal preference → stay consistent with local code, else author wins. Equally-valid design alternatives → author wins. Stuck threads escalate to synchronous discussion, with the decision recorded on the change.

Author-side discipline
The review is only as good as the artifact. Author obligations:
Small, atomic changes
One logical change per CL/PR; ~100–250 lines is the commonly cited sweet spot, 400 the hard ceiling. Include tests in the same change. Splitting strategies for large work:





























StrategyMechanismStacked changesBranch the next change off the previous one while it’s in review — author never blocksFile-basedOrthogonal pieces to different domain experts in parallelHorizontalSlice by layer (API stub / data model / client)VerticalSlice by feature, full stack per micro-interactionRefactoring separationMechanical moves/renames reviewed separately from behavioral changes — never hide logic in a movement diff
Horizontal × vertical compose into a matrix: each cell is one reviewable unit.
The description is a first-class artifact
The PR description is the permanent public record of why; future readers (and AI tools) navigate history through it. Shape:

Title: imperative, stands alone (“Delete the FizzBuzz RPC and replace it with X”).
Why / context: bug, feature, or debt — the semantic frame the reviewer judges against.
How: approach taken, alternatives considered and rejected (pre-empts the reviewer re-proposing them).
Risks / trade-offs: points the reviewer’s limited attention at the vulnerable spots.
Testing instructions: how to validate manually.

The reviewer hierarchy
Evaluate top-down, broadest first — never line-by-line from the top:

Design / system integration — does the change belong here, does it couple things it shouldn’t, is it over-engineered (solving hypothetical future problems instead of today’s)?
Functionality, security, user impact — edge cases, race conditions, deadlocks (the things deterministic tests miss); injection/XSS/CSRF, input sanitization, sensitive-data handling; demo/screenshot for UI changes.
Complexity — “too complex” = a peer can’t understand it quickly, or a future modifier will likely introduce a bug. Cleverness is not a defense.
Tests — present in the same change, meaningful (not coverage theater), deterministic, fail only on real breakage. Error handling: graceful failure, useful messages, logging.
Naming, comments, docs — names communicate purpose; comments explain why, never what (a what-comment is a refactoring signal); READMEs/docs updated in tandem.

Psychology: egoless programming
Weinberg, The Psychology of Computer Programming (1971): programmers fuse identity with output, turning review into perceived personal attack. Operative commandments for review:

You are not your code — a defect is an artifact to fix, not a verdict on the author.
Mistakes are statistically certain; a found problem is the system working, not a failure.
Critique code, not people: “this function lacks a null check,” never “you forgot again”; “we” over “you”.
Respect and patience — reviews are the highest-leverage mentoring channel; include genuine praise for elegant work.

Communication: Conventional Comments
conventionalcomments.org — machine-parseable label prefix per comment: <label> [decorations]: <subject>.


















































LabelMeaningBlocking?issue:Bug/security/structural problem; pair with a suggested fixYessuggestion:Concrete improvementPer decorationquestion:Reviewer lacks context — burden on reviewer, softens critiqueUsually nonitpick:Trivial style preferenceExplicitly nothought:Architectural musing, seed for laterNochore:Process task (ticket, CI run)Process-leveltodo:Small necessary follow-upMinorpraise:Sincere positive — aim for ≥1 per review—
Decorations: (non-blocking), (blocking), (if-minor) — give the author explicit autonomy.
Anti-patterns this counters

Bikeshedding: arguing trivia while architecture rots. Counter: nits explicitly optional, or “no nits” during the core pass.
Priority inversion: days of typo rounds, then “by the way, the design is wrong — rewrite.” Counter: the hierarchy above — verdict on design first, nits only after the foundation is approved.

Speed and emergencies

Slow review compounds: context evaporates, feedback loops stretch to weeks, pressure builds to approve junk. Maximum first response: one business day; healthy teams complete multiple round-trips per day. Track time-to-review.
But never interrupt flow state to review — batch at natural breakpoints. The speed of the individual response matters more than time-to-approval: if you can’t review now, say when, suggest someone else, or approve with non-blocking comments.
Real emergencies (production-down, zero-day, rollback-avoidance, legal) reduce review to one question — does this safely fix the emergency? — with retroactive full review after. Fake emergencies (sprint deadlines, Friday deploys, “I’ve worked on it so long”) get no bypass; that bypass is a primary technical-debt vector.

Human/machine split

Deterministic layer (linters, formatters, SAST: ESLint/Prettier, SonarQube, Semgrep, Codacy): hard CI gates. Humans must never spend cycles on what these catch — formatting arguments are automation failures.
Semantic layer (LLM reviewers: CodeRabbit, Greptile, Qodo, GitLab Duo, Devlo (last one unverified)): understand context and intent, catch cross-caller logic issues, draft summaries. Non-deterministic → unusable as compliance gates; quality is capped by how much repo context they see beyond the diff (the “monorepo problem”; enterprise tools add codebase-wide retrieval).
Human layer: final architectural validation and accountability. “An AI reviewed it” is not an auditable position in regulated industries; a human owns the merge. Emerging pattern: adversarial AI review — one model writes, a different model attacks, human arbitrates both.
2026-typical pipeline: AI feedback at draft time → static gates in CI → human architectural pass.

Implications for a code-review skill
What the research says a Claude code-review skill should encode (vs. what /lean-review and built-in /code-review already do):

Altitude-ordered output — verdict on design/approach before any line-level findings; never emit nits if the design verdict is “rewrite” (priority-inversion guard).
Label taxonomy — emit findings as Conventional-Comments-style labels with explicit blocking status; issue: requires a suggested fix.
Net-improvement verdict semantics — the approve/request-changes call is “does this improve code health,” not “is this perfect”; minor items are non-blocking by default.
Size guard — flag diffs beyond ~400 changed LOC as needing decomposition and name the applicable splitting strategy, rather than pretending one pass covers them.
Don’t duplicate the machine layer — skip anything a linter/formatter/SAST gate would catch; spend tokens where automation is weak: logic edge cases, concurrency, intent-vs-implementation drift, coupling.
Description review — review the PR description as an artifact (imperative title, why, rejected alternatives, risks); a missing description is itself a finding.
Hunt where tests can’t see — race conditions, swallowed errors, invariants the suite doesn’t encode; check tests for coverage theater (connects to evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests’s hollow-tests finding).
Tone rules are cheap to encode — comment-the-code-not-the-author phrasing, ≥1 praise when warranted.

Related

evaluating-ai-code-beyond-tests — judgment layer for AI-authored code after green CI; overlaps on “what tests don’t prove”
ai-assisted-code-review — the AI-as-reviewer leg (2026-07): pipeline placement, noise economics, measurement; extends this note’s human/machine split section
ai-verification-stack-web — the tooling this note’s “deterministic layer” gates with
.claude/skills/lean-review/ — existing token-frugal diff review; the future skill would add the altitude ordering and label taxonomy above

Sources
Primary source: user-provided deep-research report (2026-06-05), AI-generated with citation trail. Key references spot-checked against prior knowledge:

Bacchelli & Bird (2013), “Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review”, ICSE — verified real; basis for the motivations-vs-outcomes finding
Czerwonka, Greiler & Tilford (2015), “Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs”, ICSE SEIP — the usual source of the ~15% figure
SmartBear/Cisco study, Cohen, Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review (2006) — vendor research, see caveat above
Google eng-practices: google.github.io/eng-practices (Standard of Code Review, What to Look For, Small CLs, CL Descriptions, Speed, Emergencies) — verified, claims match
Weinberg (1971), The Psychology of Computer Programming — verified; Ten Commandments popularized via Coding Horror
conventionalcomments.org — verified; label set matches
Tool landscape (CodeRabbit, Greptile, Qodo, GitLab Duo, Devlo, SonarQube, Semgrep) — as of 2026-06; tool claims not independently verified

tech/flutter-enterprise.title: Flutter in the Enterprise — the Shared-UI-Everywhere Lane
tech/flutter-enterprise.content:
Flutter in the Enterprise — the Shared-UI-Everywhere Lane
As of 2026-08-29. Deep dive on one lane of multiplatform-app-architecture-options: Flutter/Dart rendering one UI codebase across iOS, Android, web, and desktop. Where the React Native lane shares a runtime and the KMP lane shares a core, Flutter shares the pixels — it ships its own renderer everywhere. Sibling deep dives: react-native-expo-enterprise, rust-shared-core-enterprise, and the KMP cluster (kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise).
The architecture in one line
One Dart codebase — widgets, state, logic — compiled to native ARM on mobile and to JS/Wasm on web, drawing every frame with Flutter’s own rendering engine rather than composing platform-native views; the platform supplies a canvas and input events, Flutter supplies everything above them.
Status pins: Compose-style stability claims and the 2026 roadmap (“we intend for WebAssembly (Wasm) to become the default” on web; Impeller completion on Android; “day-zero support for Android 17 and upcoming iOS releases”) were verified 2026-08-26 in multiplatform-app-architecture-options and are reused here, not re-checked.
Shared-layer map
Same row taxonomy as the sibling deep dives, for comparability.



























































LayerShared?MechanismEnterprise caveatDesign tokensYes, within FlutterThemeData/token packages apply identically on every Flutter targetSharing tokens with anything outside Flutter (an existing React web app, native menu-bar surfaces) needs a separate token pipeline — Flutter’s consistency stops at Flutter’s edgeUI componentsYes — all targets, the whole pitchOne widget tree, Flutter’s own renderer; pixel-identical by constructionFidelity cuts both ways: perfect brand consistency, but the UI is not built from platform-native controls, so platform idiom drift is permanent and OS-level UI innovations arrive only when Flutter reimplements themScreens / navigationYesNavigator/router layer with web URL and deep-link support (mechanism-level claim; specific router capabilities unverified in this pass)Web back/forward, URL-as-state, and crawlable routes need deliberate work — the abstractions are mobile-firstPresentation / stateYesDart state management (BLoC, Riverpod, etc.) shared across all targetsSolid — same language, same runtime, no boundaryBusiness logicYes, within the appPlain Dart packagesThe Dart-island problem: the shared core is consumable only by Flutter clients. An existing React web app, a JVM backend, or a data team cannot import it — unlike a TS core (web-native) or KMP core (JVM-native). Judgment call, not a sourced claim: production consumption of compiled Dart cores from non-Dart clients is effectively unheard ofData / persistenceYesDart SQLite/ORM packages on all targets; offline/sync per axis 4 of multiplatform-app-architecture-optionsSync-engine ecosystem (PowerSync et al.) does ship Dart SDKs (unverified in this pass)API contract / clientYesOpenAPI/gRPC/GraphQL codegen to DartContract-first REST/OpenAPI remains the safe answer; a tRPC-style end-to-end-typed shortcut exists only if the backend is also Dart (Serverpod-shaped — rare in enterprises)Cross-cutting (analytics, i18n, flags, auth, testing)Mostly yesDart SDKs (Firebase ecosystem is first-class); intl for i18n; Flutter’s built-in test pyramidTesting is a documented strength — Nubank: “Flutter shined with its excellent testing capabilities that fit nicely with our mindset” (unit/integration/E2E without rendering to screen). Auth still diverges per platform (Keychain/Keystore vs browser), as in every lane
The structural headline is the inverse of the RN lane: Flutter shares the most at the top of the stack and the least beyond its own borders. Everything inside the app is one codebase; nothing inside it is reusable by systems outside Flutter. It is an all-in bet per product, not a layer you can adopt incrementally under existing clients.
Decision view for a large enterprise
Pros

Named enterprise adoption at scale, including regulated fintech. Nubank — “the largest independent digital bank outside Asia” at the time of writing — chose Flutter in 2019 after scoring Flutter, React Native, and Kotlin Native against 11 criteria (building.nubank.com, 2019-09-30). Google’s Nubank case study adds that a life-insurance product launched “in just three months — their fastest launch ever” versus a previous several-months-to-a-year cycle (flutter.dev/showcase/nubank) — a vendor-published timeline claim that deserves the same discount as the percentages below. Google’s showcase lists Google Pay, Google Classroom, NotebookLM, Toyota (infotainment), Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, SoFi, Betterment, talabat, Whirlpool (flutter.dev/showcase) — vendor-published case studies; the productivity percentages they carry (77%, 33%, 50%) are marketing figures with no visible methodology and should not be decision inputs.
True pixel consistency across every channel — the design-system enforcement problem that plagues three-codebase orgs (design-system-scaling) becomes a non-problem, because there is exactly one implementation of every component.
The maintenance surface that hurt React Native is structurally smaller. Nubank’s 2019 evaluation flagged precisely this: “React Native has more dependencies than the other alternatives. Therefore, it is much more vulnerable to maintenance and upgrading pains.” Flutter bundles its renderer and core widgets, so the framework-vs-ecosystem seam is narrower.
Testing infrastructure scored as a differentiator in Nubank’s 2019 evaluation (see layer map) — a single adopter’s assessment, now several years old, but the built-in unit/integration/E2E pyramid it describes is still the framework’s design.
Desktop and embedded come almost free — the same codebase reaches Windows/macOS/Linux and embedded targets (Toyota’s infotainment bet). Compose Multiplatform also has Stable desktop support (multiplatform-app-architecture-options, axis 1b), so the unique part of this reach is embedded plus the single-codebase web/desktop combination, not desktop alone. (Desktop maintenance vigor is contested — see the Flock item below.)

Cons

The Dart-island problem is the enterprise-architecture con. Choosing Flutter means the business logic layer is written in a language that nothing else in the org can consume, and the org must hire/train for a language with no other use. The talent-portability argument that carries the RN lane (web engineers contributing to mobile) and the KMP lane (Android/JVM engineers) has no Flutter equivalent — Dart proficiency is Flutter proficiency. (Authored judgment; hiring-pool statistics in circulation are untraceable and deliberately omitted.)
Web is the weakest channel, and the accessibility posture is disqualifying-by-default for some orgs. Flutter web renders to canvas and exposes meaning through a translated semantics DOM — but “For performance reasons, Flutter’s web accessibility is not on by default. To turn on accessibility, the user needs to press an invisible button” (or the developer calls ensureSemantics() at startup) (docs.flutter.dev web accessibility). A public-sector or EU-accessibility-directive org must budget for enabling and auditing this path, and the canvas approach shares the concern family documented for Compose Web in kmp-web-accessibility — though Flutter’s semantics layer is more mature than Compose’s; the two are not equivalent. SEO follows the same logic: no crawlable content DOM by default, so document-centric public web is the wrong fit.
Single-vendor governance risk is live, not theoretical. In October 2024 a former Flutter team member forked Flutter as “Flock,” citing a ~50-person Google team serving a massive user base, 2023 headcount freeze, 2024 layoffs, stagnant desktop targets, and slow triage (devclass, 2024-10-30). The counter-signal: Google’s 2026 roadmap makes concrete forward commitments (Wasm-default web, day-zero OS support — verified in multiplatform-app-architecture-options), and Google’s own products (Google Pay, NotebookLM, Classroom) are showcase-listed on it. Both signals are real; a risk register should hold them together. No public Google response to Flock was found in this pass (absence-claim, unverified).
Platform idiom is permanently emulated. OS design-language updates (new iOS visual styles, Android dynamic theming) arrive on Flutter’s schedule, not the OS’s. For a consumer brand that wants to feel native-of-the-platform, this is a standing cost the RN lane (real native views) and KMP lane (fully native UI) don’t pay.
No OTA-update lever. Compiled Dart is store-gated like native; the RN lane’s EAS-Update delivery advantage (axis 5 of multiplatform-app-architecture-options) has no supported Flutter equivalent. (Third-party Flutter code-push products exist but were not evaluated in this pass.)
Nubank’s own caveats apply to brownfield adoption: integrating Flutter into existing native apps required build-pipeline changes, platform channels, and four-way routing interop (React Native, Flutter, Kotlin, Swift coexisting) — and they kept native developers for GPS, camera, and watch surfaces.

Question marks (genuinely open — and what would resolve each)

Does Wasm-default web materially close the web gap? Resolves when: the roadmap’s Wasm-default intent ships as stable default and a named enterprise reports a public-facing Flutter web property meeting WCAG AA and acceptable Core Web Vitals.
Is Flock a pressure valve or a fragmentation risk? Resolves when: either Flock demonstrates sustained divergence with meaningful adoption, or it quietly re-merges/stalls. Secondary 2025 coverage describes it as pressure-valve-shaped; treat as (unverified).
Is there any named large-enterprise Flutter walk-away? None surfaced in this pass — the discourse risk is governance (Flock, layoffs), not documented abandonment. Same absence-of-evidence caveat as the other lanes: absence of postmortems is unknown, not safety.

Verdict
Flutter is the right call when ALL of these hold:

The product’s brand consistency across channels matters more than per-platform idiom — one pixel-identical UI is a feature, not a compromise.
Web is app-shaped (dashboard, tool, companion) rather than document/SEO-shaped — and the org will budget the accessibility-enablement work if the audience requires it.
The org accepts an all-in, Flutter-only stack: no incremental layer adoption, no sharing the core with non-Flutter clients, hiring for Dart as a dedicated skill.
Google-single-vendor risk (with the Flock/layoffs signal on the register) is acceptable.
Mobile-pair + desktop/embedded reach is valuable — this is the lane’s unique surface coverage.

It is the wrong call when: an existing React web app or JVM backend is supposed to consume the shared logic (the Dart island blocks it — use the TS monorepo or KMP lanes); the public web is a primary, content-heavy channel; or platform-native feel is the product bar.
What we couldn’t establish

Any named enterprise Flutter walk-away or abandonment postmortem.
Independent verification of any showcase productivity/cost figure — all are vendor-published.
Current default web renderer and Wasm rollout status beyond the roadmap-intent quote (the renderer docs page fetched does not state the default).
Dart hiring-pool size from a traceable source.

Related

multiplatform-app-architecture-options — the option space this note deep-dives one lane of (axis 1b/1c)
react-native-expo-enterprise · rust-shared-core-enterprise — sibling deep dives
kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise — the shared-core rival; Nubank’s 2019 bake-off scored “Kotlin Native” third
kmp-web-accessibility — canvas-rendering accessibility analysis; Flutter web is the adjacent, partially-mitigated case
design-system-scaling — the problem Flutter’s single-widget-tree dissolves

Sources

Nubank, “Why we think Flutter will help us scale mobile development” (2019-09-30): building.nubank.com/why-we-think-flutter-will-help-us-scale-mobile-development-at-nubank/
Flutter showcase (vendor case studies): flutter.dev/showcase
Flutter showcase, Nubank case study (vendor-published): flutter.dev/showcase/nubank
Flutter web accessibility docs: docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility
devclass, “Flutter forked as Flock” (2024-10-30): devclass.com/2024/10/30/flutter-forked-as-flock-developer-cites-company-wide-issues-at-google/

tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence.title: KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
tech/kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence.content:
KMP Enterprise Adoption Evidence — Web-Target & Finance
Case-study evidence for the “shared Kotlin core, web-native UI” architecture: who runs KMP at scale, who uses the web target specifically in production, and what walk-away stories exist. Companion to kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise, kmp-js-interop-boundary, and kmp-web-accessibility.
As of 2026-06. Adoption status is time-sensitive; re-verify before citing.
Headline: scaled adopters are overwhelmingly mobile-only
JetBrains’ own case-study aggregation lists dozens of named adopters (70+ as of 2026-06), but only a handful — Quizlet, Memrise, Mirego, Cash App — involve a web target at all; the large majority are mobile-only Android+iOS, sharing business logic / networking / persistence / presentation while keeping native UI (kotlinlang.org/case-studies). This confirms the research premise: production web-target use is the rare exception, not the norm. (Correction to one common listing: Posten Bring on this page is mobile apps with unified frontend/backend logic, not specifically a web target.)
The two strongest web-target production references
Quizlet — closest match to the evaluated pattern
Migrated shared code from JavaScript to KMP in early 2019; runs in production at 50M+ monthly active users, compiling shared Kotlin business logic (state machines / rule engines — grading, learning analytics) to JS for web clients (ankushg.com, authored by Quizlet engineer Ankush Gupta). Quizlet’s setup is the cleanest public match to a logic-only shared core with native/web UI on top.
Two load-bearing caveats:

The migration ran the inverse direction from this enterprise’s framing: web was the original home (JS core), and Kotlin was adopted to serve mobile with type safety and avoid the marshaling cost of consuming a JS core natively. It is not a “Kotlin core pushed out to web” story.
As of 2019, their own engineer flagged “not having TypeScript definitions for JS clients” as a limitation. Public Quizlet writeups give little detail on web-side day-2 friction.

Cash App / Block — Kotlin/JS at a major fintech, but a different consumption model
Cash App/Block has run KMP in production since 2018 (per the JetBrains case-studies page), sharing logic/networking/persistence across Android and iOS; the feature-flagged-rollout-with-Touchlab detail is (unverified). From 2021 it also uses Kotlin/JavaScript for shared presentation logic across clients including web (code.cash.app). But this goes through their Zipline/Redwood stack — Redwood renders to each platform’s native UI toolkit and the JS is consumed by Cash App’s own Kotlin/Compose host, not a generic React/TS frontend (cashapp/redwood). So Cash App’s Kotlin/JS use validates “Kotlin/JS in production at a major fintech” but is a different consumption model than React-consumes-Kotlin-core-via-TS-bindings.
Mobile fintech KMP at scale is real (but mobile-only)

Cash App / Block — KMP in production since 2018.
Bitkey by Block (open-source Bitcoin wallet) — shares ~95% of its mobile codebase via KMP/Compose Multiplatform. (not-checked in the dossier — treat as (unverified).)
Worldline’s Eroski app — 99% crash-free at ~800K users. (not-checked — (unverified).)

Financial-services Kotlin at scale is on the BACKEND, not shared-core-to-web
ING (payment engine, ~6M mobile users, 4.5B payments/year), N26, Worldline, Kakao Pay (server-side Spring), Memo Bank, and Flux are cited as server-side Kotlin or mobile/backend apps — not KMP web clients (kotlinlang.org/case-studies). Nuance: ING is a payment engine plus a mobile banking app, so “backend/server-side” is a slight simplification — but the load-bearing point holds: FS Kotlin at scale is not shared-core-to-web.
Maturity caveat (load-bearing)
JetBrains’ May 2025 “Present and Future of Kotlin for Web” states the current JS-export path uses the experimental @JsExport annotation “which has constraints that make it challenging to use in enterprise applications,” with seamless interop and stabilized @JsExport still on the roadmap with no firm date (JetBrains, 2025-05). Independent analysis (kt.academy, Kotlin 1.8.21) catalogs concrete friction: List and Long non-exportable, Flow/StateFlow need hand-written wrappers, union types inexpressible, TS definitions largely manual. For the CORE-sharing approach this interop friction is the central risk surface — detail in kmp-js-interop-boundary.
Walk-away / decline evidence
Walk-away evidence is thin and mostly opinion, not named-company case reports:

Donn Felker’s “Why KMP Won’t Succeed” (Nov 2023) argues talent-scarcity and platform-convention mismatch and is explicitly skeptical of web targeting, but names no abandoning company — opinion, not a documented walk-away (donnfelker.com, not-checked — (unverified)).
JetBrains discontinuing KMP support in Fleet (consolidating on IntelliJ/Android Studio) is a tooling-direction signal to track, not an adopter walking away.
A 1-year KMP production retrospective (Jan 2024) reports domain/networking/db sharing worked but flags CI/CD complexity, expect/actual workarounds for third-party SDKs (Firebase), and shared-code testing gaps — and does not use the web target (dev.to/rafalgawlik, not-checked — (unverified)).

Release-train coupling (day-2 friction)
The recurring multi-repo complaint: every shared-core change forces a release-and-consume cycle, leaving consumers “catching up” on new core versions; teams commonly move to a monorepo so core and consumers version together (which couples release cadence). The single cited primary source (Xapo Labs) supports the specific dynamic: multi-repo required “3 PRs for each multiplatform adjustment,” with the KMM PR needing to merge before iOS CI could run (Xapo Labs, 2024). But the generalization to a “common/recurring industry pattern” is unverified from one anecdote. An STRV retrospective separately reports cross-boundary stack traces became harder to read and rebuild times grew when shared code changed (iOS-centric, no web specifics; not-checked — (unverified)).
What we couldn’t establish

No named team that adopted KMP’s WEB target (Kotlin/JS or Wasm) in production and later removed it — that specific web-target walk-away story does not appear to be publicly recorded.
No named financial-services company shipping a Kotlin shared core consumed by a web-native JS/TS frontend in production — FS KMP evidence is either mobile-only or backend server-side Kotlin.
Team-size / codebase-size figures for the web-target success cases (Quizlet, Cash App web) beyond MAU/install counts — not established.
Quantitative production data (bundle size, runtime perf, latency) for Kotlin/JS shared cores consumed by React/TS at enterprise scale — not found.
Cash App’s exact extent of web sharing, and whether any non-Redwood (plain React/TS) consumption exists in production — not establishable from the sources fetched.
Whether Quizlet’s web client today consumes the Kotlin core via Kotlin/JS bindings or a different bridge — not confirmed.

Sources

Quizlet shared-code writeup (Ankush Gupta): ankushg.com/posts/shared-code-kotlin-multiplatform/
Cash App, Kotlin Multiplatform summer: code.cash.app/kotlin-multiplatform-summer
cashapp/redwood: github.com/cashapp/redwood
JetBrains, “Present and Future of Kotlin for Web” (2025-05): blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/05/present-and-future-kotlin-for-web/
kt.academy, JS interop (Kotlin 1.8.21): kt.academy/article/ak-js-interop
Donn Felker, “Why KMP Won’t Succeed” (2023-11): www.donnfelker.com/why-kotlin-multiplatform-wont-succeed/
Xapo Labs monorepo journey (2024): medium.com/xapolabs/unifying-our-workflow-the-journey-to-monorepo-with-kotlin-multiplatform-mobile-a3231a266918
KMP-in-production 1-year retrospective (dev.to): dev.to/rafalgawlik/kotlin-multiplatform-in-production-1-year-later-55po

tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary.title: The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
tech/kmp-js-interop-boundary.content:
The Kotlin → JS / Wasm / React Interop Boundary
What crosses cleanly from a shared Kotlin core to a web-native React/TypeScript consumer, what doesn’t, and how the library is packaged and debugged. Companion to kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise and kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence. For the Compose-renders-the-UI alternative and its accessibility ceiling, see kmp-web-accessibility.
As of 2026-06 (packaging, bundle-size, bundler-consumption, and Wasm sections locally verified 2026-07-06 against Kotlin 2.3.20). This boundary moves fast — @JsExport is experimental and several limitations were only addressed in late-2025 Kotlin releases. Re-verify version-pinned facts before relying on them.
Target choice: Kotlin/JS, not Kotlin/Wasm
For a logic-only core handed to a JS frontend, JetBrains recommends Kotlin/JS: it “is the better fit because it provides a better interop experience” (JetBrains, 2025-05). Kotlin/Wasm’s strengths are near-native compute, faster UI rendering, and smaller binaries — all UI/compute-oriented, and largely irrelevant when you only ship a library that must hand rich typed objects across the boundary.
Stability (as of 2026-06):

Kotlin/JS web target — Stable; Kotlin/Wasm (wasmJs) web target — Beta, in the KMP supported-platforms table (kotlinlang.org).
Kotlin/Wasm’s wasm-js target reached Beta with Kotlin 2.2.20 (Sept 2025); Kotlin/Wasm overall is Beta with Stable expected late 2026 (InfoWorld, 2025-09; the “Stable late 2026” date is not in that source but is not contradicted). WasmGC reportedly reached all major browsers including Safari in late 2024 (the Safari 18.2 / Dec 2024 specifics are (unverified) — no source was fetched for this sentence).

The @JsExport mechanism — experimental, top-level only
The current JS-export path is built on the experimental @JsExport annotation. JetBrains acknowledges its constraints “make it challenging to use in enterprise applications” (verbatim, JetBrains 2025-05). JetBrains is working to let the “majority of Kotlin declarations” be exported and to stabilize the annotation — not yet done.

 Note: the dossier attributed stabilization to ticket KT-80310, but that ticket number could not be confirmed against the cited blog or YouTrack — (unverified), treat the ticket number as unconfirmed even though the stabilization plan is confirmed.

What crosses cleanly on Kotlin/JS
Per the official js-to-kotlin-interop doc (as of 2026-06, kotlinlang.org) and Touchlab’s guides:

Exports reasonably: data classes, regular classes, objects, nullability, enums (since 1.6.20), interfaces (since 1.6.20).
Anything not marked @JsExport is not supported across the boundary.

What does NOT cross cleanly (per-API friction)
Confirmed against the official doc and Touchlab’s dev.to @JsExport guide:

Collections. List/MutableList/Map/Set are not exported as native JS arrays/objects — they surface as KtList/KtMutableList/KtMap/KtSet views needing conversion methods (asJsReadonlyArrayView/asJsArrayView). Must be flattened to Array / plain JS objects for a clean TS consumer.
Long. Non-exportable with no JS equivalent; breaks TS typing unless skipLibCheck = true. Exporting as BigInt requires experimental compiler flags -Xes-long-as-bigint and the language feature +JsAllowLongInExportedDeclarations (-XXLanguage:+JsAllowLongInExportedDeclarations). Kotlin 2.3.0 added experimental BigInt/BigInt64Array representation.
Unsigned integer types. Explicitly not supported.
Suspend functions. Only experimentally exportable since Kotlin 2.3.0 behind -Xenable-suspend-function-exporting (consumed as JS async functions). Before that, manual Promise wrapping via GlobalScope.promise was required.
Flow / StateFlow. No clean export; require hand-written wrappers (FlowObserver/StateFlowObserver-style), per kt.academy (Kotlin 1.8.21 reference). No clean export path was confirmed from a primary source for the callbackFlow→callbacks/Observables pattern.
Sealed-class hierarchies. Export buggily — data/regular-class subclasses export, but object subclasses are invisible.
Default parameters. Not preserved across the boundary (not confirmed by an authoritative source for either target — treat as (unverified)).
Name mangling. The compiler mangles names (e.g. hello_sv8swh_k$) unless @JsName is used.
TypeScript union types cannot be expressed in Kotlin (kt.academy, 1.8.21).

Net effect: the shared-core team must design a DTO-flattened, annotation-disciplined facade — not expose the rich idiomatic domain model. That facade is the public API the web team consumes, and it is the contract that needs semver and .d.ts-diff review.
Late-2025 / 2026 improvements (Kotlin 2.3.x)
Confirmed against whatsnew23. Kotlin 2.3.0 (released 2025-12-16) added:

Experimental @JsExport of suspend functions (-Xenable-suspend-function-exporting)
LongArray as BigInt64Array (under -Xes-long-as-bigint)
Unified companion-object access across all module systems
@JsStatic in interfaces
@JsExport.Default

Kotlin 2.3.20 (released ~2026-03) added the ability to implement Kotlin interfaces from TypeScript and experimental SWC compilation support.
Several of these remain Experimental behind flags. The broad shape of the friction persists.
Wasm boundary is more restrictive
If Kotlin/Wasm is chosen anyway: only primitives, strings, function types, JsAny subtypes, and opaque JsReference<T> handles may cross — arbitrary Kotlin classes/objects/collections cannot (Touchlab, 2024-03; kotlinlang wasm-js-interop). A Kotlin object reaches JS as e.g. fun createUser(...): JsReference<User> — awkward for a React/TS consumer wanting real typed objects.
Locally verified 2026-07-06 (Kotlin 2.3.20, same spike, wasmJs { binaries.library(); generateTypeScriptDefinitions() }):

The restriction has NOT loosened. @JsExport on a class is a hard compile error on wasmJs: “This annotation is not applicable to target ‘class’. Applicable targets: function” (verbatim). The JS-target facade cannot be reused; the Wasm facade is top-level functions only.
What works, at runtime too (Node 22 / V8 WasmGC): primitives and String cross; function types cross with real TS signatures (onNext: (p0: string) => void, unsubscribe as () => void); JsReference<Account> round-trips correctly but surfaces as unknown in the generated .d.mts — the TS consumer loses all type information for handles. Long→String flattening stays exact (2^53 + 1 verified end-to-end).
TS-declaration generation and npm packaging work on wasmJs despite the Experimental label: .d.mts, ESM glue (auto-detects browser/Node/Deno/standalone VMs), and package.json with main/types wired, at build/dist/wasmJs/productionLibrary.
Warts hit in one afternoon: the ExperimentalWasmDsl opt-in moved to org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle (old FQN is an error, removal scheduled 2.4); an incremental-compilation internal compiler error after adding an export to an existing build (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in WasmIrFileMetadata.fromByteArray) — a clean build fixes it; and the JS-side per-file granularity property breaks the wasmJs compile in the same module (“Per-file compilation can’t be used with any moduleKind except es”) — the JS tree-shaking recipe above conflicts with a co-hosted wasmJs target.

Measured Wasm bundle size (resolves the open question, one datapoint)
Production library distribution (binaryen-optimized), total = .wasm + JS glue:




















Facade reachable graph.wasm (raw / gzip)Total incl. glue (raw / gzip)logic only (DTO validation, JsReference, Map/Long/String ops)10.2 KB / 5.3 KB18.3 KB / 8.4 KB+ Flow/coroutines machinery56.0 KB / 21.9 KB65.6 KB / 25.4 KB
Two structural differences from the JS target:

DCE is automatic and whole-program. The logic-only build contains zero coroutines symbols even though commonMain depends on kotlinx-coroutines — unused domain surface just vanishes at link time, no sideEffects hand-assertion, no granularity recipe. This automatic whole-program DCE is the opposite of the Kotlin/JS default, where everything in the module graph ships.
Size verdict flips by workload. Logic-only: Wasm total (~8 KB gzip) is ~3× smaller than the JS target’s minified floor (~25–28 KB gzip). With coroutines reachable: rough gzip parity (~25 KB both). The old “Kotlin/JS larger bundles, Kotlin/Wasm smaller binaries” folklore is directionally right for lean cores, but the JS glue (~3 KB gzip) and coroutines dominate the difference.

Caveats: one local datapoint, tiny facade, library-mode distribution; browser WasmGC support and streaming-instantiation behavior not re-tested here. Interop friction (no classes, unknown handles) still makes Kotlin/JS the JetBrains-recommended and practically saner target for a rich typed facade — the size win only matters if the exported surface is genuinely function-shaped.
Packaging / build / npm
Locally verified 2026-07-06 (Kotlin 2.3.20, Gradle 8.14.5, JDK 21 — spike built from kmp-jsexport-facade-example): configure js { binaries.library(); generateTypeScriptDefinitions() } (the IR argument is no longer needed; IR is the only compiler). The jsBrowserProductionLibraryDistribution task is real and emits per-module .js files (facade + kotlin stdlib + each kotlinx dependency), .js.map source maps, one .d.ts, and a package.json with main/types wired — at build/dist/js/productionLibrary, not the build/productionLibrary in older Touchlab docs. npm install <path> and a strict-mode tsc typecheck against the emitted .d.ts both worked. The build also runs a jsProductionLibraryValidateGeneratedByCompilerTypeScript validation task.
Two consumer-relevant surprises from the same spike, both UMD-specific (see the ESM section below for the fix):

Output is UMD, not ESM, by default for a browser library. useEsModules() in the js target DSL switches the distribution to .mjs + .d.mts with real import/export statements and main/types re-pointed accordingly (verified 2026-07-06).
Under UMD, the Kotlin package becomes a nested TS namespace. A facade in package core.facade produces export declare namespace core.facade { ... }, so the consumer writes import { core } from '<lib>' and reaches types as core.facade.Money. Under ESM the nesting disappears: the .d.mts emits flat root-level named exports (export declare class Money) even from a nested Kotlin package, so consumers get the idiomatic import { Money } from '<lib>' (verified 2026-07-06).

ESM + bundler consumption and tree-shaking (measured 2026-07-06, both bundlers)
Same spike, useEsModules(), consumed by a Vite 7.3.6 production build (Rollup + esbuild-minify) and a webpack 5.108.4 production build (terser); typechecked strict with moduleResolution: bundler. Both bundlers consumed the library with zero configuration. Measured bundle sizes:















































Library configConsumer importsVite (raw / gzip)webpack (raw / gzip)per-module ESM (default)full facade (Promise + Flow paths)90.8 KB / 28.1 KB85.5 KB / 25.4 KBper-module ESMone DTO only90.2 KB / 27.9 KB85.1 KB / 25.2 KBper-module ESM + hand-added sideEffects: falseone DTO onlybyte-identicalbyte-identicalper-file granularity (kotlin.js.ir.output.granularity=per-file, 123 modules), no flagone DTO only93.7 KB / 27.6 KB—per-file + sideEffects: false togetherone DTO only2.1 KB / 0.98 KB1.6 KB / 0.77 KBper-file + sideEffects: false togetherfull facade—92.6 KB / 26.7 KB
Conclusions (item 2 corrects the first pass of this section, which tested the levers only one at a time and wrongly concluded no lever works):

Minification, not tree-shaking, sets the default cost. The ~278 KB of unminified per-module .mjs collapses to ~85–90 KB raw / ~25–28 KB gzip once either bundler minifies it — the honest consumer-side floor for stdlib + coroutines is ~25–28 KB gzip, not the raw-dist ~50 KB in the table below.
Tree-shaking is zero by default but fully recoverable — the levers only work in combination. Each lever alone does nothing: at per-module granularity the whole facade plus its imports is one module, so sideEffects: false has nothing separate to prune (byte-identical in both bundlers); per-file granularity alone still ships everything because each generated file runs initMetadataFor* calls at module scope that bundlers must assume are side effects. Per-file granularity + a hand-added sideEffects: false prunes almost everything in both bundlers: the one-DTO consumer drops from ~85–90 KB to ~2 KB raw / <1 KB gzip, with all coroutines machinery gone.
The recipe has real costs, which is why the default conclusion still stands for most teams: (a) sideEffects: false is a hand-made post-build assertion Gradle doesn’t emit — it declares every Kotlin module initializer droppable. That assertion held at runtime for this facade (full flow re-run and correct under the aggressive config) but is not a general guarantee for code relying on module-init registration; (b) per-file mode ships a dangling types path (package.json points to a root .d.mts that per-file mode doesn’t emit — declarations land per-file, e.g. <module>/core/facade/Facade.export.d.mts), so the post-build step must also fix that; (c) full-facade consumers pay a per-file wrapper overhead (~8% raw vs per-module).
So: bundle cost is set by the library’s dependency graph — unless you adopt the per-file + sideEffects recipe, in which case it’s set by what consumers import. For a facade whose web consumers use only a slice (DTO validation, a rule engine), the recipe is worth the post-build packaging step; for full-surface consumers, stick with the default per-module granularity.

Bundler note: webpack ran ~6% smaller raw / ~10% smaller gzip than Vite on identical inputs (terser vs esbuild-minify) — a minifier difference, not a KMP finding.
Measured bundle size (resolves the open question, one datapoint)
For the minimal logic-only facade library above (a handful of DTOs, one suspend fn, one Flow bridge), the production library distribution measured:



































ModuleRawGzipfacade module itself18.8 KB3.8 KBkotlin-kotlin-stdlib.js162.9 KB27.4 KBkotlinx-coroutines-core.js109.5 KB18.4 KBkotlinx-atomicfu.js + dom-api-compat4.7 KB1.4 KBTotal≈296 KB≈51 KB
So the stdlib floor is ~163 KB raw / ~27 KB gzipped, and using coroutines/Flow across the boundary adds another ~110 KB / ~18 KB. Caveats: this is binaries.library() per-module output measured locally for a tiny facade (Kotlin 2.3.20) — one datapoint, not a benchmark; consumer-side bundler DCE on the UMD output was not measured.
Debugging
Source maps ship (.js.map, auto-generated since Kotlin 1.3.60), so web devs debug minified Kotlin-origin JS that maps back to Kotlin sources — workable but unfamiliar.
What we couldn’t establish

No concrete KB/MB measurement of Kotlin stdlib overhead in JS or Wasm library output — resolved 2026-07-06 by local measurement for both targets (JS: Packaging section, ~163 KB raw / ~27 KB gzip stdlib floor, ~25–28 KB gzip after bundler minification; Wasm: its own section, 8.4 KB gzip logic-only / 25.4 KB gzip with coroutines, glue included). No independent published benchmark was found. The load-time/UI-speed half of the reported JS-vs-Wasm tradeoff remains (unverified): ~0.25–0.5s faster initial JS load; ~3× faster Wasm UI (kmpship.app).
Vite and webpack consumption, tree-shaking, and dead-code-elimination behavior — resolved 2026-07-06 by local measurement, both bundlers (see the ESM/bundler section): both consume the useEsModules() output cleanly with zero config; minification cuts the bundle to ~25–28 KB gzip; tree-shaking is zero by default but recoverable via per-file granularity + hand-added sideEffects: false (one-DTO consumer: <1 KB gzip), with the caveats listed there.
Browser devtools debugging quality with the generated source maps (stepping into Kotlin, variable inspection) — asserted via .js.map, not independently evaluated.
Whether the Wasm interop restriction loosened by 2026 — resolved 2026-07-06: it has not. Exporting a class on wasmJs is still a hard compile error in Kotlin 2.3.20 (see the Wasm section for the verbatim error and what does cross).
Default-parameter handling — not confirmed by an authoritative source.
A clean Flow-to-JS export path — none confirmed.

Sources

JetBrains, “Present and Future of Kotlin for Web” (2025-05): blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/05/present-and-future-kotlin-for-web/
Kotlin/JS to JS interop: kotlinlang.org/docs/js-to-kotlin-interop.html
Kotlin/Wasm JS interop: kotlinlang.org/docs/wasm-js-interop.html
KMP supported platforms: kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/supported-platforms.html
What’s new in Kotlin 2.3.0: kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew23.html
InfoWorld, Kotlin 2.2.20 / WebAssembly (2025-09): www.infoworld.com/article/4056077/kotlin-2-2-20-boosts-webassembly-support.html
Touchlab, Kotlin/Wasm JS interop (2024-03): touchlab.co/kotlin-wasm-js-interop
Touchlab, @JsExport guide (dev.to): dev.to/touchlab/jsexport-guide-for-exposing-kotlin-to-js-20l9
Touchlab, distributing Kotlin/JS libraries (dev.to): dev.to/touchlab/different-ways-to-distribute-and-integrate-kotlinjs-library-1hg3
