tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-example.title: Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
tech/kmp-jsexport-facade-example.content:
Worked Example — The DTO-Flattened @JsExport Facade
The code companion to kmp-js-interop-boundary. That note ends on a design
consequence: you don’t expose idiomatic Kotlin to the web team — you build a
deliberately designed, DTO-flattened, annotation-disciplined facade, and
that facade is the public API the React/TS app consumes. This note shows what
that actually looks like in code.

Compile- and runtime-verified 2026-07-06 with Kotlin 2.3.20 / Gradle
8.14.5 / JDK 21: this facade was built as a real Kotlin/JS library
(binaries.library() + generateTypeScriptDefinitions()), published to a
local npm consumer, typechecked under strict TS, and exercised at runtime
(Promise, Flow bridge, precision round-trip). Corrections the build demanded
are folded in below and listed in §5. Flag names and stability remain
time-sensitive — re-check against kmp-js-interop-boundary. As of 2026-07.

The shape of the problem
Two layers, one boundary:
┌─ commonMain (idiomatic Kotlin) ─────────┐
│  rich domain model: sealed classes,     │   ← internal, NOT exported
│  List/Map, Long, Flow, suspend fns      │
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
               │  mapping / flattening
┌──────────────▼─── jsMain (the facade) ──┐
│  @JsExport DTOs: Array, Double/String,   │   ← the public API surface
│  Promise, observer callbacks, @JsName    │      .d.ts is the contract
└──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
               │  npm package (.js + .d.ts)
┌──────────────▼─── React / TypeScript ────┐
│  import { ... } from '@org/core'         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. The idiomatic core — what you do NOT export
This is normal, rich Kotlin. It lives in commonMain, serves the native
Android/iOS clients directly, and is never annotated with @JsExport.
// commonMain — idiomatic domain model. Internal to the shared core.
 
data class Money(val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String)   // Long: no JS equivalent
 
sealed interface PaymentResult {                                 // sealed: object subclasses
    data class Approved(val txId: String, val settled: Money) : PaymentResult
    data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : PaymentResult
    object Pending : PaymentResult                               // ← object subclass: invisible to JS
}
 
enum class DeclineReason { INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, FRAUD_SUSPECTED, EXPIRED_CARD }
 
class Account(
    val id: String,
    val balances: Map<String, Money>,                            // Map: surfaces as KtMap, not a JS object
    val recentTransactions: List<Transaction>,                   // List: surfaces as KtList, not an Array
) {
    suspend fun authorize(amount: Money): PaymentResult = /* ... */   // suspend: needs Promise/async
    fun balanceUpdates(): Flow<Money> = /* ... */                     // Flow: no clean export
}
Every line here has at least one feature from the “does NOT cross cleanly” list
in kmp-js-interop-boundary: Long, Map/List, a sealed hierarchy with
an object case, a suspend function, and a Flow. Hand this to @JsExport
as-is and you get name-mangled symbols, KtMap/KtList views the TS team must
convert by hand, an invisible Pending case, and broken Long typing.
2. The facade — flattened, annotated, the actual public API
This lives in jsMain. It is the only thing marked @JsExport. Every
boundary-hostile type is converted to something a TS consumer reads as native.
// jsMain — the export facade. THIS is the published API surface.
// Both opt-ins are required (warning-level in 2.3.20): @JsExport is still
// experimental, and GlobalScope.promise is a "delicate" coroutines API.
@file:OptIn(ExperimentalJsExport::class, DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)
 
@JsExport
@JsName("Money")                                    // @JsName: defeat compiler name-mangling
data class MoneyDto(
    val amountMinor: String,                         // 64-bit Long flattened to String, NOT Double.
    val currency: String,                            // JS Double is exact only to 53 bits — see Security.
)
 
// Sealed hierarchy flattened to a tagged DTO — the discriminated-union shape
// TS already understands. The 'object' case (Pending) survives because it is
// now just a tag value, not an invisible object subclass.
@JsExport
@JsName("PaymentResult")
data class PaymentResultDto(
    val status: String,                              // "approved" | "declined" | "pending"
    val txId: String?,                               // present iff approved
    val settled: MoneyDto?,                           // present iff approved
    val declineReason: String?,                       // present iff declined
)
 
@JsExport
@JsName("Account")
class AccountFacade internal constructor(private val account: Account) {
 
    val id: String get() = account.id
 
    // Map -> plain exportable Array of entries. No KtMap leaking across.
    val balances: Array<BalanceEntryDto>
        get() = account.balances.entries
            .map { BalanceEntryDto(it.key, it.value.toDto()) }
            .toTypedArray()                          // List -> Array at the boundary
 
    // suspend -> Promise. Consumed as a normal async function in TS.
    // Requires GlobalScope.promise (kotlinx-coroutines) or the experimental
    // -Xenable-suspend-function-exporting path (Kotlin 2.3.0+).
    fun authorize(amount: MoneyDto): Promise<PaymentResultDto> =
        GlobalScope.promise { account.authorize(amount.toDomain()).toDto() }
 
    // Flow -> hand-written observer wrapper returning an unsubscribe handle.
    // There is no clean Flow export; this callback bridge is the idiom.
    fun observeBalance(onNext: (MoneyDto) -> Unit): () -> Unit {
        val job = account.balanceUpdates()
            .onEach { onNext(it.toDto()) }
            .launchIn(GlobalScope)
        return { job.cancel() }                      // call to unsubscribe
    }
}
 
@JsExport
@JsName("BalanceEntry")
data class BalanceEntryDto(val currency: String, val money: MoneyDto)
 
// --- mapping functions: the only place domain <-> DTO conversion lives ---
 
// String<->Long, NOT Double math — no precision loss on 64-bit values.
private fun Money.toDto() = MoneyDto(amountMinor = amountMinor.toString(), currency = currency)
private fun MoneyDto.toDomain() = Money(amountMinor = amountMinor.toLong(), currency = currency)
 
private fun PaymentResult.toDto(): PaymentResultDto = when (this) {
    is PaymentResult.Approved -> PaymentResultDto("approved", txId, settled.toDto(), null)
    is PaymentResult.Declined -> PaymentResultDto("declined", null, null, reason.name)
    PaymentResult.Pending     -> PaymentResultDto("pending", null, null, null)
}
The when on the sealed interface is exhaustive — if someone adds a new
PaymentResult case in the core, the facade fails to compile until the mapping
is updated. That compile error is the feature: it forces the boundary
contract to stay in sync with the domain instead of silently dropping a case.
3. What the web team actually consumes
Gradle’s generateTypeScriptDefinitions() emits a .d.ts from the facade. The
React/TS app imports it as an ordinary npm dependency — but the import shape
depends on the module format (both verified 2026-07-06):

Default (UMD): the Kotlin package becomes a nested TS namespace — a
facade in package core.facade emits export declare namespace core.facade,
and the consumer reaches types as core.facade.Money.
With useEsModules() (recommended for Vite/modern bundlers): the
distribution becomes .mjs + .d.mts with flat root-level named exports
even from a nested Kotlin package — idiomatic import { Money } from ...,
as below. Vite consumes it with zero config; bundle economics are in
kmp-js-interop-boundary. Short version: ~28 KB gzip floor after
minification, and tree-shaking across the boundary is effectively zero, so
the facade’s dependency graph — not the consumer’s import list — sets the
cost.

import { Account, Money } from '@org/core';  // ESM output: flat named exports
 
async function pay(account: Account, amount: Money) {
  const result = await account.authorize(amount);                    // Promise -> await
  switch (result.status) {                                            // tagged union, all cases visible
    case 'approved': return showReceipt(result.txId!, result.settled!);
    case 'declined': return showDecline(result.declineReason!);
    case 'pending':  return showPending();                            // Pending survived the flatten
  }
}
 
// Flow bridge consumed as subscribe/unsubscribe:
const unsubscribe = account.observeBalance(m => updateUi(m));
// later: unsubscribe();
// Footgun (observed at runtime): launchIn dispatches asynchronously, so
// subscribing and unsubscribing in the same tick silently drops every
// emission. A React 18 StrictMode effect (mount -> immediate cleanup ->
// remount) hits exactly this shape — inference, not separately tested.
 
// balances is a real Array — .map works, no KtMap conversion call needed:
account.balances.map(b => `${b.currency}: ${b.money.amountMinor}`);  // exact decimal string
No KtMap/KtList views, no BigInt surprises, no mangled symbol names, no
missing union case. The TS team sees idiomatic TypeScript because the facade did
the flattening — not because Kotlin exports cleanly (it doesn’t).
4. Why the facade is a versioned contract
That generated .d.ts is the public API. Two practices follow, and they are the
“semver + .d.ts-diff review” half of the design consequence:

Semver the facade, not the core. The internal domain model can churn
freely; what the web team pins is the DTO surface. A change that alters a DTO
field is a breaking change even if the domain logic is untouched.
Diff the .d.ts in review. A .d.ts diff is the precise, mechanical
record of what changed at the boundary. Treat an unexpected .d.ts diff the
way you’d treat an unexpected public-API change in any published library —
because that is exactly what it is. A renamed DTO field is a silent break for
the consumer unless the diff is read.

The facade is small surface area on purpose: the smaller and flatter it is, the
cheaper the .d.ts diff is to review and the less the web team is exposed to
the experimental @JsExport friction documented in kmp-js-interop-boundary.
One caveat the generated contract adds (verified 2026-07-06): the .d.ts is
noisier than the facade source suggests. Every exported data class leaks
copy(), toString(), hashCode(), equals() and a deprecated $metadata$
namespace into the public surface, plus module-level Nullable<T>/KtSingleton
helpers. The .d.ts-diff reviewer must learn to read past these Kotlin-isms —
and consumers can call copy() even though the facade never advertised it.
5. What the build actually demanded (verification log, 2026-07-06)
Built and run with Kotlin 2.3.20 / Gradle 8.14.5 / JDK 21 / TS 5.9 strict.
The §1–§2 code compiled essentially as written; the full delta from
illustration to working library:

Opt-ins: @file:OptIn(ExperimentalJsExport::class, DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)
(both warning-level), plus ordinary imports (kotlin.js.Promise,
kotlinx.coroutines.promise, etc.). No experimental compiler flags were
needed for this facade — the GlobalScope.promise path avoids
-Xenable-suspend-function-exporting.
A factory is mandatory. internal constructor becomes
private constructor() in the .d.ts, so TS cannot instantiate
AccountFacade; the facade must export a factory function (the snippet as
originally drafted showed no construction path).
Package placement decides the import shape — see §3.
Runtime behavior confirmed: authorize() awaits to the flattened DTO;
the observer bridge delivers values and unsubscribes; the tagged union
switch sees all three cases.
The precision trap is real and the flatten defeats it: the demo balance
2^53 + 1 (9007199254740993) survived Kotlin Long → String → TS
end-to-end exactly, while Number("9007199254740993") rounds to
9007199254740992 — the silent corruption the Security section warns
about, observed.
Bundle cost of this facade and its stdlib/coroutines floor: measured in
kmp-js-interop-boundary — ≈296 KB raw / ≈51 KB gzip as shipped in the
library dist, collapsing to ≈90 KB raw / ≈28 KB gzip after a consumer
Vite build (minification does the work; tree-shaking contributes nothing).
ESM follow-up (same date): with useEsModules() the library was
consumed by Vite 7 and webpack 5 production builds with zero config and
typechecked strict under moduleResolution: bundler (TS 6.0); the .d.mts
exports are flat, so §3’s idiomatic imports work as written. Tree-shaking
is zero by default, but the combination of per-file granularity +
hand-added sideEffects: false prunes a DTO-only consumer to <1 KB gzip
in both bundlers — each lever alone does nothing. The full flow was
re-run correctly under that aggressive config; details and caveats in
kmp-js-interop-boundary.

Security implications
The facade discipline argued for on maintenance grounds is also the security
lever. Most of the implications below are general frontend-security truths —
but KMP’s “share the core across platforms” value proposition actively pulls
you toward the mistakes, because logic that is genuinely protected in a native
app feels like it’s still protected once the same core compiles to browser JS.
It isn’t.
The facade is a convenience boundary, NOT a trust boundary
Anything in the shared core that compiles to web ships to the browser, where the
user can read and modify it. So validation, authorization, pricing, limits, and
fraud rules enforced in the core are advisory on web — an attacker calls the
server API directly or edits the running JS and the checks evaporate. The core
shares a rule’s implementation across platforms; it cannot share the rule’s
authority. The server must re-validate everything the core “already
validated.” The real-world failure is cognitive: a green account.authorize(...)
tempts teams to weaken the server check that is the actual enforcement point.
This is why kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise keeps regulated logic
server-side (counterfactual c).
Keep the @JsExport surface minimal — it’s also the XSS-reachable surface
Everything exported is callable by any script on the page, including injected
script. A minimal facade is therefore least-privilege, not just cheaper to
review. Exporting an internal or admin operation “because it was convenient”
hands it to an XSS payload. Name mangling (hello_sv8swh_k$) is not
obfuscation and must not be treated as a protection.
Don’t ship secrets or production source maps

Embedded constants ship verbatim. Any key, salt, internal endpoint, or
fraud threshold baked into the shared core lands in the public JS bundle — a
grep away in devtools. A constant that felt “buried in the core” on Android
is exposed on web.
Source maps leak the original Kotlin. The .js.map files that make
debugging work (per kmp-js-interop-boundary) reconstruct your Kotlin
source, names, and comments. Gate them out of production builds, or restrict
who can fetch them.

Flatten 64-bit values to String, never Double (integrity)
This is why §2 flattens Money.amountMinor: Long to a String, not a Double.
A JS Double is exact only to 53 bits, so a 64-bit amount or account/transaction
ID flattened to Double silently loses precision — wrong amount, wrong account,
a corrupt-integrity bug that no exception flags. The DTO-flattening step is where
a type-safety guarantee the Kotlin core had can be quietly destroyed at the
boundary; treat every numeric flatten as a correctness decision.
Provenance gap across the language boundary

Two supply chains converge. The Kotlin stdlib + kotlinx libraries are
pulled into the bundle, then re-packaged as npm. The Gradle dependency-
verification story covers the inputs (see
kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise); the emitted npm artifact needs its
own SBOM/provenance, and SBOM tooling is weaker across the Kotlin→JS
boundary.
Reproducible build is unestablished. No confirmed reproducible-build /
SLSA-provenance story for transpiled-Kotlin frontend artifacts (open
condition 5 in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise) — so you cannot cleanly
attest that the shipped .js corresponds to the audited Kotlin source.

Checklist

 Server re-validates every rule the core enforces; core checks treated as UX only
 Exported facade is minimal — no internal/admin operations reachable from page scripts
 No secrets/keys/thresholds in any code path that compiles to web
 Production builds strip or gate .js.map source maps
 64-bit numerics and IDs flattened to String, not Double
 npm artifact has its own SBOM; provenance gap to Kotlin source acknowledged in the risk register

Related

kmp-js-interop-boundary — the per-API friction table this example
implements against (collections, Long, suspend, Flow, sealed, mangling)
kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise — the enterprise decision view; the
facade-discipline cost is one of its Cons
kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence — who runs this at scale

tech/kmp-web-accessibility.title: KMP Web Accessibility — WCAG Under a Canvas-Rendered UI
tech/kmp-web-accessibility.content:
KMP Web Accessibility — WCAG Under a Canvas-Rendered UI
As of 2026-08-31 (second pass; first pass 2026-08-26). Fast-moving: source claims below were read against jb-main on that date, tracker state against the YouTrack REST API on that date. Re-verify before citing.

Second-pass summary. The WCAG verdict below is unchanged and re-verified against live jb-main: no aria-checked, aria-valuenow, aria-live, aria-level, or tabindex is emitted, so 4.1.2 and 4.1.3 still fail at the framework level. What changed is the investment reading, in both directions. JetBrains merged three web-a11y PRs in August 2026 — two of them after 1.12.0 shipped, so they are queued for the next release and invisible in any release note. One of them resolves an open question this note raised. Meanwhile the near-complete fix for the ARIA gap exists as an unmerged external draft PR, stale since May. See What changed since the first pass, below.

“Does KMP web support WCAG” is two questions, because “KMP web” names two architectures with opposite accessibility profiles. Getting the split right is most of the answer.
The split — which architecture are you asking about
(1) Shared Kotlin core + web-native DOM UI. Kotlin compiles to a JS/Wasm library; React (or any DOM framework) renders the UI. This is the architecture evaluated in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise, with the boundary detailed in kmp-js-interop-boundary.
Here KMP is invisible to assistive technology. The compiled Kotlin never touches the DOM — it returns values that your React components render as real HTML. Accessibility is exactly the accessibility of your component layer: the same problem, the same tools, the same answers as any React app. See design-system-accessibility. WCAG imposes no KMP-specific constraint in this architecture, and this note’s findings do not apply to it.
(2) Compose Multiplatform for Web (Kotlin/Wasm). Compose renders the entire UI into a single <canvas> via Skia. To a browser and to a screen reader, the app is one opaque graphic. Accessibility exists only insofar as the framework synthesizes a parallel DOM that mirrors the semantics tree.
Everything below is about (2).
Status of the target itself

Compose Multiplatform 1.12.0 released 2026-08-25 (GitHub releases).
Web is still Beta on both stability tables — “Web based on Kotlin/Wasm: Beta” for core KMP and for the Compose UI framework (kotlinlang.org supported-platforms; that page’s own footer reads 10 September 2025, so it may lag the 1.12 release).
Web accessibility first shipped in 1.9.0 (2025-09-16) via PR #2188, merged 2025-07-07, closing CMP-7675. The umbrella request CMP-5937 (“Compose Multiplatform Web / Wasm support accessibility”) was resolved 2025-11-17.
1.12.0 is still the latest release as of 2026-08-31 (no 1.13.x, no newer prerelease). Two of the three August accessibility merges below postdate it, so the shipped artifact lags jb-main.
It is on by default; ComposeViewport(configure = { isA11YEnabled = false }) turns it off (What’s new in 1.9.0).

How it actually works
Verified by reading compose/ui/ui/src/webMain/kotlin/androidx/compose/ui/ on jb-main, 2026-08-26.
The DOM ComposeViewport builds (comment block in window/ComposeWindow.web.kt):
<container>
  <positioning_container>
    <shadow_container.shadow>      ← open shadow root
      <style/>
      <app_container>
        <canvas/>                  ← tabindex="0" role="generic" draggable="true"
        <a11y_container/>          ← the mirror, position:absolute, 100%×100%
      </app_container>
    </shadow_container>
    <interopContainer/>
  </positioning_container>
</container>

platform/accessibility/ComposeWebSemanticsListener.kt walks the Compose semantics tree and mirrors each node into a position: fixed <div> inside a11y_container, sized and placed to overlay the canvas pixels it represents. Screen readers read the mirror; clicks on the mirror are forwarded to Compose. Architecturally this is the same trick Flutter Web uses.
Two properties of the sync worth knowing:

It is debounced. DEBOUNCE_MS = 100, MAX_TIME_IN_DEBOUNCE_MS = 1000 — the tree syncs 100 ms after changes settle, or is force-synced if changes have been arriving continuously for 1 s. Under sustained animation or typing the accessible tree can trail the visual UI by up to a second.
Reordering was destructive; it no longer is. Until 2026-08-28 a child-order change called removeAllChildrenOf(htmlNode) and re-appended — by its own comment, chosen because “the code is more simple with this approach.” PR #3349 (“Update the Web A11Y DOM without rebuilding unchanged nodes”, JetBrains, merged 2026-08-28) replaced this with insertBefore-based reconciliation that leaves unchanged nodes in place; removeAllChildrenOf survives only for full teardown of the root. Verified on jb-main 2026-08-31. Not in any release yet — 1.12.0 shipped 2026-08-25, three days before the merge.

The exact semantics vocabulary that crosses
This is the most useful finding, and it is checkable in one grep. Across both web accessibility source files, the properties read are exactly eleven (was ten on 2026-08-26; LinkTestMarker added by PR #3331, merged 2026-08-27):
ContentDescription · Text · EditableText · TestTag · Disabled · Role · Heading · IsDialog · CollectionInfo · LinkTestMarker · SemanticsActions.OnClick
Links now render as interleaved <div role="link"> children inside the text node’s div, with the surrounding text split around them so a screen reader doesn’t read the link text twice — a genuine quality improvement, and a narrow one.
SemanticsProperties.kt on the same branch defines 87 capitalised properties and actions. Everything else is silently dropped on web, including:
StateDescription · ToggleableState · ProgressBarRangeInfo · Selected · SelectableGroup · LiveRegion · Error · Password · IsSensitiveData · Focused · TraversalIndex · IsTraversalGroup · HideFromAccessibility · PaneTitle · MaxTextLength · ContentType · ImeAction · HorizontalScrollAxisRange / VerticalScrollAxisRange · CollectionItemInfo · CustomActions
Silently is the operative word — Modifier.semantics { stateDescription = "…" } compiles, runs, is correct on Android/iOS/desktop, and produces nothing on web. There is no warning.
Re-verified 2026-08-31 on jb-main: StateDescription, ToggleableState, ProgressBarRangeInfo, and LiveRegion are still absent from both files, as are the strings aria-checked, aria-valuenow, aria-live, aria-level, and tabindex. The attribute set written is unchanged: aria-modal, aria-disabled, aria-label, role, contenteditable, plus innerText, id, and inline bounds.
And the DOM attributes that come out
Everything syncNodeProperties writes:









































WrittenFrominnerTextText, and EditableTextaria-labelContentDescriptionaria-disabled="true"Disabledaria-modal="true"IsDialogrolethe role map belowcontenteditable="true"EditableText (on create)idTestTaginline left/top/width/heightnode bounds
Role map (A11YImplementationUtils.kt): button · checkbox · switch · radio · tab · img · menu · heading · textbox · list · grid · dialog. Role.ValuePicker and Role.Carousel map to nothing, both marked // TODO: Any web alternative?. Anything clickable with no role defaults to button under an in-source acknowledgement: // TODO: Not everything with OnClick is a button!
Two mapping choices are questionable on their face (my reading, not a filed issue): Role.DropdownList → role="menu" where ARIA would want listbox or combobox; and role="heading" is emitted with no aria-level, so every heading is level 2 by default and heading-level navigation carries no structure.
No aria-checked. No aria-valuenow/aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax/aria-valuetext. No aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-current, aria-haspopup, aria-required, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, aria-live, aria-level, aria-setsize/aria-posinset. No tabindex on mirror nodes. No landmark roles.
What that costs you against WCAG 2.2 AA
Mapping is mine; the underlying gaps are source-verified or tracker-cited as marked.







































































Success criterionLevelStatusBasis4.1.2 Name, Role, ValueAFails for stateful widgets — checkbox/switch/radio expose no checked state, sliders and progress bars expose no valuesource: no aria-checked/aria-value*; CMP-8621, CMP-8612, CMP-8619 all open4.1.3 Status MessagesAAFails — no live-region support at allsource: LiveRegion unread; CMP-10413 open, filed 2026-07-011.3.1 Info and RelationshipsAPartial — headings have no level, no landmarks, list/grid only via CollectionInfosource2.4.1 Bypass BlocksAFails inside the canvas — no landmark or heading-level structure to bypass to; a skip link would have to live in the host page outside Composesource: no landmark roles, no aria-level2.4.3 Focus OrderAAt risk — traversalIndex explicitly unsupported; DOM order is semantics-tree DFS orderofficial docs; CMP-8630 open2.1.1 KeyboardAAt risk — Tab/Shift-Tab focus movement is a long-standing open request; keyboard handling is Compose-internal, not DOM tab orderCMP-4714, open since 2024-04-271.4.4 Resize Text / 1.4.12 Text SpacingAAStructural gap — canvas text is pixels; browser text-size settings and user stylesheets do not reach itCMP-10692, filed 2026-08-241.4.3 / 1.4.11 ContrastAAYour problem, unaided — contrast must be met by your own theme and measured from rendered pixels, not from CSS; no forced-colors / Windows High Contrast response (the forced-colors part is inferred from canvas rendering plus CMP-10692’s scope, not separately tested)CMP-106922.3.3 Animation from InteractionsAAAGap — prefers-reduced-motion not honoredCMP-106921.3.2 Meaningful SequenceAAt risk — mergeDescendants behaves incorrectlyCMP-8624 open
Screen-reader behaviour reported against 1.9.0-beta01. Thirteen months on, eight are still Open and one (CMP-8627) moved to In progress on 2026-08-31 — the batch’s first state change. All nine were filed by a single reporter in a three-day burst (2025-07-21…23) two weeks after PR #2188 merged, each with a structured repro — the shape and timing of a QA sweep over the new implementation rather than user reports arriving late (reporter’s role is inferred from that pattern, not stated in the tracker):
CMP-8612 · CMP-8619 · CMP-8621 · CMP-8624 · CMP-8627 (VoiceOver scroll doesn’t work) · CMP-8628 (mobile VoiceOver skips elements, highlights invisible ones) · CMP-8629 (alpha(0f) nodes still highlighted) · CMP-8630 (isTraversalGroup doesn’t work) · CMP-8634 (VoiceOver + TextFields incorrect).
Later additions: CMP-10457 context-menu gaps (2026-07-08), CMP-10679 no way to assert focus state in web tests (2026-08-17), CMP-10692 OS/browser preferences (2026-08-24). The collector epic is CMP-9678, open since 2026-01-22. As of 2026-08-31 it carries 23 linked issues, 14 unresolved. The nine resolved ones are a better investment record than the release notes give: CMP-9440 (LinkAnnotation), CMP-8614 (disabled attribute), CMP-9388 (tab focus), CMP-9368 (semantics after dialog close), CMP-10554 (tab focus to HTML interop), CMP-7230 and CMP-8456 (zoom/positioning), CMP-10623, CMP-9247.
What changed since the first pass (2026-08-26 → 2026-08-31)
Re-verified against jb-main, the GitHub API, and the YouTrack REST API on 2026-08-31.
Unchanged — the verdict holds. Every ARIA gap in the table below is still present in source. All nine July-2025 QA tickets are still unresolved. CMP-10652 (password leak) is still Open. compose-web-accessibility.html still 404s.
Changed — three things.
1. A JetBrains-staffed August burst that no release note shows. Three web-a11y PRs merged, all authored by eymar (GitHub author_association: MEMBER):





























PRMergedSizeWhat#33082026-08-14+119/−9SemanticsProperties.Disabled → disabled attribute (CMP-8614, Fixed)#33312026-08-27+658/−18LinkAnnotation support — interleaved role="link" children (CMP-9440, Fixed)#33492026-08-28+465/−85DOM reconciliation instead of rebuild-on-reorder
Two merged after 1.12.0 shipped (2026-08-25), so they land in the next release. #3345 (RTL a11y test coverage) is open. This is the correction to the first pass’s investment reading: that pass counted release-note entries across 1.9.0→1.12.0 and found one feature plus one bug fix. That count was accurate about release notes and understated the repo. Ongoing web-a11y work exists and is JetBrains-staffed.
2. First movement in the July-2025 QA batch. CMP-8627 (VoiceOver scroll) moved Open → In progress on 2026-08-31, by a JetBrains engineer — the first state change in that batch in thirteen months. The other eight remain Open.
3. The near-complete fix exists, unmerged, and has been stale for three months. PR #3016 “Revamp A11y for Web platform” rewrites the whole web accessibility layer (+1522/−384, 8 files). It adds, in one PR, almost everything this note lists as missing:

aria-checked (true/false/mixed), aria-valuemin/-valuemax/-valuenow/-valuetext, aria-live (off/polite/assertive), aria-selected, aria-invalid, aria-readonly, aria-orientation, maxlength, tabindex set/remove, and the grid set (aria-rowcount/-colcount/-rowindex/-colindex/-rowspan/-colspan)
reads for StateDescription, ToggleableState, ProgressBarRangeInfo, LiveRegion, Selected, TraversalIndex, Focused, Error, MaxTextLength, HideFromAccessibility, CollectionItemInfo, and both scroll-axis ranges, plus the SetProgress, ScrollBy, and RequestFocus actions
slider and progressbar roles, and Role.DropdownList → combobox — which fixes the mismapping flagged below as my own reading

Why it hasn’t landed, and why that matters more than what it contains. The author is ApoloApps, author_association: NONE — an external contributor, not JetBrains. The PR is a draft, mergeable_state: dirty (conflicted), and untouched since 2026-05-27, when the author wrote: “I’m still doing changes to fix to rough edges with the PR and I might open a new one replacing.” No replacement PR has appeared — that contributor’s subsequent PRs are all performance and UiMediaScope work. Two reviews exist, both COMMENTED, neither approving.
So the state of web accessibility is not “unsolved problem.” It is “solution drafted by a volunteer, not staffed to completion.” That is a different risk, and a worse one for planning purposes: the technical path is known, so the gap is not a research question anyone can wait out, but the timeline is owned by nobody with a delivery commitment.
Two things PR #3016 does not fix, which is worth knowing before treating it as the answer: it never touches Password or IsSensitiveData (the leak below survives it), and it adds no aria-level and no landmark roles (so 1.3.1 and 2.4.1 stay broken).
A security wrinkle, for the finserv reading
CMP-10652 “Compose Web accessibility-DOM password leak” — open, filed 2026-08-11, subsystem UI. Accessibility, platform Web, affected 1.11.1. The claim: the accessibility DOM writes a password-marked field’s live text into innerText, so anything with DOM access reads the unmasked value.
The mechanism is confirmed in source. syncNodeProperties executes htmlNode.innerText = config[SemanticsProperties.EditableText].text with no guard, and neither SemanticsProperties.Password nor IsSensitiveData appears anywhere in the web accessibility layer. And JetBrains has reproduced it. The single tracker comment, from a JetBrains engineer, reads: “Thanks, reproduced. […] document.body.shadowRoot is null, but the problem can be observed from accessibility tree.” That both confirms the leak and corrects the ticket’s repro line — the shadow root is attached to an inner div, not body, exactly as the source shows. The issue remains Open with priority Normal as of 2026-08-26. I have not run the reproduction myself.
Adjacent and also open: CMP-7553 “[Web] SecureTextField. Clipboard operations are allowed” (2025-02-04).
This sharpens the point already made in kmp-jsexport-facade-example: anything Compose puts on screen it also puts in the DOM, in plain text, by design.
Why “the audit passed” won’t save you
Automated scanners are actively misleading on canvas-rendered apps. axe and Lighthouse grade the DOM; a canvas app has almost no DOM to fail, so it scores well while being unusable. The Flutter community has written this up directly — “Lighthouse gives your Flutter app a perfect accessibility score. It’s lying”. The same logic applies here, with an extra twist: WCAG 1.4.3 contrast has to be measured from rendered pixels, not from CSS, because there is no CSS.
If you evaluate this, evaluate it manually: NVDA + Firefox/Chrome, VoiceOver + Safari (desktop and iOS), TalkBack + Chrome, keyboard-only, 200% browser zoom, browser text-size-only zoom, Windows High Contrast. Inspect the mirror by opening the shadow root and reading the a11y_container divs.
The escape hatch, and its limit
HtmlElementView (renamed from WebElementView in 1.11.0, PRs #2636, #2641; moved to webMain in #2614) embeds real, absolutely-positioned HTML inside a Compose Web app. The original request, CMP-6858, was motivated in the reporter’s own words by “the Compose Web canvas accessibility is not great.”
But interop is one of the two areas the official docs name as unsupported: “Accessibility for interop and container views with scrolls and sliders” and “traversal indexes.” So the escape hatch is real for rendering and not yet covered for accessibility. Using it at scale also means writing the accessible parts of your UI in HTML — at which point the honest question is why the shell is a canvas.
The documentation gap worth naming
kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/compose-accessibility.html states that the framework “enables the design of applications that comply with the requirements of the European Accessibility Act (EAA) and the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).”
That page then links per-platform deep dives for iOS and desktop only. There is no web section on it, and compose-web-accessibility.html returns 404. The sole web accessibility documentation is a short section in the 1.9.0 what’s-new page. A compliance claim sits on the general page; the platform with the largest gap has no page.
Regulatory stake, for the finserv framing in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise: the European Accessibility Act has applied since 2025-06-28 and covers consumer banking services, with EN 301 549 as the harmonized standard referencing WCAG 2.1 AA. (EAA date, banking scope, and the EN 301 549 → WCAG 2.1 AA reference are from secondary compliance-vendor sources — Level Access, Deque — not read from the directive or the standard text; confirm with counsel before relying on the specifics.)
The outside view
This is not a “wait two releases” problem. Flutter Web has shipped the same canvas-plus-semantics-overlay architecture for years longer, with far more resourcing, and screen-reader support on canvas-rendered content is still the standard caveat in 2026 practitioner writeups. The reference class says the overlay approach asymptotes below DOM-native accessibility rather than converging on it — because the overlay only ever carries what the framework chose to mirror, while real HTML carries browser-native behaviour the framework never has to reimplement.
That does not make CMP Web unusable. It makes the accessible-surface decision architectural rather than schedulable.
Verdict

Shared Kotlin core + React/DOM UI: WCAG is unaffected by KMP. Counterweight, so this doesn’t read as motivated reasoning: that verdict is not really evidence for the chosen architecture. Architecture (1) was picked on interop, hiring, and bundle grounds long before accessibility came up, and its accessibility profile is simply “React’s” — a wash, not a win. What this note actually does is close off the alternative some reader will eventually propose (“why not just share the UI too?”) and put a price on it.
Compose Multiplatform for Web, consumer-facing and regulated: not viable at WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA today. Stateful widgets fail 4.1.2 at the framework level; there is no framework path to 4.1.3 (you would have to mount your own live region through HtmlElementView and drive it yourself); text sizing and high-contrast are structurally out of reach.
Where it is defensible: internal tools with a known user population and a documented accommodation path; prototypes; surfaces outside EAA/Section 508 scope; apps whose accessible surface is entirely HtmlElementView.
Beware the middle case — a mobile-first CMP app growing a web target “for free”. iOS and desktop get first-class semantics support and visible ongoing investment (they carry open a11y tickets of their own — CMP-7939, CMP-9360, CMP-10207, CMP-10640 — but the vocabulary is there); the web build silently doesn’t, and the same Modifier.semantics block that works on mobile is dropped on web without a warning. The parity assumption is the trap, not the framework.

What would change this — falsifiable conditions

The July-2025 QA batch (CMP-8612, CMP-8619, CMP-8621, CMP-8624, CMP-8627, CMP-8628, CMP-8629, CMP-8630, CMP-8634) closes. CMP-8627 went In progress 2026-08-31 — the leading indicator to watch.
aria-checked, aria-valuenow, and aria-live appear in ComposeWebSemanticsListener.kt — grep the file; this is a one-minute recheck. (Still absent 2026-08-31.)
PR #3016 merges, or JetBrains opens a staffed replacement. This is now the single highest-information signal, because it converts the question from “will this be solved” to “will this be shipped.” Watch for either the draft flag clearing on #3016, or a new webMain/.../accessibility PR authored by a MEMBER account. Its author said on 2026-05-27 they might open a replacement; as of 2026-08-31 they have not.
The ten-property read set grows to include StateDescription, ToggleableState, ProgressBarRangeInfo, and LiveRegion.
A dedicated web accessibility documentation page ships (currently 404).
JetBrains publishes a VPAT / Accessibility Conformance Report or an EN 301 549 statement for CMP Web. None found as of 2026-08-26 — and the absence is informative rather than incidental, because JetBrains does publish ACRs against EN 301 549 for other products (IntelliJ IDEA, TeamCity). The capability and the template exist; the framework hasn’t been put through them.
A third-party audit of a shipped CMP Web app reports AA conformance. None found.
CMP-10652 moves off Open — it is vendor-reproduced but unfixed as of 2026-08-26.

Open questions

Does the destructive child re-ordering disrupt an in-progress screen-reader traversal? Moot as of PR #3349 (merged 2026-08-28) — reconciliation now leaves unchanged nodes in place. Whether it did disrupt traversal in 1.9.0–1.12.0 was never tested by me; the fix’s existence is suggestive but not proof that it did.
Does the 100 ms/1 s debounce produce audible staleness with NVDA during typing? Untested.
Is there any production CMP Web app with a published accessibility audit? None found — consistent with kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence, where web-target production use is already the rare exception.
Does CMP-8619 still reproduce? Source maps Role.Switch → "switch", yet the ticket says Switch has no role attribute. Either Material’s Switch doesn’t set SemanticsProperties.Role on web, or the ticket predates a fix and was never retested. Needs a runtime check.

Related

kmp-js-interop-boundary — the other web target, where Kotlin never renders
kmp-jsexport-facade-example — the security section this note’s DOM leak extends
kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence — why there is so little production web-target evidence to audit
design-system-accessibility — what accessibility work looks like when the DOM is real
multiplatform-app-architecture-options — the wider option space

Sources
Read 2026-08-26 unless noted; second-pass re-verification 2026-08-31. YouTrack IDs resolve at youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/<ID>; #NNNN are JetBrains/compose-multiplatform-core PRs.

tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise.title: KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
tech/kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise.content:
KMP for Web in a Finserv Enterprise — Shared Kotlin Core, Web-Native UI
The architecture under evaluation: Kotlin shares the core only — business logic, domain models, validation, networking/serialization — across Android, iOS, and web. The web frontend stays web-native (React or similar), consuming the compiled Kotlin core via Kotlin/JS (or Kotlin/Wasm) with TypeScript bindings. This is explicitly not Compose Multiplatform for Web and not Kotlin-rendered UI.
Companion notes: kmp-js-interop-boundary (what crosses the Kotlin→JS/Wasm/React boundary), kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence (who runs this at scale), and kmp-web-accessibility (why the other KMP web architecture — Compose rendering the UI to canvas — cannot currently meet WCAG AA, and why this one is unaffected).
The architecture in one line
A shared Kotlin module compiles to a JS library (.js + .d.ts + package.json), is published to npm, and is imported by a React/TypeScript app the same way any other JS dependency would be — while the same Kotlin core also serves true-native Android and iOS clients.
JetBrains’ own guidance points this architecture at Kotlin/JS, not Kotlin/Wasm. For the scenario of sharing business logic with a JS-predominant native UI, the May 2025 “Present and Future of Kotlin for Web” post states Kotlin/JS “is the better fit because it provides a better interop experience” (JetBrains, 2025-05). Kotlin/Wasm’s advantages are UI/compute-oriented and largely irrelevant to a logic-only library that must hand rich typed objects across the boundary. Detail in kmp-js-interop-boundary.
Decision view for a large financial-services org
Pros

One core, three clients, real type safety. Kotlin’s null-safety and stronger correctness guarantees apply to high-assurance domain/validation logic across Android, iOS, and web. Quizlet migrated its shared code from JavaScript to KMP in early 2019 specifically to gain type safety, and runs it in production at 50M+ monthly active users (ankushg.com). Note that all cited adopters are self-selected published successes — the failure distribution is largely unrecorded; see the walk-away section of kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence.
Kotlin/JS web target is Stable. In the KMP supported-platforms table, “Web based on Kotlin/JS” is Stable while “Web based on Kotlin/Wasm” is Beta (as of 2026-06, kotlinlang.org). The conservative web target for this architecture exists today.
Near-zero interop overhead on Kotlin/JS. No unnecessary data copying when handing objects to JS; selective module loading means a page loads only the logic it needs (JetBrains, 2025-05).
Mature JVM/Gradle supply-chain audit story for finserv. Gradle dependency verification covers both checksums (integrity) and signatures (provenance) (Gradle docs); CycloneDX/SPDX SBOM plugins exist for Gradle.
Predictable release cadence. ~6 months for language releases, ~3 months for tooling; Kotlin 2.3.0 shipped 2025-12-16 (kotlinlang.org releases).
KMP is the “C++ shared core without the C++ costs” pitch. It uses a standard toolchain and Kotlin is already the Android language, avoiding the niche-hiring and custom-tooling traps that sank Dropbox’s C++ core (see counterfactual (d) below).

Cons

The JS-export interop is experimental and JetBrains itself flags the gap. The current path uses the experimental @JsExport annotation, “which has constraints that make it challenging to use in enterprise applications” (verbatim, JetBrains 2025-05). Stabilization and broader export support are roadmap items with no firm date.
Idiomatic Kotlin does not cross the boundary cleanly. The shared-core team must design a DTO-flattened, annotation-disciplined facade (@JsName, @JsExport) rather than expose its rich domain model. Collections, Long, suspend functions, Flow, and sealed hierarchies all need handling. Full per-API list in kmp-js-interop-boundary; worked facade code in kmp-jsexport-facade-example.
The web facade is a convenience boundary, not a trust boundary. Sharing the core to the browser tempts teams to treat client-side validation/authz/limit logic as enforced, but anything compiled to web is readable and modifiable by the user — core checks are advisory, the server must re-validate. Plus secret-in-bundle, prod source-map leakage, and a 64-bit→Double precision-loss trap at the DTO flatten. Security section in kmp-jsexport-facade-example; reinforces counterfactual (c) below.
TypeScript-declaration generation is Experimental on Kotlin/Wasm and “may be dropped or changed at any time” (kotlinlang wasm-js-interop). (The same source makes no such claim for Kotlin/JS .d.ts, which has existed for years.) Locally that Wasm .d.ts generation did work as of 2026-07-06 (Kotlin 2.3.20) — but object handles surface as unknown in the declarations, and classes cannot be exported at all; see kmp-js-interop-boundary.
Single-vendor concentration for web specifically. Kotlin is driven by JetBrains; the Kotlin Foundation (co-founded by JetBrains and Google) protects the trademark and gates incompatible language changes via a Language Committee, but does not own the roadmap or diversify the bus factor (kotlinfoundation.org). Google’s “Kotlin-first” stance is about Android, not Kotlin/JS-for-web. A finserv risk committee should treat KMP-for-web as JetBrains-single-vendor, distinct from “Kotlin the JVM language,” which has broad institutional backing.
Smaller hiring pool. US Kotlin job listings number in the low thousands, concentrated in Android/backend (Glassdoor, as of 2025-11), versus JS/TS being the dominant frontend skill (Glassdoor). The exact count is unverified — job-board figures are volatile. A JS-first frontend org must fund Kotlin/JVM capability and absorb Gradle/JVM build infra.
Slow multiplatform Gradle builds. Tasks compile the same code once per target; mitigation needs remote build cache and target-scoping, and the plugin historically lagged on configuration-cache support (fixes still landing in 2.3.0-Beta2, Dec 2025; corroborated, YouTrack KT-44900).
Release-train coupling. A monorepo couples the web release train to mobile, and it is the common remedy for publish/consume friction. Multi-repo setups force a release-and-consume cycle on every core change (single-case evidence from Xapo Labs; the generalization to a “common pattern” is unverified — see kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence).

Question marks (genuinely open — and what would resolve each)

Will @JsExport stabilize, and when? JetBrains states intent without a timeline. Resolves when: a Kotlin release notes @JsExport as Stable with the “majority of Kotlin declarations” exportable. (Late-2025 releases shipped incremental fixes but stabilization is not done — the fixes were suspend export and interface-implementation-from-TS in 2.3.20; see kmp-js-interop-boundary.)
Is there any finserv precedent for shipping compiled-from-Kotlin JS/Wasm in an audited frontend? Resolves when: a bank/regulator engineering writeup or audit guidance addresses reproducible-build/SLSA provenance for transpiled-Kotlin frontend artifacts. None was found.
What is the real bundle-size overhead of the Kotlin stdlib in JS output? Resolved 2026-07-06 by local measurement (Kotlin 2.3.20, minimal logic-only facade): the library dist ships ~296 KB raw / ~51 KB gzip (stdlib + kotlinx-coroutines), which a consumer Vite/webpack production build collapses to ~85–90 KB raw / ~25–28 KB gzip — minification does the work. Cross-boundary tree-shaking is zero by default, so cost scales with the core’s dependency graph — though a per-file-granularity + sideEffects: false packaging recipe recovers it fully (a DTO-only consumer drops to <1 KB gzip), at the cost of a hand-maintained post-build step. The Wasm target measured smaller still for a logic-only core (8.4 KB gzip incl. glue; ~25 KB with coroutines — parity with JS), and it gets automatic dead-code elimination, but its interop is function-only. One local datapoint, not an independent benchmark; details and caveats in kmp-js-interop-boundary. For a finserv decision: ~25–28 KB gzip next to a typical React app bundle means bundle size is not the blocking con it was open as.
Does a React/TS team consuming a Kotlin core hit a maintainable breaking-change workflow? Resolves when: a first-hand writeup describes semver of the exported facade and .d.ts diff review. None found.
Is the shared-core team an org bottleneck for the web consumer specifically? Resolves when: a named web-specific incident, not general KMP advice, documents it. None found.

Compared to the alternatives
KMP’s real competition is four baselines a finserv enterprise already knows. (Counterfactuals (a) and (b) now have full deep-dive notes: react-native-expo-enterprise and rust-shared-core-enterprise; the shared-UI alternative neither counterfactual covers is flutter-enterprise.)

(a) TypeScript-first shared core in a monorepo (pnpm/Turborepo/Nx/Yarn workspaces) is the default web-dev answer and KMP’s strongest rival. It is structurally the same “share core, native UI” shape — validators, API clients, auth, domain services in a shared package consumed by React (web) and React Native (mobile), UI per-platform (greenmod.it). It beats KMP on hiring, tooling maturity, zero FFI/binding layer, and no JS-interop tax. KMP wins only where the other consumer is a true-native Android/iOS app and where Kotlin’s runtime correctness guarantees matter more than TS’s. If “mobile” means React Native, the TS monorepo dominates and KMP adds little.
(b) Rust→Wasm + native bindings is the most direct architectural analog and has stronger web production proof than KMP-for-web. 1Password ships a headless Rust core (business logic, crypto, DB, server comms) under thin native UI across Mac/Windows/iOS/Android/browser (Serokell, 2021-01); Mozilla’s UniFFI auto-generates Kotlin/Swift bindings and runs in Firefox (github.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs). Rust beats KMP on web maturity (Wasm is Rust’s first-class story), memory safety, and crypto. KMP beats Rust on hiring for a JVM/Android shop, near-zero Kotlin/JS interop overhead, and a far gentler learning curve (Rust’s borrow checker is a real adoption tax).
(c) No client-side sharing — thin clients + server-side logic via generated (OpenAPI/gRPC) clients is the classic finserv pattern and the most important counterfactual. The cited banking-architecture writeup supports the server-side-enforcement shape — API gateway as the single point enforcing authz/validation, immutable audit trails as “a natural output of the architecture” (scrums.com). The stronger conclusion that this overrides any client-side-sharing approach for regulated rules is (unverified) — the source does not contain the often-quoted “single source of truth at the client level” phrasing. Still, this incumbent beats every client-sharing approach on auditability; shared-core wins only on offline capability, latency, and client-side UX richness.
(d) C++ shared core is the cautionary tale. Dropbox abandoned it (~2019) for native after custom-tooling overhead (Djinni/json11/nn), a C++/Java deadlock that “took weeks” to debug, and a sustained inability to hire/retain C++ mobile engineers; Slack hit the same hiring and merged-release-cycle problems (InfoQ, 2019-11). This is more an argument for KMP than a live alternative — but the failure modes (bridging overhead, niche-skill hiring) are exactly what a finserv buyer should stress-test KMP/Wasm against.

Verdict
KMP-shared-core / web-native UI is the right call when ALL of these hold:

There is a genuine true-native Android/iOS client (not React Native) — otherwise the TS monorepo (counterfactual a) dominates.
High-assurance domain/validation logic benefits materially from Kotlin’s correctness guarantees over TypeScript’s.
The org can fund Kotlin/JVM capability and Gradle build infra, and accept JetBrains-single-vendor risk on the web target.
The shared core can live behind a deliberately designed DTO facade (not the rich domain model), and the team budgets for the experimental @JsExport friction.
Regulated business rules either don’t need to be client-authoritative, or the org has cleared reproducible-build/provenance audit of transpiled-Kotlin frontend artifacts.

It is the wrong call when: mobile is React Native (use TS monorepo); web maturity and memory-safe crypto dominate (consider Rust/Wasm); or the bank’s risk org will insist regulated logic stays server-side anyway (use generated thin clients) — that last case shrinks the shared-core value to near zero.
The load-bearing unknown is condition 5 plus @JsExport stabilization timing — both are open as of 2026-06. Re-test this verdict when JetBrains stabilizes @JsExport.
Sources

JetBrains, “The Present and Future of Kotlin for Web” (2025-05): blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/05/present-and-future-kotlin-for-web/
Kotlin Multiplatform supported platforms: kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/supported-platforms.html
Quizlet shared-code writeup (Ankush Gupta): ankushg.com/posts/shared-code-kotlin-multiplatform/
Kotlin Foundation: kotlinfoundation.org/
Gradle dependency verification: docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/dependency_verification.html
1Password Rust core (Serokell): serokell.io/blog/rust-in-production-1password
Mozilla UniFFI: github.com/mozilla/uniffi-rs
Dropbox/Slack shared-code costs (InfoQ): www.infoq.com/news/2019/11/mobile-share-code-costs/
TS shared-core monorepo pattern (greenmod.it): www.greenmod.it/blog/posts/share-business-logic-between-reactjs-and-react-native/
Banking architecture / server-side enforcement (scrums.com): www.scrums.com/blog/modern-banking-architecture-building-for-scale-and-compliance

tech/multiplatform-app-architecture-opti.title: Web + iOS + Android + Backend: The Architecture Option Space
tech/multiplatform-app-architecture-opti.content:
Web + iOS + Android + Backend: The Architecture Option Space
As of 2026-08-26. Version numbers and stability tiers are the fastest-moving claims in this note; re-verify before citing.
The framing correction
“Which cross-platform framework?” is the wrong first question, and it is the one every comparison article answers. It collapses five decisions that are actually independent:

UI sharing — how much of the rendered interface is one codebase
Logic sharing — how much non-UI code (domain, validation, networking) is one codebase
Client↔server contract — how the three clients talk to backend services
Data and state topology — request/response versus a local store that syncs
Delivery cadence — how you ship to three platforms whose release gates differ by orders of magnitude

You can pick independently on each axis. React Native + REST + no offline + weekly releases is a valid combination; so is native Swift/Kotlin + shared Kotlin core + GraphQL + local-first. Most “framework wars” content only argues axis 1 and silently assumes defaults for the rest.
The five-axis split is an authored frame, not a standard taxonomy — no source in this research pass proposes it. Its claim to usefulness is only that it separates decisions that can be made independently; if a real project finds two of these axes genuinely coupled, the frame is wrong for that project.
Axis 5 is the one that distinguishes this problem from ordinary web architecture, and it is the most under-discussed. See design-tokens for the cross-platform consistency layer that sits orthogonal to all five.
Axis 1 — UI sharing
A spectrum, not a binary. Ordered by how much UI code is shared:
(a) No UI sharing — native Swift/SwiftUI + Kotlin/Compose + a web SPA
Three UI codebases, three teams (or three hats). Still a legitimate default, and the correct answer more often than framework marketing admits.

Wins on: platform fidelity, day-zero OS feature access, hiring in each silo, no framework-abandonment risk, no interop tax.
Loses on: 3× UI cost, three-way feature drift, design-system enforcement becomes a governance problem rather than a code problem (see design-system-failure-modes).
Pairs naturally with heavy sharing on axis 2, which is where most of the reuse value actually lives.

(b) Shared mobile UI, separate web — Compose Multiplatform or Flutter for iOS+Android
One mobile UI, a web app built with web tooling. This is the sweet spot for a lot of products, because the iOS/Android pair are far more similar to each other than either is to the web.

Compose Multiplatform is Stable for Android, iOS, and desktop as of the current supported-platforms table (kotlinlang.org, checked 2026-08-26). Its web target (Kotlin/Wasm) is Beta.
Flutter covers both plus web and desktop from one codebase. Its 2026 roadmap states “On the web, we intend for WebAssembly (Wasm) to become the default,” and commits to completing the Impeller migration on Android by “removing the legacy Skia backend on Android 10 and above,” plus “day-zero support for Android 17 and upcoming iOS releases” (flutter.dev).

(c) Shared across all three — React Native + React Native Web (Expo), or Flutter Web
One UI codebase for web, iOS, and Android. The most-shared option, and the one with the sharpest hidden costs.
Expo is the mainstream path here. Verified against primary sources on 2026-08-26:

Expo SDK 57.0.0 targets React Native 0.86, React 19.2.3, react-native-web 0.21.0; iOS 16.4+ (Xcode 26.4+), Android 7+ (compileSdkVersion 36), Node 22.13.x minimum (docs.expo.dev).
npm registry, queried 2026-08-26: expo latest is 57.0.16 (published 2026-08-24); react-native latest is 0.87.0 (published 2026-08-11). React Native’s own release line therefore runs ahead of the SDK’s pin — an SDK upgrade, not a package bump, is how you move.
Expo’s docs describe web output as statically rendered “for SEO and performance, or client-rendered for a more app-like experience,” and note React Native Web is optional but recommended “when building across platforms as it maximizes code reuse” (docs.expo.dev).

The caveat that matters: the web output is not a normal web app. RNW renders <View>/<Text> primitives to DOM. You inherit a component model designed for mobile, and web-native concerns (semantic HTML, CSS-native layout, third-party web widget ecosystems) get harder, not easier. React Server Components are “[e]xperimentally available. This is a beta release and subject to breaking changes,” with EAS Update not yet supporting them and production deployment explicitly not recommended (docs.expo.dev).
The honest version of option (c) for most teams: share the mobile pair, treat web as a first-class separate surface, and take the sharing on axis 2 instead. Which is option (b) with extra steps.
(d) Web-first wrapper — Capacitor / PWA
Ship one web app; wrap it in a native shell for the stores. The web build is the product; the native projects are packaging.

Cheapest path to three platforms if you already have a web app and mobile is a companion surface, not the primary one.
Cost is a WebView, which means the performance ceiling and platform-idiom ceiling are both lower. For content, forms, dashboards, and internal tooling this is frequently fine and frequently under-considered.
Capacitor produces standard native projects, so store submission is a normal native submission (Xcode/Android Studio or CI), whereas Expo’s EAS Submit handles it from CI without a local macOS requirement — (secondary sourcing; verify against current EAS docs before relying on the macOS claim).

(e) The .NET lane — MAUI + Blazor Hybrid
Relevant only if the org is already C#/.NET end to end, in which case a single language from UI through API is a real advantage. Outside a .NET shop it has no pull. Treat 2026 status claims for MAUI as (unverified) — I found no primary Microsoft roadmap source in this pass.
Axis 2 — Logic sharing (usually the higher-value axis)
Independent of the UI decision. The reusable mass in most products is domain models, validation, API clients, auth flows, offline queueing, formatting, feature flags, and analytics — not pixels.

TypeScript shared core in a monorepo. The default when web is React and mobile is React Native. Zero FFI, zero binding layer, one toolchain. Structurally the same “share core, native UI” shape as KMP, and it dominates KMP if mobile is already RN.
Kotlin Multiplatform core, native UI on each platform. The strongest option when mobile is true-native and the backend is JVM. Stable on Android, iOS, JVM server, and Kotlin/JS for web (kotlinlang.org). The mobile pair is solid; the web consumption path still goes through the experimental @JsExport, and Swift Export is still pre-stable — JetBrains’ August 2025 roadmap lists it as experimental with a stable release targeted in 2026 (JetBrains). (A secondary summary described it as moving Alpha→Beta; the primary post says experimental. Check the current tier before planning around it.) This option has its own cluster: kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise for the decision view, kmp-js-interop-boundary for what actually crosses the boundary, kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence for who runs it in production.
Rust core + generated bindings (UniFFI/Wasm). Strongest web story of the compiled-core options, highest learning tax. 1Password’s headless Rust core under thin native UI across desktop, mobile, and browser is the standing production reference; Mozilla’s UniFFI generates the Kotlin/Swift bindings for this shape.
Share nothing on the client; put the logic on the server. The classic and still-underrated answer — thin clients, generated API clients, all rules enforced server-side. Costs you offline capability and client-side latency; buys you a single place to audit and change behavior. Worth remembering that anything compiled to a client is readable and modifiable by the user, so client-side validation and limit checks are advisory no matter which sharing option produced them — the server re-validates or it isn’t enforced.

Monorepo tooling follows from language mix, not preference: Turborepo or Nx if the shared code is JS/TS; Bazel/Buck2/Pants if the repo is genuinely polyglot and large. Remote caching is the feature that pays for the migration, not the task graph. (Tool-to-scale mapping here is from secondary comparison articles — treat specific package-count thresholds as unverified.)
Axis 3 — the client↔backend contract
Three clients means the contract is the integration surface that breaks. Options:

REST + OpenAPI, contract-first, with generated clients. Generate TypeScript, Swift, and Kotlin clients from one spec so a backend breaking change fails the client build rather than production. This is the boring answer and it survives client-framework churn better than anything else — the spec outlives the framework you picked on axis 1.
GraphQL (+ Federation for multi-service backends). Earns its complexity when clients genuinely need different shapes of the same graph and you would otherwise proliferate endpoints. Federation composes domain subgraphs into one schema.
tRPC. End-to-end type safety with no codegen step, but only inside TypeScript. If iOS/Android are Swift/Kotlin, tRPC cannot serve them — it is a web+RN answer, not a three-platform answer. Easy to mis-select, because tRPC’s DX is genuinely excellent inside the half of the problem it covers.
gRPC / Connect. Strong typing and streaming across polyglot clients; browser support needs a proxy layer.
BFF per client. Orthogonal to the above: one thin service per client surface, shaping responses for that client’s needs. Buys independent evolution and per-client caching; costs you N services to keep alive. Worth it when the web and mobile clients want genuinely different payload shapes; wasteful when they want the same data.

The BFF also solves an auth problem, which is why it keeps reappearing: web and native have different correct token stories. Native apps store tokens in the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore, which are hardware-backed and unavailable to other apps. Browsers have no equivalent — anything in localStorage is readable by any XSS that achieves execution. So the standard shapes diverge: OAuth 2.0 + PKCE with OS secure storage on native, versus a BFF/token-handler pattern that keeps refresh tokens server-side and hands the SPA only a short-lived access token in memory. (Sourced from secondary security write-ups in this pass; verify against the current OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Apps BCP before implementing.)
Axis 4 — data and state topology

Request/response with a cache (TanStack Query and equivalents). Right for most products. Cheapest to reason about.
Local-first / sync engine. A local database on each client with a sync protocol to the server. Buys real offline, instant interactions, and conflict handling as a designed feature rather than an incident. Costs you a hard distributed-systems problem inside your product.

Current contenders: PowerSync (Postgres → client SQLite with a write-back path; the most mobile-mature of the three), ElectricSQL (Postgres sync with “shapes” defining what reaches which client), Zero from Rocicorp (query-based sync; Replicache was sunset in its favor). (All characterizations here come from secondary comparison articles, not vendor docs or hands-on use — treat maturity rankings as unverified.)


The decision driver is not “would offline be nice.” It is whether a user in a tunnel, a warehouse, or a hospital basement is a real user. If not, this axis costs more than it returns.

Axis 5 — delivery cadence, the constraint web developers underestimate
Web ships continuously. Mobile ships through a review gate, and users on old versions persist for months. Any architecture spanning both has to answer: how do we change the product without a store release?
Options, roughly by power and risk:

Just ship native releases. Fine at low change frequency. Version skew becomes the API’s problem — you now support every client version in the wild.
Server-driven UI. The server sends UI structure, not just data; clients render generically. Airbnb (Ghost platform), Netflix, and Lyft are the canonical references, and Shopify reported escaping a weekly release cadence with it. The cautionary half is equally well documented: Spotify’s HubFramework, the earliest serious generic SDUI at scale, was deprecated, with engineers describing debugging it as archeology. (Both halves are from secondary write-ups — the Shopify and Spotify specifics are unverified.) The lesson in that pairing: SDUI works when scoped to a surface that genuinely needs frequent change, and rots when generalized into a whole-app rendering framework. Note also that every named reference here is a company with a dedicated platform team to maintain the renderer and its tooling — that standing cost is the part of the economics that doesn’t transfer to a small team.
JS bundle OTA updates (EAS Update and equivalents). Push a new JS bundle without a store review — available only if axis 1 put you on a JS runtime.
Sidestep the store entirely. If the audience is employees or a known enterprise customer base, MDM/managed distribution (and Apple’s business-focused distribution programs) removes App Review from the critical path and with it most of axis 5’s difficulty. Worth checking before designing around a constraint that may not apply — (programme names and current terms unverified in this pass).

Get the Apple rule right, because it is widely misquoted. App Store Review Guideline 2.5.2 reads, verbatim:

“Apps should be self-contained in their bundles, and may not read or write data outside the designated container area, nor may they download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app, including other apps. Educational apps designed to teach, develop, or allow students to test executable code may, in limited circumstances, download code provided that such code is not used for other purposes. Such apps must make the source code provided by the app completely viewable and editable by the user.”
— App Review Guidelines, retrieved 2026-08-26

Note what is not there: the widely-cited “code run by WebKit or JavaScriptCore is exempt” carve-out. That language lives in the Apple Developer Program License Agreement §3.3.2, not in the review guidelines — several secondary sources attribute it to 2.5.2, and they are wrong. The substance of the permission is that downloaded scripts must not change the app’s primary purpose or add functionality inconsistent with what was reviewed. (The §3.3.2 wording and the reported June 2017 rewrite to engine-agnostic language are from secondary sources; read the current DPLA text directly before betting a release strategy on it.)
Guideline 4.7 is a separate provision covering “HTML5 and JavaScript mini apps and mini games, streaming games, chatbots, and plug-ins” — it is about hosting third-party software inside your app, not about updating your own. Don’t conflate them.
Practical read: bug fixes, copy, and UI iteration within the reviewed purpose are the safe zone; shipping a materially different app post-review is the violation.
Combination archetypes
Constructed here as a reasoning aid, not observed in a survey — each row is internally consistent, but the set is not exhaustive and the labels are mine.















































ArchetypeAxis 1 (UI)Axis 2 (logic)Axis 3 (contract)Fits whenJS everywhereExpo/RNW all threeTS monorepo coretRPC or REST+OpenAPISmall team, TS-native, web and mobile want the same productNative pair + webCompose MP or Flutter for mobile; web-native SPAKMP core, or server-side onlyREST+OpenAPIMobile UX quality matters; web is genuinely a different surfaceAll native, share the coreSwift + Kotlin + ReactKMP or Rust coreREST+OpenAPI or GraphQLPlatform fidelity is the product; you can staff three silosThin clientsAnythingNothing shared client-sideREST+OpenAPI, BFF per clientRegulated/audited domain; rules must be enforceable server-sideWeb-first companionCapacitor/PWAN/A — it’s one web appRESTMobile is a companion, not the primary surface
How to choose — the drivers that actually decide it
Ordered by how often I’d expect each to be the binding constraint. That ordering is an authored judgment, not a measured one — but note that every driver on it outranks the benchmark numbers that comparison articles lead with:

Who you can hire and retain. The clearest documented shared-core failures — Dropbox abandoning its C++ mobile core around 2019, and Slack hitting the same wall — were killed by hiring, retention, and custom-tooling overhead rather than by the technology failing on its own terms (InfoQ, 2019-11). Whether that generalises to most failures is unmeasured; it is placed first here as a judgment, not a statistic. This driver is really Conway’s law surfacing in the option space — each archetype implies a team shape you have to be able to staff and fund; multiplatform-team-topology works that through per archetype.
How different the three products really are. If web is a marketing site + dashboard and mobile is the app, sharing UI across all three is solving a problem you don’t have.
Whether offline is a requirement or a wish. Decides axis 4 outright.
How often you need to change the product. Decides axis 5, and axis 5 can retroactively decide axis 1.
Regulatory posture. If client-side logic can’t be trusted as enforcement, axis 2 collapses toward thin clients regardless of what’s technically shareable.
What the backend already is. A JVM backend makes KMP nearly free on axis 2; a Node backend makes TS sharing nearly free.

Framework benchmark numbers are near the bottom of that list, and near the top of every comparison article.
Evidence quality warning
Searching this topic in 2026 returns an unusually high proportion of SEO content-farm output — “X vs Y vs Z 2026” articles that recycle each other’s numbers without primary sourcing. Adoption statistics in this space (KMP “7%→23%”, Flutter 46% vs React Native 35%) circulate widely with no traceable methodology and should not be used as decision inputs.
Claims in this note traceable to primary sources: Expo SDK/RN version pins, npm registry versions, KMP/Compose stability tiers, the Flutter 2026 roadmap quotes, Expo’s RSC status, and the verbatim Apple guideline text. Everything else is labeled inline.
Also unfound in this pass: credible recent postmortems of teams abandoning a cross-platform framework. The 2018-era Airbnb React Native writeup is still the most-cited example, which is itself a signal — either the failure mode has genuinely receded with the New Architecture and Compose MP stabilizing, or failures simply stopped being published. Treat the absence as unknown, not as evidence of safety.
