tech/multiplatform-team-topology.title: Multiplatform Team Topology: Who Owns the Shared Parts
tech/multiplatform-team-topology.content:
Multiplatform Team Topology: Who Owns the Shared Parts
The companion question to multiplatform-app-architecture-options. That note frames the architecture as five independently choosable axes; this one covers the constraint that couples them: every sharing decision creates a shared artifact, and a shared artifact needs an owner your org chart can actually produce.
Why this is not a sixth axis
The five axes work as a frame because they are independent technical choices. Org structure is not a sixth choice alongside them — it is the medium the other five are chosen in. Conway stated the mechanism in 1968:

“Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization’s communication structure.”
— Melvin Conway, “How Do Committees Invent?”, Datamation, April 1968 (quote as given on melconway.com, retrieved 2026-08-29)

Martin Fowler’s gloss names the consequence for sharing decisions specifically: “Conway understood that software coupling is enabled and encouraged by human communication,” and where architecture clashes with org structure, “module interactions that were designed to be straightforward become complicated, because the teams responsible for them don’t work together well” (martinfowler.com/bliki/ConwaysLaw). A shared core is deliberate coupling between platforms; it holds only if the communication structure behind it holds.
The inverse Conway maneuver — “change the communication patterns of the designers to encourage the desired software architecture,” coined by Jonny LeRoy and Matt Simons in the December 2010 Cutter IT Journal (attribution via Fowler’s bliki) — is the org-side lever: pick the architecture, then reshape teams to fit it. The bound on the maneuver is the labor market. You can redraw the org chart; you cannot redraw who is hireable and retainable — which is why multiplatform-app-architecture-options ranks hiring as driver #1 and why the failure evidence below is mostly hiring evidence.
Vocabulary: the four team types
Team Topologies (Skelton & Pais, 2019) is the standard vocabulary. The four types, as defined on teamtopologies.com/key-concepts (retrieved 2026-08-29):

Stream-aligned team — “aligned to a flow of work from (usually) a segment of the business domain”
Platform team — “a grouping of other team types that provide a compelling internal product to accelerate delivery by Stream-aligned teams”
Enabling team — “helps a Stream-aligned team to overcome obstacles. Also detects missing capabilities.”
Complicated Subsystem team — “where significant mathematics/calculation/technical expertise is needed”

Applied to the three-client problem (the mapping is authored here, not from the book):

A shared TS/KMP core consumed by client teams is a platform in this sense — an internal product with the client teams as customers, served “X-as-a-Service.”
A Rust core behind UniFFI bindings leans complicated-subsystem: the point of that lane is concentrating scarce expertise behind a boundary so client teams don’t need it (rust-shared-core-enterprise).
Design-system and build-tooling teams are platform teams whether or not anyone calls them that.

Team Topologies’ own warning applies directly to shared cores: the “Thinnest Viable Platform” concept exists because “most internal platforms become bloated monstrosities that slow teams down rather than accelerate progress” (same page). A shared core is subject to the same bloat gravity as any internal platform.
The implied team shape per archetype
The combination archetypes from multiplatform-app-architecture-options each imply a team topology. This column is the authored core of this note:



































ArchetypeImplied team shapeThe org bet you’re makingJS everywhereStream-aligned feature teams over one codebase; no sharing boundary between teamsEveryone is a TS generalist; web-platform and native-platform depth atrophiesNative pair + webPer-surface stream-aligned teams + a core-owning teamYou can fund the core team permanently, not just for the migrationAll native, share the coreThree platform silos + a complicated-subsystem core teamYou can hire and retain for four skill pools, including the rarest oneThin clientsBackend team owns all logic; client teams consume a contractThe API spec is the coordination point; client teams accept being downstreamWeb-first companionOne web team; native shells are packaging workMobile stays a companion — if it becomes the product, the topology is wrong
Two structural observations fall out of the table:

Sharing inside one team is cheap; sharing across teams is what Conway taxes. The JS-everywhere archetype works for small teams not because JS is special but because there is no team boundary running through the shared code. The moment the org grows enough to split teams, the boundary has to land somewhere — and wherever it lands becomes the interface that degrades first.
The pure states are stable; the hybrid state is where org costs concentrate. Airbnb, from direct experience: “The path of a world that is 100% native or 100% React Native is relatively straightforward. However, once you have a mix within your codebase, many new issues arise. How do you split up your teams? How do teams collaborate? … How do you hire and allocate resources across your organization?” (Building a Cross-Platform Mobile Team, Gabriel Peal, 2018-06-19, read in full 2026-08-29). Every migration between archetypes passes through that hybrid state — so the transition cost is an org cost more than a technical one, and it is paid even if you eventually retreat.

Who owns the shared core
The practical question every sharing decision on axis 2 reduces to. Three ownership options recur; the failure modes are the same ones the design-system cluster has already documented one layer up (design-system-governance).
1. Dedicated core team (platform model). The core is an internal product with an SLA and a roadmap. This is the only model with named production evidence in this cluster’s research passes — but it needs standing funding, not project funding. The design-system parallel is exact: Nathan Curtis, across 80+ design systems, reports the number thriving without centrally allocated people as “Zero. Zero. Zero percent.” A shared code core is the same economics one layer down: unfunded, it rots into the thing product teams route around (design-system-failure-modes gives the rule-of-thumb 12–24-month timeline for the design-system version). Risk: the core team becomes a bottleneck and loses touch with client-team friction — the same centralized-model weakness as in the governance table.
2. Strongest consumer owns it. The team that uses the core most (usually the largest client team) stewards it. Cheap to start; drifts predictably — the core evolves toward the owner’s platform, and the other clients become second-class consumers whose PRs wait. (Failure mode reasoned from the Conway mechanism and the design-system parallel; no named public postmortem for this specific shape found in this pass.)
3. Federated stewardship (“everyone owns it”). Contribution from all client teams, no central owner. This is the model Curtis publicly retracted for design systems — “Favoring federated was and is wrong … federated is not a choice, it’s a facet. In practice, it’s never pursued first and never without central investment” — and the mechanism is the same here (an unfunded shared artifact, contribution without an owner), so the correction should transfer: federated contribution is a maturity phase a funded core earns, not a way to avoid funding one. See design-system-governance for the full retraction.
What the documented failures were actually about
The two best-documented shared-core walk-aways are org failures wearing technical clothes:
Dropbox (shared C++ mobile core, abandoned by 2019). Eyal Guthmann’s postmortem (dropbox.tech, 2019-08-14, re-read 2026-08-29) itemizes the costs: a custom build system that “was a big drag on our resources as it needed to be constantly updated to support changes in two build systems”; a hiring-and-retention wall — a year-long specialist search failed, and “mobile developers simply did not want to work on a C++ project”; and the summary judgment, “this overhead ended up being more expensive than just writing the code twice.” Toolchain maintenance and hiring are both team-shape problems: the architecture assumed a standing C++-platform team the labor market wouldn’t staff.
Airbnb (React Native, sunset June 2018). The org half of the five-part series (part 3, cited above) lists the mechanisms: the technology was polarizing (“wildly different opinions varying from praising it as a silver bullet … to being wholly against any use …”); root-cause attribution blurred across the native/RN boundary (“it wasn’t clear which team an issue should be attributed”); hiring perception suffered (“many Android and iOS engineers were hesitant to apply”); and split teams fragmented expertise (“the code became fragmented … engineers no longer had the expertise to work across the entire flow”). Note the caveat Airbnb later appended to the post, still on the page: the technical points reflect end-of-2017 React Native and should be revalidated; “[a]ny organizational points should also be considered within the context, size, and culture of your organization.”
Both are big-company stories with parallel native teams already in place — the hybrid state from the table above. Neither says shared cores fail; both say shared cores fail when the team shape they imply can’t be staffed or funded. Which is the note’s claim in one sentence.
The checklist form
Before committing to a sharing decision, answer for the shared artifact it creates:

Who owns it in eighteen months? A named team with standing funding, or “the team that built it” (which is a migration crew, not an owner)?
Can you hire for the implied skill pools — including the rarest one — at your location, comp band, and brand? (Dropbox’s veto.)
Which team boundary does the sharing boundary cross? If the same team owns both sides, the coupling is cheap. If not, that interface is where drift starts.
What happens to the org during the migration, given the transition passes through the hybrid state even on a later retreat? (Airbnb’s cost was concentrated there.)
Is the core scoped as a thinnest-viable platform, with a mechanism for saying no to scope, or will it accrete until client teams route around it?

What we couldn’t establish

Any named public postmortem for the “strongest consumer owns it” model. Its failure mode below is reasoned from the Conway mechanism plus the design-system parallel, not observed in a published case.
Any multiplatform-native evidence for the federated-ownership correction. Curtis’s retraction is design-systems evidence, transferred here on the argument that both are unfunded shared artifacts. The transfer is an argued claim, not a measured one.
Team sizes, funding levels, or cost figures for any of the three ownership models. No source in this pass gives numbers, so the note can say which shapes exist and how they fail, but not what one costs.
How often the hybrid state is actually transited versus avoided. The claim that transition cost concentrates there rests on one company’s account of its own migration.
Recent walk-away evidence. Both documented cases are 2018–2019, from large orgs that already had parallel native teams — the same recency and selection problem multiplatform-app-architecture-options flags for the technology-side evidence. Airbnb’s own appended caveat says the organizational points “should also be considered within the context, size, and culture of your organization.” Treat both as existence proofs of a failure mode, not as base rates.

Scope guard
This note covers the org structure implied by sharing decisions — ownership, staffing shape, governance of the shared artifact. General org design (reporting lines, funding models, team sizing) is out of scope here; if that material ever earns a note it belongs in knowledge/general/, not this cluster.
Related

multiplatform-app-architecture-options — the five-axis option space this note is the org-side companion to
rust-shared-core-enterprise — the lane where the complicated-subsystem team shape is most pronounced
react-native-expo-enterprise — the Airbnb walk-away’s technical half
kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise — a shared-core decision whose counterfactuals are largely staffing arguments
design-system-governance — the same ownership problem one layer up, with the federated retraction this note leans on
design-system-failure-modes — what an unfunded shared artifact decays into, with timelines

Sources
Retrieved 2026-08-29 unless noted.

Conway’s Law original statement — “How Do Committees Invent?”, Datamation, April 1968
Martin Fowler — Conway’s Law — the coupling gloss and the inverse-Conway attribution to LeRoy and Simons
Team Topologies — key concepts — the four team types and Thinnest Viable Platform, quoted verbatim
Dropbox — The (not so) hidden cost of sharing code between iOS and Android — Eyal Guthmann, 2019-08-14, re-read 2026-08-29
Airbnb — Building a Cross-Platform Mobile Team — Gabriel Peal, 2018-06-19, part 3 of the sunset series, read in full 2026-08-29
Nathan Curtis’s federated-governance retraction is cited via design-system-governance, where it is sourced

tech/pc-build-matx-9070-xt.content:
Micro-ATX Gaming PC Build — RX 9070 XT (silence-first)
Compact mATX build, 1440p, optimized for acoustics and build quality. Budget €2,200–3,000 incl. VAT. No purchase date. Current spec lands at €2596.40 across two retailers (2026-07-27 pricing, excl. Windows and shipping).

⏸ Deferred as of 2026-07-31 — this build is not being made for now. oxzo’s current 7900 XTX machine stays in service as his daily driver, and the household’s other machine is the kid-tier pc-build-matx-kids-9060-xt, which was bought and is being assembled. Everything below remains a valid spec, but treat prices as stale and re-price before ordering. One knock-on recorded during the kids’ build: the €104.10 fan line here is a candidate for deletion, since the current machine already holds 6× Noctua 140 mm fans and this case’s top takes 2× 140 (rear is 120 only) — reuse rather than repurchase when this build reopens.

Verdict as of 2026-07-26: compatibility is sound; the shopping list is not. Build it, but renegotiate RAM, SSD and fans first.
For the kid-tier counterpart — same form factor and retailers, RX 9060 XT 16 GB + Ryzen 5 7500X3D + 32 GB, 1440p, €1717.82, Bazzite — see pc-build-matx-kids-9060-xt. It reaches the opposite conclusion on retailer splitting (€10.09 spread, so one order), and it resolves the Linux question the same way this build does, by moving the anti-cheat games to a console instead of buying Windows.

Pricing and SKU detail below come from a build audit dated 2026-07-25, supplied by oxzo. Not independently re-verified here.

Why mATX and not Mini-ITX
The 9070 XT is a 304 W part. In ITX volumes that heat leaves via fan RPM, and quiet cards are physically fat cards — so silence pushes volume back up. The premium ITX cases are also thermally compromised: the Fractal Terra caps the CPU cooler at 48 mm once a ≥50 mm GPU forces Max GPU mode, the Mood’s fabric restricts airflow, and the Ncase M1 is discontinued. mATX also returns ~€150–250 in ITX board and SFX PSU premiums.
Design rule: large volume, many fan mounts, everything spinning slowly. Airflow beats sound-damping foam for a 300 W GPU — foam muffles a fan working hard, airflow means it never has to.
Why not a “premium quiet” case instead (considered and rejected 2026-07-27)
The category barely exists at this size, and the reason is physical. Dampened cases work by solid foam-lined panels, restricted intake, and enough volume to run big fans slowly — a formula that needs volume (Define 7 ≈ 45 L, Silent Base 802 ≈ 55 L). At 26 L with a 304 W GPU, restricted intake makes the fans spin faster, and fan noise at source exceeds what foam removes downstream. The one dampened mATX case, Fractal’s Pop Mini Silent, is documented as running hot with powerful parts and suited to efficient mid-range components.
The A3-mATX’s real weakness is cable management, not acoustics — GN: “no channels or covers and there isn’t really any space behind the motherboard. Tie-down points are limited,” while otherwise rating it easy to work with and solidly built. A premium swap buys assembly experience, not quiet.
Fractal Design North (€174.90, Jimm’s) is the only serious alternative and fails on three counts: it is 45.1 L vs 26.3 L (there is no mATX North — it is an ATX mid-tower that accepts mATX boards), its cooler clearance drops to 145 mm with the front fan bracket fitted against the NH-U12A’s 158 mm, and it is itself a mesh airflow case rather than a damped one — the same philosophy for €88 more and nearly double the volume.
The build’s two loudest parts are already handled (NITRO+ at 26 dBA measured; NH-U12A with two NF-A12x25). GN’s zero-case-fan run landed within 1.5 °C of their best config, which bounds how much the chassis is contributing. Case swapping is the lowest-leverage money in this build; the open value problem remains the €519.90 RAM.

Fan layout
Resolved 2026-07-27 against GamersNexus’s bench test of this chassis. The case ships with no fans at all — all three are a purchase.
3× 120 mm, all exhaust: 2× top (rear-most positions) + 1× rear. Side and bottom stay empty.









































PositionFansDirectionWhyRear1ExhaustSits behind the NH-U12A’s rear fan and continues the cooler’s front-to-back path out of the case. Highest-value single fan.Top, rear two slots2ExhaustLifts the hot column off the CPU/VRM area.Top-front0—Sits above the front-mounted PSU at F2; would recirculate front-panel air instead of pulling from the CPU region.Side0—Feeds the GPU intake passively — see below.Bottom0—Forced by the 64 mm card.
Side intake is the trap. GN measured ~11 °C worse GPU temperature with 2× side intake versus none, and traced why: under top/rear-exhaust-only negative pressure the GPU pulls near-ambient air through the bottom mesh and inward through the unused rear PCIe slot covers. Side fans form a competing pressure system that shoots air above the card, stops the lower third of the side panel feeding it, and reverses the PCIe slot covers from intake to exhaust. GN names this build’s situation directly: a GPU this large “will effectively cut the case in half… will only be able to pull from the bottom and rear PCIe slot covers, meaning side intake will significantly hurt its performance.” Side fans do help the CPU substantially — it is a real trade, decided for the 304 W part over the ~120 W one.
GN’s own optimal config is unavailable here. Their winner was wood front + top exhaust + 2× bottom intake (GPU 47 °C over ambient, CPU 44 °C, 32 dBA). A 25 mm bottom fan caps GPU thickness at 61 mm; the NITRO+ is 64 mm.
Caveat on transferring GN’s numbers: they tested with a 240 mm AIO up top, which exhausts CPU heat directly. The NH-U12A dumps it into the case instead, so this build depends on top exhaust more than theirs did — hence two fans there rather than one.
Why not more. GN’s “wood stock” run — zero case fans, cooler only — finished just 1.5 °C behind their best CPU configuration. The chassis is ventilated enough that marginal fans buy very little thermal headroom while each adds a noise source. Three is the sweet spot; two (1 top + 1 rear) is defensible; four or more is spending acoustics for nothing.
Fan choice — 3× Noctua NF-A12x25 PWM chromax.black.swap, €34.70 each (€104.10) at Gigantti (oxzo’s brand preference, 2026-07-27). Matches the NH-U12A chromax.black, which already carries two of the same fan. Cheapest of the three retailers for this SKU (Verkkokauppa €34.99; Jimm’s does not stock the chromax at all) and it joins the Gigantti order, so no third shipment. Supports Zero RPM, so the fans stop entirely at idle; ships with Low-Noise Adapters.
Priced alternatives: NF-S12A ×3 €77.97 (Verkkokauppa); NF-A12x25 G2 ×3 €104.70 (Jimm’s, brown/beige); NF-A12x25 brown ×3 €101.97 (Verkkokauppa); NF-P12 redux-1300 ×3 €50.97 (Verkkokauppa); Corsair RS120 PWM 3-pack €29.90 (Gigantti); ARCTIC P12 Pro PST ×3 €32.70 (Jimm’s).
Open counterpoint worth revisiting if noise disappoints: Noctua splits its range by application — the S-series is airflow-optimised for unrestricted positions, the A- and F-series are pressure-optimised for radiators and heatsinks. All three positions here are free-air exhaust, which is exactly the S12A’s design case, at €26 less for the set. The chromax A12x25 was chosen on aesthetic match and order consolidation, not on blade-type fit; at the low RPMs expected the difference should be small, but this is the assumption to test first if the build is louder than hoped.
Traps checked while pricing Corsair (recorded in case the brand question reopens): iCUE LINK QX120/RX120 need a System Hub that only the “Starter Kit” SKUs include, so “Expansion” fans bought alone will not run; RS120 MAX is a 30 mm-thick static-pressure fan wrong for free-air exhaust; and the AF120 Elite appears discontinued (0 kpl at Verkkokauppa, Jimm’s page 404s).
Assembly constraints
These are build-defining, not preferences:

PSU mounts at the front-offset bracket position F2.
No bottom fans. The case’s GPU thickness limit drops to 61 mm when a 25 mm bottom fan is fitted; the NITRO+ is 64 mm, so a bottom fan is now ruled out by clearance, not just by preference. (The PURE at 61–61.6 mm was already over the line.) The GPU instead draws fresh air directly through the filtered bottom mesh, with its own fans sitting close to that intake. The limit only binds with a bottom fan — Lian Li’s baseline clearance is a 4-slot GPU up to 415 mm — but every extra millimetre of card is a millimetre less intake plenum above the mesh, which is the cost of the NITRO+ over the PURE.
Top-front position: leave empty.
Rear and top: exhaust. All-exhaust negative pressure is the point, not a compromise — it is what lets the GPU feed off the bottom mesh and rear PCIe slot covers. See Fan layout.
No side fans. Bench-measured ~11 °C GPU penalty in this chassis. Helps the CPU, costs the GPU more.
If bottom intake later proves necessary, use 15 mm slim fans only — and test GPU temperature and noise without them first. With the 64 mm NITRO+ even this needs re-measuring before ordering fans.
Cooler ceiling is 165 mm. be quiet! Dark Rock Pro 5 and Noctua NH-D15 G2 are both 168 mm and do not fit. Verified fitting: NH-U12A chromax.black (158 mm), Dark Rock 5 (161 mm), Thermalright Phantom Spirit 120 SE (155 mm).
Case accepts ATX/SFX/SFX-L PSUs up to 220 mm. Radiators if switching to liquid later: top 360/240, side 360/280/240, bottom 240.

GPU model selection
Re-verified 2026-07-27 against the full Verkkokauppa 9070 XT range. The PURE holds — but availability, not merit, is what decides it.
Case clearance filters nothing: Lian Li’s baseline is a 4-slot GPU up to 415 mm, and the widest 9070 XT on the market (XFX Mercury, 349 × 142 × 72 mm) still fits. The binding filters are acoustics and stock.
TechSpot’s 14-card roundup names five best-in-class models — XFX Mercury, Sapphire Nitro+, Sapphire Pure, PowerColor Red Devil, ASRock Taichi. Verkkokauppa stocks three, and the Taichi is out of stock. That leaves the PURE and the Nitro+.
Verkkokauppa range, 2026-07-27:













































































ModelPriceStockDispositionASUS Prime XT OC€669.80Ei saatavillaBottom of both thermal and gaming testsASRock Steel Legend€699.99Ei saatavillaHottest + loudest tierGigabyte GAMING OC€769.99Heti, >25Hottest + loudest tier — best stock, wrong cardGigabyte GAMING OC ICE€787.99Heti, 1Same coolerSapphire PULSE€789.99~1–2 wkRejected — see belowASRock Taichi OC€814.99Ei saatavillaTop tier, unobtainableGigabyte AORUS ELITE€829.99Ei saatavillaMid-tierASUS TUF Gaming OC€836.99Ei saatavillaWell built, unremarkable thermalsSapphire PURE OC€899.99~1 wkPickSapphire NITRO+ OC€955.99~1 wkDefensible upgradeNITRO+ PhantomLink / Polar€1129.99 / €1139.99~1–3 wkNo case for the premium
Why not the Pulse, despite looking like the value pick. TechPowerUp measured it at 25.5 dBA / 57 °C and called it the quietest 9070 XT they had tested. GamersNexus, testing in a hemi-anechoic chamber, found what buys that figure: memory at 90 °C (“90 becomes 95 inside a case pretty fast”), and a fan that cycles 1560 → 1400 → 1300 → 1390 → 1100 → 1258 → 1000 → 1170 → 1130 RPM under a fixed workload — “an irregular and annoying ramp/de-ramp rapidly cycling within a 2-3 minute period.” The VBIOS chases core temperature, so the fans never learn the memory is cooking. Perceived annoyance tracks variation, not absolute level: a steady 28 dBA beats a cycling 25.5 dBA. This also explains TechSpot’s independent finding of the Pulse running the warmest average GPU temp (62 °C) and hottest VRM (86 °C) — same relaxed curve, different instrument.
Two caveats on the PURE. No top-tier lab published a sound-pressure figure for it — TechPowerUp reviewed the Pulse and Nitro+ but not the PURE. Its acoustic standing rests on TechSpot’s noise-normalized results (strong) rather than a measured dBA number; the 31.9/33.6 dBA figures cited under Sources are from a weaker outlet on a non-comparable methodology. And it is white (black PCB, silver heatsink, non-white bracket) against a Wood-edition case.
Defensible upgrade — Sapphire NITRO+ OC, €955.99 (+€56). TechPowerUp measured 26 dBA under load and an 83 °C hotspot, and rated its cooler the strongest of the four tested. The 12V-2x6 connector hides behind a magnetic backplate and routes toward the motherboard — worth real money in 26.3 L with the PSU at F2, and the Seasonic ships a native 12V-2x6 cable so no adapter is involved. Against it: 64 mm vs 61 mm costs 3 mm of the bottom-mesh intake plenum this build’s cooling depends on, 1894 g vs 1233 g, and the RAM line already strains the budget.
Prices and stock as of 2026-07-27; re-check at order time.
PSU selection
Resolved 2026-07-27 against Verkkokauppa stock. The two hard requirements — a zero-RPM (semi-passive) fan mode and two independently usable PCIe cable runs, meaning two separate cables rather than one daisy-chained pair — eliminate most 850 W ATX 3.1 Gold units on the shelf.
Pick: Seasonic FOCUS GX-850 ATX 3.1 (2024), €140.90 at Jimm’s. 80 PLUS Gold, ATX 3.1 / PCIe 5.1, fully modular, selectable semi-passive mode, 135 mm FDB fan, 10-year warranty. Ships 3× PCIe 6+2 on three separate cables plus a 12V-2x6 600 W cable. At 140 mm deep it is 20 mm shorter than the Corsair — real cable-bend room at the front-offset F2 bracket in 26.3 L. Stock was thin (3–4 units).
Alternative: Corsair RM850x ATX 3.1 (2024), €163.99. Same boxes ticked, plus Cybenetics Gold, a 140 mm FDB fan, and a manual fan-override knob; also 3× PCIe 6+2 all on separate cables. 160 mm deep, €21 dearer, but deep stock (>25 units) — the safer order if buying is not immediate.
Rejected and why:

ASUS Prime 850W Gold ATX 3.1 (€118.99) — no zero-RPM, one PCIe cable in box, not shippable at time of check. Fails both requirements.
MSI MAG A850GL PCIE5 — no semi-passive operation; 4× PCIe on two daisy-chained cables; 5-year warranty.
Cooler Master MWE Gold 850 V3 ATX 3.1 (€122.99) — has zero-RPM, but a 120 mm ball-bearing fan at 2300 RPM max; reviewed with “high fan noise at max load” and thermal stress. Wrong unit for a silence-first build.
Asus TUF Gaming 850W (€104.90) — cheapest, but the fan profile is tuned for component temperature rather than noise.
Corsair RM850e (€148.99), ASUS ROG Strix 850W Platinum (€161.99) — both advertise zero-RPM / 0 dB; PCIe cable-run counts not verified, and neither undercuts the RM850x enough to justify chasing.

Both shortlisted units supply three independent PCIe runs, so the choice holds whether the ordered 9070 XT variant takes 2× or 3× 8-pin.
Prices and stock as of 2026-07-27; re-check at order time.

Order from two stores: Jimm’s + Gigantti. No third order improves it. With the PURE the optimum is €2465.30; with the NITRO+ chosen it is €2492.30 — see the order sheet for the per-store split and links.
Jimm’s alone is €2537.20 (+€71.90) if one order and one warranty contact is worth that. The premium is three lines — CPU €459.90 vs €419.00 (+€40.90), SSD €194.90 vs €169.90 (+€25.00), cooler €135.90 vs €129.90 (+€6.00); Jimm’s wins the rest. Net of Gigantti’s shipping the real gap is smaller. Verkkokauppa alone is €2656.92 (+€191.62) and is cheapest on none of the eight lines — it held the SSD line at 2 TB (€298.99, and Gigantti didn’t stock that capacity), so dropping to 1 TB took its last win. An all-Gigantti build remains impossible: no Wood case, board unavailable.
Price isn’t the only axis. Verkkokauppa and Jimm’s can each supply the whole build; Gigantti cannot. Verkkokauppa also has five pickup points and 1-hour Helsinki delivery against Jimm’s shipping from Turku, so the €191.62 narrows once shipping is priced — and it is the fallback if Jimm’s thin RAM stock or 5–10 day GPU lead time bites.
The NITRO+ is the chosen GPU as of 2026-07-27 — at €855.90 from Gigantti it costs €27.00 over the Jimm’s PURE while shipping immediately instead of on a 5–10 day supplier order, and it is the only 9070 XT in the shortlist with a published load-noise measurement.
Three conclusions that outlive the prices:

The board campaign is dated. Jimm’s B850M-PLUS WIFI at €169.90 against €244.90 list runs to 16.8.2026 or 30 units. This is the campaign the parts table flagged as “worth pursuing.”
Retailer arbitrage does not solve the RAM. €519.90 / €519.90 / €529.99 — a €10 spread on a €520 part. The largest value problem needs a different kit or a delay, not a different shop.
Two stock traps in the all-Jimm’s basket: RAM down to 2 units (Gigantti has 50+), and the GPU is a supplier order (5–10 days), not own stock.

Totals exclude fans (no SKU chosen), Windows and shipping.
This changes the GPU verdict. Gigantti’s NITRO+ at €855.90 is €44 below Verkkokauppa’s PURE and only €27 above Jimm’s PURE, with 25+ units shipping immediately. The NITRO+ was previously reasoned about as a +€56 upgrade; at +€27, against a card with a lab-measured 26 dBA where the PURE has no equivalent measurement, the case is much stronger. The counterweights are unchanged and marginal: 64 mm vs 61 mm costs 3 mm of bottom-mesh intake plenum, and 1894 g vs 1233 g.
Two cards from TechSpot’s best-five that Verkkokauppa never stocked are available at Jimm’s — PowerColor Red Devil Spectral White €869.90 and Hellhound Spectral White €852.90 (mid-tier performer). Jimm’s also has the ASRock Taichi OC in stock at €1099.90, €285 over Verkkokauppa’s dead listing — not worth it.
Two verification notes:

A cached search result advertised the PURE at Jimm’s for €739.90. That campaign expired 31.1.2026; the live price is €828.90. Price-comparison and search snippets for this vault’s Finnish retailers go stale — open the product page.
⚠ Gigantti’s Seasonic listing (product 854300) claims a 120 mm fan and six 6+2-pin connectors. Hardware Busters measured a 135 mm fan and three PCIe 6+2 cables on the GX-850 V4 ATX 3.1. The price matches the ATX 3.1 model but the spec copy appears lifted from an older SKU — confirm before ordering there. Jimm’s and Verkkokauppa list it unambiguously.

Prices and stock as of 2026-07-27; re-check at order time.
Value problems to resolve before ordering
In priority order:

RAM (€500–520). The single largest value problem. Replace or postpone. The AI-datacenter DRAM shortage tripled DDR5 prices through 2026 and mid-2026 forecasts point to continued tightness — so waiting is a gamble, not a plan. If 6000 CL30 EXPO is unavailable, a 5600–6000 CL36 kit in stock beats waiting.
SSD. Substitute a better-priced 2 TB TLC drive for the KC3000. Resolved 2026-07-27 — dropped to WD_BLACK SN7100 1 TB at €169.90, saving €129 against the 2 TB option and €155 against the rejected KC3000 2 TB. Accepted tradeoff: 1 TB is roughly a five-or-six-game working set once Windows or Bazzite is on it, so installs get managed rather than hoarded. Expansion is deliberately cheap — the B850M-PLUS WIFI has 3× M.2 slots and the case has 3 drive bays, so a second NVMe later needs one drive and a side panel, no rebuild.
Case fans — deliberately not economised. The original concern was that three premium fans are over-spec, and on thermal grounds that still holds: cheaper sets were priced at €29.90–€50.97 and GN’s zero-fan run was within 1.5 °C of their best config. Three NF-A12x25 chromax.black at €104.10 were chosen anyway, on brand preference and match with the chromax cooler. This is the cheapest line to revisit if the budget tightens — roughly €55 recoverable. See Fan layout.
Cooler. A cheaper AM5 air cooler is fine if acoustics and long-term Noctua mounting support are not priorities.
Windows. Add its cost to the finished-system budget if needed. (Not required if running Bazzite/Fedora — see Linux notes.)
Retailers. Consolidate only after weighing component savings against added shipping and return complexity.

Pre-order checklist

 Recheck every SKU and live price — all eight lines repriced 2026-07-27 across three retailers (fans still unpriced)
 Confirm stock, shipping, return terms, campaign expiry
 Confirm RAM SKU KF560C30BBEK2-32, EXPO support, motherboard QVL listing
 Confirm the GPU choice against the field — PURE re-verified 2026-07-27; thickness is not a binding constraint without a bottom fan
 Do not order 25 mm bottom fans
 Confirm the PSU ships two independently usable PCIe cable runs — Seasonic FOCUS GX-850 ATX 3.1 ships three separate PCIe 6+2 cables
 Plan PSU installation at F2
 Include Windows in the budget if required
 Compare mixed-retailer savings against single-retailer warranty simplicity — done 2026-07-27; two orders (Jimm’s + Gigantti) hit the €2465.30 optimum, Jimm’s alone costs €65.90 more
 Order the board before the Jimm’s campaign ends 16.8.2026 (or accept €244.90 list)
 Pick case fans — 3× Noctua NF-A12x25 chromax.black.swap, 2× top + 1× rear, all exhaust; side and bottom empty

All lines are compared across Verkkokauppa, Jimm’s and Gigantti above. Not yet checked: Proshop.fi, Datatarjous.fi; cross-check Hintaopas.fi.
Search snippets and price-comparison sites go stale on these retailers — open the product page. Three expired campaigns surfaced as current during this pass: the PURE at Jimm’s for €739.90 (expired 31.1.2026), the A3-mATX Wood at Jimm’s for €69.90 (expired 31.3.2026), and the 9800X3D at Gigantti for €439.90 (a dated April figure; live price €419.00).
Undervolting
The 9070 XT undervolts well — around −100 mV with a reduced power limit trades roughly 10 % performance for a substantial power drop (figures reported for the non-XT 9070; XT is directionally similar, not separately verified). At 1440p there are frames to spare, so this is close to free acoustic headroom. Tune after assembly rather than buying more cooling.
Linux
See wine-proton-gaming-linux, bazzite-brainhost-ops-runbook.

RDNA 4 is well supported on current kernels/Mesa (RADV); Bazzite and Fedora 42+ handle the 9070 XT out of the box, avoiding NVIDIA driver-packaging friction on atomic distros.
GPU undervolting needs amdgpu.ppfeaturemask set for full overdrive access; LACT is the usual tool (unverified against current Bazzite releases).
FSR 4 works through recent Mesa/Proton paths (unverified — check Bazzite release notes at build time).

Micro-ATX Kids’ Gaming PC — RX 9060 XT 16 GB (Hogwarts Legacy class, 1080p/1440p)
Comparison build against pc-build-matx-9070-xt. Same form factor and same retailers, different goal: a machine for a 9- and a 7-year-old playing Hogwarts Legacy-class single-player games. The Roblox/Fortnite layer that normally comes with that age group is not this machine’s job — it lives on the household Xbox Series X, which is what makes the Bazzite decision below possible.
Verdict: build it as a 1440p machine. The resolution question has no price attached. Inside the box, 1080p and 1440p cost the same — €0 difference — because the cheapest GPU worth buying is already a competent 1440p card and the 8 GB variants are not cheaper in Finland. On the display side a 27” QHD gaming panel (€170.99) sits inside the 1080p gaming-monitor price band (€110–200). Nothing in this build gets cheaper by targeting 1080p.
Box total as planned €1717.82 from Verkkokauppa alone (2026-07-30 pricing, excl. monitor and shipping; the fan line changed at purchase — see the order sheet) — €878.58 less than the 9070 XT build’s €2596.40, at 66 % of its cost. No OS line: this is a Bazzite machine (decided 2026-07-30, see below), so the €139.00 Windows licence the anti-cheat situation would otherwise force never gets bought.
Spec upgraded 2026-07-30 to Ryzen 5 7500X3D + 32 GB (+€295.00 over the original Hogwarts-Legacy-only draft). Both changes are driven by the same thing: WoW and Dragon’s Dogma 2 are on the list, and both are CPU- and memory-bound in ways a Hogwarts Legacy-class library is not. Neither is a resolution decision.
The remaining money fork is the 9070 GPU tier-up (+€213.09), and it is the one to skip — it buys nothing in either of the two games that drove this upgrade.

Asked 2026-07-30, and the answer promoted the 7500X3D and 32 GB into the default spec. Both games are CPU-bound, and both are exactly the workload 3D V-Cache exists for. AMD’s spec page confirms the 7500X3D is a real 3D V-Cache part: Zen 4, 6C/12T, 96 MB L3 against the 7600X’s 32 MB, 4.0/4.5 GHz.
World of Warcraft. The GPU is enormous overkill; a 9060 XT 16 GB will not be the limiter at 1440p in any scenario. The limiter is single-thread CPU and cache in the three places WoW gets heavy — 20-man raids, dense M+ pulls, and capital cities. A 7600X is comfortable questing and in the open world; a 96 MB L3 part is the one that holds the floor when a raid boss and forty nameplates arrive at once. Linux side is proven ground here: the Battle.net/Lutris path works, and the known failure mode is already documented in voice-proxy-crash-linux-fix (rename WowVoiceProxy.exe and the ERROR #132 mid-fight crashes stop).
Dragon’s Dogma 2 is the problem child, and no CPU in this price class fixes it. GamersNexus’s benchmark piece is titled “Dragon’s Dogma 2 is a Mess: GPU & CPU Benchmarks, Bottlenecks, & Crashes,” and the shape of the problem is structural rather than a hardware shortfall:

Vernworth is severely CPU-limited. Reported testing found a negligible gap between Low and Max settings inside the city — the graphics settings barely move the frame rate, which is the signature of a CPU wall. A Ryzen 5 5600X + RX 6600 at 1080p on lowest settings averaged 39 fps with 20 fps 1 % lows in Vernworth, and first-pass traversal drove 0.1 % lows to about 6 fps. (Figures from secondary reporting of GN/PC Gamer coverage, not read off the source charts.)
Outside the cities it is a normal GPU-bound game and the 9060 XT 16 GB handles 1440p fine. DD2 is also VRAM-hungry at higher settings, which is another mark against ever considering the 8 GB variant.
A 7600X is a solid step up from the 5600X in those reports, and a 7500X3D more so, but the honest expectation is good frame rates in the world and compromised 1 % lows in Vernworth. That is DD2 on every PC.

Hogwarts Legacy is Gold/Deck Verified; DD2 is ProtonDB Silver, and the reports that run well lean on custom Proton builds (GE-Proton, CachyOS Proton) plus launch options rather than working untouched. It runs — dragons-dogma-2-mods-linux already documents the REFramework mod path under Proton on this household’s hardware — but budget setup time, and do not hand it to a child as a first-run experience.

Adding two more 8 GB sticks later does not work well (corrected 2026-07-30)
The board has four DIMM slots, so this looks like a free upgrade path. On AM5 it is not, for two independent reasons:

Four DIMMs drop the memory speed. ASUS’s own spec sheet for the PRIME B650M-A WIFI II lists 4800 as the only non-OC rated speed — every rate from 5200 to 7600+ is marked (OC) — and footnotes that the supported data rate “vary[s] depending on the CPU and memory configuration [and] number of DRAM modules.” In practice four single-rank DDR5 sticks on AM5 land near 4800 rather than 6000. Because Infinity Fabric is coupled to memory speed on this platform, that is a permanent, everywhere loss of frames traded for capacity the machine may never need. (The 4800-with-4-DIMMs figure is the consistent community finding across Tom’s Hardware, Overclock.net and PCPartPicker threads, not a lab measurement I verified.)
Two kits bought separately are not a validated pair. EXPO profiles are qualified for the kit, not for two kits side by side. Even an identical part number ordered a year later can be a different die revision or batch, and it is not guaranteed to POST at rated timings.

So the real upgrade is sell or redeploy the 2×8 kit and buy a 2×16, which keeps two DIMMs and keeps 6000 CL30. That makes a 16 GB kit a full purchase rather than a down payment on 32 GB — and it is the whole reason 32 GB went into the default spec rather than being deferred.
Buying 2×16 up front is not free of that logic either: it leaves the two spare slots as an equally bad path to 64 GB. But 32 GB is where this machine’s workload actually sits, so the spare slots are decoration, not a plan.

AM5 boards will often read XMP timings anyway, but that is a hope, not a QVL entry, and troubleshooting a child’s PC that boots at 4800 MT/s is a bad trade for €120.
G.Skill Aegis 55 32 GB “(32 GB × 1)” 6000 CL36, €399.90 (Gigantti, 5 kpl) — a single 32 GB module. On AM5 that is single-channel operation and a large, permanent gaming penalty. The listing reads like a 32 GB kit. It is not.

The Crucial Pro OC 32 GB CL36 at €449.00 is the only 32 GB kit under €500 that looks legitimate; its EXPO support is unverified — confirm on the product page and the board QVL before treating it as an option.
Storage — 1 TB, and the one upgrade path that actually works
Yes, an old 3.5” spinning disk fits — with two caveats
Asked 2026-07-30. Cooler Master’s spec sheet gives the S400 4× 3.5” bays, 4× 2.5” bays and one 5.25” bay, and the HDD cage is removable and mountable in three positions — forward for a longer PSU, backwards for radiator room, or out entirely with one screw. The board has 4× SATA 6Gb/s. So capacity is not the question.
Caveat 1 — cage position versus a 304 mm GPU. Reviewers report “limited clearance to the 3.5” HDD cage, even with the cage in its furthest forward position” with a long card, fitting only after cable manipulation. The ASUS PRIME 9060 XT at 304 mm is long, if inside the 319 mm limit. Expect the cage position to be dictated by the GPU rather than chosen freely, and check it before buying extra drives.
Caveat 2 — the PSU is exactly at the limit. CM lists PSU clearance as 140 mm with the HDD cage in the backmost position. The Seasonic G12 GM-650 is 140 × 150 × 86 mm — a zero-margin fit in that position, and comfortable with the cage forward. It fits either way, but there is no slack.
The real objection is noise, not fit. A spinning disk is the one part of this machine that cannot be made quiet. In a build where €59.99 bought dampening and a fan profile that idles near-stopped, spindle whine and seek chatter become the loudest thing in the room — undoing on the noise axis exactly what the case was chosen for. The Silencio series mitigates it (dampening material behind the front panel and lining the steel side panels, rubber-padded fan mounts) but cannot remove it.
Reasonable use: bulk overflow — old game installs, media, backups — on a drive set to spin down when idle, given 1 TB is tight for this library. Unreasonable use: as the drive anything actually loads from, or as a reason to skip a second NVMe later, which the free M.2 slot makes cheap and silent.
Decided 2026-07-30: the backup disk goes in a USB dock, not in the case
Asked for a drive holding image backups rather than anything in active use, and settled the same day. Not mounting is not the same as not spinning — a SATA drive that has power spins up at POST whatever the mount state, so noauto silences the filesystem, not the platters. Solving this internally means three separate mechanisms, and solving it externally means none.
The external answer is better on its own merits, not just simpler. In a USB dock or enclosure the drive is silent, cool and unpowered whenever it is unplugged — and a backup that is physically disconnected cannot be encrypted by ransomware, deleted by a curious 9-year-old, or wiped when the machine gets reinstalled. For archive media that separation is the point, not a compromise. It also sidesteps the cage-versus-304 mm-GPU clearance question entirely.
Kept for reference — if a spinning disk ever does go inside, the pieces are:

That last row was the argument that settled it: the one mechanism that solves the actual problem is also the one that costs a package layer on a system where layers are being kept to a minimum on purpose.
Consequences of the dock decision, all favourable:

The HDD-cage-versus-304 mm-GPU clearance question is moot for this build. The cage can go in whichever position suits the GPU and the PSU, or come out entirely on its one screw.
No /etc configuration, no second rpm-ostree layer, no spin-up noise in a case bought for silence.

Silence, dust and reliability — why the case, cooler and fan lines are what they are
Asked 2026-07-30, and folded into the default spec the same day. All three goals land on the same three lines — case, cooler, fan layout — and none of them is expensive, because the thermal load here is small enough that quiet is bought with size and filtration rather than with premium fans. +€59.99 total, 3.6 % of the build.
Total heat is ~225 W (160 W GPU + 65 W CPU). That number is what makes the whole package work, and it is also what invalidates the parent build’s advice.

It named Fractal’s Pop Mini Silent as running hot with powerful parts and “suited to efficient mid-range components.”
This build is efficient mid-range components. The condition that killed the category is absent, so the category comes back.

Fans — run positive pressure, which also inverts the parent build
The parent build runs all-exhaust negative pressure, deliberately, because its 304 W card had to pull air through the bottom mesh and the rear PCIe slots. That reasoning is GPU-specific and does not apply here.
For dust, do the opposite: more intake than exhaust, so the case sits slightly pressurised and air enters through the filters instead of being sucked in through every unfiltered seam. Practical layout in the S400:

2× front intake (behind the front filter) + 1× rear exhaust. Leave the top empty.
The case ships 1 front + 1 rear Silencio FP 120, so this needs one more 120 mm fan at minimum.

As built 2026-07-31 — 2× NF-A12x25 G2 front intake, stock Silencio FP rear
This supersedes both the ARCTIC P12 order-sheet line and the 140 mm revision below it. Bought: 2× Noctua NF-A12x25 G2 PWM (Sx2-PP twin pack), plus the Peerless Assassin 120 SE as the CPU cooler.

Still 2 in / 1 out, positive pressure. Three chassis fans against the board’s three chassis headers — no splitters needed. Skip the bundled Low-Noise Adaptors — but keep them. A BIOS PWM curve covers the same range adaptively instead of capping RPM permanently, and at ~225 W in 33.9 L these fans sit near minimum regardless. The one thing an LNA does that a curve cannot is lower the floor: a curve can’t take a fan below its own minimum duty. If the front intakes turn out to be audible at idle on the flattest curve available, that is the case for fitting them.
Why the good fans go at the front. The front is the only intake and the most restricted position in the case, pulling through a dust filter. Pressure-optimised A-series blades belong there; the rear vents into open air, where the stock Silencio FP is adequate. Noctua splits its range by application — S-series for free air, A- and F-series for restriction — so an A12x25 G2 at a filtered intake is the blade type matched to the job.
⚠ The one risk this choice carries. The 140 mm revision below chose that size partly to sidestep a reported conflict between 120 mm front fan mounts and long GPUs. Going 120 takes that bet: the ASUS PRIME card is 304 mm against a 319 mm limit, so there is margin, but reviewers report front-fan interference in this case with long cards. Dry-fit the GPU with both front fans mounted before routing any cables. The front bracket is slotted, so shifting the fans vertically usually resolves it; the fallback is a single upper front intake plus the rear exhaust.

Why it was dropped (decided 2026-07-31). A fan-shuffle across machines was considered: move 140 mm Noctuas from oxzo’s current 7900 XTX machine (which has six of them) into the kids’ front, and backfill with the new 120s. Three things killed it:

The pc-build-matx-9070-xt build is deferred, and it was the only destination that actually wanted 140s — its A3-mATX top takes 2× 140 and its fan line was unbought. Without it there is no move worth making.
The 7900 XTX machine is a running daily driver cooling a much hotter card than this 160 W one. Disturbing a working, dialled-in cooling setup to marginally improve an already over-cooled box is backwards.
A 120 mm fan does not bolt into a 140 mm mount — different hole patterns, so backfilling needs adapter brackets that generally are not included. It is not the clean one-for-one swap it looks like.

The note’s original “don’t buy Noctua, buy €5.60 fans” advice is withdrawn, and it was wrong for a specific reason. It reasoned from the parent build, where €104.10 of NF-A12x25 bought quiet for a 304 W card and looked like overkill for a 160 W one. That compared the wrong thing: at 225 W the cheap fans are indeed already inaudible at their duty cycle, but the intake still has a dust filter in front of it, and blade type — not price — is what decides a restricted position. The parent note’s own open counterpoint — that Noctua splits its range by application, S-series for free air and A-series for restriction — points toward the A-series here, where all three of that build’s positions pointed away from it.

Build day — what this specific parts list needs (2026-07-31)
Not generic assembly advice; these are the things that bite this combination of parts.

The full ordered build guide is pc-build-kids-assembly-runbook (written 2026-08-01, when the build started) — bench test, case prep, cabling map, BIOS settings, Bazzite install and a no-POST table. The list below is the subset that is decisions, and stays here because it belongs with the reasoning; the runbook is the thing to have open at the desk.

Before the CPU goes in


Flash the BIOS first — and this is now a likely requirement, not insurance (corrected 2026-08-01). The board has a USB BIOS FlashBack button (ASUS techspec), which flashes with only the PSU connected — no CPU, RAM or GPU needed.
An earlier revision of this note read the ASUS CPU QVL as showing 2613 for the 7500X3D and dismissed the column as suspect because “it showed the same figure for every 7000X3D part.” That was a misreading. The column varies correctly, and the 7500X3D is on the far side of the split: the QVL gives it 3263, against 2613 for the 7600X and 7800X3D (read 2026-08-01; single read of a paginated table — re-confirm at build time).
The split is not arbitrary. 2613 is the mid-2024 BIOS that added initial Ryzen 9000 / Zen 5 support (AGESA 1.1.7.0); 3263 is the later one covering the parts that launched after that — 9850X3D, 9700F, 9500F and the PRO 9000 series all show 3263 too (this bucket structure verified directly in the QVL table). The 7500X3D launched November–December 2025, roughly a year after 2613.
So any board manufactured before late 2025 cannot know this CPU exists, and a B650 SKU from 2024 that has been sitting in the channel is a real possibility. The failure mode is total: no video, no beep, CPU Q-LED lit, nothing that says “BIOS.” It is recoverable — FlashBack works with the CPU installed and the machine fully built — so skipping the flash risks an hour of misdiagnosis rather than the build. Flash it anyway; it costs ten minutes at a point where nothing is assembled.
⚠ Target ≥3263, not “latest.” The top BIOS as of 2026-08-01 is 3886 (2026-07-02), flagged Beta on ASUS’s download page. There is no reason to run a beta here. FlashBack expects the file renamed to P650MAW2.CAP — ASUS’s BIOSRenamer utility, included in the download ZIP, does it for you.


Bench-test on the box — board, CPU, cooler, one DIMM, GPU, PSU — before anything is buried behind a 304 mm card in 33.9 L.


Case prep, before the board goes in

Remove the 3.5” HDD cage entirely (one screw). The backup drive is external by decision, so the cage has no job, and pulling it fixes two things at once: the reported clearance conflict between long cards and the cage, and the PSU squeeze — CM lists 140 mm PSU clearance with the cage backmost against the Seasonic’s exactly 140 mm depth.
Dry-fit the GPU against both front fans before routing any cable. This is the one clearance the note never closed — see the fan section.
Leave the top empty. A top exhaust would make the case 2-in/2-out and throw away the positive pressure the filtered case was chosen for.

Assembly

M.2 before the GPU. The SN7100 goes in M.2_1 (top slot, PCIe 5.0 x4 with a Ryzen 7000 CPU), which sits under the graphics card. If the board ships an M.2 heatsink, peel the film off its thermal pad.
RAM in A2 and B2 — second and fourth slots from the CPU. Two sticks in A1/B1 is the classic no-POST.
Mount the cooler on the bench; check the Peerless Assassin’s front fan does not overhang the first DIMM.

Power

The card takes exactly 1× 8-pin and ASUS recommends a 550 W PSU (ASUS techspec), so the 650 W unit is comfortable. Use the dedicated PCIe cable, not a daisy-chain off a peripheral run. The G12 GM is semi-modular — 24-pin and EPS are hardwired.
PSU fan-down, over the filtered bottom vent.

First boot

Enable EXPO. It does not turn itself on, and 32 GB quietly running 4800 JEDEC instead of 6000 CL30 is invisible unless you look.
Do not raise SoC voltage manually on an X3D part. Run EXPO and leave it — which is why step 1 comes first.
Q-Fan: flat, low curves with long ramp times on all three chassis fans. This is where the silence is actually bought; slow response also avoids the ramp/de-ramp cycling that pc-build-matx-9070-xt documents as more irritating than a steady higher noise floor.
Secure Boot — Bazzite needs it disabled or its key enrolled.

OS — Bazzite, with the anti-cheat games offloaded to the Xbox
Decided 2026-07-30: Bazzite. Fortnite and Roblox go on the household’s Xbox Series X instead of driving the PC’s OS choice, so the €139.00 Windows licence never gets bought.
This is worth recording as a division of labour, not just an OS pick, because the constraint that would otherwise force Windows is real and permanent. AreWeAntiCheatYet — the tracker for anti-cheat status on Linux/Proton — lists both games as Denied as of 2026-07-30, meaning the developer has explicitly declined Proton support:

Fortnite — Denied. Noted as having run “for a short period of time” and no longer. Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux (Rocket League shipped EAC in April 2026 with Steam Deck/Linux working), so this is Epic declining to enable it, not a technical wall — it could change, and hasn’t in years.
Roblox — Denied. Its Hyperion anti-cheat blocks the Windows client under Wine.

So the split is: PC = Steam single-player and everything Proton runs well; Xbox = anti-cheat live-service and Bedrock crossplay. Each box does what it is actually good at, and neither compromises for the other. If the kids later want Fortnite on the PC, that decision costs €139.00 and a reinstall — not a rebuild.
The flagship title is fine. Hogwarts Legacy is ProtonDB Gold and Steam Deck Verified. Reports on the page describe it as very playable with the usual caveat that it is poorly optimised on Windows too; one report notes a 2–3 second periodic freeze out of the box that GE-Proton fixed, which is the normal Bazzite tinker and something you already know how to do — see bazzite-brainhost-ops-runbook and wine-proton-gaming-linux.
GPU driver: RDNA 4 is well supported on current kernels and Mesa, which is the parent note’s finding for the 9070 XT and applies to the 9060 XT as the same architecture and the same RADV path. Not separately verified for this specific card — the 9060 XT launched later than the 9070 XT, so a current Mesa matters, which is exactly what Bazzite ships.
The one thing Bazzite costs you here
Windows would have brought Microsoft Family Safety playtime limits for free. For a 9- and a 7-year-old that is a real feature, and on Linux it is a manual build:

malcontent — app-level restrictions, part of the GNOME/Flatpak parental-controls stack.
timekpr-next — the standard screen-time limiter. It is a system daemon, so on an atomic base it means an rpm-ostree overlay rather than a Flatpak.
GNOME 50 is reported to be adding native bedtime and daily screen-time controls (reported January 2026, unverified) — but Bazzite’s flagship image is KDE, so that path may not apply.

Neither tool is verified working on Bazzite here — I found the Universal Blue forum thread asking the same question but could not read its replies. Treat parental controls as an open task with a known toolset, not a solved problem. Worth deciding before the machine lands in a child’s room, because retrofitting time limits after the fact is a negotiation rather than a setting.
The €139.00 saved is close to the €170.99 the 1440p monitor costs. That is the honest reallocation: the OS decision pays for the display.
The resolution question, priced
The framing was “1080p or 1440p if the price difference is low.” The difference is not low — it is zero inside the box, and roughly zero outside it.
Inside the box: the same GPU, CPU, RAM and PSU serve both. There is no cheaper GPU worth buying (TechSpot: least expensive card anyone should consider), the 8 GB variants are not cheaper locally, and 16 GB of VRAM at 1080p is not waste — it is what keeps Hogwarts Legacy’s texture streaming out of trouble. A 1080p-targeted build and a 1440p-targeted build are the same parts list.
Outside the box: 27” QHD gaming panels start at €170.99 (ASUS TUF Gaming VG27AQE5A). The 24” 1080p gaming field runs roughly €110–200 — e.g. LG 24U411B 24” FHD IPS €109.99 (2–3 week lead), MSI G255F 24.5” FHD €199.99. A 1440p monitor is cheaper than several 1080p ones. Buy for panel quality and refresh rate, not resolution tier.
Recommendation: 1440p, high preset, RT off, FSR in reserve. At 1080p the card is far above any refresh rate two young children will notice, which makes 1080p a legitimate fallback if a spare monitor already exists — but nothing about the purchase changes.

Kid-specific constraints
Not derivable from the parent build, and worth deciding before ordering:

Two kids, one machine — decided 2026-07-30: build one now, a second later. Nine and seven will not share a PC peacefully at the hours they both want it, so this is deferred rather than solved. When the second one comes up, re-run the Steam Machine comparison: two of those is €2,078 against €3,435 for two of this build, and that is the scenario where it wins.
Front-panel USB-A. Controllers, headsets and USB sticks in this house are USB-A. A case with only front USB-C is a daily irritation.
Glass side panels. A tempered-glass panel next to two children is a risk the parent build never had to price. The Silencio S400 is sold in both a sound-dampened steel panel SKU and a glass one — buy the steel one, and confirm which the retailer stocks.
Cheap, replaceable fans. Superseded 2026-07-31 — 2× Noctua NF-A12x25 G2 were bought. The original argument was that a machine which gets moved, kicked and repositioned does not deserve €104 of Noctua. The counter-argument that won: the front intake pulls through a dust filter, and pressure-optimised blades are the right tool for that position regardless of what the box costs. See the fan section.
Filters get cleaned or they stop working. Front/top/bottom filters plus positive pressure is the plan; it needs a rinse every few months to be worth anything. Pick a case whose filters come out without tools — this is a reliability decision, not a tidiness one.
Parental controls are the cost of the Bazzite decision — malcontent plus timekpr-next, set up by hand, neither verified here. See the OS section; decide it before the machine reaches a child’s room.

Upgrade path — keep this platform, don’t plan a rebuild
Asked 2026-07-30: is this a 2–4 year machine that gets replaced, or one that gets upgraded? Upgraded. The expensive, slow-moving parts are all adequate and the fast-moving ones are all replaceable — which is unusual for a build at this price, and mostly an accident of AM5.
The socket is the whole argument. AMD extended AM5 support through 2029 at Computex 2026, up from the previous “2027+”, covering Zen 6 and possibly Zen 7 — reported by Tom’s Hardware and TweakTown; not read off an AMD primary source here. The board already supports Ryzen 9000 per ASUS’s own spec. So in 2028 this machine takes a then-current X3D chip without touching board, RAM, case or PSU.
Clean upgrades — drop-in, no compromise:





















PathWhy it is easyCPUAM5 to 2029. The single biggest lever, and everything else stays. The Peerless Assassin 120 SE already has headroom well past a 120 W X3D.Storage1 of 2 M.2 slots free. Adding a drive penalises nothing — see the storage section.PSU / cooler / fansAll standard parts, all swappable in an evening.
Constrained but workable:

GPU — capped at 319 mm by the case. That is a real filter, not a formality: the parent build’s Sapphire NITRO+ 9070 XT is 327 mm and would not fit. Plenty of shorter mid-range and upper-mid cards do.
GPU — 650 W and 2× PCIe 8/6-pin, no native 12V-2x6. Seasonic lists the G12 GM-650 at 54 A on +12 V with two PCIe 8/6-pin connectors. A future card expecting a 12V-2x6 connector needs an adapter, or the PSU swap that is already costed in the PSU comparison.
GPU slot is PCIe 4.0 x16 (B650). Fine for x16 cards; more of a real cost on a future PCIe 5.0 x8 card, which would run at 4.0 x8.
RAM to 64 GB means replacing, not adding — 2×32 in two slots. Same finding as before; the four-DIMM path drops the speed grade.

What actually gets replaced in 2028 is a CPU or a GPU, for roughly €300–500 — not a €1717.82 machine. Against that, the case for a rebuild would have to be a socket change, and AM5 removes it for the whole window in question.
Considered and rejected: buying a Steam Machine instead (2026-07-30)
Fair question, since this build’s job description — Steam single-player games on a SteamOS-family Linux with the anti-cheat titles offloaded to a console — is close to exactly what Valve’s Steam Machine is for.
It is €678.82 cheaper and roughly half the GPU. As of 2026-07: launched 29 June 2026 at €1,039 for the 512 GB model, custom AMD Zen 4 CPU with a 28-CU RDNA 3 GPU and 8 GB VRAM. GamersNexus and others place its graphics between an RX 6600 and an RX 7600 — Cyberpunk 2077 at 1440p Medium with RT and FSR Quality managed 28 fps; Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered at 1440p, 48 fps. Valve’s own silicon runs at roughly half the wattage of desktop equivalents, which is the trade for the chassis. Availability in Finland is through a randomised reservation programme, with fulfilment reported as “the end of this year.”
Against the note’s original scoping, it was genuinely competitive. A Hogwarts-Legacy-class single-player library at 1080p is squarely inside what it does, and €1,039 sits close to the €1333.83 the first draft of this build came to.
Against the spec that WoW and Dragon’s Dogma 2 forced, it is the wrong machine — on all three axes that drove the upgrades:

8 GB VRAM, permanently. This note has now rejected 8 GB twice on its own merits, and TechSpot calls the 8 GB 9060 XT “the one you should avoid.” A Steam Machine cannot be moved off it.
No 3D V-Cache, at half desktop wattage. The 7500X3D’s 96 MB L3 was bought specifically for WoW raids and Vernworth. This is the workload a Steam Machine is worst at, and DD2’s CPU wall is severe on far stronger chips.
Nothing is upgradeable. The section above is the whole counter-argument: this build’s value is that a 2028 CPU or GPU swap costs €300–500. A Steam Machine’s answer to 2029 is another Steam Machine.

Also worth weighing: WoW is not on Steam, so it needs Lutris or Bottles in SteamOS desktop mode — doable, but more friction on a console-shaped device than on the Bazzite desktop this household already runs.
Where it genuinely wins: two of them. The unresolved “one machine or two” question below is much cheaper to answer with Steam Machines — €2,078 for two against €3,435 for two of this build. If the real problem turns out to be a 9- and a 7-year-old fighting over one PC, that is the comparison worth running, not this one.
Value problems and where to cut
In priority order:

RAM (€529.99). The largest line after the GPU, and now a third of the box. Stepping back to 16 GB recovers €245.00 and is defensible only if DD2 and WoW leave the list. Waiting for prices is a gamble, not a plan, and topping up later does not work — see the RAM section.
GPU (€449.90). The open-box Gigabyte at €376.00 is the one free saving in this build (−€73.90). Opportunistic only.
CPU (€229.99). Recovers €50.00 by reverting to the 7600X, at a cost measured entirely in WoW raid and Vernworth 1 % lows.
Case + cooler + fan (€162.97). €59.99 recoverable by reverting the silence package, and about €30 more by dropping to a €66.99 case. Both give up filtration and dampening, which are the point — cut RAM or CPU first.
SSD (€182.99). Nothing to cut at 1 TB — it is already the cheapest in-stock drive of its class. The question here is whether to spend up for capacity, not down.
Monitor. Outside the box total. €159.00 buys the 1440p panel (AOC Q27G4XF, campaign to 31.8); a spare 1080p display makes it €0.
Windows (€139.00). Resolved 2026-07-30 — Bazzite, with Fortnite and Roblox on the Xbox Series X. The line is gone, and it was the only one where this build cost more than the parent’s.

Open items

✅ Case panel SKU — closed. Verkkokauppa’s S400 is the sound-dampened steel variant, confirmed by oxzo on the product page 2026-07-30. The remaining risk is stock: 1 kpl. Fallback is Jimm’s 162726 at €113.90, which names the steel model number in its listing.
Fallbacks, in order: Lian Li A3-mATX black €87.99 — clearances already documented in pc-build-matx-9070-xt, but no dampening and no included fans; or the Phanteks XT M3 €76.99, which is cheapest and ships three fans but whose GPU and cooler clearances were never verified. Neither is filtered on all three intakes.
✅ Case clearance — resolved for the S400. Published at 319 mm GPU and 167 mm cooler, against the 304 mm ASUS PRIME card and a ~155 mm Peerless Assassin. This was an open item while the Phanteks was the default; it no longer is.
✅ PSU fan mode — closed 2026-07-30. The G12 GM’s S2FC is a thermal curve; the CORE GX-650 uses the same S2FC and is not a half-step; true fanless mode starts at the FOCUS series. Decision: keep the G12 GM-650. The FOCUS GX-750 upgrade path (+€50.00) is costed and parked in the PSU comparison. The Corsair RM650e’s zero-RPM claim remains unverified and was not needed.
✅ SSD resolved 2026-07-30 — and the flagged risk landed. The note previously specced a WD Blue SN580 2 TB at €153.99, warning it was “the kind of listing that disappears.” It did: the product page now reads 0 kpl, Ei saatavilla, price still displayed. Replaced with the WD_BLACK SN7100 1 TB at €182.99, yli 25 kpl — the same drive the parent build picked, so its reasoning already applies (newer BiCS8 TLC, faster than the rejected KC3000; DRAM-less HMB is the tradeoff).
Crucial Pro OC 32 GB CL36 (€449.00) — EXPO support unconfirmed.
7500X3D boxed-cooler status unconfirmed; the €25.99 Thermalright line assumes none is included, which is the safe assumption for an X3D part. Verify at order time.
✅ Fan count and layout — closed 2026-07-31 (as built). 2× Noctua NF-A12x25 G2 front intake + stock Silencio FP 120 rear exhaust, top empty, 2nd stock fan spare. 2 in / 1 out, positive pressure; three chassis fans against three chassis headers. The mixed 140+120 front question never had to be answered. Remaining check is physical: dry-fit the 304 mm GPU against both front fans before routing cables.
Parental controls on Bazzite — malcontent + timekpr-next, neither verified working on an atomic base here. The one open task the Bazzite decision creates.
Not priced: shipping, keyboard/mouse/headset, controller.

Pre-order checklist

 Price every line live across Verkkokauppa, Gigantti and Jimm’s — done 2026-07-30
 Confirm 16 GB vs 8 GB GPU economics — 16 GB is at or below 8 GB pricing on every comparable SKU
 Decide the resolution target — 1440p, no box cost
 Check whether a second retailer is worth it — €10.09 on the current spec, no
 Verify the anti-cheat status driving the OS decision — Fortnite and Roblox both Denied on AreWeAntiCheatYet
 Decide the OS — Bazzite, 2026-07-30; the two Denied games live on the Xbox Series X instead
 Confirm the flagship title runs on Proton — Hogwarts Legacy is ProtonDB Gold / Deck Verified
 Confirm the Silencio S400 panel SKU — oxzo verified Verkkokauppa stocks the steel-panel variant, 2026-07-30
 Price all nine lines across all three retailers — done 2026-07-30; only Verkkokauppa can supply the whole build
 Confirm case GPU/cooler clearance — resolved by moving to the S400 (319 mm / 167 mm published)
 Confirm SN580 2 TB stock — gone (0 kpl) on 2026-07-30; replaced by the SN7100 1 TB at €182.99
 Order while the board campaign lasts — €79.99 vs €126.99 list, no published end date. Same class of dated discount the parent build tracks on its own board line
 Verify every order-sheet link resolves to the right SKU at the quoted price — done 2026-07-30, product page by product page
 Check whether the Jimm’s B850 campaign is worth taking for this build — no, +€89.91 for a PCIe 5.0 slot this GPU can’t use; re-check only if the €79.99 board campaign lapses
 Confirm RAM SKU on the B650M-A WIFI II QVL, EXPO enabled
 Decide one machine or two — one for now, 2026-07-30; a second gets built later, and the Steam Machine comparison is the one to re-run at that point
 Check the open-box GPU at €376.00 at order time
 Decide the PSU — keep the G12 GM-650 at €81.99, 2026-07-30; FOCUS GX-750 costed at +€50.00 and parked as a later drop-in swap
 Decide how the backup disk attaches — external, not internal, 2026-07-30. Drive confirmed SATA, so the IDE-capable €96.90 dock is ruled out; enclosure €22.99 at Verkkokauppa or AXAGON dock €19.90 at Jimm’s
 Set up parental controls on Bazzite before handover — malcontent + timekpr-next
 Decide the monitor — AOC Q27G4XF, €159 (from €229, campaign to 31.8), 2026-07-31; beats the €170.99 ASUS anchor on both price and refresh rate, and the €149 Cepter on stand, panel and evidence
 Check whether a fourth retailer (Power.fi) beats any line — no, 2026-07-31; Power stocks none of the nine parts

Sources
