tech/react-native-expo-enterprise.title: React Native + Expo in the Enterprise — the JS-Everywhere Lane
tech/react-native-expo-enterprise.content:
React Native + Expo in the Enterprise — the JS-Everywhere Lane
As of 2026-08-29. Deep dive on one lane of multiplatform-app-architecture-options: React Native + Expo for iOS/Android, a TypeScript shared core in a monorepo, web either React (separate UI) or React Native Web (shared UI). This is KMP’s strongest rival per the verdict in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise — when mobile is React Native, “the TS monorepo dominates and KMP adds little.” Sibling deep dives: flutter-enterprise, rust-shared-core-enterprise.
The architecture in one line
One language and one runtime across all three clients: React renders to native views on mobile (via React Native) and to the DOM on web, with domain logic, state, and API clients living in shared TypeScript packages that every client imports directly — no FFI, no binding layer, no export annotations.
Current version pins (verified 2026-08-26 in multiplatform-app-architecture-options, reused here): Expo SDK 57 targets React Native 0.86; npm react-native latest is 0.87.0. The New Architecture (JSI + new renderer + new native-module system, bridge removed) has been the default since React Native 0.76 (reactnative.dev, 2024-10-23).
Shared-layer map
What each abstraction level looks like in this stack. (Same row taxonomy as the sibling deep dives, for comparability.)



























































LayerShared?MechanismEnterprise caveatDesign tokensYes, all threeTS token package (or Style Dictionary pipeline) consumed by RN styles and web CSSToken values share cleanly; component styling APIs still differ between RN StyleSheet and web CSS unless you also share componentsUI componentsMobile pair: yes. Web: optionalOne React component tree renders native views on iOS+Android; extend to web via react-native-webThe web output is not a normal web app — RNW renders <View>/<Text> to DOM; semantic HTML, CSS-native layout, and the web-widget ecosystem get harder (detail in multiplatform-app-architecture-options, axis 1c)Screens / navigationMobile pair: yes. Web: partialReact Navigation or Expo Router; Expo Router maps routes to web URLs (web-parity specifics unverified in this pass)Deep links, back-button semantics, and SEO-relevant routing are where mobile-first navigation abstractions leak on webPresentation / stateYes, all threeSame JS runtime everywhere — Redux/Zustand/XState/TanStack Query in shared packagesThe cleanest layer in this stack; nothing crosses a language boundaryBusiness logicYes, all threePlain TS packages in the monorepo (pnpm/Turborepo/Nx)TypeScript’s types erase at runtime — high-assurance validation needs runtime schema checking (e.g. Zod-style validators) where Kotlin would give compile-time + runtime guaranteesData / persistenceLogic yes; storage engines differTanStack Query caching shared; SQLite/MMKV on mobile vs IndexedDB/localStorage on web; sync engines (PowerSync et al.) ship JS clientsOffline/local-first is a designed feature, not a default — see axis 4 of multiplatform-app-architecture-optionsAPI contract / clientYes, all threeGenerated TS client from OpenAPI/GraphQL — or tRPC, which works fully here because every client is TypeScriptThis is the one stack where tRPC serves all three channels; it locks the contract to TS forever, so REST+OpenAPI stays the safer enterprise defaultCross-cutting (analytics, i18n, flags, auth, testing)Mostly yesJS SDKs for analytics/flags/i18n load in all three clients; Jest + shared test utilsAuth is the exception: Keychain/Keystore on native vs the browser’s lack of secure storage forces divergent token handling (see axis 3 of multiplatform-app-architecture-options)
The structural headline: this stack shares more layers with less friction than the compiled-core lanes in this cluster — the entire interop-boundary problem that dominates the KMP evaluation (kmp-js-interop-boundary) simply does not exist. The cost is concentrated elsewhere: runtime guarantees, native fidelity, and vendor coupling.
Decision view for a large enterprise
Pros

Hiring and talent portability, the driver that kills shared-core projects, favors this stack most. JS/TS is the dominant frontend skill; Shopify’s stated reasons for adopting RN were “Write it once,” talent portability (enabling developers to work across iOS, Android, and Web), and shipping more value (Shopify Engineering, 2025-01-13). Coinbase reported 113 contributors to its RN repo including “a large number of web engineers, who previously would have been unable to contribute on mobile” (secondary sourcing — the primary post blocked non-browser fetch in this pass).
Five-year enterprise retrospective evidence exists — rare in this space. Shopify (Director of Engineering, Mustafa Ali) reports all its apps on RN with “sub-500ms (P75) screen loads” and “>99.9% crash-free sessions” after five years, and states the limitations that historically blocked adoption “simply don’t exist anymore” (Shopify Engineering, 2025-01-13).
Fintech-scale precedent. Coinbase completed its transition from native iOS/Android to RN (200+ screens reimplemented, announced May 2021) (secondary sourcing, primary blocked). Note what this is evidence for: a money-moving consumer fintech accepted RN’s runtime and delivery model — the closest thing this lane has to the finserv precedent that kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence could not find for KMP-web. It is a bounded precedent: a 2021 US crypto exchange does not operate under a chartered bank’s change-management regime, so it answers less of the regulated-OTA question below than it first appears to.
The maintainer dogfoods at maximum scale. Meta runs the New Architecture at scale in the Facebook app and in the Facebook/Instagram apps for Quest devices; Expensify, Kraken, and Bluesky are named production adopters (reactnative.dev, 2024-10-23). Microsoft maintains React Native for Windows as open source (microsoft.github.io/react-native-windows), with react-native-macos as a separate Microsoft-maintained project — though that page does not name which Microsoft products use it, and product-level claims (Office, Xbox UI) were not verifiable from primary sources in this pass; treat them as (unverified).
OTA updates are a delivery lever no compiled stack has. EAS Update pushes JS bundles without store review — Expo’s customer page quotes MTA: “identify, patch, and deploy an OTA fix in under 90 seconds from the first user report” (expo.dev/customers). The Apple-rules analysis lives in multiplatform-app-architecture-options axis 5.
Expo has become the de-facto toolchain, absorbing build/submit/update infrastructure that enterprises would otherwise build (EAS Build/Submit run from CI without local macOS). Named production users include MTA, incident.io, Mollie, Cameo, Phantom, Partiful (expo.dev/customers) — mostly startups/scale-ups; the large-enterprise-shaped evidence is Shopify/Coinbase on RN itself, not on Expo’s cloud. And as with every lane in this cluster, the pros rest on published successes — mid-size RN failures don’t write retrospectives, so the visible record is survivor-weighted.

Cons

The upgrade treadmill is real and acknowledged by the friendliest witness. Shopify, in its pro-RN retrospective: “Updating an app to each new version of React Native takes a significant amount of work,” debugging “is flakey” compared to native tooling, and the stack leans more heavily on third-party libraries than native does (Shopify Engineering, 2025-01-13).
Native expertise is still required — the pitch says otherwise. Shopify calls 100% React Native “an anti-goal”: hardware-intensive features (scanning, on-device AI), memory-constrained surfaces (widgets, watch apps), and background sync stay native. An org budgeting zero native engineers is planning against the evidence.
TypeScript’s guarantees are weaker than a compiled core’s. Types erase at runtime; unsound boundaries (JSON parsing, any leakage) need runtime validators. For the high-assurance domain logic that motivates shared cores in finserv, this is the direct trade against KMP’s Kotlin type system (kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise, verdict condition 2).
Sharing UI to web is the weak layer. RN Web inherits a mobile component model; React Server Components in Expo remain experimental and not production-recommended (verified 2026-08-26 in multiplatform-app-architecture-options). The honest enterprise default is: share the mobile pair + the TS core, build web UI web-native.
Two-vendor concentration. Meta owns the framework’s direction; Expo (the company) owns the build/update cloud that has become the recommended path. Both are healthier bets than a single niche vendor — but an enterprise risk review should note that EAS is a paid SaaS in the critical release path, and self-hosting equivalents is real work.
OTA updates cut both ways in a regulated org. The same mechanism that patches in 90 seconds means production code changes without store review or (by default) internal release gates. A compliance regime that requires reviewed, versioned releases must either gate EAS Update behind its own change-management process or forgo the lever entirely. (Inference from the mechanism; no regulator guidance on OTA JS bundles was found either way in this pass.)
The canonical walk-away story belongs to this stack. Airbnb sunset React Native in June 2018 after two years, citing “a variety of technical and organizational issues” — hiring polarization, unclear native-vs-RN boundaries per feature, and maintainability at their scale (medium.com/airbnb-engineering; body details via secondary summaries — Medium blocked non-browser fetch; the widely-quoted survey figures 63%-would-choose-again / 74%-would-consider are (unverified)). Udacity is reported to have dropped RN the same year (ADTmag headline, unverified). Both predate the New Architecture by six years; no comparable post-2024 walk-away was found — the same absence-of-evidence caveat as in multiplatform-app-architecture-options applies.

Question marks (genuinely open — and what would resolve each)

Does RN Web reach web-parity for a content/SEO-relevant enterprise web surface? Resolves when: Expo ships RSC as production-recommended and a named enterprise reports a public-facing website (not a dashboard) on RNW at scale.
Will regulators/auditors accept OTA JS bundles in regulated apps? For an EU finserv org this is specifically a question about DORA-era ICT change-management expectations, not just Apple’s rules. Resolves when: a bank or health-sector engineering/compliance writeup documents an approved EAS-Update-style change-management process. None found — same evidentiary hole as KMP’s condition 5.
Is the New Architecture migration complete across the long tail of libraries an enterprise app actually uses? The 2024 launch post claimed 850+ compatible libraries covering all >200K-weekly-download packages; the current figure was not re-verified in this pass. Resolves by: auditing your actual dependency list, not the ecosystem statistic.

Verdict
RN + Expo + TS monorepo is the right call when ALL of these hold:

Web UI is React (or web UI sharing is explicitly not attempted) — the TS core then serves all three channels with zero interop tax.
The org’s engineering base is JS/TS and hiring plans stay that way; the ability to move web engineers onto mobile work is worth more than compile-time domain guarantees.
Mobile UX target is “excellent app” rather than “day-zero platform showcase,” and the org still funds a small native-specialist bench for the layers Shopify keeps native.
OTA delivery either passes the org’s compliance regime (with its own gate) or isn’t load-bearing to the case.
Meta + Expo vendor coupling is acceptable in the risk register.

It is the wrong call when: the mobile apps are hardware/AR/background-heavy native showcases; the org is JVM-based and mobile is already true-native Kotlin/Swift (KMP’s home turf — kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise); or regulated change-management rules the OTA lever out and the runtime-typing gap matters, at which point the compiled-core lanes (rust-shared-core-enterprise, KMP) or thin clients win.
What we couldn’t establish

Primary-source text of the Airbnb and Coinbase posts (Medium and coinbase.com both refuse non-browser fetch; tools/snapshot failed on their Cloudflare challenge) — details above marked secondary.
Microsoft product-level RN usage from a primary source.
Any named post-New-Architecture (2024+) enterprise walk-away from React Native.
Independent (non-vendor) verification of Shopify’s performance figures — they are self-reported in a celebratory retrospective.

Related

kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise — the rival lane; its counterfactual (a) is this note
flutter-enterprise · rust-shared-core-enterprise — sibling deep dives
design-tokens — the token layer in the shared-layer map

Sources

Shopify Engineering, “Five years of React Native at Shopify” (2025-01-13): shopify.engineering/five-years-of-react-native-at-shopify
React Native blog, “The New Architecture is here” (2024-10-23): reactnative.dev/blog/2024/10/23/the-new-architecture-is-here
Gabriel Peal, “Sunsetting React Native,” Airbnb Tech Blog (2018-06-19): medium.com/airbnb-engineering/sunsetting-react-native-1868ba28e30a (body via secondary summaries)
Coinbase, “Announcing Coinbase’s successful transition to React Native” (2021-05): www.coinbase.com/blog/announcing-coinbases-successful-transition-to-react-native (body via secondary summaries)
React Native for Windows: microsoft.github.io/react-native-windows/

tech/rust-shared-core-enterprise.title: Rust Shared Core in the Enterprise — the Compiled-Core Lane
tech/rust-shared-core-enterprise.content:
Rust Shared Core in the Enterprise — the Compiled-Core Lane
As of 2026-08-29. Deep dive on one lane of multiplatform-app-architecture-options: a headless Rust core — domain logic, crypto, storage, sync, networking — under three thin, fully-native UIs (SwiftUI, Compose, React), bound via UniFFI on mobile and WebAssembly on web. The maximal-assurance, maximal-fidelity option, and the one with the steepest people cost. Sibling deep dives: react-native-expo-enterprise, flutter-enterprise; the KMP cluster (kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise) is the adjacent compiled-core rival.
The architecture in one line
Everything below the screen is one Rust crate compiled per platform — a shared library with generated Kotlin/Swift bindings on mobile, a Wasm module on web — and everything on the screen is written natively per platform, three times.
Shared-layer map
Same row taxonomy as the sibling deep dives, for comparability. This lane’s profile is the mirror image of Flutter’s: nothing shared on top, everything shared underneath.



























































LayerShared?MechanismEnterprise caveatDesign tokensNo (orthogonal)Token pipeline (e.g. Style Dictionary) feeding three UI codebases — see design-tokensConsistency is a governance problem again, as in any multi-UI setup (design-system-scaling)UI componentsNo — deliberatelyThree native UIs; platform fidelity is the pointFull 3× UI build-and-maintain cost; feature drift risk across clients returnsScreens / navigationNoPer-platform navigation idiomsSame 3× cost; deep-link parity is manual disciplinePresentation / statePartial — a design choiceThe core can own app state and expose view-ready data (libsignal implements the full Signal protocol below the UI; frameworks like Crux push this further — Crux’s own README calls it production-ready but pre-1.0 with occasional breaking changes), or stay a passive library under per-platform view modelsWhere this line sits is the architecture’s key internal decision; too little in the core and sharing evaporates, too much and the FFI boundary churnsBusiness logicYes — home turfOne Rust crate; UniFFI generates Kotlin/Swift/Python/Ruby bindings (built-in), with third-party bindings for JS/React Native/Wasm, KMP, C#, Go, Dart (mozilla/uniffi-rs)UniFFI is “ready for production use, but … a long way from a 1.0 release” (verbatim, same README); the JS/web binding path is third-party, not Mozilla-maintainedData / persistenceYesCore owns the database and sync (1Password’s core owns DB and server comms per the Serokell writeup cited in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise)On web, storage backends differ (IndexedDB vs SQLite) — the core needs a storage abstraction seamAPI contract / clientYesCore owns networking + serialization once; clients never talk to the backend directlyConcentrates the contract in one place — strongest version of axis-3 discipline; but browser networking constraints (CORS, no raw sockets) make the web build a variant, not a copyCross-cutting (analytics, i18n, flags, auth, crypto, testing)Crypto/auth logic: yes. Rest: mostly noCrypto is the flagship shared layer — libsignal implements the Signal protocol, primitives, and zero-knowledge groups once in Rust for every client (signalapp/libsignal). Core logic tested once; analytics/i18n SDKs stay per-platformTesting asymmetry is favorable: the highest-assurance code gets one test suite; the 3× cost lands on UI tests, the lower-assurance layer
The structural headline: this lane shares the least code but the most assurance. What crosses platforms is exactly the code where correctness matters most — and it crosses as one memory-safe, singly-audited artifact.
Decision view for a large enterprise
Pros

The strongest production evidence of any shared-core-to-web architecture in this cluster. Signal’s libsignal is “platform-agnostic APIs used by the official Signal clients and servers, exposed as a Java, Swift, or TypeScript library” with implementations “written in Rust,” consumed by the Android, iOS, and Desktop apps and server-side (signalapp/libsignal). That is one core serving every channel including TypeScript — the exact web-consumption story that kmp-enterprise-adoption-evidence could not find a finserv precedent for in KMP.
1Password is the standing commercial reference: headless Rust core (logic, crypto, DB, server comms) under thin native UIs across desktop, mobile, and browser, with the browser-filling engine ported to Rust/Wasm (Serokell, 2021-01 — already sourced in kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise).
Mozilla runs UniFFI at browser scale — “used extensively by Mozilla in Firefox mobile and desktop browsers” (README verbatim) — so the binding generator itself is production-exercised infrastructure, not a hobby tool.
Memory safety + no runtime. For crypto and money-math cores, Rust removes the GC pauses, runtime bundle, and memory-unsafety classes that every other lane carries in some form; Wasm is Rust’s first-class compilation target, giving web the same audited logic rather than a reimplementation.
Web gets automatic dead-code elimination and small artifacts relative to runtime-carrying alternatives — directionally consistent with the local Wasm measurements in kmp-js-interop-boundary (that measurement was Kotlin/Wasm, not Rust; treat the size advantage as an expectation, not a number).
Server reuse is real. The same crate that ships in clients can run server-side (libsignal does exactly this), collapsing the client/server duplicate-validation problem that axis 2 of multiplatform-app-architecture-options warns about — the server re-validates with the same code.

Cons

The people cost is the documented killer of this architecture’s ancestors. Dropbox abandoned its C++ shared mobile core (~2019) over custom-tooling overhead and a sustained inability to hire and retain; Slack hit the same wall (InfoQ, 2019-11 — sourced in the KMP cluster). Rust improves the tooling story (Cargo, UniFFI vs hand-rolled Djinni) but the structural risk — a niche-skill core team as a single point of failure between three UI teams — is the same shape. Rust’s learning curve is a real adoption tax on top.
You pay full price for three UIs. Every design-system, feature-parity, and review-load cost of the no-UI-sharing baseline (option (a) in multiplatform-app-architecture-options) returns. This lane only makes sense when that cost was going to be paid anyway for fidelity reasons.
The FFI boundary is a designed artifact with ongoing churn. Like KMP’s @JsExport facade (kmp-js-interop-boundary), the UniFFI interface layer must be deliberately shaped (object model, serialization at the boundary), and UniFFI’s own maturity statement — production-ready but pre-1.0, “more advanced things might break as you upgrade over time” — puts upgrade risk on the roadmap permanently until 1.0.
The web binding path is the least institutional. Mozilla maintains Kotlin/Swift/Python/Ruby; the JS/React-Native/Wasm bindings are third-party per the README. An enterprise betting its web channel on this lane should evaluate those bindings as dependencies with their own bus factor — or hand-roll a wasm-bindgen facade, which is more work but first-party tooling. (wasm-bindgen characterization is general knowledge, not verified in this pass.)
No delivery lever. Compiled core + native UIs means store-gated releases on mobile everywhere (axis 5); no OTA escape hatch.
Async/threading models don’t cross the boundary cleanly — Rust async, Kotlin coroutines, Swift concurrency, and JS promises each need adapter discipline at the FFI seam. (Mechanism-level claim from general FFI experience; not sourced in this pass.)

Question marks (genuinely open — and what would resolve each)

When does UniFFI reach 1.0, and what breaks on the way? Resolves when: a 1.0 release with a stability contract ships. Until then, budget for binding-layer maintenance on every upgrade.
Is there a named enterprise (non-security-product) running this lane? The strong references — Signal, 1Password, Mozilla, Firefox — are all security-centric products whose crypto core justifies the Rust investment. Temporal presented a shared-Rust-core case for multi-language SDKs at QCon SF 2025 (secondary search-result mention, unverified). Resolves when: a mainstream consumer/enterprise app (retail bank, commerce, SaaS) documents this architecture in production.
What does day-2 look like for a web team consuming a Rust/Wasm core? No first-hand enterprise writeup of the TS-consumer workflow (semver of the Wasm facade, debugging across the boundary) surfaced — the same evidentiary hole as KMP’s web-consumer story.

Verdict
A Rust shared core under native UIs is the right call when ALL of these hold:

The org was going to build three native UIs anyway — platform fidelity or product bar demands it — so the 3× UI cost is sunk, not incurred by this choice.
There is a genuinely high-assurance core (crypto, E2E messaging, credential handling, money math, sync engine) whose single-implementation, single-audit property is worth a dedicated systems team.
The org can hire and retain that Rust team and accepts it as a structural dependency for every client team — with the Dropbox/Slack failure shape explicitly on the risk register.
Web consumption is either modest (a Wasm module for the hot core, not the whole app) or the org accepts third-party/hand-rolled binding maintenance.
Server-side reuse of the same core is valuable — it’s this lane’s unique bonus.

It is the wrong call when: the motivation is reducing UI cost (this lane increases it — use react-native-expo-enterprise or flutter-enterprise); the “core” is ordinary CRUD/validation logic (TS monorepo or KMP does that without the systems-language tax); or the org is JVM-centric with true-native mobile, where KMP delivers most of the sharing at a fraction of the hiring risk (kotlin-multiplatform-web-enterprise).
What we couldn’t establish

Any named non-security-product enterprise running a Rust shared core across all three channels in production.
UniFFI 1.0 timeline or a stability contract.
Quantitative boundary-overhead or Wasm-artifact-size data for Rust cores at enterprise scale (the local measurement in the vault is Kotlin/Wasm, not Rust).
Signal’s or 1Password’s internal team-size/cost economics for the core team.

tech/web-page-typologies.content:
Web Page Typologies — Intent-Driven Taxonomy
What it is
A compact reference mapping common web page types to the user intent they serve and the UX principles that follow. Each typology exists to reduce cognitive friction for a specific search-intent mode — informational, navigational, commercial, or transactional — and mixing the wrong pattern with the wrong intent is a primary source of conversion failure.
Why it matters
Most “bad” pages aren’t ugly — they’re misaligned: a transactional checkout designed like an informational article, or a landing page with homepage-style navigation that bleeds attention. Knowing which typology applies is upstream of layout, copy, and component choice.
Scope caveat
This taxonomy is biased toward commercial web (marketing, e-commerce, SaaS). Content-first and community sites — documentation, forums, wikis, UGC feeds, academic sites, civic tech — don’t map cleanly onto any of the listed types. Read the patterns below as “applicable when the page is part of a conversion or info-retrieval funnel,” not as universal web UX.
Search intent (the foundation)



































IntentQuery modifiersPages that serve itUX focusInformational”how / what / why / guide”Articles, FAQs, resource hubsScannability, objective toneNavigationalBrand names, “login”, “contact”Homepage, about, loginWayfinding, speedCommercial”best / vs / review / alternative”Category, pricing, portfolioComparison, filteringTransactional”buy / discount / SKU”Landing, checkout, signupFriction removal
The four-bucket model is SEO-derived and simplifies reality — real queries are often mixed (info + commercial), exploratory without clear intent, or hedonic browsing that fits no bucket. Use it as a design prompt, not a classifier.
The AI shift: users increasingly state desired outcomes in natural language and supervise, rather than executing click-sequences. Pages are becoming context-aware (predictive suggestions, starter templates, inferred workflows) rather than pure command surfaces.
Foundational / navigational

Homepage — Digital storefront, routing hub, “safe harbor” for disoriented users. Logo top-left is the convention for LTR cultures; centering or right-aligning measurably hurts navigational recall in LTR contexts (specific multiplier unverified). RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew) invert this. Above-the-fold area carries disproportionate attention; avoid “false floors” that trick users into thinking the page has ended — full-width dividers, hero media that perfectly fills the viewport. Modern homepages trend toward high element counts and heavy third-party scripts — watch a11y regressions.
About Us — Humanize the entity. Mission, values, authentic team imagery, testimonials. Stock photography reads as hollow.
Contact — Bridge for inquiries. Minimal fields (name / email / message), multiple contact modalities, set response-time expectations to reduce anxiety.
FAQ — Self-service support + long-tail SEO. Categorized, jargon-free, searchable when large. Audit periodically.
Privacy / Terms — Legal compliance + trust signal. Plain language over legalese. Always reachable from the footer.

Content / authority

Article / blog — Fulfills informational intent, builds domain authority. Users scan, not read: well-structured content surfaces “layer-cake” scanning (jumping heading-to-heading), while text-heavy pages force the weaker “F-pattern”. Countermeasures: descriptive (not clever) subheadings, inverted-pyramid structure, bullets, bolded keywords, short paragraphs, line lengths ~50–75 chars, generous line-height, sticky TOC for long-form. Avoid “marketese” — subjective promotional prose users actively filter out.
Press / newsroom — Serves journalists on deadline. Central repository, tight click-depth, downloadable media kit (vector logos, headshots, fact sheet), direct PR contact — never a generic web form.

E-commerce

Category / PLP — Commercial investigation; acts as digital assistant over a large catalog. Faceted search with live match counts, OR-logic multi-select, prominent active-filter chips with one-click removal, uniform thumbnails, clear price/title hierarchy. For goal-directed catalog browsing, “Load More” or pagination tends to beat infinite scroll — infinite scroll disrupts spatial memory and hides footer content. (Infinite scroll is fine for hedonic feeds — social, discovery — where there’s no return trip.) Preserve scroll position on back-navigation from PDP.
PDP (product detail) — Single-item evaluation. Not deeply expanded in source; pairs with PLP.
Checkout — Transactional execution; highest-stakes UX on an e-commerce site. Unexpected costs and forced account creation are top abandonment drivers (often cited via Baymard Institute — specific percentages time-sensitive, unverified). Strip global nav and footer, offer a prominent guest checkout, use address autocomplete, default billing to shipping, trigger appropriate mobile keyboards, replace “shipping speed” with concrete delivery dates, mark both required and optional fields explicitly. Tradeoff on stripping nav: users sometimes need policy/shipping info mid-flow — inline accordions or slide-out panels often outperform total removal.

SaaS / conversion

Landing page — Singular conversion goal, engineered for low attention ratio (interactive links ÷ conversion goals, ideally 1:1). Strip global nav and competing CTAs. Enforce message match with the ad/email that drove the click. First-person CTA phrasing (“Start my free trial”) is commonly reported to outperform second-person (specific lift figures unverified — Michael Aagaard / Unbounce A/B test is the usual citation). Tradeoff: users who want more context before committing bounce back to search instead of exploring the site — for considered-purchase products the 1:1 ratio can underperform a lightly-linked page.
Pricing page — High commercial intent; cognitive overload kills it. Transparent pricing (avoid “Request a Quote” unless genuinely bespoke), three-to-four tiered columns with a “Most Popular” anchor exploiting price anchoring, monthly/annual toggle defaulting to annual with savings made visible, feature matrix with tooltips, adjacent social proof, money-back / free-trial risk reducers.
Signup / login — Utilitarian gateway. Offering SSO and social login reduces password + verification burden for most users, but don’t force it — privacy-conscious users actively avoid social login, and social-only signup locks out that segment. Keep email fallback. Email as primary identifier is the mainstream choice; know it opens email-enumeration attack surface and makes email changes more involved than username-based systems. Confirm-password fields are widely criticized — a single input plus visibility toggle is often better on mobile, but the confirm field still catches typos in contexts without paste support or in sensitive flows (banking, recovery) where double-entry is the user’s only error check. Inline validation in real time. Visually differentiate signup vs login states to prevent wrong-state attempts.
Onboarding — Shepherds a signup to “activated” (first core-value action). Minimize time-to-value. Prefer progressive, contextual disclosure over modal step-through tours. Gamified checklist widgets exploit the Zeigarnik effect (drive to complete interrupted tasks) — pre-fill the first step to bootstrap momentum. Never ship a blank empty state: seed dummy data, sample projects, or starter templates.
Dashboard — Operational command center for B2B apps. Progressive disclosure: summaries and alerts above the fold, drill-downs hidden. Left vertical sidebar for primary nav (LTR assumption), top-right for profile/notifications. Modular / rearrangeable widgets for diverse role needs. Tradeoff: power users resent drill-down friction — surface a “detailed view” or “raw data” escape hatch so progressive disclosure doesn’t become progressive concealment.

Safety nets / post-conversion

Search results (SRP) — Fallback when nav fails. Always-visible open search box (not icon-only), autocomplete, typo tolerance, persistent query display, format results per data type (grid for products, list for docs, facets for refinement). Zero-results states must offer alternatives — curated recommendations, popular categories, parameter suggestions — never a dead end.
Portfolio — Credibility arbiter for creatives and agencies. Curate ruthlessly over archiving everything. High-resolution imagery with minimal UI chrome. Narrative case studies (challenge → approach → outcome + quantified result) beat bare image galleries.
Thank-you / confirmation — Peak-trust moment, commonly underused. Confirm and reassure first (order number, next steps, delivery dates) to blunt post-purchase anxiety. Then leverage momentum: related-product cross-sell, post-checkout account creation, social share prompts, reinforcing social proof.

Emerging shifts (2025–2026)

Hyper-personalization — AI + first-party data driving persona/geo/history-aware layouts; returning users see dynamically reordered grids.
Intent-driven UIs — Natural-language outcome specification replacing click-by-click workflows; user becomes supervisor.
Aesthetic pivot — Millennial minimalism giving way to Gen Z maximalism, brutalist typography, WebGL/3D product showcases. Gate against perf and accessibility cost.
AI-generated layouts — Accelerate prototyping; still require human UX strategy for hierarchy and cognitive-load discipline.
Complexity creep — Homepages trending toward very high HTML element counts and heavy third-party frameworks; a11y regressions widespread.

Caveats on specific statistics
The source article this was condensed from contained many precise-looking figures (exact percentages, “×6” effects, element counts, completion-rate ranges). Most of these figures trace loosely to Baymard Institute, Nielsen Norman Group, or UX vendor A/B-test posts, but the specific numbers were not independently verified here. Treat any percentage you see in web-design literature as directionally useful, not authoritative — rerun the measurement on your own funnel before citing.
